[Commentary]: "If one can see that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding and identical to ultimate truth" means that it refers to the Three Jewels of Identical Character (*sādharmya-triratna*).

[Commentary]: "Because of the skillful means of both the object to be disciplined and the discipliner" means that regarding the sentient beings to be converted, there is the cultivation of skillful means capable of disciplining them.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the Tathāgata only rejoices when the time for the offering of the four riches arrives," the intended meaning is this: if one were to offer material wealth to the Tathāgata, he would not rejoice;

rather, it is when one practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) that the Tathāgata truly rejoices. Furthermore, the joy [spoken of] here refers only to the planting of the seeds of the Tathāgata’s original Buddhahood, which is called "joy";
it does not mean that the abandonment of diligence is called "joy."
[Commentary: Regarding "the two natures," the meaning refers to the two natures of the one who pays respect and the object of respect. The one who pays respect is Vasubandhu and others;

the object of respect is the Triple Gem. Furthermore, the "two natures" refers to the Triple Gem of common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and the Triple Gem of specific characteristics (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*).
"The meanings of the various gates" refers to the twelve divisions of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "from this fourth [point] up to 'non-Dharma,'" the intended meaning is as follows:

although the fourth point previously mentioned spoke of revering the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, it is now explained again with reference to the third point. Therein, the fourth also speaks of revering non-humans and non-Dharma;
here, "non-Dharma" refers to the Buddha, and "non-human" refers to the Dharma.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the seventh [case] reaches full purity with respect to the object," the intended meaning is that while the fourth [case] is applied to that which is venerated, the term for the "object" (*viṣaya*) in the seventh case cannot itself be venerated.
[Commentary]: First, "by virtue of wisdom" refers to the arising of understanding through self-benefit; second, "by virtue of grace" refers to [the benefit of others]. Bodhi...

The intention behind the Master’s composition of this treatise is that benefiting others immediately manifests the Bodhisattva’s virtues of grace; for the sake of self-benefit, he generates great wisdom, and for the sake of benefiting others, he generates great compassion.
This is intended, in total, to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time and to rescue all sentient beings.

Alternatively, it is for the purpose of seeking the fulfillment of the two bodies—the Wisdom Body (*jñāna-kāya*) and the Grace Body (*upakāra-kāya*). Generating great wisdom is for the sake of attaining these; therefore, there is a reason for composing this treatise.
It is said that since those dharmas belong to the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, explaining them demonstrates the possession of wisdom and virtue;
furthermore, explaining them gives rise to great wisdom in others. Since they bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, this demonstrates the possession of benevolence and virtue;
because sentient beings, having obtained benefit, successively enable others to also obtain benefit and happiness, it is said that great compassion is thereby generated.
[Commentary]: That which is called "meaning" (artha) refers to the meaning of "sinking into constancy.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement from "these sentient beings" up to "no separate capacity," the intention is as follows:
this first interpretation holds that the category of living beings is called "sentient" (sattva) because they possess sentience; thus, there is no separate capacity or possession [of selfhood].

[Commentary]: Regarding "the provisional" (*prajñapti*) as that which possesses [something], this is the second interpretation; it takes the provisional person (*pudgala*) composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the possessor and the distinct eight consciousnesses as that which is possessed.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding "sentient being" (*sattva*) as "nature" (*svabhāva*), the phrase "because one possesses this nature" constitutes the third interpretation; its intended meaning is to explain this as a collective provisional designation.
This refers to the existence of a distinct *dharmatā* (dharma-nature). This *dharmatā* is precisely the twelve *āyatanas* and so forth.
[Commentary] Furthermore, "sentiment" (*qing*) means craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Regarding the phrase "because there is that which can give rise to craving":

the intention of this fourth interpretation is that the "sentient being" (*sattva*) as a conventional designation possesses the eighth consciousness; because it exists, it is able to produce craving and so forth, as explained below.
Because it speaks of "loving the ālaya" and "delighting in the ālaya," and because the third [verse] states, "If the fundamental consciousness did not exist,
upon what other dharma would the existence of sentient beings (*sattva*) be established," we know that the substance of "sentient being" (*qing*) is precisely the eighth consciousness;
whereas the Sarvāstivādins call the six consciousnesses by the name "sentient being," which differs from the Mahāyāna.
[Commentary: Sentient beings differ in sixty-two ways. Furthermore, according to the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot), the verse on sentient beings states:
"Five, four, three, three, four, three, two, and seven; thirty-nine, four, four, and one—these constitute the sixty-two types of sentient beings.
The "five" refers to the five destinies: hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas. The "four" refers to the four castes.
The three [classes] are: first, the Brahmin; second, the Kṣatriya; third, the Vaiśya; and fourth, the Śūdra. Another set of three is: first, male; second, female;

and third, neither male nor female, which refers to those with both sexual organs (dviliṅga). Furthermore, there are three types: inferior, middling, and sublime, which correspond to the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior.
It is also said that the Desire Realm is inferior, the Form Realm is middling, and the Formless Realm is sublime; this interpretation is somewhat more excellent.
The fourth [category] consists of four types: first, householders; second, renunciants; third, those who practice asceticism; and fourth, those who do not practice asceticism.
Regarding householders, there are two types: first, householders with wrong views; and second, householders with right views, which refers to those who have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma and so forth.
Regarding renunciants, there are also two types: first, renunciants with wrong views, such as non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); and second, renunciants with right views.
That is to say, those who have faith and incline toward the True Dharma are of three types: first, those with restraint (wholesome); second, those without restraint (unwholesome);

and third, those with neither restraint nor non-restraint (neutral). Regarding the second [category], there are two views: one says they are free from desire, while the other says they are not yet free from desire.

An ordinary person who suppresses afflictions through the six modes of practice and is born in a higher realm is called "one free from desire"; one who does not suppress afflictions through the six modes of practice is called "not yet free from desire."

Regarding "those who have not yet abandoned desire" (*avītarāga*), this generally refers to those within the human realm of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who possess wives; they are called "not yet having abandoned desire. Those who do not commit sexual misconduct from their youth are called "having abandoned desire" (*vītarāga*).
There are three types: first, those of false certainty (*mithyātva-niyata*); second, those of right certainty (*samyaktva-niyata*); and third, those of no certainty (*aniyata*).

As for "false certainty," it refers to being fixed in error, such as by committing the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*). "Right certainty" refers to being fixed in correctness, namely the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

The sixth mind is necessarily non-retrogressive; therefore, it is called "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and others, while situated within the categories of the wrongly fixed (*mithyātva-niyata*) or the rightly fixed (*samyaktva-niyata*), do not yet cultivate [the path], have not yet reached the sixth mind of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), and have not yet committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karman*).

Thus, it receives the name "indeterminate. "Determinate" (*niyata*) has the meaning of being certain; it does not refer to the concentration (*samādhi*) among the triad of concentration and wisdom (*prajñā*). Seventh: first, the bhikṣu.
Second, bhikṣuṇīs; third, śikṣamāṇās; fourth, śrāmaṇeras; fifth, śrāmaṇerīs; sixth, upāsakas; seventh, upāsikās.
Ninth, first, the cultivation of abandonment (*abhyāsa-prahāṇa*). There are three types of cultivation of abandonment:

first, the cultivation of wholesome dharmas such that afflictions do not arise is called the cultivation of abandonment; second, the suppression of afflictions so that they do not arise is called the cultivation of abandonment.

First, the "abandonment of habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā-prahāṇa*) refers to the three types of abandonment—such as the suppression of afflictions through the six practices—and is spoken of in relation to the noble ones (*ārya*).

Second, "reciting and studying" refers to the study and recitation of the holy teachings, which applies to both laypeople and monastics alike. Third, regarding the four propositions on "pure giving" (*śuddha-dāna*):
first, the giver is pure while the recipient is impure; second, the recipient is pure while the giver is impure; third, both the giver and the recipient are [impure]; [and fourth, both are pure].

Regarding the fourth [category], "impurity in both giving and receiving," there are four types of elders (*sthavira*): those who are elders among the laity and those who are elders among the ordained.
Among the ordained, those with more than twenty years of seniority are called elders; among the laity, those aged fifty and above are called elders. Regarding the fifth, "middle age":
among the laity, those aged thirty and above are called middle-aged; among the ordained, those with ten or more years of seniority are called middle-aged. Sixth...
A "youth" (*kumāraka*) refers to one who has been at home for a short time and has been ordained for less than nine summer retreats (*navavārṣika*).
Seventh, the Preceptor (*ācārya*); eighth, the Teacher (*upādhyāya*), also known as the *śāstr*;

ninth, the co-resident disciples (*sahavāsika*) and the near-resident disciples (*antevāsika*), each of whom is of two kinds: first, those who recite the *Prātimokṣa* together, called "co-residents"; second, those who dwell in close proximity.
The first is the name "Upādhyāya" (Preceptor). Second, one who dwells in the same place as the Upādhyāya is called a "Co-resident" (Sahavāsin);
one who dwells in close proximity to the Upādhyāya is called a "Near-resident" (Upavāsin). Tenth, there are two types of "guests": laypeople and renunciants.

Eleventh, regarding the management of monastic affairs, there are also two [categories]; the first says that if one does not take pleasure in managing monastic affairs, one transgresses ten [precepts].

Second, those who crave gain and offerings include both monastics and laypeople; thirteenth, those who feel weary and renounce include both ordinary beings and sages, as they respect the contaminated (*sāsrava*) while aspiring for the higher;

fourteenth, "much learning" (*bahuśruta*) applies to both the correct and the false, as well as that which is neither false nor correct—referring specifically to the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
fifteenth, regarding the arising of great merit and wisdom through the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), there are also two types: first, the mundane...

Among these, there are two types of contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*). The second is uncontaminated knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), which consists of the sixteen aspects of the noble ones (*ārya*).

"Practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipatti*) refers to the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*). "In accordance with the Dharma" means the Teacher’s Truth-Dharma; "practice" (*pratipatti*) refers to [the application of] that.

Seventeenth is the upholder of the Sūtras; eighteenth is the upholder of the Vinaya; nineteenth is the upholder of the Śāstras—these include both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*). Fourth, there are three types: first, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); second, [noble learners]; third, [noble non-learners].

The path of seeing (darśana-mārga) is the first, the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) is the second, and the path of culmination (niṣṭhā-mārga) is the third. Regarding the fourth [classification], there are four: first, the Pratyekabuddha; second, the Śrāvaka; third, the Bodhisattva;

and fourth, the Tathāgata. As for the first [category], although there are four types of Wheel-turning Kings (cakravartin)—those with wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron—they are combined into one because their names are identical. Thus, the sentient beings benefited by them are of sixty-two kinds. Question: [What are these?]

Regarding the question of whether there are those among these sentient beings who lack the lineage (agotra), the answer is that they are only [excluded] from having the lineage, not from being [included in] the lineage-less.
As it is said: "O Victorious One, I shall expound [it]," and again: "It also includes those without the lineage.

Since they hear the teaching and each attains the fruit within their own vehicle, the previous statement regarding "the Victorious One" refers specifically to those who have entered the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "benefit (*hita*) and happiness (*sukha*) are one essence with different names," the intended meaning is that benefit and happiness are indeed a single essence, yet they are designated by two distinct names—benefit and happiness—based on the specific object being benefited.
Question: In the previous section on the ten benefits, it was also stated that benefit and happiness are distinguished based on the object benefited;

how does this differ from the present case? Answer: The former merely distinguished benefit and happiness according to worldly benefit, without analyzing their essential nature (*tattva*); the present [analysis] does so.
There is a distinction based on their essential nature.
[Commentary: Regarding the ten kinds of understanding that bring benefit and happiness mentioned above, there is a verse as in the commentary.

However, when these are sequentially assigned to the ten benefits and five joys, "the world" refers to both future relief and present relief, as well as present benefit and future benefit; the first and second [points] are these.
"Nature" (性) refers to the gathering of what is good and the abandoning of evil; that which is the opposite of this constitutes the third and fourth [categories].
"Suffering and pleasure" (苦樂) refer to the emergence from suffering and the attainment of pleasure; this is the fifth. "Wisdom and merit" (智福) refer to the sixth.

"The supramundane and the mundane" (出世世) refer to the seventh. "Small and great" (小大) refer to the eighth. "Differing in name from their substance" (與名異) refers to the ninth. These are the ten benefits.
The "five benefits" are a summary; they are subsumed within the tenth benefit mentioned above. [Commentary]:
Regarding the phrase "or, in this verse, because it ultimately leads to benefiting others," the intention is to explain the purpose for composing this treatise. To explain that statement:
it is solely for the sake of sentient beings, desiring to cause them to have faith and practice, that this treatise was composed; thus, it is composed based on a single condition.
Question: Previously, it was stated that the treatise was composed based on two conditions; why, then, is it now said to have been composed based on only one condition? Answer:

Because the Bodhisattva’s fundamental aim is to benefit others, and because sentient beings abide in the Dharma through faith and study, there is no contradiction in saying it was composed based on one condition, even though both conditions are present.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "taking the previous explanation based on the complete conditions as the primary meaning," this intends to explain the reason for composing the treatise.
Thus, there is no contradiction between the previous explanation concerning the complete conditions and the subsequent explanation concerning great compassion.

Since the purpose of causing the Dharma to endure for a long time and rescuing all sentient beings is preeminent, this is the interpretation provided by Dharmapāla, Sthiramati, and others regarding that teaching.
Also. *Cheng weishi lun shu yi yan*, Scroll One (The preceding portion of the treatise).
*Cheng weishi lun shu yi yan*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Ruli of Fushou Monastery in the Western Capital.

[Commentary: Although the three meanings are distinct, they correspond to the three masters. Regarding the two intentions for composing this treatise, it is said that both are "for the sake of persons and the Dharma," because [the purpose] is to cause the Dharma to endure long and to deliver all sentient beings.
[Commentary]: "The above constitutes the opening, the heading, and so forth" means: initiating this treatise is called the "opening";
pointing out and explaining it partially is called the "heading"; selecting this treatise while setting aside other schools is called "selection and retention";
and refuting erroneous attachments regarding what one has composed oneself is called "pointing out and refuting."

[Commentary]: Those who hold a false understanding of the principle of emptiness are, namely, Bhāviveka. Although he asserts that the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is empty, he negates both the *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) natures as being entirely non-existent;

thus, while he claims it is "emptiness," it does not accord with the true principle of emptiness and is therefore termed a "false understanding. This is because, within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not [non-existent].
[Commentary]: Ignorance (*avidyā*) is called "delusion" because, due to ignorance, one does not understand all phenomena;

thus, that which does not understand is termed "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the essence of false view is error. Question: What is the distinction between this and the previous explanation of delusion and error? Answer: There is indeed a distinction.

The former refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), who are designated as "deluded" by their very nature because such persons are themselves deluded; [this is distinct from] the Śrāvakas.
The same applies to the Pratyekabuddhas; their very nature is designated as "deluded persons," for the person is indeed deluded. Hereafter, the explanation shall be based solely on the dharmas.

Since ignorance (*avidyā*) is understood to be the essence of delusion, it is clear that the designation of "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is likewise made with reference to dharmas. Thus, there is a distinction between these two explanations.

When it is stated below that "a person possessing delusion and false view is called 'deluded and mistaken,'" this concludes the preceding point. Furthermore, there are persons who possess both delusion and false view.
[Commentary]:
"Not being deluded or mistaken" refers to the meaning of generating understanding from the text within the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. [Commentary]:
What was previously called "person-self" (*pudgala-ātman*) refers to the emptiness of person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "wisdom arises by taking emptiness as its object," [the questioner asks]: "If sentient beings cling to existence, it is taught that this is 'emptiness,' and thus the gateway of emptiness reveals the true principle.
Likewise, when sentient beings cling to emptiness, could one not also say it is 'existence,' and thus the gateway of existence reveal the true principle?

The answer is: Not so. Sentient beings cling to existence much more than they cling to emptiness; therefore, it is spoken of from the perspective of the majority in order to destroy their clinging to existence.
Therefore, it is said to be "empty. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "just as a diamond is difficult to sever," the intent is to correctly explain the reason why the obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and the attachments (*grāha*) are termed "heavy" (*guru*).

There are five explanations in total. The first four apply to both types of obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), while the fifth applies only to the two types of attachment (*grāha*). The first four explanations clarify the sense of "heaviness."

The obstructions are divided into three; regarding the first explanation, it says: "Because they are as difficult to sever as a vajra" means that the seeds of the two obstructions follow sentient beings and are not severed until one reaches the state of an Ārya.

"Bearing this difficulty of crossing the flow of birth and death" means that the active manifestations of the two obstructions incite karma and bring about rebirth, making it difficult to achieve liberation. They "oppress sentient beings in the four [states]."

Regarding "because they are born": this refers to the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) bringing about their results, which are subsumed within the four modes of birth (*yoni*). Question: To which mode of birth does the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya* or *pariṇāmikakāya*) belong? Answer:
Since its original body is of the fragmented nature (*bheda-lakṣaṇa*), it is subsumed under the womb-born (*jarāyu-ja*) category of the fragmented type;

alternatively, it may be considered to include the transformation-born (*upapāduka*), because it transforms the coarse into the subtle without fixed limits and follows sentient beings as they sink into the three realms (*tridhātu*) without rest. This means drifting through the three realms without cessation.

Therefore, the second explanation states: "Because it is like a vajra, difficult to sever" means that the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) must be completely severed only upon attaining Buddhahood;
"because it bears this burden and crosses over the stream of birth-and-death" means that the efficacy of the afflictions (*kleśa*) in inducing rebirth is superior;
and "because it oppresses weak sentient beings within the four modes of birth" refers to their following along with the *pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death).

Regarding "because sentient beings are submerged within the three realms": this refers to the fact that the place of transformation and rebirth (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) is situated within the three realms.
The third interpretation states: "The term 'heavy' is explained by way of analogy; it is like a diamond (*vajra*), which is difficult to sever. This explains the meaning based on the name:

because one must carry this heavy burden across the difficult-to-cross flow of birth and death (*saṃsāra-srotas*). It is like a person carrying a heavy load who cannot emerge from a pit as they follow it. [This] suppresses weakness.
Regarding "sentient beings dwell in the four modes of birth": it is because, like a body burdened by a heavy load that cannot rise, they fall;
regarding "sentient beings sink into the three realms": it is because those so designated are suddenly submerged.
[Commentary: Regarding the meaning of the previous four [categories] as "heavy" in the sense of severing all two obstacles (*dvaya-āvaraṇa*):

this means that the four preceding meanings are called "heavy" in reference to the difficulty of severing the two obstacles in general. Now, the two attachments (*dvaya-grāha*) are called "heavy" because they are fundamentally deep-seated;
it is precisely due to the obstacle of these two attachments that birth arises.

[Commentary]: "What obstacle prevents the principle from stating only the two emptinesses, yet it simultaneously includes the elimination of phenomena? This objection concerns the meaning of the four previous explanations regarding the "heavy obstacles. The objection states:
"If, as previously established, there are only the two emptinesses, then when they are severed, one should only sever the two attachments.
Why, then, upon the arising of realization, do you say that the two heavy obstacles are severed along with other factors such as greed and so forth? Emptiness is..."

Regarding the phrase "the two attachments," the intended meaning is that the two attachments are capable of acting as obstacles. This refers exclusively to the manifestation of the principle of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) through the abandonment of these two attachments.
[Commentary]: The passage beginning with "furthermore, only the two attachments" etc., addresses the fifth point concerning the meaning of "repeated" (*punar*). The objection states:

"If one intends to say that the substance of the two obstacles (*dvi-āvaraṇa*) extends to greed and so forth, then since greed and the rest are also eliminated when the repeated obstacles are abandoned later on, one must know that [greed] should not be considered an obstacle to the principle."
If it is understood that the two attachments to self and phenomena alone are what are grasped, and since greed and the other afflictions are likewise abandoned,
why is it stated only that there is emptiness of self and phenomena, without saying that greed and the others are also empty?

[Commentary: "Furthermore, because the afflictive hindrances [reach their limit], only the two emptinesses are taught regarding ultimate truth"—this explains the two hindrances and answers the first question.
"This is based on the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) up to the abandonment of the afflictions"—the intent here is that this refers to the stage of ultimate abandonment of the seeds;

that is, when the seeds of the dualistic grasping at self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) are abandoned, all other afflictive and cognitive hindrances (*kleśa-jñeya-āvaraṇa*) are likewise eliminated.

The phrase "all are exhausted" means that the remaining stages are not so; the underlying intent is that once one is free from afflictions (*kleśa*), the subsequent abandonment of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is like that of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas:
they first abandon eight grades of affliction, and only then do they abandon the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) in the ninth grade, because that view of a self is extremely subtle.
As for the statement that "the view of a self in the fourth stage is likewise," the meaning is that [it is abandoned] in the same manner as the aforementioned.

Bodhisattvas on the fourth stage and those training as followers of the Two Vehicles practice the contemplation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), such as the impurity of the body;

thus, although the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) does not arise, it is not like [the state of an Arhat] where it has been eliminated. This is because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) such as greed, which act as its companions, still remain.

For this reason, it is known that [the view of self] is not called "completely severed" (*prahīṇa*). Therefore, the claim that it is "eliminated" (*vibhāvita*) at this stage is incorrect; furthermore, the term "eliminating the companion" (*sahāyakṣaya*) refers to this.

Regarding the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed and so forth, the intention of the one who abides [in them] is as follows: "The view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is the master, and greed and so forth are its attendants. When the view of self is harmed, it is called "harming";
that is, the latent tendencies of greed and so forth are the attendants that harm the self. [Question: In the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), these are abandoned.

Now, when it is said that the "attendant latent tendencies" are harmed, do they arise in association with the view of self? [Answer: What is being referred to here as the latent tendencies of greed and so forth.
These are merely independent forms of greed, anger, and so forth, which can be induced by the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) acting as their remote cause. Question:
How is it known that they are not associated (*saṃprayukta*) [with the view of self]? Answer:

Regarding association, since greed and the like are said to be abandoned simultaneously with the view of self, and yet [the text] states they are not [abandoned together], we know that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of greed and so forth that harm their companions are not associated. This also applies to the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

Question: For what reason does a bodhisattva, while training in the abandonment of hindrances, practice the contemplation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) common to the two vehicles?

[As stated in the text... Answer: It is because the bodhisattva desires to gather and transform those of the two vehicles. Regarding these two types of universal study, that which is not studied is not called "universal knowledge. Question:

What is the distinction between the contemplation of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna factors of enlightenment? Answer: If the two vehicles were to abandon even one type of practice or understanding, their realization would only then be complete.

This is because it differs from the bodhisattvas who take the two types of wisdom as their skillful means, and because the followers of the Lesser Vehicle have already previously studied [the path], whereas here one is beginning to study for the first time;
thus, the Lesser Vehicle takes the wisdom of emptiness that removes obstacles as its skillful means.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the general explanation up to the point where the two subtle questions above are answered:

this constitutes a general explanation of the two attachments and the two obstacles combined into a single section and discussed in one place, rather than distinguishing between the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

As for answering the two questions above according to their respective meanings—from "Furthermore, regarding the general explanation" up to "because they have not yet been extinguished accordingly"—the second question is answered first.
Question: From "if one realizes the two emptinesses" up to "realizing emptiness without interruption," this answers the first question.
The statement "clinging refers to the grasping of mind and mental factors" explains the essential nature of the term "clinging."

[Commentary: The meaning of this general fourfold response to the second question is that one directly answers the second inquiry using the fourfold textual passage as a whole, without providing any further separate explanation.

[Commentary]: If the first two phrases constitute the answer to the first question, then they specifically cite two phrases from the four-phrase treatise to provide both a specific and a general response to the first question.
The first two phrases answer the question regarding the adherence to emptiness (*śūnyatā-grāha*), while the latter two phrases clarify the reason for severing the heavy obstacles;
therefore, they are explained separately. [Question: How is this one section distinct?
The answer to the two questions is given through the distinction between the general and the specific, which accounts for these words.

Furthermore, one interpretation holds that from "first, the afflictive hindrances" up to "only the two emptinesses are taught" answers the first question; then, providing a general explanation up to "realizing emptiness without interruption" answers the second question.
As the commentary states: "Now, this general fourfold response answers the second question," which refers back to the preceding answer.
The second question is the text itself; if the first two sentences pertain to the answer to the first question, they then belong to the preceding section answering the first question.
According to the commentary (*śāstra*), this interpretation is slightly superior.
[Commentary]: "The six consciousnesses grasp external objects" refers to the dharma-grasping (*dharmagrāha*) of the sixth consciousness; "understanding" refers to the five sensory consciousnesses.
"Among the five consciousnesses and so forth" means within the five sensory consciousnesses there are factors such as craving for dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and so on.

"The five consciousnesses and so forth" includes, by implication, craving for dharmas, aversion, and pride (*māna*) within the sixth consciousness. Now, these forms of pride and so forth are merely hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) and not grasping (*grāha*).

Because it is inferior and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), or because wholesome minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) do not generally grasp objects as such, one should know that the grasping-obscuration within the sixth consciousness is likewise so. [Commentary:

Regarding the statement that those comprised within the "born-of-maturation" (*vipākaja*) are necessarily inferior, the meaning is that the nature of the entity of the feeling born of maturation is inferior.
It is not that it possesses powerful function, but rather that it is comprised solely within the category of what is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and is definitively inferior in nature.

This means that this feeling is definitely of an inferior nature and is therefore subsumed under the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Question: How is this feeling an obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?

[And so forth. Answer: Because it causes the mind to become submerged and agitated when experiencing the objects of the five desires, such that one cannot attain concentration; furthermore, it leads to craving for various things even up to the higher stages (*ūrdhvabhūmi*).
The failure to cultivate the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) is entirely due to sensation (*vedanā*); therefore, sensation is said to be an obstacle to concentration.
Although other factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) are present at the same time, sensation is specifically mentioned because it is the strongest factor in obstructing concentration.

[Commentary: The meaning of "attaining the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) up to the two lower obstacles" is as follows: when ideation and sensation do not function, one attains the unconditioned of the cessation of ideation and sensation (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-asaṃskṛta*);
when pleasant sensation does not function, one attains the unconditioned of the imperturbable (*āniñjya-asaṃskṛta*). It is called "imperturbable" because it is not moved by pleasant sensation.
Now, when it is said that one attains the unconditioned by ceasing these sensations, this is stated with reference to sensations that are not associated with afflictions (*kleśa*).
If it is associated with afflictions, it is abandoned together with those afflictions and is not said to attain non-existence;
this feeling is defiled in relation to the Mahāyāna, yet it is unobscured-neutral in relation to the Two Vehicles.
[Commentary]: One who practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) asks: "What is the distinction between *dhyāna* and *samādhi*? (and so forth). The answer is:

*Dhyāna* refers to the four dhyānas, while *samādhi* refers to the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), as well as the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). "Attainment" (*samāpatti*) is here translated as "equilibrium" (*snyoms par 'jug pa*).

As will be explained below, *dhyāna* is here translated as "calm contemplation" (*zhenli*). "Calm" (*zhen*) refers to concentration (*samādhi*), while "contemplation" (*li*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). The underlying intention is that the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) is characterized by concentration.
"Wisdom and meditative concentration are equally attained, hence they receive the name 'dhyāna' (静虑). Furthermore, it is explained that 'dhyāna' means 'tranquility' (静).
Because wisdom is entirely dispersed while one is in a state of concentration, [it is called dhyāna]. Question: "Does the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) not possess wisdom? [And so forth. Answer:
"Although wisdom exists there, because wisdom is inferior and concentration is predominant, it receives only the name 'concentration' (定) and does not obtain the designation of 'dhyāna' (静虑)."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the two vehicles [attain] the designation of the superior fruit," the meaning is as follows: this refers to the fourfold classification (catuṣkoṭi) in contrast to Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and the two vehicles at the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
This can be understood according to the text. "The two fruits" refers to the *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles.
[Commentary]: Regarding the fact that everything in this treatise is termed "continuation" (*anubandha*), the intention is as follows:

the statement that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are capable of continuing rebirth is made because they share this common name. Now, one should distinguish four logical possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*): there are cases where something continues rebirth but is not an affliction;

namely, the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) acting as a condition to constitute the transformation-death (*nirmāṇa-cyuti*), which is also called "continuation. Although it does not initiate karma, it nevertheless functions [to sustain rebirth].

The coarse [factors] are made subtle so as to possess the sense of continuity and rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*). Among these, there are those that are afflictions (*kleśa*) but do not themselves constitute continuity and rebirth; these serve as the seeds of affliction.

There are also those that both constitute continuity and rebirth and are themselves afflictions, namely, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), and so forth, which manifest as active karma.
Finally, there are those that are neither afflictions nor constitute continuity and rebirth, namely, mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) and the like.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the various practices cultivated by ordinary beings are temporarily extinguished," the intent is as follows: Ordinary beings practice the six contemplations by aspiring for the higher realms and loathing the lower ones, reckoning those higher states to be *nirvāṇa*.
Consequently, the afflictions (*kleśa*) that arise simultaneously with deluded phenomena are temporarily suppressed and do not manifest.
The principle revealed by this suppression is what is termed *nirvāṇa*; this quiescent principle is called *tathatā* (Suchness), yet it is not the *tathatā* of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, regarding the explanation of "true liberation," one should analyze it through the fourfold logical permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*), which can be understood by consulting the text.

[Commentary: The meaning of the statement "liberation is not true because it is provisional" is that the two vehicles possess two kinds of nirvana—namely, *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) and *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder)—which are termed "liberation" merely because they are free from bondage;
they are not true liberation, and thus they are called "provisional. Therefore, in the *Lotus Sūtra*...
The Sūtra states: "To merely be free from delusion is called liberation; in reality, one has not yet attained all-encompassing liberation.

Because such a person has not yet attained the Unsurpassed Way, it is said that true liberation is not yet achieved. The meaning is that as long as a Bodhisattva’s afflictions (*kleśa*) are not exhausted and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not eliminated, they cannot be called liberated.

[Commentary]: Regarding the provisional nature of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the intent is as follows: "deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to wisdom, and "cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because the afflictions are extinguished by means of wisdom, it is termed "cessation through deliberation. Therefore, names such as "non-existence," "removal," and "cessation through deliberation" are all merely provisional designations.
Furthermore, these are established according to what is abandoned; based on the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), one attains eighty [types of cessation] by abandoning the eighty-one grades of afflictions.
Because the first category is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), we know that it is designated as "provisional" (*prajñapti*) by means of the names of the expressive designations; its reality is *tathatā*.
If one looks toward the principle of *tathatā*, it is real; if one relies on the expressive designations such as "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is provisional.

Question: Why does this passage appear? Answer: The intention is to distinguish between the two vehicles' [attainment of] *nirvāṇa with remainder* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) and [the state] relative to...
The Mahāyāna clarifies that the two vehicles’ nirvāṇa is provisionally designated as such because two types of names are established based on their designating expressions;

however, since the essence of true thusness (*tathatā*) is not manifold, it is real. Furthermore, because those of the two vehicles delight in dwelling within the two types of cessation (*nirodha*), it is provisional;
the principle revealed by these two cessations is precisely the reality of true thusness. Another interpretation:

Regarding the statement that the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) is provisional: when the practitioners of the two vehicles realize the principle of selflessness (*anātmatattva*), they take suffering, emptiness, and non-self as the gates of skillful means (*upāyamukha*) to realize that principle.
At the moment of actualizing the realization of the principle, they do not perceive the characteristics of subject or object;

the sphere of mental activity (*cittagocara*) ceases and all [mental functions] fall into sleep. Furthermore, after emerging from meditative equipoise (*samādhi*), they re-examine the aforementioned principle by means of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Since he was no longer attached to his contemplation, he subsequently perceived non-self.

Having seen the principles of the skillful means—suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self—that preceded his contemplation, he realized the principle of *nirvāṇa* and let out a lion’s roar, saying:

"Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence. Since he reckoned that the skillful means preceding his contemplation were [the cause],...
Knowing clearly that this nirvana is provisional and not real, the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of the parable of the conjured city;

since the conjured city is not real, it serves as a metaphor for the two types of nirvana. Because the nirvana of the two vehicles is not ultimate, it is termed "provisional," which refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), while the "real" refers to true suchness (*tathatā*).
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the general and the particular... because they do not fail to abide," the intention is as follows:

Having previously completed the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) of true liberation in contrast to ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the Hīnayāna, the present section further clarifies its provisional and ultimate aspects in contrast to non-Buddhists and followers of the two vehicles;
thus, it differs from the preceding discussion. "General" refers to the Mahāyāna, while "particular" refers specifically to non-Buddhists and followers of the two vehicles. Thus it is said.
This explains the conventional and the real by means of the general and the particular. Furthermore, the phrase "not non-abiding" may also be understood as "not being without a place of abiding.
Why? Because it is explained through the relative relationship between the general and the particular.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "as for that which is known," up to "it shall be explained in detail later," the intent is as follows: To clarify the nature of the obscurer, one must distinguish the obscured;

because it obscures that which is known, it is called the "obscuration to the known" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). However, when presenting the essential nature of the phenomena that constitute the "known," there are generally two levels.

First, the presentation by way of the existence or non-existence of all phenomena—that is, the term "obscuration to the known" is already used [in this context]. What follows is the second [level], which concerns only...
Regarding the section from "The substance of the phenomena that constitute the objects of negation" (*yōu-hō-shutsu-tai*) down to "the detailed explanation," another interpretation states:

From the point after "the objects of knowledge" (*sho-shi*), the nature of the obstructions (*nō-shō-tai*) is clarified. If this is so, why is it said "the phenomena that are the objects of the obstruction of knowledge" (*sho-shi-shō-hō*)? [The answer is:

By citing the phenomena that are the objects of the obstruction of knowledge, the nature of the obstructing agent is revealed. Otherwise, on what basis could they receive the name "obstructing agent"? Second, the clarification of that which is obstructed (*sho-shō*).
The explanation that "Dharma" refers to the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*) and so forth is excellent.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "Although ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cultivate the two kinds of selflessness... up to "...because they do not reach both kinds," the intent is as follows:
this section of the commentary generally establishes a threefold fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, it takes the bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and the two... [text fragment].
Question: If this is so, since they are already bodhisattvas, why are they called ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)?

[And so forth. Answer: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that there are two kinds of ordinary beings: first, those who are ordinary beings within the Dharma (*adhyātma-dharma-pṛthagjana*); second, those who are ordinary beings outside the Dharma (*bāhya-dharma-pṛthagjana*).
Now, bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), as long as they have not yet ascended to the level of the noble ones (*ārya*), are designated only as ordinary beings within the Dharma. Second.
The first four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established by contrasting ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles;

the third set of four alternatives is established by contrasting those of the two vehicles with Bodhisattvas. If one were to perform a detailed analysis of each of these three sets of four alternatives individually, there would be twelve statements;
however, according to the method used in the text, there are only eight statements. Regarding the statement "Greatness is not Bodhi," this refers to Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), they are called "Great" [but] as long as they have not attained untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*), it is not termed *bodhi*.

[Commentary: The section beginning with "Another interpretation" below further correlates the text of the treatise with its five stages (*pañcāvasthā*) to explain the severing of hindrances, the attainment of the fruit, and the reason for composing the treatise.
Question: If that is so, why does the commentary speak of "four stages"? Answer: Within the five stages, the first two are combined into one.
"One person speaks of four stages.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the stage of practice through resolute belief" (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) and so forth, the intended meaning is that although there are two stages prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*), because one generates resolute belief (*adhimukti*) toward all teachings heard, these two preliminary stages are collectively termed the "stage of resolute belief."
[Commentary: The intention of the previous textual explanation is as follows:

from the passage in the treatise beginning with "For the sake of the two emptinesses" up to "attaining great bodhi," as well as the commentary text down to "one should know that below," these passages are all the interpretations of the Tang Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra.

[Commentary]: First, regarding the purpose for which this was composed: it was written in order to generate understanding and sever the obstacles of sentient beings who cling to a real self and real dharmas. [Commentary]:
Regarding the phrase "the Mūlasarvāstivādins and others," one asks: since the Vātsīputrīyas, the Sautrāntikas, and others all maintain that such a person is an Arhat, why...

"What is this 'attachment to a self' (and so forth)? In response, Cè says: "This refers to the time when one has not yet attained the fruit. This is Cè’s account of the Tripiṭaka Master’s interpretation.

[Commentary: Regarding "the truth of consciousness-only," the intent is to explain that "consciousness-only" corresponds to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while "truth" corresponds to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That is to say, because one is blinded by ignorance, one externally clings to a self and phenomena; this is called delusion regarding consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Because of incorrect understanding, one erroneously clings to a self and phenomena, failing to comprehend the two gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Furthermore, Ximing states:

"To cause one to realize the two emptinesses is the ultimate (*paramārtha*) wisdom of consciousness-only; to understand the principle of consciousness-only as it truly is is conventional (*saṃvṛti*) consciousness-only."
Wisdom. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "differing from the preceding" for the sake of those such as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the intended meaning is that this preceding section contains three general explanations;
these are the three distinct purposes for which this treatise was composed. As for the statement "differing from the first":
To say there is a difference means that it differs from the first explanation; to say it differs from the former means that it differs from the second explanation.

Furthermore, it is said that each individual [point] differs from the position of the master Sthiramati presented previously in the first [explanation], which can be understood through careful examination.
To cite the previous treatise for the purpose of contrasting and clarifying this passage means to open up and reveal this text of the teaching on *vijñapti-mātratā*.
To demonstrate this meaning for the sake of engendering faith, the exposition of the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is presented;
specifically, this section of the commentary records Master Huìbiàn’s account of how the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed the treatise based on three intentions.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement in the sutras that "it is mind-only" and so forth, Bhāviveka explains: "In conventional truth, both object and subject exist together;
however, the sutra speaks of 'mind alone' from the perspective of what is predominant, not because objects do not exist."
[Commentary]: Regarding the "teachings of intentional terminology concerning the twelve bases," the meaning is as follows:

The Tathāgata taught the doctrine of the twelve bases without distinguishing between faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*, *dhātu*), yet he did not fail to differentiate between internal and external. Although he did not explicitly distinguish them, the mind (*manas*) is situated within;

because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not separate from consciousness, the followers of the Hīnayāna failed to understand the Tathāgata’s teachings of intentional terminology and consequently engaged in conceptual construction.
The statement that the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) exist substantially apart from consciousness is spoken with an underlying intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*);
this is the intended meaning here. [Commentary: Regarding the phrase "now, in terms of the Middle Way, there is no contradiction," the intent is as follows:

when it says "like the objects external to your mind," it does so by recourse to the doctrine of the Mahāyāna Middle Way; thus, it speaks of "objects external to the mind" according to the Mahāyāna Middle Way.

Because there is no object, if one considers this from the perspective of Bhāviveka’s own school, it constitutes the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*svavacanavirodha*), since for him there is indeed an object;
thus, these two positions present a formal logical refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) based on contradiction with the Master’s inference.
[Commentary] A certain class of Bodhisattvas, fearing that they might contradict the ultimate teachings, asserts that there is but one consciousness (*eka-vijñāna*). Their intention is as follows:
these Bodhisattvas base their assertion on five kinds of analogous scriptural passages that speak of "one consciousness. Regarding the term "analogous":

for example, although the teaching on the "far-reaching" (*dūra-gama*) speaks of various consciousnesses, these Bodhisattvas cannot accept it; thus, when explaining the "far-reaching," they say that there is only [one].
The teaching that "one consciousness" is like saying "one similarity" is called the teaching based on similarity. The "teaching of distant travel" refers to the *Dharmapada-sūtra*.
When it says that the mind and the faculties each can receive the teaching, this explains that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) functions at the gates of the five sense organs;
it means that there is only the mental consciousness and no other five consciousnesses. This is like how many reflections appear upon a single object.

Regarding the "teachings through images" (*nimitta-dharma*), the term *yoga* refers to how, just as many reflections appear upon a single mirror, so too do many objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) appear within consciousness.

Regarding the "teachings through analogies," the intention of the analogy of many waves arising from a single body of water is that the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) is capable of producing the waves of the seven consciousnesses.
However, this bodhisattva did not understand the Buddha’s intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) and consequently grasped it incorrectly.
To establish a single consciousness (*ekavijñāna*) in this manner contradicts the fundamental intent; therefore, it is what is being refuted.

As for the statement that "only one [consciousness] proceeds," this refers to the fact that at the very moment a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, there is no other simultaneous mental consciousness; thus, it is said that there is no second.

Regarding the claim that "there is only one consciousness" while referring merely to the first six, this is the interpretation of Master Tse (Fazhuan). This is logically impossible, as the Master of the Commentary (Yuanze) explains.
This is a refutation.
[The *Śāstra*] states: "That which Buddhadatta maintains is also based on the sūtras" means that the master Buddhadatta is one teacher within the Sautrāntika school;
his name in Sanskrit is Buddhatideva, which translates as "Awakened Heaven" (Jue Tian). The doctrine he now establishes is likewise founded upon the sūtras.
Because this is our tenet, it is said that it is "also based on the sūtras. Their position is as follows:

"Since the sūtras state that the conjunction of three factors is called 'contact' (sparśa), we know that this proves there is only consciousness (vijñapti-mātra) and no mental concomitants (caitta). This is their cited proof. [The opponent asks:

"If there are no mental concomitants, why does it say that the conjunction of the three is called contact? Is contact not indeed a mental concomitant? [And so forth. The answer is: "Although such contact exists, it is also..."

It is called "non-existent" because it is like the small amount of water in a river, which is also called "waterless. Furthermore, regarding the statement that the contact between the sense organ, the object, and consciousness lacks substantiality, the phrase "the person consists of the six elements" means that the four great elements are established because they are the basis for form;
"space" is mentioned because it is the basis for movement; and "consciousness" is established because it is the basis for mind. Thus, the body is said to be composed of these six elements.

As for the claim that there are only sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*): [Note: The provided text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on Abhidharma or Yogācāra doctrine concerning the nature of the person (*pudgala*), the lack of intrinsic substance in the sensory process, and the composition of the body.]

As for the inclusion of volition (*cetanā*) and so forth, it is because they also describe the master Buddhadatta’s position that faith (*śraddhā*) and the like constitute the initial stages of entering the path;

therefore, they must be established [as mental factors]. Furthermore, they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Moreover, regarding those established as mental factors based on their being functions that accompany the mind:

with the exception of faith and so forth, and excluding greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and the like, those which are merely specific functional differentiations of the mind are established by the name "mental factor" (*caitasika*).

Question: It cannot be called either name or reality. I ask: I have not yet understood whether faith is provisional or real. Answer: Other forms of faith are provisional, whereas faith that accords with the Buddha-dharma is real.
Question: Are sensation, perception, mental formations, volition, and so forth provisional or real? Answer: That which constitutes an aggregate (*skandha*) is real;
that which does not constitute an aggregate is provisional.
[Commentary]: As for the statement, "However, what mind could there be when Bhāviveka maintains that [the ultimate] has been reached? the intention is as follows:

Bhāviveka maintains that in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), both object and mind are empty, whereas in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), both object and mind exist. Why, then, does he now specifically maintain that consciousness is non-existent while not saying the same of the object?

The answer is: according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), both object and mind exist; it is now, because of contradicting your own assertion that [the mind] exists, that he asserts the mind is non-existent.
[Commentary: If one were to analyze this meaning according to the fourfold logical categories (*catuṣkoṭi*), there are two layers of such analysis within the text;
furthermore, in the *Shuyao*, there is a ninefold analysis based on the sequential relationship of the four dharmas. First, clarifying the momentum of simultaneous arising (small/large, large/small);
second, establishing the momentum of the Dharma-realm (large/small, small/large); third, the momentum of adorning the jeweled stupa (large/small, small/large).
The fourth is the posture of the layered lotus (small-large, large-small); the fifth is the posture of the king leading his carriage (small-small, large-large);
the sixth is the posture of the dragon dragging its tail (large-large, small-small); the seventh is the posture of the ten-thousand great jewel cords (large-large, large-large);

the eighth is the posture of the thousand-fathom royal sash (small-small, small-small); the ninth is the posture of the hundred-jointed *lǚbǔ* (small-large, large-small). Question: There are four total counts; for what reason are they explained?

There are many assertions regarding "large" and "small," and although there are four types of calculations, the number of people involved is vast; because the ritual procedures (*dharmasaṃketa*) are established according to the number of persons, there are numerous calculations for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that those with wrong views claim there is no mind or object at all, the intent is to say that Bhāviveka maintains that, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), neither mind nor object exists.
Both [schools] share the same view as the Ekavyāvahārikas; these two aforementioned schools raise an objection against the Master based on contradiction with the authoritative scriptures (*āgama*).
[Commentary]: The Dharmaguptakas maintain that when the mind takes associated factors as its object, it is taking the mental concomitants (*caitta*) that arise simultaneously with it as its object.

[Commentary: Regarding the Mahīśāsaka school’s tenet that [the mind] takes co-existent dharmas as its object, there are three interpretations: first, it refers to the mutual cognition of mental factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth occurring at the same time;

second, it refers to the objects of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their corresponding bases (*viṣaya*) occurring simultaneously; third, it asserts that multiple minds occurring at the same time can also take one another as objects.

Furthermore, it is said that "co-existent dharmas" refers specifically to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that coexist with wisdom (*prajñā*). Although there are these three interpretations, the intended meaning is taken to be the first.
[Commentary:
Regarding the statement that Dharmatrāta asserts the essence of mental factors (*caitasika*) is precisely volition (*cetanā*), he was one master within the Sarvāstivāda school.
As for the Dharmaguptaka and Mahīśāsaka schools, they will both be refuted below.

[Commentary]: "If its object is real" means that because one understands the profound and subtle principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) according to reality, the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* is the object realized by wisdom. [Commentary]:

"However, within the first object, it reaches the point where there are only these two" intends to say that within the objects, there are both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Although the two truths are distinct, because the ultimate and the conventional are mutually dependent, they are taken together as the object. Question:

Since the ultimate and the conventional each have four levels, why are only the two truths mentioned here? Answer: Because all that is knowable is comprised solely within these two. Furthermore, question:
Why, among objects, are only the two truths mentioned and not other phenomena? Answer: Because all that is knowable is comprised solely within these [two].
"Because there are two.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the same as the initial nature and characteristics," the meaning is that within the present context of the objects of cognition, the text concerning the two truths is identical to the passage on the characteristics and nature found in the first section.
[Commentary]: Regarding the introduction of the treatise by means of a question to prompt its commencement, there are generally five types of questions:
first, questioning due to lack of understanding; second, questioning due to doubt; third, questioning for the purpose of testing; fourth, questioning out of disrespect or provocation;
and fifth, questioning with the desire to benefit and bring happiness to sentient beings. Herein, we rely upon the fifth type of question.

Regarding the intention for the benefit and happiness of others, it may be objected: "If there is only consciousness and no external objects apart from the mind, why do worldly convention and the sacred teachings speak of a self and dharmas?
In this context, "worldly" refers to non-Buddhists and ordinary beings, as they are subject to refutation and destruction;
"sacred teachings" refer to what is spoken by the Noble Ones, as they cannot be refuted or destroyed.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the meaning of designating one as "sage" (*śramaṇa*) because they accord with principle and penetrate the divine: it means that the mind accords with the principle and the wisdom penetrates the divine, both taking the *tathatā* (suchness) as their object.
As for why it is called "divine," it is because its spiritual subtlety is identical to that of the divine.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the mind merges with the object," when fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the mind are considered in relation to the object, they are called "merging with the object";

when mental factors (*caitta*) are considered in relation to the object, they are called "the intellect merging with the spirit. Furthermore, Xi explains that "the mind merges with the object" means the mind merges with the reality of the object, while "the intellect merges with the spirit" refers to the presence of superior spiritual function.

[Commentary] Regarding the intent behind explaining the origin of the question: it means that if, as in the preceding dialogue, there were only consciousness and no self or dharmas, how could the worldly and sacred teachings speak of a self and dharmas?
This explanation of the origin of the question is as stated in the *Śūyao* (Essential Pivot).
[Commentary]: "Although there are none such as those... up to "...therefore they are said to be provisional. The intent of this passage is to explain away an external objection. The objection states:

"If it is said that the self and dharmas have no substantial reality, how can one speak of the existence of provisional selves and dharmas? (and so forth). The answer is as given in the text of the commentary.
[Commentary]: "Although there is a substantial entity (dharmatā), it is called 'provisional' because [it is merely] designated"—the intention of this passage is to resolve an objection.

The objection asks: "If there is already a substantial entity, why is it termed provisional? The answer, as stated in the commentary, arises from the two preceding types of provisional self and phenomena.
Regarding the phrase "arising from the two": this explains the underlying purpose of the first two lines of the verse.
And regarding the explanation of the two phrases:

[The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Merely by means of the two kinds of conventional designations (*prajñapti-vyavahāra*)" means that it is solely by means of the two preceding kinds of conventional designations that verbal expressions arise, which are called the "two kinds of conventional designations" for the existence of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "one should explain the verse down to the prose commentary that follows," the intended meaning is as follows: In the preceding text, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) were explained first, followed by the transformation (*pariṇāma*), and finally the seeds (*bīja*).
Now, having first explained the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*), one subsequently explains the various characteristics and transformations;
this is in accordance with what follows below regarding the "various characteristics of the self" and the "various characteristics of phenomena."

[Commentary]: This merely explains the meaning of *vijñāna* (consciousness), while incidentally including the mental factors (*caitta*). This explains away an external objection. The objection states:

"Since the substance of consciousness undergoes transformation, and based on this [transformation] one speaks of 'self' and 'dharmas,' the mental factors—which possess these two divisions [of grasping at self and dharmas]—should also be said to involve 'self' and 'dharmas.

Why, then, do you speak of the reality of consciousness alone and not mention the mental factors? [And so forth. The answer is: "This merely explains the meaning of consciousness, while incidentally including the mental factors."
[Commentary]: If this were so, then True Suchness (*tathatā*) would not be "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*). This refers to an external objection:

[the opponent] argues that while the self and dharmas are unreal and thus called "representation-only," True Suchness is not unreal; therefore, it should not be "representation-only. The statement, "it is called 'representation-only' because it is not separate from consciousness," and so forth, is the response.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "The Noble One" to "provisionally designating the names of self and phenomena," this correlates with what is taught in the holy scriptures concerning the self and phenomena.

Question: For what reason must the holy scriptures teach about the self and phenomena? Answer: It is for the sake of severing erroneous grasping at purity; therefore, it is necessary to teach about the self and phenomena.
As it says: "Since they are great men, I am likewise so; one should not disparage oneself and become disheartened. Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "Do not cling..."

The realization that sentient beings truly exist or do not exist does not serve as the basis for generating intense compassion and the vow [for awakening]. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Even one who gives rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru can still generate the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is the intended meaning of this passage;
therefore, both the self and phenomena (*ātman-dharma*) in worldly and noble teachings are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the second interpretation up to the phrase "is spoken of as self and phenomena": this second [interpretation] further explains the basis upon which self and phenomena are provisionally established.
That is to say, based on the aspect of deluded perception (*vikalpa-bhāga*), one speaks of the existence of self and phenomena; these are the names for worldly self and phenomena.

Because they lack a real substratum, they exist only as provisional designations. Moreover, since the aspect of deluded perception is itself a transformation of the aspect of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), it is described as "also [the product of] deluded perception."
"Conditioned by these, grasping can arise. [Commentary:

Regarding the statement in the holy teachings that "the meaning relies upon the substance," this means that within the holy teachings, the existence of self and dharmas is explained as being based upon the substance of the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) of consciousness;
thus, the meaning relies upon the substance because it is provisional (*prajñapti*). (From the Ximing Commentary)

Question: Why do you say that the self and dharmas are not explained based on the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*)? [And so forth. Answer: Because it is easy to understand according to their characteristics, we speak of the image-portion (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-portion (*darśanabhāga*);
furthermore, there is no harm in relying on the actual meaning.

[Commentary]: "The particular depends upon the general" means that "self" (*ātman*) and "dharmas" (*dharma*) are termed the "particular," while the "self-verifying division" (*svasaṃvittibhāga*) is termed the "general.
That is to say, within the single, general self-verifying division, one speaks of the two particulars: self and dharmas.
[Commentary]: The meaning of the statement "that which is grasped is taken as self and dharmas" is as follows: "that which is grasped" refers to the self and dharmas;
"the mind that performs the grasping" is the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving division); and "the dharmas that are expressed" are the *nimitta-bhāga* (imagined division).
Thus, these grasped selves and dharmas, as well as the *darśana* and *nimitta* divisions, are all transformations of consciousness.

[Commentary]: Regarding these two preceding interpretations, both are the intent of Dharmapāla’s explanation. His meaning is that these four types of distinctions between self and dharmas arise from the following:
in the first interpretation, there are two kinds of self and dharmas; in the second interpretation, there are likewise two kinds of self and dharmas. Question:
If there were no distinction between self and dharmas, it would be inappropriate to establish four types.
Question: Since the two types of self and dharmas have four kinds of characteristics each, how do they differ? Answer: Regarding the first interpretation of the two types of self and dharmas:
these "self" and "dharmas" are designated by name based solely on the conventional expressions used for the means of cognition;

they are not established as "self" and "dharmas" based on the actual substance of phenomena (*dharma-tattva*) or internal consciousness (*vijñāna*). As for the second interpretation of the two types of self and dharmas:

However, it is based on the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as the perceiver, the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as the perceived, and the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), that the sense of "self" and "dharmas" is predicated;
thus, these "selves" and "dharmas" are said to be subsumed within the fundamental substance of consciousness itself, which is not separate from it.

Therefore, the sense of self and dharmas exists upon the substance of consciousness. Consequently, this differs from the second interpretation mentioned previously, which relied solely on verbal expression.
The latter statement is based solely on the fact that the substance (*dharmatā*) and the functional utility (*artha-vṛtti*) differ, and thus the two types are distinct.

[Commentary]: "The particular non-existence is based on the general non-existence" means that the two types—the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*)—are the particular non-existences; these exist upon the basis of the general non-existence.
This refers generally to the two divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), which are termed the "general non-existence. Alternatively, [it may refer to...].

It can be seen that because the two aspects—the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)—are given the collective name "non-existent," the objective aspect is entirely non-existent;

on this basis, the subjective aspect as well is likewise [non-existent]. For Master Sthiramati, these two aspects—the objective and the subjective—are also conventionally non-existent, just as a snail’s head has two horns:
although the horns have no substantial essence, they arise from the head.
[Commentary: Regarding the difference from Dharmapāla’s interpretation, Nanda relies solely upon the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) to establish this as self and phenomena;
Dharmapāla, however, penetrates both the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect) and the *nimittabhāga* to establish this as self and phenomena. Thus, there is a distinction between them.
[Commentary]: "The name has many meanings" refers to the fact that the *vipākavijñāna* (retributive consciousness) has multiple designations, as explained below.
