[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "all dharmas are stored within consciousness," the seven evolving consciousnesses are stored within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); that is, the fundamental consciousness is that which performs the function of storing.

Thus, the fundamental consciousness serves as the two types of conditions for the various consciousnesses. As for the statement that "consciousness [is] with respect to dharmas," this refers to the fundamental consciousness.
Because it is stored within the seven evolving consciousnesses, the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) is that which is "stored" (*cita*).

[Commentary: First, regarding "nurturing those seeds in the present life," this means that the active states (*pravṛtti*) of the seven consciousnesses, through their capacity to perfuse (*vāsana*), gradually cause the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vāsanā*) in the eighth consciousness to increase in the present dharma. Second, regarding "storing and planting them in future lives..."

"Seed" means: how could it be that future dharmas are allowed to arise? Therefore, the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma from the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) are gathered by the eighth [consciousness] within its seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), causing them to increase and bring about fruits in the future.

Regarding "mutually producing one another," this concludes the preceding point that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the evolving consciousnesses are mutually the results of one another; furthermore, it explains their mutual gathering and planting.

"Seed" (bīja) signifies that which encompasses planting; it has the sense of being an auxiliary. That is, the karmic seeds act as auxiliaries to the seeds of verbal designation (*nāma-kalpa*), enabling them to possess the capacity to bring about future heterogeneous maturation (*vipāka-phala*).
The phrase "that which is produced is the fruit, and that which arrives is the cause" explains the reason why the two aforementioned types of consciousness serve as mutual causes and effects.

[Commentary] Explaining the verse to clarify the preceding inquiry: the "preceding inquiry" refers to the difficult question posed prior to the verse, such as the statement, "If it exists only as the fundamental [nature],...
up to "...serving as the nature of causes and conditions. This verse now explains that which was previously questioned and clarified—that it is not merely the fundamental [nature].
Within this, there are three parts: first, explaining the verse to establish the nature of causes and conditions; second, citing scriptural authority to establish the preceding point.

Regarding the statement that "the three meanings of the causal conditions are not external dharmas because they are also produced," the intended meaning is that since the seven consciousnesses are both perfumers and,
furthermore, produced, they serve as mutual causes and effects.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "like reeds leaning against one another," a question is asked: since the conditions for dependent origination consist of three factors (*tridharma*), how can two factors serve as a metaphor?
The answer is: although the [number] two and three differ, because the two reeds exist simultaneously, they are like the three factors of dependent origination existing at the same time.

Furthermore, as explained below, it is solely by relying on these two that dependent origination is established; namely, the two factors of the seed (*bīja*) and the manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*). Now...
If one asks what error there is in taking two reeds as a metaphor, it is known that this merely serves as a metaphor for the two phenomena of cause and effect.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the conditions for the cause and effect of the substance are exhausted," the intention is as follows: when the seed is viewed in relation to the manifest, it is called "viewing in relation to the substance."

[Commentary]: Regarding "the essence of causes and conditions is exhausted": this refers to seeds producing the manifest and the manifest producing seeds, which collectively exhausts all causes and conditions. Question:
Since it is said that seeds produce the manifest and the manifest produces seeds, there are thus three factors; how then can you say that causes and conditions are established based on two? Answer:
Although there are three factors when considering their mutual production, in terms of the actual essence of the causal relationship, it consists solely of seeds.
"Two dharmas manifest.
[Commentary] If one considers the distinction between cause and fruit, yet speaks only in terms of their essential nature (*tattva*), the intended meaning is as follows:

for example, when speaking of "causal conditions," this refers only to seeds in relation to the essential nature of the manifest state (*samudācāra*). If one speaks in relation to distinct fruits, the production of a seed from a seed may still be designated as a "cause."
As for "conditions" (*pratyaya*), they merely distinguish between preceding and succeeding moments; as for "cause and effect," they differ in their types.

When it is said that "the arising of the manifest from the seeds refers only to the statement regarding their substance," this means that one takes what has been perfumed (*bhāvita*) to receive the name "seed," and this seed, in relation to the eighth consciousness's manifest state, serves as its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
[Commentary]: Furthermore, the meaning of the statement "it is not exhaustive because it does not mention the untainted (anāsrava)" is as follows:

when the aforementioned explanation of causes and conditions was distinguished based on new perfuming (navasaṃskāra), that discussion of causes and conditions was not exhaustive because it did not mention the untainted; this is because [the untainted] has never been perfumed and thus lacks untainted seeds.
Consequently, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* only states that defiled phenomena (saṃkleśadharma) serve as the causes and conditions for the ālayavijñāna, and does not mention the untainted.
[Commentary]:

As for the meaning of the phrase "merely causing [the seeds] to increase," it is intended to say that when karma manifests and increases its own seeds, these are called "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

One might argue that when karma manifests and increases the eighth consciousness, this too should be called a "causal condition. This objection is raised from the perspective of another school (the Sautrāntika), as Dharmapāla does not accept this.

The manifestation and growth of seeds such as the wholesome are termed "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), because they must be perfumed to produce various types of manifest activity as their direct causal condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because the resultant seeds reach the stage of growth," this explains that it is not by virtue of being a causal condition, but rather due to one's own karmic seeds.
"Because increase does not serve as a causal condition.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement "the indeterminate mind perfumes indeterminate seeds, etc.," this is the intended meaning of the answer:

for example, when an indeterminate mind perfumes indeterminate [seeds], or when a wholesome or unwholesome mind perfumes its own wholesome or unwholesome seeds; these seeds then give rise to their own respective manifest activities (*samudācāra*).
In your own school, you define *pratyaya* (condition) merely as that which causes the seeds of the fruit and the seeds of karma to increase;
how then can you challenge me? Even if both were newly perfumed (*navābhyāsita*), why would they not simply be called *pratyaya* because they arise anew? Therefore, your challenge is inconsistent.

Question: Since the mind of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and its objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*) are all capable of perfuming the seeds of the fruit, why do you say only that the "unconscious" (*acittaka*) states lack perfuming?

Question: Why does the discussion of the seeds of recording (*vijñapti*) not mention [the seeds of] the wholesome and so forth? Answer: According to the actual state of affairs, seeds are perfumed by minds of all three natures, and both the causal seeds and the resultant seeds are indeed perfumed as objective divisions (*nimitta-bhāga*) of karma.
However, for now, when we speak of perfuming by the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), this is done to set aside the wholesome and unwholesome without further discussion.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "all contradict that doctrine," if one were to admit [the seeds] exist inherently (*svabhāva-vāda*), it would contradict all the scriptural citations adduced by those masters.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "all contradict that doctrine," the textual passages cited concerning newly perfumed seeds (*navasaṃskāra-bīja*) would all contradict the three meanings of inherent existence.
Based on the subsequent text, this interpretation is correct.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the antidotes produced by those in training (śaikṣa) [counteract] the outflows (āsrava)," this implies that the noble path (āryamārga) produced by those in training must have the various outflows as its cause, because you admit that contradictory factors can exist in a causal relationship.

[Commentary]: It may be so for the Hīnayāna that [a mind] acts as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), for they allow that an unwholesome mind arises immediately after an indeterminate mind through causes such as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

As for the statement that wholesome and unwholesome karma of the Hīnayāna brings about a body of maturation (*vipāka*) through causal conditions, what is called "homogeneous" refers to that which belongs to the same realm (*dhātu*) bringing about a body of that same realm; this is termed the "homogeneous cause."

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "The original is Mahāyāna" up to "the teacher," the question is whether the Mahāyāna proponent of new熏 (newly perfumed) seeds and the Mahāyāna proponent of the blending of mind (*citta*) are one and the same or distinct.
The answer is: this teacher is a specific name within those who allow for new perfuming—the "Proponent of the Blending of Mind" or the "Proponent of New Perfuming.

Alternatively, the Proponent of New Perfuming and the Proponent of the Blending of Mind are distinct. As for "blending" (*hun*), the *Qieyun* states that it means "to occupy together"; "occupying together" means "to mix."

[Commentary]: Since it is granted that [conditioned phenomena] act as conditions, there must be taking and giving. A questioner asks: what is the distinction between taking and giving? The answer is: when the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) has not yet appeared, it lacks the function of taking the fruit;

whereas when the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) has passed, it possesses the function of giving the fruit. This is because, like the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), although it itself has ceased, the fruit arrives in the present.
Furthermore, the Commentary states that all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) serve as objects of cognition (*ālambana*); this is merely a provisional [explanation].

The seeds that produce manifest activity are called "seeds yielding fruit" (*phalada-bīja*); the seeds that induce subsequent moments [of seeds] are called "seeds grasping fruit" (*phalagrahaṇa-bīja*).

Regarding those who raise objections against the Mahāyāna teachings: they claim that while unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) can be apprehended as objects of perception (*ālambana*), they cannot serve as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) for any phenomena.
[Commentary: "That is, the essence of the mind is capable of cognizing dharmas" clarifies that this is the definitive principle distinguishing the cognizing mind [from other entities]. [Commentary:
"It is not because the preceding essence has ceased that one speaks of its permanence" means that when this treatise speaks of "permanence and unity," it is intended to refute [the opposing view].
"Always one.

[Commentary: If it were the case that the substance of the preceding untainted state ceases and the substance of a subsequent untainted state arises, this refers to the refutation of that hypothesis in the following passage.
The Commentary states: "If it were unconditioned... because True Suchness is wholesome," which means that if one says the nature of the mind is pure, it is emptiness.

In principle, that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—as refuted above by you—is faulty for you, yet it is without fault for me. Furthermore, it is commonly accepted that *tathatā* (suchness) and *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) are not associated with faith and the like.
Since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of your unwholesome minds and so forth is itself wholesome, why do they not associate with faith and the like?
Moreover, the nature of your unwholesome and neutral minds is a factor that is associated (*saṃprayukta-dharma*). As such...
"Why is this called unconditioned goodness?
[Commentary]: "If it were like the goodness of form and sound, which lack faith and so forth," is a restatement of an external objection.

"My unwholesome and neutral mental natures, though their essence is good, are still like the goodness of form and sound, as they lack association with faith and so forth"—this refers to the following discussion in the treatise: "What kind of dharma is this? and so on.
The main point refutes [the objection].

[Commentary]: The meaning of the statement "this defiled [phenomenon] serves as the cause for acquisition" is that because it is designated as "defiled," the cause universally includes all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), taking them collectively as the cause. Furthermore, this inference takes the unwholesome (*akuśala*) as its subject.
Regarding the analogy: it is because that which has already been refuted can serve as an analogy.

[Commentary] As for the meaning of "bondage by the object-condition" (*ālambana-bandhana*), the intention is this: a wholesome mind with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala-citta*) is called "defiled" (*saṃkliṣṭa*) because it is bound by the objects of those afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, it is termed "defiled."

[Commentary]: Regarding this [fallacy] where the *dharmin* (the subject) is not universally established (*aprasiddha*), one asks: "If that is so, why was the previous reason (*hetu*) not considered a fault, even though it was not untainted (*anāsrava*)?

Answer: The former [reason] served as the *pakṣadharma* (the property of the thesis), whereas this [subject] is the *dharmin*. A *dharmin* must be admitted by both parties; therefore, it constitutes a fault.
A *pakṣadharma*, however, contradicts the opponent's position while being acceptable to oneself; therefore, it is not a fault.
[Commentary] The meaning of the phrase "there should be no superior nature" is that since the contaminated (*sāsrava*) is that which is to be countered, how could it possess a superior nature?

[Commentary] Furthermore, the meaning of the statement "it is the seed-nature of supramundane consciousness" is that if there were originally existing uncontaminated seeds (*anāsravabīja*), why would one say that the contaminated perfuming by hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) serves as the seed for supramundane consciousness? As for the word "and":...

"Causes and conditions" refers to the contaminated seeds (*sāsrava-bīja*). This means that the permeation of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) arises from its own seeds as contaminated manifest activity (*sāsrava-saṃmukhībhāva*), and in turn perfumes them to form seeds that serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the growth of those uncontaminated seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).

Furthermore, there is an interpretation which states that "and its own causes and conditions" means that supramundane mind (*lokottara-citta*) takes its own seeds as its cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, it arises only when the outflowing habituation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*) acts as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). Although there are two interpretations, both are valid.

[The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "According to their distinctness" means that it is explained according to the distinctness of the innate (*prakṛtistha*) and the newly perfumed (*navasaṃskṛta*). "Innate" refers to...
"The outflow-free newly perfumed [seeds] are themselves outflowing.

[Commentary: Therefore, regarding the charge of contradiction with the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, these two interpretations do not conflict with the passage on the "perfuming by hearing" (*śrutavāsanā*) in that treatise.

[Commentary]: One who correctly grasps the intent of the Abhidharma is as follows: while the *abhisamaya-bhāga* (decisive factor) roots of goodness are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), here the intent is expressed by way of the coarse, manifest, and superior dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Since it speaks of the seeds of supramundane mind as being accessible to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated, it is said that one correctly grasps the intent of the Abhidharma.
Thus, the roots of goodness perfumed by hearing are themselves contaminated; originally, they are not uncontaminated.
The seeds are themselves untainted (*anāsrava*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because the inferior grade increases," the intended meaning is that within the stage of the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), the increase of the inferior grade of tainted (*sāsrava*) hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*) causes the inferior grade of untainted seeds to increase;
the other cases should be understood accordingly.
[Commentary: Regarding "transformative extinction," the intended meaning is that the seeds, taken as a whole, comprise three grades:

by transforming the inferior grade into the middling grade, and transforming the middling into the superior grade, there are thus three grades; yet in terms of their essential nature, they belong to a single category.

According to the third master, when transformation is simultaneous, the seeds possess these three grades; if they undergo perfuming, the inferior and middling grades transform simultaneously, and the middling grade transforms with...
In the superior grade, once the untainted seeds have fully increased, one is able to realize untainted wisdom and enter the Path of Seeing.
[Commentary] "The seeds of the three untainted faculties" refers to the seeds of the untainted dharmas of the three vehicles.
"Because their natures are each distinct" means that the lineages (gotra) of the three vehicles are each distinct.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that hell and so forth are spoken of in terms of what is "about to arise," this refers to the passage in the preceding section concerning the attainment of the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) in hell.

Regarding the passage from "The dharmas consist of five aggregates" to "the distinctions are exhaustive," the meaning is as follows: Among the five aggregates of dharmas, by merely excluding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), the distinctions are fully exhausted.

That which accords with the Dharma cannot serve as a seed; external material dharmas can possess the six characteristics [of a seed], whereas this [internal mind] does not.
This lack of distinction clearly indicates that other dharmas are likewise not termed "seeds.

[Commentary]: Regarding the exclusion of its own locus while establishing other categories—this explanation holds that the reason for introducing those other categories is merely to briefly exclude its own [locus].
The establishment of the remaining second, fourth, fifth, sixth, and subsequent gates within the section on seeds does not serve to exclude other phenomena from being seeds;

rather, the intent of establishing these remaining gates is as follows: since the meaning of the "seed" has already been fully established by the single third gate through its exclusionary definition, I shall now briefly mention that, beyond the section on one's own seeds, the terms for the remaining second gate and so forth are established, though they will not be further detailed here.

The meaning of this statement is that, according to the second gate and others, the seeds are established in accordance with their respective locations and are distinguished without being presented out of sequence.

[Commentary] Regarding the fact that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* does not distinguish between specific differences: the intent is that while that treatise does not distinguish between the differences of external seeds, it does distinguish the differences of internal seeds;
by possessing these seven characteristics, they constitute seeds and so forth, having the functional capacity to produce fruits. If, in the world...
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* encompasses both internal and external [dharmas].

[Commentary]: That is to say, even though that treatise distinguishes each [category] individually regarding external [dharmas], when it comes to "simultaneous existence with the fruit" (*phala-sahabhū*), it speaks only of internal seeds and not of external ones.
How, then, can we know that external dharmas possess the meaning of "simultaneous existence with the fruit"? Therefore, at this time, [the focus is] exclusively...
The citation is raised for inquiry as explained in the *Śāstra* itself. [Commentary:
Regarding "the seeds giving and taking the fruit": when a seed possesses the power to produce a manifest state (*pravṛtti*), it is called "giving the fruit" (*phaladāna*).

Subsequently, the seed of the succeeding moment is called "taking the fruit" (*phalagrahaṇa*). Furthermore, it is said that the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*)—which functions in the future as a seed capable of producing—is the subsequent moment.

The fruit is said to "take" [the fruit] when it reaches the past; although it remains in its own state, it bestows its power upon the subsequent fruit, causing it to reach the present, which is called "giving" the fruit.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the four schools, such as the Mahāsāṃghika, do not undergo transformation, the meaning is as follows: namely, the Mahāsāṃghika and the Ekavyāvahārika schools.

The Lokottaravādins and the Kaurukullakas maintain that certain members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); likewise, the Mahīśāsakas collectively maintain that certain members of dependent origination are unconditioned.
Although these two schools differ at present, what they maintain is the same; therefore, it is explained in one place.

[Commentary]: If one were to argue that [the cause] does not exist in the initial stage during the subsequent period, this is an external defense. The following is the direct refutation of that defense:
it is said that in the initial stage there is no superior cause of the cause; rather, it must reach the end of its full term before the cause for grasping the fruit becomes manifest.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the seeds of all," the masters of old held that True Suchness is the support (*āśraya*) of all phenomena, and thus they designated True Suchness itself as the "seeds. [Commentary]:
As for the phrase "If it were so... up to 'becoming the seeds,'" this passage from the main text below contains two intended meanings. The first meaning is that if, at the moment of the *kṣaṇa*...

If that cessation were the seed, then the preceding moment as a seed would have to produce the subsequent moment as a manifest phenomenon; this is the first point, raising an objection regarding the production of a manifest phenomenon from a seed at different times.

Alternatively, even if they are of the same moment, [the objection] concerns the relationship between the seed and the phenomenon within the same moment by comparing one's own body and another's body;

this is the second point. As for the term "seed" (*bīja*): *Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a commentary on a philosophical debate concerning the nature of seeds (*bīja*) and their relationship to manifest phenomena (*dharma*), specifically addressing the temporal and simultaneous dynamics of causal efficacy.*

If one maintains that [the seventh consciousness] must share the same mental moments as the manifest [consciousness], then its own seeds would have to serve as the seeds for the manifest [consciousness] of another body;
thus, the treatise was composed with these two points in mind.

[Commentary]: By this, it is meant that for those of no-nature (icchantika), the seventh consciousness does not manifest until the fruit [of Buddhahood] is attained. This explanation serves to distinguish [them from others].

Question: Regarding those with the potential for enlightenment (*gotra*) and those without it, why is it that although the first seven consciousnesses can act as perfumers (*vāsana*), they cannot collectively be designated as seeds?
Furthermore, what is the intention behind distinguishing only those without the potential for enlightenment regarding the seventh consciousness at this point?
Answer: Because the seventh consciousness of those with the potential for enlightenment lacks two essential conditions, it does not [function as a seed].
The first [type] lacks the quality of being "ever-present" (*nitya-anuvartana*) because it undergoes transformation once one has entered the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The second lacks the sense of "manifestation" (*prabhāsvara-artha*). Although the seventh is indeed capable of perfuming (*vāsanā*), its seeds and fruits do not manifest;

because their characteristics are submerged and obscure, it cannot be called a "seed. Since this meaning is fully established, there is no need for further distinction. Question: Even if one were to distinguish them...
What prevents you from answering that it is not so? Since the seeds of the *manas* must possess six characteristics, and since two of these are lacking, the seeds are not established;

why then is there a need for further discrimination? Question: For those of no spiritual lineage (*agotra*), the seventh consciousness lacks something; why then is there a need for immediate discrimination? Answer: For those of no spiritual lineage, the seventh consciousness lacks only one characteristic;

therefore, discrimination is necessary. Question: How does it lack one characteristic? Answer: [The text continues: ... [it lacks the characteristic of being] the support for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Thus, because it lacks this one characteristic, it is distinguished as not being a seed.

The seventh [consciousness], although it can indeed permeate (*vāsanā*) seeds, has its characteristics submerged and hidden rather than manifest; because it lacks this one factor, it must be distinguished [from the others].

Question: How can it be said to "constantly follow and transform" (*nitya-anuvartana*)? Answer: It refers to those of no spiritual disposition (*agotra*), who ultimately never give rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

Since the seventh consciousness does not attain the untainted (*anāsrava*), and because there is no untainted state, it is uninterrupted and ceases to exist [only upon the attainment of the untainted].

Because it is abandoned at the time [of cessation], it possesses the sense of "constantly following and evolving. Question: Since it constantly follows and evolves, why can it not be called a "seed" (*bīja*)? Answer:
Because the characteristics of the perfumed seed do not manifest, this is precisely the seventh [consciousness] lacking its fruit;

it possesses only the aforementioned [general] meaning. Therefore, it is excluded here. Question: If the seventh consciousness is not a seed because its characteristics are submerged and hidden, then for the time being, its characteristics are submerged...
Question: Among the six characteristics of a seed, why is it said that if even one characteristic is missing, it cannot constitute a seed?

Answer: "Manifestation" refers to the characteristic of being co-existent with its fruit. If the fruit and the seed are mutually submerged and not manifest, this constitutes the deficiency of the characteristic of being co-existent with the fruit.
Therefore, the seventh consciousness (*manas*) is not called a seed. As for those of the nature of having a spiritual disposition (*gotra*):...
For those who lack this nature (the *anātmaka*), the first six consciousnesses do not function during the five states, such as the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*);
because they are absent and lack constant, concomitant transformation, they are not what is being discussed here. Question: How can seeds and fruits be "submerged" (*līna*)? Answer:

Because the seventh consciousness does not pass through the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), but is of one class of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature, it is constantly associated with the four afflictions (*kleśa*). It spontaneously and internally grasps at a self (*ātman*), and thus perfumes the seeds.

Question: Since these various characteristics are submerged and obscure, how does this differ from the seventh consciousness (*manas*) of those who possess the nature [of Buddhahood] (*gotra*), such that it is distinguished here as being "alone"?

Answer: The seventh consciousness of those who possess the nature lacks constant, continuous transformation (*anuvartana*). In this context, it is not distinguished because, as in the third section on the gate of constant transformation, it has already been distinguished there;

therefore, it is not mentioned in this text. Question: For one who possesses the nature, the seeds perfumed by the seventh consciousness give rise to the seventh [consciousness]. Is this not the case? [End of excerpt]
Question: Can that which is currently functioning (pravṛtti) be called a seed? Answer: It receives the name "seed" because it is asked about [in this context]. Question:

If it is argued that whatever constantly follows along (anuvartate) may be called a seed, then why can the seventh consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*), which constantly follows along, not be called a seed?

Answer: Because the seeds constantly follow along and give rise to manifesting active states (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) which appear as objects, they are called "seeds. The non-existent [seventh consciousness] does not do so. Therefore, it cannot be called a seed.
Although the seventh consciousness (the *ālayavijñāna*) functions as a concomitant (*anuvartaka*) and is perfumed to produce various resultant characteristics, it remains submerged and latent;
therefore, the seventh consciousness lacks the nature [of being a seed] and cannot be designated as a "seed.

[Commentary]: This passage specifically excludes the principle that a preceding dharma serves as the seed for a subsequent dharma, intending thereby to distinguish the "seed" as that which produces its own kind through self-reproduction.
Regarding "one's own position" [the *shu* (commentary) states]: Some say, "How is it understood that... The intent of this is as follows:

according to the master Vasumitra, the seeds that produce the manifestation of mindfulness are not a single moment, but rather successive moments. That is to say, how does the master Vasumitra understand this?
Since there is a textual passage stating that this fruit co-exists [with its cause], it is asked: "How is this to be understood? [The *Śū* (Commentary) states:

"That is, while the cause is in the state of arising, the fruit is in the state of ceasing. This means that the prior cause is in the state of arising (*utpāda*) and the subsequent fruit is in the state of ceasing (*nirodha*).

The intended meaning is that for a mental factor (*citta-dharma*), a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) is so brief that it exists simultaneously across both the two phases of arising and ceasing; thus, it is the mental factor itself.
When the mind is in the process of arising, it is said to "repay" its prior cause; this means that while the cause is present and about to cease, it can project a subsequent effect.
When the effect is in the process of ceasing, it is said that "the cause was present during its arising. Why is this? Because it is able to project a subsequent effect.

Furthermore, when the effect is in the process of ceasing, it is said to be "in relation to the preceding moment," because it repays the prior cause. Thus, the initial arising of the mind is considered in relation to [the subsequent].

The subsequent moment serves as the cause; when it ceases, it is viewed in relation to the preceding moment as the effect. Thus, the cause exists at the time of arising and the effect exists at the time of cessation.

Therefore, although the master Saṃghabhadra provisionally clarifies that the Sautrāntika school establishes both the times of cause and effect as arising and ceasing, they nonetheless remain together in the present.

Consequently, this does not contradict the scriptural statement that [the characteristics] exist simultaneously with the dharma. Question: Since the sūtras state that there are four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), why...

Therefore, it is said that only the two moments of arising and ceasing are mentioned in response, as the Buddha stated: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are dharmas of arising and ceasing.

He did not mention "abiding" (*sthiti*) and "alteration" (*anyathātva*). Thus, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra. Question: Since the manifestation of material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) possesses the characteristic of abiding, why is it not said that they have all three characteristics, but only the two characteristics of arising and ceasing?
Answer: Arising and ceasing apply to both matter and mind, whereas the characteristic of abiding applies only to matter. Here, we are relying on [the fact that]...

In general, it is said that there are only two characteristics: arising and ceasing. Question: Since both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are equally existent, why are two characteristics established for mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), while three characteristics are established for material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*)?
Answer: Material phenomena are sluggish and thus can possess the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti*).

Mental phenomena are extremely rapid; therefore, two characteristics are established for them. Because extremely rapid phenomena cease immediately after arising, they may lack the characteristic of abiding. Furthermore...
In the third fascicle, there is an extensive analysis [of this point]. The master Vasumitra—that is, the patriarch Nanda—raises an objection:

[The *Śāstra*] states, "If that were so, regarding the seed in relation to that which is not co-existent with its fruit... The intent of this passage is as follows: this is a hypothetical objection. The objection states:

if one allows that the seed produces the manifest state (*pravṛtti*) while permitting that cause and effect are simultaneous—which is termed "co-existence with the fruit"—then it would follow that the seed produces the seed itself.
If this cause and effect were to be simultaneous, they should be called "coexistent with the fruit" (*phala-sahabhū*). [Objection: If that were so, what would be the fault? [Response:
If that were the case, what difference would there be between the production of seeds and the production of seeds manifesting as actualities?

[Commentary]: What is the meaning of this brief clarification regarding the intention not to distinguish these fetters? Furthermore, it contradicts the principle of "different times" in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, for the *Yogācāra* does not permit the simultaneous arising of seeds from seeds.
There is also a citation stating that the master Vasumitra said:

"The cessation of the cause and the arising of the fruit exist simultaneously within the present; this is what is called 'co-existence with the fruit' (phala-sahabhū). This would imply that the arising of seeds from seeds [is simultaneous]. However, this should be...
Furthermore, the meaning of the objection regarding the "simultaneous existence of cause and effect" (*sahabhū-hetu*) is as follows: What is the purpose of this brief clarification?

If Master Saṃghabhadra were to make such a statement, what would be the point of briefly distinguishing [the types]? For if seeds produced various [results] and those produced manifest as one, there would be no distinction in their simultaneous nature;
moreover, it would contradict the principle in the *Yogācārabhūmi* that they occur at different times.
[Commentary] Regarding the objection that two destinies arise simultaneously:

the meaning is this—if the human destiny has attained cessation but has not yet ceased, while the heavenly destiny has already arisen, would this not constitute the objection of two destinies arising simultaneously? Therefore, the *ālayavijñāna* of a single body cannot arise simultaneously in two destinies.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "distinguished from other bodies because they do not harmonize," the meaning is as follows:

although the seeds within one's own body exist simultaneously with the manifest activities (*pravṛtti*) of another body, because they do not harmonize, the seeds within one's own body cannot be designated as "seeds" in relation to that other body.
[The mention of] the Sautrāntikas and others is because the Sautrāntikas and the Sthaviras maintain that cause and effect are distinct.
At that time, they are not yet designated as seeds; therefore, they are negated here. As will be explained separately below in the refutation, one should understand this by analogy with form:
the mind possesses the function of cognitive engagement (*ālambana-cintana*), whereas the seeds of the mind do not possess the function of cognitive engagement;
thus, it should be understood through the example of form.
The meaning of the statement, "The same should apply to seeds in relation to their respective categories," is that according to the Master’s interpretation,
since two manifest states cannot coexist within a single moment of thought, it is said that two seeds cannot exist simultaneously within a single moment. There is another interpretation,
as explained in the *Yanmi*.
[Commentary: "If that is so, how [can it be]?"—this refers to the contradiction between their essential natures (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*). This means that the objection follows from the preceding point:

if one does not admit that two seeds arise simultaneously, then for instance, within the state of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), there would be no simultaneous arising of an untainted seed (*anāsrava-bīja*) and a newly perfumed seed (*navasaṃskṛta-bīja*) in the same moment, because their essential natures are contradictory.
As described in the *Yǎnbì* (Exposition of the Secrets), the intent of this objection is extensive; read the *Yǎn* (Exposition) for a detailed account.
Esoteric Text. [Commentary]:

Regarding the meaning of "this is not the same as the fault of the seed producing the seed at a different time," the intent is that this answers the previous objection by clarifying the reason why they are not simultaneous.

It explains that it is because within the *laukikāgra-dharma* (the supreme mundane dharma), there is the wisdom perfumed by hearing (*śruta-vāsanā-jñāna*), and through this wisdom perfumed by hearing, [the seeds] are purified.

Because it is the true Dharma flowing equally from the *dharmadhātu*, and because the contaminated mind of preparatory effort (*prayoga-citta*) is predominant, it acts as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to perfume the innate uncontaminated seeds existing within the stage of the "World-Highest" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

It is precisely because these seeds possess such power that they can serve as the cause for subsequent moments of their own kind—the seeds that arise through the natural law (*dharmatā*) of their own nature. Furthermore, that which serves as the cause for these subsequent moments is the preceding moment of the uncontaminated [mind].

Furthermore, the seeds of outflows (*āsrava*) can serve as causes; that which is capable of functioning as the seed for the arising of a single subsequent moment is precisely the originally existing untainted seed (*anāsrava-bīja*) within the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
It possesses two functions: first, it draws forth the seed of its own kind for the subsequent moment through the natural law (*dharmatā*);
second, it serves as a cause to induce the seed for the arising of the subsequent moment, which is the second moment.

By the nature of things (*dharmatā*), since the causal power of the seeds of their own kind and the seeds that arise simultaneously is equal, the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) manifests upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Therefore, there is no fault of seeds producing seeds within the same moment of thought. The Commentary refers to these "arising" seeds as "newly perfumed" (*navasaṃskṛta*) seeds.
In response to the question of whether these arising seeds produce further seeds, [it is said]: they do not arise from original seeds; thus, they may be called "new."
If [the seeds] arise from what is originally present (*mūla-vidyamāna*), how can they be called "newly perfumed" (*nava-vāsita*)? To this, the response is:

because the *laukikāgra-dharma* (the supreme mundane dharmas) are perfumed by outflowing taints (*sāsrava*), although these arise from originally present untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*), they are said to acquire "newly perfumed seeds" in terms of their causal lineage (*gotra-pratyaya*).

However, since the meaning of "generating seeds" is not the correct interpretation according to the Master [Vasubandhu], this point is jointly transmitted and accepted as the teaching of Dharmapāla’s disciples.
One should form this understanding. [Commentary]:

This is also difficult to understand; its meaning is that it refutes the previous interpretation. If one were to follow the previous explanation, then within a single moment there would be four factors:
first, the spontaneous, self-similar, and natural seeds; second, that which is originally present and gives rise to [the result].
The third is the seed produced by both the original and the new [types of seeds], which gives rise to actualized manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
The fourth is the seed produced through the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of these actualized manifestations, because it is said that "perfuming the seed" occurs when the actualized manifestation arises.

Since there are thus four dharmas, how can they together constitute the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and furthermore, how can one say that these three dharmas mutually serve as causes and conditions for one another? This is the question.
Difficult to understand. [Commentary:
Now, to explain that this is not so is to collectively refute the preceding objection and reveal the reasons and conditions for its existence.
[Commentary: To say, "It is precisely the originally existing seeds... therefore there are only three dharmas," is the establishment of the principle. Although this principle exists, however—
The innate seeds (*prakṛtistha-bīja*) do not serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the perfumed seeds (*vāsanā-bīja*), as stated in the *Yanmi* (Exposition of the Secrets).

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the interpretation from "Moreover, the innate... up to "...serves as the causal condition": since the previous meaning was incorrect, it must be explained further.

The intended meaning is that the innate seeds give rise to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) manifest activity (*samudācāra*), and because this manifest activity perfumes and forms seeds, they are able to serve as such.

The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) refers to seeds producing manifest activity as the "present condition" (*pratyutpanna-pratyaya*), and manifest activity perfuming seeds to form seeds as the "causal condition.

Seeds are not taken as the causal condition in relation to seeds themselves, because they are separated by manifest activity. Although there are three interpretations, the latter interpretation is taken as correct.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "by this, the prātimokṣa-saṃvara, etc.," the intended meaning is as follows: a single moment of seeds possesses a superior efficacy that gives rise to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) manifest activity;

this manifest activity then perfumes the seeds, resulting in the wisdom of clear understanding and the *vimukti-śīla* (liberation-precept). This precept serves to restrain the seven branches of body and speech;
however, it is merely an increase in function, not an increase in essence.
[Commentary: Although this section clarifies the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*) by reference to the subsequent treatise, an external critic raises an objection.
First, the Master of the Commentary explains the objection, and subsequently presents the objection from the external critic. The intent of the objection is as follows:

since it is stated that "simultaneity with the fruit" (*phala-sahabhū*) constitutes a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), just as a seed is a causal condition, it is not yet clear whether [the cause] is simultaneous with its fruit. The answer is as provided in the Commentary: although the cause... [text truncated].

Regarding the term "the fruit": this explains away an external objection. Does not the objection state that since both cause and fruit pertain to all three time periods, how can it be said that [the fruit] exists simultaneously with [the cause]? Therefore, this clarification is made.
[Commentary: Since the term "cause" (hetu) applies both to seeds (*bīja*) and to existing seeds (*sadbīja*), the first mention of "seeds" refers to seeds acting as causes to produce the present;
the subsequent mention of "existing seeds" refers to seeds acting as causes to produce future seeds. Taken together, they are termed "seeds and existing seeds," though their intended meanings differ.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because it can produce the perfuming," some say that by the power of the seeds, the manifest [phenomena] are able to be perfumed and only then arise;
therefore, the name "seed" is established based on its ability to produce manifest fruits.
[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "not identical to this very moment" is that the seed is not identical to this single moment; it must necessarily exist in preceding and succeeding moments.

If one were like the master Saṃghabhadra, who holds that cause and effect belong to the same temporal period (*ekakāla*), how could one explain this text stating that [the seed] is "not identical to this very moment"?
[Commentary]: As for the meaning of the subsequent explanation regarding the passage on "that which has already arisen without seeds," the intent is as follows:

If, according to Vasumitra, cause and effect were simultaneous within the same moment, how would one explain the passage in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* concerning "that which has already arisen without seeds"? Since "seeds" and "that which has already arisen" are designated as distinct moments, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* speaks of 'that which has already arisen without seeds'. Therefore, Vasumitra reconciles this by stating that "without seeds" refers to...
"Arising" refers to the final moment of consciousness of an Arhat; because it lacks the power to produce further seeds for subsequent fruits, it is "without seed.
It is called "without seed" because the seeds that would have produced fruit have already ceased. The Arhat's present body arises from prior karma and is thus termed "already arisen.
This is the reconciliation within the school that maintains the simultaneity of cause and effect. If cause and effect were of different times...
This text is the correct statement; those who have compiled it as such refer to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "in reality, it also excludes matter (*rūpa*)," a question is raised: "Previously, based on the mere exclusion of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the evolving consciousnesses were fully distinguished.
Since material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) possess all six characteristics, they were not excluded. How can it now be said that 'in reality, it also excludes matter'? Answer: If...

Since the provisional designation (*prajñapti*) of seeds and material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) can possess six meanings, it is not distinguished from mindfulness; thus, the essence of the seed is said to be material phenomenon.
Furthermore, this excludes the Sautrāntika position, as they do not admit that material phenomena can maintain seeds.
Alternatively, there is no fault here because this exclusion refers to internal matter and does not concern external matter.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the mind’s three feelings undergo transformation," the intended meaning is that because the mind is associated with the three feelings such as suffering and so forth, its engagement with objects is easily detached;
therefore, it is not a seed. [Commentary]:
Regarding the question, "The seventh consciousness is only severed [at the stage of] the Immovable," the intent of the question is to ask whether seeds and the seventh consciousness merely coexist.
Question: Since the meaning of "constantly following and transforming" persists until the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) where it is finally severed, why can it not be called a "seed"? Answer:
Although the seventh consciousness is ultimately severed at the stage of Buddhahood, from the moment one first attains the first bhūmi, a transformation occurs.

Furthermore, when the sixth consciousness enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasunyatā*), the seventh consciousness then becomes associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). Therefore, it is said that [the seventh] has not yet been confronted [by its antidote].
Because it undergoes transformation prior to being cured, and because it is designated as an "antidote" (pratipakṣa) based on the state of Buddhahood, it is interrupted and thus not called a seed;

furthermore, it does not constantly follow [the person] and therefore differs from the sixth [consciousness]. Regarding that which is interrupted: the sixth consciousness is not an appropriate example because it does not function during the five states [of meditative absorption, etc.].

Although the second vehicle attains the untainted (anāsrava) upon entering the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), the sixth and seventh consciousnesses always coexist with the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha).

Therefore. [Commentary: "If that were so" up to "the seeds of the characteristics of sensation" marks the intent of the question. From "the indeterminate of names and phrases" onwards is the explanation of the answer to the question.

The question asks: "Or rather, because the previous explanation of 'understanding' and the subsequent one regarding the two types of perfuming are distinct in their particulars yet identical in their general nature, they are differentiated as wholesome."
The statement that "the production of fruit from seeds has limits" reveals the meaning of the absence of perpetual persistence.

Although the flow of maturation within the three realms follows karma and its duration is brief, and there is a limit to the existence of retribution as beings transmigrate among the six destinies, this is called the characteristic of having an end to what is experienced.

How, then, can seeds possess the sense of perpetual persistence? The intent of the commentary in answering this is that, while the capacity of the seed’s power to produce fruit does indeed have limits...
However, because the substance of the seeds must be severed by the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*), they possess the characteristics of being acquired and persisting as a continuous transformation.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding "partial perfuming," "partial" (*bhāga*) refers to a constituent part; it is the seed of karma.

[Commentary]: "The two principles of constant transformation through arising and ceasing" refer precisely to the two gates of "momentary" and "constant following-transformation" among the six characteristics.

[Commentary]: "It is not that the manifestation of the six [characteristics] constitutes the seed itself"—the intent of this statement is to refute the previous objection regarding the transformation of the mind (*manas*). You may... [the rest of the sentence follows].
Because the seventh [consciousness] lacks the meaning of "constantly evolving," it is analogous to the case where a seed and its fruit are not simultaneous and yet both are designated as "seeds";
even if the seventh were to possess the six characteristics, it still could not be called a "seed."
[Commentary]: This clarifies that those seeds of one's own category which do not receive the name "seed" upon reaching the stage of the counteractive path (*pratipakṣa*) are as follows:

for example, the seeds of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñin*) and so forth do not produce their fruit when one reaches the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); therefore, this is called the "counteractive path. These seeds are only severed by the Diamond-like Mind (*vajropamasamādhi*).
From the point of the Path of Seeing onward, they no longer produce fruit; because they lack such nature, they are designated as "seeds of the same category" (*jātīya*) based on this.
In this treatise, it is held that for Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the seeds of afflictions (*kleśa-bīja*) no longer give rise to actual manifestations;
they are merely subsumed under their generic categories (*jāti-gata*). This applies equally to the seeds of the three evil destinies (*durgati*) and so forth.

Although other seeds may lack the conditions in the interim and thus lack the capacity to produce fruit later on, they are still called "seeds" because they do not differ in nature from those that do. Otherwise, they would not be designated as seeds.

Question: What is the distinction between the "seed-category" (*bīja-jāti*) as explained in this treatise and that in the *Anāśraya* (Treatise on the Non-Existence [of Seeds])? Answer: Regarding the meaning of "seed" in this treatise:

although it is of a category that would not arise if intermediate conditions were lacking, it is designated as a "seed" based on the fact that, in terms of its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it possesses the capacity to produce a fruit simultaneously with that fruit.
In contrast, the *Anāśraya* treatise maintains that [the seed] exists only until the diamond-like path of antidotes (*vajropama-pratipakṣa-mārga*) has not yet arisen.
From the point of its arising until the conditions for producing a fruit are lacking and that fruit has not yet arisen, it is merely termed a "category" (*jāti*).
This is because the fruit does not yet exist; since it lacks the superior activity (*adhipati-prayojana*) of the fruit, it is called a "category.

In this treatise, the essence of the seed is not defined in terms of the active manifestation (*samudācāra*); therefore, it is collectively termed a "seed. Furthermore, because it draws forth its own kind, it is provisionally called a "seed."

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) reveals the distinction between these two stages," this refers to the distinction between the two stages of the seed (*bīja*) and the genus (*jāti*).

[Commentary: To the objection, "If that were so, it would not be called a 'seed,'" the previous argument states: "If there is no nature, the seventh [consciousness] lacks the capacity to bestow its fruit."
If neither [of these] were the seed, then it would follow that when the seed has not yet produced its fruit, it could not be called a "seed.
Since this objection exists, it must be further explained. [Commentary:

The meaning of "the seed is abandoned by the Path of Seeing" is as follows: the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is established based on the seeds of a mind of revulsion; if [this state] reaches...

Regarding the statement that those in the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) who are in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva) will ultimately never again experience [birth there], this is said in terms of the seeds of what is abandoned by the Path of Seeing;

it means that once these seeds are severed, they will not arise again. In reality, however, the substance of these seeds is severed by the Diamond-like Samādhi (vajropamasamādhi). These seeds are wholesome and do not obstruct the Noble Path.

[Commentary]: The meaning of "it is not necessary for this momentary thought [to possess all six characteristics]" is that while the seeds possess the six meanings when considered over a long duration, it is not required that they possess all six meanings within every single momentary thought.
If they were to possess the six meanings within a single momentary thought, there would be the fault that a single realm could not establish the seeds of the three realms.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "one realm does not constitute three realms," etc., this is because seeds from other realms do not produce manifest activity and thus are not designated as "seeds.

If this were the case, one might argue they should be called "ripened seeds"; since those seeds are indeed termed "ripened," it is known that they may coexist with their fruit and yet still be called "seeds.
It is not necessary for them to be constantly coexistent with the manifest activity in every single moment.

[Commentary]: The meaning of the passage from "refuting the Sarvāstivāda" up to "serving as a causal condition" is as follows: this refutes the tenet of the *astitva-vādin* (the school asserting existence) which maintains that a cause of a different nature produces an effect of a different nature, yet possesses the status of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The intention of that school is to say that dharmas of the same nature—such as those belonging to their own realm (*dhātu*) and their own stage (*bhūmi*)—act as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), and because they are such, they constitute a causal condition.
For example, wholesome dharmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) induce obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas of the desire realm.

Taking these as causes and conditions because they belong to the same category is called the "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*); because they are all contaminated (*sāsrava*), they are called "outflowing fruits" (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Thus, the homogeneous cause is reckoned as a cause and condition that induces outflowing fruits, as will be explained and refuted below.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and so forth, this describes his own position while demonstrating that other views are incorrect.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement "the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) results in an indeterminate fruit": they maintain that the ripening fruit—the body composed of the five sense faculties—is produced by wholesome and unwholesome karma;

therefore, because it is a fruit distinct from its [specific] causes, the body of the five sense faculties is termed the "ripening fruit" (*vipāka-phala*). It is called "distinct" (*viśiṣṭa*) because it differs [from those causes].
At that time, it therefore receives the name "vipāka" (maturation).

[Commentary: Regarding the fact that the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) has results of a different nature: they maintain that the two views—view of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*)—universally act as causes for the defiled dharmas of the five categories, giving rise to the unwholesome and the indeterminate;
hence it is said that it obtains results of a different nature. If this is so, how is it [to be understood]?

Regarding the term "outflow" (*niṣyanda*): it is answered that both defiled and impure results are called outflows. Furthermore, what is the fault [in this definition]? Question: What is meant by "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*)? Answer:

According to our own school, the view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) act as causes for all five categories of defiled phenomena within their own respective levels.

This is because, as the treatise states, there is no one who sinks into the mire of existence without being caused by the arising of the view of self and so forth. Thus, the treatise says: "Those who cling are the view of self; they sink into the depths."
Question: Regarding the statement that the view of selflessness can realize nirvāṇa within the cycle of birth and death, what are the five categories (pañcavarga) called? Answer:
They are the afflictions belonging to each of the four noble truths and the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation; these are termed the five categories.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) reaches results such as the immediate result (*anantara-phala*) and the virile result (*puruṣakāra-phala*), the intended meaning is as follows:

A simultaneous cause obtains the ripened result (*vipāka-phala*). For example, just as one’s present body was brought about by past karma, once that karma has ceased, the body remains because the karma still exists;

thus, this karma is given the name "simultaneous cause. Furthermore, while this is a ripened result, it is also considered a virile result in a remote sense, because they belong to different time periods.
Regarding the "immediate fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*): this refers to the fact that the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) obtains the immediate fruit of human effort.
For example, when the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) exert mutual influence to arise, they are all termed fruits of human effort. This is what is intended:

when a mental factor of the present moment is considered in relation to the mental king (the primary consciousness) of the same present moment, it acts as a co-existent cause and obtains the co-existent fruit of human effort; this is precisely what is meant here.

Regarding the statement that "the collection of mind and mental factors which can induce subsequent moments of mind and mental factors is the immediate fruit of the soil" and that "taking this as a cause is for the time being acceptable":

the intent of this is to say that these causes are asserted by certain schools to be *hetupratyaya* (causal conditions). However, according to the preceding [analysis], since they are *sabhāgahetu* (homogeneous causes), they are not *hetupratyaya*.

Therefore, it is said that "taking them as causes is for the time being acceptable. Since their essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not established and they do not mutually accord, [they cannot be causal conditions].
In what sense is this "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*)? It is not called the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*), for that school itself states it is not a causal condition;
therefore, it is not mentioned here.
[Commentary: "From the various conditions" refers to mental attention, the sense faculties, objects, and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "The Sarvāstivādins' adherence to the existence of the three time periods means that the substance [of dharmas] reaches a state where it is not non-existent," the intended meaning is as follows:

The Sarvāstivādins maintain that the substantial entities (dravya) of acquisition (*prāpti*), the characteristic of birth (*jāti*), and so forth, truly exist throughout the three time periods and are eternally non-existent. Consequently, they argue that effects should be produced instantaneously. If they were to offer this defense:

"Although the substances of the past and future exist eternally, their functional activity (*kāritra*) has not yet arisen; therefore, the effects produced by them do not arise constantly or instantaneously," the Master [Vasubandhu] replies: [the following].
[The opponent] objects: "If you claim that the fruit [of an action] exists at all times because it is never separate from its substance (*bhāva*), then it would be like the substance itself.
Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* provisionally adopts this argument.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "taking wholesome form as the cause for the four aggregates," the intention of saying "it serves as the cause" is to explain that it is by means of performing physical actions [that the result is produced].

The verbal and physical karmas of good and evil act as causes to induce the four [mental] aggregates in the future; alternatively, the four aggregates such as consciousness can induce the fruit of the future physical body.
Therefore, in the Hīnayāna, the two karmas of body and speech take form (*rūpa*) as their essence, while the karma of mind takes volition (*cetanā*) as its essence.

They maintain that matter and mind act as causes for one another in a reciprocal succession, which they define as the meaning of "conditioned cause" (*hetu-pratyaya*). Now, this is not the case; it refers only to the self...
The fruit receives the name "seed" only when it is like a barley seed, which produces only barley and not rice or other grains.
[Commentary] The meaning of the seventh characteristic, which clarifies why it is not called a seed, is as follows:

although the seventh aspect is manifest, the characteristics of the fruit produced by the perfumed seeds are submerged and obscure; therefore, the seventh is not called a seed. Question: What about this seventh [characteristic]?
Question: Is it not the case that the seed is not called a "seed"? Answer: It is not so. In this treatise, the seventh *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness) is not described as a seed. Question:
Since there is no person [who lacks it], and the seventh consciousness constantly functions in accordance [with the ālayavijñāna], it should be called a seed.

Answer: It is because the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of that which is perfumed (*bhāvita*) are submerged and hidden; therefore, the seventh active consciousness is not called a seed. That is to say, among the six characteristics [of a seed], it lacks the characteristic of being a fruit (*phala*).
The meaning of "coexistent" [is established] because the fruit of the seed does not manifest.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the eighth, the manifest consciousness, is likewise," the intended meaning is that since the eighth consciousness cannot perfuse [the ālayavijñāna], it lacks a produced fruit;
thus, being deficient in the fruit with which it would be coexistent, it is not designated as a "seed."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because they are manifest phenomena": external objects such as wheat and so forth are produced from seeds within consciousness;
because they are transformations of consciousness, they are manifest phenomena and are not termed "seeds."
[Commentary]: Regarding the gain and loss of performing or not performing [actions], some say that if one performs wholesome karma oneself yet does not obtain a wholesome fruit, this is a "loss.

Alternatively, it is a "loss" because one fails to obtain a wholesome fruit by not relying on oneself; furthermore, it is a "loss" because it contradicts the principle that "one must act for oneself and obtain for oneself.
As for the contradiction: if one acts for oneself and only obtains [the result], it constitutes a contradiction. Now...

The commentary on the first [verse] explains: if one performs wholesome actions and the like, yet does not immediately obtain wholesome fruits, or if one obtains fruits despite not performing them, then one could say that [the fruit] belongs to non-action and lose [the principle] that it belongs to action; because this would lead to the aforementioned fault, there is a contradiction.
To explain the reason for this, we know that external seeds are all produced by the perfuming of internal consciousness; therefore, it says, "by depending upon that perfuming."
The following citation from the verse proves that [the object] arises through the transformation of consciousness.
[Commentary: "By depending on those latencies" means by depending on the latencies within that ālayavijñāna;
therefore, both external seeds and internal seeds serve as conditions.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it is a repeated transformation," the intended meaning is that a repeated transformation is not a transformation of the seed. For example, one might argue that the eye-faculty undergoes repeated transformation yet lacks the function of producing consciousness;
however, this is also incorrect. Furthermore, we are currently discussing what constitutes a seed and what does not, rather than the relationship between the producer and the produced.
There is also another interpretation, as explained in the *Yanbi* (Secret Commentary on the Manifestation).
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "As for the seeds of internal consciousness" to "is the projecting cause," the intent is as follows:

This section on the absence of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) distinguishes between the two causes—production (*janana*) and projection (*ākṣepa*)—and their respective near and distant results. For instance, when ignorance (*avidyā*) initiates karma and that karma invites the five fruits beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), the seeds of consciousness produce their own manifest consciousness;
this is called the "near fruit. Thus, these seeds of consciousness are considered in relation to the name (*nāman*).
The *rūpa-aṅga* (form factor) is the cause that projects its own *nāmarūpa-aṅga* (name-and-form factor), which is its distant fruit; the rest should be understood extensively in the same way.

That is to say, the seed of *nāmarūpa* itself is the cause of production (*janana-hetu*) in relation to its own manifest state, and it is the cause of projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*) in relation to what follows, because it projects [the subsequent].

Regarding the twelve factors, the cause in the state where the seeds have already been moistened is explained in terms of producing and projecting fruits in relation to their results. In contrast, the fruit is established as being near or distant in relation to its cause. Question: What is meant by the "cause of projection" (*ākṣepa-hetu*)?
Regarding the cause that produces distant results versus the cause that produces proximate results: because it is separated from the manifest consciousness, it is able to receive the name "distant.
By analogy with that, one should understand that in relation to itself and in relation to others, there is a distinction between producing and inducing the proximate and the distant.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the remaining fruit is called the projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*), one might ask: as the commentary indicates, there are both immediate, primary fruits and distant, residual ones.

Why is it that Asaṅga and Vasubandhu do not mention them both? The answer is that there is no contradiction. Asaṅga speaks in terms of the contrast between the distant and the immediate, without mentioning the primary and the residual;
Vasubandhu speaks in terms of the contrast between the primary and the residual, without mentioning the distant and the immediate. This is based on their respective intended meanings.
Each case is distinct and cannot be criticized as being uniform.
[Commentary: Since both the internal and external are absent when one reaches the state of emaciation and leprosy, consciousness has already departed from the body;
thus, at the present time, the seeds of consciousness have already ceased.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the principle of being without nature (niḥsvabhāva) is superior," the intended meaning is as follows: If, among the four modes of birth (*yoni*), all possess both the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the producing cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*), then the principle of being without nature is superior.
Why is this? Because "being without nature" is explained in reference to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Thus, while the apparitional birth (*upapāduka*) possesses both the projecting and producing causes, it does not include the "Vasubandhu" [position], because Vasubandhu maintains that the projecting cause remains as a residual fruit after death.
The corpse is said to be thus; for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), there is no corpse after death, as they suddenly cease at the end of life.
[Commentary: This means that if there were no projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), when sentient beings die, they would be like something that ceases spontaneously.

The reason why those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) do not undergo death followed by spontaneous cessation is that they lack the "inducing cause" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*); this is further explained by the existence of the fruit of the withered mulberry tree.

[Commentary: Regarding the fact that Vasubandhu’s explanation is abbreviated, the intent is that Vasubandhu only applied this principle to a single lifetime (*ekakāla*) and did not extend it to those born by transformation.
Regarding the statement that "there is no nature (niḥsvabhāva) because there are no withered mulberry fruits for those born by transformation (*upapāduka*)," the detailed explanation is as follows:

Since the absence of nature is discussed here in relation to the stage of "already moistened" (*ārdrībhūta*) within the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), and since fish born by transformation possess both the projecting cause (*ākṣepaka-hetu*) and the producing cause (*abhinirvartaka-hetu*), it is called "detailed.
This merely represents a difference in brevity or detail; it does not contradict the underlying principle. What has been cited above is precisely from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.

[Commentary: Regarding the passage from the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treatise on the Higher Dharma) stating "the projecting and the projected" and "the producing and the produced," the meaning is as follows:

what the *Abhidharmakośa* describes as the projecting causes and the projected effects, and the producing causes and the produced effects, is identical to this treatise. For example, within the twelve links [of dependent origination], ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*)—these two links—are the projecting causes;
consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other five links are the projected effects. This is based on their state prior to being moistened by craving, referring to their future existence.

Since the fruits such as birth are still being excluded [at this stage], they are termed "projecting causes" (*ākṣepa-hetu*); as for the "producing causes" (*janaka-hetu*), the three links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are established as producing causes based on their state of moistening [the seeds].
These are proximately responsible for bringing about the future fruits of birth, aging, and death; thus, these fruits are termed "that which is produced."
[Commentary]: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter nine, states that the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepa-hetu*) refers to the totality of both the projecting factors and the projected factors.

Although the seven members beginning with ignorance constitute both the projecting and the projected, because they have not yet been moistened and are distant from the fruit to be produced, they are collectively termed the "projecting cause.

The two members of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), which act as the moisture, and the member of existence (*bhava*) which is moistened by them, are close to the fruit; therefore, they are designated only as the "producing cause" (*janaka-hetu*), and the former [projecting factors] are not so called.
This is the result and not the cause; therefore, we do not discuss the tenth yoga, but merely explain the preceding cited passage.

Question: Does the Buddha-fruit have production, and are two types of causes cited? Answer: From the *nirmāṇakāya* up to the *sāmbhogikakāya*, there is a cause for production, but no cause for projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*), because it arises from seeds.
Some say that one may provisionally possess both causes when first attaining the fruit of Buddhahood.

The arising of the body is called the "generative cause" (*janakahetu*) with respect to its subsequent continuities, while it is called the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepakahetu*) because it is said that "dharmas possessing intrinsic nature" exist;
this means that all dharmas possessing intrinsic nature must necessarily be perfumed (*vāsanā*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "arising from internal seeds of common characteristics (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa-bīja*)," the intended meaning is that external seeds such as barley arise from internal seeds of common characteristics for barley within consciousness.
That is to say, after seeds have been perfumed by the common perception of barley and so forth, subsequent seeds take these as conditions to arise later;
therefore, external seeds do not arise without causes and conditions.
[Commentary]: "To practice (*xi*) means to be proximate (*jin*)" refers to being simultaneous and adjacent with that which perfumes (*neng xun*), rather than occurring in successive moments.

Furthermore, it is said that "proximate" means this seed can produce its manifest fruit (*xian guo*) in close proximity; this is the sense of "practicing through proximity" (*lei xi jin sheng guo yi*).

[Commentary]: First, regarding the refutation of the notion that "categories of consciousness" (*vijñāna-jāti*) receive perfuming—specifically, the Sautrāntika masters' view that categories of consciousness receive perfuming because they are perfumed by preceding moments of wholesome consciousness and so forth—it is now refuted.
The meaning of "categories of consciousness" will be explained below in its own section.
[Commentary: "The seventh consciousness is not at all that which is perfumed" explains an external objection. The external objection is as follows:
If that which is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) is what undergoes perfuming, then since the seventh consciousness is also indeterminate, it should likewise undergo perfuming. Answer:

Although the seventh consciousness is indeterminate, it is associated with the four afflictions and is thus "obscured-indeterminate" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), which differs from the eighth [consciousness]; therefore, it is not that which is perfumed.
[Commentary]: This is identical to the explanation provided in the section on "Returning to the Middle" (*fùzhì zhōng*).
