The *Aṣṭānirhāra-yoga* (Treatise on the Eight Non-attachments) bases its argument on the fact that sound is not separate from the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the four great elements; thus, sound is also the eighth [category] of internal appropriated objects (*upātta*).
Therefore, these two treatises do not contradict one another.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the meaning of "appropriation" (*upādāna*): the intent is to state that the eighth consciousness is that which is capable of appropriating seeds, the sense organs (*indriya*), and so forth.

Regarding what is appropriated (*upātta*), there are three different explanations according to the Mahāyāna. Some maintain that it is called "appropriated" solely because it gives rise to suffering and pleasure;
thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "The five material elements (*rūpa-dhātu*) and a portion of the four [other] elements are called 'appropriated'.

Since sound is not mentioned therein, we know that it is called "appropriated" solely because it gives rise to suffering and pleasure. Others maintain that it is defined solely by way of inclusion (*saṃgraha*).
That which constitutes one's own body is termed "appropriated" (*upātta*), as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 51, and elsewhere:

"If there were no eighth consciousness as a basis for appropriation, it would be impossible to obtain [such appropriation]. Furthermore, fascicle 56 states: "There are five types of appropriated [bases], five types of non-appropriated bases, and the remainder are exclusively non-appropriated.
Based on these passages, "appropriation" is explained solely in terms of grasping [the elements] as one's own body.

Regarding "appropriation" (*upādāna*), there are instances where both meanings are applied together to clarify what constitutes appropriation. As stated in the fifty-third [fascicle]: "As for whether consciousness appropriates or does not appropriate:
if a form is called 'appropriated' because it is the support (*āśraya*) of consciousness, how is this so?

It means that which consciousness relies upon, wherein safety and peril are shared, and which grows together through their harmonious integration. Furthermore, this serves as the basis from which all sensations (*vedanā*) arise; that which is contrary to this is non-appropriated."
However, in this treatise, the term "appropriation" (*upādāna*) is explained solely from the perspective of grasping [the body] as its own substance.
Were it not so, the seeds of all phenomena would not constitute appropriation.

[Commentary]: The general explanation of the above summarizes the points stated in the preceding verse; that which is called "appropriation" and "location" both refer to the objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
[Commentary]:
The meaning of "taking linguistic conventions (*nāma-dharma*) and so forth as the essential nature" is that all things possess an essential nature;
even when one contemplates a non-existent object (*asat*), one takes linguistic conventions and so forth as its essential nature.

[Commentary] The meaning of the phrase "this concludes the brief explanation" is as follows: regarding the characteristics of the practice and its objects of focus, there are two types—brief and extensive.
The brief explanation has now been completed; the extensive explanation will be set forth below.

[Commentary]: First, regarding the passage from "the transformation of arising" to "is called the transformative [consciousness]," the intended meaning is that "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) signifies "evolution.

When seeds evolve to produce manifest mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), the seeds act as the cause for the arising of manifest results; this maturation is what is termed the "transformative arising" (*janma-pariṇāma*).
This is as previously explained regarding the two types of causal habituation: the *niṣyanda-hetu* (homogeneous cause) and the *vipāka-hetu* (maturation cause).

"Qi" (vital energy) is precisely this. Question: While it may be that the seeds of the seven consciousnesses possess such a meaning of "arising-transformation" (*janmavikāra*), I do not yet understand whether the seeds of the eighth consciousness and the manifesting consciousness (*darśanavijñāna*) also possess this meaning of arising-transformation. Answer: They also do. Why?

Because within the substance of the eighth consciousness, there exists the functional capacity (*śakti*) to produce all manifest phenomena; therefore, this manifesting consciousness is also called "arising-transformation. It is capable [of this].

Because it performs the function of producing the manifest consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and so forth, the eighth [consciousness], the manifest consciousness, is called the "seed-consciousness" (*bīja-vijñāna*). Question: Since you have already described it as the manifest consciousness, how can it be called a "seed"?
Answer: That which possesses the capacity to produce all various active mental states (*citta-dharma*) and so forth is designated as a "seed.

Alternatively, because the seeds of the eighth [consciousness] mutually induce one another across preceding and succeeding moments, they are also termed "arising and transforming" (*utpāda-pariṇāma*).
This does not reach the previous interpretation.

[Commentary: Regarding the distinction between "arising" and "maturing," "arising" refers to the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*) and "maturing" refers to the resultant stage (*phala-avasthā*); hence they are called "distinguished. [Commentary:

Regarding the second, the name "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to the transformation of the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) as it takes objects; it is like the eighth consciousness taking seeds and the sense organs as its objects.

The body and so forth are called "transformation through conditions" (*pratyaya-pariṇāma*), just as the seven consciousnesses are called "transformation through conditions" when they take form and so forth as objects. The *Śāstra* states: "Transformation of the mind has transformation through conditions.

[Commentary: If birth is called transformation, up to and including all [other states] being called transformation, this means it is a re-explanation of "birth-transformation" (*utpāda-pariṇāma*). This refers to the second...

The eight [consciousnesses] and the seven consciousnesses, etc., each possess seeds that have the functional capacity to produce the seven consciousnesses; these are collectively termed "evolution as production" (*janma-pariṇāma*).

Furthermore, the seven consciousnesses, etc., can also regenerate the seeds of the seeing and image divisions (*darśana-bimba-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness; these are likewise termed "evolution as production."
[Commentary]: "If that which transforms through being taken as an object is the respective self-characterized portion (svabhāva-bhāga), this means:

if it transforms through being taken as an object, then at the time when the mind and mental factors take an object, the image-like portion (nimitta-bhāga) of that object manifests upon the mind of the perceiver;

this is called 'transformation through being taken as an object. 'That which is the respective self-characterized portion' means that each respective seeing-portion (darśana-bhāga) faces its own [object]."

The aspect of the objects such as blue and so forth is called the "self-evident portion" (*svasaṃvittibhāga*). Alternatively, each self-evident portion, corresponding respectively to its own admitted "seeing portion" (*darśanabhāga*) and so forth, is called the "self-evident portion.

[Commentary: According to this, one should reflect upon the meaning of the phrase "all phenomena," which intends to explain the breadth, narrowness, and quantity of the objects perceived by the various consciousnesses.
[The text states: "Each and every part of the mutual division is entirely a transformation through conditions (*pratyaya-vikāra*).

[Commentary: Alternatively, the intention behind establishing three types of transformation is that what is termed "appropriation" (*upādāna*) is itself a transformation; thus, by including the two preceding transformations, there are three transformations in total.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the seeds of the faculties up to 'can be understood,'" the meaning is as follows: one should consider how many types of transformation the seeds of the faculties and so forth possess when they serve as the support for the sense organs and their objects.

For instance, the seeds within the body that support the faculties and their objects possess the meaning of three types of transformation; this can be understood through reflection. However, the external receptacle world possesses only one type of transformation.

It is called a "transformation" because it is conditioned by [the ālayavijñāna]; since the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) takes it as an object, the seven consciousnesses likewise possess one [type of transformation].

"Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to arising; thus it is called transformation, as previously explained regarding how [the eight consciousnesses] arise from one another. Why is it called "arising-transformation"? Question:
If it is said that the seven consciousnesses possess arising-transformation, why do some passages state that the eighth consciousness is unchanging?

Answer: That which is called "unchanging" is spoken of according to the second and third criteria. Because the eighth consciousness does not take the seven consciousnesses as its objects, it lacks an object-condition (*ālambana*). Therefore, it is unchanging.
Because the transformation [of consciousness] cannot grasp or maintain the seven consciousnesses, it lacks the name "appropriating root" (*upāttendriya*).

Regarding the statement that "the transformation arises," as explained in the *Yanmi* (Secret Commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), the meaning of the phrase "in the Mahāyāna, because there is no arising from non-existence, and because objects lack intrinsic substance" is as follows: one must take an existent thing as an object for a mind to arise;

a mind does not arise by taking a non-existent thing as an object. This point refers to the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) [of the cognitive object]; whatever is taken as an object-nexus necessarily exists.

Because it arises by depending on the aspect of the image (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the aspect of the seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) within the dependent nature, it is called "arising from conditions" (*pratyaya-ja*).
This does not refer to the primary object (*svabhāva*). Why? Because the primary object may be non-existent; for example, when one perceives the past or the future, there is no primary object.
As for the statement that the mind does not necessarily possess a formal image, the intention is this: when the mind arises, there is no image upon the mind itself.

As for the "parts" (*bhāga*), they should be understood as the arising of consciousness without an objective referent (*ālambana*). Why is this? Because upon that mind there is no *paratantra* aspect of the "part" (*nimitta-bhāga*).

[Commentary: As for the phrase "like the view of self," the meaning is that when discussing the conditions of objects, it is as previously explained regarding whether there is a reflected image (*pratibimba*) or not.
In the *Ātmadṛṣṭi-nirdeśa*, it is stated that [the self] alone does not arise, nor can it give rise to mental factors such as discernment (*vitarka*) without being accompanied by consciousness;

this point should be examined in the first commentary. From this, one understands the intended meaning: if there were no objective essence in the form-part (*nimitta-bhāga*)—the reflected image upon the mind—then the arising of consciousness would lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just as in the case of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Although the view of self is indeed a subjective cognizer (*ālambaka*), it lacks a [real] self.
Because the self-substance is seen as the object-condition (*ālambana*), this view of self possesses only an object-condition but lacks the sense of an actual objective referent.
Why? Because there is no self-substance.

[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of "distinguishing and retaining" (*jianchi*): among the four parts [of consciousness], one distinguishes away the other three parts and retains the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*); therefore, it is so called.
"In this [context]" (*atra*) means that one may exclude other categories and retain only the single category of "aspect" (*ākāra*); therefore, it says "in this.

[Commentary]: "However, there are two types of aspects... 'having the same object of cognition' (*ekālambana*)"—the meaning of this is that, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, two categories of aspects are established.
For example, taking the "seeing-part" (*darśanabhāga*) as an aspect refers to the direct characteristic upon consciousness.

The term "object-condition" (*ālambana*) is applied [to the object], yet this image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is necessarily existent. Since the mind, when arising, always transforms into an image-aspect, the similarity between these image-aspects is termed "having the same object-condition.
The distinctness of each seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) is termed "not having the same mode-of-apprehension" (*ākāra*).
Second, the image-aspect as a reflected image is itself termed the "mode-of-apprehension"; thus, among all consciousnesses, it may either exist or not.

Regarding the statement "either existent or non-existent": it is "existent" in the sense that the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) possesses the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*); it is "non-existent" because the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), when taking suchness as its object, lacks an image.
Thus, it is said to be "either non-existent. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that they share the same object of cognition;
this proves that the image-aspect is the object of cognition. They are said to be "the same" because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are similar; the intent is that although it is an image...

The image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is the aspect of the mode of activity (*ākāra*), yet because the modes of activity are similar, their number is equal, and their names are identical, they are said to have the same object (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, regarding the explanation based on the primary substance (*svabhāva*), it is called "having the same object" but not "the same mode of activity. Briefly, there are three interpretations: 1.

One says that the primary substance is called the "object," while the image-aspects are distinct from one another and thus called "different modes of activity. 2. Another says that the image-aspects are similar [to one another].

Regarding the statement that "the name and the object of cognition are the same, while the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), the experiencing-part (*anubhava*), and so forth, are each different," this means they are "different in name" and "identical in their single mode of activity. As for the third point, it states that "the fundamental and the image are both called 'identical in object,' because the substance is the same;

they are called 'identical' because the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is similar; yet the seeing-part is called 'different' because its functions, such as discerning and experiencing, are distinct. This refers to the fact that while the name and the object of cognition are identical, the seeing-part, the experiencing-part, and so on, are each distinct. Furthermore, the fundamental consciousness and its images are both termed "identical in object" because their substantial basis is the same;

they are termed "identical" because the objective aspects are similar; however, the seeing-part is termed "different" because its functions—such as discernment and experience—are each distinct. This is what is meant by "identical in their single mode of activity."

[Commentary]: Now, regarding the intention of the speaker here, it means that while the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of all consciousnesses within cause and effect possesses non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), their image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is entirely absent.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) is called the mode of activity (*ākāra*) when it is distinct in substance from the Lesser Vehicle," the intention of the commentator is as follows:

This is said based on the tenets of the Lesser Vehicle school, which maintains that the image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is called the mode of activity and the aspect of seeing is called the object (*vastu*).
Therefore, the teachers of the Lesser Vehicle say that while there is an appearance resembling the object upon the mind and mental factors, this [image] is not the actual object.

The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is not itself the aspect (*ākāra*) of the cognitive process; rather, it is the mind that, by bearing the image of that object, takes the preceding object as its condition.

Therefore, it is called the "aspect" (*ākāra*). This definition of yoga is the same as that of the Hīnayāna schools. However, because this treatise differs from them, it speaks of a "distinct substance.
In this treatise, the division of "view" (*darśana-bhāga*) is taken as the aspect, which possesses two meanings: first, it is explained in terms of what is definitely present in all consciousnesses.
The second [explanation] is stated in terms of distinguishing it from the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) as having a separate essence.
[Commentary]: However, regarding the statement "only the first interpretation exists and the second does not," up to the phrase "the aspects (*ākāra*) are not the same," the intended meaning is this:
if one takes only the first interpretation and excludes the second, then the eighth consciousness and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*) would not share a common object of perception (*ālambana*).
How can it be said that they share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*) yet have different modes of apprehension (*ākāra*)? "How" means as follows:

in the case of the seven consciousnesses and so forth, their "seeing-portion" (*darśana-bhāga*) is called the mode of apprehension; thus, there is the principle that they share the same object of cognition while having different modes of apprehension.

For example, when the visual consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) manifests as blue, it all takes what is transformed by the eighth consciousness as its substantial basis (*bimba*), [with] the mind of the visual consciousness itself [as the seeing-portion].
The mental factors (caitta) rely upon the same objective essence (ālambana-svabhāva), yet they each transform themselves into the aspect of the image (nimitta-bhāga).

However, because their respective modes of activity—such as feeling, discernment, and volition—are distinct, they receive different names. While they share the same object of cognition (ālambana), they do not share the same mode of activity (ākāra).
If this is so, how can it be said that the eighth consciousness and its five simultaneous mental factors, which have transformed [the object] differently, share the same [object]?
Question: Since the objects of focus (*ālambana*) differ, how is it that the eighth consciousness and its mental factors transform into different aspects (*ākāra*)? Answer:

For instance, when the eighth consciousness transforms into the sense organs (*indriya*), the body, and so forth, it directly transforms the sense organs and the rest as having practical utility. However, the five mental factors rely upon what is transformed by the fundamental consciousness (the eighth) as their objective substance (*viṣaya-bhūta-vastu*);
they themselves then transform into images (*pratibimba*). These images lack practical utility. Just as [the original object has utility while the reflection does not], so it is here.
How can it be said that they have the same object? Now, regarding the second interpretation, which posits that the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) is the mode-of-apprehension (ākāra):
although the mind and its transformations—such as the sense-faculties and the body—are different, they are called "having the same object" because their image-aspects are similar.
This means that although the transformed faculties and so forth differ in being either functional or non-functional, they are both transformations of the faculties and so on.
Because many images are similar, they are said to have the same object of cognition (*ālambana*);

however, since the essence of the mind and mental factors differ—such as their distinct functions of discerning (*vijñapti*) and experiencing (*anubhava*)—they are said to have different aspects (*ākāra*). Therefore, a second interpretation is required.

Furthermore, this is intended to establish that the image-portion (*nimittabhāga*) within the *Saṃtānāntarasiddhi* (or *Pramāṇasamuccaya*) constitutes the aspect (*ākāra*). This point is not accepted in the *Yanyi miyi*, which remains consistent with the former [position].

[Commentary]: "From the semblance of the aspect of the cognizer to what is called the 'semblance of the cognizer'" means that the term "semblance" (sādṛśya) is not yet fully understood as being like [the actual cognizer]. [Commentary]: "The statement by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati establishing one part" refers to the meaning established by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati regarding the portion of the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) up to the signless (*animitta*).

[Commentary]: "The intention of the passage from 'the semblance of the aspect of the cognizer' to 'is called the semblance of the cognizer' is that the word 'semblance' is not yet examined as being like [the actual cognizer]."
How is this answered? In the Mahāyāna, the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) is called "resembling the cognizer" (*sādṛśa-ālambaka*) because it resembles the *ākāra* (mental aspect) of the Hīnayāna.

Since the Hīnayāna maintains that the *ākāra* belongs to the cognizer and possesses the functions of both the subject that grasps (*grāhaka*) and the object that is grasped (*grāhya*), it is said to be "resembling.

Thus, while the Mahāyāna resembles the Hīnayāna in this regard, the same principle applies to the *nimitta-bhāga* (image part) resembling the "object" (*ālambana*). This should be understood accordingly.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it does not exist herein," this means that within the Mahāyāna, one does not posit the existence of dharmas external to the mind.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "it is not the same as Sthiramati... because it can take itself as its object," the intended meaning is that [this school] establishes that mental factors (*caitta*), like the primary mind (*cittarāja*), possess the two-fold division [of aspect and substance].
This is different from Sthiramati; that is to say, that master [Sthiramati] maintains that there are two parts: the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Because this [object] is non-existent as a parikalpita (imagined nature), it must be distinguished [from the object];

furthermore, it must also be distinguished from the Sāṃmitīya school’s view that the mind directly grasps the external object—just as a lamp illuminates things or the sun radiates light—and that there is no *nimittabhāga* (image-part).

Nor is it the same as the Sarvāstivāda, which holds that the external object is the *ālambananimitta* (the objective image) called the *ākāra* (aspect), while the *darśanabhāga* (perception-part) is called the *vastu* (substance). Now, in the Mahāyāna...
The aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) takes blue and so forth as its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*); since these are different entities, they must be distinguished. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "because there are no minds or mental factors that can take themselves as objects," the intended meaning is this: in that Lesser Vehicle school, the "aspects" (*ākāra*) are merely the subjective capacity to perceive;
they take external objects while bearing those aspects, but the mind that acts as the subject of cognition does not itself take those aspects as its object. Therefore...
Those modes of activity (*ākāra*) are subsumed under the category of the cognitive object (*ālambana*), as stated in the *Yanmi* (Exposition of the Secrets).
[Commentary]: "Or like the objects of other persons" means that it is like the objects of other persons which are not taken as cognitive objects.

[Commentary: "Others are also like this" means that one's own mind, when taking itself as an object, should likewise take the minds of others as its objects, because it lacks the characteristic of an objective referent (*ālambana-nimitta*). Furthermore, the analytical explanation states:

"Others are also like this" means that when others take sound and so forth as objects, they should likewise take the present form (*rūpa*) as their object, because [the latter] is admitted to lack the characteristic of an objective referent, just as in the present case.
"Object-color. [Commentary:
The meaning of "others are also like this" is that, apart from oneself, other persons and so forth must be taking their own minds as objects;

for there is no characteristic of an external object, just as when one takes one's own mind as an object. Alternatively, others may take their own objects as objects, just as one does. Or, they may take themselves as objects.
"The object is like another's object, and it is also the condition.
[Commentary]: That which is common to the Mahāyāna is that other Hīnayāna schools also admit the existence of a semblance of objective form (*nimitta*).

[Commentary]: Regarding "the four wisdoms and three disputes," there are three masters who dispute differently concerning the existence or non-existence of the *parikalpita* (imagined) aspect, as will be explained below.

The explanation states that the difference between this [treatise] and that [other treatise] lies in whether the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) exists in the latter, while the *darśanabhāga* (perceptual aspect) exists in the former; thus, there is a distinction. [Commentary:

To claim that one who admits the existence of real functional activity is not a "Son of the Śākya" (a Buddhist) is a critique by Bhāviveka against the Madhyamaka school; it is the position of a non-Buddhist.

If you maintain that intrinsic nature and so forth possess real causal efficacy, and you further maintain that this [consciousness] also possesses real causal efficacy, how does it differ from those [other views]?

By what right do you claim to be a "Son of the Śākya"? In terms of the actual Middle Way, consciousness is dependently arisen; thus, it is not the same as the non-Buddhists. How then can you, O Son of the Śākya, be considered at fault?

[Commentary]: All the masters of the Hīnayāna schools possess these characteristics; furthermore, the Saṃmitīya school also possesses that objective aspect (*nimitta*), though the Saṃmitīyas do not admit its existence.
All twenty schools possess this subjective cognitive activity (*ālambana-pratipatti*). For the time being, we shall clarify this based on two points.

[Commentary]: The phrase "excluding those of the Mahāyāna-Saṃmitīya school" means that the Mahāyāna does not posit external objects apart from the mind, whereas the Saṃmitīya school does not posit the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect).
Therefore, they must be excluded. As for the remaining nineteen schools and so forth, these are all the targets of refutation. Regarding the Saṃmitīya school’s question:
"When the mind perceives an object, why is it necessary to further posit a *nimitta-bhāga*? The answer is: Other schools all maintain that the mind and its associates perceive objects [directly].

All [of these] possess three meanings: first, the object of cognition (*ālambana*); second, the aspect of activity (*ākāra*); and third, the substantial entity (*vastu*). Question: Does the statement "the aspects of seeing and being seen" now refer to what is established in the Hīnayāna?
Answer: There are two explanations. First, it is said that the Hīnayāna schools also establish them, though their conceptualizations differ.

Second, it is said that the Mahāyāna meaning is applied to those schools' doctrines; thus, the two divisions of the aspect of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) and the aspect of seeing (*darśana*) are themselves the Hīnayāna.
"Riding upon the aspects and the objects.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the mind of the Mahāsāṃghika school attains its own nature, its own object, reaches the focal point, and the object itself," the intent is as follows:

this school holds that the subjective and objective aspects have two meanings. First, because the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the image (*nimitta*) as its object, it is the same as the other eighteen schools; thus it is said...

The meaning of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) taking the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object—where both are identical to each other in being self-reflexive—is that it lacks a cognitive aspect (*ākāra*).
As described in the commentary, this is identical to the position of the Saṃmitīya school; therefore, it must be excluded.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the aspect of the image (nimittabhāga) of the Mahāyāna is precisely what that school establishes as 'name' (nāman)," etc., the meaning is as follows:

that Hīnayāna school and others do not possess the terminology of "image-aspect" and "seeing-aspect" (darśanabhāga); here, one uses the Mahāyāna terms for the image-aspect and seeing-aspect to designate the names established by that school.

[Commentary]: "Because it bears that aspect" means that the "aspect of activity" (*ākāra*) is precisely the "reflected image. This refers to the fact that upon the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*), there is the bearing of aspects such as blue and so forth;
this is called the "aspect of activity. It is because this seeing-division operates toward the object-aspect while bearing that aspect.
Thus, because it is an aspect resembling the object rather than the object itself, and because it belongs to the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*), the Westerners call it the "aspect of activity."

For example, when taking an object such as impermanent form (*rūpa*) as a condition, the specific meanings of suffering, impermanence, and so forth within that objective field serve as the aspect (*ākāra*).

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the self-nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) as its object: one asks, why is it not said to take the "substantial entity" (*vastu*) as its own nature?
If one asks, "Does this refer to the self-nature (*svabhāva*) or the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? the answer is:

if one were to speak of the "self-nature" (*svabhāva*) as a functional entity (*vastu*), there would be the danger of confusing it with the self-cognizing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the Great Vehicle, because the self-cognizing portion is the very entity of the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*). Therefore, it is simply called the "self-nature characteristic" (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the mind and mental factors share the same support (āśraya) and the same object (ālambana)," this possesses four meanings: first, they share the same supporting faculty (indriya);

second, they share the same objective sphere (viṣaya); third, their modes of activity (ākāra) are similar; and fourth, their substance, function, and number are equal. For now, three of these meanings are cited.

Although their modes of activity are individually distinct, because they are both directed toward the color blue and are thus collectively similar, it is simply stated [that they share the same object].
"Similar" does not mean "identical.
[Treatise] Although they are equal in number, this refers to the fact that sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth each constitute a single entity;

yet their "respective modes of activity" (*ākāra*) are distinct, meaning that the essential characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the others—namely, discernment (*vijñapti*), experiencing (*anubhava*), and so forth—are each distinct. This passage from the treatise explains the "modes of activity" as established by the Hīnayāna school.
The objects of focus (*ālambana*), the views (*dṛṣṭi*), and the entities (*vastu*) are that from which the three dharmas arise.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because their essential natures (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are each distinct," the intended meaning is that upon the self-nature (*svātman*) there exist distinct characteristics such as reception (*anubhava*) and so forth.
Question: What is the purpose of the statement in the treatise, "Although the mental objects (*manojalpa-vastu*) are equal in number"? What is its significance?
Question: Although the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) here encompasses both gain and loss, there may be one who asks:

"If names such as 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*) and so forth are each single, then their designations and entities are equal; therefore, the mental aspects (*ākāra*) of consciousness and so forth should also be called 'equal.

Why, then, do you say that the mental aspects are distinct? Answer: Although the substance and entity of consciousness, sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth are equal in number, their mental aspects are distinct. Why is this?
It is said that they are each distinct because consciousness has "discernment" as its mode of activity (*ākāra*), and so on, up to attention, which has "arousing the mind" as its nature.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that their modes of activity are "similar" and that there is "no difference," this is because within this context, even things such as "number" can be described as "number."

Since "resembling" (*sādṛśya*) and "being equal" (*tulya*) regarding the aspect of the mental mode (*ākāra*) likewise allow for the designation "equal to the mental mode," there is no difference in meaning between "resembling" and "equal. [Commentary:

The intention behind that school’s assertion that the objective part (*nimittabhāga*) is not the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is to state that the mental mode itself is not the object of cognition.

[Commentary]: That which is "resembled" refers to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect). The mode of appearance (*ākāra*) of that which is resembled—the reflected image—is precisely the *nimitta-bhāga* of the Mahāyāna.
The intended meaning is that what exists upon the subjective perceiver as the aspect of the object is that which is "resembled," and is therefore the *nimitta-bhāga* of the Mahāyāna;
that which "resembles" it is the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) of the Mahāyāna.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the Hīnayāna does not establish self-cognition (svasaṃvitti) because it fears a counter-reflexive cognition," this means that fearing the fault of a counter-reflexive cognition, they raise the objection:
"A sword should be able to cut itself," and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "The mind of the past was never an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) in the present," this means that when a single wholesome mind arises in the present, its simultaneous power of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is able to recollect that [past] mind.

If there were no self-cognition, then the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of that wholesome mind, being unable to cognize itself even for a single moment, would immediately perish; how then could it be recollected?

Furthermore, one can later recollect this wholesome mind; however, just as an object once served as the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) and was perceived by the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect), when one recollects this wholesome mind, it does not serve as the *nimittabhāga* for another [consciousness] to perceive it.
Therefore, because it was never taken as an objective aspect (*nimitta*), it is said that "it was not previously taken as an objective aspect."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as one who has never experienced color and so forth," the meaning is that because one has never experienced color, one cannot later recollect it;

since the mind likewise has never experienced [it], one cannot later recollect it either. Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* cites the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* composed by Dignāga as proof, as explained in the *Yanyi piyu*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the mind and mental factors "reach" [their objects] differently from the Hīnayāna, the intent is as follows:

this discussion distinguishes between the similarity of the objective referent (*ālambana*) and the difference in the mode of activity (*ākāra*). This is explained with reference to this consciousness; therefore, it is based solely on the similarity of the name "same objective referent.
Within this, there are four points: first, the same supporting faculty (*āśraya*); second, the similarity of the objective referent; third, the difference in the respective modes of activity.
Fourth, regarding the question of the equality of substance (*dravya*), entity (*artha*), and number (*saṃkhyā*): Why does the treatise state, "Although the entities are equal in number"?
What is the intended meaning? Answer: Here, the word "although" (*yady api*) carries a dual sense of both gain and loss. One might ask:

"If it is called 'equality of entities' because the entities such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) are each singular, then the mental factors (*caitasika*) such as *saṃjñā* (perception) should likewise be called 'equal. Why, then, is it stated [that they are not]?"

Question: Are their modes of activity (*ākāra*) distinct? Answer: Although the substance and function of consciousness (*vijñāna*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth are equal in number, their modes of activity are distinct. Why is this?

It is because consciousness has the mode of activity of discerning (*vijñapti*), up to and including mental attention (*manasikāra*) which alerts the mind; thus, their modes of activity are distinct. As for what distinguishes this from the Hīnayāna:

in the Hīnayāna school, the "substance" (*vastu*) refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) that takes the object as its support, whereas the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

In the Mahāyāna, the aspects (*ākāra*) [of cognition] are distinct because, although the mind and mental factors share the same supporting faculty (*āśraya*), the same objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), and the same object of perception (*ālambana*), their aspects of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) are each separate,
and they differ in terms of their self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), substance, events, and number.

[Commentary]: Although both are blue, as for the statement that their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ—when the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes blue as its object, the mode of understanding is also blue—how can it be said that their modes of activity are different?

The answer is: because the grasping of images (*nimitta-grahaṇa*) differs; for consciousness (*vijñāna*) functions through discernment (*vijñapti*), while sensation (*vedanā*) functions through experiencing (*anubhava*), and so forth, according to their respective distinctions.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the aspects therein are each not one," the intended meaning is as follows: "aspects" (*ākāra*) refer to the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Because the objective parts of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are distinct from one another, they are called "not one.

Furthermore, because the subjective part (*darśana-bhāga*) possesses different functions such as discernment (*vijñapti*) and sensation (*anubhava*), it is also called "not one. Moreover, since the object is considered in its totality, it is termed "reaching similarity" (*sādṛśya*). There is [a reason for this].
It is said that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* meet in their dual sense.

Regarding the "object" (*ālambana*), although the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors (*caitta*) differ, when perceiving a blue object, the images of both the mind and its mental factors are all blue;

therefore, based on this principle, they are called "a single object. Regarding the "seeing" (*darśana*), because it refers to the specific [aspect], it correctly accords with this treatise’s statement of "a single basis" (*ekāśraya*).

The treatise (*śāstra*) states that because each portion of the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) arises carrying its own respective *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part), it is said that the "objects of cognition (*ālambana*) are similar," which is not contradictory.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* bases this on the object being one and the same, thus calling it a "single common object of cognition.

This treatise, however, bases it on the similarity of the *nimitta-bhāgas* upon the *darśana-bhāgas*, thus naming it a "single common object of cognition. Therefore, the explanations in this treatise and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* differ, as also noted in the *Yanyi-pimi*.
Furthermore, regarding those [objects] as "distant" objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*), they are called "one" because their yogic objects are designated as such based on their totality;

this refers to the explanation in terms of the substantial object (*svabhāva-viṣaya*). This treatise, however, calls them "identical" based on similarity, which refers to the explanation in terms of the image-aspect (*pratibimba-nimitta-bhāga*) as the immediate objective condition (*sākṣāt-ālambana-pratyaya*).

[Commentary: Therefore, it is called "only" (*kevala*) because it is distinct from consciousness; thus one speaks of "consciousness-only. Regarding the statement that "aspects" (*ākāra*) serve as the "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), the intention is this:
since the aspects of the Hīnayāna are not themselves the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*), how can they be termed the means of valid cognition? The answer is:
because they are subsumed under the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*), they are also termed the means of valid cognition.
[Commentary: Regarding the "six teachers," these six teachers differ in their explanations of the distinctions between the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).

[Commentary: From here below is the third section, which explains that there are four parts (*catur-bhāga*). A question is raised: For instance, the sixth [consciousness], the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part), is common to all three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the seventh [consciousness] is exclusively non-valid (*apramāṇa*).
Since this [seventh consciousness] cannot serve as the third result (*phala*), it is necessary to establish a fourth part.

If the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the five and eight consciousnesses were exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it would follow that they should constitute only the third fruit; yet a fourth division is not established.

The answer is: this is not so. Because the seeing-division only takes external objects as its objective support, its functional capacity is fixed and cannot turn back to take the self-witnessing-division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) as its object.
Furthermore, because the state of the cause is inferior, the state of the fruit is not so.

[Commentary]: Of these four points establishing the principle, the first uses the logic of inference (*anumāna*) to prove the existence of the fourth [cognition]; the second cites the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove the existence of the fourth;
the third refutes alternative defenses; and the fourth explains that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) does not cognize the third [cognition]. This is the first point.

The statement, "All [cognitions] cognize their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and their results are also exclusively manifest," intends to mean that it is not only the seeing-part that takes the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as its object, but that both are manifest.
If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would also be exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[Commentary: If the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) could be only direct perception or inference (*anumāna*), it would refer to the "seeing portion" (*darśana-bhāga*);
if the result could be only direct perception, it refers to the "self-verifying portion" (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

[Commentary: Regarding the meaning of "the two types of inference are not the essence of direct realization," it is intended to show that since the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion) is known to be inferential (*anumāna*), it clearly does not take self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) as its object.

Therefore, it does not serve as the *darśana-bhāga* for direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Since the *darśana-bhāga* is the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), there must be a result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*).
As for the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying portion), which is also a means of cognition, what serves as its result of cognition? The answer is: the third [portion] itself serves as the result.
If it is because one knows the fourth by means of the third that [this objection] is raised, then the object of cognition (*prameya*) and the result (*phala*) would be indistinguishable.

To this, the explanation is as follows: within the third division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), there are two aspects, namely the objective aspect (*grāhya-amśa*) and the subjective aspect (*grāhaka-amśa*), which should be understood respectively as the object of cognition and the result.
This is because when the self-cognizing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes the fourth [division] as its object, it takes that fourth division as both its objective field and its result.
Although they are of one essence, there is no loss of distinction or confusion.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement, "The question-and-answer regarding whether direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) serves as the basis for inference (*anumāna*) rather than being its result is likewise," the intent of the commentary is simply to cite the answer-text;

however, this presupposes a prior question. The question would have been: "Since inference is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), if it is the result of direct perception, then direct perception should not be [the basis]."

Regarding the response that this [self-cognition] is the result of inference (*anumāna*): as stated in the Commentary, "Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the result of inference, but inference is not the result of direct perception. Therefore, although self-cognition takes the seeing-part as its object, it does not become external. This is the second interpretation. Thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, it is said: "If one were to say that the seeing-part is external because it takes the external as its object, then since self-cognition takes the seeing-part as its object, it would follow that self-cognition is also external. This is the first interpretation. The second interpretation is as follows: "It is not the case that the seeing-part is external simply because it takes the external as its object. Rather, it is called 'external' because it is distinct from the self-cognition of the self-cognizing part. Therefore, although self-cognition takes the seeing-part as its object, it does not become external. This is the second interpretation. Thus, there is no fault. Question: Since the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) takes the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) as its object, how can the *darśana-bhāga* be called "external"? Answer: This objection arises because the treatise states:

"The first two are external; the latter two are internal. Secondly, it is said that the essence (*svabhāva*) of the *darśana-bhāga* is internal, but because its object is external, it is termed "external.
However, the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of the *darśana-bhāga*—in which both the perceiving subject and the perceived object are internal—cannot be so [termed].

Furthermore, for example, if it is argued that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the external object as its object and the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), while the self-cognition takes the internal seeing-part as its object and the seeing-part should be the result;

the answer is: the seeing-part pertains to all three types of valid cognition and thus cannot be the result of valid cognition, whereas self-cognition is exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and can serve as the result for the seeing-part.

[Commentary] Regarding the objection concerning "bondage through conditions," the Sautrāntika school objects as follows: "If it is held that the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part) is bound by its object, the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part), then the *svasaṃvedana* (self-cognition) should likewise be so.

The meaning is this: if the *darśana-bhāga* perceives the *nimitta-bhāga* and is bound by that image, then the *svasaṃvedana*, which perceives the *darśana-bhāga*, should also be bound by that seeing-part.

This is because the *nimitta-bhāga* binds the *darśana-bhāga*, and since the *darśana-bhāga* acts as the binder, [the self-cognition would be bound]. Furthermore, he objects: "The *darśana-bhāga* perceives..."

Question: Since the substance (*svabhāva*) of the *dṛśya-bhāga* (perceived aspect) is bondage, and since the *svasaṃvedana* (self-cognition) takes that *darśana-bhāga* (seeing aspect) as its object, the *svasaṃvedana* itself should also be called bondage.

Answer: There is no fault in calling it bondage. Its substance is *sāsrava* (with outflows) and it is associated with defilement (*kliṣṭa*), so it may also be termed "bondage. This is spoken of in terms of the cognizing mind;

it is called "bondage" because when the bound mind perceives the *nimitta* (objective aspect), it does not clearly comprehend the object. Thus, there is a distinction between the two types of bondage. Furthermore, [the following] objection is raised:

Question: Is it said that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is called "bondage" because the seeing-part is generally non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*), its essence is bondage, and the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is subsumed under non-valid cognition?
Answer: This is not so. To provide an example: the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are designated as "bondage," yet the five consciousnesses are valid direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Although they are bondage according to our own treatise, what prevents them from being subsumed under direct perception? Furthermore, another explanation states: the seeing-part takes the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object and is bound by that aspect; however, the self-cognition [is not].

Regarding the response that "being bound by the seeing [aspect] constitutes being bound by the seen": this is acceptable. Although the five consciousnesses are bound by the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), they remain direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

and although the self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is bound by the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), it does not cease to be direct perception. It is not the case that something is no longer direct perception simply because it is bound by the seeing aspect.
According to the commentary, the latter interpretation is adopted, as it is more consistent with the principle.

[Commentary: "As in the Chapter on Manas" means that because the seventh consciousness possesses the attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*), it causes the first six consciousnesses to be unable to forget the characteristics (*nimitta*) when perceiving objects;
therefore, the five consciousnesses are said to have "bondage by characteristics. "Chapter" (*zhāng*) refers to a section or division of a text;

alternatively, it is said that "chapter" means a "gate," as that treatise fully elucidates the meaning of manas, and thus it is given the name "chapter. There is also a variant reading: "As in the Manas... (omitting *shi*).

That obstruction arises precisely from the ego-grasping within the seventh consciousness; it acts as an obstacle that causes the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the five consciousnesses and so forth to become defiled.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the "seen-part" (*dṛśya-bhāga*) cannot simultaneously be both valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*): the meaning is that the seen-part cannot [be both].
Within a single moment of thought, one aspect is non-perceptual cognition (*anumāna*) while another is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);

it is impossible for two aspects of seeing to arise simultaneously because they are mutually contradictory. Therefore, the meaning of these four divisions is established here solely in terms of a single instant;
they are merely four functional divisions conceptually distinguished within the single substance of consciousness.

[Commentary]: If it is argued that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is called "external" because it reaches [the object], the underlying objection is: "If the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) manifests as direct perception, it should constitute a third fruit.
The answer is: It is merely because the seeing-portion resembles something external that it is called "external.
Although the seeing-portion is indeed direct perception, it does not become a third fruit, nor does it take a third portion as its object.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "Even if one takes the mind as the object, taking the mind as its aspect" up to "because it cannot take [itself] as an object," the meaning is as follows: Among the four divisions, the first—the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect)—is exclusively the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition);
the latter three are common to both [as object and dominant condition]. Question: Regarding the latter two [divisions], they mutually take each other as objects.

However, since the latter two are common to both [subject and object], how can the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) be common to both subject and object when it does not take the *svasaṃvedana* (self-witnessing aspect) as its object? Answer: As for the *darśana-bhāga*, if...

Regarding the latter two [aspects], although they do not take the latter two as objects, when considered in relation to both the preceding and succeeding [aspects], they may be categorized as either the subject (the cognizer) or the object (the cognized).

If one considers them in relation to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), they are called the "cognizer"; if in relation to what follows, they are the "cognized. Question: For instance, does self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) take the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object by transforming it into an image?
Answer: It does not transform it into an image. Why? Because it functions inseparably from the consciousness itself. Question: If it does not transform it, how can it take it as an object?

Regarding this, how is it explained? The *Śāstra* states: "Because the mind of the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) cannot take [the *darśana-bhāga*] as its object. The answer provides this hypothetical objection (*pūrvapakṣa*):

"Based on the fact that self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) takes the *darśana-bhāga* as its object without transformation, even if one were to allow that the *darśana-bhāga* transforms into the *nimitta-bhāga* and takes that *darśana-bhāga* as an object, it still could not take [the original *darśana-bhāga*] as its object.
Why? Because it is subsumed under the category of the mind of the *nimitta-bhāga*. This is known to be a hypothetical objection. Furthermore, it says: "The mind of the *nimitta-bhāga* does not..."

Regarding the term "that which can be the object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it means that when the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of one mind takes the *darśana-bhāga* of another mind as its object, that other *darśana-bhāga* is also called the "object-condition," because the *nimitta-bhāga* (imagined aspect) of a mind cannot serve as an object-condition.

[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "it may also be so" is that it can also be termed an "object-condition" (*ālambana*), because it is only taken as an object by self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) and cannot, in turn, take self-cognition as its own object.
Just as the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) cannot take the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) as its object and is thus called a "mere object-condition," this [self-cognition] is likewise.
This is stated provisionally from the perspective of the causal stage; however, at the stage of Buddhahood, the seeing-part is also able to take self-cognition as its object in turn.

Regarding the term "manifesting as a reflection" (*pratibimba*): since it is said that [the mind] takes what is external as its reflection, it takes what is taken as an object (*ālambana*) as its object-condition.
If one were to raise the objection that the text does not mention "name" (*nāma*) when referring to "form" (*rūpa*) and so forth, this should all be considered accordingly.

If one were to argue that because it takes what is external as external, it should likewise take form as form, the answer to this objection is that there is no impediment to using "name and form" (*nāmarūpa*); for these are designated according to their respective objects.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "When the self-witnessing [consciousness] takes the seeing-part as its object, it is like the mind that is the image-part," the intended meaning is this:

when the self-witnessing [consciousness] takes the seeing-part as its object, this seeing-part should not be able to take [the self-witnessing consciousness] as its object, because it is a mind that is an image-part, just as the mind that is an image-part transformed by the seeing-part cannot take [that seeing-part] as its object.
[Commentary]: "Only that much" means that the limits are sufficient; this intends to prove that there are four aspects (*catuṣkoṭi*). [Commentary]:
"As in the case of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) of the formless realm, it takes its own self-cognition as the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*)"—this is an illustration.

Question: How is it known that the third cognition takes the fourth as its object, and that the fourth, in turn, takes the result of the fourth as its object? And how is it known that the fourth takes the third as its object?

Third, is the third [moment] also taken as the fruit? Now, following this analogy: when the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) takes seeds as its object, it takes its own self-witnessing-division (*svasaṃvitti*) as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), which then becomes its fruit. What prevents the third and fourth moments from mutually taking each other as objects and likewise becoming fruits for one another?
Question: Since the seeing-division of the fundamental consciousness universally takes the seeds of all three realms as its objects, why is it [the case that... exclusively...?
Question: Does this refer to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)? Answer: In terms of actual fact, it universally takes the three realms as its object;

however, the two lower realms also include sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*). For this reason, the discussion does not focus on the two lower realms. Because the formless realm lacks sense organs and objects, seeds and their characteristics manifest in mutual reflection;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned that there are "no other characteristics," meaning there are no distinct seed-characteristics, as the seeds themselves undergo transformation.
Supplementary Note: The self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) itself takes the self-verifying [portion] as its objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga).

Because the seeds are not separate from consciousness and because it takes those seeds as its object—meaning it takes the seeds of the self-verifying portion as its object—the capacity within consciousness to produce a fruit is termed a "seed."

[Commentary]: However, regarding the point that it does not take as its object the capacity for cognition (*ālambana-śakti*) residing upon the self-substance (*svabhāva-bhāga*), the meaning is to prove—as previously explained—that the eighth [consciousness] seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) does not take the capacities and functions of various phenomena as its objects.
As extensively explained before, it is not admitted that it takes non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and so forth as its objects.
Furthermore, the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) possesses two capacities: first, there is the capacity for cognition (*ālambana-śakti*), which is...
The self-witnessing division (svasaṃvittibhāga) takes the seeing division (darśanabhāga) as its object;

these two possess the functional capacity to produce an effect, and because that which is taken as an object by the seeing division is [the self-witnessing division], it is known that even in the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu), since the seeing division of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) possesses a perceived aspect (nimittabhāga), it is evident that there is the meaning of four divisions.
By this analogy, the other two realms also possess the four divisions.

[Commentary]: Regarding the question, "If direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth definitely do not take external objects as their referents, and since the third part is already established as direct perception, what further phenomena does the word 'and so forth' (*ādi*) include?"—the intended meaning is that the three parts are definitively established as direct perception and so forth;
therefore, the third part does not take external objects as its referent. This is not the case at the stage of Buddhahood.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "The acquisition of acquisition and non-acquisition do not establish a fourth [dharma]," the intent is as follows: This takes the meaning of the Hīnayāna as a point of contention.
It states that "acquisition of acquisition" refers to the great acquisition and the small acquisition, while "non-acquisition" refers to the essence of the dharma being acquired;

therefore, it is called "non-acquisition of the dharma. Thus, there are only these two acquisitions along with the single essence of the dharma, and no fourth dharma, such as the characteristic of arising (*jāti*).
It is also thus. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "because the measure is fixed," the intended meaning is that because the substance (*vastu*) is fixed, the measure is the measure of the substance itself.

Furthermore, it is said that the measure refers specifically to the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), which is able to cognize and deliberate; because its mode of apprehension is fixed, it is said that the three or four divisions are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "contradiction with the immeasurable," the intended meaning is as follows: You may not take "arising" and so forth as a contradiction with inference (*anumāna*) to challenge what was previously stated regarding the "immeasurable.
Furthermore, because the measure is fixed and because that which is an object of cognition differs from that which is not, these cannot serve as a valid challenge.

[Treatise] Regarding the statement that "the two natures of the sentient beings' mind extend to their various distinctions," the intended meaning is as follows: the nature of the mind of sentient beings (*sattva*) possesses two aspects.

That is to say, internally it transforms into all such internal and external [objects], wherein within both there exist the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), which constitute the entanglements.

Specifically, within the external [aspect], the characteristics (*nimitta*) serve as the grasped and the grasper; within the internal [aspect], there is self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) and the cognition of self-cognition (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti*), which arise in succession.

When viewed in relation to one another, each possesses the dual sense of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*); because these four parts are mutually interconnected, they are termed "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*).
This applies even to the untainted (*anāsrava*), and it is not merely the entanglement of afflictions (*kleśa*) that is meant by "seeds.
Among these four parts, the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) comprises various distinct meanings, such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
[Treatise] The meaning of this verse is that the two parts of the sentient beings' mind-nature are synthesized;
this explains the first line, which states that the internal and external two parts constitute two kinds of nature.
[Treatise] "Whether circular or external, reaching that which binds the grasper" explains the meaning of the next two lines, establishing the fourfold division (*caturvidha-bhāga*).

[Treatise] "In this context, 'seeing' refers to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*)" explains the word "seeing" in the verse; it is so named because it is subsumed under the seeing-division among the four divisions.
It is called "seeing" not because it has the sense of an object of perception (*ālambana*), but because it is the act of seeing. If it were otherwise, then...
The *pramāṇa-bhāga* (the aspect of cognition) and so forth should all be termed "seeing" (*darśana*), because they possess the capacity to be the subjective cognizer.

[Commentary: The meaning of the phrase "this belongs only to sentient beings... because it possesses the two bonds" is as follows: the four aspects (*ākāra*) possess the two bonds and are spoken of only in reference to sentient beings.
Why? Because they abide in the state of outflows (*sāsrava*). Thus, being constrained by the objective marks (*nimitta*), they come to possess the marks.

The essence of bondage consists of being associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) and being conjoined with afflictions (*kleśa*), whereby there is the acquisition of the "bondage of heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulyabandha*).

Based on this, although the four parts [of the mind] are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are not bound by the afflictions. Although the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is not conjoined with afflictions, its essence is still characterized by outflows, and thus it receives the name "heaviness."

[Commentary: The meaning of "nor can it take [the *svasaṃvitti*] as its object" is that the *darśana-bhāga* cannot take the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* as its object; this concludes the previous point regarding non-apprehension.

That the *darśana-bhāga* does not take the *tathatā* (Suchness) as its object is not the primary doctrine; rather, since the function of the *darśana-bhāga* is directed outward, for the sake of conforming to this principle, it is said that it does not take *tathatā* as its object.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the essence of the fruit is one": the second [moment] serves as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the third serves as the fruit (*phala*).
Since the fourth moment takes the third as its object, the third itself becomes the fruit; because the essence of the fruit is one, the fourth is not established, and only the third is retained.

[Commentary]: As for the *Pramāṇasamuccaya-kārikā*, if one were to discard the fourth [cognition] and establish only three parts, this would refer to the verses in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya* such as "the object-like appearance (*viṣayābhāsa*) is the object of cognition (*prameya*), etc. Furthermore, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* establishes two parts;
here, we likewise establish two parts, because the third part is subsumed within the second part.
[Treatise] Regarding the statement that "seeing" (dṛṣṭi) means "that which is capable of cognition" (ālambaka): this explanation of the meaning of "seeing" differs from what preceded.
It means that among the four [mental factors], only that which can cognize the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is called "seeing. Here, the term "seeing" signifies the capacity for cognition;
therefore, all three parts [of the cognitive process] are called "seeing," and thus both mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) are termed "seeing."
[Commentary: Regarding the distinct meanings of each of these four categories mentioned above: first, mental factors (*caitta*) are associated with the mind (*citta*);

second, form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are transformations of the mind; third, *tathatā* (suchness) is the true nature of consciousness; and fourth, the four divisions are explained according to the functional meaning of consciousness.

Although there are these four categories, they do not contradict the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*); therefore, it is said that "only mind exists. This concludes the preceding section.
Regarding the four categories, as previously stated in the second major section clarifying the meaning of the fourfold division, they are divided into four parts:

first, establishing two divisions; second, establishing three divisions; third, establishing four divisions; and fourth, establishing one division. Thus, these four aforementioned categories each represent a distinct interpretation.
[Treatise] Thus, when it is stated in various places that there is "only one mind," this refers to the passages on "one consciousness" (eka-vijñāna) taught in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*,
the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and so forth. As extensively cited in the seventh fascicle,
the passage concerning "one mind" in the *Daśabhūmika* refers specifically to the text on "one mind" from the *Daśabhūmika-parivarta* within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as there is no other object apart from the realm," the meaning is that by reading it as a continuous sequence, the sense becomes self-evident.

[Commentary]: "Returning to what was originally clarified" means that while the original ten gates explained the eighth consciousness, this section has thereby distinguished how all minds and mental factors possess four divisions (*caturbhāga*).
Now, stating that "discernment" (*vijñapti*) is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of consciousness, one returns to conclude the discussion on the eighth.
The Eight Consciousnesses.

[Commentary: Regarding the meaning of "relying on the principles of the Four Teachings," it refers to Dharmapāla’s interpretation that the four kinds of noble teachings establish four distinct divisions;
it does not mean that only the fourth division is established.
[Commentary]: Regarding the meaning of the phrase "these four parts, when viewed in relation to one another, serve as objects of cognition, as has already been explained above":

for instance, when the four parts are compared with one another, three questions should be posed. First: what is that which serves as the object of cognition and yet also functions as an aspect (*ākāra*), and is further termed the self-witnessing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*)?
Second: what is that which serves as the object of cognition but is neither termed an aspect nor [a self-witnessing part]?

Regarding the third [type of] self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), what are its modes of activity (*ākāra*) such that it is designated as "object-condition" (*ālambana*) but not designated as "self-cognition"?

Although the commentary does not fully capture the intended meaning, it sets forth three questions and answers the first one as follows: "The fourth [cognition] has [the preceding cognition] as its mode of activity because it is the cognizing subject;
the third [cognition] is also designated as 'self-cognition' when it serves as the object-condition. Why? Because it takes its own essence as its object."
This is the fourth section. Regarding why the third [aspect] serves as the basis for the fourth, the reason the third receives the name "self-cognition" (*svasaṃvitti*) is as follows:

in response to the second question, it was stated that the "object-aspect" (*nimittabhāga*) is called the "object-condition" (*ālambana*), but it cannot be called the "mental mode" (*ākāra*) nor can it be called "self-cognition," because it lacks the capacity to cognize.
In response to the third question, it was stated that the "seeing-aspect" (*darśanabhāga*) is the mental mode and is thus named the "object-condition."

The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) cannot be called "self-cognition" because it does not cognize itself. Furthermore, the third [cognition], as the aspect (*ākāra*), can be called both the "object-condition" and the "self-cognizing part" (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*);
although these are distinct, their meaning does not exceed this. One may investigate this in detail. Question:

Since the third and fourth [cognitions] internally take each other as objects, how can they be called "aspects"? Answer: They are called "aspects" simply because they do not abandon their nature as the subject that cognizes (*ālambaka*).
"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) does not refer to the "aspects of activity" (*ākāra*) that result from conceptual discrimination.
[Commentary: Furthermore, the objection states, "The two parts are definitely not defiled," etc. The intent of this objection is as follows:

If it is claimed that the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) is universally valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and that the latter two parts are always direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then even when the seeing-part is defiled, [it would remain so] at other times.
Regarding these two parts, they should not be considered defiled; however, in terms of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), both are called defiled because they are of the same substance.

In terms of their cognitive capacity (*pramāṇa*), the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is said to be either valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), whereas the aspect-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) is exclusively non-valid cognition. This is because the nature of phenomena is broad while the seeing-part is narrow.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the objection that "if the distinction between valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) results in a difference in suffering, pleasure, and equanimity," the intent of the external critic is as follows:

"If the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) can be both valid and non-valid, while the other two parts are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then when the *darśana-bhāga* is associated with the feelings of suffering or pleasure, the subsequent two parts should correspond only to the feeling of equanimity.
The answer is: "Not so. Because the nature of the dharma is broad, it is identical to the *darśana-bhāga* and accompanies whichever feeling is present; thus, it is valid [cognition]."
According to the *Vibhāṣā*, it is stated that there are both valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) and non-valid cognitions (*apramāṇa*); other difficult points may be understood by analogy with this.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is sometimes non-valid while the other two parts are necessarily valid," the intended meaning is as follows:

If the seeing-part is either mistaken or non-mistaken, are the other two parts—namely, the mental aspect (*manasikāra-bhāga*) and the self-witnessing aspect (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*)—necessarily non-mistaken? Or do they too become mistaken when the seeing-part is mistaken?

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "if the mind takes itself as its object," the meaning is this: the object of cognition (*ālambana*) serves as the cause for the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*), which is the fruit.

Now, if one asserts that self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, then all such causal relationships would fail to be established, because both are of the same nature—namely, the mind.
However, if the seeing-part takes the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object, there is no fault at all, because their natures are different.
[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "nor should one say that it reaches [the object] and thus produces consciousness" is as follows:

one cannot say that consciousness is produced by the two conditions of the sense organ and the object, nor that it is produced by the conjunction of these three. Why? Because it is consciousness that produces consciousness.
[Commentary: Furthermore, one should not say that an evil mind reaches a state that is not inherently evil. The meaning of this is as follows:

if the self-witnessing division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes the self-viewing division (*svālambya-bhāga*) as its object, one cannot say that this person’s evil mind is entirely unwholesome throughout. Why?

Because if the self-witnessing division knows itself to be unwholesome, it would logically follow that it is wholesome. Consequently, one must also say that the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) would likewise not exist.

The opponent’s intention is as follows: When the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) takes the body as its object during the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) by contemplating the impurity of the body, it is called "mindfulness of the body.

If one allows that self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) takes the *darśana-bhāga* as its object, then that *darśana-bhāga* would be subsumed under the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), and thus named "mindfulness of phenomena.

By extension, this objection should apply to the other three foundations of mindfulness; since there would be no distinction [between them], they would all become identical. Furthermore, regarding the Four Noble Truths...
If wisdom were to have no distinctions, then untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) would be identical to the wisdom of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya-jñāna*).

This is because when it takes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as its object, its self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti*)—the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) that takes the untainted as its object—is itself the wisdom of the Path; this applies likewise to the other Truths. Consequently, there would be no distinction between the four types of wisdom.

Furthermore, [the wisdoms] of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) and knowing the minds of others (*paracitta*) would both fail to be established, because when their self-verifying aspects take the seeing-part as their object, they are all merely taking themselves as objects and are present [only to themselves].
In the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), why is it called "taking past lives and the minds of others as objects"?
[Commentary]: Furthermore, if one knows another's mind just as one knows one's own—this means that the following objection is being cited:
