Since there is no principle by which another's sense organ could give rise to one's own consciousness, while one's own object can be experienced by another, there is a difference in meaning;
thus, one cannot demand that [the object] transform [into the organ].

[Commentary]: This passage concerning the five kinds of power common to all consciousnesses distinguishes these powers according to the various types of consciousness. As for the power borrowed from consciousness, it belongs only to the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body.
As for the power of great vows, it belongs only to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). As for the power of the Dharma, all six consciousnesses possess it;

because they uphold this sutra, they attain such things as the mutual functioning of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃprayoga*). Furthermore, the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) also belongs to the mental consciousness.

Answering the eighth question regarding why the other three powers are not the eighth: For the most part, they arise spontaneously (*svarasena*) and cannot serve as conditions to bind and activate the root consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) so that it projects and produces form (*rūpa*).

Therefore, when the body in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) gives rise to the divine eye or ear of the second dhyāna and above, and these faculties perceive the forms and other objects of those higher stages by borrowing the consciousness of a lower stage, the eighth consciousness is required for the desire for form.

Is it not the case that the color-form (*rūpa*) of that stage is transformed by virtue of borrowing the power of consciousness? Answer: Such a transformation is brought about by the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) acting as the conditioning cause for binding;

however, it is fundamentally not for the purpose of borrowing consciousness. Question: When one born in the Second Dhyāna or above borrows consciousness to take the Eighth [Consciousness] of a lower stage as an object, why is this not a transformation?
Answer: Although it takes the lower stage as its object, it does not necessarily transform it; this is because it is not due to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or supernormal powers.

If one asks: "Does the transformative power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) allow for the transformation of objects belonging to a different level? The answer is no. Regarding the transformative power established by the protection of the Dharma through the fruits of karma, it is not permitted to transform objects of a different level.

To explain: although the Desire Realm fundamentally lacks the fruits of meditative concentration, if there is a location where such fruits are provisionally present, they do not undergo transformation.

This is because that which belongs to a higher level does not arise from a lower level; therefore, the matter produced in the higher levels merely resembles that of the lower levels while actually belonging to the higher levels.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "if the eighth transformation involves only meditative concentration and supernormal powers," the intended meaning is as follows: the objects transformed within the power of meditative concentration and supernormal powers are precisely those transformed by the eighth consciousness.

This is because the sixth consciousness entering such meditative concentrations and so forth acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that induces the eighth consciousness to undergo this transformation.
Furthermore, the objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth that are thus transformed are all substantially existent (*dravyasat*), being the actual objective bases (*bhāva-viṣaya*).
It is said that sentient beings are enabled to enjoy [wealth], such as gold and silver;

alternatively, the statement regarding "the four powers" intends to mean that there are only four powers and not five, because the power of great aspiration is subsumed within the power of the Dharma.

[Commentary]: "Excluding the Tathāgata, those who attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through the cultivation of higher meditative concentrations (*samādhi*)—that is, those possessing outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) powers—when their bodies are in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), give rise to the higher divine eye and divine ear. These powers induce the divine eye and ear to arise within the body;
that is, the *ālayavijñāna* of the lower realm takes as its objects the sense faculties, sensory objects, and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the higher realm."

Taking seeds and so forth as objects, this constitutes taking the bodies of other stages as objects; all such cases arise from one's own attainment of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), for the eighth [consciousness] taking the bodies of other stages as objects does not do so through the supernormal powers of another.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the eye, ear, visible form, tangibles, and so forth" involve two faculties (*indriya*) and possess both color/form (*rūpa*) and tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*):

since these initially draw the body toward them and cause mutual contact, some explain that "there are tangibles" because the existence of the body allows for the presence of the *upādāyarūpa* (derived matter) such as the tangibles that support the sense faculties (*indriyāśraya*).
Detailed Examination: This is also not correct. When the two faculties of the eye and ear are activated, through what location does this commonality arise?
Is there a body-faculty (*kāyendriya*)? If there were a body-faculty that does not belong to a higher stage, it would be a body of the desire realm;

this is what is being discussed regarding the presence or absence of form and tangibility. As for tangibility, since the higher stages do not rely on those of the lower stages, and the lower stages already possess their own [tangibility], why would it need to be mentioned again?
For this reason, [the objection] is incorrect. Alternatively, the two faculties of eye and ear are parts of the body and thus receive the name "body"; there is no logical contradiction in this.

Furthermore, there are also cases where sound exists. Generally speaking, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are inseparable and mutually dependent; because the produced characteristics (*bhautika-lakṣaṇa*) can come into contact, sound is thereby obtained.
Thus, it is said that when one plucks, supports, or shakes dust, there is sound. Moreover, since the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) exists, how could there be no sound? [The opponent] says:

"It must be due to the power of both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal penetration (*abhijñā*). Here, "penetration" refers to the transformation within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), while "concentration" refers to...
It is not so; first, there is no scriptural statement [to that effect], and second, logically it is incorrect. If one asks:

"Should the two faculties of nose and tongue also exist in the higher realms, since they perceive fragrance and flavor? The answer is: No. Fragrance and flavor are known through contact, but in the higher stages there is no consciousness, and thus no fragrance or flavor.
The two consciousnesses of eye and ear are known through separation; because the ear faculty exists, sound may be present.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "there is no textual passage specifically stating [it exists] up to the point that it would be useless," the meaning is as follows: Within the sacred teachings, we do not see any text stating that sound exists [in the higher realms].
Furthermore, it is not admitted that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of a lower stage can arise in a higher stage. Why?

Because there is no supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) [to sustain it], and even if it were to arise, it would be useless. Moreover, since there is no need for contact, desire, or other such functions, it does not arise.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "from the two unsurpassed stages up to because there is no textual authority," the intended meaning is that from the second dhyāna upward, one does not give rise to the divine eye or divine ear of the first dhyāna.
Why is this? Because they are useless; since the higher is superior and the lower is inferior, they do not arise.

Furthermore, because there is no scriptural authority stating otherwise, it is impossible to rely on the faculties of a lower stage within the faculties of the second dhyāna and above; by principle, this is certainly not the case.

However, if one merely borrows the consciousness of the first dhyāna to take an object in a higher stage, yet claims that this does not obstruct the statement that "rejoicing in the lower and aspiring to the upper can give rise to the upper," then this interpretation fails to address the following objection:
The objection states: "If the desire realm gives rise to the upper [realms], it must rely on the upper;

and if it relies on the first dhyāna, then the two faculties of eye and ear arising in the upper stages—which borrow the lower, lower consciousness—should likewise rely on the two faculties of the first dhyāna. [Answer: This is answered as follows.

Regarding the following [verses], the joy [of the second dhyāna] arises based on two faculties within the first dhyāna. As for the second dhyāna and the stages above it, because they involve a sense of aversion toward the lower stage, they merely borrow the consciousness of the lower stage and do not arise based on the faculties of that lower stage.
An objection is raised: Since the faculties of the lower stage are inferior, the second dhyāna and the higher stages would not arise from them at all.
Furthermore, since the two types of consciousness of the first dhyāna are already inferior to the higher stages, the higher stages should not borrow the lower ones to arise.
Answer: It is not so. While the two consciousnesses belong to their own respective levels, they do not possess the sense organs (*indriya*) of those higher levels;

rather, they borrow them from the lower levels. Therefore, they do not arise from the sense organs of the lower levels. Furthermore, an objection is raised: since the higher levels lack the eye and ear, they must borrow the consciousnesses of the eye and ear from the First Dhyāna.

Yet, the First Dhyāna lacks the nose and tongue; it should likewise borrow the consciousnesses of the nose and tongue from the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). Answer: The eye and ear perceive objects through contact with external space (*prāpyakārin*); thus, [the consciousnesses] can arise on the higher levels.
Regarding the objection that while the lower consciousnesses are known within the union of the nose and tongue, the first dhyāna does not give rise to nose or tongue consciousness:

it is argued that just as the higher stages do not give rise to the consciousnesses of the lower body within the union of the nose and tongue, so too [the first dhyāna] should not give rise to them within that same union. The response is: "It may be so.

However, the eyes and ears possess the faculty of *abhijñā* (clairvoyance and clairaudience), which is why they can give rise to the consciousnesses of the lower body; since these [nose and tongue] lack such *abhijñā*, they do not arise. Thus, the objection is resolved.

It is said: "If that were so, then body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna) should likewise be bound to the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu), because it does not arise in the higher stages, just like nose-consciousness and tongue-consciousness. The answer is:
this is also not the case. Although it is bound to the higher stages, there are instances where body-consciousness can arise;
for when conditions permit its arising, it does indeed arise, because the object of touch (spraṣṭavya) exists.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage, "Just as the Bhikṣu Aśvajit, by means of his supernormal powers, went to the *upādāya-rūpa* (the great elements supporting the sense organs) of the Brahmā realm," the meaning is as follows:
Because Aśvajit possessed supernormal powers, he manifested himself and traveled to the Brahmā palace in the first dhyāna of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and beheld the Great Brahmā King;

the phrase "and so forth" includes the Brahmakāyika devas and others. Therefore, the intention is that Aśvajit’s eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) takes as its object the *upādāya-rūpa*—the great elements supporting the sense organs—within that [Brahmā’s] body.

It is said that Aśvajit, by means of his own supernormal power, transformed the bodies and the receptacle-worlds (*bhājanaloka*) of other stages; that is, the "body" was the primary subject of the preceding section.
Why, then, is it not mentioned here, but only the transformation of the receptacle-world? Question: Since this clarifies the receptacle-worlds of other stages, why is the "body" mentioned?

Answer: Although the body is cited, the intention is to clarify the receptacle-world. That is to say, the dwellings and clothing of those beings are all included within the category of the receptacle-world.
[Commentary: "Also by means of supernormal power" (*ṛddhibala*)—the meaning of this phrase is that there are two senses here.

First, celestial beings of the upper realms, by means of their own supernormal power, come to this world to hear the Dharma from the Buddha; in doing so, they transform the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) of this different realm.
Second, although the sentient beings of this realm have not yet attained supernormal powers themselves, they see the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) through the supernormal power of others.
The "devas and others" refer to sentient beings of the lower realms who transform the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) of another realm.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "beings of the upper realms see those below, even down to the *rūpa-dhātu*," the meaning is as follows: it is through the supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*) of other Buddhas that Brahma Kings and others perceive the magnificent radiance of the Buddha;
this constitutes seeing those below from above. It is by following this light that the sentient beings of this world perceive that [upper realm].

O Deva, this is a case of those in a lower realm seeing those in a higher realm. If one sees the sentient beings of the lower realms, even without the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*), the Brahmā King is also able to see them himself.

Furthermore, regarding matters such as the eighteen thousand worlds of the eastern direction seen by the sentient beings of this world-system and the Brahmā Kings and others, it is because the Brahmā Kings and others also see through the Buddha’s supernormal power, for their own supernormal power is inferior.
Because they are unable to perceive objects in distant realms of other directions for the reasons stated above, all [beings] rely on the supernormal powers of themselves or others;

this refers to the eighth transformation of the ground and the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) of sentient beings. Furthermore, when Aniruddha cultivates and attains the divine eye power (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), he perceives the trichiliocosm as if it were in the palm of his hand;
this is because he relies on the supernormal power of transformation to manifest the ground and the vessel-world. Thus it may be said.
That which perceives the five sensory objects is the "resultant color" (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*), such as gold, silver, and so forth.

[Commentary: Although the passage concerning the eighth consciousness reaching the internal body intends to say that both the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*) and the power of supernormal faculties (*abhijñā-bala*) are transformations of the eighth consciousness—whereby the eighth consciousness transforms the internal sense-faculties and the physical body through the power of supernormal faculties, while through the power of meditative concentration it only transforms the eighth consciousness itself.

Although the five objects of the [lower] stages exist, there is no textual explanation that the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can transform the internal body into a body of a different stage.

[Commentary: Furthermore, the fact that the power of concentration does not induce the arising of a body from another stage or a lower stage is intended to clarify that the power of concentration is not like the supernormal power (*ṛddhi-bala*) which transforms bodies of the higher realms;
for it is heard that the power of concentration is like the supernormal power in transforming the divine eye and ear faculties.
The fact that one cannot answer while in a body of a different realm is certainly not because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can perform such a task;

for the power of concentration can only transform the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), but cannot transform the physical body (*indriya-kāya*). This is an immediate re-explanation of the reason why the internal body cannot be transformed.

[Commentary]: "The phrase 'In the formless realm there is no supernormal power, etc. explains the meaning through the subsequent text. It is not only that one does not transform the upper body by relying on a lower-body concentration;

even when the body is in a formless concentration, one does not transform the body. This is because the transformed body lacks real material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), or because it is called a 'body' only in the sense that it is an accumulation [of atoms].
Since it is stated that one enables others to see it, it is clear that this is a provisional manifestation."

Although the form-body (rūpakāya) manifests as a form-body, it possesses only a locus of support; it is like a clay figure that lacks the function of generating consciousness and has no real sense organs.
Why is this? Because the four factors—the sense organs, mind, and so forth—cannot be transformed. Therefore, with respect to the actual body, it is said to be without sense organs.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, as well as for the Buddha, supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) necessarily reach the transformation of the body:

Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above, relying on their innate divine eye (*upapatti-pratilambhika-divyacakṣus*), cannot manifest supernormal powers because the power of their innate divine eye and ear-faculties is inferior.

If they wish to manifest supernormal powers, they must further cultivate and give rise to the divine eye and ear-faculties; these are called "supernormal powers of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-abhijñā*) and "transformation of the body," which are equal to those of a Buddha. Why is this so?

Question: Since this [state] exists, can it also be said to undergo transformation? Answer: Because the Buddha’s eighth consciousness is eternally endowed with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there is no fault in its undergoing transformation.

Question: Is it not also the case that in the higher realms, one borrows the visual and auditory consciousnesses of the *vikalpa* (scattered) state, which are not supernormal powers? Answer: There is no scriptural authority for this in the Mahāyāna.

Because a maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) cannot arise from a different level (*bhūmi*), it cannot be borrowed. One may only borrow those [consciousnesses] associated with deportment (*airyāpathika*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).

Because the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) possesses the skillful activity of speech, it is said that the visual and auditory consciousnesses resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala*) are attained there, as well as those possessing a virtuous nature (*kuśalatva*).

This includes cases such as the Brahmā kings of the higher realms employing the vitarka and vicāra of the lower realms to produce vocal karma, as well as borrowing the visual and auditory consciousnesses of the lower realms to receive the precepts from a Buddha.

It should be understood that receiving the precepts is a virtuous mind of the lower stage. Furthermore, it is explained that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the higher stages [performs this function] by means of...

Volition (*cetanā*) is the cause of speech; it does not depend on the subliminal consciousness (*manas*), but rather, induced by that [volition], visual and auditory consciousnesses arise in other stages (*bhūmi*).

Question: Do the five faculties of eye and ear perceive postures (*airyāpathika*) and so forth? Answer: If they are correctly perceiving postures or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), then only visual and auditory consciousness perceive them.
This is because they perceive the craftsmanship of speech. As for the "path" of postures and craftsmanship—here, "path" refers to posture (*iryāpatha*).

The "place where one treads" refers to the locus where skillful effort (*kauśalya*) is applied; if it concerns the skillful effort of deportment (*īryāpatha*), it is perceived solely by the sixth consciousness. [Commentary:
To interpret it in this way—to ask, "How could the eighth consciousness perceive it?"—is entirely a challenging objection.

This objection contains two points: first, it challenges the superior [consciousness] to see the inferior; second, it challenges the inferior to see the superior. If one adds the previous interpretation regarding the Bhikṣu Aśvajit and the eighth consciousness...

Question: It is said that those who obtain the bodies and environments (*āśraya-bhājana*) of other stages can also transform the three calamities (*trividha-vipatti*) and so forth; this refers to the eighth [Brahmā] of the Brahmā-world.
What logical fault is there in the claim that the eighth [Brahmā] of the higher realms could transform the three calamities?

Answer: Not so. The previous statement applied only to those of one's own stage within another realm. Since the eighth [Brahmā] cannot transform the Brahmā-world and so forth—which are not of his own stage—how could it be otherwise?
Can there be transformation? Furthermore, when the body is in a lower realm, one uses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) belonging to a higher realm to see the forms (*rūpa*) of that higher realm;
how could the eighth consciousness possibly undergo such transformation? According to principle, the eighth consciousness merely transforms the divine eye and the ear faculty;

it does not take those forms as its objects. Why is this? Because they are too distant. Since it does not take them as objects, it is clear that even though Aśvajit went to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), [the eighth consciousness did not transform].
"It must be the eighth [consciousness] that takes Brahmā and others as its object.

[Commentary: "If they were separated, it would reach even to those who transform"—this answers the objection. It means that when Aśvajit’s body reaches the higher realms and manifests there, this is the eighth consciousness;
it attains the ability to take Brahmā and others as its object, seeing the three calamities below, for although they are distant from his own level, they are not remote.
Therefore, it does not change. [Commentary:

From this, one should know up to "it should be considered. If one says that although they are separated, the eighth consciousness is seen as unchanging, then when the divine eyes and ears perceive color-form and sound, there would be no objective essence; this would be like Brahmā and others seeing the three lower calamities.

Regarding the eighth [consciousness], although it does not undergo transformation, the eye-consciousness also takes this as its object; thus, it is an instance of taking something without a manifest form (*nirākāra*) as an object.
This should be reflected upon: [the eye-consciousness] takes the transformation of another person’s [eighth consciousness] as its substantial object (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, as for the contradiction with the subsequent text stating that "there must necessarily be a remote objective condition" (*viprakṛṣṭa-ālambana-pratyaya*), it is because the five sensory consciousnesses must rely on the objects transformed by the eighth consciousness as their remote objective conditions. My current explanation also does not contradict this.

Although there is no self-eighth consciousness that transforms [into an object], it nevertheless becomes an indirect objective condition (*parokṣālambana-pratyaya*) because it takes as its object what is transformed by another’s eighth consciousness;

this should be understood from the text as it appears. Question: Could it be that one’s own five consciousnesses rely upon what is transformed by another’s eighth consciousness as their own substantial essence (*svabhāva-bimba*)?
Answer: There would indeed be five consciousnesses that perfume seeds into another’s eighth consciousness, provided they belong to the same realm (*dhātu*).
Since this treatise now relies on [the perspective of] other realms, it is accepted that one may "strike" another.

If that were so, one would have to accept that the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) of a different stage belonging to the eighth [consciousness] could perfume seeds in another; this point should be carefully considered.

As for what the commentators see—namely, the objection that the eighth [consciousness] does not take the three lower calamities as its object—the Master [of the Commentary], anticipating this difficulty, suggests that one should borrow from the present case where those who have attained meditative concentration perceive objects beyond their own realm.
Why would one claim that the transformation by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) acts as an obstacle to the treatise’s own statement?

For if the bodies, vessels, realms, stages, and the selves and others were transformed by the power of concentration and so forth, they would not be determinate; thus, even if one were to posit an eighth [type of] transformation of the lower [realms], it would contradict the principle.

[Commentary: As stated in the *Shuyao*, the intended meaning is that the eighth consciousness of Brahmā-rāja also transforms the three calamities. Why? Because it is permitted that there is an intervening condition (*vyavahita-pratyaya*).
Thus, we know that the five consciousnesses also do not contradict the fundamental object (*bhāva-vastu*) mentioned in the subsequent text.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "the receptacle world of the other stages" to "benefiting sentient beings," the intended meaning is as follows:

That which is distinct from matter within the *dharmāyatana*—namely, gold, silver, ghee, and so forth—is called an "object" (*viṣaya*) because it is the spontaneous object of meditative concentration. It is called "resultant matter" (*phala-rūpa*) because it moves toward and seeks [its end] for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
Although these are what is expected, they are distinguished by being named "object" and "result. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* says: "That object, that..."

Because it is a fruit, this [eighth consciousness] encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). This is because it is manifested by the Buddhas and the great Bodhisattvas;
thus, while the contaminated objects of the eighth consciousness of a Bodhisattva are themselves contaminated, the Buddha’s are not, and are therefore purely uncontaminated.

Alternatively, if one refers to the sixth consciousness of Bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), its objects are likewise called uncontaminated; however, the eighth consciousness is designated as having contaminated objects only [in their case].
Consciousness.
[Commentary] However, regarding the statement that the eighth consciousness exclusively takes only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as its object, the intent is as follows:

from this point onward, the nature of the eighth consciousness will be analyzed through six topical sections (*ṣaḍdvāra*) to distinguish the differences in how it perceives objects through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The first section concerns the contaminated.
1. The first [classification] is by way of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). 2. The second is by way of the three realms (*dhātu*). 3. The third is by way of the five objects (*viṣaya*). 4.
The fourth is by way of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*bhautika*). 5. The fifth is by way of the fixed and the common [powers]. 6.

The sixth is by way of the transformation of the faculties (*indriya*) and the non-transformation of the faculties. The first [category], which is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), takes only the contaminated as its object; it is fixed upon form (*rūpa*) and is generally [of the nature of] supernormal power (*abhijñā*).

To say that they are not distinct yet do not resemble one another means that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) which is transformed does not resemble the substance of the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*). [Commentary:

Furthermore, the interpretation that "because the first dhyāna has utility" should be connected to the preceding section; it is not necessarily the case that there must be an original basis (*mūla*) here.

This is corroborated by the subsequent text. If it were not so, why would the eighth [consciousness]—which is shown in the first section on "differentiation" to have both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects—be discussed in the middle [section] regarding the eye and so forth? From this, we know that it should be combined with the preceding explanation.

These three consciousnesses refer to the three consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and body; their objects and their distinct levels of attachment (*bhūmi-bandhana*) are also [to be understood in this way].

The former [passage] concerns transformation through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) within the same level (*bhūmi*), while this [passage] concerns transformation through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); therefore, there is no contradiction.

[Commentary]: Second, although this [transformation] exists in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it also extends to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding the statement "down to shedding tears," the intended meaning is that concentration and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) exist across all three [realms].
The mention of their existence in the formless realm refers exclusively to the power of concentration, because there is no supernormal power in the formless realm.

Therefore, the statement that the gods of the formless realms shed tears is based solely on the power of meditative concentration; it refers to the "matter produced by concentration" (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*). Question: Is there no supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) at all in the formless realms?

Answer: There is indeed supernormal power. Question: Why then is it said that there is none? Answer: It is said to be "none" because their wisdom (*prajñā*) is inferior; it does not mean that it is entirely absent.
For example, when one says that the supernormal powers in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) are strong, does this imply they lack meditative concentration (*samādhi*)? This case is exactly the same.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "The third [consciousness] transforms only matter and touch, while it also transforms other objects," this question asks:

"Furthermore, within meditative concentrations, supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), and so forth, does the eighth consciousness transform only matter and touch, or does it also transform other objects? The answer to this previous question is that these [transformations] encompass all five sense-objects because they are capable of transforming everything.
As stated in the *Triṃśikā-vijñapti-kārikā* (Verse 7), "By the power of supernatural faculties, the eighth consciousness is able to transform the four [objects]."

Regarding the "dusts" (viṣaya), gold, ghee, milk, and so forth all have the four dusts as their substance. This means that the substance of sound is empty and sparse, and because it is not a sense-object that supports the faculties (indriya), it does not transform when one leaves the realm of sound;
however, upon entering a Pure Land, it transforms into the five dusts, for the water-birds and forest trees all preach the Dharma, and thus sound exists there.
Furthermore, the fifty-third [fascicle] states that even the form produced by the formless meditative absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti) can likewise transform into the five dusts.

Therefore, it is said that they can transform all things, just as the *pāramitās* do; for when the minds of Śrāvakas enter the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), they comprehend the objects of the three realms.
Thus, by relying on the formless attainments, they are able to transform the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) without needing to enter a pure land.

Some say that these attainments are of two kinds: those that generally transform the five sensory objects, and those that, if based on the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), transform only visible form and tangible objects. If based on...
Regarding the transformation in the desire realm, it refers to the universal transformation of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
[Commentary: As for the statement in the *Fifty-fourth [Treatise]* up to "because it allows for utility for oneself and others," this reconciles the contradiction. If one asks:
"If it is said that there are truly five sense objects, why does the *Fifty-fourth [Treatise]* state that one transforms only visible form (*varṇa*) and not odor or taste? The answer is: Five...

Regarding the fourteenth point, which states that the matter resulting from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) consists solely of visible color (*varṇa-rūpa*) and lacks odor, fragrance, and so forth:

this is said with reference to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in the form realm who have attained meditative absorption and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), as well as with reference to Śrāvakas who have not attained the *pāramitās* in the formless realm.

Therefore, while they cannot transform odor and fragrance, they are able to transform the three objects of visible color, tangible objects, and sound; they are unable to produce the other two types of objects.

First, because the cause of fragrance is absent; second, it would be useless, as explained in the *Yanmi* (Secret Commentary on the Yogācārabhūmi). Furthermore, it does not allow for utility for oneself or others;
even if one were to grant that it transforms, it would not be like visible form, which has utility for both self and others.
Thus, while visible form is color, tangible objects are yellow and other such colors.

[Commentary: Regarding the fifth point, "the distinction between supernormal power (*abhijñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*")—this asks what difference there is between the mind of supernormal power and the mind of meditative concentration.

The answer now states: the mind of meditative concentration taking an object is invariably wholesome (*kuśala*), whereas the mind that is the fruit of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Why is this? For example, when those of the Two Vehicles or ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) attain a superior state of concentration while seated, if they give rise to supernormal powers for the sake of play; [it is the latter].
The fruit is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not virtuous (*kuśala*). Why? Because it arises from a mind of playful speech;

thus, among the four types of indeterminate states, it is the indeterminate mind of transformation (*nairmāṇika-avyākṛta-citta*). If it is produced for the sake of benefiting and gladdening sentient beings, it is subsumed under the virtuous.

Question: What is called "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*)? Answer: "Supernormal" (*abhijñā*) means wisdom (*prajñā*). Because this wisdom arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "supernormal power. "Power" (*abhijñā*) [is so named because]...

This is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound meaning "the result which is itself the supernormal power," referring to inferior wisdom (*hīna-prajñā*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta*).

If one says it refers generally to "resultant matter" (*rūpa*), this means that matter is transformed into gold, silver, and so forth by the power of supernormal abilities; thus, the matter that is the result of supernormal power is called "supernormal-resultant matter.

This is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive) compound, as the matter is induced by supernormal power. Question: Is this supernormal-resultant [wisdom] concentrated (*samāhita*) or distracted (*asamāhita*)? Answer: It is neither concentrated nor distracted. Why is this?
Whether one places them in a state of distraction or in a state of meditative concentration, neither can transform such things as gold or ghee;
it is just as when a person is about to wake from sleep—neither placing them in sleep nor placing them in waking applies universally, for they are neither fixed in concentration nor in distraction.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the first is the fundamental object and the second is the liberation object": the name "fundamental" refers to the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) itself and not to a distracted state;

the "resultant mind of penetration" is termed "liberation" because it occurs after the concentration and is not itself the concentration, just as the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) follows the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*).

[Commentary]: As for the question, "From the eighth stage onward, what is the difference? the intent of the inquiry is to ask: since those from the eighth stage onward are constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one wonders precisely how their transformations (*nirmāṇa*) differ from those of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "there is a distinction between the two because the power of supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) has been attained," this answers the preceding question.

That is to say, from the seventh bhūmi and below, there is a distinction in terms of fundamental liberation; from the eighth bhūmi and above, there is a distinction in terms of whether there is preparatory effort (prayoga) or no preparatory effort.

However, upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, even without preparatory effort, there is no difference between meditative concentration (samādhi) and supernormal knowledge, because transformations arise spontaneously through the effortless mind.
Therefore, it is asked: "How can Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onwards possess a mind of application (*prayoga*)?
The answer is that there are two types of application: 1. Application as application (*prayoga-prayoga*), which refers to the practice of applying effort and is thus called application;

2. Spontaneous application (*anābhoga-prayoga*), which refers to spontaneous contemplation. Therefore, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage onwards arise through spontaneous contemplation.
[The text] speaks of the meditative power (*samādhi*) that effects transformations such as gold through the universal penetration of the various directions.
[Commentary: Regarding the sixth point, from "furthermore, relying on supernormal powers" up to "resembling but not real," there is a question:

Since it is stated that the sense organs (*indriya*) do not change, why was it previously said that supernormal powers can induce changes in both the organs and their objects (*viṣaya*)? The answer is: This [current statement] concerns the non-transformation of other organs, whereas the previous [statement] concerned...

It induces the transformation of its own consciousness into its own sense organs; that is, just as it induces the transformation of the divine eye and ear faculties, these too are transformations induced by the eighth consciousness as its object.
Furthermore, it is said that it can also transform, as stated below: "Because the spiritual power of the Unsurpassed Enlightened One is inconceivable, he is able to manifest formless phenomena.
Question: How does karma transform its fruit? Answer: Gold, ghee, horses, barley, roots, and so forth.
It merely manifests as a semblance and is not real; this is for the purpose of subduing arrogant sentient beings, and other sages do not manifest such faculties.
[Commentary] This refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 54. Regarding the phrase "transforming the body and the vessel of another stage," the intent is as follows:

within the explanation of transforming the body and the vessel, one first explains the transformation of the body of another stage, and subsequently explains the transformation of the vessel of another stage. There are two reasons for explaining the transformation of the body first.

One interpretation states: When the gods of the form and formless realms come before the Buddha to hear the Dharma, they manifest billions of bodies that stand together upon the tip of a single hair without obstructing one another;
this refers to "different bodies. Question: Since there is no supernormal power (*abhijñā*) in the formless realm, it must be solely through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

How is the meaning of this [the existence of supernormal power] in the form realm? Answer: Although the form realm possesses supernormal powers, this does not preclude them from being transformations produced by the power of meditative concentration.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are two kinds of matter: first, matter manifested by meditative concentration (*samādhi-citta*), and second, matter resulting from karmic retribution (*vipākaja-rūpa*).

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only one kind, namely that manifested by meditative concentration. This explanation distinguishes between different types of bodies based on their specific names.

Second, it says that the gods of the realms of form and formlessness can transform their bodies to descend into the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and stand together with beings of the desire realm upon the tip of a single hair, without obstructing one another, so as to allow the multitudes of the desire realm [to perceive them].

Because they give rise to the perception [of him], sentient beings of the lower realms are able to see his transformed body through the power of another's meditative concentration; this is the eighth transformation.

It is called "another realm" (*anyabhūmi*) because it refers to the *upādāya-rūpa* (the supporting physical elements) of a different level; here, "different realm" is used as a designation for a "different body.

Furthermore, when those celestial beings manifest bodies in the Desire Realm, these are called "bodies of another realm"; however, these are still their own original material bodies (*rūpakāya*), as there is no meditative concentration in the Desire Realm.
The "pervasive" and other forms of matter are similar to the first interpretation mentioned above.

[Commentary: Regarding those who smell the fragrance of the palaces of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is because Bodhisattvas of that realm enter the concentration of the formless realm (*ārūpyasamādhi*) and consequently smell the fragrance of the palaces of the formless realm...
up to "like a fine spring rain. Here, "rain" refers to external [matter].

The "receptacle" refers to the gods of the form and formless realms who, by means of their meditative power (*samādhi*), transform their minds. This transformation results in rain and so forth that differs from their original state;
thus, it is called a "different stage" (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, the sentient beings of this realm also perceive that rain and so forth.

Similarly, when the gods of the form and formless realms stand beside the Buddha, or when [beings such as] Śakra and others come before him, they all transform themselves into bodies belonging to the desire realm—a different stage—coming from their original state.
Because those heavens lack this body, sentient beings of this desire realm who perceive those heavens also take the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) of the desire realm as their object.

[Commentary: Regarding that which is "actual form" among the objects of meditative concentration, this refers to the palaces and celestial vehicles of the formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*), which are actual forms belonging to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and serve as the objects of concentrated consciousness.
Furthermore, there is an interpretation which states that these celestial vehicles of the form and formless heavens descend below.
That which resembles rain is merely an imitation and not real, because it lacks the function of moisture and lubrication.

However, when Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage onward transform the great earth into gold or the waters of the ocean into clarified butter (sarpis), these then possess actual utility; the matter of such meditative objects is likewise subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the question, "How is it that the gods of the form and formless realms possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)?"—this inquiry asks:

since the gods of the form and formless realms all manifest through the power of supernormal faculties, why is this [manifested] form not considered a supernormal power, but rather a distinct form? The intended meaning is that it is called "the form produced as a result of supernormal power" (*abhijñā-phala-rūpa*).

What fault is there in this? Next, the passage beginning with "According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*... and ending with "...therefore they lack supernormal powers" provides the answer. [The text then] asks: what is the difference between the "result of supernormal power" (*abhijñā-phala*) and the "result of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-phala*)?

What is the distinction between the matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) and other forms? The answer is: there are two types of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*): first, the supernormal power itself; second, the matter produced by supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-rūpa*).

Regarding the former, "supernormal power" is the fruit because it is induced from meditative concentration; thus, it is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*), meaning "the fruit which is the supernormal power.

Regarding the latter, the matter transformed by supernormal power is "the fruit of the supernormal power"; thus, it is a *tatpuruṣa compound*, meaning "the matter which is the fruit of the supernormal power. As for the matter within the objective sphere of meditative concentration (*samādhi-viṣaya-rūpa*), this refers to gold and so forth that arise spontaneously within the state of concentration.

The term "meditative object" (*samādhiviṣaya*) refers to this very form produced from meditative concentration; it is called the "fruit of concentration" (*samādhiphala*). Although these names differ according to their specific meanings, there is no difference in their essential substance (*dravya*).

Furthermore, it is said that the reflected image transformed by concentration is called the "meditative object," while the actual form (*rūpa*) within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)—such as gold and so forth—transformed by the eighth consciousness when concentration acts upon the object as a condition, is called "form that is the fruit of concentration. This latter definition refers to a distinct substantial entity.
[Commentary]: "Interruption for a short duration" refers to those who die prematurely. It means that by the arising of even a single thought-moment, one's life comes to an end;
as with mayflies and the like, although they may endure for a brief time, because their time is so constrained, it is said that they die as soon as they are born.

According to this section of the treatise, it merely distinguishes that the bodies and environments transformed by supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) belong to [the level of] the supernormal powers of the second dhyāna and above, and are not transformations produced by the supernormal powers of the first dhyāna.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that "one kalpa" refers to the kalpa of formation and destruction. Regarding the phrase "because of being bound and triggered, sounds and so forth are then produced":
internal sounds are produced only when triggered by being bound to conditions such as the throat, lips, and tongue; external sounds are produced by conditions such as a ritual mace (*vajra*).
[It] is bound precisely at the moment of arising. [Commentary]:
Regarding "outflowing matter" (*niṣyanda-rūpa*), there are three types, namely: retributive (*vipāka*), nurtured (*aupacayika*), and intrinsic (*svabhāva*) matter.

Retributive matter refers to matter that arises from seeds within the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); it is thus called retributive matter. Alternatively, it is [matter] produced by karma...

The five faculties and so forth that are categorized as neutral (*avyākṛta*) are called "maturation-form" (*vipāka-rūpa*). From the perspective of their mutual induction across preceding and succeeding moments, these are also termed "outflow-form" (*niṣyanda-rūpa*).

As for "nourishment-form" (*puṣṭi-rūpa*), it is so called because it is nourished by food and clothing; from the perspective of its mutual induction across preceding and succeeding moments, it is also an outflow-form.

Regarding "natural outflow" (*svabhāva-niṣyanda*), this refers to the sense-bases that support the faculties (*indriya-adhiṣṭhāna*) and to colors such as blue and yellow, which are self-inductive across preceding and succeeding moments.

The term "outflowing matter" (*niṣyanda-rūpa*) refers to that which is produced by mutual succession; however, since retributive and nourished matter also involve mutual succession over time, those are not being considered here.
Rather, the difficulty is raised specifically regarding outflowing matter that arises from its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the seventh manas," etc., the meaning and the objection are as follows:

If it is argued that [the sixth consciousness] does not take [the ālayavijñāna] as its object because the mind and mental factors are subject to interruption, then why does the seventh [manas], which is constantly continuous, not take it as its object?
The words "If that were so" and following represent the opponent's objection, which is clear.
[Commentary]: "The limits of the spheres" refers to clarifying the boundaries of the eighth consciousness's objective sphere based upon the twelve *āyatanas*. [Commentary]:

"The five objects are common to both external and internal" means that they are considered "internal" in relation to the entire body; it does not mean they are internal in contrast to the sense organs (*indriya*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "although the mind takes [them] as objects" and so forth, there is an external objection which states:

"Since seeds are said to have the mental base (*manāyatana*) as their object, they should be subsumed under the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*); therefore, among the eight consciousnesses, the latter three consciousnesses are all subsumed within the mental base."

[Commentary] Question: Does the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) not take the provisional as its object, such as the [factors] dissociated from mind (*viprayukta*)? The intention of this question is:
for instance, why does it not take the four types of form included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) as its object?

Answer: That which is the object of the eighth consciousness is invariably real; because these forms are provisional, it does not take them as its object. Question: Since there are five kinds of form, why do you speak of only four? Answer: Within the five kinds of form...

The four types of form—extreme reduction (*paramāṇu*), extreme distance (*dūratama*), that which is derived from feeling (*vedanā-niṣyanda*), and that which arises from conceptual construction (*parikalpita*)—are exclusively nominal (*prajñapti-sat*).

The eighth [consciousness] does not take them as its object. As for the form produced by meditative mastery (*vaśitā-ja-rūpa*), it includes both the nominal and the substantial; gold and so forth are substantial, while the ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality spheres) are nominal.
The eighth [consciousness] does not take these as its objects. This refers to the fifth type of form, which, although subsumed under the *dharmāyatana*, is pervasive.

The reason why the provisional and the real are not discussed here is that we are only inquiring about the first four types of matter. What is meant by "matter resulting from extreme reduction" (*paramāṇu-saṃghāta-rūpa*)?

It refers to the sixth consciousness, within its conceptual mind, breaking down coarse matter into subtle matter until it reaches the ultimate atom; this is called matter resulting from extreme reduction. "Reduction" (*lve*) means "subtle.

Alternatively, it may be understood as reducing the coarse to the subtle, hence it is called "matter resulting from extreme reduction. As for "matter resulting from extreme distance" (*paramāvaccheda-rūpa*), it refers to the light within space.

Regarding "darkness and distance" (*tad-āloka*): when color is reduced from large to small until it reaches a single atom (*paramāṇu*), and one then removes that single atom, the space revealed by its departure—measuring the extent of a single atom—is called "color of extreme distance" (*prabhāva-varṇa*).
"Extreme distance" (*prabhāva*) refers precisely to empty space. Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states:
"Color of extreme distance is that which, having been broken down from coarse matter to a single atom, is this very atom free from obstructive contact."

The form that is induced is called "extreme distance" (*prāntakoṭika-rūpa*). Furthermore, regarding the question of how it differs from the "empty space" (*ākāśa*) among the primary colors (*varṇa*), which is also observed by the sixth consciousness through the analysis of mental factors:
there is indeed a distinction. To explain: that which is observed horizontally as the color of empty space is called "extreme distance";
that which is observed looking upward at the void is the "empty space" among the primary colors.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "among those derived from undertaking, such as those concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the Path (*mārga*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

Among the various types of matter derived from undertaking (*upātta-rūpa*), there are many—namely, manifest action (*vijñapti*), non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), that which is concomitant with meditative concentration, that which is concomitant with the Path, and so forth. Now, in order to distinguish these from the others, it says "among" (*madhye*).

The underlying sense is that the precepts concomitant with meditative concentration and the Path are called "matter derived from undertaking" because they are obtained through receiving instruction from a teacher; thus, they internally prevent wrongdoing.

Established based on the seeds of volition. [Commentary] Regarding the principle of subsuming the general under the particular: the eighth consciousness’s objects of perception—namely, the sense bases (*āyatana*) such as the faculties and their objects—are collectively termed the "dharma-base" (*dharmāyatana*). The dharma-base is the general category, while the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) and others are the particulars.

Here, the general is subsumed under the particulars, meaning the ten bases and so forth are included within it. As for "subsuming the dark by means of the light": *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The commentary likely proceeds to explain how obscure categories are clarified through more specific or luminous designations.*

The eighth object of focus (*ālambana*) is darkness, whereas the objects of the six consciousnesses are light; this is because the objects of the six consciousnesses now encompass the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and so forth.

[Commentary: It is said that these are all subsumed under their respective original bases. Furthermore, there is an interpretation which states that even the objects of the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), such as the sense organs and their objects, are all...

The *dharmāyatana* (sphere of phenomena) is termed "general" because it subsumes names collectively, yet it is termed "particular" because it also subsumes them individually. The same applies to the transition from darkness to light:

the five consciousnesses and their simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are termed "light" because they perceive objects individually and because they apprehend through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises independently and clings with stubbornness is termed "darkness. Furthermore, there is an interpretation which states that the seeds of the twelve spheres (*dvādaśāyatana*) are termed "general."

The "darkness" follows the twelve bases (*āyatana*) individually, while the "light" is subsumed under the general category of the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*), yet it is also subsumed under the individual twelve bases. [Commentary]:

Regarding the phrase "among the forms produced by meditative concentration... because it does not take the conventional as its object," the intended meaning is that the contemplations of the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) also...

Question: Since these are established within the mind by means of the sixth consciousness and are therefore merely provisional, why are they included here within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?

What is meant by the "ten universal bases" (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*)? Answer: They are the four great elements, blue, yellow, red, white, consciousness, and space; these are called the ten. Question: What is meant by "universal base"? Answer:
For example, when observing earth, one perceives everything collectively as the aspect of earth, and so on, up to the observation of space.
At that time, because they are collectively characterized as empty, these ten dharmas are provisional (*prajñapti*), being established through the observation of the sixth consciousness;
the eighth [consciousness] does not take them as its object.

[Commentary]: "However, regarding the statement that 'all dharmas have two kinds of self,' the intention is that the following treatise intends to provide a brief clarification; therefore, the commentary [proceeds]."
The phrase "the family first presents the document" refers to the subsequent passage that initiates the text.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and so forth possess deliberation":

this means that subsequently attained wisdom possesses spontaneous discernment (*pravicaya*) when explaining all phenomena, and thus it receives the name "deliberation. However, it is not like forced conceptualization (*vikalpa*), wherein names and meanings are mutually linked to one another.

Therefore, the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) takes non-existence as its object. Furthermore, there is an interpretation which states that the mind taking non-existence as its object has two causes:

first, because of false discrimination; second, because of deliberative calculation. Thus, the sixth consciousness, by virtue of possessing discrimination, is able to take non-existence as its object.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the various six consciousnesses, etc.," the term "etc. (等) refers to the inclusion of wholesome and unwholesome [states], as well as the associated mental factors (*caitta*).

It does not include the first five consciousnesses, because those do not take non-existence (*abhāva*) as an object. Since subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) involves deliberation, it can take formless phenomena as its object;
however, the eighth consciousness lacks both of these two conditions, and is therefore unable to take non-existence as its object. Thus, the conclusion below states:
Regarding the eighth [point], "it does not take the self as its object": since the substance of a self (*ātman*) does not exist, the eighth [consciousness] does not take a self as its object.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "among conditioned phenomena... it takes the real and not the provisional," the intention is as follows:

Within the category of conditioned phenomena—namely, matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitta*), and non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*)—although these have been analyzed as before, specifically within the category of matter, [the consciousness] takes only real matter as its object and does not take [provisional matter].

It is not yet certain whether the eighth consciousness takes as its object "borrowed matter" (prajñaptirūpa), the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta), the non-associated formations (viprayuktasaṃskāra), and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta);
therefore, the following question is posed.

[Commentary] As for the statement, "due to the absence of seeds of karma and of names-and-phrases (nāma-vyañjana)," this interpretation holds that [the object] must arise by means of these two causes and conditions.

The capacity to actualize this [object] refers to the transformation of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as they manifest; it is truly functional, or alternatively, all that is transformed arises from two causes.
The mention of "necessarily having a blade" excludes the five [mental factors] associated with the eighth consciousness and so forth.

The term "spontaneous" (*svarasa*) excludes the seventh and sixth consciousnesses, as well as eye-consciousness and others that are not produced by karma; or, even if the five sensory consciousnesses are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, they are not [spontaneous] if they are not produced by karma.

The commentary states that this refers to the power of the mind arising spontaneously and the transformation of causes and conditions; it specifically identifies these as the five and the eighth consciousnesses, without distinguishing between the wholesome or unwholesome natures of the five sensory consciousnesses. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "thereby the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] take non-existence as their object," the intended meaning is to explain how the sixth consciousness can take non-existence as its object, and how this relates to the seventh.

"Is it also conditioned by non-existence? Answer: Because one internally clings to the eighth consciousness as a self, and since the substance of that self is non-existent, it is said to be "conditioned by non-existence.

As for the statement "it is also conditioned by existence," this refers to the objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) such as blue and so forth, which are produced from conditions and are therefore called "existence.

Regarding the phrase "or the first [consciousness] pervades five, the eighth entirely, and the sixth partially," this refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses; this interpretation is somewhat... [incomplete].

Kuan (Guang) states that it is not only karma that induces [transformation]; rather, whatever undergoes transformation through the power of spontaneous functioning is a transformation due to causes and conditions.
Therefore, the sub-commentary below says: "That which does not follow the substantial entity and its seeds as they transform due to causes and conditions is a transformation of discrimination.

The phrase "the entirety of the seventh and a small portion of the sixth" intends to refer to the subsequent transformation of discrimination. The "small portion of the sixth" refers specifically to the *manas* (the solitary mind).
The head-consciousness (manovijñāna) gives rise to transverse conceptual discrimination.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage beginning with "conforming to that which has function" (*yong*), the intended meaning is as follows:

taking the entirety of the fifth and eighth consciousnesses, along with a small portion of the sixth, as the transformation of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) conforms to the subsequent textual passages in the treatise—specifically those stating that [the first five] necessarily have function while the latter [the eighth] serves only as an object. This conforms to the initial section of the Commentary (*Śū*).

From the passage beginning with "due to causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) up until this point in the commentary, it has not yet been clarified which of the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) constitutes these two transformations (*pariṇāma*) distinguished by causes and conditions.
Within the commentary, there are four explanations in total: first, from the initial section "following causes and conditions" up to "the principle" (*yukti*), is the first explanation;
furthermore, from "another interpretation" (*apara-vyākhyā*) down to "fire in a mirror," is [the second].
The second explanation is that [the transformation] proceeds from causes and conditions until it merely becomes an object for that [consciousness].

The third interpretation is that it proceeds from the mind and mental factors associated with the five consciousnesses until no obstacles or difficulties arise. (This is the explanation of Master Yin.

Furthermore, regarding the analysis of the transformation of causes and conditions, according to the *Shuyao* commentary on the *Shu*, Master Fa [Zang] stated that there are four interpretations; however, he said that [only the first] is correct.

Furthermore, because there are four explanations following the initial explanation, it is explained again: first, the statement "only the eighth [consciousness], the ripening [result]" constitutes the first explanation;
second, the passage beginning with the question "If it transforms according to causes and conditions" constitutes the second explanation;

third, the passage beginning with "From this, it is further said that it follows causes and conditions" constitutes the third explanation; and finally, the statement "Furthermore, 'causes and conditions' refers to the reality of all phenomena" constitutes the fourth explanation.
The actual [explanation] below is the fourth interpretation; however, the *Śubhākarasiṃha-ṭīkā* (Shūyō) arranges them out of order.

Specifically, the first interpretation in this commentary (*Sūtra*) corresponds to the second interpretation in the *Śubhākarasiṃha-ṭīkā*, and the third interpretation in this commentary corresponds to the first interpretation in the *Śubhākarasiṃha-ṭīkā*.

Furthermore, the first two interpretations in the *Śubhākarasiṃha-ṭīkā* represent Dharmapāla’s own view; because his reasoning was not exhaustive, there are supplementary explanations [in the subsequent ones]. For this reason, in this commentary...

It is often said that this refers to the "subsequent interpretation. Furthermore, the *Shuyao* states that the "third interpretation" refers precisely to the third interpretation within the *Sūtra Commentary*.
Although such an interpretation exists, its meaning is extremely difficult; I request that you, a gentleman, examine it more closely once again.

There is also an interpretation which says: as the *Sūtra Commentary* states, "If [one follows] the Yogācāra commentators, etc.," there arises the fault of producing a single body based on the subsequent text.

The commentary on the third interpretation states: "The various divergent explanations by previous scholars all stem from their failure to grasp the original intent of the Master of the Sub-commentary (*śāstrakāra*).
Upon examining his sub-commentary, it is evident that he is capable of explaining this meaning; thus, the first interpretation should be regarded as superior in principle."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "first, transformation according to causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*), the intended meaning is that while the eight consciousnesses are transformations according to causes and conditions, and although the eighth and the five [sensory] consciousnesses transform objects spontaneously (*svarasena*), they lack practical utility (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, these are excluded for the time being.

When it says "namely the seven consciousnesses," etc., the intention is to include the seventh consciousness in its entirety and a small portion of the sixth consciousness—excluding the sensory consciousnesses associated with the five [objects] that are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, [the commentary] states: "The first refers only to the eighth [consciousness], etc. This second explanation of the transformation of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*) receives its designation as "the first" because it is contrasted with the subsequent "discriminative transformation" (*vikalpa-pariṇāma*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the color, tangibles, and so forth transformed by the remaining seven consciousnesses" in the latter part: it is called "latter" because it is contrasted with the initial causal conditions.

As for "color, tangibles, and so forth," "tangibles" refers to the object-field of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*), and "and so forth" includes the mental factors (*caitta*) that are transformed; none of these possess actual utility.
[Commentary: Since this is so, regarding these two meanings from the five consciousnesses downward, the intention of the Bodhisattvas Dharmapāla and others in their interpretation is as follows:

This commentary, from "Since this is so, the five consciousnesses... up to "...should not be real," intends to evaluate the relative merits of the first two interpretations. Specifically, from "Since this is so, the five consciousnesses...
up to "...should not be real," the intention is that the first master challenges the second interpretation. [The first master] says: "If one claims that the other seven consciousnesses are all..."

If [the object] were a transformation through conceptualization (*vikalpa*), then the five consciousnesses would have to take the conventional (*prajñapti*) as their object; furthermore, the blue and other colors apprehended by the five consciousnesses would lack practical efficacy (*artha-kriyā-śakti*).

According to the answer provided below, the transformations of the five consciousnesses also possess unimpeded efficacy—this refers to what follows—and the principle is the same: they likewise possess unimpeded efficacy.

This is precisely the point of the text. Thus, in response to this objection, the *bhāga-lakṣaṇa* (aspect-part) of blue and so forth apprehended by the five consciousnesses also lacks any real obstruction.

Regarding the statement that the five consciousnesses have "practical utility" when perceiving blue and so forth, this is said in reference to the objective essence (*bhāva*) transformed by the eighth consciousness;

thus, it is said they possess practical utility. Although they lack practical utility when perceiving blue and so forth, they likewise do not perceive conventional designations (*prajñapti*) such as length or shortness.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the phrase "if [the objects] change according to causes and conditions," the intent is as follows: Suppose external atoms constitute the second interpretation; how does this differ from the first interpretation? Answer:
The first interpretation explains the objects transformed by the five consciousnesses and the eight mind-kings (*citta-rāja*);
this second interpretation refers exclusively to the objects transformed by the eighth mind-king and does not include the five consciousnesses. This is the reason for the difference.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "therefore it further says... leading to the first interpretation," the intention is as follows: wishing to establish the first interpretation, he first asks about the meaning of its causal conditions.

Now, the explanation states that "according to the sense of spontaneity (*anābhoga*) and the sense of seeds (*bīja*)," which means that the five consciousnesses and the eight consciousnesses, as appropriate, arise spontaneously from their own direct linguistic seeds (*nāma-vākya-bīja*) and transform objects spontaneously. This refers to the seeds of transformation.
The statement that "having equal practical utility is called transformation through causal conditions" accords with the first interpretation.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "the eight and five categories" up to "cannot produce eye-consciousness and so forth," these all serve to establish the aforementioned first interpretation.
When it says that the sixth consciousness and other retributive minds (*vipāka-citta*) take objects, this means that both the five categories and the retributive mind are spontaneously active.

Since there is a fear that the "objective realm as a condition for arising" (*janma-pratyaya-viṣaya*) might be confused with the "transformation through causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*), it must be distinguished. Furthermore, what is the distinction between the "conceptual transformation" (*vikalpa-pariṇāma*) subsumed under the mind and mental factors and [the aforementioned]?

This is the question that must be clarified. How should one answer the question regarding the fivefold simultaneous mental consciousness (*pañca-sahaja-manovijñāna*)? It also takes objects through transformation.

When it is said that it does not follow the actual substance (*dravya*) but rather the seeds (*bīja*) and causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) transform the aspects of the object and so forth, the intended meaning is that the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) spontaneously (*svarasena*) takes objects through transformation in accordance with reality.
Because it is the seed, it is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Regarding the five categories [of consciousness], they spontaneously transform their images based on seeds.

This means that although contact and the other [mental factors] share the same objects as the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) regarding their seeds, the seeds transformed by the fundamental consciousness possess actual efficacy and are thus termed "transformation as a causal condition.
However, the seeds transformed by the mental associates (*caitta*) are like fire in a mirror; they lack actual efficacy.
The name "image-seed" is also like the visual faculty and so forth, which are transformations of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that possess the function of producing consciousness;
whereas contact and so forth are transformations that lack the function of producing consciousness—this case is likewise.

[Commentary]: Question: Regarding the passage from "contact" (*sparśa*) onwards, which relies on the second interpretation—prior to establishing that second interpretation, an external objection is first posed, and the subsequent answer accords with that second interpretation.

[Commentary]: If the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (the "Yoga School") were to reach the point of not contradicting this text, its intended meaning would be that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*—as interpreted by the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (the "Shengzi" school)—asserts that the sense objects (*spraṣṭavya*) and so forth transform simultaneously with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
This does not contradict the textual passage concerning "transformation through causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*) in this treatise.

Thus, with respect to the roots and objects transformed by the fundamental consciousness and its associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*), they are termed "having practical utility" (*sa-phala*) as a transformation through causes and conditions. Although... [text truncated]
This contradicts the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, yet it also contradicts the *Karma-siddhi-prakaraṇa* regarding the fault that multiple [causes] produce a single [result].

As explained below in the third treatise, my own previous interpretation was superior; this refers to the first interpretation, which accords with the third section below, namely the passage refuting the notion that multiple [causes] produce a single sprout.
[Commentary: Furthermore, the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*) is that all phenomena arrive [at the consciousness]; thus, it is merely taken as an object.

The intention behind this third interpretation—that the seeds possess true utility—is as follows: it means that these seeds are transformations of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) which possess substantial reality and function;
they are therefore termed "true. These seeds give rise to form, mind, and so forth, and because they possess actual efficacy, they are termed "conditions."

The transformations that correspond to the five categories of seeds transformed by the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) are called "provisional seeds" because they lack actual functional utility.

That is to say, the manifestations of sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth, which are transformed by contact (*sparśa*) and other factors, lack the function of generating consciousness and are thus said to "arise from provisional seeds."

[Commentary: The phrase "the untainted is also like this" means that if, as in meditative concentration, the untainted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) strikes and activates the eighth [consciousness] such that it transforms things like fish or jewels with actual utility, this is termed "transformation by causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*), as in the case of the ten *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality) contemplations.
However, when the objects transformed lack actual utility, they are merely subsumed under "transformation by conceptualization" (*vikalpa-pariṇāma*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "The five consciousnesses associated with... to "...there are no obstacles or difficulties," these points constitute the fourth interpretation of the five and eight consciousnesses.

As the text states, they arise simultaneously with the five [sensory] consciousnesses; the mental factors (*caitta*) of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses also undergo transformation through causes and conditions and arise from actual seeds (*bhūta-bīja*).

However, the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by the mental factors of the eighth consciousness arises solely from provisional seeds (*prajñapti-bīja*), which differs from those of the fifth and sixth consciousnesses.

However, the gold, silver, and so forth transformed within meditative concentration arise from actual seeds and are subsumed under "transformation due to causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-pariṇāma*);
