whereas the remaining objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*) of form and mind associated with other minds and mental factors are merely semblances and not real, like fire in a mirror which lacks the functional capacity to serve as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "If one discusses the dependent nature as arising through false causes and conditions," the intended meaning is that although the perceived aspects (nimitta-bhāga), such as blue, which are transformed by the discriminative consciousness, do not possess the quality of physical obstruction like those transformed by the fundamental consciousness (mūla-vijñāna), they nonetheless possess the function of generating consciousness.
This is because blue and so forth are dependent phenomena produced by relying upon causes and conditions, and therefore they are functional.

[Commentary]: It is not the case that [the transformed aspect] corresponds to its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in the same way that matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth do. This is the intended meaning.
According to this interpretation, the transformed aspect produced by the five consciousnesses should likewise possess this function of obstruction;

for that which is transformed through conceptualization has the function of taking the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its object, being produced by relying upon causes and conditions. Therefore, when it is said to correspond to its own-characteristic, the transformed objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is [identical] to the original [consciousness].
Because their substance is extremely similar, they are designated as "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*).
[Commentary] Regarding the sixth, the retributive mind (*vipākacitta*), up to the point where it "may have function":

the intention here is that when the mental states of the sixth faculty are subtle and weak, arising spontaneously in conjunction with the five consciousnesses, they transform according to causes and conditions; however, if they arise spontaneously by themselves, they are only...
"Transformation through conceptualization.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the statement previously made that "if it were to transform according to conceptualization, it would ultimately be entirely useless," the word "previously" refers to the three preceding explanations.
Excluding the second interpretation, the objection is raised: for instance, in the case of transformation through conceptualization, the appearing aspect can only serve as an object.

If that which does not serve as the substantial basis for another lacks unimpeded function, then the objects transformed by the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) and the five consciousnesses would likewise lack such function, because they do not serve as the substantial basis for others in the same way that the objects transformed by the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) do for others.

Answer: This statement refers to those [objects] produced from seeds that correspond to their actual substance; it intends to speak of the objects transformed by the five consciousnesses and the concentrated mind.
The image-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) arises from actual seeds within the fundamental consciousness; therefore, it is functional and differs from [mere] discrimination (*vikalpa*).

[Commentary: Regarding the meaning of "following preparatory application (*prayoga*) up to deliberation": this means that the discriminating mind must be induced by preparatory application to become strongly discriminative.

Although the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) has the induction of preparatory application, and the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are difficult to induce through others, they do not strongly deliberate.
[Commentary on] "Discrimination.

[The Sub-commentary] states: "That a single moment of mind can become two kinds" means that when a single moment of concentrated mind shares the same object as the five consciousnesses—namely, the five real sense-objects—it is a transformation based solely on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
This very concentrated mind, however, is able to universally perceive objects of the past and future, as well as minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*); this is termed [discrimination].

"Differentiation-transformation" (vikalpa-pariṇāma) refers to the fact that the mind and its associated mental factors cannot take the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect) as their object; therefore, it is called "differentiation-transformation. [Commentary:

Regarding "the objective realm (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) does not follow the mind": "nature" (*svabhāva*) means essence or substance. This refers to the essence of the sense organs (*indriya*), the objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth.

Although the seeing (*darśana*) takes the objective aspect as its object, because the seeing and the objective aspect belong to different levels of existence (*bhūmi*) in terms of their binding (*bandhana*), the objective realm does not follow the mind in terms of its level-binding. This is what is meant by "nature."

When the object does not follow the mind, it is as in the case of the sixth consciousness and the five consciousnesses, where the causes and conditions sometimes belong to different levels (bhūmi) in terms of their perceived aspect (nimitta-bhāga) and seeing aspect (darśana-bhāga).

For example, when the eyes, ears, and so forth of the first dhyāna serve as causes and conditions for a mental consciousness belonging to a higher level, the perceived aspect belongs to one level while the seeing aspect belongs to another,
as has already been explained previously.

[Commentary: Regarding "solitary images with or without a substrate": when taking past or future objects as conditions, there is no actual substrate; only an image appears upon the mind, which is called a "solitary image.
This is categorized solely under the aspect of the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-part). Regarding "with a substrate" (*sadravya*)—which applies to both the mental faculty and the substrate:

when the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its substrate, it is categorized under the *darśana-bhāga* as "obscured-undefined" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and categorized under the object (*ālambana*) as "unobscured-undefined" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

Because it is recorded [in the treatises], it is said that they "penetrate" [their objects]. "Sentiment" (qing) refers to deluded sentiment; that is, the seventh consciousness (*manas*), which is associated with the four afflictions and erroneously clings due to non-comprehension.

Therefore, the five sensory consciousnesses and the simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) undergo "discriminative transformation. This is spoken of in terms of "objective realms" (*xingjing*); they also undergo "causal transformation" (*yinyuan bian*).
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "arising from the eighth and also arising from itself," the meaning is as follows:

although the first seven consciousnesses are not perceived by the eighth consciousness, when they subsequently experience objects, they arise individually from their own seeds within the eighth consciousness. One cannot claim that because the eighth does not perceive them, it prevents them from arising;
thus, even though the eighth does not perceive them, it does not hinder them from also arising from the eighth [consciousness], such as in the case of the outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-citta*).
Because among the eight [consciousnesses], they arise from seeds.
[Commentary: That which is truly unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is precisely *tathatā* (suchness).
[Commentary: Regarding the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the treatise, it refers back to the preceding passage of the treatise. Question: For what reason are they unable to transform and appear as mind?

Regarding the passage: "The mental factors... now, in this treatise, it further states 'transforming into the unconditioned,' etc."—it is not yet clear what each of the two instances of the word "etc.
(等) refers to. Answer: The first instance of "etc. refers only to the mind and mental factors—that is, it refers inwardly to them.

The second instance of "etc. refers to the unconditioned; by saying "etc.," it includes the non-associated formations and conventional dharmas. Therefore, the previous [explanation] has answered this.
In the middle [of the text], he answers only regarding the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), without mentioning "immediate succession" (*ānantarya*) and so forth.
Now, regarding the explanation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) up to the phrase "and with the unconditioned," this further explanation states that the word "etc.

(*ādi*) in the previous question refers to the mind, mental factors, and so on, thereby including the unconditioned, the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and conventional dharmas (*prajñapti-dharma*); there is no fault in this either. The intention of taking this explanation as the primary one is to state that it refers back to the previous question.

Since the intermediate [categories] such as syllables take as their objects unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and nominal designations (*prajñapti-dharma*), it is said that the eighth [consciousness] does not take mind,
mental factors, unconditioned phenomena, dissociated phenomena, or nominal designations as its objects.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the statement that "in the state of outflows (sāsrava), [consciousness] up to all [objects] should take the real as its object," the intended meaning is this: when there is transformation through causes and conditions, there must necessarily be a substantial entity and characteristic.

However, the characteristics of conceptual construction (vikalpa) do not necessarily possess a substantial entity. If this is so, then for instance, in the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness, once they reach the state of non-outflows (anāsrava), since conceptual construction is absent, they should not take the non-existent as their object.
Why? Because if it were so, then all transformations through causes and conditions would necessarily have to take transformations as their objects.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "that is, taking the text as an object" to "therefore it takes non-existence and so forth as its object," the intended meaning is that although the eighth [consciousness] in its untainted (*anāsrava*) state lacks conceptual discrimination and transformation, it nevertheless manifests their images within that untainted stage.
These "images" refer to the images of the unconditioned mind (*cittāsaṃskṛta*) and so forth.

If this is so, and since it is said that they "manifest images," how can one say that there is "direct realization"? The answer is: it is not so, because [in the untainted state], due to the absence of... [the text continues with the term *anāsrava*].

The eighth [consciousness] is associated with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*); because it is extremely clear and pure and free from delusive inversion, when it takes objects as its domain, it differs from the tainted consciousnesses that grasp at signs and engage in discrimination.

This is called "direct realization" (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) when speaking in terms of subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), for while the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes reality directly without casting a reflected image, this [subsequently attained wisdom] does so by way of an image.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) perceives the associated mind, all phenomena are exhausted," the intended meaning is as follows:
It is not necessary for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) to mutually perceive one another for this to be called "omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*). Why?

Because when a single seeing-part is able to perceive the associated mind and mental factors, as well as perceive all phenomena, it simultaneously has its own self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) perceive that very seeing-part; thus, omniscience is established.

The Wisdom [of the Commentator] distinguishes this from the previous explanation by asking: "If the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object, how can it be said that they share the same object?
The answer is: "This refers to their being the same with respect to the seeing portion; it does not mean that the self-verifying portion itself is the object. What fault is there in this?
Some say that the seeing portion apprehends the associated mind (*samprayukta-citta*); this concludes the previous explanation."
[Commentary] The phrase "because all phenomena are exhausted" and "because self-realization can further take the seeing-part as its object" concludes the second interpretation.
As the commentary states, "What fault is there [in saying that]... this explains away an objection.
This is because in the second explanation, it was not stated that the self [realizes] itself... [text fragment].
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the sixth and seventh consciousnesses should be distinguished," the intended meaning is as follows:

among these three types of cognition, the two cognitions of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) involve a mind that possesses function; the non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*) involves a mind lacking function, because it lacks practical utility.
Therefore, it is said that they "should be distinguished. Some say that the minds of direct perception and inference are the same as the preceding [discussed] objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*).
This should be analyzed.

[Commentary]: Master Candragupta’s position that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also transforms the body and the environment means that he asserts Master Somaśri permits the maturation (*vipāka*) in the formless realm to take the objects of the three lower realms as its conditions.
[Commentary: "Taking all locations as objects" means that it takes all form-locations (*rūpāyatana*) as its objects. As the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"The formless meditative absorptions (*ārūpyasamādhi*) attain mastery over all forms. This proves that the ālayavijñāna of the three realms all transforms into the perception of form as its object.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the first dhyāna covers a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*), according to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is said that if one follows the Mahāyāna, the first dhyāna covers the four continents;
the second dhyāna covers a small chiliocosm; the third dhyāna covers a medium chiliocosm (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*);

and the fourth dhyāna covers a trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). Qiu says there is another explanation: the first dhyāna covers a small chiliocosm, and the second dhyāna covers a medium chiliocosm.

The third dhyāna is equal to a great trichiliocosm, while the fourth dhyāna has no equal standard; as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 51), "it takes as its object a limited sphere of appropriation (*upātta-viṣaya*)," etc.
Since the term "appropriation" is used, this refers to the internal body and is not based on the external receptacle world. The same applies to the other two realms.
As for what can be known regarding the magnitude of the body: in the first dhyāna, the height of the body is one and a half yojanas. Thus...
In the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, the body height is sixteen thousand yojanas.
[Commentary: Regarding "taking immeasurable objects of appropriation as its object," this refers to the seeds of the mind that takes immeasurable modes of activity and understanding as its object;
it is the eighth [category] of "objects of appropriation. To say that the name is derived from the fruit means that the seeds receive the name "immeasurable" based on what they produce.
Because it arises from a mind of conceptual understanding (*vikalpa*), the eighth [consciousness] takes only seeds as its object and does not take conceptual understanding as its object.

Regarding the statement that "the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and so forth should be understood accordingly," this means that the sphere of nothingness takes the subtle grasping (*upādāna*) of objects as its object,
whereas the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) takes the extremely subtle grasping of objects as its object.
[Commentary]: "This also belongs among those established" means that this state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is also included among the items established in the preceding text.

[Commentary]: "The two schools have different interpretations" refers to how the Sautrāntika school maintains that both the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the state of non-ideation possess consciousness, whereas the [Vaibhāṣika] school maintains that both attainments are devoid of consciousness;
yet, they are like a tertian fever, and thus the body is still designated as a sentient being.
Therefore, there is no indeterminate [state]. Suppose it were the case that cessation exists whether consciousness is present or absent.
[In the Sarvāstivāda school,] beyond the profound state of mindlessness, there is further...
[as will be extensively established below by oneself... However, it is not [accepted as such].

Because the fault [of mutual contradiction] is not admitted by both parties, or because it may be included as an equivalent, the states such as the non-conceptual [heaven], other states of fainting, and so forth are cited;
that these various states possess the eighth consciousness will be established in detail below.
*Commentary on the Meaning of the Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll Three, Part Two (Upper). [Commentary]:
This statement that the three states of its own essence are "common to both" means that the *ālayavijñāna* exists throughout these three states.
Only two stages are associated with the five mental factors (*caitta*), while the fruit of Buddhahood is associated with twenty-one dharmas.

Regarding the three stages: first, the stage of being appropriated as the object of self-love (*ātma-sneha*); second, the stage of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma; and third, the stage of maintaining the continuity [of existence].

Of these, the former two pertain exclusively to the cause, while the latter pertains to both cause and fruit. Here, however, we cite only the first stage to explain the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "Although they neither increase nor decrease" to "is therefore called omnipresent": Question: Since contact (*sparśa*) and the other factors neither increase nor decrease in relation to consciousness (*vijñāna*), why are they termed "omnipresent" (*sarvatraga*)?
Answer: Although there is no increase or decrease, they are termed "omnipresent" because they arise and cease simultaneously with the substance of consciousness.
This explains the reason why, within the causal state, these five factors are always associated with it.
[Commentary]: "Although the two vehicles [attain] up to the five [factors], they correspond [to them]"—this explains an external objection. The objection says:

Since those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles have already abandoned the name of the *ālayavijñāna*, how can they correspond only to five factors? The answer is: Because their attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not yet been eliminated, they correspond [to these five].
[Treatise] "Contact" refers to the conjunction of the three; this is a brief explanation of its essence and function. To constitute contact as a self-nature, it must possess three meanings:
first, the conjunction of the three; second, the differentiation and transformation [of the sense organ];

and third, having the nature of causing the mind and mental factors to contact their objects, and functioning as the basis for sensation, perception, volition, and so forth, as will be explained in detail below. Regarding the analysis of contact, there are three main sections: first...

Regarding the sequence of explaining the essence and function, there are two parts: first, citing evidence to establish [the meaning], and second, resolving contradictions in the text. Within the explanation of the essence and function, there are two sections:
first, the general, and second, the specific;

this [passage] is the general section. [Commentary]: "Second, causing them to come together" means that once the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth have arisen from their own seeds, they are brought into contact by *sparśa* (contact).

Because they mutually accord with one another, it is said that they cause [the contact] to be joined; this is not by causing them to arise, but because of these two meanings, contact is called the "conjunction of the three. Question:

It has been stated that contact arises from the conjunction of the three, yet now you say that contact gives rise to the conjunction of the three. How can these two statements not be contradictory? Answer:

At the very moment that the conjunction of the three factors gives rise to contact, those same three factors also attain their conjunction precisely through that contact. Thus, there is no contradiction.
Therefore, they are simultaneous; for example, although the wick and the flame exist together, the flame burns the wick, and thus they are simultaneous.
Although the wick produces the flame, it is only by means of the flame that the wick exists as "contact" arising from that [flame] and causing them to be conjoined;

the meaning is similar. It is also like the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) perceiving the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*): although it is said that the function arises from the object, at the time when consciousness and the object arise together, the perception of the object-part necessarily [occurs].
This is stated with reference to the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) which arise simultaneously [with their objects], not with reference to those that are equal or immediate.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement, "The object is in the future while the organ abides in the past," etc.: this is a question posed from the perspective of the mental organ (*manas*) that has just ceased in equal immediacy (*samanantara-niruddha*). The question asks: "How can an organ in the past and an object in the future constitute contact (*sparśa*) in the present? How could they form a cause-and-effect relationship? The answer is as follows: ...as if... [text continues] ...just as when one sees a painting, one perceives the various colors and forms all at once; although the brushstrokes were produced sequentially, the observer grasps them simultaneously. Similarly, although the organ and the object belong to different times, the resulting contact occurs in the present.

Furthermore, it is like the case of a lamp: when the lamp is lit, its light illuminates the objects before it instantaneously. Although the lamp and the light are simultaneous, the light does not exist prior to the lamp. Likewise, although the organ and the object are separated by time, the causal efficacy of the contact is established in the present moment. Thus, there is no contradiction in the temporal sequence of cause and effect.
Commentary:

[The Commentary asks: "Who says that what is produced is itself that fruit? This follows the intent of the objection, which holds that the cause is future while the fruit is present—that is, the cause precedes the fruit.
My current explanation, however, intends to show that it is not that very fruit; this is based on the fact that it is not directly obtained.
Regarding the statement that "for those who view the fruit as distant, it may be said to serve as that fruit," the subsequent text explains this accordingly.
In the *Śū* (Commentary), the character "wei" (爲) in the phrase "for those who take the present as the time" (*wei xian qu shi zhe*) is pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

[The *Śū* states: "The substance exists only in the present, yet it resembles the past and future. This means that while the substance of the objective realm exists only in the present, it is said to "resemble the past and future."
However, this is spoken of solely in terms of cause and effect; since the cause comes first and the effect is explained afterward, the subsequent treatise states:

"Regarding present phenomena, because they possess the characteristic of repaying what preceded, a 'past cause' is provisionally established in contrast to the present effect; and because present phenomena possess the function of projecting what follows, a 'future effect' is provisionally established in contrast to the present cause.
This is identical to the present text, which appears to treat the past and future as [real] entities. Therefore, contact is designated as the effect.
The meaning does not deviate from the subtle and accords with correct principle. [Commentary:
Regarding the statement "abiding in the seed and prior to union," a question is raised: since "seed" is itself the time prior to union, what further purpose does the word "and" (*ji*) serve?
Answer: The term "seed" is explained according to the Mahāyāna, while the phrase "prior to union" is explained according to the Hīnayāna. Furthermore, it is said:
Although the faculties and so forth have already arisen from seeds, they are said to be "not yet combined" because they do not yet possess the capacity to produce the mind and mental factors;
whereas when the capacities of the latter three dharmas are combined and harmonized such that they can produce the mind and mental factors, this is called "transformed combination.
This is because there is a distinction between the time of non-combination and the time of combination.

[Commentary]: Regarding the name "discriminating father" (*pitṛ-vikalpa*), the intended meaning is that the son resembles the father; thus, "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) refers to the sense of "discerning" (*vi-*) what is similar (*kalpa*).

Another interpretation states: "discrimination" consists of "dividing" (*vi-*), which means "discerning," and "separating" (*kalpa*), which means "resembling. Contact discerns what is similar to the sense faculties (*indriya*);
because it possesses the capacity to produce subsequent mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is called "discrimination."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "it is also called 'discrimination' because it accords with what arises," the underlying intention of the objection is as follows:

Since contact (*sparśa*) possesses a function similar to that of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth in producing mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it is termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). However, one should rather say that contact is called "discrimination" because it possesses a function similar to the faculties in producing contact itself.

The meaning is this: the objection does not concern how [contact] produces feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth by resembling the faculties; rather, it concerns its production [of contact] by resembling the faculties.
It is difficult [to maintain] that contact itself acts as its own condition.
[Commentary: One should state the difficulty regarding the claim that "contact, resembling contact, serves as a condition":

If contact, which resembles the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, also produces contact, then how can it be said within the twelve links of dependent origination that "with the six sense-bases as condition, there is contact," and "with contact as condition, there is feeling"?
Regarding the statement, "Because it is called 'discrimination' (vikalpa) when it accords with the arising of feeling," this is cited as an example to pose a challenge:

if contact (*sparśa*), which resembles the sense organs and so forth, is said to have the function of "discriminative contact" (*vikalpa-sparśa*) because it accords with the arising of feeling, then contact—which arises resembling the sense organs and so forth—should likewise be called "discrimination.
"Accordance with the arising of feeling" means that feeling takes contact as its condition, and contact accords with the arising [of feeling].
Regarding "feeling" (*vedanā*).

[Commentary: If one does not personally conform to what is called "discrimination," the meaning is that if contact (*sparśa*) arises without such conformity, yet it merely resembles the arising of feeling and so forth from the sense faculties and other factors, and is thus named "discrimination"—this restates the original intent and constitutes a formal objection to the following text.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "Just as dharmas such as feeling (*vedanā*) cannot produce others, there is no sense of 'experiencing what resembles [the object]' (*anubhava-sādṛśya*)," the meaning is as follows:

Feelings merely experience prior objects such as pleasure and pain; they do not possess a functional capacity—similar to that of the sense faculties—to produce subsequent minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Therefore, they lack the sense of "experiencing what resembles [the object]. Now, contact (*sparśa*), however, resembles the sense faculties in its capacity to produce subsequent minds and mental factors; thus it is termed "part" (*aṃśa*).
Furthermore, that which is distinct from and unlike the sense organs (*indriya*) and so forth that produce contact is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). Moreover, Zhou says:

"Just as phenomena such as sensation (*vedanā*) cannot produce others—for instance, because sensation is not the same as contact in producing other mental states—there is no sense of 'apprehending a likeness.
Since it cannot produce itself, there is also no apprehension of a likeness produced by itself."

[Commentary]: Regarding the two functional capacities—the capacity of the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) to produce both consciousness (*vijñāna*) and contact (*sparśa*), and the capacity of contact itself—it is not the case that contact functions in the same way as those two.
While the organ and the object can produce both consciousness and contact, contact does not do so.

[Commentary: If one considers the principle of the mutual arising of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), the seeing-part may also be termed "discrimination" (*vikalpa*).

This is because the self-witnessing-part gives rise to the seeing-part of touch; thus, the seeing-part arises based on the self-witnessing-part, and furthermore, it perfumes seeds which give rise to the self-witnessing-part.
This is the meaning of "arising from one another."
[Commentary]: Furthermore, when one does not distinguish the exhaustion of functional capacities, one merely distinguishes the capacity of the sense organ (*indriya*) to produce feeling (*vedanā*);

one does not further distinguish the capacities of the sense organ to produce consciousness (*vijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), and so forth. Therefore, it is said that this is not in opposition to the *Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, as it is explained according to what is predominant.
Thus, contact (*sparśa*) only experiences the functional capacities belonging to the three feelings produced from the sense organ, because feeling is proximate to contact.
"Because it is that which is produced" explains the reason [for its arising]. [The *Śū* (Commentary) states:

"To distinguish the three feelings" means that the intention is to explain how contact (*sparśa*) experiences [objects] and produces the three feelings similar to the faculties, in accordance with the text of the *Abhidharma*.

"Because it conforms to the three feelings" means that the function of contact—which can experience [objects] and produce feelings similar to the faculties—is such that it conforms to the three feelings.
[Commentary]: "Slightly broader than the *Abhidharma*" means that this treatise’s analysis of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth is more extensive than the text of the *Abhidharma*. [Commentary]:
"In this context, 'equally taking' and so forth" means that this treatise explains that contact (*sparśa*), which resembles the faculties and so forth, is capable of producing all [phenomena].

The functional capacity of the mind and mental factors is not exhausted by considering only the three types of feeling (*vedanā*); thus, [the previous explanation] does not fully capture the principle.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the meaning of that treatise up to this point, the intention behind the statement "this interpretation is superior" is as follows:

This explanation takes *vikalpa* (discrimination) to mean "differentiation of states" (*avasthā-bheda*), and *bheda* (distinction) to mean "diversity. That is to say, it refers to the differentiation of the three states of feeling (*vedanā*)—namely, those associated with the sense organs, objects, and so forth—by means of the discriminating faculty.

This is a distinction of specific names. Now, regarding the phrase "this current interpretation is excellent," some point to the *Abhidharma* texts, while others point to the treatises of this region [China]. [Commentary:

To say that something is not "superior" because it is "partially deficient" in two meanings is because these two [meanings] serve only to distinguish the object (*ālambana*). Thus, it is called "partial."
Regarding the "one meaning" (the sense of being pervasive): this pervasive one-meaning excludes only the mind; therefore, it is said that [the mind] lacks the pervasive one-meaning.

Zhou [Zhouzhuang] states that the character *piān* (partial) should be changed to *biàn* (pervasive). Although this mind possesses the two meanings of being primary (*zhǔ*) and proximate (*jìn*), because it does not arise from itself, it lacks the pervasive meaning.

The intended explanation is that while the sense-faculties possess all four meanings, and the objects (*viṣaya*) possess the pervasive meaning, they are neither primary nor proximate; whereas the mind is both primary and proximate.
This is not the sense of "universal relaxation," for both mind and object are absent.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because consciousness arises in dependence on an object": this interpretation means that both mind and object are missing from the sense of continuity. That is to say, consciousness is able to transform the object, and the object exists because of consciousness;
the object serves as the grasped (grāhya), and consciousness relies upon the object to arise. Since they are thus mutually dependent causes, there is no sense of continuity.
Furthermore, Zhou says that the reason consciousness exists is because it arises from objects; thus he says, "Consciousness exists because objects arise.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "when mind does not arise, there are no mental factors," the meaning is that there is never a time when mind arises without the various mental factors such as sensation (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā).

[Commentary]: The intention behind not mentioning [mental attention] here is that, for the time being, we are discussing the sense faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) as the bases of consciousness, rather than mental attention (*manasikāra*).

[Commentary]: The intention behind saying "now, based on the analysis of the essence of seeing" is that what is currently stated refers to consciousness depending upon the conjunction of both the sense faculty and the object.

The statement regarding "arising through conjunction" refers only to the view that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) possesses a distinct individual substance; it does not refer to the view that the seeing-part and the self-witnessing-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) share the same substance. [Commentary:

The reason why the self-witnessing-part being the basis for the seeing-part in the sense of having the same substance is not what is being discussed here is as follows: the self-witnessing-part serves as the basis for the seeing-part precisely because they are of the same substance.
This explains that the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of consciousness arises from three factors: namely, the two—sense organ and object—and the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

[Commentary: If one were also to explain it in this way, up to the point where each [factor] relies on its own basis, then since mind and mental factors each arise based on their respective self-witnessing portions, consciousness would necessarily arise based on three factors;
contact would arise based on four; and feeling would arise based on three factors.
Therefore, it is said that "each relies upon its own. [The *Śū* (Commentary) states:

This explanation refers to the immediate basis (*pratyakṣa-āśraya*) and does not mention the remote seed-basis (*bīja-āśraya*). Regarding the statement that "when reaching the dharma, there are many," the intention is this:

it speaks only of the causes of contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth, which arise from the conjunction of two, three, or four factors; this is based on the reliance upon the present sense-faculties (*indriya*), consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and so on.

The "distant support" (*viprakṛṣṭa-āśraya*) refers to the sensory bases (*indriya*) that assist the objects (*viṣaya*), as well as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and so forth.

The "seeds" refer to those of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the like. Although you yourself admit that when mind and mental factors arise, they also depend upon distant conditions and their own seeds, we speak here only of the immediate supports—consciousness and its roots—and do not mention the distant ones, for fear that the categories of phenomena would become overly numerous.

[Commentary: Regarding the "six groups of volition" (*ṣaṭ-cetanā-kāya*), these refer to the volition associated with each of the six consciousnesses. As for feeling, perception, contact, and so forth, they are also to be assigned accordingly. Question:

Since there are five types of universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), how can they arise simultaneously with all eight consciousnesses? Answer: Not so. According to the *Mahā-śāstra*, each of the eight consciousnesses possesses its own set of universal factors.
The reason only five types are mentioned here is that they belong to the same category; therefore, they are not enumerated separately.

Question: As stated in the treatises, it is said that the eighth consciousness is associated with five factors, beginning with contact (*sparśa*), and that it is exclusively non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, its essential nature and functions are described as having specific distinctions, specific activities, and states of conformity or opposition.

Is this so? Answer: The mental aspects (*ākāra*) of the non-obscured and indeterminate [eighth consciousness] are subtle, hidden, and profound, making them difficult to know. Now, we shall discuss contact.
Statements regarding functions such as these refer only to those associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), not to those associated with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

For example, while the world knows that there are six consciousnesses, how could it know of the seventh and eighth? Furthermore, it is said that these are explained in accordance with what is commonly accepted by the Hīnayāna, because the Hīnayāna does not believe in the existence of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;
this will be established later, as should be understood below.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because they induce [the result] with extreme proximity," the meaning is as follows: "extreme proximity" refers to the similarity of the objective aspect (*ālambana-ākāra*), which explains "proximity";
"because they induce [the result] with excellence" refers to the similarity of the subjective aspect (*ākāra*), which explains "excellence."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the aspects that accord with and benefit the sensation (vedanā) which is the grasped object," the intended meaning is that these aspects of the grasped—such as being agreeable—which belong to this contact (*sparśa*), are themselves able to serve as aspects that accord with and benefit the sensation.

As for the statement that its aspectual mode (*ākāra*) is extremely similar to the aspects that accord with and benefit [sensation], this is based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which applies the term "aspectual mode" (*ākāra*) to the "objective aspect" (*nimittabhāga*), speaking here in terms of the object.
[Commentary]:
Regarding the statement that "when contact contacts suffering and so forth, feeling experiences the feeling of suffering and so forth," the intended meaning is as follows:

when contact directly contacts an object of suffering, suffering itself perceives that object of suffering; therefore, contact is superior in its capacity to induce feeling. This is why it is not said that [feeling] acts as the basis for contact.
[The *Abhidharmasamuccaya*] states that [craving] serves as the basis for other mental factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it is a state (*avasthā*) of volition (*cetanā*)," one asks: since craving is said to be a reality (*dravya*), how can it be called a state of volition? Answer:
Although craving has a distinct substantial entity (*svabhāva*), it arises only when there is prior deliberation (*vitarka*). Therefore, craving is described as being of the nature of volition.
The "state" (*avasthā*) is mutually dependent and resembles a subsumption; for example, although regret (*kaukṛtya*) has a distinct substantial entity, it is nonetheless a state of delusion (*moha*).
This case should be understood accordingly.

[Commentary] The term "mental factors" (*caitta*) serves to distinguish them from the aforementioned two [the mind and its objects]; that is, it distinguishes them from the first three among the six groups of six dharmas in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
[Commentary]:
Regarding the phrase "the touch of the four great elements is real": a questioner asks how this passage can be justified.

The answer is that the Sautrāntika school maintains that while the touch of derivative matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is conventional, the touch of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is real. Therefore, using the touch of the four great elements as a metaphor here is without fault.

[Commentary]: The statement that "the four great elements (mahābhūta) are the actual [object] of touch" is intended to explain the reason why the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) is considered real.

This is because one takes the touch of the sense-objects—the four great elements which serve as the basis—as the sense-object of touch itself, since the object of touch encompasses both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*upādāya*).

Some say that since it is admitted that fragrance, taste, and touch are real, this is stated in reference to atoms (*paramāṇu*); however, this remains difficult to understand, as atoms do not constitute food.

[Commentary]: "Alternatively, mental factors (*caitta*) should also extend to the lower [realms]" means that, as in the first reason previously stated—"because they are of the nature of mental factors"—if this were applied within the causal context of these four nutriments (*āhāra*), then those nutriments would not be taken as the illustrative example. The formal argument (*prayoga*) would be:

contact (*sparśa*), as a mental factor, is the subject of the proposition (*dharmin*); it is not identical to the phenomenon of the "threefold conjunction" (*trikasamnipāta*). The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is one of the four nutriments.
Because it is the nature of the central mind, just like volition and consciousness; by excluding [the other nutriments], faults are completely eliminated, as it excludes edible food.
[Treatise] Regarding "being able to act as a condition": this means that contact serves as a condition for feeling, and so on up to craving serving as a condition for grasping;
these are merely conditions by way of causal dependence, not conditions by way of cognitive apprehension.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "In the system of others" to "because there is no reason for it to be otherwise," the intended meaning is as follows:

If that [opposing] school admits that the members such as *tṛṣṇā* (craving) all partake of both the provisional (*prajñapti*) and the real (*dravya*), then they can serve as an analogy. Why? Because their own school admits that the member of *sparśa* (contact), in its partial aspects, is similar to the provisional;
yet they do not admit that a small portion of the member of *sparśa* partakes of the real. Why? Because there is no reason for it to be otherwise. What [reason] could there be?
Regarding the statement that one part of the branch of contact (*sparśa*) is "semblance" (*pratibimba*) while another part is "real" (*bhūta*), there is an interpretation which says:

"If it is accepted that a small portion is real and the remainder is semblance, this cannot be established. The intended meaning of this is that if one accepts that a small portion of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth is real, then contact would not be semblance.
Since both are members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), what reason could there be for craving to be real while contact is semblance? Therefore, [the former position] is untenable.
It is said that there is no different cause; however, this does not equal the previous explanation.
[Commentary] The phrase "craving and so forth" refers to citing the first analogy to include the latter two analogies, as well as "craving, grasping, and so forth" within the first analogy.
[Commentary: It may also be described as the second *siddhāntadharma* (tenet). What has been presented above is a single, actual, and not merely apparent *siddhāntadharma*;
this present one is neither identical to that [first] nor is it the second *siddhāntadharma*.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "this being the thesis-property (*pakṣadharma*) poses no obstacle," one asks: "Does the preceding first thesis-property not have the fault of being unestablished in the subject (*asiddha*)?
The answer is: "The fault of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) having an unestablished probandum (*sādhyāsiddha*) has already been excluded previously."
[Commentary]: What is meant by "startling the mind"? This asks for the name of the startling. How does it startle the mind? This asks for the method of startling.

At what stage does it startle the mind? This asks for the sequence of the stages of startling. The answer below is that the seeds of the mind-king can arise and move toward their objects, like a sleeping person being called by another.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "should startle all," the intended meaning is as follows: since it is said "all," mental attention (*manasikāra*) is included within that "all.
If this is so, how can mental attention—which has not yet arisen—startle them? Furthermore, if "all" has not yet arisen, how can it startle anything?
What, then, is the contact that startles the mind? Within the explanation of mental attention, there are also two parts: first, the explanation of its essential nature and function; next...
Refuting divergent views, there are two parts to the initial section: first, explaining the essence and function; second, resolving external objections.

[Commentary]: "Alternatively, it is not contradictory to reason that attention (*manasikāra*) arises simultaneously with consciousness"—this means that although attention and consciousness arise together, the statement that "attention startles the seeds of the mind" is established by principle as referring to its actual manifestation; this is not...
Regarding the phrase "When Righteousness (Dharma) arises again, one is only then startled," this explains the second interpretation’s refutation of [the opponent's] non-reasoning.
[Commentary: Within this objection, it should be stated that at the stage of the seed of functional power (*kāritra-bīja*), the three types of "non-knowing" do not yet exist;
furthermore, there is no difference between mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) regarding their contact with objects. The intended meaning is that at the stage of the seed, it is merely...
Regarding the characteristics of the seeds of the three factors—the faculties and so forth—it is said that they are latent and do not yet possess the sense of the three being discordant;
it is only upon reaching the stage of active manifestation (*samudācāra*) that there arises the sense of the non-conjunction of the three factors: faculty, object, and consciousness.

While in the state of seeds, there is as yet no sense of the mind and mental factors being distinct from their contact with objects; it is only upon reaching the stage of active manifestation that the mind [and its concomitants] arise.
The meaning of the mental factors (*caitta*) being different from the mind’s contact with objects is as follows:

if, through subsequent conjunction, they possess the capacity to produce the mind and mental factors, this is called having the sense of "conjunction" (*saṃprayoga*), and it also possesses the sense of causing the mind and so forth to come into contact with their objects. Question:

Since it has been stated that the three factors—the faculty (*indriya*) and so forth—only possess the sense of "conjunction" when they are in a state of active manifestation (*pravṛtti*), does it mean that at the moment contact arises, it causes the faculty and the others to enter a state of conjunction?
Regarding the point that contact (*sparśa*) is what brings about the threefold conjunction (*trikasamnipāta*), why does the treatise state that "the threefold conjunction gives rise to contact"?
The answer is: it is not so. As the treatise states, because contact arises depending on them and causes them to be in conjunction, it is described as being "of them.

Thus, one should know that contact and the sense faculties (*indriya*) etc. are simultaneous. When the commentary explains the sequence of before and after as cause and effect, it refers to their mutual dependence (*apekṣā*). Therefore, contact...
[Only when] currently active do they have utility.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "feeling and so forth arise from the conjunction of the three," one might ask: since feeling and the others already arise conditioned by contact (*sparśa*), why further state that they arise from the conjunction of the three?
The answer is: contact serves as the proximate cause (*āsanna-hetu*), while the conjunction of the three serves as the remote condition (*dūre-pratyaya*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "this essence is not fixed," it is as explained in the *Yanbi* (Explication of the Secret): one may also say that the substance of the mind is not itself the agent of alarm;

rather, it is only when attention (*manasikāra*) arises that it can produce alarm. Why then laboriously seek further alarm? It is like a person who only becomes aware of other things at the moment they awaken from sleep;
attention functions in the same way.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "This [mental engagement] should not be universal because it is absent when abiding in this object," it means: You of the Hīnayāna claim that mental engagement (*manasikāra*) is that which causes the mind to turn toward a different object.
If mental engagement were merely to abide in this very object, it would have no functional activity. Why?
Because when it merely abides in this object, it cannot cause the mind to turn away from it toward another object; therefore, it is absent when abiding in this object.
[Commentary: "If the characteristics are subtle and hidden, by what means is their existence known? This takes up the opponent's defense and refutes it again. The opponent defends by saying:

"Although it abides briefly in this object, there is still the sense of turning the mind toward another object; it is simply that the characteristics are subtle and hidden. [The author] replies: "By what means is its existence known?
For when one discusses turning toward another object, there must always be a manifestation; since the characteristics are subtle and hidden, how can it be said [to exist]?"
"How do we know it exists?

[Commentary]: In the third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, up to the point where it says "this will serve to exhaust the principle," this section of the *Yogācāra* treatise states that the "revolving of the mind" is explained according to its conforming characteristics;
however, this does not exhaust the principle, as it differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which is about to exhaust the principle. Therefore, it is now refuted.
[Commentary]:

Regarding the claim that these are not non-universal mental factors (*asarvatraga*), the opponent offers this defense: "In other states, although their characteristics are obscured, this attention (*manasikāra*) nevertheless exists;

therefore, it is said that these ten are not non-universal. Regarding the second point, [the opponent] says they reach [the object], yet they differ from meditative concentration (*samādhi*); the intended meaning is as follows:
Since the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* also relies upon this [type of] attention (*manaskāra*), it is said that these ten are not non-pervasive.

[Commentary: To resolve the second point, it is stated that because they differ from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*—referring to the cultivation of superior concentration—provisionally explains that maintaining the mind so that it abides is called "attention. This is because when cultivating concentration, there must necessarily be a decisive and superior attention.

Therefore, this is not an exhaustive account of the principle. However, the masters of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* failed to realize the intent of that treatise and consequently treated this interpretation as the definitive truth, which is why it is refuted here.
Some say that during the three stages of cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there must necessarily be a superior mental attention (*manaskāra*).

What is now stated—that "mental attention holds the mind and causes it to abide"—is merely an explanation of "mental attention" by way of its preparatory characteristics (*ākāra*) for the practice of concentration; it does not represent the actual [nature] of mental attention.

It is not that one holds the mind by means of stabilization; otherwise, since attention (*manasikāra*) already exists simultaneously with concentration (*samādhi*), why would one need to rely on the aspects (*ākāra*) of concentration to distinguish attention?
One should rather say: cultivation consists of first directing attention toward the object so as to prevent the mind from scattering—this is the function of attention.

[Commentary] Regarding the point that it differs from the Sarvāstivāda: the intended meaning is that the Mahāyāna and that school explain the functional activity (*karmavṛtti*) of attention (*manasikāra*) as being distinct, as explained in that [Sarvāstivāda] commentary.

[Treatise] "Because it can give rise to the desire for union, separation, or neither" explains that its function is to give rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*); that is to say, toward both the agreeable and the disagreeable.
It is not the case that the three objects can respectively give rise to the desires for union, separation, or neither, because [the third object] cannot produce such desires. Question:

Since desire (*chanda*) fundamentally arises only from craving (*tṛṣṇā*), why is it said to be "desire"? Answer: Because desire has the nature of seeking with joy; it is called "desire" because one gives rise to craving toward objects such as pleasure.

[Commentary]: This means that regarding the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), "not yet having given rise to the desire for union" and so forth refers to the intention that, based on the sensation of pleasure, one gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) for an object of pleasure that has not yet been obtained, desiring to unite with it or having united too soon.
Although the sensation exists in its causal state (*bīja-avasthā*) and has not yet arisen [as a manifest experience], this is still craving arising conditioned by sensation.
If the sensation has already arisen, it is precisely the desire for non-separation; therefore, it is based on both unarisen and already-arisen sensations.
Two kinds of desire arise; "desire" here refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

[Commentary: The present explanation, which relies solely on craving produced by contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja-tṛṣṇā*), describes the karmic function of defiled feeling (*kliṣṭa-vedanā*) and is not an exhaustive exposition of the principle.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the eight fundamental consciousnesses do not give rise to craving," the intended meaning is that the sensation (vedanā) currently under discussion is not the sensation associated with the eighth consciousness.

Why? Because it does not give rise to craving. As for the statement, "Furthermore, there is no contradiction in [sensation] coexisting with the eighth [consciousness]," this means that when the sixth consciousness arises in relation to objects such as suffering or pleasure—which are transformed by the eighth consciousness and the five [sensory] consciousnesses—[sensation occurs].

The commentary on "the middle [state] of joining and separating from desire" explains that when the eighth consciousness experiences a wholesome object, the six consciousnesses give rise to "joining with desire";
when it experiences an unwholesome object, the six consciousnesses give rise to "separating from desire.
As the sub-commentary states, "because one experiences wholesome and unwholesome objects, various feelings arise," this explains the reason for the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "Just as the perception arises, the speech also arises," this means that when the eighth consciousness spontaneously grasps the boundaries of an object,

the six consciousnesses take it as their objective support (ālambana), transforming it into what they experience and giving rise to verbal expressions and so forth— just as a master painter and his disciples work together on tasks such as filling in the colors.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that desire is not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*), this is said in reference to its predominant function.

Since the function of craving within the category of "craving" (the *tṛṣṇā*-aggregate) is like the feeling (*vedanā*) associated with the eighth consciousness, when that craving is absent, [desire] likewise ceases to exist. As for the statement that it is "not determinate," this is said in reference to its predominant function;

that is, the karma of craving and desire is spoken of according to its most eminent aspect, rather than being defined by the universal principle. The same applies to the characteristic of manifest action (*vijñapti-karman*).
Furthermore, this is stated based on its predominant function and is not explained according to the principle of universal concomitance (*sarvatraga*).
[Commentary: Although the Mahāyāna maintains that contact (*sparśa*) is what experiences, the term "experiences" here carries the sense of "resembling.

This is because contact possesses aspects such as being agreeable, while feeling (*vedanā*) possesses aspects such as being beneficial; they are similar in this way and thus called "experiencing. However, this is distinct from the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) based upon it.
The meanings are distinct and thus not contradictory; this [passage] addresses that contradiction. [Commentary:

Regarding contact (*sparśa*), there are the feelings of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity, all of which are capable of being experienced. Question: Since this is also the case for [feeling] itself, how can one challenge the other?
This refers to what was stated previously: the aspects of "agreeable" and so forth taken up by contact, and the aspects of "conducive to benefit" and so forth taken up by feeling.
[Objection: They are so extremely close that, by this standard, they are no different from what belongs to another. [Response: Although our own school holds such a view, it is not the case here;
for "appropriation" (*upādāna*) consists merely in perceiving an object and taking it as one's own.
Because it is distinct from that [external appropriation], it is now refuted.
[Commentary: Furthermore, it contradicts your own tenet because you do not allow for simultaneous mental factors to perceive one another.
For instance, how could feeling (vedanā) experience touch (sparśa) when they arise simultaneously? Therefore, it is said that this contradicts your tenet.
[Commentary]: If contact occurs first and sensation arrives later, how can it be called "experiencing"?

This means that if contact were prior and sensation were subsequent, one could say that the later sensation experiences the prior contact. However, since contact and sensation are simultaneous, the [sensation] does not take contact as its object;
how then can it be said to experience contact? If you claim it takes the simultaneously arising contact as its object, this contradicts your own position.
Thesis. [Commentary]:

"Alternatively, it should be that contact and feeling do not coexist in a single moment" means: if one were to concede that feeling takes the preceding contact as its object, then contact and feeling would not coexist in a single moment.
If they do not coexist, they cannot be termed "universal" (sarvatraga). If they were to coexist, then [feeling] should take [contact] as its object.
If you claim that both [cause and effect] are touched [by the same entity], then you contradict your own tenet. Thus, these subtle points leave no room for escape whether one advances or retreats;
they shatter the false and preserve the true. One must firmly question their existence.
[Commentary]: Or, if the cause is identical to the effect—just as a seed is both cause and effect—it exists in relation to what precedes and what follows.
"Because of their differentiation.

[Commentary: Regarding the question, "Should 'feeling' (vedanā), which receives contact (sparśa), not be called 'discrimination' (vikalpa)?"—the intent of the question is as follows: Contact resembles the sense-faculties and objects, and thus it is called "discrimination" of the faculties and objects;
feeling arises resembling contact, so the mental factor (caitta) should be called "discrimination" of contact. The answer is that there is no error.
Because discernment (vikalpa) apprehends that which resembles an object, this question is not placed here; it should be combined with the preceding question.

To clarify the first three mental factors—namely, contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), and feeling (vedanā)—the commentary establishes this boundary to include the arising of names and so forth through their common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in various treatises that "name is its perception" (*saṃjñā*), the intended meaning is as follows: according to our current explanation, the essence and function of perception are themselves the cause, while "name" is the effect.
When it is said in certain passages that "name constitutes perception," this is spoken from the perspective of the cause;
when "perception" is called "name," this is spoken from the perspective of the effect.
[Commentary]: As worldly people say, "What is your perception?"—this is like people asking one another for their names and saying, "What is your perception?
This is speaking of perception from the perspective of its result (*phala*).

If someone were to ask, "What is your name?", this would be speaking from the perspective of its cause (*hetu*), saying, "The name is 'perception'. Some say that the phrase "What is your perception? is found only at Ximing Monastery.
Regarding this common term, it is not seen in the Chinese translation [of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*].
[Commentary: This karma is not pervasive because, when explaining the arising of perception (*saṃjñā*), it is designated as "karma"; thus, it is not pervasive. Why?

Because the perception associated with the eighth consciousness does not give rise to verbal expressions (*nāma-vyavahāra*). If that is so, by what [is the perception associated with the fundamental consciousness] characterized?

Regarding the definition of "activity" (*karman*): it consists simply in the spontaneous grasping of an object, and there is no separate activity; or, it may be understood as the arising of conventional designations (*nāma-vyavahāra*), as explained in the section on sensation (*vedanā*).
[Commentary: The following provides a general explanation of "concomitance" (*sahabhū*); this interprets the meaning of the association of the five mental factors (*caitasika*).
[Commentary]: When there is no arising of mind, it is said that not even one of the intentional impulses (*cetanā*) arises;
this means that among the five [mental factors] beginning with understanding (*adhimokṣa*), not a single one is absent, as all of them arise.

[Commentary]: Regarding the previous statement that the two characters "corresponding" (*xiāngyìng*) appear in the verse, a question is raised: "Previously, you explained the character 'together' (*jù*) in order to distinguish correspondence;

why then do you now explain 'correspondence' once more? Is this not redundant? Answer: The previous mention of "together" was intended to explain the term "correspondence" appearing at the beginning of the treatise. As the treatise begins by stating:

"It is always associated with contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*). Now, I am explaining "correspondence" once again [in the context of the verse].

Since it must be associated with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), the verse states that its association is "only with neutral feeling. Because this association applies to both locations, it is necessary to further specify them separately.
As for the mention of "locations" (*sthāna*) and so forth, these are synonyms for the "locations" (*sthāna*) of the objects of perception (*ālambana*)—that is, the objective spheres (*viṣaya*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the five aspects such as contact [arise], they are called 'equal' (samāna)," the intended meaning is as follows: the aspects transformed by the mind and mental factors all rely upon the objective aspects of the mind-king;
because these objective aspects of the mind-king are entirely similar, they are termed "equal."

[Commentary: The tenet clarifying *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) holds that since the tenet has already clarified consciousness-only, one cannot take an external substance (*bimba*) as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, it differs from the Hīnayāna; for the Hīnayāna takes the external substance as the object-condition, whereas [in our system] the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) is called the "mode-of-apprehension" (*ākāra*) and the "perceiving-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) is called the "function" (*vastu*), thus distinguishing it from the former.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "both the co-existent and the immediate," the meaning is that they function together as a single faculty (*indriya*). "Faculty" here refers to the co-existent faculty, which is contrasted with the immediate faculty, as will be clarified below. [Commentary]:

Alternatively, even if they are not identical, one may also include the other; this "alternatively" can be understood to apply to both the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Although this differs from the present time—which takes both [the object and the aspect] together—the five meanings are fully present and it is thus called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*). Question:
Since the aspects (*ākāra*) are different, how can they be named "associated"? Answer: Because the faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) are identical, they may also be termed "associated."
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from the first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that states, "nor are they mutually inconsistent," the question is:
how does this text come to be here? The answer is: because the preceding section also includes the aspect (*ākāra*), there is a sense of correspondence;

based on this, one then understands the reason why the objects of focus (*ālambana*) in the *Yogācāra-vijñaptimātratā* system differ, as stated below: "Because the objects are similar... up to "...in reality, they are each distinct. This is [the explanation].
Regarding the clarification of the identical meaning of the "object-condition" (*ālambana*) in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*:

although the six aspects, such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth, are distinct from one another, they are designated by the same name based on their similarity. This is because when perceiving blue, all these aspects are simultaneously blue.

Thus, when this treatise refers to them as "the object-condition" and so forth based on their real meaning, it means that each of the six aspects—the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*)—is designated by the same name because they are similar in number and other attributes.
Because the objects of cognition (*ālambana*) and so forth, like the entities themselves, each possess a single nature.

Regarding their being called "identical objects of cognition" based on their common characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), this is according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, because when perceiving blue, for instance, their characteristics are all blue.

[Commentary]: "Because it is admitted that there are two" means that, as in the following section of the treatise, it is admitted that there are two types of conditions: the immediate (*samanantara*) and the remote (*ālambana*). [Commentary]:
"The aspect of activity (*ākāra*) is called 'activity' because its basis is the same" means that, for example, the sixth and eighth consciousnesses both rely on the seventh;
now, the sixth is excluded because its objects are distinct, and thus it is not associated. Zhou says it is like a single eye.

Although cessation relies upon the same single faculty, because they arise sequentially and their respective objects are distinct, the term "functioning" (*cāra*) is used here to distinguish it from preceding and succeeding consciousnesses.
[Commentary]:

Regarding the phrase "the object distinguishes the seeing," "object" refers to the *ālambana* (the perceived object), which distinguishes the "seeing. The intended meaning is that while the "seeing" is identical in taking this as its object...

The object-condition (*ālambana*) is precisely what is called "concomitance" (*samprayoga*); for if it were like the various views where the subjective aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) each take different objects separately, these would not be called concomitant.
Therefore, the term "object-condition" and so forth serves to distinguish [the mental factors] from the various subjective aspects.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as in the case of the five [sensory consciousnesses] and the mental consciousness, they are distinguished solely by way of their objective basis (*vastu*)," the meaning is as follows:

although the objects perceived by the mental consciousness concomitant with the five [sensory consciousnesses] are identical, their substantial entities (*svabhāva*) differ in number. The remaining five [sensory consciousnesses] possess multiple entities, whereas the mental consciousness possesses only one;

since their entities are not the same, they cannot be associated (*samprayukta*) with the same mental factors (*caitta*). Furthermore, the entities of the bases are likewise not the same. To distinguish them by way of their objective basis, consider for instance the relationship between the mental consciousness and the eye.
When consciousness arises, there are simultaneously two cessations and two feelings; how could two feelings and so forth be associated?
Furthermore, it is not associated with the eighth [consciousness], because feeling is not associated with feeling, and the same applies to contact and the other factors.
Alternatively, the objects of the sixth [consciousness] and those of the five sensory consciousnesses are also not equal, because mental consciousness can take all eighteen realms as its objects.

[Commentary]: It would follow that it could not sustain and benefit the continuity [of the personal series]. This means that if the eighth consciousness were to have a clearly manifest mode of activity (*ākāra*), it would be unable to maintain itself and cause its own continuity to increase.

[Commentary: "None of them are able to mutually sustain those seeds" means that if one were to allow for easy detachment, then at the same time as a pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) arises, it should be unable to maintain the seeds for rebirth in common with it, because they are mutually contradictory;
the opposite holds true for a common sensation (*sāmānya-vedanā*).
[Commentary]: "It would not then be born from that" means that if one allows for an interruption, it would not be produced by the propelling karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*) of that destiny (*gati*).
The intention is that since the eighth consciousness is interrupted, it is not produced by the propelling karma of that destiny; for that which is produced by propelling karma is uninterrupted.
"Because its life-force has already been relinquished" means that since there is an interruption, the eighth consciousness has relinquished its nature as life-force (*jīvita*).
Furthermore, how could it be capable of receiving perfuming and maintaining seeds?

[Commentary] Regarding the exclusion of other objects and so forth among the remaining four conditions: this refers to the section in the Commentary from "Another explanation" (*yòu jiè*) up to "therefore there is no desire" (*gù wú yù*).
Within this, the second point specifically excludes [the possibility of the eighth consciousness being associated with] the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Suffering, pleasure, the wholesome, and the defiled must necessarily correspond only with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*);

as for the other four meanings, they distinguish [these mental factors] from the "object-specific" (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*) factors and others, and thus they receive their respective names based on that second meaning.

[Commentary]: Because of these five meanings, the second point—which correctly reveals the intended meaning—states that among the five meanings, the first meaning must be associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
This is because the second meaning says that one "cannot distinguish between the characteristics of favorable and unfavorable objects," which correctly reveals association with equanimity;
the remaining meanings merely serve to exclude other dharmas.

[Commentary]: Among the eight proofs, regarding the first, "appropriation" (*upādāna*), as explained below under "appropriation," there are five subsequent reasons within the latter part of the first proof.
This current passage corresponds to the meaning of the first of those five reasons: the sense of arising spontaneously (*svarasena*).
[Commentary: "This reveals the reason" refers to the establishment of the cause (*hetu*).

[Commentary: "Not because of tranquility... nor by evil karma" is the text that explains away an external objection. The external objection states: "Since meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is also tranquil, it ought to be produced by evil karma.
This passage is raised as a response; its intended meaning is that this equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) merely differs from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Agitation is called "equanimity" (upekṣā) in relation to external objects, while tranquility in meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) is called "equanimity.

[Commentary: The meaning of the phrase "this has no capacity to act" is that this feeling of equanimity differs from the tranquility of meditative concentration because it does not eliminate grasping toward its object;
thus it is said to have "no capacity to act. Furthermore, it differs from wholesome and unwholesome states which possess distinct functional capacities, because wholesome and unwholesome...
Karma is capable of inducing both [pleasure and pain].

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the other seven evolving consciousnesses are said to give rise to shared fruits such as pleasure," one asks: since the seventh consciousness is always accompanied by equanimity (*upekṣā*), how can it give rise to suffering and pleasure?
The answer states: while the general meaning is thus, the specific intent refers to the six evolving consciousnesses.

Alternatively, it acts as a remote cause for the arising of suffering, pleasure, and so forth in the first six consciousnesses; that is to say, because of the constant internal grasping at a self, it causes suffering sensations and the like to arise in the first six consciousnesses.

[Commentary]: If, alternatively, suffering and pleasure arrive simultaneously, they are said to be "contradictory" by intention; this refers to the eighth consciousness when it has not yet received [the seeds].

Regarding "concomitance" (*sahagata*): among humans and devas, one should not experience suffering and so forth, because they are mutually contradictory; thus, the concomitance with painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) should be understood by analogy, such that in the hells there would be no [resultant] outflow (*naiṣyandika*) kings and so on.

[Commentary]: "If, according to the place of birth, the feelings shift accordingly" means that if one is born in a favorable realm, one is accompanied by pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*), whereas in [unfavorable realms], it is suffering.
To reverse this intention, one must acknowledge that it contradicts reason for the eighth consciousness to coexist with suffering and pleasure; the fault is as previously stated.

Since the two feelings of suffering and pleasure are subject to transformation, change, detachment, and so forth, the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) which coexists with them must likewise be subject to transformation, change, detachment, and so forth.

[Commentary]: Having understood that it is associated only with equanimity (*upekṣā*), one then raises the objection regarding its association only with the five universal mental factors (*pañca-sarvatraga*). An external critic asks:
"If you admit that it is associated with the feeling of equanimity, why does it not also correspond with the other specific object-mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*)?"

[Commentary]: Regarding this specific exclusion of those whose mental aspects (*ākāra*) are all-pervasive: "all-pervasive" here means that it specifically excludes those whose mental aspects are all-pervasive, as only they are associated with this consciousness.
