Since the *viṣayaviśeṣa* (distinct objects) are not all-pervasive, they must be excluded.

[Commentary]: Regarding the word "etc.": it also includes [the other categories] up to "is also included therein. Question: Since the four indeterminate dharmas have already been explained separately, why is it necessary to include them with the word "etc."?
Answer: Although the four [indeterminates] pervade the three natures, in the separate explanation they are only clarified as being neutral (avyākṛta).
Therefore, the "etc. here takes in both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "not vipāka" to "up to kaukṛtya (remorse)," the meaning is that not all things designated as *vipāka* are true *vipāka*.
Some are indeed *vipāka* while others are not true *vipāka*, such as those produced by *vipāka* (*vipākaja*) and so forth.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the Mahāyāna also possesses intrinsic goodness (*svabhāva-kuśala*) and so forth," the intention is to say: it is not only your school that clarifies this in the *Abhidharmakośa*;
my Mahāyāna school also possesses [this teaching] as explained in the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa).
[Commentary]: These three natures consist of combining the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) into one.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "conditioned wholesome dharmas do not reach the state of being secure," the meaning is as follows: conditioned wholesome dharmas encompass both the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) fruit and the two types of heavy burdens (*dausthulya*).
Those belonging to worldly fruits are subject to arising and ceasing, and thus they are not secure; those belonging to supramundane fruits are likewise not secure.
Because it is hidden, it is explained as encompassing two types of fruits: those that are desirable in the world and those that are desirable in the supramundane.
Desirable worldly fruits refer to worldly fame, profit, wealth, status, as well as the human and celestial bodies endowed with perfect physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and signs (*anuvyañjana*).

Desirable supramundane fruits refer to the subtle, exquisite, and superior form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) obtained by Bodhisattvas from the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) onwards; these possess great wisdom, are complete with all the marks, and are augmented by merit and rank.
Their physical forms are suffused with the rain of Dharma and endowed with the marks of a great man; they cast off the dregs of clamor and remain unstained by worldly dharmas.

Able to teach and transform sentient beings across all realms of existence, they emit great radiance that illuminates all darkness. In accord with ultimate truth, both names and characteristics have ceased to exist;
as their untainted qualities gradually increase, afflictions are naturally subdued. Such noble ones are called "transcendental," for they have already surpassed the two [realms].
That which is still subject to arising and ceasing is not yet true awakening and is therefore not called "Buddha"; because it possesses birth and extinction, it is termed "not secure.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage from "conditioned and indeterminate" to "up to unwholesome": A question is asked: Why is it designated only as "conventional indeterminate" and cannot be called "ultimate indeterminate"?
The answer is: Because its intrinsic nature is coarse and heavy (*dausthulya*), it is confused with the unwholesome; for this reason, it is not so named.
The ultimate indeterminate (*paramārthāvyākṛta*) is the intrinsic heaviness (*svabhāva-dauṣṭhulya*); because it cannot produce fruit in the conventional sense, it is called "indeterminate.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "empty space" to "so as not to cause confusion": one asks, since there are six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), why are only two mentioned?

The answer is that the unconditioned states of the immovability of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitāniñjya*) are subsumed under the "wholesome" (*kuśala*), because they are wholesome by virtue of the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*) that seeks to become weary of them.
[Commentary]: "Virtuous through skillful means" refers to the virtues associated with the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that follows the untainted [wisdom] (*anāsrava*).

That is to say, untainted wisdom itself is called "skillful means," and the virtuous dharmas cultivated by it are also called "skillful means" because they follow the wisdom that performs the cultivation.

[Commentary: Regarding the three types of "concomitant origination" (*samutthāna*) that are wholesome, according to the intended meaning, it is as follows: bodily and vocal actions are called "wholesome by concomitant origination" because they are initiated by a wholesome mind, such as the Prātimokṣa vows.

Furthermore, non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) initiated by a wholesome mental consciousness are also called "wholesome by concomitant origination," such as the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), as well as the seeds of the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) that are wholesome.
This explanation holds that wholesome seeds are also subsumed under "origination" (*samutthāna*), because they are perfumed by wholesome manifest conduct;
unwholesome seeds should be understood accordingly.
[Commentary]: "Seeds are also like this" means that seeds perfumed by an indeterminate mind are termed "indeterminate."
[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "Because it should not produce evil and should constantly produce good":

since it is admitted that the eighth consciousness is of a virtuous nature, within the happy realms (sugati) it should always tend toward the good and never toward evil, because its governing principle is virtuous;

thus, it is said that the maturation (vipāka) arises spontaneously and in constant succession. If it were virtuous, the transmigration through the five destinies (pañca-gati) would be impossible, as the evil destinies could not exist.
If this were reversed, one would constantly give rise to evil and there would be no goodness; if that were so, the processes of saṃsāra and its cessation could not be established.

What, then, is meant by "saṃsāra"? It is called *pravṛtti* (flowing) because the cause of accumulation (*upādāna*) ceases and the fruit of suffering (*duḥkha-phala*) subsides. It is called *vartana* (turning) because the fruit of suffering arises while the cause is overturned.
This is as explained in the Commentary.

[Commentary]: Regarding the first point, "wholesome [karma] has desirable fruits": a question is raised as to how that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and currently active can be said to "predict" (*vyākaraṇa*) a tainted, desirable fruit, since it cannot actually summon such a fruit.
The answer is that it is called "prediction" in the sense of the second meaning, because its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is preeminent.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "because it can be harmonized," etc.: "harmonization" refers to the wholesome, while "the field" refers to the unwholesome.
[Commentary] "The same analogy applies to the mind" means that mental factors (caitta) are treated according to the same principle as the primary mind (citta).

[Commentary]: Regarding the first, second, and fourth [explanations] which are said to accord with Dharmapāla—among the various masters, those whose meanings accord with Dharmapāla’s are identical to his in these three interpretations.
These multiple "repetitions" (punarukta) refer only to the exposition of a single master;
they do not mean that there were explanations by three different masters.

[Commentary: This section consists of three parts: first, a brief presentation of the correct meaning; second, from "There is another interpretation" onwards, an extensive refutation of divergent views;
and third, from "Therefore, by this... onwards, a concluding demonstration of the correct meaning.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "both the object and [the mode of activity] may be unknowable," the intent is to take the one gate of being "unknowable" as the primary point, rather than taking the aspect of the mode of activity (*ākāra*).
[Commentary:

However, the reason both are said to have four [aspects] is that "unknowability" is outside the count of the ten gates; it serves as an analogy for the fact that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) possesses only [these specific characteristics].

Regarding the four gates, with the exception of the four gates, it is not analogous; that is to say, the characteristics of the body, all types of mental formations, and the characteristic of sensation must first exist, and then the latter two gates follow—this is also the case for the latter part. This explains what is not analogous.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this does not constitute a rebuttal because it is identical to [the fault] itself," the intent of this objection is as follows:
If consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which cognizes while contact (*sparśa*) is not, then the analogy of the five factors associated with consciousness cannot be applied to contact and the others.

Since the analogy applies equally to the mind and its concomitants, consciousness and contact should likewise be mutually associated; for it has already been stated that the other categories apply by general analogy.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "it is associated with both contact and non-contact," the intention is that it possesses distinct characteristics according to what is appropriate; however, because contact does not coexist with contact itself, it is associated with both contact and non-contact. [Commentary]:

Regarding the phrase "if it were associated with equanimity (upekṣā), it would lead to a logical fallacy by analogy," the intention is that since discernment (vijñapti) resides in consciousness, one must then apply this principle to cases where they are identical.
It is called "consciousness. Since it has already abandoned association [with feeling], it does not reside in the faculty of sensation (*vedanā*).

The intention of the text is that if it were associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*), it would not be included among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) categorized as sensation. Furthermore, the intention is to state that the same fault would apply by analogy to sensation and the others;

for if one were to take the universal factor of sensation as an example, it would follow that equanimity must also possess a specific mode of activity (*ākāra*), and thus they would be analogous. However, since sensation does not possess such a mode of activity, [the analogy fails].
"How should one obtain the characteristics of the object?
[Commentary: "If the correct meanings do not contradict each other, they may be combined into one.

This means that although there are many masters above who have explained the meanings, and these are called 'principles' because they do not contradict one another, it is not problematic to combine them all into the doctrine of a single master. However, if the meaning of Master Ya is erroneous...
All of these are protectors of the Dharma who appear as distinct masters; this is stated to establish that there is no difference from other masters.

[Commentary: Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states that "only [the ālayavijñāna] can receive perfuming. This means that within the four types of perfumable objects in this treatise, the meaning of "sovereignty" (*vaśitva*) is subsumed.
However, according to the four types of perfumable objects in the *Saṃgraha*, the meaning of sovereignty is established separately as something external, and thus it is so named.

It is taught that all which is perfumed belongs to the eighth consciousness; it does not matter how the five [mental factors], such as contact (*sparśa*), are treated. How can the five, beginning with contact, be used as examples for the category of "all seeds"? [Commentary:
When mental factors act as a result and possess power, this refers to the power of having an object (*ālambana*), grasping (*upādāna*), and so forth. Question: Is it not the case that the mind...

Do the appropriated [aggregates] and so forth possess actual utility? Although they lack actual utility, because they arise simultaneously with the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and take objects as their conditions, they are said to be "powerful" by association.
In reality, however, the objective images (*nimittabhāga*) of the objects of contact and the other [mental factors] are like fire reflected in a mirror;
they possess no actual utility.
[Commentary: As for the question "Why... not six produced simultaneously," the meaning of the inquiry is:
how is it that what is perfumed by the mind causes the six [results], such as the *vedanā* (feeling) aggregate, to be produced simultaneously, given that there are six types of perfuming agents?

Since mental factors (*caitta*) are designated as perfuming agents, why are the subsequent results not produced all at once as six? One should answer: a single perfuming agent can indeed perfume the seeds of six results simultaneously.
As clarified in the Commentary: [The Commentary states:

"The *bhāga* (aspects) of the object and the subject within the mental factors (*caitta*) that act as perfumers (*vāsaka*) merely follow their own respective counts; even up to the point where six fruits do not arise simultaneously. The intent of this is as follows:

among the mental factors that act as perfumers, take for instance the five universal factors (*pañca-sarvatraga*); each of these possesses its own two parts, namely the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*). If...
At the time of perfuming, it is perfumed only according to its own category of universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), and not every single dharma possesses all six types.
It is not the case that a single contact (*sparśa*) perfumes and produces five categories as well as the seeds of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).

Since this is so for contact, the same applies to the remaining factors such as perception (*saṃjñā*) and the mind-king itself. Thus, there is no fault of the perfumed [basis] suddenly producing six results.
[Commentary: "The mind-king takes the fundamental consciousness as its object... it merely produces its own *svabhāva-vibhāga* (self-aspect) as a manifesting phenomenon.

This means that while the mind-king, as a perfuming agent (*bhāvakatva*), can produce actual minds (*citta*), as a perfumed object (*bhāvyatva*), it can only produce its own self-aspect and cannot produce other fundamental consciousnesses and so forth.

[Commentary] Answer: Regarding the statement "if that which can perfume is one," etc., and the six types [of seeds] that are co-perfumed by meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the intent of this passage seems not to answer the question as posed.
Furthermore, regarding what is able to perfume its own substance: subsequently, the six fruits are produced from seeds; thus, it does not answer the objection.

As for the mental factors (*caitta*) not being produced, their substantial nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be discussed. Whether their fundamental substance is produced or not is like the sixth consciousness.
Since there are six bases— namely, the foundational consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the five [sensory] cognitions— as the locus perfumed by these,
one accordingly perfumes six seeds for the essential nature of the sixth mental king (*manovijñāna*). When these subsequently arise as actualized functioning (*pravṛtti*),
it cannot be argued that while the seeds within the foundational consciousness can produce the actualization of contact and so forth, the seeds perfumed therein cannot produce actualization.

[Commentary: "One may at best discuss its essential nature and its reflected image" means that, at best, one may discuss how seeds are perfumed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) to produce the essential nature, and how seeds are perfumed by mental factors (*caitta*) to produce the reflected image.

[Commentary]: The meaning of "that which is perfumed is not so" is that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), its contact (*sparśa*), and the other [mental factors] are all equally that which is perfumed;
it cannot be said that seeds within the storehouse consciousness produce the seeds of the primary mind, while seeds within the mental factors produce the reflected images.

[Commentary]: This is also not the case; the meaning of the phrase "the analogy for reception should be thus" is that, following the analogy of the perfumed (the object) to the perfumer (the subject), it should first be the case that seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) produce the original object (*bimba*), and seeds within the contact (*sparśa*) and other factors produce the reflected image (*pratibimba*).
[Commentary: Regarding the statement "the six kinds [of perfumings] arise together to produce a single fruit... because their substance is one":

this now explains that it is not contradictory for the six capable perfumings to arise together to produce a single fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), just as a single grain of barley consists of many atoms. That which "maintains the oneness" is the fundamental consciousness itself.
The reason this is not contradictory is that it is the locus where the single perfumed object resides.
[Commentary]: The meaning of the statement "they are not distinct causes and conditions that together produce a single resultant seed" is as follows:

although there are six types of perfuming agents (*vāsana*), they do not function as distinct causes and conditions to collectively perfume a single resultant seed; therefore, it is used as a metaphor.

[Commentary]: Regarding this discussion on the matured seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) acting as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*), if one were to rely on the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) or the original essence (*bimba*), there would be thirty-six types, as stated in the treatise.
In that case, the other five types would be rendered useless; therefore, we know that this is explained with reference to the seeing-part and not the object-part.
[Commentary]: How does Dharmapāla explain this passage? If one does not admit that multiple kinds [of causes] co-arise to produce a single effect, how would Dharmapāla explain this?
For Dharmapāla admits that both new and old types of causes co-arise to produce a single effect.
[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "the difficulty regarding the co-arising of a single fruit is likewise" is as follows:

if multiple things were to co-arise as a single fruit, there would be the contradiction of many distinct entities arising together as a single sprout; if they do not co-arise, there would be the fault that one arises while another does not.
Since that which does not arise would be without a cause, the intent of the objection is thus.
[Commentary: This is a case of contradicting oneself, so there is no need for others to challenge you. I originally challenged you, saying:
"If a fruit arises from a single type [of cause], then the remaining five types would be useless. You now, in turn, challenge me, saying:

"If multiple perfuming factors (*vāsanā*) together produce a single fruit, then there is the obstacle that multiple types would together produce a single fruit; if one [type] produces it, the others would not."
Since that which has arisen and that which has not yet arisen would both be useless, the intent of this objection is merely to contradict oneself while attempting to support our own school;
thus, it fails to constitute a valid refutation. The following response provides the explanation.

[Commentary: To "harm oneself" means that while one challenges others by asserting that multiple types of fruits cannot arise together, one fails to provide a prior explanation for how one admits that two kinds of seeds—new and old—can jointly produce a single fruit; therefore, this is self-harming.
[Commentary: Regarding the objection, "This is not so... as for the claim that the eye arises from that," the intention is as follows:

The opponent says, "Since the Dragon King already possesses eighty thousand eyes and so forth, it is clear that there are six kinds of eyes; what logical contradiction is there in this? Therefore, [the author] objects:

My statement that the six eye-consciousnesses and so forth arise simultaneously is not [correct], because one can say that the seeds within the mind produce this eye, and [it arises] from among the mental factors (*caitta*).

Regarding the seeds that can produce those eyes, the Master of the Treatise (the *śāstrakāra*) raises an objection, saying: "In that case, there would have to be six root consciousnesses (*mūlavijñāna*) in a single moment.
He further objects that this is not so, yet it would follow that there are six root consciousnesses. Some say:

"If you claim that a dragon king possesses eighty thousand eyes, then there must be six root consciousnesses arising simultaneously in a single moment; it cannot be said that they arise within the mind."
The seeds of this [eye] arise within the mental states (*citta-caitta*) of this eye, while the seeds of that [eye] arise in those eyes and so forth.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the passage from "those with many eyes" to "is considered virtuous," the Master of the Treatise raises an objection:

If one says that the Dragon King has eighty thousand eyes, this would prove the existence of six eyes without contradiction; however, since there are naturally dragons who do not have many eyes, how could [the power] be pervasive in their case?
[Commentary]: "Furthermore, as with a person’s two eyes" up to "the consciousnesses are many" is the Master’s objection. [Commentary]:
"Moreover, if one grants... up to "is not of a single substance" means that this is based on the previous defense;
it is the formal objection raised in reliance upon that.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "this [transformation] is also capable of transforming and is thus called 'semblance-seeds' (sādṛśya-bīja)," the intended meaning is as follows:

the seeds transformed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) possess actual efficacy. However, when mental factors (*caitta*) rely upon the seeds transformed by the mind-king as their objective basis (*ālambana*), they themselves transform and give rise to image-seeds (*pratibimba-bīja*).
Because these lack actual efficacy, they are termed "semblance-seeds."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that these six sense organs, such as the eye-organ, exist simultaneously and in the same location, the intended meaning is that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are termed "transformations" (*pariṇāma*).
This explains the reason why a single organ can exist simultaneously and in the same location without mutual obstruction.

[Commentary]: Regarding the meaning of the "analogy of the characteristics" (lakṣaṇa-sādharmya) that follows the text down to the section on contact (*sparśa*) and so forth, an external objection states:

"If this analogy applies to the 'gate of relinquishing' (*prahāṇa-mukha*), why is it not stated at the very end, but rather stated in the middle, saying that contact and the others are likewise? The answer is:

The reason the "gate of analogy of characteristics" is stated in the middle is to demonstrate that there is an analogy between the beginning and the end; it is not for the sake of the meaning of the analogy itself.
If one were to explain the final section on the "gate of analogical application" (*dṛṣṭānta-mukha*), there might be the fear that it would imply that everything is to be subsumed under this analogy.
[Commentary: Sentient beings give rise to a discriminating mind and conceive of a self because they take the eighth consciousness to be the self;
the present mention of "arising and ceasing" is intended to refute that conception.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "external contact, sensation, and so forth," the intended meaning is as follows: "internal habitual tendencies" refers to internal seeds;
"external contact, sensation, and so forth" refers to the five mental factors beginning with contact (*sparśa*). Because contact is distinct from consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is termed "external."

[Treatise] Regarding the torrent, these three metaphors are used to explain the substance of consciousness. As for the three metaphors, according to the Ximing Commentary (*Ximing shu*), the first is the metaphor of the difficulty of escaping birth and death;
the second is the metaphor of the interruption and succession of the waves of consciousness; and the third is the metaphor of the mutual accompaniment of two dharmas.
Regarding the three kinds of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are as explained in the *Yanmi* (Exposition of Secrets).
[Commentary]: "The initial 'resembling the Sarvāstivāda and others' refers to this [text] resembling the Sarvāstivāda and other schools in raising objections against the Mahāyāna.
As for the phrase 'as below, this intention raises an objection,' etc., it means that the Sautrāntika school and others present their words of objection."

[Commentary]: "Because the present does not abide and because the future has no substance" means that because the present does not remain and the future fruit lacks substantiality, it is established as being non-interruption (*anuccheda*).
[Commentary]: "The former arises and the latter ceases" means that the preceding cause is able to produce the subsequent effect; that which ceases is precisely what serves as the cause.
Furthermore, it cites subsequent effects, such as a seed producing a seed; moreover, regarding the prior arising and the subsequent ceasing, as the treatise states:
"Because the effect arises, it is not annihilation; because the prior cause that arose has ceased, it is not eternal. This refers to the subsequent cessation.

[Treatise] Who is it that departs from [the extremes of] annihilationism and eternalism? A difficult objection from the perspective of the Hīnayāna states: "If cause and effect do not exist, then the principle of being neither annihilated nor eternal does not exist.
It is clearly understood that one cannot avoid the fault of falling into annihilationism and eternalism; and since one does not avoid annihilationism and eternalism, cause and effect do not exist.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the dharmas of the characteristics and the uncharacterized," the intended meaning is as follows: the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are the characterizers (*lakṣaka*), while the substance of conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is the characterized (*lakṣya*).

Although the substance of future dharmas exists, it has not yet been characterized by the characteristic of arising (*jāti*); therefore, they are called "dharmas of the characteristics and the uncharacterized.

The former [point] raised a difficulty based on activity (*kāritra*), whereas this raises a difficulty based on the relationship between the characterizer and the characterized; thus, the two are distinct.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the conditions do not coincide," the intended meaning is as follows: although the essence (tǐ) and function (yòng) both exist, because the conditions have not yet coincided, the function does not arise.

"Conditions" refers to the four types of conditions, such as the augmenting condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and so forth; "causes" refers to the six causes, namely: the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

[Commentary: If it is argued that conditions (*pratyaya*) and so forth may be non-existent in the future, the opponent offers this defense: "When dharmas arise, they necessarily rely upon causes and conditions.
While the cause may exist in the future, the condition is absent; therefore, no activity arises in the future. If this is the case, the Master (Vasubandhu) rebuts:
"In your own system, it follows that not all dharmas exist in the future."
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the future should be called the present," [the author] cites that school's position and raises an objection:
since the present possesses activity and functional efficacy, the past and future—being devoid of such activity—should likewise be called the present.
That school asserts that the substance of a dharma exists in the future because the characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) functions there; yet, if this dharma...
"In the past, there was the taking of a fruit; in the future, there is also the taking of a fruit.
[Commentary]: His defense is not tenable, as the Master of the Treatise rebuts him, saying:

"Since you state that the future possesses functions such as arising and so forth, and that these functions are themselves the causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), why do you defend your position by claiming that although the substance exists in the future, it does not conform to the conditions? This refers to the following.
He therefore rejects the previous defense from afar, stating that "that defense is not tenable. Furthermore, another interpretation states:

"Now, examining this passage closely, it seems to follow the Master’s [Vasubandhu’s] observation of the opponent’s error: since the 'function' (*kāritra*) has not yet been employed, it cannot be called 'present.

This is precisely what the sub-commentary below states: 'The term "function" here refers to the activity of grasping and giving; it is spoken of as "present with function" because it possesses both grasping and giving.'"
Now, the opponent’s defense is cited and refuted: since that defense is untenable, it is known that this interpretation of the textual analogy is superior.

As follows, this constitutes the formal objection: "What is the distinction between 'appropriation' (*upādāna*) and 'giving' (*pradāna*)? The answer is: that which currently possesses the functional capacity to grasp a fruit is called "appropriation";
that which, at the point of extinction, does not obstruct the arising of a subsequent fruit is called "giving. Therefore, there is a distinction between them.

[Commentary]: The objection states that while the *samanantarapratyaya* (equal-immediate condition) is said by former masters to possess the function of "taking the fruit" (*phalagrahaṇa*), the present author cites the orthodox teaching of the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which maintains that the past possesses the function of "taking the fruit," to challenge those masters.

He argues that if [the past] were to take the fruit, it would follow that the past would possess half of its functional activity, just as, for example, matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) both exist simultaneously.
Past minds and mental factors function as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) by virtue of having the capacity to grasp a fruit;

since this is not the case for matter (*rūpa*) and so forth, it is said to be "half. The statement "because they have the capacity to grasp a fruit" explains the reason why [the mind] is half-possessed of activity.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "in the future world there are three dharmas... which should be called present," the intended meaning is as follows:

the dharma of light (*āloka*), the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), and the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*)—these three dharmas have utility in the future.
How so? For example, a future dharma only attains birth by means of the characteristic of arising; thus, one knows that the characteristic of arising has utility only in the future.
Regarding "light," it is like the sun about to rise: one must first have light before the sun actually rises;

thus we know that light also exists in the future and yet performs its function. As for the "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), it possesses efficacy in relation to the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) and has the capacity to sever afflictions.
Since this capacity to sever [afflictions] also exists in the future, the objection that it should be called "present" is precisely the point of contention.
Since the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there is a "function" (*kāritra*), it should be designated as "present.

[Commentary: If you say, "Because the giving of a fruit reaches the point where there is no longer the function of grasping the fruit," and you claim that in our school, although past dharmas are said to give a fruit, this is merely a "capacity" (*śakti*) and not a "function," then we raise the following objection: It would be like an Arhat...
The final mind of an Arhat at the end of his life should not be called "present. Why? Because it lacks the functional activity of taking up a fruit (*phalādāna*), just like past dharmas.
Since that school maintains that all three time periods are substantially real, they argue: because past dharmas lack functional activity, they are designated as "past";
therefore, the final mind of an Arhat, being likewise without functional activity, should also be designated as "past."

[Commentary: Furthermore, if this mind reaches [the state of] "furthermore" and is again said to be extinguished, this is a restatement of the defense followed by a double refutation of that defense. It asks:
"How can it be that the mind of an Arhat, though initially lacking functional activity, likewise lacks functional activity at the time of its extinction?
The objection states: "If the mind of an Arhat initially lacks functional activity, it should already be termed 'extinguished,' just like that which is past."
"How can it be said later that [the entity] is further extinguished?
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the objection, "If that capacity (*śakti*) is renamed 'activity' (*kāritra*), how does it differ?", this challenges the preceding text. The preceding text stated:
"If one says that [the cause] bestows its fruit, this is merely a capacity and not what is called activity," etc. Now, the challenge asks: "What difference is there? [in this case?]

[Answer: It is different. [Commentary: If one says, "If it is not this [state], the fruit will not arise," this restates the opponent's defense. The defense states: "It is not that the final mind of an Arhat (aśaikṣa) cannot take the fruit;

it can indeed take it, but because the conditions for the subsequent moment are lacking... [The rest of the text] may be understood from the remaining words; thus, [the opponent's position] would contradict their own [tenets].

Regarding the phrase "the thesis and so forth," the author of the treatise challenges your position: the final mind of an Arhat in the stage of no-more-learning lacks the condition of equal and immediate antecedence (*samanantarapratyaya*) because there is no subsequent mind;
yet, if it possesses the function of grasping a fruit, it ought to be an equal and immediate antecedent condition.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "once the fruit subsequent to the final mind is determined not to arise," the intended meaning is that the final mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) does not give rise to a subsequent fruit.
[Commentary:

As for the statement, "If it is asked why the subsequent fruit cannot produce a fruit when it arrives," the intention is as follows: the external opponent provides a rebuttal, saying that if the conditions...

Regarding the objection that the final mind of an Arhat is also deficient and thus cannot induce a subsequent fruit: [the response is] that since the causes and conditions for the final mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are not deficient and it possesses functional efficacy, why can it not produce a fruit?
Since the cause does not produce [the fruit], it is clearly known to lack functional efficacy.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "contemplating present phenomena" and so forth, Zhe says: one contemplates the causes and effects over a long period of time.
One contemplates this body as a result, just as one contemplates causes such as giving and so on. Next, one definitively knows that one will obtain great wealth, status, and rank.

If one contemplates that this body possesses great wealth and status, a full complement of retinue, an exquisite physical form, complete and upright sense faculties, and majestic power, [one should know...]
[One] knows that it is produced by causes such as generosity, patience, and the abandonment of heterodox practices in previous lives.

[Commentary: Regarding "the characteristics of ripening and transformation": "ripening" (shu) refers to the state where the preceding [cause] has changed from its original nature; thus, it is called "ripening. "Transformation" (bianyi) refers to the resulting fruit; "characteristics" (xiang) refers to the commonalities between them.
Thus, it means "the characteristics of the fruit of ripening and transformation."

[Commentary] This answers the question regarding the dharmas of the stages of arising and ceasing. That which was previously described as "constantly revolving" refers to the principle that causes cease while effects arise;
because it is neither permanent nor unitary, it constitutes the stages of arising and ceasing. This refers to the section on the metaphors for the causal dharmas of the eighth consciousness.
[Commentary]: To say that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists while excluding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is to admit that the imagined has no essence;

this avoids the extreme of existence and serves as the cause for [realizing] non-causality. To say that the dependent nature exists while excluding the imagined is to avoid the extreme of non-existence and serve as the cause for [realizing] differentiation.

Therefore, it is said to be "free from the two extremes," which accords with the Middle Way. The two extremes of existence and non-existence are precisely the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "all [texts] speak of the distinctions of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) among the three vehicles (*triyāna*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

although it is reckoned that persons of the three vehicles all obtain the six supernormal powers, there are distinctions of clarity and obscurity, as well as universality and restriction. Since the question is asked in reference to these specific points of distinction, why are the supernormal powers of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and divine ear (*divyaśrotra*) not mentioned?
The answer is that the underlying principle is equivalent; however, the commentary selectively cites [only certain powers] and thus one cannot demand the reason for such partiality.
The supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear take only the present as their object; the five consciousnesses do not take the past as their object. One may ask:

why does the knowledge of birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) take the future as its object? The answer is that the knowledge of birth and death belongs to the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhiviṣayābhijñā*). This is because one gives rise to supernormal powers by taking birth and death as their object;
one exercises these powers with the desire to cause sentient beings to escape from birth and death.
[Commentary]: Regarding the principle of the three time periods, it is based on seeds that there is the principle of the past, future, and present;
thus, one speaks of the three time periods by way of conventional designation upon the phenomena of the present.

[Commentary: "When that wisdom arises" refers to the wisdom of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). "By the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), there is such power" means that by their very nature, they all possess the power to take the past and future as objects.

"The capacities of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) differ" means that while ordinary beings and non-Buddhists may cultivate and attain five of the supernormal powers, they cannot attain the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*); therefore, they differ from the noble ones.
Since there is no difference in the distance or clarity of the objects perceived, it is said that "each sees differently, yet all are real.
Because these are not false, they truly enable one to know such things as dying here and being born there.

[Commentary: Regarding the previous second statement, "appearing as their reflections," this refers to the fact that the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) described in the second fascicle realizes purity;

thus, it also manifests the reflections of those past and future [dharmas]. This meaning establishes that the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) take as their objects dharmas—whether existent or non-existent—across the three periods of time.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "By extensively cultivating this [wisdom], these phenomena of the past and future naturally manifest," the meaning is as follows:

through the extensive cultivation of this wisdom, once that wisdom has attained purity (*viśuddhi*), at the time of its subsequent arising, these phenomena of the past and future naturally manifest according to their respective degrees of force.
This occurs at whatever duration of time is appropriate; it is not like the transformations produced by the deluded mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Therefore, it is so stated.
"All are real.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Although this meaning applies universally," etc., the external objection asks: "In the Vijñaptimātra (Cognition-Only) system, how could the three periods of time not have a distinct substantial nature apart from the former two?
Therefore, the response states: "Although this meaning applies universally," and so forth.

[Commentary: The meaning of the phrase "the various conceptualized false minds manifesting appearances resembling past and future" is that these manifestations of past and future by false minds differ from the two aforementioned types of the three periods of time.

[Commentary: Regarding the passage in this treatise up to "there is only consciousness," it means that within this treatise there is only the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*) throughout the three periods of time.

[Commentary: Alternatively, regarding the further explanation up to "therefore they are divided into three types": based on the actual principle of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), the three periods of time are distinct from the principle of Consciousness-Only.
If one does not separately distinguish them, then even when speaking of supernatural powers, they are identical to Consciousness-Only.

Because there is still this confusion regarding false objects, three types of principles are distinguished. Regarding the three time periods (*adhvan*), they are established based on the principles of "having been" (*bhūta*) and "will be" (*bhāvin*) in relation to present dharmas;
it is not that they are not *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), for the meaning of consciousness is broad enough to encompass the other two [past and future].

*Cheng weishi lun shu yi yan*, Scroll Four. [Commentary]: The Buddha wished to eliminate that [wrong view] for those who are extremely foolish as well as those who understand. When they heard the World-Honored One say that the purpose of teaching "food" was to eliminate that meaningless asceticism, their derisive laughter increased all the more. How is this affliction to be dispelled? The World-Honored One replied: [The verse says: "Because it is not the case that there is no fruit, And because it is not the case that there is no cause, One should know that the two types of selflessness Are established by means of these two. [Commentary]: This verse explains the meaning of the preceding verse. It is said that the Buddha taught the existence of food to eliminate the affliction of those who hold the view that there is no fruit and no cause. Now, he teaches the non-existence of food to eliminate the affliction of those who hold the view that there is no self. Why? Because it is not the case that there is no fruit, and because it is not the case that there is no cause; one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two [truths]. What are the two types of selflessness? They are the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena. What are the two truths? They are the truth of suffering and the truth of origination. Why? Because the truth of suffering is the fruit, and the truth of origination is the cause. Since both the fruit and the cause exist, one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two truths. Furthermore, the truth of cessation is the fruit of selflessness, and the truth of the path is the cause of selflessness. Since both the fruit and the cause exist, one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two truths. Thus, the two truths establish the two types of selflessness. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha taught the existence of food to eliminate the affliction of those who hold the view that there is no fruit and no cause, and taught the non-existence of food to eliminate the affliction of those who hold the view that there is no self. This is what is meant by "because it is not the case that there is no fruit, and because it is not the case that there is no cause, one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two. This concludes the explanation of the verse. Now, the commentary will explain the meaning of the prose. Regarding the phrase "the Buddha taught the existence of food": this refers to the teaching of the four nutriments. Regarding "to eliminate the affliction of those who hold the view that there is no fruit and no cause": this refers to the teaching of the four noble truths. Regarding "the Buddha taught the non-existence of food": this refers to the teaching of the two types of selflessness. Regarding "to eliminate the affliction of those who hold the view that there is no self": this refers to the teaching of the two truths. Why? Because the four nutriments are the fruit of the four truths, and the two types of selflessness are the fruit of the two truths. Since both the fruit and the cause exist, one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two truths. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha taught the existence of food to eliminate the affliction of those who hold the view that there is no fruit and no cause, and taught the non-existence of food to eliminate the affliction of those who hold the view that there is no self. This is what is meant by "because it is not the case that there is no fruit, and because it is not the case that there is no cause, one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two. This concludes the explanation of the prose. Now, the commentary will explain the meaning of the subsequent verse. Regarding the phrase "it is not the case that there is no fruit": this refers to the teaching of the four nutriments. Regarding "it is not the case that there is no cause": this refers to the teaching of the four truths. Regarding "one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two": this refers to the teaching of the two truths. Why? Because the four nutriments are the fruit of the four truths, and the two types of selflessness are the fruit of the two truths. Since both the fruit and the cause exist, one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two truths. Therefore, it is said that "it is not the case that there is no fruit, and it is not the case that there is no cause, one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two. This concludes the explanation of the subsequent verse. Now, the commentary will explain the meaning of the final verse. Regarding the phrase "it is not the case that there is no fruit": this refers to the teaching of the two truths. Regarding "it is not the case that there is no cause": this refers to the teaching of the two types of selflessness. Regarding "one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two": this refers to the teaching of the four nutriments. Why? Because the two truths are the fruit of the two types of selflessness, and the two types of selflessness are the fruit of the four nutriments. Since both the fruit and the cause exist, one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two truths. Therefore, it is said that "it is not the case that there is no fruit, and it is not the case that there is no cause, one should know that the two types of selflessness are established by means of these two. This concludes the explanation of the final verse. Now, the commentary will explain the meaning of the subsequent prose. Regarding "it is not the case that there is no cause": this refers to the teaching of the two types of selflessness.
