The Dharma is not for the sake of a single person; though this may provoke derisive laughter, those who awaken to it are immeasurable.
Thus, other beings, by means of this, come to disparage the non-Buddhist outsiders and their meaningless ascetic practices; this is of great benefit.

[Commentary]: "There is not a single sentient being who, in a single moment, lacks the four nutriments" means that although the four nutriments are mentioned, the intent is to speak of the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).
If this were not the case, how could it be that edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) pervades all three realms?
To say that the intent is to distinguish them by speaking thus—that all sentient beings subsist by depending on nutriment—means that the intent lies in the nutriment of consciousness.
[Commentary]: Regarding the reason why the term "realm" (*dhātu*) is not mentioned for the latter three types of nutriment, the intention is as follows:

while the explanation of the names of the latter three provides the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the food, it does not specify them as belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and so forth. By using only the term "edible food" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) and specifying it as "bound to the desire realm," the underlying meaning is that all three realms are understood to possess all three types of nutriment.

[Commentary]: "In reference to a single lifetime" means it does not refer to other lifetimes; rather, it refers only to those sentient beings within this realm who can consume it, and thus it is called "nutriment.
It is not said with reference to other lifetimes, because although there is contact in the form realm, it is not considered nutriment.

[Commentary: Regarding "the matter that is the fruit of superior meditative concentration" and so forth: such as the actions performed by Bodhisattvas, as well as the category of matter such as the comparison between milk and curd, these are also not edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Because they belong to the same class as the sense-base of matter (*rūpāyatana*), they are not included within the category of food.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "form is coarse and manifest, and separated from the sense organ," this means that it serves as an object for its own visual consciousness by being separated [from the organ];
this is what is meant by "cognition of the separated.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "it is not necessary to specifically correspond to what is apprehended by its own consciousness," the intended meaning is that it is not required to be designated as corresponding to what is apprehended by its own consciousness.

Each consciousness individually cognizes its respective object; however, at the time of transformation and decay, it first sustains its own faculty and subsequently sustains the other faculties so that they may give rise to clear and sharp consciousness, thereby receiving the name of "nutriment.
[Treatise] To "sustain" means that contact is capable of producing joy and pleasure; this capacity to produce is what constitutes sustaining. These three are able to provide sustenance.
Are joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) themselves the contact (*sparśa*)? If it is contact that possesses these functions, what is its mode of activity (*ākāra*)?
If joy, bliss, and equanimity are what is appropriated, they should be the nutriment of joy, bliss, and equanimity; why then is it called the nutriment of contact?

Since joy, bliss, and equanimity are able to nourish [the mind] in three ways, if one were to say that when the fundamental object is attained, joy and bliss have not yet been appropriated and thus do not provide nourishment, how could they be called "nutriment"?

[Commentary]: Regarding the increase of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), it is because contact now increases feelings such as joy (*prīti*) and so forth that are capable of sustaining and benefiting the body;
only then is it termed "nutriment.
[Commentary]: "Sustaining equanimity that is not conducive to benefit" refers to equanimity associated with suffering (*duḥkha*) and other [unpleasant] states.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "there are those which are not the substance of nutriment," the intended meaning is that there are also contacts that are not the substance of nutriment;
these are precisely the contacts that give rise to suffering, grief, and non-conducive equanimity.

[Commentary: Regarding "attaining the fundamental object": it means that when one first makes contact (*sparśa*), one subsequently experiences (*vedanā*) and then fully apprehends (*saṃjñā*) it. Because contact is obtained first, it is called the "fundamental.

Some say that the "fundamental object" refers to the fact that whenever any mind or mental factor (*citta-caitta*) takes this object as its focal point (*ālambana*), the mental factor of contact has already obtained this object;
thus, it is named the "fundamental object."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the essence of this nutriment of contact consists entirely of the contact associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and so forth," the intended meaning is as follows:

because contact (*sparśa*) is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) and is associated with all consciousnesses, the mention of "contact" here refers generally to the contact of the eight consciousnesses. However, in terms of the actual substance of the nutriment, it belongs to the contact associated with the six consciousnesses, as this is predominant.
The same applies subsequently to the nutriment of volition (*manahsaṃcetanā*).

[Commentary]: If one aspires for a desirable object that is either future or present, and if this aspiration is conjoined with volition (*cetanā*), it is only when it takes a desirable object of the future or present as its focal point (*ālambana*) that it is termed "nutriment" (*āhāra*).
This is because that which has already ceased in the past cannot be joined [with the present mind].

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "desire is not diminished when it does not take the three periods of time as its object," according to the Abhidharma, desire takes the future as its object;

thus, "desire is not diminished when it does not take the three periods of time as its object" is stated here in terms of its manifest characteristics. In reality, however, desire universally takes all three periods of time as its object.

[Commentary]: "All that which is associated with desire" means it is associated with the three periods of time. If this is so, what prevents the desire associated with volition (*cetanā*) from also taking the three periods of time as its object?
Question: Regarding the characteristics of volition as the primary cause of formation and so forth, why is it now described as "aspiration"?
Answer: All mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) possess both general and specific modes of activity (*ākāra*). The "general mode of activity" is understood by way of association.

It is said that these are all identical in their activity (*ākāra*). For instance, mental contact (*citta-saṃsparśa*) and the like, when associated with feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, all have "apprehension" (*anubhava*) as their characteristic;
when mental contact and the like arise together with desire (*chanda*), they all have "aspiration" (*abhilāṣa*) as their characteristic.

This does not contradict reason, because the mind and its concomitants can each give rise to multiple activities. As for their distinction, it refers to the specific individual characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and activities of the mind and mental factors themselves. Just as...

Because it is taught that [the mental factors] have discernment as their nature, up to having volition and so forth as their nature of activity, this *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that they share the same object of cognition (*ālambana*) but differ in their modes of activity (*ākāra*).
This does not contradict [other teachings], as it is based on what is generally accepted.

[Commentary: "The category of mindfulness has no loss, and its objects also have no loss" is the answer to an external question. [The question is: "For instance, if desire fundamentally aspires toward the future, it is admitted that it takes the past as its object.
Since mindfulness already takes the past as its object, it should likewise obtain the future. [The answer is: Mindfulness can also take the future as its object.
Although its essence is not itself the future, because it arises taking future phenomena as its object, those very phenomena are [in fact] past.
"Past recollection" refers to such things as recollecting one's family home and the like; if it occurs at the present time, it may also be called "recollection of the past class.

The intended meaning is that while the future object is said to be a continuation of a past object, this "recollection" is able to take it as its object; it is not a recollection of a mental aspect (ākāra), but rather truly takes the future as its object.

[Commentary: Regarding "profound and superior aspiration": if it is a profound aspiration directed toward the primordial source (*ādikarmika*), it consists solely of volition (*cetanā*) associated with the mental consciousness (*manas*), and not other associated factors.

Furthermore, Vasubandhu says: "Just as one who sees water from afar on land might mistake it for a mirage, or as one who sees sand might think it is rice, or as one who thinks of poverty might think it will never end—all such things arise because of deep reflection, which then leads to [further] thought."

[Commentary]: "That which also corresponds to the six consciousnesses" means that if the volition (*cetanā*) associated with the six consciousnesses were to take [the object] as a consciousness, then the essence of the food of volition would have to be consciousness itself.

[Commentary]: "Causing consciousness to be clear and sharp so that it manifests before one" indicates that these three types of nutriment support consciousness, making it lucid; this applies to all [consciousnesses].

Consciousness-consciousness (*vijñāna-vijñāna*) is further able to nourish the sense faculties and the great elements; since this is the eighth consciousness, Vasubandhu states that "consciousness as nutriment" (*vijñānāhāra*) refers to that which is capable of appropriation (*upādātṛ*).
Because of this appropriation, the basis (*āśraya*) endures for a long time; therefore, it is called "nutriment."

[Treatise] Regarding the statement, "Although this consciousness (vijñāna) pervades the self-substance of all [eight] consciousnesses," the intended meaning is that the substance of the *vijñānāhāra* (consciousness-food) pervades the eight consciousnesses.
To cite the intent of the *Caturāhāra-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Four Foods) as proof for the eighth [consciousness], one asks: Why is the substance of food said to pervade consciousness? The answer is:

By using the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), it already encompasses all eight consciousnesses, because the meaning of "consciousness" is identical in all of them. Furthermore, since the other seven consciousnesses are its derivatives, when the fundamental [eighth consciousness] is mentioned, [the others are included].

Since it includes the derivative [consciousnesses], the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are neither identical nor different; thus, the term "consciousness as nutriment" (*vijñānāhāra*) applies generally to all eight consciousnesses.

However, the actual substance of consciousness as nutriment is the eighth consciousness and none other. If this is so, how is it that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that the six consciousnesses are also called "consciousness as nutriment"?

The answer is that "nutriment" has the meaning of providing sustenance and benefit. When the six consciousnesses take joy and pleasure as their objects, they are likewise able to sustain and benefit the sense faculties.
Because they are equal [in their function], the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* explains that the six consciousnesses are called "nutriments" based on this meaning.

[Commentary]: These are subsumed within three aggregates (*skandha*), five bases (*āyatana*), and eleven elements (*dhātu*). This reveals that the four nutriments are subsumed within the five aggregates and so forth.
As for the seven mind-elements (*citta-dhātu*)—namely, the six consciousnesses and the mind-faculty (*manas*)—the mind-faculty refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna* and its associates.

[Commentary]: As for the phrase "However, that [text] says," it refers to the *Abhidharma*, which explains that the three aggregates, five bases, and so forth, pertain to both the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) and the outflowing (*sāsrava*).
Since this treatise takes up only the outflowing portion, it speaks of "one part. This treatise omits the term "outflow-free" because it deals with the outflowing; thus, it does not say "one part.
Furthermore, its failure to mention the outflow-free is precisely what constitutes the abbreviation of that "one part."

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement that those [four nutriments], including outflow (*niṣyanda*), nurtured (*aupacayika*), and so forth, up to the three types of sensation (*vedanā*) and so on, the *Abhidharma* treatise explains that the four nutriments are subsumed within the three aggregates (*skandha*), five bases (*āyatana*), and eleven elements (*dhātu*). This is stated generally with respect to outflows and the other categories.

However, if one considers the nutriments themselves, they refer only to a portion of the four nutriments that are tainted (*sāsrava*). This treatise omits the portions consisting of outflows and so forth, and takes only [the remaining portion].
"Leakage (āsrava) serves as their nutriment.

[Commentary: "Nor are they that which constantly maintain the various faculties" means that the six consciousnesses are also not that which can constantly maintain the various faculties so that they do not become severed or destroyed, unlike the eighth consciousness, which is constantly able to maintain the various faculties.
If "nutriment" refers merely to the cessation [of craving], then consider the six consciousnesses: they are interrupted during the five states [of meditative absorption] or in the higher realms;
even if the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) were present there, how could it possibly sustain the various sense organs so that they do not decay?

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because that school does not admit the non-existence of essence and function": if one were to cite "the non-existence of essence and function" as a reason, that school would not accept it, because they maintain that past and future phenomena possess substantial existence (*dravya-sat*).
Therefore, such a reason commits the fallacy of being unestablished for one party (*anyatarāsiddha*). Our own school merely negates the existence of the essence and function of food;

there is no fault in citing "not being present" as a reason. The intent of the treatise is to state that while "non-existence of essence and function" cannot serve as a valid reason within this context, [the point remains that] food lacks such essence and function.
This can be applied to establish the *pakṣadharma* (the property of the subject). According to the *Ximing shu*, it is also used as the *hetu* (reason). [Commentary]:
Regarding the phrase "past and future consciousnesses, etc., are like space," this refutes the view that past and future consciousnesses possess the nature of nutriment (*āhāra*).
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Past and future consciousnesses, etc., do not have the nature of nutriment; this is because they are not present, just as [the reason] is.
By means of these analogies such as space, one should understand that those which are present but not of the nature of nutriment constitute the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).

Even though they are present, those that are not of the nature of nutriment are also included within the similar analogy (*sapakṣa*); therefore, by citing "space and so forth," this [category] is also subsumed.
Question: If that is the case, since the reason (*hetu*) does not pervade one portion of the similar analogy, how can it constitute a valid reason (*saddhetu*)? That is to say, it is not present.
Regarding the response that it is also incorrect because [the reason] exists in one part of the present within the non-pervasive example (*asādhāraṇa-dṛṣṭānta*), this is not so.

Although the reason applies to only one part of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), it still constitutes a valid reason (*saddhetu*). This is because it possesses the property of being definitely present in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattvam*) and absent from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣe 'sattvam*);

thus, it corresponds to the eighth of the nine positions (*navavikalpa*) in the *Hetucakra*, which is the position where the reason is present in the similar class and absent from the dissimilar class. As the verse states: "Two and eight."
These are the four correct reasons (*saddhetu*) among the six contradictory ones; by subsuming the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth, they all become indeterminate reasons (*anaikāntika-hetu*).

[Commentary] Regarding the statement "because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not nutriment," this explains the reason for the illustration. The intended meaning is that the unconditioned, such as space (*ākāśa*), is included within the present, yet it does not possess the nature of nutriment.

[Commentary: The subsequent specific refutation of dharmas refers to mental dharmas (*caitta-dharma*). Previously, by means of the refutation regarding the past and future, it was established that consciousnesses of the two time periods do not possess the nature of food;

here, by summarizing, it is shown that mental dharmas likewise do not possess the nature of food. This continues down to the refutation of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), which are also shown not to be food, and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding "the rest are Vasubandhu’s exegesis," this means that, excluding one section, the remaining portions of the refutation are Vasubandhu’s exegesis. [Commentary:

As for the passage stating, "If there were those who possess the nutriment of physical food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) within the desire realm, it might be conceivable that consciousness exists without such food to sustain the body so that it does not perish;
however, in the higher realms there is no nutriment of physical food. After consciousness, what would serve as nutriment for the untainted (*anāsrava*) state?"

[Commentary]: Regarding the claim that untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) constitutes the substance of edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), if one were to say that untainted consciousness is designated as food because untainted seeds exist within it, this is also incorrect. The refutation states:

"As explained in the Commentary, this refutation refers to the fact that in this stage there is no conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*). This stage is precisely the fourth [dhyāna], because it extends only up to cessation (*nirodha*).
"In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is certainly no inhalation or exhalation. [Commentary:

The Mahāyāna school maintains that one may remain in concentration for more than a single *kalpa*. This is because the Sarvāstivāda school does not admit that one can survive on food other than "morsel-food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) beyond seven days;

after the seventh day, they hold that one would die upon emerging from concentration. The Mahāyāna is not like this, and thus it allows for remaining in concentration for such a long duration. This is explained in detail in the Ximing Commentary (*Ximing shu*).
The Master Kūi’s *Yuanqi shiyu* [in ten-plus fascicles].

[Commentary: His answer regarding the "two minds" intends to say that within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are termed the "two minds.
Although there is no defiled seventh consciousness, there is the pure *manas*; therefore, it is mutually dependent upon the eighth. It is by means of these two...

There is indeed a distinction; some say there are two types of mind: first, the "accumulating and arising mind" (*saṃcitotpādaka-citta*), and second, the "variegated mind" (*vicitra-citta*), which is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

[Commentary: The phrase "not for the sake of counteracting this, nor because it arises from cessation" means that it is not intended to say that one gives rise to it out of a sense of revulsion toward this eighth [consciousness].
The meditative attainment of cessation is said to be so called only because one enters the attainment through aversion toward the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

[Commentary: This measure can be understood: in your position regarding the state of cessation, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) should also not be extinguished, because they arise again later, just as you admit [the existence] of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
As for the statement that "both schools lack [it]," this refers to the Mahāyāna and the Sautrāntika.

[Commentary: Regarding the objection that this stage possesses matter and thus must possess the root consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), it has already been established previously that matter is not separate from consciousness.
Since you admit that matter exists in this stage, there must be consciousness; and because consciousness itself undergoes perfuming, one knows that this consciousness is the eighth, and none other.

[Commentary]: Fundamentally, three great mental factors are established—namely, sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—which are the three mental formations (*caitasika-saṃskāra*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "because practice is superior in the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*)," the intent is to explain that "meditative concentration" refers to the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and "formless" refers to the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*); it means that when practicing these meditative states, sensation and perception...
These two dharmas possess superior efficacy because their obstruction of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is powerful; therefore, they are specifically emphasized.

[Commentary: The statement "the two are called mental activity (*citta-saṃskāra*) and furthermore, having reached cessation, it does not cease again" is a response to an objection. It is, for the time being, a rhetorical question.

[Commentary]: In the Mahāyāna, even the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the Buddhas and others are not characterized by universal activity. According to the Mahāyāna intention, when the activity of speech (*vāk-saṃskāra*) ceases, speech itself does not cease.
To now challenge another by saying that "when the activity of speech ceases, speech should not cease" does not contradict one's own school’s tenets.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "Now, raising an objection that contradicts one's own tenets while proceeding according to another’s system," the intended meaning is as follows:
when one objects that speech should not cease at the moment of its cessation, this is an argument conducted from the standpoint of the opponent's own tenets; therefore, there is no fault.

This is because, according to the Mahāyāna school, vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought) are not universal mental factors (*sarvatraga-hetu*), whereas according to the Hīnayāna school, vitarka and vicāra are indeed universal. Thus, [the Buddha] spoke [in accordance with the latter].
This is also because vitarka and vicāra differ [from other mental factors]. A Mahayana treatise states:
"Those that are omnipresent (sarvatraga) are spoken of from the perspective of the Hinayana. [The Sub-commentary] explains that this specific passage means:

inhalation and exhalation are called "functioning" (cārin) only with reference to the lower stages, as they are said to function by having power over the body; therefore, it says "only this passage," meaning that [vitality] is not omnipresent.
Therefore. [The *Śū* (Commentary) says: "There is nothing other than this" explains the reason why [feeling and perception] are not pervasive. [The *Śū* says:

"Because they are like vitarka and vicāra; that which is contested by inference (*anumāna*)" means that inference contests the two dharmas of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*). Furthermore—
Just as vitarka and vicāra are also universal [mental factors], the same applies to the treatises and commentaries; this is what is intended here.

[Commentary: As for the phrase "if one relies on the states of existence... because the objects of reference differ," the meaning is that even based on volition (cetanā), one may establish concentration (samādhi) and so forth.

That is to say, the original Sautrāntika masters established three types of mind—namely, feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and volition (cetanā)—and this is stated according to the actual dharmas.

One may also establish concentration (*samādhi*) upon volition (*cetanā*), because this volition is capable of dwelling single-mindedly on a single object; thus, it may also be termed "concentration. Question:

Since you have stated that it is volition, why is there concentration? Answer: Because the referent of a single moment of volition differs [from the referent of concentration]. If one considers its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it is simply called volition;
however, when established as a provisional designation based on its state (*avasthā*), it also extends to other dharmas, provided they dwell single-mindedly on one [object].

The limit of the object is called concentration (*samādhi*); if one pursues the limit of recollection, it is called mindfulness (*smṛti*); and if one pursues the limit of discernment, it is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Therefore, it is said that within a single moment of thought, what is expected differs according to the specific function.

As for the statement "it applies to all three natures," the intended meaning is that if one discusses them based on their application to all three natures and their presence with or without applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), then the ten dharmas—namely the universal (*sarvatraga*) and the object-specific (*viṣayaviśeṣa*) factors—are all termed the "great ground" (*mahābhūmika*).

Regarding the phrase "furthermore there are other dharmas," it means that in contrast to feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*), there are other [mental factors] which are termed "the rest.
[Commentary: Why do you say exclusively that there is no feeling or perception? The intention [behind this question] is:

since all mental factors (*caitta*) exist in the state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), how can you say that feeling and perception alone are absent from this state while other minds [or mental factors] are present?
[Commentary]: Regarding the distinction made by the *Śāstra* between informative action (*vijñapti*) and the contact that gives rise to sensation (*vedanā*), the intention is as follows:

it has never been stated that "in this state of distracted mind, contact can give rise to sensation," nor has it been stated that "in this state of cessation, contact does not give rise to sensation. Since there is no such distinction, how can it be used as an analogy?
[Commentary: "It differs slightly from the preceding" means that the previous passage was based on the difficulty regarding the existence of contact (*sparśa*);

since contact exists, it necessarily entails feeling (*vedanā*), and because feeling and perception (*saṃjñā*) are invariably concomitant, the principle that they must coexist is certain. This present passage, however, concerns the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), where there is volition (*cetanā*).
Since volition exists, there should likewise be feeling and perception, for this state is like other ordinary, non-concentrated states; thus, it differs from the preceding.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, "up to the heterodox masters of the Sautrāntika," the intended meaning is that Vasumitra is a heterodox master of the Sautrāntika school who enumerates the number of mental factors (*caitta*). [Commentary]:

Regarding the phrase, "the two dharmas serve as seeds; originally it was held that the attainment of cessation is mindless," the intended meaning is that the Sautrāntikas originally maintained that the attainment of cessation...
After a state of meditative absorption without mind (*acittaka*), the subsequent arising of the mind occurs only by means of two kinds of factors: first, by way of the mind itself;
second, by way of the seeds existing within form (*rūpa*). Regarding the initial question, the passage from "If there were no mental factors (*caitta*) following this [state]...
up to "...how could there be consciousness while being without mind? constitutes the entirety of that first inquiry.
The phrase "as when defilement arises" means that just as when defilement arises, although faith and so forth are absent, it does not preclude the existence of the mind;

this meditative absorption is likewise, for it does not preclude the presence of the mind alone even in the absence of [associated factors]. That which is called the "associated dharma" here is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*), its purpose in including this [category] as not being a cognitive subject (*ālambaka*) is that it implies:

not only is there no objective support (*ālambana*) or basis (*āśraya*), but the mind itself could not even be established as a cognitive subject. Thus, it includes this as being "not a cognitive subject.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and so forth" when including this as a "cognitive subject," it is intended as a formal proposition (*pakṣadharma*) for the objection: "Your mind in the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth should not be a cognitive subject, and so on."
Regarding "because it is not mind," as the *Treatise* refutes it by saying: "Just as with dharmas such as form, because [this] is also not a compassionate mind... The commentary explains:
"Because it is not mind, there are no associated dharmas.
[Commentary on the *Śāstra*]: The question "How does it apprehend images, etc.? intends to explain the reason why there is no perception (*asaṃjñā*).

[Commentary]: As for those who employ inference, their formal argument is as follows: Within the meditative attainment of cessation, there must exist feeling, perception, and other mental factors, because there is contact resulting from the conjunction of the three, just as in other states.

[Commentary: There must also be contact (*sparśa*), because it is admitted that ignorance (*avidyā*) exists; since craving and defilement arise from ignorance, it is now stated that where there is defilement, there must necessarily be contact.
Since there is contact, there must also be feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the meaning of the analogy of the non-defiled neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*): it is intended to establish a proportional measure (*dṛṣṭānta*).

According to this analogy, the measure states that the mental consciousness within this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) must not be a dharma characterized by non-defiled mental factors (*caitta*), because it is like other instances of defiled mental states.

Since it is clearly understood that there are no defiled mental factors in the state of meditative concentration, it is known that the mental consciousness within that concentration is likewise neither defiled nor neutral.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "this [reasoning] may also be applied in reverse," the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:

Your mind prior to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) must not be a distracted mind, because it seeks an object that is tranquil, just like the mind seeking an object that is nirvāṇa. How could there be a mind seeking an object that is bodhi which is yet a distracted mind?
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because all mental factors (*caitta*) are non-existent," the reason is based on analogies such as *bodhi* (enlightenment) and so forth;

by extension, this includes states such as [the perception of] form and sleep. The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: Within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there should be no mind, because all mental factors are non-existent, just like a mirage or water [that appears to exist where there is none].

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the dispute with others concerning the meditative absorption of cessation" up to "or it is said that there is no mind," the intended meaning is as follows: this refers to the subsequent discussion on the lower [stages], which concerns the dispute with others over whether the absorption of cessation possesses mind.

One should understand this by analogy with the states such as the non-conceptual attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) discussed below; the dispute below concerns the distinction between the defiled and the pure.
[Commentary]: Regarding "abiding in consciousness," non-Buddhists (tīrthika) reckon that among the four aggregates of form, sensation, perception, and formations, consciousness is the self;
thus, the four aggregates abide within it.

[Commentary]: "Taking the present seeds of the fundamental consciousness as the defiled and pure mind" means that one universally includes both the eighth consciousness in its active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) and its seeds.
"Mind" (*citta*) refers to the "collecting-and-arising mind" (*saṃcetana-citta*), because it collects the seeds of all phenomena and gives rise to all phenomena.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "conditioned phenomena, etc.," the intended meaning is as follows: conditioned phenomena depend upon the mind; therefore, when the mind is defiled, the mental states are defiled, and when the mind is pure, the mental states are pure.
This is called the "comprehensive statement" (*sāmānya-pada*), for it collectively establishes both defilement and purity. However, there is no... [text ends].
Although phenomena depend upon this consciousness, they do not become defiled or pure by means of this consciousness; therefore, it is distinguished from consciousness as a separate category.
Furthermore, it is called a "separate category" because its categories are distinct.

[Commentary]: The first phrase is as explained previously; that is, the phrase "taking the mind as the basis" was already interpreted in the initial explanation and need not be further explained here. [Commentary]:
Alternatively, if the essence of the mind is the sentient being, this refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

[Commentary]: "That which subsumes the three kinds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) taught in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* refers to the three kinds of affliction explained in this treatise [the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*]. [Commentary]:

"The prior statement that 'it maintains the seeds' was made to refute the Sautrāntikas; it was also for the purpose of refuting them first, which is why it was stated first that it maintains the seeds."
[Commentary] The "consciousness that is defiled" refers to the sixth consciousness at the very moment of initial rebirth; it is a defiled dharma,
which is precisely the consciousness at the time of the first linking of existence (*pratisandhi*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "by virtue of the basis and its perfuming," the meaning is as follows: the "basis" refers to the consciousness that can maintain the seeds (the *ālayavijñāna*), and "its perfuming" refers to the seeds that are maintained by it.
Since the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are intermittent, both the maintaining consciousness and the maintained seeds would have passed into the past.
When the subsequent consciousness at the moment of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhivijñāna*) arises, how could it obtain seeds for production if no seeds existed? [The answer is: It is said...
The basis is the body, and that which is perfumed by it refers to the seeds perfumed in the past within the desire realm;
for these to arise without a cause within the consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking in the past would constitute a great error.

[Commentary]: "Liberation by nature" (prakṛti-vimukti) means that because it is liberated by its very nature, it does not arise simultaneously with other afflictions (kleśa) or secondary afflictions (upakleśa).
"The two times" refers to the time of returning to the realm and stage of abiding, and the time after the mind is free from defilement;
these are called the two times. "Because there would be no holding of seeds" means that if the eighth consciousness did not exist, there would be no consciousness to hold the seeds.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "because it is not the eighth consciousness, it is like form, sound, and so forth," [the opponent] asks:

Since outflows (*āsrava*) and the absence of outflows (*anāsrava*) are directly contradictory, does the defiled (*sāsrava*) [eighth consciousness] not maintain the seeds of the undefiled? [Response: These cases are not analogous.

Because the eighth consciousness and the other consciousnesses are distinct, their faculties, objects, and activities differ, as do their seeds. While the defiled eighth consciousness can maintain undefiled seeds, your sixth consciousness cannot.
At that time, there being nothing else remaining, how could they sustain the outflowing [dharmas]?
[Commentary]: The meaning of "the past does not arise as the present" is that the past does not serve as the cause for the present.
[Commentary: As for how this is refuted by analogy, we do not employ a formal inference (*anumāna*) here.
Although this treatise does not explicitly refute "attainment" (*prāpti*), by combining it with similar categories of meaning, such a refutation is established.
[Commentary] This is analogous to the refutation found in the "Chapter on Purity" below; here, we now provide a rebuttal that parallels the refutations in that section.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the holding of seeds is briefly attained," the reason it is not explicitly stated is that this passage refutes the Sautrāntika position on the holding of seeds.

Because the treatise provides only a brief summary, it does not state that if one refutes the existence of the [past and future] entities, one merely refutes the past, the future, and "acquisition" (*prāpti*), but does not refute the "retention of seeds.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the substance of other seeds is certainly unobtainable," this means that for you, who lack the eighth consciousness, there is nothing else capable of retaining the seeds.
There is no arising of seeds from a mind of a different category.

[Commentary]: Regarding "after the two periods," this refers to the first period when the counteractive consciousness (*pratipakṣa-vijñāna*) arises, and the second period when one returns [to the world];

therefore, it is said that after these two periods, the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*) would be without cause. Furthermore, there is a commentary which states that this passage does not exist [in some versions].
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... up to 'should cease,' etc.," the intended meaning is as follows:

If the eighth consciousness did not exist, then for example, when one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and gives rise to the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) there, at the moment when the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) arises—which is neither in that place nor in another place—the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception would have ceased, yet it would not be subsumed under the sphere of non-perception; furthermore, the untainted mind would likewise be neither in that place nor in another place.

Because the latter is not subsumed under "arising," it is said that both types should be abandoned and departed from, and so forth. [The Treatise] states: "There is no place where non-arising exists. [Treatise]:

The defiled consciousness at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*) is not produced by *saṃskāra* (formative forces). How does this passage respond to that [opponent's] position? It answers by stating: "It is called *saṃskāra* because..."

That which is experienced must necessarily be the maturation (vipāka) and the indeterminate (avyākṛta), namely, the third moment of consciousness. However, the first moment—the consciousness at the moment of linking rebirth (pratisaṃdhi)—is exclusively defiled (kliṣṭa);
this is the established tenet of the Sautrāntikas, and all [schools] agree. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"When one passes away from the various stages such as the Unconscious Heavens (*asaṃjñisattva*) and is born here in this world, at that time, the first consciousness, being defiled by the corresponding [afflictions], links rebirth. Thus, Vasubandhu says:
"The consciousness that is defiled" refers to the very first consciousness arising upon coming to this realm after passing away from a previous one. As An-hui (Wu-xing) states:
"The 'first consciousness' refers to the consciousness at the initial stage of the moment of rebirth. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says:

"If one passes away from here and is born in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*), one briefly connects the continuity of rebirth through a non-equipoised, defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Therefore, [the opponent's position] is now refuted.

If it is argued that the consciousness at rebirth (*pratisandhi-vijñāna*) is not produced by the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) because it is defiled, and since the mind produced by the formative forces is categorized as resultant (*vipāka*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*),
then how can the defiled consciousness at rebirth be produced by the formative forces?
[Commentary]: The Sautrāntika masters ask, "What fault is there in [the position that] formations (saṃskāra) are the conditions for consciousness? Their intention in offering this defense is to say:

although it differs from the Sarvāstivāda school, which asserts the existence of past and future time and posits distinct temporal stages, within our own system—wherein the seeds exist within the "linking consciousness" (pratisandhi-vijñāna) that is capable of producing name-and-form (nāmarūpa)—consciousness is called "formations as the condition for consciousness.
This is because, according to the Mahāyāna, present karma and conditioned phenomena are capable of projecting [future results]. This is what is meant by the term "condition."

In our own school as well, it is the same regarding consciousness within the stage [of name-and-form]: although the consciousness that links rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi-vijñāna*) is not produced by the impelling karma (*saṃskāra*), because it can be summoned by the seeds of the impelling karma, the consciousness within the stage of name-and-form may also be designated as "conditioned by formations" (*saṃskārapratyaya*). The tenets of our school are likewise.

If one discusses this according to the analysis of stages, since the mind and mental factors associated with the stage of name-and-form are collectively termed "name-and-form," it is said that "consciousness is conditioned by name."

Regarding the statement that "consciousness" refers to the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) induced by karma: this is a matter of whether it is based on the condition or not based on the condition.
If it were explained based on the condition, it would be called only "name-and-form" and not "consciousness. Therefore, [the term "consciousness"] does not refer to the condition.

[Commentary]: Although the defiled consciousness is not that which is perfumed (*vāsya*), one might raise an objection: "If you say it is called 'consciousness' because it is perfumed, that too cannot be established. Why?
Because the defiled consciousness at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*) is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);

only indeterminate dharmas can receive perfuming. Furthermore, [the claim that it is] 'induced' is also untenable; that which is induced by prior karma must necessarily be an indeterminate dharma of maturation (*vipāka*). If...
The statement that "consciousness within name-and-form" is the meaning [of the condition] is not so, for it would be somewhat difficult [to maintain].

Therefore, the Sautrāntika school speaks only of "perfuming" (vāsanā) as the condition for consciousness in order to avoid the fault of excessive remoteness; thus, they say it is called a condition merely because of perfuming.

[Commentary]: These three passages explain them together. Since the point that there is no resultant consciousness is explained in the following sentence, it says "because the meaning of 'no object' is not established.

Therefore, what follows is also not established; this means that if the condition of *saṃskāra* (formative forces) cannot be established, then the condition of *vijñāna* (consciousness) for *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) likewise cannot be established.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "appropriation conditioned by existence cannot be established," Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: "That is to say, if existence were absent, then appropriation conditioned by existence would also be inconsistent.
The intended meaning is that since appropriation is already non-existent, existence conditioned by appropriation cannot exist either.
As for the phrase "because there is no consciousness to maintain the seeds," this means it would not be real. How, then, could craving and appropriation now give rise to the future link of existence?
Is there a condition? One should understand that the term "reversal" (vaiparītya) follows the preceding [explanation].

That is to say, regarding "reversal," since every defense and every refutation follows the precedent above, one should understand that everything from the initial objection concerning the cognition of conditions (*ālambana*) up to the objection concerning the vast temporal gap (*kālaviprakarṣa*) follows the same principle as stated above.
[Commentary: If it were possible for each stage to relate to the others in such a manner, then the sequential order of "consciousness conditions name-and-form" and so forth would not be established.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because they condition one another within the fruit," this is because that school asserts that the five members beginning with consciousness are exclusively results.

[Commentary: "Cessation is the fruit" refers specifically to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because it is attained through the abandonment of afflictions; thus, it receives the name "cessation. Furthermore, the unconditioned is that which attains [the state of] both the abandoned and that by which they are abandoned.

Moreover, since the unconditioned pertains to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it provisionally receives the name "cessation" based on its relationship to that which is abandoned and that by which it is abandoned.
This is stated twice because it refers to the unconditioned as the fruit of cessation.

[Commentary]: This means that from the time one has not yet abandoned the fetters of desire (*kāmacchanda*) up until the point of diligently practicing the preparatory application (*prayoga*), the intention is as follows:

since one still possesses a mind bound by the fetters of desire, one uses that very mind bound by the fetters of desire to suppress the greed and other afflictions of the desire realm, while diligently practicing the preparatory application to seek the wholesome minds bound by the form-realm fetters (*rūpāvacara*).
"Mental states" (*citta-cetasika*) is the general term for these contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement "because the mind bound by the form-realm (rūpāvacara) does not arise simultaneously [with the mind bound by the desire-realm (kāmadhātu)":

if they were to arise at the same time, the mind bound by the form-realm could be perfumed by that mind bound by the desire-realm, and thus the seed for that mind bound by the form-realm could be produced within this mind bound by the desire-realm.

If it were not perfumed by that [desire-realm mind], it would be illogical for this mind to serve as the seed for that mind bound by the form-realm. This principle may be applied analogously to the arising of a pure manifest mind (*śuddha-vijñapti-citta*).]
[Commentary]: Furthermore, this mind associated with correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) is the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukika-agra-dharma*);
that which is associated with right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth constitutes the untainted gateway of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the question, "When defiled dharmas—both manifest and seeds—are abandoned, what remains?

this means that if there were an eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna) to maintain the manifest and the seeds, then the sixth consciousness could, through an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), abandon those manifest states and seeds.

Now, since you [the opponent] do not admit the foundational consciousness (mūlavijñāna), when the sixth consciousness records an untainted state, the afflictions and so forth have already ceased; what, then, does the untainted wisdom abandon? Furthermore, it is said:
This refutes the Sautrāntika position by stating that because there is no grasping (*upādāna*), the fruit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-phala*) cannot be established. The commentary explains:
according to the text of the sub-commentary, it first presents the Sarvāstivāda defense and then refutes that attempted defense; its underlying principle is thus a refutation of the Sautrāntika.

Why is this so? Since the Sarvāstivāda school does not establish the existence of seeds (*bīja*), and since it is clearly stated that "defiled dharmas exist neither as present nor as seeds," it is evident that this refutes the Sautrāntika.
It is superior. [Commentary:

Regarding the Sarvāstivāda position that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions coexists with them: although their own school does not admit seeds, because the meaning of the acquisition of afflictions is similar to that of seeds, they also refute this.
Their position is that [the acquisition] exists during the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Question: All manifest activities are entirely non-existent; there is only the attainment (*prāpti*) of afflictions that is extinguished by the path of liberation. How can one respond to the objection:
"If the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises and all [afflictions] have already been severed, how can you say that the untainted path is able to sever afflictions?
Does it mean that in the Mahāyāna, when the untainted path arises, afflictions still exist? Answer: Not so. This is because the eighth consciousness contains the seeds (*bīja*).
When the path of no-outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises, the seeds that ought to manifest should be able to arise; yet since they do not arise, they are termed "severed.

According to your school, there is no prior perfuming and thus no seeds. If this is the case, when the path of no-outflows arises later, the preceding moment’s active manifestation has already ceased.
I do not understand what the essence of this outflow-free wisdom would be. As for your school’s [assertion of] "attainment" (*prāpti*) and so forth, these have already been refuted as being non-real.

Therefore, [the commentary] states: "One cannot say that it exists either in the past or in the future," because the dharma obtained is past or future, while the essence of the present capacity to obtain it extends into the past and future;
thus it is said, "or in the future," and so forth. This is the Sautrāntika school's position.

Because there is no past [existence] and no acquisition (*prāpti*), it is not said that there is an "acquisition of acquisition" (*prāptiprāpti*) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the future life.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "there is no fault even if the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) maintain the seeds," this is a hypothetical concession (*abhyupagama*) based on the Sautrāntika position that the life-faculty and the homogeneous character maintain the seeds.
[Commentary: It is not correct to say that [the result] is produced because there is no basis, for it is merely *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) and is not called by the name "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
[Commentary: He further attempts to defend his position, asking, "What fault is there from the perspective of principle? This is his revised argument.

His previous position was that within "name" (*nāman*) there is the *vipākavijñāna* (retributive consciousness), which he termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*) as the productive cause; the treatise refuted this, stating that one should rather say "material form" (*rūpa*) acts as the condition. Therefore, [he now argues... Sa...
Having encountered this difficulty, Vasubandhu then further rescued [the argument] by saying: "I shall now distinguish dependent origination according to its stages (*avasthā*).
Question: What is meant by 'stages'? Answer: For instance, within the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*), all associated phenomena (*saṃprayukta-dharma*) are called the factor of ignorance;
likewise, within the factor of consciousness (*vijñāna*), all associated mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as well as the maturation (*vipāka*)."
Form and so forth are collectively termed the "consciousness link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*), and this applies to each subsequent link as well.

Consequently, one might mistakenly calculate that within the consciousness link there exists form whose nature is maturation (*vipāka*), and thus it too is called the consciousness link; this is because they are explained in terms of their distinct states (*avasthā*).

Therefore, it is difficult to understand that while the consciousness at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi-vijñāna*) within the consciousness link is defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it is not itself the consciousness link [in its entirety], whereas the form existing simultaneously with it, which has maturation as its nature, is indeed the consciousness link in its totality.
Regarding the question, "What logical fault is there in naming the *rūpa* of maturation within the consciousness-link (*vijñāna-aṅga*) as the essence of that link?"—it is refuted as follows:
because there is no sense of "conditioning" (*ālambana*) when time periods are widely separated.

"Separated" refers to the refutation of the consciousness-link by means of the preceding conditions for *rūpa*. "Widely separated" refers to the refutation of the subsequent rescue-argument. If you...

Regarding the statement that the *vijñāna-aṅga*—which consists of the maturation (*vipāka*) possessing form—is said to have "formative forces as its condition" (*saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam*), this does not refer to [the immediate] maturation, because the temporal distance is so great that there is no sense of "conditioning.
For example, from this desire realm, one first creates karma for humans or devas and then creates karma for the Naivasamjñānāsamjñāyatana heaven;
when one dies from here, one is born in the Naivasamjñānāsamjñāyatana because that karma is predominant, and there one experiences [a lifespan of] eighty thousand [great kalpas].

Once the kalpa has ended, one is subsequently reborn in the realms of humans or devas; why then would the karma of humans from a previous time obstruct the retribution of the Non-ideation Heaven (*asaṃjñisattva*), and yet again induce human retribution?

The same logic applies to the realm of the devas. It is difficult to claim that because the previous time was so remote, the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) does not exist [there], for such a view would entail this error.
Furthermore, even if you grant that there is the possibility of inducing [rebirth] in the present life, as in the case of the Non-ideation Heaven, [the same difficulty remains].

The retribution of the stage is different and cannot be summoned; furthermore, no further karma is created in the interim. Moreover, since the prior consciousnesses and so forth have already fallen away and perished, there is nothing to be perfumed;
therefore, it is said that [the result] is not established. Now, following this line of reasoning, we shall refute the opponent's position regarding "time.

As for the statement that "there is no connection and no seed because they are separated by a vast interval," the meaning is that, because there is no foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) to serve as a basis, [the subsequent consciousness] could not arise.
The seeds also do not exist. [Commentary:

As for establishing "the fruit of abandonment," it means that the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) is the fruit of abandonment. According to the Sautrāntika school, there is no separate unconditioned entity;
rather, the very absence [of the seeds] is what is meant by "non-existence."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "when they arise later," the meaning is that when the path of cultivation arises again, it is because the seeds of affliction are maintained by the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
[Commentary]: "Summarizing the chapter" refers to concluding this section of the sutra’s prose; it clarifies the meaning within this scripture.
The textual evidence for the existence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) having been fully established through the proof of its principle, this now serves as a concluding summary.

[Commentary: Regarding the "combined evidence" (*saṃgraha-sādhana*) that corroborates the "fundamental evidence," it refers to the fact that the three texts—the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*—all provide evidence for the fundamental consciousness;
thus, they are termed "combined evidence. The ten proofs presented here encompass the essential intent of all those various treatises mentioned at the end of the previous fascicle.
This refers to the end of the third commentary.
[Commentary: "Not the primary proof" means that the three proofs—the initial arising, the clarity, and the karmic function—are not the primary proof for the eighth consciousness.

[Commentary] The question "Why [is it said that the seventh] reaches its support? intends to convey that because the meaning of the fundamental realization (the eighth consciousness) being the support for others is manifest, it is not stated that [the seventh] is supported by them.
Because the meaning of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses being supports for one another is obscure, their supporting essence is not set forth;
thus, it is simply stated that the seventh depends on the eighth, rather than stating that the seventh and eighth are mutual supports. As explained in the commentary.

Regarding why it is said that the basis (*āśraya*) emerges from its substance (*svabhāva*): this is because the seventh [consciousness] takes the eighth as its basis. As the treatise states: "Depending upon that, it evolves;
taking that as its object. [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement that the object of perception emerges from the substance of consciousness, the intended meaning is that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) serves as the basis for others, evolving perpetually.

Regarding the statement that "the outflow arises from the objective support (*ālambana*) which is the basis (*āśraya*) of the essence of consciousness," the verse clarifies that "the locus of appropriation" refers to the objective support of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, concerning the statement that "it arises from the objective support which is the basis of the essence of consciousness," some say that the essence of consciousness itself serves as the basis for its objective support;

this is because the seeds, the sense organs, and the body are dependent upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), and thus it is said that the fundamental consciousness [serves as the basis] for them.

Regarding the statement that "that which serves as the basis for the objective support (ālambana) of its own consciousness-body is precisely the objective support of its own consciousness-body, such as a seed and so forth," while it is said that [the seed] serves as the basis for another [consciousness], the intention is to show that it emerges from its own objective support; thus, this interpretation is somewhat superior.

[Commentary: Regarding the explanation of the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*): because the manas takes the eighth consciousness as its co-existent faculty (*sahabhū-indriya*) and also as its object (*ālambana*), it is said that "it evolves depending on that and takes that as its object.

[Commentary: This case should likewise be understood; as for the phrase "it follows the bondage of that," this is the opponent's objection. If one were to say that the eighth [consciousness] follows...

If the maturation of a particular realm is itself bound to that realm—thus clearly indicating it is bound to the luminous realm (*prabhāsvara-dhātu*)—then the seventh [consciousness] should likewise be so.
Since it is stated that it coexists with defilement, it would be bound to whichever defilement it accompanies, just as the eighth consciousness is.
Once it is established that it is bound to the luminous realm, why is it necessary to subsequently state that it is bound according to where it is produced?
[Commentary]: This is not to be taken as a general rule; therefore, it is explained here now. This answers the underlying intent of the objection:

for instance, just as the first six consciousnesses are associated with defilements, when they arise, they are not necessarily bound by the same level (*bhūmi*) as those eight [defilements]. The seventh consciousness is also associated with afflictions;

except when it arises in the state of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) cognition, in all other states involving outflows, it is always bound by the same level as them. Since this one type [of consciousness] possesses defilement, how [is it different from the others]?

The first six [categories] are also bound, yet they are not necessarily bound in the same way as the seventh; are they not bound in the same way? Now, in order to distinguish these first six, the phrase "bound according to where they arise" is stated.

[Commentary]: It says, "Fearing they might be categorized with the first six," and thus it is said now. Furthermore, regarding "fearing they might be categorized with the first six": if one did not say "according to where they arise," [the error would follow].

Regarding the phrase "fearing it will be like the first six, which are tied to all times like the seventh": some say "fearing it would be similar to the first six" means to draw an analogy. Furthermore, the commentary on the *Śāstra* states, "this should also be so," meaning that since the eighth [consciousness] arises in its own stage and is tied to its own stage, this seventh [consciousness] is likewise so; yet it has already been explained—where [is the point]? The answer is as follows: [The point is that] while the eighth consciousness arises in its own stage and is tied to its own stage, the seventh consciousness does not necessarily arise in its own stage. Therefore, although the eighth is tied to its own stage, the seventh is not necessarily so. Consequently, the seventh is not tied to all stages at all times, just as the first six are. This is why it was said, "fearing it would be similar to the first six. As for the statement "this should also be so," it refers to the fact that because the eighth is tied to its own stage, the seventh should also be so; however, since this has already been explained previously, where is the contradiction? The answer is that there is no contradiction. The intent is that although the eighth is tied to its own stage, the seventh is not necessarily so, and thus they do not share the same characteristics. This is why it was said, "fearing it would be similar to the first six. The statement that "being associated with defilement" already constitutes the explanation refers to the association with the four afflictions; this makes it clear that the seventh consciousness has already been discussed regarding its connection to the realms (*dhātu*).
The phrase "it follows that very connection" means that the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of the seventh consciousness follow that same connection. Question:

Why is it that for the six consciousnesses, one does not say they follow their respective place of birth or their respective connection, whereas for the seventh, one does say it follows its respective place of birth and its respective connection?

The meaning of the statement in the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary), "Therefore, citing this as an answer does not serve as a general rule," is as follows: The reason for stating that the seventh consciousness is bound in the same way [as the eighth] is that there is no distinction between them;

thus, it is said to be bound according to the eighth. However, the first six consciousnesses do not necessarily share the same binding as the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). Therefore, they are not described in the same way.

This is because one fears that the seventh consciousness—except during the state of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) cognition—would be classified as always being bound in the same way as the fundamental consciousness across all other states, just like the first six.
Therefore, it is now said that there are seven [consciousnesses] according to what they are bound to.

[Commentary: If the seventh entity—the mind—did not exist as a substantial reality, it would mean that the term "mind" has no referent. This implies that if the seventh consciousness exists, the function of deliberation (*manana*) can exist;
however, if one does not admit the existence of the seventh consciousness, then there is merely the name "mind" while its actual meaning is absent. Some say:
This refutes the Sautrāntika school.
[Commentary: Regarding the third point, "the essence of mind," one enumerates the mind, thought, and consciousness.
[Commentary: Although the general term is indicated, as the treatise says, "that which is consciousness" indicates the general name; here, when we speak of "mind" (manas), it refers to this.
It is separately assigned to this seventh [consciousness].
[Commentary]: Regarding the term "provisional designation" (prajñapti): because the supramundane mind is without deliberation (*vitarka*), it is not truly so;
thus, although it is designated as "manas," it is merely a provisional designation and does not necessarily correspond to its literal meaning.

[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "all [terms] are established by correlating two factors" is as follows: for instance, when explaining the six types of compound names (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti-nirukti*), one always distinguishes their specific differences by correlating two factors.

For example, the two factors in a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) are the "storehouse" (*ālaya*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); the two factors in a *tatpuruṣa* (determinative compound) are the "eye" and "consciousness," and so forth.
Even in cases such as "contradictory" (*virodha*) or "proximate" (*sāmīpya*), they are all distinguished by correlating two factors; thus, the meaning is without error.
If one speaks only of "mind," it serves as an analogy for a single dharma and lacks the sixfold analysis (*ṣaḍvidha-vyākhyā*). Therefore, it is said below:

"It is not that each individual dharma exhaustively encompasses the principle; the sixfold analysis does not fully explain all dharmas, such as non-attachment (*alobha*) and others, which lack the sixfold analysis."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because they are equally conceptualizing," one asks: since the seventh [consciousness] lacks the three types of discrimination, such as recollective discrimination (*anusmaranavikalpa*), how can it be said that they are equally conceptualizing?
The answer is: because they both possess grasping (*abhiniveśa*), they are said to be equally conceptualizing; thus, there is no contradiction.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the alternative explanation that it "continuously deliberates" (*saṃtati-pariccheda*), this is the Master of the Commentary’s distinct interpretation based on other texts;
specifically, it relies on the passage stating that it is superior to other consciousnesses because it is "constantly and thoroughly deliberative" (*nitya-paricchedaka*).
[Commentary]: Regarding "the uncommon support," this means that the seventh [consciousness] serves as the uncommon support for the sixth.
Why? Because all six [consciousnesses] possess an uncommon faculty (*asādhāraṇendriya*). Furthermore, it is said "uncommon support" to distinguish them from the common support.

The mental faculty (*manas*) that has just ceased in immediate succession is shared by all consciousnesses; the former induces the latter, and the latter induces the former. Thus, this applies to all consciousnesses alike.

To distinguish this [case], the term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) is used. Although the eighth consciousness relies upon the seventh, here the discussion is based on the six consciousnesses and does not rely upon the eighth;
therefore, there is no contradiction. [Commentary]:
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the six kinds arise based on the seven kinds," it is intended to mean that if the seeds of the sixth consciousness are about to arise...

When the manifest consciousness arises, it must be triggered by the seeds bound to the seventh [consciousness] before it can be produced; as will be explained below, the six manifest [consciousnesses] depend on the seventh.
When [the sixth] is present, it depends on the seeds of the seventh according to seven principles. What are they?

[Commentary]: Regarding whether it is wholesome or defiled: when the sixth consciousness enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the seventh consciousness is associated only with the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).
When the sixth consciousness enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the seventh consciousness becomes associated with the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*);

this is what is transformed into the wholesome. However, when the sixth consciousness emerges from contemplation, the seventh consciousness again becomes associated with the innate grasping of a self (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*).

It immediately turns into defilement; if one enters this path of vision for the first time, when entering the sixth pair of contemplations on the two emptinesses, it is only at the seventh that it becomes untainted;
therefore, by means of the sixth and seventh, they become wholesome and defiled respectively.
[Commentary] Questioning the latter master regarding the phrase "up to 'it still says it relies [on something]'": this has two meanings. The first meaning states:

Since the transformation in the First Ground is produced by the drawing forth of the sixth consciousness, and thus both the wholesome and the defiled are established, why would one need the eighth manifest-consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) as a support for the seven [subsidiary] consciousnesses to arise?
Furthermore, what superior power does the eighth possess in relation to the seventh? The second question means: For instance, within meditative concentration (*samādhi*)...

When the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) hears a sound through sudden occurrence (*ābhoga*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes a different object; it does not, like the ear-consciousness, simultaneously grasp [the same object].
Since the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are in a state of continuous activity (*pravṛtti*), why is it said that the ear-consciousness arises based on the seventh and eighth?

For what reason? Because even though they lack the power of attraction (*ākṣepa-śakti*), they are still said to be its basis. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Ear-consciousness in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) must take the seventh and eighth consciousnesses as its basis. Why? Because...
Although it lacks the power of attraction, it is still said to be a support (*āśraya*), just as the seventh consciousness from the first bhūmi upward;

this is illustrated by the statement that when the first bhūmi arises, the eighth does not attract the seventh, meaning the eighth is declared to be the support for the seventh. Furthermore, in meditative absorption, the seventh and eighth do not attract the ear-consciousness; likewise, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should also serve as the support for the ear.

As for the claim that the mental consciousness does not share the same object of apprehension as the ear: *Note: The original text contains a complex argument regarding the relationship between the storehouse consciousness (eighth), the manas (seventh), and the sensory consciousnesses, specifically addressing the concepts of "non-attraction" (*anākṣepa*) and "support" (*āśraya*) within the context of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.*
Regarding the question of one's own lack of right principle:

[The Commentary] states that for the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and seeds to reach the point where consciousness (*vijñāna*) can arise, it must first be explained that the seeds of the faculties draw forth the seeds of consciousness;
once the seeds of the faculties have produced the manifest faculties, the seeds of consciousness are then able to produce consciousness.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the sixth consciousness... up to establishing seeds," this reconciles the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Now, from the seventh [consciousness] downward, our own specific doctrine is established.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "if one says it depends on the manifest... because the modes of activity (*ākāra*) are distinct," the intent of this objection is: if one relies on the eight [consciousnesses] as manifest...

The manifestation of the eighth consciousness must share the same object as the seventh, just as the eye-consciousness relies on a manifest sense organ and both the organ and the consciousness apprehend the same object;

this case should be understood accordingly. Regarding the statement that their modes of activity differ: since the modes of activity of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are distinct, it is clear that if they do not share the same object because their modes of activity differ, the eighth does not rely on a manifest [seventh] but rather relies on its seeds.
[Commentary: If this is so, how can it be said that "the six [consciousnesses] depend on the seven [bases]"? This is a rebuttal of the previous master’s position.

If one argues that because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ, they do not depend on those [bases] as manifest, then since the sixth and seventh consciousnesses both differ in their modes of activity and their objects (*ālambana*), how can it be said that the six depend on the seven? [The opponent replies:
It is not like the case of visual consciousness, where the consciousness, the faculty, and the object are distinct; rather, the term "dependence" here carries the sense of similarity.
"Because both see the visible object.
[Commentary] The answer states: "The two persons rely on different [bases]," etc. The first master says: although the two bases are distinct, what obstacle is there to their being relied upon?
It is not contradictory for the sixth and seventh consciousnesses to be established as having different bases.
[Commentary]: If this is so, how do you know that the seventh [consciousness] serves as the support for the sixth? To this challenge, the first master replies:

"How do you know that the seventh possesses a functional capacity (*śakti*) to serve as the support for the sixth, while you do not reckon the eighth, which possesses such power, as the support for the seventh?
Since the reasoning is thus contradictory, we know that the eighth is actually the support for the seventh. The opponent answers in substance: "Because... [The text continues from here.]
The Master answers the previous objection by responding and then further questioning [the opponent], as follows: "This is the Master’s critical response to the previous teacher;
its meaning is easy to understand and requires no further elaboration.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "If there were no eighth... to "...therefore it is said they are not the seven supports," the intended meaning is that if there were no eighth [consciousness], yet there were seven...

Furthermore, because the eighth [consciousness] does not exist, the seventh consciousness cannot serve as the support for the sixth; this is what is meant by the statement that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is not so.
The intended meaning is that if the eighth were absent, there would be no obstacle to the existence of the seventh consciousness;

therefore, the mental consciousness does not take the seventh as its support. This implies that since it is clear the sixth does not take the seventh as its support, it must evidently rely upon the eighth.
[Commentary]: "As in meditative concentration, when reaching that [object], they must necessarily take it together"—this answers the previous objection. The objection stated:
"When the ear-consciousness alone hears a sound within meditative concentration, it should take the present seventh and eighth consciousnesses as its support. Now, this response states:

"Because when hearing a sound in empty space, the ear must necessarily share the same object as the mental consciousness (*manas*); therefore, the ear-consciousness takes the sixth consciousness as its support, not the seventh or eighth."
Regarding the question of what fault there would be if these [consciousnesses] numbered seven and eight were to rely on [the mental faculty] until the end:
although they do not take up objects in the same manner as the fifth and sixth, it is nonetheless not erroneous to say that they rely on the seventh by virtue of its functional power.
[Commentary]: Regarding the objection, "If there were no seventh consciousness, then even the seventh would not have the five consciousnesses as its support;
