yet the seventh does not serve as the support for the five consciousnesses. If the eighth consciousness did not exist, the seventh would not exist—how then can the eighth be said to be the support for the seventh?
This objection is based on an incorrect principle, as it fails to answer by distinguishing between supports in terms of defilement and purity.
In the latter part of the commentary, the response based on the correct principle states: "The eight cases are likewise; the seven are also thus.

The intent of this statement is that there are neither seven nor eight, and since neither seven nor eight are taught as the basis (*āśraya*), this objection regarding the basis is based on an incorrect principle.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The seven [consciousnesses] are not fundamental and do not provide support," the intended meaning is that the seven do not serve as the basis for the five [sensory consciousnesses];
this is the correct principle of the treatise. As for the seventh [consciousness], it serves as the basis for the defilement and purification of the five consciousnesses.
The expression "the above from this text" refers to the fact that within this second section on the evolving consciousness, the explanation of the meaning of the "basis" (āśraya) has been concluded.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "based on the main text below, it is the meaning of the secondary vehicle," the intended meaning is that the passage below which clarifies the three kinds of bases is precisely the meaning of the secondary vehicle.
[Commentary: Regarding "constant" and "not constant," the intent is to state that these specify the essential nature of the basis; "constant" and "fixed" refer to the eighth [consciousness].

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is neither constant nor fixed; it is not present in the five faculties such as the eye, nor does it exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and thus it is neither constant nor fixed.
The eighth [consciousness] possesses all [of these], and is therefore called "constant" and "fixed. That is to say, the six internal faculties serve as its supporting basis (*āśraya*).

The eighth is subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*), and because its causes and conditions are immediate, it is not non-constant. This is as explained in the *Yanyi* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning). Therefore, these three types are now discussed together.

Regarding the terms "constant" and "inconstant," if that which is the dependent (the supported) is designated by the name of its support (the basis), this is all a figurative designation (*prajñapti*). How is this known?

It is as cited below from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, where it says: "Whether the support is taken as the supported, or the supported as the support, these are all figurative designations made according to what is appropriate.
This is precisely what those words mean.
[Commentary: That treatise designates "reason" (*yukti*) as its title because it concerns the basis of names, the objects of dependence, their correspondence, and so forth.

Now, this commentary designates "condition" (*pratyaya*) as its cause because the mind and mental factors have three types of bases: first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); second, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
and third, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Thus, there is a distinction between the two treatises. Furthermore, regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the second...

One interpretation states that the "co-existent support" (sahabhū-āśraya), the "immediately preceding support" (samanantara-āśraya), and the "seed support" (bīja-āśraya) are all designated according to their underlying principle.
[Commentary] The term "only the seed-consciousness" refers to taking both the seeds and the manifest [consciousness] together as the "seed-seed-consciousness."

According to the intention of those who maintain the universal basis (*sarvatra-āśraya*), it is said that this refers universally to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Regarding the intention of those who do not maintain the simultaneous basis (*sahabhū-āśraya*):
the mental faculty (*manas*) is not called the simultaneous basis; rather, they are both termed the equal-and-immediate basis (*samanantara-āśraya*) because they do not exist simultaneously.
[Commentary]: This means that when the preceding [moment of] mind has ceased, it does not take up the mental factors (caitta).

What is intended by this is that both the mind and its mental factors, as appropriate, all take the immediately preceding ceased consciousness as their "opening and guiding" (āvarjana-nayanam) cause. Because this [preceding consciousness] opens the way and guides them into arising, these mental factors are not independent;
therefore, the treatise speaks of "mind and mental factors" based on the totality of the aggregate.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "because *kālanta* has the meaning of 'arriving here'": the intent behind this passage is that it was an error for the ancients to call the *samanantarapratyaya* (immediately preceding condition) the *anantarapratyaya* (condition without interval).
Now, in order to distinguish between the false and the correct, the Sanskrit original is cited to provide a comparative clarification.
[Commentary]: If one says "the support of seeds," the intended meaning is that seeds, in relation to the manifest states they produce, are called the "support of seeds";

that is, the seeds and the manifest states serve as support for one another. The purpose of this passage is to provide a detailed analysis, fearing that there might be confusion regarding the three types of supports.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the seed, when viewed in relation to the seed itself, should lack this basis," it means that a seed is not designated as a "seed" [in its own right] because it is merely subsumed under the category of "seed-type.
An alternate version of the text states: "The manifest, when viewed in relation to the seed, should lack this basis"; this is precisely correct, as explained in the *Yanbi*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the seed and its fruit are simultaneous," the intended meaning is as follows:

If one were to speak only of the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) without mentioning the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), then the seed producing its manifest fruit at the same time would have to be called a co-existent support.

However, because it is distinguished by the term "condition" (*pratyaya*), even though the seed produces the manifest fruit simultaneously, it is not called a co-existent support; therefore, it is said that "it is not the seed."

[Commentary]: "Therefore, the double exclusion" refers to the fact that when the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is said to be based on the [mind], this excludes the seeds and the mental factors (*caitta*).
[Commentary]:
Regarding the passage from "discerning the essence" to "it must not arise," the intention is to state generally that there are differences among these three types of bases.
The seed is called the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). "Dependence" refers to its arising as the direct producer of the essence that gives rise to all phenomena;
for if one were separated from this causal dependence, no other distinct phenomenon could possibly arise. The [remaining] three below should be understood accordingly;
thus, the distinction between the three dependencies is established, as explained in detail within the treatise in the section on the three types of dependencies.

[Commentary]: Now, the hypothetical case—such as that of the Hīnayāna, where [the meditative attainments] are not called "having a basis"—intends to mean that when one speaks specifically of the Hīnayāna masters, their *samādhi* and so forth cannot be called "having a basis. This is not the same as the preceding case of form (*rūpa*).

For instance, regarding form, it is reckoned as having only causes and conditions as its basis, arising from its own nature; therefore, because it lacks the other two bases, it cannot be called "having a basis."

Furthermore, even according to the Hīnayāna, if you grant that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) possesses the fruit of being an immediately antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), it cannot be called "having a basis" (*sāśraya*).

How, then, could it be called the fruit of an immediately antecedent condition? If you argue that when one first abides in this mindless state, the preceding moment of mindlessness acts as the cause that draws forth the subsequent moment of mindlessness, and thus this [subsequent] is named the fruit of the immediately antecedent condition—[we reply:

no. *Note: The original Chinese text contains a parenthetical argument regarding the definition of the *samanantarapratyaya* in the context of the *nirodhasamāpatti*. The translation reflects the logical structure of the refutation.*

Regarding the fruit: the preceding moment serves as the basis for the succeeding moment. This constitutes both the immediate condition (*samanantarāśraya*) and the causal condition (*hetupratyayāśraya*).
That is to say, the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) is the causal condition; because the preceding and succeeding moments are similar, it is termed a "homogeneous cause.

Since one of these types is a mindless state, it can still be said to possess a causal condition. This is because it relates to the meaning of the simultaneous presence (*sahabhū*) and dominant (*adhipati*) conditions as bases.

It cannot be said that [the cessation-attainment] has a basis (*āśraya*). The intention here is merely to state by way of analogy that the cessation-attainment cannot be called "having a basis," and this is not an analogy to the preceding discussion of form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "now there is no moment-to-moment arising and ceasing," that master says: "The great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth do not cease moment by moment;
according to the Sāṃkhya school, there is impermanence through transformation (*pariṇāma-anityatā*), but not impermanence through destruction (*vināśa-anityatā*)."
[Commentary]: People of that time claimed it was composed before [Vasubandhu] had entered the Mahāyāna;

those in the West all maintain that this treatise was composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu before he turned his mind toward the Mahāyāna. Formerly, Vasubandhu propagated the tenets of the Sautrāntika school.

[Commentary]: "There are cases where there is an eye but it is not the eye-element; the same applies [to other instances]. This means that although there is an eye, it is not the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*).

"Element" (*dhātu*) refers to the cause. This implies that while the manifest eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) may exist, the seed of that faculty is absent—such as, for example, the final eye-faculty of one in the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this refers to both the prior and the subsequent," this master’s intention is to say that the extinction of the seed and the arising of the sprout—the cause and effect—are not simultaneous.

If that is so, how does he interpret the scriptural passage stating that among the six characteristics of the seed, two are "simultaneously present with the fruit" (*phala-sahabhū*)? This master explains it as follows:

the term "simultaneously present with the fruit" is based on the designation of "prior and subsequent," and "simultaneous" itself refers to the period of the sprout's arising; thus, simultaneity can indeed exist.

The meaning does not require that cause and effect be simultaneous in every moment. Regarding "arising and ceasing together," the intended sense is that it merely states that the two dharmas of cause and effect both arise and both cease together;
it does not state that cause and effect arise and cease simultaneously in every single moment.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* stating "it is not this very same thought," this master explains that [the seeds] acting as causes for other natures refer to seeds producing manifest states (*pravṛtti*), whereas acting as causes for their own subsequent natures refers to seeds producing seeds.
These two phenomena do not belong to the same moment of thought; this general critique accords with the intended meaning of various teachings.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "at this time the conditions are lacking," this refers to the final aggregate (*skandha*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and does not refer to the production of seeds from seeds at other times.

[Commentary]: As for the statement "the meaning of the inference below should be understood," one should formulate an inference against the former master as follows: "The production of the manifest (*nimitta*) from the seed must necessarily..."
Because they are simultaneously cause and effect, like a flame and its wick, etc.

[Commentary]: Alternatively, if those external phenomena were not caused by internal seeds as their causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), then external phenomena such as barley would not have real causal conditions.
You may maintain that these are causal conditions, but since I do not maintain this, they are not causal conditions.
I merely intend this [seed] to be the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and do not say that those conventional dharmas (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) are the causal condition.
As for the statement that they are "not similar," this refers to the production of manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) from the seeds of form and mind.

[Commentary]: Regarding this Great Dharma Master’s statement up to "different moments of thought arise," the master’s intention is to say that because the faculties are the cause and consciousness is the fruit, they do not exist simultaneously.
Furthermore, this is stated according to the Sautrāntika school. Moreover, regarding the five faculties arising in different moments of thought within the same category:

some say that since the five material faculties belong to the same category, two eye-faculties from two different realms cannot arise concurrently; therefore, it is said they arise in different moments of thought.

Furthermore, although the seeds of the faculties have already ceased, the present faculties still exist, as in the case of the final aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa); thus, they are not the same as the basis for mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Since this section distinguishes between other-nature (*parabhāva*) and self-nature (*svabhāva*), it should be understood that this [interpretation] does not correspond to the current text.
Although there are three interpretations, the former is superior, as it challenges the opponent’s admission that visual consciousness occurs at a different time.

[Commentary]: Regarding that which "should be analyzed," the analysis of whether seeds and manifestations are simultaneous or occur at different times is explained in the tenth fascicle, in the section on the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "The World-Honored One" to "the teaching of non-self," the intended meaning is as follows: what does this text state? The answer is that it explains the seed as...
Regarding the "faculties" (*indriya*): because people cling to the body as being the self, he then explains to them: "This body possesses only the five faculties and the five objects such as form;
where is there a self? Those capable of receiving the teaching of non-self will then attain understanding.

Although there are twelve bases (*āyatana*), for now he speaks only of the five faculties such as the eye and the five objects such as form, without discussing the two bases of mind (*manas*) and mental phenomena (*dharma*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that Dharmapāla provides the commentary: for the time being, it is established that both the verses and the prose of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* were composed by Vasubandhu himself.

As for the question of why it is said here that Dharmapāla provides the commentary, the answer is as follows: Dharmapāla’s commentary was indeed composed separately in two fascicles, titled the *Dacheng Weishi Lun Shi* (Commentary on the Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi), which explains that *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
[Commentary]: The intention of this master is to state that both the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) are called "one's own seeds.

This means to show that the five consciousnesses arise from the seeds of their respective image-parts as their dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); thus, it is said that consciousness arises from its own seeds.
This is the explanation regarding the seeds of karma.
[Commentary]: The Buddha spoke of these two, namely the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the three explanations, they are as previously stated; that is, in the preceding explanation of the verse, there were three interpretations of the term "one's own seeds" (*svabīja*).
Therefore, the Commentary states: "There are three types of 'own' (i.e., *sva*), such as the 'own' of causal conditions," and so forth. Now, within this prose commentary, five [points] are explained.
The seed of consciousness is explained according to the preceding interpretation.

[Commentary: This means that just as each of its own seeds has three types, it is intended to show that not only do the "own seeds" mentioned in the preceding verse have three types, but the functional capacity upon consciousness also has three types;
thus, both explanations are termed "having three types. There is indeed this [distinction].
Regarding the correlation of the three meanings: one will see that the three meanings—division (*bheda*), seed (*bīja*), and so forth—are correlated with the functional capacity (*śakti*).
[Commentary: The passage from "producing the consciousness of form" (*rūpa-vijñāna*) to "is not, in its essence, form" (*na rūpam eva*) is to be read as a continuous sequence.

[Commentary] Alternatively, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is called "form" (*rūpa*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); because these two share the same seed, they are termed "form-consciousness" and so forth.
The intent of this passage is as follows: within the commentary on "form-consciousness," there are three interpretations.

From the section beginning with "it is not necessary to differentiate" up to "therefore it is said that manifest consciousness is named form-consciousness," the first interpretation is that the subjective aspect of consciousness transforms into something resembling form; thus, they are one. This constitutes the first solution.

Alternatively, because the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the form (*rūpa*) are not separate, this is the second interpretation. These two interpretations hold that both the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*) and the perceived aspect arise from distinct seeds.
Or, the perceived aspect is called "form" (*rūpa*); this is the third interpretation, which represents the position of those who maintain that the two aspects arise from the same seed.

Regarding the first of these two interpretations involving distinct seeds: as for "consciousness," it refers to the functional capacity of the eighth consciousness; as for the "seeing aspect," it refers to the seeds of the five sensory consciousnesses.

Because the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of consciousness manifests as resembling form, it is called "form-consciousness" (*rūpavijñapti*). This consciousness is the seed of form-consciousness and is termed the "functional capacity for form.
Since this capacity serves to establish the distinctions among the ten bases (*āyatana*), it is metaphorically designated as the "fundamental.

Because this [consciousness] and its objective form have mutually depended upon one another since beginningless time, they are said to be "mutually conditions" (*anyonyapratyaya*). The term "condition" (*pratyaya*) carries the sense of cause, basis, and reason.

Furthermore, because the sense organ (*indriya*) exists in dependence upon its object, and because the object exists in dependence upon the organ, the organ possesses the functional capacity to illuminate [the object].

Since they rely upon one another, the organ is the *pratyaya* (condition) for the manifest consciousness; thus, the seeds of the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving portion) are called "illuminating" because they depend on the organ.

Regarding the second interpretation, the *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Alternatively, that which is not separate from the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective portion) is the color-function of the eighth consciousness. This means:
The seeds of the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the five consciousnesses rely upon the [storehouse consciousness] to constitute the ten bases; these are explained as the five sense organs.

From beginningless time, these [seeds] act as perfumers (*vāsaka*) of the objective aspects and, together with the perfumed (*vāsya*), form the seeds of the five objects. These perfumers and the perfumed serve as mutual causes and conditions;

because the perfumers produce various manifestations of active states (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), they act as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) in relation to the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).

Based on this, the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is called "form" (*rūpa*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). This master asserts that "consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness.

As for the "functional capacity," it refers to the seeds of the objective and subjective aspects of the five consciousnesses; because they share the same seeds, these seeds of the objective and subjective aspects are designated as the "five faculties" (*pañcendriya*) in the sense that they serve as the basis for their respective locations.

These, together with the objective forms (*viṣayarūpa*), have from beginningless time been mutually related as the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed (*vāsya*), acting as causes for one another.
Furthermore, according to this master, when these characteristics meet, they collectively constitute the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*).

The relationship between the five faculties and consciousness is likewise one of causal condition (*pratyaya*), meaning they act as causes for one another. These three points should be thoroughly examined by all subsequent commentators.

This is also detailed in the *Yanmi* (Secrets of Exposition), which fully explains the functions of the aforementioned [three] interpretations and distinguishes the objective spheres (*viṣaya-rūpa*) based on the latter three interpretations.
[Commentary]: Because the preceding two moments of the characteristics of consciousness do not contradict reason, there is a specific explanation:

the characteristics of the preceding moment of consciousness induce a functional capacity within the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) regarding matter; this capacity then arises and produces the consciousness of matter. "Resembling itself" means resembling matter.
"The fruit" refers to the manifest consciousness of matter. "Functional capacity" refers to the seed. That is, the characteristics of the preceding moment of consciousness induce [the capacity].
It is logically consistent that the capacity within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) which resembles its own fruit causes the manifest consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) to arise;
this is a general statement, which will be explained in detail below.
[Commentary: "That which gives rise to the present manifest" refers to the seeds of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) perfumed previously, giving rise to the present manifest objective aspect.

It is also said that "form-consciousness" (rūpa-vijñāna) refers to the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) inducing the five simultaneous sensory consciousnesses, which are thus called form-consciousness.

Others say that the objective aspect produced by the seeds of the objective aspect from the preceding moment arises as the present active objective aspect; because this objective aspect is not separate from consciousness, it is termed form-consciousness.

[Commentary]: The passage from "As for the direct objective aspect (*sākṣāt-nimitta-bhāga*)" to "is called the object-condition (*ālambana*)" intends to explain that the simultaneous direct objective aspect arises as a reflection (*pratibimba*) for the production of the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*).

Because it has substance, the objective aspect is produced by conditions; thus, it is "with substance. The term "reflection" refers to the consciousness perceiving the objective aspect through two transformations of the reflection;

that which is perceived is the reflected objective aspect. Regarding the phrase "called the mode of activity (*ākāra*)," it means that which manifests upon the consciousness is named the mode of activity.
"To serve as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) refers precisely to the image-aspect (nimitta-bhāga) of the representation.

[The Sub-commentary] states: "Regarding the statement 'mutually acting as causes' down to the point where it says 'this is based on the prose section,' this explains the reason why seeds and the consciousness of form act as mutual causes, according to the prose commentary."

[Commentary]: If one holds that the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) reaching [the object] is the cause, then one is asserting that the seeds of the seeing-part serve as the condition (*pratyaya*). In this case, the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) becomes the consciousness of form;
thus, there would be no principle of causal conditionality between the sense organ (*indriya*) and its object (*viṣaya*), for "cause" refers to the fundamental reason.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the object requires the function of the faculty," the intention is this: this interpretation means that they act as mutual causes because, through the functioning of the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) serving as a condition for the *darśanabhāga* (perceiving aspect), once the *darśanabhāga* has arisen, it perfumes [the consciousness] to produce various functions capable of generating future resultant consciousnesses;

thus it is said that "the object requires the function of the faculty. If the faculty requires the function of the object, then the manifest faculty serves as the condition to give rise to the manifest consciousness, which then undergoes transformation.

Because it resembles the preceding object, it is said that the object must be employed; this means that the functional capacity (*śakti*) and the objective sphere (*viṣaya*), as well as the faculties (*indriya*) and the objects (*rūpa*), act as causes for one another.

[Commentary: The meaning of "there is no separate, substantially existent [entity]" is that one takes only the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*) as the faculty (*indriya*); apart from these, there is no substantial reality.

[Commentary]: At times when the characteristics are concordant, they provide momentum; for example, when the sixth consciousness enters the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-darśana*), the seventh [consciousness]—being with-outflows (*sāsrava*)—does not provide assistance, whereas at other times it does provide assistance.

[Commentary]: Although there is in reality no form, it appears as if it were form and so forth. This is because the master Ananta (Anhui) posits that the two parts—the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) and the aspect of the object (*nimitta-bhāga*)—are both products of universal conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

To refute this, [the text] states: "Because they appear as if they were form. Thus, although the master Ananta previously [raised objections], among the ten difficulties regarding the non-universality [of consciousness], these are:
first, the difficulty of the confusion of the elements; second, the difficulty of both being non-existent; third, the difficulty of the contradiction with the four conditions; fourth...

The fifth difficulty concerns the difference in the attachment of the sense organs and consciousnesses; the seventh difficulty concerns the lack of parity; the ninth difficulty concerns the deficiency of one among the three bases;
the tenth difficulty concerns the claim that the sense organs are merely seeds. Regarding the commentary’s statement, "the seeds of form as well," the intended meaning is this:

if you take the seeds of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of consciousness to be the seeds of consciousness capable of producing the five sensory consciousnesses, then the confusion [of categories] is established.
This is a confusion.

[Commentary: This differs from the previous objection regarding seeds. The former objection, based on the identity of the perceived object (*nimitta*), argued that if the seed of the object were identical to the seed of consciousness, then the seeds of the eighteen realms would become intermingled and confused.

[Commentary]: In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the four propositions concerning the fifty-six elements (*dhātu*), it says: "For example, there is that which is not an element (*adhātu*) yet possesses its own eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*);
this is not an element, because 'element' has the meaning of being a seed-cause (*bīja-hetu*). There is also that which possesses its own element but is not the eye-faculty;

all internal factors (*dharma*) such as these are likewise [to be understood]. There is that which is a manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) but not a seed-element-cause; therefore, there is that which is a seed-element but..."
The current operation [of the faculties] and so forth should be understood by analogy. Furthermore, regarding the fourfold classification (*catuṣkoṭi*) in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it asks:
"If there is an eye, is there also the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)? Or if there is the eye-element, is there also an eye? It should be answered by means of a fourfold classification:
"There may be an eye but not the eye-element," and so forth, as explained at length therein; one should abandon [any other views] in accordance with that.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the four elements pertain to a portion of the remaining form-realm (*rūpadhātu*)-bound [factors]," the intent is as follows:

the "four elements" refer to the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue, along with the two objects of odor and flavor; thus they are called the four elements. The "two bases" refer to the two bases of odor and flavor. These are exclusively bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As for "a portion of the remainder," this refers to the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body, and the three objects of visible form, tangible objects, and sound—these six.
The dharmas generally pertain to both the desire realm and the form realm; however, since we are currently speaking only of those that exist within the desire realm, it is said:

"and a portion of those bound to the form realm. This excludes the four elements and two bases mentioned previously; the remaining portion pertains to both the desire realm and the form realm. Since we are now discussing those existing in the form realm, it is said:
"the remaining portion" refers specifically to the five faculties, as well as the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body, along with visible form, tangibles, and sounds.
[This refers to] the three objects.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that because those [objects] possess sense-faculties (*indriya*), it is clear that manifest consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) exists—the intended meaning is that if the seeds of consciousness serve as the faculties, and since those [seeds] exist there, manifest consciousness can also be obtained.

[Commentary: Regarding the two "reversals" and two "concessions," the intent is as follows: If one concedes that the seeds of consciousness are themselves the sense organs, then since the organs would be identical to consciousness, they should belong exclusively to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

If one concedes that the seeds of the two types of consciousness are themselves the two organs, then since the consciousnesses would be identical to the nose and tongue organs, they would also pertain to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), because those realms possess the organs [and thus could have manifest consciousness].
The refutation states: both of these reversals and concessions contradict the scriptures.

[Commentary]: It is not so; otherwise, it would contradict reason. "Appropriation" (upādi) means to grasp [the seeds] as one's own essence and cause them to produce sensation and awareness; this is called appropriation.

Seeds are not called appropriation in this sense. However, from the perspective of the eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which maintains and preserves [them] without loss, seeds are also considered appropriation.
If one does not rely on the production of sensation and awareness, but merely states that the sense organs (indriya) possess appropriation while seeds lack it, [it would be incorrect].
This would contradict the passage concerning the "appropriation of seeds.
[Commentary: The meaning of the statement that "one portion of the five types is not appropriated" is as follows: the five sense objects (pañca-viṣaya) pertain to both the internal and external;

since those within are appropriated and those without are not, it is said to be "one portion. However, although sound is insubstantial and sparse, it is also termed "appropriated," according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
It is said that there are those who maintain that the sound of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is non-appropriated (*anupātta*), and so forth.

[Commentary: If the seeds of the five faculties and the five consciousnesses are taken as the subject for the sake of establishing a commonality, the formal argument (*prayoga*) would be as follows: The sixth faculty, the mental faculty (*manas*), is the subject;

it must have the seeds of the mental consciousness as its property (*dharma*), because it is included within one of the six faculties; the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is like the visual faculty," etc., which serves as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the fifth point, "The same logic should apply to the other dharmas," the intent is as follows: If the sixth consciousness possessed manifest sense organs (*indriya*), then the five material sense organs would clearly not be seeds.
It is said that the five organs are definitely not seeds because they are included within one of the six organs, just like the mental organ (*manas*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "First, there would be no seeds" to "the six faculties would lose their status as seeds," the intent is this:

if one were to take the seeds of karma as the five faculties, then the aforementioned six types of faults would not occur. However, these six types of faults are all arguments from the treatise itself directed against the previous master.
Those six [faults] can be understood from that treatise.
[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of Sthiramati’s refutation of the ten objections below: the previous master avoided this fault by taking the seeds of karma as the root.

Thus, Sthiramati presents his ten points of refutation to challenge the previous master: (1) the fault that karma, which encompasses both good and evil natures, would have a root that is exclusively indeterminate;
(2) the fault that vocal and mental karma would lack the nature of being appropriated (*upātta*); (3) the fault that karma would encompass the body... [text truncated].

1. The fault that the vocal faculty (*vāg-indriya*) and the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) would both pertain to two aggregates (*skandha*). 2. The fault that the fourth [action]—action pertaining to form, sound, phenomena (*dharma*), and mind—would not be an internal base (*ādhyātma-āyatana*).

3. The fault that the fifth—the seeds of the faculties of nose and tongue—would belong only to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). 4. The fault that the sixth—the consciousness and the action induced by the mental faculty—would have to be the manas-consciousness (*manovijñāna*). 5.

The fault that the seventh—the material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) which are themselves seeds of action—would lack the quality of being present (*pratyutpanna*). 6. The fault that the eighth—action—is material (*rūpa*).

[If] sound were [the result of] volition, it would follow that it is not a material sense-faculty (this is the ninth fault). [If] the five consciousnesses were exclusively indeterminate, it would follow that they are not produced by karma (this is the tenth fault).

[If] wholesome consciousness were not produced by karma, it would follow that the faculties are not co-existent [with it] (this is the eleventh fault). It is said that for wholesome karma, such as visual consciousness and so forth, there are no co-existent faculties because they are not produced by karma.
[Commentary: Second, regarding those based on the matter of bodily karma (*kāyakarma-rūpa*) and so forth: the seeds of mental karma (*manaskarma-bīja*) pervade all three types of karma.

If one reckons the seeds of karma as being the five sense-faculties (*indriya*), then take, for example, bodily karma: it refers to the karma created in dependence upon the physical body (*rūpakāya*).

Because there is appropriation (*upādāna*) with respect to the physical body, the perfumed seeds (*vāsana-bīja*) are taken as the faculties. These faculties may indeed possess appropriation; however, this is not the case for the two [kinds of karma], namely speech and mind, which do not previously exist [as such].

Because it takes as its root the seeds of karma that are appropriated (*upātta*) and perfumed (*vāsita*), the argument that "the sense-faculties would incur the fault of being non-appropriated" is merely a statement of sound.
[The opponent] asks: "Are the three types of sound non-appropriated? [The respondent] answers: "Sound is not separate from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*); therefore, sound is appropriated.
If it were separate from the primary elements, its substance would be hollow and sparse, and thus it would be non-appropriated."
[Commentary]: Regarding the fault that the sense bases (*āyatana*) would consist of both the form (*rūpa*) and formation (*saṃskāra*) aggregates:

since karma has volition (*cetanā*) as its essence, and volition is classified within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), all three types of karma have volition as their essence. Volition is the substantial karma, while body and speech are nominal (conventional) karma.
Because the nominal and substantial are here spoken of together, there is the fault that the sense bases would consist of both the form and formation aggregates.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "karma extends to form, sound, and mental phenomena (dharma)," the intended meaning is that when form and sound are said to extend to both internal and external phenomena, this refers to volition (*cetanā*).
"Karma" is a general designation that encompasses both the provisional and the real; therefore, it is said that karma extends to form, sound, and mental phenomena.

As for the inclusion of mental karma within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), this is because the essence of mental karma is volition, and among the twelve spheres, volition is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects; thus, it is [included] in its entirety.
The meaning is this: through volition (*cetanā*), wholesome and unwholesome forms and sounds are impelled, and these perfumed impressions constitute the various types of karmic seeds.

If one takes these karmic seeds as the "root," then that root is not merely an internal sense-base (*ādhyātmikāyatana*). Some claim that "dharmas" refers to the dharma-object (*dharmālambana*), and that since dharma-objects encompass both internal and external factors such as the wholesome and unwholesome, [this is the case].
This is not so; for how could there be karmic seeds of the dharma-object serving as the root of sound? The former interpretation is superior.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "these two or three consciousnesses... it is likewise," above, because the faculties were challenged by way of the consciousnesses, it was said that the three faculties should not be bound to the five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*) and so forth.
Now, as the consciousnesses are being challenged by way of the faculties, it follows that the consciousnesses should also be pervasive across the five stages;
therefore, it is said that the counter-challenge is likewise.

[Commentary]: "The essence of the five consciousnesses should be identical to their karmic seeds" means that since the karmic seeds of the five consciousnesses are identical to the material sense organs (*rūpindriya*), the karmic seeds of the sixth mental consciousness should likewise be identical to the manas (the seventh consciousness).
Regarding the absence of the fault of non-manifestation for the seventh [consciousness] and the eyes and so forth:

the Sage taught that the essence of the eye organ (*cakṣurindriya*) actually comprises both the manifest and the seed; if the organ were constituted solely by its karmic seeds, then the five organs would be nothing but seeds.
There is no manifestation.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "karma consists of form, sound, and volition," the intended meaning is that form, sound, and volition are explained as the karma of form and sound, taking volition as their essence.
The Commentary takes the seeds of karma as the root; the root should therefore not be material form, as explained in the Ximing Commentary.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because its substance is subsumed under form, sound, and mind," the meaning is as follows: the substance of the three types of action (*tri-karma*) is precisely the volition (*cetanā*) that initiates body, speech, and mind;
because it is associated with these three types of action, it is said to be "subsumed" by them.
[Commentary]: If one says that it reaches the stage where it is not merely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), then this karmic seed could potentially give rise to the five consciousnesses;

however, since the five consciousnesses are themselves indeterminate, and because the karma has not yet matured to actually summon the five consciousnesses, the five consciousnesses rely upon those karmic seeds and thus can pertain to all three natures.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the faculties are designated according to their conditions," karma itself is the condition. Karma acts as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that summons and brings about the five material faculties (*rūpīndriya*), which are capable of generating the five consciousnesses.

To say that those [faculties] are "karma" is based on the fact that they are summoned by it; conversely, to say that the faculties are "karma" is stated from the perspective of their capacity to summon [the consciousnesses].
[Commentary]: "Consciousness arises and transforms into something resembling an object" means it is like an external realm.

[Commentary]: "That which resembles the eye-faculty" refers to the refutation of the real material sense-faculties; it clarifies that "resembling the faculty" means resembling the grasping at a real faculty within the deluded mind.

[Commentary]: For example, when one born in the Desire Realm possesses the eye faculty, why does one not see objects? Since one possesses visual consciousness, that consciousness cannot be without its seeds;
these seeds are precisely the faculty. Why then, at the time when the material faculty is absent, does consciousness not arise to see objects?
Since one does not see objects [without it], it is clear that there must be a distinct faculty which, by giving rise to consciousness, enables one to see.

[Commentary: Regarding the "original transformation of the two views," the two verses previously cited and their explanation concern the original view (*mūla-kalpa*), which holds that [the self] arises from existence (*bhava*).

To avoid the aforementioned logical fallacies, there follows the "transformed view" (*parivṛtta-kalpa*). Since both are now reconciled simultaneously, they are referred to as being "doubly restated. Thus, the treatise states:
"It is not meant that the physical sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) are identical to consciousness or the seeds of karma."
[Commentary]: "If the former master says... up to "...is not the basis for the manifest" is a restatement of the former master’s position.
"It should be said that there is the *ālayavijñāna*... which exist in mutual dependence" is a critique of the former master. The critique states:

If you say that [the manifest consciousness] depends upon seeds, then the treatise should have stated, "Because the *ālayavijñāna* exists, the *manovijñāna* arises. Why, then, does it speak of them in a reciprocal manner?
Because the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) exists, the manas exists; and because the manas serves as its support, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is able to function.
Why is it that these [consciousnesses] exist in relation to one another in such a successive manner?

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the former master speaks of the "successive progression" up to the sixth [consciousness], this refers to the former master’s repeated defense seen previously.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) exists, the manas exists; depending upon the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises.

This is said in general terms based on the manifest functioning (*pravṛtti*) of the faculties, not based on their seeds. Consequently, the former master, relying on this passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, attempts to defend his own position, stating:
"When the sixth [consciousness] seed intends to produce its manifest functioning, it must necessarily follow along with the seventh [manas]."
If the seventh seed gives rise to its manifest activity, only then does the sixth seed give rise to its manifest activity;

it is with reference to this successive process that it is also said to have the seeds as its support. Thus, the treatise states: "Because of the existence of the manas, the mental consciousness can function," and so forth.
[Commentary: It is not so; the same logic applies to the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*). Furthermore, there is another objection:

"If it is argued that the sixth [consciousness] depends on the seventh and thus can be described through a series of dependencies, then the five consciousnesses should likewise depend on the five sense-faculties.

As for the statement in the *Śāstra* (the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*) that "it is because of the existence of the eighth consciousness that the five sense-faculties exist, and the five consciousnesses further function in dependence upon the five sense-faculties," since the existence of the five consciousnesses is already admitted...

If it is argued that the sixth consciousness, as a manifest state, depends on the seventh as its co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), and that the seventh seed in turn depends on the sixth, such that they are said to depend on one another, then when the five consciousnesses depend upon the sixth, they too should depend on the sixth seeds. This objection is raised because the former masters do not allow the five consciousnesses to depend on the sixth seeds.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: if the sixth consciousness-seed wishes to arise as a manifest state, it must necessarily follow the [seventh].

Regarding the manifestation of the seven types [of consciousness] through conditions: for example, when the seed of one consciousness is about to arise and manifest, it should likewise follow along with the seeds of the five sense-faculties (*indriya*) before it can arise as an active manifestation (*pravṛtti*).
Why? Because each type possesses its own distinct seed. As for the "distinct faculties," this refers to the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*).
Furthermore, in response to the objection: "Do the five consciousnesses not have distinct faculties?"—it is not accepted that the seeds of the sixth consciousness possess such [distinct faculties].

The distinct faculties (*bhinna-indriya*) should likewise be sixfold and not follow the sevenfold [classification]. Furthermore, it is explained that the former master took the seeds of the five consciousnesses as the five faculties;
since the six [consciousnesses] arise from the seeds of the six when manifesting in dependence upon the seventh, he said that the six depend on the seven.
Now, this is refuted: such is not possible; rather, one should speak of the five consciousnesses.
If it is granted that seeds arise following those five sense-faculties as their seeds, then one must likewise grant that the five consciousnesses have distinct faculties;
how then can it be said, as previously stated, that the seeds of consciousness constitute the five faculties?

[Commentary]: This is as explained in the *Abhidharma* regarding the sense-sphere of consciousness belonging to the eye. As for the explanation in the second chapter of the *Abhidharma* concerning the basis of visual consciousness, it states:
"The consciousness that depends on the eye is the consciousness belonging to the eye," which is explained in detail in the text.

Regarding the commentary’s mention of "the six having simultaneous dependence," the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: The seventh [consciousness] has simultaneous dependence because it possesses the quality of transition, just like the preceding six.
[Commentary on] "Consciousness": The commentary states that by analogy with the seed-consciousness, the manifest [consciousness] should also have a basis.
This means that since the manifest consciousness already has a basis in the seeds, by analogy, the manifest [consciousness] should likewise have a basis.

[Treatise]: If it is granted that the manifesting consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes seeds as its support, then it must also be granted that the seed-consciousness takes the manifest consciousness as its support.

This clarifies that the eighth [consciousness] as a seed has two kinds of supports: first, its own eighth manifest consciousness; second, the seven perfuming consciousnesses. This is an explanation by way of implication (*arthāpatti*);
what harm is there in the meaning that the functioning of the manifest consciousness takes seeds as its support? By implication, how could this not apply to seeds?
The eighth [point] takes the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) as its basis; "manifest" here refers to the eight consciousnesses collectively.

Therefore, it is said that the seeds depend on their own eighth consciousness, yet they also depend on the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*). As the treatise below states: "In the initial stage of perfuming, one also depends on the perfumer.

Furthermore, regarding the question of why the seeds of consciousness must be admitted to depend on the manifest consciousness, Master Mǎo says: "Although there is an explanation in the *Śū* (the *Cheng weishi lun shuji*), I shall now further..."

The commentary states: Master Jingyue, having seen that Nanda says the five consciousnesses take their own five consciousness-seeds as simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*), also asserts that seeds take the manifest consciousness as their simultaneous support.
Therefore, it is said below: "In the initial stage of perfuming, they also depend on the perfumer;
later, they depend on the eighth [consciousness]; both are simultaneous supports."

[Commentary: Regarding the point that both parties agree that active consciousnesses take seeds as their support—just as it was previously stated that "seeds depend on [consciousness]" and so forth—the present argument intends to show that seeds must likewise depend on active consciousness;

specifically, it means that the eighth consciousness’s seeds depend on the active consciousness. Therefore, the text below states: "In the stage of initial perfuming, they also depend on the capacity..."
Furthermore, perfuming also depends upon the manifest consciousness that is perfumed; as the subsequent treatise states:

"The perfuming agent and the ripening [consciousness] serve as the basis for the growth and abiding [of seeds]," which explains that the perfuming agent acts as the basis for the growth of the seeds, while the eighth ripening consciousness acts as the basis for the abiding of the seeds.
Moreover, when this treatise maintains that seeds depend upon the manifest consciousness, it refers to all eight consciousnesses, not merely the eighth.

The eight [types of consciousness] exclude only those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind, because they do not perfume to form seeds, nor do they serve as a support for seeds;
therefore, they are not included. [Commentary:

If it is argued that the treatise falls into the fallacy of lacking a similar example (*asādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), [we reply]: if, as the treatise states, one admits that the manifest consciousness takes seeds...

If you claim that the "cause-condition support" (*hetu-pratyaya-āśraya*) refers to the present establishment of the relationship between the active manifestation (*pravṛtti*) and its seeds (*bīja*), then there would be no analogous example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Why? Because the seed is the cause-condition support for the manifestation, whereas the manifestation is the co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) for the seed.
How could one take the cause-condition support as an analogous example for the co-existent support? However, if one follows exactly what is stated in the treatise (*śāstra*), there is no fault.
Now it should be said that seeds take the present activity as their co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).

The reason is that they are subsumed under either one of the two—seeds or present activity—and the analogy is that, when considering the present in relation to the seed, it is difficult for the present alone to be the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the seed. The intention of this master is as follows:
if considered in relation to the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*), its essence is subsumed under the causal condition; if considered in relation to its simultaneous efficacy, it is a co-existent support.
The inclusion of "presently grasping" as the illustrative example here serves to capture the meaning of the "simultaneously existing support" (sahabhū-āśraya).
If it were not so, there would be no analogous example; for this reason, the treatise does not state that the manifest [state] takes the seed as its causal condition (hetu-pratyaya).
[Commentary]: Why is it now stated that "it should also serve as a basis," and so forth?

According to the intent of the objection, since this seed is already admitted to serve as a basis within the category of "basis for present conditions," why is it now stated that it "should also serve as a simultaneous basis"?
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Now, those who assist in the explanation," there are three interpretations below: first, taking all manifest activities (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*);
second, taking all maturation (*vipāka*) consciousnesses; third, the interpretation that it refers exclusively to the manifest eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
[Commentary]: Now, regarding this master’s point that [the present] establishes the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), the intent of this answer is as follows:

Previously, it was explained that the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is broad and pervasive, thus applying to both seeds and the present. However, here we are specifically analyzing the support of seeds in relation to the present;

since the manifest state is not the support for seeds, the support of seeds is called a "simultaneous support" only insofar as it relates to the present. Although this interpretation states that the present and the seed constitute the causal condition, it is merely...

Because it serves as the basis for the growth and development within the substance that emerges from below, it constitutes a co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*); furthermore, the support for remaining and abiding is also a co-existent support.

[Commentary: Moreover, although the manifest state (*pravṛtti*) in relation to seeds is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), when considering the manifest state in relation to the remainder, all are capable of perfuming (*vāsana*).

This point means that although it was previously established within the discussion of causal conditions that the manifest state serves as the support for consciousness, this only includes those things capable of perfuming.

According to the eighth [consciousness] and other resultant (*vipāka*) minds and mental factors, which are incapable of perfuming, they lack power with respect to their own seeds because they do not serve as the support for those seeds;
therefore, this does not mention other active minds. Why is it not mentioned?
It is because these [other minds] are subsumed under the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the support condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*), and for that reason, they are not mentioned here.
[Commentary: The statement "because all others are capable of perfuming" explains why it does not mention the reason for the manifestation of other mental states.
The phrase "in relation to the manifesting of the ripening [consciousness]" (*vipāka*) serves to identify the simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
Although this is stated generally, the intention is specifically to refer to the eighth consciousness, because other types of ripening do not serve as supports for seeds.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the fact that all manifesting consciousnesses (*vijñapti*) and their maturation (*vipāka*) possess simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*), which are not mentioned here in brief:

this explanation applies universally to all manifesting consciousnesses and their maturations, as they all possess simultaneous supports. The seeds cited as examples are the same as the manifest states;
thus, they too should possess simultaneous supports. This point will be demonstrated below when defining their essential nature.
It is not said that the maturation (*vipāka*) of these various consciousnesses is omitted for brevity.

Next, because [the other consciousnesses] lack power over their seeds and cannot serve as a support, and because the eighth consciousness serves as the support of abiding (*sthiti-āśraya*), when identifying the essential nature [of the seeds], one specifically takes this eighth consciousness’s maturation as the support of the seeds.

Why is it not analogously applied to the other perfuming consciousnesses in their active manifestation (*pravṛtti*)? The answer is: because those [other consciousnesses], in relation to their own seeds, are themselves capable of perfuming.
Because it serves as a support (*āśraya*), it is not treated as an example for what follows; that which serves as a support within the middle [category] is also taken as a support.
However, this takes the sense of being a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) and does not take the sense of being a causal condition support (*hetu-pratyaya-āśraya*).

If one were to follow the previous inquiry, the seed-support of the manifest consciousness would be the eighth consciousness alone, and the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) would not be mentioned. Yet, according to the following text, the seven evolving consciousnesses are also included as superior supports. Furthermore...
Regarding the phrase "because it is abbreviated," the six active consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) cannot simultaneously perfuse seeds;
nor, in relation to those seeds, do they function as *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions), unlike the eighth consciousness. Because this is abbreviated in the text, it is not mentioned separately.

Furthermore, these six consciousnesses induced by karma lack the power over seeds and cannot maintain them, unlike the eighth consciousness. Since they appear incapable of perfuming, they differ from the others.
"Seventh, it is the basis in relation to seeds and non-seeds.

[Commentary: Only the eighth consciousness, in relation to its manifest state, is this "basis. This refers specifically to the eighth consciousness's manifest state as the simultaneous basis (*sahabhū-āśraya*).

Among the three previous explanations, the first and last interpretations are taken as superior. In the first explanation, the seed-basis consists of both the perfuming agent (*vāsaka*) and the perfumed object (*vāsya*).

Regarding the seeds of subsequent liberation for all active manifestations, they rely solely on the eighth consciousness; according to the two interpretations in the following section of the treatise, this [eighth consciousness] must be accepted as the superior one.
Next, below that, the reason why the manifest consciousness serves as the support for the seeds is explained; therefore, all eight consciousnesses are supports for the seeds.

[Commentary]: This statement—that the seeds of maturation take the manifest state as their support—intends to explain that the function of the seed takes the manifest state as its simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
When it says that the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) of the seed takes the manifest state as its causal substance, it uses the simultaneous support of the manifest state as an illustration;
that is, it illustrates how the function of the seed takes the manifest state as its simultaneous support.
Regarding the basis, the treatise states: "If one admits that the manifest consciousness takes seeds as its basis, then one must also admit that seeds take the manifest consciousness as their basis.

It is said that since the manifest state is both a cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) in relation to the seeds—because the manifest state produces and nurtures the seeds—and since the ripening consciousness (*vipāka*) serves as the support for their persistence, this constitutes the fundamental [basis] for both the original and newly perfumed [seeds].
This is because the meaning of the various schools' doctrines is fully established.
[Commentary] "Entirely not relying on that which can grasp and maintain" means that the sixth consciousness does not rely on the five sense organs;
unlike the five consciousnesses, which each rely individually on the eye and so forth, it is therefore said to be "entirely not relying. This refers to what follows: "there is none."
The reason is that it does not have even a partial dependence on material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*). Therefore, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated as follows:
The sixth consciousness is the subject (*dharmin*); it is also capable of appropriating a body possessing material sense-faculties, which is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).
It lacks even a partial dependence on the seven faculties; this is the reason (*hetu*). This is analogous to the eighth consciousness as you yourself have admitted.
[Commentary]: It is said that "the first six consciousnesses are also capable of appropriating [the body]," etc. To establish a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*) based on this text is a great error.

Since these [six consciousnesses] do not rely upon the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) even in part, how could they appropriate that which possesses material sense organs? Therefore, it constitutes an error.
[Commentary]: "Lacking the proper measure" refers to the refutation of the eighth [consciousness], which lacks the measure of being appropriated (*upātta*).
[Commentary]: "The five consciousnesses are not established" because their respective individual supports (*āśraya*) do not constitute appropriation.

[Commentary: The reason the sixth consciousness does not rely separately on the material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*) is that the sixth is distinct from the five [sensory] consciousnesses, which do rely separately on the material sense organs.

In the proof concerning the "appropriated" (*sopādāna*) nature of the fourth [consciousness], it states that they "rely separately," because this is due to the fact that [the reliance] is not universal for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Here, we present the universal cause for that [separate reliance]. Now, to reconcile this: what was stated there regarding "relying separately" is precisely intended to reveal...
It is not a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and thus there is no fault of being indeterminate (*anaikāntika*).

[Commentary: The meaning of the phrase "because this is indeterminate" is that the eight bases (*āśraya*) as they manifest are indeterminate; for while there are faculties (*indriya*) when one relies on the form realm, there are no faculties when relying on the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), hence it is called "indeterminate."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it is indeterminate thereafter": this refers to the stage of initial perfuming, where it is said that the seeds depend on the manifest [dharmas]. Thereafter, however, they are indeterminate. Why?

Because from the stage of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) onward, there can be interruptions; since the seeds do not depend [on the manifest] during those periods of interruption, they are called "indeterminate."
[Treatise] Since the supported (āśrita) and the support (āśraya) have not yet been distinguished, this section clarifies the difference between the support and the supported;
thus, it first explains the supported and subsequently explains the support.

[Commentary]: Based on the statement that "the unasked cause and the other three conditions are all bases," this interpretation explains that within the treatise, the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*) is taught in relation to the basis for phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
"The staff-like cause" refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), while "relying upon conditions" refers to the other three conditions.
The intended meaning is that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) arise in dependence upon these four conditions; thus, phenomena that previously did not exist come into being.

That which is called "arising" (jāti) is the phenomenon that momentarily halts; this is described as "abiding" (sthiti). Thus, all such phenomena, by depending upon conditions, are said to have a basis.
This is because, with respect to conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma), the four conditions possess the power to cause those conditioned phenomena to arise and abide;
therefore, in relation to the conditioned, they are designated as the "basis" (āśraya).

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "all unconditioned phenomena" to "these conditioned phenomena," the intended meaning is that unconditioned phenomena, acting as conditions, can give rise to conditioned phenomena and are thus also called their "basis.

This is like taking True Suchness (*tathatā*) as an object to give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and so forth; it is also like [the bases of] increased envy, cessation, and the path, all of which are valid measures.
[Commentary: Regarding the meaning of "that upon which it relies" (*āśraya*) and the substance of that which is relied upon: this refers to the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).
As for the meaning of "that upon which it relies," each individual faculty must possess four characteristics to constitute a basis; this is the intended meaning.
[Commentary]: "There is no time when one does not rely on this for birth" means that because one always relies on this for birth at all times, it is called "definitive.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the exclusion of the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] and taking the fifth and sixth as the basis, although there is no explicit textual passage in the treatise, it may be inferred through the logic of the meaning.

That which is indeterminate cannot serve as a basis for the seventh or eighth [consciousnesses]. [Commentary: This excludes only the universal [factors] and a small portion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). These five universal factors are all determinate; therefore, they are not excluded. As for the universal factors such as contact (*sparśa*) and volition (*cetanā*), they are determined by following the mind. Regarding the "small portion" of the aggregate of formations: *The Treatise on the Five Aggregates*, fascicle 1, states: "What is the aggregate of formations? It refers to the various mental concomitants associated with the mind, excluding feeling and perception. Furthermore, it says: "It is because these two [feeling and perception] are substantial entities that they are established as separate aggregates. Therefore, this aggregate of formations is established separately from feeling and perception. However, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Why are feeling and perception not included within the aggregate of formations? Because they are gross and distinct, and because they are the primary causes for the arising of afflictions. Feeling is gross because it experiences the maturation of karma; perception is gross because it grasps the characteristics of objects. They are distinct because their modes of activity differ. Furthermore, they are the primary causes for the arising of afflictions. Afflictions arise primarily from feeling, and once afflictions have arisen, they grasp characteristics primarily through perception. For this reason, these two are established as separate aggregates. Thus, the aggregate of formations is established separately from feeling and perception. Now, regarding the statement "excluding a small portion of the aggregate of formations," this refers to the mental factor of non-conformity (*vaimukhya*), which is a portion of the aggregate of formations. Why is this so? Because the aggregate of formations is established based on the mental factor of non-conformity. That is to say, the aggregate of formations is established by taking the mental factor of non-conformity as its essence. Therefore, when one speaks of "excluding a small portion of the aggregate of formations," it refers to this very mental factor of non-conformity. This means that because volition (*cetanā*) and so forth, as well as the seeds of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and even unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are likewise determinate, they are not excluded.
If this were the case, they would also serve as the support (*āśraya*) for all phenomena, since they too are determinate.
[Commentary]: From "If that were so" down to "and because it is determined," all of this constitutes a series of objections.

These objections are raised solely with respect to the other [faculties], and not with respect to the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*), because the five sense organs are, by nature, the foundational bases (*āśraya*).
[Commentary]: "Excluding the four great elements and the five material sense-objects" means to distinguish [them from] those excluded within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

Although these are determinate, they are certainly not objective spheres (*viṣaya*); therefore, they must be excluded. "The four great elements" refers to the four primary elements that constitute the five sense faculties.
"The five material sense-objects" intends to include both the auxiliary objects (*upādāya-rūpa*) of the five sense faculties and the four primary elements themselves.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "and the various seeds with the manifest phenomena," the intention is as follows: although seeds are determinate and likewise serve as the basis for manifest phenomena, they do not possess an objective referent (*ālambana*);
therefore, they must be excluded [from the category of objects].

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "although its substance is provisional," the intended meaning is as follows: although the substance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and other such non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), they are like [the case of] seeds and so forth in that they serve as supports;
however, they do not possess an object (*viṣaya*). Therefore, this [definition] excludes them. Some say:

"Although its substance is provisional" means that just as with the non-associated formations such as the life-faculty, although their substance is provisionally established upon form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), [they lack an object].
However, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth are also determinate, in that they do not have objects; therefore, they are excluded [from the category of supports].
[Commentary: Thus, the previous objection—that those [faculties] are not the support—is as explained before.
[Commentary: As for the statement, "If that were so, the five universal [factors] would extend to all objects of cognition," these are all words of objection. Now, regarding the objection raised:
those [universal factors] are not the basis [of the mind].

[Commentary: The intent of the phrase "thereby excluding the universal [factors] and [extending to] other bases" is that it is admitted that these mental factors and others possess the quality of having a basis.
"And it does not serve as the basis for other dharmas"—read this with a long pause.
[Commentary] To summarize up to the phrase "the basis of measure," the meaning is as follows: among the five aggregates, some are bases while others are not.
For instance, within the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), according to the standard, the five sense organs and the mental organ (*manas*) are...

Since the remaining [factors] are not the basis (*āśraya*), it is said that they are "only a small portion. The seventh and eighth consciousnesses are subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*);

however, when the eight consciousnesses are compared with one another, the mental faculty refers specifically to the seventh and eighth, while the other three aggregates—feeling, perception, and formations—are entirely excluded from being the basis, and thus they are also distinguished [and set aside].
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "taking one's own consciousness as the basis" up to the point of "the meaning of this support," the intention is as follows:

although the four meanings previously established excluded the sense organs (*indriya*) and so forth from being the support of the mind, by extension of that logic, because they possess even fewer [of those] principles, these various factors are now further excluded from being the support.
This is the general indication; the specific exclusions follow in order, proceeding from below upward.
First, let us simplify this. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "others are like those that are indeterminate," etc., this is the sequential clarification. Question: For what reason are others not the basis for oneself?
Answer: Although one’s own mind relies upon others as its objects, other bodies are indeterminate, as they do not exist at all times.

Since there is no reason [to do so], it is said that [the body faculty] is not the support (*āśraya*) of its own consciousness. Question: Why is it that when [the faculties] are viewed in relation to one another, the preceding serves as the support for the succeeding, yet it is not considered its "support" (*āśraya*)?

Answer: Because the preceding constitutes the substance (*svabhāva*) of the succeeding, it is subsumed under the category of the "opening and guiding" (*mukha-avakāśa*), which is not what is being elucidated here;
therefore, it is not included. Question: Since the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) is a general designation, should all five consciousnesses likewise take the body faculty as their support?
Yeshé-dé replied: "This is also not so; there are briefly two interpretations, as explained in the *Śubhāṣita-saṃgraha* (The Essential Points), which may be consulted and recorded.
[Commentary: Why does he exclude the others by first stating 'having an object' (*sālambana*) and so forth? The intention of the question is:

for what reason, among the factors established as the supports (*āśraya*), is 'determination' (*niyata*) mentioned first, followed by 'having an object,' up until the point of being grasped by the present mind, and reaching its own respective objects?"
In the concise version of the method, it first states that there is an object, next states that it is determinate, and finally states that it is the primary factor. Why are these two texts different?
The answer is that both are expressed through mutual implication, and thus there is no fault in the wording. As for the mention of the three reasons, they are:
because it is not an object, because it is not determinate, and because it is not the primary factor. Therefore.

[Treatise] Regarding the phrase "the others are not the objects [of cognition] because they are definitely the subject": the character *fei* (not) applies to the two following characters; the character *gu* (because) applies to the two following characters;
and the character *gu* (because) applies to the two preceding causes. Thus, all three causes are explained through mutual correspondence of antecedent and subsequent terms.

This is intended to distinguish them from other phenomena (*dharma*), for there is no further distinct meaning. The intent is to clarify that, apart from the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), other phenomena are not the objects of cognition and are definitively the subject.

Therefore, it is not [the mind] that serves as the support (*āśraya*). Furthermore, regarding the explanation that "others are not the support because they are not necessarily the master (*prabhu*)," this means that two reasons exclude other dharmas:
those other dharmas are neither "not necessarily having an object" (*aniyataviṣaya*) nor "necessarily being the master. Thus, they are not the support.
Although [the text] does not explicitly state "necessarily," the term "master" (*prabhu*) below clarifies the support from within the context; therefore, this explanation is superior.

[Commentary]: The phrase "only that which is the constant basis serves as this measure" means that these six sense-faculties alone are constantly the basis and serve as this measure—which is equivalent to their essence—or that the six sense-faculties, being exclusively the constant basis, constitute the definitive measure.

[Commentary: "Because each is singular, it is not like form and so forth" means that since both the sovereign and its objects are each singular, they possess a basis [of support], unlike form and so forth, which exist in many varieties.
[Commentary]: "The meaning of 'determination' (*niścaya*) herein refers to the fact that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is the sole and constant basis for this valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
