This text [the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*] establishes the meaning of determination within this treatise; Dharmapāla relies on this sense to briefly distinguish [it].

Only when these four meanings are established does it become a basis (*āśraya*). Therefore, this citation from the *Yogācārabhūmi* serves merely to prove the sense of being a 'basis,' and it is not necessary for it to be identical to these four [meanings]."
This is the meaning.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "not the six bases (ṣaḍāyatana) as the basis," the intention is as follows: the six bases serve as the basis (*āśraya*), while the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) serve as that which depends upon it (*āśrita*).
This is not like a king and his ministers, who mutually depend on one another; here, we speak only by taking the sense of being the basis from one side alone.
This refers to their mutual relationship as cause and support.
[Commentary: It is not a "correct correspondence" because it lacks the four meanings; the King is not the cause of the six sense bases.
Since this is based on a partial characteristic, it is a figurative analogy rather than a correct one, and thus cannot be described as a "correspondence."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "The eyes and so forth, as effects, lack an object of cognition," the intended meaning is this:

while the mind and mental factors possess both an object of cognition (*ālambana*) and a basis (*āśraya*), the eyes and so forth lack an object of cognition; therefore, they lack a basis. Furthermore, although the eyes and so forth have objects, because there is no place for them to be cognized, they do not possess a basis.
Moreover, it is asked: first, according to the [exclusion] among the four preceding meanings, the sense organs and so forth are distinguished by their possession of objects.

The term "basis" (*āśraya*) serves to distinguish [the mind] from other factors such as form (*rūpa*). Now, since non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*) lack an object of cognition (*ālambana*), this refers specifically to the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) to distinguish them from the sense organs (*indriya*) and form.
If one were to distinguish them by saying they "lack an existing object," to what kind of object would that refer?
Answer: If one distinguishes the sense organs and so forth by reference to the cognizing mind, then [the mind] is distinguished by the sense organs.

Because there is no object of cognition (*ālambana*), it is now stated that "there is no objective sphere" (*viṣaya*). This is to distinguish [the mind] from the specific knowledge [of the senses], as the sense organs and so forth do possess an objective sphere.

[Commentary: Regarding the "fivefold equality," this refers to the equality of time, the equality of basis (*āśraya*), the equality of object (*ālambana*), the equality of the substantial entity (*vastu*), and the equality of the mode of activity (*ākāra*). That is to say—

"Similarity of name and so forth—this is called the fivefold equality. The meaning of this passage is that, regarding the basis mentioned in that text, "that which relies on names" refers to the mental aspects (*ākāra*) and the names themselves.
Therefore, one should know that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), along with its associated mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), is also termed the "supported" (*āśrita*).

Why, then, is it said here that the eighth consciousness is exclusively the "basis" (*āśraya*)? The answer is that these are all conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Furthermore, in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and in this [text]...
The treatises all state that the mind and mental factors have supports, namely the seed-support (*bījāśraya*) and the immediately preceding ceased support (*samanantaranirodhāśraya*).
Why, then, do they not mention only the co-existent support (*sahabhvāśraya*), which consists of the six sense organs? This will be explained below.
[Commentary]: "According to what is appropriate for the disposition" means that one follows what is suitable for the disposition because one intends to take that which is relied upon as the basis;
"according to what is convenient for the text" means that one speaks in such a way according to what is expedient regarding the wording.
[Commentary: Regarding "when the mind is distracted, the five do not arise," this means that because the mind does not abide in the five objects, it is called "distraction.
[Commentary:
Regarding "among the five similar dharmas," the five consciousnesses serve as the analogies for the similar dharma; therefore, they are called the "five similar dharmas."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "acting as the causal basis for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and so forth," judging by the meaning, the character 即 (*jí*, "identical") must be an error for the character 與 (*yǔ*, "with/as").
The character 草與 (*cǎoyǔ*) is a graphical corruption of 即 (*jí*), as the two characters are easily confused; one should further verify this against other texts.

[Commentary]: Although the text mentions four, this refers to the four co-existent supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*) of the five consciousnesses, namely: the five material sense organs, and the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.
[Commentary]: Regarding the subsequent instances where each of these is cited more than once, as demonstrated below, they serve as the support for the sixth and seventh consciousnesses.
All of these are derived from the first passage of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*. That "these are not one" means that the cited passages for proof mentioned above are not singular.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "three causes," etc., this refers to: first, clarity; second, attention (*manasikāra*); and third, the reliance upon and nourishment of the faculties (*indriya*).
"These [faculties] are precisely the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*), because they are nourished by material food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that one hears sounds within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) over a long period, the commentators reconcile this by saying:

although within concentration there is no simultaneous engagement with multiple objects (*asamāna-ālambana*), the present claim of "simultaneous engagement" (*samāna-ālambana*) is made on the basis of the majority of cases or over a long duration. This interpretation relies on the fact that [the mind] does not [remain fixed on a single object].

Righteousness (nyāya) and righteousness are permitted to share the same object (ālambana). Because the concentrated mind (samāhita-citta) is non-conceptual (avikalpaka), it does not share the same object as the five sensory consciousnesses;

the statement that they share the same object here is made with reference to the state of distraction (vyutthāna-avasthā). At a later time, the concentrated mind is also termed conceptual, provided it excludes correct knowledge (samyag-jñāna).

[Commentary: "Because it belongs to that same category, there is no fault of non-pervasiveness" means that because subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is of the same nature as the conceptualizing mind that takes phenomena as its object, it is said to belong to that category.

If one were to say that subsequently attained wisdom is devoid of conceptualization, then it would follow that the distinct faculties do not pervade the untainted (*anāsrava*) state or the meditative mind.
Now, it is stated that subsequently attained wisdom possesses conceptualization; thus, there is no lack of pervasiveness.
[The text says] "lost.
[Commentary: Regarding "not leaking into the five consciousnesses," the seven ultimate purities (sapta-pariśuddhi) do not further leak into the five consciousnesses;
this is because from the sixth consciousness up to the eighth stage and beyond, the sixth consciousness is constantly non-leaking (anāsrava).

[Commentary]: As in the preceding *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the passage concerning the "common basis" (*sādhāraṇa-āśraya*) and so forth refers to the aforementioned five points of commonality regarding the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*);
it is because these constitute the common basis that they are referred to as "textual.

[Commentary]: According to this, taking the former as the basis serves as a superior proof; by reference to this scriptural passage, one may also correlate it with the five bases mentioned previously.
Sixth, regarding the reliance on [the *ālayavijñāna*] as a superior proof, it is not only these seven [points].
[Commentary: From the first master up to "this is also of this category," it means that these are also of the same category as having the simultaneous support (*sahabhv-āśraya*).

How is this known? It is because the first master stated: "Since the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are both constantly continuous and possess superior intrinsic power, they are clarified [as such]."

Regarding the understanding that there is a sense of mutual dependence, the interpretation that "this is also of the same category" means that, like the preceding three stages, the seventh consciousness exists here;
this interpretation is superior.

[Commentary] The consciousness that does not obstruct those vehicles is the unobscured-neutral consciousness (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-vijñāna*), because when viewed from the perspective of the attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*) in relation to the two [vehicles], it does not create an obstacle.

According to the explanation based on the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, if one considers it from the perspective of a Bodhisattva, this consciousness is also "obscured" (āvṛta) because it exists during three stages; therefore, it is called "non-obstructive" (anāvaraṇa). [Commentary]:

Alternatively, it is because the untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) can also exist [in these states]. That is to say, both the supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*) of a Bodhisattva and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) possess the seventh consciousness.

The followers of the Two Vehicles do not possess it, because they have not attained the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). Thus, for them, the seventh consciousness does not exist.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the reason that [the first seven consciousnesses] have distinct supports:

this third master cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which states that because the six consciousnesses each have distinct supports, they cannot grasp and maintain the physical body with its material sense organs (*rūpīndriya*). Because the eighth consciousness has universal support, it is able to grasp and maintain the body along with the sense organs.
If this is so, why is it not stated that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are the supports for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
The intended meaning is that the eight [consciousnesses] function with the seven as their support; the seven transform, and the eighth also transforms.

[Commentary: The third master says that the seeds of the various consciousnesses should be the supported, while the seven and eight manifesting consciousnesses possess the three meanings as previously explained by reason.
The intention of this passage is to introduce what follows below. The master’s intention is that since the seeds already possess [the three meanings]...
The three meanings should take the seven and eight consciousnesses in their active state (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) as their basis.

These three meanings are what were previously described as the basis for arising and the basis for abiding during the stage of growth. As the treatise states: "Because the seeds of consciousness do not grow or abide apart [from them].
The term "they" refers collectively to the seven and eight consciousnesses in their active state.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "initially only four, up to one," the meaning is as follows:

This fourth master asserts that the five consciousnesses possess four bases (*āśraya*), namely the five material sense organs, the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses. The sixth consciousness possesses two, namely the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;
the seventh possesses one, namely the eighth; and the eighth possesses one, namely the seventh. Furthermore, each of the mental factors (*caitta*) additionally includes itself.
The associated mind refers to the five consciousnesses and their five bases, up to the eighth consciousness and its two bases, etc. [Commentary]:
Regarding the meaning of "entering the commentary" and "following the length," Nanda holds that even a single moment of the five consciousnesses is eternally abiding.
The meaning of "綱" (the framework) is broadly divided into five; the "five consciousnesses that continue for a single moment" refers to a detailed, specific explanation.

[Commentary] Regarding the passage "as in the first [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, among the six beginning with the five consciousnesses," the intended meaning is that the first chapter of the *Yogācāra* elucidates...
The five consciousnesses possess six characteristics: first, they cognize only their own respective objects; second, they cognize only their own specific characteristics;

third, they cognize only the present; fourth, they cognize for only a single moment; fifth, they arise and function following the mental consciousness and in accordance with defilements and the production of karma;
and sixth, they further are able to grasp desirable and undesirable fruits.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "two moments arising simultaneously," "simultaneous" (*sahaja*) refers to their arising either before or after one another.

[Commentary: Furthermore, it is not the case that they arise in immediate succession (*anantara*). This is because within the five consciousnesses, there is no mutual, immediate succession between different categories of self and other;
thus, after the visual consciousness arises, auditory consciousness must necessarily arise.

[Commentary]: The statement that "immediately following this, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) necessarily arises" serves as proof that the five sensory consciousnesses do not continue in succession;

it does not prove that the five sensory consciousnesses arise from the sixth [mental consciousness]. This point is as follows: since the sixth [consciousness] arises from the five sensory consciousnesses, the sixth takes the preceding six consciousnesses as its immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "That [seventh consciousness] first arises of itself" to "constantly follows its own nature," this answers the previous question.

The question asked: "For instance, when the Wisdom of Equality first arises, why is the sixth consciousness not its support? Now the answer is given: "That [seventh consciousness] first arises of itself.
This means that the seventh consciousness has been continuously self-sustaining since beginningless time; prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is never interrupted or severed.
However, when one gives rise to the emptiness-contemplation of dharmas that is free from outflows (*anāsrava*) through the sixth consciousness,

it causes the preceding moment of the seventh consciousness with outflows (*sāsrava*) to cease, while the subsequent moment of the seventh consciousness arises together with the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*).

Therefore, that preceding moment of the seventh consciousness with outflows functions solely as its own preceding kind of outflowing seventh consciousness to induce the subsequent moment of the seventh consciousness free from outflows.

The wisdom of equality does not arise from the sixth consciousness at this time; rather, it is by taking the sixth as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that it causes the seventh to transform.
Because it is remote, the wisdom of equality relies directly upon the seventh and does not rely directly upon the sixth;
therefore, it is said to be "remote."

[Commentary: Second, regarding the stage of encountering an object with suddenness (*saurtarya*): the character "encounter" (*yu*) in the treatise implies suddenness, as seen below in the section on "seizing.

Since there are two types [of seizing] mentioned there, by analogy with that section on seizing, it follows that there should also be two types here in the section on "abiding. This is explained in detail in the *Yanmi*.

[Commentary]: The statement "the preceding stage applies to the following two places" and "extending even to the second" means that this refutation of the previous master must first proceed by way of exclusion (*apavāda*).
Furthermore, even granting (*prasajya*) that there are three stages—as listed in the commentary—it is as the treatise states: "Now, regarding the first five consciousnesses, up to what can be known.
This refers to what is explained according to the treatise; although the stage of "sudden engagement" (*tatrastha*) is not explicitly mentioned in the text, it exists by logical inference.
As explained in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya*, there are furthermore three positions which are established as the opposites of the preceding three positions.

As the treatise states: "If it were in a state of sovereignty (*vaśitva*), how could it not be continuous? This reverses the first position. "The five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) that are outflows (*niṣyanda*) arise in mutual succession";
this reverses the second position. "If the objects are particularly intense (*adhimātra*)," and so forth; this reverses the third position. One.
Regarding the statement that "the positions encompass the two lower stages," this means they pervade the two lower stages of the sequence of turning over (*parivṛtti*).

Regarding the statement that "the position encountered" (*yu-wei*) encompasses the third explanation, the character "encounter" (*yu*) in the third stage of the sequence of turning over applies to the second stage above; both are assigned according to the treatise (*śāstra*). Question:

Why is the character "encounter" (*yu*) not assigned to the stage of mastery (*svatantra*)? Answer: "Encounter" refers to something inferior; it pertains only to the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) and does not concern [the stage of fruition].

Regarding the fact that "sovereignty" (vaśitā) does not apply to the second stage because it is continuous [in the first], this is because within the treatises on the first three stages there is no second stage;
however, it is said to exist by way of implication. Therefore, the character "encountering" (yu) does not apply to the second turning-stage.
[Commentary: From this point downward, within the section on "Refutation," there are three refutations: first, the refutation that views phenomena from the perspective of principle;
second, the refutation that establishes teaching through principle; and third, the refutation that establishes principle through teaching.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "by transforming the five consciousnesses," if one follows the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* (or *Abhidharma-samaya-pradīpikā*), it is stated that upon attaining the first bhūmi, one transforms and obtains uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) five consciousnesses, which is also termed the "state of mastery.

[Commentary: As for the statement "from the eighth bhūmi onward, one is able to act spontaneously," a question is raised: from the eighth bhūmi onward, are there still medicinal remedies and diseases?
However, since they do not yet possess spontaneous knowledge, how can it be said now that they are "also equal"?
The Bodhisattva’s answer here is based for the time being on the aspect of self-benefit; thus, they have attained spontaneity. Otherwise, the term "equal" would exclude them.

[Commentary: The phrase "the untainted [faculties] are superior because they differ from the preceding stages" means that the Buddha’s various untainted faculties function interchangeably with increased excellence, which is unlike the tainted faculties of the eight stages belonging to the preceding tainted states.
[Commentary: "Not depending on conceptualization" means that one does not need to apply deliberate mental attention or discrimination before beginning to take it as an object;
rather, at all times, one spontaneously and continuously takes this preceding object as one's focus.

[Commentary: "It should also be said that the Buddhas have no *sa-ter-lin* (sudden/arbitrary) mind up until their first perception" means that this is a provisional designation of the presence of a *sa-ter-lin* mind within the stage of Buddhahood, because at the very first moment [of cognition] it follows the object; in reality, however, the Buddhas have no *sa-ter-lin* mind.
[Commentary: If all [mental states] have already reached the stage of "having seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), why are there only three? This is based on the actual meaning:

since there is no "seeking" (*paryeṣaka*) to serve as an example for the absence of the "sudden" (*ābhoga*) mind, because at the time of the sudden mind it is already identical to the three minds such as "ascertainment" (*niścaya*).

Because it has been previously seen, ascertainment arises; furthermore, there is no further mention of the "sudden" mind. As for "consequent" (*naiṣyandika*), it is named "consequent" in relation to the preceding mind that had already seen.
Nor is this very thought itself designated as "outflow" (*niṣyanda*), because it is the initial moment; it is called "outflow" only by virtue of its similarity to what precedes and follows it.

Thus, it is said that there are only three types of mind: the determinative, the defiled, and the pure outflowing mind. There is no "sudden" (*ābhoga*) or "investigating" (*paryeṣaka*) mind, as explained previously.
Some say that the statement "there are only three minds" refers to the Buddha’s path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), which consists of only three [moments].
The mind has no outflow; the mind has [the states of] sudden onset, determination, defilement, and purity—these are the three minds.
[Commentary: The phrase "the preceding and succeeding moments of the intentional mind" refers to the state of being a cause (*hetu-bhūmi*).

Because there is a sequence of moments for the mind during this stage, the five minds are established based on the stage of non-mastery (*asvatantra*). If one were in the stage of mastery (*svatantra*), these five minds would not be complete.
[Commentary]: Regarding the difficulty of reconciling phenomena with principle: this refers to the fact that Buddhas and others possess mastery over their objects.

For instance, transforming the great earth into gold and silver, or the waters of the ocean into ghee and curd—such instances, based on these very phenomena, pose a logical challenge to the continuity of the five sensory consciousnesses.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "for that which is not the first [moment]," there is also a commentary that uses the character *ci* (this). Following this character, the superior interpretation states:

"For that which is not the second [moment], namely the stage of encountering an object with suddenness (*sūr-er*), which is precisely the inversion of the second position. The former master calls it a "fault" because it is not [the correct] name.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the mind of equal outflow (nisyanda-citta) may also continue after [a moment of] it," the meaning is as follows:

if one encounters an object in a state of sudden impulse (ābhoga), the mind of equal outflow is inferior and cannot continue. However, if one encounters a superior object and has not yet relinquished the consciousness, the subsequent moments of the mind of equal outflow may indeed continue.
[Commentary: This meaning is also like the intention of one who has not yet attained the state of mastery (*vaśitā*), which says:
"Even if you do not continue [the stream] while in the state of non-mastery, how could it be that you do not continue it even in the state of mastery? This case is likewise:

even if there might be non-continuity while in the state of sudden occurrence (*ābhoga*), how could there be non-continuity in the state of uniform flow (*nisyanda*)? Therefore, the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) do attain continuity in the state of uniform flow.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "when the five consciousnesses arise, three types of mind are obtainable," the *Yanmi* (Secret Exposition) explains that these "three minds" refer to the *sū-ěr* (sudden encounter), *xún-qíú* (seeking), and *jué-dìng* (ascertaining) [minds], as stated in the first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
Specifically, it refers to the sudden encounter, the defiled or pure [mind], and the *děng-liú* (natural outflow).

It further clarifies that while the sudden encounter and the ascertaining [minds] may involve seeking, the seeking and ascertaining [minds] themselves belong exclusively to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

[Commentary]: It may be said that the five consciousnesses arise in mutual succession; however, this does not mean that the five consciousnesses cease in a single moment and then mutually succeed one another—this is what is meant by "succession.
[Commentary]: If it were the case that they proceed in succession, this would constitute an objection.
[Commentary: "That which arises in a continuous succession" refers to the preceding master’s response regarding the meaning of continuity.

"It is not the case that once visual consciousness has ceased, it can subsequently continue in mutual succession" is a restatement of the negation of that [preceding] position, serving as the introductory phrase for the following series of difficulties.

[Commentary]: If that is so, as for the statement "this is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising in a continuous succession until it can mutually continue," this is a self-inquiry [by the opponent].

[The opponent asks: "Since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* merely states that when the eye [consciousness] is active, mental consciousness is not absent, what does this proof of the continuity of the sixth consciousness have to do with the five sensory consciousnesses?
Since this is not the case, the Master [Xuanzang], in the following section, explains the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; his intention is not [as the opponent suggests].
Some say that the passage beginning with "If this were so" and ending with "the five consciousnesses continue in succession" is a challenge from the former master;

it points out that the treatise clarifies the continuity of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), not the five sensory consciousnesses. Therefore, the commentary states that from the point "at the time of visual consciousness" onwards, the Master [Vasubandhu] explains their mutual continuity of arising, showing that the *Yogācārabhūmi* is not like this.
Between the two types of subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)—that of the mind and that of the two [sensory] consciousnesses—the latter is superior.

[Commentary]: Even if one were to grant that [the consciousnesses] do not continue in succession, we ourselves also grant that within this context, there are times when the five consciousnesses do not continue with respect to their objective fields.
[Commentary]: Regarding the four heavens above the Desire Realm—excluding the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa—heavens—it is said that these two heavens can harm one another;
however, the statement "only because pleasure increases" refers specifically to the Heaven of Increasing Delight (*Nirmāṇarati*), as it is there that anger increases.

[Commentary] Regarding the four propositions stated in the fifth [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: 1. Self-harm and not harm by another refers exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), without regard for its specific locations;
this includes the four heavens of the desire realm above, such as the Heaven of the Gods of Volition (*manomaya-deva*) and the Heaven of the Gods of Heedfulness regarding Anger (*abhimukha-deva*). 2.

Harm by another and not self-harm refers to the three miserable destinies (*durgati*) in their states of extreme suffering, as well as while within the womb. 3. Harm by both self and other... [text continues]

Humans and the two lower heavens constitute the four [realms] where one does not harm oneself or others; this refers to the gods of the upper realms and those such as the Middle and Northern Uttarakurus.
[Commentary]: One explanation states that those who dwell on the terraces of Mount Sumeru refer to the four ridges of Mount Sumeru, which are called the "Four Wondrous High Terraces."
"Level" refers to the abodes of the Four Heavenly Kings; secondly, it refers to the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) residing on the summit of Mount Sumeru.

[Commentary]: Regarding those to whom these objects are attached—whether virtuous persons or non-virtuous persons—the objects of virtuous persons are such as the image of the Buddha, while the objects of non-virtuous persons are such as the instruments of suffering in the three miserable realms.
Because these objects are so powerful, the five sensory consciousnesses do not cease.
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the passage on "only a single thought-moment": this reconciles the preceding *Yogācārabhūmi* text.

Since it was previously stated that the five consciousnesses are continuous, why does the *Yogācārabhūmi* say that once the five consciousnesses have arisen for a single kṣaṇa, immediately thereafter (anantara) the mental consciousness must necessarily arise?

Therefore, the commentary reconciles this by stating: "This is based on the transformation of the object during the 'sudden encounter' (*saurei*), which occurs within the interval of equanimity; there is a sudden encounter..."
If your mind increases [its power] regarding superior objects, you might claim that the five consciousnesses continue in succession, saying, "These [five] are collectively one recollection.

[Commentary: Because the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 52) states that they are "mutually penetrating," it is clearly understood that the six consciousnesses serve as mutual roots and conditions for one another. Question:

When An-hui (Sthiramati) decisively cites this passage as proof, it would imply that the six consciousnesses are mutually immediate; why then does the sixth [consciousness] not [arise from the others]?
Are the first five [consciousnesses] immediate [conditions]? This should be understood by referring to the *Dharmapāla-saṃgraha*. This interpretation is briefly difficult to understand;

below is the detailed explanation. Furthermore, it says: "If these six consciousnesses reach the mental faculty (*manas*), the meaning is that Master Sthiramati cites the *Yogācārabhūmi* to prove that the six consciousnesses serve as mutual conditions for one another.
This was because previously, Nanda had maintained that the five consciousnesses have only the sixth consciousness as their "opening and guiding" support (*kai-dō-e*).
Therefore, the Master Sthiramati asks: "The sixth [consciousness] certainly does not take the preceding five as its *āśraya* for opening and leading (*ābhimukhya-āvāhaka*).

How then should one interpret the *Yogācārabhūmi* statement that 'if these six consciousnesses [arise], they serve as the opening and leading conditions for those six consciousnesses'? It may be possible for the five consciousnesses to serve as the opening and leading conditions for those six consciousnesses;
however, the sixth mental consciousness is not like this. He answers: "In general, the meaning is the same, and there is no contradiction even in the specific details regarding the preceding five."
Consciousness acts as the precursor for those six consciousnesses; thus, the sixth consciousness takes its own kind as its precursor, and therefore they do not continue in succession.
[Commentary]: If the five consciousnesses are interrupted until the five consciousnesses arise again, this explains the previous objection that the five consciousnesses do not continue.
Once a single thought-moment has arisen, consciousness necessarily arises; if this were so, then fifty-two [moments] should be called "equal" [in sequence].
[Commentary: The phrase "at times distracted" indicates that the five types of mind do not arise in a fixed succession.

[Commentary: Regarding the two points: first, it refutes the intention [of the opponent] by taking the five [consciousnesses] as the basis; second, it challenges that intention by requiring the seventh or eighth [consciousness] to serve as the basis.

[Commentary: Regarding the presence or absence of the seventh [consciousness], the meaning is that various masters allow for the absence of the seventh consciousness within the state of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), as is the case in ordinary discourse.
Because it is asserted that at this present time there is a seventh consciousness, [it follows that] within the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) there exists a pure seventh consciousness.

According to Master An-hui, the seventh consciousness consists solely of the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*). If one enters the attainment of cessation by means of the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) as its preparatory application (*prayoga*), then there is no grasping of a self;

thus, in the attainment of cessation, there is no seventh consciousness. This is because it is not admitted that the seventh consciousness can be of a pure nature (*anāsrava-bhāga*). As for the rest...

The Master [Sthiramati] allows for this question: since Sthiramati does not allow for a seventh consciousness in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), how can it be said that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses exist therein?
The answer is: this refers to the statement of other masters within Sthiramati’s own school.

That is to say, regarding the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which does not depend on the five sensory consciousnesses, it does not take the five as its "opening-and-leading" support (*āśraya*).

[Commentary]: This is also the case for the sixth [consciousness], which takes the seventh and eighth as its objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*). The former masters maintained that the five [sensory consciousnesses] take the mind (*manas*) as their support;
now, since the sixth should likewise take the seventh and eighth as its support, it is treated analogously to the five sensory consciousnesses.

[Commentary]: The phrase "it is revealed that the name 'manas' applies to the untainted [state], and so on up to 'is likewise'" means that when the sixth consciousness first performs the two-fold emptiness contemplation (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā) regarding both the person and phenomena as being tainted during the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), it can induce the subsequent moment of untainted wisdom of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
At the precise moment this [untainted wisdom] arises, the tainted seventh consciousness, along with the four afflictions and the discriminative [afflictions], are all... [omitted].

Regarding the simultaneous suppression and severance of the innate [afflictions]: as for how one knows that "suppression" refers to this, it is because the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) contradicts the two types of grasping.
According to the school of Sthiramati, there is only the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*) and no grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Since the extinction of the seventh consciousness brings forth the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), which is empty of these two graspings, why is this wisdom established based only upon the sixth consciousness and not established as being based upon the seventh?
Therefore, it is said that the fundamental tenet of Sthiramati does not admit that the seventh consciousness can be untainted (*anāsrava*). Question:
If this is so, why is it stated that "the manas associated with the wisdom of equality" and so forth, and that it should also be applied as the "opening and guiding" [consciousness]?
Since there are explicit scriptural authorities for this, why is it not admitted despite contradicting [your position]? Answer: There exists a manas associated with the wisdom of equality.

This means that while it possesses only a name, it lacks a substantial entity; this reveals that the seventh consciousness, termed "defiled mind" (*manas*), is a mere nominal designation lacking actual substance.
Because one attains the Wisdom of Equality by transforming the defiled seventh consciousness, it is said that the Wisdom of Equality is established based on *manas*.
In reality, however, it relies solely upon the sixth consciousness. Question: Even if one does not provisionally establish [this seventh consciousness],...

Question: What is the extent of the untainted (*anāsrava*) manas? Answer: There is the fault of contradicting the sūtras. A sūtra states that at the first moment of mind in the first stage (*bhūmi*), the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) arises in conjunction with the manas.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this refers to the birth and so forth of a portion of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) who are bodhisattvas":

it means that during the stage of taking birth as an ordinary being, one must necessarily rely upon a defiled mental consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manovijñāna*) to undergo birth; this is because the mind at the point of death (*cyuti-citta*) and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) always arises in a defiled state.

Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the eighth consciousness is projected by the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, and that the defiled consciousness comprises both the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. As for "those in training," [it refers to] one...

Regarding those who are still in training (*śaikṣa*), there are two types of faculties: sharp and dull. Those with sharp faculties attain Arhatship directly from the first fruit and do not undergo further rebirth;

they are not what is being discussed here. As for those with dull faculties, they undergo rebirth in succession, and it is by means of the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] that the eighth is induced.
When a Bodhisattva undergoes rebirth, it is through a virtuous mind associated with compassion and vows, which consists of the two wisdoms.

Regarding the associated wholesome mind, it pertains to the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. As for the question of the resultant (*vipāka*) mind, upon what basis is it said to rely on the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*)?

The answer is: this is stated solely with reference to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), not regarding noble ones (*ārya*). Furthermore, it is explained as applying generally to both vehicles (*yāna*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*), because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) exists [for them].
Moreover, the mind at the moment of passing away from the intermediate state is defiled. As for the question: why is the initial mind of the intermediate state [defiled]?

Question: Does one not give rise to defilement until the final moment of mind at the point of death? Answer: The initial moment of mind in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) does not give rise to defilement because it is still proximate to the Noble Path;

that is, within this body, one has attained the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state. Therefore, it is only at the final moment of mind in the intermediate state that one gives rise to the intention of defilement.
The reason is that the outflow-free path is incompatible [with defilement]. Question: This may be the case for those who have attained the first and second fruits, but what about the third fruit?

Question: How does one give rise to defilement? Answer: A person who has attained the third fruit (anāgāmin) dies in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and is reborn in a higher meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

There, they experience the "tasting" (*āsvādana*) of that absorption, thereby giving rise to the fruit of the higher realm. Question: Do Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) possess an intermediate state? Answer: There are two explanations. One says there is no intermediate state;

the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that Bodhisattvas take rebirth through wisdom (*jñāna*). Another says they do indeed rely on it; the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that they also rely on compassion and vows (*karuṇā-praṇidhāna*).
Because it is associated with a wholesome mind, one takes rebirth by means of the assistance of compassion and vows; thus, the *Mahā-śāstra* states:

"A Bodhisattva takes birth knowingly, not unknowingly. Second, for Bodhisattvas from the seventh stage downward, those whose compassion is predominant take on a *paricchinna-kāya* (segmented body) in order to save sentient beings, and there is also an intermediate state (*antarābhava*);
this is what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts regarding the two divisions of the desire and form realms.

Because there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and furthermore, because the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Samuddeśa*) provides proof that Bodhisattvas on the great stages do not take up bodies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), we know from this that they accept the existence of the intermediate state.
Question: Does the intermediate state of a Bodhisattva involve defilement (*kliṣṭa*)? Answer: There are two explanations. One says:

although he takes up an intermediate state, he does not give rise to either defilement or purity; the Bodhisattva knowingly undergoes rebirth, it is not out of ignorance, and moreover, it is due to compassion (*karuṇā*).

First, because they assist in the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), they are not defiled. Second, although Bodhisattvas lack innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), they still possess conceptual afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) regarding things such as medicine and disease;
because they have not yet attained universal knowledge, there is innate craving (*sahaja-tṛṣṇā*) within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Based on this, it follows that the intermediate state is accompanied by defilement. Of these two interpretations, either may be adopted; further details should be verified in other texts. Question: For what reason is it said that compassion (*karuṇā*) alone is predominant?

The Master did not provide an answer regarding the predominance of wisdom; as for the "predominance of wisdom," because one receives a body of transformation (*pariṇāmika-kāya*) in order to seek bodhisattvahood, this question and answer are omitted here. [Commentary:

Whether it be the body of分段 (*bheda-śarīra*, fragmented/limited) or the body of變易 (*pariṇāma-śarīra*, transformative), up to the point of being conditioned by wholesome roots—while it may be acceptable to ask about the fragmented body, since the transformative body... [is different].

Question: Since there is no separate rebirth [in the case of the transformation body], how can it be that the eighth consciousness is also induced by the two types of wisdom taking a wholesome mind as a condition? Answer:

When Bodhisattvas undergo the birth of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-janman*), it is all due to the assistance of meditative concentration, compassion, vows, and so forth, which cause their prior karma to induce this body of segmented existence (*bheda-deha*).

This body gradually becomes subtle and minute; it transforms the coarse into the subtle and makes the short long. It is like the practice of increasing the duration of a dharma, which continues without interruption for a long time.
That which is called "transformation" (pariṇāma) arises entirely from entering meditative absorption through the two wisdoms, supported by compassion and vows to achieve longevity;
it is based on this principle that the two wisdoms are said to induce transformation-birth. This will be explained below in the eighth chapter, within the section on the two kinds of birth and death.

[Commentary: Regarding the "three proofs," these refer to the previously cited *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Asvabhāva, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Vasubandhu, and the fifth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. [Commentary:

By stating that "the preceding eight consciousnesses are all proven by refutation," the intended meaning is that the preceding eight consciousnesses are all proven by refutation to mutually attain one another.
[It] serves as a basis.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "by analogy with the five bases," it is like how the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) existing prior to meditative absorption serves as the basis for the five sensory consciousnesses;
likewise, in the state of no-mind (*acittaka*), since the mental faculty (*manas*) has been interrupted, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses must serve as its basis because they exist perpetually.
[Commentary]: "The first untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of the Mahāyāna" refers to the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) of the First Stage (*prathamabhūmi*).

[Commentary]: "The four conditions herein are explained extensively below" refers collectively to the four conditions—causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), and so forth—as explained in the seventh fascicle.
Some say that the fourth condition herein, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), specifically refers to what is explained in the seventh fascicle.
It should be understood that the statement "it serves as this basis" means it serves as the *āśraya* (support) for opening and guiding.
[Commentary] Regarding the objection that the place where another consciousness arises does not obstruct my own brief [moment], the intent is to ask:

if, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, it does not obstruct the path of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), why is the mind (*manas*) not used as the *āśraya* for opening and guiding? It must be that the mind ceases before [the subsequent consciousness] can begin to open.
Since the "leading" (nirvāhaka) has already manifested, it does not obstruct the path after its arising, yet it is not the "opening and leading" (ābhimukhya-nirvāhaka);

therefore, we know that the eight consciousnesses cannot serve as one another’s equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), unlike the case of one's own preceding mind. Furthermore, if the preceding mind of its own kind does not cease, it obstructs that path and the subsequent mind cannot arise;
thus, it is only upon the cessation of the preceding mind of its own kind that the subsequent arises, thereby constituting the "opening and leading" of the latter.
Since there is no obstruction, they do not mutually open the way for one another as distinct categories. How then can you say that "the other" serves as the basis for "this"?
[Commentary:

The passage from "As in the Sarvāstivāda... to "...should be the path of immediate succession" (*ānantarya-mārga*) is a refutation of the previous master. For instance, according to the school [in question], the mind...

Those that do not arise simultaneously cannot serve as mutual *āśraya* (support) or *samutthāna* (inducement). Since the Mahāyāna accepts that the eight consciousnesses arise together, there should be no mutual inducement;
for if they arise at the same time, how could they act as mutual inducements? Therefore it is said: "Since they now arise together, there should be no mutual inducement.
If you claim that consciousness is the support (*āśraya*), then they should not arise simultaneously. This next passage raises an objection based on the treatise.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the nature of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*) should be thus": if consciousness, which is indefinite in its number [of moments], can serve as a condition (*pratyaya*), then by this same principle, form-dharmas should likewise be thus;
since they too are indefinite in their number, they should also constitute an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Furthermore, it says:

"If one follows the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 51), according to the reasoning that the former masters held that [dharmas] of varying numbers act as mutually equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the principle should indeed be thus."

This is not so. [Commentary] "Equality of substance" (*tulya-dravya*) means that each mental state and its associated mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are individually unique and non-dual; their simultaneous arising as sensation and so forth is termed equality of substance.

"Equality of function" (*tulya-kāritra*) refers to the mental states and their associated mental factors sharing the same basis (*āśraya*), the same object (*ālambana*), and having a mutually corresponding mode of activity.
"Appearing as if they pervade the three natures" is what is meant by "functioning as such" [the *śū*].

Regarding the phrase "arising in immediate succession," the intent is as follows: for example, when consciousnesses are compared with one another across preceding and succeeding moments, and this applies even to mental factors such as volition (*cetanā*) and so forth;
thus it is said they "arise in immediate succession. Question: Why is it necessary to make this statement? Answer: If we discuss the "opening and guiding" [of the way], [this statement is required].
If it were based on a single mind-king acting as the precursor for the many subsequent mental factors such as sensation, that would not be the case;

rather, this is explained in terms of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which requires that each individual mind and mental factor must sequentially induce its own successors. Therefore, the term "immediate succession" is employed.

[Commentary]: "Without any other mind intervening" means that when a mind and its mental factors arise from their own preceding states, there is no other mind or factor capable of intervening between them;
thus, they are called an "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*). If there were a different mind intervening, it could not be termed "immediate."

[Commentary]: "Not like form and so forth" means that since form and its concomitants are difficult to determine in terms of quantity and are not fixed, they cannot be the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*);
the phrase "the eye and so forth should be likewise" includes the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the further objection raised by the former master, he cites the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) to challenge the Dharmapāla’s position that matter (*rūpa*) serves as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

That treatise challenges the Sautrāntika view with the following logic: if one allows that the subsequent mind acts as the seed, then the final mind of an Arhat should be able to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, because a subsequent seed would still be capable of producing [a new existence]. The passage concludes below by stating: "Therefore, we know that it is matter..."

It is possible for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) to possess the conditions of immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*), yet they cannot be called "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*);

the commentary briefly cites this [view] as a summary. As for those referred to as the "Sthavira masters," these are those within the Sthavira school who rely on scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*), and are thus designated as the Sautrāntika;
they are not the Sautrāntika school as a distinct sect within the Sthavira tradition.

[Commentary]: This means that even if one were to grant that matter (*rūpa*) possesses this condition [of immediate antecedence], the statement "the meaning of 'cause-condition' (*hetu-pratyaya*) does not apply" would be redundant.
The intention behind these words is as follows: the Sautrāntikas do not establish an eighth consciousness; rather, they designate matter following matter and mind following mind as "cause-conditions.

Our interpretation, however, is not so. Even if you were to regard matter and mind in their successive relationship as "equal and immediate conditions" (*samanantara-pratyaya*), [it would still not constitute a cause-condition].

If this were not the case, the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*) could not be established; for if one does not interpret it in this way, the use of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) would be purposeless.
Now, the word "and so forth" refers to the fact that one phenomenon from the preceding [moment] and one from the succeeding [moment] are similar, which is why they are called "equal.

If you now allow that matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) can establish an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) between themselves across time, then since their quantity and nature differ between the preceding and succeeding moments, how could they be called "equal"?
Because they are equal, it is known that [the opponent] merely concedes this hypothetically, even though it is not actually accepted.

[Commentary]: First, as for the question of how we know that the school in question accepts that matter (rūpa) possesses this condition—namely, the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantarapratyaya)—the answer is that the formal text of their own treatise serves as proof.
Since the formal text of the third chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* already raises this objection:

The passage states: "It is said that preceding matter and mind can only accommodate the condition of equal and immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and cannot take on the meaning of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);

this makes it clear that they admit that matter possesses the condition of equal and immediate antecedence. If this were not admitted, why would it be said that it 'can only accommodate the condition of equal and immediate antecedence'?
Thus, by means of the third main text, the Sautrāntika position that matter possesses the condition of equal and immediate antecedence is proven."
[Commentary]: If this is so, why is it that [the text] refers to it as an "uninterrupted condition" (*samanantarapratyaya*)?

This is the objection. If one says that the Sautrāntikas admit that both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) possess uninterrupted conditions, then why does the first [section] state that it is not the Sautrāntika masters who maintain that only dharmas such as matter are called uninterrupted conditions?

[Commentary] The third fascicle, concerning the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), answers the preceding objection by stating that the meanings of "having an object" (*sālambana*) and "having no object" (*anālambana*) are distinct.
Furthermore, as for that which "has [an object]," within the third category of material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), various seeds are contained;
because it possesses both matter and seeds along with the mind, that matter is admitted to be an equal-and-immediate condition. That first [category], however, speaks of matter alone and lacks seeds.

Because it is consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is not admitted as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Furthermore, it is said that these may represent the individual tenets of different schools:

the first is the Sautrāntika master, and the third is a Sautrāntika master from the "Upper School" (*Uttarīya*); since there are differences in the doctrinal positions of these two branches, they need not be reconciled.
[Commentary]: Regarding the second point, "up to being the equal-and-immediate condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*): the intent of this second interpretation is as follows.

According to the first fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it was originally maintained that form (*rūpa*) is not admitted to be an equal-and-immediate condition because there is an inequality in the quantity [of preceding and succeeding moments].

Now, in the third fascicle of the *Saṃgraha*, although it provisionally allows for the existence of an equal-and-immediate condition for the sake of refuting the [opponent's] claim regarding causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is still not the original position that admits form [as such a condition].
It serves as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "this interpretation is correct," although this treatise provisionally accepts it as the correct meaning, it does not mean that the opponent's school admits that matter (*rūpa*) possesses conditions.
[Treatise] Regarding the mental factors (*caitta*) that should be explained as depending on and following consciousness (*vijñāna*), the text first poses the question:

"If all minds and mental factors cause consciousness to serve as their *āśraya-pravartaka* (opening and guiding support)," it then provides the answer: "Mental factors depend on this [consciousness]; they should be explained as following consciousness.
That is to say, this consciousness is the *āśraya-pravartaka* for those mental factors, and that consciousness is the *āśraya-pravartaka* for these mental factors."

[Commentary: From here below, the main text explains the objections; therein are five objections: the fourth is the objection raised by others, and the fifth is the objection regarding the mutual contradictions among various treatises and teachings. [Commentary:
"One cannot establish them as distinct because they do not differ in the four meanings and so forth" means that since they are not separate, one does not allow them to be different.

Regarding the four meanings, why are the words "at times," "based on," "having the same object," and "equal" used? Why are sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth taken as the basis for perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth?
[The answer is: because they constitute a long-continued continuum of their own nature. [Commentary]:
How is it that the meaning of "śramaṇa" is not understood as it truly is? The intention [of the text] is this: these śramaṇas reckon sensation, perception, and so forth [to be the self].
Each [mental factor] arises in succession from its predecessor; the intent of the present objection is as follows:

Why is it not the case that, just as one who is designated by the name "śramaṇa" is a true śramaṇa, [the mental factor of] feeling (vedanā) induced by contact serves as the basis for the subsequent perception (saṃjñā), rather than the feeling co-arising with the preceding moment of consciousness serving as the basis for the subsequent moment of perception?
This is the objection raised because feeling, produced by contact, is the basis for perception. One who merely bears the name "śramaṇa" is not a true śramaṇa.
The gate is similar to that of a śramaṇa.
[Commentary: "Because three conditions are reduced" means it is reduced to three conditions.
[Commentary: "If that were not the case" means that the intended meaning is that if the preceding thought does not cease, the subsequent mind cannot arise.
[Commentary]: It is called "immediate" (*ānantarya*) but is not actually so; for that treatise also states that "the mental consciousness arises immediately after the five consciousnesses.
As for the phrase "immediately after the mind," this is said in terms of its predominant influence (*adhipati*).

[Commentary] Regarding the detailed analysis of the meaning of the four conditions: the detailed analysis of the meaning of these four conditions—such as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and so forth—is also similar to what is explained here.

[Commentary]: The phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) refers to the definitive arising; it indicates that following this immediately preceding mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-samanantara*), all subsequent consciousnesses and so forth will definitely arise.
It is said "up to" because it points to that passage in the treatise.

[Commentary: The meaning is that it takes determinate consciousness (*niyata-vijñāna*) and does not take all [consciousness]; it means taking that which is determined as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and not taking anything else.
Therefore, the term "all" (*sarva*) is used as a general statement.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "one dharma not yet fully known," the intent is as follows: the purpose of citing this passage is to demonstrate that while the words are general, the meaning is specific.
According to this treatise, the words are general while the meaning is specific; however, according to the *Saṃgrahaṇī*, the words are specific while the meaning is general.

That is to say, "one dharma not yet reached" refers specifically to [the ignorance of] the principle of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), whereas it generally encompasses the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā). Thus, by means of this [realization], one realizes the principle of the emptiness of persons.
Therefore, there are intentional explanations (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) and other alternative explanations, as explained extensively in the *Yanmi* (Secret Explication). Furthermore, as it is said:

"If one dharma is not yet understood, one may simply remain without understanding that one dharma"—this too is a case where the words are general but the meaning is specific, which is identical in intent to the present point.
[Commentary: If it were not so—that is, if one did not provide this interpretation—then the basis of the causal conditions would not exist.
Why? Because [the mind] would not be taking the basis of the causal conditions as its object.

[Commentary]: This principle is definitively non-existent because it is close to reason that [the seventh consciousness] does not manifest as a support for the immediately preceding moment of cessation.

Why? Because the seventh consciousness does not take its own preceding moment of consciousness as an object. Even if it were to take it as an object, the support and the object would be identical; however, since the seventh consciousness does not take the eighth consciousness as its object, [such a support cannot exist].

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "the basis which is that" to "the consciousness which is the basis," it explains the reason why it is precisely that eighth [consciousness] and not something else distinct from it;
therefore, it is designated by its names "basis" (*āśraya*) and "object-condition" (*ālambana*) in relation to the "subjective perceiver" (*ālambaka*).

[Commentary]: This refers to the general interpretation; the treatise merely states that the Sage taught this consciousness takes the *ālaya* as its object, and does not mention that it takes the *vijñapti*, the *nimitta-bhāga*, or mental factors (*caitta*) as its objects, because these matters will be debated separately below.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Because that which is not superior cannot be reckoned as 'mine'": since seeds lack the superior function of cognitive apprehension (*ālambana*), they cannot be reckoned as belonging to a self (*ātman*).

[In the original text,] the character "所" (suǒ) has been omitted, or perhaps the characters "可" (kě) and "我" (wǒ) were combined for the sake of brevity. [The question is: Since they cannot be reckoned as "mine," [how can they be a self?]

[Commentary: Regarding the "aspect of what belongs to me" (*mamakāra*): the aspect of "what belongs to me" takes the same object as "self," performing functions such as receiving, grasping, and forming an image.
Now, when [the mind] takes "self" as its object, it simultaneously carries that aspect; therefore, it is said to "proceed by carrying the aspect of what belongs to me."

[Commentary]: The *Śāstra* does not state that [the five consciousnesses] are the objects [of the seventh], because within the discussion of "associated factors" (*samprayukta*) in the treatise on the first transformative consciousness (*pariṇāma*), it is not stated that the five consciousnesses serve as the objects for the seventh;
nor do other treatises say so. How, then, can one recklessly follow one's own deluded nature and falsely reckon the five pervasive mental activities (*sarvatraga*) as being "mine"?
[Commentary]: Regarding that which "belongs to others" among what I possess: "what I possess" refers to the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect).

Because the *nimittabhāga* has the function of giving rise to consciousness, it is connected to the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect), and because it can give rise to consciousness, it is said to have the function of belonging to others.

[Commentary: Regarding "objects that are outflows" (*niṣyanda-viṣaya*): the five external sense-objects (*pañca-bāhyārtha*) which are the objects of the five consciousnesses are the outflows of the five internal objects.
"Outflow" has the meaning of similarity; although there is a distinction between internal and external, because the internal consists of the five sense-objects, they are similar.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it does not distinguish between active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and seeds (*bīja*)," this means that in various treatises, it is simply stated that the seventh consciousness takes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object, without specifically distinguishing whether it takes seeds, active manifestations, or both as its objects.

[Commentary]: Why is it that they calculate that the seeds have no distinct entity? It is because Ananta (An-hui) calculates that seeds are merely like functional capacities and do not exist as separate, real entities, as they do not conform to the classification of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

[Commentary]: This passage distinguishes [the seeds] from the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) up to the point that they are not non-existent. According to Sthiramati, seeds are functional capacities upon consciousness and are not the thoroughly imagined nature.
If one were to conceive of them as being the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga), they would be subsumed under the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika).

Even if one grants that they are the thoroughly imagined nature, they are still produced from seeds. Now, if these seeds are merely functional capacities upon consciousness and have no separate substance:
Why was it stated above that the eighteen *dhātus* would result in confusion and other such difficulties? In response, it is said:

within the school of Sthiramati, this is the interpretation of other masters and not the view of Sthiramati himself; alternatively, it may be that Sthiramati raised these objections from the perspective of another school rather than as his own position, for according to him, the *dhātu* has no substantial reality (*svabhāva*).

[Commentary: If one were to separately give rise to the view of "mine" by taking the various aggregates as the object of that "mine," then since you maintain that the aggregates are taken as the self, you would necessarily have to separately grasp other aggregates as "mine.
Therefore, all three of the aforementioned masters fall into this error.
[Commentary: This refers to citing an example to show that [the two views] are clearly not held simultaneously. For now, we cite a common worldly case as an illustration;
by reading it continuously, one will realize the meaning oneself. It means that the two views of annihilationism and eternalism cannot coexist within a single body;

it is clearly known that within the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*), the grasping of "self" and "what belongs to self" likewise cannot arise. This is merely an analogy and does not explicitly state that [such grasping] exists within the seventh consciousness.
This immediately entails the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
[Commentary: This also serves to exclude those who reckon other consciousnesses as the self; since other consciousnesses are not of a single homogeneous type, they are not clung to as the self.
This is a general exclusion and does not imply that such a reckoning exists within this specific context.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the aspect of activity being most manifest": because the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) is intermittent, it cannot be reckoned as the self; among the other three parts, the aspect of activity within the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) is the most manifest.
[Commentary]: Alternatively, "reckoning this within a single moment up to the seventh" refers to what is reckoned by the mind (*manas*). This means that within a single moment, regarding the self...

Regarding the statement "mine" (*mamakāra*) as explained in the preceding section, a question is raised: As previously refuted, there cannot be two types of wisdom (*prajñā*) within a single moment of mind.

Why, then, is it said here that in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) there is both "I" (*ātman*) and "mine"? Answer: Both [notions] are forms of grasping (*abhiniveśa*), and they cannot coexist within a single mind.
The term "mine" is used merely figuratively (*upacāra*). Thus, while they appear to coexist in a single thought-moment, this "mine" exists only in dependence upon the "I."
Because one sees the meaning explained above and does not cling to it, there is no fault in giving rise to a single thought that "this is this.
The intent here is that within a single moment of thought, one calculates that "this self is this very self," and thus it is explained according to its meaning.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "this is my self," Ximing says: [the meaning is as follows].
The phrase "this is me" clarifies that this seventh [consciousness] conceives the eighth as the self;

the meaning of "self" here clarifies that the seventh does not conceive anything else, but takes only the eighth as its self. Thus, within a single view, two terms are used for the sake of the meaning.
Furthermore, another interpretation states: the meaning of "this is me" excludes the selfhood of others, while the sound and meaning of "me" exclude what is not-self. This is the actual principle.
The *manas* associated with the view of self lacks this kind of discrimination.

[Commentary: It may be so in the case of wholesome minds and the like, for it is admitted that these lack grasping and can arise simultaneously with the three natures; however, it is not so when grasping is present.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "nor can it be analogized to 'not obtaining,'" the intended meaning is that within a single moment of mind there cannot be two simultaneous modes of activity (*ākāra*);

since a subsequent cognition would necessarily take two objects, there is no possibility for these two to arise together. Therefore, among the four interpretations, the fourth—that of Dharmapāla—is correct.

[Commentary]: Regarding the exclusion of the four types of persons—namely, those who have deviated from the three [stages] of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas—it is necessary to distinguish them.

Specifically, although Bodhisattvas of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and above are not among these four types of persons, they give rise to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds and do not take the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as an object;
therefore, they must be distinguished. Within this [section], the commentary on the tenth [chapter] concerning "ultimate merit" refers to the first great eon (*mahākalpa*).
All merits are fully perfected upon reaching the first bhūmi, which is termed "ultimate";
it is not that the merits within the latter two kalpas are perfected at the first bhūmi.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "knowing all sentient beings up to the image of the Buddha," Ximing states that this cites the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* as proof that the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) universally perceives all things.

It is because the Wisdom of Equality knows the distinctions in the faculties of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) that it manifests the image of the Buddha for the sake of others as a Body of Reciprocal Enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Thus, when the ten kinds of Wisdom of Equality enter the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), they are immediately capable of [this].
Regarding the attainment of the successive stages of cultivation up to the stage of Buddhahood, there are two explanations for how one obtains the answer.
One says that through the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) onward, bodhisattvas are able to manifest the images of Buddhas.

For instance, if bodhisattvas even at the stage of the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*) are already able to achieve the eightfold path of enlightenment (*aṣṭalakṣaṇabodhi*), how much more so for a bodhisattva of the first stage who has attained the hundredfold gate of dharma-illumination (*dharmaprakāśamukha*) and the ten [mastery-powers]?

How could it be that, being equal, one does not manifest the image of the Buddha? Second, although the ten kinds of equality are attained in their essential form at the first stage (*bhūmi*), they reach full perfection only upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood;
only thereafter do they manifest for the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage as the *parasaṃbhogakāya*.
As stated below in the fourteenth [chapter], the "equality of wisdom" which accomplishes the three bodies is the wisdom capable of manifesting the *sāmbhogikakāya* for those in the tenth stage.

When a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, their wondrous discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) likewise possesses ten causes, as detailed in the *Tattvārtha-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Principles). [Commentary]:
Each takes its own object; because the seventh [consciousness] is capable of thorough deliberation, the seventh is called *manas*.
It is said that among the three—mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—each takes its own respective object, while the seventh is specifically named *manas*.
[Commentary: Regarding the two characters "bing" (並) and "qian" (竝) in the latter explanation, upon examining the commentary, there should be three characters: first, "bing" (並); second, "fan" (煩);
and third, "nao" (惱). Thus, there should be three in total.

[Commentary]: These first five characters up to the phrase "because it is not a single dharma" refer to the five characters in the verse concerning the four afflictions that are always concomitant (*sahaja*).
Therefore, in this prose commentary, the word "concomitant" (*ju*) is explained first, followed by the explanation of the four characters;
these four characters are termed "four" because they are not one, as stated below: "these are called the four kinds."
[Treatise] To be deluded regarding the mark of self means that the deluded are in darkness; they obscure this illusory body and falsely cling to a self that is solid and permanent.
This is to be ignorant of the phantom-like person while following one's own sentiments and calculations—is this not indeed darkness?

Therefore, that which accompanies this consciousness is exclusively the non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) that is confused about principle, as will be clearly distinguished in the subsequent proof.

[Treatise] Regarding "the conceit of self" (*asmimāna*), there are two types of conceit: first, looking down upon others; second, relying on oneself. Because this [conceit] relies solely on internal conditions and depends on the internal, it is called the "conceit of self.

[Treatise] Regarding the phrase "simultaneously expressing conceit, feeling, and so forth," the term "simultaneously expressing" has two meanings: first, it expresses conceit and craving; second, [it expresses...]

Regarding the two [types of] phenomena that arise simultaneously with the visible (*sanidarśana*), there are several explanations in the Ximing Commentary concerning how craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and pride (*māna*) arise together.
[Commentary]:

The meaning of "not depending on others for subsequent arising" is that the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) does not arise based upon the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and so forth; therefore, this consciousness...

Regarding the statement that "the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and so forth arise simultaneously with consciousness, and furthermore do not depend on others for their subsequent arising," the intended meaning is this:

since the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) internally takes the marks of the aggregates as its object and arises through dependent origination, it does not rely on anything else; therefore, the view of extremes regarding "self" and "mine" arises subsequently. This interpretation is excellent.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the view of 'mine' is subsumed under the name [of the former]," the intended meaning is as follows:
Is the view of "mine" subsumed within the aforementioned *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity), or is it subsumed within the view of "I"? Question:

What is the distinction between *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and the view of "mine"? Answer: In the Mahāyāna, *satkāyadṛṣṭi* is translated as the "view of shifting and turning," which is what is termed "body" (*kāya*).

The view of identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth are included [within the view of self] because they involve the transition toward existence and so forth, as well as the attainment of what is "mine," and because the views of the self and the objects of the self also possess the sense of transition.
Therefore, they are included. If one were to speak only of the "view of self" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), it would be too narrow and fail to encompass [all instances];
however, while there is a difference in breadth and scope, the view of identity is indeed the view of self.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, the meaning of the statement that "the first two views can take both internal and external objects" is intended as an answer to the preceding question. The previous question asked:

"For what reason do the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of mine (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*), as well as the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), not arise in succession with one another? The answer provides two points. The first point states:

because the view of self associated with this consciousness is of a single homogeneous type (*ekajātīya*) and occurs without interruption (*nirantara*), it does not allow for the arising of the view of mine and so forth. That is to say:

Regarding the preceding passage on "always internally grasping" and so forth, it says: "Furthermore, the view of self-identity (*asmimāna*) and the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) take both the internal and external as their objects;
however, because the views associated with these [other afflictions] always take the internal as their object, they do not arise simultaneously. Question:

Since you do not admit that the seventh consciousness possesses the view of self-identity, the extreme views, and so forth, how can you say that these two views exist within both the internal and external? Answer: This refers to what was previously stated regarding the sixth consciousness.
