[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the statement "if there is the wisdom of equality in the lower stages," the intent is that whenever the sixth consciousness of the upper or lower stages enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (dharmas), it invariably induces the wisdom of equality;
therefore, the wisdom of equality exists throughout both the upper and lower stages.

This is because the untainted (*anāsrava*) seventh consciousness and the sixth consciousness must necessarily belong to the same stage. However, if the tainted (*sāsrava*) manas and the sixth consciousness [are considered], [they do not necessarily share the same stage].
Alternatively, they may be bound by different stages (*bhūmi*), as explained in the *Yanmì* (Secret Exposition).
[Commentary: “If one is in the ten stages... all possess this wisdom” is a general statement, which will be explained in detail below.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "Relying on the mind of that stage [serves as] the support for the Peak of Existence," the intended meaning is as follows:

within the fixed positions, if one relies on the sixth consciousness of the Peak of Existence stage and enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by means of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmadhātu-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one induces the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

This Wisdom of Equality is not absent from the pure seventh consciousness during the absorption of cessation; therefore, the sixth consciousness of the Peak of Existence likewise takes the Peak of Existence itself as its support.

Since the seventh consciousness of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) takes the seventh consciousness as its support, it cannot be definitively stated that the seventh consciousness of the lower stages takes the sixth consciousness of the Peak of Existence as its support.
This is because the untainted (*anāsrava*) manas must belong to the same stage as the untainted sixth consciousness;
whereas the tainted (*sāsrava*) manas may, in some cases, belong to a different stage.

[Commentary]: Although it is said that throughout all stages [of meditative concentration] there is only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), the intention is as follows: this explains an external objection. The objection states: "It was previously mentioned that the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) is induced by the sixth consciousness; since this applies to all stages, it should likewise be mutually induced.

Thus, whichever stage one occupies, the sixth consciousness should correspond to whatever feeling is present, such as joy (*prīti*) or pleasure (*sukha*) in the first and second *dhyānas*, and so forth. [Private Note on the Meaning]: I have examined the meaning of this passage. It addresses the difficulty raised by an opponent who argues that if the Wisdom of Equality is induced by the sixth consciousness across all stages, then the specific mental factors associated with each stage—such as joy or pleasure in the lower *dhyānas*—should also be present when that wisdom arises.

The commentary resolves this by clarifying that while the Wisdom of Equality is indeed associated with equanimity throughout, its specific manifestation depends on the particular stage and the corresponding feeling-state of the sixth consciousness at that time. However, the primary nature of the Wisdom itself remains characterized by equanimity. This distinction allows for the coexistence of the wisdom’s fundamental quality with the variable experiences of the various meditative levels.

In the *Dīpa* (Lamp), the fifth fascicle, second section, on the left, from the fourth line downward, there is a question-and-answer session similar to this one; however, the *Dīpa* is more detailed in its exposition, whereas this text is not.
Since both are exclusively associated with neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), that which should be reflected upon is intended to have the same meaning as the previous explanation.

[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "not necessarily similar in all respects" is as follows: the cause and effect of the mind and mental factors are not necessarily similar, because they always take their objects equally.

Therefore, in terms of their association with feeling, they are exclusively associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*). However, regarding the number of other mental factors (causes and effects), they are not necessarily similar;
for it is the nature of the untainted wholesome mind to inherently possess this single-pointedness of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
The functions performed are all directly similar.
[Commentary]: Because of the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the higher realms, they may be termed "obscured" (*nivṛta*).

This means that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the upper stages must first be suppressed by the power of concentration before they can become obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*); were it otherwise, they would constitute an unwholesome (*akuśala*) nature.
[Commentary: As for the question, "Why is this consciousness termed 'indeterminate' (avyākṛta) and is also included within the indeterminate? the intended meaning is as follows:

Although the four afflictions associated with this consciousness would, by their nature, be unwholesome (akuśala), they are nonetheless of an indeterminate nature because the consciousness upon which they rely has subtle mental aspects, functions spontaneously, and is of a uniform character.
Nevertheless, the afflictions that depend [upon it] also take on the nature of the consciousness upon which they rely.

Regarding the statement that "the indeterminate does not obstruct the wholesome" because it does not obstruct the wholesome within the six consciousnesses—which are pervasive across the three natures—it is said that the seventh [consciousness] and its mental factors (*caitta*) are able to serve as the basis for the three natures.
This means they are pervasive across the three natures in terms of their function (*vyāpāra*), not that their essence (*svabhāva*) is pervasive across the three natures.
Therefore, the seventh serves as the basis for defilement and purity for the preceding six consciousnesses; furthermore, those that are pervasive across the three natures refer to the preceding six.
The consciousness arises with the three natures simultaneously; because the seventh [consciousness] is constantly active and arises together with them, it is said to "pervade the three natures.
[Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "this subtle" up to "all are the first explanation," the intended meaning is that the term "subtle" refers to both [the seventh and the eighth consciousnesses].
All of these are explained in the first [chapter] of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

[Commentary: Regarding the two interpretations presented here, the intention is that the current explanation of the "obscured-neutral" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature has two interpretations that differ from the two interpretations stated in that treatise, as detailed in the commentary.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "because the substance of the mind is subtle, it is called 'obscured' (*nivṛta*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

the mental king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) mutually manifest one another's characteristics, thereby establishing the state of being obscured. Why is this so? Because the afflictions associated with such phenomena are inherently unwholesome (*akuśala*), yet since the essence and marks of the mental king are extremely subtle, they manifest as such;
consequently, they cause the associated mental factors to also become indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) in nature. This is precisely...

The afflictions constitute the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta); however, when the mind-king (citta-rāja) becomes obscured, it is so because it is covered by the afflictions, whereas its essential nature is not itself obscured, as it does not obscure itself.

[Commentary]: Regarding "those that are simultaneously defiled and obstruct the noble [path]," this refers to the four afflictions which, being simultaneous with the mind, cause the mind itself to mutually obstruct the noble path.

As for "those that are simultaneously defiled and obstruct the noble [path]," this refers exclusively to the four simultaneous afflictions and does not include the *manas*, because the nature of the *manas* is not defiled.
Thus, the former interpretation is superior.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in the sixth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* concerning "conditions belonging to other realms," this is said in the context of analyzing afflictions that take other realms as their objects;
it means that one does not perceive worldly phenomena belonging to other realms as being "self" (*ātman*) and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) is bound to itself and others according to its object," when the seventh [consciousness] takes the eighth as its object, it is called "bound to itself and others" because it shares the same level (*bhūmi*) as its object.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this is based on the spontaneously arising (*sahaja*) up to its mode of activity (*ākāra*)," the intended meaning is that spontaneous self-view functions effortlessly.

Regarding the grasping of a self by taking both the general and the specific as its object: among the seventh and sixth consciousnesses, if the view of self generally reckons the five aggregates as the body to be the self, it then takes the dharmas of all three realms as its object, because within this very body there are dharmas belonging to all three realms.

If it specifically takes the self as its object, it then follows that it reckons one particular aggregate as the self according to what it perceives. Now, this consciousness truly possesses the view of self; it is only...
To take the eighth consciousness as the self by way of grasping it is precisely to grasp it as the self through a distinct objectification;

for this reason, we know that the seventh consciousness does not take seeds or the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) as its objects. If it were to take them as objects, it would necessarily take them all universally. Question:

It may be so regarding the seeds, but how is it with the *nimitta-bhāga*? Answer: If one takes the *nimitta-bhāga* of the eighth consciousness as "mine," consider, for instance, the case of the three faculties (*indriya*).

Suppose there is one who suddenly attains the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear; they are then led to bring forth the divine eye-faculty and divine ear-faculty of the higher realms within their own body, and only then are the two consciousnesses of the divine eye and divine ear able to arise.
However, these faculties of the two realms are the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective image portion) of the eighth consciousness.

When the seventh consciousness takes them as its object, it does so by taking the dharmas of the higher stages as its "mine" (*ātmīya-dharma*), rather than taking the *nimitta-bhāga* itself as its object.

[Commentary]: If that is so, as for the statement "the mind at the moment of death reaches this distinct object of the self," this question concerns the sixth consciousness, and the answer is as follows.
[Commentary]:

One must not object that the two fetters of association (*samprayoga*) and objective referent (*ālambana*) cannot be termed "bonds" (*bandhana*), even though the intention of the mind possesses an objective referent.
This does not define their connection by means of a fixed objective referent (*ālambana*), but rather defines their connection based on their mutual correspondence.
[Commentary: These three explanations of this passage constitute the three sections of the analysis.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "belonging to the stage of that object-condition," the intention is to cite the objective realm upon which the eighth consciousness relies in order to demonstrate that the seventh consciousness belongs to this same stage as the eighth consciousness.
[Treatise] If one asks: why is it that the passage beginning with "if the *ālayavijñāna* of maturation belonging to that stage arises" constitutes the correct interpretation? The answer is:

the preceding mention of "spontaneous [arising]" and so forth reveals the underlying reason (*yoniśas*), whereas the subsequent passage beginning with "if that [ālayavijñāna] arises" and so forth explains the specific application of the meaning.

[Commentary]: Although this interpretation exists, the previous explanation is superior. In the introductory section, there is the passage "or for the various afflictions of that stage" (*tadbhūmikakleśādi*).
Although this present text offers a different interpretation, it does not equal the previous one based on the objective conditions (*ālambana*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this exists within the causal stage until it becomes untainted": read this as a continuous sequence, and its meaning will become clear by itself.

From the first bhūmi onwards, it is called the "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti). Because the consciousness associated with this [basis] is untainted, and because this consciousness associated with it is untainted, [it is so named].
[Commentary: "Because it belongs to that class" means it belongs to the class of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). [Commentary:

Furthermore, regarding the statement "it says up to 'not for those beyond training' (*aśaikṣa*)," the intention is as follows: among the sixty-three [states], it is said that the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) suppresses afflictions (*kleśa*) but does not suppress the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Based on this, it speaks of the supramundane path; it does not speak of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Therefore, the Bodhi... [text continues].
Question: Since [the Sūtra] speaks of only two categories, why does it not mention the absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)? Answer:

Because the absorption of cessation is not the Path (*mārga*), and because it is neither a state of one in training (*śaikṣa*) nor beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is not mentioned. Furthermore, in that context, the two categories are distinguished in terms of persons (*pudgala*);

since it speaks of only two categories while encompassing both phenomena (*dharma*) and persons, [it mentions only two]. However, because the absorption of cessation is counted as a phenomenon itself, three categories are spoken of.

[Commentary]: However, regarding the eighth consciousness, it receives the name "ālaya" (storehouse) solely from the perspective of its afflictions. As for the explanation based on its own essential nature:
this eighth consciousness acquires the name "ālaya" merely from being grasped by the affliction of self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and the cognitive hindrance (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) is not mentioned therein.
Furthermore, the reason the seventh consciousness is called "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*) is that it is so named not only because of its afflictions, but also...
The pervasive attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) is explained according to its own essence (*svabhāva*), because it is not established by relying on other dharmas.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "it does not function in either" for those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the term "no-more-learning" comprehensively includes all three vehicles; therefore, it is said that it does not function in either.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "since the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is subtle, the Bodhisattva does not derive his name from it," the intended meaning is as follows: The name *ālaya-vijñāna* (store-consciousness) is established based on the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Since the Bodhisattva has already suppressed the afflictions, although he still possesses attachment to phenomena, the eighth consciousness cannot be designated by the name *ālaya*.

This is because the attachment to phenomena is incapable of grasping the eighth consciousness as "self" (*ātman*) or "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*). Even if the attachment to phenomena were capable of grasping the eighth consciousness, [the name *ālaya*] still could not be applied.
It is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
[Commentary: It is named "the storehouse" (*ālaya*) because Bodhisattvas should not abandon it, as their attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) still persists.

[Commentary: Regarding those of the Two Vehicles who attain sudden enlightenment—within the Two Vehicles there are those of sharp and dull faculties, who are termed "sudden" and "gradual"—now, in this case...

Regarding those of sharp faculties, it is said they attain "sudden enlightenment" (*tunwu*). Alternatively, the first stage of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles, or the initial stage of a Bodhisattva, may be called "sudden enlightenment" in order to distinguish them from Bodhisattvas who attain enlightenment gradually.
[Commentary] Furthermore, the interpretation that the worldly path involves the contemplation of phenomena (*shiguan*) and so forth is also based on the sixty-third passage of the text.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "not that which is to be countered" up to "differentiated transformation," the meaning is as follows: if one discusses the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), because it observes [objects] as being real entities, it is limited to this;
thus, the afflictions of the seventh consciousness and so forth are not what is to be countered by the mundane path.
Furthermore, the phrase "the power of the object-condition" means that the delusions of the seventh consciousness and so forth are also not the objects of the mundane path.
This is because worldly paths do not take [such objects] as their cognitive conditions.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "non-conceptual wisdom... because it contradicts the grasping at a self," this explains the reason why [this wisdom] must first arise from the untainted minds of the three vehicles in order to suppress [the grasping].

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "both contradict themselves," it means that the Bodhisattvas' attachment to phenomena and persons contradicts their own contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), while the followers of the Three Vehicles' attachment to self and person contradicts their own contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); therefore, they are said to "contradict themselves."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "either a portion or the whole," the intended meaning is as follows: "a portion" refers exclusively to the uncontaminated outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);

"or the whole" refers to the outflow of both the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Regarding the statement "not currently manifesting," the intention is this: entering a contemplation on one portion contradicts the manifestation of that [corresponding] portion;

if one enters the contemplation on both emptinesses, it causes the contradiction of all manifestations. Thus, it is said that they are mutually [contradictory]; this is the intended meaning. "I" [is the speaker].
Because the two attachments to phenomena (dharma) directly contradict [the realization], they do not function.
[Commentary: The subsequent passage clarifies that after the two attachments have been extinguished, they arise again once one emerges from contemplation.

This means that after the extinction of the two attachments to self and phenomena, they re-emerge upon exiting the meditative state. This is like the Hīnayāna, which [regards] the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā).

When a bodhisattva induces the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) through the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) does not arise;
or, by entering both contemplations simultaneously, both types of grasping do not arise. Subsequently, upon emerging from that state, they attain birth.

When it is said that "grasping at birth and grasping at phenomena" [arise], the intended meaning is that for those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), when they enter the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) does not arise, and for the bodhisattva, the grasping at phenomena likewise does not arise.

Therefore, it is said that they arise according to what is appropriate. Furthermore, the phrase "arising after the two types of cessation have been manifested" clarifies that after the two types of cessation—namely, the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*)—have been manifested, they subsequently arise.
This is because for an Arhat who has attained these two types of cessation, the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) do not function within these two states.

Upon emerging from contemplation, one attains the subsequent arising of the Śrāvaka’s contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the statement, "The contemplation of emptiness induces the cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*) such that the two types of grasping do not function, and the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) likewise does not function as appropriate," this refers specifically to the grasping at phenomena in relation to Bodhisattvas.
As for the non-mention of the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*), it is because this grasping likewise does not function for them, just as it does not for those of the Two Vehicles;
therefore, it is not mentioned again.
[Commentary]: "The meaning of 'having no basis' reveals that for an Arhat, there is no basis for the grasping at a self.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that this consciousness and its defiled dharmas are subsumed within the ninth stage (*navama-bhūmi*), the intent is as follows:

when discussing the afflictions within the seventh consciousness, they constitute a single category that cannot be divided into distinct grades. For now, we shall discuss them according to the three realms (*tridhātu*) to demonstrate how they exist."
The nine grades correspond to one grade within each of the nine stages (*bhūmi*). Within each stage, that which is most settled and whose characteristics are subtle is designated as the "lower grade.
If one considers this in relation to the nine grades of afflictions of the sixth consciousness within its own respective stage, it corresponds to the ninth grade; this is the case for every stage.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "all stages" to "because their power and influence are equal," the intended meaning is that within all stages, the afflictions of the seventh consciousness are simultaneously and instantaneously severed at the same time as the ninth, lowest-of-the-low grade of the sixth consciousness of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) stage;

this is because their power and influence are equal, and they equally obstruct the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). This implies that although the afflictions of the seventh consciousness exist in each respective stage...
In each category, all [afflictions] are abandoned simultaneously with the ninth category of affliction within the sixth consciousness of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
This means that although there are nine categories, they are all abandoned at once along with the lowest-of-the-low category of the Peak of Existence;
thus, the seventh category of affliction bound to the Desire Realm is similar to that lowest-of-the-low category of the Peak of Existence, because its activity cannot manifest [its own fruit].
"Because karma moistens birth and so forth.
[Commentary: If there is an objection stating that since there are nine grades, the principle of "no ninth grade" is untenable, the intent is as follows:

this is an external objection consisting of two points. The first objection is that coarse and subtle factors are not of a single category; the second objection is that since there are indeed nine grades...

The coarse and the subtle should not be of the same category. The meaning is this: if one says that the three realms, when compared with one another, have nine grades, and that these are severed by a path of nine grades, then they would not be of a single category.
For instance, within the form realm there are four stages, and thus there are four grades; how could these be of a single category?
The rest should be understood accordingly. Regarding the statement that this consciousness does not exist up to the ninth grade, it is difficult for there to be a first grade without a ninth grade.

The meaning of the second objection is as follows: when it says "in reality there are nine grades" at the end, it answers that there are indeed nine grades rather than the sense of being only one grade.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "he, by means of his preparatory practice, reaches the point where there are in reality nine grades," this refers to the Master of the Treatise’s response concerning the person who has transcended two fruits.
Because their faculties are extremely sharp, the power of their preparatory application (*prayoga*)—which consists of eighty-one grades—is consolidated into nine grades.

Although nine types of liberation paths (*vimukti-mārga*) and nine types of uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) sever [the afflictions], there is no contradiction in a single path severing a single grade; rather, it is simply that each grade contains nine sub-grades.
Question: Why is this so? Answer: Because these obstructions pertain to the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the eighty-one grades are consolidated into nine.
What prevents the simultaneous abandonment of the afflictions of the sixth [dhyāna] and those of the lower grades of the *bhavāgra* (the Peak of Existence)?
Why would there be nine grades?

[Commentary]: However, the meaning of this seventh [point], up to the phrase "simultaneous sudden abandonment," intends to explain that it is like the seventh [affliction] of its own level within the desire realm.

Although the afflictions of the intermediate state are not subsumed within the nine grades, these afflictions are similar to the ninth-grade view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) within the sixth consciousness of oneself and others;
thus, they are abandoned simultaneously in a single moment. [Objection:

Since there is one master who maintains that the view of self within the sixth consciousness is abandoned gradually rather than instantaneously, how can you say it is identical to the ninth grade of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception?

Duanzhi’s answer explains this in terms of those who leap over two fruits: when one abandons the ninth grade of the desire realm, it is simultaneously the abandonment of the ninth grade of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Why is this so? Because the nine grades are bound together as a single unit;
thus, this is called "breaking the bamboo," for when one node is broken, the entire section is likewise broken. Therefore, the eighty-one grades are collectively condensed into nine.

If one were to grant that the nine grades of affliction are similar across the three realms in terms of their coarseness and subtlety, this would contradict the previous master’s refusal to accept the doctrine of the nine grades;

for in that case, the seventh consciousness of those beings lacking the nature for liberation (*agotra*) would have no capacity to be perfumed, as there would be no increase or decrease [in its state].
Therefore, the nine grades do indeed exist.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as in the case of the roots of goodness being severed by wrong view, which is divided into nine grades," the intended meaning is as follows:

This analogy implies that the seventh consciousness also possesses nine grades, just as the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of wrong view is intensified. Although the ninth grade of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) consists of only a single grade, it is nonetheless further divided into nine grades;

likewise, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of this seventh consciousness are also divided into nine grades within each of their respective grades. Furthermore, wrong view is capable of severing the roots of goodness.

Regarding the roots [of goodness], according to two explanations in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*: one says that a single grade of wrong view can suddenly and simultaneously sever all nine grades of roots of goodness, just as when the afflictions are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whichever grade of knowledge it may be, it simultaneously abandons the nine grades of afflictions;

the second says that they are severed gradually, like the abandonment of afflictions through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), wherein a weak root of a low grade of wrong view is able to sever superior wholesome [roots].
When a supreme (uttama) false view is able to sever the lower roots of goodness, it may do so by taking each individual Truth (satya) as its object;

thus, it can give rise to the nine grades of false views either simultaneously or sequentially. Alternatively, one may first take the four Truths as objects in succession before the nine grades of false views arise.

Whichever false views take the four Truths as their objects, they are all capable of severing the innate wholesome states (upapatti-lābhika-kuśala) accordingly, as explained extensively in that *Vibhaṅga*.
The Master Jizang asked: "How can a single grade (ekavidha) be divided into nine grades? He replied:

"What is called 'one grade' refers to the nine grades collectively being termed one grade. Furthermore, within the seventh consciousness, across all stages (bhūmi), they are all subsumed under the ninth grade.
Since these nine instances of the ninth grade are all equally subsumed under the ninth grade, they are combined to form a single grade."
In fact, there are nine grades, such as wrong views and so forth.

[Commentary: As explained previously regarding the second type of perfuming agent, the meaning is that the number of afflictions in the seventh consciousness and the ninth grade of feeling within the sixth consciousness of the *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana* (the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception) constitute a single grade; therefore, they are simultaneous and identical.
If cessation refers to a single grade rather than nine grades, how then can it function as a perfuming agent? The answer is:

this is discussed in terms of the three realms and nine stages; according to the relative coarseness and subtlety across these stages—where the lower stages are coarse and the upper stages are subtle—it functions as a perfuming agent.

[Commentary]: "Because one severs the bonds of that" means that because the bond of self-grasping prevents the two vehicles from attaining liberation, severing this view of self at the present time is called "severing the bonds of that.
[Commentary]: "If a bodhisattva severs non-defilement, they also eliminate it" means that while the two vehicles regard non-defilement as the absence of defilement, the bodhisattva is able to...
[The text says: "Severed. [Commentary: If one were to define "severance" as non-functioning, then this consciousness could be eliminated.

However, if we rely on the fact that a portion of the eighth consciousness is absent due to the retribution of evil karma, then simultaneously a portion of the seventh consciousness is also non-functional. If "abandonment" is defined based on this non-functioning, then...

To hold such an interpretation is equivalent to asserting that the cause has perished while the fruit remains severed. If this is so, why is it said that [the afflictions] are abandoned simultaneously with the lowest-of-the-low grade of afflictions of the Peak of Existence?
The answer is: that statement refers to the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*), whereas this concerns the sense of non-arising; thus, their meanings differ.

[Commentary: The meaning of the phrase "one cannot use this case as an analogy for that" is as follows: while the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*) that trigger the production of karma may not arise once they have been severed, this is not the case for the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Because the latter are not triggered by the production of karma, one cannot use these afflictions of cultivation as an analogy for the former, which are severed so that they do not arise.
If that were so, then even the wholesome dharmas within the bodies of those in the evil destinies and women would likewise [not arise].

Regarding how the afflictions of discrimination arise and why they are called "non-arising" and "abandoned": it is because those afflictions only arise when one has acquired a body within a particular realm of rebirth (*gati*).
If that were the case, the seventh [consciousness] would also be included, as it too is induced by karma; however, while the eighth consciousness arises first, the seventh only arises later.
Although this objection exists, it does not apply here as it did previously.

[Commentary]: Regarding the questioner who adopts the position of the first master concerning the abandonment [of the seventh consciousness] by the eighth consciousness—namely, that this seventh consciousness is also abandoned when one in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) turns the mind toward the Mahāyāna—the present text provides an external interjection: "If this turning-mind *aśaikṣa* also abandons the seventh consciousness, why is it not mentioned here?
The answer is as follows: as that [text] states within the third fascicle, in the section clarifying the abandonment of the *ālayavijñāna*, that first master [holds that] the three...

Relying on the *ālayavijñāna* of one who has attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it does not refer to a bodhisattva. When that [text] asks why it does not mention a non-retrogressive bodhisattva, this case is likewise the same;
therefore, it is said to be "the same as that. The first master poses the question to examine the preceding passage.

[Commentary: Regarding "they should be explained separately in sequence," it means that those who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment] from the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) should be explained separately from those of sudden awakening.

[Commentary: Regarding "to what example do they correspond? this refers to whether these non-retrogressive bodhisattvas correspond to the example of bodhisattvas or to the example of those at the stage of no-more-learning.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the textual force is general," as explained above, the absence of a seventh [consciousness] was clarified generally across three positions; now it is clarified specifically.
As for this absence of a seventh within these three positions, does it constitute its *substance* (tattva) or its *name*? Below, various masters hold differing disputes on this point.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Sthiramati and others," the word "others" refers to his own disciples or to those in the West who hold such views. [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement that the supramundane manas does not actually engage in deliberation, it means that it does not deliberate on the notion of a self; this is what is meant by "not engaging in deliberation."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "these, such as the undefiled manas," it is said that the sixth consciousness must necessarily have a co-nascent, non-common support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*), which refers to the existence of the pure seventh consciousness.

[Commentary: Regarding the sequential and inverse exclusion of the eighth consciousness and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) as seeds—one should assign these inversely to the three conditions previously analyzed under the second transformation.
Since it was first necessary to establish the non-common [condition], one speaks of "inversely excluding" that non-common support;
this excludes the eighth consciousness from among the co-existent supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*). This is because the eighth consciousness...

Because it serves as a common support for all dharmas, the term "arising" (*jāti*) is used to distinguish it from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), since the immediately preceding condition does not arise simultaneously.

The term "simultaneous" (*saha*) is used to distinguish it from the seed (*bīja*), because the seed is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Here, this "simultaneity" reveals the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Although there is this interpretation—where "arising" distinguishes it from the seed and "simultaneity" distinguishes it from the immediately preceding condition—it does not accord with the literal text.

Next, the term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) is explained as follows: as previously stated, the two characters "co-arising" (*sahaja*) serve to exclude both the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*) and the seed-condition (*bīja-pratyaya*).
This is because the immediate condition depends on what precedes and follows and is therefore not co-arising;
furthermore, the seed is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), whereas the co-arising [condition] is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), as indicated by the word "co-arising."
[Commentary]: "This refers to the majority" means it is stated based on other occasions, but does not refer to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

[Commentary]: "However, regarding the difficulty that the number of consciousnesses arising as cited cannot be seven," the meaning is that this poses a question by citing the preceding *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* passage.
For instance, as the aforementioned treatise states: "The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is definitely always associated with one..."
The passage stating that "consciousnesses arise together, up to seven arising together," refers generally to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

However, the passage stating that "if one abides in the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), up to two [consciousnesses] arising together," represents the Master’s (Vasubandhu’s) primary point of refutation.

If, as Master Sthiramati maintains, the seventh consciousness does not exist during either the state of the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) or the meditative attainment of cessation, how could the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* state that when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, there are then two [consciousnesses] arising together?
The meaning of this original objection is that [the mental consciousness] arises up to seven times simultaneously, and so forth. A question is raised:

If there are those beyond training (aśaikṣa) who likewise lack the seventh consciousness, why is this not treated as an objection equivalent to [the objection regarding] the Noble Path? Furthermore, regarding the present objection that those beyond training lack the seventh consciousness:
if the five sensory consciousnesses arise, they should only be accompanied by six consciousnesses; if that were so, what then?
The *Śāstra* asks: "If five consciousnesses arise suddenly and operate simultaneously with the seventh [consciousness], would this not likewise contradict the Noble Path?
This objection is similar to that regarding the Noble Path. As for the meaning of "not an objection concerning simultaneous operation with the seven":

it asks why this is similar to the objection regarding the Noble Path and so forth, stating that if one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) were to suddenly give rise to the five consciousnesses, they would then operate simultaneously with the seventh; thus, it is called "not an objection concerning simultaneous operation with the seven. This, then, is the general [point].
The meaning of citing the preceding *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* passage is that there is no difficulty in the sense [of the argument]. The entire preceding section is a series of questions. [Commentary:
The meaning of the text seems to be that from the statement "there is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)" up to "there is no storehouse consciousness," the intent is to say:

this is the answer to the aforementioned question. The intent is to say: it is also consistent with the noble path (*āryamārga*) and so forth to raise such an objection regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The text contains the term "ālayavijñāna," which is why [the objection] is not difficult. Why?
Because those beyond training (aśaikṣa) lack the ālayavijñāna, and they also lack the seventh consciousness; therefore, it is not difficult.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the defiled mind (kliṣṭamanas) does not exist because it is accepted by both parties," if one were to speak merely of the non-existence of the defiled mind, this would be mutually accepted.
However, if its substantial entity (svabhāva) were also non-existent, that is not accepted by Dharmapāla and others; therefore, it is here refuted.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the wisdom which relies on one consciousness as its support," this master maintains that the Wisdom of Equality (samatājñāna) relies solely upon the sixth consciousness;
or, among the six consciousnesses, it may rely on any one of them, with that specific consciousness serving as the support and the Wisdom of Equality serving as the supported.

[Commentary]: The meaning of "not the wisdom associated with the six consciousnesses" is that the Wisdom of Equality is not a wisdom associated with the six consciousnesses, because wisdom associated with the six consciousnesses is subject to change and fluctuation.
Furthermore, the meaning of "not the wisdom associated with the six consciousnesses" is that it does not refer specifically to the stage of Buddhahood;

rather, regardless of which vehicle one speaks of, when explaining the sixth sense-base (*ṣaḍāyatana*) or the cultivation of the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), this wisdom is always subject to change and fluctuation.
Whether tainted (*sāsrava*) or untainted (*anāsrava*), they arise through mutual influence; if it pertains to the stage of a Buddha, it functions constantly and without interruption.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "if the noble path were present, there would be the fault of their coexistence," the intended meaning is as follows:

the two versions of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* explain the seventh consciousness by means of the five "common characteristics" (*pañca-sādharmya*) as the support for the sixth consciousness. If one followed the view of Master Sthiramati, there would be no supramundane [consciousness].
Regarding the *Manas* [consciousness], the syllogisms (sādhya and hetu) established in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* both contain fallacies.
[Commentary: The meaning of the phrase "if stated generally... because there is no basis" is that the *Yogācāra* treatises establish it in this manner;
however, the master Sthiramati does not accept the supramundane *manas*, and thus such faults arise for the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Furthermore, regarding the faults that follow below, the intention is that they are all faults of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). It says:

"If one does not take [the six consciousnesses] as the fundamental tenet, but merely establishes the tenet that 'only the sixth consciousness exists,' then there is the fault of contradicting one's own tenet by asserting 'the sixth consciousness and so forth' [when the 'and so forth' implies more than just the sixth]."
[Commentary]: If one says that excluding the Noble Path (āryamārga) serves as the basis for inference (*anumāna*), the intention is this:

if one alters the thesis (*pakṣa*), there is the fault of contradicting the inference because it has been established by scriptural authority (*āgama*). The authoritative statement is: "The sixth consciousness, such as the Noble Path, must also have a support (*āśraya*), because it is a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

just like the mental consciousness that excludes the state of non-conceptualization (*anyathā-manasikāra*). Thus, there are two faults within the thesis: first, [the fault of contradicting inference].
This [reason] is partially contradictory to the thesis (*siddhānta*) and secondly, it contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

[Commentary: "If, because they are subsumed under the six consciousnesses, [they] reach the point where the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has no support"—the meaning is that by taking the subsumption under the six consciousnesses as the reason, one establishes the previous general thesis;
however, this reason possesses the fallacy of being "uncertain due to self-inclusion" (*svato-anaikāntika*). As for the general thesis, as stated in the commentary: "If one speaks generally..."
The sixth consciousness reaching its superior, distinct basis (*adhipati-viśeṣa-āśraya*) is the general thesis (*siddhānta*). Furthermore, it is said:

"If [the seventh] is subsumed under the six consciousnesses, then according to the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, it would constitute a distinct thesis; thus, there is no seventh. The intent of this is as follows:

if one were to take the six consciousnesses as the reason for establishing the subsequent distinct thesis, two faults would arise: first, contradiction with the self-characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa-viruddha*); second, contradiction with the certainty (*niyama-viruddha*). Why?

Regarding the subsequent distinct school’s response as stated in the commentary: "If, excluding the noble path and the mental consciousness of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), all other mental consciousnesses must necessarily have this support," how can this latter position avoid the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic of the phenomenon (*dharma-svalakṣaṇa-viruddha*)? The response is as follows:

To establish the formal argument (*prayoga*): "A portion of the remaining mental consciousnesses would also lack a support, because they are subsumed within the six consciousnesses, just like [the mental consciousness] you [accept]."

Because the noble path (*āryamārga*) that is being excluded is the consciousness of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), this is the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon;

it contradicts the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*). [Commentary: The fallacy of "contradiction by determination" (*niścayaviruddha*) arises from the aforementioned reason (*hetu*); however, it is simply a modification of the preceding reason.

The reason given is that since the cause is subsumed solely within the six consciousnesses, there is only the fault of contradicting the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property itself (*dharmin*), and not the fault of a definitive contradiction (*niścita-viruddha*). Why is this?

Because a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a definitive contradiction would overturn the preceding cause; how, then, can it now be said that there is the fault of a definitive contradiction?
Furthermore, according to the *Śūyao*, it is also stated that both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*) each have two faults, but it does not mention "definitive" [contradiction].
This is because the Master’s original pen-draft contained an error; alternatively, one might reformulate the preceding reason as a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) as follows:

"The sixth afflicted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must lack a coexistent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), because it is subsumed under either the afflicted or the pure [categories], just like the sixth consciousness during the Path (*ārya-mārga*) and so forth.
Since the preceding reason has been thus modified, it results in the fallacy of a contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*) in their three stages are "unstained" (*akliṣṭa*) with respect to the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), the intent is as follows:

although the two vehicles in these three stages possess the afflicted *manas* associated with clinging to phenomena, they are still termed "unstained" because it does not obstruct the noble path-factors (*ārya-mārga-aṅga*) of the two vehicles.
This is not the case for Bodhisattvas; if the sixth consciousness enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*), the seventh...

That which is associated with the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is defiled; the sixth [stage], the entry into the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), is associated with the wisdom of non-equality (*asamatājñāna*) and is purely immaculate and untainted (*anāsrava*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the distinctions to be considered according to what is appropriate," the meaning is that the seventh [stage] constitutes the distinction of the accomplishment of purity.
The power of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) also depends on the sixth [consciousness] inducing the seventh before the distinction between defilement and purity can be established.

[Commentary]: Whichever vehicle one follows, it is taught that for those who do not posit the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) sever the defiled view of self, while Bodhisattvas sever both the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma*).
However, since the grasping at phenomena is not defiled for the two vehicles, it may also be termed "pure"; yet because Bodhisattvas are able to eliminate it, [it is considered defiled for them].

Regarding the statement, "The defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) is never without the substance of the seventh consciousness; there are four stages," these are the three vehicles’ stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and the stage of non-retrogression.

[Commentary: Regarding the subsequent explanation of "the distinctions of this [mind]" and so forth, it refers to what the treatise says starting from: "The distinctions of this manas are briefly of three kinds," and so on.

[Commentary]: This is said with the intention that for those who have not previously [attained it], the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is first abandoned when entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Thus, "abandoning the name" refers to abandoning the designation of the view of a personal entity (*pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
[Commentary: This meaning refers to the intention that when one enters the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), [the defiled manas] is abandoned.
It explains that while in the state of outflows (*sāsrava*), this consciousness is able to be associated with the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) without abandoning the defiled *manas*.

However, upon reaching the state of outflowlessness, there is no longer a *manas* associated with self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*), because the realization of true selflessness (*anātman*) contradicts self-clinging.

[Commentary: "As below, so too for the abandonment of these associated [factors]" means that as stated in the subsequent text regarding the abandonment of these four associated factors, the same applies to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the others.
[Commentary: One cannot say that they are mutually abandoned; one must not claim that the temporary absence of the seventh [consciousness] constitutes abandonment.

The eighth [consciousness] is also called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) when it is temporarily not grasped by others; however, one cannot use the term "permanent abandonment" for the eighth to imply that the seventh is also permanently abandoned.

Why is this not possible? Because the defilement of the seventh is severed by its own nature (*svabhāva-prahīṇa*), and thus it is termed "abandoned" even during the period when it is temporarily absent.
The eighth, however, is severed through its objects and fetters (*ālambana-bandhana-prahīṇa*); it requires that others never grasp it again before it can be so designated.
This is called "abandonment" (*śānti*).
[Commentary: Since those in training (*śaikṣa*) of the Two Vehicles are not yet said to have attained abandonment, there is no scriptural passage stating that they abandon the *ālayavijñāna*.
Therefore, one cannot say that the seventh consciousness is temporarily abandoned in order to manifest that the eighth is also temporarily abandoned.
[Commentary]: If it were admitted that [the seeds] are temporarily relinquished, then they would also have to be called "relinquished" [permanently].

If it is admitted that even the eighth consciousness is temporary, then why is it that the untainted [minds] of those in training (śaikṣa) of the two vehicles also do not temporarily grasp or store [seeds], yet these are not called "relinquished"?

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because the defiled, secondary false [manas] contradicts the outflow-free," the intended meaning is that when one enters the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the seventh [consciousness] is temporarily relinquished;

some say it is the manas associated with the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) that does not function when entering the outflow-free state. Others claim this refers to the temporary relinquishment of the name "ālayavijñāna" when the eighth [consciousness] enters the outflow-free state.
This interpretation is incorrect, as it contradicts the aforementioned explanation.
[Commentary]: If this [state] exists in the initial stage, it necessarily involves this state of grasping; this refers to the position associated with the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

The intended meaning is that when there is grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), there must be grasping at phenomena; however, when there is grasping at phenomena, there is not necessarily grasping at a self. This is because the stage of grasping at phenomena is extensive, whereas the stage of grasping at a self is brief.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena" to "the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena," the intended meaning is as follows:

entering the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasunyatā-vipaśyanā*), the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) induced by that contemplation, and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) induced by it—all these involve the sixth consciousness entering the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena;
however, they induce the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) associated with the seventh consciousness.

[Commentary: "The outflow is likewise because its essential category is identical" means that as for "outflow," it refers to the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā-jñāna*).

When explaining this fruit, the seventh consciousness is also accompanied by the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), because it belongs to the same essential category as the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "if one contemplates [them] as not so": when one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) and so forth within the sixth consciousness, it does not induce the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna);
however, if one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā), it is then able to induce the seventh wisdom of equality.
[Commentary]: However, regarding the statement that "the distant fruit within the fruits [of cultivation] reaches the [ultimate] dharma-contemplation," this also refers to the two proximate fruits;
that is, each of the two subsequent attainments (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) is called a "proximate fruit" in relation to the two contemplations of arising and of dharmas (*dharmālambana*).

[Commentary]: Based on this, one should explain the "proximate fruit. According to this principle, because the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmadharmatā-śūnyatā-jñāna*) necessarily induces the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) regarding the emptiness of phenomena immediately thereafter, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that the subsequently attained wisdom of the contemplation of phenomena manifests;

it is not a distant fruit, as is the case with the subsequently attained wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Question: Why is the subsequently attained wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons not considered the proximate fruit? Answer: With respect to the [emptiness of] phenomena...

Because the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) does not belong to its own category, it is not called "proximate. If that is so, then the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is its own category. The answer is:

based on the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), the absorption of cessation is also considered to be of its own category. Furthermore, the meaning of the statement that there is no "immediately proximate fruit" is as follows: it refers to the subsequently attained wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);

when viewed from the perspective of the subsequently attained wisdom regarding the emptiness of phenomena, this [wisdom regarding the emptiness of persons] is called a "remote fruit" in relation to the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena.

If it is the distant fruit, it refers to the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arising from the person-observation (*pudgala-darśana*); if it is that which manifests immediately, it refers to entering the subsequent [knowledge] from the dharma-observation (*dharma-darśana*).
At the time of the arising of the observation, both the fundamental [knowledge] and the subsequent [knowledge] are the fruits of the dharma-observation;
because the text is abbreviated, it mentions only the subsequent knowledge as the distant fruit.

[Commentary]: Alternatively, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) reaches up to the subsequent wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that arises after the contemplation of persons.

This commentary provides a further explanation: it is certainly not the case that the subsequent wisdom following the contemplation of phenomena (*dharma-vipaśyanā*) cannot induce the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
It is likewise not problematic that this [emptiness of persons] serves as a remote fruit (*viprakṛṣṭa-phala*) in relation to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

[Commentary]: Regarding this, as for the first interpretation—that "this reaches the entirety of the treatise on the fruit"—it refers to what was stated above: "Therefore, it should be explained," and so forth.

As for the latter meaning—that "it is perhaps from the eighth stage onward, etc."—the term "entirety of the treatise on the fruit" means that it does not distinguish between near and far, but speaks of the fruit in general;
thus, the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons is also induced by the emptiness of phenomena.

Because it refers to the fruit [of the path], as the treatise states, when the wisdom that realizes the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna) is present, the seventh consciousness—which clings to phenomena—no longer functions;
since there is no mention of a distant fruit other than this, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of the "defiled seventh" in its entirety.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "loss of the two objects, the contaminated and the uncontaminated," the intended meaning here is as follows:

since one fears that within the context of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one might simultaneously take both the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and True Suchness (*tathatā*) as objects, this question is posed.
[Commentary: "And all" means that at all other times, one enters the true contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharmatā-śūnyatā-dhyāna*), which is the essential body (*svabhāva-kāya*).

[Commentary: In reality, it is only conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); that is, the semblance-aspect of True Suchness (*tathatā-nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) is called "conditioned" because it is a reflection upon the mind.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that [the seventh consciousness] universally takes both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as its objects: this means that the subsequent Equality Wisdom (*samatājñāna*) takes the contaminated maturation (*vipāka*) as its object, while the uncontaminated [aspect] takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
Question: Why is this so? Answer: Because the seventh [consciousness], being induced by the sixth [consciousness] which takes True Suchness as its object, also takes True Suchness as its object.
[Commentary: Here, the general statement "taking the ripening [consciousness] and so forth as objects" includes *tathatā* (suchness).
This interpretation of the treatise is based on the fact that within subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one attains the taking of what resembles *tathatā* as an object. Question:

Why does the treatise speak only of taking the ripening consciousness and the immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) as objects, and not mention *tathatā*? Answer: Because subsequent cognition does not take *tathatā* as its direct object through a mode of grasping (*grāhaka*). Therefore...
Because it does not state that [the mind] takes both the ultimate and the conventional as its dual objects.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the previous interpretation is superior," this means it is superior because it universally takes the conventional as its object, as if it were the ultimate.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because their nature has not yet been abandoned," it is because the eighth [consciousness] has not yet been able to completely abandon grasping; some say it is because their nature has not yet been abandoned.

The intended meaning is that prior to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), if one does not enter the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), even at the seventh stage one remains associated with the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*), because one has not yet abandoned such grasping;
therefore, it is correct to understand that the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) takes the ālayavijñāna as its object.

[Commentary]: "The characters 'consciousness' (識) and so forth" means that when combined with the term "and so forth" (等), it refers to the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation consciousness), the *amala-vijñāna* (stainless consciousness), and others. [Commentary]:

"The self of persons (*pudgala-ātman*) is the primary [subject], while the reference to the self of phenomena (*dharma-ātman*) is secondary and narrow" means that one distinguishes between these two types: the self of persons and the self of phenomena.

Regarding the essential dharma of differentiation, I take the "self of persons" (*pudgala-ātman*) as the primary basis for its arising. Question: Why is it called the "self of persons"? Answer: Because one conceives of a self based upon the person, it is called the "self of persons.

Since the "self" possesses the function of mastery (*adhipati*), it is the master; it possesses the function of sovereign control (*svatantra*), and the "ruler" (*īśvara*) possesses the function of decisive severance.

Furthermore, it is because one also conceives of the functions of being an agent (*kartṛ*) and an experiencer (*bhoktṛ*). As for the "self of phenomena" (*dharma-ātman*), it refers to that which is based upon phenomena.
The essence possesses the superior functions of maintaining its own nature and so forth; these are the superior functions of mastery and so forth.

Here, when speaking of the "self of phenomena" (*dharmātman*), it is in the sense of mastery and not in the sense of a sovereign ruler, because the "self of phenomena" is broader than the [personal] self, and one conceives of a self based upon phenomena;
hence it is called the "self of phenomena."

[Commentary]: Regarding the metaphors used here, there are varying depths of meaning. As for the intent of those who hold to the grasping of dharmas (*dharmagrāha*): the "shallow" metaphor refers to being deluded by a tree stump, which represents being deluded by dharmas;
this is the grasping of dharmas. If the tree stump is taken to be a person, it represents the arising of the grasping of a self (*ātman-grāha*) based upon the grasping of dharmas.
[Commentary]: The "deep" metaphor refers to the intention of those who give rise to grasping at phenomena among human beings; it means that the preceding dharmas possess depth.

Those who are deluded regarding the stump serve as a metaphor for being deluded regarding the principle of the emptiness of dharmas. When one mistakes the stump for a person, this serves as a metaphor for the grasping at persons (*pudgala-grāha*). Question:

What is the distinction between this "deep" metaphor for grasping at persons and the "shallow" metaphor for grasping at persons? Answer: There is no difference in kind; it is merely based on the delusion regarding the stump.

The [distinctions between] shallow and deep are divided according to human attachments, which are of a single kind. To the question, "Why is it that while human attachments are of one kind, the dharmas are not?
the answer is: regarding the dharmas, the explanation is based on the delusion concerning principle (*li*); regarding humans, it is based on the arising of phenomena (*shi*).

Therefore, within the dharmas there are analogies of both shallow and deep, whereas human attachments are but one kind and lack such distinctions of depth. In reality, even the person who is deluded is deluded regarding principle; however, they must first be deluded regarding the emptiness of dharmas.
Only when one grasps that phenomena have a basis and that these phenomena possess power does the attachment to a self arise;

even when one grasps the Buddha-nature as the self, one still grasps that phenomena have a substantial essence, and it is based on this functional activity that the attachment to a self arises. To speak from this single perspective, it is said that one is deluded regarding both principle and phenomena;
yet according to the ultimate reality, one is also deluded regarding the principle of self-emptiness (*ātmaśūnyatā*).

[Commentary] Question: It may also be said that among humans there is "reaching up to the grasping of phenomena" (*vastu-grāha*). The intention [of this question] is to pose a counter-question by reversing the analogy to the grasping of persons (*pudgala-grāha*).

The question asks: If it is the case that within phenomena (*dharma*) one is deluded regarding principle (*li*), whereas among humans one gives rise to the grasping of phenomena, then might it not also be the case that the grasping of persons is deluded regarding the principle of non-self (*anātman*), while giving rise to the grasping of phenomena within phenomena?

Answer: Because the grasping of phenomena is broad in scope, it universally encompasses all delusions; the grasping of persons is [narrower], being limited to [the delusion regarding] non-self. Therefore, [the former] pervades [the latter].
The narrow [interpretation] relies on the person to calculate the self; thus, it is only by relying on the person’s body that one gives rise to attachment, calculating it to be the self.

[Commentary: Regarding the difficulty of the "shallow" analogy, the phrase "it is not an attachment to dharmas" means: for instance, among the analogies there are shallow and deep ones. The deep analogy refers to the body, which is difficult to escape from.
The shallow analogy refers to being deluded regarding a tree stump. However, as long as one dwells in delusion regarding dharmas, that is precisely attachment to dharmas. It is shallow.
The meaning of the objection regarding the "person" (*pudgala*) clinging [to a stump] and the theory of body and life is as follows:

If one says that clinging to a stump can be used as an analogy for the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), while the bark of a tree trunk serves as an analogy for the phenomena themselves, then being deluded about the stump should not be an analogy for the clinging to phenomena. Therefore, the Commentary states: "Being deluded about the stump should not be the clinging to phenomena.

However, the intent of the response is this: "Being deluded about the stump" refers to a lack of understanding; this lack of understanding is similar to the clinging to phenomena, which is why it is called the clinging to phenomena.

Furthermore, one does not understand phenomena (*dharma*). Because this lack of understanding is identical [to the former], the delusion regarding the stump is used as a metaphor for the clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

In reality, however, being deluded about the stump does not constitute clinging to phenomena; although one is indeed clinging to the stump, it is only when there is an actual stump that one can speak of a person.
Question: Since you say that "not understanding" resembles clinging to phenomena, I do not yet know in what sense this "lack of understanding" differs [from it].

Regarding the response to doubt: although this [response] does not provide full understanding, it is certain that there is no understanding; the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of one who doubts is characterized by hesitation, and thus cannot be used as a point of comparison.
[Commentary: The passage from "Just as a single visual consciousness" to "arises with two modes of activity" takes only a small portion as a metaphor.
Furthermore, it is only the aspect (*ākāra*) of consciousness that is taken up, not the two objects; this is the intended meaning of the "minor analogy.

The essence of wisdom (*prajñā*) is one, yet its two functions—recollection of the past and present, and the grasping of self and dharmas—are distinct, just as a single visual consciousness has a self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) that can produce many aspects of seeing, such as blue and other objects.
Thus, while the self-verifying portion is one, the functions of the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) are as numerous as the objects. This is also commonly accepted.

Regarding the "shared cognition" (sādhāraṇa-vijñāna), Dharmapāla and Sthiramati both agree that the multiple aspects (*ākāra*) of consciousness are termed "shared"; thus, this shared cognition serves as the metaphor.

Regarding the "non-shared grasping mind" (asādhāraṇa-grāhaka-citta), Dharmapāla maintains that when the grasping for a self (*ātma-grāha*) arises, it necessarily entails the grasping for phenomena (*dharma-grāha*).

Sthiramati does not grant this, asserting that the seventh consciousness possesses only the grasping for a self and lacks the grasping for phenomena; therefore, it is called the "non-shared grasping mind."
In total, those permitted to study this text are numerous; the text here is merely an abridgment. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "doubting the principle and sealing the phenomenon," etc., this is for the time being left as an objection based on an incorrect interpretation.

As for the objection that it is not a matter of dogmatic adherence, this too is for the time being left as an answer based on an incorrect interpretation; for, from the perspective of the Dharmapāla school, it is not admitted that doubt and sealing arise simultaneously. Therefore, for the time being...
[Question: Regarding the doubt as to whether the next world exists or does not exist, what desire, resolve, and so forth arise therein?
[Commentary: Since this does not contradict it, we allow that they arise together; because their object is one, we allow that they arise simultaneously.

[Commentary]: Regarding those who possess the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*), since the grasping at a person already entails the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), the latter need not be stated explicitly as it follows naturally;
this is because the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) necessarily arises based upon the grasping at phenomena.

[Commentary]: Regarding the two vehicles of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) up to those who have entered the paths of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-mārga*): the intent is that in these stages, the grasping at phenomena arises concurrently.

Apart from this, there are also those who hold to the view of a person (*pudgala-grāha*). Apart from the Noble Path, the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and so forth, [the view of a person] also arises at other times.

Question: For example, regarding the Noble Paths of the two vehicles, the meditative attainment of cessation, and so forth, as was already explained previously, what is the purpose of stating them again now?

Answer: Although it was explained previously, it was not in terms of the abandonment of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa-prahāṇa*); now, it is stated specifically in terms of the abandonment of conceptual differentiation.
Do not repeat this error.
[Commentary: If one contemplates with these three minds, the meaning is that these three minds constitute the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*); this is the correct interpretation.

The first of these three minds gives rise exclusively to the contemplation of persons (*pudgaladṛṣṭi*), while the margins of the latter two minds pertain to the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmadṛṣṭi*). Therefore, these three minds involve the attachment to phenomena within the Path of Vision.
There are instances when there is practice and instances when there is no practice.

[Commentary: "And the two fruits" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

[Commentary: If one abides in a distracted state of concentration, the mind is distracted; this is the stage of the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) distracted mind. Concentration itself is the state of the concentrated mind, excluding [the distracted state].

Because other meditative concentrations, such as the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), involve coarse mental states that do not obstruct the subtle grasping at dharmas (*dharma-grāha*).

[Commentary: As for the phrase "however, all these are similar to the Great Power," the meaning is that because these bodhisattvas frequently give rise to grasping at dharmas, they are said to be "similar" [to those with self-grasping].
Since self-grasping has already been subdued or severed, it does not arise again; this is the case from the seventh ground upward.

In the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), the two attachments to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) and to a self (*ātma-grāha*) may arise intermittently; this differs from the eighth ground (*bhūmi*) and beyond. From the eighth ground onward, attachment to phenomena may either manifest or not.
If the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) continues uninterruptedly, it does not manifest.

However, if the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) continues, attachment to phenomena will manifest until the final moment of the tenth ground (*daśama-bhūmi*), at which point it is permanently severed. As for those in training who turn back...
Regarding the mind and the self-grasping of the Bodhisattva of Sudden Enlightenment: from the seventh bhūmi up to the completion of that stage, it is suppressed and exhausted;

at the completion of the tenth bhūmi, its seeds are severed. The self-view of the sixth consciousness is suppressed at the fourth bhūmi, while the self-view of the seventh consciousness is suppressed so that it no longer functions by the final moment of the seventh bhūmi.
[Commentary: Regarding the faults of the two obstacles in the three locations, these are explained as in the commentary on the tenth [chapter]. [Commentary:

As for the statement, "If it is said that the sixth consciousness can give rise to the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of dharma-grasping (*dharmagrāha*), and that the seventh is its support," the intended meaning is this:

if an opponent were to say that the seventh consciousness does not possess dharma-grasping, yet the sixth consciousness is permitted to arise [with it] and is said to have [the seventh] as its support—[is this not so?]
However, it is not yet known upon which phenomena this treatise relies as its basis. Since the treatise is intended for those who practice, it must rely upon various phenomena as its support.
Yet, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the sixth consciousness is eternally untainted (*anāsrava*), and all afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) no longer function.
How, then, can the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) still serve as its support? It is clear that [the attachment to phenomena] cannot serve as its support.
It is known that the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) consisting of the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) within the seventh consciousness serves as its basis. An external questioner asks:
"Next, you say that the cognitive obscuration within the seventh consciousness serves as its basis; upon what dharma does it depend? The answer is:
"It depends on the afflictive and cognitive obscurations within the first six consciousnesses. The questioner asks: "What about the sixth consciousness up to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*)?"

Since the aforementioned [seventh consciousness] constantly arises as untainted (*anāsrava*), how can it be said to serve as the basis for the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth of the preceding six consciousnesses?
The answer is: it is indeed as you have questioned. Therefore, the treatise cites a sutra which says: "From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, afflictions no longer manifest;

there remains only their basis. This refers to the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). It is proven that from the eighth stage upward, within the seventh consciousness, there exists [the basis] that serves as its support.
Regarding the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), its dharma-attachment does not depend on the afflictions at all times as its support;
however, because it previously served as the support for the manifest afflictions within the six consciousnesses, it receives the designation "support.
It is said that while the first six are not supports, the seventh is the support; this means that within the six consciousnesses, the cognitive obscuration cannot [function independently].
It serves as the basis for the cognitive obscurations within the seventh consciousness, which is the fundamental [basis];
thus, when afflictions arise among the six consciousnesses, they all derive from the afflictions and so forth within the seventh consciousness.
[Commentary]: Why does the preceding statement, "up to the words 'possessing [the seeds],' " refer to the previous passage concerning the continuums of ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas?
This serves as the introduction to the following section.
