[Commentary]: "It is not that which arises from good or evil as a maturation-born [phenomenon]" means that the mind and mental factors resulting from the specific retribution induced by good or evil karma are fruits born of maturation (*vipākaja*);
what is being discussed here is not the same as those.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "this is a general name that encompasses [the specific]," the intended meaning is as follows:

Although the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) is subsumed under the general name "unspecified arising from maturation" (*vipākaja-avyākṛta*), this general term "arising from maturation" is itself a specific name when contrasted with other categories such as "postures" (*airyāpathika*) and so forth.
This is because it is not one of the other three types [of unspecified states]. Thus, a specific name can function as a general name, just as the case of the "body-faculty" (*kāyendriya*).
[Commentary: Now, although this second section—which summarizes the preceding [sections] into three positions—is explained within the tenth gate, there are two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the seventh consciousness by means of the ten gates; second, the summary of the preceding [sections] into three positions.
This refers to the third segment, which groups [the material] into three positions.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement "it exists in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna," the intention is that it is accepted by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the uncontaminated [seventh consciousness] takes the eighth as its object," the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) used in the treatise is that the uncontaminated seventh consciousness takes the principle of selflessness—that is, *tathatā* (suchness)—as its object, as well as the eighth retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) and so forth; therefore, the word "and" has been placed above [in the commentary].
Because it is admitted that upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood, [the mind] can take all phenomena as its objects, the treatise uses the term "etc.

(ādi). [Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the mental faculty (*manas*) can recollect an object," "recollection" (*smṛti*) has the meaning of deliberation (*tarka*). To say this is a "mistaken reversal" is an error.
Recollection has the nature of clearly remembering the past, whereas the mental faculty has the nature of deliberation; since their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are distinct, [they cannot be equated].
How can it be said that the mind contemplates objects? Therefore, this is an error.

[Commentary] Next, that which reveals the proof is the verse immediately following concerning the mind being eternally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Thus, the subsequent verse says: "The mind is eternally indeterminate;
dharmas range from wholesome to unwholesome. This verse is also erroneous, for the intended meaning does not adopt these two extremes. Indeed...

If one holds that the two extremes consist in the practice of annihilationism and eternalism, this is an error; for the seventh [consciousness] cannot practice annihilationism or eternalism, as it merely takes the eighth [consciousness] as its object while grasping at "I" and "mine," rather than calculating annihilation or eternity.
[Commentary]: Regarding the term "Vimukti-āgama," the intended meaning is that this sutra is named the *Vimukti-āgama-sūtra*.
"Āgama" here is translated as "Pure Teaching" (*viśuddha-śāsana*); thus, this "Vimukti" refers precisely to the Pure Teaching, and not to the liberation of *nirvāṇa*.

[Commentary]: However, there is a slight difference here; for while that treatise presents self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and self-conceit (*asmimāna*) first, followed by self-love (*ātma-sneha*), this sutra presents self-view and self-love first, followed by self-conceit and so forth. Thus, it is said that there is a slight difference.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because this mental state exists as it corresponds [to its object] in the past and future," the intended meaning is that when the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) arises, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of this mental state are immediately extinguished.
Why is this? Because the afflictions and their antidotal path do not arise simultaneously, and because the seeds [of the afflictions] have already been severed.
When the untainted path arises, these afflictions are not only absent in the present, but they also do not exist in the past or the future. Why is this? Because... [the past...]

Because the past and future lack substantial reality, yet according to their own tenets, the untainted path arises and its afflictions, though severed, still possess substantial existence in the past and future;
therefore, they cannot be called Buddhas. When we say that the past and future lack self-nature, we are refuting that school's position.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this sutra is believed by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna" up to "constantly offering food," the intent is as follows:

it cites a verse from this sutra which states, "The afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas) is at all times co-arising and co-ceasing with the various afflictions. This sutra is accepted by both vehicles, Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as teaching its existence;
however, while the two vehicles agree on its existence, their interpretations of its name differ. Specifically, what the Mahāyāna refers to as being taught in that sutra is...

Regarding this seventh consciousness, if explained according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) interpretation, it is identical to the sixth consciousness. Within the various schools of the Small Vehicle, there are further distinctions;
for instance, the Sthavira school states that the "defiled mind" (*kliṣṭa-manas*) is constant.

This is precisely our own school’s subtle mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which we admit arises simultaneously with the afflictions and is perpetually active, just like the mind at the moment of taking birth. This subtle mental consciousness is what undergoes rebirth.
It is called "defiled manas" because it arises continuously throughout its final state; this is also like the Mahāyāna teaching that the *ālayavijñāna* exists constantly during the stage of rebirth.

Furthermore, if the Mahāsāṃghika school explains it thus: although this defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) may temporarily have interruptions in the interim, it is still termed "constant" because it arises and ceases simultaneously with all afflictions (*kleśa*). This is also the case here. Thus it is said.
This person constantly gives food and so forth; does this mean they give food at all times? It is not problematic that there may be interruptions in the interim;

this case is also like that. If the Sarvāstivādins maintain that the scriptural term "constant time" (*nityakāla*) refers to a correspondence between preceding and succeeding moments rather than a simultaneous requirement, it means being "concurrent" (*sahagata*) with the afflictions (*kleśa*) in the same moment, just as in the case of "constant giving."

Regarding the statement that [the seventh consciousness] "always coexists with afflictions," this refers to the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*) and not the sixth consciousness; this differs from the views of the Hīnayāna. The descriptions concerning eating and so forth are spoken in terms of the majority of cases, and the constant experience of pleasure and so on should be understood accordingly. Now, regarding the Mahāyāna, the sūtras state:
"It always coexists with afflictions," which refers to the seventh consciousness and not the sixth consciousness; thus it is different from the Hīnayāna.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "The non-common [ignorance] does not establish a self as a sentient being based on the two conditions," the meaning is as follows:

To prove the existence of a seventh [consciousness], the six teachings are collectively cited as a single verse, as in the commentary. As for "non-common," this refers first to the Sūtra which clarifies non-common ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*).
Regarding "the two conditions," the subsequent treatise states: "With the eye and forms as conditions, visual consciousness arises; and so on, up to the mind..."

With the dharma as a condition, mental consciousness arises. Regarding the term "mind" (*manas*), the subsequent treatise states that the Sūtra says "that which cogitates is called mind," and so forth.
As for the distinction between the two meditative attainments, the subsequent treatise says: "The attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation are distinct;

if this consciousness did not exist, they would have no distinction. Regarding the defilement of the state of non-conception, it is said below: "Non-conception has defilement; if this consciousness did not exist, it would have no [defilement]."

Regarding the defiled sentient being’s notion of self, as the treatise states: "The sūtras teach that the wholesome, defiled, and neutral minds of ordinary beings are always accompanied by the grasping of a self;
if this consciousness did not exist, then in the states of those three natures of mind, there would be no sense of 'I' and so forth."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "or there are two kinds of conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta*), the intended meaning is that ignorance (*avidyā*) may be broadly divided into two types:
first, the common (*sādhāraṇa*), and second, the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "the meaning has two senses... as for 'that which is principle' (*tattva*)," the intended meaning is that the meaning has two senses; the first is easily understood.

Regarding the two meanings: "meaning" (artha) refers to the principle (li), and the principle is suchness (tathatā). Question: What is the difference between the principle of suchness and the meaning of the object?
Answer: The first meaning is distinct. That [latter] refers to the object in relation to the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga);

this refers to the principle itself, which is the principle of suchness. Question: Since this section of the treatise does not specifically analyze the meaning, why is this meaning explained in advance?

Yes. The answer provides a general preliminary clarification; logically, there should be no discrepancy, as this meaning is precisely what will be restated later in the text as the "revelation of the true meaning.
[Treatise] Regarding the statement from the verse up to "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*), this cites the first verse of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She-lun) as scriptural proof.
There is non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*).

[Commentary: Ignorance that operates constantly throughout all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*)—because of this ignorance, when the first six consciousnesses perform wholesome acts, the giving and so forth initiated therein cannot be free from the perception of signs (*nimitta*), let alone when other unwholesome or neutral states of mind arise.
Therefore, it operates constantly throughout the three natures of the mind; if it were otherwise, it would contradict the scriptural statement regarding its "constant operation.
Thus, it is said: "if not so, it does not operate constantly."
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that both the sūtra and the verse speak of "ignorance" (*avidyā*), the sūtra and verse cited previously are precisely the verses from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

[Commentary: As for the phrase "if the six groups of consciousness... because they are associated," the intended meaning is this: the six groups of consciousness are fundamentally common to all three moral natures (wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral).

If they were associated with non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), they would then be associated exclusively with the defiled and could not pertain to the three natures. Why? Because it is accepted that they are associated with...
"Because it is constantly associated with ignorance.

[Commentary: If one were to claim that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) becomes defiled by virtue of those afflictions, and if the opponent asserts that this mental consciousness becomes defiled specifically through uncommon ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), the objection is raised:
"This mental consciousness should not be restricted to being wholesome or pure. Why is that?"
Because this ignorance functions constantly, it is for this reason that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* raises this objection.
[Commentary] Regarding the passage from "this ignorance" to "it is not that it does not accompany the secondary afflictions," the meaning is as follows:

although the essence of ignorance within the seventh consciousness is indeed a root affliction, it does not coexist with other root afflictions; rather, it coexists only with the secondary afflictions.

The name "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikāvidyā*) refers to its association with the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). According to this master’s view, the three [afflictions] beginning with craving (*tṛṣṇā*) within the seventh consciousness are termed secondary afflictions.
Question: If it is said that ignorance is called "unshared" because it does not coexist with the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), then with which root affliction is it not shared?
Answer: One may simply say it is not shared with the root afflictions; however, it is also not the case that it is not shared with them at all.
To say that [the mental consciousness] does not coexist with the fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) within the sixth consciousness is certainly not the case;
rather, it can only be stated generally that it does not coexist with the fundamental afflictions.
[Commentary: "The fundamental states as appropriate" refers to such things as wrong desire (*mithyā-chanda*), wrong resolve (*mithyā-adhimokṣa*), and the feelings of joy or aversion.
All such [states] are subsumed under the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of the Bodhisattvas, yet they are termed "secondary afflictions.
[Commentary: The reason the twenty secondary [afflictions] are not called "afflictions" (*kleśa*) is intended to mean that they are not designated as root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the meaning of the statement that "those which follow [the primary afflictions] but are not fundamental are not called afflictions," it is intended to show that there are indeed those which follow [the primary ones] yet are not themselves fundamental.
Furthermore, those which are capable of following [them] and are also subsumed under the category of "obstructions" are the fundamental afflictions themselves.
This is as stated in the *Abhidharmapāda* (Dharma-saṃgraha). The phrase "because what follows is not called an affliction" explains why the secondary ones (*anuvartaka*) are not designated as such.

Regarding the origin of the afflictions (*kleśa*): if the former masters maintain that the three beginning with craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are established as states of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), this is not so.
Why? Because [the text] does not mention the word "affliction" (*kleśa*) in connection with them. Therefore, it is incorrect to designate craving and the others as "secondary afflictions.
Thus, we know that these three are merely called "afflictions" and cannot be classified as "secondary," because they are not mentioned among the categories of primary and secondary afflictions.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the time of returning through cultivation," "cultivation" (xiū) means returning through cultivation.

[Commentary]: Regarding "not seeing this term 'not shared with greed and so forth' in various treatises," this is an explanation based on the specific stage; it means that within those various treatises, there is no textual passage stating that [this factor] is not shared with greed and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the various treatises generally speak of delusion (*moha*) up to the name 'unshared' (*āveṇika*) in contrast to other forms of delusion," the intent is to synthesize the various treatises, which do not mention an unshared [affliction] corresponding to greed (*lobha*). There are two interpretations of this:

first, "in contrast to others" means that while delusion and so forth within the other six consciousnesses are mentioned, only the delusion within the seventh consciousness is called "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikāvidyā*); second, "delusion" refers to... [text fragment].

Regarding the remainder of greed and other afflictions within the seventh consciousness, we shall now discuss greed in relation to the remaining ignorance within that same consciousness, focusing on its relationship with ignorance.
In reality, greed and the others are also termed "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*); however, there are two senses in which greed and the others are called "unshared.
One interpretation states that the greed and other afflictions within the seventh consciousness are termed "unshared" because they do not coexist with other afflictions such as pride.
Because pride is characterized by loftiness while greed is characterized by downward movement, they are not associated; therefore, it is called "unshared" (*āveṇika*).
Second, the statement that greed and so forth which operate independently among the six consciousnesses are called "unshared greed" is the correct interpretation, according to the following text.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "However, this master [holds that] up to [the point where it] does not take [it] as primary," the intended meaning is as follows:
This master asserts that among the six consciousnesses there exists a non-common *rāga* (greed) and so forth, which is not the seventh consciousness.

However, because the *rāga* within the seventh consciousness does not coexist with the *māna* (pride) and other afflictions of the six consciousnesses, it is termed "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) only by virtue of being associated with the afflictions within its own [seventh] consciousness; thus, because it is not...
Because it is the primary [factor], it cannot but share its name with the primary one; thus, although ignorance (*avidyā*) is not differentiated, it is termed "unshared" (*āveṇika*).

[Commentary: As for the statement that this primary ignorance also exists in other consciousnesses, this refers to its presence within all six consciousnesses; here, "primary" refers specifically to the independent (*svatantra*) [ignorance].
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the views and so forth of the former master are also called 'unshared' (āveṇika)," the intention is as follows:

The former master challenges the former master by arguing that when delusion (*moha*) increases among the other six consciousnesses, greed (*lobha*) and the like, as well as views (*dṛṣṭi*), should be termed "associated" (*saṃprayukta*).

This is because the former master admits that greed, views, and so forth exist as unshared factors within the other six consciousnesses; thus, he specifically mentions the occasion when delusion increases.

[Commentary]: "If it were predominant, it should be called 'unshared' (āveṇika)"—this objection regarding greed and so forth is raised by the former master based on the time when greed and so forth increase.
However, according to our school, this principle is accepted by both; now, each raises an objection based on what they themselves accept.
[Treatise] There is an interpretation that the passage from "this delusion exists" up to "because it exists only in this consciousness" represents the correct tenet of Dharmapāla.
[Commentary] Regarding the second type, "independent and non-common," which means it does not arise together with others:
the intention is to explain that there are two kinds of "non-common. First is "associated non-common," which refers to the seventh consciousness; second is "independent non-common."
Regarding the term "unshared" (*āveṇika*): it is called "unshared" because it does not coexist with the root afflictions; this is the explanation of the name "unshared.

Furthermore, there are two types of the second category, the "independently occurring" (*ananyasamprayukta*) ignorance: first, the non-primary independently occurring type, which is associated with anger (*krodha*) and so forth, and is thus termed "non-primary independently occurring.
If that is so, why is it called "independently occurring"? The answer is: because it does not coexist with attachment (*lobha*).

It is called "acting alone" (*ekavīcāra*); since acting alone implies being unshared (*asādhāraṇa*), such ignorance does not exist as a seventh [mental factor], whereas the second [ignorance] is the primary one that acts alone.
It is called "acting alone" because it is not shared with the root afflictions; it is called "primary" because it is not associated with anger (*krodha*) and the others.
That is to say, it is not associated with other [afflictions] such as greed (*lobha*) or the ten [secondary afflictions] beginning with anger.
This is because it is designated as "acting alone" (*ekavartin*).

[The Commentary] states: "Or, although it does not arise together with others [of its own class], this does not mean it does not arise together with other secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as those belonging to the categories of anger (*krodha*) and so forth.

However, at the end of the fourth fascicle, in the explanation of the secondary afflictions, there are four general theories; according to this, that which acts alone is generally considered capable of being associated (*samprayukta*).

Furthermore, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), [ignorance] is associated with both *āhrīkya* (lack of shame) and *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread); this is not the case in the higher realms, as explained below.
[Commentary:
This is to establish that the ignorance (*avidyā*) mentioned subsequently is what gives rise to the following text, and to establish the subsequent "unshared" (*āveṇika*) [ignorance].
Because of ignorance, the *Yogācārabhūmi* is cited as proof.

[Commentary: Regarding "concomitant with the latter five secondary afflictions," this refers to the five that are concomitant among the eight great secondary afflictions—namely, torpor, restlessness, lack of faith, laziness, and heedlessness—which corresponds to the first interpretation among the four masters at the end of the fourth fascicle. In contrast to...
The preceding [passage] refers to the minor and intermediate [degrees], hence it is called "subsequent.

[Commentary]: As stated in the sūtras, etc., that [ignorance] is exclusively conceptual (*vikalpika*), because the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states that noble ones have already permanently abandoned the non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Therefore, we know it is exclusively conceptual. That [sūtra] relies solely on this as the primary explanation; it is not based on [other types].
That which is not a primary cause is not cultivated for abandonment through non-commonality.
[Commentary] The passage from the second fascicle of the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa-sūtra* refers to the text of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*.

[Commentary]: Regarding this term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) used in accordance with the Hīnayāna: although the Mahāyāna permits it, since the Hīnayāna also permits it, it is said to be "in accordance with" [the former].

It does not mean that it is not constantly active, nor that it is unshared with the Hīnayāna. There are those who claim that the Mahāyāna has no teaching in accordance with the Hīnayāna, but this is not what the Mahāyāna permits.
The "unshared ignorance" (*avidyā*) of the Mahāyāna, which resides within the seventh consciousness, is the interpretation presented previously.
"Because the Victorious One taught them himself.

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation from the perspective of "light characteristics" (*laghu-nimitta*): this refers to the ten types beginning with mindfulness (*smṛti*), which are established based on the fundamental [consciousness]. This applies equally to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are coarse and mobile, and they frequently manifest, they are termed "light characteristics. This is not the case for greed (*rāga*) and the other [afflictions], and thus they are so named.
Regarding the "unshared" (āveṇika) mental states, those that are grave are called the "roots," while those that are light are called "anger" and so forth.
[Commentary]: Although these are divided into two categories, they consist precisely of the primary and non-primary types;

however, they are not subsumed under "ever-present ignorance" (mūla-avidyā), because ever-present ignorance does not pervade minds of all three natures (tridhātu-citta), whereas ever-present ignorance does pervade all three natures.

[Commentary]: Vasubandhu speaks only of the non-universally accepted conditions, up to the point where he explains that [consciousness] arises from two; this is the total interpretation of Vasubandhu’s intent in the *Vyākhyāyukti* (or *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*).
That passage seems to challenge a different Mahāyāna master—namely, Sthiramati—who asserts that in the uncontaminated state (*anāsrava*), the seventh consciousness does not exist.
Now, it is said that just as the visual faculty and the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) give rise to visual consciousness, so too do the mental faculty (*manas*) and...

Regarding the statement, "The fundamental consciousness gives rise to the mental consciousness," the phrase "the mind [is] as if" serves to refute the views of other masters and to prove the existence of a seventh consciousness.

[Commentary]: As for the passage from "However, with respect to the support... to "...it is precisely because of the dharmas of sense organs and objects," the intended meaning is as follows: it explains the reason why there is a difference between the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) and this treatise.
Vasubandhu distinguishes the two types of roots solely on the basis of their support (*āśraya*), whereas this treatise distinguishes them based on both the root and its object (*ālambana*).

The second [type of] object-condition is used to explain the seventh [consciousness]. If one were to posit the *ālayavijñāna*, it would not be commonly accepted; therefore, based on this principle, it is clearly understood that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) refutes the "Heterodox Master" (*anyācārya*).

[Commentary]: To assign them in reverse order means to assign them in reverse order to distinguish the sequential cessation of the "mind" (*manas*) within the aforementioned second transformative consciousness.
The phrases "and the causal conditions," "the basis," and so forth, are excluded by proceeding from the end toward the beginning.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement, "Included within the middle... because it is subsumed under this single consciousness":

this means that if one were to say only that they are subsumed under the six consciousnesses without mentioning the "middle," it would be for the purpose of establishing the six consciousnesses; however, in order to clearly establish the sixth consciousness, the term "middle" is placed there.

Regarding the statement "because it is subsumed under a single consciousness," the intended meaning is that since the sixth consciousness is already subsumed under a single consciousness, one cannot use the fact of being subsumed by the six consciousnesses as a logical reason.
[Commentary] The clarification of what is not the case concludes the preceding text; this explains that the Sarvāstivādins and others do not fail to admit the existence of a seventh consciousness.
Because it contradicts the aforementioned sūtra.
[Commentary: The Sthavira school’s defense regarding the material entity within the chest is as described in the Ximing Commentary; one may consult and record that account. [Commentary:
As for the meaning of "following their words," it refers to the second interpretation. If the five consciousnesses lack the three types of discrimination, what [is the case]?
Therefore, the initial explanation states that there is "intrinsic discrimination" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), and so forth;

this is answered by following the doctrine of the Sautrāntikas, who maintain that intrinsic discrimination exists because the Sautrāntikas admit that the five consciousnesses possess intrinsic discrimination. This will be explained in detail later in the seventh fascicle.
[Commentary: Regarding the objection that the concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is unestablished, the Sautrāntika objects:

"If one uses the five consciousnesses as a concordant example to prove that the sixth consciousness has a simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*), this concordant example is unestablished, because the five consciousnesses and their sense organs are not simultaneous."
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "one should know that it is likewise for those things established by worldly perception," the formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
Your five consciousnesses are necessarily simultaneous with their respective sense organs, because they arise in dependence upon them, just like a sprout and its shadow.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "The mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) share the same object of cognition until the meaning of cause and effect is established," the intended meaning is as follows:
By using volition (*cetanā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) as a common analogy, it is proven that the five sense organs (*indriya*) and their respective consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) share the same object;

therefore, they are necessarily simultaneous. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: Your eye organ and its consciousness are necessarily simultaneous because they share the same object, just like volition and feeling. If this is so, then...

The proof [of your position] commits the fallacy of being "uncertain" (*anaikāntika*) with respect to others, because the Sautrāntikas maintain that although mental factors such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth share the same object as the mind, they are merely states of volition (*cetanā*) and arise either before or after the mind; thus, it incurs the fallacy of uncertainty with respect to others.

The objection is stated as follows: Are the five consciousnesses simultaneous with their respective faculties in the same way that volition and feeling (*vedanā*) share the same object? Or are they like craving?
Since [desire] and the mind take the same object, there would be this fault [of their arising at different times].

Therefore, it should have been established previously that desire is necessarily simultaneous with thought and feeling, because mental factors such as desire are necessarily simultaneous and share the same object, just like thought and feeling.
Once this has been established, one may then use it as an analogy to establish that the sense-faculties and consciousnesses are necessarily simultaneous.

Since it is established that the five consciousnesses are simultaneous with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the same applies to the sixth [consciousness]. It is determined that they are simultaneous; the simultaneous mental faculty (*manas*) is precisely the seventh consciousness.

[Commentary: "Extremely established" (*prasiddha*) serves to exclude other schools. As for the purpose of this exclusion, the intention is that by using the term "extremely established," one excludes those who do not [accept this].
The term "universally established" (*prasiddha*) serves as its own qualification according to the literal text;

if this term were not placed to qualify it, then to state merely that "the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)" is the subject (*dharmin*) would result in the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the subject (*asiddha-dharmin*), as it would encompass all instances of mental consciousness, including those that are not established for either the proponent or the opponent.
For instance, the Hīnayāna school accepts that a Bodhisattva in his final existence possesses a contaminated (*sāsrava*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) mental consciousness, such as that of *Sītā*.
The Crown Prince taking a wife, fathering a son, and enjoying the five sensory pleasures are things not permitted by the Mahāyāna;
if these were included within the category of "existent phenomena" (*dharma*), one would incur the fault of the "unestablished for oneself" (*svato 'siddha*).

Conversely, if the Mahāyāna asserts the existence of Buddhas in other directions and so forth, which the Hīnayāna does not accept, one incurs the fault of the "unestablished for others" (*parato 'siddha*). Thus, in order to avoid such faults, [the definition] is established as follows:
The term "universally established" (*prasiddha*) serves as a qualification for brevity.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the non-common [qualifies] the present eighth consciousness up to 'the thesis is unestablished,'" the intended meaning is as follows:

one now uses the term "non-common" to distinguish it from the "common," meaning that the present functioning eighth consciousness acts as the common support (*sādhāraṇa-āśraya*) for all dharmas; furthermore, with respect to the eighth...
The six [sense bases] are not "non-common" (asādhāraṇa) because they are not produced by non-relatives and because they are not proximate;
that is to say, they are called "non-common" in reference to the dominant supporting basis for the arising of the five consciousnesses.

If the term "non-common" were not included and one were to state only in general that the established mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must have a dominant simultaneous supporting basis, then for the proponent, the thesis would suffer from the fault of having an unestablished specific qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*).

The Hīnayāna does not admit the existence of an eighth consciousness; yet, in this present school, by failing to distinguish [the subject] when positing it as the support (*āśraya*), one commits the fallacy of the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-asiddha*).

Specifically, the subject (*dharmin*) in the antecedent member (*pūrvapakṣa*) is called the "qualified" (*viśeṣya*), while the predicate-property (*pakṣadharma*) in the consequent member (*uttarapakṣa*) is called the "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Because no such distinction is made within the thesis (*pratijñā*), this error is incurred. Furthermore, there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*), for the other school does not admit that the five sensory consciousnesses depend upon the eighth consciousness.

Therefore, if one were to propose the five consciousnesses as the corroborative example (dṛṣṭānta), there would be the fault of the "unestablishedness of the probandum" (sādhyāprasiddhi) within the example.
Since the probandum is the property of the subject (pakṣadharma), and that property cannot be applied to the example, the absence of the probandum— the thesis—
within the example is termed the fault of the unestablishedness of the probandum.

[Commentary: "The phrase 'to manifest its own name as its basis' up to 'because it is already established' means that, for example, the eye-faculty is itself called the 'eye-base,' and so on up to the mind-faculty being itself called the 'mind-base'; thus, one manifests its own name as its basis. The intended meaning is this:

we now set aside the manifestation of names as their respective bases because the term "basis" (āyatana) has a specific purpose here—it serves to exclude what the Sthavira school asserts to be a subtle matter within the chest.
If it were a physical object, it would function as the sense organ of mind; however, this is not the case, because the mind is not material.
Therefore, since this material sense organ is the object of the sixth consciousness, it is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) among the categories of form.

[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "this principle is not so" is as follows: the Elder’s (Sthavira) reckoning that material objects constitute the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is not logically tenable.
If these colors were the objects of the sixth consciousness, they would have to be subsumed under the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*), and should not be subsumed under the internal mental faculty.
It is to avoid such faults that the term "manifesting its own name-base" (*svanāmāyatanapradarśaka*) is placed; if it were not...

In the section setting forth the explicit designation, the term "discriminating" (*vikalpa*) is used; it simply states that the "established mental consciousness" (*vijñāna-manas*) is the *dharmin* (the subject), and that there must necessarily be a co-arising, non-common, predominant "mental base" (*manāyatana*) as its *dharma* (the property).
This avoids the fault of lacking a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), because the five sensory consciousnesses do not rely upon the mental base and thus cannot be employed as a similar instance.
Therefore, it is stated in general that "manifesting the name and its own base" explicitly indicates this.
Because each of the various consciousnesses relies upon its own respective sense organ (*indriya*), the five consciousnesses can serve as a common example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

[Commentary: As for the statement that "it is not the thesis to be established" (*asādhyapakṣa*): if one were to say merely that what is co-arisen and non-common is the mental base (*manāyatana*), then the thesis itself would not be something to be established.

Why? Because the Sautrāntika-Sthavira school (Śrīlāta) maintains that matter (*rūpa*) constitutes the mental faculty (*manendriya*), and thus it would also be included within the thesis to be established.
Because it is [already] established, the Mahāyāna does not admit that form (*rūpa*) is the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*); therefore, this thesis is not something to be proven.

If one were to admit that form is the mental faculty, it would further contradict one's own school’s tenets, as our own school does not admit that form is subsumed under the sphere of mind (*mana-āyatana*).

If one were to establish this against the Sthavira, it would commit the fault of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhana*), because the opponent has already established it; thus, it is the fault of redundancy (*punarukta*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it is accepted that [the mind] is not included in the 'immediately preceding' (samanantara) and so forth," the intended meaning is as follows:

The purpose of stating "not included in the immediately preceding" is to exclude the mental faculty (*manas*) that has ceased in immediate succession, because this [mental consciousness] constitutes its simultaneous support (*sahabhū-āśraya*).

If one did not say "not included in the immediately preceding" and instead merely said "it is universally established that mental consciousness must have an uncommon [basis]," it would fail to manifest its own name, its locus, and its predominant production.

As for the "basis" (*āśraya*), it constitutes the fault of the unestablished nature of the thesis (*sādhyāsiddha*), because the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is also included within the thesis;

since its substance is not co-existent (*sahabhū*), it cannot serve as a basis. Furthermore, if this were addressed to all Hīnayāna schools, there would be the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), for all Hīnayāna schools admit that the past mental faculty (*manas*) can produce the present consciousness.

[Commentary]: If one raises the five consciousnesses as a homologous example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the property to be established (*sādhyadharma*) is not present; this means that the property of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*) does not apply to the example.

Consequently, the property to be established is missing from the example. This is because the Hīnayāna schools do not admit that the five consciousnesses take seeds as their specific support (*asādhāraṇāśraya*).
Therefore, one does not oppose [this argument] to the Sautrāntikas, for they also admit the existence of seeds. If one were to oppose it...
[This] is because [the opponent] has already established [their position] and also admits that the five consciousnesses rely on seeds.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it is not a direct producer," this means that the seventh [consciousness], in relation to the eighth, serves only as a co-existent support (*sahabhū-āśraya*) and is not a direct producer.

[Commentary]: That which is not proximate—the seventh [consciousness]—is not proximate in relation to the first five consciousnesses; therefore, it does not serve as their generative support (*jananāśraya*), but only serves as their defiled and purified support (*kliṣṭa-śuddhāśraya*).
Question: What is the difference between the seventh consciousness serving as the generative support for the sixth consciousness and the production of actualities (*pravṛtti*) from seeds?

Answer: The production of actualities from seeds refers to the arising of the essence itself (*tattva-janman*); here, however, [the seventh consciousness] merely acts as the support for that which is capable of immediate transformation (*sākṣāt-pariṇāmin*).
The naming [of the mind] indicates that its basis for arising is distinct from the various [mental factors] that manifest simultaneously.

[Commentary: Furthermore, the exclusion of simultaneous mental factors (*caitta*) means that although these simultaneous mental factors also serve as a basis for the sixth consciousness, they are not subsumed under the category of "basis for arising" (*janmanāśraya*);
therefore, they must be excluded. Question: How does the sixth mind-king (*cittarāja*) depend upon the mind?

The answer is as stated in the preceding treatise: it is accepted that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) are mutually dependent, just as a sovereign and his ministers are mutually dependent.

Regarding the mention of "mental factors arising simultaneously," this is intended to distinguish them from the mental factors associated with the seventh consciousness (*manas*), even though they arise simultaneously;
for while they coexist with the seventh, they do not share the same status as the basis upon which the seventh arises.

[Commentary]: Regarding the previous point that there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the subsequent fault of establishing what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), the intended meaning is as follows:

If one merely states that the "universally established mental consciousness" (*vijñāna-manas*) necessarily has an "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) basis up to an "overriding" (*adhipati*) basis, but does not include the qualification "the basis from which it arises," then the seventh [consciousness] would also be included among the factors of the thesis (*pakṣadharma*), as it serves as the co-existent (*sahabhū*) and defiled/pure basis for the five [sensory consciousnesses]. Consequently, the thesis would also have to possess [such a basis].

The first point is that the thesis is unestablished (*asiddha*) because there is no similar example (*sapakṣa*); since the Hīnayāna does not admit that the five consciousnesses depend upon the seventh [consciousness], it is said that there is the fault of lacking a similar example.
This first meaning excludes the mental factors (*caitta*) that arise simultaneously, as they are not the support (*āśraya*).

The second meaning excludes the case where one does not speak of the "support of arising" (*utpatty-āśraya*) for those simultaneous mental factors, but speaks only of the "predominant support" (*adhipatya-āśraya*) and so forth.

Since mental factors (*caitta*) serve as the support for the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and are also included within the category of the thesis-property (*pakṣadharma*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Because the opponent’s own school has already accepted the former and now accepts it again, establishing it once more constitutes a redundancy (*anuvāda*). Question:

How do mental factors serve as the support for the mind? Answer: If they were supports in the sense of being the supported and the supporter (*āśraya* and *āśrita*), then mental factors would not be the support for the mind-king. If they were [supports] in the sense of mutual induction...
If one relies on the metaphor of "borrowing the name" (*nāmopacāra*), then mental factors (*caitta*) would also be "kings" (i.e., primary minds), just as kings have ministers.

Regarding the questions raised previously concerning the lack of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), why was it not stated that these two fallacies are specifically addressed here?

The answer is as follows: the previous analysis relied solely on a single sense [of the term], which is why those [fallacies] were not mentioned; however, in this present context, [both senses] are taken into account.

The basis of arising possesses two meanings, which serve to exclude [other possibilities]; within a single meaning, one fault is excluded, and thus the two faults are specifically singled out without contradiction.
Furthermore, the term "basis" (āśraya) refers to the third meaning, as it excludes all that depends upon it (āśrita).

If this were not excluded, there would also be the fault of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana); why, then, is this not mentioned? The answer is: by citing one category, the others are implied.
Furthermore, there is no further discrimination.

[Commentary: Regarding the mutual exclusion of each of these meanings herein, one takes the meaning of "predominance" (*adhipati*) and contrasts it with the meaning of "coexistence" (*sahabhū*), and likewise takes the meaning of "coexistence" and contrasts it with the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*);
in this manner, each of the various meanings is mutually distinguished in relation to the others.

[Commentary: Is the dharma also substantially existent? The answer is: The sutra merely states that consciousness arises from the object (*viṣaya*); it does not state whether the object has a substantial essence or lacks one.
Therefore, the dharma cannot be used as an example [for this].
[Commentary] The meaning of the question, "Although dharmas lack intrinsic nature, they serve as conditions to produce mental consciousness;
although the five sense-objects serve as objects to produce the five consciousnesses, should they likewise lack intrinsic nature? is as follows:

Although this analogy holds true for such characteristics, the Master [Vasubandhu] does not accept it, and thus he excludes it by stating that "the analogy is not established. This means that one cannot take those dharmas as a universal standard for what is non-existent.
Principle Five: It also applies to non-existence. [Commentary:
"It should also arise from two conditions" up to "and acts as the mind"—this is an objection by an outsider. The Sūtra states that dharmas arise from two conditions;
non-existence also gives rise to consciousness. The Sūtra states that when the substance of the sense organ arises from two conditions, consciousness also arises, just as...

[Question: Although past consciousness has already ceased and lacks a present substantial entity (*dravya*), it can still induce the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the present cessation; therefore, it is established as the mental faculty (*manas*). [Answer: As explained in the Commentary.
[Commentary:
"Therefore, dharmas cannot be analogized to the five [faculties]" means that one must not take the nature of *dharmas* and apply it as an analogy for the five sense faculties.

Because for those [faculties] to serve as either objects (*viṣaya*) or faculties (*indriya*), they must possess power; therefore, one cannot use the case of non-existent phenomena (*abhāva-dharma*) as an analogy for the five faculties to render them likewise without substance.

Some say that since the five [faculties] are not analogous [to the others], one cannot use the case of non-existent phenomena as an analogy for the five faculties to render them likewise without the seven [consciousnesses].
[Commentary: "Even if it had an essence previously, it is now useless" means that although its existence was asserted before, it is now useless because it has entered the past.
Since it lacks both essence and function in the future, upon what could they be established? Therefore, it says, "its function is logically non-existent.
The phrase "even if it had an essence previously," etc., refutes the Sarvāstivāda; for if the Sarvāstivādins maintain that there is an essence, that has already been refuted above.
Because the past lacks function and the future lacks substance, the Sautrāntika masters are refuted;
since their own school admits that the past lacks substance, it is logically impossible for its function to exist. Thus, the former interpretation is superior.

[Commentary]: Regarding the Sautrāntika school’s statement, "it is metaphorically designated as having the function [of mind]," the intent is to explain the reason why the Sautrāntika masters designate past consciousness as "mind" (*manas*).

Subsequently, they refute this by stating that although the four Sautrāntika masters claim that although the past lacks substantial existence, it is said to possess the function of reflection (*manana*) at the time it was present—and thus, even though it has now ceased, it can still serve as the support for subsequent consciousness—how is this so?
Therefore, regarding that which resembles the function of present deliberation (*manana*), the Mahāyāna refutes it, saying: "It is not so.

When your consciousness (*vijñāna*) is in the present, it possesses only the function of discernment (*vijñapti*); although it may be designated as 'consciousness,' it cannot be designated as 'mind' (*manas*), because it lacks the function of actual deliberation.
Thus, the objection is raised: "If there is no actual deliberation, upon what basis is [the designation of] 'mind' established? If you claim there was deliberation previously..."

[Question: "The past can appear to possess the function of deliberation; since you [assert that] prior to this there was no function of deliberation, how can the past appear to possess the function of deliberation as it does in the present? [Commentary:

Regarding the statement in the *Śāstra* (Sūtra) that "the Mahāyāna refutes the preceding [systems] up to the meaning of the preceding vehicle," the intention is as follows: the preceding refutation of the Vaiśeṣika heretics states, "Furthermore..."

"It cannot be said that the provisional (*prajñapti*) must necessarily depend on this; how then can you now challenge the Sautrāntika school by saying, 'Since there is no correct deliberation (*tarka*), by what is the provisional established?
Is this not contradictory? [Commentary]: This is not so.

According to the principle, that which reaches to the level of "existence" appears to function [as such]. This refers to the Master’s response: speaking according to the principle, it does not depend [on the aforementioned basis].

In reality, there is only that which resembles transformation; it is merely due to deluded attachment that we conventionally speak of "resemblance" and further establish positions and refutations, as explained in the second fascicle, where one should consult that text.
The intention of the master of the treatise lies in the meaning of the transformation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
[Commentary: Regarding the absence of the fault of contradicting the teachings: if one considers the intent of the Mahāyāna, there is present correct deliberation;
the statement here that "there is no correct deliberation" is made from the perspective of challenging the other school’s tenets.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "now setting aside one’s own position to follow another," the meaning of the objection is as follows: If it is granted that the Mahāyāna exists during the present process of correct contemplation, yet it is now said that it does not exist, by what basis could this [absence] be established during that correct contemplation?
This objection—stating that one sets aside one’s own doctrine and follows the opponent’s school—is raised not to discuss one’s own tenets, but solely from the perspective of the other’s system.
Thus, it is called "setting aside one’s own position to follow another."

[Commentary: Furthermore, the previous discussion regarding the difficulty of reaching the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) while analyzing the conventional (*prajñapti*) was intended to mean this:

the prior refutation of the non-Buddhists—who claim that the conventional does not depend on the real—was made from the perspective of the ultimate truth, wherein mind and language are cut off and it is impossible to debate whether something is true or false.
The present statement regarding "correct contemplation" and so forth is spoken from the perspective of the conventional truth; within the conventional, there exists the real.
Because it is provisional, it is called "provisional"; because it must rely on the real, the two difficulties are distinct.

[Commentary: Therefore, it is merely named "manas" (mind) and not "vijñāna" (consciousness), because consciousness lacks the sense of having a support, and thus does not resemble the manifest consciousness;
furthermore, it possesses the sense of deliberation (*manana*).

[Treatise]: If there were no defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) within the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), such that it existed in one and was absent in the other, what would distinguish those two?
[The answer is: Where there is a defiled mind, there is a distinction; where there is no defiled mind, there is no distinction. This means:
if you do not admit that this defiled mind exists in one attainment and is absent in another, then I ask: what difference is there between these two attainments?
Therefore, the difficulty regarding the distinction between the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) arises from this afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*). The treatise states in summary:
"If the afflicted mind were absent during the two attainments such that it exists in one and is absent in the other, how could that one [attainment] be distinguished as being long and continuous?"

[Commentary: If the Hīnayāna maintains that there are only twenty-one [mental factors], this refers to five universal factors, five object-specific factors, ten wholesome factors, and the ten wholesome factors associated with the mind-king (*citta-rāja*).
According to their school, the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*) is considered a provisional designation, as it is a sub-component of wisdom (*prajñā*). In the Mahāyāna, this is not the case;

thus, there are twenty-two factors. Regarding the phrase "the cessation of the mental consciousness through the signless" (*animitta-nirodha-manovijñāna*), this refers to the cessation of the sixth consciousness within the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Regarding the "two consciousnesses," this refers to [the sixth and] the seventh consciousness; the five consciousnesses are not mentioned because they have already been abandoned during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), and because all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) lack the physical basis of the five consciousnesses, they are not discussed here.

[Commentary]: Regarding the question of what difference there is if both [attainments] involve the cessation of the same factors: if it is the seventh consciousness that ceases in both meditative attainments, then twenty-two dharmas cease in both;
yet one wonders what distinction exists between these two attainments.

Now, the only difference between the two attainments is that in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), twenty-two dharmas cease, whereas in the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), twenty-three dharmas cease, because a portion of the defiled aspect of the seventh consciousness also ceases therein. Thus, the latter is superior.
"Established upon the seeds of the absence of ideation (*asaṃjñika*)" means it is established upon the seeds of that which is capable of generating aversion.

[Commentary] Regarding "the two acquisitions (*prāpti*) up to the five aggregates (*skandha*) or four aggregates": the first acquisition is that obtained through skillful means (*upāya*), namely preparatory application (*prayoga*);

the second is that obtained through the abandonment of defilements (*vairāgya*), meaning the sense of being free from passion. The state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) is obtained solely through preparatory application, whereas the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) pertains to both.

The attainment of Buddhahood is acquired solely through spontaneous effort (*anābhoga*), whereas the other two noble attainments are acquired through applied effort (*prayoga*). Regarding the two names:

the first refers to the four aggregates of the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which depend on the mind of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); the second refers to the five aggregates of the non-conceptual state (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), which depend on the mind of the Fourth Dhyāna.
Thus, they are called "the two names."
[Commentary]: If there were no seventh consciousness, there would be no ordinary person to loathe and no sage to admire.

It is because the seventh consciousness clings to a self that ordinary beings undergo saṃsāra and are thus defiled and loathsome; it is because the purified seventh consciousness corresponds with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) that one becomes a sage, which is what is to be admired.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the two explanations are as follows," some say that they should be combined into three characters, and that the [current] commentary erroneously has only two characters;
this is as explained later in the seventh fascicle.

One should consult other editions. [Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "long duration" because the first and last are excluded: this takes the intermediate period as "long duration," whereas the initial birth and final passing away are not.
Because the time is extremely brief, the text below states that there is a fault because [the entity] does not exist during the long interval between [past and future].
[Commentary]: Your argument that the past and future worlds fall under the category of "self" is measured as follows:

your past and future worlds should not be considered past and future, because they are not subsumed within the present world, just like permanent unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Furthermore, it says: because they are "past," they are not permanent; they differ from the permanent.

Furthermore, that which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not exist in the future nor is it present, being like a flower in the sky; since both its coming and going are non-existent, the absence of self-clinging (*ātmagrāha*) therein would constitute a fault. [Treatise:

Because the apprehended object (*grāhya*) is non-existent, the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) is likewise mutually non-existent. This negates their attempted rebuttal; for they attempt to defend themselves by claiming that there is "non-conception" (*asaṃjñika*).
It is not the case that sentient beings possess the acquisition of self-grasping such that the Noble Ones revile and loathe it.
Since the world that is acquired does not exist, the acquisition of self-grasping cannot exist; how then could there be self-grasping?

Furthermore, as for that which is said to be the "acquirer"—the three types of "I" that acquire the past and future worlds, which are the objects acquired—it is said that although the past and future worlds do not exist, the acquirer still exists.
Regarding those non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), they possess the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).

[Commentary: Next, from the Mahāsāṃghika school up to the point of "grasping at a self," this refers to the four schools—the Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, and Gokulika—as well as the Mahīśāsaka and others, who maintain that there exists a separate *anuśaya* (latent disposition) which is like a seed and is an *viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha* (a formation dissociated from mind).

Because the state of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) is comprised within [the category of] "possession" (*prāpti*), there is the grasping of a self (*ātman-grāha*); for this reason, both the noble ones (*ārya*) and the wise alike censure and loathe it. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "obtaining the category and not losing it, but rather increasing it," the meaning is as follows: "not losing it and increasing it" refers to the flow of what is obtained;

hence it is called "obtaining the category. The Saṃmitīya school states that because of the existence of this "category of obtaining," although the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) are absent within the Heaven of Non-conception, [the continuity of the mind persists].
[Objection: "If there is also attachment to a self (*ātma-grāha*), why must there necessarily be a seventh consciousness? [The Master replies:
"This has already been refuted previously among the non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
[Commentary: The statement that "the self and both matter and mind can all receive perfuming" means that in our own school, it is accepted that matter and mind mutually [perfume one another].

Regarding the statement that "the mutual perfuming of characteristics occurs even in the state of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñika), for since the material sense-faculties are present there, the seeds are stored within them, and from this, self-clinging (ātma-grāha) can arise":

[The Commentary] states that the characteristics of defilement (saṃkleśa) pertain to all three natures (trividha-svabhāva); the meaning is that it is because of the existence of the seventh consciousness’s self-clinging that [defilement is established].

The six consciousnesses, such as those engaged in giving through speech and so forth, cannot eliminate signs; thus, signs are themselves defilement. These six consciousnesses exist within the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) of the mind.
[Commentary]: The intention behind stating that "the three natures of the outflowing [mind] all lack self-grasping" is to clarify that they should both be without self-grasping.
"It is defiled. [Commentary:
Regarding the statement, "The mode of activity (*ākāra*) of this self’s external conditions is coarse and violent," etc., this interpretation differs from the one above. [Commentary:

Regarding the statement, "By means of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), one gives rise to wholesome dharmas such as giving (*dāna*)," etc., that [arising] is initially caused by the seventh [consciousness], the *manas*.
When practicing generosity within the six consciousnesses, one cannot eliminate the perception of signs (*nimitta*). This explanation refers to the "sixth self" (*ātman*);

however, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun), based on the fact that one can practice generosity and so forth through the "self," posits a seventh consciousness to prove its existence. This is merely cited to clarify the sixth consciousness by means of the seventh;
it means that because of the self in the seventh [consciousness], the self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) within the six consciousnesses becomes distinct and sharp, such that one says, "I."

When one is able to practice giving and so forth, it means that the three natures arise in an intermingled manner within the mind; it does not mean that "I am the one who practices giving"—this refers to the seventh consciousness (*manas*).

Since the seventh consciousness is constantly characterized by self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), how could one possess giving that is free from the signs of a self (*nirnimitta-dāna*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and thereby accomplish the practice of perfection (*pāramitā*)?
Therefore, we know that the statement regarding the "signs of a self" being extinguished refers solely to the "I" within the sixth consciousness. Thus:
There is no such thing as "giving with a mark of self" within that sixth [category], because it is called the "extinction of marks.
[Commentary] This explanation is superior because it is the fundamental one; this second explanation is the fundamental one and is superior to the first. Why is this?
Because the former explanation lacks the extinction of marks regarding giving with outflows (*sāsrava*) and so forth. For what reason? Because of the one...
Because one constantly clings to a self at all times, it is not truly revealed;

this is the intended meaning of the statement that it is solely due to the seventh consciousness’s clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*) that the mode of activity of self-clinging becomes intensified within the six consciousnesses.

Therefore, it is said that because the object of the seventh consciousness’s clinging to a self is present, acts such as giving cannot be without signs (*animitta*); the seventh consciousness does not truly reveal a self, and thus giving does not lose its signs. Hence, the question is asked: "This..."

Question: What is the difference between this treatise (*Śāstra*) and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*? Answer: This treatise explains it in terms of the seventh consciousness’s grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*), stating that "because of grasping at a self, [practices such as] giving (*dāna*) and so forth cannot eliminate signs (*nimitta*).
The *Saṃgraha*, however, bases its argument on the "self" spoken of within the sixth consciousness, stating that "I am able to practice giving," and so forth.
Since each is based on a different meaning, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, it is because of the seventh consciousness that the first six consciousnesses are unable to eliminate signs.
Master Zhao says that this refers to the "seven increases" and the "six. Furthermore, it is because of the sixth consciousness that karma is created and delusion arises again.
[Commentary: According to the statement regarding the "consciousness that directly produces," the seventh consciousness is taken as the direct producing basis for the sixth.
[Commentary]: As for the statement, "Since the afflictions of the seventh [manas] are extinguished in the two vehicles," etc.:

when the two vehicles enter the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), although the seventh [manas] is still associated with the attachment to dharmas (*dharma-grāha*), it is not termed "afflicted" from the perspective of the two vehicles.

Nevertheless, because the attachment to self (*ātma-grāha*) is absent, it is said that the afflictions are extinguished. Why, then, does the fifth consciousness still possess the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*)? The answer is as stated in the commentary.

[Commentary]: "Alternatively, because the bondage by way of causal category still persists, it follows that there should also be bondage by way of characteristics" means that the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) during the causal stage possess bondage by way of characteristics due to the seven [mental factors];

even in the stage of the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), although the seven [defiled factors] are absent, these [consciousnesses] themselves, as their own category, likewise give rise to bondage by way of characteristics.
To say "it is not so" means that if one does not take the causal category as the interpretation, but takes only the second...

If it is said that the seven types of existence involving attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) are called "bondage by signs" (*nimittabandhana*), then the untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) of the two vehicles would also possess bondage by signs, as it likewise involves attachment to the seventh type of existence.
Alternatively, if it is said that this is not so—that one does not grasp this cause for liberation—why is that?

If you claim they belong to the same category, then the mind of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmyajñāna*) should also possess [bondage], as it belongs to the same category as the preceding state of contaminated causal conditions.

Question: What is the difference between the bondage of characteristics (*nimitta-bandhana*) and the bondage of the object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*)? Answer: There is no difference, as they both pertain to all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
Objection: If that is so, why speak of two types of bondage? Answer: They are distinguished into two kinds based on their breadth and narrowness.

The bondage of the object-condition is broad because it encompasses both the original [nature] and its reflection; the bondage of characteristics is narrow because it refers only to the characteristic portion (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the reflected image. Some say there is a slight distinction.

That which is bound by the object of cognition (ālambana-bandhana) receives the designation "bond" from that which can cognize it; whereas that which is bound by its own substance receives the designation directly.

Therefore, it is said that while the followers of the Two Vehicles (dvayāyānika) sever the bond of the object of cognition, they do not sever the bond of the characteristics (nimitta-bandhana), because the bond by which the object of cognition is bound by the subject of cognition is termed the "bond of the object of cognition.
There is a school of thought that maintains: although the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) does not currently possess afflictions, due to the present [influence] of another...

Because they are bound by the objects of delusion, they become "outflow-tainted" (*sāsrava*); this is called "binding by the object. The Master of the Treatise refutes this below, for [taint] is not established by other delusions;

otherwise, one would have to concede that [the mind] becomes untainted (*anāsrava*) through the understanding of others, and so forth. If it were binding by way of the object, then the subject—the mental state—would be called "bound by the aspect" (*nimitta-bandhana*).

Since all such binding by aspects arises from the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), the followers of the Two Vehicles do not sever it. However, this [grasping at phenomena] is inferior to the former [grasping at a self].

[Commentary]: That which possesses the characteristic of conceptual discrimination refers to the outflow-tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) that, when taking an object as its condition, gives rise to discrimination through forgetfulness;

because this discrimination fails to comprehend [the object] and is constrained by its characteristics, it is called "bondage by characteristics" (*nimitta-bandhana*). The aspect of vision (*darśana-bhāga*) of the outflow-free [mind] (*anāsrava*) does not cling to characteristics, and therefore it is not bound by characteristics.
[Commentary]: "The substance is coarse and heavy" means it is hard, rough, and lacks a supple nature. [Commentary]:

Alternatively, regarding the views that are bound, they are provisionally termed "bondage by characteristics" (*nimitta-bandhana*). This explains that the state of the views being bound is easily manifested;
the reason is that the aspect of the views that are bound is either non-perceptual (*anumāna*) or inferential (*anumāna*), and it involves conceptualization corresponding to grasping (*abhiniveśa*).

To explain, it is said that the characteristic of bondage (*bandhana-lakṣaṇa*) applies to both the internal and external; the internal refers to the sense organs (*indriya*), while the external refers to the true objects (*viṣaya*).
Because various forms and appearances (*ākāra*) are easily manifested within the relationship between the binder and the bound, we speak only of "bondage by characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-bandhana*).
[Commentary: "Because it is detested by afflictions" means that it is bound because it is augmented by the primary afflictions, their derivatives, and so forth. [Commentary:
"Because it is augmented by the tainted manas" means, as stated previously, that it is caused [to arise] by the seventh [consciousness], the *manas*.
The fact that giving and other virtues induced within the six consciousnesses cannot eliminate characteristics such as [the marks of a Buddha] is precisely this point.

[Commentary]: The phrase "because of the presence of *dausthulya*" (coarseness/heaviness) intends to mean that contaminated states possess the bondage of *dausthulya*—namely, rigidity, harshness, and lack of pliancy—and that uncontaminated states are not like this, and thus cannot be used as an analogy.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "The essence of the bondage of heavy dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) also extends to the contaminated (*sāsrava*)," the intended meaning is that not only is the bondage of characteristics (*nimitta-bandhana*) contaminated, but the very essence of the bondage of heavy dysfunction also extends to the contaminated.
Question: What constitutes the essence of the bondage of characteristics? Furthermore, how many types of bondage of heavy dysfunction are there?
Answer: As explained in the Ximing Commentary (*Ximing shu*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because that [text] explains based on the predominant manifestation," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) maintains that the aspect of "I" being able to perform giving is predominant;

thus, it speaks from this one perspective. However, if one were to rely on this [present] treatise as well, the principle should be the same. Furthermore, if one considers it in relation to the six consciousnesses, it is distinct from this.
Moreover, Ximing states that this citation of a verse reiterates the reason for being bound by characteristics and not yet liberated, namely: "Such is the manas."
Thus, as long as this defiled manas—the basis of consciousness—has not been extinguished, the six consciousnesses will never be liberated from the bonds of their phenomenal characteristics.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "past and future afflictions arise and serve as conditions":

this means that wholesome states and the like are rendered outflowing (sāsrava) because they are triggered by past afflictions serving as conditions, and because they are conditioned by future afflictions.

Since [the wholesome and so forth] are already established as "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) by virtue of being associated with the wholesome and so on, why would one need to rely on their mutual coexistence? Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* and other texts state:

"At the time when the wholesome and so forth arise, although there are no present outflows, they are bound by past and future afflictions that take them as objects; thus, those wholesome states and so on are called 'with outflows'.
To refute this, [the author] says: "The principle of being bound by objects in the past and future does not exist."

[Treatise] Regarding the claim that something becomes "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*) due to the afflictions of others, our own school asserts: Although the World-Honored One’s body has already exhausted all outflows, it nevertheless becomes "with-outflows" through the conditions of the afflictions of others.
For example, it is said that Aṅgulimāla gave rise to anger toward the Buddha; because of this, the World-Honored One also became "with-outflows.
Therefore, this refutation [of the opponent's view] is not based on the idea that [the Buddha becomes with-outflows] through the afflictions of others.
Because it constitutes a contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomenon.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "not losing and increasing," this refers to the intention that the Saṃmitīya school maintains that "not losing and increasing" occurs by means of the *prāpti* (possession) of the Sarvāstivādins.
[Treatise]: Nor can it be said that because the wholesome states and so forth arise from tainted seeds within the sūtras, they become tainted. The intended meaning is this:
you may not say that although manifest afflictions are absent, the manifest wholesome states and so forth nevertheless become tainted because they are produced by tainted seeds;
for prior to those seeds, there would be no cause by which they could be established as tainted. This explains [the opponent's] objection.

It may be asked: by what means can it be said that [the seeds] are contaminated (*sāsrava*)? For when you say that seeds are perfumed by the wholesome and so forth, since the manifest afflicted *manas* does not exist at that time, upon what basis could manifest outflows form contaminated seeds?
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "past karmic bonds are led by afflictions," the Sautrāntikas say, "I do not agree with the Sarvāstivādins on this point.

This establishes the definition of *āsrava* (outflow). Within the body, the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and so forth arise solely from the seeds of the outflows; therefore, they are called "with outflow" (*sāsrava*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the same applies to the wholesome and so forth," this analogy means that internal material sense faculties which are results of maturation (*vipāka*) likewise arise from seeds of the outflows.
Therefore, they constitute the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*).
[Commentary: Regarding that which is bound by the outflows (*āsrava*), it is like the wholesome course of action (*kuśala-karma-patha*) produced by ignorance (*avidyā*);

the intention is that wholesome tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*) invite future existence (*punar-bhava*) through the power of the outflows. Regarding that which is followed by the outflows, it is like attaining the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the divine eye and ear in the higher realms.

Furthermore, because the various *dausthulya* (dysfunctions) of the higher stages continue to pursue them, the divine eyes and ears become *sāsrava* (with outflows). Therefore, the *Abhidharma* states:

"That which is pursued by outflows" means that due to these roots of goodness, they again conform to the state of being with outflows, causing the goodness of the stage of application (*prayoga*) not to become untainted (*anāsrava*).
Thus, the *Abhidharma* says: "That which is followed by outflows" refers to the roots of goodness of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), even though...

Although it is accompanied by the heaviness (*dausthulya*) of afflictions, it can be established as having an untainted nature (*anāsrava*), because all [these factors] are conducive to their respective antidotes. [Commentary:

The meaning of "even though it is also produced by these" is that, at the time of performing the sixth [act of] giving, although it is produced by the preceding [afflictions] within the current consciousness...
The arousal of craving and so forth does not arise simultaneously [with the primary cause]; they are merely auxiliary conditions (*pāratantrya-hetu*) and not the direct cause (*mukhya-hetu*).
[Commentary: The meaning of the statement that "the binding by the afflictions of others is also an auxiliary condition" is as follows:
