even if one personally practices giving and other virtues, if at that time another person’s mind is bound by afflictions, this too is an auxiliary condition and not the direct cause.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the bondage of others' conditions is also a secondary cause," the meaning is as follows: although one may personally practice giving and so forth, if at that time another person's mind is bound by afflictions, this [affliction] is still a secondary cause.
For it to be a primary cause, it must necessarily arise in accordance with [the wholesome action] simultaneously.

[Commentary]: "This means that it is not the case that each [consciousness] transforms individually. The intent is as follows: if they were to become outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) due to being bound by external conditions, then they would not be transforming individually.

Furthermore, if they were to become outflow-tainted through mutual binding by conditions, then when I practice giving, another person’s desire for the fruit [of that giving] and so forth should also [become tainted].
Since this is not the case, we know that each [consciousness] transforms individually. In the Mahāyāna school, [the seeds of] the wholesome and so forth..."
Since it is not bound by external conditions, one knows that each transforms this extremely fresh *vāyu* (wind/energy);
because the interpretations of the Tripiṭaka masters differ, it is called "new" (*xīn*) in meaning.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the term "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) precisely indicates that this dharma co-exists with the outflows, the intended meaning is as follows: at the time of practicing giving and so forth...
All [minds] possess a seventh [consciousness], because the mind of the three natures becomes defiled (sāsrava) precisely through its simultaneous occurrence with the mind of self-grasping;
thus, afflictions such as self-grasping constitute the primary cause of defilement.

[Commentary]: If it is argued that being bound by other conditions is also refuted as before, this is the same as the previous refutation that liberation through others cannot result in the attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*), and so forth. [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmapada* and other treatises, "furthermore, they do not mutually augment one another," the intended meaning is that [the state of being bound] arises solely from tainted afflictions (*sāsrava-kleśa*).
The seeds and so forth that follow this body arise in other realms and stages, yet it is not said that they bind sentient beings of those other stages;
furthermore, the outflowing seeds do not mutually augment one another in relation to the wholesome and so forth—this corresponds to the text of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
[Commentary]: "Mutually augmenting" means that the seventh [consciousness] augments other dharmas to establish them as outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*).

When the sixth consciousness is untainted (*anāsrava*), the seven afflictions do not function; however, when this ignorance itself is not yet untainted, it augments the defilement of the seventh [consciousness].

Furthermore, regarding "mutually augmenting," Ximing [Master] explains that this reveals that because the nature of outflow-tainted [dharmas] and the nature of the outflows themselves are identical, they mutually augment one another.
Because [a dharma] is established as *sāsrava* (with-outflows) only through augmentation, the term "one's own" (*svakīya*) excludes the Sarvāstivādins;
"actualized by other afflictions" excludes the Sautrāntikas; "affliction-seeds" excludes the Mahāsāṃghikas;

and "simultaneous arising and ceasing with latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*) excludes the Vātsīputrīyas. Because past and future afflictions and outflows can establish [a dharma] as *sāsrava*, this clarifies that [it is established] by...

[The seventh consciousness] becomes *sāsrava* (with outflows) only when it arises and ceases simultaneously with the afflictions currently active within its own continuum, thereby mutually augmenting them.

[Commentary: The phrase "the same applies to those in training (*śaikṣa*)... because it is associated with the wholesome" means that for one in training, the seventh consciousness has not yet been extinguished and thus remains associated with afflictions.
When the seventh consciousness is absent, there can be no afflictions within the other consciousnesses to accompany acts such as giving.

Because it is associated with a wholesome mind, and since it is known that other consciousnesses become contaminated (*sāsrava*) by being accompanied by a wholesome mind, it is clear that this must necessarily be due to the simultaneous presence of the afflictions of the seventh [consciousness].

[Commentary: This is intended to resolve the preceding doubt and give rise to the explanation in the following passage, which clarifies that the state of being contaminated is not established by the afflictions of another [consciousness].
[Commentary] "The category of outflows" (*āsrava-jāti*) refers to the fact that the various contaminated (*sāsrava*) aggregates of an Arhat are produced by afflictions from previous lives.
This means that the various contaminated phenomena of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), such as contaminated wholesome states and so forth, arise from previously existing contaminated seeds;

thus they are established as being contaminated. This further implies that it is entirely due to the seventh [consciousness], the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and so forth, at a prior time, in conjunction with the six consciousnesses...

The three natures (trisvabhāva) and the mind together permeate the seeds of outflows (*sāsrava-bīja*); subsequently, when the body of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) possesses outflows, these [outflows] are established as being of the same category as the previous outflows.

If the Lesser Vehicle does not admit that there is a seventh consciousness co-arising with the six consciousnesses and the mind, then how could the mind and so forth become possessed of outflows at a later time? Furthermore, it cannot be said that they are the outflows themselves.
[This refers to] the category [of the afflictions].

[Commentary: Regarding the fault that "self-grasping would not exist," if you do not establish the seventh consciousness, then self-grasping would be non-existent; this is what is meant by the fault that it "would not exist."

[Commentary] Regarding the third passage on principle: as previously stated, "having already cited the sacred teachings, one shall now manifest the correct principle," this refers to the third scriptural passage within that section manifesting the correct principle.

[Commentary]: Regarding the reason why consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not separately established within the category of the "bases" (*āyatana*), this principle applies universally. Question: Why is consciousness not separately established among the twelve bases? Answer:
For the time being, the bases are defined by distinguishing between the unique faculties (*indriya*) and their corresponding objects (*viṣaya*).

Thus, they are collectively termed "bases," without separately discussing consciousness. This will be explained in detail in the respective analyses in the eighth fascicle. [Note: The commentary is redundant.]
Since consciousness exists within the "realm" (dhātu) and its "gate" (dvāra), it is not what is being elucidated here;

alternatively, it may be that within the realm the eight consciousnesses are not opened up, but only the six consciousnesses are mentioned, which would likewise be unobjectionable when speaking of the six in relation to the sense organs (indriya) and their objects (viṣaya).
*Commentary on the Exposition of the Meaning of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Scroll Five;
*Commentary on the Exposition of the Meaning of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Scroll Six, Part One.

[Commentary]: Regarding these nine verses that summarize the "transforming consciousness" (*pariṇāma*), they are analyzed through nine categories. First, the distinctions of the first transforming consciousness...
Chapter Two: The Separate Gate; Chapter Three: The Self-Characteristic Gate; Chapter Four: The Aspect Gate; Chapter Five: The Three Natures Gate; Chapter Six:
The Association with Mental Factors Gate; Chapter Seven: The Co-arising with the Three Feelings Gate; Chapter Eight: The Basis Gate; Chapter Nine:
The Simultaneous Operation Gate; Chapter Ten: The Arising and Ceasing Gate.
[Commentary: Regarding the latter two verses, this refers to the seventh verse of the subsequent treatise, which states:
"Relying upon the fundamental consciousness, there are [states such as] sleep and fainting," and so forth, comprising these two verses.

[Treatise] Regarding the phrase "next, among [the three transformations]," it is called "next among" because the second transformative consciousness is situated between the [first and third] of the three transformative consciousnesses.
[Commentary] First, regarding the explanation of the six causes: "cause" (hetu) carries the meaning of "basis," "reason," or "motive."
[Commentary: "Nor are they fixed as distinct" means that it is not the case that the six consciousnesses are fixed as distinct, for there are additionally the seventh and eighth consciousnesses.

Furthermore, it is said: "Nor are they distinct" because, in terms of their general characteristics, they are subsumed to form a single consciousness, just like the single mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
[Commentary]: Is it not the case that this refers to only one [sense organ]? Answer: It is because the sense faculty (*indriya*) is impaired that consciousness becomes dull and inferior.
Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) relies upon that dull and inferior gateway, it is not distinct; thus, regarding what is actually blue, it falsely interprets it as yellow.
It is certainly not the case that the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) sees blue as yellow.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "when the latter seven are untainted (*anāsrava*), the six are necessarily untainted," the meaning is as follows:

if the six are untainted, the seventh is not necessarily untainted—this refers to those such as the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). However, if the seventh is untainted, the six are necessarily untainted—this refers to those such as Bodhisattvas.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "not the basis for defilement or purity" to "the basis for elicitation," the intent is as follows: the eye-faculty and so forth serve only as the generative basis (*janmāśraya*) for the five consciousnesses;

they do not serve as their basis for defilement or purity (*saṃkleśavyavadānāśraya*), nor as their basis for elicitation (*ākṣepāśraya*). Therefore, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the fundamental basis (*mūlāśraya*);

the seventh consciousness is the basis for defilement and purity; and the sixth consciousness, in relation to the five consciousnesses, is the basis for elicitation, as it is capable of eliciting them.
Because the five consciousnesses arise [from them], these [bases] are not bases of arising; therefore, they are what is excluded.

[Commentary]: This matter is sometimes transformed by the mental consciousness. Matter must be transformed from consciousness to become a sense organ (*indriya*), for the mind can produce consciousness and see matter.
Since consciousness necessarily knows that there is an organ, according to this principle, it relies upon the organ and does not rely upon matter.
[Commentary: "How can it be that the seeds of consciousness do not arise following form?"—these two phrases are the question; what follows is the answer. [Commentary:
"Form that is separate from consciousness," etc.—this cites a concrete instance to clarify the intended meaning:

it is only because the sense organ and consciousness are conjoined that consciousness is able to apprehend an object and cause the sense organ to undergo benefit or harm; it is not the case that the four types of form and consciousness each separately cause form.
When there is benefit or harm, it is just as when external matter such as color-form undergoes benefit or harm;
yet, because consciousness itself is neither benefited nor harmed, this is like the case where rice seedlings and the like are damaged by frost and hail.

Since it is evident that while the matter is damaged, the consciousness is not, it is clear that the benefit or harm of the matter does not occur through a conjunction between matter and consciousness. That which damages the matter externally is, for instance, the frost.
"Crops and the like are [examples of this].

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it is associated with the untainted (anāsrava) sixth consciousness," the intent is as follows: if the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) enters only the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it does not preclude the seventh consciousness from being tainted (*sāsrava*).

However, in the present case, that is not what is being taken into account; rather, it refers to when the sixth consciousness also enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

The seventh [consciousness] is untainted (*anāsrava*), and now both are untainted; the intent of "now both are untainted" is that they enter together into the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), wherein the sixth consciousness assists the seventh faculty.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "Why... to "...is acceptable," the intended meaning is as follows: The sixth consciousness alone is called *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness); because this name is prone to confusion [with the mental faculty], it is said "it is not so.

As for the visual consciousnesses and the others, they are established by names according to their respective faculties (*indriya*) and thus are not subject to such confusion; hence it is said "they are acceptable. The underlying point is that all six consciousnesses possess the immediately preceding mental faculty (*manas*) as their basis.
Even if you grant that the five consciousnesses are designated by distinct names such as "visual" and so forth according to their unique faculties (*asādhāraṇa-indriya*), it is still said...
If that were so, for what reason is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) alone designated as such? Therefore, it is said: "Not so. Some say: "The mental faculty (*manas*) is not [the same];

the mental consciousness should not be based on a non-common sense-organ (*asādhāraṇendriya*), because other consciousnesses are also based upon what is called 'mind' (*manas*). Eye and the others may be so;
eye and the others may be called non-common sense-organs because other consciousnesses do not rely upon them."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the five bodies of consciousness also depend upon the mind," the intended meaning is that since the five consciousnesses depend upon their own specific, non-shared faculties (indriya), the sixth [consciousness] likewise depends upon its own specific, non-shared mental faculty (manas-indriya), just as the five consciousnesses do.
[Commentary] Question: Regarding the previous statement that the sixth [consciousness] relies on five, eight, or seven [bases], the intent is as follows:

since it was previously stated that the sixth relies on the five sense organs as well as the seventh and eighth consciousnesses, why is it said that the sixth has an "unshared basis" (asādhāraṇa-āśraya)?

[Commentary]: Regarding the seventh consciousness in relation to the five and the eighth, both are its supports (*āśraya*). In relation to the five, it serves as the support for defilement and purification;

in relation to the eighth, it serves as the simultaneous support (*sahabhv-āśraya*). However, when considering what is proximate and conducive to its arising, it relies solely on the sixth consciousness and not on the fifth or the eighth;
therefore, it receives the name "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).

[Commentary]: This means that regarding the five [consciousnesses] such as the eye reaching the two bases, it is intended to say that the five consciousnesses—eye and so forth—not only rely on the immediately ceased mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), but also rely on the five material faculties (*rūpa-indriya*).
Therefore, it is stated below that "the five have both the mental and material as their two bases.
The sixth [consciousness] is not like this; because it relies solely on the mind, it receives the name "mental consciousness" (*mano-vijñāna*).

[Commentary]: If that is so, since the seventh and eighth consciousnesses also rely solely upon the manas, they are collectively termed "manas" because these two consciousnesses are both the sphere of mind (manāyatana);
this is explained here according to their own specific definitions.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses also possess the name "mind" (*manas*) based on their support, the intention is as follows:

since the sixth consciousness, relying upon the *manas*, is named "mental consciousness" (*mano-vijñāna*), one knows that the seventh and eighth also rely upon one another; thus, they likewise ought to be named "mind," "heart," or "consciousness. Therefore, it is said that this principle also applies here.

Now, I maintain that according to various treatises, the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is established based on its own preeminent capacity for discernment (*vijñapti*), while the term "mind" (*manas*) is established based on its capacity for reflection (*manana*).
"Manas" (mind) is named for its accumulation; "citta" (thought) is named for its basis; and "vijñāna" (consciousness) is named for its preeminence.

This is why they are not called by the names Manas, Citta, or Vijñāna [in this specific context]. [Commentary]: Furthermore, explaining the distinct reasons why the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are named "Manas," the meaning is as follows: this term "Manas" does not refer to the act of deliberation (*manana*).
The term "intention" (*manas*) is also like when people say, "this intention intends such-and-such," which is just as it was said that "mind" (*citta*) refers to gathering and storing;
this is a further explanation of the reason for the distinction between the names "mind" and "intention."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it conforms to and explains the general and specific meanings of *vijñāna* (consciousness)," the intended meaning is as follows: that which discerns (*vijñapti*) is the general name for consciousness;
alternatively, from "consciousness of form" (*rūpa-vijñāna*) up to "consciousness of phenomena" (*dharma-vijñāna*), these are the specific names.

Therefore, the treatise states: "That which discerns the six objects is called consciousness," which refers to the general name; and it further states: "The five consciousnesses, such as those of form, etc., [proceed] up to the discernment of all phenomena."
This is another name [for the sixth consciousness]. Furthermore, it is said that "it is capable of attaining the designation 'dharma-consciousness'";
this is a re-explanation of the reason why the sixth consciousness receives the name "dharma-consciousness.

[Commentary]: This means that while the external bases (āyatana) are collectively termed "dharmas," when referring specifically to the external objects of perception, they are established as such; yet, among them, it is the sixth [consciousness] alone [that is designated as dharma-consciousness].
It is called the *dharmāyatana*. [Commentary:
It is also named after the consciousness that apprehends it exclusively (*asādhāraṇa*). This is because both the consciousness and its object are distinct from one another;
thus, they are each termed "unshared consciousness. Since it discerns phenomena (*dharma*) without being shared, the treatise states: "Alternatively, it is that which can discern phenomena."
[The text] alone receives the name "consciousness of dharmas" (*dharmavijñāna*).

[Commentary: Alternatively, among those within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), that which is capable of discerning is the sixth consciousness alone, and thus it is specifically named "consciousness of dharmas. Furthermore, it is said that there is also this meaning:
the sixth consciousness possesses the sense of discernment, which differs from the previous explanation of "dharmas."

[Treatise]: Following this, from the point where it says "depending on the object" up until "or name-and-form and consciousness," this section has already established the general principle that names are established based on objects, as spoken from the perspective of the stage of non-mastery (*avaśa*). If one were in a state of mastery (*vaśa*), it would not be so;

for it is admitted that the four [bases] and consciousness can each take other objects as their conditions. Although they possess this capacity, [the designation] should proceed from the sense-faculties (*indriya*) to avoid confusion.
[Omission].

[Commentary]: The *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* serves as scriptural proof for this treatise. That sūtra is based on the fact that the five consciousnesses, which have not yet attained mastery, perceive only their own respective objects.
If the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) were designated as "dharma-consciousness" (*dharmavijñāna*), then both cause and effect would be universally applicable; therefore, it is so intended.

[Objection: It may be so [in name], but if that were the case, while the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) in the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) are admitted to have five objects of perception (*ālambana*), they are not admitted to do so in the causal state (*hetu-avasthā*) when one has not yet attained mastery.

If you admit this [mutual perception] even in the causal state, how would you explain the *Saddharma-smṛty-upasthāna-sūtra*, which says that the five consciousnesses in the causal state are also admitted to perceive each other—just as a snake’s eye hears sound?
[Response: The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) itself explains: "This is the doctrine of the Saṃmitīya masters; it is not the Mahāyāna."
The Mahāyāna school does not admit that the "snake-eye" can hear sounds, because the snake-eye may possess the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and other such factors.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement, "In the first bhūmi, one is immediately called 'sovereign' because the five untainted (*anāsrava*) consciousnesses manifest": Question:
Since the five faculties in the first bhūmi are still tainted (*sāsrava*), how can they give rise to the five untainted consciousnesses? Answer: The five consciousnesses prior to the bhūmis are...

Regarding the statement that the seventh [consciousness] establishes the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) nature of the others: because the seventh clings to a self, it prevents the arising and other functions produced by the five sensory consciousnesses from transcending their objective characteristics;
thus, they become outflow-tainted. Therefore, the seventh serves as the basis for defilement and purification.

Since the sixth consciousness acts as the inducing basis for the five sensory consciousnesses and can follow both natures (wholesome and unwholesome), the latter do not become untainted (*anāsrava*), even upon reaching the initial [stage of the path].
Because the stages (bhūmi) attain the untainted (anāsrava) state by means of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, they also induce the five sensory consciousnesses to become untainted.
Therefore, the untainted five consciousnesses exist in the first stage; this will be further explained in detail in the tenth fascicle.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "However, there is another meaning: 'that which is produced by the power of conditions leading to the inconceivable,'" the intent is as follows:
the five consciousnesses are produced by the sixth consciousness through the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that realizes the emptiness of phenomena;

it is permitted that within the Pure Land, they manifest supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), such as emitting water and fire, performing miracles, and preaching the Dharma. This refers to the distinct stages found within the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.
To provide this explanation is not the primary meaning.

[Commentary: Alternatively, there is another interpretation: that prior to the seventh stage, one is not yet called "sovereign" (vaśitā). This refers to the fact that only from the eighth stage onward is one termed "sovereign";
although there is mutual interchangeability prior to that, one has not yet attained sovereignty. This is also found within that treatise.

There is also a separate master’s interpretation that they may be used interchangeably; according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, even those prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva path] may use them interchangeably.
Thus, the Sūtra says, "The pure physical eye born of one's parents," which refers precisely to the two meanings explained above.
[Commentary: "Either at the first stage (bhūmi) or upon entering the eighth stage" means that it is precisely at these times that they function interchangeably and no longer lack autonomy;
it does not mean that such was not the case prior to this.
[Commentary: "How is it that the various faculties reach all objects?"—this is entirely a question intended to provide proof for the meaning of this consciousness.
The intent is to demonstrate that these consciousnesses function interchangeably.
[The *Śū* (Commentary)] states: "To cite the sense organs as the support in order to reveal the consciousnesses supported by them" is the response.
[The *Śū*] asks: "How can they function interchangeably... is this not confusion? This is the second question. Alternatively, it says: "This, however..."

The objection is merely this: if the eye is defined by its grasping of visible form (*rūpa*), yet it is also called the "eye" when it grasps tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*) through contact, how can this not be a confusion?

This refers to the naming of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) based on their apprehension of objects; the reason for the term "confusion" lies in the naming of the faculties themselves, not in the naming of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Now, by naming consciousness after its faculty, there is no ambiguity. To say that [the sense-organ] does not reach the object but is the "apprehender" (*grāhaka*) refers to cognition through separation (*prāpyakāritva*).
Because it is free from cognition through contact, the objective form does not reach the perceiver; therefore, it is said that "it does not reach the perceiver.

Regarding the phrase "as discussed in the Dharma-lakṣaṇa (Yogācāra)," this refers to the principle of the Dharma-lakṣaṇa which teaches that [the object] is not reached and is known through non-contact; thus it is said, "as discussed in the Dharma-lakṣaṇa.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "causing it to reach" and so forth, this refers to cognition through conjunction (*saṃyoga-jñāna*); it means that the eye now takes up the tangible.
If one perceives the five consciousnesses and the five faculties within a synthesis, what distinction is there such that it is called "confused"?
Furthermore, this would contradict the principle explained above regarding the discernment of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) through analytical separation.
[Commentary]: Regarding "name" (*nāman*), the intended meaning is as follows: "Name" is like a guest, for a guest has no fixed affiliation;
names are likewise so. Therefore, names lack substantial reality and cannot definitively designate a single phenomenon.

Thus, they receive the designation "guest," being merely based on conventional discourse and not constituting an ultimate standard of measurement. As the Sūtra says: "Names are mutually guests. Furthermore—
Since the designations "name" and "mutually guest-like" lack a fixed determination, the eye does not exclusively take form as its object to receive the name "eye";
now it also takes touch as its object and is called "eye. Therefore, the established name "eye" is not of fixed determination.

[Commentary] Therefore, regarding the phrase "those who obtain the name based on two," this refers to the previous establishment of names based on the two factors of sense-faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*);
[in this case], one may rely solely on the sense-faculties, as there would be no risk of confusion.

[Treatise] According to the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) definitively discerns the distinctions in the mental activities of sentient beings; it reaches the point where such capacity no longer exists.

Therefore, this explains that [the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*] universally takes the six objects as its cognitive domain. Since the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states that the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* discriminates the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings, we know it does not take only form (*rūpa*) as its object.
Furthermore, since it is said to be able to initiate the transformations of the three types of action (*trividha-karman*), we know it universally takes mental action (*manas-karman*) as its object.
Moreover, since it is said to compose the four types of indeterminate treatises (*avyākṛta-śāstra*), we know that the five consciousnesses take only one [object] as their domain.
All these categories of meaning have been fully explained as cited from the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* in the *Yanmi*; therefore, they are not recorded here.

[Commentary] There are three types of bodily transformation (*kāya-nirmāṇa*): first, transformation through the manifestation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), such as the body expanding or contracting, or emitting water and fire;
second, transformation through taking birth, namely being born in a royal palace or taking birth according to various species; third, transformation through manifesting the fruit [of maturation].
This refers to the retribution for accepting gold and rejecting the horse-barley [offering], as examined in the *Huiri lun* (Treatise on the Sun of Wisdom).

[Commentary] The "three hundred and fifty" intends to state that from the initial generation of the bodhicitta and the practice of the six pāramitās, up until the distribution of the śarīra relics, there were in total this many instances of those to be saved and the locations where they were saved; that is, each and every one.
In each station, all six perfections are present; thus, taken together, there are two thousand one hundred.
Each individual perfection serves as an antidote for four types of sentient beings—namely, those characterized by greed, hatred, delusion, and those with equal proportions of these afflictions.

This means, for example, that there may be a sentient being who gives rise only to superior greed toward an inferior object; or another sentient being who gives rise only to superior hatred toward an inferior object; or yet another sentient being...
In inferior objects, one gives rise only to superior delusion; these constitute the three types.

Furthermore, just as a single sentient being might give rise only to inferior greed toward an inferior object, to middling greed toward a middling object, and to superior greed toward a superior object—the same applies to hatred and delusion—and is therefore called an "even-parted" (*sabhāga*) sentient being.
That is to say, when the mind and the object correspond to one another, it is termed "even-parted. However, regarding a single...
The person who manifests discursive thought (*vitarka*) does not possess these four types of mental activity;

however, those beings to be converted by others—whether belonging to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the body (*kāya*), or the various categories (*jāti*)—may possess these four. Therefore, the arising [of discursive thought] is also that which is to be remedied.

Thus, each individual practice cultivated in opposition to these four types of mental activity counteracts the faults arising from the four great elements and the six objects of no meaning (*anartha*).
Regarding the fourteen thousand questions, it is said that from "radiance" (*ābhāsa*) up to "the distribution of the Buddha-body," what is the meaning of "radiance"? What is its stage?

Answer: At the very beginning of practicing the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthiti-citta*), when one performs the contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and forms the perception of light, it is called "radiance.
Alternatively, it is said that when the mind arises toward the Dharma, it is called "radiance. Although this interpretation exists, [it is not definitive].
The original text has not been seen.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement here that "there are differences between persons and dharmas," the intended meaning is to explain how these four types of transformation apply to both persons and dharmas, such that there are four distinct ways of answering questions (*vyākaraṇa*).
Why, then, does the separate excerpt state this?

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the Buddha’s transformations lack real, superior function, yet even those resembling transformations may be so called," the intent is as follows:

Although the Buddha is able to manifest through the four factors of faculties, mind, karma, and the fruits of mental states (*caitta*), these manifestations—when compared to the Buddha’s own fundamental essence of mind and so forth—are not more excellent, clear, or sharp.
Because they do not equal the original mind in terms of their objective conditions (*ālambana*), they are said to lack real, superior function and are thus termed "resembling" [transformations].
When asked why transformation (nirmāṇa) is necessary, the answer is: because each of the objects of the four types of knowledge (jñāna) pervades all places, transformation is required.
However, the Buddha’s own mind and mental factors are not transformations of the minds and mental factors of others.
[Commentary: The phrase "below it reveals that which is not stated" means that it reveals that the root verse does not state the non-common basis (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*).

The phrase "the common basis is stated below" means that it reveals that the common basis is stated in the subsequent [prose] commentary. This is as stated in the seventh fascicle of the treatise: "relying upon the fundamental consciousness," and so forth.
Furthermore, the purpose of revealing the non-common basis here is to provide a specific explanation for why the non-common basis is not mentioned within the verse itself.
These six consciousnesses are explained as having a common support, namely the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and so forth.

[Treatise: Previously, for the sake of convenience in accordance with the meaning, the supports were discussed; this was intended to mean that because the sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) are coarse and manifest, they were not mentioned in the root verses (*kārikā*).
In the prose commentary (*bhāṣya*), "previously, for the sake of convenience in accordance with the meaning, the supports have already been discussed" refers back to what was stated before.
The fourth fascicle extensively explains that the basis has been understood.
[The Commentary] states: As previously discussed at length, this refers back to the same point.

If one were to say, "If a phenomenon is determined to have an object as its primary factor, causing the mind and mental factors to apprehend their respective objects, it refers to the six internal bases"; or, if pointing more specifically, "it is the well-established *manas*."

Regarding the statement that "the consciousness-mind has its own unique [characteristics], such as manifesting its own name, not being subsumed by the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), and so forth—even up to the point where the meaning of the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) for these, such as visual consciousness and the like, is to be explained," this refers to the following passage: "As stated in the Sūtra:
'How does visual consciousness, depending on the eye-faculty, discern various forms (*rūpa*)? etc. If it is asked whether the object-condition is also discussed below, [it is].
Why is it that the response is not stated within the verse? Because the treatise clarifies *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), it does not explicitly discuss external objects.

[Commentary] Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the preceding text was not intended to clarify that the verse lacks the long passage on selflessness; thus, it is not explained separately. The meaning of this interpretation is as follows:
"the preceding text" refers to the immediately preceding section concerning the six transformations and so forth. The intent is to state that this [verse] is not meant to clarify...

The verse does not explain the reasons for [the order of] the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). The Commentary states: "Because they are coarse, manifest, and universally established, these are not explained here.

This means that I have simply not mentioned the faculties and objects in my prose commentary because they are coarse and manifest. Question: If that is so, why does the Commentary say, "Since the meaning follows as a matter of course, it shall be explained"?
Answer: It is merely stated because the meaning follows as a matter of course; it is not stated because it is the primary subject.

When it is said that there is "seeing" and "resistance," this is intended to mean that the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya) has the sense of illuminating objects; thus it is called "having seeing" and "having resistance.
Furthermore, the faculty itself arises from its own seeds.
[Commentary] To say that the meaning of "category" (*jāti*) refers to "differentiation" means that, as previously stated, the categories of the six sense organs and their objects are distinct;
this is precisely the meaning of "differentiation" within the verse. Therefore.
[Commentary] It is said that this explains the reasons for the distinctions [of the consciousnesses] by following the objects of the six sense faculties, up to the point where there are six types.

[Commentary] Regarding the subsequent reconciliation with the sūtra, the intention is as follows: the previous statement that "taking the apprehension of objects as its nature and characteristic" explains the passage in the verse regarding "taking the apprehension of objects as its nature and characteristic.

The subsequent statement, "as it is taught in the sūtra," serves to establish [the meaning] through scriptural authority. The final statement, "that sūtra speaks only of [the case where] it does not... [is intended to show that the sūtra’s teaching is partial].
The phrase "to reconcile" (*hui*) refers to the fact that the preceding section cited the sutra text as a question; therefore, it is necessary to reconcile [the apparent contradiction].

[Commentary: The statement in that sutra, "it is merely provisional and not ultimate," means that the previous sutra taught that the five consciousnesses only take the five objects as their conditions.
Regarding the phrase "among all supports" (*yi*), this refers to the fundamental supports for both defilement and purity, and so forth.

[Commentary: As for the statement that "in reality, the five consciousnesses also cognize consciousness and so forth," this refers, for example, to the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) taking the seeing portion (*darśana-bhāga*) as its object.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the meaning is not fixed," the intended sense is that once the self-witnessing portion has undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it does not only take the seeing portion as its object, but also cognizes sounds and so forth;
hence, it is said to be "not fixed. For instance, when consciousness arises based on the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) to hear a sound, how could it possibly cognize the color of the sun?

Regarding the passage: "The object [is such] because a single sense-faculty gives rise to consciousness which takes all objects as its condition; therefore, it is said that this is based on a partial [perspective]," this refers to what is taught from the standpoint of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).

[Commentary: There is an interpretation that this explanation does not accord with the treatise. Therefore, I shall now provide a further, more detailed explanation of the treatise itself, which should be consulted in the relevant section.
Knowing this, one’s intention is slightly superior.
[Commentary] Next, regarding the citation of that sūtra on the six consciousnesses to establish the proof, this refers to what is stated in the treatise:
"That sūtra speaks, for the time being, of the uncommon support (*asādhāraṇa-āśraya*), and so forth."

[Commentary]: This is not intended to address the meaning of the preceding objection; rather, it is solely for the purpose of clarifying the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the six consciousnesses by citing scriptural authority to establish them.
It does not serve to resolve the previous difficult question, as this passage is established for that reason.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the eighteen *dhātus* differ as conditions," this means that when the eighteen *dhātus* serve as the objects of perception (*ālambana*), there are differences in the number of the perceiving consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) that arise.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "five, three, six, and two lead to mastery and so forth through differentiation," the intended meaning is to apply the principle of cause and effect to the eighteen [realms].

Because the objects of perception—the *dhātus*—differ in their number, the causes and the perceptions each correspond accordingly. "Cause" refers to the stage of the cause; "perception" refers to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).
"Each corresponding accordingly" clarifies that each perceives its own respective object; thus it is said they "correspond accordingly. There are five, three, and six, with two [categories].

The "five" refers to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); the "three" refers to the three consciousnesses that perceive them; and "each one is three" means that each of the five [objects] is perceived by all three [consciousnesses].

Regarding the objects of consciousness: the five consciousnesses, the sixth consciousness, and the eighth consciousness take form as their object and are established as eye-consciousness, along with the simultaneous mental consciousness and the eighth consciousness;
this continues up to the taking of touch as an object, which is established as body-consciousness, along with the simultaneous sixth and eighth consciousnesses.

The seventh consciousness takes the internal as its object, and therefore it is not mentioned here. As for "the six having two": the "six" refers to the six sense bases, and the "two" refers to [the two types of objects].

"These" refers to two consciousnesses, namely the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. The sixth consciousness universally takes the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) as its objects, while the seventh consciousness takes only the eighth consciousness as its object;
since the eighth consciousness is included within the mental faculty (*manas*), it is said that both consciousnesses take the six sense organs as their objects in general.

Regarding "the sixth and the one are each indeterminate": "six" refers to the six consciousnesses, and "one" refers to the sixth consciousness. Now, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of this [sixth consciousness] universally takes the six [sense organs] as its objects.
Regarding the "one indeterminate consciousness": this refers to the single *dharmāyatana*. The *dharmāyatana* is the object (*ālambana*) of the sixth [consciousness].

Just as the *dharmāyatana* includes the actual matter (*rūpa*) of the fruit of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala*), which is also the object of the five and eight consciousnesses—the five consciousnesses being induced by the sixth consciousness and thus able to take the actual matter of the *dharmāyatana* as their object—and just as the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) also transforms this actual matter, so too do other mental factors (*caitta*) and so forth when the sixth consciousness takes them as its object.

Regarding the statement that the six and seventh consciousnesses take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as their object, and that the sixth and seventh wisdoms arise from the cessation and path [truths], and thus realize *tathatā*—this refers to the single category of the *dharmāyatana*.
Now, concerning the analysis of "indefinite" and "sovereign" [consciousnesses], this is distinguished according to the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*).

At the stage of fruition, all five consciousnesses are able to mutually take one another as objects, which differs from the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*), as explained in the *Juyao*. Furthermore, it is said that the sixth [consciousness] and each of the others are indefinite.
However, at the stage of Buddhahood, the six consciousnesses take objects in an indeterminate manner, such that each one universally takes all objects as its domain;
this kind of universal knowledge is distinguished from the state of ultimate mastery.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the verses concerning the basis have already been explained as before," this refers to the fourth line, which states:

"The fifth, fourth, sixth, and second, seventh, eighth, and first [lines] all rely upon the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the leading cause (*āksepaka-hetu*); each of these is twofold. This is a question asking why these words appear here;

the answer is that since the previous section discussed the verses on the *ālambana* (object-condition), the verses concerning the *āśraya* (basis) now follow in sequence. This indicates they are identical.

As stated previously [in the Commentary]: "According to the preceding text, up to the point 'because they share a common basis,' some say that this refers back to the analysis of how the six consciousnesses are named based on their specific (asādhāraṇa) bases, which possesses five characteristics.
Regarding the term "specific" (*asādhāraṇa*), it serves to exclude the efficient cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
"Shared basis for defilement and purity" and "shared basis for the same object": the latter refers to the sixth consciousness having the five consciousnesses as its shared-object roots;

thus, it serves as a further distinction. Regarding "common basis" and so forth: if this refers to the fundamental eight consciousnesses themselves, they serve as the root; thus, these too are excluded.
The term "and so forth" includes the aforementioned shared-object bases and others.

[Commentary]: "If it reaches the dharma through the power of another" means that this explains the term "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) in the verse concerning the object (*viṣaya*) mentioned immediately above.
[Commentary]:

"To show that this aggregate is likewise" is a preliminary question regarding the first transformation (*pariṇāma*). It takes that [previous case] to illustrate this aforementioned attainment of mind (*citta-labdhi*).

Regarding the question concerning the nature (*svabhāva*) mentioned subsequently: among these mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), there are those that do not necessarily correspond to all three natures (*tri-svabhāva*);

how then can they be said to be like the reflection that manifests [the mind]? Answer: This is merely stated with respect to the fact that when this aggregate arises, its nature is the same [as the mind]; it does not mean that they are necessarily restricted to corresponding with all three natures.

Furthermore, another interpretation is that because the nature of these associated factors (*samprayukta-dharma*) is not fixed as being identical [to the mind], their nature is explained after the mind; for that king [the mind] alone is the totality.
"One nature" refers to what is clarified subsequently.
[Commentary: Furthermore, while those various phenomena do not necessarily pervade all three natures, this [present case] definitely does.
This is explained before and after in order to let later students know this distinction; because the natures are not fixed, they cannot be definitively equated.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "because names are hidden, they are explained first," the intended meaning is that they are explained first because their names are obscure. [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement "the untainted (anāsrava), conditioned (saṃskṛta), and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) are likewise," the intended meaning is that these two [categories] are called "wholesome" (kuśala) because they can bring about benefit in this life and future lives;
"with attainment" (prāpti) refers to the untainted with attainment, and "with realization" (sākṣātkriyā) refers to the unconditioned with realization.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding those who attain both benefits for the present and future lives through *nirvāṇa* and the attainment of *bodhi*: this means they obtain peace and happiness in the present life and will not be reborn in the evil realms in the future.

Some say it is like an *aśaikṣa* (one beyond training) who realizes *nirvāṇa with remainder*; this is the benefit for this life, and upon death, entering *nirvāṇa without remainder* is the benefit for future lives.

[Commentary: The meaning of the statement "now, explaining up to 'it is merely an indeterminate fruit of suffering'" is that the fruits of suffering in the evil realms are merely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not unwholesome (*akuśala*).
This is because they do not cause distant harm in future lives; thus, although they cause bodily pain, they are not unwholesome in terms of future rebirths.
[Commentary: In the Mahāyāna as well, each of the three natures possesses four types. It is the same for the wholesome;
the indeterminate also has four types, as was extensively analyzed previously in the third fascicle within the discussion on the indeterminate nature of the eighth consciousness.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the various treatises collectively subsume [them] because they are established separately," the meaning is as follows:
the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) taught in all treatises are subsumed within the four types of three natures presented here; therefore, it is said they are "collectively subsumed.

Furthermore, there is this sense that it is not merely that the three natures taught in this specific treatise are being discussed, but rather that the three natures found in all treatises are also encompassed; hence it is said, "there is also this meaning."
Because this meaning does not contradict reason, it is established separately; that is, the general principle of the three natures found in all treatises is not contradicted by this treatise,
which establishes four kinds of three natures, such as the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and so forth,
as explained in the third fascicle.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "only ten factors are present," this refers to the non-concentrated states (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) where *praśrabdhi* (serenity) is excluded; thus it is said there are ten factors.
The mention here of eleven is a general enumeration of the entire group for the sake of discussion, not implying that all [eleven] are necessarily present together.
[Commentary] This means that when "hatred" (dveṣa) reaches ten, it refers to the two among the seven minor [afflictions]—namely, anger (krodha) and so forth—combined with hatred itself to total ten.
The three—flattery (śāṭhya), deception (māyā), and arrogance (mada)—are excluded because they are generally indeterminate (avyākṛta).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "because it encompasses the previous two," the intent is as follows: it encompasses both the previously mentioned wholesome and unwholesome, as well as the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), all as explained at length in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
Some say that because the indeterminate is neither the aforementioned wholesome nor the unwholesome, it is said to "encompass the previous two."
[Commentary]: Furthermore, these two, three, and four categories have already been briefly explained. For example, there are two types of "wholesome" (*kuśala*):

those acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) and those produced through application (*prāyogika*). There are two types of "unwholesome" (*akuśala*): specifically unwholesome (*svabhāva-akuśala*) and unwholesome by association (*saṃprayoga-akuśala*). There are also two types of "neutral" (*avyākṛta*):
obscured neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and unobscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), as extensively clarified previously.

[Commentary]: "If conditioned phenomena that possess seeds are subsumed within those natures" means that if the three natures possess seeds, they are all subsumed under those natures in accordance with their active manifestation (*samudācāra*).
[Commentary: As for the statement, "However, these two, three, and four gates each rely on a single meaning," the intent is as follows:

within this treatise, there are two, three, and four gates that distinguish the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). In the *Abhidharma* treatises, the distinction of the three natures is generally of two types:

first, the general, and second, the specific. Regarding the general, it is perhaps by means of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and so forth that the three natures are distinguished; the second is the specific.

"Distinguishing the three natures" means distinguishing them as follows: the wholesome is analyzed by way of thirteen categories, the unwholesome by twelve categories, and the indeterminate by fourteen categories;
this constitutes the specific distinction. The explanations in this treatise differ from those in the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa);
these differences should be examined and compared. As for the distinct terminology used, each is based on a particular meaning, and thus they do not contradict one another.

[Commentary]: "The five consciousnesses cannot transform the mind to initiate karma" means that "transforming" refers to arising. The five consciousnesses cannot cause the mind to arise and initiate the two types of karma—bodily and vocal.
Even if they are granted the name "karma," it is merely a provisional karma and not a substantial karma.

This is because only the sixth [consciousness] is capable of initiating the mind and giving rise to karma; therefore, it is called the "concomitant-transforming mind that initiates karma. It follows the sixth [consciousness].
Because the six consciousnesses arise subsequently, some say that the "transforming mind" (pravṛtti-citta) initiates karma;

this refers to the sixth mental consciousness creating wholesome or unwholesome karma, which transforms the eighth consciousness (ālayavijñāna) to cause rebirth in various realms of existence. Such a functional capacity is absent in the five sensory consciousnesses.

Furthermore, while they follow the transforming mind of the sixth consciousness to initiate the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—the five consciousnesses cannot initiate the karma of deportment (airyāpathika). However, [the eighth consciousness] can.

Regarding the question of how the five consciousnesses can take postures (*īryāpatha*) as their objects, since the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses do not take postures as their objects, the answer is: it is not so.

What is meant here by "taking as an object" refers to taking the paths of posture (*īryāpatha-mārga*) as objects; "path" (*mārga*) means location (*sthāna*). Location refers to the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
Since the five consciousnesses have the five sense-objects as their objects, they are said to take postures as their objects through the medium of these five consciousnesses. This is the meaning.

It is said that when the five consciousnesses take postures (*īryāpatha*) as their object, they are subsumed under the indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*). Question: How is it that postures pertain to all five sense objects? Answer:
There are those that are the actual crafts and postures, and there are those that are designated as such by way of association.

For example, the bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*) of form and sound are the actual crafts and postures; whereas odor, taste, and touch are the bases upon which craft-activity depends. Generally speaking, these are termed "craft."

Because they skillfully engage with the five sense objects, the five consciousnesses take them as their conditions. Corporeal intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) is the primary deportment (*airyāpathika*), while fragrance, taste, and touch are the bases for the karma of deportment;
taken together, they are called "deportment" because they pervade the four sense objects and are thus conditioned by the four consciousnesses.
However, since sound is not subsumed under walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, sound is not deportment. These two types of neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), if practiced repeatedly—

All [of these] are present before one. Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the correct principle (*nyāya*), what are called the "paths of craftsmanship" (*śailpasthānika*) and the "paths of deportment" (*airyāpathika*) are precisely what constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

[Commentary: "Excluding the transformation [minds]" means that the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are also not transformation minds; therefore, the five consciousnesses do not [possess them].
This refers to the indeterminate mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-avyākṛta-citta*).

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "not the five consciousnesses... arising together in succession," the intended meaning is that the five consciousnesses occur for only a single moment and cannot arise simultaneously for two moments;
nor does it mean that they arise from one another without interval in mutual succession. This is what is being stated.

Visual consciousness arises first, followed by auditory consciousness, and then olfactory consciousness, and so forth; they cannot arise in such immediate succession. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Once the five consciousnesses have arisen in a single moment, immediately thereafter, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) necessarily arises.
Question: When mental consciousness arises after the five consciousnesses have arisen, do the five consciousnesses arise simultaneously? Answer: No. The term "a single moment" [is used here].

Regarding the arising of the five consciousnesses, the intended meaning is that within the five consciousnesses, once any one consciousness of a corresponding type has arisen, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) immediately arises;

it does not necessarily mean that all five consciousnesses must arise simultaneously. Therefore, although the statement is general, its intent is specific. Consequently, the three moral natures (trividha-svabhāva) of the five consciousnesses do not coexist.
[Commentary: "That hearing sounds within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is not what I allow" means that this master does not permit hearing sounds within meditative concentration.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "even if one were to allow that the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) arise together": this master says that even if one were to allow the simultaneous arising of the three natures, this would only be possible within meditative concentration;
in the state of distraction (*vikṣepa*), it is not so.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the five [sensory consciousnesses] arise simultaneously and share the same object," this means that it is precisely through the guidance of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that the subsequent mental consciousness arises simultaneously with the five and shares their objects.

[Commentary: Even if one grants that the five consciousnesses can arise simultaneously with all three natures, one should raise the objection that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) must likewise arise simultaneously with the three natures.

Although the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states "in successive order," this refers to the citation from the third chapter of the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*) in the preceding section, which says:
"The wholesome and defiled [states] of the five consciousnesses necessarily arise guided by the mental consciousness. This is cited to prove that they share the same nature.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "because of discerning [the object] up to the mental consciousness," the intended meaning is as follows: there are two types of mental consciousness.
First, the mental consciousness that discerns the object of meditative concentration (samādhi) takes only a single object within that concentration as its cognitive domain.

Second, the mental consciousness that takes various objects as its domain refers to the mental consciousness contemplating suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and so forth, while within concentration.
The mind is called "various objects" because its objects are not uniform; this refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

When auditory consciousness arises, it is by means of these two types of mental consciousness that one can hear sounds within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Although this is a distinct, esoteric interpretation, it is also the explanation of Master Puyang.

[Commentary: Therefore, the statement that "the [three natures] are definitely not simultaneous" intends to clarify that while it is certain they do not coexist, this does not preclude their coexistence within a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This means that the two consciousnesses (the mental consciousness and the manas) may simultaneously take the object of sound as their common object and likewise share the same wholesome nature.
If this is so, the statement that "sudden [cognition] is indeterminate according to the body" refers to the stage prior to mastery.

[Commentary: "Nor do the five consciousnesses arise in succession" means that within the five consciousnesses, as soon as one consciousness arises, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) immediately follows;

there is no room for the ear-consciousness to arise subsequently to the eye-consciousness. Therefore, because they do not arise in succession, the other consciousnesses should be understood accordingly.

[Commentary]: Regarding the previous statement that the five consciousnesses understand only in a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), this was explained above as meaning that the five consciousnesses do not comprehend the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) in a single moment;

furthermore, when explained based on multiple moments, it is likewise not admitted that the five consciousnesses comprehend the three natures, because the inducing mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cannot simultaneously comprehend the three natures.
[Commentary: "From the conventional up to the non-arising moment" explains the "single mind-moment" (*ekacitta-ksana*) mentioned in the sutra;
this is stated with reference to the ultimate intent of this [teaching]. The phrase "taking one place as the basis" refers to the locus of reliance.
Furthermore, the statement "a similar continuity because it is extremely similar" explains the term "within a single mind," based on its extreme similarity.
Therefore, it is collectively termed "one mind.

[Commentary] To clarify that the eighth consciousness does not coexist with the three natures simultaneously means that the eighth consciousness cannot at one time be concurrent with the three natures within the five consciousnesses;
as the treatise states, "the three natures coexist" refers to whichever [nature] is present among the eighth, seventh, and five [consciousnesses].

"One wholesome" refers to the simultaneous presence of the three natures. As for "naturally indeterminate," this refers to the eighth consciousness, which is called the pure indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

[Commentary] This citation from the text on the continuity of the five consciousnesses—up to the point where it says "the five consciousnesses may be simultaneous"—clarifies that within the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, there are two explanations regarding the five consciousnesses.
One states that the five consciousnesses exist for only a single moment and are simultaneously associated with the three natures; the other states that the five consciousnesses...
Xu Zuer and others maintain that many moments of thought continue in succession and that the three natures (trisvabhāva) operate simultaneously;

this is the second interpretation of the orthodox tradition of Dharmapāla, and this passage concerning their continuity was cited together with the preceding section on the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) in the fourth fascicle.
[Commentary]: Although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) also takes visible objects as its object, it first shares the same object with the visual consciousness;
however, because the auditory object is more prominent, it shares the same object with the auditory consciousness, even arising as an unwholesome auditory consciousness.

[Commentary]: "Alternatively, the phrase 'the preceding single visual consciousness reaches the point where the three natures are simultaneous' means that although the sudden (*sutarā*) and continuous (*prabandhika*) [mental states] are indefinite as to their quantity, it is nonetheless admitted that the three natures can coexist at the same time.
The intended meaning is as follows: first, a visual consciousness arises to contemplate a Buddha image;

before this has ceased, a subsequent mental state of investigation (*paryeṣaka*) arises. While this investigation has not yet reached a definitive cognition of what kind of image it is, the image again emits light, and the eye..."

When a strong condition arises again, it is called "sudden" (*saṃtīraṇa*); this refers to the preceding "seeking" (*paryeṣaka*) which was not yet determinative—both are sudden and do not reach the stage of "equal outflow" (*niṣyanda*).
Later, when a material object comes into range and its consciousness arises, the initial arising is merely "abrupt" (*ābhoga*).

Subsequently, there is seeking and determinative cognition of whether the sound-object is wholesome, unwholesome, or otherwise; the subsequent mental states that arise thereafter are what constitute "equal outflow."

Because the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of the *citta* are numerous while the resultant streams (*nisyanda*) are few, the five consciousnesses can coexist with all three natures (*tri-śīla*). As for their simultaneous occurrence in a single moment:
for example, when visual consciousness perceives a form, if that is a wholesome state, it shares the same object as the eye;

furthermore, if there is simultaneously an unwholesome sound-object or a neutral (*avyākṛta*) odor-object, all three natures coexist. Since odor is neutral, the six consciousnesses are permitted to arise together.
There are three natures that are necessarily all present at all times;

the statement that they are "sudden" and "many moments" does not refer to the number of names for their simultaneous presence, but rather to the duration of their temporal sequence. That is to say, because many "sudden" minds arise in succession, they are called "many moments."
[Commentary] Furthermore, the meaning of the phrase "explaining that the *saurta* [immediate] and *nisyanda* [flowing-on] states extend up to arising together" is as follows:

whereas previously, in the first instance, the number [of consciousnesses] was clarified in terms of *manasikāra* (attention), now, in this second instance, the number is clarified in terms of *vijñāna* (consciousness).

For example, when the two minds of *saurta* and *nisyanda* arise, either three or four consciousnesses may arise—the *saurta* arising with one or two consciousnesses, and the *nisyanda* likewise—or conversely, it may be otherwise; however, this applies only to...

Regarding the five consciousnesses, which arise as sudden encounters (*saṃbhrama*) or as continuous flows (*nisyanda*), their number and quantity are also indeterminate, as are the specific names assigned to those consciousnesses.
They arise simply according to whichever object arrives; it is not said that one consciousness arises first and another arises later.
Because they take an object as their condition precisely as it arrives, the word "or" (*vā*) is employed here.
[Commentary]: Although the five consciousnesses, a single moment of thought, and the three natures can all coexist, this is the intention of the former masters. [Question]:

If the former masters do not allow for the three natures to coexist within the five consciousnesses, how should one interpret the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*? It states: "Regarding the five consciousnesses having the three natures simultaneously, there are two explanations.
One says that the five consciousnesses having the three natures simultaneously refers to a continuity of multiple moments. The former masters do not accept this.
Regarding the passage stating that "the three natures occur simultaneously," how is this to be reconciled? The former master says:

although the five consciousnesses may possess the three natures simultaneously within a single moment, when the visual consciousness and the mental consciousness (*manas*) are both perceiving a wholesome object, even if there is an auditory consciousness perceiving a tangible object, it does not perceive sound.

If it were to perceive sound, the wholesome visual consciousness would have to cease, and only then could the mental consciousness and the auditory consciousness perceive together. Thus, the wholesome visual consciousness [does not persist].
"When it ceases, the mind no longer takes sound as its object"—this is the interpretation of that master [Vasubandhu].

According to the intention of Dharmapāla, although a single mental consciousness (manovijñāna) may take the same objects as the five sensory consciousnesses, their natures are not necessarily identical.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the previously raised objection is capable of inducing the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and so forth," the intended meaning is as follows:

although the mind (*manas*) arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, it does not necessarily share the same nature (wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral) due to its prior causes; therefore, the previous objection—that at that time the mental consciousness should necessarily correspond to all three natures—is rendered futile in this context.
"Futile" (*táng*) means empty (*xū*); "discarded" (*juān*) means abandoned (*qì*). The reasoning of the former master was merely a vain turning of the wheel.
This means that Mo Xu has abandoned his argument. The citation of scriptural evidence following these words is an answer to the previous question.
It intends to prove that although the two consciousnesses share the same object, they do not necessarily have the same nature; one may be wholesome while the other is neutral (avyākṛta).

[Commentary]: As for the statement that Mahāmaudgalyāyana emerged from meditative absorption immediately upon [hearing a sound], this serves as proof that the three natures (trisvabhāva) are distinct.

According to the treatise, however, there are only two natures present in such a state. For instance, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) during meditative absorption is of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*).

Furthermore, the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) that suddenly hears a sound during absorption is of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), because in a state lacking mastery, sudden occurrences follow the mind and are thus indeterminate. How, then, could there be anything unvirtuous (*akuśala*) in this state?
The nature of the answer implies that the natures of the cognitions differ; it is not necessary for all three natures to be present. [Commentary]:
Alternatively, "that which arises" refers to the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). This means it is distinct from what preceded;

previously, it was explained that within meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the ear-consciousness associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to apprehend this sound. Now, the intention of this interpretation is that one hears the sound while in meditative absorption.

Auditory consciousness arises immediately; it is not said that it arises in association with mental consciousness, for mental consciousness can arise even during meditative absorption (*samādhi*), whereas auditory consciousness cannot.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*) that there are "various kinds of mental consciousness," the treatise explains that there are two types of mental consciousness:

first, the mental consciousness that exclusively discerns the object of meditative absorption, which is exclusively of a wholesome nature; second, the mental consciousness that apprehends various objects of perception.

Since consciousness (vijñāna) penetrates all three natures (trisvabhāva) and takes the eighteen spheres (aṣṭādaśadhātu) as its objects, the statement that "it is not only the mental consciousness associated with meditative absorption that can apprehend this sound" implies that the treatise also acknowledges that the auditory consciousness (śrotravijñāna) hears it together with it.

This serves to demonstrate that the mental consciousness within meditative absorption is wholesome (kuśala), whereas the auditory consciousness that suddenly hears the sound is indeterminate (avyākṛta); therefore, their natures are different.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the ear-consciousness does not perceive within meditative concentration": if there were no ear-consciousness perceiving sound during concentration, upon what would the mental consciousness rely to give rise to the aspiration to emerge from concentration?

Question: Since it is already admitted that the mind of the formless realm cognizes all things, what prevents the mental consciousness from perceiving sound during concentration and thereby emerging from it?
Answer: It is said that the mind of the formless realm cognizes the phenomena of the three realms.
Those of inferior capacity can only perceive it through preparatory effort (*prayoga*); since this [state] lacks such effort, it cannot perceive it. [Commentary:
The mental consciousness that emerges from meditative absorption at the very end refers to the final moment of mind within the state of concentration itself.
According to that school, this [consciousness] intends to hear sound; therefore, one emerges in the very next moment, rather than emerging only after having already heard the sound. Thus...

The formulation of the logical proof (*pramāṇa*) and the objection is as set forth in the Commentary: "One who emerges from meditative absorption should not [do so] at the very moment of hearing a sound" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
However, the intention of that thesis is as follows: because one wishes to hear a sound, one therefore wishes to emerge from absorption. The contradiction in the thesis is stated thus:

"Your consciousness emerging from absorption at the final moment, for the sake of wishing to hear a sound, should not [occur] at the very moment of hearing the sound. The reason (*hetu*) is stated: "Because..."

In this state, because sound is not heard, it is as with the mind during the preceding meditative absorption (*samādhi*). That school maintains that during the final moment of consciousness within absorption, sound has not yet been heard;
only after emerging from this state does one hear sound. Therefore, we now establish a formal inference (*pramāṇa*) for this reason.

[Commentary: Yet, how could the former master not have understood this passage? According to the preceding commentary, he reconciled it through a single interpretation, permitting both explanations—that one hears sounds within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and that this is possible within concentration but not in the state of distraction (*vikṣipta*).
That "it is not so in the state of distraction" refers to the first master’s explanation of the text;

it points to the previously cited argument from the *Treatise on the Five Consciousnesses and the Three Natures Not Being Simultaneous* (*Wǔshì sānxìng bùqū lùn*), along with its commentary, which states: [text omitted].
Does the former master not understand the meaning of this passage? Does he not understand the explanation in the nineteenth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*)?

As for the explanation, it has already been clarified above. "The explanation" refers to the former master’s interpretation of the nineteenth fascicle of the *Xianyang lun*, as stated in that treatise:

"If one allows that the five consciousnesses function simultaneously with the three natures, then at that time, the mental consciousness should also be associated with all three natures. It is because [the former master] understands it according to this passage.
The phrase "as previously explained" refers to this superior interpretation. [Commentary:

Some masters cite scriptural evidence, while other masters cite this very text as proof, stating that during the state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), the five sensory consciousnesses do not exist.
Therefore, it is said: "Although this is not direct proof, it is cited for the sake of reconciliation."

[Commentary]: One who possesses extensive knowledge [states] that it is as if one were in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), permitting only the arising of ear-consciousness while the other four consciousnesses do not arise;

therefore, it is said that within the state of *samāhita* (equipoise), the five consciousnesses are absent. Furthermore, regarding the "many people" mentioned—referring to those such as the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*)—they do not give rise to the five consciousnesses during meditative absorption.
Based on this principle, it is said that in the state of *samāhita*, the five consciousnesses are absent; this does not apply to Bodhisattvas.

Therefore, it is permitted for a Bodhisattva to give rise to auditory consciousness and so forth while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Even from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, although they are constantly in concentration, their activity is perpetually quiescent;
thus, there is no impediment to their fully giving rise to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). Lesser Bodhisattvas, however, are not like this.
This [point] reconciles the treatise on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
