[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "As it is said that great compassion (mahākaruṇā) is accompanied by [the root of] non-harming, its essence is not merely non-harming," the intended meaning is as follows:
Although it is taught that great compassion has non-harming as its essence, even when one is in a state of other wholesome minds that lack great compassion, non-harming still exists.

Therefore, since non-harming exists precisely at the time of not causing injury or affliction, what hindrance is there to its existence during other states of wholesome mind? This is because all... [text continues].
This is because a wholesome mind does not harm any sentient being.

[Commentary] As for why the four qualities beginning with diligence are not mentioned—since their meaning is identical—the text here should logically include them as well, as they constitute a set of four dharmas.
This is just as when gathering sentient beings, or as how great compassion, once it possesses these four dharmas, becomes effective.
If this state also possesses four factors, how can it be that non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is absent?

[The Treatise] states: Regarding the explanation in the *Maulī Bhūmi* that the ten factors beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) pervade all stages, since among the four "all-pervading" categories in the *Maulī Bhūmi*, these eleven factors including faith are common to all stages, we know that pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) may exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Otherwise, [it would not].
If pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) does not exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how can it be said to pervade all stages (*sarvabhūmi*)?

[Commentary: To resolve this doubt, consider that during the stages of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*) within the desire realm, when one cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*), at the very moment prior to the actual concentration, one attains pliancy through the preparatory application (*prayoga*).
This is also called a "stage of concentration" (*samāhitabhūmi*) because it possesses a subtle sense of composure and flexibility; thus, one understands that point.
The reason why the wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-caitta*) pervade all stages (*sarva-bhūmi*) is that they are explained as "resolving doubts.
[Commentary: One should speak according to the majority, because those ten factors arise together and are constantly present. To provide an analogy:

if you say that *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) is difficult to find in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet it is said to pervade all stages based on the majority, then one should likewise say that *praśrabdhi* is difficult to find. It would not be right to claim otherwise.
It should also follow that when arising together with others, it does so from the majority; for [the ten universal factors] always arise together.
Since lightness (*praśrabdhi*) is associated [with them], it is not known from the majority, nor is it stated to exist in all stages (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, one knows that the desire realm possesses lightness, because this master’s intention is that the distinct wholesome mental factors (*kuśala-caitta*) are said to pervade all stages.
[The Commentary] states: "As for the phrase 'if there were no fundamental, superior, subtle, and light ease (praśrabdhi) in the higher realms,' etc.,

this master [interprets] the *Vyākhyāyukti* and other texts as meaning that the statement 'there is no light ease in the desire realm' refers to the absence of the fundamental dhyāna stages of the higher realms."
The supreme and wondrous pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is not, in fact, without being induced during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the gathering of the mind is called 'harmonious flow' (*sukha-praśrabdhi*)," the intention is as follows:

although one may temporarily attain the gathering of the mind in the desire realm, it is not a meditative state (*samāpatti-bhūmi*); therefore, there is no moistening or harmonious flow. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 63, states regarding the desire realm: [...]

If the realm (*dhātu*) lacks *praśrabdhi* (pliancy), it is called an "unstable stage" (*asamāhita-bhūmi*). If this were not the case, one would have to say that [the desire realm] reaches the unstable stages.

The intention [of the objection] is: if you claim that *praśrabdhi* exists in the desire realm, yet say there is no *praśrabdhi*, it is because the fundamental meditative concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) of the higher realms lack *praśrabdhi*;
therefore, it is called an unstable stage. The rebuttal says: Not so. One should state, according to the treatises, that it is the various minds of the desire realm [that are meant].
The phrase "Because it lacks the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of the upper realms, it is called an 'unfixed stage' (*anibhūmi*)" represents an external rebuttal to the preceding text.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "There is nothing among all states of mind that is not thus," the meaning is that because the three stages beginning with *vitarka* (investigation) are universally present in all states of mind, it is said that "there is nothing that is not thus."

[Commentary: As for the statement that "the duration of vitarka (applied thought) and so forth varies," the intended meaning is as follows: all mental states are present throughout the three stages characterized by vitarka and so on.

Within the stage of *savitarka-savicāra* (with applied and sustained thought), all mental states and their objects exist throughout the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) of the first dhyāna;

these are all designated by such names. Furthermore, within the first dhyāna there is *praśrabdhi* (pliancy), and within the stage of *avitarka-avicāra* (without applied or sustained thought), there is the desire realm.
Although the *dhātu* possesses vitarka and vicāra, it lacks *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) and is thus termed "short. The commentary (*śū*) repeatedly explains the principles of the text;
it does not mention the desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).
[Commentary: Because the remaining meanings herein are identical, they are called "no different explanation"; that is to say, among the eleven factors, with the exception of *praśrabdhi*.
The remaining ten dharmas are all identical and without difference from the Master’s explanation.
[Commentary: That is to say, in the sixth section, which discusses the "gate of co-arising with the sixth consciousness," all points are consistent with the preceding fifth section.
This location merely sets forth the correct meaning; it does not mean that there is no incorrect meaning within that [fifth section]. This is...
This is the section on the association with the sixth consciousness.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "it is thus in both the causal and resultant stages," this master’s intention is to say that in both the causal and resultant stages, the five consciousnesses are outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and lack pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), because they are by nature distracted and agitated.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "as in the case of the supernormal powers" to "possessing pliancy," the intended meaning is as follows: the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear are of an indeterminate nature, whereas those that are wholesome are of a wholesome nature.
As for those that are indeterminate, regardless of the supernormal powers, how can they be of a wholesome nature? The answer is:

when a Bodhisattva gives rise to the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear, there are two intentions. If he gives rise to them with the thought of wandering freely for his own sake, they are of an indeterminate nature.

If it is argued that because the arising [of mind] through teaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings is itself of a virtuous nature, one may say it is "virtuous" and thus possesses *praśrabdhi* (serenity),

[the commentary] refutes the previous claim that while the five [mental factors] are absent in the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), they are admitted to exist in the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*). This interpretation establishes that [these factors] coexist with the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing activities).

This passage explains that the very nature of consciousness possesses pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) in the state of fruition; thus, it generally refutes the previous master’s position that both cause and effect lack [pliancy].
It does not mean that the Master [Asaṅga] admits the presence of pliancy only in the state of fruition. One should understand it in this way.

Therefore, the treatise states: "The 'wholesome induced by meditative concentration' (*samādhi-niṣyanda-kuśala*) refutes the five [factors] in the causal stage, and 'accompanied by the knowledge of accomplishing activities' (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna-sahagata*) refutes [the absence of pliancy] in the resultant stage."
[The five] stages lack [this].

[Commentary]: If one is at the stage of Buddhahood, this constitutes correct goodness; for the Buddha possesses both active wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), which is the correct meaning.
It is not as the literal statement suggests—that active wisdom is attained immediately upon the first stage—which is incorrect. This refers to what was stated previously in the [first] chapter.

Regarding the first interpretation, although the second interpretation holds that the causal factor lacks the accomplishment of the activity of wisdom (*jñāna*), it is said that there are various acquisitions (*prāpti*) which induce the five sense-consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) and bring about pliancy (*praśrabdhi*);
however, if a contaminated meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) induces the five sense-consciousnesses, there is no pliancy.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "If one interprets it thus" to "because there is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)," this interpretation is incorrect.

If one were to say that the *jñāna-kṛtya-anuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (the wisdom of accomplishing activities) is attained at the first stage (*bhūmi*) and that pliancy arises [therein], this would contradict the text of the second master in the preceding treatise which states:

"There is an opinion that pliancy exists only within meditative concentration (*samādhi*)," and so forth. That master maintains that pliancy does not exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); yet here, it is said...

The claim that the wisdom of accomplishing activities (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna) attained on the level of the cause possesses pliancy (praśrabdhi) implies that there is pliancy in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), because the nose and tongue faculties are bound exclusively to the desire realm;
thus, this contradicts the former master’s position.

[Commentary: That previous [position] merely asserted that it is non-existent based on the distinct natures (*vijātīya*) and the subordinate consciousnesses (*adho-manas*). This explanation reconciles the difficulty of the preceding [argument] by adopting such an interpretation.

As the second master stated regarding the absence of *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) in the desire realm, this was said in reference to the subordinate mental states of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those who have not yet attained the noble stages (*ārya*).
Question: Since the five consciousnesses are admitted to be induced by others, they are necessarily accompanied by subordinate pliancy; how is this determined?

The mind induces the mental consciousness (*manas*), and the mental consciousness possesses pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); there is no answer [to the claim] that this is not so. It is accepted that the five sensory consciousnesses are associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since they are induced by another, it is possible for them to possess concentration.
However, since the mental consciousness does not exist simultaneously with both [the sensory consciousnesses], the distracted mental consciousness lacks concentration.
[Commentary: The preceding passage merely addressed the first master up to the point where it stated that this does not exhaust the full principle;

this was to harmonize with the words of the second master, which claimed that there is no *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) in the desire realm. This was said specifically in relation to the first master and does not exhaust the principle.
In reality, however, the five consciousnesses induced by the subsequent attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of Bodhisattvas in the desire realm do possess *praśrabdhi*. Thirdly...
Although the commentators state in their texts that all five consciousnesses [possess pliancy], in reality it pertains to only three;

this is because the olfactory and gustatory consciousnesses exist only in the desire realm and thus lack pliancy. Question: This section of the treatise presents three distinct interpretations; among these three, which should be taken as correct? Answer:
As explained in the *Yanmi* (Exposition of the Secrets), one should take the third interpretation as correct.

[Commentary]: If that were so, then although the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are induced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they should lack pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). The intent of this objection is as follows:

since the five consciousnesses induced by concentration possess painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*)—such as the physical pain of diligent effort or the sacrifice of one's own flesh and body to save sentient beings—it follows that the five consciousnesses should lack pliancy.

Answer: Although there is no [sensation] associated with suffering within the five consciousnesses, there is that which is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) and pleasure (*sukha*). Thus, pliancy is present.

The five consciousnesses possess pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). That is to say, apart from the sensation of suffering, other sensations such as pleasure and equanimity in the subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) possess pliancy;

other sensations may also be present. As for the "resultant of supernormal power" (*abhijñā-phala-citta*), this indicates that the sensations of joy, pleasure, and equanimity associated with the resultant of supernormal power possess pliancy.
The "resultant of supernormal power" refers specifically to the supernormal powers of the divine eye and divine ear.
[Commentary: If this is so, how are the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body to be reconciled? This leads to the following inquiry:

since this question has already arisen, one cannot say that the resultant mind is weak and thus possesses pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Why? Because the subsequent text allows that the five sensory consciousnesses possess pliancy.
[Commentary: Although the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), it is not said to be accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
This explains the reason why the faculty of suffering is termed outflow-free. [The opponent] raises an objection: "If the faculty of suffering is already termed outflow-free, how can it lack pliancy?
This text provides the direct answer to that prior objection: I merely stated that it is "outflow-free in general," but...

It is said that they are accompanied by pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); in reality, this is because the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) following the five sensory consciousnesses induces the attainment of pliancy in all feelings except for painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*).

Because painful feeling is parched, it lacks pliancy. [The phrase "the three consciousnesses of the upper realms"] refers to those accompanied by the three consciousnesses of the upper realms, while "[the five consciousnesses of the lower realm]" refers to those accompanied by the five consciousnesses of the lower realm.
Regarding the statement that the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is designated as untainted because it is induced by the untainted sixth consciousness.
"It is not that its essence is untainted.

[Commentary]: This is the objection: "If there is nothing to be remedied, how can there be a remedy? To say that sentient beings in the desire realm possess torpor and pliancy is to cite an example to challenge this point.
The intent is to say: if there is no object to be remedied, one cannot admit the existence of a remedy.
If the desire realm possesses *styāna* (sloth), how could there be *praśrabdhi* (pliancy) as its antidote?
[Commentary]: The phrase "because they are not produced [by such causes]" means that the eleven factors beginning with faith are not produced by false teachings or false teachers;
therefore, unlike the afflictions of discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*), they are not abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*).
[Commentary: The passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (57) stating "up to the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*ājñātāvya-jñendriya*) is cited in its entirety as proof.

Its intended meaning is to demonstrate that the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*) pervade both what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and a portion of what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).

Regarding the latter, they are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in terms of conceptual afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*). Furthermore, [the text implies] that those who are eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and so forth will certainly not be reborn, as they possess the capacity to attract [such a state].
Since the afflictions have been eliminated, the fruits they would otherwise have summoned will certainly not arise; this is what is meant by "abandoned through seeing.
As for those wholesome dharmas abandoned through cultivation, their essence is outflowing (sāsrava), because they obstruct the outflow-free (anāsrava) fruit.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "those two sets of six... and the uninterrupted," the intent is as follows: the following is the Master’s (the *shujiā*) explanation of the treatise (*lùwén*).

The five sensations (*pañca-vedanā*) and the mind-faculty (*manas*), because they are common to both the [view-based] abandonments (*darśana-heya*) and the uninterrupted [path], constitute the first six; these are designated as the "first six" in relation to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) are common to both the uninterrupted and the cultivation-abandonments; these are designated as the "last six" in contrast [to the former].

The Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is called "subsequent" (*uttara*). As for the faculty of "having already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) and the faculty of "perfectly knowing" (*ājñendriya*), they are exclusively not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

Question: Previously it was stated that twelve [faculties] are partially to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and partially not to be abandoned; why then is it said here that only the two untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are exclusively not to be abandoned, without mentioning the others?
Answer: This is stated by taking those that are entirely untainted as the primary case; in reality, however, this also applies to the six faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).

These untainted (*anāsrava*) factors also pertain to the non-abandonable (*aprahātavya*); since they are established by their very nature as being practiced by the practitioner, they are not mentioned [in this context]. Question:

If the five sensations (*vedanā*), the mind (*manas*), and the six faculties (*indriya*) also pertain to both what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and what is non-abandonable, why are they not mentioned at all?

Answer: Here, we are discussing only the last six [faculties] which are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*). This serves to demonstrate that the eleven wholesome roots—beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)—pertain to the non-abandonable; therefore, they are not mentioned.

The faculties such as sensation (*vedanā*) differ from these because their causes encompass all three natures; this is why they are not explained here among the faith-faculties (*śraddhā*) and so forth.
Furthermore, if they were included in the untainted (*anāsrava*), they would pertain to that which is not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*).

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the passage from the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* up to "wholesome karma abandoned by seeing," the intended meaning is that the suffering fruits of the three miserable realms are mostly produced by karma incited by conceptual afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*), and that these can be permanently severed upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). What contradiction is there in wholesome karma also being severed by the path of seeing?
As for the claim that the *Abhidharma* states all karma leading to rebirth in the evil destinies and their fruits are [all] abandoned by seeing—
"Severance" (prahāṇa) refers to taking as one's teacher the distinct retributive karma and its fruits that lead to rebirth in the evil destinies.
[Commentary: That [text] does not state that the severance of the conditions and fetters of wholesome dharmas is what is called "severance by seeing" (darśana-heya).

The intention here is that the Abhidharma merely states that all karma and fruits leading to the evil destinies are severed by the Path of Seeing; it does not say that the conditions and fetters of wholesome dharmas are severed. Therefore, [wholesome dharmas are not severed by seeing].

This is called "abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-heya*). The meaning here is that although afflictions may bind wholesome dharmas, one does not say that the afflictions are abandoned by the path of seeing;

rather, one calls the wholesome dharma itself "abandoned by seeing. Nor is it called "abandoned by severing the object-binding," for the *Abhidharmapāda* (Treatise on the Dharma) does not speak in such a manner.
[Commentary]: "If it were not so, up to 'the wholesome is not abandoned by insight' (dṛṣṭiheya)" means that the author raises a counter-objection against the previous master, saying:

"If you claim that something is abandoned by insight because it severs the fetters of its objects, then as stated below, the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) also assist the afflictions of the path of insight in bringing about the fruit of rebirth in evil destinies;
thus, when one enters the path of insight, one would also have to sever the objects of the afflictions of conceptual discrimination."

How could the fetters and so forth be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), while the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanākleśa*)—though they indeed assist in bringing about rebirth in the evil destinies—are not abandoned upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)?
If it is argued that [the fetters] are abandoned by the path of seeing and thus serve as proof [that they are not abandoned by the path of cultivation], the intention is this:
if one says that wholesome views are abandoned, then one is treating the path of cultivation as if it were the path of seeing.
If one realizes the wholesome by means of the afflictions, yet does not perceive the path of abandonment, then it cannot be attained; therefore, it is said that this realization is incorrect.
There is another interpretation, as explained in the section on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
[Commentary] The answer is as follows: Regarding the statement that "all results reaching the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) are termed 'abandoned,'" the intended meaning is this:
even if a result is abandoned while its cause has not yet perished, there is no fault of contradicting reason. Why is this?

For example, regarding the results of the signless state, Uttarakuru, and the eight difficulties—when one enters the Path of Seeing, although these results will certainly never arise again in the future, the causes of those results, namely the wholesome karmas, [remain].
Since the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) still remains and these wholesome dharmas do not obstruct the noble ones, what logical contradiction could there be based on this principle?

From this, it is known that the fruits of the three evil destinies (*durgati*), which are summoned by both wholesome and defiled causes, are all termed "abandoned" (*prahīṇa*), because they are abandoned by the path of seeing.

Thus far, we have discussed abandonment in terms of the fruit; as for the karma of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it may be abandoned either by the path of cultivation or by the path of seeing.

Regarding the "severance of the lower": this refers to the severance of the fruits of the three evil destinies and the fruit of the *asaṃjñisattva* heaven, which are summoned by the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*).

Once these conceptual afflictions have been eliminated upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the fruits such as that of the *asaṃjñisattva* heaven are also severed. Because they will never again arise—since the cause is subsequently non-existent—they are called "severance through the extinction of the cause.
Thus, it is also termed "the severance of the fruit through the extinction of the cause."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that both the causes and effects of the wholesome and the defiled reach [their limit] and are thus termed "abandoned":

the causes of the three evil destinies (*durgati*) as distinct retributions, as well as the wholesome states such as the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), are all termed "wholesome causes. As for "defiled causes," there is one interpretation which holds that the afflictions (*kleśa*) that give rise to karma producing distinct retributions during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are termed defiled causes;
another interpretation holds that defiled causes refer to the conceptualized afflictions (*parikalpita-kleśa*) and the [erroneous] arising of the attainment of non-conception.

When one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) through the [four] equal realizations (*samyaktva-nyāma*), there is a simultaneous abandonment of both the afflictions and the fruits they produce; yet, there are distinctions between them.

Specifically, the term "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) generally refers to the distinct states such as the non-arising of those [afflictions] while remaining in their own nature. Regarding the causes of defilement, such as wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), this is abandonment by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*);

regarding the fruits, such as rebirth in the three evil destinies, it is called abandonment by way of non-arising (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*). Furthermore, it may also be abandonment by way of the destruction of the fruit and the extinction of the cause. As for wholesome karma, its intrinsic nature must... [text ends].

Regarding the statement that when one abandons the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the seven causes are abandoned and their fruits follow suit as well: this refers specifically to the fruit of non-conceptual maturation (*asaṃjñisamāpatti-vipākaphala*).

[Commentary: It is said that if one has attained that fruit but has not yet entered the state of a noble one (*ārya*), it is not a fruit of grasping afflictions (*kleśopādāna*), nor is it necessarily a fruit of the wholesome states induced by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

[Commentary]: As in the section on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) below, where "non-arising" is termed "cessation," this also refers to the cessation of the fruit while the cause remains unceased, as is explained in the case of the afflictions (*kleśa*) during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement that "the cause is also ceased until [the fruit] reaches [its end], there is no contradiction," the intended meaning is that even in cases such as the extinction of the causes in the Heaven of No-Characteristics (*animitta-deva*), it is likewise so.

That which is called "abandoned" (prahīṇa) refers to the abandonment of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); it also receives the name "abandoned" based on this. However, according to its actual substance (*dravya*), it is abandoned only by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). An objection is raised:

"If that is so, then wholesome karma of the miserable realms (*apāya*) should also be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because its fruit enters into being abandoned by the path of seeing;

for when the cause ceases, the fruit follows in its disappearance. The reply is: If one were to speak according to the actual fruit, the cause would also be called "abandoned by seeing," since the fruit is now abandoned. However, we are currently speaking in terms of the bondage of the object-condition.

"Because 'abandonment' refers to abandonment through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is no contradiction. This is not based on a statement regarding the result, but is restricted to its own nature because it pertains solely to the path of cultivation; therefore, there is no contradiction.

[Commentary] "Others should all follow this example and reflect according to reason" means that those points concerning retribution and non-retribution which have not yet been explained should be considered in this manner.
That which is designated as "other" refers generally to the phenomena produced through the methods of the three realms and so forth;
that which is designated as "this" refers to the agent who has not yet acted but intends to act by emulating this agent who has already acted. All others are likewise emulators of this.

[Commentary]: To clarify that [the afflictions] penetrate both the dull and the sharp faculties and pervade both the preceding and the succeeding stages—where "preceding and succeeding" refers to the sequence from pride downward—the ignorance (*moha*) following pride is distinguished as dull, while desire (*rāga*) is distinguished as penetrating both the preceding dull and the succeeding sharp;
thus, pride and its like are termed "dull," while doubt (*vicikitsā*) and its like are termed "sharp."
[Commentary] "Existence" (*bhava*) refers to future existence (*punar-bhava*). It is called "future existence" because the function of craving to moisten and nourish rebirth increases therein;

thus, one develops defiled attachment toward the fruit of future existence. Because the present body has already been moistened [by craving], one cannot give rise to craving for that very present body;
however, in reality, one does indeed give rise to craving for the present.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "If it refers to the arousal of karma, it does not mean that [craving] only moistens [rebirth]," the intended meaning is as follows: one cannot say that craving only moistens the arising of birth;
rather, when the arousal of karma occurs, it also causes the arising of the *upādāna-skandhas* (grasping aggregates). Why is this?

For instance, both innate (*sahaja*) craving, which can moisten birth and cause the five aggregates to arise, and discriminative (*vikalpita*) craving, which can arouse karma, also cause the *upādāna-skandhas* to arise. Therefore, [the text] says this.
If it is asked: "Is it not merely moisture? How then are they the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*)? The answer is: "Clinging" (*upādāna*) is a synonym for afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because the five aggregates are produced by afflictions, they are called the aggregates of clinging; alternatively, because the body of the five aggregates can give rise to afflictions, it also receives the name "aggregates of clinging."

[Commentary]: Alternatively, even when beings in the two higher realms undergo rebirth through the aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*), it is due to their prior craving for meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) that they attain those concentrations;

the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages are thereby increased by this craving, and thus they also undergo rebirth through the aggregates. This is because the term "aggregates of grasping" (*upādāna-skandha*) refers to the afflictions themselves.
From this, we know that craving (*rāga*) not only moistens rebirth but also causes the aggregates of grasping to arise. Some say that this [craving] is precisely that very "thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*).
The afflictions such as *manas* (ego-thought) also cause the arising of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*), which is the fruit; this differs from what was stated previously.
[Commentary: The fact that the eighth volume of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* agrees with this means it is consistent with the *Abhidharma*.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the passage from "fifty-eight" to "possessing the instruments of suffering," it says:

this refers to giving rise to a mind of fear toward the Truths of Cessation and the Path, and giving rise to a mind of cowardice and distress through acts of harm; thus, because such anger and hatred are deluded regarding the Truths of Cessation and the Path, one knows that even the untainted (anāsrava) serves as a condition for suffering.
[Commentary]: This refers to when others perceive sentient beings as being harmful toward those who have benefited them, or as performing harm toward those who have not benefited them.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice), Chapter 58, there are two types: first, generating anger toward the perception itself because it harms one;
that is, if another person gives rise to such a view that harms one's own body, one then generates anger toward that very perception. Second, [regarding]...
1. Regarding sentient beings who cause harm: it refers to giving rise to anger toward those sentient beings who wish to damage one’s own body.
2. Regarding those one loves: it refers to giving rise to anger toward one’s wife or children when they act in a way that is not beneficial to others.
3. Regarding those one does not love: it refers to [giving rise to anger] toward an enemy when they act in a beneficial way.
One who acts for the benefit of others gives rise to anger toward them.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the aforementioned are merely conditioned by what has arisen," the intent is that "the aforementioned" refers to the four types, such as the views of others.

Regarding the phrase "the grasper is the five aggregates of grasping," the intent is to state that anger arises based upon the five aggregates of grasping belonging to sentient beings, and not based upon non-sentient things.
"Arising" is discussed in reference to a primary locus; however, this is still limited to its actual application, as anger can also arise toward insentient objects. [Commentary:
"The mental consciousness acts as the initiator" means that the mental consciousness is capable of initiating karma; "initiating" is synonymous with "arousing.

"The five sensory consciousnesses act as the followers" means that it is said the five sensory consciousnesses also follow the mental consciousness in being able to initiate karma, just as those five sensory consciousnesses themselves cannot directly [initiate karma].

The karma-initiating [mind] is able to give rise to the karma-sustaining mind; the karma-initiating [mind] arises and sustains [the action], just as an arising [moment] arises in accordance with another arising and is thus able to initiate karma.

[Commentary: This means that regarding the hesitation concerning the Truths and so forth due to ignorance, the intended meaning is that one first becomes deluded about the Truths because of ignorance.
The reason why doubt arises is that because it is not yet resolved, wrong views and other afflictions subsequently arise.
[Commentary] The statement "because ignorance gives rise to craving and so forth" refers to the functional activity of ignorance during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
therefore, ignorance does not necessarily give rise to doubt, wrong views, and the like in all instances.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because those with wrong views have an increase of ignorance, [ignorance] comes first," the intended meaning is as follows:
According to the Abhidharma, because people with wrong views have an increase of ignorance, wrong view is mentioned first and doubt is mentioned later.
Since it is the case that there is an increase of ignorance, why is it said that ignorance should be mentioned first and wrong view later, yet it is stated here that wrong view comes first?

[Question: Is it as stated later that doubt [comes first]? [Answer: No; this does not concern the sequence of ignorance (*avidyā*), but rather discusses the sequence between wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt.

[Commentary: The inclusion of the seven types of non-knowledge (*ajñāna*) is as previously explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, Chapter Nine. Regarding the "seven types of non-knowledge": first is delusion regarding the world (*loka-moha*).
The inclusion of these [seven] delusions— namely, (1) delusion regarding the two matters, (2) delusion regarding transmigration, (3) delusion regarding the supreme, (4) delusion regarding reality,
(5) delusion regarding defilement and purification, and (6) delusion regarding overweening pride— is as explained in the ninth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "here, 'remote' is spoken of from the perspective of the root," this refers to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. It states that the mind becomes uplifted because of the self (*ātman*);
this is said because pride (*māna*) is associated with the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, pride is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the view of self;
it is produced by the view of self and its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is similar to it. Or, the view of self is the root of pride; here, "remote" is used in reference to that root.
Because this is explained in the original [text], it says: "Due to the self, the mind becomes haughty.
[Commentary] Regarding the three types of pride mentioned in the Sūtra, the type of pride consisting of the nine prides is a sub-classification of the seven prides.

[Commentary]: Regarding the two explanations of the "Great and Broad" (*mahāvaipulya*) based on the *Mūla-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇapāda*: this refers to citing both the Great and Small vehicles' treatises.
The *Mūla-śāstra* is the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, while the *Prakaraṇapāda* is one of the six *pāda* treatises of the Hīnayāna. Some say that the *Mūla-śāstra* is the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*;
because the *Jñānaprasthāna* serves as the body [of the Abhidharma], it is called the "Root" (*mūla*), and the six *pādas* are its limbs. Others say that the *Mahāvibhāṣā* is the "Root."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that among those of the Hīnayāna, the Noble Ones (Āryas) possess teachers who do not manifest the pride of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmāna*), the intention is as follows:

In the Hīnayāna, it is held that as long as there is the pride of the path of cultivation—meaning the mental aspect of being loftily uplifted and looking down upon others—it does not manifest once one has definitely attained the state of a Noble One;
thus, they are said to be "without pride. In the Mahāyāna, this is not the case, for it is permitted that such pride may arise.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in the fifty-eighth [section], "Based on the five characteristics, they are distinguished until they exhaustively encompass those," the intended meaning is as follows:

Among the various doubts concerning the future life up to those arising regarding the Three Jewels that are taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, all are subsumed under "doubt regarding the Truths" (*satya-saṃśaya*).

Specifically, if one doubts the future life based on the gateway of the Four Noble Truths, it is termed "doubt regarding the world" (*loka-saṃśaya*); likewise, if one doubts the Three Jewels based on the gateway of the Four Noble Truths, it is subsumed therein.

This is precisely because it is a doubt regarding the [Noble] Treasures (*ratna*). Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, fascicle one, states: "Doubt regarding the Truths (*satya*) is also subsumed under doubt regarding the Treasures;
as appropriate, it is subsumed within the Truths of Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*). However, there is no such thing as "doubt regarding an object" (*vastu-vicikitsā*).

While doubt arises regarding an object—for instance, doubting whether a tree stump is a person—this is indeed doubt, yet it is not the "doubt that is an affliction" (*kleśa-vicikitsā*). Doubt regarding an object is merely...
The *vipākaja* (maturation-born) mind and mental factors, etc.
[The Commentary] states that for this master, doubt has the discernment (*prajñā*) among the object-specific mental factors as its essence;

he says this because doubt is a hesitant investigation lacking decisive judgment. However, according to the correct principle, doubt merely causes discernment to be indecisive—it is not discernment itself.

[Commentary: "Vi" has the meaning of "various. Because this meaning of "various" assists "mati" (intellect) to form "vicitra-mati" (diverse wisdom), the Great Treatise further states that "different cognitions" (*anya-buddhi*) and "differences" (*nānātva*) are synonymous terms.
Therefore, it is known that "differentiated wisdom" (*anya-prajñā*) constitutes the essence of doubt;
this is the intention of this master. "Qi" (祇) is pronounced as "Zhi" (只).
[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "What serves as the auxiliary condition such that the essence remains as it was before?
Master Hu says: *mūḍhi* (delusion) is not yet wisdom; because it is assisted by *vī* (discernment), it becomes an aid. Thus, since it is within doubt and cannot be called wisdom, doubt is not wisdom.

For example, if one says the word "leader" (*nāyaka*), when the character for "lead" (*nī*) acts as an auxiliary, the resulting word is called "various characters" (*nānākṣara*) and cannot be called the word "leader. Now, the character *vī* assists *mūḍhi*.
This is immediately stated to be "arising" (utpāda) and cannot be called "wisdom" (prajñā).

If, as the former master claimed, that which has not reached the bottom is called wisdom—despite the presence of the syllable *vi* acting as an auxiliary—it still retains its original name of "wisdom. To this, the objection is raised:

if the essence remains as it was and it is merely by virtue of the assistance of *vi* that it is named "various kinds of wisdom," then we reject this interpretation. Since there is no alteration [in the essence], one knows that it is merely an auxiliary.
Why is it that, just as in the world, when a letter has an auxiliary, it must undergo transformation? Therefore, the later master’s [position] is the correct statement.
Why is it that the substance [of the cognition] remains as it was even when conditions arrive? This is an objection against the former master.
Since the substance assisted by the *prajñā* (wisdom) remains as wisdom itself, you doubt where its substance resides; therefore, you know [the former position] is incorrect.

[Commentary]: Although there are degrees of intimacy regarding the objects of perception, the meaning of the intimacy or distance of delusion with respect to the Truths will be explained below in its own section.

Furthermore, the phrase "delusion regarding principle" (*li*) and so forth means that although there are degrees of intimacy regarding the objects of perception (the Truths), because the sense of being deluded regarding principle is equivalent, it is termed "inverted conceptualization."

[Commentary] This means that regarding those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) pertaining to the higher realms cannot incite evil karma that brings about suffering;
furthermore, this excludes the innate self-view (*sahaja-ātmadṛṣṭi*) and so forth of the desire realm, as these cannot directly bring about the fruit of suffering.
Since it is only the conceptualized afflictions (*vikalpita-kleśa*) that incite evil karma.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "sa" has the meaning of "falsehood," it is not possible for this single syllable alone to convey the meaning; rather, it must be assisted by other syllables before the meaning of "falsehood" is established.
[Commentary]: In the term *cintati-sa*, it is only through the preceding four syllables that the syllable "sa" is manifested as having the meaning of "falsehood."
The first four characters have the meaning of "falsehood" (*mṛṣā*). The interpretation of the term *bodhisattva* in other schools may be understood by analogy with this. [Commentary:

Regarding the Mahāyāna interpretation from "should be explained" (*yīng jiě*) up to "the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* is shifted" (*sēng qì làn dǐ sà*): in the Mahāyāna interpretation, the name "view of a self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is shifted to refer to the "view of the body" (*kāyadṛṣṭi*). Question:

Why is the name "view of a self" shifted to refer to the "body," while the name "mind that takes as its object" (*nengyuán xīn*) is shifted to refer to the "object of observation" (*suǒyuán*)? Answer: It is because [in this context] it refers to the object of observation.

Question: Why is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of the self said to be "transferred"? Answer: According to what is explained below, because the objective sphere of the self undergoes transformation, the view that takes the self as its object is said to be "transferred.
This is because the aspect-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) that resembles the self is a dependently originated phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing;

it is on this basis that it is called "transferred. Question: Is the mind not also transferred? Answer: Although it is indeed transferred for the time being, it is spoken of [as such] based on what is manifest.
Xian also discusses this in terms of the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Regarding the differences among these three schools of thought, they are as explained by Ximing.
[Commentary: That which is the support of the self (*ātman*) refers to that which resembles the self; it is the support of the self because it is a phenomenon subject to transformation by others.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "discriminative and innate [ignorance] may take either general or specific objects," this explains that both general and specific objects are common to both discriminative and innate [ignorance].
[Commentary: This refers, for example, to the conceit: "Form is the self; I possess forms; forms belong to me; I am within forms."
The meaning is as follows: the first phrase constitutes the essence of the self (*ātman*), while the subsequent three phrases constitute that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*).
"I possess various forms" reveals the *ātmīya* that is associated with the self—namely, the self's ornaments.
"Forms belong to me" reveals the *ātmīya* that is pursued by the self—namely, the self's servants. "I am within forms" reveals the *ātmīya* that is inseparable from the self—namely, the self itself.

The cave-dwelling [of the self] is questioned as follows: "How does one reckon form (*rūpa*) as the 'object' (*āyatana*)? The answer is: as it is said, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) encompasses all forms;
one reckons the internal sense-faculties of form—the body—as the "self," while the remaining objects that support those faculties and so forth are reckoned as the "objects.

This applies to all the other aggregates as well. However, among the two interpretations in the *Yanyan mimi*, the latter interpretation states: "Each individual aggregate contains one 'self' and three 'objects. Regarding this:
"That which belongs to others is not what belongs to me; it is within the aggregates that 'mine' resides. To sever this [false] understanding is the correct [view].

[Commentary: Regarding the analysis of the formations conditioned by the aggregates, though the *Śāstra* explains in detail how they arise without distinguishing their specific locations, this present text provides a general analysis of the modes of activity (*ākāra*) of "I" and "mine.
This is done so that students may easily understand the manifestation of these modes of activity.
Regarding the phrase "discriminating the aggregates as objects of activity" (*vikalpa-gocara-skandha-viṣaya*): "discriminating" (*vikalpa*) means the sense of thorough comprehension.

That is, in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, it is explained with such a distinction. "Aggregates as objects of activity" refers to discriminating the characteristics of the aggregates that serve as the objects of the notions of "self" and "mine.
"Not discriminating the place from which [activity] arises" means not discriminating from which aggregate the notion of "mine" subsequently arises.
Question: When one conceives of form as "I" or "mine," such as "my necklace" or "my servant," is this not a conceptualization arising from a specific locus?
Answer: It is not so. To say that form is "I" or "my necklace" and so forth merely refers to what is called "mine" (ātmīya), which arises following after the self;
it possesses such a mode of activity (ākāra) that it is not distinct from this aggregate (skandha).
Because it arises from those aggregates and so forth, it is said that "the place of arising is not discriminated. The intended meaning is this:

if one discriminates the aggregates as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the formations (*saṃskāra*), yet does not discriminate the place of their arising, there are sixty-five propositions; if one discriminates the formations as the object-condition for the aggregates but does not discriminate the place of their arising, there are only twenty propositions.
If that is the case, it should be understood according to the later explanation in the *Yuanmi* (Secret Commentary), as in the following passage: "As when one grasps..."

"Form is the self, feeling is the self, ornaments and servants are the self"—since these arise from the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) as objects of conceptual discrimination, the former interpretation alone is incorrect. [Commentary:
Regarding the statement "the sixty-two views and so forth should be understood accordingly," one should apply this twentyfold formula by dividing it across the three periods of time.

Regarding the sixty-two views established separately: the view that the life-principle (*jīva*) is identical to the body and the view that the life-principle is different from the body constitute sixty views.

As for the statement "these arise from conceptual discrimination" (*vikalpa*), this means they are views arising from the conceptualization of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), not innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "all these are mental engagements" (*manasikāra*), the meaning is that all these views of self arise by taking the aggregates as their object through the modes of activity of mental engagement, contemplation, and conceptualization.

[Commentary] The meaning of "also including conceptual discrimination" (*vikalpa*) is that the view of a self that takes the aggregates as its object (*pañcaskandha-ālambana-ātmadṛṣṭi*) arises not only through innate tendency (*sahaja*) but also through conceptual discrimination;
it also arises from false teachers and other such causes by conceptually discriminating the five aggregates as a whole as being "self" and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the mind takes the self-clinging as its object and [gives rise to] views of annihilationism or eternalism," the meaning is that these views arise after the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), taking that self-clinging within the object of perception as their basis to produce notions such as annihilationism and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "after the Tathāgata’s death" and so forth, it refers to those non-Buddhists who maintain that their own object of devotion, Brahmā, is the one who teaches the Dharma for the Tathāgata;
they thus inquire whether Brahmā exists or does not exist after the Tathāgata has passed away.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "taking other realms as objects for the purpose of severance and so forth is explained in detail among the conditions of other realms," this refers to what follows below in the section on conditions of other realms.

It is accepted that taking other stages (*bhūmi*) as objects constitutes taking others as self; thus, notions such as annihilationism (*uccheda*) and eternalism (*śāśvata*) arise toward them, as will be explained in detail below.

[Commentary]: That which arises subsequent to the view of self is not [the view of extremes]; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the practice of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) does not arise after the view of self.

This treatise, however, concerns that which arises after the innate (*sahaja*) view of self; therefore, both are subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), as they are identical according to this discourse.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding this view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and the various excerpts and commentaries that discuss it, an external objection is raised as follows:

"If [the view of extremes] takes the view of self (*ātman*) as its general object and is thus permitted to take dharmas of the higher realms as 'self,' why is it not permitted for other types of conceptual views (*vikalpaka-dṛṣṭi*) to take dharmas of other realms specifically as 'self'?
Therefore, how can it be distinguished [from them]? Thus it is said: "The others do not take other realms as their objects; how then can they be distinguished?"
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) takes the Brahmā kings of other realms as permanent; furthermore, it is taught that the view of extremes arises after the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Yet, [the view of extremes] does not take phenomena of other realms as its object, because the conceptualized view of self does not take phenomena of other realms as its object.

Therefore, the question is raised: "How can the view of extremes take [other realms] as its object separately from the view of self? The intent of this objection is thus resolved by the subsequent passage, which states: "It is only [the view of extremes] that clings... [and so forth].
Because the dharmas of other stages are not obtained as one's own self but are obtained as the self of another, it is admitted that they are indeed the self of the Brahmā-deva.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "twenty eons of formation and destruction" and so forth: the meaning is that these non-Buddhists, having sat in meditative equipoise and attained the higher dhyānas, obtain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).

This refers to the universal perception of events throughout twenty *kalpas* of the past. Question: According to the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya*, the names of the formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness [of a world-system] constitute twenty *kalpas*.

Calculated collectively, eight minor *kalpas* (*antara-kalpa*) form one great *kalpa* of formation and destruction. Why, then, is the term "twenty *kalpas*" here directly taken to mean a *kalpa* of formation and destruction?
Answer: Regarding the term "twenty *kalpas* as a *kalpa* of formation and destruction," it is simply because these twenty *kalpas* consist of ten periods of formation.

Regarding one interpretation of the *saṃvarta-kalpa* (the eon of destruction): as for why it is said to consist of twenty eons, that which is called "destruction" is spoken of in relation to "formation";

it does not necessarily have to be explained according to the *saṃvarta-kalpa*, but may be explained based on the *vivarta-kalpa* (the eon of formation). The subsequent eons should also be understood according to this principle.
Question: Why do we observe different numbers of eons? Answer: This is because the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) practiced therein possess the distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior.

The three grades are not the same, and those they initiate also differ in being inferior or superior. The reason they are inferior is that [those with] the lesser grade see little, while those with the superior grade see much.
Regarding the "knowledge of past lives" (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*): this superknowledge (*abhijñā*) is able to know the events of past lives;

thus it is called the "superknowledge of past lives. Subsequent explanations should be understood according to this. Regarding the term "concealment and manifestation": this explains the cause for its destruction. What is called "destruction" refers merely to concealment.

[The text] clarifies that "manifestation" (khyāna) refers to "destruction," yet this destruction is not the same as total annihilation; rather, "destruction" means that at the very moment the aggregates (*skandha*) arise, they are called "manifestation.

Therefore, they are reckoned as permanent. [Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "that is to say, there is the view of permanence in the Path of Seeing... all of which are permanent," the intention of the objection is as follows: since this view of permanence...
If these conceptual afflictions are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), how could they also take phenomena of other realms as their object and regard them as permanent?
This is because one contemplates that both the self and the world remain constant throughout eighty eons; thus, the "world" refers to the three realms collectively as its object.
How then could it be that such a perverted view of permanence does not take phenomena of other realms as its object?
[Commentary: However, the passage from "relying on this subsequent arising" to "the solitary-image object is said to follow only the seeing-part" answers the aforementioned objection.

The meaning is that because non-Buddhists have previously attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they give rise to the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) based on that concentration. Since they constantly perceive phenomena belonging to the higher realms, these [past lives] can be understood as being connected to the higher realms.

Although they constantly perceive [phenomena] across the three realms, when they collectively take the objective part (*nimittabhāga*) as their object, it follows the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*) and thus belongs to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).

"Because they are bound [to a realm]. [Commentary: It asks: "Since the objects are bound to the realms and stages to which they correspond, why must the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) follow the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect) in its realm-bound status?

The answer explains the reason: "The *pratibimba* (reflected image) alone is said to follow the *darśanabhāga*. It further asks: "What is meant by a 'solitary reflection' (*kevala-pratibimba*) object? The answer is: "By means of the body..."
In this context, when one gives rise to the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), one takes distant objects of the higher realms as a condition;

because these are not directly perceived, they are called "solitary images" (*kevala-pratibimba*). Although they possess an objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), they lack an underlying essence (*svabhāva*). How could there be a real self or a real permanence as their essence?
Therefore, because they lack an essence and possess only an objective aspect, they are termed "solitary images. Question: What is meant by "non-solitary images"? Answer: [To be continued...]

Question: How is it that the five types of objective spheres (*viṣaya*), as well as the *nimitta-bhāga* (image-part) of transformation and the movement of conditions, are not all merely "shadow-only" (*tadākāra-mātra*) objects, since they possess substantial bases (*sadravya-viṣaya*)?

Answer: Regarding the distinction between these *nimitta-bhāgas* and the seeds of the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-part): when the body resides in a certain stage (*bhūmi*) and perceives dharmas of its own stage, the transformed *nimitta-bhāga* and *darśana-bhāga* are distinct, arising from separate seeds.

However, if the body is in a lower stage and perceives dharmas belonging to another [higher] stage, [the relationship is different]. (Note: This passage addresses the Yogācāra theory of the three natures and the dual-aspect (*dvayākāra*) consciousness, clarifying how the objective images and the subjective perceiving aspect arise from distinct seeds depending on whether the perceiver and the perceived belong to the same or different levels of existence.)
The *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) transformed by [the seeds of] permanence and so forth is perfumed together with the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect), forming a single type of seed;
this is because the reflected object (*pratibimba-viṣaya*) manifested alone in another realm lacks substantial reality and cannot be separately perfumed by its own seed.
[Commentary: Regarding the second point, "hearing that the Brahmā King has such views," the intended meaning is that the Brahmā King possesses such a mode of understanding.
To hold such a position—that the great elements, such as earth, are eternal while the mind and so forth are impermanent—the intention is this:

the non-Buddhists regard Brahmā as fixed and authoritative, and they place their trust in his words. If Brahmā maintains such a calculation that "the great elements, such as earth, are eternal," then I likewise calculate them to be so.
As for the claim that the mind and so forth are impermanent because they are visible, it is because the mind and its associates are subtle.

Because it is difficult to perceive and because it arises and ceases rapidly; furthermore, those who reckon the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) to be permanent and the mind to be eternal do so because they maintain that for non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), the mind has ceased while the body remains.
Conversely, others hold the mind to be eternal because they maintain that while the mind persists, form (*rūpa*) has ceased.
Moreover, it is said that the mind is eternal because its function of discernment operates over a long duration; if it were impermanent, [it could not do so].

If one cannot maintain discernment for a long duration, yet is able to discern clearly over a long period as usual, my statement that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are impermanent is based on observing that mountains and rivers undergo destruction; thus they are impermanent.

"Mutual endurance" (*sahamati*), as explained in the commentary, carries the meaning of mutual confirmation—that is, fellow practitioners confirming one another—or it refers to those dwelling in the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*). "Dwelling" means to abide.

Regarding the phrase "hearing the Brahmā-king speak in the Brahma-heaven, or hearing it through successive transmission," this refers to how certain non-Buddhists residing in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) hear the teachings of the Brahmā-king and so forth through repeated oral transmission; these non-Buddhists, having heard them from others,
form such attachments.
[Commentary]: These eight views are precisely the four theories of universal permanence and the four theories of partial permanence. [Commentary]:
Regarding the statement that the self of the form realm takes its own level as the object of the self-view, the intended meaning is this:

among these eight views, there are those who take the self-view of the form realm to apprehend the Brahmā King of their own level within the form realm as the self; that is to say, there are non-Buddhists who rely upon the mind...
The subsequently arising view of self is that which is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); this is why it is said to take phenomena of its own level as its object.

Alternatively, although one may use the view of self belonging to a lower realm to conceive of the Brahmā King of a higher realm as "self," even though he is not one's own self, we do not exclude such a case from being considered "another self."
[Commentary] "If it were not so, it would not be subsumed under the view of extremes" means: if one merely conceives of a self and reckons it as permanent, it would be the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi);
if one does not reckon it as permanent, it would be a false view (mithyā-dṛṣṭi) and not subsumed under the view of extremes.
To reckon another as a self is called a false [view].
[Commentary: As for those whose views of permanence and so forth do not contradict one another, they are likewise categorized as partial-eternalism (*ekāṃśa-śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

Although they take other phenomena as their object, even if not intentionally, since it was previously stated that "the self and the world" are also thus in the case of full eternalism, it is clearly known that one's own self is also included therein.
Therefore, this is subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), just like the reckoning in the case of full eternalism mentioned before.
[Commentary]: Regarding "one extreme [of views] extending upward and downward," the meaning is as follows: for instance, if one takes the Brahmā King as eternal, this is the "upward" calculation;

if one calculates one's own self as impermanent, this is the "downward" calculation. While it is acceptable that calculating [the self] as eternal is so categorized, what kind of view does the calculation of [the self] as impermanent fall under? This is explained by the Commentary itself.
[Commentary]: Of the initial four views, three are established as distinct views based on their respective supports.

There are other non-Buddhists who give rise to these three views that are not included within the count of the sixty-two views. First, the soul is identical to the body; second, the soul is different from the body;
third, this general view of a self extends up to the infinite—this constitutes the third view. It is named as one view based on the two preceding views, relying upon them.

The latter [view] refers to the first two views mentioned previously: "the life-principle is the body" (*jīvaḥ śarīram eva*) and "the life-principle is identical to the body" (*jīvaḥ śarīram evātmā*).
As for "I am united with the body," it means that some reckon the life-principle and the body together as the self; thus, the commentary states: "This is the total self.

This is because some reckon the self to be identical to the body, some reckon the self to be distinct from the body, and some reckon the self and the body together as the self. Therefore, the commentary says: "This is the total self."
That is to say, they reckon the five aggregates as a single self and perceive no further distinctions or limits;

this is because they reckon that the five aggregates pervade all places. Second, they reckon only a single self and nothing else; thus, there is "no difference," meaning their own self has no variation.
As for "number," it is because the self is all-pervading and cannot be diminished by any number.

[Commentary]: Those who grasp the characteristics (*nimitta*) of phenomena are called "possessors of perception" (*saṃjñin*). This is because, through the existence of perception within themselves, they are able to grasp the characteristics of phenomena;
thus, after death, they are born in the realm of the gods characterized by perception. This explains the meaning of "possessing perception."

[Commentary]: The intention behind the calculation that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also possesses form is as follows: it refers to a certain class of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who calculate that the formless realm has form;

therefore, they calculate form to be the self (*ātman*). Consequently, after death, they are reborn in the three lower formless realms. This is because, although there is no coarse form (*audārika-rūpa*), there is subtle form (*sūkṣma-rūpa*).
If one does not allow for the existence of form, then they would neither calculate [form] to be the self, nor would they be reborn there.

The Three Heavens asked: "Why is it that one is not reborn in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)? The answer was: "Because the subtle perceptions (*saṃjñā*) in that heaven are extremely faint and obscure, non-Buddhists do not desire to be born there;
they only wish to be born in the heavens of those possessing perception (*saṃjñin*). Some say: "It is permitted for there to be form (*rūpa*) in the Formless Realm (*ārūpya*);

that which possesses form is the 'form produced as the fruit of meditative concentration' (*samādhiphalarūpa*), or it is the 'form of the meditative object' (*samādhiviṣayarūpa*) admitted by the Mahāsāṃghika school, which exists even in that specific stage."
Based on this calculation, according to these four views, one may attain the path by relying on the entirety of the desire realm and a portion of the upper two realms;
alternatively, one may rely on a lower body to conceive of the dharmas of the higher stages as being attained.
[Commentary: Those who grasp the formless aggregates as the self and so forth are grasping the four aggregates as the self; they reckon the life-principle (*jīva*) to be the self.

Regarding the explanation of these names, one should know them as they appear in the treatise; as the first treatise states, "sentient beings," "life-principles," and so on—these are explained in detail therein.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "in the entirety of the desire realm" and so forth, according to this inclusive formulation, if one allows that there is form in the formless realm, then [the attainment] can arise even upon reaching there—that is, when one is born into the three lower formless realms.
If one does not allow that there is form there, then it arises only in the two realms of desire and form.
[Commentary: "Pervading all places" means that one conceptually constructs a self in relation to forms in all places, not merely within one's own body.
[Commentary: "It is not that what they see can know that formless space has no limits" means that these non-Buddhists are not able to know that the world is infinite;
rather, they are only able to perceive a single trichiliocosm, which does have limits.
Beyond the three thousandfold world-system, one can no longer know [the extent], and thus one clings to the notion that it is "boundless.
[Commentary]: That the body is "immeasurable" means it is so because of its greatness; it does not mean that its measure is unknown.
[Commentary: "Limited perception" (*parīttasaṃjñā*) refers to the aforementioned attachment to the self as finite, because it relies on the attachment to the body.
"Immeasurable perception" (*apramāṇasaṃjñā*) refers to the aforementioned attachment to the self as infinite, because one takes all forms (*rūpa*) everywhere to be the self;

this infinity does not rely solely on the attachment to the body, for since form itself is the self, and what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*) is also the self, the self follows the magnitude of those forms—whether large or small.

[Commentary]: Regarding "various signs such as those of the desire and form realms," there are cases where one newly born in the first dhyāna of the fourth dhyāna sees the lower realms being destroyed;
because they become terrified and give rise to various perceptions, these are called "various signs."

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "the minor perception" (*parīttasaṃjñā*) up to "I am united with that," it means that one clings to form as the self (*ātman*) and [regards it] as "mine" (*mama*).
Because this is explained as the union of the "self" and the "possessed," it is called the "minor perception. "Minor" refers to limited form; one reckons this limited form as the self.

Subsequently, the various perceptions (*nānātvasaṃjñā*) are also explained as the union of the "self" and the "possessed. The preceding single perception and the subsequent various perceptions both belong to the "possessed" and are not the self.
[Commentary] The meaning of the phrase "purely consisting of the characteristics of suffering, etc. is that certain individuals maintain the view that [suffering] does not exist within hell itself;
they hold this view because they believe there are no afflictions of discrimination within hell.

[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "seeing others attain meditative absorption" is that one not only conceives that others possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), but also conceives that oneself possesses form;
after death, one is born into the Realm of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*). The rest should be understood accordingly.
[Commentary]: Second, regarding those who hold that the formless [aggregates] up to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) constitute the self:

they take the four aggregates themselves as the life-faculty because the aggregate of form is included within the first "self," and because that which is conceived as the life-force is precisely these four aggregates. Thus, the four aggregates are the life-faculty;
there is no separate life-faculty apart from them.

[Commentary: "Only through vitarka and vicāra does it arise; it is not for one who has attained meditative concentration. This means that one merely observes another entering the non-percipient (*asaṃjñin*) concentration and, calculating that the other has died and been reborn there, subsequently gives rise to this misconception oneself; it is not that one has personally attained that concentration.

Even if one has attained this concentration, such a misconception may still arise, or it may arise without relying on concentration at all, because the mind in [other] concentrations is not clear; it must necessarily arise [only when the mind is thus].
"One only gives rise to grasping through vitarka and vicāra. [Commentary:

It is not that those who do not arise from meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) are merely those who arise from vitarka and vicāra; the character "wei" (唯) is likely an error for "yi" (依). One should instead say:

"Based on meditative attainment, they do not arise from vitarka and vicāra. Question: How do we know this is an error? Answer: According to the first and third [sections] of the Commentary, both cases are consistent with this.

Regarding the statement that "sentient beings enter the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) with their characteristics not clearly manifest," this second passage merely says they "enter the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception" without mentioning "not clearly manifest" and so forth; based on this, it should be understood that there is an error,
and one should further examine other versions of the text.

[Commentary]: Regarding all these four types of formless self, the intention of the teaching is that these four views—such as having limits and so forth—all involve grasping the four non-material aggregates (*catur-arūpa-skandha*) as the self, which subsequently gives rise to further attachments; therefore, they are called the "four formless [views]."

[Commentary]: First, because the duration of that meditative absorption is brief, taking each individual aggregate (*skandha*) as its basis, and so forth—because the duration is brief, one cannot take all the aggregates collectively as the self;
rather, one takes them individually and separately. Thus, it is "limited" (*antavān*). "Each one" refers to taking any single aggregate as the object.
Following the conclusion of the absorption, one takes the aggregates and so forth from within that prior absorption and clings to them as being permanent.
"Extremes" (*anta*) refers to these [two].

[Commentary: This excludes a third [alternative], as there is no further dharma beyond these; it is only that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) hold this view, and thus it is specifically the third that is excluded.
[Commentary]: The phrase "existing yet being non-existent" means that one currently perceives existence [of the self] and subsequently perceives its non-existence after death.

[Commentary]: The statement "the present body may also arise, and another body may also arise" intends to explain that one may conceive of the self as being annihilated after the death of the present body, or likewise conceive of the self as being annihilated in each subsequent body in future lives, provided one investigates through vitarka and vicāra.
That is to say, one calculates that this body of mine will be annihilated; if based on meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), one calculates that many future births will likewise be annihilated.
Therefore, based on the attainments involving vitarka and vicāra, [the view of self] can arise in all cases. One might ask:

"Just as in the two realms of desire and form, one equally calculates form to be the self and conceives that it may be annihilated in the future, since there is no form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), I do not understand what dharma is calculated to be the self? Thus he speaks.
"Is there annihilation after death? He replied, "It is said so. Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who reckon that there is form among those without form, and they also reckon form to be the self.
Later, when one is in the formless realm of the heavens, they also reckon the life-faculty to be the self;
thinking that once born there, it will no longer exist, they hold that the self is annihilated."

[Commentary: However, the meaning of their fundamental position—that [the formless attainments] are separately severed and extinguished—is as follows: when one cultivates the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) within this realm, it is said that no shape or form exists there;
because the characteristics of cultivating meditative concentration are difficult to perceive, one must apply effort before the subsequent absorption can be achieved.
When the subsequent absorption arises, it necessarily proceeds from this [preceding state]; therefore, being formless and shapeless, the higher stages are not perceived.

Because of the nature of the dharmas, one should separately cultivate and separately calculate the abandonment and cessation for each respective stage, rather than calculating the abandonment and cessation as a whole. Why is this?
It is because one no longer perceives the existence of dharmas belonging to higher stages. However, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), one does perceive the existence of subsequent higher stages;

that is, within the first, second, or third [dhyānas], one perceives the existence of dharmas belonging to higher stages. Thus, in the realm of form, one perceives the existence of subsequent higher stages.
Because the Dharma does not reckon the cessation [of the self] in the first, second, or third dhyānas,
and because it is no longer perceived after the fourth dhyāna, it is reckoned as a single cessation in total.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "there is no giving, up to and including no evil conduct," the meaning is as follows:
non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) do not believe in such cause and effect. Because they hold that there is no giving, they claim that giving brings no merit and thus does not produce a result.
