Because they hold that there is no craving, they claim that rebirth is not produced through the activity of greed; for while craving moistens birth and causes one to come and go among the various realms of existence, the non-Buddhists do not [acknowledge this].
Because of their lack of faith, they have no affection or devotion; they do not perform sacrifices to the gods, nor do they bring about rebirth. They deny the existence of sublime conduct;
those who deny good deeds reject virtuous actions, while those who deny evil deeds slander unwholesome karma. Furthermore, they deny the ripening results brought about by good and evil karma.

[Commentary: As for the fact that this treatise mentions only the fruits of wholesome karma and does not mention the fruits of unwholesome karma, it cites one case to reveal the rest by analogy; thus, what ought to be said is already implied.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "there is no such world," etc., it means that there is no worldly activity, but rather things exist spontaneously; the same applies to parents.
It does not arise through the agency of parents but exists spontaneously, like the patterns on a peacock’s feathers, which are not produced by artificial means;
thus, those who deny the existence of beings born by transformation (upapāduka) are reckoning that there is no intermediate state (antarābhava).
[Commentary: "These are of two kinds" means that because there are two types of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), all five views are collectively termed wrong view.

This is because they both involve a prior inversion regarding objects of knowledge; thus, the treatise states: "Wrong view is of two kinds: first, superimposition (*samāropa*), which refers to the four views such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth;
second, denial (*apavāda*), which refers to the repudiation of cause and effect and so forth. That is to say, these are the five views.
"Afflicted by heterodox views.

[Commentary] "The first, 'mostly characterized by denial' (*apavāda*), means that among heterodox views, the majority are of the nature of denial—namely, the two types such as causelessness (*ahetuka*) and so forth.
In reality, there are also those characterized by superimposition (*samāropa*), such as the calculation that Śakra and Brahmā are eternal, immutable, and unchanging, and so forth."
[It is] so. [Commentary]: "The meaning of 'being unable to recollect all the stages prior to that mind of emergence' is as follows:

it refers to those non-Buddhists who, wishing to pass away from the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), must first emerge from meditative concentration and only then pass away from that heaven to be reborn here."

Through the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), one observes through kalpa-contemplation from where one has come and in what place one existed in previous births;
that is, one simply contemplates until the mind of that [previous] deva has already ceased, and does not observe what occurred before that mind had arisen. Why is this?

Because the contemplation of non-Buddhists reaches at most no further than eight minor kalpas (*antara-kalpa*). If that deva has already passed away eighty kalpas ago, [the non-Buddhist] cannot perceive it.

It may be as you have said; however, having passed away from that heaven and been reborn here among humans, one attains the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvajātismṛti*) and observes the various stages prior to the emergence of the mind through the vision of kalpas.
If one does not see what was previously unseen, how can it be logically maintained that there is no cause?

Answer: If one has not yet passed through eight minor kalpas, and by means of the vision of kalpas, one calculates that one ought to see those events prior to the emergence of the mind, then [one would indeed see them]. But...
When one is in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), although the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) have ceased, the physical body (*rūpakāya*) remains.

Because the objects [perceived] later are subtle, and because one subsequently attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) within this realm to perceive those heavens, one sees only the mind that has emerged from absorption and does not see what occurred prior to it.
Thus, the physical body is described as arising from the cessation of the mind; since both are not seen simultaneously, one then conceives of them as the self (*ātman*) and the world.
[The beings] in the intermediate state do not arise without a cause.

[Commentary]: This merely illustrates one case; by extension, according to this calculation, all stages of existence (*bhūmi*) possess the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), yet none of them fully understand that all things are without cause.
However, the fact that there is no cause for passing away from the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) is somewhat more evident, and thus this single instance is cited.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding "a single lifetime," this refers to the fact that prior to this present life, the preceding lifetime lacks the manifest characteristics of a cause for the thoughtless state (*asaṃjñi-citta*).

As for the others, since the four coarse [elements] are manifest, it cannot be said that they lack a cause. Based on the previous explanation, even looking back through many lifetimes, the absence [of such a cause] may likewise be termed "lack of cause."

[Commentary]: "Fourth, because of being able to recollect the stages of the kalpa of destruction" means that this fourth view calculates the self in relation to the stages of the kalpa of destruction as being neither existent nor non-existent, and neither finite nor infinite.
This is because when one observes the destruction of the world, one perceives neither a limit to the self nor an absence of limit;
for when the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*) is destroyed, nothing can be apprehended. This is the present fourth [view].

This is not merely a third alternative; rather, it is a distinct calculation. Question: What is the difference between the four views of "having limits" (antavān) and the four views of "being eternal" (śāśvata)?

Answer: Those [four views] are calculated as being eternal, but are not calculated as being pervasive; these [four views] are calculated as having limits, but are not calculated as being eternal; therefore, there is a distinction.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "these four are able to recollect the kalpas of formation and destruction": the first three views are able to recollect the kalpa of formation, while the fourth view is able to recollect the kalpa of destruction;
therefore, it comprehensively encompasses both the kalpas of formation and destruction.

[Commentary: Regarding the fourth type, "evasive equivocation concerning immortality" (*amarā-vikṣepa*), it refers to the heterodox practitioners who calculate that the Brahmā heaven is eternally abiding and immortal.
If someone asks, "What dharma is immortal? they answer, "It is the Brahmā heaven that is immortal.
Because they answer by citing this immortal heaven, there is no further confusion; thus, upon asking, one immediately gains rebirth in that heaven. Now, as for the Buddha...

The name for the dharma of "evasive equivocation" (*vibhāṣā*) is also said to be that which a disciple of the Buddha—a "deathless deity" (*amara-deva*)—is able to pose as a non-evasive question. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "first, fearing ignorance... one should not speak," it means that these non-Buddhists gave rise to fear within themselves, and consequently...

Regarding the statement, "Even I myself do not know whether [these things] are wholesome or unwholesome," this means that if someone else were to question me on this matter, I would not be able to give a definitive answer.
Why? Because if I were to give a definitive answer, it would imply that I lack knowledge, and they would consequently disparage me.
Therefore, I should simply reply, "The secret meaning of the heavens should not be spoken of. Now, in this first case, one merely harbors fear.
Being afraid, he thought thus and did not answer the person before him because the latter had not yet spoken.

[Commentary]: Regarding the second point, "practicing all manner of crookedness" up to "responding with words as before," such as "it is not I, the Pure Heaven," etc., means that the Pure Heaven does not permit me to provide a prophetic declaration (*vyākaraṇa*).
All such matters of profound secrecy can only be personally realized by oneself.
The path of purification also permits this reflection: even if one intends to deceive or act with guile toward another, one does not speak a reply.

Now, regarding "guile" (*śāṭhya*), there are two interpretations: first, that one who is guileful does not die in the Heaven of Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*), meaning they employ deception and fraud within their conduct;
second, that one may also employ various forms of evasion toward a questioner, including the remaining three types of evasive speech (*vāk-chala*).
One should also understand by analogy that for those who speak as previously described, it is stated that "one must not explain the secret meanings to the gods," and so forth;
this is to be understood by analogy.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "harboring fear and so forth," the meaning is that these non-Buddhists constantly harbor fear because they lack definitive knowledge (*avyākṛta*).
He then thought to himself: "Let it not be that my dullness and inferiority are known by others.
For this reason, he could not escape the fear that others might know him to be ignorant; because of this ignorance, he could not attain liberation.
Taking this as his dwelling, he settled therein—meaning he feared that his former state of mental derangement might recur—and he pondered this calculation within his own mind while harboring fear.
Because they are afraid, they call it "abiding in self-composure," just as a person inside a room is said to be "in a place of security. This current calculation merely relies on other matters;
it is the same as before, answered with silence. [Commentary:
Regarding "following words without cessation," this means simply following the questions posed by the preceding person to respond to them in turn, proceeding through successive verbal exchanges.

Furthermore, when one has reached that [higher realm], while my own body remains here in this world, by what means could one conceive of those dharmas as "self"? Regarding this question, some explain:

if one has attained that concentration and gives rise to a mind belonging to the higher realms, it would be possible to conceive of those dharmas as self; however, if one has not attained that concentration, one cannot obtain the dharmas of the higher stages.
Since the body still remains in this realm, it is unclear what one could possibly conceive of as "self. This is the intent of the question.
1. [Commentary]:
Regarding the statement "if one takes the desire realm as an object up to taking another stage as an object," the meaning is as follows:

even if one attains that meditative concentration and gives rise to the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) in the higher stages, such that one takes the body of the desire realm as "self," this is still taking a phenomenon of a different stage as an object; that is, the mind of the higher realm takes [the lower] as its object.
Regarding the statement that "the body of the lower realm is the self," this is as answered in the *Śū* (Commentary) itself.

[The *Śū*] states: "As for what is discussed in the lower part of the treatise, this refers to the discussion on the objects of perception—both superior and inferior—found in the subsequent sections of the treatise.
That text does not permit the grasping of dharmas belonging to other stages as one's own internal self."
[Commentary]: Regarding "that which is the cause of all things," this refers to the calculation that Maheśvara is the cause of all things and the producer of all dharmas.
If one asks what the difference is from the previous [view], the answer is: the former was calculated as being eternal, while this is calculated as being the cause;
the former is a false view under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), whereas this is a false view under the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).
[Commentary: "And their retinues" refers to the five aggregates that arise simultaneously with those views; they are called "retinues" because one does not reckon them as being able to attain purity.
Although one may reckon the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and so forth as the fruit, one does not reckon this heaven as being able to attain the pure dharma of *nirvāṇa*;
therefore, it is not subsumed under the clinging to views or precepts (*dṛṣṭi-śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*). As the treatise says: "Some recklessly and erroneously cling to various [wrong paths]."
To view those who have attained liberation as being like those in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) or the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)—
mistaking what is not liberation for liberation while regarding it as true nirvāṇa— is wrong view within the context of the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasatya).
[Commentary: To reckon that which is not the Path as the Path refers to the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

This means that according to the various dharmas established by various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they falsely cling to what is not the Path as being the Path; this "Path" is the cause [of their delusion].

It is not truly the cause of *bodhi* or *nirvāṇa*, yet they falsely cling to it as the cause of the supreme Dharma (*agradharma*), such as the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*) of the Sāṃkhya or the categories of the Vaiśeṣika.
In the six categories of meaning (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) and other systems, it is all stated that if one can cultivate knowledge, attain the wisdom of practice, and reach up to Bodhi, and so forth.
[Commentary]: Although this is not the case of "regarding what is not a cause as a cause," the term "cause" (*hetu*) is itself a synonym for "penetration" (*prativedha*).
Therefore, regarding what is not a cause as a cause is precisely the meaning of regarding what is not the Path as the Path; there is no separate distinction.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "the four extremes, etc., are included herein," the intention is as follows: among the fourteen indeterminate questions, "eternalism" is subsumed under the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*), while "non-eternalism" is subsumed under the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Both "existence" and "non-existence" are likewise subsumed under the views of eternalism and annihilationism; thus, these collectively constitute the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, the identification of the "life-principle" with the "body" is subsumed under the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). However, the four extremes, such as existence and so forth, are [also] subsumed under false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
[The text] concludes:

"Collected. [Commentary]: According to the *Śāstra* (Treatise), from section fifty-eight up to the phrase "because they are abandoned in accordance with me," the intended meaning is that if these fourteen indeterminate matters (*avyākṛta-vastu*) were views of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), they would be abandoned under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "among wrong views" to "only the truth of origination," the intended meaning is that among wrong views, the two theories of non-causality are exclusively wrong views subsumed under the truth of origination;
this is stated explicitly in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

[Commentary: "Reversing the cause of outflows and being deluded regarding the fruit of nirvāṇa" summarizes the two aforementioned theories of no-cause (*ahetuvāda*) and the reason for being deluded regarding the truths while claiming to have attained nirvāṇa in the present life. [Commentary:

Regarding the four views such as "finite" and "infinite," up until the arising of the fruit of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*): to grasp at a self as being finite is precisely the suffering of the vital breath (*jīvitapariḷāha*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not only deluded regarding worldly fruits, but is also deluded regarding supramundane fruits.

Because the *tathatā* of the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) pervades all things, and because [ignorance] takes as its object the fruit-dharmas of the three periods of time in general, it also encompasses delusion regarding the untainted fruit of the truth of cessation.

Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that among the fourteen indeterminate questions (*avyākṛtavastu*), the four such as "having an end" (*antavān*) are wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) subsumed under the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
"Included. [Commentary:
Regarding the passage from "the indecisive equivocation of non-death" to "and because of being deluded regarding the Four Truths," this is a summary of the meaning of the text's inclusion.

It explains that the indecisive equivocation of non-death arises from questions and answers concerning the Four Truths, as well as from delusion regarding the Four Truths. The intent is to explain the four types of indecisive equivocation.

This passage addresses the confusion regarding the four truths and the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; thus, it provides a dialogue on the four truths. [The interlocutor asks: "The Immortal and Pure Heaven (*amṛta-śuddha-deva*) is the fruit. What is this cessation?

This refers to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). [He further asks: "Since cessation does not arise, what kind of practice should one cultivate? This refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

According to other schools, this question concerns the tainted fruits of suffering within birth and death, as well as the self and so forth, which constitute the Truth of Suffering and its Origin (*duḥkha-satya* and *samudaya-satya*).

Furthermore, regarding those who are deluded about the Four Noble Truths: to grasp at the fruit of suffering within the three realms as being the "deathless heaven" is delusion regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
To fail to understand right view and thus practice erroneously is delusion regarding the truths of origin (*samudaya*) and the path (*mārga*).

To take no delight in nirvāṇa and falsely grasp at the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) as being nirvāṇa is delusion regarding the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Furthermore, the question and answer concerning the Four Noble Truths serves to clarify this.
The *Yang* (Exaltation) states in the tenth [chapter]: "If someone comes and, according to the worldly path, asks about the wholesome and unwholesome, or the truths of suffering and its origin;
or, according to the supramundane path, asks about the truths of cessation and the path—at that time, one should declare: 'I am the one who is undisturbed by death.
One should merely give this evasive response and say no further words."

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 58) cited above, which does not mention the four views—namely, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and the others—among the fourteen indeterminate points, the intention of the text is as follows:

although there is no such explicit statement as to whether these are abandoned under which of the truths (*satya*), one may infer by means of reasoning that they are indeed abandoned under the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), encompassing all twenty positions.
Because there is a locus of delusion but no locus of severance, this is established by inference through principle.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the twenty views serve as the basis for the arising of the sixty-two views," this means that among those twenty views, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) serves as the basis.
Furthermore, because false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) also arise in delusion based upon this view of self, the treatise states that these are the various bases.
[This constitutes] karma.

[Commentary: Regarding "all evil views" and "the five aggregates which are their basis," the intended meaning is that there is a distinct, pure faculty of perception (*darśana*) that grasps both the evil views and the aggregates upon which they depend.
This is what is meant by "grasping."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "thereby individually contradicting the various views and so forth," as stated in fascicle 58:
"The grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) refers to each of the sixty-two views and other such views being individually reckoned as supreme, preeminent, superior, and excellent;
even to the extent that one believes through these views one can attain purification, liberation, and transcendence—this is called the 'view-aspect' (*dṛṣṭyaṅga*). Now, in this treatise...
The mind not only conceives of [the self] as superior, but also conceives of it as pure; the aggregates and so forth are likewise [treated in this manner].

[Commentary: If one maintains that what is not "view-attained" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) is not "included in views" (*dṛṣṭisaṃgṛhīta*), the meaning is that, apart from the views themselves and the five aggregates, to further maintain other dharmas as superior is entirely not subsumed under views.

[Commentary]: Regarding the initial passage of the fifty-eighth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the section on delusion concerning the Four Noble Truths, those that correspond to this [treatise] are precisely the opening of the fifty-eighth fascicle and the subsequent passage on delusion concerning the Four Noble Truths; these are identical to the present treatise.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "as in the Hinayana, [it extends] fully to all instances of grasping at views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), this is as explained in the *Yanmi* and the *Chaojie*.
Furthermore, one should state that "grasping at views and so forth" (*dṛṣṭy-ādi-parāmarśa*) refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) that arise simultaneously with the views.
[Commentary] This is not so, up to the point "because it is only at that time," for this is not the explanation of the *Abhidharmakośa*.

The Hīnayāna [view] holds that the objects of the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are the same, while their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ, and they permit them to be reckoned as either simultaneous or sequential. The Mahāyāna is not so; it does not hold that the objects are the same while the modes of activity differ, nor that they are reckoned as either sequential or simultaneous.
Rather, it takes the object of focus—the view itself and the five aggregates as a single collection—and, focusing upon them, clings to them as being supreme.

Attaining purity is precisely what constitutes the view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). If the grasping of precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) takes as its object all those precepts and the five aggregates that accompany them—which are associated with that view—it is called the grasping of precepts.
Both types of grasping (*dvaya-parāmarśa*) grasp their respective objects as being supreme and capable of attaining purity.
Thus, the distinctions between the objects of these two types of grasping differ from those in the Hīnayāna.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the nature of precepts as prohibitions and distinctions," that which is by nature a precept is called a *śīla* (precept), while that which is a prohibition is called a *vratā* (vow).

[Commentary]: Regarding "and being able to serve as a cause, etc.," for example, the calculation of Maheśvara as the supreme creator who provides all things with their causes is not included within the categories of views or precepts, but is subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Similarly, the Sāṃkhya masters' calculation of the twenty-three principles (*tattva*) originating from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is also [not a precept].
It is not that the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is like the Vaiśeṣika masters who reckon that atoms can produce coarse matter;

it is also not so. [Commentary]: If this were not the case, then reaching liberation would be termed "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). According to the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise 58), these two should properly be termed "clinging to precepts.
Since they are named "clinging to views," it is clearly known that they contradict what is manifest. The same principle applies to the category of "precepts" (*śīla*) as well.
[Commentary] As for the statement that "those who explain the delusion regarding the Four Truths all have this teaching," this refers to the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 58.

[Treatise] It is not so; how could it be otherwise? Regarding the phrase "not subsumed under the two types of grasping," the intention is that this serves as a counter-establishment (*pratiṣedha-siddhi*).

If it were not as previously explained—namely, by way of the abbreviated description of reflections (*pratibimba*) and the gate of following along (*anuvartana*)—then the consciousness of cessation would not be [grasped as] cessation, and the consciousness of the Path would not be [grasped as] the Path. That is to say: [if it were not so, one would] falsely reckon what is not the Path to be the Path.
It is appropriate to include this within "clinging" (*parāmarśa*), but it is not appropriate to say that it is subsumed under "wrong view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Since the Mahāyāna is neither annihilation nor is it considered annihilation, and neither is it a path nor is it considered a path, it is stated that it is subsumed under wrong view rather than under the two types of clinging.

Therefore, we know that as previously mentioned, there are instances where it is said that "clinging to [something] as superior" is called *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views), and "clinging to [something] as capable of bringing about purity" is called *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances); it is clear that these are explained through abbreviation (*saṃkṣepa*) and according to the circumstances (*anuvṛtti*).

This is a shift in perspective, as it is taught in accordance with the Hīnayāna. Question: What is the difference between "conceiving what is not extinction to be extinction" and so forth, and "conceiving what is not supreme to be supreme" and so forth?
Answer: Conceiving what is not extinction to be extinction is precisely the same as conceiving what is not supreme to be supreme.

Regarding "conceiving what is not the path to be the path," this refers to conceiving what is impure to be pure. To speak of "clinging to what is superior as being a 'view-grasping' (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa)" is precisely the act of conceiving what is not supreme to be supreme.

As it is said that those who hold to the grasping for precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) as being able to attain purity are actually following a non-path while reckoning it as a path, or a non-extinction while reckoning it as extinction,

these are precisely wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Since there are other passages where this is termed "view-grasping" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), we know that [the present formulation] is an elliptical statement (*chāyā-saṃkṣepa*) and a teaching given according to the occasion (*anuvartana-mukha*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "Fifty-eight" up to "as explained previously in the section on wrong views," the intended meaning is as follows:

Since the estimation of what is not superior as superior under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is identical to the estimation of what is not a cause as a cause—which is subsumed under wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and not termed "two types of grasping" (*dvigraha*)—it is clear that the former [the latter case] contradicts what is explicitly stated.
As for the phrase in the commentary, "it should be among the views," the intention is to say that since it is not wrong view, it must be [a type of] view (*dṛṣṭi*).

To claim that what is here termed "Mahāyāna" constitutes wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and is not subsumed under the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) contradicts previous passages; since those earlier sections explicitly mention the two types of grasping, it is clearly evident that this [current position] violates the manifest teaching. [Commentary:

Regarding the three kinds of four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*): the three kinds of inversion refer to the inversion of views (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*), the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), and the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*). Each of these has its own distinct categories.

Since each of the inversions contains the four inversions—such as the misconception of permanence within impermanence—it is said that there are "three types of four inversions," as explained in their respective commentaries.
[The *Sūtra*] now explains this, stating: "It merely says 'reckoning suffering as a vehicle'"; this is precisely how it reconciles the three types [of inversions] in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The text of the Four Perversions states: "It speaks only of regarding what is impure as pure and regarding suffering as a vehicle, but does not mention other [factors].

The reason for this is that, in reality, one also regards the various views along with their retinues as such; the subsequent passage provides a reverse explanation to clarify those factors that are not [primary] views.

[Commentary]: The four dull [afflictions] refer to greed, hatred, delusion, and pride; the two sharp ones refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
These six all encompass both the conceptual (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*) types. As for doubt and the latter three views, they arise only conceptually.
Thus, while there are six when stated generally and ten when distinguished specifically, it is said that although the general and specific enumerations differ, [the total remains consistent].

However, because there are ten types [of afflictions], it is clarified that within these ten afflictions there are twelve gates of analysis: first, the gate of simultaneous arising (*sahaja-vibhāga*); second, the gate of association with their own kind (*sva-jāti-saṃprayoga*);
third, the gate of association with the various consciousnesses (*sarva-vijñāna-saṃprayoga*); fourth, the gate of association with the various feelings (*sarva-vedanā-saṃprayoga*);

fifth, the gate of association with the specific objects (*viśeṣālambana-saṃprayoga*); sixth, the gate of analysis by way of the three natures (*tri-dhātu-vibhāga*); seventh, the three... [text fragment].
Chapter Eight: The Gate of the Analysis of Elements; Chapter Nine: The Gate of the Analysis of the Three Trainings; Chapter Ten: The Gate of the Analysis of the Three Abandonments; Chapter Eleven:
The Gate of Objects with and without Substantial Entities; Chapter Twelve: The Gate of Objects as Names and Objects as Substantial Entities.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that, when viewed as a whole, there are no divergent explanations, this is because those four dharmas arise solely from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Therefore, concerning their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), there are no differing assertions among other masters. Some passages state that "arising" means that the four dharmas arise solely through conceptual construction.

[Treatise] Regarding the question of where the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts state that [the view of self] reaches: the following passage cites scriptural evidence. Specifically, the eighty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"At the time of cultivating the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the truths, due to one's mental disposition (*āśaya*), one fears that 'I shall no longer exist in nirvāṇa,' and so forth, even to the point of thinking, 'I shall be annihilated and destroyed.
This is what the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other texts all refer to as the innate view of extremes (*sahaja-antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)."
The "view" refers to that which is subsumed under the view of annihilationism; because of this view, the mind recoils from the realm of nirvāṇa and gives rise to great fear, thinking:
"Where am I, and where has my self gone now?"

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "not seeing the path of cultivation because one constantly perceives characteristics," the intention of this master is to say that, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the path of cultivation there is only the characteristic of severing [views], and no characteristic of constant perception.
[Treatise] Therefore, when birds, beasts, and the like give rise to fear and terror, this is cited as evidence that innate (*sahaja*) nihilistic views exist.

Since birds, beasts, and others are terrified by the prospect of their own annihilation, these views are innate and not conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*). Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 58, states:
"There are two types of self-view: the innate and the conceptually constructed. The innate is present in all foolish worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*)."

Even down to birds and beasts, all who manifest [afflictions] arising from discrimination are those among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who give rise to them through speculative calculation (*parikalpa*).

[Commentary]: Regarding those who give rise to fear and the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) by taking *nirvāṇa* as their object: when first emerging from meditative observation, because they take *nirvāṇa* as an object through innate extreme views (*sahaja-antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and discriminative self-views (*vikalpita-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), they give rise to fear and the view of annihilation; that is, the innate view of annihilation relies upon [these].

To conceive of a self as distinct [from the aggregates] and subsequently give rise to this notion is what is called the "coarse characteristic. Some say that "conditioning" (ālambana) means "arising from":

because one realizes a portion of the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), one perceives that the conceptualized self does not exist and thus gives rise to fear, thinking, "I have accepted a self; where does it reside?"

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "fearing that the self might be annihilated," this refers to those with the view of annihilation who naturally fear cessation; now, those with the view of eternalism likewise naturally conceive of permanence and accumulate the requisites for its maintenance.
As for the term "explaining the clear realization" (*abhisamaya*), it refers to the later master's explanation of the preceding passage on clear realization.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this is based on general terminology," the former master explains that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises cited later—stating that "clinging to the five aggregates of grasping as either annihilated or permanent, whether arising innately (*sahaja*) or through discrimination (*vikalpita*)"—is a statement concerning their general characteristics.

[Commentary]: If that is so, as for the phrase "greed and its concomitants," the intended meaning is this: greed arises toward objects of attachment, whereas suffering and the like arise from being oppressed by objects that are contrary;

since their mental aspects (*ākāra*) are mutually contradictory, how can they arise together? The answer is as follows: when greed encounters adverse conditions, it coexists with sorrow and suffering;
when hatred encounters favorable conditions, it coexists with joy and pleasure—this is precisely what the text means.
[Commentary]: The phrase "stated as co-occurring" (*saha*) below refers to the textual passage concerning greed (*lobha*), pride (*māna*), and so forth, occurring together.
[Commentary]: Regarding the word "stated" (*ucyate*) in the treatise (*śāstra*) up to the point where it says "stated as co-arising," this is an explanation of the word "stated" within the treatise;
thus the treatise says, "it is stated that they attain association. This has two meanings: first, it is according to the internal logic of this treatise itself.

It may be said that there are two ways of speaking regarding "being associated with that": first, according to this principle, it is spoken of as arising simultaneously [with the afflictions], such as in the case of *yoga*;
second, as stated in the treatises (*śāstra*), there is no fault in saying that greed (*rāga*) is associated with the five views (*dṛṣṭi*).

This is because the statement of association has two meanings: one refers to the treatises, and the other refers to *yoga*. It is not the case that the characteristics of greed and pride (*māna*) actually exist within the treatises themselves.
The text here is not part of the passage corresponding to the latter five mental factors (*citta-mahābhūmika*).
[Commentary: However, regarding the "one dharma" mentioned herein, one first takes greed (*rāga*) as the primary factor and enumerates it across the remaining nine dharmas;
then, taking hatred (*dveṣa*) as the primary factor, one enumerates it across the remaining eight dharmas. In this manner, one proceeds sequentially through them all.

It is called "the practice of a single direction" because it proceeds toward others in a single-minded manner. Regarding "arrogance based on relying on oneself," this refers to the arising of pride by relying upon one's own self.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, as for the statement that one must certainly not give rise to anger and so forth toward oneself—what is the intent behind including this here? The answer is that previously, the discussion was restricted to pride (*māna*).
Regarding the statement that [ignorance] co-exists with hatred (*dveṣa*), this explains its co-existence with pride (*māna*); the rest should be understood accordingly.

As for the claim that each [affliction] may or may not co-exist [with ignorance], while it is possible for those that oppose the Middle Way (*madhyama-pratipad*) to co-exist, this is likewise permissible for those that accord with it.

[Commentary]: Regarding the two passages from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that state it can arise [simultaneously], these two passages refer to the *Yogācāra-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, which the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-paryāya) does not accept. [Commentary]:
The meaning of "this applies to both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*)" is that this anger is said to arise simultaneously with views; thus, it applies to both.
This refers to both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptual (*vikalpita*) [afflictions].

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "view (*dṛṣṭi*) is clarified as a single category," the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "When anger (*pratigha*) is associated with view, it is distinguished [from other views];

however, when stated generally as being 'associated with view,' this clarifies the meaning of view as a single category. It further states that the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are not actually associated with anger.
[Commentary]: "The three treatises all speak [of this]" refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 58), the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* (fascicle 55), and the *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* (fascicle 6);
hence they are called the "Three Treatises.

[Commentary]: "If one suspects that the object of service is superior" means that because of its inferiority; if one suspects that the preceding object is superior, it is because it is an inferior object.
Because it has not yet been determined, pride does not arise.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the treatises on the three locations all equally state that it is associated with views," this means that all treatises agree in clarifying the sense of being associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-samprayukta*).
As for the "three locations," they are as in the three treatises mentioned previously.

[Śāstra]: "The same applies to a portion of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of wrongness (*mithyādṛṣṭi*. This explains that a portion of the view of a self-identity and the view of wrongness does not coexist with pride (*māna*).

Specifically, when one clings to an extremely suffering aggregate as a self, it does not coexist with pride; however, when one clings to an aggregate that is not extremely suffering as a self, it can coexist with pride.
Therefore, the text states: "Because one relies on an inferior, suffering aggregate, it is associated with sorrow (*daurmanasya*). As for the view of wrongness, it negates [the existence of things].

The aggregate of suffering is neither associated with pleasure nor with pride, because it contradicts one's own feelings; thus it is said that the same applies to a portion of the body and to false views.
[Commentary:
According to the first master’s explanation below regarding association with sorrow, the intention of this master is that one who conceives the aggregate of suffering as a self...

It does not coexist with pride because painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) resides in the five sensory consciousnesses; thus, a portion of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is likewise [not associated with pride].

If one relies upon inferior aggregates (*skandha*) conditioned by suffering and conceives them as a self, this gives rise to pride accompanied by sorrow (*daurmanasya*), as it is contrary to one's desires.

The *Pañcāśatka* states: "Pride is of two kinds: first, loftiness (*unnati*); second, submissiveness (*nīcatva*). Loftiness arises from the perception of being superior or equal, and therefore it is associated with joy (*saumanasya*).
Furthermore, if [the view] is associated with inferiority or pride (*māna*), it is permitted to be associated with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), as explained in detail there.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "associated with the suffering-aggregate" up to "not arising together with pride," this explains one portion [of the view].
The meaning of the text is that when one perceives the aggregates associated with suffering as "self," this specific portion of self-view does not arise together with pride. Why is this?

This means that because one does not give rise to pride (*māna*) regarding the inferiority of the aggregate of suffering (*duḥkha-skandha*), and because even when wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) negates the principle of the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*), pride does not arise either.
How is this known? Within the Buddha’s teaching, there exist the truths of suffering and its origin;

however, upon understanding [the path], one may develop aversion and resentment, giving rise to wrong view and negating it by asking, "How could there possibly be the truths of suffering and its origin? This very [wrong view]...

Because [the view of self] is seen to be exclusively a practice of dejection (*daurmanasya*), it is associated with pride (*māna*); for pride arises only by taking up practices of elation (*abhimāna*) as its object.
[The commentary] states that "in reality, it may also be so" because this is spoken according to the actual state of affairs:

even the false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) that denies the truths of suffering and its origin may be associated with pride, since one relies on oneself to deny the dharmas of others; thus, it is said that it "may also be so" when considering the objects of both self and others.
Question: It was previously stated that wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) does not coexist with pride (*māna*); why is it now permitted? Answer:
Previously, it was held that pride does not arise when [wrong view] shares the same object (*ālambana*). Now, because the objects are distinct, their coexistence is permitted.

Alternatively, even self-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) coexists with pride; while one grasps the inferior aggregates of suffering as "self," one gives rise to pride toward others, as their objects are different.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement in the subsequent text that "pride reaches as far as suffering and inferiority," the intended meaning is that pride can also be associated with the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) which conceives of the aggregates of suffering as a self.
As stated below, because one relies on the inferior aggregates of suffering, it is associated with sorrow; thus, it is clearly known that pride coexists with the view of self.
Since one conceives of the aggregates of suffering as a self, a specific form of pride arises, and because this view and pride coexist, sorrow subsequently arises.

Fear and pride can also coexist with wrong view; as it says below, when one employs wrong view to repudiate cessation and the path, because one relies on one's own [erroneous] dharma to disparage and destroy the path, they are able to be associated [with it].

[Commentary]: Now, regarding the phrase "based on coarse characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), this establishes the meaning within this context. It is stated according to coarse characteristics that [the view of self] takes the aggregates associated with pleasure as its object and functions together with pride (*māna*), while the denial of cessation and the path functions together with pride.

Furthermore, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) taking the aggregates associated with suffering as its object, and a portion of the false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) denying suffering and its origin, do not function together with pride;
therefore, it is said that a portion of the view of self regarding the body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is likewise so, as is the case elsewhere.
"Namely, the spirits, humans, and so forth.

[Śāstra]: Regarding the phrase "because the five views develop into many," this is explained by contrasting view with view; since there are no two simultaneous cognitions (*prajñā*), they certainly do not coexist.
Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (58), because the five views are of the nature of cognition (*prajñā-svabhāva*).

Question: If that is so, how can the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) within the seventh consciousness coexist with the discernment (*prajñā*) of the "object-specific" mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*), given that they are mutually incompatible by nature?
Answer: Among the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), these are explained according to their distinct functions;
therefore, there is no contradiction here, as this [present discussion] is based on their essential nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, they do not conflict.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "pride and so forth necessarily arise from the conceptualization of recollective mental application," one should explain that pride and so forth arise from both recollective and constructive conceptualization.
Since the five sensory consciousnesses lack such conceptualizations as recollection and the like, they are devoid of pride.
[Treatise] Question: Greed, hatred, and delusion—whether innate (*sahaja*) or discriminative (*vikalpita*—are all compatible with the five feelings?
Answer: How is it known that both the innate and the discriminative are compatible with all five? Therefore, the *Pañcāśatka-praśna* asks:

"Of these afflictions, how many are associated with the [five] faculties, and so forth, up to how many are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)? Answer: If they arise spontaneously (*svarasena*), one...

All afflictions are found to manifest within the three types of sensation (*vedanā*); therefore, those that pervade all classes of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) are associated with all faculties (*indriya*) of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
The commentary explains: based on this, greed, hatred, and delusion are associated with five and three faculties respectively.
Furthermore, it states: "Not all afflictions arise spontaneously; they are associated with various faculties according to their respective requirements."
I shall now explain that greed is sometimes associated with pleasure and joy, and at other times associated with sorrow and suffering;

as it is with greed, so it is with hatred and delusion. Since delusion pervades all objects, its meaning is evident and can be understood accordingly. Based on this text, it follows that there are also afflictions involving conceptualization within the five sensory consciousnesses.

Otherwise, how could conceptual greed and the like be associated with painful feeling? [They would not be so associated. It is only by distinguishing them [from non-conceptual states] that they are so designated.
Since the intention to pursue other afflictions, evil destinies, or mental suffering does not exist in the happy destinies, one should not raise an objection based on that;

rather, it should be analyzed according to recollection and so forth. As for the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other texts stating that greed is associated only with joy, pleasure, and equanimity, while hatred is associated with sorrow, pain, and equanimity, this is as stated below:
it is described according to their coarse characteristics.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "only with joy, pleasure, or equanimity," the *Fifty-five [Treatises]* says this refers to the majority of cases.

This merely explains the feelings associated with the category of attachment (*rāga*) and does not concern other types such as aversion (*dveṣa*), because the coarse activity of aversion is associated only with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) and physical pain (*duḥkha*).

[Commentary]: Now, regarding the general explanation of the two types of craving and other mental formations here, "two types" refers to the distinction between conceptual (vikalpita) and innate (sahaja) craving.
Furthermore, the claim that craving arises together with sorrow and suffering is a tenet unique to the Mahāyāna; it is not accepted by the Hīnayāna.

[Commentary]: Among the five and six consciousnesses, those associated with sorrow and suffering are as follows: those in the five consciousnesses are associated with the sensation of suffering; those in the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) are associated with sorrow.
Hatred is the reverse of this. [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement that "within the five consciousnesses there are also greed and so forth arising from discrimination," the intended meaning is that since the treatise states "greed... [it implies these arise through conceptualization].
Hatred and delusion arise together with all three types of discrimination and are compatible with all five feelings.
As for greed, since it is non-discriminative, how could it be associated with painful feeling? This is because painful feeling exists only within the five sensory consciousnesses.
Therefore, we know that there are discriminative afflictions within the five sensory consciousnesses, which are induced by the discriminative afflictions present in the mental consciousness.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "it is not so, because it would coexist with suffering," the intended meaning is as follows: Since the five consciousnesses can possess conceptualized greed and other such afflictions, they are able to correspond with the sensation of suffering.
This is because the sensation of suffering exists only within the five consciousnesses; within the mental consciousness (*manas*), there is no suffering.

If one does not allow that the five consciousnesses possess conceptualized greed and the like, then this greed would not coexist with the sensation of suffering within the five consciousnesses. Furthermore...

As for the pride of discrimination (*vibhava-māna*), it exists only on the mental level (*manobhūmi*) and does not coexist with painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*), because the mind does not tend toward suffering.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "in the miserable realms (*durgati*) it coexists with grief (*daurmanasya*)," the meaning is as follows: one gives rise to pride by relying upon an inferior physical aggregate within the miserable realms;
yet, seeing suffering and fearing its oppression of the body, one gives rise to grief. Therefore, it is said that pride is associated with grief.

[Commentary]: This refers exclusively to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Regarding the definitive statement that [afflictions] arise together with suffering: while greed born of discrimination (*vikalpita-rāga*) occurs across all five sensory consciousnesses and is definitively stated to coexist with suffering, pride (*māna*) exists only in the mental consciousness.
Although pride includes both discriminative and innate types (*sahaja*), it does not coexist with suffering.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "In the aggregate as a whole, there is only the sense that it is associated with all feelings," the meaning is this:

it is only within the aggregate as a whole that one admits the possibility of being associated with suffering and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure; it does not mean that each individual [mental factor], such as the innate pride (*sahaja-māna*) and so forth, is individually permitted to be associated with them.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "doubt and so forth should be understood accordingly," since it is clearly evident that pride of discrimination (*vibhava-māna*) does not correspond with suffering, one should know that doubt (*vicikitsā*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and the others likewise do not correspond with the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*).

[Commentary: Furthermore, we know that the previous master’s claim—that those who create karma for rebirth in evil destinies do not give rise to afflictions such as volitional deliberation (*vitarka*) within hell itself, but rather that "discriminative" (*savikalpa*) refers only to the power of strong discriminative delusions from a previous life by which various karmas are created—is incorrect.
[Objection: How could one further create evil karma while in hell?
The Master Yājñavalkya replied: "The former teacher formulated this view because he did not understand the correct principle.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "In the Abhidharma... up to "...are all like joy and pleasure," etc., it is as stated in the *Abhidharmapada* and other texts that in the desire realm, [mental factors] are associated only with joy (*saumanasya*) and pleasure (*sukha*).
This text continues until it asks: "How is it that they are associated with four or five feelings (*vedanā*)? I do not yet understand how this is so. Please explain.

As before, regarding the "conjunction with greed," the previous commentary stated: "The conjunction with greed involves being accompanied by sorrow and suffering due to adverse conditions (*vipakṣa*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the four feelings, suffering is excluded because in the hell realms there is no conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) or doubt (*vicikitsā*). Doubt and the three views do not correspond with the feeling of suffering.
As for "arising according to the mind," this means that within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there is both conceptual discrimination and non-discrimination.

This explains the reason why [the mind] does not coexist with suffering (*duḥkha*), as stated above. The intended meaning is that because the mind in states of extreme suffering lacks discursive delusion (*vikalpa-kleśa*), it does not coexist with suffering;
whereas in other states, because discursive delusion is present, it can be associated with other feelings (*vedanā*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the term 'universally established' (*prasiddha*) in the context of a collective aggregate":

here, the association with feeling (*vedanā*) is based on a single mental aggregate (*citta-saṃghāta*), which can be understood as applying to a specific location (*sthāna*). It does not mean that every individual affliction (*kleśa*) of every individual realm (*dhātu*) or stage (*bhūmi*) universally applies;
rather, it simply indicates that they may coexist. Because there is no divergent teaching, the term "universally established" is used; it is not a mere verbal convention. Question: How is this known?
Question: Is doubt associated with sorrow? Answer: First, when one has performed virtuous deeds and doubts whether there will be no virtuous fruit, it is associated with sorrow.
Furthermore, in whatever worldly affairs one undertakes, doubting whether one will succeed or fail involves a degree of sorrow; this is easy to understand.
[Commentary]: "If that which takes as its object [the view] associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is the 'clinging to precepts and observances' (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)," the meaning is this:

previously, one saw that [the view] was associated with mental distress—thinking, for instance, that because of such distress one could not quickly attain *nirvāṇa*. Now, since one further grasps those very views and precepts, it is said that the two types of clinging are associated with mental distress.
Question: If this is so, why did it previously state that hatred (*dveṣa*) is necessarily dissociated from the two types of clinging, yet here they are held to be the supreme path?

It is not because one does not hate others that it is explained as being "contrary" (*ekānta-virodha*) to hatred and the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*); rather, it is because the two types of grasping are not invariably contrary to mental distress (*daurmanasya*).
Therefore, it is said to be "possessed" [of them].

[Commentary: The statement "it is not associated with the five consciousnesses and is exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*)" explains the reason why it is not associated with suffering (*duḥkha*) or mental distress.
Because the two views do not exist within the five consciousnesses, they do not coexist with painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*), but are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, they do not coexist with mental grief (*daurmanasya*), because grief possesses both wholesome and unwholesome natures. Question:

If painful sensation exists only in the five consciousnesses and does not coexist with the two views, how can the two views coexist with pleasant sensation (*sukhavedanā*), which also exists in the five consciousnesses? Furthermore, if it is said that [the two views] coexist with mental grief...
If the two views are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they do not coexist with the two natures; the same applies to the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*). How, then, can they coexist?

The answer is: because there is pleasure (*sukha*) on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*), it can coexist [with the views]; since the feeling of joy is pervasive across the indeterminate states, it can be associated with the feeling of joy.

[Commentary: Regarding those who grasp at the aggregates associated with suffering while in states of extreme suffering, this former master maintains that there are afflictions involving conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) in the hells.

As for the latter master, he holds that within the realms of humans and devas, the "conceptual view of self" takes as its object the body and such things as the suffering of illness; thus, it grasps the aggregates associated with suffering.

Therefore, when the subsequent commentary states it is "the same as the first master," it means that [the latter] does not grasp [the self] as being co-existent with suffering, unlike [the case of] the evil destinies.

This concerns the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*). A detailed explanation is as previously stated, namely, as explained in the section on the distinctions among the five types of sensation (*pañca-vedanā*).

[Commentary] The statement "the two views of conceptual discrimination up to those that are not contradictory to the co-emergent" means that the two views of conceptual discrimination are identical to the position of the first master [who held they do not coexist with suffering].
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Chapter 59) likewise agrees with the intention of the first master in stating that there is no sensation of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*) therein.
The Master [Vasubandhu] holds that in the hells there are no afflicted states of non-discrimination; for this reason, these two do not coexist.

In this context, the *Pañcāśatikā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Fifty) states that the two innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*) coexist with suffering; this is according to the actual meaning. As for the fact that both masters do not contradict one another, it is because, regarding the two discriminative views (*vikalpita-dṛṣṭi*), neither contradicts the text of the *Pañcāśatikā*.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the analysis of the afflictions is explained up to the *Pañcāśat-sūtra* (Treatise on the Fifty-nine)," both masters agree that the two types of views (*dṛṣṭi*) are all associated with the four feelings (*vedanā*), as stated in the *Pañcāśat*.

However, the former master’s position—that the views of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) do not coexist with the feeling of suffering (*duḥkha-vedanā*)—contradicts the text of the *Pañcāśat*, because the former master maintains that there is no feeling of suffering in the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*). The latter [master] does not hold this view.
[The afflictions of] suffering (*duḥkha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are associated with the two views [of self-existence and extremes].
[Treatise: Greed (*rāga*) is associated with the four views, pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

This means that greed and pride (*māna*)—the four views excluding wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—are all associated with the three feelings, excluding sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*), because they grasp at favorable objects. Ignorance (*moha*) can be associated with all five feelings.

Because delusion (*moha*) is explained as being in accordance with the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is discussed as coexisting with five [mental factors]. Regarding the view of wrongness (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), they are discussed as coexisting with four [mental factors], excluding suffering (*duḥkha*).
The underlying intention is that there are two reasons for excluding suffering: first, they exist only on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*);

second, they do not exist in places of pure suffering. For these two reasons, suffering is excluded. Regarding greed (*lobha*) and delusion (*moha*), they are associated with both pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*saumanasya*), and this applies throughout the lower four stages (*bhūmi*).

This refers to greed and delusion being associated with the five consciousnesses. If one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are associated with the five consciousnesses, being accompanied by pleasure (*sukha*).

In the first dhyāna, they are associated with both the mental consciousness and the [first] five consciousnesses; in the second and third dhyānas, they are associated only with the mental consciousness and are accompanied by pleasure.

Question: Does the first dhyāna possess the five consciousnesses? Answer: This is stated according to the majority of cases; however, there are only three consciousnesses present—the nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses.

Because the tongue faculty is associated only with the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), [the treatise] discusses the remaining seven faculties. Regarding the seven faculties of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), excluding those of the Desire Realm, they are associated with all three [types of feeling].

This is because, by removing greed, hatred, and delusion, the seven faculties of pleasure are associated only with the lower three dhyānas; these are all associated with mental pleasure (*manobhūmi-sukha*). Why is this?

Because the five views, pride, and doubt exist only on the level of the mind. As for the treatise stating that "doubt is exclusively associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*) when it occurs independently," this refers to the specific case of doubt occurring alone.

It is difficult to explain why these two [doubt and pride] are not associated with the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) in the desire realm; this is as stated in both the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya*:

doubt in the desire realm is associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*) or equanimity (*upekṣā*), but not with joy, because a mind that is not resolved does not arise unless it is stilled and extinguished.

As for doubt in the form realm—specifically doubt regarding the dhyānas—it is associated with joy and bliss, because it is sustained by meditative concentration (*samādhi*). It is not uncommon [for doubt to exist there].
The *Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya* also explains that [the feeling of] equanimity (*upekṣā*) is associated with both sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and renunciation (*tyāga*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because the feeling of equanimity arises at the final stage," the intention is to demonstrate that this feeling of equanimity exists as a continuous stream throughout the entire body.
Regarding the phrase "because it arises at the final stage," the intention is to state that in the three lower dhyānas, there are minds associated with joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*).
If the mind is about to cease, it always possesses the stages of *sthiti* (abiding) and *upekṣā* (equanimity), because the mind of equanimity exists at all times;
therefore, one knows that [the mental consciousness] is also associated with craving and so forth.

[Commentary: The fourth dhyāna is excluded because the mental consciousness of the fourth dhyāna is accompanied only by the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and lacks the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).
The above excludes hatred (*dveṣa*), as it exists only in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

[Commentary: Regarding doubt (*vicikitsā*) concerning the higher dhyānas—such as doubting whether that concentration (*samādhi*) is superior or inferior—it remains within the stage of concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*).

Thus, doubt is a defilement belonging to the stage of concentration; however, because it is first produced by the power of the mind’s concentration characterized by joy and bliss (*prīti-sukha*), it is classified as doubt.
Regarding the question of how the seven factors, such as pride (*māna*), arise once the higher meditative attainments (*dhyāna*) have been obtained:

the answer is that the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride, and doubt are associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and not with the five sensory consciousnesses. Because one has attained those meditative states, one falsely conceives them to be supreme, most excellent, and capable of purification;

thus, there arises the view of [wrong] views and the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Due to this attachment to precepts, one subsequently calculates [the self] in terms of annihilation or permanence, whereby the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arise.

Considering this concentration to be supreme, one negates the paths of action and thus gives rise to wrong view; having attained this superior concentration, one develops overweening pride (*abhimāna*).

These five types of afflictions are induced by the mind entering and emerging from concentration, for they cannot exist within the state of concentration itself, as such matters are known only through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, doubt regarding the realms does not coexist with joy, as it pertains to objects that are to be scrutinized.
Because ignorance that acts alone does not arise when the seeking mind has not ceased and hesitation remains undecided, it is said that it is like doubt regarding principles;
since doubt is already known to coexist with the aforementioned joy and pleasure, one should know that ignorance likewise coexists with joy and pleasure.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because coarse aspects of suffering and pleasure do not reach the level of mental consciousness," there are two interpretations. First, it means that if one speaks in terms of coarse aspects, doubt does not coexist with suffering or pleasure;
since the object of suffering is predominant and fixed, and since the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of doubt is already distinct from it, they cannot coexist.

Second, it means that in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are no feelings of suffering or pleasure; since doubt resides in the level of the mental consciousness, there is no suffering [to coexist with it].
Regarding the statement that [the first two dhyānas] are associated with pleasure because they possess coarse characteristics:

this is said because the suffering and pleasure found in the desire realm, among humans and devas, and in other realms of mixed sensation, all reside in the five sensory consciousnesses and not in the mental consciousness; thus, one knows that there is no simultaneous presence of both suffering and pleasure.
[Commentary]: Greed and the other [afflictions] are associated with pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*saumanasya*).

This means that, according to the intention of the author, all afflictions are associated with joy and equanimity (*upekṣā*) throughout the lower three stages (*dhyāna*), excluding the third *dhyāna* because there is only the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) there.

Within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), one excludes the places of extreme suffering in the hells, because in the hells there are no afflictions involving conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). This applies to all other places characterized by mixed feelings.
Because the mental level (*manobhūmi*) possesses craving, joy, and equanimity. [Commentary:

The phrase "the remainder of the meaning already explained following the difficult points" refers to what is stated in the treatise: that greed and delusion are associated with both pleasure and joy; up to doubt and independent delusion;

and that desire is associated only with sorrow and equanimity—and so forth. All these are "following the difficult points to explain the remaining meanings. The treatise states: "The remaining [mental factors] are associated with all feelings (*vedanā*)."
"Arising" refers to the meaning of this passage concerning the difficulty of resolving the doubt; it is a supplementary explanation.

[Commentary] However, because the mental aspect (*ākāra*) of doubt is profound, the statement that it "occurs simultaneously with concentration" intends to say that the acquisition of doubt can be associated with concentration. Question:

Since the mental aspect of doubt is still indeterminate while concentration is focused on a single object, how can they be associated? Answer: There is no fault in their association, just as in the case of seeing three [colors].
Although the Jewel is indeed certain regarding the merits of the Triple Gem, one may still give rise to hesitation, wondering: "Does making this offering bring merit, or does it not?
Based on the mode of its mental activity (*ākāra*), what is described as "attaining a corresponding concentration" is precisely defiled concentration (*kliṣṭa-samādhi*).

[Commentary] Regarding the question that the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*) are not universal (*sarvatraga*) because they are distinct: since "feeling" (*vedanā*) shares the characteristic of being distinct, it is not universal;
the meaning of "universal," as explained above, is that [the universal mental factors] arise in association with all states of mind, and thus there is no need to question this.

[Commentary]: It is not asked whether [the afflictions] correspond with the nature of goodness (*kuśala-dharma*), because goodness is contrary to defilement (*kliṣṭa*); therefore, this is not discussed here. [Commentary]:

"Because what follows must necessarily inquire about what precedes" means, for instance, that while the specific objects of cognition (*viṣaya-viniyata*) and so forth, along with the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*) and the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), have already been explained previously, one subsequently uses the later afflictions to inquire about the former. As it is said: "With which consciousnesses do these ten afflictions correspond?"

Regarding the principle that one should explain what precedes before asking about what follows: as was not clarified for the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*) because they appear later, we shall now not analyze their association (*samprayoga*) and so forth by contrasting them with the four indeterminate factors.
[Treatise] Regarding the statement that "hatred is exclusively unwholesome because it harms oneself and others": it brings about undesirable fruits and harms both this life and future lives;
thus, it is said to "harm oneself and others," as analyzed previously.

[Treatise] Regarding the phrase "the two upper realms, etc.": the remaining nine afflictions in the two upper realms are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as they are suppressed by meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

As for the nine factors such as attachment (*rāga*) belonging to the desire realm that arise through discrimination (*vikalpaja*), they are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), because they give rise to evil conduct.
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter two, states: "Intrinsic unwholesomeness refers to [afflictions] excluding those associated with the defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*)."
Regarding the defilements and so forth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that can give rise to unwholesome conduct, as well as the secondary defilements (*upakleśa*), they are unwholesome.
The fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* explains: "Those bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that do not arise spontaneously are of an unwholesome nature;
if they arise spontaneously and can give rise to unwholesome conduct, they are also unwholesome. The remainder are obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). This is the interpretation.

Among the nine afflictions, doubt and the latter three views arise solely through discrimination (*vikalpita*). Greed, delusion, and pride are common to both discrimination and innate arising (*sahaja*).
Regarding those that arise through discrimination, doubt and the other three views share the nature of being unwholesome (*akuśala*).

Among those that are innate, if they incite unwholesome conduct, they are also subsumed under the unwholesome; however, if they are innate and do not incite unwholesome conduct, they are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Thus it is said.

[Treatise] It is said that the remaining indeterminate [factors] include those subtle ones that do not obstruct the wholesome and so forth; this clarifies the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

As for the single dharma of hatred (*dveṣa*), it exists only in the desire realm; regardless of whether it is innate (*sahaja*) or discriminative (*vikalpita*), it is exclusively categorized as unwholesome and is not analyzed separately.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "a small portion of the remaining three," the intended meaning is as follows: that portion of greed (*rāga*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*) which is innate (*sahaja*) and gives rise to unwholesome conduct that harms oneself and others is of an unwholesome nature (*akuśala-dharmatā*).
That portion which functions spontaneously (*svarasavāhin*) without giving rise to such action is of a neutral nature (*avyākṛta-dharmatā*).
Because it possesses four causes, it is subtle and does not obstruct the wholesome, and so forth.
[Commentary: The phrase "along with these four causes" distinguishes this teaching, principle, and practice as being likewise possessed of the four aforementioned causes.
Although they frequently arise as manifest activities (*samudācāra*), because they do not cause harm, they are categorized as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

[Commentary: The reason for treating this as identical to the preceding [case] is that the explanation for its being indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) is the same as the three or four causes mentioned above.
[Commentary: As for why the former interpretation is superior—it is because most treatises state that this view is subsumed within the ninth category;

thus, it is said that there are not nine categories. Furthermore, as for the argument that if one follows the latter [interpretation], there would indeed be nine categories—if one adheres to the latter interpretation, that too is acceptable.
Furthermore, for instance, even though the formless realm lacks a path capable of counteracting it, there are still nine grades; why then could the two views not also have nine?
Moreover, within the seventh [view], the view itself is already reckoned to have nine grades—how much more so for the two views?
Since the extensive texts above and below clearly allow for nine grades, we shall adopt the latter position here.

[Commentary]: That is to say, the "not-yet-attained concentration" (anāgamya-samādhi) does not admit of defilement; for the treatise states that one may give rise to afflictions of the higher realms while having attained the fundamental [dhyāna], yet it does not state that one gives rise to afflictions of the higher realms while in the not-yet-attained concentration. Therefore, the not-yet-attained concentration does not admit of defilement.

The meaning is that the not-yet-attained concentration is precisely the preparatory stage (prayoga-mārga) prior to the fundamental dhyāna; in the Mahāyāna, at this stage there is no distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).
Furthermore, there is no room for the arising of afflictions [in the *anāgamya* stage]; if one attains that concentration (*samādhi*), there is room for a mind that can give rise to afflictions.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "If this were so" to "for what purpose," the intent of this question is as follows:

If it is said that afflictions do not arise in the *anāgamya* stage, then consider one who passes away while still in the *anāgamya* stage; it is uncertain whether such a person would have given rise to afflictions and passed away without receiving further birth.

Because one must abide in a distracted state of mind, the answer is that this is certainly impossible; it is only after having attained the fundamental dhyānas (mauladhyāna) that one either regresses from them or passes away.

Although there are cases where one has previously attained the higher dhyānas but, after emerging from them, regrets practicing meditation—this is termed "regression from dhyāna"—such a person may still pass away while afflictions arise.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "at this time," it refers precisely to the time of this *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration.
It means that within this stage, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm have not yet been completely subdued or exhausted;

thus, it is said that if the ninth grade [of affliction] is not free from defilement, one can only enter the fundamental concentration once they are subdued, but as long as they are not yet exhausted, one cannot attain the higher concentrations. This interpretation asks whether there is still defilement present within the *anāgamya*.
