If one is able to suppress the afflictions of the desire realm entirely within the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration, can afflictions of the higher realms arise therein?

One cannot give rise to such afflictions, because they are bound to the higher realms. Question: Regarding what was said about "suppressing the afflictions" (*kleśa-vinodana*), which afflictions are suppressed?
Answer: According to the principle of suppression, it suppresses the innate (*sahaja*) afflictions but does not suppress the conceptualized (*vikalpita*) ones.
[Commentary]: The statement that "there is no defilement of the ninth grade because it only exists when the time arrives" establishes a distinct meaning.
This intent explains that there is no such thing as being able to enter the fundamental dhyāna while the ninth-grade affliction of the desire realm still remains;

rather, one must first exhaust all desire-realm defilements before entering the fundamental dhyāna, and only then does one subsequently give rise to the afflictions of the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration. As for what is called "un... [the text here is incomplete].

That which reaches meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) is itself the preparatory absorption (*prayoga-samāpatti*); it is both the preliminary application (*prayoga*) prior to absorption and the absorption itself, or it is called the "neighboring absorption" (*sāmantaka*).

Because it is the cause for the fundamental absorption (*maula*), it is named the neighboring absorption. According to this latter sense, the "not-yet-reached" absorption (*anāgamya*) may be defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
[Commentary: From "Because [they] have not yet attained mastery" onwards, this summarizes the meaning: even the words cannot give rise to afflictions that have not yet arisen;
this is true for both ordinary beings and sages alike.
[Commentary: "Because they do not commit evil" means they do not, out of lack of self-mastery, commit evils such as killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct.
[Commentary]: From the second fascicle of the *Xiǎnyáng shèngjiào lùn* (Exposition of the Manifestation of the Sacred Teachings) down to the fine examination, it is not found there;
among the three types of concentration—pure, defiled, and untainted—it is never stated that the "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*) stage exists within them. How could it give rise to defilement?

[Commentary]: Regarding "only the afflictions of meditative concentration" (*samādhi-kleśa*): "afflictions of meditative concentration" refers to the arising of afflictions after one has attained that concentration, whereby one relishes (*āsvādana*) the concentration thus obtained.
"Afflictions" refers to the delusions produced at the moment of birth; it means the afflictions that arise when one is born into that particular stage (*bhūmi*).
Some say, furthermore, that only those afflictions which moisten birth are "birth-afflictions," and that these do not take meditative concentration as their object.

And yet they give rise to relish, such as when one grasps at the Brahma King and gives rise to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); all these are termed "afflictions based on meditative concentration" (*samādhi-kleśa*).

[Treatise]: Regarding those who attain the fundamental dhyānas through the various contaminated paths (*sāsrava-mārga*) up to the level of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), this explains the following objection:

How can it be said that the various contaminated paths do not suppress the discriminative afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) of lower stages, nor the subtle co-emergent afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the view of self and what belongs to self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*)?
Because it is capable of giving rise to the various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages, this general principle states:

although one cannot suppress those [afflictions] arising from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-ja*) and the like, one is nonetheless able to suppress and eliminate the coarse afflictions arising simultaneously with birth (*sahaja-audārika-kleśa*), thereby gradually realizing the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) of the higher realms.

Furthermore, "subtle" simultaneous afflictions refer to the production of the two views (*dṛṣṭi*) and the nine modes of rebirth (*upapatti*). One must not object that this contradicts the lower treatises.
Regarding the statement that "the contaminated [attainments] can suppress [defilements]," this refers to the inability of the sixfold practice (*ṣaḍākāra*) to suppress them;

whereas the other statement refers to the ability of the discernment of the truths (*satyavipaśyanā*) to suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*). Because these refer to different meanings, they do not contradict one another; this shall be analyzed in detail when we reach the ninth intermediate stage.
[Commentary]: Why is it that the mundane path subdues the cultivated [afflictions] but does not subdue the views? A questioner asks:

For what reason does the treatise state that the mundane path subdues the coarse innate afflictions, but does not subdue the conceptualized [afflictions] or the subtle innate views of self and extremes (*satkāyadṛṣṭi* and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?
[Commentary]: First, regarding "merely deluded about phenomena... because it is obstructed by the obstruction of phenomena," this answers the intent of the preceding question.

Because innate coarse afflictions possess these four characteristics, the six stages [of practice] are able to suppress them, whereas the one [type of affliction] is merely deluded about phenomena. This distinguishes them from the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which are delusions regarding principles (*tattva*).

Second, "functioning according to an external orientation" means they function by being deluded regarding external objective phenomena; this distinguishes them from the [afflictions of the path of seeing].

Regarding the statement that these [afflictions] such as craving arise only by taking internal [objects] as their conditions—just as the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, or the sixty-two views, arise only through delusion regarding the principles (*tattva*)—this is because these conceptual cravings arise subsequent to the view of self.

Thus, while it is said that "view" is excluded [from this category] because it differs from the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), in fact, this refers specifically to the external gate; that is, there is a distinction between the internal and external aspects of principle and phenomena.
The innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of the three [realms] are abandoned because their substance is distracted; they are coarse and agitated, arising repeatedly.

Because these coarse afflictions directly obstruct the cognitive aspect of the practice of *vastu-vipaśyanā* (contemplation of things), they can be suppressed by the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*). This suppression differs from that of the innate subtle afflictions (*sūkṣma-sahaja-kleśa*), which are abandoned through analytical discernment (*vibhāga-vipaśyanā*).
By suppressing these [coarse ones], one realizes the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*); otherwise, it cannot be said that this is the practice of *vastu-vipaśyanā*.

This is not an observation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); rather, it is the observation that the obstacles to that concentration—namely, the obstacles of suffering, coarseness, and so forth—are the objects of this contemplation.
[Commentary: There is an interpretation stating that when one attains the third fruit, the intent of this question is as follows:

if, during the time of suppressing afflictions through the sixfold practice of the contaminated path (*sāsrava-mārga*), one does not suppress the two views of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), then it is like a person who has already attained the fruit [of stream-enterer] by means of the prior contaminated path.

One must first subdue the afflictions before entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*). At the time of severing the afflictions, although one may sever the six categories of both discriminative and innate afflictions, one does not realize the second fruit;

rather, one proceeds directly toward the third fruit. Since the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) were not previously subdued [at the stage of the first fruit], it is clear that they are not severed [at the second];
how, then, could one attain the third fruit?

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "as with the seventh consciousness" up to "it only obstructs those in the stage of no-more-learning," the meaning is as follows: this is an answer to an objection.

The response states that although one does not suppress the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) [at this stage], nor can one sever it, this does not prevent one from realizing the third fruit (*anāgāmiphala*).

Just so, the view of self within the seventh consciousness cannot be severed until one reaches the diamond-like path of immediate succession (*vajropamasamantamārga*), at which point one realizes the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*).
In this context, it is also possible that one attains the fruit of realization only upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), at which point one finally abandons [the defilements].

However, if one interprets it in this way, it contradicts the lower treatise, which does not permit a noble one (*ārya*) to first arise in a higher realm and subsequently abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) of a lower realm. Because of this difficulty, there is a second interpretation, which states:
"They are also abandoned"—an illustrative example of which can be understood [from the text].

[Commentary]: "Those who do not submit to delusions regarding principles" refers specifically to those who do not submit to delusions of discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*). This is because once that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) has been attained, it is possible for all [delusions] to manifest;
furthermore, having already attained it, one is able to freely access the fundamental dhyāna (*mauladhyāna*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "The subsequent discrimination... to "...for us," the meaning is as follows:

Although one does not suppress the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—both discriminative and innate—while practicing meditative concentration, once that concentration is attained, the discriminative [view of a self] and the view of a self of the higher stages can arise. Question:

If this is so, why does the text below ask, "Since one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the lower stage, why do the afflictions of the higher stage not arise? Answer: It is based on the fact that they have not yet...
"One who has attained meditative concentration" refers to the questioner.
[Commentary] "As with the mind at the moment of death, one may also give rise to a higher [state]" is an illustration;

that is, among the nine types of minds at the time of death, after having already attained meditative concentration, at the moment of death one may give rise to higher afflictions and be reborn in a higher realm. Now, one attains that concentration.
Nor does it obstruct the arising of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth belonging to that [future] stage,

because this mind at the moment of death gives rise to craving by taking as its object the phenomena of the stage where one is to be reborn; thus, while it takes the future location as its object and gives rise to craving,
it does not grasp the phenomena of the stage where one is to be reborn as "self."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "fearing lest they become confused": if it were as some claim—that an ordinary person who has not yet abandoned the defilements of a lower realm can give rise to [afflictions] of a higher realm—this would be incorrect, for there are two faults.
First, there is the fault of contradiction: if the defilements of the lower realm have not been subdued, how could one give rise to those of the higher realm?

Second, there is the fault of confusion: the afflictions of the two realms would then tend to become intermingled; or else, the afflictions of the higher realm ought to be considered defiled [by the lower]. Such would be the consequence.
The defiled dharmas of the two realms are so because they are mutually intermingled.
[Commentary]: If this is so, regarding whether the delusions of view arise or do not arise when one emerges from meditative absorption, the intent of the question is as follows:

Suppose a person here first attains the fundamental dhyāna of a higher stage, and subsequently, after emerging from that absorption, gives rise to a mind of the desire realm; at that time, would the delusions of the desire realm arise?

Question: Did the afflictions of the realm (*dhātu*) not previously submit to the delusions of discrimination (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*)? Answer: It is said that they arise as "superior" (*śreṣṭha*), as explained in the *Yanmi* (Secret Commentary).

If one were to regress from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they would invariably arise; however, since this treatise concerns non-retrogression, their arising is determined according to the commentary.

There is no explicit textual judgment in the answer, but it refers to the *Shuyao* (Essential Pivot), which permits the meaning that they arise as "superior. This is what is meant by the statement: "Having become free from the defilements (*rajas*) of this stage..."

Regarding the phrase "those in that stage" (*tadbhūmikāḥ*) and so forth, the intended meaning is that one who is free from the defilements of a particular stage and is born in a higher stage gives rise only to the craving and views of the higher stage, but does not give rise to the discriminative afflictions (*vikalpaka-kleśa*) of the lower stage;

this is exactly the same as the present case. As for the statement in the *Pañcāśatikā* (Treatise on the Fifty) that "one born in a lower stage gives rise to [afflictions] of the higher stage," this is identical to the present case;
it does not mean that by attaining a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of that higher stage, one gives rise to the afflictions of the lower stage—this is what is identical to the present case.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because at this present time there arises a subsequent existence" (*paścādbhava*): "this present time" refers to being precisely in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
"Because there arises a subsequent existence" means that since one has already received a body in the intermediate state, it is clearly evident that a subsequent existence-body will follow;
therefore, the intermediate state arises. Below, the false view of denying the existence of *nirvāṇa* is mentioned; this explains the intent behind such a denial of *nirvāṇa*.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement, "Because wrong views in the form realm do not bring about suffering of the lower realms," the intended meaning is as follows:

since wrong views in the form realm cannot produce the karmic fruit of suffering in the desire realm, it is clearly understood that wrong views pertaining to the desire realm must arise within that [form realm].

[Commentary: The statement that "the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises at the time of birth" refers to the Abhidharma teaching that the intermediate state arises when one gives rise to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
[Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "the intermediate state of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) reaches the ordinary state (*pṛthagjana-bhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) until the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*)," the intention is to challenge the Sarvāstivāda.

"Many" refers to their calculation that because one perceives the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) while in the fundamental existence (*pūrvabhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one then gives rise to slander.
Therefore, the present objection asks: "Since the fundamental existence of the desire realm is neither fixed nor supernormal, how could it perceive the intermediate existence of the form realm?

The intended meaning is that even the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhibala*) is permitted to see the intermediate existence, yet it is not permitted to see the fundamental existence, let alone death.
At birth, one must necessarily abide in a distracted state of mind.
[Commentary: It is not the case that one arrives at this understanding of "non-existence" by giving rise to wrong views regarding the higher realms; rather, one should raise the following objection:

"It is not by means of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) giving rise to wrong views regarding the form realm as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that the karma of the desire realm destined for retribution in hell ripens and leads directly to rebirth."

Regarding the *naraka* (hell realms), there is the view of ancient masters who claim that it is due to wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) belonging to the upper realms acting as a condition that causes the fruit of karma to ripen for a future retribution in hell;
this is incorrect. [The *Śū* commentary states:

Nor is it the case that those [beings] originally possess such wrong views, because the power [of such views] would be too remote; nor is it the case that they [originally] belong to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*).
"There are those who give rise to false views.
[Commentary: If that were so, then the thought directed toward the realm [of form] would itself be [the karma]. This objection regarding the mind states:

if one says that within the realm of form there arises a view belonging to a lower realm, then unwholesome karma of the lower realms must be set in motion by the factor of ignorance (avidyā) of the upper realm; thus, it would follow that this [upper realm] is itself the karma.
This refers to volition (cetanā) associated with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, regarding the statement "as below, so above," it may be objected:
"If [a dharma] of a higher stage functions by being activated by ignorance (*avidyā*) of a lower stage, what prevents [a dharma] of a lower stage from being activated by ignorance of a higher stage?
Therefore, it is said, "as below, so above, is likewise. This will be analyzed in the section on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the craving that moistens rebirth arises from the lower realms down to the neutral [states]," the meaning is as follows:

when one is in a higher realm and is about to be born into a lower one, one gives rise to innate, neutral greed and other afflictions of the lower realm to moisten the process of rebirth. Thus, we know that while in a higher realm, one gives rise to craving and ignorance of the lower realm.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "the craving that moistens rebirth arises from the lower realms down to the neutral afflictions," some say it refers to "moistening."

[Question: "The arising of craving should also be associated with false views; the same applies to the moistening by thought. [Answer: That is also the case; it should likewise be understood that [craving] is produced by the ignorance of the higher realms.
[Commentary: Regarding the point here that [the text] does not mention [this], the intended meaning is that when one is in a higher realm and is about to be born into a lower one...

When the ground arises, moisture, birth, and craving occur simultaneously; at that same time, the four factors of self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), conceit (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and [craving] are also obtained.
For instance, while ignorance and craving must definitely be accompanied by the other two factors, their presence or absence is not fixed.
Therefore, only self-craving and ignorance are mentioned, and conceit and the other two are not. They are not mentioned because they are not fixed.

Regarding the statement that craving arises toward the place of rebirth (*upapatti-bhava*) alone: this refers to the arising of craving toward the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) that is about to be born;
it does not refer to the initial arising of craving toward the fundamental existence (*mūla-bhava*) of the place of rebirth, because the latter is remote.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it arises by way of analogy," the intended meaning is as follows: This second interpretation allows for the arising of pride (*māna*) and so forth, just as when craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises toward phenomena belonging to a future birth, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) can occur.
This is because the mode of activity of the view of self—which requires taking a self as its object—is concordant with the mode of activity of craving;
since craving arises only when there is a view of self, one also gives rise to pride by conceiving the preceding object to be superior. Thus, [this includes] ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because this is universally established, it is not mentioned here. It is asked:

regarding what was said about the four [afflictions] beginning with self-love (*ātmasneha*), do these arise toward external objects, or do they arise toward one's own person, or do they arise at the very beginning of existence? Answer:

These four dharmas can arise toward both external objects and one's own person. According to the treatises, their arising toward external objects is predominant, because of what was stated previously.
"Because [other factors] arise therein.

[Commentary: The intention behind citing this as a partial illustration is as follows: if one were to say that four dharmas arise, why does it specifically mention the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)?

The answer is that, according to the actual reality, pride (*māna*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and so forth also arise; however, because this is merely a brief citation of a general principle (*pradeśa*), they are not mentioned here.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the other three views, doubt, and so forth arise from these," this refers to the text of this assembly. As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states, that one born in the higher realms does not give rise to [afflictions] of the lower realms has two meanings: first, it is based on the majority; second, it conforms to our own school’s tenets. When it says "does not arise," it is based on the majority.

Within this basis on the majority, there are two aspects: first, regarding the period of time; second, regarding the number of afflictions. As for the latter: ... [The text continues with a detailed analysis of the relationship between the higher and lower realms, the nature of the afflictions, and the conditions under which they may or may not manifest. ... Regarding the period of time: although one born in the higher realms may have previously cultivated the seeds of lower-realm afflictions, because those afflictions have been suppressed by the power of the superior meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), they do not manifest during that lifetime. However, if one were to fall from that state, they would again give rise to them. Therefore, it is said that they "do not arise" based on the fact that they do not manifest during the specific period of that birth. Regarding the number of afflictions:

among the various categories of afflictions, those of the higher realms are fewer in number and less intense than those of the lower realms. Because the afflictions of the higher realms are subtle and weak, they lack the power to trigger the manifestation of the grosser afflictions of the lower realms while one remains in the higher state. Thus, it is said that they "do not arise" based on the quantitative disparity between the two. (Note: The ellipsis indicates the continuation of the technical commentary on the *Yogācāra* system.)

Regarding "time," it refers to the time of denying cessation (*nirodha*) and the time of moistening rebirth (*upapatti-pratisaṃdhi*); only during these two times do [afflictions] arise, while at other times they do not.

As for the number of afflictions that arise, either three or six do so—namely, the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), anger (*krodha*), and false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), etc.—whereas doubt (*vicikitsā*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) never arise at all.
This is based on the fact that these latter ones do not arise; for the most part, they are conducive to existence (*bhava*).
"School" (zong) refers here to the Sarvāstivāda school; according to that school, because one who has attained a higher stage does not give rise to [afflictions] of a lower stage.
[Commentary: Regarding the question, "Can the remaining afflictions—both discriminative (*vikalpita*) and innate (*sahaja*)—also arise? the intended meaning is as follows:
apart from the three views and doubt, can the remaining six factors—which comprise both the discriminative and innate types—arise collectively? This is the general inquiry.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "seeing that anger, delusion, and wrong view are severed up to the point where they do not arise," the meaning is as follows:
In the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), anger, delusion, and wrong view arise at the stage of reviling cessation (*nirodha*), but do not arise at other times.

As for the afflictions of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), such as pride, they arise during the stage of "moistening birth" (*janma-sneha*)—that is, when craving and so forth are active—but it is not admitted that they arise at other times; furthermore, there is no further path of cultivation [beyond this].

Because hatred (*dveṣa*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) do not arise during the stage of moistening birth (*upapattibhava*), as they lack the aspect of volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*), there is also no [hatred or extreme view] at the stage of deceiving regarding cessation (*nirodha*).
There are those who say that hatred on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) does not arise therein;
however, it is admitted that at the initial stage of moistening birth, one may give rise to both hatred and affection toward one's parents. Thus, the view of extremes is also absent.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that there is no explicit textual authority for the general explanation of the arising [of afflictions], the intended meaning is that the absence of such a text serves to prevent their arising.
As for the other commentaries’ analysis of innate (*sahaja*) and acquired (*parikalpita*) [afflictions] according to what is appropriate, this follows the preceding [discussion].

Furthermore, the assignment of those aforementioned arising [afflictions] and the subsequent innate and acquired afflictions is to be correlated exactly as was done previously according to what is appropriate.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "The lower [levels] give rise to the upper, up to the point where there is no fault," the intended meaning is as follows: If one is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and attains the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), it is possible for five kinds of afflictions (*kleśa*) to arise.
These are: (1) the view of grasping at views (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*), because one may grasp the dharmas of the higher stages as being superior and capable of purification;

(2) pride (*māna*), because one may possess pride regarding those meditative absorptions; and (3) doubt (*vicikitsā*), because one may doubt whether the dharmas of the higher stages are superior or inferior.
Since it is universally established that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) serve as conditions for rebirth in the higher realms, the text does not explicitly mention them.

However, when one desires to die and be reborn in a higher plane of existence, there must necessarily be the "I-making" (*asmimāna*) and the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) to moisten the process of rebirth; therefore, these are called the "afflictions of birth.

These arise specifically through the moistening influence of the view of self and so forth. Furthermore, the term "afflictions of birth" applies generally to the aforementioned [lower realms] as well, and other three [types of afflictions] may also arise.

The non-arising [of views] is distinguished by the commentary itself regarding the arising of the nine dharmas above; because there is no hatred toward the higher realms, only nine are mentioned. [Commentary]:

To attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives and reckon the Brahmā King as eternal is wrong view. This is because reckoning the Brahmā King of the higher realm as eternal does not arise based on the view of self (*ātman*).
If it were based on the view of self, yet one further reckons him as either annihilated or eternal, then it is [wrong view].
[Included] within the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

[Commentary: As for the statement that one has not yet seen the arising of the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), it refers to the text concerning its conceptualization. According to the *Saptabhaṅgī-vicāra-śāstra*, one conceives of the lower realms as giving rise to the view of annihilation in the higher realms;
based on the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), and because that conception arises from the self, one gives rise to [the view of annihilation] by reckoning that there is cessation after death.

Regarding "that view of annihilationism" (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*), it may be that this view of annihilationism relies upon the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) while conceiving of the cessation and extinction of the bodies belonging to the higher realms.

[Commentary]: Regarding the question, "In how many of the nine stages of the three realms can one give rise to views of the higher [realms]?"—this is a general inquiry concerning how many dharmas of the higher realms can arise from within each of the nine stages of the three realms.
It should be understood that this applies even down to the two realms and eight stages; one should reflect upon how many such dharmas can arise from below.
Excluding the desire realm, for the two realms and eight stages, it is all as in the *Juyao* (Essential Points).

[Treatise] Regarding the statement that "the afflictions of lower stages also take higher stages as objects," there are two passages in the treatise: first the heading and then the explanation; this is the heading.

The section beginning with "The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, etc. is the explanation. Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, taking higher stages as objects, and second, taking lower stages as objects. As for the former:

Regarding the first [type of craving], which takes the upper realms as its object, there are four [afflictions]: first, greed; second, hatred; third, the view of self-existence (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and pride; and fourth, the explanation of the remaining [afflictions].
This is the first, greed. [Commentary:

"Because the case of hatred taking the upper realms as its object is analogous to the principle" means that this treatise uses the example of delusion regarding the upper realms to illustrate what is logically equivalent.
If one is still deluded regarding even profound principles, how much more so regarding shallow matters!

[Commentary]: Regarding the "inherently mixed and co-arising entities" belonging to the lower and upper stages—that is, all the co-arising phenomena within a single body in this desire realm that extend across the lower and upper realms—one fails to discern their distinctions and instead grasps them collectively as a mere mixture.

I am also [the object] of the innate, generalizing view of self (*sahaja-sāmānyālambanātma-dṛṣṭi*); the discriminative view of self (*vikalpitātma-dṛṣṭi*) is not mentioned here because it arises by taking specific phenomena as its objects.
Therefore, it is said that the view of self on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) clings to one's own body as being the self.
[Commentary] "The blending of the body" means that the dharmas of the upper realms and the self-substance of the five aggregates of the lower stages are blended together in one place.
When taking them as an object, because one does not observe their distinctions but takes them collectively as an object, one is able to take the dharmas of the upper stages as objects.
"As explained previously" means that, as stated before, this should be applied analogously to the Truth of Suffering; it need not be explained for each individual truth.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "the worldly path up to pride," the intended meaning is that the sixfold worldly path is able to suppress the greed and hatred of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), as well as the pride that is proximate to such greed.
This is termed "proximate" because it arises simultaneously with and is associated with views of self and what belongs to self (*ātma-ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, since it does not mention the suppression or abandonment of other dharmas, we know this refers to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, why is it that the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), along with greed and the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), cannot be subdued simultaneously?

It is because they arise in close proximity to the view of self. However, the previous statement regarding the eighty-eight [defilements]—that the view of self is not subdued—takes the view of self as the primary basis;
thus, while the view of self is explicitly mentioned, other factors such as greed are omitted for brevity. Moreover, this treatise states "in general."

Regarding those who, based on conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), grasp at a self and what belongs to a self, and harbor views of annihilationism or eternalism along with pride— the term "those who are greedy" is also used here as an abbreviation.

As for the mention of a separate treatise by the commentator, this refers to the aforementioned passage from the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi* concerning the seeking of birth in higher realms and the savoring of higher meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).

[Commentary]: This statement that the sixth consciousness is severed only by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) means that the universal objectifying view of self (*sarvatraga-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) within the sixth consciousness is an innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and therefore it is severed through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
[Commentary]: There is another interpretation which holds that the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) extends even to taking the three realms as a combined object to constitute a self.
This is because one first takes all phenomena of the three realms as a general object and conceives of them as a self; based on this, one subsequently conceives of them as permanent.

Since one conceives of the self and the world—whether belonging to others or oneself, or to higher or lower realms—as permanent, the totalizing objectification (*parikalpa*) thus also includes the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). This is the intended meaning.
The conceptualized view of self (*parikalpita-ātmadṛṣṭi*) is said to be distinct because it takes [the aggregates] collectively as its object.

Since there are scriptural passages stating that the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātmadṛṣṭi*) also takes them collectively as its object, this [distinction] specifically clarifies their similarities and differences. If they were not different, how could one conceive of another's self?
Therefore, the conceptualized view of self first grasps the phenomena of the three realms collectively as "self," and only thereafter conceives of it as being entirely permanent and so forth.

Furthermore, for example, if the view of permanence arises after the view of self based on the view of self, and if one does not aggregate the three realms and take them collectively as a self, how could there be a view of permanence that conceives of [the self] as entirely eternal? Since the view of permanence universally applies to the conception of total eternity, the view of self is likewise so; therefore, it is said that the four [views] are entirely eternal. Question: Is that which is regarded as "mine" grasped as the self? Does it encompass both one's own and others' selves? Answer: Some say that although this is a conceptual discrimination, it is a universalizing view of self (*sāmānyātma-dṛṣṭi*).

Because it perceives the five aggregates over twenty kalpas and so forth, it collectively reckons the five aggregates of both oneself and others as being one's own or another's self, and as permanent.
This grasping conforms to the view of a world that is coextensive with the view of a permanent self.
Furthermore, those that are subsumed under "commonly seen" (sādhāraṇa-dṛṣṭi) are, when they arise subsequently, simply false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

[Commentary: Hatred (*dveṣa*) has only specific objects (*viśeṣālambana*), as it takes the dharmas of oneself or others as its object; this differs from view (*dṛṣṭi*) and pride (*māna*), which take the dharmas of the three realms collectively as their objects, such as by conceiving them as "self" or "mine."
[Commentary] There is an interpretation that the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) reach up to and take the higher realms as their objects.

This explanation holds that when ordinary beings in the desire realm hold the Brahmā King of the higher realms to be the self, they give rise to the view of extremes based upon this; thus, these two views are conceptually constructed and can take dharmas of other stages as their objects.

Regarding the statement below that "one does not see [the self] in the world," which refers to holding the dharmas of another stage to be the self, the subsequent passage clarifies that this is not the case.
There is no logical contradiction in regarding [the self] as "I" or regarding another as "I.

[Commentary: One who attains superior dharmas by disparaging others does so because they have attained the superior dharmas within the body through meditative concentration (dhyāna) gained by disparaging others with the pride (māna) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "it takes one portion of the Brahmā King as its object, such as permanence," the intended meaning is that the view of permanence arises subsequent to the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) in the higher realms;

it is not a view belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Since he has already attained the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of those upper realms, how could he further give rise to the views of self and extremes (*ātmagrāha-antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) of the lower realm to take that Brahmā King as its object?
Therefore, this view of permanence is bound to the higher realms, and thus there is no acquisition of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
The phrase "subsequently arising alongside the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth" may also refer to what arises after emerging from meditative concentration.

[Commentary: The statement "speaking according to coarse characteristics" is intended to resolve textual contradictions. This means that the minds of the Hīnayāna are coarse and their understanding is shallow;

they only give rise to greed by taking present objects as their conditions, and it is not permitted for them to give rise to craving by taking dharmas of higher stages as objects. The rest should be understood accordingly.
[Commentary]: "Or, as for the passage in the *Abhidharma* (the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*) from the sixth chapter up to 'it should be so,' this refers to the preceding Abhidharma text which states:
'That view of self does not take the higher realms as its object; it is omitted that the view of extremes [does not do so]. How is this known? The explanation says:

Since the view of extremes must necessarily rely upon the view of self, how much more so when it does not take those [higher realms] as its object—it is clear that the view of extremes likewise does not take them as its object. Therefore, it is said, 'it should be so.'"

[Commentary: Therefore, from the fifty-eighth [verse] up to the point where it says "arising with respect to the higher [realms]," this statement that one takes the Great Brahmā King as being permanent is merely a *dṛṣṭi* (view), not an *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* (extreme view).

This is because it does not arise subsequent to a *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (self-view) directed toward that object. Furthermore, even the *mithyādṛṣṭi* (false view) below can take the higher realms as its object.

If one were to say that this is an *antagrāhadṛṣṭi*, it would necessarily follow that it arises subsequent to a *satkāyadṛṣṭi* regarding other phenomena; however, since such a *satkāyadṛṣṭi* does not exist...
The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) in the higher realms cannot exclusively take phenomena of other [lower] levels as permanent.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "all sixty-two views arise subsequent to the view of permanence and so forth," this means that even those who hold a complete view of permanence do so because it arises after the view of self (*ātman*) in the higher realms.
As for the previous commentary’s mention of "some offer a different interpretation," this was merely intended to guard against [the possibility of] misinterpreting the object of cognition.

This is an explanation based on a different interpretation; the previous [explanation] stated that the lower [level] conditions the upper, but the present intention is not so. The subsequent proof states:
"Next, the Commentary says it is the 'view of extremes regarding other levels' (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which arises following the 'view of self regarding other levels' (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, the phrase "as previously explained" refers back to what was stated above—or perhaps there is an alternative textual interpretation. The latter statement, "it is the view of extremes regarding other levels," etc., is precisely the explanation.
This is one sense of the meaning of "eternalism" (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
[The *Śū* (Commentary) states: Regarding the passage from "One interpretation says... to "...because it arises in dependence upon that," the intended meaning is as follows:

Since the conceptual view of a separate self (*pṛthag-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) cannot be apprehended within the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is clearly understood that the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) is likewise [inapprehensible] regarding the phenomena (*dharma*) of other stages (*bhūmi*). Why is this? Because of the view of extremes...
"Because it necessarily arises subsequent to the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), this [view] is not permitted to take that as its object.

[Commentary: This second interpretation, which reaches this point, is highly reasonable. It permits that one portion of those with the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) may take the aforementioned [Brahmā] as their object.
How is this known? It is because there are non-Buddhists who, having studied that meditative concentration (*samādhi*), attain the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) to universally perceive Brahmā.

The King, for my sake, gave rise to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); because he subsequently clings to one part as being eternal and so forth, the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) can also be said to take the higher realms as its object.

This statement is extremely reasonable. However, is it not the case that this is not universal? Answer: It is admitted that those who give rise to [the view] based on the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) may take the higher realms as their object, as has been stated.
However, if it arises from a distracted mind involving discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), then it cannot take the higher realms as its object.

Therefore, it is said that these are not "beyond" (na-ūrdhva-bhūmika). The meaning of this external [objection] is as follows: although what was stated previously is indeed highly reasonable, the principles involved differ.

If [the mind] can access [a higher level], it is permitted to take the higher level as its object; if it cannot access it, taking the higher level as an object is not permitted. Thus, they are different. As for the phrase "as previously explained":

if one considers the state of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) within a distracted mind, then one cannot take the higher level as an object, just as in the first explanation above.
The refusal [of this] is because I perceive that there is a self belonging to a higher stage.
[Commentary: Now, another interpretation should state that it is merely the self belonging to one's own body within the desire realm; even from the perspective of ultimate truth, this is not denied.
This interpretation is no different [from the previous one], but it further provides a reasoning to show that one does not perceive the grasping of dharmas belonging to other stages as [one's own].

Regarding the statement, "My teaching and this [text] should be spoken of as either based on specific conditions or as being real," if one attempts to reconcile these points, the underlying principle is difficult to fathom.

[Commentary: Furthermore, the alternative explanation that "specific conditions" refers to "the self as a condition" is an interpretation of the term "self-condition" (*ātma-pratyaya*) within the treatise.

Therefore, the meaning is clearly revealed: these two periods are distinguished based on their respective objects. For the most part, the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not take the higher realms as its object;

however, according to the actual fact, a portion of this view of self that takes the eternal as its object can indeed take the higher realms as its object. Regarding these two periods: first, it is based on coarse characteristics;

second, it is based on specific objects. It is stated that the view of self does not take the higher realms as its object based on these two periods, yet there is also the claim that specific objects are for the most part [those of the higher realms].

The meaning is that, apart from these aforementioned views of self that take the aggregate as their object, there are no other views of self—whether innate (*sahaja*) or conceptual (*vikalpita*)—that take phenomena of other stages as their objects;
it is based on this principle that they are said to be "for the most part" [not so].

[Commentary]: Regarding "condition" (*pratyaya*), it refers to the reason for reaching that [object]. As for "not conditioning" (*na pratyayati*), the intended meaning is that there is a distinct condition; "distinct condition" carries the sense of "reason.
Because one does not conceive of the phenomena of other stages as being the self, based on this reason, it is said that there is no conditioning of the higher [stages].

Some say that "distinct condition" has the sense of "for the most part" (*bhūyastvena*); the intention is that, apart from these cases of collective conditioning and so forth, other afflictions possess distinct conditions.
"Because they are distinct, they do not take the higher [realms] as objects. "Distinct" (*bhinna*) means "in many parts," while "taking as an object" (*ālambana*) means "the reason for [cognition].

[Commentary: Another interpretation states that when the Hīnayāna speaks of "distinct objects," it refers to the assertion of the *Vibhajyavāda* school that they do not take the higher [realms] as objects.
However, within our own school (*svayūthya*), those who maintain that a portion of [phenomena] is eternal may also take the higher [realms] as objects.

[Commentary: Regarding the principle that it is admitted that the arising of views lacks a "shaft" (i.e., a specific object), this is the same as what was stated above; however, there may be alternative interpretations of the meaning.

That is to say, within the context of the "permanence" [view], the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) through discrimination can also take the totality as its object. Nevertheless, while there is no explicit textual evidence proving that the view of self on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) takes the totality as its object, there is indeed textual evidence for it.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because of doubting the Buddha of the realm," this means that by citing the Buddha, the doubt concerning the higher realms is revealed—specifically, the act of requesting his disciples to preach the Dharma and so forth.
Since the World-Honored One is not bound to the Desire Realm, he is not included [in that category].

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "denying the principle of suffering and its origin in the lower realms," this refers to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) which denies the principle of suffering and its origin in the lower realms, as well as doubt (*vicikitsā*) regarding that principle.
Because cessation and the path do not belong to the lower realms, they are not mentioned; therefore, it speaks only of the principle of suffering and its origin in the lower realms.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the two types of grasping (dṛṣṭi-grāha and śīla-vrata-parāmarśa) arise, with those previously generated through hearing and reflection in the desire realm serving as the predominant causes," some say:
first, in the desire realm, one gives rise to false views through hearing and reflection, such as reckoning [wrong views] to be *nirvāṇa*;

subsequently, when one is born in a higher stage, one then gives rise to the grasping of those prior views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), and further grasps the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) associated with those views as being the [true] precepts (*śīla*). This is what is meant.
"Grasping at a superior cause" means precisely grasping at that which is a superior cause as being a superior cause.

[Commentary] Regarding the "as before" in the phrase "the mode of activity is as before": it refers to the fact that, by depending on conditions within the desire realm, the two types of grasping (dualistic attachment) can arise from past hearing and reflection;
therefore, it is said to be "as before."
[Commentary]: "At all other times" refers to all other occasions when [the mind] does not take [them] as objects.

"Because they are all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)" means that since those ordinary beings do not hold views such as the eternalism of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they do not take [those objects] as their focus; therefore, it is said they are "mostly" [not so].
Furthermore, if the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) take the self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as their general object, they may also take lower realms as their object.

[Treatise] Regarding the question of which of these ten afflictions are abandoned by what means, within the ninth "Gate of the Threefold Abandonment," there are four sub-sections. First is the "Gate of the Threefold Abandonment.
Now, regarding the delusion concerning the characteristics of the Truths (*satya*), there are both general and specific aspects.

The following two sections—the "Gate of General and Specific Delusion Concerning the Truths" and the "Gate of Direct and Indirect Delusion Concerning the Truths"—specifically address how doubt and three views are directly deluded regarding the principle of suffering (*duḥkha*), and so forth. The treatise provides a detailed analysis of these.
The following four points clarify the gate of delusion regarding principle and phenomena.

[Commentary]: Now, as for the question of whether what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) is the same as the Lesser Vehicle’s abandonment of the Four Truths through nine grades, this is intended to raise an inquiry into the meaning of the treatise;
it asks whether it is the same as the Lesser Vehicle’s abandonment through the sixteen moments of mind during the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
Are the afflictions of the cultivated stage (*bhāvanā-heya*) abandoned through nine distinct categories?

[The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Because it corresponds with the wisdom of up to three categories regarding the destruction of the conditions of the truths. The intended meaning is as follows: "Destruction" (*huài*) here means "intermingled" (*zá*).

This untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), associated with untainted mental attention (*manasikāra*), intermingledly takes the suchness (*tathatā*) of the four truths as its object; this is called "comprehensive objectification" (*sāmānya-ālambana*).
Question: Since afflictions are indeed of nine grades, how can they be severed all at once? Answer:
Although there are nine grades, because they contradict the one True Suchness—or the three minds—they are both severed instantaneously within these two types of paths.
Question: Regarding the contradiction of the one True Suchness, if one realizes the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one may obtain the instantaneous dharma, as in the case of the three minds.

Question: Since the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the path of seeing through images (*sākṣātkāra-darśana-mārga*), how can it also sever the afflictions (*kleśa*)? First, the internal elimination of the provisional designation of sentient beings through wisdom that takes conditions as its object, which can eliminate the inferior-grade latent tendencies of conceptualization;

second, the internal elimination of the provisional designations of both sentient beings and phenomena through wisdom that takes conditions as its object, which can eliminate the middle-grade latent tendencies of conceptualization;

third, the universal elimination of the provisional designations of all sentient beings and phenomena through wisdom that takes conditions as its object, which can eliminate the superior-grade latent tendencies of conceptualization. These constitute the three minds.
Question: Do the three grades of wisdom in the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) collectively eliminate all afflictions? Answer: They do collectively eliminate them.

Specifically, the lower-grade wisdom eliminates the lower-grade afflictions and the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) associated with those afflictions; the middle-grade wisdom eliminates the middle-grade afflictions and the two obstacles associated with those afflictions;
and the upper-grade wisdom eliminates the upper-grade afflictions and the two obstacles associated with those afflictions. It is only thus.
Regarding the three grades of afflictions based on their conditions, the wisdom attained is likewise of three types, with differences in the mental states.

In each case, one gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), until the third mental state is fulfilled; at this point, it is termed the fulfillment of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

If, as previously mentioned, one were to realize the principle of the path of seeing through only one or two mental states and so forth, the realization would be partial and not complete. Therefore, such a person possesses dull faculties and inferior wisdom; however, if they are sharp...

Regarding the "roots," because the single mind of the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) suddenly cuts off the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is asked: among these three minds of the path of seeing, are they real or provisional?
Now, when it is said that they cut off afflictions, are they real or provisional? The answer is: since it is stated that they cut off afflictions, how could they be called provisional?

Therefore, they are simply called real. According to this treatise, these three minds—whether they be the path of seeing of characteristics (*lakṣaṇadarśanamārga*) or the three minds of yoga—are [all real].

How should one interpret this regarding the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)? The answer is that the *Yogācārabhūmi* explains it based on the individual paths of seeing for those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and thus there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "because it corresponds with the mental application (*manasikāra*) directed toward the truths and persists until it contradicts one or three grades of knowledge," some say that the meaning here differs from the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), where the sixteen moments of mind (*ṣoḍaśa-citta*) involve distinct mental applications directed toward each object.

This refers to the severing of delusions (*kleśa*). This answers the previous point regarding how [the Mahāyāna] differs from the Śrāvaka vehicle in severing delusions through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).

While those Śrāvakas sever delusions by focusing on the truths collectively through mental attention (*manaskāra*)—wherein the universal object of cognition (*ālambana*) is the principle of the truths, yet because the individual aspects of the cognition (*ālambaka*) are unable to sever the delusions—here in the Mahāyāna, "collective focus" (*samastālambana*) is termed "embracing focus" (*parigrahālambana*).
This means that while it universally focuses on the Four Truths, it does not engage in separate analytical contemplation of each one; thus, it is called "embracing focus. Furthermore...
To designate [feelings] as "neither-suffering-nor-non-suffering" and so forth is called "embracing conditions. This contradicts the view that there is one mind for each [truth].

If there are three minds for the path of seeing (darśanamārga), then there are indeed three minds for the path of seeing. This answers the previous objection regarding the abandonment of the nine grades through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Furthermore, another interpretation states that these ten afflictions collectively constitute the Four Noble Truths; thus, when one contemplates the suchness (tathatā) of the Four Noble Truths...
Because these ten afflictions are abandoned simultaneously through the four [noble truths], they are associated with the attention that takes the truths as its object in their entirety—
that is, with untainted true knowledge (*anāsrava-bhūta-jñāna*). At the time of taking the truths as an object in their entirety,
one is able to abandon the afflictions because they are mutually contradictory and do not arise together.

[Commentary]: This means that unlike the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), which consist of nine grades and oppose nine grades of wisdom—whereby a single arising of an innate affliction requires the arising of nine paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) to sever and realize their abandonment—the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are not like this, and thus they are severed all at once.
Furthermore, this excludes those of sharp faculties who have reached the attainment of the fourth [dhyāna].
As for the "fruit," the intended meaning is to exclude those of sharp faculties; that is to say, this person, by the power of prior hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*),
subsequently applies effort (*prayoga*) through the mind, and bundles the eighty-one grades of afflictions across the nine stages of the three realms into nine categories,
taking the highest-grade afflictions of the lower stages together with the highest-grade afflictions of the upper stages as a single category, and so on down to the desire realm.
The lowest-of-the-low grade of each realm and the non-total lowest-of-the-low grade are also combined into a single grade;

thus, they are collectively nine grades, through which one gives rise to nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) to realize the fourth fruit.
[Commentary]: "General" refers to the ten types [of afflictions] up to those that are deluded regarding the Four Truths.
The meaning is that whenever any single affliction arises, it universally deludes the principle of the Four Truths; therefore, they are called "general."
[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the various afflictions have distinct modes of activity," the explanation is as follows:

when one is deluded regarding a single Truth, such as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), at that time, wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and so forth, are direct delusions; the subsequent arising of independent greed (*rāga*), pride (*māna*), and so on, following this view and doubt, are all termed "distinct delusions.
Regarding the phrase "in each individual Truth, it is called 'delusion of this,'" the intended meaning is that although there is a general mode of activity, there are also specific ones.
Regarding the nature of these modes of activity (*ākāra*), if one were to claim that they are distinct for each truth—

such that one is deluded only by suffering and not by the other three truths like origination and so forth— how could such [limited] modes of activity be called afflictions? They must, in fact, possess all ten delusions beneath each respective truth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "If it were only thus" to "subsumed under which truth," the intent is to challenge the previous master’s position. It says:

If you claim that those [afflictions] arising after doubt following the view of suffering (duḥkha-satya) can be designated as having distinct modes of activity (ākāra), then consider, for instance, false views, doubt, and delusion (*moha*), which collectively delude one regarding all four truths.
What truth would the greed (*rāga*) and other afflictions arising after such doubt be subsumed under? Would they follow the preceding [truth]?
The intention behind saying that [the specific aspects] are included within the general aspects is as follows:
if one speaks according to the specific aspects, one cannot encompass the general aspects; therefore, it is necessary to further explain the general aspects.
Regarding the statement that "if one speaks according to the specific aspects, the aspects are subsumed up to the object and doubt arises," the meaning is that this refers to the general aspect.
The "aspects" (ākāra) are like the "doubtful view" (*vicikitsā-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth;

since these are universally deluded regarding the Four Truths, it is clearly known that the greed and other afflictions arising subsequently are also called "universal delusion," because the aspects of greed and the others follow the aspects of the views and doubt. Regarding the phrase "Universal delusion may be so":

this concludes the meaning of universal delusion. As for "If [it were] distinct delusion regarding the aspects," and so forth: this is a counter-objection to the previous objection concerning distinct aspects.

If, as I have stated, that which is called "collective mode of activity" (*saṃmugdha-ākāra*) is not as you claim, then under which Truth (*satya*) would independent greed (*kevala-rāga*) and so forth be subsumed?
For independent greed and the like cannot individually delude one regarding the Truths.

Furthermore, it is impossible to say that greed and so forth—which arise subsequent to collective doubt or views—are included within "individual delusion," even though greed and so forth may arise subsequent to doubt during the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
It is known that ignorance, along with doubt and views, are all collectively delusions, as they are equally afflictions of discrimination and arise conditioned by views and doubt.
Regarding these four, when it is said they are "collective," does this refer to their number being collective, or their names being collective?
Or does it mean that their initial modes of activity (*ākāra*) are collective, or their names are collective? Answer: There are two kinds of what is here termed "collective."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that there are now two general types [of objects], up to the "contemplation of the bases as the conditions for destruction," the intended meaning is as follows:

if one calculates them collectively, all four truths each possess ten types; if one considers them by their modes of activity (*ākāra*), every single affliction has the capacity to universally delude regarding the four truths, which is what is meant by "modes of activity.
However, when considering the universal delusion regarding the four truths as a whole, there are eleven phrases, consisting of combinations of two by two.

There are six propositions: (1) confusion regarding suffering and its origin; (2) confusion regarding cessation and the path; (3) confusion regarding suffering and its cessation; (4) confusion regarding the origin and the path;

(5) confusion regarding the origin and its cessation; (6) confusion regarding suffering and the path. If three and two are combined, there are four propositions: (1) the first three, excluding the path;
(2) the last three, excluding suffering; (3) the first two and the fourth; (4) taking the first three as one proposition. Furthermore, there is confusion regarding the whole.
Because the Four Truths constitute a single phrase, there are eleven phrases; alternatively, if one is confused regarding each of the Four Truths individually, there are four phrases.

Combined with the preceding, there are fifteen phrases in total. Regarding those who destroy the mindfulness-establishment based on objects (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*): if the mindfulness-establishment based on objects gives rise to two, three, two, three, or three [subsequent establishments], these are the mixed-object (*vyavakīrṇālambana*) types.
Question: Since there are already two types in the aggregate, I do not yet understand how they are distinguished subsequently.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "There are also two types of distinctions... because they are individually deluded," the meaning is as follows:

"Distinction in number" refers to the fact that there are ten types [of afflictions] under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), whereas under the remaining three Truths there are only eight; this is the distinction in number.

Furthermore, "distinction in mode of activity" (*ākāra*) means that, for example, when greed and other afflictions of the ten realms arise through strong discrimination independently, each is individually deluded regarding suffering.

At the time of suffering, one is deluded only regarding suffering and not regarding the other three; the other three [delusions] regarding the other three [truths] are to be understood by analogy with this, and are therefore called "distinct delusions.
[Commentary]: The first, the locus of causes, is the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya); the second, the locus of dependence, is the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya).
[Commentary]: "Furthermore, because they serve as the basis for these ten" explains the reason why suffering serves as the basis. [Commentary]:

"Cessation and the Path are the objects of their fear" means that because the Truths of Cessation and the Path are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas capable of severing afflictions, certain non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) hold such views regarding the Truths of Cessation and the Path, saying: "Since Cessation and the Path can sever afflictions and so forth..."
This refers to the fear that "I" might exist or the fear that "I" might be annihilated; thus, one gives rise to afflictions and denies the two truths.

Regarding the statement that the ten afflictions arise from delusion regarding the two truths: some say that a "place of fear" (*bhaya-sthāna*) refers merely to conduct that is inconsistent [with one's nature], where such confusion does not increase;
this is explained as creating that fear. Furthermore, it is not the same as suffering (*duḥkha*) or its origin (*samudaya*).
[Regarding] "conjunction with delusion":

[The Commentary] states that because their nature is not conducive to the growth of the ten types [of afflictions], it is explained that the Truths of Cessation and the Path are definitely untainted (*anāsrava*).
Since these [afflictions] can only be diminished and do not increase, one merely gives rise to confusion, denial, hesitation, and so forth regarding the Truths of Cessation and the Path.
"Delusion" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), which negates [the truth] as wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), or is hesitation as doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Furthermore, it is said that because it gives rise to various kinds of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), one may conceive of things as a self (*ātman*) or as arising spontaneously (*svabhāva*), and so forth; this refers to the Truths of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) and the Path (*mārgasatya*).
It is also like the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who conceive of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) as being like the Truth of Cessation, transforming and evolving into the subsequent truths.
[Commentary: Both possess these two; that which is not a causal basis and the locus of fear are called the "two conditions. [Commentary:

Regarding the statement "in reality there are also [cases] reaching the specific and the general," the intended meaning is as follows: if one attains a coarse aspect (*sthūla-lakṣaṇa*) that is specific, then one does not say it possesses both conditions.

However, even according to the subtle aspect (*sūkṣma-lakṣaṇa*), there are cases where there are specific and general [conditions], such as the afflictions (*kleśa*) under the category of suffering (*duḥkha*).

The affliction of *pradāsa* (malice) is exclusively deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and does not extend to the other three truths; the same applies to the other three truths. These are distinct because they are contrary [to the Truth of Suffering] and do not extend [to the others].

This is the specific mode of delusion regarding the characteristics [of suffering]; yet these very afflictions of specific delusion all possess the functional capacity for general delusion regarding the four truths.
Thus, the existence of two conditions is due to the fact that within the former, there is both a general name and a specific one.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the meaning of the passage from "How can it be... up to "...all are deluded regarding the Four Truths," how is it that the three truths of origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*) are reckoned by the two views of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?

Answer: It is said that these two views deeply grasp their objects and fail to understand the three truths, falsely adhering to them as a self (*ātman*) and as phenomena (*dharma*) that are permanent (*nitya*) and so forth;
thus, the two views exist with respect to the three truths. If this is so, then all afflictions (*kleśa*) would be the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Question: Should not all [of these views] be deluded regarding the Four Noble Truths? Why, then, is it said that they arise based on the fruit-aspect of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*)? Answer: It is not so.

When the two [types of] views are deluded regarding the Truth of Suffering, they directly fail to understand and instead cling to the fruit of suffering as being a self, or as being subject to annihilation or permanence (*uccheda-śāśvata*).

As for those that arise by clinging to the other three truths, they merely involve the arising of afflictions (*kleśa*) under the influence of those three truths, along with their false conceptualizations and their concomitants.
To take the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth as a self is not a direct delusion, as it differs from the nature of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*);
therefore, one cannot say that both views are delusions regarding all four truths.

[Treatise] "Specifically" means arising from a specific delusion regarding the characteristics of the four truths, etc.; this explains "specific delusion," meaning [delusion] regarding suffering and the other [truths] individually.
The first, lack of understanding, is called "distinctive delusion. [Commentary:

Regarding the three truths of origin, cessation, and the path, their distinct modes of activity (*ākāra*) are as follows: the origin has the aspects of cause (*hetu*), accumulation (*samudaya*), production (*prabhava*), and condition (*pratyaya*); cessation has the aspects of cessation (*nirodha*), tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*);

the path has the aspects of path (*mārga*), method (*nyāya*), practice (*pratipad*), and deliverance (*nairyāṇika*). These are not like the aspects of emptiness (*śūnya*), selflessness (*anātman*), and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "because the non-concomitant ignorance is deluded regarding the three truths, eight [factors] are established," the intended meaning is as follows:

In the second major section, which explains the specific delusions, there is a question concerning why there are eight factors in relation to the three truths such as the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). For instance, while the other seven [factors] are exclusively delusions regarding the three truths individually, this is not the case here.
Since the associated ignorance is a pervasive delusion, how can it be said to specifically pertain to the three truths of origination and so forth?

If one asks, "Are there then eight [types]? the answer is: because one does not take up associated ignorance (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*), but takes up only unshared ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*), the number eight is established.
Since associated ignorance is a universal delusion, it is known that the specific delusions are spoken of based on the unshared [ignorance].

Because [associated ignorance] cannot directly delude regarding the aspects of the formations (*saṃskāra*), the principle follows what was stated previously: specific delusions are also based on the unshared and solitary [ignorance].

Regarding the statement that "ignorance (avidyā) acts as delusion," if one says this refers to ignorance in its general sense, it is strictly speaking only in reference to associated ignorance (*saṃprayukta-avidyā*).

[Commentary: The reason many reckon the tainted resultant dharmas as being the two views is that they intend to explain the five tainted aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as being the self and reckon them as being subject to annihilation or permanence;
these are precisely the view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). Therefore, these two views mostly operate with respect to the resultant state.
Question: Does the arising [of delusion] occur with respect to the three truths? Answer: It should be understood that the response is "no.

This means it is only a case of being deluded regarding the fruit and grasping it as a self; it does not mean that the arising occurs with respect to the three truths and that one simultaneously realizes the three truths.
[Commentary]: However, in reality, the delusion regarding the three truths also gives rise to two views.

As for the phrase "because it serves as our [object]," this means that the view of self actually takes the three truths as its object—unlike the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which arises only with respect to the fruit.

Since the view of self also arises from afflictions (*kleśa*) underlying the three truths, it is said here that because one is deluded, one subsequently takes those underlying afflictions as an object and clings to them as a self.

[Commentary: However, regarding the distinct conditions for realizing the Truths, there is no contradiction in the subsequent explanation. Emptiness and non-self each have two types: one general and one specific.
The general refers to the Four Truths—namely, the four truths of suffering and so forth—all of which are non-self; therefore, they are termed "non-self. It is not that... [text fragment].

"I speak of it as empty because it is 'mine'"; thus the Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "The general emptiness of non-self applies to all four truths, because it takes the truths collectively as its object.
This is precisely what was established previously when it was said that the True Path of Seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*) takes the truths collectively as its object.

Therefore, the two views [of self and mine] can also take the other three truths as their objects, because they arise from them. Specifically, the suffering of the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is not-self.

Because it is by nature [devoid of self], it is called "non-self"; because it is not "mine," it is described as "empty. Now, this specific principle of emptiness and non-self is subsumed within the Truth of Suffering.
The view of a transitory collection (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) specifically errs regarding the side of non-self, while the view of permanence errs regarding the middle;

the view of annihilationism also errs regarding the side of impermanence, for it mistakenly conceives that what is impermanent does not continue into the future, thereby contradicting the principle of arising and ceasing. Therefore:

The two views are deluded only regarding the Truth of Suffering; now, among the sixteen aspects, the specific aspects of emptiness and non-self belong exclusively to the Truth of Suffering, which does not contradict the previous general [teaching on] emptiness and so forth.

[Commentary] The answer states that those who grasp at the subordinate factors of those lower views—such as precepts and so forth—as being "precepts" are manifesting an adherence to precepts based on and conforming to those specific deluded false views.

They take these precepts, along with the five aggregates co-arising with them, to be supreme and purifying. Therefore, the grasping at precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) extends across both the truths of origination and cessation.
The intended meaning is that there are non-Buddhists who observe the "pig-precepts," "chicken-precepts," and so forth, and they grasp these as being [the means to liberation].

To grasp at the cause of a superior fruit as being the means to attain purity is the attachment to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Furthermore, to conceive of what is not cessation as cessation and to grasp it as the most excellent means for attaining purity is the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Following this attachment to views, one accepts rules and observances; grasping these rules and observances as supreme and capable of purifying is precisely the attachment to rules and observances.

This is a heavy affliction. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (58), with the exception of the two views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), [the remaining views constitute the attachment to views].
Regarding the existence of other truths externally, each is examined and described through the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, "viewing the retinue" means that "view" refers to the false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) under the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), while the "retinue" refers to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) co-arising with them. "Precepts" refers to the precepts of pigs and chickens;

if one further clings to these precepts as being superior and capable of purifying [one], this is called the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). This interpretation is somewhat superior and accords with the Yogācāra.
