Now, according to the Sanskrit original, there is only the term *vicāra* and no mention of the word *vitarka*.

If one relies solely on the Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras and śāstras, there is no mention of "correct study"; and even when relying on the Sanskrit, there is only "contemplation" (*cintā*), with no mention of "correct characters.

Since correct characters are absent, how can there be talk of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought) in the mantras? For "seeking" (*mīmāṃsā*) is precisely what constitutes *vitarka* and *vicāra*.

[The opponent asks: If the Sanskrit manuscripts already contain the term "contemplation" but lack the phrase "pure awakening" (*viśuddha-bodhi*) and so forth, for what reason does the new translation of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* include it?
As for the passage stating that there is "pure awakening," this is merely an addition by the translators; it should have simply said "pure reflection.
This new translation of the treatise relies on the Sanskrit originals of the sūtras and śāstras, and does not cite the older Chinese translations.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "The preceding eight stages" up to "still possesses," "self-benefit" refers to the stages prior to the eighth;
"no stage of benefit" refers to those subsequent to the eighth. As for the question of how this is known, the answer is that according to the following text, it says:

"Because Bodhisattvas in the ninth stage eliminate the obstacle of non-willingness to practice within the context of benefiting others. Therefore, [the absence of self-benefit] pertains to the stages from the eighth upward.
He then exerts effort.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the explanation that among the ten dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the factor of right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is absent because it is unimpeded:
the intention of this master is that right thought is identical to vitarka and vicāra; thus, it is known that among the Buddha’s ten dharmas of one beyond training, right thought is excluded.

Furthermore, since there are nine dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and given that right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) is admitted as one of the eight branches of the noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*),
it would follow that a Buddha possesses only seven branches of the noble path.

[Commentary: From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward, since the untainted (*anāsrava*) contemplative mind proceeds in continuous succession, when it reaches the tainted (*sāsrava*) primary consciousness (*vijñapti*), this constitutes a difficulty.

The objection states: "If the five sensory consciousnesses must be induced by vitarka and vicāra, then from the eighth stage onward, as the untainted mind is constantly in succession, how can the tainted five consciousnesses be initiated in the absence of vitarka and vicāra? The answer is: "It is not so."

In the meditative concentration of Maudgalyāyana, sound functions because it is induced by vitarka and vicāra; thus, one knows that when a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage arouses the five consciousnesses, it is not necessarily induced by vitarka and vicāra.
Although the continuum of untainted mental consciousness lacks vitarka and vicāra, this does not preclude the arising of the five consciousnesses.
The preceding statement clarifies that the five consciousnesses mostly arise through those [vitarka and vicāra], but it does not mean they arise at all times.

It must be that vitarka and vicāra induce the arising of the five sensory consciousnesses; this is explained according to the "concomitant gate" (*anuvartana-mukha*), which follows the tenets of the Hīnayāna schools in asserting that the two dharmas of vitarka and vicāra are universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).

Regarding the meaning of the three—vitarka, vicāra, and so forth—as explained in the *Śū-yao* (Essential Pivot), it refers to the meaning of the three types of activity (*trividha-caryā*) of body, speech, and mind as explained in the *Śū-yao*.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because from the first bhūmi onwards, [vitarka and vicāra] do not function in the inferior [stages]," the intended meaning is as follows:

throughout the ten bhūmis, the arising of untainted subsequent-attainment wisdom (anāsrava-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) always involves vitarka and vicāra. However, when one reaches the stage of the diamond-like mind (vajropama-citta), vitarka and vicāra no longer function, because one has attained superior [states] and abandoned the inferior.
This means that these very vitarka and vicāra do not function simultaneously with their associated mental states and mental factors at that time.

[Commentary: Regarding the proof provided by the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*)—from "only with subsequently attained wisdom" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) up to "neither"—the present explanation states that vitarka and vicāra only coexist with subsequently attained wisdom and do not coexist with correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*). This is because the *Seventy-three [Verses]* explain the four alternatives regarding vitarka and vicāra as follows:

"There is contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*) without observing only suchness. Here, "observing" (*guan*) means realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*), and there is also [the case of] mere reflection (*cintana*).

Only true suchness is also [the object of] contemplating true suchness; this refers to the uncontaminated subsequently attained wisdom (*anāsrava-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which, because it possesses vitarka and vicāra, is called "contemplating true suchness.
Within the mind that contemplates true suchness, there is the mental representation of what is being contemplated. Furthermore, there is not contemplating true suchness nor observing true suchness;
this refers to other minds and mental factors produced as the maturation (*vipāka*) of karmic results.
[Commentary: In the fifth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, these two are explained as being the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the three realms.

Regarding these two types of discrimination: first, the defiled mind (*sāsrava-citta*) is called "discrimination"; second, the pervasive conceptualizing mind (*parikalpa-citta*) is called "discrimination.
Explaining these two types of contaminated [minds], they are precisely the mind and mental factors of the three realms, which are termed "discrimination."

[Commentary]: Although this treatise is composed based on the perspective of the contaminated (*sāsrava*), its intention is to state that among the five dharmas, [vitarka and vicāra] belong to the third category.
It does not say they belong exclusively to the third, because vitarka and vicāra also pertain to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the first master’s explanation here concerning the nature of *vitarka* and *vicāra*, his intention is as follows:
since the first master asserts that *vitarka* and *vicāra* are exclusively *sāsrava* (with-outflows), they are absent within the five factors of the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna;

thus, the two untainted factors of *vitarka* and *vicāra* are missing, leaving only the three untainted factors of joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and concentration (*samādhi*). These three factors are common to both the tainted and the untainted.
[Commentary]:

Regarding the passage from "If one follows the second master... up to "...this meaning should be considered," it is based on the second master’s assertion that within the untainted (anāsrava) minds of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) during the causal phase and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), there exist untainted vitarka and vicāra, whereas in the Buddha [they do not].
If the fruit is entirely devoid of vitarka and vicāra, then the fruit of Buddhahood would consist only of *cintāmaya-prajñā* (wisdom born of reflection) and lack vitarka and vicāra.

When it is said that there is no "coarseness" (*audārikatva*) or "subtlety" (*sūkṣmatva*), the intended meaning is that *vitarka* is coarse and *vicāra* is subtle; therefore, they can be established as factors of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-aṅga*).

Since the *cintāmaya-prajñā* of the Buddha’s fruit lacks both coarseness and subtlety, it does not possess the factors of the antidote. As for other persons, when they first cultivate [the path] amidst the afflictions (*kleśa*)...

In the initial cultivation of the first dhyāna, there are vitarka and vicāra; because these can counteract the unwholesome states of ill-will and harm within the desire realm, vitarka and vicāra are called the "counteractive factors" (pratipakṣa-aṅga).
Joy and bliss are the "beneficial factors" (anuśaṃsa-aṅga), and the essence of concentration (samādhi-svabhāva) is the "supportive factor" (āśraya-aṅga).
This essence of concentration serves as the support for the other factors—vitarka, vicāra, joy, and bliss. Regarding the afflictions within the body of a Tathāgata...

Since [the Tathāgata] is without [faults], he lacks vitarka and vicāra as factors to be remedied. Just as non-negligence (*apramāda*) serves as the remedy for negligence, the Tathāgata possesses uninterrupted non-negligence;
thus, vitarka and vicāra are called "remedial factors" (*pratipakṣa-aṅga*). If this is so, the Tathāgata should possess the factors of vitarka and vicāra. [Response:
Dharmapāla says that while one must guard against [faults], the Tathāgata possesses non-negligent vitarka and vicāra. This is merely verbal activity (*vāk-karman*); the Buddha is without it.
Because they proceed through verbal outflows (*āsrava*), they lack the factors of vitarka and vicāra.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "those with and without outflows, those with and without objects, and so forth, all exclusively take these as their objects," the explanation is as follows:

within these four dhyānas, when taking objects such as the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) or those with objects (*sālambana*), with the exception of remorse (*kaukṛtya*), the remaining sleep (*middha*) and the three dharmas of vitarka, vicāra, and [the others] are able to take objects that are without objects (*anālambana*).

Because remorse cannot coexist with other fundamental afflictions, its associated view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*)—which is a proximate view capable of taking as its object the outflowing phenomena that lack a real basis—is said to have only remorse as its object;
it cannot coexist with the co-nascent view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) or the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Since vitarka and the others are admitted to take co-nascent afflictions as their objects, this constitutes the third point, following the aforementioned method of analysis.

[Commentary]: Regarding these two questions, the intent of the inquiry is as follows: Is there a distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva) separate from the substance of the mind, as the Sarvāstivādins maintain;
or is it merely a differentiation of the states (avasthā-viśeṣa) of the mind itself, as the Sautrāntikas and others hold?

[Commentary: As for the Lankāvatāra masters, even down to those who distinguish various differences, they maintain that the eight or nine various consciousnesses described in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* are like the various waves upon water;
since they do not even distinguish the eight consciousnesses as separate, how much less could they distinguish mental factors (*caitta*)?
Therefore, they do not establish mental factors. As for the Śataśāstra masters, they maintain that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty; since they do not even [distinguish] the phenomena...
If the establishment [of mental factors] is not permitted, how could one separately establish them?

The Sautrāntikas and the master Ghoṣaka maintain that only three mental factors are established—namely, feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), and volition (cetanā) among the five aggregates. All other wholesome or defiled states are merely designated based upon volition;
they have no separate substantial entity. If one were to further establish other mental factors, the sūtra text should have spoken of "many aggregates" rather than allowing for only these three.

Because there are five aggregates (*skandha*), it is known that mental factors (*caitta*) exist in only three categories. Although this [position] does not explicitly state "mental factors," it is nonetheless called "non-existent" because they are few.

The Venerable Ghosaka also made this statement regarding vitarka and vicāra; he was one of the four masters who offered critical evaluations (*vibhajya-vādins*) among the Great Virtuous Ones (*bhadanta*) in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
As for the others—namely, Buddharakṣita, Vasumitra, and so forth—they did not state that there is only one.

Regarding the statement that "all mental factors (*caitta*) are without [independent] equality," the Sautrāntika school maintains that there are three mental factors and so forth, such as initial application (*vitarka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), and wholesome states (*kuśala*).
These are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*) for specific states (*avasthā*) of volition (*cetanā*).

This principle applies generally to this objection, as explained previously in the first fascicle regarding how *vitarka* and *vicāra* are real while *sparśa* (contact) and others are provisional. Since this has already been challenged as before:

[Commentary]: As for the passage from the *Abhidharmakośa* up to "it is taught that there is only consciousness," this refers to the description of the Sautrāntika tenets within the *Kośa*'s explanation of the member of contact (*sparśa*), as well as the mention of the views of Ghoṣaka and others in the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, which state that consciousness exists through habitual cultivation.
[Commentary]: "Far-reaching" (*dūramgamā*) and "solitary" (*ekacārī*): from time immemorial, its roaming through objective spheres is called "far-reaching";

because there is no second [to it], it is called "solitary. Now, an external objection states: "If mental factors (*caitta*) exist, then it would be called 'functioning with others' and should not be called 'solitary.
Therefore, we know that there are no mental factors. Another school asserts: "Because the six consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously, it is said to be 'solitary.'"
Regarding its "solitary wandering": according to the Sautrāntika school, because they maintain there are no distinct mental factors (*caitta*), it is said to wander alone;
according to a certain class of Mahāyāna masters, because they maintain that the five consciousnesses do not exist and only the mental consciousness exists, it is called solitary wandering;

and according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, because each of the various consciousnesses evolves separately and lacks a sovereign master, it is called solitary wandering. As for its being "bodiless and sleeping in a cave," it means:

Regarding the statement that the present mind is formless: because it is formless and invisible, it is said to be "bodiless. Yet, while dormant, it resides within the cave of the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
To say one "trains" this [mind] is difficult to justify; for if one speaks of training the mind, one does not speak of training the mental factors (*caitta*).
This clearly demonstrates that there are no mental factors.

[Treatise] Regarding the "six elements of a person" (*ṣaḍdhātavaḥ puruṣasya*): this fourth [point] cites many sūtras which state that the great elements (*mahābhūtāni*), space (*ākāśa*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) constitute the body of a sentient being, but do not mention mental factors (*caitta*).

However, various schools differ in their interpretations of this passage; while their specific tenets vary, they are all in agreement with the Mahāyāna. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 56, states:
"The 'six elements' are spoken of with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*); it is intended solely to manifest this form (*rūpa*)."

The mind and mental factors have the most excellent basis for their movement; this is the intended meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣya*) of the Sūtra’s statement that the four great elements are the most excellent basis for form, space is the most excellent basis for movement, and consciousness is the most excellent basis for the mental factors. This "mind" (*manas*) is spoken of because it serves as the most excellent basis for these three.
Thus, it is said with intentional meaning that the six elements constitute the sentient being's body, although in reality there is no such thing as "mind."

Regarding the comparison: if one follows the Sautrāntika school, their assertion that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and space are the same as the Mahāyāna teaching—that mental factors (*caitta*) have no separate intrinsic nature apart from the mind—is challenged by the view of the master Buddhadatta, who states that outside of the four great elements there is no separately produced derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), and that outside of the mind there are no separate mental factors;
thus, the objection is raised based on the Sautrāntika position and the view of Buddhadatta.

[Commentary]: Or, it may manifest as the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*). Question: What is the difference between the grasper and the grasped on one hand, and the two parts—the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) and the aspect of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*)—on the other?

Answer: They differ in terms of being grasped or not grasped, and in terms of being the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) or the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). This concludes the first alternative.
[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of "restating what has already been established," the intent is as follows:

The meaning of this first phrase refers to that which was previously discussed in the treatise—namely, that within the eight consciousnesses (the mind-kings) and the six stages of mental factors (the caittas), upon the establishment of these mind-kings and mental factors, all are capable of manifesting as if they were the two divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), or manifesting as if they were the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*). This is the main point of the Sub-commentary; however, Master Zhe says:
Regarding the interpretation that "the mind appears as two": this refers to the mind appearing as greed and so forth, and appearing as faith and so forth; this is called "appearing as two.

Of these two interpretations, the latter is somewhat closer to the original intent. By citing verses to prove that there are no mental factors (*caitta*), it is shown that the appearance of the two parts—the seen (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*)—is not discussed.
Therefore, the Master of the Commentary (*Ṭīkākāra*) has either misinterpreted this passage, or perhaps he was not mistaken in citing the mind’s appearance as the seen and the seeing parts.
For example, defilement and purity are also manifestations of the mind.

[Commentary] Regarding the initial proof by means of scripture, this refers to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and others; regarding the subsequent establishment by means of reasoning, this refers to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the ninth and tenth scrolls of the ten-scroll *Laṅkāvatāra*," this refers specifically to the ninth and tenth scrolls of the *Laṅkāvatāra*.

[Commentary: As for the passage from "intrinsic nature" to "two entities do not coexist," the intended meaning is that, just as two minds or two texts cannot exist simultaneously in their own essence, the same applies to other cases by analogy.
[Commentary]: Regarding the light that exists outside the solar disc, there are two kinds of light: first, light near the disc; second, light far from the disc.
A sutra states: "The sun has a thousand rays; five hundred shine downward and five hundred shine sideways."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the "Chapter on the Five Dharmas" explains the five dharmas—characteristics, names, and so forth—it is called the "Chapter on the Five Dharmas.

As for the phrase "consisting of ten fascicles," this refers to the work being composed in ten fascicles; alternatively, it may mean that within these ten fascicles, the seventh fascicle establishes that mind and mental factors possess distinct substantial entities.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement by Deva-buddhi and others that these are not separate entities but are merely distinct temporal stages (*avasthā*) of the mind, such that five [mental factors] are posited:

the explanation is as follows. Deva-buddhi and others maintain that the distinctions between preceding and succeeding stages are what are described as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.

For example, at the very moment of initially apprehending an object, that stage is called "feeling"; subsequently, in the second moment of apprehending the object, there is the "designation" (*prajñapti*) of names and words.

Furthermore, when taking an image or the like as an object, the sequential stages of conceptualization are called "saṃjñā" (perception). When the mind conditions an object through the activity of the three successive moments, it is called "saṃskāra" (volitional formations).

Subsequently, when there is the discernment of that object, it is called "vijñāna" (consciousness). Thus, within the single substance of consciousness, the distinct states at different times while conditioning an object are designated as vedanā, saṃjñā, saṃskāra, and vijñāna.
Apart from the mind itself, there are no separate mental factors; all others, such as greed and faith, are likewise [subsumed within these].

Because they are conventionally established based on the primary consciousness (*citta*), one knows that there are no separate mental factors (*caitta*). That is to say, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are spoken of as distinct states within the sequence of the same [consciousness].

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because both existence and non-existence would result in fallacies," the intended meaning is: since it is but a single consciousness, how could there be distinct prior and subsequent states?
The establishment of the five aggregates and so forth is as explained below regarding the reasons for their faults. If there are various states and functions, they ultimately reach the signless;
thus, one understands that there is the fault of existence. Once functions have ceased, the following explains the differences regarding the absence of lineage (*agotra*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because things such as milk undergo transformation from prior to subsequent states," this serves as proof that while material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) undergo change, mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) do not.
There are those who calculate that, like the mind, the basis and conditions [of mental phenomena] undergo prior and subsequent transformations;

however, the intended meaning is that mental phenomena differ from material phenomena—such as milk and the like—which undergo transformation—only in that they vary according to their dependence on sense faculties and conditions.
[Commentary: Regarding the claim that within a single present moment there are various differing mental aspects (*ākāra*), we now raise this objection:

if one asserts that consciousness in a single moment possesses multiple aspects—namely, the aspects of experiencing (*anubhava*), grasping images (*nimittodgrahaṇa*), volitional formation (*abhisamskāra*), astonishment (*vismaya*), and discernment (*vijñapti*)—and yet maintains that there is only a single consciousness, for what reason is this so? This is because...
The meaning [of the objection] is that there would be many modes of activity (*ākāra*) within a single moment of consciousness due to various causes and conditions.
[Commentary: To say that even when the sense organs and objects undergo transformation over multiple moments and appear similar, there is no distinction, also constitutes a fault;

this is a refutation of the transformation occurring over multiple moments. Even if you were to grant that there are multiple preceding and succeeding moments, it would cause a single consciousness to possess various [distinct] aspects.

Regarding the distinction between their modes of activity (*ākāra*), the present objection is stated as follows: For instance, in the case of a single visual consciousness, the preceding moment of visual consciousness relies upon the eye-faculty and takes visible form as its object;
the subsequent moment of visual consciousness likewise relies upon and takes this same faculty and object.

Since the faculty and object of the preceding and succeeding moments of visual consciousness are identical, how can it be said that one visual consciousness possesses distinct functions such as discernment (*vijñapti*) and experiencing (*anubhava*) across these successive moments?
Because there would be distinctions in the characteristics of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, this results in a logical fallacy.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement that "these various dharmas are a combination and not a non-combination," etc., this is intended to distinguish that there are multiple factors which can be called a "combination.
Just as many people are called a "combination" while a single person is not, since it is only...
If there were a consciousness alone without mental factors (*caitta*), how could it be called "conjoined" (*samprayukta*)?
Since it is explicitly stated that they are conjoined, it is clear that there must be multiple mental factors; thus, "conjoined" carries the meaning of "associated" (*samyukta*).

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the scriptural passage on the metaphor of the lamp’s light, as well as how it was previously cited—just as many rays of light arise depending upon a single lamp, so too do many mental factors arise depending upon a single mind—the prose section cited previously refers back to the preceding text.
The current citation of the metaphor of the lamp’s light intends to draw out its significance, similar to the metaphors of the sun and its radiance or the practice and its illumination.
The light and the lamp are simultaneous; this is the meaning corresponding to the metaphor.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the contradiction with the three metaphors, up to "there is only mind or only perception," the meaning now applies only the latter three phrases to correspond to the former three realms.
What is the matter? The statement "there is only form" corresponds to...

Previously, regarding the desire realm, it was stated that within the desire realm the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are designated as the self. How could this be so if the desire realm possessed only form?
We know that there must also be mind, mental factors, and so forth; the mention of "mind" and "mental factors" (or simply "mind") refers precisely to this.

Furthermore, regarding the form realm, since it is said that "the mind arises from the mind," this refers to the mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). How could it be that the form realm possesses only mind?
Regarding the statement that "there is also form, mind, and mental factors," if one were to say that there is only perception (*saṃjñā*), this would correspond to the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Within the Formless Realm, it is stated that "formless perception arises. How could it be that within the Formless [Realm] there is only perception and no other minds or mental factors?
Therefore, we know that there are indeed other minds and mental factors. Alternatively, it is said: "From milk, curd, and ghee... down to 'only'..."

Regarding "perception" (*saṃjñā*): now, by citing this analogy, the meaning is explained as proving that where there is mind, mental factors (*caitta*) must also exist. How could there be only matter (*rūpa*) without necessarily having mind?

There must also be perception, feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth. That which is called "matter born of mind" (*manomaya-rūpa*) refers precisely to transformation-birth (*upapāduka*), which arises immediately according to one's will.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that those who take the coarse four great elements as the self—this refers to humans and devas in the desire realm, all of whom grasp these coarse four great elements as being the self.
[Commentary: Therefore, in such texts as the *Ṣaḍdhātu-sūtra*, when various [objections] are raised against this, the rebuttal states:

"If you claim that the teaching of the six elements of a person (*pudgala*) refers only to the mind, then consider the *Kṣīra-upama-sūtra*, which speaks of the elements as having coarse great primary elements (*mahābhūta*), from milk up to the arising of formless perception like clarified butter (*sarpis*).
How could it be that the Desire Realm possesses only coarse great primary elements? The same principle applies to the two upper realms."
This should be examined.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "namely, the five sūtras," if one were to claim that there is only mind and no mental factors (*caitta*), it would contradict the teachings of the five types of sūtras;
thus, it is said that this contradicts the holy scriptures. As detailed in the commentary, the five sūtras are cited in full.

[Commentary]: "Constantly and invariably" means that while the consciousnesses [of the five universals] are always present, their objects are not necessarily fixed. This implies that although they are constantly present, the objects are indeterminate;
for instance, greed, hatred, doubt, and wisdom do not arise simultaneously. Question: Are the five universal mental factors not also constantly and invariably present? Answer:

Although they are constantly and invariably present, they do not function as the primary factor, nor do they serve as the basis [for the others]; therefore, [the term "invariably" is used] in this specific sense.

Because [the Sūtra] distinguishes the mind from the mental factors (*caitta*) by means of four meanings, such as "predominance" (*adhipati*), it speaks only of "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) and not of the mental factors and so forth.
[The Commentary] states that the six elements (*dhātu*) are mentioned only because they reveal the three dharmas of matter, motion, and mental factors;

therefore, it now speaks collectively of the "mind" being predominant, intending to mean that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) serve as the support for the eleven kinds of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
This means that the five internal sense-faculties (*indriya*), the five external objects (*viṣaya*), and non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) are all absent;

as for the "space-element" (*ākāśa-dhātu*), it is not the "unconditioned space" (*asaṃskṛta-ākāśa*) among the six unconditioned phenomena. Rather, it refers to the interstices between the bones and joints within the bodies of sentient beings, which is designated as the "space-element.
This space-element is capable of performing actions such as coming and going, as well as [the movement of] the hand.
The movement and shifting of the eyes and so forth can be known as that which the mind depends upon;
this is the cause of the realms (*dhātu*) and the meaning of the Sūtras. It is said that the "space element" (*ākāśa-dhātu*) also includes external empty form;

if there were no external space-element form, then even a purely wholesome state with characteristics would be merely a solitary movement and could not proceed forward, for it lacks excellence. Therefore, the movement of sentient beings' forms must rely upon internal space.
"The elements serve as the support.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "the body of form and mind moves by depending on space," the intended meaning is as follows:

when a person wishes to travel a great distance, it is by means of the motivating mind (*samutthāpaka-citta*) that it draws forth the resultant form (*nisyanda-rūpa*); only then do activities such as moving, walking, or staying occur by depending upon space. This is what is meant.

The text instructs that one should first move forward [the argument] and then explain the basis of the mind and mental factors. [Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the sutra on the analogy of milk and so forth cited immediately prior, it should be used as a counter-interrogation; that is, one should counter-interrogate the earlier Buddhadeva and others by saying: "If you admit that the mind undergoes successive variations and distinctions, then you must be interrogated regarding milk, curd, ghee, and so forth. What was there before? What becomes later? If you say they are different, then how can you claim that the mind is permanent? If you say they are not different, then how can you claim that milk transforms into curd? Thus, the same fault applies to both positions. Therefore, the meaning of this sutra is that the mind and mental factors are momentary and perish in each instant. This is because the nature of milk and so forth is established through the power of conditions, and since these conditions are impermanent, the nature of the substance must also be impermanent. Consequently, the mind and mental factors, which likewise arise from the power of conditions, must also be impermanent. This is the intended meaning. It is not the case that the sutra intends to prove the impermanence of the mind and mental factors by using the example of milk and so forth. Why? Because the nature of milk and so forth is established through the power of conditions, and since these conditions are impermanent, the nature of the substance must also be impermanent. Consequently, the mind and mental factors, which likewise arise from the power of conditions, must also be impermanent. This is the intended meaning. It is not the case that the sutra intends to prove the impermanence of the mind and mental factors by using the example of milk and so forth. Why? Because the nature of milk and so forth is established through the power of conditions, and since these conditions are impermanent, the nature of the substance must also be impermanent. Consequently, the mind and mental factors, which likewise arise from the power of conditions, must also be impermanent. This is the intended meaning. It is not the case that the sutra intends to prove the impermanence of the mind and mental factors by using the example of milk and so forth. Why? Because the nature of milk and so forth is established through the power of conditions, and since these conditions are impermanent, the nature of the substance must also be impermanent. Consequently, the mind and mental factors, which likewise arise from the power of conditions, must also be impermanent. This is the intended meaning. If you maintain that the subsequent transformations such as curd and so forth are what is called "form" (*rūpa*), then since you admit that the substance of the mind undergoes transformation from moment to moment,
the substance of the mind should likewise be called "form. Furthermore, you argued that if the six elements of the person (*pudgala*) consist only of mind, then the analogy of milk and so forth—
stated in the sutras where it says that in the desire realm there are coarse four great elements like milk, up to the arising of perception in the formless realm— is contradicted.
Sū: Is it only in the Desire Realm that the coarse four great elements exist? The other two realms should be understood accordingly. [Commentary]:
This does not mean that the [mental states] resembling greed and so forth are also non-existent. The intent of the statement is that the mind-king resembles the mental factors (caitta).
When the mind-king arises in a defiled state, it resembles greed and so forth; when the mind-king arises in a pure state, it resembles faith and so forth.
Therefore, the verse maintains that the mind appearing as two is the mental sovereign (*citta-rāja*) itself that can appear as such;
"appearing as greed" and so forth, or "appearing as faith" and so forth, refers to the greed, faith, and other factors that it appears as.
[Commentary]: The meaning of "not taking one as the example" is that both meanings are taken collectively.

If only the latter meaning were taken, others would then take the two divisions of appearance and seeing as the example [for their argument], because they lack a separate substance and because the mind arises [from itself].
Furthermore, the meaning of "not taking one as the example" is that both meanings are taken together and termed "semblance" (*sādṛśya*); it does not mean taking one meaning alone as the example.
"This interpretation—that they are 'similar'—is the fundamental one.
[Commentary: "The preceding sutras can be understood" refers to the previously cited sutras concerning defilement and purity, etc.
[Commentary: "If that is so, from greed and faith... what is it? This is the question. The intent of the question is: the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is that which is capable of being similar.

Mental factors (*caitta*) are that which is similar [to the mind]. If one says that the mind is admitted to appear as two and that this also includes mental factors, then mental factors would be subsumed within the "that which appears.
Now, it is further asked: regarding such appearances as greed (*rāga*) and so forth, it is not yet clear what they appear as.
This is the question. The passage from "Among mental factors in general" down to "they are also included therein" constitutes the answer.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the categories of general and specific aggregates differ when explained according to their meaning," the intended sense is as follows:

although mental factors (*caitta*) are subsumed within the general aggregate of mind (*citta*) and thus constitute a single unified aggregate, when explained according to their meaning, they are divided into general and specific aggregates—the primary mind (*cittarāja*) constitutes the general aggregate, and the mental factors constitute the specific aggregate.

This means that while the sovereign mind manifests as the two divisions of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the seen-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), the mental factors themselves—such as faith (*śraddhā*) and greed (*lobha*)—manifest individually.
In each of the cognizing divisions (*sākṣātkāra-bhāga*), there appear two aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*);

thus, it is said that within the aspect transformed by the self-cognizing division (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of greed or faith, there are both greed and faith, and within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) arising from the self-cognizing division of faith, there are likewise both faith and greed.
This demonstrates that the following two phrases are not a general summary of the preceding. This interpretation accords with the *Śāstra*, which states: "The mind-king itself..."
Within the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) manifested upon the *sākṣin-bhāga* (subjective aspect), there are the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*) of greed, faith, and the indeterminate;
likewise, within the *nimitta-bhāga* arising from the *sākṣin-bhāga* of correct faith, there are also the three natures of faith, greed, and the indeterminate.

Furthermore, within the *nimitta-bhāga* manifested upon the *sākṣin-bhāga* of defiled greed, there are also the three natures of greed, faith, and the indeterminate. Therefore, [there is no contradiction].
Regarding the teaching that dharmas have both wholesome and defiled aspects, the *xiangfen* (objective aspect) contains all three natures, as explained in other notes.

Furthermore, according to this interpretation, when the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its associated mental factors—such as greed and faith—undergo transformation, they are all capable of manifesting as greed, faith, and so forth;
this differs from the previous interpretation.
[Commentary]: "Because it does not exceed the two states of defilement and purity" explains the anticipated objection. The objection is as follows:

If, for instance, the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitta) largely pass through the three natures (trividha-svabhāva) across many stages, why is it said that the mind is admitted to manifest only in the two states of defilement and purity?

The answer is: Among all stages, no function is more powerful than that of the two states of defilement and purity. When these two states are mentioned, the mind is described as appearing similar to greed (*rāga*) and so forth. This is because, in those specific states, the activity of defilement and purity is most predominant.

Because manifesting the superior and concealing the inferior is also similar to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the Commentary states: "Therefore, this general statement also includes the indeterminate, as it does not contradict wholesome or defiled dharmas.

[Commentary] Regarding indeterminate dharmas, there are those that accord with defilement; for example, when one gives rise to a defiled mind by taking one's wife and children as an object, there are [others] that accord with...
"Wholesome [states] are such as when one gives rise to a wholesome mind upon seeing a plain image in a decorated shrine.

[Commentary]: Among the various schools, those that maintain there are no indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas—namely the Mahāsāṃghika, Ekavyāvahārika, Lokottaravāda, and Kaukkuṭika—these four schools establish only the two categories of wholesome and unwholesome, and do not establish the indeterminate. This is the mountain [of their tenet].

Regarding the phrase "since rivers and so forth have that which they conform to," it is as follows: objects such as mountains, rivers, and the world are produced by virtuous karma, while impure worlds, the earth, and so forth are produced by non-virtuous karma.
The intention of the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna is that pleasant and unpleasant mountains, rivers, and so on are induced respectively by non-virtuous and virtuous karma;
since these possess the nature of being good or evil, this [case] is likewise so, though it is merely said to be "similar."
Greed, faith, and so forth are not said to be "similar to the indeterminate.
[Commentary] The summary of what preceded up to the phrase "not explaining the subsequent category" means that there are two senses here.
First, it is a summary of the preceding sūtras and śāstras, stating that there is no fault of contradiction. Second, it says: "Alternatively, this subsequent [category] applies generally..."
Regarding the previous interpretation that this section does not explain the subsequent category:

the intended meaning is that while the text of this category only connects forward to the cited sūtra—namely, the passage stating "how can the holy teaching say 'there is only consciousness'?"—it does not explain the subsequent category's passage which admits that "the mind appears as if it were two.
Question: If the second interpretation does not admit the subsequent category, how can this text state that "it also appears as if it were those [objects] and so forth"?
Wen replied that because there is no contradiction with reason, the two statements need not yet be reconciled.

[Commentary: Regarding what is now stated—that among the four types of conventional truth, the second, the conventional truth of reason (yukti-saṃvṛti), up to the fact that dharmas and their causes and effects are neither identical nor distinct—this treatise states that this relies on the conventional, namely the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
That the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) each have their own distinct identities is an understanding based on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) according to reason.

As for the statement in the text that, "if one speaks from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the mental factors and the mind are neither identical nor different," this is based on the second of the four types of ultimate truth;
for within that second ultimate truth, the cause and effect of all phenomena are neither identical nor different.
Taking the mind-king as the cause and the mental factors as the effect, they are neither identical nor separate; taking the mental factors as the cause and the mind-king as the effect,

they are likewise neither identical nor separate, because the mind-king and the mental factors stand in relation to one another as associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the third [level], the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), up to the point where the eight [consciousnesses] are not definitively separated, the intent is as follows: if one speaks according to the expressive designations (*vyañjana*), the eight consciousnesses are each distinct;

however, if one refers to the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), all eight consciousnesses are the two kinds of selflessness, because all eight consciousnesses are subsumed within the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*).

[Commentary: Furthermore, even when investigating within the first of the four ultimate truths (*paramārtha*), there is neither identity nor separation; how then could there be a fixed state of separation?
Now, according to the first of the four ultimate truths, there exists that which is neither identical nor separate.

Since it is taught that all phenomena are like illusions, transformations, reflections of the moon in water, and mirages, how could there be any fixed separation? Therefore, this is explained by means of such superior principles as being like an illusion and so forth.
This clarifies that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are neither identical to nor separate from [the mind].
[Commentary: Alternatively, this refers to the fourth [section], where the text itself provides its own interpretation:

if one speaks according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the fourth [level], it cannot be definitively stated whether the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors (*caitta*) are identical or separate; yet, the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) likewise cannot be said to be one.
Because their modes of activity (*ākāra*), bases (*āśraya*), objects (*ālambana*), and associations (*samprayoga*) differ; because when one ceases, the others do not necessarily cease;
and because they are not definitively distinct—as the Sūtra states that the eight consciousnesses are like water and waves, as explained in detail below.

[Commentary]: Regarding the meaning in the verse where both the basis (*āśraya*) and the co-arising (*sahabhū*) are concealed, the intention is as follows: according to what is asked in the treatise, only the state of manifestation (*vartamāna-avasthā*) is questioned;
however, according to the answer, there are three gates—namely, the basis, the co-arising, and the manifestation—and so forth.
Here, because the manifestation is the most prominent aspect, it is specifically questioned, whereas the other two gates are not questioned because they are concealed.

[Commentary: If one addresses the second [level of] ultimate truth specifically, it is neither identical to nor separate from [the conventional], because its nature as cause and effect is such that it is neither identical nor separate;
this is the reason why the principle of cause and effect regarding the Four Noble Truths is neither identical nor separate.

As for the first [level of] conventionality, it refers to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), which exists nominally but lacks reality, such as the imagined self (*ātman*) and so forth. The second [level of] conventionality refers to the explanation of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

First, the individual distinction between the three conventional [truths] clarifies that the cause and fruit of the Four Noble Truths are distinct: the fruit is not the cause, and the cause is not the fruit.

Second, the individual distinction between cause and fruit clarifies that they are mutually exclusive. Third, the conventional truth of the two emptinesses being distinct clarifies that by severing the grasping at a self, one manifests the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and by severing the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), one manifests the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
although True Suchness (*tathatā*) has no differentiation, it is through the severance of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa-dvaya*) that these two emptinesses are realized as distinct.
If explained according to the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it cannot be definitively stated [that they exist], because all phenomena are indeterminate.

Regarding the first ultimate truth, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are all like illusions, transformations, the moon in water, and so forth—the eight similes—and are thus not real.
Regarding the second ultimate truth, cause and effect are neither identical nor separate; this is because suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) constitute all causes and effects.

Regarding the two emptinesses: whether the mind-king (*cittarāja*) is the cause and the mental factors (*caitta*) are the effect, or the seeds are the cause and the manifest consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) is the effect, they are neither identical nor separate.
If one relies on the third ultimate truth, the *tathatā*, its essence is one;

however, because it is distinguished according to how it is expressed and revealed, the two emptinesses are conventionally said to be distinct. If one relies on the fourth ultimate truth, it is simply the single *dharmadhātu* of *tathatā*.

Because the path of mind and speech is cut off, although the second conventional and the first ultimate have the same essence of reality (*dharmatā*), they are distinguished based on whether they are [viewed] as truly real or as being like an illusion and so forth;

the others should be understood accordingly. Question: Since the essence of the latter three conventionalities and the former three ultimates is all one and the same, how can one distinguish between the ultimate and the conventional within a single phenomenon? Answer: Based on their essence, they are one; however, both are [conventionally] designated...

The reason for this distinction in what is taught is as follows: For the sake of sentient beings who enter the Buddha-dharma and other sentient beings, the Buddha teaches that, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) definitely exist;
that causes and effects are real; and that each phenomenon is individually true.

However, for those who have long practiced the path and have each entered the stages of the noble ones (*ārya*), the Buddha explains all phenomena according to their manifestation (*samudācāra*) and their sequential order, just as they truly are.
Because the four ultimate truths—such as the non-separation of illusion from cause and effect—differ in their underlying motivations, they cannot be held equally accountable.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because both rely upon the eighth consciousness," this means that the five consciousnesses and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) together rely upon the eighth [consciousness].

[Commentary: This phrase generally extends to all six consciousnesses. Regarding the intent of the explanation on "simultaneous transformation," it means that the single phrase "this relies upon the fundamental consciousness" applies throughout the following three phrases to clarify the meaning of the simultaneous transformation of the six consciousnesses.
[Commentary] Regarding the "two phrases," these refer to either "together" or "not together," such as the two phrases concerning waves depending [on water] and so forth.
Now, in this verse, there are three phrases in total, with the addition of the phrase "the five consciousnesses manifest according to conditions."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "and the term 'mindless' (*acitta*)," up to the point where it says "one may incur the fault of [thinking] the mind arises," the two characters "mindless" (*acitta*) in the verse apply generally to the following four states.
One should state: "the mindless attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the mindless attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), mindless sleep, and mindless fainting.

If the other four states were not described as "mindless," one would fear that they would be considered equivalent to states with a mind, such as ordinary sleep and so forth. Thus, the intention [of the verse] is also [to distinguish them].
The term "arising" is employed to exclude this fault; the word "unconscious" (*acitta*) is placed [in the text] because one still fears such confusion.
[Commentary: The meaning of "pervasive" is that the *ādāna-vijñāna* exists throughout the stages of ordinary beings and sages, as well as in both defiled and pure states;
however, the *ālaya-vijñāna* is restricted [to certain states], being entirely absent in the stage of the Arhat of the Two Vehicles and in the eighth stage of the Bodhisattva.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "The root is the origin of arising," the explanation states that "origin" (*shi*) means "beginning.

This is precisely the meaning of "root," referring to the eighth consciousness as the causal source from which all other consciousnesses arise. Furthermore, in relation to the arising of this specific physical body, the eighth consciousness alone may be considered the initial point of arising;
one must not interpret this "beginning" (*shi*) as "without beginning" (*anādi*). Thus, it refers to the eighth [consciousness].
Consciousness is beginningless; however, its "end" and "beginning" are established only within the temporal limits of a single lifetime in the present existence.
[Commentary] Why is it that, although the seventh consciousness is free from obstruction when reaching its objects, only the first six evolving consciousnesses are said to have an immediate support?

Why is the seventh [consciousness] not mentioned as the eighth? Now, regarding the "immediate support" (*sākṣād-āśraya*), since the seventh and eighth [consciousnesses] are taken together as the simultaneous support (*sahabhv-āśraya*), it is not called the immediate support. This is because the seventh consciousness has objects that are always unobstructed;
the meaning is that the eighth and seventh consciousnesses abide in mutual dependence, and their objects are always present without obstruction.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "excluding the seventh," the meaning is as follows:

since the basis upon which it transforms and the object upon which it depends were already clarified based on the aforementioned second *pariṇāma* (transformation), the text here excludes the seventh [consciousness].

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the passage from "another interpretation of the eighth consciousness" up to "the text that manifests through reflection," it clarifies the stages of abandoning the outflows for both the seventh and eighth consciousnesses.
This is as previously analyzed in the verse on the first transformative consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which states:

"In the stage of Arhatship, [it] is abandoned. This explicitly clarifies the stage of abandoning the outflows for the eighth consciousness. Furthermore, as previously explained, this also applies to the seventh consciousness.
The second verse on the transformation of consciousness states: "In Arhats, in the meditative attainment of cessation, and in the supramundane path, it does not exist," and so forth.

This clarifies that the seventh [consciousness] is absent during the stages where outflows (*āsrava*) are severed; it does not clarify the stages of its arising and ceasing. Now, regarding the six evolving consciousnesses, their stages of arising and ceasing are clarified; thus the verse says:
"The five consciousnesses appear according to conditions," up to "even in sleep and fainting," and so forth. Therefore, we know [the nature of] the six.

The *vijñānas* that transform are explained only in terms of their arising and ceasing, and not in terms of their cessation of the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*). My current interpretation is as follows:

because the seventh and eighth consciousnesses function at all times and are therefore constant and uninterrupted, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses only clarify the cessation of the state of being with outflows and do not clarify the stages of their arising and ceasing;
this is also intended to indirectly indicate that the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) likewise have times when they are interrupted.
The six consciousnesses merely clarify the states of arising and ceasing; by implication, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses also possess states of arising and ceasing.
This is what is suggested by the preceding and subsequent passages of this treatise.
Here, "arising and ceasing" means that "ceasing" refers to the five states of mindlessness, while "arising" refers to the constant manifestation of the conscious [eighth] consciousness.
[Commentary: "Because all consciousnesses are common" means that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) all commonly rely upon the eighth manifesting consciousness (*darśana-bhāga*).

Question: How can the seventh and eighth consciousnesses undergo arising and ceasing? Answer: This refers only to the designation of these two consciousnesses as having arising and ceasing; it is not said according to their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

This is because within the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there exists the pure seventh consciousness. Therefore, throughout the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), the seventh and eighth consciousnesses...

Because both the observation of arising and the observation of ceasing involve transformations within the states of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they are designated as "arising" and "ceasing" based on these.
[Commentary: The phrase "this very [consciousness] relies upon the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*)" applies to both verses;
for within these two verses, it is explained that the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) all rely upon the fundamental consciousness.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the two [types of consciousness] having the same object of form," this refers to the five sense objects collectively being termed "form" (*rūpa*); it does not mean that they are the "same object of form" in the sense of a single shared entity.
[Commentary]:
If, according to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), the five consciousnesses are of three types—arising by means of five, four, or three [objects]—then there are these three categories.
First, visual consciousness constitutes one category that arises by way of five conditions: namely, space, light, the sense organ, the object, and attention.
Second, auditory consciousness constitutes one category that arises by way of four conditions: namely, those same five conditions minus light and darkness, as sound is also heard.
Third, the three consciousnesses of the nose, tongue, and body constitute one category that arises by way of three conditions: namely, the sense organ, the object, and attention.

[Commentary]: Regarding the absence of a fundamental support (*mūlāśraya*): if the first six [consciousnesses] rely on the eighth as their fundamental support while relying on [the seventh] as a remote support, and if the seventh and eighth rely upon each other, then they are merely termed "simultaneous supports" (*sahabhv-āśraya*).
However, if the seventh and eighth [are considered], it is the correct principle that the seventh arises by way of three conditions.

[Treatise] It refers to the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*). Regarding the internal reliance upon the two bases within the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), the question is now asked: by what meaning are "internal" and "external" clarified?

Answer: There are two interpretations. First, one interpretation states that because they are subsumed under the twelve bases (*āyatana*)—specifically the mind-base (*manas-āyatana*)—they are called "internal," whereas because they are mental factors (*caitta*) subsumed under the dharma-base (*dharma-āyatana*), they are called "external.
Alternatively, it is said that only the eighth consciousness, whether in its state as seeds (*bīja*) or as manifest activity (*vṛtti*), arises [therein].
Because it is fundamental, it alone is called "internal"; the remaining conditions are not fundamental and are therefore all called "external. This is explained based on what follows in the treatise.

If this is so, since there is yet another analogy of a mirror surface within the previous analogy, should it not be further illustrated by an example below?
Regarding the word "equal" (*samam*) used here: just as when one mentions water waves, one further mentions the surface of a mirror;

so too, since within the Dharma [of the teaching] there are only the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*), once the five consciousnesses are mentioned, there is no further phenomenon to be equated. Why, then, is the word "equal" used below?

It is because this is a general exposition using the term "equal" to encompass all things; thus it says, "these equalities of Dharma and analogy are explained at length as in the Sūtra, etc. (*ity-ādi*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that while there are seven consciousnesses [discussed] previously, only five are specifically mentioned here, this is the objection.

The response is: "The five are necessarily accompanied by the sixth and seventh, as these two arise constantly. This means that when the five are present, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is necessarily present;

since the mental consciousness must arise based on the seventh [consciousness], it is said that consciousnesses are like waves. When the seven consciousnesses encounter conditions, they immediately arise.

[Commentary]: As for the statement that "the momentum of the five consciousnesses at the stage of Buddhahood is the same as in the cause," this means that if the five consciousnesses of the Buddha-stage possess objects (ālambana), their quantity is similar to that of ordinary beings in the causal state.

Furthermore, the five consciousnesses of the Buddha-stage are frequently interrupted and only partially continuous, because the various conditions upon which they depend are often not fully present. Within the stage of Buddhahood, the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) also possesses nine [faculties].

Since that which arises through conditions is called "fleshly vision" (māṃsa-cakṣus), it possesses nine conditions; whereas the Buddha’s divine vision (divya-cakṣus) possesses seven conditions, excluding space and light.
[Commentary]: Regarding "subtle and profound": their mode of activity (ākāra) is subtle, which is termed "profound"; this does not mean they are investigating objects.
"Fine" (*sūkṣma*) means "profoundly discerning.

[Commentary: "Alternatively, those who are weary in mind" refers to the two states of non-cognition (*acittaka*). "Alternatively, those hindered by other objects" refers to the three other states, such as the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and so forth.

[Commentary: The meaning of "therefore it differs from the previous [explanation]" is as follows: The previous interpretation held that while one portion of the defiled aspect does not function, this does not preclude the existence of a portion of the non-outflow (anāsrava) seventh consciousness.

The present interpretation, however, holds that it merely causes the substance of the consciousness to undergo a transformation such that it becomes either defiled or pure; it does not mean that [the defiled aspect] ceases to function entirely.

Therefore, because it differs from the previous view—wherein one portion of the defiled is extinguished while one portion of the pure remains—it is said to be different from the former. Some say: "Therefore it differs from the former..."
The distinction is that it is not like the sixth consciousness mentioned previously. This is because the sixth consciousness does not function at all when its objects are obstructed.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement "it is called 'constantly manifesting,'" the meaning is that when the eight consciousnesses are compared, the sixth consciousness differs from the first five.
Although the sixth consciousness is intermittent, coarse, and mobile, the conditions upon which it relies are never lacking; therefore, it is not like [the others].

The first five consciousnesses differ from the latter two in that the seventh and eighth consciousnesses have subtle mental aspects (*ākāra*), are frequent, and are mostly continuous, whereas the sixth consciousness is frequently interrupted;
thus it differs from the latter two. Excluding the five states [of unconsciousness], it exists at all other times and is therefore said to arise constantly.

[Commentary]: Regarding the second alternative mentioned in the subsequent passage, which states, "For this reason, the sixth [consciousness] is not mentioned in the verse, up until the double conclusion," this refers to the end of the second alternative explanation in the treatise, which says: "For this reason, the sixth consciousness is not mentioned.

This text, which appears according to the conditions of the occasion, should likewise be situated at the end of the first alternative explanation in the treatise; it should also conclude there by stating: "Because of its cessation..."

It is not said that this [non-attachment] manifests according to conditions; rather, in the first interpretation of the present treatise, the words "by these and so forth" are not yet applied, whereas in the second interpretation, those words are applied below.
This is because one wishes to provide a double conclusion for the two preceding interpretations.

[Commentary]: "Because they do not internally take seeds, faculties, or principles as objects" means that "seeds and faculties" refers to the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), while "principles" refers to the principles of the Four Noble Truths (*caturāryasatya*).
The five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) do not take these as objects. Some say that the five consciousnesses only take external objects and do not take internal seeds as objects;
this is because the principle by which the five faculties give rise to consciousness is such that they are restricted to their respective domains.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "or when there is a deficiency," the intended meaning is that when the sense faculties (*indriya*) are deficient, the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) do not arise.
For example, during the *kalala* stage in the mother’s womb, when the five faculties are not yet complete, consciousness does not arise.

Or, in cases such as those born blind, deaf, or with a nose like a jar, or those suffering from bodily wind-disorders, paralysis, or loss of taste, the five consciousnesses do not arise at all. Even if the physical faculties (*rūpīndriya*) are present, [the consciousnesses may still fail to arise].
The reason they do not arise is that their conditions are lacking; such instances are frequent. [Commentary:

Regarding the dharmas of the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth, the intended meaning is that they collectively take both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) as their objects. The intention is this:

the former master, when correlating the six consciousnesses with the eight or seven [consciousnesses] to explain the internal and external gates, cannot explain the internal gate based on principle. Why is this? Because...

Regarding the phrase "the five, seven, and eight consciousnesses are the same": they are the same because they arise by taking external objective realms as their objects and do not arise by taking internal principles as their objects.

If one follows the latter master’s explanation regarding the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the six consciousnesses, then there are indeed the categories of "internal" and "external" gates: the first five consciousnesses arise by taking the external gate as their object, while the sixth consciousness universally takes both the internal and external gates as its objects;
this is what is meant by "being subsequent to the six. This intends to explain that [the seventh] takes both the internal and external as its objects.
The "gate" (*dvāra*) refers to the sixth consciousness. Question: Does the former master admit the existence of internal and external gates? Answer:

If one considers the principle of objective conditions (*ālambana-vastu*), the former master cannot maintain that there are internal and external gates. However, if one merely distinguishes based on the eight consciousnesses, there can indeed be internal and external gates;
for instance, the five consciousnesses take the external as their object, while the seventh and eighth consciousnesses take the internal as their object, and the sixth consciousness pertains to both.
The first interpretation, which is fully established both internally and externally, belongs to the former master; the second interpretation belongs to the latter master.
Therefore, in the treatise, the section from "the five consciousnesses" onwards represents the explanation of the latter master.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the word 'etcetera' includes [them]," in the treatise, the word "etcetera" following "the non-conceptualizers" (*asaṃjñin*) includes the two lines of the verse that follow. [Commentary]:

As for the statement that "conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is the cause of birth and death," this means that even among the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they do not establish other mental factors (*caitta*) such as sensation (*vedanā*) or volition (*cetanā*);
rather, it is only conceptualization that is able to perceive all objects and grasp at notions such as "male" or "female. Therefore, [birth and death] arise because of conceptualization.

One creates karma for birth and death and receives a body of birth and death because of this perception; since this perception is the cause of birth and death, non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) particularly loathe it.
[Commentary]:
Although it is said in general that six are distant, three are near, and one is immediate, these refer to the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body, which do not exist above the second dhyāna.

Therefore, it is called "distant" (dūra). Regarding the three types of "one" (*eka*): the first is the sixth consciousness, which ceases at this stage; this is called the "near one" (*antika-eka*). Question:

When one is first born in that heavenly realm, these three also arise there; why are they not called "near"? Answer: With respect to the distance of the plane (*bhūmi*), because they do not exist [there], they are called "distant.
It is not based on their arising at the moment of initial birth that they are designated as "near" or "distant."

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the passage from "In all places of birth" to "the manifestation of all branches can be obtained," the intent of this question is to ask whether all twelve branches are complete in every place of birth and so forth. Since it is not stated here, the text below has been omitted.
*Samāpatti* (三摩躰底) is translated here as "equipoise" (*tingzhì*). Equipoise has already been explained in the previous commentary.

[Commentary: Regarding this master’s interpretation of *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 59, up to the point "one should not subject [them] to interrogation," this refers to how this master reconciles the passage from *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* 59 cited by the later master.
This master states that the statement in 59—that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) take birth through the moisture of active afflictions (*kleśa*)—is said according to the majority of cases;
it does not mean that all do so. That is to say, those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*) possess only the seeds [of affliction].
Master Zhunsheng says that once one has entered the Path of Seeing as described, one immediately uses the seeds of the *anuśaya* (latent defilements) to moisten rebirth;
however, those who have attained the first two fruits also moisten rebirth through both seeds and active manifestations (*samudācāra*).

Only those who have attained the third fruit use the *anuśaya* of their own stage’s final mind to moisten rebirth, because they have exhausted the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm and have not yet been able to give rise to [the higher paths].
Because afflictions manifest in the first dhyāna, they merely moisten the seeds.

[Commentary] Furthermore, the explanation on page fifty-six regarding the phrase "for the sake of convenience" means that this interpretation refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* passage cited by the later master.
That text states that when subsequent perceptions and so forth arise, one immediately passes away from there; the intended meaning is that this describes death.

Since the arising of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is designated as the "arising of perception" (*saṃjñotpāda*) and so forth, when that subsequent perception arises, one passes away from that heaven after death;

it is not the case that one is said to pass away from there while still alive. Therefore, we know that after death, when the perception of the intermediate state arises, one then passes away from that [heaven].

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the nourishment of birth for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) up until the time of death for these non-Buddhists," generally, when discussing the nourishment of ordinary beings, it refers exclusively to the nourishment provided by seeds and manifest states.

Here, however, one master [argues] that since those in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) lack both initial and final mental activity, it is clear that when these non-Buddhists die from that heaven, [their rebirth] is brought about solely by the power of the potentiality (*śakti-bala*) of the previously mentioned seeds. Thus, he cites only the former seeds.
Ordinary beings born in the desire realm who possess only the seeds moistened [by craving] and do not give rise to evolving consciousnesses and so forth—
excluding this single class of ordinary beings and non-Buddhists— the others are moistened by both.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "nine types of mind that moisten rebirth," this means that at the time of death for sentient beings throughout the nine stages of the three realms, all give rise to present craving which moistens [the process of rebirth].

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "having already been born, one immediately passes away from there," this refers to the final moment of the mind in the *pūrvakālabhava* (existence prior to death), which is termed "conception" (*saṃjñā*).

From the stage of "presently arising" up to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the perception arises that one has been born; once the perception that one has already been born has arisen, one then passes away from that state.
Therefore, the Commentary states: "The perception having arisen, one then passes away from there"—this is the intended meaning here.

[Commentary]: Although it serves as an analogy for the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) because it reaches a state of "yū" (extreme), one might raise a latent objection based on the implications of this passage:
if there is thought at the very end of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), how can it serve as an analogy for the mindless attainments?
It is precisely for this reason that this text exists. Nevertheless, its status as an analogy for the mindless attainments is due to the fact that for a long duration in between, there is no mind.
Because it resembles the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), it serves as a metaphor; for there is no mind during the interval of the mindless attainment.

[Commentary: If one argues that there is mind in the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*), this "existence at birth" refers to what is called the "fundamental existence" (*mūla-bhava*), not the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), which is termed "existence at birth.
This is because, according to the Mahāyāna school, the eighth consciousness performs the linking of rebirth and does not involve mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "by the nature of things, one undergoes birth until the initial stage of 'original existence' (*pūrvakālabhava*)," the intent is as follows:

In discussing the process of taking birth, there must necessarily be a *pravṛttivijñāna* (evolving consciousness) at the very beginning. This is not yet the "existence at birth" (*upapattibhava*), but rather a general classification of the three types of existence within a single lifetime:
namely, existence at birth, original existence, and existence at death. "Existence at birth" refers to the very first moment of entering the womb; "original existence" refers to...

From the second moment onwards until the end of the hundred years, this is collectively termed "existence at birth" (*pūrvakālabhava*) and "existence at death" (*maraṇabhava*), which refers to the actual moment of dying.

When it is now said that this is not "existence at birth," the intended meaning is that when this evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) first arises, there is one moment during which it has not yet arisen;
it only arises at the time of the first moment of "existence at birth. Therefore, this evolving consciousness exists precisely within "existence at birth."

Considering that these evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) have not yet arisen, this is not the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*); therefore, at the very beginning of the fundamental existence (*mūla-bhava*), evolving consciousnesses must necessarily arise.

[Commentary] However, this is not a text stating that they are identical to the evolving consciousnesses; rather, its intended meaning is that, by the nature of things (*dharmatā*), there are six consciousnesses at the initial moment of taking birth.

It does not mean that consciousness arises immediately upon birth; rather, it refers to the initial stage of the "prior existence" (*pūrvabhava*) after the "birth-existence" (*upapattibhava*) has already begun.

It is not the case that it occurs at the second moment following the birth-existence. Although it is said that the six consciousnesses exist in the initial stage of the prior existence, it is not said that they exist at the second moment following the birth-existence.
What is called the "second moment" is precisely the initial stage of the prior existence.
This refers to the first moment of mind of the state of existence at birth (*upapattibhava*); it is said to be "after" the state of existence at birth because it is in contrast to it.
