It is said that the mind which transcends [the lower stages] based on a particular stage is bound to that very stage; that "subtle mind" refers to the mind at the point of entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Question: Since Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas enter this absorption without having undergone [the gradual] cultivation [of the stages], upon what basis is the absorption of cessation established?

Answer: For masters such as the sovereign Bodhisattvas, when they say they are entering the absorption, they immediately form the mental conception of the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*) by virtue of this [power].
Because of the mind, it remotely induces the seeds of the "subtle-subtle" mind (*anulakṣaṇa-citta*) that existed prior to the attainment of cessation when one was formerly not yet self-mastery;

it causes these seeds to regain their potency. Furthermore, by means of the function of the mind of revulsion (*nirveda*) which guards the mind, it establishes the attainment of cessation so that the mind does not arise.
This is also like the method of prolonging life: although the old karma is said to be exhausted, one further abandons [the previous] robes and bowl to provide nourishment and benefit.

Karma can likewise draw forth the lifespan; this is also the case here. By means of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) preceding meditative absorption, one draws forth from afar the ancient seeds of the mind of revulsion (*nirveda*) from former times, enabling them to function so as to prevent the mind from arising; it is with this intent that the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is established.

Regarding those who first practice, the attainment of cessation is established based on the seeds newly perfumed by the extremely subtle mind (*sūkṣma-citta*) preceding the absorption. As for Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery:

Because the uncontaminated mind preceding meditative concentration has already drawn forth [the seeds] before mastery is attained, at the time of entry, the mind’s aversion causes the old seeds to gain potency;
the functional capacity to restrain the mind is precisely what is established as the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodha-samāpatti*) upon this basis.
[Commentary]: Regarding the Buddha’s manifestation of various dignified postures (*īryāpatha*) while not arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*):

if the Buddha, a Great Bodhisattva, or others were to grant permission for someone to come on the following day or the day after to preach the Dharma or manifest dignified postures, they would first enter the supernormal power of the knowledge of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*) and make a formal vow, saying:
"After I have spoken, seven days or one year hence, I shall enter the meditative absorption of cessation. If it is later...
When sentient beings come, even though I am in the concentration of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*), I am able to manifest majestic deportment and preach the Dharma to transform those beings.
Once the limit of the period for which the vow was made has expired, I immediately enter the concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Even until the next day when people come here, although these bodhisattvas are within the concentration of cessation, they appear as if in a state of mind and are thus able to preach the Dharma and manifest majestic deportment.
Because they are equal, it is said that one does not arise from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) while manifesting the various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*).

[Commentary]: The meditative absorption of cessation actually proceeds from present activity; however, it is categorized as neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). This means that the absorption of cessation involves the seeds of mental aversion;
through the preceding outflow-free (*anāsrava*) present activity, it causes those preceding present activities to subsequently perfume the seeds.

According to its capacity, one enters this meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). It is not included within the category of those in training (*śaikṣa*), because it is the cessation of this very state, being extremely tranquil and lacking further progression.
Furthermore, because the aspect of its superior stillness resembles *nirvāṇa*, it is neither included among those in training nor among those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);

rather, it is included among those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*). This is because this meditative absorption of cessation is subsumed under the category of dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Therefore, it is not [included in the other two categories].
"Identical to wholesome form, mind, and so forth.
[Commentary]: Although it belongs to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), because it is not included therein, it is "neither of the two. This explains the external objection. The objection asks:

Since the seeds of the outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-bīja*) that produce revulsion belong to the Truth of the Path, how can the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) not be included among those who are in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)? The answer follows.
The following passage is not clear; it is feared that characters may have been omitted, as some [versions] include this under the category of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

[Commentary: "It is not the same as other seeds, because those are not yet stilled" means that if the seeds within the body of one in training (*śaikṣa*) are increasing and progressing toward [the goal], they are categorized as belonging to those in training.
If, however, the seeds within the body of one beyond training have already progressed in the past...
Upon reaching the ultimate fruit, there is no further dharma to advance toward; therefore, it is called "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*) and is also termed "the cessation of seeking.

Within the body of one beyond training, seeds that have already advanced toward [higher stages] are subsumed under the category of "beyond training. However, because they do not share the same lack of further advancement as the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they are not subsumed under either of the two [categories of the unconditioned].
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "it encompasses both conditioned and unconditioned because it is not subsumed under either of the two," the meaning of this passage is as follows:

that which is "neither of the two" (non-dual) encompasses both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Within the conditioned, it also encompasses both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Among the conditioned, the uncontaminated encompasses those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), namely the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Furthermore, the unconditioned uncontaminated also encompasses those who are neither in training nor beyond training.
That which is neither training nor beyond training is precisely the primordially pure *parinirvāṇa* within the very bodies of all sentient beings.
This, too, lacks any progressive advancement because sentient beings are neither those in training (*śaikṣa*) nor those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

It is just as the afflictions, indeterminate factors, and so forth within the bodies of those in training and those beyond training are subsumed under that which is neither training nor beyond training; thus, it is "training" [in the sense of being the ground].
All contaminated wholesome dharmas and all uncontaminated dharmas present within the body of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are subsumed under both the state of training (śaikṣa) and beyond training;
however, because the faculties of grief and suffering are both contaminated and uncontaminated, and can lead toward the uncontaminated, they pertain to both training and beyond training.
That which exists within the body of one in training is the state of training, and that which exists within the body of one beyond training is the state beyond training.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "lay disciples also exist in the Form Realm," this means that those Anāgāmins in the higher realms who have attained Arhatship all assume the physical appearance of laypeople. [Commentary]:
Although the text concerning the Six Desire Heavens does not explicitly mention this, there is no contradiction in meaning; the intent is to state that they possess bodies within the heavens.
Regarding the realization of non-returning and the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) by those newly practicing it:

this is stated as being "exhaustive" from the perspective of human beings alone, because they are proximate [to the teaching] and superior [in capacity]. As for the statement that it is "not yet exhaustive," this refers to the fact that the treatise specifically mentions attainment among humans; the text is not exhaustive if one considers attainment among both humans and devas.
If one were to include both humans and devas, then it would be considered exhaustive from the standpoint of ultimate principle.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "However, there is no subsequent arising in the desire realm" and so forth, the intended meaning is as follows:

Suppose one has realized the body-witness (kāyasākṣin) state as a non-returner (anāgāmin) in this life, having first attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) within the desire realm. If one attains it again in a future birth, it will be re-manifested while still in the form realm.
Why is this? Because a non-returner who is born in the form realm does not return to take birth in the desire realm again.

Therefore, because one can arise in the higher realms after passing away from the desire realm and attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is said that "later, in the two upper realms as well, it manifests.
[Commentary] This refers to the period before the doctrine of the eighth consciousness was established; this passage from the *Śāstra* reconciles the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Regarding that treatise’s statement that one later attains the present [ālayavijñāna] in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), this is said on the basis of the position that the eighth consciousness does not yet exist;
it speaks of the subsequent arising of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in the form realm without mentioning its attainment in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Now, in this assembly, when the treatise states that one also attains the present [ālayavijñāna] in the two higher realms, this is based on the fact that [the existence of the eighth consciousness] has already been established.
This is the exposition on the true meaning of the eighth consciousness.
[Commentary] The Udāyin-sūtra serves as proof for this point; furthermore, it does not exclude those in the formless realm from being able to enter this meditative absorption.

For example, when Śāriputra was in the midst of the great assembly, he spoke of the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), saying: "Suppose there is a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who previously [resided] in the desire realm..."

Having attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), he subsequently transcends the realm of those sustained by physical food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) and is reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*).
According to whichever celestial abode he occupies, he is then able to enter the absorption of cessation. Later, having arisen from that state, he is reborn in the Heaven of the Yāmas (*Yāma*).

According to whichever celestial abode he occupies, he is then able to enter the absorption of cessation. At that time, the novice Śrāmaṇera was present among the great assembly and heard what Śāriputra had said regarding this matter.
When the śrāmaṇera who had attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) among the mind-made devas (manomaya-deva) said, "Śāriputra,

what you call 'mind-made devas' refers to those who have entered the meditative absorption of cessation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," the śrāmaṇera then rebuked Śāriputra before the assembly,

saying, "Elder, that is not so. Śāriputra spoke again, explaining that the mind-made devas arise from the realm of devas who subsist on solid food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra), and that they follow according to their experience.

When one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in a single location, the novice likewise acts as before; thus it is repeated three times, yet each time the Elder says, "It is not so.
The old sūtras and śāstras state: *manomaya-deva*; here, *manoma* refers to the "mind-made" (*manomaya*) devas.
If the new sūtras and śāstras say *manas-maya*, *manas* means "mind" and *maya* means "made"; that is, it is the mind itself.
"Mind-born devas" (manomaya-deva) refers to those beings who are born by transformation (upapāduka) and are produced according to their will;
thus, the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm and all the gods of the form and formless realms are born by transformation and are all called mind-born devas.

However, those born from the womb, egg, or moisture are not produced according to their will. Nevertheless, even though there are beings born by transformation in the desire realm, they are also designated as "mind-born."
Now, we do not take [that specific case], but rather take the various devas of the form and formless realms;

since humans and devas of the desire realm all subsist on edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), and it is now stated that they "surpass" edible food, it is clearly understood that this refers to being born in the form realm beyond the desire realm, specifically among the mind-made devas (*manomaya-deva*).
As for the phrase "because it says 'any one'," the intention is to explain that since the Udāyin Sūtra states "any one," it is clearly understood to be precisely this.

Because one enters and emerges from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in whichever realm one has received a body, it is known that this also includes the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This means that the followers of the Lesser Vehicle do not understand this sutra; they claim that the novice (*śrāmaṇera*) mentioned here is Śāriputra, yet this is not so.

It was not spoken with the intention of referring to a novice, but rather to one who is a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) distinct from the former [type], who had previously suppressed the craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) within the desire realm.

Having attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) and being non-retrogressive, one passes away from the desire realm and is immediately reborn beyond the desire realm among the gods who subsist on solid food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra).

There, one gives rise to the perception of compassion; however, within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), although one is born among those gods, one cannot attain the meditative absorption of cessation.

This is because they lack a formless body and fear that [the continuum] would result in annihilation. Since Udāyin does not establish the eighth consciousness, it is said that even the Hīnayāna does not establish it.

As for why Udāyin said that Śāriputra was not "not non-[attainment]," how could one claim, based on the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings, that Śāriputra had already attained the fruit of Non-returner,
first achieved the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) within the desire realm, and then, without falling away,
passed away and was reborn among the mind-made gods (*manomayakāya*) who transcend the desire realm— that is, in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)?

One who has attained entry into the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) may, if they previously regressed from that absorption, later be reborn in the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*).

Even if they are reborn in any one of its celestial abodes, they can still give rise to the absorption of cessation. However, since the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) does not establish an eighth [consciousness], there is no non-percipient heaven (*asaṃjñi-sattva*) within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*);
thus, fearing total annihilation, one cannot attain the absorption of cessation there. For this reason, Śāriputra’s path is not like that of the Mahāyāna.
The explanation given in the *Madhyama-āgama* regarding Śāriputra’s reasoning is correct, whereas the reasoning of the śrāmaṇera is incorrect. Furthermore, Śāriputra’s intention was as follows:

suppose one who has attained the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) has previously suppressed the afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) within the desire realm and subsequently attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Later, having regressed and given rise to defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), he immediately regresses from that celestial absorption of cessation and passes away, being reborn within the form realm—excluding [the case where he had not yet suppressed them].

Because noble ones are not born among the Great Brahmā Heaven or the Heaven of Non-conception, when one is reborn in any other heaven, the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) can again be induced to manifest.

Furthermore, if one who has attained the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmin) does not fall away from the meditative absorption of cessation, then after passing away from there, they will be reborn in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-perception within the Formless Realm and attain the meditative absorption of cessation; this refers to Śāriputra’s understanding of the Mahāyāna.

Because there is an eighth consciousness, one can also attain the meditative absorption of cessation within the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; since the Hīnayāna does not admit this, their path is incorrect.
The Mahāyāna maintains that because the eighth consciousness exists, it is said: "Śāriputra was but a śrāmaṇera. [The opponent asks:

"Does Śāriputra say that the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is called the 'Mind-made Heaven'? [The respondent answers: "He speaks of it only in general terms and does not distinguish it specifically."

By subsuming the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception under the category of mind-made beings (*manomaya*), the Buddha himself did not preclude the possibility that the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is not a mind-made heaven;
it is for this reason that the two vehicles, Great and Small, have resulted in a persistent and unresolved controversy down to the present day.

[Treatise]: Regarding the phrase "because [the state] from the storehouse consciousness up to its non-interruption and non-extinction," the treatise explains that those of fixed nature among the *śrāvakas* do not believe that there is an eighth consciousness in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) where one is born;

thus, even when they enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) in the formless realm, they do not give rise to this absorption because they do not believe in the existence of the eighth consciousness.
Therefore, they do not enter the absorption of cessation.

[Commentary: Regarding the point where the former masters say that this [Great Vehicle] is the same as that [Small Vehicle], their intention was as follows: the former masters held that what is established is called "Great," while what is not established is called "Small";

thus, they considered it "Small" because it is not established. Now, however, this is not so. To say it is "established" means there is the sense of having faith in its existence, as explained previously.
How is this known? For example, even within the Mahāyāna, it is said that the Small Vehicle is established therein.

The eighth refers to the experience of pleasure, joy, and so forth within the ālayavijñāna. Although one knows this to be the case, there are those who do not say that an eighth [consciousness] exists.

This is because those born in the desire and form realms, as well as those abiding in the *anāgāmin* stage, speak from the perspective of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), asserting that it exists; thus, for them, it is called "established.
However, for those who do not believe in its existence, even though it has been established, it is not called "established" because they lack faith in its existence. Furthermore—
Just as one may have faith in the existence of the Hīnayāna within the Mahāyāna yet not regard it as ultimate,

we know that this discussion of belief and non-belief pertains only to the Hīnayāna and not to the Mahāyāna, because [the latter] is already established as such. Therefore, this treatise, like the *Yogācārabhūmi*,
follows the former masters in not permitting the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
[Commentary] Question: "If that is so, how can one believe that those who attain this meditative absorption exist, etc.? The intention behind the Noble One’s question is as follows:
One who attains the absorption of cessation must be a Non-returner (Anāgāmin) or higher;

furthermore, such a Noble One must be one whose lineage is fixed (*niyata-gotra*) and cannot be one whose lineage is unfixed (*aniyata-gotra*), because a Noble One of unfixed lineage will certainly not be reborn in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Because they belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) who are non-returners (*anāgāmin*) will not be reborn even in the very place where they have already been born once;

how much less would they be reborn in a lower realm? Thus, those of fixed nature do not take birth in the lower realms. As for those of indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*), it is not that the Buddha does not save them because their faculties have already matured;
rather, the meaning of this passage is to say that when the faculties of those of indeterminate nature—who are destined for the Great Vehicle—have matured, the Buddha will certainly [save them].
He saves them as if they were those of fixed nature; however, if those with the roots of the Mahāyāna are not yet mature, the Buddha likewise does not save them.
[Commentary: It is also not the case that those of indeterminate nature with great faculties will necessarily fail to mature and enter the stage of Nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa.

The meaning of this passage is to state that there are no persons of indeterminate nature who, possessing great faculties, would fail to mature and enter the stage of Nirupadhiśeṣa; it is intended to mean "indeterminate" [in the sense of being potentially determinate].

Regarding the question, "If those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*) whose faculties are not yet mature do not enter the nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), how does this differ from those of determinate lineage (*niyata-gotra*)?"—the intent is to ask:

if it were the case that those of indeterminate lineage whose faculties are necessarily not mature do not enter the nirvana without remainder, then what distinction would there be between them and those of determinate lineage?
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, furthermore, how could those of either determinate lineage believe [in such a distinction]?
Is it the eighth consciousness? Furthermore, a bodhisattva would certainly not be born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

If one who is fixed in their nature (*niyata-gotra*) were to have faith in the Mahāyāna, they would not be a person fixed in that [inferior] nature. If they were indeed a person fixed in that nature, how could they believe in the existence of the Mahāyāna and the eighth consciousness?
[Commentary] The answer is: among those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*), there are those who are deluded regarding the Dharma and those who believe in the teachings of the Hīnayāna.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "If there be a bhikṣu who has truly attained arhatship, yet does not believe in this Dharma, such a thing is impossible.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* explains this by stating that there are two kinds of śrāvakas: first, those of fixed nature who, although they believe in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [do not realize its ultimate meaning].
Those of indeterminate lineage who are unwilling to practice will, upon hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, develop deep faith and resolve to practice.

Even if the Buddha were present in the world, those of fixed lineage who are dull-witted and attached to the *Hīnayāna* would hear the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Mahāyāna and all produce faith, yet they would still not practice the Mahāyāna;
this is just as one might have faith in the Mahāyāna while remaining attached to the *Hīnayāna*.

Because they do not regard [this attainment] as ultimate, those who are not "confused regarding the Dharma" (a-dharmasthāyin) can also give rise to the meditative attainment of cessation within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who are not confused regarding the Dharma will give rise to faith, whereas those who are confused regarding the Dharma will not.
In this first interpretation, half will give rise to faith and half will not.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "this general meaning differs from that of [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] fascicle 56," the intent of fascicle 56 is based on the establishment of the eighth consciousness (the ālayavijñāna);
therefore, it holds that all beings give rise to this meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This present text, however, is based on a teaching where the ālayavijñāna has not yet been established;
therefore, it maintains that those born in the formless realm do not give rise to this meditative absorption.
[Commentary]: The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter ten, states: "As for those who do not enter this meditative absorption...

According to the text of the *Abhidharmakośa* itself, it simply says, "mostly dwelling in the maturation of tranquility (*śamatha-vipāka*), they do not enter this absorption," and there is no character "not" (*na*). Thus, the Master of the Commentary has cited the text erroneously.

The intended meaning of the *Abhidharma* text is that when disciples such as those in the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) are born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), by virtue of their dwelling [in tranquility], [they do not enter this absorption].

The first liberation of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which is supremely peaceful and possesses a distinguished maturation (*vipāka*), for the most part does not require the exertion of effort to enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because one desires to abide in that peaceful maturation.

Therefore, the lower realms and so forth all possess sensations associated with adverse maturations and are thus not called "peaceful"; the formless realm is not like this, and thus it receives the name "peaceful. This, then, is the [reason for its] attraction.
Since the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* provides this second interpretation, it says, "furthermore, for this second interpretation.

Alternatively, the character "not" (不) may be a corruption of the character "partly" (可), as it is often used in the sense of "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) and so forth. Some say that the commentator (*śāstrakāra*) made no error; the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states:
"It means that those who do not abide in the formless realm and do not enter this meditative absorption [do not attain it]. This refers to the state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Because the evolving consciousnesses, which are coarse and active, as well as conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) and so forth, do not function, the *vipāka* (maturation) obtains the name "tranquility.

Since that treatise states that those who lack faith in the teaching of the eighth [consciousness] are for the most part unable to abide [in this state], noble beings (*ārya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) do not enter this meditative absorption.
[Commentary]: Regarding those for whom the *yoga* is supreme, this refers to those of fixed nature who are not deluded regarding the Dharma;
they take faith as their object and possess the eighth [attainment], even if they are born in the formless realms, they mutually obtain this meditative absorption.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because it is spoken of in terms of the ultimate stage of the path of abandonment upon which this concentration relies," the intended meaning is that all levels of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) are the basis for the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Furthermore, because one abandons the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and thereby achieves the state of an Arhat (*aśaikṣa*), it is called the "ultimate stage of the path of abandonment."

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "There are those who say that dharmas are empty... up to 'it is not so,'" although ancient masters made this assertion, it is incorrect because it contradicts the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*.
Therefore, one should take the text of this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* as authoritative.

[Treatise] Regarding the passage in the *Śāstra* commentary stating, "Among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the lower eight stages," there are two masters' interpretations within the treatise.
The first master relies on the third chapter of the *Saṃgrahaṇī*, which speaks of five types of persons who attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

The treatise states that one must completely abandon desire, while the remainder are either suppressed or abandoned, because [among them] there is the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), who has completely abandoned the desire realm. The second master, however, bases his explanation upon the [opposing] view.
Regarding the phrase "in the ninth [verse] of the Dharma, among the four lines," this master explains it based on this very meaning:
one must first sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) and transformations of the lower four stages before the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) can arise.

According to the treatise, regarding the cultivation of the afflictions of the eight lower stages, it states that one must completely sever those of the desire realm, while the remaining afflictions are either suppressed or severed. Since it says "completely severing within the eight lower stages," [this implies the aforementioned requirement].

Regarding the statement that "the remaining afflictions of the desire realm are suppressed and abandoned," since it has already been stated that within the lower eight stages (*bhūmi*) all [afflictions] of the desire realm are completely abandoned, and that in the upper [stages] there are seven stages where [afflictions] are abandoned—having already excluded the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)—why is it now said that there are eight stages?
One should rather say that the afflictions of the upper stages are either abandoned or suppressed; however, the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) cannot suppress the afflictions of the Peak of Existence.
Therefore, even the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) is able to suppress the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because these are both obstacles and the obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is strong," the intended meaning is that the obstacle to concentration has as its essence the ripening-born sensations of inferior joy and bliss belonging to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
These sensations arise simultaneously with the afflictions of those two natures; it is by this that one is obstructed.

Because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is strong, inferior sensations (*vedanā*) serve as the primary obstacles, while afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like serve as secondary obstacles.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the intent behind the statement that those who have attained the first two fruits—having abandoned six grades [of afflictions] and so forth—do not attain it:

since those who have attained the first two fruits have exhausted both the six grades of afflictions and the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), why is it not permitted that they attain the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)? That is to say:
Because one proceeds from the first fruit to the second fruit, they are called the "first and second fruits";

it is not that a person who has attained the first fruit can abandon the six grades of afflictions associated with the cultivation of the desire realm. Alternatively, although the text is general in form, its intent is to inquire about the second fruit.
[Commentary: "It is said that only the five types of persons, such as the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and so forth, attain [this]" means:

among them, the Non-returners include those who have attained liberation through both meditative concentration and wisdom (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), while among the Arhats (*aśaikṣa*), it includes those liberated through both concentration and wisdom, but excludes those liberated by wisdom alone (*prajñā-vimukta*).
The phrase "because they first cultivate it in the Desire Realm" intends to explain that this occurs for the first time there.
Cultivation occurs only among humans in the desire realm; subsequently, it also becomes manifest in the two higher realms.

If that is so, how do you reconcile this with the second of the four propositions in the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharma* (the *Dharmapada*), which does not even mention "having already attained the first dhyāna" and so forth?

The intent of the question here is precisely the objection raised by the second master against the first: that one does not abandon the afflictions of the lower three dhyānas [while cultivating the path].
Regarding why one who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is said, in the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* among its four propositions,
to attain it only after attaining the fourth dhyāna, and not by attaining the lower three dhyānas,
the full text of those four propositions is as extensively set forth in the *Abhidharmakośa* and other secret treatises; this has been recorded in my notes.
[Commentary] To answer the objection that there is no contradiction in saying that one attains [the attainment of cessation] based on the fourth dhyāna alone:

the first master explains that the *Abhidharma* does not state that the attainment of cessation is attained based on the fourth dhyāna alone, nor does it exclude the three lower dhyānas from being the basis for the non-abandonment of afflictions and the failure to attain the attainment of cessation.
Therefore, it is known that although the defiled seeds of the three lower dhyānas are not abandoned, they coexist [with the attainment].
Since one can attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) while suppressing the defilements of the three lower dhyānas, what obstacle is there?

[Commentary]: Regarding the suppression or abandonment of the remaining five higher stages: this means that for the four upper stages, one uses the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) to suppress them, whereas for the fifth upper stage, one uses the supramundane path (*ārya-mārga*) to abandon them;
this is because the mundane path cannot suppress the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

[Commentary]: Among the lower three dhyānas and so forth, the seeds of affliction that can obstruct meditative concentration (samādhi) coexist with the various changing sensations of sorrow and suffering in the Desire Realm, and with the various changing sensations of suffering and pleasure in the lower three dhyānas.

This means that both the active afflictions and their seeds, when associated with sensation, are all capable of obstructing concentration—just as the unconditioned state of immovability (āniñjya-asaṃskṛta) does not.

Regarding the establishment [of the immovable unconditioned] based on the lower stages, the intended meaning is that it is established through the cessation of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and the attainment of the lower stages;

it is not otherwise. This is because pleasant feeling is largely characterized by movement and agitation of body and mind; therefore, the cessation of pleasant feeling and the perception of phenomena should be established as the immovable unconditioned.

Thus, the immovable unconditioned is not established based on the lower three dhyānas, but is established based on the higher stages. Now, regarding the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*): *Note: The provided text contains a complex argument concerning the Abhidharmic classification of the "immovable unconditioned" (*aniñjya-asamskṛta*) and its relationship to the levels of meditative absorption (dhyāna) and the attainment of cessation.*

It is likewise for the following four stages (*bhūmi*): because their afflictions are manifold and their obstacles to concentration are powerful, one must first sever them before attaining this concentration;

subsequently, one may give rise to it. Regarding the five upper stages, its initial arising occurs only among humans in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because their wisdom and understanding are extremely sharp and keen.

[Commentary] As for using the four propositions from the *Abhidharma* (the *Mahāvibhāṣā*) as proof, this refers to what was previously cited from the four propositions in the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharma*:
"It is said that the noble ones, having attained the fourth dhyāna, do not seek rebirth in the formless realms and so forth, and thus enter the attainment of cessation.
Since it states they have "attained the fourth dhyāna," it implies that they have severed the seeds of affliction within the [lower] three dhyānas.
According to this textual evidence, even the second master’s position that [the unconditioned] is superior is reasonable;
for example, it establishes that the unconditioned "immovable" (āniñjya) does not depend on lower stages, thereby refuting the logic [of those who hold otherwise].
[Commentary]: Regarding the intention of those who wish to clarify that the first two fruits [of the path] lead to the realization of the nine meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), it is said:

Suppose there were someone who claims that one who has attained the first two fruits can suppress the attainment of the cessation concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*). There are three faults in such a position.

First, according to your reckoning, one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has exhausted all the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*) of the three realms and uses the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) to suppress the nine grades of the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm, or the nine grades of the first dhyāna.

Furthermore, it is not the case that one who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by suppressing and exhausting all nine grades of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) [does so immediately].

Rather, a person on the path to the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), having exhausted the six grades of the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) through cultivation and suppressed the lower three grades of the desire realm up to the suppression of all afflictions of the sphere of nothingness, attains the meditative absorption of cessation. Now, as for the present objection, let us first set forth three faults; for instance:

How can those who have attained the first and second fruits of the path enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) when they have not yet completely abandoned the two natures—unwholesome and neutral—of the desire realm that obstruct concentration?

Furthermore, since the shifting sensations of joy and bliss within the lower three dhyānas also obstruct concentration and have not yet been abandoned, how could those in the first and second fruits attain the absorption of cessation? This constitutes the first [objection].

Furthermore, another objection states: "If it is said that those who have attained the first and second fruits of the path can attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), then one must also establish the 'body-witness' (*kāyasākṣin*) and the 'non-returner' (*anāgāmin*) within the context of those two fruits. This constitutes a second fault. Furthermore, another objection states:

"If those who have attained the first and second fruits can attain the meditative absorption of cessation, then those in the first and second fruits should also be able to realize the nine successive absorptions (*navānupūrva-vihāra-samāpatti*). This constitutes a third fault. Since these three faults logically follow, [the position is untenable].
Because it is difficult to achieve, those in the first two fruits cannot attain the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

[Commentary: This meaning is as follows: although the seeds already subdued may be lost or not lost, even until one is reborn at a stage where they have not yet been severed by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The intent is that, for example, a person in the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*) has completely severed the afflictions of the desire realm; based on this, regarding the eight stages above...
In the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), with the exception of the single level of non-perception (asaṃjñika), this meditative absorption can be attained whether afflictions are abandoned or not;

however, for the remaining seven levels, one must either suppress or abandon the afflictions before attaining the absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). This refers to a person who has attained the fruit of a Non-returner (anāgāmin) and has suppressed the afflictions of the first dhyāna and so forth such that only their seeds remain.
If, upon falling away, they give rise to the active manifestation (pravṛtti) of the afflictions of the first dhyāna and die, they will be reborn in the first dhyāna.

By means of seeds, one moistens birth in the higher realms; according to this principle, if one regresses and gives rise to afflictions, it should involve the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of seeds acting in conjunction with moisture.

This interpretation is indeed found among various schools of thought. Since one who has regressed from the *nirodha-samāpatti* gives rise to afflictions, how could it be that they do not employ the active manifestation of moisture?
If one does not regress and give rise to active afflictions, then there would simply be the seeds of delusion in the first dhyāna.

In a state where [defilements] have not yet been severed by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*)—that is, at the very moment they have been suppressed—one arises in the first dhyāna solely by means of seeds.

Within the first dhyāna, there are three heavens; if one is born into any of these three heavens, it is not precluded that the active defilements (*samudācāra*) of that stage may provide the moisture [for rebirth], because one dies and is reborn within that same stage. However, if one is to be born in the second dhyāna, it must necessarily...

When one gives rise to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), one immediately severs the seeds of this first dhyāna; it functions like the seeds of the earth where one is currently born, moistening the birth in the second dhyāna.
This applies to all other stages as well; therefore, there is no fault of severing a lower stage while one has already been born in a higher one.
[Commentary]: If that were so, then ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should only moisten [the seeds] through their seeds. To this, the objection is raised:

the holy teachings state that those who have entered the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) moisten birth by means of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); that is, even those in the first and second fruits moisten [birth] through active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
If the holy teachings state that ordinary beings moisten [birth] through seeds, it could also follow that ordinary beings should only moisten [birth] through seeds.

[Commentary]: However, regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they manifest the six types of cultivation that moisten [the seeds of existence] and do not suppress craving and so forth; since they are currently seen to have attained birth, it is difficult to claim that noble ones (*ārya*) do not possess the seeds.

The intention behind saying "though the seeds exist" is that while the seeds for rebirth in the higher realms should indeed arise, [the noble ones differ from] ordinary beings whose bodies, while remaining in a lower stage, give rise to the six types of cultivation that suppress afflictions—specifically, the path that can only suppress the afflictions of the lower stages within the *bhāvanāmārga* (path of cultivation) concerning delusions regarding phenomena (*vastu*).

Although afflictions such as vexation (*pratigha*), delusion (*moha*), and pride (*māna*) cannot suppress conceptual craving (*vikalpita-rāga*) or the subtle, innate views of self and what belongs to self (*sahaja-satkāyadṛṣṭi*),

they nevertheless arise because they serve to suppress other delusions regarding objective phenomena (*vastu-moha*). Furthermore, since afflictions of a higher stage arise in order to be born in a higher stage,

it follows by analogy that a noble one (*ārya*) would not sever the seeds of the lower stages and should thus be able to be reborn in a higher realm, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is moistened [by those seeds].

The passage beginning with "relying on companions" up to "attaining rebirth in higher realms" intends to convey the following meaning: Just as the afflictions that properly moisten birth— namely, the innate delusions regarding phenomena such as greed,
ignorance, and pride that arise during the path of cultivation— are able to be suppressed by the sixfold path while an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) resides in a lower realm, so too,
even though other forms of craving associated with the path of seeing and innate views of self and what belongs to self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi-ātmīyadṛṣṭi*) exist, they cannot [arise].
Because it moistens birth, one attains rebirth in a higher realm. As for "having no remaining delusions as companions," this means there are no co-arising delusions regarding phenomena (*vastu*).
[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "The noble ones' moisture for rebirth does not rely on companions; though they have seeds, they do not ascend to birth," the explanation is as follows:

such a person possesses only the moisture of the seeds and does not rely on manifest activity (*pravṛtti*) as a companion before beginning to moisten and produce birth. Thus, through the moisture of the seeds alone, birth occurs, and the afflictions (*kleśa*) have already been suppressed.

If one is reborn in the ground of affliction immediately, according to the first master, one is reborn in a place where the seeds of existence have already been suppressed in the First Dhyāna, but is not reborn in the higher ground of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).

According to the second master, one is reborn in a place where the seeds of existence have already been severed in the Fourth Dhyāna and suppressed in the lower grounds, but is not reborn in the higher ground of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception; therefore, there is no fault of severing the lower [grounds] while being reborn in the higher.
[Commentary]: Because the virtuous karma of a noble one (ārya) is superior, it is necessarily determined;

even when compared to the strong karma of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), if that ordinary person is at the stage of a worldling (bāla), the fruit received later from their own created virtuous karma is one degree inferior.

Furthermore, when one enters the state of a noble one from the stage of a worldling, the fruit received from this very same karma is one or two degrees superior compared to its previous reception during the stage of being a worldling. This case is also like that.
The seeds of the Noble Ones are moistened by the power of their wholesome karma and further nourished by the untainted (anāsrava), and thus it is only their seeds that are moistened.

If they were otherwise, the seeds of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) would be stronger than those of the Noble Ones; however, because the wholesome karma of ordinary beings is weak and lacks the support of the untainted, it is their manifest states (dṛṣṭadharmika) that are moistened.
Otherwise, the seeds of the Noble Ones ought to be stronger than those of ordinary beings.
[Commentary]: Now, regarding the Non-returner (anāgāmin) who, while dwelling within the stage of a Non-returner, necessarily only plants the seeds [of rebirth]—the meaning here is as follows:

Suppose one who has previously attained the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) as a fruit of Non-returning later regresses from that attainment of cessation and, at the end of life, dies from the desire realm and is reborn in the Brahmakāyika heaven of the first dhyāna stage; such a person necessarily only plants [the seeds].
It is moistened because the seeds of the afflictions of the desire realm have been exhausted and the mind of fulfillment has arisen;
thus, although it is only the seeds that provide moisture, even while one is born among the Brahmakāyika devas, one does not yet abandon the afflictions of the Brahmakāyika and other heavens.

When one passes away from the Brahmakāyika heaven and is born among the Brahmapurohita devas, it is only the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) that provides moisture, because the path that remedies these [afflictions] is not yet perfected. It is precisely from within the state of the Brahmapurohita devas that one abandons the first [level].
When the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the first dhyāna are exhausted, one uses the seeds of the second dhyāna to moisten rebirth among the Parīttābha (Limited Light) devas of the second dhyāna.

Since this is still a level of the first dhyāna, the outflowing mind (*āsrava-citta*) uses only the seeds to moisten rebirth; although one is born among the Parīttābha devas, one does not yet sever the afflictions.

It is only when one is born among the Ābhāsvara (Immeasurable Light) devas that one severs [the afflictions], and once the afflictions of the second dhyāna are exhausted, one is born in the Parīttaśubha (Limited Purity) devas of the third dhyāna.

This applies likewise up to the third and fourth dhyānas; the intended meaning is that for those born in their own respective realms, there is only the moisture of manifest activity, whereas for those born in other realms, there is only the moisture of seeds.

Furthermore, when one is born from the fourth dhyāna into the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), there is also the moisture of manifest activity because one gives rise to afflictions through falling back [from a higher state].
All the above refers to the moisture of manifest activity; the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks only in terms of attaining the abandonment of the afflictions of the desire realm.
Regarding the statement that the path of counteraction arises in its entirety in the form realm as merely moistening the seeds, this treatise is likewise:

if one who has attained the fruit of non-returner is born in the three heavens of their own level or other levels and attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), such that they neither fall back nor give rise to afflictions,
these are all cases where [the path] merely moistens the seeds.

[Commentary: The meaning of the remaining two phrases is clear: there are those in lower stages who abandon the afflictions of the lower [stages], such as those in the second fruit and the candidate for the second fruit (*dvitīyaphalapratipannaka*), as well as those in the third fruit (*trtīyaphala*) who, while in a lower stage, abandon the afflictions of the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and realize the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).

There are also those in higher stages who abandon the afflictions of the upper [stages], such as those among the *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who flow upwards) who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), upon being born (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), or after having been reborn (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*).

In the cases of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and so forth, they all exercise mastery over the higher stages, severing the afflictions of the higher realms and realizing the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*). [Commentary: However, regarding the unconditioned of immovability (*āniñjya-asaṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-asaṃskṛta*), which are established based on the abandonment [of defilements] and the cessation of feeling, the intention of the statement that they constitute a portion of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is as follows: if one merely suppresses defiled feelings and so forth, the unconditioned obtained thereby is only the unconditioned of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*). For this reason, because the seeds have not been severed, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) obtained by severing the seeds of sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth is termed the unconditioned of immovability (*āniñjya-asaṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned of the cessation of perception and sensation (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, this unconditioned is but a portion of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it is obtained through the severance of specific seeds;
it cannot be entirely subsumed under analytical cessation, for analytical cessation as an unconditioned phenomenon applies to the severance of many [defilements] and is established as manifold.

In this chapter, the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is now established in relation to the abandonment of the seeds of feeling and so forth; this makes it clear that the "unshakable" (*āniñjya*) and other such states are but a portion of analytical cessation.
The intended meaning here is as follows: if one suppresses the defilements of the lower two dhyānas, one attains the unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

if one suppresses the defiled dharmas such as feeling in the third dhyāna, one attains the unconditioned state of non-analytical cessation known as the "unshakable. This is the sense in which it is explained.

This unshakeable unconditioned (*āniñjya-asamskṛta*) is a portion of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because non-analytical cessation is established by the non-arising of all phenomena due to the absence of conditions;
since a portion of present feeling and so forth does not arise, the unshakeable unconditioned is a portion of non-analytical cessation.
If one severs the seeds of feeling and so forth of the third dhyāna, one immediately attains this unshakeable unconditioned. This is that unconditioned.
Because this is one portion of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is subsumed under the unconditioned state of immovability (*āniñjya-asamskrta*).

By abandoning [the defilements] of the third dhyāna—such as the pleasure that undergoes transformation—one establishes the unconditioned state of immovability and attains one portion of the unconditioned state of analytical cessation, because one has attained the abandonment of one portion of feeling and so forth.

If one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the fourth dhyāna and so on, one attains only the unconditioned state of analytical cessation, and does not [attain the unconditioned state of immovability].
Regarding the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-asamskṛta*):

if one abandons [the defilements of] the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and so forth, one attains only the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha-asamskṛta*), but does not attain the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling.

If, however, one abandons the afflictions from the sphere of nothingness downward until they are exhausted, one attains both unconditioned states—namely, the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling and the unconditioned state of analytical cessation—or at least a portion of the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling.
This is comprised within a portion of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation), as previously explained.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if one suppresses the afflictions of the lower eight stages or five stages," the intent is to say that the two aforementioned masters suppress the afflictions of the eight stages or five stages.

This means that, in comparison with the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), these are both termed "lower. If one suppresses the afflictions of the eight stages, there are two kinds of non-existence...
Are they all comprised within non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? Because their seeds have not been severed.

If one suppresses [the afflictions] of the five stages, this is merely the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-asamskṛta*), which does not constitute analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). However, the unconditioned state of the "Immovable" (*āniñjya-asamskṛta*) is comprised within analytical cessation, because the afflictions of the four lower stages have all been severed.
Nevertheless, the general statement in the commentary (*śāstra*) should be formulated in this way; upon examining the treatises (*śāstra*), the positions of the two masters are indeed present.
The commentary states that "one character" is an error; it should correctly be read as "eight characters.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "not one who is non-body-witness, wisdom-liberated, etc.," the meaning is this:

those who first attain this meditative concentration and subsequently turn their minds toward awakening (pratyāvṛtti) are merely body-witness *anāgāmins* or those who are both liberated (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*); they are not persons who are "non-body-witnesses."
Why is it that only those liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) [attain this]? Because they had not previously attained it.
[Commentary]: The phrase "there is a certain class [of practitioners] in the seven stages" intends to say that it is not the case for superior Bodhisattvas;
rather, when arising amidst afflictions to benefit sentient beings, one is only able to permanently subdue all afflictions and attain this at the fulfillment of the seventh stage.
"Because it is concentrated, it is said to be 'of one kind'.

[Commentary] This refers to what is stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*: regarding those who give rise to afflictions within the bodhisattva’s subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). A question is raised:

since subsequently attained wisdom is already untainted (*anāsrava*), how can it give rise to afflictions? Furthermore, do the wisdom and the afflictions exist simultaneously? Some say that it is indeed subsequently attained wisdom.
If it is the case that the afflictions associated with the five consciousnesses arise simultaneously, how can an outflow-free state give rise to unwholesome afflictions?

Answer: It is by way of intentional engagement (*abhiprāya*) that it is called "associated," yet because there is no defiled perception (*saṃjñā*), it also receives the name "unassociated. Because it does not increase the outflows (*āsrava*), it is termed "without defiled perception."

[Treatise] The commentary contains a citation from the third fascicle [of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] stating that from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, one is able to permanently suppress all afflictions (*kleśa*).

As stated in the third fascicle: "There is an interpretation that Bodhisattvas from the first stage upward have already realized the principle manifested by the two kinds of emptiness and have already attained the two kinds of superior wisdom; thus, they are like Arhats who have already severed the afflictions..."

[The text mentions] "affliction" (*kleśa*) and so forth. [Commentary]: Furthermore, another interpretation is that although "compassion and wisdom are equal," this refers to the state within the body of a single person where compassion and wisdom are balanced.

The underlying intention is to say that although this Bodhisattva possesses equal compassion and wisdom, because of the distinction between the lineages of those who fear and those who do not fear, there is therefore affliction.
Regarding the arising or non-arising of afflictions (*kleśa*): if one fears afflictions, one suppresses them so they do not arise, for fear of their becoming faults;
if one does not fear them, one intentionally causes them to arise for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. Thus, there is this distinction between suppressing and not suppressing.

For those who suppress [afflictions], they attain this meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) at the first stage (*bhūmi*); for those who do not suppress them, they attain it only upon reaching the seventh stage, where they then suppress [them] and achieve cessation.

[The section on] Determination. [Commentary]: Regarding "there are noble ones" and "there are ordinary beings," this is stated intentionally to distinguish between those of the Two Vehicles who have turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna].

Those who are noble ones refer to those from the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) up to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); these are the noble ones who have turned their minds. Those who are ordinary beings refer to those who were previously practitioners of the Two Vehicles.

One who, while practicing the path of the Hīnayāna according to their spiritual lineage, turns their mind toward enlightenment before even attaining the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) while still at the stage of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) within the Hīnayāna—
this is a bodhisattva who has turned the mind while remaining an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
[Commentary]: Regarding "attaining Buddhahood" as that which has already been accomplished up to its full perfection:

if the Buddha had previously attained the *nirodha-samāpatti* (attainment of cessation) while on the causal stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), then at the very moment of initial Buddhahood, it is said he "accomplishes" it.

At the time of attaining Buddhahood, he immediately relinquishes the stages of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) as well as all inferior out-flow-free states (*anāsrava*) and inferior attainments of cessation belonging to the ten grounds.
This refers to the attainment of the unprecedented, most supreme, and excellent meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) at the very moment of attaining Buddhahood.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "if one follows the two masters, all three vehicles reach [this state]," this clarifies that the number of persons who attain this concentration differs.

In the Mahāyāna, there are those Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment who, while still in the desire realm, attain the supernormal powers and reach all ten stages (*bhūmi*); as for those of gradual enlightenment...

Regarding Bodhisattvas, they attain [the meditative absorption of cessation] throughout both the desire and form realms, and across all stages—both prior to and upon entering the bhūmis—because they have already attained it previously;

however, for those who have not yet attained it in the interim, they must first attain it because they had not attained it before. As for Pratyekabuddhas, specifically the rhinoceros-like Pratyekabuddhas, they appear only in Jambudvīpa in the southern continent;
even when they attain the meditative absorption of cessation within the supramundane state, they do not proceed to the other three continents.
The attainment of meditative concentration in the higher realms occurs because one does not turn toward the supramundane there; thus, only a single person attains it.

As for the *pratyekabuddhas* who travel in groups (*vargacārin*), they likewise do not reach the heavens; with the exception of the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*), they appear in the other three continents and attain the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Regarding the Śrāvaka vehicle, if distinguished by location, it is attained among humans—excluding the Northern Continent—in the other three continents, as well as [in the heavens].

The six heavens of the desire realm obtain all nine [attainments]; in the form realm, excluding the Great Brahma Heaven of the first dhyāna and excluding the heaven of non-perception, there are sixteen heavens in total that obtain them.

Those who attain the fruit while residing in these places are all those who are "bodily witnesses" (kāyasākṣin) of the non-returner (anāgāmin), as well as those who are "liberated through both parts" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
Furthermore, those in the four heavens of the formless realm also obtain them; in total, there are three [categories].
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*), there are twenty-nine locations where one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);

this is because these twenty-nine locations all contain non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arhats. In terms of the stages (*bhūmi*), this refers to the nine stages; in terms of the "divided bodies," it refers to these twenty-nine locations.

Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), all noble ones (*ārya*) possess superior, middling, and inferior capacities. As for the nine grades (*navavidha*), they are categorized according to the abandonment [of defilements] in the first dhyāna.

One person attains the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by suppressing the nine grades of defilement of the first dhyāna through the first grade of defilement of the second dhyāna, thereby subduing the remaining eight grades of defilement of the first dhyāna as well as the defilements of the higher stages;

thus proceeding in succession, there are nine such persons who attain the cessation attainment by gradually severing the nine grades of defilement of the first dhyāna while subduing the defilements of the higher stages.
Likewise, there are nine persons for each stage up to the severance of the nine grades of defilement within the second dhyāna, and so on.
The same applies to all nine grades of defilement in the sphere of nothingness, up to the attainment of the cessation of the nine grades of existence in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);
since there are likewise nine persons who attain meditative concentration, it is said that there are "nine grades. This is according to the first master’s explanation.

According to the second master’s explanation, for example, there is a person who is a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who has exhausted the defilements of the lower three dhyānas but has not yet abandoned even one grade of defilement within the fourth dhyāna. This person...

This refers to nine types of persons: from those bound by all fetters in the fourth dhyāna up to those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by severing the nine grades of defilement in the fourth dhyāna;
this applies likewise up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Thus, according to the first master, within the eight stages (*bhūmi*), there are nine grades in each stage, and thus nine types of persons in each. According to the second master, within the five stages, there are nine grades in each stage.

All of these possess nine types of persons who attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); if categorized according to superior, middling, and inferior faculties, there are many varieties.

Regarding those termed "certain" or "uncertain," this clarifies that they have definitely attained the absorption of cessation. Those who include the body-witness non-returner (*kāyasākṣin anāgāmin*), the one liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*), the rhinoceros-like solitary realizer (*khadga-viṣāṇa-pratyekebuddha*), the group-dwelling solitary realizer (*vargacārin-pratyekebuddha*), and the bodhisattvas of the ten stages all attain the absorption of cessation. As for the "uncertain," they are those who [have not yet definitively attained it].

Regarding those of the two vehicles who are liberated through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*), as well as those who are not "bodily witnesses" (*kāyasākṣin*) or those of indeterminate nature— the latter refers to persons of indeterminate lineage who attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
[Commentary] This means that among those in the first six stages who follow the path of the Śrāvakas, up to those capable of entering this absorption— if they are in the first six stages...

Based on the stage of the perception of compassion (*karuṇā-saṃjñā-bhūmi*), by taking as an object the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the four aggregates associated with the perception of compassion, a bodhisattva is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*);
that is to say, within the first six stages, the bodhisattva, in common with the śrāvakas, performs conditioned formations and is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "In the seventh stage, one is able to enter this samādhi in every thought-moment, even to the point of being free from the conceptualization of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena," this means that when a Bodhisattva in the seventh stage wishes to enter the samādhi of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they take as their object the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*) and the unconditioned true suchness (*asaṃskṛta-tathatā*).
Only after departing from the signs of existence and non-existence do they enter the samādhi of cessation; this is unlike the Śrāvakas, for Śrāvakas are unable to produce the signless [object].

Because it belongs to the realm of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*), it merely acts as a condition and serves as a basis for the perception of compassion; thus, one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by means of the conceptual characteristics of the sphere of infinite space.

Therefore, a Bodhisattva enters this absorption by relying on subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) while maintaining conceptual images (*sanimitta*) that take suchness (*tathatā*) as their object.
How does wisdom attain suchness while maintaining conceptual images? The answer is: because one enters the meditative absorption of cessation through subsequently attained wisdom.
[Commentary: If "determined nature" (*niyata-gotra*) refers to those who attain [the fruit] throughout all ten stages, this is a general explanation of the meaning of the passage;
it refers to the person who is determined to attain [enlightenment], and not to the "determined nature" of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
This is because it encompasses both the sudden and gradual determinations, or alternatively, it may refer exclusively to the Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment.
[Commentary]: As stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* regarding the first stage (*bhūmi*) and so forth, up to the description of those who practice by taking conditioned phenomena as their object—

this passage means that while that sūtra speaks of attaining the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) from the first stage and so forth, it also accords with the text in this treatise which states that one may attain the meditative absorption of cessation from the first stage.

[Commentary]: Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Great Wisdom), fascicle 62, which states that one can enter [the meditative absorption] in every thought-moment up to the point of non-conceptuality (*animitta*), this explains the reason for the differences between the sutras and śāstras in this context.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of the "Far-Reaching" (*dūraṃgamā*) stage because it concerns the ability to enter [this state] in every thought-moment;
the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, however, discusses it in terms of attaining the concentration, and thus applies it to all ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Therefore, there is no contradiction between them.

[Commentary]: Although the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (in its eighty fascicles) states that one enters this cessation-samādhi (*nirodha-samāpatti*) by taking the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*) as an object when entering the nirvana-without-remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), there is no contradiction here.
The intention of this assembly is as follows: it refers to Bodhisattvas who take the true signless realm as their object when entering cessation-samādhi, rather than those who take a semblance of it;
thus, those Śrāvakas of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) are excluded because they transform the signs [of reality]. This does not conflict with the meaning of the eighty-fascicle version.

This is a contradiction. Although Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles both possess subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), there is a distinction between their direct and indirect engagement with transformations;

thus, they are divided into the "true" and the "semblance. To provide another explanation: from the seventh stage upward, Bodhisattvas take the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*) as their object, whereas the reverse—taking signs as objects—is not the case.

Consequently, they do not enter cessation by relying on subsequently attained wisdom. Furthermore, because those of the Two Vehicles cannot enter meditative absorption moment by moment, they are not included here.
Because bodhisattvas of different capacities are able to enter this state in every moment of thought, there is no contradiction in explaining it specifically [in this way].
[Commentary: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, asks, "To what state of mind does one emerge? The intent of this question is as follows:

when entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there is no conceptual discrimination; since one neither thinks, "I shall enter samādhi," nor "I shall emerge from samādhi," while actually within the state of concentration...

Because the mind is tranquil, one is free from applied effort (*prayoga*). Since the mind ceases first at the time of emerging from meditative absorption, how can there be mental attention (*manasikāra*) for emergence?
The answer is: because one has previously well-cultivated the preparatory resolve (*cittābhisaṃskāra*).

If there are certain modes of conduct, signs, or characteristics that enable entry into absorption and emergence from absorption, by practicing and repeatedly cultivating them, through that cultivation—

"Therefore, one can enter spontaneously and emerge spontaneously. The commentary explains: "By the power of cultivation, although there is no conceptual discrimination, one is able to enter and emerge from this meditative absorption spontaneously.

Previously, because of having cultivated the meditative absorption with mental activity (*sacittaka-samādhi*), there were various marks and signs of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) for entering and emerging from the absorption.
Regarding 'marks and signs of conditioned phenomena,' the explanation is as follows: when, at the time of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for entering the absorption, [one perceives]..."

When all minds and mental factors arise with the various characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), one generates revulsion and is able to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Upon emerging from this absorption, because three kinds of contact and three kinds of objects serve as conditions for emergence, it is said that they are all identical to the characteristics of conditioned phenomena in their ability to enter and emerge from cessation.
This is intended to mean that through the power of extensive cultivation and the application of detachment from mind and its associates, one is able to do so.

One is able to enter and emerge [from meditative absorption] spontaneously; alternatively, this may be explained from the perspective of those who have attained mastery. If one has not yet attained mastery, one only emerges from concentration through a prior vow.

Now, considering this passage, it applies generally to all who have long practiced the great treatises. The statement "having previously formed a mental resolve" refers to beginners because they must cultivate the preparatory purification thoroughly.
As for those who have long practiced, this is stated in reference to the most eminent among them; specifically, it refers to those who have long engaged in cultivation at the very beginning.
The details of the practitioner’s cultivation are omitted here. [Commentary:

Furthermore, it is stated that at the time of emerging from meditative absorption, one contacts three kinds of contact (*sparśa*), namely the immovable contact (*āniñjya-sparśa*) up to the contact with the objects of the three cessations (*nirodha*).

Herein, this refers specifically to the three kinds of contact contacted when, having already emerged from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), one perceives the three types of objects; "contact" (*sparśa*) refers precisely to this.

This contact associated with the sixth consciousness is called "contact" because it contacts and confronts the preceding objects; it is not the contact of the body-consciousness that is called "contact.
This is because the body-consciousness cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), whereas only the sixth consciousness can enter this absorption.
Accordingly, it is designated as "immovable contact" (*aniñjya-sparśa*). To provide a further correspondence: the "possessor of the object" refers to the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*).
When there are objects and sense faculties that possess the designation of "possessors of objects," it is intended to mean that my former view of self arose based on these faculties and objects;
