now, since that view of self has been severed in the attainment of cessation, the faculties are not moved by such views, and thus it is called "immovable.

When the mind emerging from meditative absorption takes this as its object, it is called "contact with the immovable," because one contacts the immovable object; hence, it is "contact with nothingness."

Regarding "the object of the object of the object of the object": this refers to the sense-faculty objects that emerge from meditative absorption; when the mind emerging from absorption takes these as its objects, those objects are the "objects of the objects of the sense-faculties" of the emerging mind.

This means that there is no grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). When the mind emerging from absorption contacts that [object], it gives rise to the "contact of nothingness" (*ākiṃcanyasparśa*) and the "contact of signlessness" (*animittasparśa*).
These are assigned to the "object of cessation. "Signlessness" (*animitta*) is precisely *tathatā* (suchness), which is the object of cessation.

This is precisely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). It is the object of the mind emerging from meditative absorption; in relation to this object, it is called "contact with the signless" (*animitta-saṃsparśa*).

Alternatively, in reverse order: "contact with the immovable" (*āneñja-saṃsparśa*) corresponds to the object of cessation; "contact with nothingness" (*ākiñcañña-saṃsparśa*) corresponds to the state of non-existence;

and "contact with the signless" (*animitta-saṃsparśa*) corresponds to the possessor of the object. Furthermore, according to the *Śāṣṭha-śāstra* (or *Saṃghabhadra*), in response to question 153, these three types of contact exist as follows: [text continues].
Regarding the distinctions between them, there are four explanations. The second explanation states: emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the contact of immovability;

wishlessness (*apranihita*) is the contact of non-existence; and signlessness (*animitta*) is the contact of non-contact. These are assigned to the three contacts based on the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).

Other details are not recorded here, as further distinctions are explained in the *Śubhākarasiṃha-śāstra* (or *Jiuyao*). Some say that "possessing an object" refers to the five aggregates being called "possessing an object."

This mind emerging from meditative absorption takes an object that possesses a domain and establishes the "unshakable contact" (*aniñjya-sparśa*), because it is not moved by the grasping of the conceit of "I am.

As for "domain upon domain" (*viṣaya-viṣaya*): this refers to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). The substance of these five sense objects is collectively one domain; furthermore, because each of the five consciousnesses individually apprehends them, they are also called domains.

Thus, they are termed "domain upon domain. When the mind emerging from absorption takes [this] as its object, it establishes the "contact of non-existence" (*ākiṃcanya-sparśa*) once it has initially entered meditative absorption.
After severing greed and the other [afflictions], upon emerging from meditative absorption, there is no longer greed and so forth;

there is nothing at all, but only mind and that which is perceived by the mind, which should contact the remaining [objects] as described before. As for Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained mastery, they emerge from absorption based on the former two objects;
as for Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery, they emerge from absorption based on the latter object.

[Commentary] Question: Since the five object-specific mental factors (*pañca-viṣaya-niyata-bhūmika*) arise even when not associated with outflowing consciousness (*sāsrava-citta*), why are there only twenty-two [mental factors] in this context?
The intent of this question is as follows: Just as among the five object-specific factors associated with outflows, desire may arise toward an object of longing alone;

or, regarding an object of grasping, concentration may exist without wisdom, or wisdom may exist without concentration—such that these five object-specific factors do not necessarily arise simultaneously—how is it that [only twenty-two are established]?
Question: Does the cessation attainment (nirodha-samāpatti) have the extinction of twenty-two factors as its essence? Answer:

It is so for the outflow-free (anāsrava), because the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) do not coexist and their characteristics are distinct; however, in the state of the outflow-free, the five constant [faculties] are fully present, because within a single practice one cultivates all practices.
[Commentary]: Regarding the first point, "what time did the Buddha attain that which was previously attained and that which was never before attained? The intention is this:

the Buddha’s attainment of the *nirodha-samāpatti* (attainment of cessation) is also called "never before attained," because other wholesome dharmas and defiled dharmas of the Buddha have been attained hundreds and thousands of times throughout kalpas;
thus, they are termed "previously attained. As for wholesome and unwholesome dharmas and so forth, at the very moment their characteristics arise from the future, the dharma-dhātu itself arises.
The "previously acquired" (*pūrvaprāpta*) refers to those wholesome and other dharmas that are acquired simultaneously with the dharma itself upon reaching the present;
these are called "previously acquired" because they were already acquired prior to the arising of the dharma, and because they are now acquired again simultaneously with that dharma.

Conversely, the "not previously acquired" (*apūrvaprāpta*) refers to those such as the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), which have not been acquired since time immemorial; they are so named because they are acquired for the first time in the future.

Because there is no acquisition prior to the dharma (*aprāptapūrva-prāpti*), if the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) relies on the present, it gives rise only to the simultaneous acquisition (*sahajā-prāpti*), which constitutes a single layer of acquisition;

yet it is called "acquisition not previously obtained" (*aprāptapūrva-prāpti*) because it is a fresh, new acquisition at each moment. Since there is no acquisition prior to the dharma, it is termed "not previously obtained.
If it relies on the past, there is only the subsequent acquisition (*paścātprāpti*) of the dharma; therefore, the Buddha’s attainment of cessation is named "not previously obtained."
In this current passage, since there is not even one character less than what is required, let alone two, we know that it is improper to place an extra character in the preceding text.
Furthermore, this "one character" should be the word "yi" (以), as in the phrases "that which was previously attained" (*yì céng dé*) and "that which was never attained" (*wèi céng dé*).

Moreover, the meaning of "previously attained" and "never attained" has already been explained and examined in the discussion of the proofs for the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*) and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). Furthermore, regarding the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...

It is certain that there is an attainment through detachment (*vairāgya-lābha*) distinct from other noble ones, which is attained solely through application (*prayoga*). This is why the Buddha is specifically questioned and answered regarding this:

it is discussed with reference to its perfection. Although it has already been attained during the stage of a cause (*hetu-avasthā*), it is not yet perfected; it is only upon reaching liberation (*vimukti*) that one realizes its perfection.

[Commentary]: Regarding emerging from meditative absorption due to a prior vow: when one wishes to enter absorption, one must first establish a specific period—whether it be seven days, ten days, or even as long as one day or one kalpa—before emerging from it.
This means that once the previously established period has elapsed, one immediately emerges from the absorption.
[Commentary]: Regarding those who possess extremely heavy sleep and so forth, there are two types: light and heavy.

If it is light sleep, it is an indeterminate mental factor (*aniyata-nirvedha*), as explained in various treatises. As for fainting (*mūrchā*), it is precisely the sixth consciousness along with its associated mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
Thus, the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "Fainting is the non-common karma (*asādhāraṇa-karman*) of the mind."

[Commentary: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 1, states that fainting (*mūrchana*) is the unique activity of the mind (*manas*), because at the time of fainting there is only mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

If one refers to the moment when fainting first arises, there is indeed only mental consciousness; however, during the subsequent stage of extreme and heavy fainting, there is no mental consciousness.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of fainting as being [the activity of the mind] based on the initial occurrence of fainting, when mental consciousness is present.
The mental karma that is not shared has fifteen types of differentiation:

discerning objects, deliberating on objects, intoxication, madness, stupor, waking, dreaming, awakening, initiating karma, the ability to leave desire, the ability to leave [the state of] detachment, severing the roots of goodness, reconnecting the roots of goodness, death, and birth.
[Commentary]: Regarding "striking the *marmans*," *marman* here means "vital point of death" (*mṛtyu-cchidra*) or "joint of death" (*mṛtyu-parvan*).
Thus, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, fascicle 30, states: "The *marmans* are not separate entities; they are distinct from the joints of the body.

If one strikes them, death immediately ensues. Therefore, there are one hundred and twenty-eight joints of death upon the human body; if these joints of death are struck, one immediately falls into a state of fainting and death. As it is said:
The Noble One is well-liberated from the fetter of death; he merely faints upon touching the fetter of death, yet he obtains objects without needing to die or be supported.
[Commentary]: "Fainting" refers to fainting at the point of contact; this fainting is the "fainting" among the twenty kinds of touch.
The twenty kinds of contact (*spraṣṭavya*) are explained in detail below. [Commentary:

Alternatively, it may be that only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is called the "unshared activity of the mind" (*asādhāraṇakarma*); this interpretation refers to the state of being in a swoon.

Prior to the swoon, when the five sensory consciousnesses have ceased, at the time of the swoon itself, only the mental consciousness exists, and thus it is termed the unshared activity of the mind. Furthermore, this is not [the same as] the mind (*citta*).

Although there is a state of mental distress (*mūrchā*), it is nonetheless not a mental factor (*caitta*). When one reaches the stage of being without mind (*acittaka*) due to distress, it is termed "extremely heavy fainting.
[Commentary: This means that the state produced by the mental factor of sleep is not like the state produced by the phenomenon of fainting. To explain briefly: as for the phenomenon of fainting...
It is only by depending on conditions such as wind and heat that fainting occurs; it does not arise without such conditions.
However, sleep can arise even in the absence of wind, heat, and so forth, as when it is induced by factors such as physical food, exhaustion, or mental dullness.
This state of the body and mind that is thus induced is what constitutes sleep. Sleep is a mental factor (*caitta-dharma*) and is distinct from fainting.
As for the statement that "it is not like the state produced by what the sleeping mind can induce," the intended meaning is this:
that which is induced by the sleeping mind is precisely this inducing factor itself reaching its ultimate limit as a state [of extreme sleep] within the stage of the mindless state;
therefore, it is metaphorically called "sleep. In reality, when there is no mind, it is not termed "sleep"; thus, it is said that the inducing factor of sleep is the mind.
[Commentary]:
"Abandoning all activities" means that just as when a person is actively engaged in work, they remain sleepless until the task is finished, at which point they fall asleep;
for this reason, these ten factors are said to be able to induce sleep.

[Commentary]: In reality, one is not truly asleep. If there is mental activity during sleep, it may be designated as "sleep"; however, when there is no mental activity, it is not called sleep—it is merely a conventional designation of sleep. [Commentary]:

As for the explanation, it is like a person whose internal orifices are blocked by accumulated undigested food and drink; because the gases cannot be expelled, they become congested and cause distress.
[Commentary]: "Led by supernatural power" means being affected by the power of ghosts or spirits such that the mind becomes faint and unconscious.
As the Vaipulya Sūtras state, various great powerful deities addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there are those who disturb the reading of the sūtras, we shall strike this person until they die or reach a state of mindlessness"—this refers to the supernatural power of bringing about their fainting and unconsciousness.
[Commentary]: Alternatively, both of these are portions of the *spraṣṭavya-āyatana* (the sense base of the tangible). This is the second interpretation; the preceding was the first interpretation.

Alternatively, both are portions of the *spraṣṭavya-āyatana* among the twelve *āyatanas*. "Sleep" refers to the touch of fatigue and exhaustion; "fainting" (*mūrchā*) is precisely this state of collapse.

Among the twenty kinds of tangibles, this refers to the "superior touch" (*uttara-spraṣṭavya*) within the *spraṣṭavya-āyatana*; that which is superior to the objects of touch (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*) all depend upon it.

[The sensation of] "fainting" (*mūrchā*) is conventionally established upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); however, in this treatise, it is said to be a portion of the sense-object of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*).

Furthermore, this is explained with reference to fainting within the two realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*), and not with reference to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because the tangibility based on the four great elements does not exist in the formless realm.

Question: Is there fainting in the formless realm? Answer: There is indeed fainting in the formless realm as well, such as that occurring during death and rebirth; however, this [term "fainting"] is used here with intentional restriction (*abhiprāya*).
Since fainting is also included among the fifteen types of karma, we know that there are cases where fainting is a tangible object (*spraṣṭavya*) and cases where it is not.
Question: In the later explanation of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, both sleep and fainting are both explained as having the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) as their essence.
I do not yet understand what the essence of sleep and fainting was taken to be in the initial explanation within that same treatise. Answer: This will be explained below.
[Commentary]: "When there is consciousness, it reaches this point where contact occupies a small portion" clarifies the reason why *mūrchā* (fainting) has contact as its essential nature.
[Commentary]: "Or when there is consciousness... explains that the state of unconscious sleep (*asamprajñāta-nidrā*) has contact as its essential nature.
"Byo (Yu).

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "a small portion of the state of arrival," the intended meaning is that these two tactile sensations of exhaustion and fainting are exclusively objects of the eighth consciousness. Why?
Because they are subtle and not consciously perceived; thus, it is said that when one is in a state of extreme deep sleep or fainting, it is designated as a time when there is no mind.
Because the subtle state of non-awareness takes fatigue as its essence, the eighth consciousness also takes it as an object. Furthermore, Ce (Cè) states:

"Moreover, this sphere of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) is the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness; the seventh does not take it as an object, and the first six do not function [with respect to it].

Some say that the eighth consciousness does not take these two types of tangibility—fatigue and vexation—as its objects. Why? Because all twenty kinds of tangibility are merely provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*) that depend solely upon the four great elements.
The eighth [category] established here as a designation refers only to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that serve as the basis for contact and so forth;

it does not refer to contact itself. The phrase "a portion of the sense-base of contact" mentioned in the summary statement of these two [categories] points to this very passage in the treatise, or indicates that both are included within the sense-base of contact.
[Commentary]: Regarding the previous separate explanation of the two [states] as taking the mindless state (*acittaka*) up to this point as their essence:

in the treatise, the former explanation of mindless sleep and fainting establishes these mindless states upon the specific phases (*avasthā*) of the material body (*rūpakāya*), its faculties (*indriya*), and their objects (*viṣaya*).

Since the mind does not function therein, it takes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as the essence of this mindless sleep and fainting. This differs from the latter explanation, because the latter [explanation] holds that...
Because it takes the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*) as its essence.
[Commentary: As for the question, "Why is it not so?"—the intent of this question is: why are the two stages of death and birth not mentioned?
Since the stage of "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) has already been mentioned, the two stages of death and birth should likewise be mentioned.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "One should say that eight states are called 'mindless,'" this answers the previous question:
if one follows the former masters' assertion that there are only the two states of death and birth, then the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* should have stated that there are eight mindless states.

[Commentary: Regarding the "single contradictory interpretation" (*ekānyathā-vyākhyāna*), an examination of other editions reveals that not a single character [of this term] exists there; alternatively, the meaning of the treatise itself contains two parts:

first, to manifest the contradictory interpretation, and second, to clarify the reason for not mentioning entry into the nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa. For the time being, since we are explaining the manifestation of the contradictory interpretation, it is called "one."

[Commentary]: Regarding "coarse and shallow dharmas," the intended meaning is that the two factors of sleep (*middha*) and stupor (*styāna*) are coarse and shallow dharmas; therefore, the Buddha does not possess them at all from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) onward.
Any mention of their presence is merely a manifestation for the sake of skillful means in teaching and transforming others, appearing as if identical to sentient beings.
The character "zai" (財) used in the *Śāstra* is an error.

[Commentary]: Regarding the three vehicles (*triyāna*), the distinction between those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the analysis of the three realms (*traidhātuka*) and so forth, all should be contemplated according to reason.

As for the others: the noble ones (*ārya*) possess the latter three [attainments]; the Buddhas possess eight stages; and only one possesses the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Those in the three realms who possess sleep exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

those in the meditative attainment of cessation exist in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); and those in a state of fainting exist throughout the three realms. Death and birth occur within the three realms.

Therefore, both death and birth are comprised within the state of being without mind (*acittaka*), and "being without mind" is itself subsumed under *mūrchana* (fainting). Otherwise, the categories of the five states of being without mind would not exhaustively encompass all phenomena.

[Commentary] In explaining the six simultaneous [mental factors], eight simultaneous occurrences are also mentioned; however, the verse text originally intends to clarify the six simultaneous [factors].

The statements that "the five consciousnesses manifest according to conditions" and "the mental consciousness constantly arises," and so forth, are also spoken here for the sake of following the flow of the text;
thus, they also indicate that the eight consciousnesses arise together. Therefore, the passage concerning the "eight consciousnesses, etc. is precisely an elucidation of their simultaneous arising.

[Commentary]: This refers to the objections raised by the original masters of the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, such as those of the Sarvāstivāda school. The "original master" is Kātyāyanīputra himself.
As for the "objections," these consist of the questions and answers found within the *Jñānaprasthāna* itself, such as:

"Why is it that many consciousnesses do not exist in the present? All such instances are the questions and answers from the *Jñānaprasthāna*; they are somewhat superficial, extending even to the passages in this present treatise.

Since these are all passages from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the Sarvāstivādins and others maintain that for a single sentient being, only one consciousness arises at a time and they do not arise simultaneously.
Therefore, when Kātyāyanīputra was formulating his own school’s tenets, he used this to challenge the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna:
"If multiple consciousnesses were to operate, how could it be said that there is only one sentient being? Thus, this treatise is the fundamental text of the Sarvāstivāda.

Regarding the question of who composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, some say it was composed by Kātyāyana during the Buddha’s lifetime, while others say it was composed by Kātyāyana after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
this is the fundamental tenet of the Sarvāstivāda school.
[Commentary]: If it is the case that [the same applies] even up to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) when one belongs to another realm, then consider this:

suppose a person whose body is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) attains a meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). When they enter a meditative absorption of a higher level belonging to another realm, how can such a person be said to belong to their own category (*svabhāga*) of sentient beings in the desire realm, and so on up to the formless realm?
This is the objection; it is to be understood by analogy with the case where one whose body is in the desire realm enters [a state].
When the untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*) manifests before one, how can this person be said to be a "tainted sentient being" (*sāsrava-sattva*)?
They ought to be an untainted sentient being.

[Commentary: According to the master of the *Nyāyānusāra*, the term "sentient being" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*), because there is a succession of preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness. Thus, it is the *Nyāyānusāra*.

The Master of Reasoning explains that "sentient being" (*sattva*) refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), while "sentience" (*sattva*) refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Because the life-faculty is capable of possessing this consciousness, it is called a "sentient being.
Even when one is in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), although present consciousness is absent, the life-faculty should still persist;
it is capable of possessing past and future consciousness. Since the former is the past and the latter is the future, it is said that the life-faculty is capable [of possessing consciousness].
There are preceding and succeeding consciousnesses.
[Commentary: This is discussed in common with what is accepted by the Hinayana schools;

when this treatise states that "sentient beings are established based on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)," it refers to the statement that sentient beings are established based on the life-faculty as accepted in common with the Hinayana. Seeds are capable of...
Because there is the eighth consciousness, that which is the provisional establishment of seeds is what the treatise states:

"In dependence upon the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), the life-faculty is a provisional [establishment] based upon seeds. That which follows is the actual dharma of manifest activity (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*);
this refers to what the treatise establishes as "sentient beings" or "the maturation-consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*). This maturation-consciousness is a manifest consciousness, and thus it is real.

[Commentary]: Regarding the second point, "establishing sentient beings based on the quantity [of seeds and manifestations]," the meaning is that sentient beings are established based on the duration of life (āyus) resulting from these two factors—the seeds and the active manifestations.
Question: Why are other consciousnesses not used to establish sentient beings, but only the eighth?
Answer: Because that [eighth consciousness] alone is always present as a single entity, whereas the other consciousnesses...
[This is] because there is both transformation and interruption.
[Treatise]: How can multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously when a single body has only one *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition)?

The intention [of this question] is that according to the Small Vehicle’s own school, they challenge the Mahāyāna by asserting that within a single body, various consciousnesses do not arise concurrently, following the six [sense bases].

Question: When a single consciousness arises within a stream of consciousness, there is only one immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). How then does the Mahāyāna allow for multiple consciousnesses to arise simultaneously?
Answer: As stated in the *Shu* (Commentary). [The *Shu* states: This is not so.
Regarding the claim that multiple immediate conditions exist within a single moment, the Hīnayāna objects: "In our school, there is only a single consciousness."
When [a cognition] arises, there is within that single moment only one immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Since you, in the Mahāyāna, admit that multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously in a single moment, it follows that there must be multiple immediate conditions in a single moment.

Although the Hīnayāna raises this objection, according to the Mahāyāna, multiple immediate conditions are indeed admitted in a single moment, because multiple consciousnesses arise simultaneously within that single moment.
[Commentary: It is not the case that within the Mahāyāna, one consciousness induces multiple consciousnesses to serve as the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

According to the correct principle of the Mahāyāna, the eight consciousnesses each relate to one another as equal-and-immediate conditions; that is, one consciousness of the preceding moment takes one consciousness of the succeeding moment as its equal-and-immediate condition.
[Commentary]: Alternatively, this refers to the interpretation of the former masters regarding the mutual relationship of the six consciousnesses as conditions.
As the former masters stated that the six consciousnesses stand in relation to one another as equal-and-immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the preceding text says:

"If this one consciousness serves as the equal-and-immediate condition for those six consciousnesses, or if those six consciousnesses likewise serve as [the condition] for this one consciousness—this is what is meant by these consciousnesses being equal-and-immediate conditions."

[Commentary]: Regarding the principle that each [consciousness] individually possesses many conditions capable of inducing the arising of multiple resultant consciousnesses: this means that among the eight consciousnesses, each one individually has many equivalent and immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
For example, a preceding moment of visual consciousness acts as a condition capable of inducing the arising of a subsequent moment of visual consciousness;
the same applies to the other consciousnesses. What is called "many equivalent and immediate conditions" refers to their arising and ceasing moment by moment (*kṣaṇa-utpāda-vināśa*).
Therefore.

[Commentary: This "proof of arising" regarding the fifty-first *samāpatti* refers to the passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter fifty-one, which corresponds to the first of the eight proofs for the *ālayavijñāna* mentioned previously—the proof of its arising. Now, this passage is cited here based on reasoning.

It is difficult to maintain [the position that consciousnesses do not arise simultaneously]. For instance, suppose sentient beings at one time desire to apprehend the five objects, such as visible forms;

when the conditions—the sense faculties, their objects, and so forth—are all assembled and their respective potencies are equal, why would the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) exist therein where consciousness does not arise?
There is no other reason for its non-arising than [the absence of simultaneous consciousnesses]. Because of this, it is known that various consciousnesses function concurrently.

[Commentary]: Regarding the similarity of the six consciousnesses when conditions converge: if the sense organs are unimpaired, the objects are present before one, and attention is correctly aroused, these three conditions are fully present for all six consciousnesses; therefore, they are said to be "similar.
As for other conditions such as space or light, there are differences in their presence or absence.

[Treatise] Furthermore, although mental factors (*caitta*) do not differ in their nature as such, when they arise simultaneously with those of different categories, this raises an analogy regarding the primary mind (*cittarāja*).

The intended meaning of the response is as follows: If it is accepted that various mental factors—such as sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)—which are identical in their general definition yet distinct in their specific types, may coexist;

why then should one not likewise allow for the simultaneous arising of consciousnesses of different categories, such as the visual and auditory consciousnesses, which are identical in their general definition as being "mind" (*citta*)?
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "within a single thought-moment there are four functions," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 51, states:
"When various consciousnesses arise simultaneously, within a single kṣaṇa there are four kinds of functions: first, the function of discerning the vessel-world;

second, the function of discerning the basis; third, the function of discerning the self; and fourth, the function of discerning objects. The explanation says: the "vessel-world" refers to the [first]...

Regarding the eighth consciousness’s function of being the support for the vessel-world and its karmic activity: this refers to the eighth [consciousness] discerning the five sense organs (*indriya*), their auxiliary objects (*viṣaya*), and their seeds.
This is because the five organs and their seeds each serve as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the consciousness;

thus, the organs and seeds are called the "support" (*āśraya*) of the eighth, and by discerning these, it acquires the name of the "karmic activity of support. Regarding the "karmic activity of the self": the manas is constant...

The eighth is reckoned as the "self," whose function is the discernment of the self; the remaining six consciousnesses each discern their own respective objects, which is termed the function of discerning objects.
This means that if various consciousnesses arise simultaneously, there are four functions; if they do not arise simultaneously, these four functions are not established.
If one does not admit the existence of these four functions, it contradicts the words of the Sage. If there is a fourth function, it must necessarily exist.
If the first three karmas exist, it does not necessarily follow that the fourth karma exists, because in the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), the six consciousnesses do not exist. [Commentary:
Now, there are some who claim that the eight consciousnesses are not distinct; this fails to exhaust the full principle, as is the case with those who study the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.

It is said that the eight consciousnesses are not distinct from one another, just as waves arise depending on seawater and are thus not distinct from the water, or as a face and its reflection appear depending on a mirror and are not distinct from the mirror.
Although this is not the case here, within the sūtras and śāstras it is taught that the seven consciousnesses depend upon the eighth consciousness;
therefore, analogies such as waves arising from the sea are cited. Because waves arise from the sea, that treatise relies [on this analogy].
This is explained through a partial analogy; in reality, the eight consciousnesses are each distinct. Furthermore, Master Zhe said:

"If you argue that because waves depend upon water and there is no difference between the water and the waves, the eight consciousnesses must likewise be without distinction, then it would follow that the conditioned depends on the unconditioned and the unconditioned depends on the conditioned, and thus the unconditioned and the conditioned should have no distinction."

[Commentary]: The statement "now it is said that [the mind] takes the past as its object" means, for example, that the scattered mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes as its object events that ceased long ago.

[Commentary]: This distinguishes [this case] from the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), which would result in the fallacy of being indeterminate. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The sixth mental consciousness is the subject (*dharmin*);

the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it should not clearly apprehend the objects perceived by those five sensory consciousnesses; the reason (*hetu*) is that it is not permitted [to claim] that the mental consciousness [is indistinct].

Because it is concomitant with the five consciousnesses, it is the reason (*hetu*); like a distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) taking as its object a past event long since ceased, this is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
If the term "distracted" were not included in the example, there would be the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika-doṣa*) regarding the reason.

Thus, the opponent brings up the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) as an instance of inconclusiveness, asking: "Is it not the case that, just as the knowledge of past lives takes as its object a past event long since ceased..."
Because it is clear and distinct, why does the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the five [sensory consciousnesses] not perceive the five objects clearly?
Is it because, like a distracted mental consciousness that perceives objects long past and extinguished, this [simultaneous mental consciousness] also fails to perceive the five objects clearly?
Therefore, the term "distracted" (*vikṣipta*) is employed to exclude the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), for [the latter]—due to its connection with the past...

Because the cognition of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), there is no fault in its being an inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, as the *Ximing* [commentary] on valid cognition states:

"According to your own school, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) induced by the five sensory consciousnesses should not be clear (*vyakta*), because it does not take the past as its object while in a state of concentration; it is like a distracted mental consciousness taking that which has long since ceased as its object.

Although the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*) takes the past as its object, it is nevertheless clear; therefore, it is said that [the clarity of] a distracted mind—"

The statement that "because it is not an object of a distracted consciousness and has long since ceased, it is clear," as well as the claim that "a distracted consciousness apprehending an object is not clear," would result in the fallacy of uncertainty (*anaikāntika*) regarding the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*).
If a distracted consciousness, being distracted, were to clearly perceive an event that has long since ceased, this would constitute the fallacy of uncertainty;
thus, this passage constitutes the third proof among the eight proofs, namely "clarity" (*spaṣṭatva*).
This is the proof.

[Treatise]: How is it that when five [sensory consciousnesses] arise together, there is only one mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that apprehends one or many objects? This is the meaning of the objection raised by others:

according to the Master’s own school (*siddhānta*), the six consciousnesses are admitted to arise simultaneously; how then can there be only one mental consciousness when five [sensory consciousnesses] are present with respect to visible forms?
[Question: Among these [five consciousnesses], does one take on one or more objects according to the number of the five consciousnesses?

[Commentary (Sū): The meaning is that it is not admitted that a single moment of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises simultaneously with the five consciousnesses, nor that a single mind grasps multiple objects.

This refers to the intention of the Sarvāstivādins, who do not admit that the six consciousnesses arise together; why then would they not admit a mental consciousness co-arising with the five [sensory] consciousnesses (*pañca-sahaja-manovijñāna*)?

It is clearly understood that this refers to the apprehension of the five objects; however, it is also admitted that a solitary mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising alone in a single moment can likewise take eighteen realms (*dhātu*) and many other objects as its conditions.

Therefore, the text states: "That school does not admit a single moment of mental consciousness associated with the five [sensory consciousnesses] (*pañcaka-sahaja-manovijñāna*) that perceives multiple objects;
yet, there is no impediment to a single moment of solitary mental consciousness perceiving the eighteen realms, as their own system explains. There is no place where they do not so state.
It is impossible for two consciousnesses to arise simultaneously in a single moment; it is impossible for two wheel-turning monarchs to appear at the same time and in the same place;
it is impossible for two rhinoceros-like pratyekabuddhas to appear in the world at the same time and in the same place;
and because it is impossible for two Tathāgatas to appear in the world at the same time and in the same place, we do not admit that two [consciousnesses] exist in a single moment.
Regarding the simultaneous arising of two consciousnesses, the present assembly understands it as follows:

there is no possibility and no occasion for two wheel-turning kings (cakravartin) to appear simultaneously within the same world-system (*sādhāraṇa-lokadhātu*); yet, it is permitted that many wheel-turning kings may appear at one time in other distinct world-systems.
Furthermore, there is no possibility and no occasion for two eye-consciousnesses (*cakṣurvijñāna*) to arise simultaneously from a single eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).

[Commentary]: Furthermore, excluding those such as the Mahāsāṃghika school who do not admit that [the six consciousnesses] arise simultaneously—the intention of the proponent here is that this objection does not apply to the Mahāsāṃghikas;
if it refers to the Mahāsāṃghika, the Ekavyāvahārika, the Lokottaravāda, the Kukkutika, and other such schools, they do admit that the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously.
However, regarding others such as the Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika schools, the Master of the Treatise (the author) does not admit that the six consciousnesses arise simultaneously.

Now, in response to the Sautrāntika position that one apprehends the five objects, the Vaibhāṣika challenges the Sautrāntika regarding the meaning of the Master’s statement concerning the apprehension of one or many [objects].
As for the phrase "the mental consciousness occurring in the single moment immediately following the five sensory consciousnesses," up to the point where it says "is obtained" (*prāpnoti*),

the intended meaning is that the Vaibhāṣikas and others do not admit that the mental consciousness in the single moment immediately following the five sensory consciousnesses can clearly perceive the five kinds of objects.

The object may indeed be so; for within that school, it is accepted that a distinct, independent manovijñāna (mental consciousness) arising subsequent to the five sensory consciousnesses possesses a clear and distinct function regarding the five kinds of objects.
Question: Why does the Sautrāntika school not accept that the manovijñāna following the five sensory consciousnesses perceives the five kinds of objects with clarity?

Answer: The Sautrāntikas and others state that the single moment of manovijñāna following the five sensory consciousnesses— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content as given.*
At one and the same time, five kinds of clear objects are perceived.

Once the visual consciousness has perceived the object of form in the first moment, and that visual consciousness has ceased in the second moment, the mental consciousness arises and perceives the preceding object of form with equal clarity.
Once the mental consciousness has ceased, in the third moment, the auditory consciousness arises and perceives the object of sound; as soon as the auditory consciousness has ceased—
In the fourth moment of attention, when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises taking sound as its object, it is clearly manifest;

however, if it takes as its object that which was not the object of the preceding visual consciousness, it is not clearly manifest because it is separated by a momentary cessation of the mental consciousness.

When the fifth moment arrives, olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*) arises taking fragrance as its object, and upon this, the olfactory consciousness ceases and the mental consciousness arises again, taking the previous [object] as its focus.

The olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*) attains clarity only when it perceives its own object; if it takes as its object the preceding visual or auditory consciousnesses rather than the objects of form or sound, it is not clear because it is separated by many moments of thought.
The gustatory and tactile consciousnesses, etc., should be understood according to this same principle:

they can only perceive one object clearly at a time, and cannot perceive five objects clearly simultaneously. If other independent mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*) take the five [objects] as their objects...
The objects would then become clearly manifest.

[Commentary: Although this objection is raised to show that even in the Mahāyāna, clarity is not attained—just as in the Mahāyāna, if the sixth consciousness arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, the mental consciousness (*manas*) perceiving the five objects cannot also be clear at that same time.

Although the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses, if the mental consciousness and the visual consciousness focus together upon the same object of form, the mental consciousness attains clarity;
it does not share this capacity for clarity regarding sounds and other objects in the same way as the auditory consciousness and its counterparts.
This objection and others like it were intended by the Master [Vasubandhu] to demonstrate his point.

Although it is difficult to refute others by claiming that the objects of those five consciousnesses should not be perceived with clarity and so forth, within the Mahāyāna, the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) co-arising with the five [sensory consciousnesses] also has instances where it does not perceive its objects clearly;

this is because the mental consciousness co-arising with the five consciousnesses functions merely through spontaneous engagement (*anuvartana*) and lacks deep apprehension or conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

However, one must carefully examine the distinction between this co-nascent [mental consciousness] and that of the Hīnayāna schools. Question: How is it that you previously spoke of "co-arising with the five"?

The statement that "the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) apprehends the five objects clearly" means only that it shares the same objects as the five sensory consciousnesses; because it is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it receives the name "clear.
It is not as clear as the independent mental consciousness (*svatantra-manovijñāna*), which possesses an extremely clear function; therefore, it is said to be "not clear.
Alternatively, even if this objection were raised, it would be a Mahāyāna critique leveled by a follower of the Hīnayāna; that is, one from the Hīnayāna school posing this challenge to the Mahāyāna.

If one wishes to maintain that the fivefold simultaneous mental consciousness (*pañcaka-sahabhū-manovijñāna*) also apprehends objects without clarity, this accords somewhat more closely with the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*).
[Commentary: Just as the visual and other consciousnesses each apprehend one or twenty types of form (*rūpa*), the present commentary states that "visual consciousness takes twenty types of form.
This is either in accordance with the assertions of those schools that maintain such a position, or because that school permits twenty types [of form].

Form (*rūpa*) is substantially existent and is entirely the object-condition (*ālambana*) of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Furthermore, the commentary states that "visual consciousness takes twenty kinds of form as its objects";

this refers to the position of those masters who previously asserted that visual consciousness can take conventional forms (*prajñaptirūpa*), such as length and so forth, as explained in the preceding commentary.

Moreover, when it says "visual consciousness takes twenty kinds [of form]," this is stated in terms of their number; however, regarding the principle of the twenty kinds of form, they are indeed substantially real.

It is said that visual consciousness does not take as its object [such] conventional forms as length and so forth; for length and other such forms are all specific varieties of shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*).

Visual consciousness likewise takes as its objects light, shadow, brightness, darkness, and so forth, because these are all specific varieties of manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), such as blue, yellow, and the rest.
As for the twenty types, they are: blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, high, [low, straight, crooked, cloud, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, sunlight, brightness, and darkness].
"Below, [there are] the regular and irregular, smoke, clouds, dust, mist, light and shadow, brightness and darkness.

[Commentary: As for the phrase "the object possesses many characteristics because it is the aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) grasped by the functioning of multiple consciousnesses," this refers to the *nimitta-bhāga*.

Since that which is grasped by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*)—namely, the various mental aspects (*ākāra*) of the perceiving seeing-part itself—is manifold, we know that the *nimitta-bhāga* which serves as the objective support (*ālambana*) must likewise be manifold.
[This refers to] various characteristics.

[The Sub-commentary] states: "Because they do not arise from the same conditions as the three natures" means that if the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) shares the same object as the visual consciousness, then the mind is able to induce the arising of the five sensory consciousnesses.
If this were so, the mental consciousness of the three natures would then be of the same nature as the five sensory consciousnesses.

If mental discourse (manojalpa), though assisting the five [sensory consciousnesses] to arise, were not to share the same object (*ālambana*), then the mental consciousness would likewise be unable to induce the arising of the three natures within the visual and other sensory consciousnesses.

How, then, could the five consciousnesses possess these three natures? Since it is evident that the mental consciousness shares the three natures with the five when they are simultaneous, it is clear that they share the same object.
From this, it is known that the mental consciousness has two functions: first, it assists the five [consciousnesses] in their arising.
Regarding the phrase "the two are alike in being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet differ from the visual consciousnesses and so forth":

this means that although both are alike in being direct perceptions, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able to clearly and distinctly discern and deeply apprehend the characteristics (*nimitta*) of the object, whereas the visual consciousnesses and so forth cannot clearly and deeply apprehend their respective objects;
thus it is said they are different. This does not mean [the mental consciousness] is useless.

The intended meaning is that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) assists the five [sensory consciousnesses] in their arising, and because it is also capable of having the function of clearly apprehending and deeply grasping the object of perception (*ālambana*), it is said that it is not without utility. [Commentary]:

Regarding the phrase "the intention arises here... further assisting the five to arise," the mental consciousness that accompanies the five has two aspects: first, [it acts as a simultaneous support].

It is understood that two [conditions] are required to assist the five [sensory consciousnesses]. Even if the two eye-consciousnesses are clear, they do not serve as an analogy because they lack the assistance to induce the five [other sensory consciousnesses].
Not all clear mental consciousnesses (*manovijñāna*) are capable of inducing the five;

for instance, although the mental consciousness within meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is clear, it cannot assist the five. Question: Is it the case that the five consciousnesses are entirely absent in all states of meditative absorption? Answer: [No.]

It is accepted that those who have attained mastery may give rise to the five sensory consciousnesses even within meditative concentration (*samādhi*); however, for those who have not attained mastery, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within concentration cannot induce the arising of the five sensory consciousnesses.
Question: Is the mental consciousness that arises simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses always direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? Answer:

Just as the sixth consciousness can function through inference (*anumāna*), it may also share the same object of cognition as the five sensory consciousnesses; if it arises within concentration as direct perception, the mental consciousness may likewise be direct perception along with the five.
Question: If that is so, why does the treatise state that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising simultaneously with the five [sensory consciousnesses] is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

Answer: This refers to the case where the mental consciousness spontaneously engages its object and is necessarily accompanied by the five; it is therefore called direct perception. However, when the mental consciousness arises at other times, its status as direct perception is not fixed.

Regarding the statement "not having the same object" (*asamānaviṣaya*), this refers to those among the eight [types of mental consciousness] that do not share the same object, which exist in their entirety.

Those that differ even partially regarding their objects are likewise not associated; for example, the five consciousness-bodies are not associated when viewed in relation to one another, and it should be understood that the same applies to the relationship between the fifth and the seventh [consciousnesses].

Furthermore, those that differ slightly regarding their objects are not associated, such as the relationship between the fifth and the sixth or eighth, and between the sixth and the seventh or eighth.

[Commentary]: "This means that because the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses have different ranges of objects—some broad and some narrow—it clarifies that among the eight consciousnesses within the causal state (*hetu-bhūmi*), there are differences in the breadth or narrowness of the objects they perceive.
To perceive many phenomena is called 'broad,' while to perceive few is called 'narrow.

For example, the sixth consciousness can perceive all eighteen *dhātus*, which is the broadest; the eighth [consciousness] perceives only eleven *dhātus*, namely the five material sense-faculties (*pañca-rūpīndriya*)."
Furthermore, because it comprises the five types of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) and a portion of the *dharmāyatana* as substantial form (*rūpa*), the preceding treatise states:

"As for the substantial form transformed by the *dharmāyatana*, if its seeds are categorized according to where their manifest activity (*samudācāra*) occurs, then this [definition] is broader than the following.

If the seventh consciousness (*manas*) takes only a single dharma as its object, it is termed "narrow"; whereas each of the first five [consciousnesses] calculates that they each take a single dharma—such as visible form—as their object.

It is also called "narrow. If one asks: since every single [cognition] at the stage of Buddhahood universally takes all phenomena as its object and possesses both fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), then if that is so, how can the wisdom that accomplishes activities (*krtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object when it lacks fundamental wisdom?

There are two explanations for this: some say that the wisdom that accomplishes activities also possesses direct cognitive wisdom (*sākṣāt-karaṇa-jñāna*); others say that it possesses only subsequently attained wisdom.

Regarding the attainment of wisdom, there is no "essence-wisdom" (*svabhāva-jñāna*). The commentary states: Having realized the conventional and attained the ultimate, it is termed "subsequently attained" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*);
thus, even the subsequently attained wisdom of the Buddha-fruit takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its object. Even if essence-wisdom is absent, it is possible to take suchness as an object.

Some say that the five consciousnesses of the Buddha-fruit possess both essence-wisdom and subsequently attained wisdom; while this may be logically superior, it is taken here according to common sentiment.

[Treatise] As for the statement, "Even if they share the same object, they are incompatible because their substance and number differ," this is intended to dispel an external doubt. The external doubt is as follows: "If they do not share the same object, it may be as you say;
but since they do share the same object, why are they not compatible? To address this, the following clarification is made:
Even if they share the same object, they are still incompatible because the substance and number of their respective bases differ according to where they are located. This is what is being stated.
Although there is some partial similarity among the eight [consciousnesses], they are nonetheless not congruent, as in the case of the fifth and sixth [consciousnesses].
Regarding the sixth [consciousness] in relation to the seventh and eighth, their respective bases—the substance and number of the faculties—differ.

[Commentary]: Even if there were partial similarity, it would be because the substance and number of the faculties that serve as the respective bases for the eye-consciousness and so forth differ; that is to say:

The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, possess four types of supporting faculties (*āśraya*), namely: the faculty of the common object (*sabhāga-viṣaya*), the faculty of discernment (*vikalpa*), the faculty of defilement and purity (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna*), and the fundamental faculty (*mūla*).
As for the sixth consciousness, it relies upon only two faculties: the faculty of defilement and purity and the fundamental faculty.

As stated in the commentary (*śāstra*), the claim that "the mental consciousness relies upon three faculties" is an error; one cannot say that the six [consciousnesses] rely on the immediately preceding and ceased mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), because [the eighth consciousness...]

Since all consciousnesses possess the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that has just ceased as their immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), they are said to be "associated" (*samprayukta*). This association necessarily possesses four equalities:
equality of time, basis, object, and substance. Now, we shall distinguish them by means of a single equality.

"Exhaustive" refers to this single equality, namely, the equality of the supporting faculty (*āśraya-indriya*). Among the four equalities of association, it is distinguished by the equality of the supporting faculty.
Therefore, because the substance and number of the faculties upon which they rely differ, they are not associated.

Regarding the statement that "the two differ in number because the four and three rely on different [bases]," one should rather say: "The four and two rely on different [bases], while five rely on four faculties, and the sixth relies on two faculties."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because their associations differ," this means that each has its own distinct [associates]. However, as previously stated, "association" (saṃprayoga) refers to having the same object of cognition (*ālambana*), the same function (*kārya*), and equal mental factors (*caitta*);
these are termed association. Now, when the eight consciousnesses are compared with one another, they cannot be associated.

First, their modes of activity (*ākāra*) differ, namely their seeing-aspects (*darśana-bhāga*). Second, their bases (*āśraya*) differ, namely that visual consciousness relies on the eye-faculty, and so forth, up to body-consciousness relying on the body-faculty.
The consciousnesses differ in their bases: the first five depend on the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), the sixth depends on the seventh, and the seventh depends on the eighth, each being distinct.

They differ in their objects: visual consciousness takes form as its object, up to tactile consciousness taking touch; the sixth takes all things as its object; the seventh takes the eighth as its object;
and the eighth takes three kinds of objects. They differ in their association: the eight consciousnesses may arise simultaneously or not.
Because they arise in varying degrees and cannot be associated, one cannot say they are definitely one.

Furthermore, if one were the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and the others were mental factors (*caitta*), then association would be possible; this is because association occurs with that which has a different nature, not with its own nature.
Since all eight are consciousnesses, it is impossible for a king to associate with another king. Moreover, as for the difference in association:
This is because the number of mental factors associated with each of the eight consciousnesses differs individually, as has already been explained previously;
Ximing [Master] also holds this interpretation.
[Commentary: Furthermore, from "the seven are perfumers" up to "the eighth is the fruit," that sutra also clarifies the relationship between the perfumer and the perfumed.
"Meaning 7: 'Cause' refers to that which can permeate (*vāsana*) herein; meaning 8: 'Effect' refers to that which is permeated herein. [Commentary]: This is neither identical nor different;
based on the four ultimate truths (*paramārtha-satya*), it corresponds to the four conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*). One should reflect upon this in accordance with reason.
Regarding the first ultimate truth in contrast to the two conventional truths: within the first conventional truth, there is the grasping at all phenomena as having individual identities;
and within the second conventional truth, there is the notion that the aggregates, bases, and elements truly exist, and that the eight consciousnesses truly exist as distinct entities.

If, regarding the first ultimate truth, all phenomena are like illusions—unreal and existing only as designations—then the eight consciousnesses do not exist conventionally as previously described. As for the third [ultimate truth]...

If conventional reality is substantially existent as the worldly causes and effects—namely, the truths of suffering and origination—and supramundane reality is substantially existent as the transcendent causes and effects—namely, the truths of cessation and the path;

and if within the eight consciousnesses, seeds serve as the cause that produces the seven manifest states as the effect (with the seven consciousnesses acting as the perfuming causes and the seeds within the eighth consciousness acting as the perfumed effects), such that cause and effect are distinct from one another; then...
Entering the second [section on] the ultimate truth, the causes and effects of the eight consciousnesses are all conventionally existent. This refers to what the preceding treatise stated:
"The future effect is established as a conventionality in relation to the present cause; the past cause is established as a conventionality in relation to the present effect.

That is to say, within the eighth consciousness, the seeds act as the cause and the first seven consciousnesses act as the effect. Thus, the cause viewed in relation to the effect is not different [from the conventional], or alternatively, the seven [consciousnesses] serve as the perfuming cause.

Because the seeds within the eighth consciousness are the fruit, the cause, when viewed in relation to the fruit, is also not different from it; otherwise, they would lack the nature of cause and effect.
If the aspects (*ākāra*) of the eight consciousnesses were compared with one another, one could not say they are not different, because their active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) are each distinct.

As for the third, ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), in contrast to the four types of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the first three types of conventionality are as previously described; the fourth type of conventionality is... [text ends].

If there is a direct realization of the principle of the two emptinesses, and this is subsumed within the third ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is merely based on provisional designations (*prajñapti*) to speak of "the two emptinesses and one reality" as the true principle.
If the third is the ultimate and the fourth is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), then there is reliance on designations to speak of "realizing the principle through the two emptinesses.

Now, regarding the fourth ultimate truth, which sets aside designations to discuss the fundamental intent (*artha*), it transcends words and thought; furthermore, there is no fixed [existence of] the eight consciousnesses.
[The first four] are indeed different; the four conventional [truths] and the four ultimate [truths] are neither identical nor different.
[Commentary: Regarding the fourth, "the true ultimate truth," "ultimate" (paramārtha) answers the fourth [question], meaning it is exclusively the true and not the conventional.
Therefore, the fourth is named "ultimate" because if the first were conventional, it would be merely conventional and not true; thus, the first conventionality is so named.
The conventional (*saṃvṛti*) is also called the worldly conventional (*loka-saṃvṛti*). "Worldly" refers to the conventional;
"principle" (*li*) refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*), because the essence of the eight consciousnesses is precisely True Suchness. Thus, a sutra says:
"All phenomena are also suchness."

[Commentary: Therefore, "neither identical nor different, transcending the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*)," etc.—the "four propositions" are: (1) the proposition of identity, (2) the proposition of difference, (3) the proposition of being both identical and different, and (4) the proposition of being neither identical nor different.

[Commentary: Regarding the preceding statement that "the mental factors look toward the mind as their counterpart," this refers to the citation from the *Śrīmalādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra-śāstra* (Zhuangyan lun) which allows for the mind to appear as two.

Within this, the relationship between the mental factors and the mind they look toward is examined in terms of identity and difference. This second point—concerning conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) in contrast to the remaining ultimate truths (*paramārtha-satya*)—is explained as follows:
this second conventional truth is also subsumed under identity and difference; by "subsuming the branches back into the root," it is not separate from the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

Therefore, they are "one" in name because the mind subsumes its sovereign [the mental factors], yet they are "also different" due to the distinction in their functions, as the functions performed by the sovereign and its [factors] are not the same.

If one considers them in relation to the second truth (paramārtha-satya), they are neither one nor different, because the characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions and thus cannot be discussed in terms of oneness or difference;
this applies even when comparing the second conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) [to the ultimate].
The ritual procedures for the third truth and the fourth truth are likewise. Question: Why is the second conventional truth not paired with a single truth?
Answer: Because the first truth is itself the second conventional truth; they are identical in their application of the eighteen *dhātus* and so forth.
[Commentary: Now, regarding the intent of this treatise in discussing the second conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) in contrast to the fourth ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya):
it means that here, in this section of the treatise, the eight consciousnesses are distinguished by being compared with one another, rather than being contrasted with mental factors (caitta).

As for "distinguishing the eight consciousnesses by comparing them," and "discriminating the second conventional truth in contrast to the fourth ultimate truth": the second conventional truth is both identical and different [from the ultimate].
Regarding the Fourth Noble Truth, it is neither identical nor different;

because all phenomena are like illusions and transformations, within the heart of the Truth, words and thoughts are cut off, and thus its identity or difference cannot be discussed. Therefore, it is distinguished from what preceded it.

As for the previous statement that "identity and difference cannot be spoken of" at the conclusion of the ultimate principle, the intended meaning is that this follows the preceding discussion on the single text concerning the eight consciousnesses themselves.
Because their nature cannot be said to be definitively one, nor does it have a definitive nature up to [the point of] "no-nature," the explanation is concluded; "concluded" (*kṣipta*) means finished.

Within the second True Truth (*satya*), the explanation of cause and effect has been completed. Now, we shall merely take the eight consciousnesses and clarify their non-identity and non-difference by correlating them with the ultimate and conventional truths (*paramārtha-saṃvṛti*), rather than explaining them in terms of cause and effect. This is why we correlate only the second conventional truth with the fourth ultimate truth.
Furthermore, it does not contradict the second [type of] true equality and clarity.

[Commentary: The meaning revealed here, regarding the phrase "as for confronting the second truth," intends to say that although the treatise’s original text distinguishes between the eight consciousnesses as being neither identical nor different when viewed in relation to one another, if one applies this principle by way of its underlying meaning, these eight consciousnesses may likewise be accepted as being the same as the preceding *citta* (mind).
The fact that mind and mental factors appear as if they were two is also not contradictory when their cause and effect are distinguished in relation to the second ultimate truth;
this is because, as previously stated, the mind and mental factors are similar, and thus it is said that "they are also obtained," and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the mental factors and the mind reach the fourth [truth] as the ultimate," the intended meaning is that one may also take the preceding mind and its mental factors together with these eight consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it is also possible to distinguish them by contrasting the second [truth], the conventional, with the fourth, the ultimate;

this merely serves to mutually clarify the principle, and there is no contradiction in the reasoning. Question: Since the Commentary speaks of the third truth, why does it not mention it here? Answer: The Commentary states:

Regarding the "third truth," this is an interpolated passage. If one were now to discuss the third truth alongside [the others], it would not differ from the preceding statement that "the mind appears as two" and so forth.
Furthermore, according to the treatise, it mentions only the second and fourth truths and does not mention the third.
Alternatively, another interpretation suggests that here too, the mind-king and mental factors may be treated together with the aforementioned mental factors.
This is explained by correlating the second conventional [truth] with the second, third, and fourth ultimate [truths], and so forth.
[Commentary: In reality, as for the conventional and ultimate truths, they arise from the second conventional level below;
when correlated with the ultimate truths, there are four, three, and two layers of numerical distinctions, as explained below.

[Commentary: Regarding the second section, "the conventional exhausts its ultimate reality, even unto that which is beyond words": because they are now contrasted as opposing entities, there are four layers.

Just as the second conventional [level] of the aggregates, bases, and elements consists of the eight consciousnesses, so too, when contrasted with the first ultimate [level], there are the eight consciousnesses and so forth.

This is because they are contrasted as opposing entities relative to the second conventional level. As for the contrast with the first ultimate level, there are the eight consciousnesses and so forth.

Furthermore, because these are illusory phenomena, it is impossible to discuss their identity or difference. This is because, in relation to the second ultimate truth, they possess the nature of cause and effect;
thus, one speaks of a present cause in contrast to a conventionally established future effect, or a present effect in contrast to a conventionally established past cause.

Therefore, they are neither identical nor different. In relation to the third ultimate truth, there is no self whatsoever. In relation to the fourth ultimate truth, all verbal designations are set aside to speak of the ineffable.

The essential meaning is that because words are cut off, the third conventional truth is contrasted with the second ultimate truth; as for cause and effect not being different, this is because when contrasted with the third ultimate truth, there is no self at all.
Because mental discourse is cut off in relation to the fourth ultimate truth, the fourth conventional truth has two layers.
Since the fourth conventional truth uses the gates of emptiness and existence to express the principle, it is "coarse. If one opposes the substance [of the fourth] to the third ultimate truth...
The realization of principle through the two gates of emptiness is subtle; thus, when contrasted with the fourth [truth], the True Mind, both [subject and object] are transcended.
When compared to the preceding three truths, the True [Mind] is such that even the words "mind" and "transcendence" are absent.

[Commentary]: This means that taking function as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and substance as the characterized (*lakṣya*) is as follows: for example, within consciousness, the function of discernment is the defining characteristic, while the substance of consciousness itself is the characterized;
likewise, for sensation and so forth, functions such as experiencing are the defining characteristics, while their respective natures as substances are the characterized;
and for non-sentient phenomena, functions such as arising and abiding are the defining characteristics, while the substance of the phenomena such as form is the characterized.

[Commentary]: Among the four truths, one calculates the grasped objects based on the attachment to their existence as real entities; because there is no intentionality [regarding them], it is said that the first conventional truth is contrasted with the four truths.

For example, in the first conventional truth, the grasping at the existence of a real function of the self constitutes the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), while the grasping at the existence of a real essence of the self constitutes the "characterized" (*lakṣya*).
This applies even up to the grasping at phenomena as having real essences and functions; it is the same.
All are non-existent because they are merely false attachments. [Commentary:

As for the phrase "if one takes the second conventional reality... because the characterized object is non-existent," this means that just as the first conventional truth consists of false attachments whose essence is non-existent, when contrasted with the four true realities (*satya*), it has no distinct existence of its own;
for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks both substance and distinction.

If the second conventional truth possesses the distinctions of the eight consciousnesses and so forth in its own substance, it is nonetheless without distinction when contrasted with the three truths of ultimate reality.

This is because within the three truths of ultimate reality, there is no actual functioning of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) or the relationship between the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*).

Therefore, the intended meaning is not that the second conventional truth is non-existent in relation to the four truths of ultimate reality; rather, it means that just as it is non-distinct from the first [truth], it is likewise non-distinct from the latter three truths of ultimate reality.

You [should understand that] when it is said that "within reality (tathatā), seeing is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the seen is the defined (*lakṣya*)," and so on for all things that ought to be considered, this is distinguished according to the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*) in terms of seeing and the seen.
Seeing is the defining characteristic because the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) takes the characteristic as its object;

the seen is the defined because it is characterized by that which is grasped by the seeing-part. Question: Is this not the same as the "defining characteristic" referred to previously as "activity" (*kāritra*)?

What is the distinction? The previous response was based on a general presentation, while this subsequent explanation distinguishes them specifically. Within a single object, there are both the characterized (lakṣya) and the characterizing (lakṣaṇa).

The seven consciousnesses function as the characterizing because they act as the perfuming agents (*vāsaka*); the eighth consciousness functions as the characterized because it is that which is perfumed (*vāsya*).

Furthermore, when distinguishing the characterized and the characterizing according to the fundamental and the derivative, the eighth consciousness is the characterized because it serves as the support (*āśraya*), while the seven [consciousnesses] are the characterizing.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) because it serves as the basis (*āśraya*). It is just as water and its waves are related:
waves arise dependent upon water, such that the waves are the defining characteristic and the water is the defined (*lakṣya*). This case should be understood in the same way.

Alternatively, the eighth consciousness is the defining characteristic and the other seven are the defined, because the seeds of the eighth consciousness—which are capable of transformation—give rise to the actual manifestation (*pravṛtti*) of the seven consciousnesses; this is stated with reference to this [relationship].

In principle, one may distinguish between the aspect of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*), or between the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) and the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*), such that the aspect of seeing is the grasper and the self-verifying aspect is the grasped.

This is because the aspect of seeing depends upon the self-verifying aspect; as the preceding treatise states: "The aspects of seeing and grasping both arise in dependence upon the self-verifying [aspect]," just like the horns of a cow, as previously explained.

Alternatively, regarding material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), there is the substance (*dravya*) and its function (*kāritra*); the function serves as the grasper, while the essence of matter (*rūpa-svabhāva*) serves as the grasped.
The characteristics—such as the four characteristics of arising and so forth—are the defining attributes (*lakṣaṇa*), while the substance of the dharma is that which is defined (*lakṣya*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "also non-existent in relation to the two truths": the third truth (the conventional) exists only as a distinction between cause and effect; yet even in relation to the two truths, it lacks any distinct third truth, because both truths are devoid of self.
Furthermore, the fourth truth (the ultimate) sets aside the means of expression to discuss the intended meaning. This is why [it is said to be non-existent].
Within the ultimate truth as well, there is no distinction between cause and effect; this fourth conventional truth corresponds to the fourth ultimate truth in the same way.
