if the three categories of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*) collectively encompass all twelve links, yet when one considers the twelve links individually, they do not exhaustively encompass the three categories of afflictions, karma, and suffering—what is the reason for this? This is the inquiry.
[Commentary] The meaning of the response from "If one excludes these" up to "because they are not among the twelve links" is as follows:

If the three types—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—are considered, they are subsumed within the link of ignorance and the links of craving and grasping among the twelve links.

If all other afflictions are considered, they are not subsumed within the twelve links; rather, they are subsumed under the general category of the delusions contained within those three. If one can correctly...

Karma that brings about retributive results in future lives is subsumed under the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) known as *saṃskāra* (formative forces) and *bhava* (existence).

As for other karma that can bring about results in the present life— such as performing evil deeds that result in leprosy or the like, or committing unwholesome acts against one’s parents with a rebellious or harmful intent,
resulting in death by strangulation, death by a magnet, and so forth— this constitutes other distinct types of retributive karma within the body of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
Retributive karma that is with outflows (*sāsrava*), such as the aforementioned types of karma, is not subsumed under the member of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) within the twelve links;
rather, it is included within the category of "karma" among the three preceding general categories.

If this is so, then the internal bodies of sentient beings produced by the Buddha’s activities are subsumed under the members of "aging and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*) and so forth within the twelve links, whereas external things such as mountains and rivers are not subsumed under those links but are instead included within the category of "suffering" (*duḥkha*) among the three general categories. Both cases are thus accounted for.

Regarding the exclusion of those with distinct retributions (*viśeṣa-vipāka*): for example, when a person in the present life commits evil by slandering the Buddha and thereby incurs a distinct retribution such as white leprosy, this is not included within the twelve links [of dependent origination].

Furthermore, in the case of the Tathāgata, the distinct retribution of Aṅgulimāla—such as the heat of the fires of hell upon his body, as well as the suffering experienced while his body was still joined [to the world]—is entirely not subsumed under the twelve [links]; these constitute the three general [exclusions].

The suffering of the intermediate state, up to and including the suffering of practicing the path with diligence, should all be understood according to this principle. [Commentary] Regarding the statement that "the essence consists of one part out of the five matters in total," the intention is as follows: the specific and general essences of the twelve links will be set forth individually below. Question: What constitutes the essence of the twelve links in their totality? Answer: It is fully as follows: * **Ignorance (avidyā):** Its essence is the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the past life. * **Volitional formations (saṃskāra):** Their essence is karma (*karman*) performed in the past life. * **Consciousness (vijñāna):** Its essence is the seed of the future life. * **Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana):** Their essence is the body of the present life. * **Contact (sparśa), feeling (vedanā), craving (tṛṣṇā), grasping (upādāna), and becoming (bhava):** These have the same essence as the aforementioned consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases. * **Birth (jāti):** Its essence is the body of the future life. * **Old age and death (jarāmaraṇa):** Their essence is the suffering of the future life. As for the statement "one part out of the five matters in total": the first four links—ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, and name-and-form—have the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their essence. The remaining eight links—from the six sense bases through birth and old age and death—each have one aggregate as their essence. Therefore, it is said that the essence of the twelve links consists of one part out of the five aggregates in total. This is because the five aggregates are the substance of the twelve links; they are not distinct from them. Consequently, the essence of the twelve links is established by taking these five aggregates as the basis. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one part out of the five matters in total": the first four links have the five aggregates as their essence. The remaining eight links each have one aggregate as their essence. Thus, the essence of the twelve links consists of one part out of the five aggregates in total. This is because the five aggregates are the substance of the twelve links; they are not distinct from them. Consequently, the essence of the twelve links is established by taking these five aggregates as the basis. Moreover, regarding the phrase "one part out of the five matters in total": the first four links have the five aggregates as their essence. The remaining eight links each have one aggregate as their essence. Thus, the essence of the twelve links consists of one part out of the five aggregates in total. This is because the five aggregates are the substance of the twelve links; they are not distinct from them. Consequently, the essence of the twelve links is established by taking these five aggregates as the basis. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one part out of the five matters in total": the first four links have the five aggregates as their essence. Regarding the five categories (*pañcavastu*), they take only the two dharmas of *nimitta* (the sign) and *vikalpa* (conceptualization) as their essence. Question: Why are the "name" (*nāman*) and "substance" (*vastu*) not included? Answer:
According to the five dharmas discussed below, "name" belongs to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), which is a dharma without intrinsic reality;

therefore, "name" is not taken [as an essence]. These twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) are *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent origination). If one defines their essence according to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), one simply takes the dependent [nature] as the basis.

Since its essence consists of that which arises dependently (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—and because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks intrinsic reality—it does not take the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as its substance;

this is not what is being discussed here. If one were to define its essence according to the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements], it would only take those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) within the aggregates, bases, and elements, and thus would not take the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) portion of these three.
Why is this? The answer is: because it does not have the nature of an aggregate (*skandha*). Question: Is it the case that being contaminated is itself the essence?
Question: Are only the six external bases among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the six external elements among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), considered "limbs" (*aṅga*)?
Answer: No. This is because they are designated as limbs only insofar as they are contaminated (*sāsrava*); those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) do not constitute the substance of a limb.
It is not distinguished by way of internal or external. Why? Because external objective phenomena (*bāhyālambana-dharma*) do not constitute the substance of a limb. [The text must continue...]
Bian further explains that some interpret this as subsuming the objects within the mind, whereby the mind as a whole constitutes the constituent parts.

He also explains that "one part" refers to taking the internal six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) from among the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its substance, rather than including the external six objects; thus it is called "one part.

The same principle applies to the realms (*dhātu*). Question: Since discrimination (*vikalpa*) is itself the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), how many constituent parts are included within this discrimination?
Furthermore, regarding how many members (*aṅga*) are subsumed within the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the answer is that the characteristic subsumes twelve members.
As for the distinction, it subsumes only the mind and mental bases (*citta-caittāyatana*);

this may be understood by analogy. [Commentary: Regarding the eleven specific excellences of initial ignorance (*avidyā*), as will be explained below, there is no need to elaborate further. The Commentary cites:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, also explains the seven types of ignorance and so forth in the following section. [Commentary:

Regarding the statement that they are "provisionally designated as the causal conditions for formations (*saṃskāra*)," the intended meaning is that because they are associated with ignorance and are similar in their shared delusion regarding the world, they are provisionally designated as the branch of ignorance as a whole;
thus, it is established that they serve as the causal conditions for formations. It is not [the case that ignorance alone is the cause].
This refers to the causal conditions (*nidāna*).

[Commentary: According to the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and this treatise below, when it is said that one does not take other dharmas because they constitute a single matter, this means taking the single dharma of ignorance (*avidyā*) as the "ignorance link" (*avidyā-aṅga*), which is then termed a "single matter. If one were to further include other factors, it would become manifold.
Because the dharmas do not function as a single entity, other dharmas are not grasped [as the primary cause].

[Commentary]: When karma is actually initiated, it is exclusively ignorance (*avidyā*) that acts as the primary factor; the others are merely auxiliaries. However, when initiating non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karma*), both greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) are also termed "primary initiators.
When initiating meritorious (*puṇya*) or immovable (*āniñjya*) karma, only ignorance acts as the primary initiator; as for greed, it... [is an auxiliary].
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to those factors that assist in the arousal of karma, yet these are also not included.
[Commentary: This is not like the method of the Hīnayāna, which distinguishes based on temporal stages (*avasthā*). The meaning of "stages" here is one of mutual conformity;

as in the Hīnayāna, when the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are distinguished by stage, although all five aggregates (*skandha*) exist simultaneously, they are collectively designated as "ignorance" (*avidyā*), and so on.
The "limb of consciousness" (*vijñāna-aṅga*) refers to the stage of initial birth when one is within the mother's womb; in that single moment, it is called the limb of consciousness.
Although the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are present simultaneously at that time, this is collectively termed "consciousness.

From this point onward, until the completion of the first four weeks (twenty-eight days), it is subsumed under the limb of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa-aṅga*). Although the five aggregates are likewise present simultaneously during this period, they are collectively termed "name-and-form."

Having already explained that [the factors] are subsumed within the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it should be understood accordingly that while in the mother’s womb, visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) does not arise because of the absence of the two conditions of space and light;
although the other four types of form exist in the womb, they are called "capable of hearing sounds, smelling odors, tasting flavors, and feeling contact, pleasure, and pain.
When the six faculties, such as the eye, have arisen, this is called the member of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). If [one dies] in the mother’s womb, [the process stops at five].

From seven days after birth until emerging from the mother’s womb, and up until the age of three, although one has not yet been able to distinguish between good and evil, and though encountering the fire of the sun, one feels no fear;
even when touching with the hands, the perception of pleasure and pain is all termed the stage of "contact" (*sparśa*).
From the age of four until the age of ten, although one can distinguish between pleasure, pain, and so forth, one has not yet given rise to craving or consciousness (*vijñāna*).

When "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) and "karma" are collectively termed the "appropriation of a state," then from ten years of age until old age and death, if one can give rise to misconduct and craving, and through such misconduct and craving creates karma such as killing, at that stage, although ignorance (*avidyā*) and other factors exist, they are collectively termed the "member of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-aṅga*);
and although the member of volitional formations exists, it is collectively termed the "member of existence" (*bhava-aṅga*). Thus, in this present life, ignorance and volitional formations arise.
If one looks toward the past, these present factors of ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) are termed the members of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*);
if one looks toward the present, the five results beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) are termed the member of ignorance (*avidyā*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "there are nineteen, seven, five, and six kinds of various forms of ignorance, as explained in the ninth fascicle of the *Mahā-śāstra*," the nineteen types of ignorance are as follows:
first, ignorance regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). What is this?

It refers to the arising of improper conceptualization (*ayoniśo-vikalpa*) regarding past conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), such as: "Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was I in the past? and so forth.
"What kind of ignorance does its essential nature possess?"—this is the intended meaning of the text. "Essential nature" refers to the essential nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
"Kind" refers to the kinds of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). Ignorance (*moha*) is always accompanied by doubt (*vicikitsā*);
it doubts whether past formations (*saṃskāra*) were spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Regarding the past, for the most part one doubts the cause, and to a lesser extent, one doubts the result.
Because past [factors] act as causes capable of producing present effects, there is ignorance regarding the future limit.
What is meant by this? It refers to the arising of improper conceptualization (*ayoniśo-vikalpa*) concerning future conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), such as:
"Will I exist in the future, or will I not exist? What will my nature be? What will my kind be? Such is the meaning of the text regarding this ignorance.
This delusion is accompanied by doubt regarding the future body; "all practitioners" refers to the fruit. This doubt concerns the future life:

for the most part it doubts the fruit, and only to a small degree does it doubt the cause, because the future constitutes the greater portion. Third, regarding ignorance of the prior and posterior limits: what is meant by this?
It refers to the arising of improper hesitation within oneself, such as: "What is my self? Who am I?"

Regarding the passage, "Why is it that these sentient beings now come from where, having passed away here, will they go to where?"—the meaning of this statement concerning "ignorance" regarding the prior and posterior limits (*pūrvānta* and *aparānta*) is as follows:
the "prior and posterior limits" refer to the present; for the present is the beginning of the future and the end of the past.
Thus, it is called the "prior and posterior limits. The phrase "arising within" refers to the body itself; it is the basis for doubt.
Regarding the present internal body, what is it that is the self? Of what kind is the self? Is the body the self, or is craving the self?
What kind of self is it, and what kind of karma can this body perform? As for where these sentient beings have come from:
it is precisely this present body that manifests as the prior cause for the future, capable of producing its fruit.

Therefore, it is said that the present is designated by the terms "prior limit" and "subsequent limit. The aforementioned ignorance regarding the three periods of time is explained here in conjunction with doubt;

for one doubts the three periods of time. Since the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of ignorance is subtle and difficult to discern, its mode of activity is clarified by reference to the modes of activity of the afflictions that coexist with it. The following sections should be understood accordingly. (4)

Regarding "ignorance with respect to the internal," what is meant by this? It refers to the improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) directed toward each of the various conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), whereby one conceives of them as "mine.
The meaning of this passage is that "ignorance with respect to the internal" refers precisely to the internal body.

This text thus demonstrates that ignorance (*avidyā*) coexists with the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), and it is associated with the grasping of the internal body as a self, as expressed in such phrases as "form is the self" or "the self possesses form."
Regarding these five types of ignorance concerning the external, what is meant by "ignorance regarding external formations belonging to the category of sentient beings,

which gives rise to improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) by conceiving them as 'mine' (*mama-īya*)"? The meaning of this passage is to show that ignorance arises together with the view of "mine" (*mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*),
and that it grasps external things— such as fields, houses, clothing, and so forth— which are included within the category of sentient beings, as being collectively like "mine."

Sixth, regarding ignorance concerning the internal and external: what is meant by this? It refers to the arising of improper conceptualization (*ayoniśo-vikalpa*) toward the formations (*saṃskāra*) within the continuums of others—namely, ignorance regarding those who are enemies, friends, or neutral persons. This passage does not define the "internal" as one's own person;

rather, it establishes the "internal" and "external" in relation to other sentient beings, whether they be enemies, friends, or neutral, because the bodies of other sentient beings are included within the category of sentient beings.
That which is internal is called "external" because it belongs to another body. Ignorance arises together with greed and hatred;
one gives rise to anger toward enemies and love toward kin. Seventh, regarding ignorance of karma: what is meant by "arising of improper conceptualization regarding all karmas"?
It means the ignorance that there is a self as the creator. This passage clearly shows that ignorance is conjoined with the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
8. Regarding ignorance concerning maturation (*vipāka*): what is meant by this?
It refers to the improper conceptualization regarding those formations (*saṃskāra*) subsumed under the fruit of maturation, [thinking] that there is a recipient;

such ignorance is that which arises together with the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), grasping the fruit of maturation as being the recipient. 9. "I" is merely another name for the agent who performs actions. Thus it is said.
What is ignorance regarding maturation (*vipāka*)? It refers to the ignorance consisting in improper conceptualization regarding karma and its fruit.
This ignorance arises together with the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), grasping at the fruits of karmic maturation as being the agent and the experiencer.
What is ignorance regarding the Buddha? It refers to either not reflecting upon the Buddha’s enlightenment or reflecting upon it erroneously.

Whether due to negligence (*pramāda*), or due to doubt (*vicikitsā*), or due to the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that consists in disparagement—this passage explains that it reveals how ignorance arises together with negligence, doubt, and false views; or "not reflecting" means not reflecting upon the Buddha;
or "wrong reflection" means regarding the true Buddha as not being the Buddha, or regarding others as [the Buddha].
Those who regard gods and others as true Buddhas rather than the Buddha, or who give rise to slander toward the Buddha, or who act with negligence regarding the Buddha—
such as the woman Anupamā who conceived lustful attachment upon seeing the Buddha, or those who harbor doubt as to whether the Buddha exists or not,
or who give rise to wrong views toward the Buddha through disparagement— the following ten cases should be understood accordingly.
First, regarding ignorance of the Dharma: what is meant by "the well-expounded nature of the True Dharma" or "not reflecting upon it," etc.?
As for those who should know the Dharma according to the Buddha, this refers to the teaching, the principle, the practice, and the fruit.

Regarding the "well-expounded nature," whether it be the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, the two vehicles, or ordinary beings, all are termed the "well-expounded nature. Within this Dharma, there are also five [aspects].

"Kinds" refers to non-reflection and wrong reflection, which is to say, erroneous understanding. Alternatively, it arises from the dharma through heedlessness, or doubt regarding the dharma, or slander of the dharma;
this reveals that ignorance, doubt, heedlessness, false views, and so forth, coexist [with it].
Because one does not have much knowledge regarding the dharma, it is called "ignorance. (12) Regarding "ignorance concerning the Saṅgha," what is meant by "concerning the Saṅgha"?
Regarding "right practice" or "non-mental engagement," one should understand these according to the Buddha’s intent:
if there is right practice accompanied by attachment, it is called the Saṃgha; if there is no right practice, it is not called the Saṃgha.
As for "wrong mental engagement," "heedlessness," and so forth, it is as described in the Sūtras: after a woman approached, a young arhat saw her and subsequently gave rise to defiled desire.
13. Arising of a mind of misconduct through the accumulation of domestic merit; what is meant by "ignorance regarding suffering"?

It refers to not reflecting on, or otherwise failing to comprehend, that suffering is of the nature of suffering; this should also be understood according to the Buddha’s teaching. 14. Ignorance regarding the origin [of suffering];
15. Ignorance regarding cessation; 16. Ignorance regarding the path is likewise. 17. What is ignorance regarding causes?
This refers to the ignorance that arises from improper conceptualization—either by postulating no cause or by postulating Īśvara as the cause.
This shows that ignorance is conjoined with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) in its grasping at what is not a cause as being a cause.

Regarding the eighteen [instances] of ignorance concerning the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) produced from causes, one should understand them by analogy with the ignorance concerning the cause itself; this passage thus clarifies that [ignorance] involves such grasping.
The notion that all fruits arise from Īśvara or from *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and so forth is also ignorance associated with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Nineteenth, regarding the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*), there is non-penetration and lack of knowledge as they truly are. What is meant by "arrogance" (*abhimāna*)?
It refers to the ignorance consisting in distorted reflection regarding what has been realized. The meaning of this passage is that it concerns the six contacts.

It is not that the six types of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśa*) are defined as being associated with the six consciousnesses; rather, according to the commentary, they are specifically called "the six contacts" because they pertain only to the contact within the sixth consciousness.

This person of overweening pride (*abhimānika*), by means of the contact of the sixth mental consciousness (*manas-sparśa*) and so forth, claims to have attained the first dhyāna and says, "I have attained the first fruit," up to claiming to have attained the fourth dhyāna and saying, "I have attained the fruit of Arhatship."
"At this time of meditative concentration, one cannot penetrate [reality] as it truly is. Below, the inclusion of the nineteen types of ignorance within the seven types of ignorance is explained.
Regarding the "seven ignorances": first, ignorance regarding the three times (*adhva-moha*), which refers to the first three ignorances;

second, ignorance regarding phenomena (*vastu-moha*), which refers to the next three ignorances; third, ignorance regarding transmigration (*saṃkrānti-moha*), which refers to the preceding and subsequent three [ignorances].

"Knowledge" refers to the karma that enables the attainment of results and causes those results to shift and transform. The four types of supreme ignorance refer to the [ignorance regarding] the next three Jewels.
The five types of ignorance regarding reality refer to the [ignorance regarding] the next four Truths. The six types of ignorance regarding defilement and purity refer to the next two.
The seven types of ignorance regarding overweening pride refer to the final one. These five types of ignorance are subsumed within the nineteen forms of non-knowledge mentioned previously. First...
"Delusion regarding meaning (*arthamoha*)" refers to "reasoning" (*yukti*); that is, this delusion regarding meaning completely subsumes the preceding nineteen [delusions].

"Delusion regarding views (*dṛṣṭimoha*)" subsumes the first six and the eighteenth among those preceding nineteen. "Delusion regarding negligence (*pramādamoha*)" subsumes the next three, four, and five [categories].

"Delusion regarding the true meaning (*tattvārthamoha*)" subsumes the seven [categories] consisting of the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths. "Delusion regarding the supreme (*adhimānamoha*)" [subsumes the remaining categories].
Pride and delusion are subsumed solely within the nineteenth [category]. Question:

Why is it that among the five types of delusion (*moha*), the delusion regarding the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha-moha*) subsumes the Three Jewels (*triratna*) and the Four Noble Truths (*catuḥsatya*), whereas among the seven types of delusion, the delusion regarding reality subsumes only the Four Noble Truths? Answer:

Within the seven types of delusion, the Three Jewels are indeed subsumed because they are the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); thus, they are included within the "most excellent" (*agrya*). As for the Four Noble Truths, they are included within the "subsequent stages" (*anupūrvika*).
Because it pertains to the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*), it is subsumed within the delusion regarding the meaning of reality.

Among the five types of delusion, since the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths are all real and not false, it is subsumed within the delusion regarding the meaning of reality; thus, there are seven. Regarding the six types of lack of wisdom (*ajñāna*): first, lack of wisdom; second, lack of vision;
third, lack of clear realization (*abhisamaya*); fourth, darkness; fifth, delusion; sixth, the darkness of ignorance (*avidyā-andhakāra*). Next, [the lack of] wisdom...

Regarding the mutual inclusion [of categories], the treatise only explicitly states that the six and seven [factors] mutually include one another, and does not mention the nineteen; this meaning should be understood by inference.
Thus, the treatise says: "In this way, the distinctions of the six types of ignorance should be understood as following the sequence of the seven objects of non-knowledge previously explained.
As for the latter two objects of non-knowledge, they are combined together into one; this is the final darkness of ignorance."
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, chapter ten, up to the words "all are said to be real," that tenth chapter states:

"Nine [links] are real and three are provisional. This is the same as what this treatise clarifies. Furthermore, verse fifty-six says: "One should know that the links of birth and old age and death are phenomena that exist provisionally (*prajñapti-sat*);

all other links are phenomena that exist substantially (*dravya-sat*). As for the term "skillfulness in dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*), a question is raised: what is meant by "condition" (*pratyaya*)?

One who possesses skill in arising and skill in answering knows this; that is, because they understand the arising of conditions and explain them accordingly, it is called "skill in dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda-kauśalya*).

Furthermore, among the fifty-five [topics], within the explanation of whether the various afflictions are provisional or real, it is stated that the five views are provisional, whereas ignorance (*avidyā*) and the others are all said to be substantially real.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the textual force is the same as in the tenth [chapter] of the *Abhidharmakośa*," it is because the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* also explains that ignorance (*avidyā*) is a substantial entity. [Commentary]:
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that there are two types of ignorance, namely, the time of the seed and the time of the fruit. As for "the time of the seed," it is precisely...

"The time of the seed being the fruit" refers to the time when the seed is the fruit, which is to say it is the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*); this is established according to the older sūtras and śāstras.

However, in the newer sūtras and śāstras, it is stated that the seed is the manifestation; the intended meaning is that within the link of ignorance (*avidyā*), there are both the seed and the manifestation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "ignorance has four types, namely the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and so forth," the intended meaning is that the four types of ignorance refer to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), the associated (*samprayukta*), and the unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
By citing this passage, it is proven that ignorance encompasses both the seeds (*bīja*) and the manifest states (*vṛtti*).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the three types of ignorance—meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable—are distinct," the intended meaning is that while there are three kinds of karma produced (meritorious and so forth), there are only two types of ignorance that produce them.
According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, "non-meritorious karma is produced by ignorance regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*).
Because this ignorance is exclusively of a defiled nature, when it is present, it necessarily does not allow for the presence of receptivity (*kṣānti*).

Regarding the explanation of understanding the aspect of maturation (*vipāka*) through right view: it is said that when ignorance (*avidyā*) and karma conjoin, they necessarily do not allow for the arising of the True Dharma and right view upon the maturation of the practitioner.
Regarding the explanation of the performance of meritorious and immovable actions arising from delusion regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha*):
"true meaning" refers to the Four Noble Truths; delusion with respect to them is called "delusion regarding the true meaning."

Regarding the delusion of meaning (*artha-moha*): even if one who has not yet seen the Truths (*adṛṣṭasatya*) gives rise to a wholesome mind, because they are bound by those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), they are also called "deluded.

By the power of that [delusion], they fail to know the suffering of the three realms as it truly is, and are thus able to initiate meritorious and immovable formations (*puṇyāneñjya-saṃskāra*), which serve as the causes for future existence (*punarbhava*).
Question: According to the Abhidharma, based on the two types of ignorance (*avidyā*), three kinds of formations are initiated. How is this so?
Why is it not stated that there are three distinct types of ignorance? Herein, the three grades of ignorance are capable of initiating karma:
specifically, superior-grade ignorance, because its affliction is heavy and it accords with unwholesome karma, is able to initiate non-meritorious formations (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*);

middle-grade ignorance, because it is somewhat slighter, is able to initiate meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*); and inferior-grade ignorance, because it is extremely subtle, is able to [initiate immovable formations].
Regarding the motivation for immovable karma (*āneñjya-karma*): if this ignorance (*avidyā*) accords with unwholesome karma, it is termed "superior" (*adhimātra*);

if it accords with wholesome karma, it is termed "middling or inferior" (*madhya-mṛdu*). Now, since the *Abhidharma* states that two types of delusion (*moha*) can motivate the three types of karma, one should say:

the superior delusion of maturation (*vipāka*) motivates non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karma*), while the middling and inferior delusions in terms of ultimate reality motivate meritorious karma (*puṇya-karma*).

Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If one is deluded regarding the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), one produces non-meritorious formations (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*), because [the conventional] is coarse, shallow, and easy to understand.

If one is deluded regarding the ultimate (*paramārtha*), one produces meritorious and immovable formations (*puṇya- and āniñjyābhisaṃskāra*), because only noble ones (*ārya*) are able to know that there is suffering.
Here, the explanation is made solely by contrasting the true and the conventional; it is not based on the fourfold classification of the ultimate and the conventional.
This also clarifies the intent of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the two branches of conduct up to the three types of conduct constitute the essence," the meaning is as follows:

the "three types of conduct" refers to the volition (*cetanā*) associated with the three—body, speech, and mind—which are taken as the essence; alternatively, it may refer to the volition associated with the mind and the nominal (conceptual) karma of body and speech.

That is to say, one takes form (*rūpa*) and sound (*śabda*) as the three formations (*saṃskāra*). This is based on their essential nature (*svabhāva*). Alternatively, some manuscripts state that "mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) constitute the essence";

this refers to taking the mind and mental factors occurring simultaneously with volition (*cetanā*) collectively as the branch of formations. This is because it defines the essence by way of its attendants (*parivāra*).
Thus, the treatise states: "The attendants of karma are also designated by the name 'karma'."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the three consciousnesses persist as constant accompaniments," at first glance, the cited passages such as 93 and so forth seem to state that the member of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) refers exclusively to seeds and does not include other consciousnesses.
However, the actual principle is that they constantly continue and assist [the rebirth-linking] as a member;

this distinguishes them from the other evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), and thus the meaning—that it is not the seeds themselves being posited as the member—is established of its own accord.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "in the mother’s womb, with consciousness as the condition," the intended meaning is as follows: the seeds of consciousness perfumed by the past *saṃskāra* (formative) factor are called "causal consciousness" (*hetu-vijñāna*).
This consciousness is able to produce the initial consciousness at conception within the mother’s womb. This consciousness at conception is precisely the "resultant consciousness" (*phala-vijñāna*).
Once this resultant consciousness has continued [into existence], it is able to sustain the various forms of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) during the stage of the *kalala*.
"Maintain it until the end of life so that it does not cease.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "this very consciousness in the future," "this consciousness" refers to the consciousness of the middle period (the present). The name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) of the subsequent period is called the "future";
because the consciousness of the middle period is able to project the factor of name-and-form in the subsequent period, it is called the "seed of name-and-form."
"Following along with that consciousness. Question: What does "following along" clarify? It clarifies that it can be drawn forth. That very treatise states:
"The seeds of name-and-form are further followed along with by the seeds of the future six sense bases," and so on, up to the functioning of the link of craving.
How can this prove that it is the eighth consciousness? Answer: If "consciousness" refers to the eighth, which is capable of maintaining all seeds—[the rest follows].
Eighth, because it is able to maintain all seeds, the seeds of the future limit can follow along with the seeds of the middle limit;
if it were not the ālayavijñāna, what would possess these seeds such that they could be said to follow one another, the former leading the latter?

[Commentary]: If this is so, why does the end of the ninth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* state that the six consciousnesses constitute the "consciousness link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*), and further explain that while there are six types [of seeds] in the form realm, there are only four in the formless realm, and only one in the desire realm? The intent of this question is:

if only the eighth consciousness’s seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are designated as the "consciousness link," for what reason does the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its ninth fascicle, designate the six consciousnesses as such?
Regarding the limb of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*): if one is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the six consciousnesses—eye and so forth—are collectively called the limb of consciousness.

If one is in the first dhyāna of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the two consciousnesses of nose and tongue are excluded, and thus the four consciousnesses of eye, ear, body, and mind are called the limb of consciousness.

Furthermore, from the second dhyāna upward, one likewise relies upon the three consciousnesses of eye, ear, and body from the first dhyāna, together with the mind consciousness, as the limb of consciousness.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are no first five consciousnesses; there is only the sixth consciousness, which alone is designated as the "consciousness limb" (*vijñāna-aṅga*).
[Commentary: Because volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) act as conditions, they cause consciousness to undergo transformation.

Although this consciousness in the present life possesses only the nature of a cause, the nature of the cause fundamentally refers only to the seeds of the eighth consciousness, which are designated as the "consciousness limb," until the various consciousnesses arise as the result. Therefore...

The eighth [link] of the middle period is the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*). From this point downward, the six consciousnesses are collectively treated as the link of consciousness because they constitute the fruit of all consciousnesses;
therefore, the eighth [link] of the middle period is designated as the link of consciousness. From this point downward, the six consciousnesses are collectively treated as the link of consciousness.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "designated according to all continuities until the arising of retribution," there are three interpretations concerning the six consciousnesses as the *vijñāna-aṅga* (consciousness link).
First, it is said that when that treatise designates the six consciousnesses as the *vijñāna-aṅga*, it does so by referring to the "continuity-body" (*saṃtāna-śarīra*) of all sentient beings;
this refers to the entire body of a sentient being from beginning to end.
If one is in the desire realm, the six consciousnesses are present; in the form realm, four are present; and in the formless realm, only one.

A second interpretation states that when that treatise identifies the six consciousnesses as the "consciousness link," it is speaking from the perspective of the Hīnayāna school, because that school has not yet established the eighth consciousness.
A third interpretation states that identifying the six consciousnesses as the "consciousness link" may be made with reference to a single sentient being.

Regarding the statement that all consciousness within the body exists from beginning to end as the six types of sensory consciousness (the six *rūpa*-based consciousnesses) and the four formless ones (*ārūpya*), there is another interpretation which says:

"Since at the very moment of initial rebirth there is only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is permissible—by way of its continuity—to consider the body as the 'consciousness link' (*vijñānāṅga*).

This too is not correct; for in the Mahāyāna, at the time of initial birth, there is only the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). To claim here that it is the mental consciousness would therefore contradict [that doctrine].
Regarding the present assistance in explaining the fault in our own school's position: in reality, it is the eighth consciousness that undergoes rebirth;
however, because the six consciousnesses may exist according to the subsequent continuity, the six consciousnesses are designated as the "consciousness link."

[Commentary: Because it is taught that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and [consciousness] act as mutual conditions for one another, the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) at the very moment of entering the mother’s womb is able to act as a mutual condition for name-and-form;
this clearly demonstrates the meaning of their mutual dependence.

Since the other seven consciousnesses cannot act as mutual conditions for name-and-form, only the eighth is designated as the "consciousness link" (*vijñānāṅga*), persisting and evolving continuously until the end of life.

Therefore, it is only the eighth consciousness that constantly continues and evolves without interruption; because the first six consciousnesses do not function during five states, they are not the "consciousness link.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "suffering from the embryonic stage" in the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, according to that treatise, it asks: "How many can produce suffering? It says: "Namely, five."

How many members of the *duḥkha-garbha* (womb of suffering) are there? It is said they are five. How many are exclusively suffering? It is said they are two. The commentary explains: ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*)—these five are able to produce future suffering;

thus they are called "producers of suffering. Consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—these five are seeds;

they are the causes for that future birth and death, and are thus called the "womb of suffering" (*duḥkha-garbha*). Birth (*jāti*) and old age-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*)... [are the manifestation of that suffering].

The second [category] consists solely of suffering. Since it is stated that consciousness and the other [links] are called the "womb of suffering" (*duḥkha-garbha*), it is clear they are not the suffering itself.

Furthermore, since it is stated they are the "womb of suffering," it is evident they are capable of producing suffering. Why, then, are they not included within the category of "that which produces suffering"?

Answer: Because the causes are not yet complete, there is a distinction. As for the result, because it is imminent, it receives a different name. Birth, old age, and death are themselves designated as "suffering," whereas their causes are termed "suffering" [metaphorically].
"Garbha" (womb) is a name based on its primary referent. [Commentary:
The frequent rendering of this as "the suffering of the womb" (*garbhaka-duḥkha*) is an error in transcription and transmission. Question:

Even if one were to say that it is named by way of a *karmadhāraya* compound—namely, "the suffering of the womb"—what would be the discrepancy? Answer: Although the substance of all outflows (*sāsrava*) is indeed suffering, the intent of the cited passage is to clarify... [text ends].
Since the two fruits, birth and so forth, are designated as suffering, the link of ignorance is called "that which gives rise to suffering.
Because both saṃsāra and death are exclusively suffering, one knows that the embryonic state (garbha) is the cause of suffering; thus, the *tatpuruṣa* compound (*adhikaraṇasaptamī*) is superior.
[Commentary] Question: If this is so, why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 9, state that "this applies even up to birth, old age, and death"?

The intent of this question is as follows: if the five members—consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—are merely seeds and lack manifest activity, why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 9, speak of the seeds perfumed by the three types of formative action (*saṃskāra*): meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable?
When the six consciousnesses and their seeds produce their resultant fruits, are these six consciousnesses called the "consciousness link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*)?
To speak of the "seeds of the six consciousnesses" means that the seeds of the aforementioned six consciousnesses are capable of producing the fruits of the six consciousnesses.

Furthermore, since various sacred teachings state that the "formations link" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*) perfumes the consciousness, and that consciousness and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) serve as mutual conditions for one another, it is known that [the seeds] are present.

Since it is taught that consciousness (*vijñāna*) functions as a seed for conditions but cannot itself act as a condition [for the next life], and because it is further stated that consciousness enters the mother’s womb, we know that it is the active (*pravṛtti*) eighth consciousness that enters the womb;
the seeds of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) do not. Furthermore, according to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, it says:

"Ignorance has both the time of the cause and the time of the fruit," and this applies likewise up to birth, old age, and death. Therefore, we know that all members of the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are...
The presence of seeds and their active manifestation is termed the "consciousness link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*), because the sacred teachings state that this term applies to both seeds and manifestations.
[Commentary: The statement that there is a sequence of before and after is made with reference to the stage of the fruit that is to arise;

the intention is to explain that when the manifest consciousness arises, it conditions future birth and old age and death, and thus it is said that the manifest consciousness exists within that intermediate process.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "Alternatively, in the present... to "...only seeds," the intended meaning is as follows:

The ten factors of the cause belong to the past, while the two factors of birth and so forth constitute the fruit in the present; thus, these present fruits of birth and so forth are themselves the ten causes of the past.
Within this stage of birth, old age, and death, the manifest consciousness (*vijñāna*) is described as the *vijñāna* link; however, in reality, it refers only to the seed.
"Taking *vijñāna* (consciousness) as the member [of dependent origination] is the correct meaning.

[Commentary: "If it were not so, it would contradict [the teachings on] the suffering up to the fetal stage (*garbha*). This indicates a contradiction with both the tenth [chapter] and the fifty-sixth [verse];
that we now mention only the contradiction with the fifty-sixth verse is because that term serves as a general summary. As for "the fetal stage," it refers to the tenth...

The ten points are as previously cited. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 55, states: "In the present life, consciousness is said to be perfumed by meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma;
it is followed by successive seeds and is capable of inducing the suffering of birth, old age, and death in future bodies, such as consciousness and so forth.
It further states: "Consciousness [is one of] the members of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling."

The nature of the seed, having previously received the designation "cause that draws forth various sufferings" according to the time of its support, now receives the designation "birth, aging, and death" as it yields its fruit, and further receives the name "suffering.
According to these scriptural passages, the five members beginning with consciousness are understood solely as seeds.
The commentary explains: "The five members are the seeds of the previous life. 'According to the time of its support' means that these seeds, following their prior..."
Regarding the body: when that very same body previously experienced various sufferings, these seeds already acquired the designation of "projecting causes.
Now that they produce the fruits of birth, aging, and death, birth, aging, and death are likewise designated as "suffering.
Based on such textual passages, one should know that the link of consciousness also possesses seeds.
[Commentary: As for the statement that "feeling (*vedanā*) also has two kinds," this refers to the two types: the seed (*bīja*) and the manifest (*vṛtti*). [Commentary:
Regarding the passage from "the feeling of objects" to "all should be understood accordingly," the intended meaning is that feeling extends to active manifestations (*samudācāra*).

The reason for this is that the feeling of objects serves as the condition for the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and other formations; this is also stated with reference to the future arising of manifest feelings as the basis for the explanation.

Because it is taught that, in terms of its essential nature (*tattva*), [the link of consciousness] is precisely the seed, it is said that the links such as feeling (*vedanā*) encompass both the seed and the manifest (*bīja-vyakti*).

[Commentary: Regarding the first point—that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are included, even extending to the maturation (*vipāka*) and other natures—the intention here is to state that there are two ways of defining the essence of the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*):
first, by way of a composite definition including other factors; second, by way of a distinct definition.
To define the essential nature [of this limb] by means of "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is to define it in a confused manner.

This text takes all members of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) as "form" (rūpa), and all minds and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) as "name" (nāma). Regarding the phrase "the roots and supports of the great elements" (mahābhūta):

"roots and supports" refers to the bases upon which the sense organs (indriya) rely; these are the four sense organs themselves, along with the four types of sensory objects (viṣaya) that assist them. Within these four objects, there are the four primary derivative elements (upādāyarūpa) that constitute them.

The four great elements (mahābhūta) arise simultaneously with the four subtle objects (tanmātra); the four great elements act as the creators (nirmātṛ), while the four subtle objects act as the created (nirmita).

These are precisely the "sustaining objects" (upādāya-rūpa) that sustain the five material sense organs (pañca-rūpīndriya). Thus, these four subtle objects that sustain the sense organs serve as the locus (āśraya) for the five material sense organs.
This implies that the four primary elements not only create the four subtle objects but also serve as the locus for the five material sense organs.

Therefore, it is said that "the faculties depend on the primary elements" (*mahābhūta*). Regarding the statement "the faculties depend on the primary elements," this explains that the five material faculties (*rūpīndriya*) also have the four primary elements as their creators;

that is, the four primary elements create the five derived faculties. Now, concerning the four primary elements that serve as the creators for the location of the five material faculties, there are two interpretations.
One says: these four primary elements can only create the five material faculties and do not [coexist] with the five faculties.
And it acts as a basis; secondly, these four great elements can produce the sense faculties (*indriya*) and also act as the direct basis for them.
Regarding the phrase "the various derived forms" (*upādāyarūpa*), this single term applies to both the aforementioned categories: the faculties and their bases.
These faculties and objects are all derived from the great elements that produce them. Furthermore, the four great elements can also produce pus, blood, and so forth.
All forms (*rūpa*) are termed "form-dharmas" (*rūpa-dharma*). As for "form within the sphere of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana-rūpa*), it refers to the five kinds of form within the sphere of phenomena;
all these are subsumed under the category of form. This is the confused explanation regarding the branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Question:

Are the "form-dharmas" and so forth, as well as the other forms, also called the branch of name-and-form? Answer: In reality, with the exception of the objects of form (*rūpārtha*) and the sense organs (*indriya*), they are not the branch of name-and-form; rather, they are simply called "form."
Because they belong to the same category, they are also designated as the link of *nāmarūpa*.

[Commentary: The meaning of the statement that the link of *nāmarūpa* subsumes the five links—*saṃskāra*, *vijñāna*, and so forth—and thus possesses the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), such that the four [links] beginning with *vijñāna* are established therein according to their predominance, is as follows:

since the link of *nāmarūpa* already includes the five links starting with *saṃskāra* and *vijñāna*, it is complete with the five aggregates; within this totality, the four [remaining] links, beginning with *vijñāna*, are established according to whichever factor is predominant.

Regarding the statement that the member of "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) has the three natures as its essence: the intention is that since the member of name-and-form subsumes the five aggregates (pañcaskandha), and the five aggregates can pertain to all three natures, the essence of the member of name-and-form likewise pertains to the three natures.
Furthermore, there is an external objection and response as explained in the *Yanyi miyi* (Secret Meaning of the Commentary on the Yogācārabhūmi).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that these factors, such as this limb [of dependent origination], are explained without being confused with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the Master of the Commentary explains:

Within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), one takes only the subtle particles that support the sense organs; thus, the five sense organs themselves are excluded, as they are subsumed within the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), one takes only the six consciousnesses of the present life, which are termed "consciousness-as-name-and-form" (*vijñāna-nāmarūpa*); thus, the [past] consciousness is excluded.
The eight consciousnesses are subsumed within the preceding member of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, the seventh consciousness is excluded, as it is not produced by karma and does not fall under the twelve members of dependent origination.

Additionally, the immediately preceding mental faculty (*manas-indriya*)—which is the six consciousnesses of the prior moment—is subsumed within the member of "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), contact (*sparśa*) is also excluded.
"Contact" (*sparśa*) refers to the link of contact (*sparśāṅga*). Furthermore, excluding the entire aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), it is subsumed within the link of feeling.

Taking the entire aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and a portion of the three aggregates of form (*rūpa*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), these are called the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpāṅga*).

Within the aggregate of formations, excluding contact and grasping, the remainder consists of the resultant (*vipāka*) mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*). Regarding this, Master Zhe explained that it refers to taking the eighth [consciousness] from within the aggregate of consciousness.
The seeds of the designation "name" within consciousness are subsumed under the link of consciousness;

the seeds of the designation "name" within the present sixth consciousness are subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*) among the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); and the seeds of the designation "name" within the five sensory consciousnesses are subsumed within "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
This interpretation is also reasonable, and one may accept or reject it according to one's own judgment; the rest is the same as the Master’s commentary.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the two entities differ in their breadth and narrowness... up to the point where the five entities are identical to one name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)," the "two entities" refer to the definition of the entities as presented previously in a disordered manner.

According to the first interpretation in the Commentary regarding the branch of name-and-form, it takes all of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and all other mental states and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) of the three natures—namely, the four aggregates—as the aggregate of name-and-form.
If one defines *nāmarūpa* as merely "name-and-form," the definition is too broad and vague.

If it were to include the members of consciousness (*vijñāna*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*), then its essential characteristics would become confused with those other members. Therefore, for the second [definition], the essence of *nāmarūpa* consists of the entire aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and a portion of the other three aggregates;
thus, the seeds of the five results—consciousness and so forth—are each distinct and do not constitute a second [definition].

If the substance [of the dependent origination] is comprised within the member "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), then how is it known that the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) each have their own distinct identities? [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "among those associated with the eighth consciousness... up to the maturation-contact and -feeling" (*vipāka-sparśa-vedanā*): the meaning is that here, we are currently excluding the eighth [consciousness].
Regarding the mental states and mental factors associated with the seventh consciousness, because they are of an obscured nature and are not the fruit of karma,
they are not subsumed under the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). In the commentary, it is stated that the contact and feeling associated with the eighth [consciousness],

as well as the contact and feeling within the six consciousnesses, are what are subsumed under the link of contact and feeling (*sparśavedanāṅga*), and are likewise not subsumed under the link of name-and-form.
[Commentary]: "And all remaining seeds of the maturation (vipāka) mental factors from past lives constitute this very substance. This is explained as follows:
if one refers to the time when the seeds of the maturation mind and mental factors were perfumed, they belong to the past;

however, if one refers only to the seeds of the maturation mind and mental factors themselves, they exist solely in the present life and lack a substance in the past. Therefore, [the text] here takes them [as existing in the present].

The textual body of this [passage] consists of the seeds of the indeterminate dharmas that are the maturation (*vipāka*) of unwholesome conduct in past lives. [Commentary: The *Śāstra* (Treatise) states at 93:
"The five sense organs that are co-nascent (*sahaja*) are called 'form' (*rūpa*), and so forth," up until "this does not mean exhausting the principle.
This refers to the branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Regarding the term "co-nascent": it refers to the five sense organs which serve as the common support for the five consciousnesses.

The underlying meaning is as follows: the ninety-third [sūtra] explains that the five material sense-faculties, such as the eye, which are co-nascent, are designated as "form" (rūpa), while the mind (manas) that has just ceased in the preceding moment is designated as "name" (nāma).
Based on this text, the interpretation of "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is not distinct from the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana).
Furthermore, that same text explains that the six consciousnesses are designated as the "consciousness link" (vijñāna-aṅga); thus, the six consciousness links are identical to "name-consciousness."
Because they serve as mutual conditions for one another, the six consciousnesses arise with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as their condition;

since these six consciousnesses arise together in dependence upon the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), it is said that the link of consciousness and the link of name-and-form serve as mutual conditions.

However, according to the ninety-third text, when explaining the single principle of "conditioning," the six sense-faculties are designated as the link of name-and-form; yet these six sense-faculties themselves are not [inherently] name-and-form.

In terms of its essential nature, it is superior in principle to take the entirety of the previously explained aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) and a portion of the other three aggregates as the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
[Commentary] The meaning of this interpretation is that the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and name-and-form are one in essence;
however, they are divided into two members based on their functional significance.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "That is, the five material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and the preceding six consciousnesses... even though it is called 'included within the middle' (*madhyāntarbhūta*), it is not yet called the 'six sense-bases' (*ṣaḍāyatana*)," the intention is as follows:
The Master of the Commentary explains that this refers to the seeds of the present six consciousnesses;

the meaning is that within the "mind-faculty" (*manas*) and the "consciousness-aggregate" (*vijñānaskandha*) among the members of the "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), these are explained in terms of the seeds of the present six consciousnesses.
When the six consciousnesses arise as active manifestations (*pravṛtti*) in a future life,

because they serve as the objective support (*ālambana*) and the causal basis (*kāraṇa*) for the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja-citta*) arising as present active manifestations of the six consciousnesses,

it is said that the present six consciousnesses themselves constitute the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) within name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). This is because the maturation-born mind that has fallen away from the present active six consciousnesses opens the way for [the future existence].

Regarding the basis for the function [of the six consciousnesses]: from the perspective of having a basis (*āśraya*), the six consciousnesses of the past are subsumed under the mental faculty (*manas*) within the "six bases" (*ṣadāyatana*) member.
This refers to a single mental faculty; that is, it is the single mental faculty. As for the explanation of the meaning:

it is explained according to the meaning based on this single mental faculty, distinguishing between the present and the past, whereby the six consciousnesses of the present are designated by their names.

Within the constituent of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) refers to the six consciousnesses of past lives; within the constituent of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it refers to the mental faculty (*manas*).

If one does not interpret it in the manner explained above—namely, that the consciousness included within the six sense bases constitutes the mental faculty—then the aggregate of consciousness would be missing from the constituent of name-and-form.
If, on the other hand, the six consciousnesses were included within the constituent of name-and-form at that time...
That which constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the absence of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) among the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).

Therefore, it is explained figuratively as being twofold with respect to the seeds of the six present consciousnesses. This is discussed in terms of the five factors—consciousness and the others—being simultaneously present at one time;
the meaning is that this is treated according to the seeds of the five factors, beginning with consciousness, which coexist at a single moment. Question: Regarding the six sense bases...

What is meant by "simultaneous"? The answer is: because the seeds of consciousness at the same time are designated as the "mind" (*manas*) in accordance with worldly convention, these five types are simultaneous.
If this is explained in terms of the stages at the time of future rebirth, it refers to the full possession of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which consists of the five aggregates.
This is like the very first moment of entering the mother’s womb in a future life, where it is designated as only the "consciousness link" (*vijñāna-aṅga*). From the second [moment]...
From the second moment onwards until the end of the fourth week, within the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), although consciousness (*vijñāna*) of the past is termed "mind" (*manas*),

it is also included within the intermediate [stage] because the member of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) has not yet arisen; therefore, from the second moment onwards until the end of the fourth week, within the stage of name-and-form,
there is also the immediately preceding mind of the six past consciousnesses, which is termed "mind."
The mind immediately following these faculties, as well as other mental states and mental factors, are all subsumed under the branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

thus, the branch of name-and-form is complete with the five aggregates. However, it is not yet called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), because as long as the function of the six bases has not arisen, they cannot be designated as the six bases.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, “In some places it is also said that they are manifest activities... all should be understood according to this,” the intended meaning is as follows:
where it is said that the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is a manifest activity and not a seed, this is based on the previous explanation of the limb of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
It is explained there that this is also stated in reference to the stages of the future birth; in reality, however, it refers only to the seeds and does not refer to the manifest activities.

[Commentary]: Regarding this treatise, if one speaks in terms of sequential stages (*avasthā*), it is only the category of contact (*sparśa*) that occurs after the stage of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) that constitutes [the link].
However, with respect to the stages of birth and aging, the six sense bases themselves serve as the preliminary condition for the subsequent arising of contact.

In this context, the factor of contact does not include the contact associated with the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭamanas*), because that is not a maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) produced by karma.

[Commentary]: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle nine, states that the "six contacts" refer to the contacts associated with the six consciousnesses, which constitute the "six groups of contact.
This is explained in terms of the stage of what is about to arise; in reality, however, it refers only to the seeds.

[Commentary: However, when the treatise states that feeling (*vedanā*) is the condition for craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and even that its very substance is subsumed under the member of birth (*jāti*), this refers to what is taught in other treatises regarding feeling and craving as conditions;
it is explained in terms of the present stage of birth and old age, as well as the future stage of birth and old age.
Therefore, this member of feeling is subsumed within the member of birth, as the future stage of birth and old age is precisely that [member].
This refers to the ten-membered fruit of the present, namely: the ten members of the cause in the present and two members of the fruit in the future.
Here, the explanation is given in terms of the stage of actual arising. That is to say, within the present body, ignorance and formations give rise to the seeds of the five fruits;
at the time of death, craving, grasping, and becoming arise to moisten these seeds, thereby producing future birth, aging, and death. Furthermore, the present...
Birth, aging, and death are the results of the ten past causes; these are the ten past links as causes and the two present links as results.
This constitutes a single layer of cause and effect, unlike the two-layered cause and effect of the Hinayana.

[Commentary] The beginning of the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Craving refers to craving within the three realms. Here, the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is exclusively the craving within the sixth consciousness.

Because this craving is able to take up the body of future existence as its object and gives rise to the cause that produces craving, it is precisely the craving of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage in the treatise below which states that "attainment serves as a causal condition," the intended meaning is that craving and aversion are called "grasping" (*upādāna*).

Therefore, it is said that the seed of craving serves as the causal condition for grasping; there is no difficulty in asserting this, for there is nothing that can be cited as a counter-example where the present [craving] does not serve as a causal condition for present action.
Furthermore, since greed is itself grasping, there is no contradiction in saying that the seed of craving gives rise to grasping as its causal condition.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, the meaning of the statement in the subsequent text that "it is exclusively abandoned through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*) is intended to show that this is based on a comprehensive treatment of the links over a long duration, because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are subtle and distinct.

[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "How does one wish to grasp... up to "...therefore disputes arise," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that craving (*rāga*) belongs exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

It further states that three views (*dṛṣṭi*) pertain to all three realms; specifically, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the three realms is called the grasping for a doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*), while the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the grasping for precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) within the three realms are called the grasping for views and precepts (*dṛṣṭiśīlavratopādāna*). However, in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is...

Regarding the arising of the four types of clinging (*upādāna*) for those who have gone forth from the household life, this is stated solely with reference to human beings within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Although there are no "householder renunciants" (i.e., non-Buddhist ascetics) in the heavenly realms, the latter three types of clinging can still arise there. However, the clinging to sensual desires (*kāmopādāna*) and the clinging to self-theories (*ātmavādopādāna*) apply universally to both what is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and what is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

As for the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭy-upādāna*) and the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*), these are exclusively abandoned by insight. The clinging to sensual desires is precisely the craving (*rāga*) belonging to the desire realm; it consists of [craving] for views and rules and observances.
Grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) refers to the grasping at [wrong] views and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) among the five views.

Grasping at the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*) refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) among the five views. Just as when various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to a self, there is only empty talk and no real essence of a self;
this is called grasping at the doctrine of self. "Grasping" (*upādāna*) means attachment; consciousness first clings by grasping at a self, and then becomes attached.
Because they are not abandoned, they are established as "grasping" (*upādāna*). Furthermore, grasping has two functions:

first, because these four types of grasping serve as the root for the arising of conflict, householders and laypeople, preceded by the grasping of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), engage in disputes over material things such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth;

second, monastics and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), by clinging to their own views as correct and denigrating the views of others as false, give rise to the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭy-upādāna*) and the grasping of self (*ātma-vādopādāna*).

Second, the two types of grasping (*upādāna*) and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) give rise to contention. Second, the four graspings serve as the root for future existence (*punarbhava*);
herein, the four graspings are capable both of initiating karma and of moistening rebirth.

Because worldly people give rise to sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), they are able to nourish and develop the five faculties, objects, and realms within the physical body of the desire realm. Because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) give rise to [the view of] future...
The three types of grasping (*upādāna*) refer to the formations (*saṃskāra*) that lead toward receiving a body within the three realms.

[Commentary: Regarding "grasping as grasping," this means that the afflictions—such as the arising of greed for one's own views, the arising of hatred toward the views of others, and the arising of pride—are all termed "that which is grasped.
Now, regarding the distinct meaning of what is said here concerning "grasping" in combination, the intention is that it refers exclusively to yoga.

The *Gaowen* (Explanatory Text) contains three different versions of the text regarding the four types of grasping (*upādāna*), which are here combined into one to clarify the distinct meanings of what is being explained. [Commentary:
As for the citation from the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*), since it is stated therein that "craving refers to the three [types of craving]," and so forth.

The craving for the realms (*dhātu-tṛṣṇā*) also pertains to both the manifest and the seeds; this should likewise be called "clinging" (*upādāna*), meaning that clinging to the three realms also pertains to both the manifest and the seeds.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the ten links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) are subsumed under the cause of origination," the intent is as follows:

these links of existence take as their substance the seeds of the preceding formations (*saṃskāra*) and the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), because they are moistened by the two dharmas of craving and clinging.
It is renamed "existence" (*bhava*). When it has not yet been moistened, the six factors beginning with consciousness merely abide in their own state and lack the capacity to produce a future result.
Once they are suddenly moistened, they possess the capacity to produce a future result; therefore, they receive the name "existence.
That is to say, because they have the power to bring about a future fruit, they are called the limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*). This, however, is merely the seed.

Regarding the question of whether [the factors] pertain to both the manifest and the latent: since the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) pertain to both seeds and manifest states—just as manifest craving and so forth moisten the seeds of consciousness and so forth, which is easy to understand—does the seed of craving and so forth also have the capacity to moisten the seeds of consciousness and so forth? Answer:

It pertains to both meanings. If one considers ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), "moistening" refers exclusively to the manifest moistening of grasping as the link of existence (*bhava*). If one considers noble ones (*ārya*)...
The third fruit also pertains to both the manifest and the seeds; it refers to the noble ones who, by means of craving, moisten the two types of seeds.
The six factors, such as consciousness, which undergo transformation through this moistening, are termed the "limbs of existence" (*bhavāṅga*). Regarding the view, there are two treatises;

one does not exclusively adopt [the other], for the limbs of existence are subsumed under the "productive cause" (*janakahetu*) and not the "projecting cause" (*ākṣepahetu*), because they are designated as the projecting cause only when they have not yet been moistened. Question: What comes before craving?
Question: Regarding the subsequent [moment], how can one say that "conjunction moistens" the preceding dharma? Answer: One does not explain conjunction based on temporal priority and posteriority;
rather, it is called "conjunction" simply because the meaning of "moistening" is the same.
[Commentary]: That which refers to the transformation and cessation of the aforementioned five aggregates is what is called "cessation" (nirodha) within the context of aging and transformation.

The intention behind stating that the two names "birth" and "aging-and-death" are provisionally established upon the five aggregates is to explain that these two links—birth and aging-and-death—are precisely the three characteristics of arising, change, and cessation (*jāti*, *jarā*, *anityatā*) among the [four] non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). It is simply that birth, aging, and death all exist upon the basis of the five aggregates.
