If "name" (nāma) is considered within the context of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), it is subsumed under the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha).

[Commentary: The present intention in taking the actual substance (dravya-svabhāva) as also being the first five aggregates is that, if one relies on the designation (prajñapti) of birth, old age, and death, these are included among the dissociated factors (viprayukta-saṃskāra);
however, if one speaks according to the essential nature (dharma-svabhāva) of the phenomena, these two branches are likewise identical to the five aggregates.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage "If one considers the stages up to the arising of existence with its fruit," the intended meaning is that existence with its fruit (*saphala-bhava*) is the very essence of the limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

This is because the two factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) moisten the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other [limbs], causing them to evolve; thus, the limb of existence is itself designated as "existence with its fruit" (*saphala*).
Furthermore, when existence with its fruit has already arisen, it is termed "birth, old age, and so forth" (*jāti-jarādi*); this explains that birth and the others are also [the limbs of existence].
There is no contradiction in [the seed] being common to both. How is this known? As stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, "arising" (*janana*) and "projecting" (*ākṣepa*) are simultaneous.
The five factors—consciousness and so forth—in their fivefold aspects when not yet moistened are called "projecting causes" (*ākṣepaka-hetu*), because they project a distant result.

Once they have been moistened, they proceed as "arising causes" (*janaka-hetu*), because they can directly produce the immediate result. Although they are identical prior to being moistened, they are both considered seeds and thus constitute a single type of cause.

It is said that arising (*jāti*) and projecting (*ākṣepa*) are simultaneous. Regarding "arising and projecting are simultaneous": "arising" refers to the fruit; the cause capable of producing it is the "existence" (*bhava*) link.
Because the seeds of the "existence" link do not perish until the fruit of birth and old age (*jāti-jarā-maraṇa*) reaches the stage of birth and old age, they are called "simultaneous.
Furthermore, if one takes the "existence" link itself as the cause of birth, old age, and so forth, then birth and the others are also applicable [as effects].
There is no contradiction in [the seeds] being the *bhava-aṅga* (existence-factor), because the very essence of the *bhava-aṅga* consists of the seeds of the preceding consciousnesses and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the consciousnesses that produce the fruit are still called 'projecting' (*ākṣepaka*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

when it is said that the *bhava-aṅga* produces the consciousness of the fruit, this *bhava-aṅga* is still referred to by the name "projecting cause. Why? Because the essence of the *bhava-aṅga* is precisely those preceding consciousnesses and so forth.
Question: Since those [seeds] have already been moistened, why are they still called "projecting causes" (*ākṣepa-hetu*)? Answer:

It is because they project the result—the appropriation of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth—thereby being called projecting causes; furthermore, since the seeds themselves are designated as the "capable projecting cause" (*śakya-ākṣepaka-hetu*), for it is only through their arising that they take up the actualized state (*samudācāra*).
Thus, the "projecting cause with light" refers precisely to the seeds of the five results, such as consciousness, which, although already moistened, undergo transformation.

It is called "existence" (*bhava*) because it reaches the stage of birth; this refers to the fruit of that birth. Regarding the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), the intended meaning is as follows:

if one speaks in terms of specific stages (*avasthā*), then when one reaches the stage of birth, old age, and death, the seeds of consciousness and so forth—which were previously cited as causes—are no longer collectively designated by the name of the "birth-link" (*jāti-aṅga*) and so on.
Therefore, it is said that the birth-link and the others encompass both the seeds and the manifest states. Question: How does one reach birth and old age?

Question: At the stage of death, do the seeds of consciousness and so forth still exist? Answer: That which follows must necessarily carry that which precedes it, but that which precedes does not necessarily carry that which follows.
It is like when the seed exists, the fruit has not yet arisen; yet when the fruit arises, the seed must have existed. It is also like the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment:
while one is practicing the four foundations of mindfulness during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), the four right efforts have not yet arisen.
Furthermore, when one cultivates the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), they necessarily involve the preceding four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*);

likewise, up until the cultivation of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), it correctly involves the preceding seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). Therefore, since the present stage of the branch of birth (*jāti-aṅga*) necessarily involves the preceding seeds, it is said that the branch of birth extends to the seeds as well.
[Commentary: According to the Sarvāstivādins, each [member] has the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

For instance, within the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), although the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) simultaneously possesses the five aggregates, it is collectively designated as "ignorance"; this applies likewise up to the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

This is explained in terms of dependent origination according to stages (*avasthika-pratītyasamutpāda*); the meaning of "receiving a name" here refers to the application of a designation based on its state.
"Obtaining the name 'arising through conditions' refers to obtaining the name based on its general meaning; it does not refer to obtaining the name based on specific instances.
[Commentary: The meaning is that there is no birth, no sovereign, no agent, and no experiencer; there is no self-exertion, and nothing attains independence.

It is said that these twelve links arise merely by depending on various conditions and lack a real self, an agent, or an experiencer, unlike the false imaginings of non-Buddhists who posit such things as an experiencing self, an agent, or the like;
because they are like illusions and transformations, they differ from those [non-Buddhist views].
The phrase "revealed solely by phenomena" means that it is intended to state that dependent origination is revealed solely by conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena.

Conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are said to be "arisen from conditions" because they arise, perish, and continue in succession. That which "moistens" refers to the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).

That which is "moistened" refers to the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding those that "fall into the continuity," "falling" means perishing, and "continuity" refers to the body.

Thus, because the personal existence (*sattva-kāya*) arises through the inclusion of both the moistening agent and the moistened object, it is called "arisen from conditions"; alternatively, it is so called because of the existence of the moistening agent and the moistened object.
Sentient beings fall into the midst of birth and death. Alternatively, it may be interpreted as applying to external phenomena as well;
for instance, seeds such as rice or wheat only produce sprouts when moistened by water and soil, and thus there is a continuous succession of arising and ceasing.
[Commentary] The tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: "Because one is bound by afflictions (*kleśa*), one receives this name.
The meaning of this passage is that it explains the characters "condition" (*yuan*) and "arise" (*qi*). "Bound by afflictions" explains the character "condition";

"repeatedly proceeding toward birth and death within the [five] destinies" explains the character "arise. This refers to the process after one has died in a single body and [is reborn] within a single destiny.

"Furthermore, because it undergoes [change] through one and many, it is called 'dependent origination' (pratītyasamutpāda). This explains the name "dependent origination" by analyzing its constituent characters (*akṣara*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "it is explained by relying on the characters *pratī* and *utpāda*," this refers to the etymological interpretation of the term itself.

As for the statement "this is not a definitive [etymological] explanation, but merely the Master of the Commentary’s provisional interpretation of the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*," according to the commentary, this is not appropriate; furthermore, the word "furthermore" (*jù*) should simply be joined [to the preceding clause].

Furthermore, the commentary explains that the passage from the *Yogācārabhūmi* concerning the characters "condition" (*pratyaya*) and "arising" (*utpāda*) provides an interpretation of these terms, such as "name" (*nāman*) and so forth. [The *Śāstra*] states:
"Furthermore, depending upon and relying on various conditions, until it pervades all phenomena. This citation from the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* is abbreviated;
here it is cited in full: "Furthermore, depending upon and relying on various conditions, having quickly perished and ceased, they continue in a state of conjunction."

Because they arise, they are called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This is explained according to the meaning of *kṣaṇa* (moment). The commentary states: conditioned phenomena necessarily depend upon various conditions to arise;
having arisen, they immediately perish; having perished, they encounter conditions again and arise once more.

Because they arise repeatedly and perish repeatedly, this explanation based on *kṣaṇa* applies universally to all conditioned phenomena—whether contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—and all are thus the same.

[The Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the various conditions have passed away yet are not abandoned," this cites a passage from the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The cited text here is abbreviated;
now it is quoted in full: "Furthermore, although the various [conditions] have passed away, they are not abandoned; based upon one's own continuum..."
It is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) because it arises [in dependence]. As it is said: "Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises.
One should understand that the explanation of its name is based on this meaning. To explain:

the intent of this passage is to state that, due to the arising of the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) within the body of a past life, it is able to project the factors of formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), which are capable of bringing about the seeds of the five fruits.
Once the body has died, although the body itself has passed away and no longer exists, the seeds of the five fruits produced by past karma are never separated from the body of this present life;
that is, the seeds of the five fruits—past ignorance (*avidyā*), formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—constitute the birth, aging, and death of this present life.
These seeds of past ignorance, formative forces, and consciousness are what is called [the cause].
Because of actions performed in this life, the birth, aging, and death of the present body arise; this is what is meant by "origination.

It is not due to anything else—neither a creator god (Īśvara), nor primordial matter (Prakṛti), nor any other such cause—that birth, aging, and death are produced. Regarding the principle "because this exists, that exists":
because ignorance exists, volitional formations (saṃskāra) are activated. This commentary states that the "agent" in dependent origination is precisely what the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) posit.
The "Self" (*ātman*), the "Lord" (*īśvara*), and so forth; now, this Dharma is a phenomenon produced from conditions, not something created by the Self, Lord, or other non-Buddhist deities.
That "this being produced, that is produced" means that because ignorance is subject to arising and ceasing, the formations (*saṃskāra*) it brings about are likewise subject to arising and ceasing.
This demonstrates dependent origination as impermanent. That which is permanent is [the non-Buddhist concepts of] primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the Lord, and so on.
The heavens, the self-nature (*svabhāva*), and so forth—these phenomena produced by such natures as darkness (*tamas*) are impermanent; yet the causes, such as the nature of darkness, are eternal.
Now, however, in the Buddha-dharma, both cause and effect are impermanent.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the statement that it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) because it arises from the past up until the present—this is also a passage from the commentary on the tenth fascicle of the *Mahā-śāstra*.
The cited text here is abbreviated; I shall now quote it in full:

"Furthermore, because one has awakened to the conditions of arising (*pratītyasamutpanna*) in the past, and so forth, [the phenomena] arise in continuous succession, it is therefore called 'dependent origination. As the Blessed One said: 'I have already awakened to this, and I am now correctly proclaiming and teaching it.'"
"Because it is transmitted from one to another by this very name, it is called 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The meaning of this passage is as follows:
while dwelling in the past and practicing the path of a bodhisattva, he heard from the Buddha the teaching on the twelve links of dependent origination.

He understood that through these factors, sentient beings cause the flow of birth and death and the cycle of saṃsāra to continue without interruption. Having heard this, he felt weary of and terrified [of cyclic existence].

By practicing, training, and realizing the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), one severs the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) and realizes the true nature of the dharmas of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma-tattva-svabhāva*), thereby attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, regarding the past, he is equal [to all Buddhas] having already awakened to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

As for the arising of the continuum, having himself awakened to the dharma-nature of the twelve links of dependent origination, he also causes sentient beings to awaken to the dharma-nature of dependent origination.
You sentient beings should likewise know the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and diligently cultivate awakening;

by giving rise to the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), severing the tainted links, and attaining perfect enlightenment, you shall realize the *dharmatā* of dependent origination. Therefore, it arises in continuous succession.
As the World-Honored One said: "I have already awakened to this and am now proclaiming it. It is precisely by means of these twelve links of dependent origination that [this teaching] unfolds.

Because it revolves, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which is precisely "continuity. Furthermore, it is said that "arising as continuity" refers to the continuity of the twelve links.

Because the formations (*saṃskāra*) continue from ignorance (*avidyā*) to consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so on until old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) continue into the link of birth (*jāti*), once the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is realized, the continuity of the twelvefold dependent origination arises, flowing and revolving without interruption. It is further stated that this is "continuity."
"Arising" refers to the continuity of the body; that is to say, the twelve links cause one body to be experienced, and furthermore, through the twelve links, one body continues in succession.
Thus, it is by means of the twelve *bhava-aṅgas* (factors of existence) that the body is made to continue.

Therefore, when the Blessed One was able to awaken to the *dharmatā* (true nature) of the twelvefold dependent origination—both the act of awakening and that which is awakened to—is called "condition" (*pratyaya*) at this time.

The meaning of the Dharma taught for the sake of sentient beings is all termed "arising" (utpāda); therefore, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This very Dharma is named "dependent origination" because it arises through being proclaimed.
Regarding the phrase "the succession and so forth" in the commentary (*śāstra*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) does not appear in the root text;
it was inserted by the commentator (*śāstrakāra*), referring to "internal [factors] and so forth."

[Commentary]: Although there are five explanations in total, I shall not cite them all for fear of being too prolix. However, the tenth chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* actually contains five interpretations;
the present commentary cites only four, which correspond to those four interpretations. The fourth interpretation in that treatise states:

"Furthermore, because it repeatedly perishes and repeatedly arises in succession, it is called 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This is explained based on the sense of repeated destruction and repeated cessation.

The commentary explains that this passage interprets dependent origination by means of the cessation of one link and the arising of another: specifically, it shows that once ignorance has ceased, formations arise;

and once formations have ceased, consciousness and the subsequent links arise. Although the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Da lun), fascicle ten, contains five such interpretations, only four are cited here;
thus, it says that further citations would be cumbersome. Furthermore, within the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), there are yet another five interpretations.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in the fifty-sixth [section] that "the cause is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the fruit is called dependently arisen (*pratītyasamutpanna*), and so it is even for old age and death":
an external questioner asks, "For what reason are the twelve links also called dependent origination and also called dependently arisen? The answer is:
the cause is called dependent origination because the seed acts as the cause capable of giving rise to the fruit; thus, the fruit is called dependently arisen.

Therefore, all twelve links are called *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination), and their fruits are called *pratītyasamutpanna* (dependently arisen). This means that all manifest fruits arise from causal seeds;

thus, all twelve links are termed "dependently arisen. As for the reason given in the commentary—that "because the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of ignorance is not severed and exists"—the "latent tendency" refers precisely to the seed.
That is to say, it is because the seed of ignorance is not severed that [existence] arises.
Therefore, "that ignorance-entrapment" refers to the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of one who possesses this entrapment;

the intended meaning is that because the seeds of ignorance exist, the actual manifestation of ignorance arises. "Because this entrapment arises" means that the actual manifestation of ignorance arises.

Because this entrapment arises, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth come into being, and even up to old age and death it is the same; the intended meaning is that [all these arise] due to the actual manifestation of ignorance.

Because the formations (*saṃskāra*) exist, the branch of formations arises; thus, the cause—the branch of ignorance—is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the result—the branch of formations—is called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
Furthermore, because the seed of formations exists without interruption, the actual manifestation of formations arises;

thus, the cause—the seed of formations—is called "dependent origination," and the result—the actual manifestation of formations—is called "dependently arisen. This continues up until the seed of the branch of birth exists without interruption.

Therefore, when the *jāti-aṅga* (the link of birth) arises through its actual manifestation, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as the cause, and "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) as the effect.

Furthermore, because the *jāti-aṅga* exists through its actual manifestation, the *jarāmaraṇa-aṅga* (the link of old age and death) arises through its actual manifestation; thus, the former cause is named "dependent origination," while the *jarāmaraṇa-aṅga* is named "dependently arisen.

Moreover, the sequence beginning with "ignorance conditions volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) and "volitional formations condition consciousness" (*saṃskāra-pratyayaṃ vijñānam*) reveals the causal efficacy (*prabhāva*).

Birth arises precisely because ignorance possesses the power to project the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), which in turn possess the power to evoke the five fruits beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Just as an arrow shot from a bow reaches a great height and distance due to the power of its propulsion, so too is it with the dependent origination of formations conditioned by ignorance, and consciousness conditioned by formations.
Therefore, know that there are three types of dependent origination in general: first, dependent origination without agency; second, dependent origination without permanence.
"Dependent origination has three functional powers.

[Commentary]: "However, regarding the five kinds of fruits viewed in relation to one another, up until the point where they function as fruits and are no longer causes—this passage is identical to the section on the 'causality of simultaneous arising' within the five kinds of causality below.
This refers to when consciousness is viewed in relation to name-and-form, or when name-and-form is viewed..."

The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and so forth are merely termed "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) among the twelve links of dependent origination; they are not [necessarily] "causal conditions" within the context of the four types of conditions.

Therefore, when viewed in relation to what precedes and follows them, they can function as causal conditions. That which is a cause at one time but not an effect at another is, for example, the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is the cause and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is the effect.

That which is an effect at one time but not a cause at another is, for instance, the link of consciousness in relation to the preceding link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); by virtue of the volitional formations, [consciousness arises].
Because it is cited [in the sūtras], and so on up to: "The same applies to craving in relation to the link of feeling.

Furthermore, when explained as being a cause but not a fruit, this refers to the five fruits—consciousness and so forth—in their state as seeds in relation to the fruits of birth and old age and death; that is, the seeds of consciousness and so forth are designated only as causes, not as the fruits of birth and so forth.
When they are a fruit but not a cause, this refers to the seeds of the five fruits—consciousness and so forth—in relation to ignorance.
The statement that "the formations of ignorance act as causes for consciousness and so forth, which are merely called effects" is Master Tai’s interpretation;

however, one might fear that this connection does not accord with other texts, as the meaning here is distinct. This differs from the cause-and-effect relationship of the four conditions mentioned previously:

the former concerns the arising of its own manifest activity from its own seeds as cause and effect, whereas the latter concerns the sequence of the five constituents, such as consciousness, in relation to one another.
Because they stand in relation to one another as cause and effect, they cannot constitute a direct causal condition (*nidāna*). Question:

For what reason is cause and effect distinguished only with respect to the five fruits of consciousness and so forth, rather than with respect to the other members? General Answer: Because the other members are not true *vipākaphala* (fruits of maturation), they are not mentioned.
Alternatively, one may follow Master Tai’s interpretation, which holds that they also apply to the other members when viewed in relation to birth and old age.
"Because it is taught as the fruit of death.

[Commentary: Vasubandhu’s own intention in the *Abhidharmakośa* is the same as this. Regarding the fact that it also receives a distinct name: within the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, it is also based on cause and effect;
since it is at the time of the fruit and not the cause, it is said to be "the same as this."

[Commentary]: Regarding the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*’s statement that it is called "dependent origination" because its various members (*aṅga*) are distinguished as such: "various members" refers to the twelve links.

"The conjunction of their respective conditions" means that each link’s own seed, through conjunction with causal conditions, gives rise to the actualized manifestation (*pravṛtti*), thereby attaining the name "dependent origination.
This serves as proof for the preceding point that one's own seeds and their manifestations function as cause and effect.

This is precisely what was stated previously: that which is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) refers to the cause, while that which is called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) refers to the effect.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement from "ignorance" (*avidyā*) up to "possessive compound" (*karmadhāraya*): this first interpretation states that "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is the wisdom that discriminates phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), and "non-" (*a-*) means non-existence.
However, that which is absent is knowledge; that which is capable of its absence is delusion (*moha*). This is because there is no other [entity] apart from it.
It is said: "Ignorance" (*avidyā*) refers to that which does not exist, and that which does not exist is a phenomenon without intrinsic substance (*avastuka-dharma*). Now, an objection is raised:
if it is stated that "outflow-free wisdom" (*anāsrava-prajñā*) is what is meant by "that which does not exist," then outflow-free wisdom should likewise be non-existent.

If, on the other hand, you say that although "ignorance" is non-existent, "wisdom" (*vidyā*)—which is the opposite of ignorance—is existent, then consider this: for example, if a person's parents have already passed away, one simply says they are "without parents."

It should also be understood that there is something distinct called "non-existence" (wu), yet the essence of the parents still exists; this remains an obstacle [to understanding]. Master Zhe’s explanation states:

"Non-existence" (wu) is not [the meaning here]; "enlightenment" (ming) refers to the penetration of wisdom (hui). Because this essence of delusion is not a transformation of wisdom, the treatise names it "ignorance" (avidyā).

[Commentary]: The old explanation states that "having no other name for its reception" refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*). As for "ignorance" (*avidyā*), it is so called because there is no other untainted illumination;
thus, ignorance is named as such. The intended meaning is that ignorance lacks any other illuminated [state] or outflow-free [clarity], and therefore it receives the designation "ignorance."

[Commentary]: Regarding the term *trimabhava*, which is here translated as "the sixfold analysis of separation and combination" (*li-he shi*), it means that within each of the six types of compound analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhāṣā*), there are both analyses of separation and of combination.

For instance, within the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) analysis, "separation" refers to cases where the substance (*tattva*) and the function (*karman*) are distinct, such as when one says "the storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*).
Here, "storehouse" (*ālaya*) refers to that which contains, while "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the act of discerning; this is called "separation. However, if one says...

"Storehouse" (*ālaya*) is consciousness; this is an *appositional compound* (*karmadhāraya*). Within the *dependent compound* (*tatpuruṣa*), as in the term "eye-consciousness," the name "consciousness" is distinct from the eye-faculty:
the eye has the sense of "illuminating," while consciousness has the sense of "discerning"; therefore, they are distinct.

If one says "the consciousness that depends on the eye" is called "eye-consciousness," this is an *appositional compound*. Within the *possessive compound* (*bahuvrīhi*), as in the term "yoga... [the text here is incomplete].
The term "yogācārya" (master of yoga) has the meaning of "one who practices" (*yukta*) and "teacher" (*ācārya*). This is an analysis by way of separation (*vyadhikaraṇa-vigraha*):
that is, within the person designated as a "teacher," there exists the dharma of practice, and thus he is called a "yogācārya. This is an analysis by way of synthesis (*sāmānādhikaraṇa-vigraha*).

It is just as when one says "a wealthy person"—the "person" is a conventional designation, while "wealth" refers to property and so forth. In the analysis by way of opposition (*virodha-vigraha*), it is like saying "capable of... [and so on].

Regarding "the establishment" (*sādhana*) and "the refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*): the establishment consists of the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), and so forth; the refuter is one who refutes the opponent's position, which is to say, they separate [it from its basis].

If one says that "establishment" and "refutation" are in a *vyadhikaraṇa-karmadhāraya* (appositional compound with different case-roles), this is a collective construction (*samāhāra*). Within the *saṃkhyā-viśeṣaṇa-karmadhāraya* (appositional compound with a numeral as a qualifier), for instance, when one says "the five aggregates" (*pañca-skandhāḥ*):

"five" is the number, and "aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of a collection (*rāśi*); this is a distributive construction (*nirbhāga-vyutpatti*). If one says "five... [this refers to the collective sense].

The *skandha* (aggregate) is an example of a collective explanation (*samāsa-vyākhyā*). As for the proximate explanation (*upapada-vyākhyā*), it is like saying that the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is able to survey the body;

"mindfulness" (*smṛti*) is able to maintain its nature, which is an analytical explanation (*nirukti*). To say "the observation of the four foundations of mindfulness" is an example of a collective explanation.

[Commentary]: This refers to the explanation of "ignorance" (avidyā) starting from "that which is not knowledge" up to "therefore it is called ignorance. This second interpretation takes *vidyā* as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). [Commentary]:
Or, because it ranges from the six types of compounds up to the six types of compounds, this states that ignorance does not apply to the *karmadhāraya*, as there is no distinction.

Because they share the same essence, although the two characters "ignorance" (*avidyā*) together express a single delusion—just as the term *tṛṇa* refers to a single thing—it is known that ignorance is not subsumed under the six types of compound analysis; this is superior from the perspective of principle.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "There is no separate explanation for 'with' (yu) and 'clearly' (ming) up to the six types of analysis," this means that what is being discussed here is the general explanation of the six types of analysis (*ṣaḍ-vibhakti*).

Generally, all six types of analysis involve the two meanings of separation (*vibhakta*) and combination (*samasta*). Therefore, the ancient sūtras and śāstras treat these separations and combinations as the six types of analysis.
Since among the twelve links of dependent origination the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) is the first, the link of ignorance is explained first.
Regarding the initial analysis that separates "non-existence" (*abhāva*) from "clarity" (*vidyā*): this refers to first analyzing the characters for "non-existence" and "clarity" individually;

what is called "separating non-existence" means it is not existent, while "clarity" refers to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*). Regarding the subsequent analysis that combines them for a comprehensive explanation:

this refers to subsequently combining the characters for "non-existence" and "clarity" into one place to explain them together, which is called a "combined explanation. Thus, "ignorance" (*avidyā*) [is explained].
This refers to the luminous, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) that is other than the absence of delusion; therefore, it is said to be "separated.

The branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is also like this: first, one separates "name" from "form" to explain them individually—this is the "separation of name," which consists of the four non-material aggregates (*skandhas*), while "form" refers to the characteristic of all phenomena of being subject to change and resistance.
Subsequently, one explains them by combining them; this general explanation describes name and form as being mutually [dependent].

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by [the six sense bases]," the branch of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is likewise explained. "Six" is the number; "bases" (*āyatana*) refers to the locations where the mind and mental factors arise and grow.
This is the analysis (*vyutpatti*). As for the synthesis (*samāsa*), it is collectively termed the "six sense bases.

It is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound consisting of two dharmas; that is, essence and function constitute the two dharmas, and because these two dharmas—essence and function—are distinct, it is called a *karmadhāraya*.

Since the factor of ignorance (*avidyā*) can denote a single dharma and lacks the two meanings of separation and combination, it does not constitute one of the six types of compound (*ṣaḍ-vigraha*). Question:
If the factor of ignorance is not a sixfold compound, why was it previously stated that ignorance is karma? Answer: This is based on the relative distinction between self and other;

when there is a relative [distinction], there is no "other" apart from the "self," and thus there is no untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*). However, if one considers its essential nature (*svabhāva*), there is neither separation nor combination.
Regarding the *ālayavijñāna*, there is both separation and union; because it does not stand in opposition to self and other, it forms a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.

Furthermore, another explanation states that the aforementioned *karmadhāraya* name has no separate interpretation for "non-existence" (*am*) and "clarity" (*vibhāsa*), or that it is not one of the six types of compounds; what follows below is the subsequent explanation that combines these as a general interpretation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "These six types of explanation depend on the distinction between two dharmas," the "two dharmas" refer to the two dharmas of separation (*viyoga*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

The intention of the phrase "only then can it be explained" is as follows: if a dharma possesses both the qualities of separation and conjunction, only then can it be explained by means of the six types of grammatical analysis (*ṣaṭ-vibhakti*).
Since ignorance (*avidyā*) is neither separate nor conjoined, it does not exceed the scope of the six types of explanation for all dharmas.

[Commentary: There is another interpretation which holds that all [the factors] are identical to "volitional formation" (*saṃskāra*) and cannot be cited separately. In that passage, it explains that the names of the remaining [factors] are all identical to the "limb of volitional formation" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*).

That is to say, "volitional formation" is a name designated based on its own essential nature; "constructing" (*abhisamskāra*) is the meaning of "volitional formation," and it is also designated by the term "function.

It refers to the function of producing a result. Similarly, "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is a name designated based on its own essential nature; "discernment" (*vijñapti*) is "consciousness," and it is also...
"Function" (kāritra) is designated as such because it possesses the capacity to discern its object. "Contact" (sparśa) is named after its essential nature because it touches upon the object;

thus, the meaning of contact is also the conjunction of the three. Furthermore, the capacity to produce sensation (vedanā) and so forth, up to the arising of the aggregates, is likewise termed "arising" (jāti).
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "because it accords with and leads toward the various meanings of the objects of perception," the term "name" (*nāman*) indicates the designation for the object.
Alternatively, because it relies on verbal expression to differentiate the various meanings of the objects of perception, it is called a "name";
this refers to the name that expresses meaning. That treatise states: "Just as a name can express an object, the four aggregates are called 'name. Furthermore—

The commentary explains that because names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*) and so forth are subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), the four [mental] aggregates are called "name. [The *Śāstra*] states:

"The meanings of planting, growing, and increasing in various locations, as well as the meaning of being subject to transformation and resistance (*rūpaṇa*)," refers to material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), which possess distinctions of the four directions, above, and below—making six directions in total.
Mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are not like this; furthermore, planting and growing do not apply to them alone.

Just as external grains and barley are so, it is likewise with the internal body; sustained by food and drink, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are able to increase.
Once they have increased, they then produce the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)—such as the sense faculties and their objects—and cause them to grow and undergo the quality of resistance (*pratigha*).

As for the meaning of "transformation and resistance," it is like the physical appearance of a person’s face, which changes when one is angry, when one is pleased, or when one is terrified. Or [it is like being] struck...
"When damaged, their color changes and they possess resistance; external forms, such as those damaged by wind, frost, and the like, all possess change and resistance.
'Resistance' (āvaraṇa) refers to substantial obstruction.

[Commentary: There are two kinds of change and resistance: first, the sense that they are immediately transformed and destroyed when touched by hands and so forth; second, the sense of spatial differentiation.
[The text] distinguishes between the meanings of various characteristics.
[Commentary]: The meaning of the passage from "it is not that the essence of the name is identical to form" up to "because it is the form possessed by the name" is as follows:

it clarifies that this member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is explained, respectively, neither by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional), *tatpuruṣa* (determinative), nor *bahuvrīhi* (possessive) compounds; rather, it is exclusively a *dvandva* (copulative) compound.
[Commentary: Regarding the meaning of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as "gateways for growth," the intent is that these six faculties are called "bases" (*āyatana*) for three reasons:
first, they are the places where consciousness arises; second, they are the places where consciousness grows;
and third, the reason the six bases are called "gateways" is that they are the places through which consciousness travels, and thus they are termed "gateways."

[Commentary]: In the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are three successive expositions regarding the first [member]. Regarding the statement "up to being the cause in sequence," the explanation is as follows:

that which must first be ignorant of the object of knowledge is the member of Ignorance (*avidyā*); that which gives rise to wrong practice is the member of Volitional Formations (*saṃskāra*). Question:
Since volitional formations encompass both the wholesome and the unwholesome, why is it referred to collectively as "wrong practice"? Answer: There are two interpretations. First, regarding only...

Regarding unwholesome conduct, it is said that there are two [types]: ignorance gives rise to the three types of formations—meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable—and since all these invite the fruit of suffering and contradict the cessation of suffering, they are collectively termed "erroneous conduct.
As for the "inversion of mind," this refers to the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Question:

Since the link of consciousness refers exclusively to the eighth [consciousness], why is it called an "inversion"? Answer: There are two interpretations. One says: formations are of two kinds; first...

The manifestation of these two types of seeds is called the seed of the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). It is named the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna*) because it is perfumed by the manifestation of volitional formations.
Furthermore, it is called the link of consciousness because it has "inversion" (*viparyāsa*) as its cause; this is to be understood in two ways.

First, at the time of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), one gives rise to a mind associated with attachment or aversion toward the parents and so forth, which is termed inversion. This occurs because tainted wholesome volitional formations are contrary to [the state of non-inversion].

If even the cessation [of suffering] can still be termed "perverse existence" (*mithyā-bhava*) and "outflowing indeterminate" (*sāsrava-avyākṛta*), what fault is there in calling the root of birth-and-death "perversion"?
Therefore, various treatises state that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) of the three realms are false; this falsity is itself a synonym for perversion (*viparyāsa*).

Alternatively, because they arise from perversion, they are also called perversions. Some say that what is termed "mental perversion" is the member of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*); according to the member of consciousness, this present [state] is likewise [so designated].
Regarding the eighth consciousness, for now we shall provisionally designate it as the "consciousness link" (vijñāna-aṅga) by way of the preceding six consciousnesses.

Since at the time of linking rebirth (pratisaṃdhi), one gives rise to mutual attachment and aversion toward the parents, this is termed "inversion. This state of inversion is a characteristic of the preceding six consciousnesses and does not belong to the eighth consciousness;
such is the meaning. Although there are two interpretations, you may choose between them as you wish. As for the continuity of the linking of rebirth:
That which is the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the period from the fifth to the seventh day within the womb;

that which is the perfection of the sense faculties refers to the link of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Regarding "the enjoyment of objects," this refers to both the links of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), as both are capable of enjoying objects.
The intention is that through contact contrary to one's inclinations, there arises the feeling of sorrow and suffering, whereas through contact conformable to one's inclinations...
This refers to the arising of the mental formations associated with feelings of joy and pleasure, which are similar and identical in their locus and clarity.
This meaning indicates that the sequence of the five factors, beginning with consciousness, is explained according to the stage at which they are about to arise.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that these take the five future fruits as causes, the intent is to show how these five—consciousness and the others—relate to ignorance and formative action (*saṃskāra*).
Since that which is the fruit immediately becomes the cause for the state of being born in the future, it is said that "the five fruits serve as causes.
That which consists of attachment and longing is the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*); that which nourishes the afflictions is the link of grasping (*upādāna*);

that which initiates karma for future existence is the link of becoming (*bhava*); the arising of the five kinds of fruits is the link of birth (*jāti*); and the deterioration once born is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This explanation is stated according to the sequential order of the stages of rebirth.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "within the first six links, the internal body is established as the object-condition," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states:

"As for the preeminence of the internal body as the object-condition, it is subsumed within the first six links; that is, one first gives rise to the grasping of 'self' with respect to the internal body, and because of this grasping of the internal body as self..."

Immediately, the factor of ignorance arises; through this ignorance, one fails to comprehend that various karmas lead to the fruits of suffering, thereby giving rise to the factor of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Once these three types of formations—meritorious and so forth—have been set in motion, one immediately gives rise to discursive thought, which constitutes the factor of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This is defined as the factor of consciousness in terms of the six consciousnesses; because karma acts as an auxiliary companion to consciousness, it is able to bring about the three kinds of suffering in the future.
Regarding the first [category], the fruit of suffering comprised by the initial arising of the faculties refers to the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

the fruit of suffering comprised by the perfection of the faculties refers to the link of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); and the fruit of suffering comprised by the enjoyment of objects refers to the link of contact (*sparśa*).
Therefore, it is said that "within the first six links, the internal body is established."
[Commentary: Regarding the establishment of the final six links as having their objects fully present, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle ten, states:

"Furthermore, within the present life, that which arises dependent on contact (*sparśa*) is the link of sensation (*vedanā*). From sensation, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is produced, which is the link of craving.

By means of enjoying objects, extensive seeking (*pariyeṣaṇā*) arises, which is the link of grasping (*upādāna*). With grasping as the precursor, there is becoming (*bhava*); and because of becoming, [birth arises]."
This causes the fruits of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) in the five destinies to arise; once they have arisen, aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) follow accordingly.

All of these are explained in terms of the stage where birth, aging, and death are actively manifesting. Therefore, it is said: "The latter six links are established as objects and conditions, because they consist in the enjoyment of objects."

[Commentary: Third, regarding the establishment [of the categories] based on the three types of sentient beings, up to the phrase "as explained extensively therein," this cites the text from the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
As it says there: "Furthermore, there is a sequential distinction, namely, by way of three types of sentient beings:
first, the class of sentient beings who delight in supramundane purity; 'class' (*gotra*) here has the sense of lineage, meaning that these sentient beings delight in..."

It is not because of renunciation, nor through profound revulsion toward dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), nor by severing the various defilements (*saṃkleśa*) and increasing pure dharmas (*śukladharma*).

Question: How does one sever dependent origination and yet increase pure dharmas? Answer: It is because those of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), having contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination both forward and backward, subsequently give rise to this thought:

"Birth for me has been exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall not undergo further existence. Thus [they sever dependent origination and increase pure dharmas].

The differentiation of the twelve links of dependent origination is precisely what is called the "increasing of the pure dharmas" (*śukladharma*). For now, let us follow the forward contemplation (*anuloma*) of the twelve links:
as it is said, because ignorance is differentiated, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are differentiated, and so on, up to:

because birth is differentiated, aging and death cease. Next, let us contemplate them in reverse (*pratiloma*): one should consider, "By the absence of what does aging and death cease? By the differentiation of what does aging and death cease? and so forth.
It is said: "Because of birth, there is old age and death; because of the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of old age and death. ...

[continuing] "...because of the non-existence of what is there no existence of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and because of the cessation of what is there the cessation of volitional formations? One should say: "Because of the non-existence of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no existence of volitional formations; because of the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.

For now, let us perform the contemplation of the pure dependent origination (*viśuddha-pratītyasamutpāda*) in both forward and reverse order, as well as the defiled dependent origination (*kliṣṭa-pratītyasamutpāda*) in both forward and reverse order.

The contemplation is as explained in the separate transcription; its meaning is that it causes sentient beings to observe dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) so that they may attain wholesome dharmas (*śukladharma*).
Therefore, the twelve links are established. Regarding the two types of assemblies of worldly and pure sentient beings:

those who do not know the principles of the truths (*satya*) as they truly are, and who thus lack knowledge of the principles of the truths, are the link of ignorance (*avidyā*). Or, if one abides in right mindfulness...

Whether one performs meritorious karma (*puṇyābhisamskāra*), or performs immovable karma (*āniñjyābhisamskāra*) induced by the cultivation of contaminated meditative absorptions (*sāsravadhyāna*), or—if one does not abide in right mindfulness—performs non-meritorious karma (*apuṇyābhisamskāra*):

these factors of volitional formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*) constitute the link of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) because they cause the mental continuum to act through the gateway of volitional formations.
Furthermore, just as the three types of karma previously mentioned sequentially induce the results of suffering in the three respective realms of rebirth, so too do they function accordingly.
Inferior non-meritorious karma brings about three kinds of painful fruits within the miserable realms—namely, the factors of name-and-form, the six sense bases, and contact.
Middling meritorious karma likewise brings about three kinds of painful fruits among humans and devas—namely, the factors of name-and-form, the six sense bases, and contact.
Furthermore, by means of superior immovable karma, one brings about the three [factors] of the two upper realms.
The fruit of suffering refers to the three links of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and contact (*sparśa*).

The "mass of sentient beings" who are attached to objects of pleasure refers to the link of feeling (*vedanā*), which is the sensation produced in relation to objects currently being experienced. From feeling arises craving, which is the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The extensive pursuit of these objects constitutes the link of grasping (*upādāna*). With grasping as the precursor, existence (*bhava*) arises.
Because the members [of dependent origination] exist as members, once the fruit of birth-and-death within the five destinies has arisen, aging and death follow accordingly.
These two are also explained in terms of the stage of the fruit that is yet to arise. To explain the sequence of the causes:

first, among the six preceding members, the internal body is established as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); second, the six subsequent members are established as the objective condition for the worldlings who delight in existence.
The first six branches are established for sentient beings who are attached to sense objects, while the latter six branches are established for them;
thus, both types are explained in terms of the stages of future rebirth.

[Commentary] Question: If this is so, why is it that when one proceeds to contemplate dependent origination in reverse order? The intent of this question is explained as follows: "If it were as previously stated..."

Question: If [the teachings] arise simultaneously and are then explained in sequence, how is it that within the purification of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-viśuddhi*), one first contemplates old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) and subsequently contemplates birth (*jāti*) and so forth?

[Commentary]: The answer, "Because it is established according to the principle of the sequential order of the Truths (*satya*)," means that this is established in accordance with the four truths (*catur-āryasatya*). It refers to the arrangement of the path.
This is the explanation according to principle: first, one explains the Truth of Suffering, meaning that it consists of old age, death, and so forth.

Therefore, by relying on the established Four Noble Truths to practice the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), one contemplates each of the eleven links as being complete with the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Consequently, there are forty-four knowledges in total; for example, old age and death possess four knowledges, and this applies likewise down to the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

Because ignorance has no cause and is therefore not observed, there are no forty-eight knowledges. Thus, one first applies the method to the branch of old age and death within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

The commentary states: "The observation of the origination of old age and death, the cessation of old age and death, and the practice leading to the cessation of old age and death—'old age and death' refers to the Truth of Suffering;
'the origination of old age and death' refers to the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*); and the Truth of Origination is..."

Because the branch of birth arises precisely with birth itself as its cause and is able to produce the branch of old age and death, it is said that the branch of birth is itself the truth of the origin (*samudaya-satya*) of old age and death.
Subsequently, one should understand by analogy that the cessation of old age and death is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

When observing the cessation of old age and death, there is necessarily a principle to be realized, which is cessation itself. The practice leading toward the cessation of old age and death is the path (*mārga*).

This is the wisdom that realizes cessation through direct insight (*nirodha-satyābhisamaya-jñāna*). Question: How is this branch of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) abandoned? Answer: It can only be abandoned by the path of the Arhats (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) of the two vehicles;

thus, by abandoning the suffering of old age and death, one attains the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). Furthermore, observing that the arising of birth is the origin of birth and that the movement toward the cessation of birth is the practice [leading to it]:
"birth" is the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); "the origin of birth" is the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*); and as for the truth of origination—

That which consists of the *bhava-aṅga* (existence-factor) having the *bhava-aṅga* as its cause and being able to produce the *jāti-aṅga* (birth-factor), and that which is the cessation of birth—that is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

That which is the practice leading toward the cessation of birth—that is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). The meaning of "abandonment" is the same as what was explained regarding the *jarā-aṅga* (aging-factor). This applies likewise up to the contemplation of the *saṃskāra-aṅga* (volitional formations-factor):

namely, the practice of observing the formations, the practice of observing their origination, the practice of observing their cessation, and the practice leading toward their cessation; these are to be understood according to the previous explanation regarding suffering, origination, cessation, and the path.

The path of abandonment is also the same as before, constituting the branch of ignorance (*avidyā*). Since there is no further truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) above this, and because ignorance has no [further] cause, ignorance thus lacks the four truths.
Consequently, among the remaining eleven branches—excluding the branch of ignorance—all are complete with the four knowledges (*jñāna*);
thus, there are forty-four knowledges in total. This is what the practitioners of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) cultivate prior to the four roots of merit (*kuśala-mūla*).
The observation of the twelve links of dependent origination through forty-four types of knowledge constitutes the contemplation of the process of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) in reverse order.

This contemplation has, for its essence, only the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). Alternatively, it may be performed even during the four stages of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Question:

Since suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are affliction, while cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are purification, how can they both be collectively termed the "contemplation of the process of affliction in forward and reverse order"? Answer: Cessation... [is included].
Although the Path is pure, because Suffering and its Origin are defiled, they are collectively termed "defilement.

If one speaks of the contemplation that accords with defilement, it refers to the links such as ignorance conditioning formations, formations conditioning consciousness, and so forth up to birth conditioning aging and death;

thus, in both the stage of the Requisite Accumulation (*sambhāra*) and the stage of Application (*prayoga*), this can be considered a commonality of defilement, following the same principle as before.

In the question within the commentary, one asks about the pure dependent origination (*śuddha-pratītyasamutpāda*); now, the commentary clarifies the contemplation of the defiled dependent origination (*kliṣṭa-pratītyasamutpāda*) by answering according to the principle of the sequence of the truths.
Since this answer contradicts the question and is entirely inconsistent with it, let the reader take note.

According to the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, there are forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*) for the contemplation of the defiled dependent origination in reverse order alone; it does not state how it is for the pure [dependent origination]. Now, as for the Master of the Commentary...

Does the explanation of the pure dependent origination (*viśuddha-pratītyasamutpāda*) also rely on the principle of the sequential order of the truths? Therefore, the commentary contradicts the text of the *Abhidharmapitaka*.

Furthermore, according to the record on the contemplation of the defiled dependent origination in reverse order, among the forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*), seven additional knowledges are further added—namely, the observation of the eleven links excluding ignorance because it has no cause—resulting in a total of seventy-seven knowledges, just as in the case of the Dharma robes.
The detailed commentary clarifies this fully, but for fear of being too wordy, it is not recorded here.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the defiled agent can be understood through reflection upon the two periods of time based on their immediate succession as cause and effect":
the "two periods" refers to the past and the present as one, and the present and the future as two. Now...
Furthermore, if we speak according to the sequence of rebirths (*upapadyavedanīya*), the past twelve links of causation (*hetu*) result in the present twelve links of fruition (*phala*).
Alternatively, the present twelve links of causation may result in either the present twelve links of fruition or the future twelve links of fruition.
If, however, we speak according to subsequent rebirths (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) that span multiple lifetimes, they are not fixed; that is to say, first:
The first seven links arise in one lifetime; the second, the three links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*), arise in a second lifetime;
and the third, the two links of birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), arise in a third lifetime.

Furthermore, these twelve links as conditions may be indefinite—meaning they do not necessarily follow a fixed sequence—whether occurring across three lifetimes, five lifetimes, or even across hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "causing sentient beings to be deluded about existence (*bhava*) up to giving rise to doubts concerning the past and future," the intended meaning is that those who are deluded about existence are those who give rise to delusion regarding the fruits of existence within the three realms.
This clarifies that it causes sentient beings to arise in existence and to become deluded;
since this is manifested by the obscuring power of ignorance (*avidyā*), one consequently fails to comprehend the three bodies of existence throughout the three periods of time.

To give rise to doubt regarding the three periods of time and so forth is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*), with which [the other afflictions] coexist; this is identical to the first three types of ignorance among the nineteen kinds of non-knowledge.
Furthermore, "existence" (*bhava*) refers to the three existences: the existence of desire (*kāma-bhava*), the existence of form (*rūpa-bhava*), and the existence of the formless (*ārūpya-bhava*).

[Commentary]: "First, the delusion regarding objects causes sentient beings to be confused; this refers to the aforementioned doubt concerning the lack of understanding regarding the objects of knowledge.
The explanation states: "Delusion regarding objects" means that delusion arises in relation to objective spheres.

Because of this delusion, one fails to understand the three realms of existence and the objects of the three periods of time, thereby giving rise to doubt. This is as stated in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
Although the phrasing differs slightly, the meaning is the same; thus, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "In this regard, ignorance is of two kinds:
first, delusion regarding conditions that causes sentient beings to be confused; second, acting as the cause for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)."

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the rest, up to old age and death," etc., according to what is stated in the commentary, the karmic function of ignorance has already been explained and will not be discussed again.

Since the karmic functions of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth have not yet been explicitly stated, and fearing that students might remain ignorant of them, I have now carefully consulted the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and appended the relevant passages here for those who read it to find them easily and derive benefit. The subsequent sūtra says:
Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) have two functions: first, they produce karmic retribution in future lives; second, they act as the cause for the arising of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Consciousness has two states: first, it enables the continuity of sentient beings; second, it acts as the cause for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Name-and-form has two states:
first, its components mutually assist and establish one another; second, it acts as the cause for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The six sense bases have two [functions]...

The first stage [of contact] has two functions: first, it can take the six sense objects as its objective conditions; second, it acts as the cause for sensation (*vedanā*). Contact (*sparśa*) has two stages: first, it can touch the objective conditions;

second, it acts as the cause for sensation. Sensation has two stages: first, it gives rise to increased craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth; second, it acts as the cause for craving. Craving has two stages:
first, it generates a mind of greed toward things that can provoke defilement; second, it acts as the cause for grasping (*upādāna*). Grasping...
Existence (*bhava*) has two aspects: first, it increases the defilements of afflictive bondage;

second, it acts as the cause for birth (*jāti*). Birth (*jāti*) has two aspects: first, it enables rebirth in other realms of existence; second, it acts as the cause for aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
Aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) have two aspects: first, it causes the maturation of the sense faculties; second, each instance of the maturation of the faculties constitutes aging.
Death has two aspects that act as causes for death. There are two states of existence at death (*cyuti-bhava*): first, the destruction of the five aggregates (*skandha*);

second, because of non-perception and non-cognition, the continuity [of existence] remains unbroken. That treatise says: "The destruction of the five aggregates can act as the cause for subsequent birth;

because of non-perception and non-cognition, it can act as the cause for subsequent birth. Commentary: Regarding "conditions" (*pratyaya*), they are the objects of perception (*ālambana*) among all those [conditions].
Because one does not awaken while amidst the objects of perception, it is called "delusion within the objects of perception" (*ālambana-moha*).

Because it arises as the cause of various afflictions and causes sentient beings to be deluded, and because it has the capacity to draw forth birth in other realms of existence, it is called "birth in other realms" (*anyabhava-janman*); it is not yet the state where birth has already been completed.
Thus, the meaning is the same as that stated in the fourth *Abhidharmapāda*: "causing the subsequent existence (*punarbhava*) of sentient beings to manifest. The rest of the text follows accordingly.

"Because they are entirely consistent with the Abhidharma, they are not cited [separately] so as not to disrupt the 'prime of youth'; this refers to aging (*jarā*), meaning that aging can destroy the physical body (*rūpakāya*).
'Because it destroys the life-span' refers to death (*maraṇa*), meaning that death can destroy the life-force (*jīvita*).

Therefore, because these two are not perceived or known, they cause the continuum to remain uninterrupted. This is now explained in connection with the commentary on the branch of death (*maraṇāṅga*).
As for those who possess vision and knowledge, at the time of their death they are unable to see the destruction of existence, nor can they perceive the various objects of the subsequent life;
yet from this death, they cause the continuity of the body in a future existence to proceed without interruption. The Noble One is not like this;

because he perceives and knows the nature of birth and death, he feels weary of and terrified by it, and thus brings about its cessation. Therefore, there is no further succession; for one beyond training, "birth has been exhausted, and I shall receive no more."
"There is a future existence.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "in the *Abhidharma*, 'old age and death' (*jarāmaraṇa*) are treated as a single unit, whereas here they are divided," the meaning is as follows:

In the *Abhidharma*, old age and death are explained together; therefore, it speaks only of "old age" and does not speak of "old age" being of two kinds. Furthermore, in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, with respect to old age...
Death has no fruit; therefore, it is not said that death is of two kinds, nor is it stated that there is no perception of the continuity of the stream of existence and so forth.

As stated in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*: "Because there is a fruit after death, and because there is no perception [of such a fruit], the subsequent continuity of the body is uninterrupted. Thus, these two points are not contradictory.

[Commentary: Furthermore, because they lack knowledge, regarding that which is not an antidote, up to the point of performing immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*), the intended meaning is that the worldly path suppresses afflictions through the sixfold practice—rejoicing in the higher realms and feeling aversion toward the lower ones—and thus there is no falling back.

The *Śāstra* explains that noble ones (*ārya*) do not perform immovable karma and so forth; whereas various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) suppress afflictions through the worldly sixfold practice and view the lower realms as suffering.

Because one regards the coarse obstacles as hindrances and views the higher realms as peaceful, sublime, and secluded, one immediately conceives of the higher realms as the transcendence of birth and death and as the ultimate state of *nirvāṇa*.
Consequently, one counteracts the afflictions of the desire realm by performing meritorious and immovable karma of the higher realms;

therefore, this is ignorance regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-moha*). One who is ignorant of the ultimate truth initiates meritorious and immovable karma toward the bitter fruits of existence among gods and humans.

Question: What is the distinction between merit (*puṇya*) and the immovable (*āniñjya*)? Answer: Merit refers to wholesome states that are dispersed (*viprakīrṇa-kuśala*), while the immovable refers to wholesome states that are concentrated (*samāhita-kuśala*). [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement that "the conventional and the ultimate [are both] suffering," and that it is called "ultimate" [in this context], the intended meaning is as follows: according to the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma-piṭaka*), one may establish a single type of suffering. Why? Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess the nature of oppression (*bādhanā*).

Alternatively, one may establish two types of suffering, namely: ... [The text continues with the definition of the two types of suffering. ... *Note: The provided source text contains a fragment regarding the classification of suffering in the Abhidharma tradition.*

If conventional suffering (*saṃvṛti-duḥkha*) and ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*) are subsumed within the eight types of suffering, then the first seven sufferings—subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)—are called conventional suffering.
If the eighth suffering is subsumed under the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), it is ultimate suffering.

The meaning is that one creates meritorious and immovable formations (*puṇya-āniñjya-saṃskāra*) due to a failure to understand ultimate suffering; it does not mean that one creates merit and so forth due to a failure to understand the suffering of suffering.
[The text says: "One performs [karmic] formations.

[Commentary: If it is argued that suffering in the form and formless realms consists of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) and so forth, up to the point where one creates non-meritorious (*apuṇya*) formations due to delusion regarding those [realms], then in this context the objection is raised:

If you say that the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*) and the suffering of change are worldly sufferings, and that because of delusion regarding them one creates non-meritorious formations, then as for the form...
Since the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*), one should not be deluded regarding it by performing non-meritorious actions (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*).

Question: How is it known that the two upper realms possess the suffering of change? Answer: In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), specifically within the lower three dhyānas, there is pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanā*). Based on this feeling, "change" is established as the suffering of change;
"change" here means loss. For example, when one dies from the lower realms and is reborn in the third dhyāna, at a later time [the pleasant feeling changes].

Because of falling away, there is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*); or, as can be seen, when one who has previously attained that meditative absorption falls away from the pleasant feeling of that stage at the time of death and is reborn in a lower realm, this too is called the suffering of change.
Although in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) there is actually no suffering of change, the present commentary states that "the realms of form and formlessness have the suffering of change.

While this phrasing mentions them collectively, the intent is difficult to reconcile with the realm of form; therefore, it says they "have" the suffering of change [to indicate its presence in the realm of form].
Because they are suffering, one should also mistakenly give rise to non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-saṃskāra*).

[Commentary: As for the meaning of the statement that "in their essence, all are suffering," it means that there is no need to correlate the two truths by means of the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkha*);
rather, one may simply state in general that the suffering of the three miserable realms and the hells is easy to understand, and is therefore called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If suffering refers to the happy realms of humans and devas, it is called "ultimate suffering" (paramārtha-duḥkha) because it is difficult to understand.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that the worldly is difficult to comprehend and is thus termed "excellent" (*śubha*) and so forth, the intended meaning is as follows:

for instance, when the happy realms of humans and devas are called "ultimate suffering," it is solely because they are difficult to comprehend from a worldly perspective that they are designated as "ultimate"; in reality, they are not ultimate. This is also the case here.
Regarding the statement that "the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) is ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*)," the intended meaning is as follows:
Since humans and devas in the happy realms are called "ultimate suffering," it is clear that because the suffering of change exists within those realms, the suffering of change is also ultimate.

How is it, then, that the *Abhidharma* previously classified the suffering of change as "conventional suffering" (*saṃvṛti-duḥkha*)? One should carefully examine this point in relation to both this treatise and the *Abhidharma*.

What is the distinction? This treatise bases its explanation on the three types of sensation within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to clarify the three types of suffering. What are their specific characteristics? First, regarding the three miserable realms (*apāya*):

in the hells in their entirety, and in one portion of the hungry ghosts and animals where there is exclusively a place of pure suffering, based upon the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*), there is the "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).

Furthermore, in that one portion of hungry ghosts and animals where sensations are mixed, there are also sensations of flow-on pleasure (*niṣyandasukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣāvedanā*); based upon these, [the other two types of suffering are established].
There is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). Here, "change" means transformation and decay;

thus, within the delusion of worldly fools, there are three types of suffering arising from that confusion, which give rise to non-meritorious formations (*apuṇya-saṃskāra*). Furthermore, even within the realms of humans and gods, there is what is called ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*), which likewise possesses three types of suffering.

For example, among the six classes of desire-realm gods (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*), there is the suffering of having one's head broken or one's waist severed by others, as well as the mental anguish of the gods of wrath (*krodha-deva*) and so forth.

Regarding suffering: because there are the sufferings of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), the heavenly realm (*deva-gati*) likewise possesses these three types of suffering.

Just as it is easy to understand that the human realm possesses these three sufferings, they are not described here [in detail]. Because of delusion regarding those [heavenly realms], one initiates meritorious formations (*puṇya-saṃskāra*).

As for the two upper realms, in the lower three dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), there is the suffering of change and the suffering of conditioned formations; this is because when the blissful sensations of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) are lost through falling away, there is the experience of their passing and ceasing.

Since the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) arises when there is the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), there is no fault in [the presence of] the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
Because there is only the suffering of conditioned formations based on equanimity and no other feelings, no other type of suffering is established there.

Furthermore, because one creates immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*) through delusion regarding those [formless states], even within meritorious karma (*puṇya-karma*)—which is a delusion regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-moha*)—there are likewise three types of suffering. This is as explained in the Abhidharma treatises, where it is stated that the determination of suffering is not fixed.
Alternatively, one may establish a single suffering, namely the nature of oppression, which is precisely the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Or, one may establish two types of suffering:
