However, if that which takes ignorance as its cause—namely, the subsequent ignorance and the prior karma and craving that act as auxiliary conditions—is unable to cause the twelve links of birth and death to continue and increase;
or if there are no wholesome links acting as mutual path-conditions, then the twelve links will not be diminished.
Although there are two interpretations regarding this basis.

[Commentary: By this, it is also revealed that "just as craving for rebirth" means that the intention is solely to clarify that old age and death are the cause and ignorance is the fruit, just as in the case of craving for rebirth and so forth.

[Commentary: "Although it is known that ignorance (avidyā) initiates [karma] and craving (tṛṣṇā) provides moisture, [craving] is used as a metaphor"—this explains a potential objection. The intent of the objection is as follows:

For instance, since the functions of ignorance in initiating karma and craving in providing moisture are essentially different, how can craving be cited as a metaphor for old age and death arising from ignorance?
Now, the answer is given: Although ignorance and craving differ in their functions of initiating and moistening, they are nonetheless equal [in their role].
Because they are "outflows" (*āsrava*), they are used as analogies. "Outflow" (*niṣyanda*) has the meaning of "similarity.

Since ignorance (*avidyā*) arises from an object and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) likewise arises from an object, both aging (*jarā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are objects; thus, ignorance and craving are similar in their nature as afflictions (*kleśa*) with respect to their objects.
Therefore, using craving as an analogy is not subject to contradiction or objection.
[Commentary: "It is not like the examples of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) regarding the attainment of results and so forth" means that this explains the doctrine of the Small Vehicle.

The intention of the Small Vehicle is that, for instance, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) existing simultaneously with the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) are all designated as the link of ignorance because they can set the process of becoming in motion;

therefore, ignorance takes the five aggregates as its *pratītyasamutpāda* factor. The statement that "craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth are likewise" refers to taking feeling (*vedanā*) and so on as the link of formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

The essential nature of the five [factors] beginning with birth and old age and death is not the same as that of ignorance; rather, they all share the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their essence.
The branches of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are also modeled after ignorance, as both take the five aggregates as their essence, since one type is a defilement (*kleśa*).

Therefore, it is said that "defilements and so forth" are all explained by way of stages (*avasthā*) to distinguish the process of birth. This is according to the Hīnayāna, and is not [the Mahāyāna view].
Regarding the meaning of the Mahāyāna: if one speaks of the meaning of the Mahāyāna, each of the twelve links has its own distinct essence, which differs from that of the Hīnayāna.
[Commentary:
Furthermore, the intent behind manifesting the refutation of the extremes of eternalism and nihilism up to the future is to explain the twelve links of dependent origination.

This refers to the refutation of two delusions regarding permanence and annihilation: first, the delusion that there was no cause for the prior existence, which leads to the view that the ten preceding members do not exist as causes;
and second, the delusion that there is no future fruit in the present, which leads to fear of the current body and the view that there will be no future fruits.
This [teaching] refutes such claims by establishing that the two [subsequent members] constitute the future fruits.

[Commentary: "To know that the causes and effects—beginning with craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arising from present feeling (*vedanā*)—are uninterrupted" means that although there are further causes from previous lives which are not mentioned here, by knowing that craving arises conditioned by present feeling, one may infer accordingly that past ignorance (*avidyā*) was likewise produced by old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
It is not only that past ignorance was produced by old age and death; [it is also not only that present feeling is produced by contact, etc.]... [the cycle continues].

The preceding ignorance gives rise to old age and death; likewise, future old age and death can also give rise to ignorance. Because of this [mutual causality], the causes and effects are not described as being without limit.
The intention behind not stating that ignorance has a cause or that old age and death have a result is that the causal chain of the twelve links is uninterrupted;
therefore, one does not further state that ignorance has a cause or that old age and death have a result, but rather treats them simply as causes.
For this reason, it is not said that those two dharmas lack cause and effect;
namely, old age and death have ignorance as their fruit, while ignorance takes old age and death as its cause.

[Commentary: From here below, the intention of establishing [the sequence] based on what is inherent in the text itself is stated. The preceding discussion on the establishment or rejection of causes and effects was an addition external to the treatise;
from here below, the establishment is based on what is inherent in the text itself. Therefore, the treatise states: "Old age is not necessarily present;
it is established as a member [of dependent origination] by being attached to death. Thus it is.

[Commentary] Question: Birth, aging, and death are the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); they do not reach the substance [of the dharma], and their nature is non-existent (*abhāva*). This summarizes the previous objection:

if one allows that these are characteristics, then why is the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) not also posited as a member [of dependent origination]? Furthermore, since the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is non-existent, how can it constitute a member of dependent origination?
[Commentary]: "If they are not characteristics, then what are these [birth and so forth]? This refers to a subsequent objection:
if birth, old age, and death are not the three characteristics, then I do not yet understand what else exists apart from these three characteristics of birth, old age, and death.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the subsequent difficulty is well-explained," this refers to the response in the commentary which states, "This is subsumed within the three characteristics. Because this response addresses the subsequent difficulty, it is called "well-explained.

Regarding "how is the preceding difficulty [resolved]? the intention is that although the subsequent difficulty was previously explained, the preceding difficulty had not yet been resolved; therefore, it is called "the preceding difficulty."

Regarding the question of how one can say that the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) [are not exhaustive] and why they are not all mentioned: this explains the difficulty raised concerning the prior state (*pūrvāvasthā*) as to why it is not designated as a member.
It states that "dependent origination" is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*); therefore, [the prior state] cannot serve as an analogy.

This explains the reason why, among the difficulties previously raised, the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) is not a member of dependent origination, whereas death (*maraṇa*) and acquisition (*prāpti*) can be members of dependent origination; hence, it is said [that the prior state is not a member].

To provide an example, the following further refutes [the objection] regarding why death can be established as a member (*aṅga*) of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the reason why the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) serves as such a member.
[Commentary: If this is so, what is the difference between the various treatises that speak of reaching death and cessation? The intent of the question is:

if the characteristic of death is established as a member of dependent origination based upon the body as a single-period continuity (*eka-kalpa-santati*), then such a characteristic is not established merely based on a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

It is also possible to establish [the characteristics] based on the body as a single continuous period (*eka-kāla-saṃtati*). Why, then, can they not be called "limbs" (*aṅga*)? What is the difference between death (*cyuti*) and cessation (*nirodha*)? [Commentary:
The answer is that while the periods of a single lifetime (*eka-kāla*) and a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) differ, the intention is as follows:

although the divisions of time for a single lifetime and a single moment are distinct, if one relies upon the *kṣaṇa*, the three time periods are also established based on past dharmas; if one relies upon the single lifetime, the three [time periods]... [are likewise established].
The world also establishes the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) upon past phenomena; although the temporal bases differ, the establishment of the characteristics is the same.
Why is this? Because each indicates that this phenomenon no longer exists at a later time. The case of death cannot be used as an analogy for establishing [characteristics] based on different times;
rather, it clarifies that the stage immediately preceding death, the actual moment of dying, and the final moment are all designated as the "limb of death."

"And the stage of dying in accordance [with the process] is also subsumed under the limb of death. The commentary explains: "At the moment of actual death, while warmth has not yet departed from the body, the eighth consciousness is in the process of departing from the body;
this is precisely what is called 'actual death. As for 'one who is about to die,' this refers to the initial onset of illness, gradually leading up to death.
Regarding the 'stage of dying in accordance [with the process],' it refers to when a sick person who wishes to die may pass ten days [or more]."
When five signs appear, death is certain beyond doubt: first, the eye sockets sink; second, the bridge of the nose collapses; third, the color of the lips and mouth changes;
fourth, the skin stretches and does not contract; fifth, the dark complexion shrinks like a drawn-up quiver.
When these five signs of decay appear in the gods, they are all termed the stage of approaching death.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement "relying on the characteristic of cessation (nirodha-lakṣaṇa) up to establishing the three members," the intended meaning is as follows: This is an external question to the text. The question asks:
"Since the essence of the characteristic of cessation is non-existent, why must one rely on the characteristic of cessation to establish the members of birth-and-death? The answer states:

"The reason for relying on the characteristic of cessation to establish the member of death is to induce a sense of weary detachment (nirveda). Therefore, one relies on the three characteristics to establish the three members. Now, as for birth...
Question: Since two characteristics of death can be established as branches, how can one establish branches while asserting that they are based on three characteristics?

Answer: As stated in the lower part of the treatise, old age is not necessarily present; thus, the intention in establishing it as a branch in conjunction with death is to say that old age should be established as a branch in its own right.
If it were merely attached to death to establish a branch, there would be no fault.
*Commentary on the Exposition of the Meaning of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten, Part One;
*Commentary on the Exposition of the Meaning of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten, Part Two.

[Commentary] Question: If birth, aging, and so forth are themselves the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of birth and so forth, then these latter two members [aging and death] should be subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). To what essence (*svabhāva*) would they then belong?
Regarding the point that there is indeed a distinction, the intended question is as follows:

If the three links of birth, aging, and death are identical to the three characteristics (of conditioned phenomena), then the final two links among these twelve should be subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), because the three characteristics—birth and so forth—are subsumed under the aggregate of formations. This is not so;

for the three characteristics are dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) and are therefore subsumed under the aggregate of formations. However, the essential nature of the two links of birth and aging-and-death is...

Because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) manifest, birth, aging, and death are subsumed within all five aggregates; this is the intended meaning of establishing them based on their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

This means that although these three members—birth, aging, and death—are established as entities based on the three characteristics of arising, change, and cessation, their actual substance is distinct from the members themselves.

Their substance consists of the five aggregates, yet among those three characteristics, they are exclusively the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Question: Since the three members are established in opposition to the three characteristics, there should consequently be thirteen [members].

Question: For what reason does [Vasubandhu] speak of twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*)? Answer: It is not so. If one were to address them individually according to the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*), one would say that three links are established because they manifest those characteristics;
thus, old age (*jarā*) may also be called a "link" as it is attached to the link of death (*maraṇāṅga*).
However, when speaking according to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are only twelve links and not thirteen.

[Commentary]: "As with one who dies upon contact, it does not immediately cease; this is subsumed under the three characteristics"—this citation is used as an example to prove that the three members [of the syllogism] are not themselves the three characteristics.

"Dying upon contact" refers to the moment when one is about to die or is in the process of dying; at that time, the wind-blade (*vāyu-śastra*) disintegrates the body, and the limbs and joints suffer excruciating pain.
At such a time, it is called "death-contact. Although it is termed "death," the physical body itself is not the characteristic; this is likewise [the case for the other members].

[The Sūtra says: "Thus it is. [Commentary: The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states, "Because death occurs upon the attainment [of birth]," etc. The meaning of this passage is to explain the reason why these two dharmas (birth and aging-and-death) are established together as a single limb.
Question: For what reason are the two dharmas of aging and death established as one limb? Answer: It is to demonstrate that [aging] exists apart from death.
Because death exists, even those who die prematurely or within the womb possess the factor of death but lack that of aging;
therefore, while the factor of death is certain, aging is not. For this reason, aging is established as a factor in conjunction with death.

[Commentary]: "It is not within the womb-born body that [the six sense bases] exist separately from name-and-form" and so forth—this passage serves as a counter-illustration to clarify the underlying intention for establishing the individual links.
It means: it is not the case that within the womb-born body there are the six sense bases existing apart from name-and-form.
This implies that the six sense bases can exist independently of name-and-form; thus, one takes name-and-form itself as the six sense bases. If they were merely within name-and-form... [text ends].

Regarding the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*): after name-and-form, when the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) become clear and predominant, they are then designated as the link of the six sense bases.

This is because a single dharma is established as distinct links according to its successive stages. Thus, the Treatise says: "When the faculties are not yet matured, the characteristics of name-and-form increase;

subsequently, when the faculties are matured, the six sense bases become clear and predominant. Based on this, contact (*sparśa*) arises; based on contact, feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth arise. This is what is intended by the term "name-and-form."

The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are a single dharma that is established as a separate limb by distinguishing between its prior and subsequent stages; whereas old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are two distinct dharmas that are combined and established as a single limb.

This is because, for example, in the case of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), the sense faculties are all acquired instantaneously; therefore, it is not said that the limb of the six sense bases arises based on name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

[Commentary]: This means that according to the principle of this treatise, those who do not suffer from minor ailments [are exempt]. The intent is that in the two upper realms (*dhātu*), there is no illness whatsoever.

Even among the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is likewise no illness due to their merit; although they possess the five signs of decay (*pañca-vyasanāni*), these are signs of death and not signs of disease.
Furthermore, in the hells, there is also no illness because they are subject to extreme oppression. As for wherever...
That which "should exist" refers to the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of humans, ghosts, and animals within the desire realm; although such illness exists there, it is nonetheless not fixed.
For instance, among the human realm, the Venerable Bakula lived past eighty without ever suffering even a minor ailment.

These cases are all based upon the scriptural teachings (*āgama*). Thus, the nature of this illness is not fixed and does not pervade the three realms; even if it were present, it would still be uncertain.
[Commentary]:

Regarding the phrase "not those who die prematurely at the end of life," the intended meaning is that when an elderly person approaches death, their faculties and consciousness differ from what they were before;
therefore, this is categorized as "decay."

[Commentary: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, from the tenth [chapter] onwards, agree with this in stating that when sentient beings of the two upper realms (*rūpa-dhātu* and *ārūpya-dhātu*) are about to pass away, the objects experienced by their body and mind become weak in their mode of activity (*ākāra*) and cannot compare to what they were before; therefore, they are termed "decayed" and "putrefied.
The phrase "those various formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to the sense faculties and the mind; they are called "formations" because they involve transition, flux, and volitional construction.
Because it is called "formative activity" (*saṃskāra*), this activity gradually weakens and is thus termed "decay. Because it is identical to this, [the commentary] states:
"The ninth [verse] etc., regarding the two modes of birth—moisture-born and egg-born—'until reaching' refers to what is certain.

The meaning is that for the moisture-born and egg-born, except for the period spent in the mother’s womb, at other times they follow the sequence of the womb-born; in all such cases, there is the member of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, among those born from moisture, although there is no mother, at the very moment they first receive birth in that moist environment, their physical form develops through successive stages just as it does for those born from a womb;
therefore, they possess the branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). This excludes those born from an egg or those born from a womb;
for when one is still in the mother’s womb, name-and-form has not yet fully formed, whereas once one has emerged from the mother’s womb, the mother provides warmth to sustain them.

Once the vital energy (*nāma*) has already formed, it is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). In this sequence, it gradually increases until the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the faculties, and so forth arise.
In the case of birth from a womb, name-and-form must specifically increase within the mother’s womb;
as for what distinguishes this from the others, it refers to its distinction from the other three modes of birth.

[Commentary]: "Not universal" means that because the birth by transformation lacks the branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it is said to be not universal; this refers to the fact that at the initial moment, all sense faculties are produced through transformation.
[Commentary]: Question: Why does the body arise instantaneously? This is cited from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* for comparison and interpretation, as is the case with moisture-born beings.
Regarding the sequential link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), why does the *Yogācārabhūmi* state that for those born from moisture or by transformation, the members of the body arise all at once?
That treatise asks: "What is meant by 'emergence' (*abhinirvṛtti*)? It refers to the fact that for those born from moisture or by transformation, the members of the body arise all at once.
This is a repeated question and answer; "emergence" means birth, as it is called "emergence" because the members of the body first arise simultaneously upon taking birth.
The nineteenth passage, beginning with "Manifestly," states that for those born from moisture, name-and-form gradually increases;
yet this tenth passage even speaks of [increase] being instantaneous—how can these not be contradictory? The answer to this may be understood as follows:

the preceding ninth passage refers to the fact that although the limbs and hands of the body exist, the various sense faculties have not yet become clear and full; therefore, it says that for those born from moisture, name-and-form [increases] next.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the body parts arise all at once" in the tenth stage of the *Pravṛddhi* [stage], this refers specifically to the limbs—the hands and feet—arising simultaneously;
it does not mean that all the sense organs (*indriya*) arise all at once. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

[Treatise] Regarding the statement that "at the stage of initial rebirth, although the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and so forth are complete," a question is raised: Why does it not say they are "complete with the six bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*), but instead speaks of the "five faculties"?

Answer: If the five faculties are complete, they are designated as the "six bases. However, if the five faculties are not yet complete, even though the mental faculty (*manas*) is present, it is not called a "limb of the six bases.
This is because at the moment of taking birth, one already possesses both the mental faculty and the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).

Furthermore, if one were without the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), one would be like insentient objects such as wood or stone; since this is not the case, at the moment of initial conception there exist both the body-faculty and the mind-faculty (*manendriya*).

This means that while the four faculties of the eye and so forth are not yet complete, it is termed "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) and is not yet called the "limb of the six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
It is only after seven days have passed and the remaining faculties, such as the eye, are fully developed that it is then termed the "limb of the six sense bases."
[Commentary: "If that is so, up to 'the sense-faculties are fully developed at birth'"—this is the question;

from "in the realm of form, those born by transformation" onwards is the answer. Since the passage beginning with "nine, thirteen," etc., is all from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this second explanation is provided within the treatise itself.
[Commentary]: "Consciousness relies upon the seeds of name-and-form" refers to the eighth consciousness; "the mental faculty (*manas*) is the seventh consciousness.

[Treatise]: Regarding the statement in this treatise that [consciousness] exists up to the two higher realms, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it says that in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all...
The consciousness of sentient beings depends upon the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and the seeds of name-and-form depend upon consciousness for their evolution.
Because the seeds of form exist within that consciousness, even though form is interrupted, it shall arise again later. Commentary:

According to the meaning of this passage, it refers exclusively to the seeds of the *retribution* (*vipāka*) and does not include the seeds of the *meditative attainments* (*samāpatti*). This is consistent with the logic of the text. [Question: Regarding the element of mind (*manodhātu*), what is name-and-form?
The mutual dependence of the answers is as follows: when ignorance gives rise to formations of the higher realms, this is the same as that [previous case].

Regarding the statement "a portion of all exists in the two upper realms," "all" refers to the twelve links. "A portion" means that while the twelve links exist within the desire realm, they are not the twelve links of the two upper realms;
thus it is called "a portion. This is like the twelve links of the form realm.
The branches are not those of the upper two realms because they are twelve branches;

thus it is said they are "one part," just as the twelve branches of the form realm are not the twelve branches of the formless realm, and thus are called "one part. The same applies to the formless realm.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement "from the beginning of dependent origination up to the principle, there is likewise no fault," this accords with a question in that sutra:
"If, during a single lifetime, there were only its name and no form at all, what fault would there be? The Buddha replied:

"If, during a single lifetime, there were only the names of the four aggregates and no form at all, this would not accord with reason. The intended meaning is that name and form exist in mutual dependence.
Regarding the commentary on the passage concerning "abiding," the Master of the Commentary (Sūzhǔ) provides three interpretations of that scriptural text: 1.

One interpretation states that the phrase "abiding in dependence on form" (*rūpāśrita*) spoken therein refers to the two realms of desire and form (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*), where a physical body (*rūpakāya*) actually arises and form is manifest; thus, these words are spoken with reference to that. 2. Another interpretation states, "or the seeds of form, etc.

The intent of this explanation is that within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there exist the seeds of form; this refers specifically to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is formless.

The name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the five mental factors, such as contact (*sparśa*), are called "name" (*nāman*); alternatively, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses may also be included under "name.

Furthermore, because in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) the eighth consciousness and its five associated mental factors abide in mutual dependence upon the seeds of form, it is said that "name and the seeds of form are the support for consciousness.
This refers to the statement that name and the seeds of form serve as the support for consciousness.

Its seeds are the *bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eighth consciousness; they rely upon its own *svabhāva-bhāga* (self-substance aspect) to serve as the support for the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect), which in turn takes them as its object.

Furthermore, the consciousness’s *darśana-bhāga* has a remote dependence on the seeds of form (*rūpa*). However, since the *bhāga* of form also relies upon the five mental factors (*caitasika*) such as contact (*sparśa*), and these mental factors mutually depend upon the mind (*citta*), it is said that in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the seeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) serve as the support for consciousness. This may also be explained as follows:

The factors of the formless realm depend upon that seventh [consciousness], because since the seventh is not produced by karma (*karmaja*), it is not subsumed within the twelve links of dependent origination.
Thus, the names and consciousness of the upper realms depend upon the seeds of matter (*rūpa-bīja*) belonging to the lower realms. Master Shi stated:

"These seeds of matter are not subsumed within the twelve links of the formless realm. A third [source] states: "One takes the seeds of matter which are the fruit of the concentration of the formless realm."

Question: It may be so for the noble ones; how is it for ordinary beings? Answer: Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) also possess the seeds of the form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) belonging to their original existence (*upapatti-bhava*), those realms are complete with all twelve links.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, if the World-Honored One were to teach that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) alone serves as the condition for existence (*bhava*) and does not condition grasping (*upādāna*), what fault would there be?

The explanation states: the intention is to say that if one asserts that craving conditions grasping, or that there is craving which does not condition grasping, or that [existence] does not arise from craving—what fault would there be in this?
[Commentary] When the World-Honored One says, "Up to this point, those born into these two fruits do not take craving as a condition," he answers the previous question.
Based on the question regarding craving and grasping (*tṛṣṇā-upādāna*), the present answer clarifies that while craving arises, it does not necessarily pervade all cases.
There are two types of persons who do not give rise to craving: first, those who have committed evil karma, who at the time of death do not crave their evil [deeds].
Although one seeks birth in a happy realm (*sugati*), because of non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karman*) previously relied upon, one is reborn in an evil realm (*durgati*).
This is called a "contradictory fruit" (*viruddha-phala*); thus, craving does not arise [for that state]. Because this non-meritorious karma is the basis for its future result, it is said:
"due to the non-meritorious karma performed. Second, the passage beginning with "Furthermore, as it has been said" below explains the second point.

The human realm arises from craving; this means that as stated in the sūtras, when those of the two vehicles are in the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*), they are still in the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

They practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to become weary of the body of birth-and-death, not seeking a future existence, but desiring to attain a body that has no further existence.
Thus, the commentary states: "They aspire for a body that has no further existence. Although...
The aspiration for a body that will not undergo further existence arises from previously performed meritorious, immovable karma;
because this subsequent fruit is contrary to one's original intention, it is called a "contrary fruit" (*vipāka-phala*). Consequently, no craving arises for this fruit.

Furthermore, those who possess the first three fruits seek the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), and thus they are all said to seek non-existence (*vibhava*), since those in the state of no-more-learning have no further fruit of rebirth.
Therefore, the arising of these two fruits is also undesirable; the "two fruits" refers to the results cultivated by the two aforementioned types of persons.
Regarding the fruit that contradicts immovable karma (*āneñjya-karma*), it is, for example, like a learned monk (*bahuśruta bhikṣu*) being reborn in the Avīci hell.

[Commentary] Question: If that is so, does this not contradict the statement that they do not return? Since they have previously subdued craving and attained cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), they do not give rise to craving;
therefore, combined with the previous cases, there should be three types of persons: first, those born in the evil destinies; second, those seeking non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*);
and third, those who have attained the fruit of non-returner through cessation—these three types of persons do not give rise to manifest craving.
[Commentary: Because the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmin) possesses the seeds for birth up to the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), this explanation resolves the previous question.

Although there is no manifest craving (*tṛṣṇā*) [in that state], it is spoken of in terms of seeds as being "fixed," just as [the term] "clinging" (*upādāna*) is used. Why is this? When the fruit arises, its function is to moisten [the seeds] through the manifest [craving];

thus, it is spoken of in terms of the manifest as being "fixed. However, for the Non-returner, the moisture comes from the seeds; therefore, the statement regarding its "fixity" is made with respect to the seeds. As for the phrase "regarding one's own body," it refers to... [text fragment].

This refers to one's own body at the place of birth in that realm. Question: At the time of rebirth, does it only employ the moisture of the seeds (*bīja*), or does it also extend to the moisture of the manifest (*dṛṣṭa*)?

Answer: It is like the three heavens of the First Dhyāna: if one is born in that very stage, it employs the moisture of the manifest; if one is born in the Second Dhyāna from a full mind of that stage, it then employs the moisture of the seeds. Question:
Since the entities of "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*) and "grasping" (*upādāna*) are identical in their essential nature, why is "grasping" specifically cited [to represent them]?

The analogy is established according to the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, which states that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is indeterminate as to its presence or absence, whereas grasping (*upādāna*) is necessarily present once [craving] has been established.
By this principle, since the seeds of grasping must certainly exist for a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) to moisten rebirth, it is cited as an analogy.

[Commentary]: Although he does not love the place where he is to be born, up to the point that "he also gives rise to craving"—the meaning is that although this person does not love the body in the place of his future birth, he nevertheless gives rise to craving for the self, and because he also generates craving for present objects, when he wishes to depart [from this life], he gives rise to feelings of attachment toward his own body.
Furthermore, regarding "my objects," these are taken as objects by means of the self.
[Commentary]:

Although the seeds and the manifest states differ, their essence is not distinct; this means that although the seeds of the five members and the manifest states such as birth are distinct, the seeds and the manifest states are simultaneous.
Since these five members—consciousness and the others—are results, they are *vipāka* (maturation).
"Relative identity. [Commentary]:
"Prior to the four seven-day periods" refers to the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) existing within these first four seven-day intervals.
From the initial stage of *kalala* at birth up to the stage of *ghana*, there are four stages in total, with each stage lasting one seven-day period.
The entire period of four seven-day intervals is termed the stage of *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the five members herein extend their influence downward," the explanation is as follows: for now, we cite "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) as referring to the consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking, because the characteristics of consciousness are manifest at that time.
Here, the term "cause" (*hetu*) extends through the subsequent four stages; thus, one should say: "namely, at the time of rebirth-linking..."

At that time, because the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is manifested, it serves as the cause for the arising of contact (*sparśa*); because the characteristic of contact is manifested, it serves as the cause for the arising of sensation (*vedanā*);

because the characteristic of sensation is manifested, [the subsequent stages arise]. The rest is as explained in the commentary. The meaning is that when the five fruits manifest as active states (*pravṛtti*), they cause the seeds (*bīja*) of those five fruits to have their causal characteristics manifested.
The stage of *praśākhā* is here translated as the "stage of possessing the sense organs."
[Commentary]: Regarding the World-Honored One’s statement from "birth and old age and death" up to the term "old age and death," the intended question is:

"World-Honored One, if within the stage of birth and old age and death one employs the factors of name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling as its characteristics, then why is it that when explaining this stage of birth and old age and death in full, five members are specified, yet in this present body only the two members of birth and old age and death are mentioned?"
Question: Does this name not include the five members beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*)? Answer: As explained in the commentary itself. Question:

Why is the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*) not mentioned in the cited text? Answer: Because the seeds of the member of consciousness encompass both the "projecting" (*ākṣepaka*) and the "projected" (*ākṣipta*).

Here, we speak only of the projected actualities—name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—as they enter the mother’s womb; therefore, only these four stages are specifically mentioned, and not the member of consciousness.
In truth, there is no branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*) followed by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth. Question:

How is it known that the seeds of the branch of consciousness pervade both the projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and the projected (*ākṣipta*) factors? Answer: As explained in the commentary on the projecting branches, consciousness is also a projecting factor;
however, because it is already present [in the previous life], the branch of consciousness is not mentioned here.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "The arising reveals the suffering of conditioned existence" up to "the three characteristics," a question is raised:
In the *Abhidharma*, it is stated that birth, aging, sickness, and death are all termed the "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Since even within the womb there is the suffering of being constrained by the fetus and so forth, why does this treatise only manifest the [other] three types of suffering (*trividha-duḥkha*) at the stages of birth, aging, and death? Are these two treatises not in contradiction? Answer: The *Abhidharma* is based upon its...

In terms of actual principle, all four types [of suffering] are called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); this treatise, however, manifests only three types of suffering based on their predominant characteristics.

Phenomena that are subject to flux (*vipariṇāma-dharma*) are termed the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) upon reaching the present life; because the loss of what one desires is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and because the destruction of the body through death is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Thus, the desire realm possesses all three types of suffering, while the form realm possesses only two: the suffering of change and the suffering of conditioned existence. It lacks the suffering of suffering.

Regarding the statement that "form-existence (rūpa-bhava) consists of the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkha)," and that this reveals the three characteristics of the two upper realms: this means that while the characteristic of suffering is predominant [in the desire realm], it is subtle [in the upper realms];
thus, speaking in terms of their respective characteristics does not contradict one another.

[Commentary] Question: If that is so, when it is said that at the stage of fruition (phala-avasthā) one reaches the five aggregates beginning with consciousness (vijñāna), what is the intention behind saying this is to reveal the three types of suffering?

Question: Since the two factors of *manas* (mind) and *vedanā* (feeling) already arise at the time of the fruit, why are the five factors beginning with *vijñāna* (consciousness) further explained? Answer: As stated in the treatise.
[Commentary]:

"Because the present reveals the subsequent, the explanation of the five is not obstructed"—this clarifies the principle of "shadow-revealing" (*yingxian*). If one follows the five factors of the present...
The stages can also be described as having five resultant phases—consciousness and so forth—within the two future stages of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

These are namely the five positions where the characteristics of the causal consciousness become manifest at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), which uses the present to indicate what follows;
that is, it uses the present to indicate the future. This is based on the subsequent [stages] of the two future states, birth and aging-and-death.
Regarding the stages: within the five resultant stages—such as the present consciousness and so forth—one may also speak of the two members of birth and old age and death.
This is because the future reveals the present; thus, the commentary states: "There is no contradiction in saying that the two [members] reveal the present by means of the future."

[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "because of this, the previous statement up to 'otherwise it would be contradictory'" is as follows: Based on the principle of mutual clarification previously established, it was accepted that [the members] were distinct yet pervasive.

Now, when it is said that there are distinctions between the preceding and succeeding [members], it is because the previous statement said that "either they are explained according to their future occurrence as the two—birth and aging-and-death—or they are explained according to their present active state as the five, beginning with consciousness. It is not otherwise.

The meaning of the objection is as follows: If one does not say so, or if one asserts that there is a distinction between prior and subsequent based on their states of arising in the future, then there is the fault of contradiction.
Since it was previously admitted that they mutually manifest [each other], how could there still be a distinction between prior and subsequent?
Therefore, it says: "If not, there is a contradiction."

[Treatise] For what reason, from the origination of karma up to its establishment as distinct [factors], are craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) separately established? According to the answer provided below, there should be four questions;

however, because the text is concise while the meaning is extensive, they are now expanded here: 1. Question: All afflictions (*kleśa*) throughout the entire realm (*dhātu*) are capable of initiating karma;

why is only one type, ignorance (*avidyā*), mentioned here? 2. Question: Since the "moistening" (*anuśayana*) of karma applies to all afflictions, why is only one type, craving, mentioned? 3. Question: Regarding this moistening...
Delusion is not merely a single part; since the two factors of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) give rise to delusion, many factors should likewise not be restricted to one.

Regarding the four questions—how grasping encompasses all delusions, why only craving and aversion are called "grasping," and so forth—the answers should be understood according to the sequence of the subsequent explanatory text.
This can be readily discerned.

[Commentary]: Why are the members [of dependent origination] not treated the same within the branches of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) as they are within the branch of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
The meaning is: why is it that within the branch of ignorance, unlike the two types—craving and grasping—only a single "ignorance" is established?
[Commentary: As stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, there are eleven kinds of excellence. First, the excellence of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya-viśeṣa*):

this refers to the fact that this ignorance universally conditions the four truths and is characterized by impurity. Second, the excellence of the aspect (*ākāra-viśeṣa*): this refers to the fact that this ignorance can conceal the true and manifest the false phenomena of saṃsāra.
Third, the excellence of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya-viśeṣa*): this refers to the fact that this very ignorance serves as the root for all afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore...

Because it serves as the fundamental basis for karma and saṃsāra, its superiority in terms of origination (*samutthāna*) means that this ignorance directly initiates the *saṃskāra* (formative) link, and also indirectly initiates the links that are "projected" (*ākṣepa*) and "arisen" (*abhinirvṛtti*).

Regarding the term "etc. (*ādi*), it refers to the superiority of the fivefold transformation of cause and effect (*hetu-phala-pañca-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*), meaning that this ignorance itself is capable of transforming.

Conversely, four types of ignorance are established: namely, those associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), those bound by the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), and the non-common [ignorance].
Regarding the superiority of its wrong practice: this ignorance gives rise to the two modes of superimposition and denial toward the Four Noble Truths;

thus, grasping at existence is superimposition, while denying it is denial, both of which arise from ignorance. Regarding the superiority of its characteristics: the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of this ignorance is subtle.
Because it functions in common with its subtle characteristics, the commentary explains that the self-characteristic essence of ignorance is difficult to know.
Since beginningless time, it has operated spontaneously; yet, while the ocean of the *dharmatā* is by nature pure, it is stirred by the wind of ignorance to form delusion.
Because such a mode of operation is unknown to anyone other than a Buddha, the Sūtra says that even Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage cannot [fully comprehend it].
Because it can be understood and realized only by the Tathāgata, it is called "subtle.
Because it is associated with craving and attachment, and arises simultaneously with anger, pride, and so forth, it is said to pervade both the agreeable and the disagreeable.

Because this *avidyā-āvasthā* (ground of ignorance) serves as the basis for all afflictions, it is said to have a common characteristic; because it shares the same objects of perception, it has a common mode of activity; and because it is defiled, it is so named.

It is called "superiority in eight shared activities" because this ignorance serves as the basis for the phenomena of the flow of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-pravṛtti-dharma*), and it acts as an obstacle to *tathatā* and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Therefore, *tathatā* is named "quiescence" (*śānti*) and meditative concentration is named "cessation" (*śamatha*).
The ninth is "superiority in nine obstacles," meaning that this ignorance can obstruct bodhi and obstruct the extensive Dharma, which is the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-bodhi*).
This refers to the name of the supreme dharma-tathatā as the "vast dharma-tathatā," because it pervades all attainments;
it is called "supreme" because the bodhisattva’s victory surpasses that of the two vehicles. Regarding the eleventh, the supremacy of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-viśeṣa*):

it is so called because it is the antidote to the two kinds of subtle wisdom. These two kinds of subtle wisdom are namely, the subtle wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) and the [subtle wisdom of] equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
Regarding the statement that there are "two types of wondrous wisdom," this refers to the wisdom of the fundamental nature (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

If one claims that the latter does not equal the former, how could the subsequently attained wisdom following the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) possibly sever ignorance and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*)?

For it is known that when the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) abandon the grasping at a self, they must also sever the cognitive obstructions; thus, we know the former [the fundamental wisdom] is superior. Alternatively, some explain that these two types of wondrous wisdom are...

Question: Since these two—the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—are also able to sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and ignorance when the followers of the Two Vehicles enter the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), [how do they differ from the four wisdoms]?

Furthermore, among the four wisdoms such as the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*, how many are for the purpose of severing [obstructions], and how many are for the purpose of unobstructed contemplation (*anāsrava-vicāra*)?

Answer: The *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing activities) and the *mahādarśana-jñāna* (great mirror-like wisdom) are exclusively for the purpose of unobstructed contemplation within the path of non-outflow (*anāsrava-mārga*). This...

Since these two wisdoms exist only in the state of Buddhahood, if the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is the path that severs the ignorance of delusions, then as for the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*), speaking according to reality, it cannot sever delusions.
If one were to say it can sever them, then the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), who lack the Wisdom of Equality, would not sever their delusions;
yet they clearly do sever them. Thus, we know that the severing of delusions does not arise from the Wisdom of Equality. Now, I shall explain the nature of this equality.
Regarding the statement that the wisdom of nature (*prakṛti-jñāna*) can sever delusions by way of mutual association:

this refers to the seventh consciousness acting as the support for the sixth, such that even though it is a remote aid to the sublime contemplation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā*), it also possesses the capacity to sever delusions. Furthermore, since the two wisdoms—the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) and the sublime contemplation—arise together, and because the sublime contemplation severs delusions, the wisdom of equality, through its association with it, is likewise able to sever delusions.
[Commentary]: Regarding the explanation of the four types of craving as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 55) states:

"What is craving? It refers to the intimacy with, concealment of, and protection of one's own personal existence (*ātma-bhāva*). This is a general definition of the essential nature of craving. "What is craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*)?

It refers to the seeking of the specific distinctions of one's own personal existence in the future. This refers to the craving of a practitioner on the path who seeks birth in a pleasant realm for their body.
What is the craving that accompanies the cultivation of bodhi and so forth, as well as poverty?

It refers to the attachment arising from the loss of the enjoyment of desirable five-fold sensual objects that were previously obtained, while being currently afflicted by delusion. What is the craving for various hopes and desires?

It refers to the craving that arises as a longing for objective referents such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth. These four types of craving are explained as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) based on their predominance.

[Treatise] Regarding the necessity of repeated irrigation for sprouts to arise: just as worldly barley seeds must be washed and watered repeatedly before barley sprouts can emerge, so too do the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma require the repeated moistening of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) to produce the sprouts of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). As for other [conditions], they are not like this;
because their influence is slight compared to that of water, craving alone is specifically mentioned.
[Commentary: "If one speaks of the sprout of birth arising from existence," this means that the sprout of the *bhava-aṅga* (existence) arises from the *bhava-aṅga*.

[Commentary: "In reality, there are many active manifestations of craving (*tṛṣṇā*)," meaning that there are the four types of craving mentioned previously, as well as the craving co-arising with the nine types of death-moment consciousness, and further, both discriminative and innate cravings; therefore, it is said that "craving is manifold."
[Commentary: "If that which grasps, that which is grasped, or that for the sake of which there is grasping are all termed 'grasping' (upādāna). To explain this:

"that which grasps" refers to the grasping that takes as its object the four types of grasping, namely the craving (*rāga*) and other afflictions that act as the subjective grasper; "that which is grasped" refers to the four types of grasping themselves as the objects of cognition;
and "that for the sake of which there is grasping" refers to the remaining afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and pride (*māna*). Thus...
The arising of afflictions such as greed for the sake of such-and-such matters is called "grasping for the sake of [something]" (*upādāna*).
For example, because one gives rise to greed, delusion, and so forth for the sake of fame and profit, all afflictions constitute grasping.

[Commentary] Question: Regarding the various factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) up to "also having those of other stages," the intent is as follows: the meaning of the question raised here is precisely to introduce the meaning of the subsequent treatise.

It asks: when a body is born in this stage of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), does it take only the factors of dependent origination belonging to its own stage as conditions, or does it also take the factors of dependent origination belonging to other stages as conditions?

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "If that were so, what fault would there be," the intended meaning is: even if one takes the factors of dependent origination belonging to oneself or another as conditions, or takes the factors of dependent origination belonging to other stages as conditions, what fault would there be? This will be addressed through a double refutation below.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "If [the members] were only of this stage" up to "ignorance and formations of another stage," the explanation says: Here the objection is raised:

if all the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) produced in this stage were exclusively of that same stage, how would one reconcile this with the preceding text of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*?
Therefore, that sūtra poses the following objection: "Bhagavān, regarding the three members of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)..."
All these are afflictions; it is taught that the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) conditions the formations (*saṃskāra*) of a different level.

Why, then, is it not said that the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) condition the formations of a higher level? Because they are devoid of mental engagement (*manasikāra*). Thus, craving and grasping are indeed the productive conditions for dependent origination. The Blessed One declared:
"Regarding the two links of craving and grasping in relation to the link of formations, they are not permitted to be of a different level; they must necessarily be of the same level."

Because [the realms] are distinct levels, it is said that they have "limitations. If it were claimed that craving and grasping in the desire realm serve as conditions for the imperturbable karma of the two higher realms, this would be unreasonable, because [those higher realms] are not their objective domain (*gocara*).

If, however, one allows that ignorance (*avidyā*) can take karma of a different level as its condition, then if one maintains that [craving and grasping] alone do so, it contradicts this very text, which further states: "Ignorance [is the condition] for karma that is free from desire in the desire realm..."

Regarding the condition of "simultaneous origination" (*samutthāna-pratyaya*): for one who is detached from the desire realm, it is the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna) that can effect detachment from the defilements of the desire realm.
This means that the ignorance of the desire realm acts as a simultaneous origination condition for the volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of the *anāgamya-samādhi*;

because they arise together, they are said to be "equally originating. Alternatively, regarding those of the form realm, this refers to the nine [levels] of the *anāgamya-samādhi* of the second dhyāna.

Because the factors of the path (*pratipad-aṅga*) in the Unattained Concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) can act as successive conditions for origination (*samutthāna-pratyaya*),
just as the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the First Dhyāna can give rise to the factors of the path in the Unattained Concentration of the Second Dhyāna acting as a condition for origination,

and so on until the ignorance of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) can give rise to the factors of the path in the Unattained Concentration of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) acting as a condition for origination; this is what is meant by "or the Form Realm."
Regarding the phrase "the same category," it means that because the subsequent *anāgamya* (preliminary concentration) is of the same lineage as the preceding *anāgamya*, it is so designated.

Furthermore, concerning the statement "in this way, ignorance [leads] to formations of a different realm (*dhātu*) and so forth," the explanation states: the intent of this passage is to admit that ignorance belonging to one stage (*bhūmi*) can give rise to the limb of formations belonging to a different stage.
For example, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), by taking the arising of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) as the cause...
That which arises is ignorance (*avidyā*), and ignorance itself is the fruit; thus, these two—cause and fruit—are called "companions.
Furthermore, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that are simultaneously associated (*samprayukta*) are also called "companions.

For this reason, while ignorance in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) can give rise to the "limb of practice" (*pratipad-aṅga*) within the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna, this ignorance necessarily cannot give rise to [the limb of practice] within the fundamental concentration (*maula-samādhi*) of the first dhyāna.
The *saṃskāra-aṅga* (volitional formations) of the second dhyāna cannot also give rise to the *anāgamya* or the fundamental dhyāna; the same applies to all higher stages.
The intended meaning is that one can give rise to [a state] by means of its immediate neighbor, but not by skipping over it.

This continues until, because the *avidyā-aṅga* (ignorance) of the *ākiṃcanyāyatana* (sphere of nothingness) can give rise to the *saṃskāra-aṅga* of the *anāgamya* of the *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana* (sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception), the outflowing (*sāsrava*) [factors] of the eight stages [are established].

Question: Within the meditative attainments (*dhyāna*), why do all members of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) arise from the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the lower stages, and why do they arise immediately following [that ignorance] rather than with an interval?

Answer: It is because they arise in immediate succession and not by skipping over stages. Question: For what reason can the ignorance that functions as a motivator (*pravartaka-avidyā*) belonging to its own stage not arise within the *anāgamya* (preparatory) concentration of the eight stages?
Answer: It is like a crown prince who, before attaining the position of sovereign, cannot commit evil deeds. Question: Since it is already granted that the *anāgamya* concentration exists...

Question: Why does the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) not, like the ignorance (*avidyā*) of its own level, give rise to the factor of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) of the "not-yet-attained" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) of its own level? Answer: It is not so.

Only when the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have been completely severed can the "not-yet-attained" concentration arise. Ignorance is able to give rise to the factor of "volitional formations" of its own level;

however, as for the factor of "volitional formations" of the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*) of the eight higher levels, it is given rise to solely by the ignorance of those respective levels.
If one attains a fundamental dhyāna, one can give rise to the afflictions of that very stage, just as a crown prince who has already attained the royal throne may commit evil deeds.
However, it is absolutely impossible for ignorance (avidyā) of a higher stage to give rise to formations (saṃskāra) of a lower stage.

If one regresses and gives rise to [afflictions] of a lower stage, there is ignorance of that same stage giving rise to formations of that same stage; therefore, we know that ignorance of a different stage gives rise to formations of a different stage.
[Branch].

[Commentary]: "If one attains a branch belonging to a different realm, it is subsumed within this very [category]" means that this refutes the notion that ignorance (*avidyā*) of one stage (*bhūmi*) can give rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) of a different stage.
Furthermore, if one were to allow that ignorance of a different stage gives rise to volitional formations, then the text of the *Pañcāśatikā* (Fifty Verses) would again... [contradict this].

How does this accord with that treatise which states: "In whichever bhūmi or dhātu one is born, it should be known that the twelve links of existence (bhavāṅgas) are subsumed under that very bhūmi and dhātu in which one is born"? [Treatise]:

For example, regarding the arising of ignorance (avidyā) belonging to a higher bhūmi, one asks: is it produced by taking the ignorance of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) as its cause, or is it used [as such]?

When ignorance arises in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it again suppresses the eight preceding grades of delusion; the remaining one grade can give rise to higher [afflictions], and is not inferior to what is explained below.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "all links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) rely upon their own stage" up to "reaching the same grasping-dependent-origination," the meaning is that if the links of dependent origination...
"All depend on their own respective levels" means that whichever realm or level the factors of the dependent origination branches belong to, they are all subsumed under that same level;
this is stated in terms of the majority. That is to say, among the twelve branches, eleven branches are entirely subsumed under their own level, while only a small portion of one branch is not.
Furthermore, a small portion of ignorance (*avidyā*) is capable of giving rise to the formations (*saṃskāra*) branch of a higher level.

Therefore, when the formations that are set in motion depend upon ignorance, this is identical to the scriptural passage on dependent origination through grasping (*upādāna*), because it is only the ignorance of a lower stage that sets in motion the formations of a higher stage;
thus, the Sūtra and the Śāstra each rely on one specific meaning and do not contradict one another.
[Commentary: Regarding the question, "How is this so? which seeks to clarify the matter down to the point of those who have set out for a higher stage—the intent of this inquiry is as follows:

since it is admitted that factors of dependent origination belonging to one stage can serve as conditions for factors of dependent origination belonging to another stage, it must then be the case that all twelve factors of dependent origination of one stage are capable of serving as conditions for the twelve factors of dependent origination of another stage; or is it only twelve [factors] that do so?

Since it is asked whether, among the members [of dependent origination], only a single member serves as a condition for a member belonging to a different stage (*bhūmi*), the text says: "Is it one or many?
As answered below: "Among these twelve members, only a single member serves as a condition for a different member. The treatise states: "As follows:
ignorance (*avidyā*) gives rise to formations (*saṃskāra*) of a higher stage."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "having abandoned the nine grades of desire," as stated in the commentary:

"If one allows that the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration possesses defilement, it is nonetheless necessary to abandon the desire of the [lower] realms and exhaust the nine grades [of afflictions] before the defilement within the *anāgamya* concentration can arise and initiate karma. Question:

When one attains a fundamental concentration (*mauladhyāna*), the afflictions of that specific level have not yet arisen; what then is it that initiates [the karma]? Answer: It is likewise [ignorance].

This is because one employs the ignorance of the desire realm to initiate the attainment of that concentration, and since one has not yet given rise to the ignorance of the higher stages, [it is said so].

However, once the fundamental concentration has been attained, when it first arises, it is the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration; there is no logical error in the position that it is initiated by the ignorance of the higher stages.

[Commentary]: This clarifies that while the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that these [twelve links] comprise eleven branches according to the majority view, here it is explained that a portion of ignorance (*avidyā*) that does not project karma is subsumed under its own level alone;
thus, only a small portion of the single branch of ignorance serves as a condition for formations (*saṃskāra*) belonging to other levels.
[Commentary]: "The intention of the Sūtra applies universally, and thus there is no contradiction" refers to this particular assembly of the Sūtra.

As stated in the *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra*, when ignorance (*avidyā*) of one stage serves as the condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of another stage, it is said to apply universally because it concerns both one's own realm (*svadhātu*) and other realms.

Thus, regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and so forth, they pertain to one's own realm, whereas ignorance pertains to other realms; therefore, it is said that [the principle] applies universally. It is stated that there is dependence upon other stages.

This means that among the twelve links, the remaining links depend on their own level (*svabhūmi*), whereas the link of ignorance (*avidyā*) depends on other levels, acting as a condition for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of different levels. [Commentary:
This passage can demonstrate that [the outflows] will ultimately not arise; this meaning specifically clarifies that the contaminated states (*sāsrava*) of the aforementioned eight levels [are so].

In the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the preparatory concentration), there are no afflictions at all; because one has not yet attained the fundamental concentrations (*mauladhyāna*), one cannot give rise to the afflictions of the eight higher stages.

[Commentary: The meaning of the statement that "all lower stages are likewise for those who have set out from the *anāgamya*" is as follows: it is like being physically situated in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
When first arising, the practice-factors of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna are produced by the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the desire realm;

likewise, when first arising, the practice-factors of the threshold concentration within the second dhyāna are produced by the ignorance of the first dhyāna, and so on, until the practice-factors of the threshold concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which are produced by the ignorance of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Therefore, [the practice-factors of each stage are produced by the ignorance of the immediately lower stage].
It is said that this [craving] arises only in such a manner when one has not yet reached a lower stage.

[Commentary: Does it arise using the *vedanā* (feeling) branch of the stage one is destined to be born in as its condition, or does it arise using the *vedanā* branch of the stage currently inhabited as its condition? The intent of the question is:

does this craving that moistens [the seeds of existence] function by taking the *vedanā* branch of the future birth-stage as its condition to produce craving, or does it function by taking the *vedanā* branch of the present dwelling-stage as its condition to produce craving?

Regarding the phrase "by means of what condition": the meaning of "borrowing" (or "relying") refers to how the factor of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises by depending upon sensation (*vedanā*). What is the intention behind this question?
The intention of one who asks this, while granting that [factors] of different levels (*bhūmi*) can serve as conditions for one another, is as follows:

since it is granted that ignorance (*avidyā*) can serve as a condition for the factor of formations (*saṃskāra*) belonging to a different level, it should likewise follow that sensation belonging to a different level can serve as a condition for craving belonging to a different level; therefore, this question is posed.
[Commentary]:

Regarding the phrase "according to what is appropriate" up to "the seeds at the prior time," the commentator explains that it refers to the defiled feeling (*kliṣṭa-vedanā*) which is simultaneously associated with the active craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This defiled feeling is also capable of producing craving; this feeling associated with craving is precisely the object (*viṣaya*).
The "reception of the realm" (*dhātu-vedanā*) and the "reception of the object" (*viṣaya-vedanā*) are precisely this defiled reception produced with ignorance-contact as its condition.
Only this defiled reception is able to serve as a condition for the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Alternatively, regarding the "seed of craving" mentioned previously:

within the five fruits such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), it refers to the seed of the branch of reception (*vedanā-aṅga*), which is the maturation-reception (*vipāka-vedanā*). This seed of the branch of reception is also capable of serving as the seed for the reception of the object.

"Taking [feeling] as a condition, craving arises. The meaning of this passage clarifies that when one dies in a particular stage and is reborn in that same stage, craving necessarily relies upon feeling belonging to that same stage.

[Commentary]: "When arising from one stage into another stage, it also necessarily relies upon feeling belonging to that same stage. The intent of this interpretation is that if one is in one's own stage...

In the process of death and rebirth within one's own stage (*bhūmi*), craving arises conditioned by feeling belonging to that same stage; thus, the limb of craving necessarily depends upon feeling of the same stage.
If one dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is reborn in the first dhyāna, craving arises conditioned by the feeling belonging to the stage of that first dhyāna where one is to be born;
thus, this craving also necessarily depends upon feeling of the same stage. This feeling of the same stage is what is subsumed under the [craving] limb.
The above constitutes the first interpretation. [Commentary:

Furthermore, there is the sense that even while currently residing in a particular realm, one experiences [feelings] that serve as remote conditions for [craving] in other realms; this is the second interpretation.

It is said that, for example, when dying from the desire realm and being reborn in the First Dhyāna, the feelings experienced within the desire realm also act as conditions for craving in the First Dhyāna. This is because...
For example, when ignorance gives rise to formations of a different stage, this feeling conditioned by those formations is itself conditioned by craving of a different stage;

yet this feeling does not constitute a [complete] link of dependent origination. This interpretation is inferior to the first one, because subsequent craving of a different stage cannot moisten the existence-link (*bhava-aṅga*) of that different stage.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the initiation of karma is the equal-arising cause," this means that ignorance possesses a superior power capable of equally initiating the three types of formations—meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable—or that these three formations are equally initiated from ignorance;
thus, the cause of equal arising is termed the "equal-arising cause."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "feeling conditions craving" and that they "extend across different levels" (*bhūmi*), this refers to my previous second interpretation:
because feeling at one level serves as a condition for craving at a different level, this question is raised. Question:

Why is it that while consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the others are presented with various combinations and omissions, *saṃskāra* (formative forces) and *bhava* (existence) are both combined into one? Answer: The intention of this question is to ask: why is this so?

Therefore, among the branches produced from the seeds of the five fruits—wherein the "projected" (ākṣepaka) factors such as consciousness are expanded—the "birth" and "aging-and-death" branches are combined into one;

thus, there is a difference between expansion and contraction within the projected branches. If that is so, why are the "projecting" branch of *saṃskāra* and the "producing" branch of *bhava* not both combined into one?

[Commentary: "It is not merely because within the *saṃskāra* (formations) there is nothing that is not of the nature of karma (*karma-svabhāva*) that they are not separately distinguished. This statement regarding their non-separation explains the reason why they constitute a single branch (*aṅga*).
The intended meaning is as follows: for instance, within the branch of *saṃskāra*, there is nothing that is not of the nature of karma;
since it is taught that they are entirely of the nature of karma, they are collectively termed *saṃskāra* and are not further divided.
[Commentary] Question: Why are the three types of karma collectively termed "karma-existence" (*saṃskāra-bhava*)? This question intends to ask:

why are the three types of karma—namely, merit (*puṇya*), non-merit (*apuṇya*), and immovability (*āniñjya*)—along with their moistening factors, collectively designated as the limb of existence (*bhavāṅga*)?
Furthermore, why are craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) distinguished separately within the stage of moistening?

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the Sarvāstivāda and other schools [assert] two causes and five fruits, the intended meaning is as follows: The Sarvāstivāda school maintains that within a single moment all twelve links are present.
For example, at the time of committing an act of killing, there is simultaneously existing ignorance, which is termed the "link of ignorance";

the simultaneous volition (*cetanā*) is the "link of formations" (*saṃskāra*); and the simultaneous consciousness (*vijñāna*) is termed the "link of consciousness. If one simultaneously forms a conceptual intention...

The four sense objects and the faculties are called the branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Simultaneously, the five faculties and the immediately preceding mental attention (*manasikāra*) are called the branch of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

Simultaneously, there is the branch of contact (*sparśa*). Simultaneously, there is feeling (*vedanā*), which is called the branch of feeling. Simultaneously, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is called the branch of craving.
Simultaneously, the remaining afflictions are called the branch of grasping (*upādāna*). Simultaneously, bodily and vocal actions are called the branch of becoming (*bhava*), from which birth arises.

The characteristic of arising (*utpāda*) is the limb of birth (*jāti*); the characteristic of change (*anyathātva*) is the limb of aging (*jarā*); and the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha*) is called the limb of death (*maraṇa*).
[Commentary: "In this school" refers to the meaning expressed in the following passage from the Abhidharma-śāstra.
It explains that according to the tenets of this Mahāyāna school, the ten causal limbs of the past are identical to the two resultant limbs of the present, and so forth.

[Commentary]: "Nor is it a fruit obtained from karma to be experienced in the present life" means that while the fruit obtained from karma to be experienced in the present life is called a "present-life fruit" because it is a fruit of prior retribution (*pūrvavedanīya*), these twelve [bases] are collectively *vipāka-phala* (fruits of maturation);
therefore, they do not share the name "fruit of present-life karma. Hence, it says: "nor is it a fruit of present-life karma."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the worlds differ based on the death and birth of the body, the meaning is as follows:

because one creates the causes consisting of ten members (*daśāṅga*) in this life, and it is only in a future life that the two members of the fruit (*phala*) are spoken of, the worlds are therefore different.

[Commentary]: If one considers the temporal divisions, even up to the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), these coexist with birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) in the future;
therefore, when explaining the meaning of the three periods of time based on the divisions of "great" and "small" durations, it is not fixed. Question:

If it is as stated in the commentary—that after having committed the seven branches [of karma] in the past, before the subsequent body has matured, the present body does not yet give rise to craving and so forth—then for that subsequent body, it would be the present...
