thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 53, states: Question: Does a noble one (ārya) perform karma that projects a homogeneous body (*nikāya-sabhāga*) in the desire realm? Some say...

Because they do not create many faults or calamities pertaining to the desire realm, they create only meritorious karma. Some say they also create [non-meritorious karma], but the former explanation is correct;
thus, the *Nyāyānusāra* (Treatise in Accordance with Correct Reasoning), fascicle 64, states:

"The noble ones (*ārya*) cannot further produce new projecting karma for future existence, because they have turned their backs on saṃsāra and are oriented toward nirvāṇa. Therefore, the Sūtra says that the noble ones only experience the results of past karma."

[Treatise] Regarding the statement that "by means of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna (*dhyāna-vyavakiraṇa*), one supports inferior karma to be born in the Śuddhāvāsa [heavens]," the commentary explains:

Furthermore, there are four kinds of support for the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). First, support by means of the contaminated (*sāsrava*): as when an Arhat, at the time of death, intends to be born [in a higher realm], he observes the future life;
having now known that he will attain [rebirth] within two or three years, he further observes the present moment among the assembly.
If a person has no sense of benefit regarding the Buddha-dharma, they may think: "Birth for me is exhausted; the holy life is established;
what was to be done has been accomplished; there will be no further existence. Thus, they refuse to prolong their life and desire to pass away.
At the time of death, their mind is free from craving and they do not cherish their body. At the very moment of dying, they experience a great joy of relinquishment.
The time for the body is like being cured of a grave illness and entering *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
If an Arhat contemplates that his own body will bring great benefit to the Buddha-dharma or to sentient beings in the present life, he may then retain this body out of fear that it would perish;
consequently, he shall relinquish all the robes, alms bowls, and material wealth belonging to his remaining body to those currently present.
Having previously dedicated this merit and the provisions for practice as a cause for the present body,

so that its fruit may continue without interruption for a long time, he then, having truly completed the act of giving, sat cross-legged within a quiet room and made this aspiration with the mind and speech of his body,
speech, and mind belonging to the desire realm: "I dedicate this meritorious conduct to prolong my remaining karma."

Having already made the vow for a long duration, he immediately entered the fourth dhyāna, the limit of the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) meditative attainment, so that the power of that concentration might support the meritorious karma of his giving to extend his life-span. Upon emerging from that concentration, he then made this vow:

"May the power of this concentration and the power of my vow, supported by the meritorious karma of my giving, act as the cause for my present body, so that I may now experience its results continuously for a long time."

Having made this vow, he subsequently enters the fourth dhyāna, the "limit of the outflow-tainted" (sāsrava-prāntakoṭika), to support his meritorious karma and the power of his vow so as to accomplish the practice of prolonging life.
Upon emerging from this meditative concentration, his life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is extended;

he may attain a lifespan of a hundred years, a thousand years, one kalpa, two kalpas, or even many kalpas. This is solely a case of an outflow-tainted concentration supporting a body belonging to the desire realm. Second, the basis.

The "untainted provisions" (*anāsrava-saṃbhāra*) refer to those of indeterminate lineage—śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of great power—who exclusively enter untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*) to transform their *pariccheda* (segmented) bodies into *pariṇāmika* (transformative) bodies; or who, by means of untainted meditative absorption, provision this body, or provision it so that what was previously coarse and inferior becomes sublime;
or provision a body originally six feet tall so that it attains a height of one hundred, a thousand, or more feet, or extends it further.
Regarding their lifespan, it may last for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to hundreds of thousands of kalpas.

As asked in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, concerning women such as Yaśodharā and Gautamī who received the prediction of attaining Buddhahood like great Arhats—when, precisely, do they cast off this female body?
Answer: When they are about to receive the transformation [of gender], they cast it off; when they are about to receive the transformation, they cast it off.
When one abandons the *pariccheda-bheda* (segmented existence), how could one not abandon the female body? This very transformation of abandonment is what is meant by "abandonment.

Regarding the resources for the arising of the three types of feeling, these belong exclusively to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). For example, when various ordinary beings cultivate the lower-grade superior concentration (*adhimātra-samādhi*) of the first *dhyāna*, through repeated and intensive cultivation, they attain birth in the Heaven of the Brahma-Pariṣadyas;
likewise, by cultivating the middle-grade concentration of the first *dhyāna* and practicing it repeatedly...

Due to habitual practice, one is born as Brahmā or Mahābrahmā; by cultivating and repeatedly practicing the medium grade of concentration within the first dhyāna, one is born in the Heaven of Great Brahmā (Mahābrahmā).

For the second dhyāna and above, the explanation follows the same principle. Although the four formless attainments, such as the sphere of infinite space, do not have three distinct heavens, within each of these four formless realms there are likewise three grades [of rebirth].
One cultivates a mixture of the four contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states.

Regarding the cultivation of the requisites: this refers to the various non-returners who, by means of the mixed cultivation of contaminated and uncontaminated meditative absorptions as their requisite, take rebirth among the five heavens—Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala—due to their past karma.
This [karma] consists of five grades, which lead to birth in the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.

When first practicing this mixed cultivation, they have not yet attained mastery; at that initial stage, they cultivate the uncontaminated absorption for ten mental moments (*daśa-smṛti*), entering the contaminated absorption with those same ten moments. Furthermore...
Ten moments of thought enter the untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*); because this is the initial cultivation, one cannot enter it in a single moment.

However, one can enter the untainted concentration in a single moment of thought. Through the power of successive and repeated practice from this point onward, one gradually becomes able to enter the untainted concentration in a single moment of thought;
this is called the maturation of mixed cultivation (*miśra-bhāvanā*). As for the five grades, they are the inferior, the intermediate, and the superior grades.

Regarding the first of the three grades within the "Supreme Excellence" (uttama-agra) category: the lower grade consists of three moments of mind—the first moment is untainted (*anāsrava*), the second is tainted (*sāsrava*), and the third is untainted.
By cultivating these three moments of mind, one is reborn in the Heaven Free from Affliction (*Avṛha*).
Second, the middle grade cultivation consists of six moments of mind: the first moment is untainted, the second is tainted, and the third is... [untainted].
The fourth thought-moment is untainted (*anāsrava*); the fifth thought-moment is untainted; the sixth thought-moment is tainted (*sāsrava*).

Immediately thereafter, one is born in the Heaven Free from Heat (*Atapāḥ*). Third, the "Superior" grade consists of nine thought-moments: namely, six untainted thought-moments and three tainted thought-moments;
following the procedure described above, one is born in the Heaven of Good Manifestation (*Sudṛśāḥ*). Fourth, the "Superior-Superior" grade consists of twelve thought-moments, namely...
Regarding the twelve moments of mind for birth in the Sudarśana Heaven: there are eight untainted (*anāsrava*) minds and four tainted (*sāsrava*) minds;
the method for the latter is analogous to what was previously established. Fifth, regarding the supreme grade: there are fifteen moments of mind, which result in birth in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
These fifteen moments consist of ten untainted minds and five tainted minds; the method for these is also analogous to what was previously established. Furthermore, according to the same principle...

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-four, states: "It should be understood that herein, the power of the untainted (*anāsrava*) permeates the tainted (*sāsrava*), causing it to bring about rebirth in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
The commentary explains: "The initial and final moments are untainted, while those in between are tainted; this is termed 'accomplishment' (*pariniṣpatti*).

Because the tainted moments in the interim are cultivated by the preceding and succeeding untainted minds, they cause that fruit to be summoned. Since it says "causing it to be brought about," this clearly indicates the creation of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*); otherwise, how could this be?

Because the sense of "inducing" (*ākṣepa*) is established, the Sarvāstivāda school maintains that the "mixed cultivation of dhyāna" (*vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna*) refers to the creation of a new projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*) that brings about the fruit of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens;
it is not based on the meaning of "perfuming" (*vāsana*). Furthermore, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* also states:

"The ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) of the mixed cultivation of dhyāna projects the fruit of the generic similarity (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens. In this context, both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative minds act as [the projecting cause].
What are the modes of activity? The answer is: there are three types of mental engagement (*manasikāra*) regarding the activities of the tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*):

First, mental engagement with specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-manasikāra*), which refers to contemplating the specific characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), the Buddha, and so forth.

Second, mental engagement with general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-manasikāra*), which refers to contemplating general characteristics such as suffering (*duḥkha*), impermanence (*anitya*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and selflessness (*anātman*). Third, mental engagement through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), which refers to [contemplating] the white [qualities].
Because one contemplates the chain of bones (*asthi-saṃkalā*) and so forth, one does not cultivate the six aspects consisting of revulsion toward the lower [realms] and aspiration for the higher.
If it is an untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-samādhi*), the mind cultivates only the aspects of suffering, impermanence, emptiness, and non-self. Question:

It is not yet known whether a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage who is born in the palace of Maheśvara practices the mixed cultivation of the higher [dhyānas]. Answer: If one is a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), one immediately practices the mixed cultivation of the dhyānas as a resource.
The exhaustion of past karma results in birth within the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) as a body subject to segmentation (*paricchinna-śarīra*).

If a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment is certain to be born within the fourth dhyāna, they will take birth in one of the three heavens—Cloudless (*anabhraka*), etc.—and receive a body of transformation (*pariṇāma-kāya*).

If a Bodhisattva at the stage of the fulfillment of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi-pūrṇa-citta*) utilizes their compassion and vows to support those in the Cloudless heaven and below, [they may be reborn there].
During the three days, by virtue of past karma, they attain supernatural powers and proceed to the palace of Maheśvara.

As for the Bodhisattvas of the Two Vehicles who have turned their minds toward enlightenment through gradual awakening, since they retain their physical birth-bodies, they undergo a transformation of body within the Desire Realm.

According to the second master’s explanation in the treatise, there are also those of the Two Vehicles who turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] within the Form Realm; these are the gradually awakened ones in the fourth dhyāna.

In whichever heaven one is reborn during the intermediate state, upon completing the tenth bhūmi, one immediately arouses compassionate vows (*karuṇā-praṇidhāna*) to support the karma of previous births within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) where one is to be born.
By means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one proceeds to the palace of Maheśvara. Therefore, the aforementioned treatise states:

"Alternatively, by the compassionate vows of the sixth consciousness, the eight consciousnesses are drawn forth to achieve the fulfillment of what was previously incomplete. Thus, it is known that this refers to the tenth [bhūmi].

A Bodhisattva on the stages does not practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna. If one who has attained the fruit of a Non-returner (anāgāmin) possesses a body of fragmented existence (*prādeśika-kāya*), they do practice the mixed cultivation of dhyāna and are born in the five Pure Abodes;
because this is a case of being "born" (*jāti*) rather than "going" (*gamana*), it is called "birth.

If a Bodhisattva, having already received a transformed body (*parivṛtta-kāya*), does not receive further birth but acts as one who "goes," it is called "going. This applies even to a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*).

From the stage of fruition up to that of an Arhat, when they undergo the transformation of the body through the reversal of the faculties, they see only a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha) within a single four-continent world-system (*cāturdvīpaka*), which is the same as what is seen by bodhisattvas of the stage prior to awakening who have attained sudden enlightenment. If they reach the four roots of goodness (*catuḥ-kṣānti*), they then see a great transformation Buddha within a single trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
This applies to those of the two vehicles who undergo the transformation of the body through the reversal of the faculties; for bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment, it is likewise so.
All Buddhas perceived by those with the segmented body (*prādeśika-kāya*) are entirely identical, and all are termed Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the Buddhas of Other-Enjoyment (*parasaṃbhoga*) perceived by those from the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward are likewise entirely identical.
[Commentary]: Regarding these karmas of total retribution and the seeds of names-and-words (*nāma-vyañjana-bīja*) created during the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*):

although these old karmas and old seeds were previously created while one was an ordinary person, they are able to mutually attract and induce their respective fruits because they are interrelated and mutually reinforcing.

By supporting the lower [karmas] and the seeds of names-and-words, one is born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). If one attains the four fruits of the path or reaches the stages prior to the seventh bhūmi...
In states such as those with outflows (*sāsrava*) during the stage of the mental consciousness, and the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) with outflows in the eight stages and above—
although within these states one does indeed perfuse the seeds of the five fruits, such as names and words (*nāma-pada*), yet no new karma is created.

Although these newly perfused seeds are termed "seeds of names and words," because they are impelled by the resonance of prior karma, these seeds of names and words become useless and cannot [produce results].
Because it arises as active manifestation.

[Commentary: Regarding the previous interpretation that "only the stage of meditative concentration (samādhi-bhūmi) is called 'immovable' (āniñjya)," this applies to all stages; thus the previous interpretation states:

"By means of abiding fixedly in the object of focus," and so forth, up to "none of these things exist. This interpretation is established based on the power of concentration (*samādhi*) to enable the mind to focus one-pointedly.

The objective realm (*viṣaya*) is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*). If one interprets it in this way, then the concentrations of the upper eight stages are all termed "immovable," which is the broadest sense of the term.
[Commentary]: If one were to define "immovable" based on not changing location, then speaking from the perspective of the majority of cases, this [definition] would also apply here.

The intended meaning is that although other lesser noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) cultivate immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*), they must experience its results in the very place where it was produced and cannot shift them to be experienced elsewhere;

thus, they receive the name "immovable. This does not preclude those who are Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) or those born in the Palace of Sovereignty (*Īśvara-bhavana*) from being born in the lower three heavens or the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), etc., just as the karma of hell cannot be shifted, yet this is still admitted.
Because it transforms the heavy into the light, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"If one has committed sinful karma in previous lives that should result in falling into the evil realms, by encountering a minor thief in this present life, those past karmic offenses will be immediately extinguished, and one shall attain Bodhi.
Furthermore, although Aṅgulimāla attained the fruit of Arhatship, he had previously killed a thousand people; consequently, he was burned by the fires of hell and his body suffered in the hells.

Regarding the statement that one who has committed heavy karma receives a light retribution for suffering: according to the scriptural text, this refers to one who has attained the fruit of Arhatship yet still undergoes the fires of hell.
Now, explaining this by means of reasoning: it refers to those who have attained the first or second fruits [of the path], as they have not yet abandoned desire;

because there is still evil karma within their bodies, they are able to undergo the retribution of suffering in hell. As for those who have attained the latter two fruits, since they have already become detached...
All evil karma of the desire realm is completely severed and exhausted, which means it does not cause one to undergo the retribution of the hells.

Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, since the seeds of an Arhat’s evil karma have already been severed, and there is no such thing as past or future evil karma, how could an Arhat possibly undergo the suffering of hell?
This interpretation would seem superior; yet, if this is so, how is it that Aṅgulimāla [experienced such suffering]?

Answer: It is because those in the stages of the first and second fruits receive the retribution of hellfire; furthermore, there are cases where it is specifically stated that an Arhat was killed or bitten by a dog.
Although such sufferings exist, they are not the retributive suffering of hell; rather, they are distinct retributions for specific evil karmas, not general retributions for karma.
Therefore, there is no contradiction.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is born in that place," it is called "birth" merely because of going there; it does not mean birth in the literal sense.
[Treatise] Regarding the phrase "there is one interpretation," etc., this first master is the Bodhisattva Huibian Nanta.

[Commentary: Regarding the section on the three types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) within the twelve links, as the treatise states, there is abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), abandonment by severing bonds (*bandhana-vipramokṣa-prahāṇa*), and abandonment by non-arising (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*);
these three abandonments are elucidated in relation to the twelve links.

[Commentary]: Some interpret this as follows: the meaning of the explanations by the two masters Jing and Tai is that the delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) because it has not yet been severed by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*);

whereas the delusion regarding the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha-moha*) is severed by the path of vision because one has already attained the state of an Arya. This is their provisional interpretation;
the Master [Woncheuk], who composed the sub-commentary below, does not accept it and raises a challenge by citing a sutra.

[Commentary]: The passage from the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* (緣起經), Part II, which states, "up to that which is not conditioned by ignorance," intends to cite the sūtra to challenge the opponent's position.

The opponent claims that the delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*) is abandoned through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), but this is incorrect. The *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, Part II, further states:

"External phenomena arise in ordinary beings through the four types of ignorance, giving rise to the three types of formations, including non-meritorious ones. This clearly demonstrates that [ignorance] is also abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), as it gives rise to non-meritorious [formations].

The practice of equanimity (*sābhisaṃskāra*) also brings about a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), because the four types of ignorance (*avidyā*) are to be abandoned through both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Furthermore, the previous argument—that if one speaks of "delusion regarding reality" (*tattvamoha*), it must logically be abandoned only by the path of seeing—is also incorrect. As stated below in the *Pratītyasamutpādavyākhyā*:

"Among ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who are heedless regarding internal phenomena, with the exception of the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), the other three ignorances give rise to knowledge and are also common to the path of cultivation."
Ignorance gives rise to meritorious formations because ignorance, through its association and so forth, permeates the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Furthermore, when it is said that "heedfulness" refers to formations whose conditions are not ignorance, the intended meaning is that they do not take manifest (*samudācāra*) ignorance as their condition;

this does not preclude them from being identical to those formations such as merit that arise from seeds, for seeds are also abandoned through the path of cultivation. This is as the former person has stated.
It is not the case that ignorance regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha-moha*) is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Why? Because it contradicts this sūtra.

Although the commentators (*ṭīkākāra*) cite the text without making such a distinction, judging by the sense, it should be understood as follows: each [type of ignorance] is individually correlated with the preceding part of the sūtra;
others do not do so. If that were the case, what would be the use of citing this text?

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Now, from the *Abhidharma* up to 'non-merit,'" the intention is as follows: What is the purpose of this passage? It is answered because there are further defenses offered by previous scholars;
thus, this text is cited to pose a challenge. An external defense states:

Although the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* says that the four types of ignorance regarding external phenomena give rise to the differentiation of external things, and the three types of ignorance regarding internal phenomena give rise to the differentiation of internal beings—such as negligence and non-negligence—and so forth, [the two sets] function together.

Since the four types of ignorance are not individually assigned [to specific categories] and are known to pertain to both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), what contradiction is there in designating the ignorance of the path of seeing as "delusion regarding the ultimate reality" (*tattvārtha-moha*), the ignorance of the path of cultivation that produces merit and the imperturbable (*aniñjya*) as "delusion regarding maturation" (*vipāka-moha*), and the ignorance that produces non-merit as "delusion regarding the unwholesome"?
Therefore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* is now cited; furthermore, it is objected: "If one distinguishes them in this way, since ignorance is inherently unwholesome..."
How could there be internal dharmas of a different nature that cause non-virtuous ignorance to produce meritorious or immovable formations?

Furthermore, since the ignorance cultivated on the path of meditation is categorized as neutral (avyākṛta) and thus belongs to external dharmas, do ordinary beings possess obscured-neutral ignorance that produces non-meritorious formations?
Indeed, those who produce non-meritorious formations all possess a mode of activity characterized by intense delusion regarding the principles of reality.
"This is an objection citing a passage from the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*. Regarding the phrase "The fifty-ninth [chapter] says... and so forth, this cites the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* as proof.
This commentary clarifies the intended meaning of the current text somewhat more clearly.
[Commentary]: "How could the afflictions of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) lead to non-meritorious action? This means:

since the afflictions of the path of seeing in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are exclusively of a wholesome nature (kuśala-svabhāva), how can they give rise to meritorious (puṇya) or immovable (āniñjya) formations?
Furthermore, how can those of an unwholesome (akuśala) or obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) nature give rise to non-meritorious (apuṇya) formations?
[Commentary]: If one says that karma which produces specific retribution (*viśeṣa-vipāka*) is not the member of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*), the meaning is as follows:

the first phrase restates the opponent's defense, while the second phrase directly refutes that defense. The intent of the refutation is this: when it is said that great merit can trigger karma leading to the three evil destinies, this refers to the production of specific retribution.
As the commentary states: "That is, the production of evil specific retribution [is what is meant by] total retribution," because the subsequent text constitutes the formal refutation.
The meaning can be understood.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement in this section that "the two explanations conclude that it is abandoned only by the Path of Seeing," there are two masters' views in this treatise concerning external causes;
both state that the ignorance which directly initiates karma is abandoned only by the Path of Seeing, whereas the auxiliary factors are not fixed.

[Commentary]: That person further says, "up to and including those abandoned by insight" (*darśana-heya*). The intention is this: this person refers to the two masters Xing and Tai mentioned previously, who further attempt to rescue their former position.
The Master of the Commentary (Suzong) had previously praised them for their grasp of the Dharma and its meaning; he does not honor their names, but merely recounts their arguments to refute them.
His purpose is to demonstrate that the delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka-moha*) is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Why is this so? Because of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Since it is stated that delusion regarding the two truths—the conventional and the ultimate—gives rise to non-meritorious actions (*apuṇya-karma-saṃskāra*), the *Abhidharma* further subsumes the two sufferings of the ultimate and the conventional within the eight types of suffering.
As for the first seven sufferings, because they involve delusion regarding the facts of ripening (*vipāka*), one gives rise to non-meritorious actions;

therefore, delusion regarding ripening is abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as it consists of delusion regarding facts. Furthermore, the seventh chapter of the *Abhidharma* states: "By means of delusion regarding the true meaning (*tattvārtha*)..."

Regarding the statement that "the true meaning of the practice of immovable merit" refers to the Four Noble Truths, one is called "deluded regarding the true meaning" because of ignorance toward them.

Since it is known that there are two types of delusion—delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*) and delusion regarding principles (*tattva*)—there is a difference between the cultivation and the vision paths for severing these two types of delusion.

Question: According to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other treatises, since the delusion regarding maturation (*vipāka*) is a delusion regarding phenomena, it follows logically that this delusion should be severed through the path of cultivation.
Question: According to the general commentaries, why do you criticize this? Answer: Examining the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the explanation of "ignorance regarding maturation" (*vipākaja-moha*) states:
"Because it is invariably of a defiled nature, when combined with ignorance, it necessarily does not admit of the correct view that understands and realizes the characteristics of maturation.
Based on this scriptural passage, how could it be that [this ignorance] refers only to innate delusions regarding phenomena? Therefore, the critique in the commentary is not contradictory.
This is the scriptural doctrine.

[The Commentary] says: Is it not so? How could one claim that the conventional suffering spoken of in the *Abhidharma* and the *Yogācāra* is identical to this conventional [suffering]? One might challenge the opponent, saying:
"If you take the two types of suffering—the conventional and the ultimate—as taught in the *Abhidharma* and the *Yogācāra*, and equate them with what was previously stated..."

If it were the case that the delusion regarding the ultimate nature of maturation (*vipāka-paramārtha-moha*)—which consists of the two defiled delusions—is abandoned through distinct dharmas via the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), then it would not be so.

Therefore, since the present conventional passage is identical to the previous conventional passage in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, one might ask: "Is the text for all instances then a single conventional passage?
To which it is replied: "It is not so. The person previously asked: "If they are not to be made identical, how then are they to be distinguished?"
Is there a distinction between suffering in the conventional sense and suffering in the ultimate sense?
[Commentary]: Because it is easily understood, it is said that "conventional" refers to non-meritorious action (*apuṇya-karma*).

This treatise, within the *Yogācārabhūmi*, states that delusion regarding the conventional leads to non-meritorious action, while delusion regarding the ultimate leads to meritorious and immovable actions (*puṇya-aninjya-karma*); this is stated in reference to their performance.

In the exposition of the gates of karma, it is said that one creates non-meritorious formations (apuṇya-karma) by being deluded regarding the suffering of the three miserable realms, which is termed "worldly suffering" (loka-duḥkha).

One creates meritorious and immovable formations (puṇya-āneñjya-karma) through ultimate ignorance (paramārtha-moha) regarding the excellence of the fruits of the human and celestial realms; this is merely establishing the conventional (saṃvṛti) in contrast to ultimate suffering (paramārtha-duḥkha).
If, within the category of merit, the first seven sufferings are termed "conventional" while the eighth suffering is termed "ultimate suffering," this is based on [the following]:
The Dharma-gate of the eight sufferings as coarse or subtle, which are difficult or easy to know, distinguishes between the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, this does not refer to the "conventional" in the sense of non-meritorious action (*apuṇya-karman*) and so forth; although the names are the same, their meanings are distinct.

When it says that non-meritorious action is "conventional," the intended meaning refers to the [first] seven sufferings. Is it not the case that these are summoned by the arising of non-meritorious action from ignorance?

Worldly suffering refers to the eight kinds of suffering: namely, birth, aging, sickness, death, separation from the beloved, association with the hated, failure to obtain what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
These sufferings are called "ultimate suffering" (*paramārtha-duḥkha*) because the conditioned intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the five aggregates is itself suffering;

when this is associated with the feeling of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*), it is termed the "five aggregates of clinging. While this is easily understood by the noble ones (*ārya*), it is difficult for others to comprehend as ultimate truth.
The remaining seven are named "easily understood" and are collectively termed "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*).

[Commentary: If this were not the case, one might ask why the first seven [stages] of suffering do not produce non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya*). The underlying difficulty of this objection is as follows:

if one does not adopt the aforementioned interpretation, then since there is no sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) in the lower three dhyānas, there would necessarily be various forms of suffering present.

Among the eight sufferings, the sixth and seventh are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter Six, it is said that the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering mutually encompass one another.

Specifically, the suffering of birth up to the suffering of association with the disliked can manifest the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), because they correspond to the intrinsic nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena that accord with painful feeling.
The suffering of separation from the beloved and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks can manifest the suffering of change, as has already been explained.

Because it signifies the destruction of the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those phenomena conducive to pleasant feeling that have been attained or not yet attained, it briefly subsumes all five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as suffering.

It is able to manifest the meaning of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), which is the state of insecurity (*anāśvāsika*) followed by the three types of impermanence (*anityatā*). The commentary states:

Regarding the two types of impermanence, first is the suffering at the stage of arising, which is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*); second is the suffering at the stage of cessation, which is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*). These two—arising and cessation—[constitute the basis for the suffering of conditioned existence].
Since all stages are subsumed under impermanence, they are designated as the two types of impermanence.

Having already stated that the first seven [stages] are suffering in a conventional sense and are capable of producing non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya*), there should be no suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) within the lower three dhyānas, because non-meritorious formations (*apuṇya-saṃskāra*) are not produced there.

If there were suffering of change in those states, why would one not produce non-meritorious karma in the lower three dhyānas? Therefore, [suffering of change] also exists within the lower three dhyānas.

There is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; for example, when one falls from the concentration of the fourth dhyāna or higher and seeks the mind of the second or third dhyānas below, such as failing to achieve them or having already achieved them lost, a state of oppression arises, and thus it is also called suffering.

[Commentary: Furthermore, how could the miserable realms (durgati) lack the eighth [type of] ultimate suffering (*paramārtha-duḥkha*)? Thus we know that although the phrasing is identical, the intended meaning is difficult to grasp.

If one were to say, "Since the miserable realms possess the eighth ultimate suffering, it is clear that ultimate suffering is not induced solely by meritorious or immovable karma," this would contradict the *Abhidharmakośa*, which states that the nine types of death-minds are associated with self-love (*ātmasneha*).
Within the three realms, one causes the continuity of birth to proceed respectively for the desire, form, and formless realms.

That is to say, for one who passes away from the desire realm and is reborn again in the desire realm, the continuity of birth is linked by the mind at the moment of death associated with self-love (*ātmabhāvābhiniveśa*) pertaining to the desire realm.
If one is reborn in the form or formless realms, the continuity is linked by the mind at the moment of death associated with self-love pertaining to the form or formless realms.

The continuity of the mind at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) is as follows: when one passes away from the form or formless realms, whether being reborn in those same realms or elsewhere, there are six types of consciousness.
Furthermore, regarding birth in the desire realm, there are three types of consciousness for rebirth in one’s own level or other levels, as appropriate;
thus, there are nine types of consciousness in total. Moreover, this craving for self-existence (*ātmabhāva-tṛṣṇā*) is merely innate (*sahaja*) and does not clearly comprehend its objective referent.

Regarding the question of whether [these minds] are subsumed under the nature of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*): the Abhidharma merely states that there are nine types of mind within the three realms (*dhātu*).

It is not yet clear whether this formulation is established by way of the five destinies (*gati*), the four modes of birth (*yoni*), or the nine stages (*bhūmi*). Answer: One may also die in the heavenly realm and be reborn in the heavenly realm;
one may die in the heavenly realm and be born in the human realm, and so on down to the hell realm. The other destinies should be inferred accordingly. (20)
There are five minds and four births, totaling sixteen minds across nine stages;
within each stage there are nine minds, and nine times nine makes eighty-one minds, all of which are to be assigned according to the three realms.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that innate craving (*sahaja-tṛṣṇā*) and innate ignorance (*sahājā-avidyā*) are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the former master says:

"If innate craving arises simultaneously with innate ignorance, because they exist during the stage of moistening rebirth (*upapatti-pratisaṃdhi-bandhana*), they are abandoned only by cultivation. [Objection:
Since innate pride (*māna*), the view of self-existence (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), and so forth also exist during the stage of moistening rebirth, why are they not mentioned, but only craving?
[Question: Are both [ignorance and the links of existence] ignorance? [Answer: Although the link of existence is not necessarily [ignorance], ignorance pervades all defiled minds;

therefore, it is specifically mentioned. [Sūtra Commentary: Regarding the passage "The treatise states... and below, the two difficulties are presented. Now, based on the treatise, there are two difficulties regarding the middle [links] that challenge the previous master.
The first difficulty follows from the statement in the treatise: "A portion of all the links. The second difficulty follows from the statement: "Furthermore, all [factors] of the entire realm..."
The first difficulty concerns those afflictions that arise and are abandoned through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*); the second difficulty, as intended by the *Śāstra-vivaraṇa*, is easily understood.

Thus, the second master’s position represents the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla. Furthermore, according to the *Śāstra-vivaraṇa*, the branch of ignorance (*avidyā*) constitutes the first difficulty, while the branches of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) constitute the second difficulty.
Based on this interpretation in the *Śāstra-vivaraṇa*, the passage in the treatise stating "the entire realm" (*sarva-dhātu*) and so forth is merely... [text truncated].
That rebuttal does not constitute a correct principle.

[Commentary: If he were to offer a rebuttal by saying that the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), in its tenth fascicle, merely relies on a general statement based on the majority, the intention of the former master’s rebuttal would be this:

excluding the three [factors], the remaining nine members are common to both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). Now, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* follows the majority regarding these minor [members].
It is taught that the three links of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) also pertain to both the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

[Treatise]: "To 'link' means to cause [the next life] to conjoin. Because craving and grasping moisten the seeds of the five fruits, causing subsequent births to continue without interruption, it is called 'linking birth' (*pratisandhi*)."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 59, etc., that "it is not only the karma-forming ignorance that initiates the conduct leading to the evil destinies," the intention is as follows:

This objection challenges the previous master by stating that if one were to claim that only the karma-forming ignorance is severed by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), then the *Yogācārabhūmi* should have stated that the conduct leading to the five destinies is initiated solely by the afflictions severed by the Path of Seeing;
it should not have stated [exclusively] that it is only the conduct leading to the evil destinies.

Since it is stated that the *parikalpita-kleśa* (conceptual afflictions) can project [rebirth], it is clearly understood that the *parikalpita-kleśa* also project rebirth in the realms of humans and gods;
however, these are projected by means of *bhāvanā-heya-kleśa* (afflictions abandoned through cultivation).

This is because the former masters maintain that while ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) projects all types of rebirth, they do not state this exclusively regarding the projection of rebirth in the evil destinies.
The conduct leading to the evil destinies is produced by discrimination.

[Commentary: If it is asked how the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) can produce karma that brings about distinct retributions for humans and gods—since those who reach the human or celestial realms must have cultivated such karma—the former master defends this by saying:

"While it is true that the afflictions of the path of cultivation can produce karma for distinct retributions as humans or gods, here we are only discussing how afflictions of discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*) produce them."
"Going toward the evil destinies" means that "evil destinies" here refers collectively to the three evil realms.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement, "This refers to the karma for specific retributions in the evil destinies," yet we are now discussing only the collective retribution—this is a critique of the previous master's position. It says:

"If it were as you previously stated, then the afflictions cultivated on the Path should only give rise to specific karmic retributions for humans and devas, and should not give rise to [collective retribution]."

Since it is admitted that the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) give rise to karma that results in the specific retribution (*pratiniyatavipāka*) of the three evil destinies, we know that the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*) speaks only of the karma for general retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*) of the five destinies.
Therefore, we know that the karma for the general retribution of the evil destinies is also triggered solely by discriminative ignorance (*parikalpita-avidyā*).
Thus, it is said that karma of the evil destinies is triggered only by discriminative afflictions; if it were triggered by the afflictions of the path of cultivation...
Afflictions can also assist in the production of karma that results in the general retribution of humans and devas.

[Commentary: Regarding the passage "Only those [afflictions] abandoned by seeing [the truths] produce karma," up to "provided they are not contradictory," this text correlates the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
First, it correlates with the *Abhidharmakośa*, which states: "The ignorance that directly produces the karma for the general retribution of humans and devas..."

Since all [of these] are exclusively abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), the *Abhidharma* explains, based on this meaning, that the two types of delusion—conventional and ultimate—are abandoned by insight. [Treatise]:
Regarding the statement "the assistants are not fixed," this text reconciles the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. It states: "If it is a person who assists and inspires..."
The karma that results in collective retribution in the celestial realms is [the object] of ignorance;

however, the ignorance that assists in producing the karma for collective retribution in the miserable destinies (*durgati*) is abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), because its mode of activity as a conceptual affliction is sharp and intense, enabling it to assist in producing the karma for collective retribution in the miserable destinies.

As for the afflictions that assist in producing the karma for individual retribution in the miserable destinies, they pertain to both abandonment by insight and abandonment by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). The *Yogācārabhūmi* speaks only of "going to the miserable destinies" [in this context].

It is said that "only the afflictions of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) can initiate [karmic action]," yet it does not mention others; in reality, those that assist in initiation also include the afflictions of both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Question: What is meant by "assisting" in the case of those that assist in initiation? Answer: This ignorance (*avidyā*) is called "assisting" because, in relation to this ignorance that initiates karma, it provides power before and after it.
Question: At the time when the constituent of action (*karma-anga*) occurs, are there also factors such as attachment (*rāga*) and aversion (*dveṣa*)?

Question: For what reason is it said that only ignorance (*avidyā*) is mentioned? Answer: Because ignorance universally serves as a condition for meritorious (*puṇya*), non-meritorious (*apuṇya*), and immovable (*āniñjya*) karma, whereas the other [factors] do not necessarily exist [in all such cases]; therefore, they are not mentioned.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the auxiliary factors are indeterminate," the intended meaning is as follows:

if that which directly moistens rebirth were only abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), then since the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states—based on these indeterminate auxiliary factors—that "all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the entire realm (*sarva-dhātu*) are capable of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi-bandhana*)," and because this uses the expression "entire realm," it follows that both afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation are capable of moistening rebirth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "all four types of clinging (*upādāna*) are called the 'clinging member' (*upādānāṅga*)," the intended meaning is to demonstrate that since clinging generally encompasses both afflictions abandoned through insight (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*),

while the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭy-upādāna*) and clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-upādāna*) are abandoned solely through insight, and the clinging to sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*) and clinging to a theory of self (*ātma-vādopādāna*) are abandoned through both insight and cultivation,
it is therefore said that the member of clinging also pertains to both types of abandonment.
[Commentary]: As for the statement that "the afflictions that initiate karma exist only as seeds until the time of death, when they arise as manifest [afflictions]," the intent is this:
it also serves to resolve apparent contradictions in the scriptures. There are authoritative teachings stating that the afflictions which initiate karma exist only as seeds;
this refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal [Buddhist] tradition who are not heedless, who, by means of the seed of ignorance, initiate meritorious and immovable karma.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the holy teachings that the delusions which moisten rebirth are exclusively seeds, this refers to the fact that for one who has attained the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin),
the seeds of ignorance moisten the seeds of their own and other births, as well as those of other stages (bhūmi).

[Commentary: Some say that "those who die from the state of non-perception" refers to the interpretation of the Master of the Mindless School regarding the location of the Heaven of Non-perception found in the seventh fascicle.
This master’s intention is to say that sentient beings in the Heaven of Non-perception are entirely without mind both at their initial birth and their subsequent death;

thus, when they pass away, they rely solely on the moisture of seeds. However, what is discussed here is the application of heedfulness by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) within the internal phenomena.
The "seeds that initiate karma" refers specifically to the seeds of non-associated ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*) associated with the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

If we rely on the auxiliary factors for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within internal phenomena, this includes the aforementioned associated ignorance (*sābhisaṃskārikā-avidyā*), which also arises in the present;

since it is from the actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of this associated ignorance that one is able to initiate and further incite karma, it is also called the "remote cause-condition" (*dūre-hetv-utthāna*).

Regarding the statement that "present intention" refers to the time of death when the seeds initiate karma: even before the seeds have been employed as the actual branches [of the path], present activity already arises;

therefore, it is said that present activity serves as the remote cause (*dūre-hetu*) and the motivating cause (*samutthāna*). This is because both seeds and present activity are capable of initiating [the process].

Furthermore, another interpretation states that for those passing away from the stage of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) or the Heaven of No-thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), the seeds serve as the primary branches and the moisture [for rebirth].
If the auxiliary conditions that moisten [the seeds] have not yet ceased before death, the afflictions that arise through those auxiliary conditions and moisten birth can also manifest.
[Commentary:
The meaning of "the nature of form is not defiled" is that all afflictions and their associated mental states and bases [are meant].

Regarding the nature of defilement as unwholesome (*akuśala*) or obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*): it is abandoned by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), because when the antidotes of both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) arise, the seeds [of those defilements] are permanently severed.
However, the nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*) is not defiled; rather, it is abandoned through the severance of bondage (*bandhana-vigama-prahāṇa*) and not by intrinsic nature.

This is just as the sense faculties (*indriya*) and so forth are abandoned when their conditions—the afflictions—are severed; since the eye-faculty becomes free from those afflictions, it is said [to be abandoned].
Regarding the question: Are the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and so forth called "bound by conditions" (*ālambana-bandhana*), while the rest are all determined accordingly?

Is that which serves as the direct objective aspect (*sākṣāt-bhāga*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) called "bound by conditions," or is it that which serves as the substantial essence (*svabhāva*) called "bound by conditions"? Answer: With respect to the direct objective aspect, it is called "bound by conditions," because it is merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
If that were so, would the eighth [consciousness] itself also [be bound] with respect to the bodies of others and the sensory bases (*indriya-adhiṣṭhāna*) that support the faculties? It is indeed so.

It is also not the case that the essence itself is bound by conditions; rather, it is said that when the first seven consciousnesses are associated with afflictions and take that objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) as their object, they are called "bound by conditions.
This is unlike the eighth consciousness, which is not associated with afflictions and for which one cannot say whether it is bound or unbound.

As for the discussion regarding the severance of those afflictions that take [the essence] as their object: the "object" refers to that which is taken as an object, and the "subject" refers to that which takes it as an object.

The "condition" (*pratyaya*) that takes [objects] as its cognitive focus (*ālambana*) and is mixed with those [defiled states] is precisely the "condition" in the sense of being a basis for reliance (*upādāna-pratyaya*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "following the objects of those seven consciousnesses, when they reach the name 'defiled' (*sāsrava*), they are said to be severed," the intended meaning here is this:

if within a mind of affliction one takes wholesome objects or non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) objects as one's cognitive focus, these are the "objects" at the locus where the perceiving [consciousness] is bound.

Objects of perception (*ālambana*) that are wholesome or neutral are not themselves bound phenomena; yet they can be bound by other perceived objects, and thus they are subsumed under the condition of the object (*ālambanapratyaya*).

When afflictions within the mind perceive other afflictions or obscured-neutral phenomena (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), those obscured-neutral phenomena are not abandoned through their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), but are subsumed under the bond of association (*saṃprayoga-bandha*). This is because they previously perceived the afflictions as their own intrinsic nature.
These bound phenomena (*baddha-dharma*) are not bound by the afflictions (*kleśa*) that serve as their objective conditions (*ālambana*).

Nevertheless, unwholesome (*akuśala*) and obscured-unneutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomena are precisely what constitute "associated binding" (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*), and thus they are subsumed within the category of "non-interruption of intrinsic nature" (*asvabhāva-prahāṇa*).

Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna, since the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are of a neutral nature (*avyākṛta-svabhāva*), the afflictions within the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) take only these neutral sense objects as their objective conditions; this is the case for those within the sixth consciousness as well.

Afflictions can take the three natures as their objects; if the afflictions within the seventh consciousness take an indeterminate object, and so forth—wherever the afflictions within these seven consciousnesses take wholesome objects and the like—they are all comprised within "bondage by way of the object" (*ālambana-bandhana*).

Furthermore, in this context, the general sense of bondage formed when the seven consciousnesses take the five sensory objects, wholesome, or indeterminate phenomena within one's own continuum is likewise considered unwholesome.

Because it forms an object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*) based on the seven consciousnesses, the five sense-objects of others' bodies, and wholesome or neutral phenomena, the treatise refutes this, stating:

"It is not by being bound by another that something becomes outflowing (*sāsrava*); otherwise, it would follow that something could become non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) simply by being liberated from another. Question:
When the afflictions within the seventh consciousness are severed, can the eighth consciousness also be said to have its object-condition binding severed? Answer: It can indeed.
This refers to the severance of the bonds of objective conditions (*ālambana-bandhana*).
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "mixed with those afflictions" up to "named as having attained severance," the intention is as follows:

this first interpretation within the commentary merely establishes the name "associated with outflows" (*āsrava-saṃprayukta*) as being mixed with those afflictions; however, this naming also possesses faults, which the Master himself will investigate below.

The difficulty is as stated in the commentary below: "If one says that the seven consciousnesses are called 'mixed' because of afflictions and so forth," this passage constitutes a critique of the first interpretation mentioned previously. [Commentary]:
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "arising alternately" being termed "mixed," and so on, up to "however, that which accords with this is called mixed"—the intent of this is as follows: this...

The second [explanation] regarding "intermingling with those afflictions" refers to the fact that within the first six consciousnesses, wholesome and indeterminate dharmas arise in alternation before and after the afflictions;

this is termed "intermingling. Due to the power of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions, each wholesome or indeterminate dharma arising before or after them becomes of a nature characterized by outflows (*sāsrava*); thus, they are said to be "intermingled with those afflictions."

An external objection is raised: "If that which arises in alternation with other states is called 'mixed,' then when those in training (śaikṣa) turn toward the Great [Vehicle] and reach the first bhūmi, or when Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment reach the first bhūmi and give rise to the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) and the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), these arise in alternation before and after the afflictions of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses; therefore, the Wisdom of Equality and the others should also be called 'mixed.'"
In the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary), those [actions] that naturally accord with one another are termed "mixed" (*miśra*).

As for the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, which are untainted (*anāsrava*), they do not accord with the afflictions (*kleśa*) because they are directly opposed to them; therefore, they are not called "mixed.

When it is said, "This is not [due to] causal motivation (*hetu-samutthāna*); all neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma is not causally motivated," the intended meaning is that what is here termed "mixed" refers to that [neutral karma].
This refers merely to the fact that [the karma] arises amidst [other factors] and thus possesses a mixed character; it does not become mixed by virtue of its *samutthāna-hetu* (originating cause).

Since indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) karma does not arise with ignorance as its originating cause, it is said that "it is not due to an originating cause. Question: What is called the "originating cause"? Answer:
For example, when wholesome karma—whether meritorious or imperturbable (*aniñjya*)—is set in motion by the member of ignorance (*avidyā*), this very wholesome conduct [is so designated].

It is reasonable that what is produced by clarity (*vidyā*) is called "arisen from a cause" (*hetusamutthāna*); however, tainted wholesome karma (*sāsrava-kuśala-karma*) is termed "mixed" (*vyavakīrṇa*).

This is because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, as well as indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena, when untainted (*anāsrava*), are not arisen from causes consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*) or ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, it is said that the untainted and the indeterminate are not termed "mixed. Thus, we know that [the term "mixed"] does not refer to those things external to "arising from a cause. This is the objection raised by the opponent.
That [explanation] is indeed a partial interpretation (*vyavasthāpana*), as it does not fully encompass the meaning of "mixed" (*saṃkīrṇa*).

If contaminated wholesome states are called "mixed" because they arise with ignorance as their cause, then since ignorance is not abandoned in the indeterminate karma and indeterminate dharmas, those should also be called "mixed.

Therefore, that [explanation] is incomplete. Furthermore, regarding the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭamanas*), there are only the four afflictions of the obscured-indeterminate nature (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*). One...
When members of a homogeneous continuum arise without being interspersed by other dharmas, it is not called "mixed.

Even though the untainted seventh consciousness, the Wisdom of Equality, arises in alternation with the tainted seventh consciousness, it is not considered mixed because they are of different natures.
However, within the sixth consciousness, when wholesome and neutral factors alternate with the branches of affliction, they do constitute a mixture.

It is called "mixed" because its nature conforms to the outflows (*āsrava*); thus it is named "mixed. Alternatively, it also extends to the first five consciousnesses, as the first five consciousnesses encompass all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the statement that even the wholesome is called "abandoned," this third interpretation intends to explain that there are wholesome karmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala-karma*).

It is termed "mixed" because it arises with merit and immovable formations having ignorance as its condition; thus, it shares the name of "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) with the indeterminate [factors], yet it does not arise from the branch of ignorance itself.
Therefore, the Commentary states that it is not the same as the indeterminate [of the other type].

Once that ignorance is severed, those wholesome karmas are termed "severed by the mixed fetter. However, regarding the second explanation of "mixed" within the Commentary, it refers to being mixed with those afflictions...

The term "affliction" (*kleśa*) encompasses both contaminated wholesome karma and neutral phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*), and is thus collectively termed "mixed" (*miśra*). This interpretation is broad.
Alternatively, the third interpretation restricts "mixed" to only contaminated wholesome karma while excluding neutral phenomena; this is somewhat narrow.

Here, we adopt the second interpretation, which accords with a portion of the third interpretation, and thus name it "mixed. From the perspective of principle, this [second] affliction is likely superior.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "When the mind is bound by association and the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) reach the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), how could there not be binding through association?"—the meaning of this fourth interpretation is as follows:
when the mind and its universal and other mental factors arise simultaneously with afflictions such as greed (*lobha*), it is called "binding by characteristics" (*nimittabandhana*).
When greed and the like are severed, the universal, particular-sphere (*viśeṣaka*), and other mental factors are also said to be severed; however, this is not a true severance.

If one collects [the afflictions] based on the nature of the universal mental factors such as the mind-king (*cittarāja*), they are not defiled; however, if one designates them "abandoned" based on the abandonment of their associated greed and so forth, then this abandonment is suffering itself.
This abandonment is mixed with those afflictions; collecting them together constitutes the fourth interpretation, which captures the original intent of the text.

If that were the case, then the passage below stating that those mixed afflictions are abandoned only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) would be consistent with the text’s subsequent explanation, which says they are "mixed with those."

Since afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the present explanation states: if the bondage of association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*) pertains to both the paths of seeing and cultivation, then when that which is associated with those [afflictions] is severed, the afflictions themselves are abandoned only through the path of cultivation.

If one were to say that severing the bondage of association is also called severing that which is associated with those afflictions, and thus belongs to the abandonment of the path of cultivation—would this not then mean that the afflictions associated with ignorance (*avidyā*) are also abandoned? Therefore, it should be...

Knowing that the first two explanations are correct, one does not adopt the fourth interpretation, but rather adopts a portion of the third—the one immediately preceding it—and a portion of the second;
therefore, it is said that the first two explanations are good and the first [of those two] is not adopted because it contains faults, as will be explained below.
Zhe says that the first interpretation is difficult to refute, stating: "If one says that the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), though pervasive, etc., is associated with greed (*rāga*) and so forth..."

When greed and the like arise simultaneously [with the mind], at the time they are abandoned, the mental sovereign (*cittarāja*), the universal factors (*sarvatraga*), and so forth still remain; thus, it is difficult to maintain that these are abandoned by their own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*).

The objection states: "Since the mental sovereign and the universal factors coexist with greed and the like, are the mental sovereign and its associates defiled (*kliṣṭa*) or are they neutral (*avyākṛta*)?
If you say that greed and the like are defiled, then one should likewise say that the afflictions such as greed are abandoned by their own nature."
If it is argued that what is not defiled must be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), then even if it were indeterminate, what would be the harm in its meaning?

If that were the case, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*)—along with the universal (*sarvatraga*), object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), and other mental factors—would have to be exclusively indeterminate and could not pertain to the three natures (*tri-dharmatā*). If it were associated with greed, hatred, and so forth, it could not pertain to the unwholesome (*akuśala*);
if it were associated with faith and so forth, it could not pertain to the wholesome (*kuśala*). This is because the category of the indeterminate encompasses all three natures.
[The text] states that knowing that the mind and so forth follow greed, anger, and so forth is the inclusion of their defiled nature through abandonment.

[Commentary: If it is said that the seven consciousnesses are called "mixed afflictions" up to the point where they are said to be abandoned when their objects of perception are exhausted—provided they are not mixed afflictions—the intention is this:
if one speaks of the afflictions within the seventh consciousness in relation to the wholesome states and so forth within the sixth consciousness.
Because the three natures coexist, and because they coexist with the fulfillment [of the path], they are called "mixed. Regarding those afflictions:

for example, when a person who has attained the fruit of *anāgāmin* dwells in the desire realm, having exhausted the nine grades of the afflictions of cultivation belonging to the desire realm, the afflictions within their seventh consciousness are simultaneously and instantaneously severed along with the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdumṛdu*) afflictions of the stage below the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), because their power is equal; thus, they should immediately [be eliminated].

The wholesome dharmas within the body of one who has attained the fruit of returning (*pratyāgami-phala*) are not called "interrupted" or "mixed" with those afflictions, because the afflictions of the seventh consciousness of the desire realm remain present.
Consequently, it is said that the wholesome and other [dharmas] are "interrupted" only because the sixth consciousness’s capacity to take them as objects has been completely severed;
this is not a case of being called "interrupted" due to the interruption of mixed afflictions, because the afflictions within the seventh consciousness [remain].
Because they still remain, they must necessarily be severed only upon reaching the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).

[Commentary: Since this is so, as for those who have naturally attained non-existence—according to the principle stated above, although the various wholesome states (*kuśala*) and so forth of superior noble beings in lower stages have not yet severed the defilements mixed with them, those wholesome states and so forth are nonetheless said to be "severed" because they have naturally become non-existent.
This clarifies that wholesome states and the like are not severed without cause by the mere presence of mixed afflictions;
rather, when one severs the desire [realm] and exhausts the nine grades of delusions capable of taking them as objects, wholesome dharmas are naturally severed. There is an interpretation which says:

although a person of the Non-returner (anāgāmin) fruit does not sever the seeds of those mixed afflictions within the seventh consciousness, if they are born into the higher realms, they cannot give rise to desire.
The active afflictions within the seventh consciousness of the *dhātu* are termed "naturally non-existent" because these active afflictions do not arise;
the active unwholesome states are termed "severed. [Commentary:

As for the statement that even those [afflictions] reached by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are called "severed," this refers to the fact that the nature of these delusions of the path of seeing is powerful, yet upon entering the path of seeing...
At that time, it occurs spontaneously because there are no bonds of the path of cultivation and no afflictions of the path of seeing;

thus, it receives the name "severance" (*prahāṇa*) due to the severance of the afflictions of the path of seeing. By analogy, wholesome states and so forth are also called "severed," as these are bonds of inferior conditions while [the path] is strong;
because the strong is absent, wholesome states and so forth receive the name "severed. Therefore, wholesome states and so forth are also termed "bonds of conditions."
"Severed.

[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "because those afflictions are powerful, it is also called severed" is that because the afflictions taking them as objects are powerful, one enters the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Since the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is contrary to the obstacles, when one takes those wholesome states and so forth as objects, the afflictions are spontaneously severed; therefore, they are wholesome.
The same applies to [the wholesome and so forth]; they are called "severed" because the bonds of conditions are severed and do not depend on the absence of those associated afflictions (*kleśa*).

[The *Śāstra*] says: "If this is so, how is it that... up to "...should be considered. If the intent of this objection is that since severance does not depend on the absence of associated afflictions, then wholesome states and the like would become outflowing (*sāsrava*) by virtue of their very existence, [we reply]: they likewise do not depend on associated afflictions. There are two answers.
One interpretation states that since there is this objection, it is explained in terms of the six consciousnesses:

those afflictions are mixed with the wholesome and so forth of the desire realm’s own level within the six consciousnesses, whereas they are not mixed with the wholesome and so forth of the non-desire realm’s own level; thus, they are said to "attain bondage" and "severance.

They become "outflows" (*āsrava*) because they coexist with outflows—that is, because the wholesome and so forth coexist with the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, [they become outflows] from a previous time.

That which arises mixed with outflows (*āsrava*) is called "outflowing" (*sāsrava*). If that were so, it would follow that [the mind] becomes outflowing solely through the afflictions (*kleśa*) within the seventh consciousness.

Answer: It becomes outflowing by virtue of being associated with outflows, such as wholesome states and the like. Regarding the severance of bonds (*bandhana*) based on the seventh consciousness, since the objects of those [afflictions] are mixed with wholesome states and so forth, when they are severed, [the wholesome states] are also severed because they are mixed with those afflictions that take them as objects.
If that is so, why is it said that "wholesome [states] are severed"? Answer: Because when the objects are severed, those afflictions mixed with them are also severed.

Regarding the two meanings of the abandonment of wholesome states such as those of the *yadṛcchika* type—namely, partial abandonment and complete abandonment—the term "abandonment" applied to wholesome states of the desire realm refers to partial abandonment.
As for the statement that they are called "abandoned" because one abandons the defilements associated with them, this refers to complete abandonment;
for at the stage of the perfection of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), both types of associated delusions are entirely absent.
[Commentary] Question: Regarding the statement that the five views are a portion of wisdom and thus should not be abandoned—the intent of this question is:
if the substance of these five is itself wisdom, then is this very wisdom what is not to be abandoned?

[Commentary] Regarding the passage from "that which should be abandoned" to "all may be abandoned," the objection is raised: if one says that [the afflictions] should be abandoned by their very nature (*svabhāva*), then the entire substance of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) associated with desire and so forth should collectively be called "abandoned. Why?

Because it is known that there is no such thing as "abandonment" apart from the associated dharmas; for the substance of the associated wisdom (*prajñā*) is itself that which can be abandoned. Furthermore, another objection is raised: if this is...

That which is severed by its own nature (*svabhāva-prahīṇa*) is the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, it is also devoid of any object-bound phenomena (*ālambana-bandha-dharma*).
Since the essence of wisdom is severed by its own nature, it is likewise devoid of any dissociation from association (*viprayukta-bandha*). The meaning is this:
if wisdom were not severed by its own nature, then this wisdom would possess both the sense of being associated with afflictions regarding its objects and the sense of being dissociated from them.

Regarding the meaning of "bondage through association" (*saṃprayoga-bandha*): if it is said that wisdom (*prajñā*) is abandoned by its own nature, this would be identical to the afflictions (*kleśa*); therefore, how could there be such things as "bondage through objects" (*ālambana-bandha*)?

This is because [wisdom] is the very essence of the factors that constitute bondage. Conversely, if it is said that the essence of wisdom should not be abandoned, then the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*) would not be included among those abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
However, within the category of afflictions, the five views are components of wisdom and are all subject to abandonment by both insight and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).
Therefore, if one says they are not to be abandoned, this meaning does not hold and contradicts the holy teaching.

[Commentary] Thus, up to the case of non-apprehension (*asamprajanya*) and so forth, one should ask according to this principle: "Since non-apprehension has discernment (*prajñā*) as its constituent essence, is this constituent of discernment something that should be abandoned?
It is not so; if one were to say it is abandoned by its own nature (*svabhāva-prahātavya*), [it would contradict the fact that it is associated with the afflictions].

Regarding the statement that "the factors associated with non-binding are not binding because the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*) is itself binding"—if one were to say they are not binding, then this wisdom would not be subsumed under the category of afflictions (*kleśa*). [Commentary:
The meaning is that those which constitute the essence of view (*dṛṣṭi*) are binding; it is intended to say that wisdom which is not view is not binding.

Furthermore, because it is seen that the faculty of "intention" (*manas*) takes the five views as its substance, those which are to be abandoned [by insight] are the five views themselves; those which are not the substance of the five views are not abandoned by their own nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*).

[Commentary: By the phrase "these ten," etc., it refers to the combination of the universal (*sarvatraga*) and the object-specific (*viṣayaviśeṣa*) mental factors. The meaning is that, with the exception of wisdom (*prajñā*), [the others are included].

The remaining nine [mental factors] pertain to all three natures; those that are defiled are included among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). However, although their essence is not outflow (*āsrava*), they are metaphorically called "outflows" because they are phenomena that are bound.
If mental attention (*manasikāra*) and the others were themselves afflictions, there would be many contradictions regarding their association (*samprayoga*) and bondage (*bandhana*);
this is shown by way of illustration.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "because that which is relied upon does not exist, the cause also does not arise," this means that because the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the collective retribution (*vipāka*) does not exist, the karmic causes of individual retribution (*vipāka*) also cannot arise. [Commentary]:
