Regarding the phrase "relying on the previous [state] of being free from bonds and severed," the intended meaning is that the wholesome [states] are those which have been bound by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Because these unobscured [neutral] factors and so forth are gradually abandoned during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it is said that the wholesome and unobscured [neutral] factors are abandoned only by the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, another interpretation states that they also pertain to both types of abandonment: if one refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called "abandoned by detachment from bonds" (*visaṃyogaprahāṇa*);

if one refers to their own substance (*svabhāva*), they are called "abandoned by the path of cultivation" because they do not conflict with the Noble Path and are only abandoned upon reaching the ultimate fruit.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the six faculties beginning with faith" up to "not abandoned":

the five faculties beginning with faith and the faculty of 'knowing the unknown' (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya)—these six factors are contaminated (*sāsrava*) and thus abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); however, because they lead toward the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), they are also termed "not abandoned."

[Commentary]: As for the phrase "that which takes this as its object and binds," the meaning is that those [afflictions] which take faith and so forth as their objects and arise during the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) are all abandoned by the path of cultivation.

[Commentary]: As for the phrase "yet they are not yet exhausted," the meaning is that although afflictions of the path of vision (darśanamārga) also take these as objects, here we are referring only to the afflictions of the path of cultivation.

If it is said that the afflictions of the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) are not mentioned because they have not yet been exhausted by the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), and that one now discusses the abandonment [of afflictions] from the perspective of their exhaustion on the path of cultivation, then the afflictions of the path of seeing are not discussed here. [Commentary:

Regarding the passage "He enters the gates of the wholesome and the neutral... which are exclusively abandoned by seeing" (*darśana-heya*), the intended meaning is as follows: for example, the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and so forth.

It may also be categorized as belonging to both types of abandonment (*prahāṇa*). If one considers the karma of the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) from the perspective of the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Why? Because wholesome and indeterminate dharmas do not obstruct the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and their nature is not defiled (*kliṣṭa*).

If, however, it is subsumed within the category of the basis (*āśraya*), then the wholesome karma of the attainment of non-conception and so forth—following the principle of being designated according to its support (*niśraya*) and its fruit—is also called "non-... [unmanifest].

Regarding the abandonment by birth (*upapatti-prahāṇa*): because the fruit of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) does not arise at the time of entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), the wholesome karma of non-conception and so forth—when compared to the wholesome and the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)—and when considered in terms of their dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*), are abandoned by both Seeing and Meditation (*darśana-bhāvanā-dvaya-prahātavya*).
This should be explained in the same way as the five faculties (*indriya*) below.

[Commentary]: As for the phrase "those are merely conceptualizations arising from the outsiders and so forth," this means that if the substance of conceptual afflictions gives rise to karma leading to the three evil destinies—just as conceptual afflictions such as wrong views can give rise to the karma of the meditative attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)—then by analogy, these are what arise among the outsiders and are abandoned upon entering the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).
If one firmly upholds the five precepts, they will not arise.
Afflictions such as desire, hatred, and pride cause the karmic retribution of a male body through these precepts;

yet, when one observes the five precepts, if afflictions such as greed arise repeatedly before and after, then by the power of this mixed karma, one receives a female body. This is likewise due to the arousal of karma through discriminative afflictions.
As for the five types of impotent beings—those born from eggs, those born from wombs, and others—the three miserable realms, and so forth.
When one enters the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), the afflictions (*kleśa*) that are to be abandoned through analytical discernment are simultaneously severed;
therefore, as in the aforementioned case of the fruit of the Dharma, these causes are ultimately not taken up, and thus the fruit is lost—this is like the severance [of karma].

Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned fruit of the Dharma, with the exception of the distinct retribution (*vipāka*) of the hells, all other distinct wholesome dharmas are absent, because when one enters the Path of Seeing, the body no longer receives them.

Therefore, when the causes of distinct retributive karma (*vyavasthita-vipāka-karma*) no longer arise subsequently, this is termed the "extinction of the fruit and the disappearance of the cause," because the causes of distinct retributive karma perish along with their fruits.
Furthermore, it is said that among the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*), the "long-lived heavens" refers specifically to the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva-deva*).

One cannot say that the four formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*), such as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), are included here, because [the former] involve long lifespans of eighty thousand *kalpas*.
This is because those who are Non-returners (anāgāmin) bound for the upper realms are also born in that heaven.
[Commentary]: Regarding *paṇḍaka* and the hermaphrodite (*ubhayavyañjana*): in Sanskrit, *paṇḍaka* is translated as "ultimate" (*atyanta*), meaning they ultimately lack virility.
In Sanskrit, *paṇḍaka* is also translated as "transverse virility," or "world-cutting," or "originally non-existent," or "harmful."
Alternatively, those who lack personal power and function are called "world-transcending" (*ati-loka*); these are the five types of *paṇḍaka*, also known as the five types of non-males.
All five of these are eunuchs (*śaṇḍha*). As for those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), they constantly manifest [sexual desire] just like the afflictions (*kleśa*);
they may thus be called "beasts among humans."

[Commentary]: "To sever" has the meaning of "abandoning," not the meaning of "attaining an antidote. If that were so, then the evil destinies and the fruits of evil karma—which are also indeterminate in nature—would likewise be examples of what was originally non-existent and would now manifest; however, this is not the case.

The intended meaning here is that when wholesome and indeterminate dharmas are "severed through non-arising," this refers only to the sense of "abandoning," not to being severed by the untainted path of antidotes (*anāsrava-pratipakṣa-mārga*). It simply means that their active manifestation does not arise.

This is termed "abandonment" because the evil karma of the three miserable destinies and their neutral fruits (*avyākṛta-phala*)—which had manifested until the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*)—no longer arise;
this abandonment also carries the sense of relinquishment (*prahāṇa*), and thus it is said that the same principle applies here.

However, regarding these seeds of wholesome and neutral dharmas, when one reaches the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), they are abandoned through the severance of their bonds (*bandhana-vigama*). This is also the case for the three [types of] non-conceptual heavens (*asaṃjñi-sattva*).

When one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the functioning of the heterogeneous ripening (*vipāka*) neutral fruits and the wholesome karma of separate retribution (*viśeṣavipāka*) does not arise;

this is called "abandonment through non-arising. If these seeds are not entirely severed until the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), when the body first becomes free from bondage, it is called "abandonment through separation from bondage."
[Commentary]: The intention behind explaining the retribution of evil fruits together with their causes is as follows:

when it is said that the fruits abandoned through the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) are explained together with their causes, this refers to the afflictions of discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*) acting as the cause for the arousal of karma. Since these afflictions of the Path of Seeing have been severed, the fruit no longer arises;
thus, explaining the fruit together with its cause is termed "severance. However, in reality, the seeds have not yet been severed.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the five faculties [of the desire realm] are also explained as being abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) in this same way," the intended meaning is as follows:

The five material faculties (*rūpīndriya*)—namely those belonging to the three evil rebirths, the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), women, *paṇḍaka*, and hermaphrodites—are called "abandoned through seeing" because they are designated as such by way of their association with the causes [of those states].

However, the seeds of these material faculties are not yet severed; it is only during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) that one becomes free from their bonds and severs them. Some say that this refers to faith (*śraddhā*).

When those of the five external paths (tīrthika) emerge from the state of non-ideation (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), they likewise sever [the afflictions] upon reaching the stage of the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga);

according to the previous principle, this is "severance by non-arising" (anutpāda-prahāṇa). If considered from the perspective of liberation from bondage, it is also termed "severance through cultivation" (bhāvanā-prahāṇa).

[Commentary]: Regarding the "four kinds," first is severance by intrinsic nature; second is severance through the removal of fetters; third is severance through the disappearance of causes and the loss of effects;
fourth is the loss of effects and the disappearance of causes. [Commentary]:
"Causing them never to arise again" is stated in conjunction with the causes.

[Commentary]: "The second point, 'the exhaustion of fruits and the concurrent severance of causes,' refers to the wholesome karma that constitutes individual retribution (*pratiniyata-vipāka*) within the three evil destinies.

This commentary provisionally uses the general term "severance," yet in reality, there is no such thing as wholesome karma constituting individual retribution in the places of extreme suffering in the hells.

As for those with wholesome karma constituting individual retribution in the hungry ghost realm—for instance, those ghosts who possess merit—all such cases are fruits of individual retribution, summoned by wholesome karma of individual retribution.

In the intermediate states (*antarābhava*) of the minor hells, there are experiences of pleasure as a result of concordant causes (*niṣyanda-phala*), such as being born among animals as horses or elephants in royal households;
their physical forms, deaths, and so forth are all summoned by distinct karmas of individual retribution (*pratiniyata-vipāka-karman*). These are each distinct karmas of individual retribution.

[Commentary]: Regarding the question of how the non-percipient attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)—which induces afflictions ranging from those associated with views to those abandoned through cultivation—can be both a cause (resulting in the non-percipient heaven as its fruit) and itself a fruit:

the answer is that it is because non-Buddhists first cultivate the non-percipient attainment by taking false views and the like as their cause; subsequently, upon reaching the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), these false views are themselves [abandoned].

Excluding the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and others, because one does not cultivate the fruit of the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-deva*), nor can one be born there, it is said that the attainment of non-conception is abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) according to its causes.
[Commentary: If ignorance, craving, and grasping were not mentioned up to the point of "not being superior," the intention was to state that these three members are themselves...

The abandonment by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*) and the abandonment through both seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-prahāṇa*) do not apply to the abandonment of non-arising due to the lack of connection with objects (*ālambana-bandhana*).

This is because these two types of abandonment are not particularly distinguished [in that regard]. However, regarding abandonment by intrinsic nature, it is based on the substance of the seeds; since the three members [of dependent origination] are abandoned by their own intrinsic nature, they are abandoned spontaneously upon entering the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Question: What is meant by "the abandonment of non-arising due to the lack of connection with objects"? Answer: Indeed, as for the connection with objects...

"Severance" refers to the severing of wholesome dharmas and so forth that are bound by afflictions or neutral states acting as conditions; it does not mean the actual destruction of the substance of the wholesome dharmas themselves.

Therefore, it is not a matter of excelling over their non-arising. Severance consists merely in cutting off the cause so that the effect does not arise; it is not the severing of the substance itself.
Consequently, the non-arising of what is bound by conditions does not apply to all three branches [of dependent origination].

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the formations [saṃskāra] have a partial [application] up to [the point where they] do not extend to those abandoned by birth" (*jāti-prahātavya*), the explanation is as follows:

Among the members of the *saṃskāra* link, there are unwholesome volitional actions (*cetanā-karma*), and among the members of the *bhava* link, there are likewise unwholesome volitional actions. These are non-defiled formations (*akliṣṭa-saṃskāra*) which are abandoned by their very nature (*svabhāva-prahātavya*).

Within that category of abandonment by nature, there are those abandoned by both seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). However, the reason the *bhava* link lacks the *saṃskāra* link is because it is transformed through the operation of the *saṃskāra* link as its cause.

Because they are factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*), it is known that the nature of the simultaneously arising mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is defiled; thus, the formations (*saṃskāra*) are also of the same nature of existence.

Regarding their abandonment: if one speaks of the abandonment of self-nature, then among the formations, wholesome volition (*kuśala-cetanā*), and within the factors of existence, wholesome karma and the five neutral seeds (*avyākṛta-bīja*), these pertain to both abandonment through severance of bonds (*bandhana-viccheda-prahāṇa*) and abandonment through non-arising (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*).
Abandonment through non-arising refers to what is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahāṇa*), whereas abandonment through severance of bonds refers to...
These are abandoned through the path of cultivation because, being non-conceptual and so forth, they are wholesome karma;
thus, when the cause perishes and the fruit is lost during the path of vision, the wholesome karma that constitutes a distinct retribution within existence is severed.

Since this wholesome karma—which is the fruit of the path of vision—is lost and its cause perishes, it is said that "existence" (*bhava*) is abandoned through both the paths of vision and cultivation.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement "the seven branches beginning with consciousness should be understood as appropriate," the intended meaning is that the five resultant seeds beginning with consciousness, as well as the branches of birth, aging, and death, are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) dharmas;
thus, they are not subject to abandonment through insight (*darśana-heya*).

Furthermore, since these seven branches—such as those pertaining to the three miserable realms, the eight difficult conditions, women, those born from eggs or moisture, and *paṇḍakas*—as well as the distinct retributive wholesome karma within the body, are likewise [indeterminate].
When entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), both the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) and the seeds of non-arising are said to be "not produced" and thus severed;

however, the seeds of distinct retributive wholesome karma and neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas still remain manifest. Therefore, when one later becomes free from bonds, this constitutes the severance of bonds through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
As for the wholesome karma and neutral dharmas within the bodies of other humans and devas—whether in their active manifestations or as seeds—they are likewise [severed].

This is the path of cultivation that abandons bondage through severance; because it does not contradict [correct] vision and because it is neither pervasive nor subject to rebirth, the Commentary states:
"The evil realms, humans, and devas should be understood accordingly.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "Although there are seven births" to "none are received again," the intent of this question is: having attained the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)...

If one who has reached the peak of existence among gods and humans attains the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) after undergoing at most seven births, they will not be reborn in the higher realms;

since there is no eighth birth in the desire realm thereafter, this constitutes the complete abandonment of the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) belonging to the higher realms. How, then, can it be said that there is no complete severance?

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage "However, as for the stream-enterer who has already become a non-returner," the intended meaning is that because a stream-enterer can attain the state of a non-returner and be reborn in the higher realms, one cannot say that [the afflictions] have been completely severed.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* provides a general discussion based on this point, stating that there is no case of complete severance;
this answers the preceding question.

[Commentary]: Regarding those who have not returned to the desire realm (*anāgāmin*) but whose attainment of all stages is indeterminate: their intention is that they have departed from the desire realm; however, their status regarding the upper realms is indeterminate.

This means that some may realize the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) within the desire realm itself; or some may, following the stage of non-returner, successively give rise to the two upper realms and attain the state of no-more-learning;
or there are those of sharp faculties who leap over the fruits and do not arise in the upper realms, while those of dull faculties proceed sequentially.
Because one has attained the fruit, it arises in the higher realms; thus it is said to be "indeterminate. This applies both before and after, answering the previous question.
If an Arhat were to sever all links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), this yoga would be exactly the same as the present text.

[Commentary: Regarding the intent of this section, which also explains the "portions of abandonment" (*prahāṇa-bhāga*) of the fruits, it means that herein it is further clarified how the twelve links are abandoned at the stages of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Specifically, as in the case of the first two fruits, all or a portion of the *bhava-aṅga* (the link of existence) belonging to the desire realm is abandoned;
for the non-returner fruit, all *bhava-aṅga* of the desire realm is abandoned; and for the Arhat, all [links] of the three realms are abandoned.
The exhaustion of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) refers to the delimitation of the twelve links through the abandonment [attained] in the four untainted fruits (*anāsrava-phala*).
Alternatively, regarding the fruit of the non-percipient heaven (*asaṃjñisattva*), it is called "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), and so forth, as previously explained.

[Treatise]: From "ten [faculties] associated with pleasure and equanimity" up to "the true meaning": in these various holy teachings (*āgama*), [the terms are used] according to the predominance of their respective characteristics.

Regarding the statement "it is not fixed," this also intends to show that while the twelve links are associated with the three types of feeling (*vedanā*), according to this treatise, ten links are associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*);
twelve links are associated with painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*); eleven links are partially subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*);

twelve links are partially subsumed under the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); and twelve links are entirely subsumed under the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

As for what is subsumed [within these categories], all of these are merely conventional designations; that is, they are designated as being associated with pleasure or equanimity in reference to the future states of birth and old age.

Now, if one speaks according to the actual reality of the meaning, among the twelve links, if the links of ignorance and formations were to take up birth, old age, and death—since within these six bases there already exist manifest minds and mental factors—[the aforementioned associations would not hold].

Therefore, within the branch of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), when it is associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) or neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), these six branches can likewise possess the modes of suffering:

the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). As for the other five branches, such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth, they all possess the nature of being seeds;

since these six branches have not yet arisen as manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), how could the mind and its mental bases (*citta-caittas*) be associated with the three types of feeling or the three types of suffering?
Regarding the corresponding question: although there are no three types of feeling (*vedanā*), does it follow that there are no three types of suffering (*duḥkha*)?

Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are suffering, if one were to establish the three types of suffering based on the three types of feeling, then since present feeling lacks the cause of suffering, how could they be established? Therefore, these six bases lack both the three types of feeling and the three types of suffering.
That which is called "existent" is entirely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*). If one says that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are... [the text continues].
Regarding the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*): the twelve links of dependent origination, without exception, are all subsumed under the suffering of conditioned formations.

The answer states that they are designated as the suffering of conditioned formations based on the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), because within these [twelve] links, the suffering of conditioned formations exists only within the six links beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, this is because the feeling of equanimity arises and becomes manifest in these stages. Moreover, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* explains that "birth" (*jāti*) manifests the suffering of conditioned formations, while "aging" (*jarā*) manifests the suffering of disintegration (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

The suffering of death manifests as the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "Ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases are called the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*);

contact and feeling are called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); and the feeling of suffering is itself birth, old age, and death, which are called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
As stated in these scriptural authorities, these are all mutually dependent designations.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this refers to the fact that [feeling] can arise simultaneously with a single consciousness," the meaning is as follows: if one considers the operation of a single consciousness, three types of feeling cannot arise concurrently;
therefore, it is said that "feeling does not associate with feeling. However, when discussing multiple consciousnesses, it is possible for the three types of feeling to arise together.

For example, while there may be pleasant feeling in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), painful feeling in the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), and [neutral feeling] in the olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*).
The meaning of "equanimity" (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is somewhat broader. [Commentary]:
The intent behind stating here that they are "associated" (*samprayukta*) and "coexistent" (*sahabhū*) up to the point of "not coexisting with feeling" is this:

it explains that the three feelings are associated with the currently active mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), which is termed "coexistence. This is like asking: with what feeling is a single consciousness associated?
They should all be called "simultaneous" (*sahabhū*). It is not that two feelings arise together within a single moment of consciousness;

thus it is said that "feeling does not coexist with feeling. When it says "it is not that what exists in the world is called simultaneous," this does not mean that two feelings arise at the same time.
"World" (*loka*) here carries the meaning of "time-period" (*adhvan*). Furthermore, regarding the twelve links of dependent origination in the future, [only] excluding...

The remaining eleven members [of dependent origination], with the exception of the member of sensation (*vedanā*), are all associated with painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*), because within the state of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) there is painful sensation;
therefore, the remaining eleven members in the state of old age and death are all associated with painful sensation, because within the state of old age and death there is suffering and affliction.
Thus it is said that in the state of old age and death, sorrow, lamentation, and other forms of suffering arise predominantly.

[Commentary]: Regarding the first point among those cited from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (the "Great Treatise") concerning what is to be eliminated, the intent is as follows: this is a citation of scriptural evidence. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that "pleasure" (*sukha*) is to be eliminated.
Second, [this refers to] that which corresponds only to the twelve links [of dependent origination]; here, one eliminates the two links of sensation (*vedanā*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

As for "suffering-sensation" (*duḥkhavedanā*) and the first among those to be eliminated, this refers to suffering-sensation and the link of old age and death among the two links previously mentioned for elimination.

Because they do not correspond with the factor of feeling (*vedanā*), it is said that within the three doors of feeling, the two factors of pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) may coexist with ten factors, while painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) may coexist with twelve factors;
thus, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and this treatise are in agreement.

[Commentary]: Regarding the intent of this section, from the specific explanation up to the statement that "sorrow and joy are explained like suffering and pleasure," it means that while the previous discussion addressed the association with the three feelings (*vedanā*), if one explains sorrow and joy specifically in relation to the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*), they are explained as being identical to suffering and pleasure, with no further distinct meaning.
[Commentary]: Because the stage of the birth-link (*jāti-aṅga*) is broad, there are those who experience pleasant and neutral sensations (*sukha-upekṣā-vedanā*).

"The birth-link is broad" means that from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until one reaches the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*) and before it undergoes decay and transformation, all are subsumed under the birth-link; during this interval, it is not precluded that pleasant or neutral sensations may arise.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "a portion of the eleventh" to "also constitutes the suffering of change," the intent is as follows:

since we are now explaining the three types of suffering (*tri-duḥkhatā*) in relation to the classification of the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), they can coexist with feeling (*vedanā*). However, the suffering of change is established upon the first eleven links, excluding only the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
This is because the suffering of change is established based on pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), whereas at the stage of old age and death, there is no longer any such pleasant feeling.

Question: Since there is no pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) in the links from old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) upwards, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*) is not established there. However, regarding the eleven links [from ignorance to existence], the question arises:

just as the suffering of change can be established for the links of consciousness and so forth, and for the link of existence (*bhava*), where pleasant feelings may potentially exist within the positions of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and formations (*saṃskāra*), how can the suffering of change also be established for those [links] that are not associated with pleasant feeling?

Answer: [The suffering of change is established there because] even though they are not associated with pleasant feeling, they are nonetheless subject to transformation. Furthermore, since the nature of conditioned phenomena is such that they inevitably undergo change, the suffering of change is established based on this very fact of transformation. Thus, even in the absence of pleasant feeling, the suffering of change is applicable.

Otherwise, if one does not recognize that consciousness and the other factors are associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), then the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) could not be established upon those members of dependent origination, because pleasant feeling would be absent there.

Now, since it is stated that pleasant feeling is admitted to exist even during the stage when consciousness and the others arise, consciousness and the rest are indeed concomitant with pleasant feeling;
therefore, the suffering of change can likewise be established upon consciousness and the other factors. This is merely in terms of their association with...
Regarding the statement that [feeling] is "concomitant" (*sahagata*), this is not said in reference to its association with a specific body of consciousness; therefore, there is no contradiction.

For instance, when a pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) arises within the sixth consciousness or the five sensory consciousnesses, because the eighth consciousness and others are constantly present, it is said to be "concomitant" with the pleasant feeling.

It is "concomitant" in the sense of being simultaneous (*saha*); based on this principle, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) is established. As for the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), it is as follows.

This should also be understood by analogy. To answer the question of why it is necessary to establish the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) specifically upon pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*):
it is because this pleasant feeling is the object of attachment for all sentient beings, and its state is characterized by being produced through conjunction.

Thus, [the Buddha] made known that while such pleasant feelings do not encompass the suffering of change, how is it that you sentient beings cling to them with the notion that they are truly happiness? Therefore, based on this...

Regarding the statement that "pleasurable feeling constitutes a portion of the suffering of change (vipariṇāma-duḥkha) within eleven [links]," this refers specifically to the suffering of change to clarify that these eleven links do not correspond to the other types of suffering;
hence it is called "a portion."

[Commentary: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts state that "a portion of the factors associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and those not associated with feeling (*avedanā*) constitute the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
The explanation is as follows: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* establishes the three types of suffering based on the three feelings;

namely, it establishes the suffering of change based on pleasant feeling, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) based on painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*), and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) based on neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Regarding the phrase "associated with feeling":

The "branches" (aṅga) refer to those previously mentioned: the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) and the ten branches, with the exception of the branch of feeling (*vedanā-aṅga*) and the branch of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa-aṅga*).
As for that which does not coexist with feeling (*na vedanā-sahagata-aṅga*), this refers to the branch of feeling itself;
since this branch of feeling is not associated (*saṃprayukta*) with feeling—because feeling is not mutually associated with feeling—it is therefore called the "non-feeling-coexistent branch. Now...

One takes up the ten factors that accompany pleasure (*sukha-sahagata*) along with the factor of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); these eleven factors in total are called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

Since this factor of sensation is also said to possess pleasure, and since it is established as the suffering of change based on its equality [with other states], one takes up the factor of sensation.
This is the same as the theory of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "one portion," this refers to the twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), which encompass the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

Here, excluding the suffering of suffering and the suffering of conditioned existence, only the suffering of change is taken; therefore, it is called "one portion. The subsequent twelve links likewise pertain to all three types of suffering, yet they exclude the suffering of conditioned existence and the suffering of change.
The commentary’s statement regarding "one portion" should also be understood according to this principle.
[Commentary] Therefore, the tenth [chapter] states: "The factors associated with painful feeling up to a portion of them constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
Regarding "factors associated with painful feeling," this refers to the previously mentioned painful feeling being associated with eleven of the members, excluding the member of feeling itself.
Furthermore, "factors not associated with feeling" refers to the member of feeling itself, because feeling does not associate with feeling. Thus it is said.

Therefore, it is said that feeling (*vedanā*) is not a factor that accompanies feeling; rather, the eleven factors [of the dependent origination] are now taken as the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Furthermore, because there is also suffering within the factor of painful feeling (*duḥkhā-vedanā*), the suffering of suffering is established based on that painful feeling. Thus, it is stated that twelve parts of the factors are subsumed under the suffering of suffering.
As for the phrase "one part," this should be understood by analogy with the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the classification based on the three types of sensation (*vedanā*), this establishes the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*) by means of those three sensations.

As previously stated, the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) coexists with ten of the [twelve] links; whereas pleasure (*sukha*) and pain (*duḥkha*) coexist with ten and eleven links respectively. Here, suffering is established based on eleven links.

By analogy, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are excluded, because within the state of old age and death there is neither pleasure nor pain. Since the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is established here based on the sensation of equanimity, old age and death are excluded.

Regarding the statement that the limb of death (*maraṇāṅga*) is explained in the same way as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*): because the suffering of change is established based on pleasure (*sukha*), and since there is no pleasure-feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) in the state of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), there is no suffering of change in that state.

Now, because [the suffering of] formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*) is established based on equanimity (*upekṣā*), and since there is no equanimity-feeling in the state of old age and death, there is no suffering of formations in that state;

therefore, it is said to be explained in the same way as the suffering of change. As for the phrase "previously accompanied by equanimity-feeling and pleasure-feeling": [this refers to the fact that] in the prior stage, it was associated with both equanimity and pleasure.
Regarding "because it is the same as feeling": in the section on the "simultaneous gate" (*sahabhū-mukha*) previously discussed, there were ten types of pleasant and neutral feelings;

however, in the stages of old age and death, pleasant feelings and so forth do not exist, and only neutral feeling (*upekṣā*) is possible. Therefore, it is said that they are the same as feeling because they share the same nature as pleasant feeling.

[Commentary]: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 10, states that all "two branches of suffering" refer to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

The underlying intent is that both the suffering of suffering and the suffering of change are subsumed under the pervasive suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), as they are all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*).

Therefore, this treatise says that twelve factors are entirely subsumed under the suffering of conditioned formations. The meaning of the statement that there are factors of the suffering of conditioned formations which are not included within the two [other] sufferings is that there are indeed such cases.
The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) does not refer to the two meanings of the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

This is because that which is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā-sahagata-aṅga*)—that is, the factors associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—is precisely the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

The intended meaning is that the feeling of equanimity, together with the factors that do not accompany feeling (*avedita-sahagata-aṅga*), constitute eleven factors in total; these are established as being categorized under the suffering of conditioned existence, rather than being subsumed within the sufferings of pain or change.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "and those factors not co-arising with feeling" (*vedanā-sahabhū-anga*), the intention is that the factor of feeling (*vedanā-anga*) does not arise simultaneously with itself; thus, it is called a "factor not co-arising with feeling.

Therefore, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are excluded. This is because within the state of old age and death, there is no possibility of relinquishing [the nature of suffering], as it is based on relinquishment that one speaks of "suffering-as-conditioned-process" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
The *Mahāśāstra* (Great Treatise) agrees with this text, also stating that within the state of old age and death, there is no...

Because it involves pleasure (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and neutrality, it is called "one part" (*ekadeśa*); it is termed "one part" in contrast to the two feelings of suffering (*duḥkha*) and pleasure.

[Commentary: Regarding the manifestation of the aspect [of suffering] in terms of time, when the state of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is manifest, it is based on that very state of equanimity that the aspect of "suffering as conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is established and made manifest.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the two [types of] suffering are made manifest when associated with the two [types of] feeling," the intention is that the characteristic of *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (suffering due to change) is most manifest when established in relation to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), and the characteristic of *duḥkha-duḥkhatā* (suffering as suffering itself) is most manifest when established in relation to painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*).

Thus, it is said that because the three characteristics of suffering are made manifest when established in association with the three types of feeling, the word "with" (*yǔ*) is placed [at the beginning].
[Commentary: This explains the two stages based on the substantial entity (*dravya*) and its manifest characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). What are these two stages? First, the substantial entity;
second, the manifest characteristics. The following passage provides its own explanation: "The actual meaning subsumes suffering.
This refers to the conclusion of the aforementioned meaning of suffering.

[Commentary: "Furthermore, within this treatise and others, there are two [categories], up to 'the majority' (*bhūyastvena*). This explains the two positions. First, "the whole entity and the majority encompass the three types of suffering" (*triduḥkhatā*);

this interprets the position of the actual substance (*dravya*). The meaning is as follows: if one discusses it according to the whole entity, then the majority encompasses the three sufferings; therefore, the treatise states:
"The twelve [links] in their entirety are subsumed under the suffering of conditioned phenomena (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); all contaminated (*sāsrava*) [phenomena]..."

Since all phenomena are characterized by the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), this [classification] is based on the majority; it does not preclude the fact that there are also other forms of suffering within them. Thus, the treatise states:
"Eleven [members] are for the most part subsumed under the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); twelve are for the most part subsumed under the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).
This explains the state where the characteristics are manifest. The intended meaning is that these [members] are simultaneous with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).

It is called "suffering of conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) because it is established based on the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), as its characteristic form is manifest therein. The *Śāstra* states:

"That is to say, the factors associated with the feeling of equanimity and so forth are called 'suffering of conditioned existence. This refers to the ten members [of dependent origination] as well as those factors not associated with feeling;

these are also called 'suffering' because they are themselves feeling. Thus, the eleven members are termed 'suffering of conditioned existence. As for the other two feelings associated with suffering, the intended meaning is that they are associated with the two [feelings] of pain (*duḥkha*) and pleasure (*sukha*)."

Because the factors associated with feeling (*vedanā-sahagata-aṅga*) are designated as "suffering due to suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) and "suffering due to change" (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), they rely upon two types of feeling to reach two types of suffering; thus, their characteristics are most manifest.
This is based on the majority of cases, yet it does not preclude that within those two types of suffering, the term "suffering" (*duḥkha*) may also apply generally.

Furthermore, regarding these two feelings, because their characteristics are distinct and manifest, they are established separately as "suffering. Thus, the Commentary states: "The other two feelings are collectively termed 'suffering' in the majority of cases," just as in the case of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).

That is to say, the eleven constituent links that function together with [the feeling of] pleasure, as well as those links that do not function together with feeling—namely, the link of pleasant feeling—are now also included.
That is, a portion of the eleven links is designated as the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), excluding the link of old age and death.

Furthermore, the eleven links that function together with painful feeling, as well as those links that do not function together with feeling—namely, the link of feeling itself—include a portion of the eleven links.

It is called "suffering as suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Therefore, in the section clarifying the characteristics [of the three types of suffering], the establishment of the three sufferings based on the three feelings is all explained according to the majority of cases.

[Commentary: The eighth stage of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states that the scripture cited is from the eighth chapter of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which quotes the sūtra itself to clarify the ten [stages].
Regarding the two branches, the Sūtra says:

[Commentary] As for the meaning of the statement that the treatise lacks an explanation: it is intended to mean that while that treatise merely states that the remaining factors of dependent origination are called "disintegration," it does not further explain that craving, grasping, existence, birth, old age, and death are termed the suffering of disintegration (*vibhava-duḥkha*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts that what accords with reason based on the universal nature of phenomena is as follows:

it has been explained above in this treatise that eleven [of the twelve links] constitute a portion of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*), one [link] constitutes a portion of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkha*), and the remaining twelve [links] in their entirety constitute the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkha*).
All of this is based on the tenth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Therefore, we know that what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* accords precisely with the truth.
The Principle.
[Commentary: Regarding the fact that various seeds are hidden and not discussed, there are two interpretations within the Commentary; this is the first interpretation.

According to this, among the five factors such as consciousness (*vijñāna*) within the causal stage, as well as the members of existence (*bhava-aṅga*), these are exclusively seeds; likewise, ignorance (*avidyā*), formative forces (*saṃskāra*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
Since these four and a half branches consist partly of seeds and partly of actual manifestations, it is said that among the twelve links of dependent origination there are three types of suffering,
though the seeds are hidden and not explicitly mentioned.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "Alternatively, it is said that at the time of the fruit, the cause is also manifested," this second interpretation means:

within these twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*), there are also the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*). Since they are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), they are all the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Because they coexist with both painful and pleasant sensations (*vedanā*), they possess two types of suffering;
thus, the treatise states, "Ten [links] are simultaneous," etc., as explained extensively above. Therefore, the first ten links also exist [at the time of the fruit].
The three types of suffering.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "conditioned phenomena are called formations because they are volitionally produced" up to "explained in accordance with their characteristics," the meaning of this text is explained as follows:
old age and death are associated with the three types of suffering; this refers to the sense of their arising.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the meaning of 'formative activity' (saṃskāra) increases the seeds for the future fruit," the intended meaning is that through ignorance (avidyā), one forms the seeds for the five fruits in conjunction with formative activities;
since these subsequently give rise to the fruits of birth and old age and death (jāti-jarāmaraṇa), the first seven members are said to be the basis for the future.

[Commentary]: This means that the substance (*svabhāva*) of the *vedanā* aggregate frequently gives rise to painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) up to the point where only the *vedanā* aggregate increases.

The intended meaning is that the substance of the *vedanā* aggregate is primarily designated as such with respect to bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*), and not solely with respect to the feeling associated with the eighth [consciousness].

Therefore, within the *vedanā* aggregate, painful feeling can arise; since both painful and pleasant feelings are collectively termed the *vedanā* aggregate, it is said that the *vedanā* aggregate frequently gives rise to suffering.

This is intended to reveal that among the various constituents of sensation (*vedanā*), these are suffering; specifically, it means that within the various links of dependent origination, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) increases primarily through sensation.

The meaning is that the suffering of all the links arises because the link of sensation grasps and undergoes transformation; thus, the suffering of suffering is established based on the link of sensation, which in turn depends upon contact (*sparśa*), and the subsequent sensations establish this suffering.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this suffering arises precisely at the time of maturation," the meaning is as follows:

"at the time of maturation" refers to the link of *bhava* (existence), because the six links [of the previous life] combined with moisture are designated as *bhava*. "This suffering arises precisely [then]" refers to the link of *jāti* (birth).

[Commentary]: "Transformation and decay" is termed *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* (the suffering of change). This statement that both old age and death are termed *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā* concludes the relationship between the primary factor (*karana*) and its result (*karya*).
As for the phrase "the suffering of change is likewise," the intention is as follows: because it results from the maturation and transformation [of the aggregates], it is called a "result" (*phala*);

within this state, one experiences this transformation and decay, which is termed *vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*. All these three types of suffering are explained according to their predominant characteristics. This concludes the preceding section.
This can be understood.
[The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "Because they are all resultant dharmas" means that the present ignorance and so forth are now the resultant dharmas of past birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "not having the meaning of being a cause," the intended meaning is that it is simply at the point of "invoking and eliciting" (*āva-han*) that it is termed "accumulation" (*samudaya*), and not that it refers to the analytical observation of causality.

[Commentary]: As for the statement that "the aggregate of suffering and the aggregate of accumulation are one and the same thing, yet two are spoken of because they are cause and effect," the intent is that the Sarvāstivādins maintain that suffering...

The two truths of origination (*samudaya*) are in fact one and the same thing; it is from the perspective of the cause that it is called origination, and from the perspective of the result that it is called suffering (*duḥkha*).
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the truth of suffering is broad, extending even to all that is origination," the intention is as follows:

because the truth of suffering is broad and encompasses everything that is suffering, the truth of origination—which consists of outflows (*āsrava*)—can also be termed suffering. However, in terms of the meaning of "invoking retribution for future existence" (*punarbhava*), suffering itself is not origination.

[Commentary]: Regarding the meaning of "accumulation" (*samudaya*) as having retribution: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 55, states: Question: What is the meaning of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*)? Answer:

It is the meaning of formations (*saṃskāra*) produced by afflictions (*kleśa*). Question: What is the meaning of the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*)? Answer: It is the meaning of that which can produce the Truth of Suffering. Question:

Can it be admitted that tainted unwholesome karma and the unwholesome nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the desire realm are capable of obtaining the accumulation of ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*)? [End of quotation]

Question: If the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the two upper realms is exclusively obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), and if the craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) that truly moisten rebirth in all three realms are likewise of an obscured-unspecified nature, how can they bring about the ripening of fruits, and how can they be subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)?
Answer: Because the member of ignorance in the upper realms, as well as that craving and grasping, are capable of producing karma, they are indeed the Truth of Origination.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the seeds of the two untainted paths are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) and are not members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are two interpretations.

First, it is said that the untainted path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are called the "two untainted paths. Second, it is said that the paths of those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are called the "two untainted paths.
Furthermore, it is argued that this is incorrect, for while there are those beyond training, there is no actual manifestation (*samudācāra*) of the untainted [path] in them.

Since it is stated that one must include the phrase "untainted seeds" (*anāsrava-bīja*), and given that the seeds of the two untainted paths are clearly understood, these are the originally existing untainted seeds of the two paths of the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the application (*prayoga*).
Based on this principle, the two paths of the provisions and the application receive the designation "untainted";

as such, they are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). If the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* is consistent with this passage, then it is what the commentary (*ṭīkā*) has cited.

The text is difficult to understand at first glance; I shall now cite it in full. Question: How many members (aṅga) are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) as suffering in the present life?
Answer: Two, namely birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarā-maraṇa*). Question: How many members are subsumed under the Truth of Suffering as suffering in the future life? Answer:

From the member of consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to the seed-nature of sensation (*vedanā*). Question: How many members are subsumed under the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)? Answer: The remaining members; therefore, there are five members [of the Truth of Origination].
[The text says:

"Aggregation. [Commentary: "If it were not so—that is, if consciousness were not considered a causal condition for name-and-form (nāmarūpa) in the manner previously explained as immediate succession—then consciousness would likewise serve as a causal condition for name-and-form through a series of successive stages."
This means that they are designated as "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) with reference to the results of birth, aging, and death that are yet to arise.

The intended meaning is that although these [factors such as] consciousness and so forth were not explained in immediate succession as in the previous case, here they are explained according to a temporal interval; thus, the five branches beginning with consciousness, when viewed in relation to the future birth, aging, and death, also qualify as causes and conditions.
That is to say, they are termed "intervening" because they are separated by the branch of existence (*bhava*) and others.
[Commentary]: The meaning of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*’s statement that "arising and drawing-forth are simultaneous" is as follows:

if the consciousness and so forth have already been moistened, then the seeds of the drawn-forth consciousness and so forth are simultaneously capable of producing the [subsequent] members of dependent origination.

[Commentary]: Now, regarding the mutual relationship between seeds and the contiguous factors of the members [of dependent origination], the intent is to explain that here, with respect to the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*) and the seed [of its subsequent member], they cannot function as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
For example, the seed of consciousness in relation to the seed of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-bīja*) is not a causal condition;

likewise, name-and-form in relation to the seeds of the six [sense bases] is also not a causal condition, and so on, up to the seed of contact (*sparśa-bīja*) in relation to the seed of sensation (*vedanā-bīja*), which is also not [a causal condition].
The meaning of "conditioned cause" (*nidāna*) is as follows: the factors of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) that have already been moistened are considered conditioned causes with respect to arising;

however, the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), while in their state as seeds and not yet moistened, are therefore not conditioned causes with respect to arising. If one speaks of them in immediate succession, these seeds may indeed function as conditioned causes with respect to the manifest states (*samudācāra*).

[Commentary]: This refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which does not state that karma is the causal condition for the branch of consciousness (*vijñāna*) within the ten stages of dependent origination.
The intent of this passage is as follows: since it does not state that karma is the cause of the branch of consciousness, the seeds of karma do not stand in a causal relationship to consciousness.
Why is this so? It is because their natures are different.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because the manifest *saṃskāra* is viewed in relation to the *vijñāna* branch of the seeds of *saṃskāra*," the intended meaning is as follows:
because the manifest *saṃskāra* perfumes the seeds of *saṃskāra*, these very seeds of *saṃskāra* are designated as the *vijñāna* branch.

Therefore, while *saṃskāra* acts as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for *vijñāna*, in the previous [section]—where it was based on their differing natures—it was stated that *saṃskāra* is not a causal condition for *vijñāna*. Now, however, because it actually brings about [the result], it is called *saṃskāra*.
The category called the "consciousness link" possesses causes and conditions, as will be explained below when reconciling conflicting passages.
[Commentary] The meaning of the phrase "this is based on distinct entities rather than sequential stages" is as follows:

within this *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, that which is designated by the name "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is taken as the "ignorance link," and other dharmas are not taken as the "ignorance link. Therefore, in relation to "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*), ignorance...

Regarding the statement that "formations (saṃskāra) are expected to have no causes or conditions in relation to consciousness," and so forth, even the limb of formations is understood by way of the name "karma.
One does not take other dharmas as being the limb of formations; the same applies to all others. In the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, this is explained by means of specific stages (*avasthā*):
when the teacher says that the five aggregates do not exist simultaneously with ignorance, he is referring to this particular stage [as the limb of ignorance].
Therefore, it is said that ignorance (avidyā) is established as a condition for formative forces (saṃskāra);

furthermore, the Sarvāstivādins also clarify the twelve links by establishing them as conditions for formative forces based on their respective stages. Since this is not the case here, they are not [mere] conditions.
[Commentary: The meaning of the statement in that treatise, "Taking ignorance as an example, the others are likewise," is as follows:

taking ignorance in relation to formations (*saṃskāra*) as an example of having causes and conditions, it is shown that [ignorance] also acts as a cause and condition in relation to consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so on, up to aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) in relation to old age and death (*jāti-jarāmaraṇa*).
This is done to demonstrate, by way of illustration, the sense of having causes and conditions for ignorance.

[Commentary]: That treatise states only that ignorance serves as three conditions for formative action (*saṃskāra*) with respect to form (*rūpa*). The intended meaning is that ignorance serves only as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for formative action with respect to form.
This is because the present link of ignorance, when compared to the formative actions of body and speech, cannot take those bodily and vocal formative actions as its object;

since these bodily and vocal formations are themselves material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), they are incapable of taking a preceding moment of ignorance as their objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Thus, for the two [actions of] body and speech, [ignorance lacks an objective condition].
Since karma is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*) and does not arise from the condition of equal and immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it lacks that condition;
there is only the single predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that it serves as three conditions for formless action (*ārūpya-karma*), the intent is to explain that the manifest member of ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as a condition for the manifest mind (*manas*).

The mental karma of the volitional formation factor has three conditions: namely, the manifesting ignorance of the preceding moment induces the manifesting mental volitional formation of the succeeding moment;

therefore, it possesses the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Because the manifesting mental volition of the succeeding moment can take the ignorance of the preceding moment as its object, it possesses the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is the broadest in scope, and its meaning is necessarily established. Question: What [is this]?
Therefore, why not state that ignorance conditions formations, rather than stating that formations are conditioned by ignorance? Answer:

Here, we speak according to the sequence of the arising of characteristics. Since the mind and its mental factors, as effects, must necessarily arise from an object, when present activity takes ignorance as its object, this is precisely ignorance producing formations.
If one says that ignorance can take formations as its object, then it is the formations that serve as the object.
If ignorance were instead produced from formations, the principle that "ignorance conditions formations" would not be established.
If one were to grant such a view, how could it be that death serves as a condition for birth? Therefore, we know this is not the case.
[Commentary] This refers to when a form-possessing [dharma], in relation to a form-possessing limb, serves as a single predominant condition;

this is the meaning of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Treatise on Consciousness-Only) compiled by the Śramaṇa Ruli of Fushou Monastery in the Western Capital, Volume Eleven, Part One.

[Commentary]: The reason for the name [of these afflictions] is precisely the derivation of the two terms "cause" (*hetu*) and "condition" (*pratyaya*). "Cause" refers to the primary delusion, while "condition" refers to that which assists the delusion. [Commentary]:

Regarding the phrase "within uncontaminated karma, excluding non-discriminative [wisdom], because it arises in dependence upon objects," this asks about the preparatory application (*prayoga*), the faculties (*indriya*), and so forth.
Question: Are both the fundamental [wisdom] and the subsequently attained wisdom called "non-conceptual"? Answer: They are not all called non-conceptual. Question:

If they are all non-conceptual, I do not yet understand what the difference between them is. Answer: Although they are non-conceptual, their meanings differ: the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) lacks inverted conceptualization;
the wisdom of the essential nature (*mūla-jñāna*) lacks investigative conceptualization; and the subsequently attained wisdom lacks erroneous conceptualization.

Since these three types are all characterized by conceptual discrimination, they are all termed "non-conceptual" [only in a specific sense]. Here, we take only the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom that arises with respect to phenomena as its object,
and do not include the non-conceptual wisdom that takes the established Four Truths as its object, because the latter has the principle of the Four Truths as its object.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the projecting and completing karma," the intended meaning is that within this [category] there are two types of karma: the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karma*), which can only project the eighth [consciousness], the primary retributive fruit;
and the completing karma (*paripūraka-karma*), which can only complete the fruit, namely the distinct retributions of maturation (*vipāka*).

Therefore, these two types of karma—projecting and completing—are termed the "limb of formations" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*). Question: Why, among the preceding twelve limbs, is it only the projecting karma that is called "karma," while the other is not?
Question: Regarding "fulfilling karma" (*pūrṇakarma*), this current passage states that karma generally encompasses both projecting (*ākṣepa*) and fulfilling karma. Answer:

Within the previous twelve links, because they cause birth and death to continue in succession, only projecting karma was mentioned; however, in this current passage, because it concerns general adornment, fulfilling karma is also included.
Since each is based on a single specific meaning, there is no contradiction between them.
[Commentary] The phrase "directly inducing," etc., intends to clarify that because of this [state], there are neither completing karmas (*pūrṇakarma*) nor contaminated karmas (*sāsravakarma*);
it is these two types of karma that cause birth and death to continue in succession.
[Commentary]: Regarding "no fulfillment," it is like the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). As for the meaning of "directly inducing":
suppose, for instance, that the impure wholesome or unwholesome ripening causes can directly induce the ripening fruit so that the continuum is obtained;

likewise, the fulfilled and discriminative karma—just like wholesome and unwholesome karma—can also cause the body to obtain a continuum by supporting the body of prior karma so that its continuum is maintained.
It is said to be "like a ripening cause" (*vipāka-hetu*) because it abides [as a support].

[Commentary: The phrase "it does not have direct power because [the result] arises from this" means that while the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) assist the two types of karma in producing birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), they do not possess direct power;
rather, birth arises from this [karma], and there is no continuous succession [of birth] apart from this.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "The obstacle of afflictions" to "taking up moisture for rebirth," the meaning is as follows: here, the afflictions that initiate karma (*karmābhisamskāra*) are not included;

although those [afflictions] were previously taken to initiate karma and produce the seeds of the five fruits such as consciousness (*vijñāna*), once that is complete, one must still rely on afflictions to provide moisture for rebirth.
Therefore, only all the afflictions that moisten for rebirth are termed the "obstacle of afflictions. Question: Why are only those that moisten for rebirth included?
Question: Does it take up the afflictions that initiate karma? Answer: If it takes up the afflictions that initiate karma, it is not equal to those that complete karma;
if it takes up the afflictions that moisten rebirth, then they are equal. Therefore, like the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they do not initiate karma.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)... or those which grasp everything like the moisture of afflictions," the intended meaning is as follows:
although the categories of cognitive obstructions are numerous, only those that take the Buddha or sentient beings as their object are designated as cognitive obstructions.

Therefore, it is said that if one does not grasp at bodhi or sentient beings as being substantially real, there is no basis for giving rise to intense compassion and vows. Furthermore, it says, "or those which grasp... [and so forth].
All cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are capable of acting as conditions for the transformation of birth-and-death (*pariṇāmika-janma-maraṇa*).
Just as all afflictions (*kleśa*) throughout the entire realm are capable of linking rebirth, so too do all cognitive obstructions assist in the transformation of birth-and-death.

Furthermore, because the cognitive obstruction serves as the basis for that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*), if this obstruction were absent, that [transformation] would certainly not exist; therefore, it is taken in its entirety.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it is easily seen," this refers to the fact that when one observes with the eye that the five aggregates have fixed limits—ranging from a maximum of eighty thousand years down to a minimum of ten years—it is easily known; this refers specifically to the wisdom of the sixth consciousness.

[Commentary]: "A portion" (*bhāga*) or "a segment" (*avasthā*) and so forth are called "divided segments" (*bhāga-avasthā*); this refers precisely to the death of the present body and the birth of a subsequent body. [Commentary]:
It is not that those in the mundane world, nor those who have turned their minds toward the various heavens and so forth, can perceive it;

even the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) who has entered the stage of transformation (*parināmika-bhāga*), as well as the *arhat* of divided segments (*bhāga-arhat*), are all unable to see it. The meaning is that [the Buddha] says this because they lack the capacity to perceive it.
What is seen is only the body of segmented birth; whether ordinary person or sage, all fail to see the body of transformation. It is said that even one who has attained the divine eye cannot see it.
Those such as the Bodhisattvas of the four fruits, once they have entered the single category of the body of transformation, each see only those of their own kind.
However, while those above can see those below, those below cannot see those above. This is like when one who has attained the first fruit undergoes the body of transformation.
Those in the upper three fruits do not see one another’s transformation-bodies; they see only those of their own kind.

If those in the upper fruits undergo transformation, they not only see those of their own kind, but also see the transformation-bodies of those in the lower three fruits, even up to the Bodhisattvas who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment] and those of sudden awakening.
Although there are cases where they share the same transformation-body, those in the lower stages do not see the bodies of those in the higher stages.

Those in higher stages can see one another, and they can also see the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of those in lower stages. Furthermore, these transformation bodies can be seen by those with physical eyes (*māṃsacakṣus*).
Even those with the *divyacakṣus* (heavenly eye) who have attained the stage of segmented existence (*bhavasaṃdhi*) cannot see them.
Question: Can a Bodhisattva in the second stage, who still undergoes segmented existence, see a Bodhisattva in the first stage who has received the transformation body? Answer: Yes.

They are able to see [beings] of the second bhūmi because their faculties are weak while their wisdom is strong; they also see the subtle bodies of the transformation-rebirth (pariṇāma-vaśika) of lower stages, which differ from those of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha arhats because the latter have dull faculties.

Furthermore, although they are all alike in being of the first bhūmi, there are those with the body of分段死 (bheda-maraṇa, fragmented death) and those with the body of 變易死 (pariṇāma-maraṇa, transformation-death);

thus, those of the same class see only one another’s *svalakṣaṇa* (specific characteristics), and even those with the body of fragmented death do not see the bodies of transformation-death. This applies to the first bhūmi as well.
Whether it be the *pariccheda* (segmented) or the *pariṇāma* (transformative) [death], Bodhisattvas cannot see one another.
Since the *pariccheda*-body of a second-stage (*dvitīya-bhūmi*) Bodhisattva is not seen, how could they see the land where that second-stage Bodhisattva dwells?

It is just as among the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*), those below cannot see the bodies or lands of those above, because their merits possess degrees of strength and weakness. Thus it is.
[Commentary]: Regarding the fact that there are already two interpretations in the seventh [fascicle], within that same fascicle there are the explanations of two masters.

The first master says that for a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment (*tunwu*), the retention of the body occurs only after [the exhaustion of karma] in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*); those of the Two Vehicles who have turned their minds toward [Mahāyāna] are equal to this, as they retain the body after [exhausting karma] in the Desire Realm.

The second master says that some allow for the retention of the body in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) for Śrāvakas who have turned their minds toward [Mahāyāna], with the sole exception of the five [types of Arhats].
The Śuddhāvāsa devas are also as extensively described previously.

[Note: Regarding the statement that through the power of compassionate vows one attains birth until reaching what is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), a question arises: according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, a bodhisattva retains afflictions (*kleśa*) in order to realize all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
yet here it is said that compassionate vows can bring about rebirth until the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood. Are these not contradictory? Furthermore...
Question: Since birth is brought about solely by compassionate vows, what need is there for afflictions (*kleśa*)? Furthermore, why do they not cease for a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva? Answer:
Prior to the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one undergoes birth through the division of segments (*pariccheda*); from the eighth stage onward, because it does not obstruct the Path, they do not cease.
Question: If that is so, they should not be defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*). As for defiled phenomena, why would they not cease? Answer: It is like the *manas*.

Although delusions are eliminated last, they may still be termed "defiled"; this is not a fault. Furthermore, because they can assist the *jñeya* (the knowable) to undergo transformation and continuity, they are not severed.

If that is so, when those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) turn their minds [toward Mahāyāna], they should not undergo transformation, as they lack afflictions.
Answer: There are the latencies (*vāsanā*) of delusions which can act as auxiliary conditions, and thus they too undergo transformation; this is stated according to the first interpretation.

[Commentary: The statement that "the limits of this karma for this continent are not fixed" intends to clarify that while the specific divisions [of rebirth] are subject to variation, the karma pertaining to a particular realm and level is entirely determinate.
"This karma" refers to contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karma and the like.

"This continent" and "this realm" refer to the place where the fruits of such segmented [rebirths] are experienced. It should be understood as meaning: "By means of such karma, one is born among humans or devas."

The phrase "middle and so forth" refers to the earth and other realms; according to their respective capacities, they abide and undergo transformation, which is designated as the fixed limit of that transformation.
[Commentary]: Here, "this karma, this continent, this realm, this earth," etc., indicates that this karma is untainted (anāsrava) karma.
This continent, realm, and earth are the locations where the fruit of transformation is received. Because this untainted state has no fixed limit, it is called "transformation."
