The *Yì* (Change) [treatise] states that because the four dhyānas and untainted (*anāsrava*) states nourish this physical basis, causing the body’s length and duration to be indefinite, it is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*).
[Commentary:
The meaning of the phrase "as nourishing the body of the Bṛhatphala Heaven in the Form Realm, so too is it for humans and devas in the Desire Realm" is as follows: this...

This refers to a specific instance and has two interpretations. One says: for example, if a Bodhisattva undergoes transformation-rebirth (*pariṇāmikī-janman*), they utilize untainted meditative concentration and vows to sustain this former body, causing it to become vast and surpass the bodies of those in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Since the bodies of those gods are sixteen thousand *yojanas* in height, the [Bodhisattva’s] body, being sustained by these [powers], exceeds that of those gods; thus it is said.
Regarding the statement that "passing sixteen thousand *yojanas* means passing sixteen thousand *kalpas*":

because the Bodhisattva has attained the transformation-body (*pariṇāmi-kāya*) and the necessarily untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, he extends his lifespan through these sustaining dharmas so that it exceeds that of the gods;

thus, he passes sixteen thousand *kalpas*, or perhaps less than that, depending on whether the sustaining dharmas are not fully perfected, or whether his body cannot exceed sixteen thousand [yojanas].
Their life span is six thousand *yojanas*, nor can it exceed sixteen thousand *kalpas*.
Thus, the dimensions of their bodies and the duration of their lives differ from those of the gods; hence it is said that they may be "less than those.
Why is this so? It is because by the power of the Bodhisattva’s vows, [the body] becomes long when required to be long and short when required to be short, being without fixed limit.
Therefore, it is said that there is no fixed limit, and the same applies to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

This means that among humans and devas in the desire realm who undergo transformation-death (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*), those who sustain their old bodies through untainted concentration and vows may now have a lifespan longer than what was induced by their former karma, or shorter than what was induced by their former karma;
since there is likewise no fixed limit, it is said that there is no fixed limit. Now...

Regarding "increasing or decreasing," this refers to the intentional resolve of the bodhisattvas. If a bodhisattva is reborn in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (the Ultimate Heaven), they do not obtain a transformation body (*pariṇāmika-kāya*).
A second interpretation states that if one is born in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, one necessarily obtains a transformation body;
that is, the very body supported by its original basis is further extended by sixteen thousand *yojanas*, and now exceeds that even more.
It is sixteen thousand kalpas; or it may be less than that because it is sustained by untainted (anāsrava) provisions, or perhaps the body merely manifests as the former body.
Why is it reduced? It is said to be so because of the intentional resolve of the Bodhisattva; the Desire Realm is likewise so. Question:
How can there be a turning of the mind in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven? Answer: Although there are Śrāvakas [there],...

Question: If those who are born there do not turn back their minds and proceed directly [to parinirvāṇa], then bodhisattvas who go straight on are also born there and likewise attain the transformation body (*pariṇāmika-kāya*).

However, according to the holy teachings, it is said that bodhisattvas of the great stages (*mahābhūmi*) are not born there. How then can they receive the transformation body in the Akaniṣṭha heaven? Answer:

Since the explanation in the previous fascicle also allows for the possibility of being born there, there is no contradiction in the sense of receiving the transformation body. For now, we rely upon this.

The previous explanation stated that the *rūpakāya* is five hundred *yojanas* in height; the present statement that it "exceeds five hundred *kalpas*" intends to say that among the Bṛhatphala deities in the fourth dhyāna, their bodies are five hundred *yojanas* tall and their lifespan is five hundred *kalpas*.

If a Bodhisattva receives a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) supported by untainted meditative concentration and vows, then because of the cause of that body, his own body and life may exceed those [of the Bṛhatphala deities].

Regarding "deva" or "that deva," the meaning is as previously explained in the commentary: the body of a Bṛhatphala (Great Fruit) deva exceeds five hundred yojanas, and his lifespan exceeds five hundred kalpas, though it may be slightly less than that.
Although the text concerning the Bṛhatphala is not recorded in this particular version of the commentary, the meaning is identical to the other versions, and thus both are acceptable.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas" up to "the untainted dharma-body of the inconceivable realm," the intent is as follows:
this text explains the reasons by contrasting the three vehicles’ state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); it does not discuss bodhisattvas attaining the body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*).

The meaning here is to address the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in their state of no-more-learning who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment]: although they have not yet attained the first bhūmi nor realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), [they are nonetheless capable of such a transformation].

Question: Since one attains the transformation body (*pariṇāma-kāya*) prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva], it is said that one has not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and has not yet attained freedom from the transformation body.
Answer: If that were so, a bodhisattva would have abandoned the transformation body upon realizing the selflessness of phenomena. Response: That is not so.

Although a bodhisattva has attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) selflessness of phenomena, they have not yet brought it to fulfillment. Why, then, have they not abandoned the transformation body? It is because they are not identical [to those who have].
The Tathāgata, by means of the Tathāgata, fulfills the dharma of selflessness;

therefore, he does not undergo the body of transformation (pariṇāmiki-kāya) but realizes the inconceivable realm of the untainted Dharma-body (anāsrava-dharmakāya). Regarding "death through transformation," the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"Death through transformation is the same as this treatise."

[Commentary]: "The arising of the various faculties of sensation" and "the ceasing of the various faculties of sensation upon death" mean that "sensation" (*vedanā*) refers to the experiencing of the five sense objects or the grasping of them;
"faculties of sensation" (*vedanendriya*) refers to the five material faculties; and "arising and ceasing" has the meaning of birth and death.
[Commentary]: "Mallikā" is translated here as "Fǎngzhě. This term has two meanings: first, a "mālā" (garland) worn upon the forehead is called *fǎng*, as it is highly esteemed by the world;
likewise, the Lady [Mallikā] was also held in high regard by the King, and thus she is called *fǎng*.

Furthermore, it is said that Lady Mallikā was originally a flower-gathering maidservant who nevertheless made offerings to the Buddha; she manifested herself to become the Queen of King Prasenajit. This...
The lady had a daughter whose appearance was so exceptionally beautiful that she surpassed her mother; thus she was named Śyāmāvatī, which means "Superior to Her Mother.
This is the very same Śyāmāvatī. Therefore, Prince Vimalakīrti is the younger brother of Lady Śyāmāvatī.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as if," it is used to illustrate the transformational rebirth (*pariṇāmi-kāya*) by means of the contrastive example of the birth-and-death body (*aupapāduka-kāya*); hence, it says "as if.
[Commentary]: Regarding the explanation of the "three kinds of mind-made bodies" (*manomaya-kāya*) produced here, these are:
the mind-made body of the *śrāvaka*, the mind-made body of the *pratyekabuddha*, and the mind-made body of the *bodhisattva* who has attained mastery.
[Commentary]: The *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states, "Outside the three realms... yet it is not outside the realms. The explanation says:
although these people are "this very [person]," that treatise speaks of three types of persons—namely, the Arhat, the Pratyekabuddha, and the sovereign Bodhisattva.

To say they are "outside the realms" is spoken in terms of their auxiliary causes; because they belong to untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) and are not bound by the realms, they are said to be "outside the three realms."
Since this body of transformation is *sāsrava* (with outflows), it does not exist outside the three realms; thus, the Commentary states:
"These three types all transform the former coarse bodies, etc. This explains why they do not exist outside the realms.
[Commentary: From "the ground of the dwelling of ignorance" up to "and arises," these five should be called the five *śikṣā-bhūmis* (grounds of training).
The *śikṣā-bhūmi* is precisely the seed; the five *vihāra-bhūmis* (grounds of abiding) are also seeds. However, regarding the two kinds of supports:

first, the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) serves as the supported, the locus of abiding, while the afflictive obscuration (*kleśāvaraṇa*) serves as the supporter, that which abides. Second, it is as follows:

The seeds of the two obstacles serve as the "abode" (*āśraya*) upon which they dwell, while the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of the two obstacles serve as the "dwellers" (*āśrita*) that depend upon it.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that there are these five *nivāsabhūmi*s (abiding grounds) such as ignorance due to repeated practice, the intended meaning is as follows:

sentient beings, through delusion and inversion, give rise to false discrimination, causing the various afflictions (*kleśa*) to increase gradually; for this reason, the Tathāgata established that there are five.

Question: Regarding the ignorance that abides in the ground (*mūla-vyavasthita-avidyā*), if ignorance did not exist previously and were newly arisen without prior perfuming (*vāsanā*), then since ignorance already existed previously, why would it arise again?
Answer: Although ignorance already existed previously, its functioning was weak;
therefore, it was not said to have the perfuming of ignorance. Because afflictions gradually increase, ignorance is established anew. Such is the inquiry.
According to the principle of reasoning, one should say that "dwelling on the ground" (*bhūmi-sthita*) means that the active manifestations dwell upon their seeds;
it is just as grasses and trees dwell depending upon the earth.
[Commentary]: The meaning of "this eighth ground" is that within the two aspects of characteristics (*nimitta*) and lands (*kṣetra*), the eighth ground has already...
"Attaining mastery" (*vaśitā*) refers to being unimpeded by the signs of objects, such as pure lands; it is so called in terms of mastery.
Furthermore, "mastery" means that whatever one transforms, such as the earth and other elements, all become gold, clarified butter, and so forth; therefore, it is called mastery.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "bodhisattvas on the great stages (*mahābhūmi*) and so forth" in the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, although the names are many, their underlying meaning is similar.
If one refers to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, a bodhisattva of the eighth stage is called a "Bodhisattva of Great Power" (*Mahābala*).
Therefore, the designation "Bodhisattva on the Great Stages" used in the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* is not contradictory [to other systems].
This is because Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are all designated as "Great Grounds" (*mahābhūmi*).

[Commentary: The phrase "merely transforming" intends to say that one merely transforms the old *paricchinna-vedanīya* (segmented) body into the present new *pariṇāma-vipākaja* (transformative-retribution) body.
This is like saying that when making clothes, one speaks of "making clothes," not "producing clothes"; for one produces something new by transforming an old object.
Therefore, [the *Shu*] states: "This does not exhaust the principle but merely follows the scriptural text.

The meaning is that the explanation in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (She lun) regarding the transformation of the body (*parināmikadeha*) for those of the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning and those bodhisattvas who have turned their minds and possess mastery, does not exhaust the principle; rather, it is presented here merely in accordance with the scriptural text.
As it is said below: for now, let us grant that those who have attained the first three fruits and Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage attain the transformation body (*pariṇāmanakāya*).
[Commentary] The meaning of the statement in the second fascicle of the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, "up to the point where there are no further faults," is that the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* grants this.
Those who have attained the first three fruits may also undergo transformation (pariṇāmanā).

For example, a person on the stage of Srotāpanna within the desire realm has only seven births remaining as fixed karma for the body of segmented birth (bheda-śarīra). Having necessarily experienced these seven births of the segmented body, they would then realize the fruit of Aśaikṣa.
However, if they do not take up the fruit of Aśaikṣa but instead turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they immediately undergo transformation. This is based on the maximum limit of seven births.
However, this does not preclude the possibility that among those [attaining the fruit], there may be stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) who, despite having fixed karma for two, three, four, five,

or six births within the realm of segmented existence (*prātibaddha-vedanīya-karma*), attain the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Or, they may have one birth remaining— such as a person of the second fruit who,

having completed the total of one birth in the human realm of the desire world through the stage of "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*), realizes arhatship (*aśaikṣa*) without subsequently taking up the fourth fruit.
Only upon turning back the mind (āśaya-parāvṛtti) does one undergo the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya);

or, for those who have eliminated [defilements] in various places throughout the upper realms, such as those in the third fruit, once they have attained meditative concentration born from the realm of form (rūpadhātu), regardless of where they are born, they need only pass through one more birth before realizing arhatship.
Because they turn back their minds and immediately undergo the transformation body, those in the first three fruits may also undergo the transformation body; this refers to those of sharp faculties.
Therefore, the body of *paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death), which is moistened by afflictions, attains *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation).
[Commentary] "Ultimately not arising" does not mean never arising forever; the intent is to say that one attains the *pariṇāma-kāya* (transformation body).

Because the *paricchinna-kāya* (segmented body) ultimately ceases to arise due to the support of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), the *pariṇāma-kāya* is able to arise; hence it is said that it is "not never-arising."
[They] are born.
[Commentary]: Regarding the eightieth [point], "attaining the transformation of birth" (*parivṛtti-janman*), that treatise states:

"Furthermore, a Śrāvaka who is dedicated to Bodhi may either be able to abandon the aspiration for the state of a Śrāvaka while still in the stage of training (*śaikṣa-avasthā*), or may do so only upon reaching the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa-avasthā*)."

Because there are differences in their faculties and differences in the various conditions upon which they depend, one knows that the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) pertains to both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Thus it is verified that this superior transformation is taught in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

However, the claim that the transformation of the basis for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) occurs from the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) up through the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) does not represent the ultimate principle.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that those prior to the seventh stage are not mentioned because they have attained the state of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*), one asks: what is meant by "fixed nature" and what is meant by "not fixed"? Answer:

If a Bodhisattva whose wisdom increases prior to the seventh stage is said to be of fixed nature, it is because from the entry into the first stage onward, they immediately undergo the transformation of support (*parivṛtti*).
As this treatise states: "There are those who, from the very first stage, attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)."

If a Bodhisattva whose compassion is predominant is termed "of indeterminate nature," it is because they only undergo transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) upon reaching the fulfillment of the seventh stage;
thus, the preceding treatise states: "Or there are those who, until the fulfillment of the seventh stage, are only then able to attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

According to this passage, since a Bodhisattva predominant in compassion only undergoes transformation-death upon the fulfillment of the seventh stage, it is said that they are "like those who have attained cessation."

It is definitively taught that since the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) extends from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the perfection of the mind, the acquisition of the *pariṇāmika-kāya* (body of transformation) is likewise so.
[Commentary: This phrase intends to state that this is subsumed under the "conjunction" category; thus it says, "this phrase.

Regarding the explanation of the conjunction of both "segmental" (*paritta-kaḍevara*) and "transformative" (*pariṇāmika*) births—namely, "because of mastery" and "because afflictions are not yet exhausted"—the term "mastery" refers to...
It is simply that one attains the name of "uncontaminated wisdom" (anāsrava-jñāna), which is called "mastery" (*vaśitā*); it is not the stage of the eighth ground that is called mastery.

[Commentary: As for the phrase "if based on afflictions... because they are extremely subtle and difficult to know," this explains the meaning of receiving the *pariṇāmanika* (transformation) versus the *paricchinnaka* (segmented) [birth].

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onwards, [the Bodhisattva] takes the place of all sentient beings to undergo the three miserable realms (*durgati*) and so forth," the intended meaning is as follows:
the Bodhisattva possesses a true body of a human or celestial being within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

When this Bodhisattva takes the place of sentient beings to undergo suffering, the Bodhisattva’s own body also corresponds to the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhavedanā*), because this body of segmented existence (*prātibhāṣika-śarīra*) is burned by the coarse fires [of affliction]. If the Bodhisattva gives rise to revulsion and detachment, then...
Regarding the exclusion of painful sensations: if a bodhisattva is in the hells, whether by providing food and drink or by preaching the Dharma, their primary concern is to bring about benefit.
Question: When a bodhisattva takes on the suffering of sentient beings with a segmented body belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), how can they experience painful sensations?
Answer: Because great compassionate bodhisattvas are always born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and are never born in the form realm, [painful sensations do not exist for them].
Furthermore, another interpretation states that even if a Bodhisattva were born in the Form Realm or were to enter the hells, they would not feel pain from being burned by fire.

This is because the body of the Form Realm is subtle, produced by its own karma, whereas the fire of the Desire Realm is coarse; since the coarse and the subtle differ so greatly, one does not feel pain when burned by the fire.
If one who has already attained the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) goes to the three miserable realms, it is the transformation body that goes there to undergo suffering and so forth.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "abandoning the insect-body," the body born of fragmented birth (*pratisaṃdhi*) is called an "insect-body" because it harbors insects.
As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 326 and 448: "Subhūti, the body and mind of a non-retrogressive Bodhisattva are pure;
they are not like the bodies of ordinary people, which are constantly preyed upon and consumed by eighty thousand families of insects. Why is this so?

What is this? Because the physical forms received by these bodhisattvas—due to the predominance of their roots of goodness—are pure both internally and externally, they are not invaded or consumed by insects.
As their roots of goodness gradually increase, so too do their bodies and minds become increasingly pure.
By virtue of this cause and condition, the bodies and minds of these bodhisattvas are as firm and solid as gold.
The adamantine [nature] cannot be afflicted by adverse conditions.
[Commentary]: Regarding the interpretation that this also reaches the meaning of "receiving" (attaining), the explanation states:

if one interprets this as the abandonment of the segmented body (*prādeśika-kāya*) and its parasites at the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), this is merely explained from the perspective of Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward who definitely receive the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). Based on this...

Speaking in terms of reality, there are also Bodhisattvas prior to the seven stages and persons who have attained the first three fruits who likewise receive the *pariṇāmiki-kāya* (transformed body). [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement that those from the first stage onward "have already attained it," this means they will certainly no longer be subject to rebirth as determined by their karma, just like an Arhat. This is the explanation.
If there are Bodhisattvas on the first stage whose wisdom has increased and who attain the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*),
they no longer possess the determinate karma of the fragmented body (*prādeśika-kāya*) like that of Arhats and others, because these Bodhisattvas of increased wisdom fear the afflictions (*kleśa*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "Mahāmati speaks of the dharma of tranquility," and so forth, up to "yet not even a single phrase [of it] is spoken herein"—the intent is as follows:
"speaking of the dharma of tranquility" refers to the Buddha’s teaching on the principle of *pudgala-śūnyatā* (the emptiness of the self).

This is because Bodhisattvas of the Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi (the Far-Reaching Stage) realize this characteristic of non-self; thus, the Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage attain mastery and are born according to their will.

Because of this body, it is known that the bodhisattvas of this stage have attained the transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*), yet because they have not all invariably attained the transformation body,

therefore, this treatise does not state that bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage attain the transformation body.

When the Bodhisattva practices the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), he perceives that all objective spheres are merely his own mind and realizes that they are consciousness-only.

To know existence and non-existence as they truly are means to know that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent, while the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) are existent.
To attain the signlessness of all phenomena, such as their being like illusions and so forth, up to the mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); this is the explanation.
The second, the mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*), also attains the signlessness of all phenomena, which is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);
"phenomena such as illusions" refers to knowing that dependently originated phenomena (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are like illusions and unreal;

"all are non-existent" refers to knowing that dependently originated phenomena lack any real essence and knowing that the self-nature of the imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is non-existent, whereby the body and mind undergo transformation.
Regarding "transformation": having already undergone the transformation of the body, the body gradually becomes more excellent, which is called the "transformation of the body";

the mind gradually becomes clearer and sharper, which is called the "transformation of the mind," whereby one attains other immeasurable meditative concentrations (*samādhi*). Regarding "immeasurable power of marks" (*nimitta-vaśitā*): "marks" refers to objective signs;
it means that the Bodhisattva attains great mastery and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) regarding immeasurable objective signs. "Power" refers to the ability to act according to one's will.

Regarding the phrase "the transformation of earth and so forth into objects such as gold and silver, because of the delight in the characteristics of dharmas": this refers to their characteristic nature (*lakṣaṇa*).

That is to say, when a bodhisattva realizes the *dharmatā*, they attain great bliss. [Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "thus those two kinds and three kinds... are also not mutually contradictory," the intended meaning is that this *manomayakāya* (mind-made body) possesses two sets of three types;

hence it is called "two kinds and three kinds. Specifically, as stated in this treatise, when the *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training) of the Two Vehicles and the Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery obtain the *manomayakāya*, these constitute the first set of three types.
Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* speaks of three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), which correspond to the second of the three types of mind-made bodies [mentioned in other texts].

Now, taking the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* as our basis, we either include those who have completed seven births and attained the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), or exclude those who have only one birth remaining.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* that "this constitutes a great error," the intended meaning of that treatise's question is as follows:

since those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning have exhausted the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within this single body and will necessarily enter parinirvāṇa without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*) forever, [how can they be said to attain Buddhahood?]"

To say they are no different from the Buddha means that while the Buddhas are those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is because they have realized the nature of *tathatā* within birth and death that they are said to be no different.
However, because the followers of the two vehicles lack the Bodhisattva’s vow to benefit and bring joy to others, it is said that the two vehicles differ from the Buddha.

As for the "beyond-training" stage of the two vehicles, what need is there to cite their transformation of birth and death (*parināmika-jarāmaraṇa*) to lead them toward Great Enlightenment? [This would require] three great eons.

Regarding the answer that one suffers for a long duration throughout the kalpas: within the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), there is no suffering; it is merely shrouded in obscurity by the *saṃskāra-duḥkhatā* (suffering of conditioned existence), because it is a *sāsrava-dharma* (contaminated phenomenon).
[Commentary] The meaning of the objection in that text is largely the same as this. To explain: the intent of the objection in that sutra is identical to that found in this treatise.
"How can it be said that the Truth of the Path truly brings about suffering? The general meaning of this passage is the same [as the previous one].
[Commentary]: Although Bodhisattvas take birth through the power of their vows, they certainly cannot be born [in the lower realms] by the force of karma.

The intent of this text is to resolve an external objection. The objection states: "If Bodhisattvas take birth through the power of their vows, how [can it be said that the Truth of the Path brings about suffering]?"
He then said: "Since they have forever subdued the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), there is no possibility for them to again receive a future body of segmented birth. The answer is:

although Bodhisattvas take birth through the power of their vows, there is no way for afflictions to manifest. When the seeds of affliction are subdued, the fruit of segmented birth can certainly not arise;
therefore, when they utilize untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) and vows to sustain their segmented existence, [they do so without the presence of afflictions].
"Because of past causes, they undergo the *pariṇāma-cyuti* (transformative) birth-and-death.

[Commentary]: Although they rely on afflictions (*kleśa*) for birth-and-death, their mode of taking birth differs from that of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvi-yāna*).

Regarding the statement that "the present and the seeds moisten birth," the transformational interpretation says: even if one suppresses the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of afflictions so that they do not arise, although the seeds of affliction still exist...

It cannot moisten birth or cause rebirth. If one asks: "If even an ordinary person or a non-returner (anāgāmin) moistens birth through the seeds of the manifest afflictions (*kleśa*), then since Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward have suppressed the manifest [afflictions], they too should use the seeds to moisten birth.
Answer: Although those from the eighth stage upward possess the seeds, these do not moisten [birth].

Because their births are not the same as those of non-returners, there is no fault; furthermore, since Bodhisattvas rely on the moisture of afflictions to take birth for the sake of benefiting sentient beings—arousing desire, anger, and so forth—they differ from ordinary worldlings and those of the two vehicles.

[Commentary]: "Therefore, it is necessary for the grasping at dharmas (*dharmagrāha*) to assist wisdom in taking birth. This is explained as follows: "Wisdom" here refers to untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom with conceptual differentiation (*savikalpa*).

Therefore, it requires the assistance of the ignorance-obscuration (*ajñānāvaraṇa*) of grasping at dharmas to enable this untainted wisdom with conceptual differentiation to undergo transformation (*pariṇāmika*).

[Commentary: "Since there is the benefit of the two kinds of altruism" means that the Bodhisattva who has attained self-realization benefits others by transforming the conditions of their existence and undergoing *pariṇāmi-cyuti* (the death of transformation).

[Commentary: "That which is not through analytical cessation yet arises again" means that once the body and karma have attained non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), they no longer arise.
Because there is no principle of re-arising, this merely serves as the condition for the karma that causes the body to be felt, ensuring the body does not cease.
According to this commentary, the character "one" (一) is missing beneath the character "more" (更); this also accords with the intended meaning. How so?

It is because it has not yet extended [the life] prior to [the hundred years], allowing [the person] to reach one hundred years. Regarding the life beyond the hundred years, it attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); it is only by virtue of the subsequent extension that [life exists] beyond the hundred years.
Because it arises through the force of life (*jīvita*) and continues in succession, it is said that "it arises again even without discernment" (*apratisaṃkhyā*).
However, regarding the allowance for arising without discernment, as will be clarified by the commentary (*śāstra*) itself later on, we shall here rely on the latter interpretation. [Commentary]:

"This is not the same as the dharmas such as the cultivation of dhyāna in the Hīnayāna" means that this [state] is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas those [dharmas] of the Hīnayāna are both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted.

There is a distinction because they are untainted (*anāsrava*). Alternatively, those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) cultivate meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and further create karma; since [the present case] merely utilizes that karma as a resource, it is said to be "not the same.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "three great kalpas" in the sutra—Question: If a Bodhisattva of sudden enlightenment attains the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) upon reaching the first stage (*bhūmi*), then...

Question: Since it is stated that [the path] takes two great kalpas, why is it further said to take three great kalpas? Answer: There are two interpretations. First, it is said that this refers generally to those before the stages (bhūmi);

thus it is called "three great kalpas" because one cultivates the causes prior to them, and the cause and fruit are fulfilled. This is known because the cause conforms to the fruit; hence it is said to take three great kalpas.
Second, it is said that this refers specifically to those who follow the circuitous route; therefore, it is called "three great kalpas."

[Commentary]: Regarding "supreme concentration" (*uttama-samādhi*), the older translations refer to it as the "limit of the fourth dhyāna. This is called "supreme concentration" because among all concentrations, this one is superior and preeminent.
It is called "limit" (*prānta*) because it is the final boundary within each respective stage (*bhūmi*). It is called "extreme" (*koṭi*) because it is the ultimate excellence;
thus, it refers to the highest grade of concentration within each stage. Therefore, all four dhyānas may be termed "supreme concentrations," or [it may refer to] only the fourth.
Because the four dhyānas also attain excellence, one may infer from this that there are two interpretations. [Commentary:

Although there is no explicit text for this now, it does not contradict the underlying principle. This refers to when a person attains those four dhyānas and obtains that which is the most excellent among what they have attained themselves;
this is called "limit" (*prāntakoṭika*). If one considers others, those below cannot know what is above them.
What is meant by "attaining the limit"? Since the limit cannot be attained, what is there to be transformed? For this reason, one must not expect [liberation] from oneself or others.

[Commentary]: Although the sutra speaks of the suffering of conditioned existence and so forth at length, the intended meaning refers to Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles who have turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna].

In the *Sūtra on the Transformation of Birth and Death*, it is taught that although one practices the bodhisattva path for three great kalpas and thus experiences the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), once the merits of the Tathāgata’s three bodies are attained, one shall certainly no longer undergo hardship. Having attained this, which accords with one's aspirations, there is great joy and bliss;
however, this is not the joy and bliss found within the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). This is explained in detail as stated therein.

[Treatise] Since this has not yet been fully realized even by those who possess fierce compassion and vows, one might ask: "If grasping at that bodhicitta is grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), why is grasping at sentient beings (*sattva*) not grasping at a self (*ātman*)?
The answer is: If one grasps at a sentient being as a single, permanent, and sovereign entity, that would indeed be grasping at a self and not a phenomenon.
However, because one merely grasps at the existence of a substance without relinquishing its own-nature (*svabhāva*), it is subsumed under phenomena alone.

[Commentary: Since one has not yet attained Buddhahood and fully realized the non-conceptual, great compassion, and the single flavor of equality—where "non-conceptual" refers to *tathatā* (suchness), "great compassion" refers to the resolve for the benefit of others, and "realization" refers to the practice of that resolve—it is intended to mean that the Buddha’s true wisdom is able to fully realize *tathatā* and thereby attain the great compassion that benefits others; all of these are [contained therein].
Because they lack attachment to phenomena despite their equanimity, although Bodhisattvas have realized *tathatā*, they have not yet fully realized it;
thus, they are unable to give rise to the single-flavored understanding of great compassion with equanimity.

It is due to this arising of the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that sentient beings and bodhi are grasped as being attainable or deliverable, and only subsequently does uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karman*) arise.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that karma is taught as the cause because it is preeminent, the intended meaning is that the power of untainted (anāsrava) karma can prolong the present body for an extended period;
therefore, untainted karma is taught as the cause. Only the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) are somewhat proximate [to this state].

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that ignorance serves as a condition because it is remote: since the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) is remote from the karma of the body, it cannot provide sustenance;
rather, it merely clings to sentient beings and bodhi as being substantially real, and thus it is "remote. It is therefore designated only as a "condition" (pratyaya).

[Commentary]: "It is not like the afflictions that provide the conditions for outflowing karma even to a small degree"—the intent of this statement is that the afflictions of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) act as conditions to directly moisten the five branches beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), which are then designated as "existence" (*bhava*).

Although the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) likewise serve as conditions, when compared to outflowing karma, they are not like the afflictions in their capacity to directly moisten consciousness and the other branches; thus, while the general sense of acting as a condition is the same, there is a distinction between direct and indirect influence.
The distinction lies merely in the adherence to substantial difference; as for the afflictions, they are said to be conditions only in a partial sense of similarity.
[Commentary]: Because of these obstacles, the co-arising factors do not become untainted (*anāsrava*).

The meaning is that "co-arising factors" refers to the bodily and vocal karma produced by the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as well as the non-associated formations (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*) produced thereby, all of which are included therein.

The *sāsrava* (tainted) states, through the arousal of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) by means of meditative concentration, are able to manifest various kinds of phenomena, and whatever is performed is accomplished.

Furthermore, desire (*chanda*), effort (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) are called the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*). These four are able to give rise to supernormal powers; thus they are named the four bases of power because they are the "feet" (*pāda*) of the "divine" (*ṛddhi*).
[Treatise] If the retained body were sustained by impure meditative concentration (*samādhi*), vows, and so forth, the correct interpretation is as explained in the Commentary.

There is a view that the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas intentionally sustain [the body] with pure (*anāsrava*) concentration; however, for what reason would this not be possible? It is simply because they lack the power of great compassion and great vows, and because their pure power is weak;
thus, the body so sustained is merely termed "segmented" (*paricchinna*). Otherwise, the cultivation of dhyāna would necessarily be exclusively impure (*sāsrava*). Details [are as follows].

It is said: Since the treatise has already stated this clearly, how could one suppress it out of mere human sentiment and refuse to follow it? Furthermore, the meaning of "perfuming dhyāna" (*xūnchán*) and the matter of "retaining the body" (*liúshēn*) are not the same.

It is difficult for "black dhyāna" (*hēichán*)—which relies on causes from a different stage to produce a fruit in a different stage—to be permeated by untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) to extend one's lifespan;
such an extension merely prolongs the retribution of this current life based on past causes. How, then, can these two cases be treated as analogous? Moreover, furthermore...

Yan-zhi [Sengzhao] maintains that because [the transformation body] is indeed real yet not eternally fixed, and because it arises differently from other things, it can be relied upon according to the treatises. [Commentary]:

The meaning of the statement "it is not admitted that one can see the superior transformation body because it is not its object" is that although the two vehicles possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), if they do not turn their minds toward enlightenment, they cannot see the superior transformation body; this is because the transformation body is not within the range of the divine eye.

It is established as a fundamental principle that those above can see those below; however, if they are of the same class who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], then both those above and below are able to see one another.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "in the Small Vehicle, up to the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), there are only outflow-tainted states," the intention is to explain that according to the tenets of the Small Vehicle school, the provisions of merit for extending one's lifespan are pervasive.

Regarding the merit that is either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), according to the Mahayana school’s teaching, since the cause for abandoning the body of merit-sustenance is necessarily only with outflows,
the body thus prolonged is subsumed under the category of the *paricchinna-bhava* (the fragmented or limited existence).

[Commentary]: Regarding this passage which serves as proof for the statement "one may also obtain the distinct [bodies]," the explanation says: the outflowing (*sāsrava*) nourishes the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) body, while the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) nourishes the *pariṇāmi-vaipākika* (transformative-retribution) body.

The transformative-retribution body is subtle and wondrous, whereas the segmented body is coarse; there is a distinction between the coarse and the subtle, and each is perceived differently according to the body one possesses.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage "the birth-and-death outside the realm up to the birth-and-death that is outflow-free," the interpretation states: according to the scriptural text, it should be said that there is birth-and-death outside the realm and birth-and-death within the realm.

"Within" refers to the fruit of outflows (*sāsrava*), while "outside" refers to that which is outflow-free (*anāsrava*). The outflow-free is the transformation-rebirth (*parināmi-jarāmaraṇa*), whereas the outflowing is the segmented-rebirth (*pratibimba-jarāmaraṇa*).
However, these are spoken of as being "outside the realm" only in terms of their auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*); in essence, this is not actually the case.
[Commentary]: There is a wondrous Pure Land that transcends the three realms, wherein Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are destined to be born. The interpretation states:

this refers to the *parabhogakāya* (land of others' enjoyment). The intent in citing this passage is to prove that *parināmika-jarāmaraṇa* (death and rebirth through transformation) is a death and rebirth outside the [three] realms, which is precisely the abode of Mahāmaheśvara.
[Commentary: Regarding the question in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 80, "Does this extend even to the realm of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-dhātu*)?", the intent of the inquiry is as follows:

Is it based on *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* that one receives the body of transformation (*pariṇāmika-kāya*), or is it based on *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* that one receives the body of transformation? The meaning of the question is thus;
the answer is as stated in the commentary.
[Commentary]: Regarding the question, "At most, there is not even one more birth," the intent of this inquiry is as follows:
If those who attain the fruit of Arhatship quickly must pass through three births, how can it be that one attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime?
Here, "one lifetime" refers to attaining the fruit of Buddhahood after undergoing the transformation-death (*parināmi-jarāmaraṇa*) only once; this is the point of the objection.

[Commentary] Answer: As for the statement that one can only achieve Buddhahood by increasing the lifespan through practice, this means that by entering the *parināmika-kāya* (transformation body), one increases the lifespan and thereby passes through three great *kalpas* before attaining Buddhahood.

[Commentary: The statement that one who has skillfully cultivated the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) can abide for an eon means that meditative concentration is indeed the basis of psychic power;
psychic power arises dependent upon concentration. Just as a person with feet is able to travel to various directions, so too is psychic power according to its support.
[Commentary: This refers to those whose progress toward enlightenment is extremely slow. The explanation says:
as the World-Honored One stated, "Those who have well-cultivated the bases of psychic power can remain for an eon," this refers precisely to those whose progress is most sluggish.

Regarding those who appear in the realm of activity and serve the Buddhas—meaning that the Buddha desires these śrāvakas to appear within the lands and serve the various Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions—he intends to cause them to do so.
Because he must rouse sentient beings [from their state], this person is said to be extremely dull-witted compared to a bodhisattva who begins practice from the outset.
If one who has turned the mind from the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) reaches the bodhisattva’s stage of faith after twenty thousand *kalpas* or ten thousand *kalpas*,

whereas a bodhisattva who begins practice from the outset and attains sudden awakening reaches that same stage of faith after sixty *kalpas*, there is also a recension of the text that omits the account of the "Manifesting Realm" (*prādurbhāva-loka*).
The Buddha’s transformation of sentient beings is consistent with both the words and their meaning, and thus there is no contradiction.

[Commentary: Regarding the four kinds of birth and death: first, the birth and death of expedient means (*upāya-janma-maraṇa*), which refers to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that serve as the preliminary practice (*prayoga*) prior to the transformation of the basis (*pariṇāmiki-janma-maraṇa*);

second, the birth and death of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-janma-maraṇa*), which consists solely of the cause of untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*); third, the birth and death of existence (*bhava-janma-maraṇa*).

"Death" refers to the initial transformation through the power of meditative vows; "gradually" refers to the fourth [characteristic], which is the absence of birth and death—meaning that this body of transformation gradually declines and deteriorates.
[Commentary] The phrase "because there are the three, such as the body" intends to explain that contaminated karma is designated by the three types, beginning with "body."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "merely attaining twenty kalpas," this means that by means of concentration (*samādhi*) and vows (*praṇidhāna*), one reaches the momentum of twenty kalpas;

when that momentum is about to be exhausted, one then uses the power of concentration and vows to support the subsequent period for another twenty kalpas. Continuing in this manner without interruption is called "the former being exhausted and the latter arising."
[Commentary: The intent of the present objection is as follows: "If one were to depart from internal consciousness, it would not be appropriate to speak of three [natures].

The meaning of this objection is that if there were consciousness but no external dharmas apart from the mind, there should be only a single *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), because this dependent nature consists of consciousness and mind;
consequently, the other two natures should not exist, since the essence of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is a non-existent thing (*abhāva*).

Furthermore, because [the perfected nature] takes [objects] as its cognitive focus, and since the essence of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is precisely suchness (*tathatā*), which is neither matter nor mind and thus cannot take [objects] as its cognitive focus, these two natures are not matter or mind.
Consequently, it would follow that there are no phenomena external to the mind;

one should have to say "only consciousness" (*vijñaptimātra*), and there would be only one nature, lacking both the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the perfected natures. Therefore, the objection is raised: "Since the Sūtras speak of three natures, it cannot be 'only consciousness'."

[Commentary] Now, regarding the analysis into four propositions based on the correct meaning: this refers to the differentiation of the four propositions according to the school of Dharmapāla, as explained in the commentary.
The third proposition states that it is both pervasive and conceptualized; this refers to the sixth consciousness and its associated mental factors when the two types of grasping arise.

At such times, these mind and mental factors pervasively take the five aggregates as "self" and pervasively take the eighteen elements as "dharmas," rather than taking only a single [aggregate or element] as their object.

Since the Dharma is not all-pervasive, according to the school of An-hui (Sthiramati) based on incorrect reasoning, the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) regarding the eight consciousnesses all involve grasping (*grāha*).
As it is said: there is that which is reckoned as non-pervasive, namely the eighth, seventh, and the first five consciousnesses;

there is that which is pervasive but not reckoned [as such], namely the untainted (*anāsrava*) and so forth; there is that which is both pervasive and reckoned, namely the sixth consciousness. If one interprets it in this way, there would be no [seventh consciousness].
The four propositions.
[Treatise: Regarding the falsely grasped self-nature and its distinctions—within the inquiry into phenomena, the self-nature and distinctions can be known;
how then can there be self-nature and distinctions within the "self"? The answer is: it is merely designated in general as "self," which is itself the conceptualized self-nature.

The various names such as "omnipresent" and "eternal" constitute the distinctions; one should understand that all such conceptualizations as being "separate from the aggregates" and so forth follow the same principle.
This is precisely what, in the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*), refers to the self-nature and its specific attributes (*viśeṣa*) of the self (*ātman*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the essence is not manifold," this refers to the fact that [the mind] universally conceptualizes.

Since the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) serves as the basis upon which all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena depend for their existence, a question is raised: "If they become contaminated by virtue of being concomitant with the outflows (*āsrava*), why then say they become contaminated by virtue of the cognitive obscuration?
The answer is: if something becomes contaminated, it must necessarily be concomitant with the outflows; it is concomitant with the outflows...

To serve as a basis, one must necessarily rely upon these obstacles; thus, the two meanings of "becoming an outflow" (*āsrava*) and "becoming a basis" (*āśraya*) are distinct, and consequently, there is no contradiction between the preceding and subsequent explanations.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the statement that even a non-existent entity as conceived can be called a "thing" (*vastu*), etc.: this second interpretation refers specifically to the *parikalpita* (imagined nature).

The nature of that which is grasped (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is termed "thing" (*vastu*) and "variety" (*nānātva*). Although its essence is non-existent, because it appears to the mind at the time of false grasping, it manifests as such.

[Commentary: The locus of dependence for this grasping differs from that of the former master; the second phrase of the former master refers to the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

The second [explanation] states that the objects thoroughly imagined by the second phrase—namely, the dependent (*paratantra*) and the perfected (*pariniṣpanna*) natures—are the basis upon which the grasped (*grāhya*) depends.

[Commentary]: However, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts speak only of the dependent nature as the "place of establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā-deśa*); the intended meaning is that the dependent nature and...
The imagined deluded mind takes the dependent nature as its place of stable footing, just as good ground serves as a place of stable footing;
this is indeed so. Question: Why is it that only the dependent nature is said to be the place of stable footing, while the perfected nature is not?
Answer: Because the two natures—the imagined and the dependent—are somewhat similar and thus compatible with one another. However, this...

The two natures are the domain of ordinary beings and are easily understood; therefore, it is taught that only the dependent nature (*paratantra*) is the place of rest, while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*) is not mentioned.
If one applies reasoning to this, the perfected nature is also a place of rest—yet would one not then be grasping at *tathatā* as being substantially existent?

[Commentary: However, regarding the latter half of this verse as presented in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the explanation given there is identical to that of the second master in this treatise. [Commentary:

The preceding section merely re-explains the meaning of the "clinging" (*parikalpita*) in the first verse; it indicates that the nature of the pervasive conceptualizer (*parikalpa*) is revealed from the opening sentence of the treatise.
Having reached this point in the commentary, the text now re-explains the previous verse on the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The phrase "what is being stated now" refers to the third line of the initial verse, which reads: "This [is] the thoroughly imagined nature. Below, the text proceeds to explain that third line.

[Treatise]: Regarding the statement, "Because they all appear as the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka)," one may ask: How is it known that appearing as the grasper and the grasped is termed "clinging" (abhiniveśa)?

Answer: The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Chapter Four, states: "The dependent nature (paratantra-lakṣaṇa) refers to that which arises based on the pervasive conceptualization (parikalpa) and recollection (anusmaraṇa) of the grasped and the grasper, [which themselves] arise based upon karma and afflictions (kleśa).
It further states: "As previously explained regarding the body and so forth..."
The nature [of phenomena] is established through the false discrimination of the grasped and the grasper by the various consciousnesses. Furthermore, it is said:
"For example, like a mirage, through the power of its own continuity, there is the false, pervasive conceptualization that establishes what appears as water as the grasped and the grasper.

This means that just as a thirsty deer, due to the power of its own arising craving, establishes the notion of water upon a shimmering heat-mirage, and thus has a grasped object and a grasping subject.
Because they arise from this, it is known that within the *paratantra-svabhāva*, both modes of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*) are termed "clinging" (*abhiniveśa*). Question:
Are the two aspects of the grasped (*grāhya*) simultaneous or not? Answer: This treatise provides a general principle:

in reality, whenever one clings according to the mind, at the time of the grasping subject (*grāhaka*), there is the aspect of the grasping subject and the grasped object (*grāhya*), and so forth. However, this does not mean that one clings to these two graspings at all times.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because a mind that does not have grasping is not called 'grasping,'" "grasping" (取) means "clinging" (執). It should rather be stated as: "because a mind that does not have grasping is not called 'clinging.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because a mind that is not without clinging appears as the two types of grasping," this is an indirect demonstration (返顯) clearly showing that both the grasper (能取) and the grasped (所取) exist.

Regarding this "clinging" (*sagrāha*): if one asks whether the two types of grasping (*dvividhādāna*) within the untainted (*anāsrava*) state should all be considered clinging, the answer is as follows:

according to Master Sthiramati alone, the two aspects—the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*)—of the untainted subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) are also clinging; however, Dharmapāla does not accept this, as will be explained in detail below.
[Śāstra]: Regarding the statement that the *ālaya-vijñāna* takes as its object the seeds of the false attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the intended meaning is as follows:
"the imagined nature" refers directly to the object that is grasped; "false attachment" refers to the mind that performs the universal imagining (*parikalpa*).
These seeds, which are perfumed by this very mind that grasps, are called the "seeds of false attachment to the imagined nature."

Question: For what purpose is this treatise cited? Answer: There are two interpretations. The first says it proves that the seven afflicted consciousnesses (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*), which act as perfumers (*vāsaka*), all possess grasping (*grāha*).
The second says it generally proves that the causes capable of producing [the seeds] in the eightfold [system] all possess grasping.

Question: According to this master, is the sixth consciousness admitted to have two types of grasping, and do both types of grasping coexist? Answer: There is one interpretation with two further explanations regarding this. The first... [text ends].

Question: [The Sautrāntika] says they are protected together, while the second [school] says they do not coexist, because—as in the seventh [chapter]—there is an attachment to a self and a lack of attachment to dharmas. Question:

According to the intention of Sthiramati, the two parts are the essence of the grasping of the parikalpita; since they are like a hare’s horn and so forth, how can they possibly perfume seeds? Answer:
What is meant here by "perfuming seeds" refers only to the self-witnessing part (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) perfuming the seeing and image parts, not [the other way around].

The intention of this Master is as follows: he maintains that the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvedana*) itself is the seed perfumed within the *paratantra-svabhāva*, yet he also states that this [seed] is merely nominal and is further described as being the *parikalpita-svabhāva*.
Question: How can a nominal seed give rise to a real self-cognizing part? Answer: This is the intended view of this Master;
it cannot yet be reconciled [with other systems]. Question: If only the self-cognizing part is perfumed, why does the later commentary state that [the seed] "is able to produce"?
The "seeds" have two capacities; these two capacities refer to the seeds of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). Why are they not contradictory? [Answer:

When the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) takes the seeing-part and the object-part as its objects, it also perfumes seeds; subsequently, the two parts arise from these seeds. Question: How does the self-cognizing part take the object-part as its object? Answer:
Its intention is to allow that the self-cognizing part is distinct from the seeing-part, which takes [the object] as its object.
The aspects of the sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and so forth, as well as the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*parikalpita-bhāga*), are provisional.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the habitual tendencies of the discrimination of marks" (*nimitta-vikalpa-vāsanā*): the intention of this master in citing this passage is to take specifically the "habitual tendencies of discrimination.
Discrimination (*vikalpa*) refers to the mind of conceptual calculation (*parikalpa*), which is false discrimination; that is, within the eight consciousnesses, there is a false...
Because of false discrimination, all eight consciousnesses possess the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
[Commentary: Regarding the three dharmas of greed and so forth, they are paths but not karma; greed, hatred, and delusion are the paths within the mind, whereas karma refers to volition (*cetanā*).
Now, defining them by their essential nature, volition is the actual substance of karmic obstruction. Because the dharmas of greed and so forth are that which volition traverses, they are so named.
The Path (*mārga*) is so called because it accords with [the nature of] action; thus it is termed "paths of action" (*karmapatha*). As for why body and speech are called paths of action:
"action" (*karman*) is explained as movement or activity, which refers to the two—body and speech—while "path" (*patha*) is so named because volition (*cetanā*) traverses them.
The fourfold analysis may be understood by consulting the text.

[Commentary: Although the remaining seven consciousnesses are also capable of conceptualization (*parikalpa*), they cannot engage in universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*). Therefore, Ananta’s fourfold classification states:

that which is conceptualizing but not universal is the five sensory consciousnesses, the eighth consciousness, and the seventh consciousness; that which is universal but not conceptualizing refers to untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*);
and that which is both conceptualizing and universal refers to the sixth consciousness.

[Commentary]: Regarding the fact that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) does not mention [the seventh consciousness], the intended meaning is as explained by Sthiramati: the *Saṃgraha* does not mention it because it cannot perform universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*).

This does not mean that the fifth, eighth, and seventh consciousnesses do not conceptualize at all; rather, while these five, eight, and seventh consciousnesses do engage in conceptualization, they do not engage in universal conceptualization.
Therefore, it is said that it is not the others that do not conceptualize. "The original commentary on the two treatises" means that "original" refers to Asaṅga and "commentary" refers to Vasubandhu.
"Non-existence, etc.
[Commentary]: "The substance conforms to that name" means that the substance of the sixth consciousness conforms to the name of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature);

therefore, it is specifically mentioned. As for the others, this is not the case, so they are not mentioned. However, one should not conclude that something does not exist simply because it is not mentioned.
[Commentary]: Therefore, the "boundless modes of activity" of the mental consciousness refer to its taking various modes of activity, such as the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), as its objects.
[Commentary]:
"If that is so, the seventh [consciousness] cannot universally conceptualize and thus should not be included herein"—this is the objection raised by Sthiramati.
The sixth consciousness is able to universally take the seventh as its object; if it were not so, it would not be a *parikalpa* (imagining).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "if it were not so," among the three types of discrimination, it refers to *vikalpa-parikalpa* (discriminative imagination); furthermore, the fifth and eighth [consciousnesses] are also not so.
Dharmapāla’s interpretation states that this refers to the *vikalpa-parikalpa* within the three types of discrimination, which subsumes the seven types of discrimination.
The seven types of discrimination are all instances of this *vikalpa-parikalpa* (conceptualizing discrimination).
However, according to the first [chapter] of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these seven discriminations are all the unique activity (*asādhāraṇa-karman*) of the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, since the seven discriminations are distinctions between *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), they exist only within the sixth consciousness and do not pervade the other consciousnesses. If one follows the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* (or *Abhidharma-kośa*), however...
The treatise explains that the seven types of discrimination are not merely distinctions between vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). These seven types are:

discrimination with signs, discrimination without signs, deeply defiled discrimination, non-defiled discrimination, seeking discrimination, examining discrimination, and spontaneous discrimination. Because they correspond to four meanings within the seventh consciousness, they constitute defiled discrimination.
If the seventh consciousness corresponds with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), such discrimination is termed [non-defiled].
Because it is not an afflicted discrimination (*kliṣṭa-vikalpa*), it is known that the seventh [consciousness] is also subsumed under "imaginary construction" (*parikalpa*).
[Commentary: Wuxing says, "The mental consciousness possesses discrimination... up to "...this is the correct interpretation.

The meaning of this is that since this treatise states that "discriminative construction" (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) is capable of universal imagining (*parikalpa*), it is identical to Asaṅga’s original *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*; therefore, there is no contradiction.
The *Xing shi* (Commentary on the Nature) states: "One should know that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of pervasive conceptualization because it possesses discrimination.

This is because it is intermingled with the display of and recollective conceptualization (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*). The commentary explains that "intermingling" (*saṃsarga*) signifies the sense of being associated (*samprayukta*) and arising simultaneously (*sahabhū*).
Thus, because the mental consciousness is accompanied by both the recollective and the deliberative conceptualizations, it is able to conceptually distinguish and display [objects]. That is to say:
This conceptualization of alternative names is also called the "function of deliberative treatise" (*cintā-śāstra-vṛtti*).

That which takes the seeds of the habitual perfuming of its own linguistic expressions as its seed refers to the seeds of the habitual perfuming of the conceptual proliferation of linguistic expressions belonging to the mental consciousness throughout beginningless saṃsāra; these serve as the cause for its arising.

The commentary explains: "It reveals that the seeds perfumed by its own seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) are the substantial entity that is the direct productive cause of its own manifest activity. This refers to both the treatise and [the consciousness].

"Taking the linguistic designations (*nāma-vyavahāra*) of all other consciousnesses as seeds" means that because they arise resembling those [objects] by taking as their cause the seeds of the linguistic designations of the infinite images of form and so forth belonging to other consciousnesses.

Therefore, all infinite modes of activity (*ākāra*) proceed as conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). The commentary explains: They are called "infinite" because their objects are manifold; that is, they take other consciousnesses as their conditions.
The linguistic habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) regarding names and images such as form (*rūpa*) are called "images" (*pratibimba*).

Furthermore, those seeds perfumed within the objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighteen realms and the other consciousnesses—which are said to be "conditions"—are collectively termed "the use of others" (*parārtha*).

Because of this, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises resembling all [objects], and thus it functions with infinite modes of activity (*ākāra*); this is not the case for the five sensory consciousnesses or the eighth consciousness.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the passage from "all eight consciousnesses" to "the sixth and seventh consciousnesses," the intended meaning is as follows:

All eight consciousnesses are equally false conceptualizations (vikalpa) and lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). When it says that "the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) possesses conceptualization," the intent is to distinguish it from the undefiled mind (akliṣṭa-citta).

Thus, it is said that the mental consciousness possesses conceptualization because it is the universal imagination (parikalpa), which does not apply to the other consciousnesses that lack such conceptualization. Furthermore...

The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* merely states that "by means of these categories, one is able to engage in pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*)," without specifying which particular consciousnesses are involved.

As for the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* that "the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses the conceptualizations of discernment (*nirūpaṇa-vikalpa*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*"), what contradiction is there in this being intended to exclude uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds?
Thus, we know that while all eight consciousnesses possess conceptualization in general, how could they all be capable of pervasive conceptualization?

[Treatise] Regarding the statement, "Those who grasp at a self and dharmas must possess wisdom": this is a question concerning Dharmapāla’s position that the five consciousnesses can coexist with wisdom.

Now, in challenging another, does he not contradict himself? There are two interpretations: first, it is said that because the five consciousnesses lack superior wisdom, they are inferior and thus cannot grasp;
second, it is said that this reason specifically challenges the eighth [consciousness]. Detailed explanation: Generally speaking, whoever possesses grasping must necessarily possess wisdom.
The claim that both [masters] do not admit the existence of wisdom (*prajñā*) is merely their own dogmatic adherence;

since the former master asserts that all contaminated minds (*sāsrava-citta*) possess attachment (*abhiniveśa*), Dharmapāla challenges this by pointing out the absence of wisdom. Therefore, these two interpretations do not constitute a sound explanation.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement by the former master that vitarka and vicāra arise simultaneously, his intention is as follows:

According to Sthiramati’s explanation, for instance, although in the Hīnayāna tradition vitarka and vicāra are distinguished as coarse and subtle respectively, and since vitarka and vicāra are innate wholesome states that are directly opposed to ignorance (avidyā), what contradiction is there in their arising simultaneously?

[Commentary: Regarding the nature of *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought), it may be granted that they arise together; however, regarding the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), this is reversed. Dharmapāla explains in general terms:

"The natures of *vitarka* and *vicāra* are mutually compatible, so we allow them to arise together. But the natures of virtue and ignorance are contradictory; virtue and ignorance cannot arise simultaneously."
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "all contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds of the three natures are [considered] unwholesome because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are slight," Anahita states:

"To say that all contaminated minds of the three natures are called 'unwholesome,' yet to say that a contaminated mind is called 'wholesome,' means that it is designated as wholesome because its unwholesome mode of activity is slight. Question: Why are all contaminated minds called unwholesome?
Answer: There are four types of unwholesome [dharmas]: first, unwholesome by intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-akuśala*), such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and so forth;

second, unwholesome by association (*samprayoga-akuśala*), namely the afflictions associated with greed and so forth; third, unwholesome by origination (*samutthāna-akuśala*), namely the actions they produce, such as bodily and vocal karma;

fourth, unwholesome in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-akuśala*), which refers to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena, for even the wholesome and neutral natures are termed "ultimate" [in this context].

Because they are unwholesome (*akuśala*), all contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*) are unwholesome; thus, it is clearly known that grasping (*grāha*) exists within all minds of the three natures.

[Commentary: If one says that all contaminated states are unwholesome up until the point where they are designated as "non-delusion" (*amoha*), Anahbuddhi states that non-delusion is wholesome (*kuśala*).
The faculties (*indriya*) and the unwholesome root of delusion (*moha-akuśalamūla*) cannot be associated;

however, if the aspect of delusion within a contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*) is slight, it is termed the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha-kuśalamūla*), whereas if the aspect of delusion is heavy, it is termed the unwholesome root of delusion.

Since there is both slight and heavy delusion within a contaminated mind, there must likewise be grasping (*parāmarśa*) within that same contaminated mind. Is this not, therefore, in accordance with correct principle?
[Commentary]: If the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is itself the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā-darśana*), how can it lead to the manifestation of the wisdom of emptiness?

If one holds that the untainted mind of the followers of the Two Vehicles is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), while for Bodhisattvas it is the untainted mind of the emptiness of both persons and phenomena (*dharma-pudgala-śūnyatā*), then if one allows that wholesome minds involve attachment to phenomena (*dharma-abhiniveśa*), how could the paths of Accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) and Application (*prayoga-mārga*)—which would then consist of minds involving such attachment—possibly induce [the realization]?
Question: Is it the wisdom of the two types of emptiness realized on the path of seeing?

If one does not admit that there is grasping within a wholesome mind, would this not contradict the scriptural passage stating that [wholesome states] are ultimately unwholesome? Answer: It does not contradict it. How so?

When all contaminated (sāsrava) wholesome states and the other three natures are called "ultimately unwholesome," this is said with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita). This is because they are contrasted with uncontaminated (anāsrava) phenomena.
To criticize [the position] for the sake of reputation is merely a claim regarding the ultimate meaning; in reality, a wholesome or neutral mind is not called "unwholesome.

It is like saying that the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) is established based on pleasure (*sukha*): at the very moment of its transformation, there is no suffering of change, yet it is so designated with reference to the future time when it can be transformed.
This is indeed the case. Furthermore, as for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), could even pleasant feeling (*vedanā*) be oppressive? It is simply...
The refutation is as follows; this is established by analogy. [Treatise:

Regarding the statement that "the grasping at existence and the realization of non-existence do not arise simultaneously," a question is raised: When those of the two vehicles enter the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), do they not rely on the contemplation of the emptiness of subject and object?
The answer is: Although they do not explicitly cultivate the emptiness of subject and object, while relying on the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, they suppress [such grasping].
The grasping at a self may also be termed "empty," yet how could it be non-existent?
[Commentary]: One might object that the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) should also be a perfuming agent (*vāsanā*).

This objection implies that, apart from the seventh consciousness, those among the other six consciousnesses produced by karma, as well as the eighth consciousness, should all be perfuming agents. This objection concerns the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state.
It is the mind. [Commentary: It should be the eighth consciousness... because it would contradict inference (*anumāna*), one establishes the following formal argument (*prayoga*):

"The subject, the eighth consciousness, must also be capable of perfuming (*vāsanā*) (the thesis-property); because it is admitted to possess grasping (*sgrub pa*, *grāha*) (the reason); just like the preceding seven consciousnesses (the example). If you say that the eighth...
Although the eight consciousnesses possess grasping (*grāha*), the fact that they do not undergo perfuming (*vāsana*) contradicts inference (*anumāna*).

[Commentary: Although in the preceding stages one practices the contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvi-śūnyatā-darśana*), these are "provisional appearances" (*prajñapti-lakṣaṇa*); the meaning is this:

even if one has previously practiced the contemplations of the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-avasthā*), because it is accompanied by the aspect of emptiness (*śūnyatā-ākāra*) and does not realize the truth, it is called a "provisional appearance."

Because the untainted [wisdom] (*anāsrava*) is able to realize reality, while [all else] is collectively termed "false conceptualization" (*abhūtaparikalpa*), the eight consciousnesses of the three realms are all false conceptualizations. [Commentary:
