The object of such fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realized through cessation is as described above; the remaining four are all subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that takes transformed appearances as its objects while realizing the conventional and the true.

Because the three types of *tathatā* and the four *tathatās* of establishment and so forth are the distinct objects of these two wisdoms, it is said that "the objects of the three and four are distinct.
If explained according to their designations, these four are the objects of subsequently attained wisdom.

Regarding the objects (*ālambana*), if one discusses their manifest essence (*svabhāva*) according to the theory of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the three—reality (*tathatā*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and so forth—are the objects of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*).
[Commentary: From "the mind of pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpita-citta*) up to "not the perfected nature" (*niṣpanna-svabhāva*), the intended meaning is as follows:

the mind of pervasive conceptualization, being associated with the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), is termed "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*); because it arises from seeds, it is termed "dependent" (*paratantra*); and its three aspects of suchness (*tathatā*) and defilement... [are explained].

Regarding the phrase "because it is dependent on others," the intended meaning is that the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*) and the origin of suffering (*duḥkha-samudaya*) are both defiled phenomena whose essential nature is dependent.

This refers to the essential nature of defiled phenomena as expressed by linguistic designations; it is not an essential nature that transcends language. Therefore, they are not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "most do not cling to consciousness-only," the explanation is as follows: because most people, through their worldly deluded sentiments, do not cling to consciousness-only as being truly existent, [this does not apply to] the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Furthermore, because there are only a few who do cling to it, it is not mentioned. As the preceding treatise states:
"If one clings to consciousness-only as being truly existent, this is just like clinging to external objects; both are attachments to phenomena (dharma-grāha)."

There is no contradiction because this is stated in terms of the majority. As for the statement that "the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) can only slightly know representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*)," the intended meaning is that there are those who have realized the dependent nature to be representation-only, but they are few; therefore, it is not taught as being the dependent nature.

This is not because it does not encompass the previous two [natures]. Regarding the "correct practice" (*samyak-pratipatti*) in terms of abandoning faults, the intended meaning is that correct practice is explained in relation to the abandonment of faults.

Because it is free from inversion, it belongs solely to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and is not subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); for the untainted dependent nature, being ultimately free from inversion, is itself the perfected nature.

[Commentary]: Regarding the sense of "successive transformation," it refers to the fact that on the basis of consciousness, space and other unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) manifest as transformed appearances.

This [nature] is the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature); one then clings to it, asserting that "this is truly existent," which is precisely what is called the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

Thus, it is said that there is a sense of mutual dependence. Therefore, the sub-commentary below states: "Since even unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are transformations conditioned by the mind, they are the *paratantra-svabhāva*."
[Commentary] The *Madhyāntavibhāga* states that "the nature grasped by form (rūpa) extends to each of the three natures. This means:

first, because one stubbornly clings to form as being form, this is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of form; second, because form arises from conditions, this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of form;
third, because it is the true nature of form, this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) of form—or alternatively, [this may refer to] the untainted [nature].

Because it undergoes a change in color within the mind, it is also subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). If it is grasped through false attachment, it is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) belonging to sensation;
because sensation arises from conditions, it is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); and because it is the actual nature of sensation, it is the perfected nature of sensation.

The same applies to perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and this should be extended accordingly even to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*); if one falsely clings to them as unconditioned, [the same three natures apply].
Therefore, that which is the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is itself unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), because the consciousness-transformation of the unconditioned arises from conditions;

that which is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is itself unconditioned, because the unconditioned is provisionally established based upon suchness (tathatā); and suchness itself is unconditioned, because it is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
[Commentary]: Here, excluding the provisional (*prajñapti*) unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the present discussion of the unconditioned is based on the unconditioned itself;

therefore, it is subsumed solely under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Why? Because it is devoid of arising and ceasing. If one holds that consciousness transforms into the provisional unconditioned as previously explained, it would pertain to all three natures.
Second, another interpretation: or the provisional unconditioned is also subsumed solely within the perfected nature, because it is a provisional designation upon suchness (*tathatā*).
Because they are established, from the outset they are comprised solely within the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature).

[Commentary: This explains that these existent phenomena (*bhāva*) are not what is imagined by the *parikalpita* (the imagined nature). The intended meaning is that if one were to discuss them individually, all six categories of phenomena would not be subsumed under the *parikalpita*.

Why is this? Because this passage distinguishes between the inclusion or non-inclusion of phenomena that possess substantial reality (*dravya*), and does not concern phenomena that lack such reality (*abhāva*).
Because the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature) is a non-entity (*avastu*), it is not included [in the five categories].
[Treatise]: Regarding the passage stating that certain locations do not include the five categories, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74:
Question: Among the five dharmas, how many are included within the first *svabhāva*? Answer: None at all are included. Question: How many are included within the second *svabhāva*? Answer: ...
Regarding the question of what is subsumed by the four [categories], as for the third self-nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), how many are subsumed? Answer: It is subsumed by one.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the first is the *yoga*," etc., the meaning is that there are four different explanations concerning the mutual inclusion of the three natures and the five categories (*pañcavastu*).
This is called "the first" because it is the initial passage [of this discussion].

[Commentary]: Regarding "the two aspects of the transformed," these refer to the signifier (the name) and the signified (the characteristic). Regarding "the transformer as one," this refers to the transforming consciousness being collectively termed a single part because it is a discernment;
thus, it does not differentiate between subject and object. Furthermore, truly untainted right knowledge (*anāsrava-samyagjñāna*) also does not differentiate between subject and object;
therefore, it is said that the untainted is without such [duality]. Otherwise, because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), it does not divide into two.
[Commentary] Question: Regarding the passage from "If [one relies on] the dependent nature" to "should be known," the intent of this question is as follows:

If it is stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) subsumes right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), why was it previously stated that the dependent nature takes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as its object?
"Should be known" means that because the imagined nature has no substantial reality, one can only "know" the dependent nature.

Regarding the statement that "that which should be abandoned is perfected" and "that which should be realized is perfected," the answer is as follows: That [text] speaks only of the defiled portion (*kliṣṭa-bhāga*) of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), not the pure portion (*viśuddha-bhāga*).

If the pure portion of the dependent nature also takes non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) as its object—where "non-apprehension" means taking the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*) as its object—then it is as follows:

the tainted, defiled portion takes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as its object, while the untainted, pure portion takes the two kinds of emptiness as its object. Thus, the untainted dependent nature is established.
It is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
[Commentary: Alternatively, regarding those instances where it is said to be subsumed under the perfected nature, according to the old *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā*, it states:

"The name is the characteristic of the imagined (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*); conceptualization is the dependent (*paratantra*); and suchness and correct cognition are subsumed under the perfected nature."

[Commentary]: Previously, this was discussed according to the gate of expression (*abhilāpa-mukha*); now, it is established based on the aspects of the perceived and the perceiver (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding the statement that "reaching the name is conceptualization" (*nāma-vikalpa*), the explanation is as follows:

As previously stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it is called "entry into the expressive" (*abhilāpa-praveśa*) because the treatise says: "That which appears as if it were the expressive is designated as 'name' (*nāman*), and it is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Now, however, the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* explains it according to the aspects of the perceived and the perceiver; therefore, even the "name" that expresses [the object] is [included].
Because the image-part (nimittabhāga) is the object-aspect of the seeing-part (darśanabhāga), it differs from the former [self-witnessing part];

furthermore, since the other [parts], such as self-witnessing and the seeing-part itself, are termed "discrimination" (vikalpa), both the seeing and image parts are subsumed under the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "that which is grasped is entirely non-existent... because it lacks substantial reality," the explanation is as follows:

The *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is without substance; among the five dharmas, it is subsumed solely within "name. This is intended to reveal that what is grasped exists only as a name and entirely lacks substantial reality.
Question: According to the commentary, even the expressive name is subsumed within "characteristic" (*nimitta*). If that is so, would there not then be four [dharmas]?

If there are no five dharmas, why is this so? It is because the name (*nāman*) is itself the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, for what reason is it said that the parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature) subsumes those names?
The answer is: not so. The intended meaning here is that although it is indeed a name, it is also described as a characteristic because it is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for views;
it is not because the name is the characteristic itself. This was the prior intention stated regarding the absence of "name" among the five dharmas.
Since this is not only a name but also extends to the characteristic (*nimitta*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* states among the five categories that "whatever exists as a name is a characteristic;

whatever exists as a characteristic is not necessarily a name," because [the name] refers to the intrinsic substance (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth. Thus, one knows that characteristics and names are distinct.

Therefore, among the five dharmas, the category of "name" is taught within the category of "parikalpita" (imagined nature) to reveal that its essence is non-existent. Question: Among the five dharmas, is "name" the imagined nature?
Since that which is grasped by the imputational nature has no essence, it is not yet clear whether it can be called "having an essence.

The answer intends to clarify that the imputational nature possesses only a name but lacks a substantial entity; even the name itself has no essence, as names are also characteristics that arise dependently.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "True Suchness and Correct Wisdom" to "are not mutually contradictory":

the *Madhyāntavibhāga* (Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes) maintains that both the wisdom that takes as its object and the suchness that is the object are included within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because both sever outflows and both eliminate inversions.

As for the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it maintains that from the perspective of the meaning of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is likewise no contradiction. Question: If correct wisdom can sever outflows, how can true suchness sever outflows? Answer: [See following section].
Correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is the essence that realizes; its realized object is untainted suchness (*anāsrava-tathatā*).

Since this [suchness] is untainted, and because correct wisdom can sever delusions, it subsumes the essence of untainted suchness. Furthermore, being free from defilement, it may also be termed "untainted.
Moreover, if the realizing subject and the realized object were distinct, neither could be subsumed as untainted; since the subject and object of realization are not different, both are [untainted].
Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), the *Madhyāntavibhāga* states that both awakening (*bodhi*) and the abandonment [of defilements] are called "awakening.
It further explains that both wisdom (*jñāna*) and its locus are collectively termed "prajñā.

[Commentary]: Regarding the ten fascicles, the term "disordered" refers to the fact that the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (or *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, depending on context) explains the five dharmas (*pañcadharma*) without following a fixed sequence; hence it is called "disordered. At the end...
This treatise should be understood as follows.

[Commentary: The phrase "because it relies extensively on names and signs" up to "explaining that reality is not names or signs" means that the mind of the dependent nature provisionally establishes what is grasped as being subsumed under names and signs;
this explains the reason for saying that the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) abounds in names.

Because one falsely conceptualizes objects first, and subsequently falsely conceptualizes names upon those objects, the first nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is subsumed solely within the two categories of name and appearance (*nāma* and *nimitta*).
This is because worldly sentient beings are mostly attached to names and appearances; thus, this [nature] is distinguished as being dependent on others (*paratantra*).

As for correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*), it is said to be subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), just as stated in the preceding text; therefore, it is not mentioned separately in the treatise.
[Commentary]: If the essence (*tattva*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) were mutually inclusive, they would constitute a contradiction.

If one were to take the two essences of "name" (*nāma*) and "meaning" (*artha*) from the *Saṃgraha* to subsume the essence of name and meaning within these five dharmas, it would result in a contradiction. Why?

Because among the five dharmas, "meaning" is itself the characteristic (*nimitta*), while "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). That treatise takes "meaning" as the primary nature; thus, it would be taking the non-existent to subsume the existent—how could this be?
There is no contradiction.

[Commentary: Regarding the establishment of these points up to the "appropriated" (upātta), this citation from the treatise clarifies that what is explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* differs from what is stated in this treatise.

[Commentary]: Regarding this term "name" (*nāman*): it is the remainder of the discussion on names. Therefore, it is stated that within this treatise, the "name" spoken of refers to the "name" among the five dharmas;
its meaning is precisely "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) and "characteristic" (*nimitta*). This clarifies that [this text] differs from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun).

Consequently, the explanations of the five dharmas in these two treatises differ, and their mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*) also varies. Here, we shall not cite them in full, but merely cite those points that correspond.
Raising this point is not intended to explicitly clarify the mutual inclusion of the five dharmas.
[Commentary: Because the name possesses the power of the expressive potential (*vācaka-śakti*), it reaches as far as the *paratantra-svabhāva*.

The meaning of this statement is that dharmas such as the mind, which are of the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra*), can be designated by names because names function as the expressers (*vācaka*); thus, the name itself is the basis for the arising of grasping (*grāha*).

The name "dependent" (paratantra) refers to that which arises in dependence [on causes and conditions]; however, because attachment is further produced toward it, it is said to be the "dependently originated phenomenon" (paratantra-svabhāva).

The passage below cites Vasubandhu as proof, thereby designating the dependently originated phenomenon itself as the "name. If one carefully examines the meaning of the treatise, this is how it should be understood.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because it is extremely remote": the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the nature of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

Now, since the grasping at the dependent nature does not rely upon the perfected nature—in order to include the dependent nature—it is said to be "remote. Even if one relies upon the grasping at the dependent nature, when explained through successive stages, the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*) is fundamentally free from names and conventions (*nāma-vyavahāra*).
[Commentary] The phrase "because there is no name that conforms to the dependent" means that while there exists the object of grasping (the imagined nature),
there is no object that corresponds to the name "dependent."

[Commentary]: Regarding the explanation that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is included within the "neither of the two" (*ubhaya-apoha*): this means that the perfected nature transcends verbal expression;

it is free from names and free from referents. Because it is free from names, the perfected nature cannot serve as a basis for names, yet it is designated as a name by being the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
Because it is free from referents, one cannot falsely imagine it to be substantially existent based on this perfected nature, nor can one establish it through mere designation.

Because it is for the sake of the meaning (*artha*), one knows that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is free from both name and meaning; therefore, it is said that it is "neither of the two" and is not subsumed by either.

[Commentary on the *Lankāvatāra-sūtra*]: Regarding the passage "the middle and extremes... even the provisional also pervades existence," the explanation is as follows: based on the two teachings and the five dharmas, there are two interpretations. The first says:
"Alternatively, 'pervading existence and non-existence' refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)," because the essence of the imagined nature is non-existent.

It is not substantially existent; even if it arises dependently, its essence is existence—this is the second point. Alternatively, if its essence were substantially existent, then the essence of the five dharmas would all be substantially existent.

However, although the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks an essential reality when analyzed, it is conventionally said to exist in accordance with deluded cognition, just as one might speak of "existent" regarding a net of hair or flowers in the sky due to deluded perception.
To grasp these as real is incorrect. Furthermore, this applies to the objects of the imagined nature.

That which serves as the basis is the *paratantra* (dependent nature); although the *parikalpita* (imagined nature) lacks any actual characteristics, it is spoken of [as such], and thus it is conventionally said that the imagined nature also pertains to existence.
This second interpretation clarifies that the five dharmas are, in their entirety, existent.

[Commentary: Regarding the various sūtras that appear disordered, one should understand them according to their underlying principle. What has been clarified above—the mutual inclusion of the five dharmas and the three natures—was cited from the four teachings;
only the first [the Yogācāra teaching] cites the text of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* without confusion.

As for the other three teachings, the textual passages explaining the mutual inclusion of the three natures and five dharmas are intermingled and lack sequential order; let the reader take note of this.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that the *Madhyāntavibhāga* [explains] the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and the ten realities (*daśatattva*) as being mutually inclusive, that treatise’s second chapter explains this inclusion in detail;
here, we shall merely cite the names and briefly clarify their intended meaning. First, regarding "fundamental reality" (*mūlatattva*):

because the other realities are established based upon it, it is established according to the three natures. To explain: within the three natures, there is the sense of "reality," and thus they are termed "realities."
Regarding "the reality within the first nature": in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, it is stated that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is eternally non-existent;
because it is eternally non-existent, one regards this nature as real and thus it is non-erroneous. The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) exists but is not real;
because it is merely existent and not real, it is accepted as being real only with respect to the dependent nature. As for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), there are two [aspects].
Because it is emptiness, it is accepted as the reality of the two characteristics; this is because it is non-erroneous regarding the fundamental characteristic of reality.
Third, the reality of non-error refers to the nature of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and selflessness;

by means of these natures, one can counteract the four errors such as permanence and so forth. Fourth, the reality of cause and effect refers to the Four Noble Truths, which are the causes of defilement and purification.
7. The reality of the distinction between results (*phala-viśeṣa-tattva*), which refers to the distinction between the two truths of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*);
8. The reality of universal consensus (*prasiddha-tattva*), which refers to what is universally established by both worldly reasoning and the two [types of] consensus; 9.

The reality of the domain of purified wisdom (*viśuddha-jñāna-gocara-tattva*), which refers to the difference in the domains of the purified wisdom that has cleared away the two obstructions—the afflictive (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) and the cognitive (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*); 10. The reality of appropriation (*parigraha-tattva*), which refers to... [the text continues].
The ninefold distinctions of reality concerning the inclusion of the three natures within the five categories are as follows: the seven aspects of true suchness are included within the three natures.
The tenfold skillfulness in reality refers to the cultivation of skillfulness regarding the ten categories, such as the aggregates, in order to counteract the ten kinds of views of self;
however, each of these ten realities is individually included within the three natures, with the first one being included within all three natures.
I have cited other [passages] as appropriate; fearing that the text would become too prolix, I have not cited them all.

[Commentary: As for "the aggregates and so forth," this refers to the ten types of skillfulness (kauśalya) regarding the aggregates and so forth taught in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, namely, skillfulness regarding the aggregates, skillfulness regarding the elements (dhātu), and so on, as will be understood below. These are not described here in advance.

[Commentary]: "From 'if that which is falsely conceptualized' up to 'the nature of the grasped' (parikalpita-svabhāva) clarifies that both the signified (vācya) and the signifier (vācaka) possess the nature of the grasped.

This means that among the five dharmas—namely, marks (nimitta), names (nāman), and so forth—both the signified and the signifier exist. For example, when one relies on a name and conceives of the name as being the signifier, there is the nature of the grasped upon the signifier;
when one relies on an object and conceives of the object, there is the nature of the grasped upon the signified."
The adherence to the nature [of phenomena] as being such that both the signifier and the signified exist belongs generally to the first nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Alternatively, it may be said that within each individual nature there are both signifiers and signifieds; this is the explanation of how signifiers and signifieds exist within the first nature.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "in the first five matters, from 'characteristic' (*lakṣaṇa*) to 'basis' (*āśraya*), they pertain to the dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*):

this explains the second point, the meaning of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) as being both innate and acquired. One may also say that within the signified and the signifier, there is the dependent nature.

As for the statement that "among the five matters, the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is entirely [the dependent nature], while characteristic and name are partially the signified," a question arises: what is the intent of this "conceptualization"? It refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Question: What is the general definition [of "name"]? Why is it said that it consists exclusively of that which is expressed (*abhidheya*)? Answer: Mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) necessarily possess names. A "name" is subsumed under that which expresses (*abhidhāna*).
When one analyzes the meaning associated with this name, that analysis is subsumed under that which is expressed.

For example, when one says "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), it means "discernment" (*vijñapti*). This "discernment" is what is expressed; it is made manifest by means of the expressing name. Therefore, [the name] is exclusively that which is expressed.
Regarding the statement that "a portion of names (*nāman*) is the signified (*abhidheya*)," [the interlocutor] asks:

"Since the conjunction of names is the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the conjunction of signs (*lakṣaṇa*) is the signified, why is it said that a portion of names is the signified and a portion of signs is the signifier? The answer is:

Because names signify names, names are included within the category of the signified. For example, in the world, when one says "So-and-so" and the like, because there is an extreme abundance of fame and profit (*nāma-lābha*), the commentary states this.

It is said that because names are also what is expressed (*vācya*), and because a portion of the characteristics (*nimitta*) are also that which expresses (*vācaka*), the intended meaning is that names are themselves characteristics.
Since names are subsumed under the characteristic-aspect when contrasted with the seeing-aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), names are indeed characteristics;

thus, the characteristics are the expressers. Therefore, the Commentary states: "Because names are also characteristics. In this way, the expressed and the expresser both belong to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because they arise from conditions, this constitutes the second nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which possesses both the signified and the signifier;

therefore, it is said that "these three dharmas, as appropriate, consist of the signified and the signifier belonging to the dependent nature. These three dharmas are namely: appearance (*nimitta*), name (*nāman*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "True Suchness (tathatā) is the entirety [of the perfected nature], while Correct Wisdom (samyag-jñāna) is a small portion" up to the point of reaching the Perfectly Established Nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva):

Question: True Suchness is that which is explained (the signified); its meaning is easily understood. Why, then, is Correct Wisdom also that which is explained? Answer: Because Correct Wisdom realizes True Suchness, their essence is not separate;
since wisdom and True Suchness are equal, a small portion of Correct Wisdom is also that which is explained. Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra...
It is said that the wisdom of all Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable; its gateway of wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter.

This gateway is the teaching (*śāsana*), and thus it is that which expresses wisdom. This is the wisdom of principle (*prajñā-jñāna*), and as such, it is that which is expressed. A small portion of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is identical to True Suchness (*tathatā*) and is therefore subsumed under that which is expressed.
A small portion of correct wisdom is that which expresses, because through subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it manifests as if it were [the object].

Because it measures names, phrases, and syllables, it is said that subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is also a signifier (*vācaka*). The treatise states: "Subsequently attained [wisdom] manifests as the semblance of a signifier.
Thus, both the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier belong to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), for they are free from inversion.

This constitutes the third nature (*trisvabhāva*), which possesses the full sense of both signifier and signified. Question: Since the mind of correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) and so forth pertain to both signifier and signified, why was this stated previously?

Question: Is conceptualization (*vikalpa*) exclusively that which is signified? Answer: It is so when referring to the distinct opening of characteristics and names within the state of outflows (*sāsrava*); this is because conceptualization therein is exclusively that which is signified.
However, in the state of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*), correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) alone exists, and thus it possesses both the capacity to signify and that which is signified.

[Commentary]: The previous statement that "there is no means of expression (vācaka) for the untainted (anāsrava) state free from faults" refers to the fact that, as stated in the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, because the untainted mind and so forth are free from conceptual proliferation (prapañca), they are collectively termed "correct cognition" (samyagjñāna) without being described in terms of the signified (vācya) and the signifier (vācaka).

Now, when it is said that the actual essence of phenomena (dharmatā) is truly untainted and yet possesses the capacity to signify, this is explained according to the essence of phenomena; it indicates that even the subsequently attained [wisdom] (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) possesses the names, phrases, and sentences that serve as signifiers.

Because the letters and so forth are equal, in the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the Bodhisattva on the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*) manifests immeasurable names, phrases, and letters;
therefore, it is not the same as what preceded it.

[Commentary: Regarding the two types of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and the objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) and so forth that accompany them, which are included within this nature—there are none.
The two types of untainted wisdom refer to fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Regarding the category of "concomitant factors":

when wisdom arises, there are the five universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the five object-specific factors (*viśeṣa-bhūmika*), the eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*), and the associated mind-king (*citta-rāja*), each of which possesses both the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).
These are termed the "pure dependent nature" (*viśuddha-paratantra-svabhāva*), and because they are entirely non-erroneous, they are subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "based on the three intrinsic characteristics," the intended meaning is that the *parikalpita* (imagined), *paratantra* (dependent), and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) natures each possess two aspects:
the signified (*lakṣya*) and the signifier (*lakṣaṇa*). These subsequent three sets of three aspects are respectively correlated with the three natures.
[Commentary]: To speak according to the actual reality, the third [nature] also possesses the latter two natures.

As for the intention behind the statement that "the mutual connection between the two characteristics is solely the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)," this is said according to what is predominant.
In actual fact, it also possesses the latter two natures. If one holds that the name and the object are connected by way of the two emptinesses, [then it is so].
This refers to the conceptualization of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

While the imagined nature itself is without essence, the two characteristics upon which that imagined nature depends—the relationship between the signifier (the name) and the signified (the object)—are both dependent on the imagined nature.
Because the grasping mind and the phenomena that serve as its basis are both of the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*), [the aforementioned] applies to them.

Since it is precisely the grasping at dependent phenomena as being truly existent that constitutes the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the intended meaning is that the relationship between the two characteristics is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

This refers specifically to the relationship between the signifier—the name—and the signified—the object—possessed by those who have not yet given rise to a mind that grasps [at true existence], which is limited to the contaminated (*sāsrava*). For example, when a signifying name expresses "eye," there is inherently...
The meaning expressed by the term "eye" is naturally subsumed within the name "eye"; how could there be any grasping [of it as a separate entity]?
When discussing "fire," its meaning is not related to "water. Since this relationship between characteristics is natural (*dharmatā*), why is there grasping?
How can that which is grasped be of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)? Answer: The two types of relationship are those between the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*).
Since both the signifier and the signified can pertain to the untainted (*anāsrava*), and because the untainted signifier and signified— being non-erroneous—
are subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one should know that these characteristics also pertain to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

[Commentary]: The passage from "That which is clung to as a characteristic" up to "merely the dependent nature" intends to explain that the basis for what is clung to also extends to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because True Suchness (*tathatā*) is also something clung to.

This is because, for example, in the Hīnayāna, one uses a mind characterized by attachment to dharmas to cling to the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) as being substantially real.
As stated previously, True Suchness is also a "thoroughly imagined object" (*parikalpya*) through indirect application; this [present] passage is based on that.

This refers to the "distant condition" (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*). [Commentary: "Non-attachment to characteristics is itself the essence of non-existence, culminating in the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) alone. The meaning of this passage is that non-attachment to characteristics also extends to all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Question: How can these characteristics extend to the first nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)? Answer: [The Commentary states: *The *parikalpita-svabhāva* is characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature; it is merely a conceptual construction based on the appearance of objects.

Because one does not grasp at the characteristics of this imagined nature as being real, it is said to be "non-attachment to characteristics. Since this non-grasping applies even to the imagined nature, the characteristic of non-attachment extends to the first nature as well.*
It is said that non-attachment to characteristics means that the essence itself is non-existent and thus cannot be grasped.
Furthermore, to conceptualize what is grasped is like the non-Buddhists who cling to a real self (*ātman*) or a truly existent *tathatā*.

If such a real self were a substantial entity (*bhāva*), it would be an object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and would fall under the category of graspable characteristics. However, since this real self lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), its essence is non-existent.
Because phenomena that lack intrinsic nature cannot be clung to, the true nature of reality (*tattva*) and so forth are indeed called "the characteristic of non-clinging.

This characteristic of non-clinging applies to both the first nature (the imagined) and the true nature of reality; since the true nature of reality is precisely the imagined nature, it is so designated.

The characteristic of non-clinging also applies to the dependent and the perfected natures, as can be understood from the text. For example, although the untainted mind and other such states do not involve clinging, they nonetheless arise from conditions.
Furthermore, because it arises in dependence upon others and is non-erroneous, it is also the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Although the five uncontaminated sensory consciousnesses (*anāsrava-pañca-vijñāna*), the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), as well as contaminated wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*, *cintā-mayī-prajñā*), and neutral minds (*avyākṛta-citta*) do not involve grasping, they are nonetheless dependently originated (*paratantra*).

When the treatises state that these characteristics are exclusively the perfected nature, this is said in reference to the fact that they are not capable of grasping; therefore, it does not apply to the other two natures.

[Commentary]: Now, from the "Section on Compendium and Explanation" (Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī) up to the "Section on Correct Differentiation" (Viniścaya), this citation from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* re-explains the distinctions between the five characteristics.
This is a general citation of the text; therein, each difficulty is addressed and re-explained. Regarding the two characteristics of "belonging" (*parigraha*) and "connection" (*sambandha*):
"that which is the basis for the grasping of the imagined nature" means that within these characteristics, there is the imagined [nature].
Regarding the nature of that which is grasped (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): this imagined nature serves as the objective basis for the mind that grasps;
that is, the object of apprehension serves as the support for the mind that performs the conceptualization.
As will be understood from the text itself, the Master of the Commentary explains this in detail below.

[Commentary]: From "clinging to signs" up to "and these latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*) refers to the mind and its mental factors that are capable of clinging, as well as the latent tendencies associated with this mind and its mental factors;
these are collectively termed "clinging latent tendencies," which are the seeds.
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "not clinging to signs" to "right discernment of liberation," the intended meaning is as follows:

Because one still possesses the imputed nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and its seeds, one cannot be said to have "non-clinging to signs. Now, because the imputed nature and its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have been severed, the "right discernment of liberation" arises;
therefore, it is called "liberation through non-clinging. This liberation is True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is right discernment.

That untainted right knowledge (*anāsrava-samyagjñāna*) which is able to dispel pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) and sever the latent tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*) is called "non-attachment.

[Commentary] The explanation beginning from "The following... up to "...is the characteristic of non-attachment" is the Master of the Commentary’s interpretation of the five characteristics as they appear across various treatises.
Regarding the passage "that which is the characterized object (*lakṣya*) up to that which is not included among the characterized objects," that refers to the aforementioned treatise.

The intended meaning is that the characterized object (*lakṣya*) which is expressed is a dharma possessing substantial reality (*savastuka*). Among the five categories (*pañcavastu*), the first four are the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the fifth is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Therefore, among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), the dependent and the perfected are dharmas that possess existence and are thus the objects of expression (*abhidheya*).

The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is a non-existent dharma and is therefore not an object of expression. Question: How can a non-existent dharma not be an object of expression? Answer: Although it is non-existent, [it is still the object of expression].
The Dharma is what is currently being explained; that is to say, non-existent dharmas lack a distinct substantial essence, unlike the eye and other faculties which possess many such distinctions.
Therefore, it is said that [non-existent dharmas] are not what is explained. Regarding the phrase "the two treatises," each of them explains its own position:

the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra-vyākhyāna* (or *Vyākhyā-yukti*) both explain that the expressive [words] are exclusively of the nature of the parikalpita (imagined). This is also not contradictory.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, and the *Vyākhyāyukti*, that which is grasped as an object of attachment is also called:

the "universally imagined" (*parikalpita*); the "constituted by conjunction" (*saṃyoga-saṃskṛta*); the "characteristic of superimposition" (*adhyāropita-lakṣaṇa*); the "falsely grasped" (*mṛṣā-parikalpita*); the "manifested by verbal expression" (*abhilāpa-prabhāvita*);
the "application of syllables" (*vyañjana-prayoga*); the "mere sound" (*ghoṣamātra*); and the "devoid of essential nature and characteristics" (*asvabhāva-nirnimitta*). This is because...

This principle does not contradict the statement in the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Holy Teachings), fascicle 12, which says that the names that express [objects] are of the nature of mere conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);

nor does it contradict the *Xianyang shengjiao lun*, fascicle 16. The sixteenth fascicle establishes two types of association based on the three natures according to the relationship between the signifier and the signified;
the twelfth fascicle refers to the association of the signifier alone as being merely conceptually constructed. Since each is based on a different meaning, they do not contradict one another.
Regarding the phrase "because these two are related and reach the point of giving rise to the conceptualizing mind": this explains the meaning of the third characteristic.

It states that within the relationship between these two characteristics, the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of being conceptually constructed) and the conceptualizing mind stand in a relationship of support (*āśraya*) and supported (*āśrita*).

This is because it is precisely due to the existence of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* that the conceptualizing mind arises; thus, the *parikalpita-svabhāva* is the support and the conceptualizing mind is that which is supported.
It is clearly known that the basis of grasping is the mind of parikalpita-svabhāva (the imagined nature), while this mind itself is paratantra-svabhāva (the dependent nature).
Therefore, the characteristic of the mutual connection between these two is exclusively parikalpita-svabhāva. One merely states that this characteristic can give rise to the parikalpita mind;
one does not say that this characteristic itself is paratantra-svabhāva.

[Commentary: Therefore, the statement in the fourth [section] regarding "the self-nature of the thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) explains the fourth of the five matters, namely the characteristic of attachment (*abhiniveśa-lakṣaṇa*).
Next, the phrase "the fourth can be known" refers to this very text;

"the fourth can be known" explains that within the characteristic of the fourth attachment, there is the mind that performs the thorough imagination (*parikalpa-citta*), as well as the seeds for severing [that mind] repeatedly within the process of thorough imagination.
The son thus clings to the characteristic of dependence on others as the fifth;

that which is the characteristic of non-clinging refers to the intention that the defiled dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is precisely the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it serves as the basis for the grasping mind.
Therefore, one gives rise to contemplation of the mind and realizes, as it truly is, that the grasped nature is empty, and likewise realizes, as it truly is, the grasping mind and—

Having completed the severance of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one realizes that the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*) grasped as real are non-existent, and that there is only the afflicted portion of the dependent nature (*kliṣṭa-paratantra-svabhāva*) along with its seeds.
Thereupon, the Noble Path arises; once the afflicted portion of the dependent nature and its seeds have been severed, liberation (*vimukti*) is attained.

Liberation is precisely the true suchness (*tathatā*). As it is said: when the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is absent and the dependent nature is freed from outflowing afflictions (*sāsrava-kliṣṭa*), one attains liberation. There is no [other] liberation.
All arise from right knowledge and are termed "non-attachment to signs.

[Commentary] Regarding these five signs, the first two differ across various treatises as each relies on a single meaning; the latter three are consistent in principle across all treatises and do not contradict one another.
This means that among the five signs, the two signs concerning the signified (*lakṣya*) and the signifier (*lakṣaṇa*) do not conflict between the various treatises.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the sixteenth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* both state that each of the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) possesses all three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

However, the eighty-first [chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] and the twelfth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* both state that the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the signified consists of the five categories (*pañcavastu*), such as characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and names (*nāman*), whereas the characteristic of the signifier is exclusively the nature of the parikalpita (the imagined).
Therefore, among the five categories, the first two—characteristics and names—are so stated in various treatises.

Each is explained differently according to its specific name and meaning; however, regarding the three natures within the Four Truths, they are all identical. For instance, as stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun) and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* (Xianyang shengjiao lun), Chapter 16:
"The two aspects of mutual dependence are exclusively the nature of the parikalpita (imagined); if one clings to these aspects, it is the nature of the paratantra (dependent);
if one does not cling to these aspects, it is the nature of the pariniṣpanna (perfected). If [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] states eighty-one... [text truncated].
The *Xiányán shìlùn* (12) explains the latter three characteristics as follows: "The characteristic of mutual connection is the nature of the thoroughly imagined (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
'Attachment' refers to the mind that performs the imagining and its seeds, because they have the nature of dependent false discrimination (*paratantra-vikalpa*).

The characteristic of non-attachment and so forth is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Within this characteristic of non-attachment, it is said that [the absence of] what is imagined and grasped is itself the perfected nature."

Regarding the statement that "one attains liberation through the characteristics and their underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*," the intended meaning is that by knowing the non-existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the impure dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one attains liberation into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Therefore, the latter three [characteristics] are identical across all treatises. Question:
The *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (12) states that within the characteristic of the relationship between the signifier and the two [signified] natures, it says that there is only the imagined nature.

Question: I do not yet understand what the distinction is. Answer: Regarding the term "parikalpita-svabhāva" (imagined nature) used within the context of the "signifier" (*abhidhāna*), it refers to the fact that the very essence of the imagined nature is non-existent.

When the term "parikalpita-svabhāva" is used within the context of the "characteristic of mutual relation," it indicates that this imagined nature serves as the objective referent (*ālambana*) for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, regarding the "characteristic of attachment," it refers to the mind that conceives of the dependent nature [as being the imagined].
This can be understood according to its meaning; it should not be criticized individually.
[Commentary: This means that "this is this" and "this is the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of this stage" is called the "truth established by the world.
This explains the intent of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, stating that this worldly truth—such as earth, water, and so forth—has existed from beginningless time.

The conventional designations "water," "earth," and so forth, which are determined through the linguistic expressions shared by oneself and others, are what are called "real" because they are conceptually constructed as water, fire, and so on.
Furthermore, it is not the case that earth and the other elements are established as real only after being analyzed and examined through external, heterodox reasoning;
rather, they are established with the name "real" solely by virtue of the linguistic conventions universally invoked in the world.
[Commentary]: "According to the observer, up to 'this is not the ultimate reality'—this explains the intent of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

It states that whether one is at the stage of a practitioner of wisdom (*jñānin*) or an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), whatever object one observes and desires to establish is established by means of such principles as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*). For example, sound is impermanent because it is produced; just as..."

Just as with a jar and so forth, that which is the object of activity and the known object for the arising of definitive wisdom through such thorough investigation is precisely the "attainment of reality" (*tattvaprāpti*) that is to be established.
This reality is established by means of the principle of common proof (*sādhāraṇasiddhitaḥ*).

The principle of establishment based on what one has personally established (*svaprasiddhasiddhitaḥ*) is the third of the four principles; it is established by means of the three measures of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
That which is to be established and proven is as stated below. However, in what stage of practice does this true reality reside?

It resides within the three stages of the person whose distracted mind has already passed beyond [the mundane] but who has not yet entered the Path of Seeing. During the thirty moments of mind and the seven preparatory practices (*saptaprayoga*), one is called a "person dwelling in the stage of an ordinary being" (*pṛthagjana*) and is also called a "wise one.
If one enters the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is no longer this true reality.

[Commentary: "This refers to all Śrāvakas reaching what is called this 'reality' (*tattva*)" clarifies that this is the reality practiced by the pure wisdom regarding the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa-viśuddha-jñāna-gocara-tattva*).

Within this context, the text provides a further explanation in response to an objection, stating: "The untainted skillful means wisdom (*anāsrava-upāya-jñāna*). Regarding this, there are two interpretations. The first states:

it refers to taking the untainted preparatory application (*prayoga*) within the first seven stages and comparing it to the subsequent uninterrupted preparatory application (*ānantarya-prayoga*). Therefore...

Regarding the four paths—preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and special progress (*viśeṣa*)—when viewed in relation to one another, preparatory knowledge (*prayogajñāna*) also extends to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
This is because the two types of untainted preparatory knowledge are essentially tainted preparatory knowledge that serves as the inducer of the untainted fundamental knowledge (*maulajñāna*);
thus, it is metaphorically designated as "untainted preparatory" by virtue of being able to induce the untainted, just as the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) can induce the untainted.
That is to say, it is conventionally designated that the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is also called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the statement "outflow-free," subsequent worldly knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-laukika-jñāna*) is so called because it is able to take as its object the established Four Truths and so forth after the outflow-free [wisdom].

Alternatively, the contaminated worldly knowledge of phenomena (*vastu-jñāna*) arising from the preceding outflow-free wisdom is also metaphorically termed "subsequent outflow-free wisdom," as it is said:

Because the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is induced by others who are untainted (*anāsrava*), it is also called "untainted. Alternatively, persons of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) also possess the three or five types of untainted subsequently attained cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that take phenomena as their objects.
Regarding the phrase "the reality that is the object of the wisdom purified of the afflictive obstructions" (*kleśāvaraṇaviśuddhajñānagocaratattva*), the meaning is as follows:
for those who have attained the four fruits of the path, as they successively abandon the afflictions, the afflictive obstructions are also said to be "purified of afflictive obstructions."
This refers to the obstacles that are to be remedied; "wisdom" refers to the wisdom that serves as the remedy. If one interprets it in this way, purity belongs to the obstacles.

Alternatively, another interpretation states: because the wisdom of purity can sever the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), it is called "the wisdom of purity that purifies the afflictive obstacles.

Since those of the Two Vehicles have not yet severed the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is specifically referred to here as the "wisdom of purity that purifies the afflictive obstacles. [This concerns] the sphere of practice.

"Those" refers to the spheres of practice cultivated by followers of the Two Vehicles; such as the untainted path of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the principles of the Four Noble Truths, all of which are the spheres of practice cultivated by those of the Two Vehicles. "Reality" refers exclusively to the principles of the Four Noble Truths;

that which is practiced is "reality," and thus it is called the "reality of the sphere of practice. It is said that by taking these as objects of cognition, one attains [liberation] regarding the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Regarding "purity" (*viśuddhi*), there are two interpretations of the term "condition" (*ālambana*). First, it is said that "condition" means "to rely upon.

This refers to the practitioners of the Two Vehicles who rely on this wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the principle of the emptiness of persons to take the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) as their conditions; thereby they are able to sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and their wisdom attains purity.

Second, it is said that "condition" refers to "cognitive engagement" (*ālambana-manasikāra*). This means that by taking the established truths as their objective domain, they sever the afflictive obstructions.
"Attaining purity of wisdom through practices such as the contemplation of the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths," and so forth;

and regarding the phrase "because one subsequently realizes non-obstruction," this means that by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), one realizes both the *sa-upadhiśeṣa* (nirvāṇa with remainder) and *an-upadhiśeṣa* (nirvāṇa without remainder).
Since one has attained nirvāṇa and is no longer bound by afflictions, it is called "non-obstruction. This is taught as its true nature.

It is indeed so. The statement that "it is called 'true reality' (tattva) because it arises from discernment," up to this point, intends to explain that "discernment" refers to the observation by means of wisdom while one is in the stages of the equipment (*sambhāra*) and application (*prayoga*) of the two vehicles;

thus, by observing the Four Truths through [the aspects of] impermanence and so forth, one attains clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Once clear realization has been attained, subsequently, the truth...

When actual knowledge (*bhūtajñāna*) arises, it takes as its object the principles of the Four Noble Truths; because these are the objects of the three types of knowledge—such as the knowledge of the path (*yathābhūtajñāna*) and so forth—the principles of the truths are termed "the real" (*tattva*).
Question: Why is *abhisamaya* (clear realization) so called? Answer: *Abhi* means "manifesting before one's eyes," and *samaya* means "observing.

Thus, by means of the preparatory knowledge (*prayogajñāna*), one observes the principles of the Four Noble Truths as they manifest before one; this is called "observation. Following this clear realization, there is no [further]...

Because the undefiled path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises to abandon the afflictions and one becomes a noble one (*ārya*), it is said that "after the stage of clear observation (*abhisamaya*), true knowledge (*bhūta-jñāna*) arises.

Regarding the question of what is meant by "true": it refers exclusively to the Four Noble Truths. Why is it stated that the "true" as the object of knowledge (*jñeya-bhūta*) consists of the three types of knowledge?
It is because the Four Noble Truths taken collectively are termed "the true," which includes both the preparatory (*prayoga*) and subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) knowledges.
Question: Can wisdom (*jñāna*) also observe *tathatā* (suchness)? Answer: No. Since wisdom is threefold, its objects of reality are not identical.
If *tathatā* within the Four Noble Truths is the object of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), it is therefore called "reality" (*bhūtārtha*).

However, the principles such as suffering and impermanence within the Four Truths are the objects of both the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); these too are called "reality. Thus, taken together, there are four [types].

Question: Since it has been stated that the principle of the Four Noble Truths is also called "reality" (*tattva*), and given that untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) belongs to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), I wonder whether untainted wisdom itself can also be termed "reality.
Answer: If that untainted wisdom takes the minds of others as its object, it may also be termed "reality," for it is then the objective domain of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
Therefore, [the Commentary] says: "Because it can obstruct wisdom within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is called 'this reality'.

Regarding the phrase "cognitive obstructions," this refers to the obstructions that are to be remedied, thereby revealing the wisdom that acts as the remedy. "Purified wisdom regarding the cognitive obstructions" means...
When a bodhisattva enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), they sever the two obstacles of conceptualization; this is collectively termed "purity" (*viśuddhi*).

This continues up to the tenth stage and the Buddha-stage, where purity is defined according to the point at which each respective obstacle is exhausted. "Pure wisdom" (*jñāna-viśuddhi*) refers either to the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*), or alternatively, purity belongs to wisdom itself;
because wisdom is pure, it is called "pure wisdom. As for "the sphere of practice," this refers to the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) and the four [means of attraction] practiced by the bodhisattva.
It encompasses the principles of the two-fold emptiness of self and phenomena, the ten true suchnesses (*tathatā*), and so forth; all of these are the spheres of practice for Bodhisattvas.
To sever delusions and realize suchness is called "true suchness," which is the objective realm of wisdom.

This true suchness transcends verbal expression, yet the Buddha provisionally establishes it through names and phrases to teach sentient beings, so that after they have heard it, they may subsequently engage in cultivation; therefore, it is so described.

Tathatā (Suchness) is called the "True Reality. Question: Since a Bodhisattva takes both the established (*prajñapti*) and the non-established (*aprajñapti*) as objects, I wonder which dharma they apprehend that is named "True Reality"? Answer:
A Bodhisattva realizes the non-established and thereby severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding the delusion of principle;

they also sever the latent tendencies regarding the delusion of phenomena by means of the sixteen moments of mind regarding the four established Truths (*satya*). However, here it refers specifically to taking the non-established Tathatā below as the object and naming it the "True Reality."

It is considered "true reality" because it is the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) that is the primary object of observation for Bodhisattvas, whereas the established truths (*prajñapti-satya*) are observed only incidentally.

Question: Since Bodhisattvas simultaneously abandon both obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) through the twofold emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), why is this reality designated only as "the true reality that is the domain of the wisdom purified of the cognitive obstacle" (*jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhajñānagocaratattva*)?
Answer: Although they realize and abandon both obstacles simultaneously regarding the twofold emptiness, [this designation] is made in order to counteract...
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks only of the purification of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the wisdom [thereof], and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from the mundane up to the stage of the Mahāyāna alone," this refers to the four levels of the four realities (*catvāri tattvāni*).

There are two ways of correlating these stages, which can be understood through careful investigation; there is a difference in their breadth and narrowness. As for the "four principles" (*catasro yuktayaḥ*), consult the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*.

Eleventh, the four principles (*yukti*): 1. The principle of dependence (*apekṣā-yukti*) refers to the fact that when conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) arise, they necessarily depend on conditions such as earth and water. 2.
The principle of efficacy (*kāryakaraṇa-yukti*) refers to the functional activity, such as the eye serving as the basis for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). 3.

The principle of logical proof (*upapatti-sādhana-yukti*) refers to the proclamation of statements that do not contradict valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in order to establish a point that is yet to be proven, such as through inference (*anumāna*).
The establishment of the thesis that sound is impermanent and so forth is accomplished through four principles of natural order (*dharmatā-yukti*):
namely, that from beginningless time the characteristics of phenomena have been established by their very nature, such that fire can burn, water can moisten, wind can move, and earth can support.

[Commentary]: "Also taking the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) as the truth, up to 'if not so, it would be diminished'" means that these Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya*) are also taken as true by virtue of including untainted wisdom.

If untainted wisdom were not taken as true, the reality of the Four Noble Truths would be diminished because untainted wisdom would not be subsumed within them; therefore, it is said that untainted wisdom is also [true].

Because it is an object of the post-attainment uncontaminated mundane wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-anāsrava-lokajñāna*) obtained after the [four] truths have been observed, the post-attainment uncontaminated wisdom is called "mundane wisdom";

since this mind also takes the conventional as its object, the "reality that is the domain of wisdom purified of the cognitive obstructions" (*jñeyāvaraṇaviśuddhajñānagocaratattva*) should also be explained according to this principle.
[Treatise] Regarding the statement that "worldly principles are subsumed within two matters": Question:

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (36), the latter two truths take the principle of the Four Noble Truths and suchness (*tathatā*) as their essence; however, in section 73, correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is also included.

What is the reason for this discrepancy? Answer: There are three explanations. 1. One explanation is as stated in the commentary (*śu*). 2. A second explanation is the traditional interpretation by the Tripiṭaka Master, which states: "This shall be verified [in the future]."

At the time when the two obstacles are purified, one also realizes wisdom; this is just as when the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part) takes *tathatā* (suchness) as its object, the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying part) simultaneously takes the *darśana-bhāga* as its object.
Therefore, correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is also *tathatā*. There are other interpretations, but fearing they would be too prolix, they are not recorded here.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "mostly based on the principles taught for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and so forth," the explanation states:

This clarifies that it differs from the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, which explains principles and reality based on what is common to both ordinary beings and noble ones (*ārya*), and therefore encompasses all three natures (*trisvabhāva*). This treatise, however, explains principles based on ordinary beings;
because it concerns only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and not the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), it is subsumed solely under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
[Commentary]: "That which encompasses both existent phenomena (*dharma*) and non-existent phenomena constitutes the fourfold essence of reality" is the general meaning of this statement.

Specifically, non-existent phenomena do not pervade the latter three types of reality; therefore, the text says: "If one defines 'reality' based on the conceptually grasped self and phenomena, then non-existent phenomena may also be called reality.
Since existent phenomena constitute the [first] three types of reality, it is said that they "pervade" them.
The four truths cannot be established [in that way].

[Commentary: Regarding the passage in the *Madhyāntavibhāga* stating "based on the one perfected nature," among the four propositions, the first clarifies the first truth based on the imagined nature;
the second clarifies the second truth based on the imagined nature and so forth; and the third and fourth clarify the third and fourth truths based on both.
Based on the single perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). [Commentary:
Regarding the statement "the absence of nature and impermanence... up to being conventionally designated as truth": the absence of nature is real while the truth is conventional;

because it is named "real by nature" despite its nature being eternally non-existent, this conventional designation is called "truth" (satya) because it is impermanent within the context of the conventional truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Thus, the name "truth" is conventional.
Because its nature is eternally non-existent and is not [ultimately] suffering, it is said that the name "Truth" (*satya*) is provisional.
[Commentary: Regarding the second point, from "arising and ceasing are impermanent" up to "is impermanent," this means that both nature and truth are real.
Since these contaminated phenomena are truly subject to arising and ceasing, they are also suffering; thus, both nature and truth are real.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the three impurities and purity, from impermanence up to existence and non-existence, constitute the meaning of 'stainless,'" this refers to the fact that while the nature is real, the truth is spoken of in a conventional sense.
True Suchness (tathatā) is truly stainless and pure; however, when it is in the state of saṃsāra, it is termed "stained True Suchness.
When afflictions are severed and saṃsāra is ended, it is "unstained True Suchness. Thus, True Suchness is a provisional designation based on its various states.
That impermanence is in reality an eternal dharma is what is called "the nature being real";
it is not that impermanence under the Truth of Suffering is called a truth, for the true nature is not suffering.
[Commentary]: Regarding this explanation that the divisions of states (*avasthā*) are designated as defiled or pure:

it means that because there are the two stages of defilement and purity—namely, concealment and manifestation—based on what is expressed, they appear similar to the mental state of impermanence (*anityatā-saṃjñā*) that takes suffering as its object.
It is conventionally termed "impermanence" because it is initially defiled and subsequently pure; however, its essence is actually permanent.
[Commentary: Regarding those who do not actually take the aspect of impermanence as their object, the aspect of impermanence takes the three truths of conditioned phenomena as its referent;
it does not take the truth of cessation, which is unconditioned, as its objective domain.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "based on all things being impermanent," the intended meaning is that this aspect of impermanence takes the nature of the beginning and end as its object.
This subjective aspect of cognition is not the "impermanence" among the sixteen aspects; rather, it is an impermanence-cognition external to those sixteen aspects.
Why is this? Because among the sixteen aspects, the aspect of impermanence takes only the three truths (*satya*) as its objects, whereas the [nature of] the beginning is not.
This is because the nature of the Truths (satya) is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and is not manifested as impermanent.
[Commentary: Regarding the six types of impermanence: first, impermanence of non-existence; second, impermanence of non-destruction; third, impermanence of transformation;
fourth, impermanence of separation; fifth, impermanence of acquisition; sixth, impermanence of what is yet to be. These are like seeds within consciousness.
Because what precedes ceases and what follows arises in a continuous succession from moment to moment without being lost, it is called "impermanence without loss or destruction.
The rest is easy to understand.
[Commentary] Regarding the eight types: first, "momentary" refers to the characteristic of impermanence among the four characteristics of a single moment; second, "successive" refers to...
This refers to impermanence among the one characteristic and the four characteristics. Next, regarding "the three within the internal form":

this means that the disharmony of the four great elements within the internal body is called "sickness," the deterioration of the sense faculties is called "aging," and the dissolution of the body at the end of life is called "death.

Therefore, sickness, aging, and death exist only within the internal body; the mind exists only within the designation "name" (*nāma*). "Name" is the collective designation for the four aggregates that are non-material (*arūpa*).
Regarding "name, vessels, and objects of enjoyment": "vessels" refers to the external vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), as it is the locus upon which all sentient beings depend.
"Objects of enjoyment" refers to the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), which are the realms that are experienced and enjoyed.

[Commentary] Regarding the classification according to the three realms: in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are only five kinds of impermanence, namely, the absence of illness, the vessel [world], and the three kinds of enjoyment.
In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are seven, excluding illness. In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all eight kinds are present.

One interpretation states that these exist among the six heavens of the desire realm, the northern continent (*uttarakuru*), the hells in their entirety, and the hungry ghosts (*preta*) in their most extreme states of suffering.
In one portion of these [realms]—namely, among humans—there is no illness; however, there are the other seven types of impermanence.

As for the three continents of the east, south, and west, as well as among ghosts and animals, all eight types are present according to their respective abodes. This is stated in terms of the majority of cases and does not exhaustively cover every possibility.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the passage from "the impurity and purity herein" to "are not the same," this further reconciles the two views. The intention here is that this treatise (*Abhidharmasamuccaya*) discusses the ultimate meaning (*artha*) by means of its designations (*vyañjana*);

therefore, transformation and impermanence pertain to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). In contrast, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (or *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*) bases itself on the substance of the designating expressions;
thus, transformation and impermanence are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*) are impermanent.
[Commentary] Regarding the fifteen kinds of impermanence, according to that treatise, among the six kinds of impermanence, the latter five are all termed "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*).
These transformations differ in fifteen ways: first, transformation of state (*avasthā-vipariṇāma*), such as infancy and so forth;

second, transformation of appearance (*varṇa-vipariṇāma*), such as the transformation from beautiful complexion to an ugly one; third, transformation of form (*saṃsthāna-vipariṇāma*), such as emaciation from hunger and so forth.
1. Transformation through prosperity; 2. transformation of the limbs and joints; 3. transformation through cold and heat; 4. transformation through injury by others; 5.

transformation through emaciation and fatigue; 6. transformation through deportment; 7. transformation through contact with [external] objects; 8. transformation through contact with suffering and so forth; 9. transformation through defilement; 10.
transformation through illness and so forth; 11. transformation through death; 12. transformation into a bluish-black discoloration.
Regarding the fifteen types of transformation, the "transformation of total non-appearance through exhaustion" refers to such things as a chain of bones, which, when burned and destroyed,
disperse until they are entirely invisible in every respect.
[Commentary]: First, regarding the suffering that is grasped as a self and as dharmas, up to the point where it is said "the nature is real while the truth is provisional":
however, in this commentary, the character *wéi* (for/as) should be pronounced with the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

This term "that which is grasped" (*suǒqǔ*) refers to the so-called "grasped nature" of the real self and real dharmas imputed by the universal conceptualization (*parikalpita*) of ordinary beings; because these are what are grasped by the two kinds of grasping minds, this nature is real.
The provisional meaning of "truth" (*satya*) is that the grasping mind takes suffering as having a substantial entity;

therefore, although this nature is non-existent, it is provisionally named "suffering," and what is grasped is also called "suffering"—this is the provisional truth. However, regarding "nature as real," this refers to the reality of the self-entity (*ātman*);
