because it is impermanent, it is the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), and thus its nature is real.
[Commentary] Regarding the suffering of the two aspects: this text states that both the nature (*svabhāva*) and the truth (*satya*) are real;

specifically, the dependent-arising nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and tainted (*sāsrava*), is the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and is also the object traversed by the practice of suffering.

[Commentary]: "Nature is real while the truths are provisional" means that because True Suchness (tathatā) is conjoined with all contaminated aspects of suffering, it is also called "suffering," though it is not actual suffering.
Thus, it is said that the truths are provisional; True Suchness is the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and therefore it is said to be "real."

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that it is called "emptiness" because there is no nature of non-existence, the intended meaning is that one contemplates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as being devoid of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and thus designates it as empty.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that taking it as an object is emptiness and that emptiness has nothing to grasp, the intended meaning is that taking the dependent nature as the object of emptiness is based upon [that very nature].
Because there is nothing to be grasped above it, its essence is called "emptiness," yet its essence is not itself empty.

[Commentary] Regarding "the absence of self in distinct characteristics": this means that within the dependent nature (*paratantra*), there is no falsely grasped self; therefore, it is called "selflessness."

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'conditioned phenomena' (*saṃskāra*) within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) extends to all truths," the intended meaning is that beneath each truth there are always associated afflictions (*kleśa*), and these afflictions all possess the modes of comprehension (*ākāra*) such as impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and non-self (*anātman*).

Therefore, it is said that the meaning of "conditioned phenomena" in the Truth of Suffering extends to all truths. If this were not the case, how could the Truths of Cessation (*nirodha*) and the Path (*mārga*) also be characterized by impermanence?
"Are they suffering, etc.?

[Commentary]: Furthermore, the intention behind dividing each of the four aspects of the truth of suffering—which eliminate the four inversions—into three categories is as follows: since there are four aspects under the truth of suffering, each is divided into three;
that is, they must be so divided in order to eliminate the four inversions. The "four inversions" refers to [the misconceptions that things are] not impermanent, and so forth.
To conceive of the impermanent as permanent, suffering as pleasure, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure constitutes four inversions.
When emptiness removes the inversion regarding purity, this very substance of false attachment is itself empty.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "first, the accumulation of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and so forth," according to the commentary there are two interpretations. The intent of the first interpretation is as follows:

because the grasping mind clings to a self and to phenomena, it perfumes [the continuum] to produce various [entities]. Although these have a substantial basis, they arise from the pervasive conceptualization of a self and phenomena;

thus, the mind that performs this calculation perfumes various [seeds], which are called the "first nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). This is not a separate perfuming of seeds for the objects of grasping themselves.

Alternatively, the seeds perfumed by that which is grasped through conventional designations (*prajñapti*)—which are themselves the objects of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*)—arise from the perfuming mind.

Regarding the second point, "the nature of the initial [moment]": it means that the grasping mind takes those habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) as its object of universal conceptualization. These habitual tendencies are the basis for what is grasped;
from that dependent basis, there arises what is conventionally designated as the grasped. This too is ultimately real, yet its nature is conventionally imputed and habituated.

"Qi" (vital energy/affliction) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); because it is truly the origin (*samudaya*), it is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). It is "truly" [conventional] because its primary nature is provisional; its nature is indeed provisional. [Commentary:

Regarding the third point, "not yet free from the bonds of the origin," etc., this refers exclusively to karma and afflictions as the essence of the Truth of Origin (*samudaya-satya*); its true suchness (*tathatā*)...

In the state of being bound by afflictions (*saṃbaddha*), *tathatā* (suchness) is conventionally designated as the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). This is a conventional designation of truth;
however, because *tathatā* is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), its nature is real.

[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "first, intrinsic cessation" to "certainly not included among the truths," the intended meaning is that intrinsic cessation refers to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not subsumed under the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*), because the truth of cessation is a conditioned phenomenon (*bhāva*).
If one now asserts that the cessation of intrinsic nature is subsumed under the truth of cessation, then intrinsic nature would be real while the truth would be provisional.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the extinction of the two graspings results in the extinction of the grasped and the grasper; because the grasped and the grasper are absent," the intended meaning is as follows:

By the power of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the two—the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*)—which arise from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), are prevented from arising; therefore, they are called the "extinction of the two graspings.

This is the conventional designation for the nature of reality (*tattva*). Why is this so? Because the non-arising of the two graspings is itself analytical cessation, which is in fact the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), yet its nature is...

It is not that the other-dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is merely so called because it is dependent upon the two graspings (*dvaya-grāha*) which are to be eliminated; rather, its nature is termed "other-dependent" because its essence is dependent.

Thus, its nature is conventional (*prajñaptika*), since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is not other-dependent. Regarding the distinct interpretations of Dharmapāla and Sthiramati:

if Dharmapāla asserts that the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) are other-dependent, then within these perceived and perceiving aspects, they constitute the object and the subject.
The two masters differ because they grasp the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
[Commentary: "Attaining cessation from that which is non-existent" means that from the cessation of the two graspings, one attains the cessation of the two graspings.

[Commentary: Regarding "the dependent is a provisional designation": this refers to the cessation of these two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*). It is not the dependent nature itself that is the dependent;

rather, it is merely provisionally designated as the dependent. Alternatively, because the two types of grasping depend upon [the dependent nature], they are called "dependent," and thus this nature is a provisional designation.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the Middle and Extremes reaching contradiction," this treatise states that intrinsic cessation (*prakṛti-nirodha*) is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).

The *Madhyāntavibhāga-ṭīkā* explains that intrinsic cessation refers to both analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and suchness; thus, there is this apparent contradiction. Question: What is the difference between analytical cessation and suchness? Answer:

Analytical cessation is established based on the attainment resulting from the severance of afflictions, whereas suchness is established by way of its essential nature (*svabhāva*). It is designated as suchness by way of convention (*prajñapti*).
Therefore, the meaning of *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) is provisionally established upon *tathatā* (suchness).

[Commentary: Third, regarding the path of realization: *tathatā* is subsumed under the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) and is not subsumed under the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) of the *mārga-satya* (truth of the path).
Now, when *tathatā* is spoken of as the *mārga-satya*, its essence is real while its designation as "truth" is provisional. A second interpretation states that if one follows...

That which can realize the path is called the "realizer of the path. This is the untainted reality, which is indeed the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*); furthermore, it is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the Truth of Nature (*dharmatā-satya*).
Both are real. [Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "the name 'thoroughly known' (*parijñeya*) is broad," the intended meaning is that although the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks intrinsic substance, it nonetheless receives this single name; thus, it should be thoroughly known solely as such.

Since there is no other meaning [beyond this], one knows the particulars universally and thus obtains the general name; that is, by means of the particular universal conceptualizations (*parikalpa*), one obtains the name of "universal thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*).

This is also like how the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) obtains its general name through its particulars. Question: Are these three types of paths the fundamental [wisdom] (*mūla*) or the subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)? Answer:
The latter two are the fundamental wisdom (*samyag-mūla-jñāna*), while the former one is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). The subsequently attained wisdom...

Because it can universally know [the nature of things] therein; furthermore, because one first universally abandons and universally realizes [the truth], and subsequently, within the wisdom of subsequent attainment (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), is able to universally know and explain [the distinctions of] medicines, diseases, and so forth.

According to this interpretation, since the former [wisdom] alone is subsumed under subsequent attainment, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* (Chapter 74) states that the ability to universally know the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and so forth is the function of subsequent attainment.
[Commentary]: "All are common to the three natures" means that the objects traversed by each of the three gates of liberation are individually common to all three natures.

[Commentary]: "That is to say, taking the dependent nature as the object, up to its being the very object of emptiness"—this clarifies that all three natures are collectively the object of the gate of emptiness.

This is the reason for the objective sphere traversed by the doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*). Because the essence of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and of "self" and "mine" is empty, it is said to be the sphere of emptiness.

That is to say, when one takes as an object that which is devoid of the imagined nature upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), this reveals the reason why the dependent nature is the sphere of emptiness;
the intended meaning is that when one realizes the absence of the grasping at "self" and "mine" upon the dependent nature, one speaks of the dependent nature [as the sphere of emptiness].
It is called the "object of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-viṣaya*). Regarding the statement that it is established as the object of emptiness because it is manifested through realization:

this reveals that the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) is the reason for being the object of emptiness. The intended meaning is that the *pariniṣpanna* must be manifested by means of the two kinds of emptiness—of self and of phenomena—and thus the *pariniṣpanna* is designated as the "object of emptiness.

According to the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*), however, it only clarifies that the *paratantra* (dependent nature) and the *pariniṣpanna* constitute the object of emptiness; therefore, [the dependent nature] is not mentioned here.

The *parikalpita* (imagined nature) is not mentioned because its essence is empty and its object is easy to understand. The first three objects of emptiness are all established in relation to the *parikalpita* (the imagined nature); therefore, regarding these three types of emptiness, they are all termed "wishless" (*apraṇihita*).

For instance, because the *parikalpita-svabhāva* lacks any substantial reality, it cannot be the object of aspiration or seeking. Likewise, because the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature) is devoid of a real self or phenomena, it is called "empty" and is thus not an object of aspiration or seeking;
that is, the *paratantra* itself serves as the object of the wishless. Furthermore, the *paratantra*...

This dharma of arising and ceasing cannot be the object of aspiration. Just as one grasps at the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) as being real within the mind of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), since this nature is the suchness (*tathatā*) that is the object of pervasive conceptualization, this suchness cannot be the object of aspiration;

it is the perfected nature as an object of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*). Question: Since the perfected nature is not unwholesome (*akuśala*), why can it not be the object of aspiration? Answer: As follows...

The commentary states that the reason *pariniṣpanna* (the perfected nature) is the object of the "wishless" (*apraṇihita*) is that one does not give rise to the aspiration for *tathatā* (suchness) as something conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).
However, this does not contradict the fact that, according to the seventy-second [verse], actual *tathatā* itself is not designated as the "object of the wishless.
Thus, there is no inconsistency.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "as space conditions these three up to the realm of signlessness," the intent is as follows: this explains that the three natures (trisvabhāva) are attained as the internal objective conditions for signlessness;

that is, the previously mentioned realm of emptiness serves as the internal realm of signlessness. Now, the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) exists only as a deluded sentiment and lacks any real essence or characteristic;
thus, the first nature constitutes the realm of signlessness. Upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature), [there is no...]

The imagined self and what belongs to the self (*ātman-ātmīya*) are also called "empty" because they lack the characteristic of dualistic grasping; this dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is itself the object of signlessness (*animitta*).

Since the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)—which is *tathatā* (suchness)—lacks any substantial reality, and since its essence and characteristics are non-existent, it constitutes the state of signlessness.

Therefore, it is said that the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the object of signlessness. Thus, the Commentary cites the object of emptiness to establish the three natures as being signless.

"Emptiness" refers entirely to the object of the non-characteristic (*animitta*) within the *parikalpita* [nature]; this is likewise the case, for since its essence is non-existent, how could it have characteristics? [Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) comprise three types," the intended meaning is that among the five categories (*pañcavastu*), the category of characteristics corresponds to the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*).

How is this known? Because characteristics correspond to both the subject that knows and the object that is known, and both of these possess the three gates of liberation. The explanation states: "The subject that knows..."
This refers to the wisdom of the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*). That which is known is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of the three gates of liberation.

As for their mutual relationship, the "known" (*jñeya*) is mostly the objective sphere that is known; thus, the "penetration" (*abhisamaya*) pertains to a small portion of what can be known, while the "penetration" itself is what can know a small portion of that [objective sphere].
Therefore, the text of this *Yogācārabhūmi* differs slightly from this treatise.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also the three kinds of objects": the explanation is that "characteristics" also encompass the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), and these objects of knowledge are precisely the objects of the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).

Question: With what intention is this stated? Answer: It is intended to clarify that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) are also the objects of the three gates of liberation.

The meaning is that since characteristics are the objects of the three gates of liberation, and since the dependent and perfected natures possess outflows (*sāsrava*), [they are thus established as such].

Since the true suchness characterized by the untainted (*anāsrava-lakṣaṇa-tathatā*) has quiescence as its characteristic, it is clearly understood that this is also the object of the three gates of liberation.
Therefore, after first citing the scriptural passage, one subsequently establishes the point. The phrase "since the abandonment is thus" serves to formally establish the argument.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement here, "it is said [they are doors] because they serve as proofs," the intended meaning is as follows: this treatise states that the three gates of liberation are untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Within untainted wisdom, there is the wisdom produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*); since one realizes *tathatā* (suchness) by means of this, it is called "attaining the three gates of liberation.
This is identical to the text in the second fascicle of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Vyākhyāyukti*), which likewise refers to them as "gates of liberation" (*vimokṣamukha*).
This refers exclusively to supramundane cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*), which differs from the seventy-two passages cited previously;
for those state that it corresponds to the three doors of liberation and also serves as their three objects.

[Commentary: "Since this is so... it is also for the sake of the signless" (*animitta*)—this establishes the underlying principle. It completes the preceding citation of the text regarding how signs (*nimitta*) constitute three kinds of objects.

"Signs" refers to the characteristic of generality (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) among the five categories (*pañca-vastu*), which is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, signs are said to be the objects of the three liberations (*trivimokṣa*).

Moreover, the distinction between the contaminated and the uncontaminated separately divides the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); there is abandonment [of the former], namely, the dependent nature.

Since the outflows (*āsrava*) are themselves the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), we know that the three objects are established based on both the dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected natures. Question:

Since the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) is associated with the perfected nature, how can it be called "signless" (*animitta*)? How can it be said to be the object of the signless liberation? Answer: The second chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"The wisdom that takes signs as its object is the path of signlessness; it acts as the path, proceeds as the path, and transcends the path—this is also the practice of signlessness. This explains it.

It is said that wisdom which takes the signless as its object is also called "signless. This means that the four types of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) belonging to the Path Truth (*mārga-satya*) are collectively termed "signless" because they take the signless as their object;
therefore, the Gate of Liberation of Signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*), when taking these as its object, is also signless.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage "The four practices of the Path lead through to the three gates of liberation," the intended meaning is that untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is the objective realm of these three gates of liberation. [Commentary]:

Regarding the passage in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 12, which states "[the dependent and the perfected] serve as the three gates of liberation": since it has already been clarified that the dependent and the perfected [natures] are...
Regarding the "objects of the three liberations," it is now stated that the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) is also an object of the three gates of liberation.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "taking these three natures as objects" (*ālambana*), "taking as objects" here carries the sense of "relying upon" or "depending on.

Because one gives rise to the three types of patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) by relying on these three natures, these three natures serve as the objects (*viṣaya*) for that patience.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "when realizing the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*, afflictions and suffering do not arise," some scholars have raised an objection: "At the time of realizing the *pariniṣpanna*, there is no distinct stage of patience (*kṣānti*);
therefore, the 'patience of non-arising' (*anutpāda-kṣānti*) is intended to signify that one realizes that object of non-arising, and thus it is called 'patience of non-arising.

Since afflictions and suffering do not arise upon realizing the *pariniṣpanna*, how could this depend on contemplation? Therefore, one should say: 'Contemplating the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*'—it is not [the realization itself]."

Because afflictions and suffering do not arise, it is called the "patience regarding the non-arising of afflictions and suffering" (*anupattikadharmakṣānti*). To explain in detail: when one realizes and realizes the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature), afflictions and suffering do not arise;
this is termed the patience of non-arising. It does not mean that at the very moment of realizing the perfected nature, one separately gives rise to this patience.

Rather, the non-arising of afflictions and suffering is itself the object [of realization]. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the commentary (*śāstra*). This is the interpretation held by some.
The principle is now clear and understood; one may proceed according to one’s own preference.

[Commentary: From "86" up to "precisely taking this perfected nature as the object," this passage cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun) to clarify that the three natures serve as the objects for the gates of liberation.
However, it is cited here merely for the sake of textual convenience; the actual clarification of the present text follows the three previous interpretations.

[The section on] "Transcending within" [explains] the second [point], the nature of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the phrase "called 'formations' (*saṃskāra*)," the commentary explains: "As for saying that 'formations' are conventional, it refers exclusively to that which is out-flowing (*sāsrava*) and subject to flux; this is what is termed 'formations.
This immediately distinguishes them from the first three of the four ultimate meanings (*paramārtha*). The first three of the four ultimate meanings are as follows: [omitted].

Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) in contrast to the fourth [category], although it is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is not the same as this conventional truth of practice. Why?
Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*). It is also distinguished from the untainted practice, which is a conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) practice and differs from tainted conventional practice.
Furthermore, when it says "distinguishing the ultimate," it specifically distinguishes the third ultimate [truth]. The third...
Although the ultimate truth is also termed "conventional" in relation to the fourth [type of] ultimate truth, their essential natures differ;

thus, it is necessary to distinguish them from the conventional truth of practice (*saṃvṛti-satya*). [Commentary: Regarding the passage from "the manifest conventional" to "the fourth conventional," the intended meaning is that this manifest conventional...

The *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) is revealed by means of the emptiness of the non-dual absence of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) upon the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) when its defiled portion has been eliminated;
this refers to the fourth of the four conventional truths (*saṃvṛti*).
Regarding this conventionality, there are two interpretations: first, that this "revealed conventionality" is subsumed under the fourth conventional truth; second, that... [text fragment ends]
The "manifest conventional" (*vyavahāra-saṃvṛti*) is also the third of the four ultimate truths (*paramārtha*), because it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
[Commentary: The passage from "Alternatively, this manifest conventional... to "...because it is untainted" represents the second interpretation. There is also an interpretation which states:
"This manifest conventional takes the third among the four; that is, it is the third conventional truth, which is distantly related to the preceding three."
The fourth truth is the ultimate (paramārtha-satya), which is also called the third conventional (saṃvṛti-satya). This third conventional truth is also that which is revealed by the two emptinesses;

because it is untainted (anāsrava), [the opponent] answers: "One takes only the third conventional within the conventional truths, for the mind reverses the tainted (sāsrava) characteristics of the four truths;
thus, it is not the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) and cannot be called 'revealed conventionality' (prajñapti-saṃvṛti). Therefore, one knows that it is exclusively the ultimate."
This is as in the third [section] of the middle [treatise].

[Treatise: Regarding the phrase "attaining the two supreme meanings" (*paramārtha*), this refers to the fact that the essence of *nirvāṇa* is a supreme fruit and is thus designated by the term "supreme" (*parama*).

"Meaning" (*artha*) signifies that which is conducive and beneficial; furthermore, because it is a principle (*nyāya*), it is called "meaning. It is both supreme and meaning, and is thus explained by the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
It is also because it reveals that which is attained that it is called "attaining the ultimate meaning.
[Commentary: From "True Suchness is established from of old" up to "therefore it is established and named," this commentary explains the reason for its name while also resolving objections;
the text is easy to understand.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "explanation of the possessive compound" (*bahuvrīhi*) for "supreme object" (*paramārtha*): this third line, "supreme object," takes uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) as its essence.
This uncontaminated wisdom takes the supreme dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) as its objective sphere; thus, it is called "practicing the supreme object.

It is a possessive compound because *tathatā*—the supreme—is designated as the "possessive property" (*dhana*), while the wisdom that takes the supreme object as its condition acquires the name "supreme object. It is like [the following example]:...
Furthermore, if one were to discuss the food basket and so forth according to the specific nature of each entity, this would also be the first ultimate truth;

because it is the manifestation of the essence and function of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), among the four ultimate truths, it is called the "First Ultimate Truth: Manifestation of Essence and Function."

[Commentary]: The meaning of "this should be thoroughly known" (*parijñeya*) is as follows: if the Buddha did not take the first nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as an object, why do various treatises state that "the imagined nature is without essence, the dependent nature should be abandoned, and the perfected nature should be realized"? Therefore, the objection is raised:
if one does not know what is non-existent, how can it further be said that "this should be thoroughly known"?

[Commentary]: "That which does not take that as an object" means it does not take the primary nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) as an object; "because that is not an existent phenomenon" intends to say that the primary nature is without substantiality. [Commentary]:

"Taking that which was originally without substance as the basis until one takes non-existence as the object" intends to say that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is fundamentally established as being without substance.

This is not the domain of ordinary cognition but that of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). However, when taking this [non-existence] as an object, there immediately arises an appearance resembling non-existence;

the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the aspect of non-existence (*animitta*), while the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) is existent. Since it is described from the perspective of its essential nature, it is called "taking non-existence as an object.
Although the objective aspect exists, because its fundamental object is non-existent, it is said that one "knows non-existence."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "If one were to take another's mind as an object in this manner, it would contradict the principles of the Holy Teachings," the meaning is as follows:

For instance, when taking another person's mind as an object, although one does not directly apprehend that other person's meditative mind (*samāhita-citta*), one instead takes as an object the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective image) which is the reflection of that mind.

According to this, since the *nimitta-bhāga* is merely a transformation of one's own mind and thus belongs to one's own mind, it is called "another's mind" only by referring back to its original source.
The wisdom that understands this meaning is as follows: when one conceptualizes through pervasive imagination (*parikalpa*), that which is conceptualized has no substantial reality;

it does not directly apprehend [an external object], nor does it transform into a distinct aspect (*nimitta*). Rather, it apprehends this objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), which, although it is a transformation of one's own mind and thus exists, is said to be "apprehending the non-existent" with respect to its underlying essence (*bimba*).
If one does not accept this, it would contradict such principles of the Noble Teachings (*ārya-śāsana*).
[Commentary: As stated in the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* regarding the cognition of others' minds, when it says "reaching the inconceivable realm," the intended meaning is as follows:

although when [Bodhisattvas] cognize others' minds and so forth, they transform a single type of mental image to perceive them, the transformations of Bodhisattvas and others do not equal those of a Buddha.

This is because when the Buddha’s wisdom realizes them, they are extremely similar; therefore, it is said that [others] do not know them as they are known by the Buddha’s realm. The Buddha’s realm, the Buddha’s realm, is inconceivable.

It is intentionally stated that the Buddha perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) because he knows reality by directly realizing its characteristics; furthermore, it is extremely clear and pure.

Although the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas of the Two Vehicles do perceive the minds of others, they do not know them as the Buddha does—knowing them as they truly are—therefore it is said they do not know the realm of the Buddha.
[Commentary: "Although this is so, it does not say 'direct object-condition' (pratyakṣālambana-pratyaya). The explanation is as follows:

"Although this is so" means that although [the mind] allows for the universal imagination (*parikalpita*) of non-existent things and the minds of others as one kind of object-condition, it does not call them "direct object-conditions. Why?
Because the purport of the preceding twenty treatises does not, for the time being, allow for direct object-conditions. The phrase "from here down to 'the two vehicles'" explains the second point.
The ten passages on *vijñaptimātra*.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "up to the point where the divine eye and knowledge of past lives do not constitute direct realization," this explains how the Buddha’s wisdom perceives the past and future;
what follows below explains the inconceivable.

[Commentary]: The phrase "it does not mean that one directly realizes that mind as something grasped externally to the mind" means that if one were to directly apprehend that [external] mind, it would constitute the grasping of an object external to the mind, and thus the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) would not be established.

[Commentary]: The Noble One takes this "contradiction" to be "non-existence. Because there is no intentionality outside the mind, he says that there are no phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—outside the mind.
[Commentary]: "One merely perceives within one's own mind," up to the two interpretations in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, refers to the Bodhisattva’s contemplative realization.

The imagined nature (*parikalpita*) does not exist; however, when a bodhisattva observes that the real self and dharmas imagined by other sentient beings cannot be found upon their minds, the mind of the bodhisattva likewise lacks the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) as an object of perception. Therefore, it should be understood that when a bodhisattva contemplates the imagined nature, it is devoid of such an aspect.
Masters such as Dharmapāla all maintain this view, just as there are two interpretations regarding the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "Seventy-fourth" to "should be known as such": because the first nature (*prathama-svabhāva*) lacks any substantial essence or characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it can only be said to be "knowable" (*jñeya*);

it cannot be said to be an "object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*), as it lacks any substantial essence. Therefore, this first nature is not within the cognitive domain of either ordinary beings or the wisdom of the noble ones (*ārya*).

[Commentary: This statement, "the other-dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is not an object directly perceived by non-ordinary wisdom," intends to say that the other-dependent nature is the sphere of mundane ordinary wisdom and of post-attainment uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), but it is not the sphere of supramundane wisdom. Why? Because it is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Since fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) takes the signless (*animitta*) as its object, the latter [post-attainment] wisdom alone is the sphere of the noble ones (*ārya*) and is not the sphere of ordinary wisdom. Among these, [the former] is the sphere of ordinary wisdom.
The intervening section on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) being the object of two types of wisdom is easy to understand from the rest of the text.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "If that were so" to "it would not be noble wisdom," the meaning of this text at number seventy-four is as follows:

If noble wisdom did not know non-existence, then it would follow that noble wisdom does not know anything at all. If that [non-existence] is already non-existent, how could there be wisdom regarding it?

Furthermore, if that which is known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) as non-existent were actually existent, then because it is a mental object (*cittasamprayukta-dharma*) that lacks characteristics (*animitta*), it would be subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
thus, the first nature [the imagined nature] would not be established as non-existent.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the principle of *tathatā* is without [duality]," the intended meaning is that if one is without the self or phenomena within the principle of *tathatā*, this is what is subsumed under the "perfectly real" (*pariniṣpanna*).
Furthermore, it is said that the principle of *tathatā* being without characteristics is subsumed under the "perfectly real.
This interpretation explains the reason why the Noble Ones do not take the first nature as an object: if the noble wisdom were to take the first nature as an object, it would be... [as follows].
If one regards the inverted [perceptions] as non-existent, that which is the aspect of the mind’s reversal is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
If, with respect to the principle of *tathatā*, one regards [the self and phenomena] as lacking real existence, this is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Therefore, the subsequent passage down to "is the same as what was previously stated" summarizes this point: that noble wisdom does not take the first nature as its object. This refers to what was previously stated regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The passage regarding "clinging is not the object of the wisdom of ordinary or noble beings" is identical [to the previous].

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "it is not that one does not realize there is no non-noble wisdom," the intended meaning is as follows: this is a reflection by way of negation; it means that even the realization that "there is nothing" constitutes noble wisdom.
As for the phrase "lest external dharmas also be able to serve as objects," this is a self-raised objection meant to establish the author's own position. It means: if...

If non-apprehension of non-existence were not the realization of a noble one’s wisdom, then external objects would have to be the objects of cognition because they are not apprehended as non-existent;
yet, since external objects are neither apprehended as non-existent nor taken as objects of cognition, we know that although noble wisdom does not apprehend non-existence,
it nonetheless constitutes noble wisdom by virtue of its capacity for cognition.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "In general, as for difficult conditions, when it is said that they are not its object," this explains away a potential objection. The objection asks:
"It was previously stated that True Suchness (tathatā) is also a pervasive object (parikalpita) through indirect dependence; how can it now be said that it is not its object?
The answer, as in the commentary, is that because it does not attain reality, it is said to be "not its object."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "because they are established as provisional or substantial upon the basis of the general and the particular," the intended meaning is that the provisional is established upon the general [whole], while the substantial is established upon the particular dharmas—as, for example, with the provisional nature of the five aggregates.
[Commentary]: Regarding the second point, "the continuity-convention (saṃtati-prajñapti) persists until now because it remains": "continuity" refers to the body itself.
Here, with respect to a single sentient being from beginning to end, although they pass through many bodies across the five destinies, they remain one and the same person.
This is stated based on this single sentient being, as the Buddha said: "The deer king of the past was my very self in this present life."
It is clearly understood that this refers only to the continuum of a single person; although there are many bodies, they constitute one [person].

Thus, it is based on the single, conventional body of a sentient being that it is called a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*). Alternatively, it may mean that a single person has continued in succession up until the present Buddha-body.
Here, "body" (*kāya*) is conventional, while "sentient being continuum" (*sattva-saṃtāna*) indicates the length of time. This is what is meant by speaking of a "conventional sentient being."

The marks [of a Buddha] now constitute the attainment of Buddhahood; this is what is called "successive designation" (*saṃtāna-prajñapti*). Since it was thus in the past, it will likewise be so in the future.

As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, when the Buddha bestowed the prophecy upon Śāriputra, saying that in a future age, after immeasurable kalpas have passed, he would attain Buddhahood under the name Puṣpārāma (Flower Light), it further said: "That very person is yourself; you should rejoice. Thus, the body of a śrāvaka and...

Although the Buddha’s bodies differ, they are not other than this one person; from the time one receives the prediction of future Buddhahood in this present body, it is only then called "conceptual continuity" (*prajñapti-saṃtāna*).
The future Buddha-body is precisely the body of Śāriputra at the present time.

[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "there would have to be multiple entities" is as follows: if outflows (*āsrava*) and non-outflows (*anāsrava*), and so forth, were substantially real (*dravyasat*), then the material forms (*rūpa*) upon which they depend would necessarily have multiple entities.
Some say: "We admit that outflows, non-outflows, and so forth, are not nominal designations based on states (*avasthā-prajñapti*) of matter;
rather, these are merely meanings attributed to matter and are not nominal designations based on states. Therefore, anger (*krodha*) and the like are taken as nominal designations based on states."
[Commentary]: "From 'Candrakīrti' to 'provisional' (prajñapti)" refers to the restatement of Candrakīrti’s tenet, which serves as the basis for the following formal refutation.
Candrakīrti asserts that within ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), all phenomena are empty; thus, even the "provisional" is empty.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it is established within the dependent nature," this refutes Bhāviveka.

If, according to him, even the ultimate truth and the dependent nature are all merely conventional, then since there would be no real phenomena (*dharma*) within the dependent nature itself, and since real phenomena are absent, upon what could a conventional designation be established?
Therefore, it is said that "there are no real phenomena, and thus conventional phenomena do not exist. Regarding the phrase "within the same category," Dharmapāla says:

Now, as for the establishment of designations (*prajñapti*), all such designations rely upon the categories of phenomena such as matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*); these designations are established based on the real.

This establishes the principle and simultaneously refutes Candrakīrti: since the real depends on the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), upon what could a designation be established? A designated phenomenon must necessarily depend upon a real phenomenon for its conceptualization (*prajñapti*). Thus it is said.

[Commentary]: If it were otherwise—if Master Bhāviveka held a view different from my own interpretation—then if there were no real entity (*dravya*), even the conventional (*prajñapti*) would not exist.

[Commentary]: Furthermore, when it is said that "the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not as it is designated, yet it is definitely existent," the intended meaning is this very dependent nature.
Its nature is not like that of a provisionally designated phenomenon, which exists only after being conceptually established. Nor does it mean that everything is definitively non-existent.
This means that this *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is also not definitively non-existent at all times.

Why? Because it arises from subsequent conditions; therefore, in every respect, it is neither existent nor non-existent. It is "not existent" because it differs from provisionally designated phenomena.
"It is not non-existent because it arises from conditions. Furthermore, it is said that "it is not existent" means it cannot be expressed by linguistic designations;
"it is not non-existent" means that the dharma which transcends language is not nothingness.
(From the *Yan-yi* Commentary on the *Cheng weishi lun*, Scroll 11, Part 1)

Is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the untainted (*anāsrava*) free from signs (*animitta*)? What is meant by "not obstructing"?

Although the subsequently attained wisdom of the untainted possesses the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), because there is no grasping toward what is apprehended, it is not conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); therefore, it is not obstructed.
As the Commentary states: "This also transcends the conceptual proliferation of those signs"—this explains the reason why the subsequently attained wisdom of the untainted is not obstructed.
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Buddhabhūmi*, there are two theories; this [present view] is not the first.

As for the statement that "all those untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) function as the dharma," the intended meaning is that they comprise all the fundamental and subsequently attained (*prsthalabdha*) wisdoms of both the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).

Thus, the Master says: "There is one interpretation that all fundamental wisdoms, etc., possess both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the vision (*darśana*); there is another interpretation that [only] the fundamental wisdom, etc., [possesses them]."

Regarding the statement, "If one sees that these characteristics do not exist, this is not so," this treatise speaks only in terms of the wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) as its essential substance;
because there are three different interpretations by the masters, it says "no.

[Treatise]: "If those characteristics do not exist... up to "...the wisdom of names, sounds, and so forth. The sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) refutes the interpretation that [wisdom] has a limited measure (*pramāṇa*), stating: "This is an objection [to the view that wisdom is finite]."

This proposed reason also lacks a supporting example; one should simply offer a direct challenge rather than establishing a formal syllogism (*pramāṇa*). To evaluate it by setting up such a measure and then directly challenging it, the underlying logic is difficult to scrutinize.

This is because the former master merely stated that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) lacks objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), but did not say that other forms of wisdom lack such aspects.
How, then, can one take the cognition of form and the cognition of non-form as the standard measure and then proceed with a direct challenge?
Now, judging by the principle according to the text, one layer of the objection and its response is missing. The objection states:

"When all minds other than non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) correctly take an object as their condition, they should lack an image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), because [according to you] they are taking an object as their condition.
To this, the former master’s response says: "Even if that were so, what fault would there be? Therefore, the treatise restates it: "If there were none..."

The opponent’s position is that the cognition which takes those [objects] as its object—namely, the cognitions that take color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth as their objects—is established through a series of arguments as being a true perception possessing an objective aspect (*sākāra*).

As for what is not explicitly stated, it is because [the author] intends to generate subsequent knowledge through skillful and concise phrasing. The cognition taking color-form as its object is now presented as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*):

"This cognition which takes color-form as its object is the subject (*dharmin*); it must be able to take the aspects of sound and so forth as its objects" is the thesis (*pakṣadharma*). This is because [the opponent] admits that there is no sound and so forth [in that cognition].

Because it possesses the characteristic [of being a cognition], it is a cause, just as the cognition of sound and so forth is; this is the illustration, and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are to be understood by analogy.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the meaning of the repeated inference based on the cognition of form and sound can be understood by analogy," the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

Your cognition apprehending form should not be a cognition apprehending form, because it lacks the objective aspect (*sākāra*) of form, just like the cognition apprehending sound. Furthermore, the cognition apprehending sound should likewise [not be a cognition apprehending sound].

Because the cognition taking sound as its object lacks a portion consisting of the aspect of sound, it can be established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like the cognition taking form as its object.
[Commentary: Although there is no direct realization of a non-conceptual aspect, that which is called "realizing suchness" is explained here as follows:

Suppose an objection is raised that if there is an objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*), then it must have an object of cognition (*sālambana*). In that case, consider for instance the direct realization of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*).
Regarding the claim that at the time of suchness there must be the characteristic of non-conceptual wisdom that directly realizes it, this master replies: "Not so.

Although there is no characteristic of non-conceptuality that directly realizes [it], when wisdom realizes [suchness], there is a subtle aspect-part (*nimittabhāga*) that is extremely similar to that suchness;
therefore, it is called 'direct realization. It is not that the aspect-part is absent, but rather it is said so because it differs from the coarse aspect-parts of other forms of cognition."
The Section on Signlessness.

[Treatise]: Regarding the statement, "Because it is said that signlessness neither grasps nor does not grasp signs," this refers to the third master, Dharmapāla, whose view represents the correct principle. According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Treatise 73), it asks:
"If one grasps a sign within the realm of signlessness (*animitta-dhātu*), it is not the grasping of signlessness; if there is nothing to be grasped, how can there be grasping?"
Furthermore, it cannot be established as a "grasping of the signless" (*animitta-grāha*). If that is so, how can it be called "grasping of the signless"? The answer is:

because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with verbal expression have already been abandoned, this grasping, although it grasps the signless realm, does not grasp signs; therefore, it is established as "grasping of the signless. Question:
If there is no apprehension (*pariccheda*), how can it be established as "grasping"? Answer: Although there is no apprehension of the various distinctions of signs, [the grasping] exists.

Although there is augmentation, because one grasps the signless (*animitta*), the grasping is established. Question: If there is no apprehension and no augmentation, how can the characteristics of this grasping be known? Answer:

Because it grasps the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) and because it grasps the signless, the characteristics of the five kinds of phenomena (*pañca-vastu-lakṣaṇa*) may all manifest as its characteristics.
These five kinds of phenomena are collectively explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. Question: If not... [text ends]

[Question: It is clear that [this] can be established as "grasping" (*upādāna*); why then is it not reckoned as the cessation of all graspings? [Answer: Because cessation and non-existence (*abhāva*) lack the sense of being something to be cultivated or performed.
One who practices contemplation does not cultivate anything based upon cessation and non-existence.

[Question: If that is so, how is its characteristic known? [Answer: It is known by the realization of one’s own internal wisdom (*pratyātma-jñāna*). [Question: If that is so, why is it not [known] in the same way as...?
Regarding the realization thus prophesied, this internal realization is not a locus for the establishment of conventional designations;
therefore, it is not expressed through such prophetic declarations.

[Commentary]: "Because this wisdom that takes the True as its object arises by narrowly grasping the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (tathatā)"—the term "narrowly grasping" (xiá dài) means to rely upon or support.
The metaphor of "relying" is like a sick person who requires a staff; only when urged by another person can they rise.

Because the essence of correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is weak, it requires the support of the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*) in order to arise; therefore, it is said to be "narrowly bound. There are two meanings of "binding":

first, binding that carries the aspect of an image is called "binding the aspect"; second, binding that carries the essence and characteristics is called "essence and characteristics without division."

The distinction is as follows: although there is no objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) consisting of a reflected image, it is nevertheless called "possessing aspects" because it directly possesses the essential nature and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Why is this? Because the seeing aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of correct wisdom is not separate from True Suchness, as it is a dharma of internal realization.
[Commentary: This is also not the case, because [the mind-king] is not that which is relied upon or entrusted to for consideration. The meaning is this:

although the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) arise in mutual dependence, and at the time of arising they take on the essence and characteristics of those mental factors, the mind-king cannot be said to "take as an object" (*ālambate*) the mental factors.

This is because the mental factors are not that which is relied upon or entrusted to for consideration by the mind-king; therefore, it is said that the mind-king and mental factors both simultaneously take the preceding [object] as their object.
The objects of each respective sense-sphere are that which the mind attends to and relies upon; thus, they may be called "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*).

Although the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) arises bearing the essential characteristics of the mental factors (*caitta*), it is not that which the mind-king itself attends to and relies upon; therefore, it is not termed an "object of cognition. One interpretation states:

"The previous objection is irrational, because that mind-king does not bear the essential characteristics of the mental factors. Another interpretation states: "The mind and the mental factors relate to one another in a reciprocal manner."
There is no fault in defining the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) as that which bears an image of its object, as explained in the eighth fascicle regarding the four conditions.
[Commentary:
"Seeing is itself the Path" means that the essence of the Path is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and all Buddhas traverse it.
Because this wisdom alone enables one to attain Buddhahood, it is called the "Path" (*mārga*); "seeing" (*darśana*) refers to illumination, which is the function of this wisdom.
[Treatise] The principle of the single true vision is precisely what is described as non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), and is further summarized as the "One Mind."

The subsequent passage states that there are three moments of mind in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while others maintain there is only one moment of mind in the path of seeing; both rely on this text concerning the "true path of seeing" (*tattvadarśanamārga*).

Regarding the statement that there are three moments of mind, it refers to the three moments of mind consisting of the cognition that internally censures sentient beings as mere designations (*prajñapti*) and so forth.

Since the treatise itself states that although it consists of many *kṣaṇas*, it is clear that there are multiple moments of mind—whereby a single moment is not called "many," yet three moments and beyond are indeed designated as such.

Because there are many [factors], all three minds are designated as the "True Path of Seeing" (darśanamārga), and it is based on this that they are established. Regarding the single mind, the Master says:
"Although it consists of many moments, they are equal. Since he speaks of them being "equal," it is clear that, in reality, there is only one mind.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement, "The distinction between gradual and sudden, one mind and many minds," the intended meaning is that "gradual" refers to many minds, while "sudden" refers to one mind.
[Treatise] From the actual realization of the two emptinesses up to the general exposition of "one mind," this single passage contains the intent of both masters; for now...
Regarding the "three minds," the Master says: Since there are many *kṣaṇas*, it is clear that there are actually three minds;

however, this is spoken of as "one mind" in general terms based on the essence and characteristics of the *tathatā* (suchness) realized therein. In reality, there are many instances of this "one mind. Regarding the "one mind," the Master says:
Since the *tathatā* realized is one, it is clear that the realizing wisdom (*jñāna*) is also one. As for the mention of "many *kṣaṇas*," it refers to uninterrupted comprehension.
The liberation and the single path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) are designated as "many moments," yet in reality they constitute a single moment of mind.

[Commentary: Regarding the passage from "the three moments of the path of seeing" to "the single-moment path of seeing," the meaning is that according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (58), because the matter within the true path of seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*) is ultimately perfected and equal, it is collectively described as the "single-moment path of seeing."

Regarding the "Three Minds" (tri-citta) school, the *Śāstra-samuccaya* states: "Since there are multiple moments (*kṣaṇa*), it is clearly known that these three minds constitute the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
This refers to the passage in the [Abhidharma] treatises concerning the fifty-eight moments within the single mind.

If the "Single Mind" (eka-citta) school speaks of "multiple moments," this is based on the designation of the three paths—the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and advancement (*viśeṣa*)—as "multiple moments," rather than referring to multiple moments within the uninterrupted path itself.
It is granted that there may be multiple moments.

[Commentary: However, the text of the *Pañcāśatikā* also states that seeing the path (darśanamārga) through three moments of mind up to the abandonment of the three grades [of afflictions] is called "sudden" (*tun*).

This master reconciles the text of the *Pañcāśatikā* by suggesting that it may mean that as soon as one first enters the contemplative mind, one abandons the afflictions of the three grades, which is thus termed "sudden."
Another interpretation states that the third stage involves the wisdom that dispels all phenomena of sentient beings as being merely conventional designations dependent on conditions;
because this is combined with the simultaneous abandonment of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations of the highest grade in a single instance, it is termed "sudden."

[Commentary]: Regarding the view that person and phenomena are distinct: the former master asserts that a bodhisattva first realizes the principle of the emptiness of persons and subsequently realizes the principle of the emptiness of phenomena;

first they sever the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and subsequently sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); and first they give rise to the coarse wisdom that negates [the self] (*pudgalanairātmya-pratisedha-jñāna*) and subsequently give rise to the subtle wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya-sūkṣma-jñāna*).
If one follows the latter master, it is asserted that within the bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the wisdom negating persons does not arise separately.

Contemplating only the emptiness of dharmas (dharma-śūnyatā) while simultaneously bringing along the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) is called "different in both respects," because there is a difference in the severing of the obstacles of persons and dharmas, and a difference in the realization of the principles of persons and dharmas;
hence it is said to be "different in both respects."
[Commentary] Regarding the intent of "providing two explanations for now," it means there are two interpretations of the term "sudden" (*tun*). First, the initial three minds are called "sudden":

namely, one mind of uninterruptedness (*ānantarya*), one mind of liberation (*vimukti*), and one mind of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*). Although these consist of many moments of mind that continue over a long duration, because they do not emerge from meditative observation (*samādhi*), they are termed "sudden.
Second, the first two minds are designated as "sudden," which refers to the arising of a single [moment of] uninterruptedness.

Because the *vimuktimārga* (path of liberation) excludes the *viśeṣamārga* (path of excellence), as one does not need to arise [from] the superior to enter the inferior, it is said that there are "two" for the time being.
This explains the meaning of "sudden" (*tadana*) within this true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which, when combined, consists of eleven expositions.

Specifically, regarding the establishment and exclusion of the distinctions among the three minds—the initial *ānantaryamārga*, *vimuktimārga*, and *viśeṣamārga*—there are eleven interpretations, as detailed in a separate commentary.

[Commentary: "Wisdom as its characteristic" refers to the essential nature (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa). The passage concerning the vision of the path of insight (darśana-mārga) being of one mind explains that it takes untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) as its essence.
To cite this now as proof is to verify the principle that [the afflictions] are severed instantaneously within a single moment of mind.
[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of "mutually explaining" these two passages here: it refers to the text where the single mind explains the three minds, and the three minds explain the single mind;
hence, they are said to be "mutually explained. First, the Master of the Single Mind explains the passage on the three minds as follows:

"Although the three minds—such as immediate realization (*ānantarya*) and so forth—are distinct, because their objective reality is ultimately identical and their nature is equal, they are collectively described as the 'one mind in three minds. This is the explanation by the Master of the Three Minds.
The *Yixin lun* (Treatise on the One Mind) states: "Based on the identity of their characteristics, the one mind is spoken of in general; in reality, there are three minds.

[Commentary: An ancient master says that regarding these three explanations, the intent of the ancient masters is that within this True Path of Vision (*tattva-darśana-mārga*), there are two teachers' views—gradual and sudden—and now, to this, is added the single True Path of Vision from the *Śāstra*, hence it is said in general that there is "one mind. This is the meaning of the text.
It is not correct to say that the first statement contains two meanings while the latter two contain one meaning, such that they are explained as three meanings in total;
for the preceding passage on non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and so forth is merely a general heading and does not constitute a detailed exposition of specific meanings.

[Treatise] Regarding the statement that there are three categories of the "contemplation of the non-established" (*avyavasthāna*), one interpretation holds that the three minds now discussed are called "non-established" in contrast to the sixteen minds;
however, if contrasted with a single mind, the path of insight (*darśanamārga*) of signlessness is termed "established," because it belongs to the third of the four ultimate realities (*paramārtha*).
To elaborate: although this reasoning exists, it is not found in any of the various scriptures.
Because this refers to the establishment [of the teachings], it is known that this establishment is spoken of solely in terms of the differentiated observation of the four truths;
thus, it differs from the establishment of the four ultimate meanings (*paramārtha*) and cannot be taken as a precedent. Therefore, the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya, chapter nine, states:
"Establishment means that the śrāvakas and others, having realized for themselves what they have attained to its culmination, desire to cause others to understand it as well."
By means of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one establishes the Truth of the Path through immeasurable varieties of sets of names, phrases, and syllables;
that is to say, regarding the various truths, there are such forbearances (*kṣānti*) and such knowledges (*jñāna*). This explanation of establishment is made solely in terms of the Four Noble Truths.

[Treatise] Regarding the phrase "the wisdom that internally dispels the conventional designation of sentient beings based on conditions," the term "internal" (*ādhyātmika*) has two traditional interpretations. First, as explained in the Commentary (*ṭīkā*), "internal" refers to one's own person;
thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* asks: "What is the wisdom that takes as its object the dispelling of the conventional designation of individual sentient beings?
This wisdom has as its characteristic that, within one's own continuum, there is no conceptualization of a self-characteristic.
"Discrimination" (vikalpa) means the act of removing. How is it removed? It is by means of the knowledge that takes as its object the conventional designation of individual phenomena;
this knowledge has the characteristic of being non-discriminative regarding the marks of phenomena such as form within one's own continuum.
Since the rest is the same as previously stated, it is known that "internal" refers only to one's own person. Second, distinguishing internal and external by way of the elements (*dhātu*). First:
First, by excluding sentient beings of one's own level within the desire realm, one establishes the conventional designation of "the second.

Second, because the conventional designations of both self and phenomena belonging to one's own and others' levels within the desire realm exist together therein, the term "internal" (*ādhyātmika*) is used; since the term "internal person" applies to both oneself and others, they are all called internal.

Third, because the conventional designations of both self and phenomena in all higher realms are universally excluded, the term "universal" (*sarva*) is used. A detailed explanation states: although the latter reasoning is generally applicable, [it is not so here].
Having no basis for reliance, I now rely on the first explanation.
[Commentary: "Taking as objects all internal and external selves and phenomena" means that externally one understands the self to be like the conception of Brahmā as the self;

this refers to the self of others. Regarding "external phenomena," this refers to the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and so forth. The statement "the three minds are the meaning of the true Path of Vision" (*darśana-mārga*) is...

The three minds taken together constitute the true path of seeing; this is the meaning of the Master’s teaching. As for the statement that the "dharma" [aspect] constitutes the true path of seeing: "dharma" means the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
"dharma" here carries the sense of "learning" or "training. [Commentary:
This initial general explanation regarding the path of seeing as characterized by images refers to what this treatise calls the "two paths of seeing with images. Furthermore...
The statement that there are two [types] is a general heading and a broad exposition; the following two masters' views constitute the correct interpretation.

Furthermore, because it is determined that there are three moments of mind within the path of insight (*darśana-mārga*), this explains the intent behind the broad exposition of the path of insight, which also states that the three moments of mind take the non-established [truths] as their object.
This clarifies the meaning of the general exposition of the path of insight.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the sixteen moments of mind, those termed *dharmakṣānti* (receptivity to the dharma) and *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of the dharma) are called "dharma," while the latter two are called "anvaya" (subsequent).

For instance, *duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti* and *duḥkhadharmajñāna* are called "dharma-jñāna," whereas *duḥkhanvayajñānakṣānti* and *duḥkhanvayajñāna* are called "anvaya-jñāna. The same applies to the remaining four truths (*satya*).
Thus, the four truths comprise sixteen moments of mind; that is, eight contemplate true suchness (*tathatā*), and eight contemplate correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
Contemplating correct knowledge is called subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*); contemplating suchness is called dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*).

[Commentary]: If one has previously cultivated the apprehension of signs regarding the higher realms, it means that a Bodhisattva, having previously practiced the contemplation of the truths of the upper and lower realms during the stage of preparation (*prayoga-avasthā*), is now able to perform the sixteen aspects of the eight truths of the upper and lower realms while abiding in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) characterized by signs.
The mental contemplation of the dharma-patience regarding suffering takes the four truths of the desire realm as its object;

the subsequent patience regarding suffering takes the four truths of the two higher realms as its object, whereby one comprehends the dharmas of the four truths of the form and formless realms through subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
[Treatise] Regarding the transition from the True Path of Seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*) to the Path of Seeing through Names and Characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-darśana-mārga*): Question:

Since the True Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) does not actually sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), why is it called "the Dharma" (*dharma*) in the third stage, where it universally dispels the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) therein? Answer: There are two explanations.

First, it is said that since this is now a provisional designation and not an actual severance or realization, one should not hold it accountable. Second, it is said that although it does not sever the seeds (*bīja*), it eliminates the heavy residues (*dausthulya*).

Regarding the statement that "the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are eliminated," what is the underlying principle? To explain in detail: the latter explanation should be superior. Now, as for the term "dharma," it carries the sense of something resembling [an entity].

Since that which is characterized (the dharmin) does not exist, how can there be a characteristic (the dharma)? Although we know this is a conventional designation, it is a provisional semblance of reality;
because it eliminates the heavy obstructions (dausthulya) and resembles the severing of their seeds, it is conventionally said to "eliminate delusion. Therefore, the latter explanation is correct.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that there are four aspects (*darśana-bhāga*) corresponding to the obstructions abandoned by oneself, it is asked: "It is not yet clear how many uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) there are. If one says there are two, this is logically untenable;
for we have not seen any textual passage stating that there are two uninterrupted paths upon entering the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
If one says there is only one, there should not be two aspects within a single mind, as two types of wisdom cannot arise simultaneously. Answer: It is indeed so.

Although the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) consists of a single wisdom with two functions, when the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) arises, it simultaneously abandons both obstacles;
therefore, in terms of the obstacles being abandoned, it is said that this single wisdom has the function of two aspects of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).
This is likewise the case for the two aspects of seeing within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); thus, there are four aspects of seeing.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "from the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) to the essence (*tattva*), there is no distinction in meaning," one asks: Are they non-distinct or distinct? Why say there is no distinction? The answer is:

There is no distinction between them as subject (*ālambaka*) and object (*ālambana*), because although the self-verifying portion is a subject, it is not a subject of an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma;
therefore, it is said there is no distinction. Furthermore, there is an interpretation that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the essence of all dharmas.

This is the characteristic of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is self-verified; furthermore, it is the essence of the two divisions of the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*).
Based on this principle, it is said to be "non-conceptual.

[Commentary: Within this, there are six types—distinguished as arising separately, uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberated (*vimukti*)—which refers to the seven [moments] within the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) consisting of the perceived and the perceiving.
Only when the mind attains ultimate realization do three types of minds sever the afflictive and cognitive hindrances:

for the lower grade of afflictive hindrances, one separately gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); for the middle grade of cognitive hindrances, one separately gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation;

and for the upper grades of both afflictive and cognitive hindrances, which are combined into a single category, one likewise separately gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation. Thus, there are three [sets of] paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation.
There are six *vimukti-citta* (liberation-minds) together with one *viśeṣa-mārga* (path of excellence), thus making seven minds in total.
[Commentary] Alternatively, the subsequent *anantarya-mārga* (uninterrupted path) is itself the preceding *vimukti-mārga*; thus, the three uninterrupted paths constitute five minds.

This is intended to mean that because the three grades arise as uninterrupted paths, it is not stated that there are separate paths of liberation for each grade; rather, the uninterrupted path of a subsequent grade immediately follows [the liberation of the preceding one].
Since the preceding chapter dealt with the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is stated here again that there are paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Within these three categories, there are three paths of uninterrupted transition; furthermore, within the third category, there is one path of liberation.

Because there is no fourth category to be abandoned, the subsequent category of liberation is designated as the path of uninterrupted transition. Thus, the three paths of uninterrupted transition and the single path of liberation are combined.

Regarding the five moments of mind during the stage of supreme progress (*viśeṣa-gāmin*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is therein that one attains the ultimate realization. Question:

Why is it that only the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is mentioned, and not the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)? Answer: Because Bodhisattvas possess sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), they do not separately give rise to a path of liberation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the fourteen interpretations found in other excerpts, this interpretation clarifies the meaning of the sudden and gradual nature of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) within this chapter on the Path of Seeing.
It is stated there as follows: "Alternatively, with respect to the thirteen moments of mind, it is called the gradual abandonment of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);

the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) likewise have three grades—superior, middling, and inferior. When one abandons the inferior grade of the afflictions, a single moment of uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises."

First, regarding the first interpretation: when one liberation (*vimukti*) severs the inferior grade (*mṛdu*) of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) necessarily arises;
the other grades are to be understood accordingly. Since there are six grades, there are six uninterrupted paths and six liberations, totaling twelve moments of mind.

Furthermore, with the addition of one superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*), there are thirteen moments of mind. This is called the gradual severance of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), whereby one finally attains the ultimate. This is the first interpretation. Furthermore...

Entering from the truth (*tattva*) into the signs (*nimitta*), there are twelve minds consisting of the stages of removal and superior progress; this is called "gradual" (*anupūrva*), which is the second interpretation.
Alternatively, immediately following [the truth], there is the aforementioned liberation (*vimukti*), which consists of eleven minds; this is called "gradual," which is the third interpretation.

Alternatively, afflictions (*kleśa*) consist of two grades—superior and inferior—and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) likewise consist of two grades—superior and inferior; thus, there are four grades of obstructions, and one proceeds by abandoning them one grade at a time.
When the obstructions are being abandoned, one uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arise for each of these four categories;
