thus, four uninterrupted paths and four paths of liberation arise in total, together with one path of special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*). These nine moments of mind are called "gradual" (the fourth interpretation).

Alternatively, excluding the path of special progress, these eight are called "gradual" (the fifth interpretation). Or, if the subsequent uninterrupted path is identical to the preceding path of liberation, then these seven moments of mind constitute the "gradual."

This is the sixth interpretation: either by taking the inferior grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the inferior grade of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) together with the two superior grades of afflictions and the objects of knowledge as a single grade, there are thus three grades of hindrances;

when these are abandoned, one gives rise to three paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), three paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and one path of special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), totaling seven moments of mind, which is called "gradual. This is the seventh interpretation; or, excluding the path of special progress...

Six moments of mind are called "gradual," which is the eighth liberation; alternatively, immediately following the preceding uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), there is this liberation. Five moments of mind are called "gradual," which is the ninth liberation;

alternatively, when only the upper and lower two grades of the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) remain, one gives rise to two uninterrupted paths and two liberations, plus one path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), totaling five moments of mind called "gradual," which is the tenth liberation; alternatively, excluding the path of superior progress, there are four.
The mind is called "gradual" (*anupūrva*); this is the tenth interpretation. Alternatively, the gate of "subsequent non-existence" (*paścād-abhāva*) refers to the aforementioned liberation;

thus there are three minds, which is the twelfth interpretation. Alternatively, the two obstacles constitute the thirteenth interpretation. Alternatively, excluding the superior progress (*viśeṣa-gāmin*), there are two minds, which is the fourteenth interpretation.

【Commentary】 The meaning of the phrase "all are judged in relation to the third grade of the grasping at persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*) as coarse or subtle, superior or inferior" is that both the lower and middle grades are distinguished as coarse or subtle, and superior or inferior, in relation to the upper grade of the grasping at persons and phenomena.

That is to say, what is abandoned first is termed "coarse," while what is abandoned later is termed "subtle"; what is abandoned first is termed "inferior," while what is abandoned later is termed "superior."

[Commentary: Regarding the fact that in all instances one first eliminates the superior grade and subsequently eliminates the inferior grade, this question refers to what preceded; the answer based on the "inferior" [grade] can be understood accordingly.

[Commentary: This, when viewed in relation to the path of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) reaching its actual essence, means that this treatise relies upon the path of the counteragent as the counteragent.
Because the path is inferior, the afflictions abandoned [thereby] are termed "low-grade. Those various holy teachings are established in relation to the actual substance of the afflictions;
therefore, the high-grade [afflictions] are abandoned first.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because the mental disposition of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is thus," this second master asserts that all three minds are [equally] such.
In the Path of Subsequent Realization (*anvaya-mārga*), one takes true reality (*tathatā*) as its object; how then can there be a real distinction of three moments of mind?

In the Bodhisattva’s Path of Preparatory Application (*prayoga-mārga*), the arousal of the thought of enlightenment is intended for the Path of True Seeing; it is directed solely toward the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) to sever hindrances and realize the truth.
It is realized all at once (*sakṛt*), not through the distinction of three moments. How can it be said that these three moments constitute the Path of True Seeing?
[Śāstra]:

First, regarding the observation of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) up to the sixteen types of mind: Question—Are these two sets of sixteen minds fully contained within all treatises?
Answer—It is not fixed; according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Treatise on the Compendium of Abhidharma), Chapter Nine, one should take the first sixteen as the standard.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* does not mention the former [sixteen moments of mind], whereas the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* mentions the latter sixteen moments of mind but does not mention the former.
Regarding why various treatises either include or omit them, the Tripiṭaka Master explains: "Bodhisattvas practicing contemplation naturally fall into three categories.

There is one category of bodhisattvas who initiate their contemplative practice based on the former sixteen moments of mind, and another category of bodhisattvas who do so based on the latter sixteen moments of mind."
Furthermore, there may be another class of bodhisattvas who employ both types of sixteen-moment contemplations (*ṣoḍaśa-citta-vipaśyanā*) in their practice.
Because the sacred teachings each rely on one door and thus provide partial or indirect explanations of the other, the present author has fully expounded both types;
therefore, this does not contradict other treatises.

[Commentary]: This refers specifically to the separate establishment of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Regarding the statement that there are sixteen distinct moments of mind, this means that beneath each of the four truths, one separately generates an uninterrupted path and a path of liberation.

For example, the "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) is the uninterrupted path, and the "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is the path of liberation.

The subsequent two knowledges merely confirm and certify what preceded them; they do not arise as separate [paths] for the remaining truths. The other truths should be understood according to this principle.

The four truths are established separately as sixteen moments of mind. Regarding the first, "Dharmajñānakṣānti" (Receptivity to the Knowledge of the Dharma concerning Suffering), its name is explained according to the distinction between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
If one follows the Hīnayāna, it is named from the perspective of the fruit;

this receptivity is able to produce the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*), and being the cause of the knowledge of the dharma, it receives the name "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma," just as a tree that bears flowers and fruit [is called a "flower-fruit tree"]. Hereafter, other cases should be understood accordingly. Now, following the Mahāyāna, [it is named] from...
Because it is designated by that name, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Juedifa) states in the ninth [chapter]: "Suffering refers to the Dharma of the Truth of Suffering. "Dharma" refers to the teaching;

"knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the wisdom of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) which takes the lower teachings on suffering as its object. Now, the untainted wisdom of patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) that directly realizes the Truth of Suffering is called "Patience regarding the Knowledge of the Dharma of Suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), because it arises from the preceding Knowledge of the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).
This corresponds to the second "Knowledge of the Dharma of Suffering" in that treatise.

If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is called "knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) because it takes the truth of suffering as its object; thus, it is named after its objective domain. If one relies on the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (the *Mahāvibhāṣā*), it is named after its cause.
In full, it should be called "receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and "knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*);

however, for the sake of brevity, it is simply called "knowledge of the dharma of suffering," which realizes liberation from the afflictions previously abandoned. Third, regarding "receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*): it refers to...

Immediately following the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), an untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) arises that internally realizes, in each case, both the preceding acceptance of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of suffering itself.
It declares: "All subsequent noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) are of this same category.
This means that the third moment of mind arises at a single instant, internally realizing the dharma-acceptance and dharma-knowledge; that is to say, it occurs only after these two moments of mind.
Because all the noble dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) arise subsequent to these two types of mind, they are all of this same category.

There are two kinds of "discourse" (*vāk*): first, verbal discourse; second, mental discourse (*manojalpa*), which refers to the path of the mind at the time of the patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) that accord with the objects of cognition.

All the subsequent noble dharmas are of this same category; it is for this reason that [the subsequent patience] is called "subsequent patience regarding the knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñānakṣānti*).
The commentary states: Regarding "category" (*anvaya*), the *Abhidharmakośa* says that because one first realizes the true principle of all phenomena, it is called "dharma-knowledge" (*dharmajñāna*).
Because the subsequent object and cognition resemble the former, they receive the name "category. The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* says:
"Because the first two kinds are the category of all subsequent noble dharmas. The explanation says: the initial patience and knowledge are the noble path produced subsequently.

Regarding the "Dharma-knowledge of the category of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), the second [moment], its explanation is the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa*. Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* XVII names it the "category-knowledge" (*anvaya-jñāna*) as the fourth [moment].
As for the "Dharma-knowledge of the category of suffering," this knowledge takes only the Dharma-knowledge of the category of suffering as its object;

thus, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Because one internally realizes and confirms within the Dharma-knowledge of the category of suffering, it is called the Dharma-knowledge of the category of suffering."

[Commentary: Regarding "the patience that endures the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*): "patience" (*kṣānti*) refers to the seal of endurance. This patience occurs during the stage of application (*prayoga*) preceding [the path of seeing], wherein one contemplates the knowledge of the dharma of suffering.

Because this knowledge universally contemplates two objects—first, the knowledge from the stage of application, and second, the true suchness (*tathatā*) observed by the true vision—it is established as ultimate.
Therefore, the commentary does not mention it separately; it simply speaks of "patience-knowledge," which is precisely this path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The untainted patience (anāsrava-kṣānti) is named after its cause; that cause is the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) during the stage of preparatory application (prayoga).
Because this patience is derived from that knowledge, it receives the name "patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering" (duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti).
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna) confirms the subsequent knowledge of suffering," the meaning is as follows:

this subsequent knowledge of suffering confirms the preceding subsequent-knowledge-tolerance (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-akṣānti), and is thus called "subsequent knowledge of suffering. This constitutes a double confirmation of the third knowledge, asserting:

"This is my object; it is untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna). It is a thorough knowledge that internally realizes the third knowledge, which was previously realized through the distinct internal realization of the dharma-tolerance (dharma-akṣānti) and dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna).

Furthermore, another interpretation is that the "Dharma-patience" (*dharmakṣānti*) and "Dharma-knowledge" (*dharmanirvedha-jñāna*) of the preceding stage act as a seal; they seal the objects of the subsequent "Subsequent Patience" (*anvayakṣānti*).

They do not directly take the "Subsequent Patience" itself as their object, but rather the objects of the "Subsequent Patience," which is why it is called "sealing the objects of Subsequent Patience. Since the Dharma-patience and Dharma-knowledge constitute the third category of patience, they seal the objects of the fourth knowledge;
hence it is said they "seal the objects of Subsequent Patience."

[Treatise] Regarding the statement that "the eight contemplations of suchness and the eight contemplations of correct wisdom" constitute the scope of the objects of the clear wisdom (*vidyā*), the *Abhidharma* states:
"There are two types of objects, namely suchness (*tathatā*) and correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*). The path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) takes suchness as its object;
the path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) takes correct wisdom as its object."

[Treatise] Regarding the statement "the true path of seeing of dharmas (*dharmābhisamaya*) and so forth," the Commentary provides two interpretations. One interpretation critiques the first explanation, stating:

"This treatise and the Abhidharma both refer to 'subsequent patience' (*anvayakṣānti*). Within the respective internal realizations of 'dharma-patience' (*dharmakṣānti*) and 'dharma-knowledge' (*dharmajñāna*), there are already the self-verifying portions (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of both the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) regarding all dharmas.
Furthermore, it is stated that 'subsequent knowledge' (*anvayajñāna*) confirms subsequent patience; it does not speak of a separate [self-verifying portion] for subsequent knowledge."

Regarding the realization of *dharmajñāna*, how can it be said that the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) consists of the *dharmakṣānti* and *dharmajñāna* as the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) and liberation (*vimuktimārga*), while the self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*) pertains to the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)? Now, two explanations are offered:
First, it is said that *dharmakṣānti* and *dharmajñāna* are distinct within the true path of seeing;

the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation consist of the aspect of seeing (*darśanabhāga*) which takes the suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, while the self-realization takes the wisdom (*jñāna*) as its object. However, because this has not yet been definitively established, the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) re-examines the dharma with certainty.

At the time of the *niścaya-mudrā* (seal of certainty), it is likewise: the *dharmajñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena) has two [aspects], the self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*) and the second [the object-cognizing]; the first three are as previously stated.

Since the fourth is described as the "seal of confirmation" (*anumodanā-mudrā*), it follows that within the two paths—the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and the liberation (*vimukti*)—the self-cognizing aspect cognizes the self-cognizing aspect;

and within the four aspects, the third [self-cognizing] cognizes the seeing aspect (*darśana*). Now, since this *duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna-kṣānti* (receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of suffering) is a *dharma*...

Regarding the self-realization of the fourth [moment], the patience (*kṣānti*) and the clear knowledge (*vidyā*) of the two paths of realization—the self-realizing portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*)—only the seeing of phenomena (*dharmadarśana*) and the self-realization itself are mentioned;
the meaning is that other aspects are omitted for brevity. To explain this in detail:

as for the mention of "phenomena" (*dharma*), it refers only to the true seeing (*bhūtadarśana*) which takes suchness (*tathatā*) as its object through distinct wisdom; it does not refer to those various individual mental aspects (*ākāra*), because within true seeing there are no distinct aspects.

The third [moment] realizes only the first two knowledges, and the fourth does likewise; alternatively, it may take the third as its object, yet it is merely knowledge that takes knowledge as its object.

Based on this one aspect, they are separately assigned to the two paths. Since there is no fault in distinguishing them by not taking the third and fourth as objects of the path of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā*), the treatise concludes:
"The establishment of the distinctions in names and characteristics is called the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); if [it refers to] the third and fourth..."
In both cases, although the meaning of the distinction between the two preceding paths as self-cognizing aspects is present, it is not explicitly revealed.
As for the principle that the self-cognizing aspect exists within the two paths, even if there is no textual evidence, there would be no fault; the text has simply omitted it.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "They are established as distinct because they seal the preceding cognition," one asks: Since the two preceding minds both possess the *dharmajñāna-darśana-bhāga* (the seeing-part of the knowledge of phenomena), and the two subsequent minds both possess the *svasaṃvedana-bhāga* (self-verifying part) of the two paths, what distinction is there between them?
Answer: The *dharmakṣānti* (receptivity to phenomena) and *anvayakṣānti* (subsequent receptivity) lack the preceding uninterrupted [seeing-part];

the self-verifying parts of the *dharmajñāna* and *anvayajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena and subsequent knowledge) take as their objects the self-verifying parts of the preceding liberation-seeing [parts]. Thus, [the distinction is established].
They differ because they are not mutually validated.

[Commentary] Furthermore, another interpretation states that when it says "this is the totality of dharmas," it refers to both the dharma-object and the suchness; since these two paths—the seeing-path and self-realization—are not differentiated, they are called the "totality of dharmas."
[Treatise]: Second, regarding the establishment of sixteen types of minds—distinguished by the contemplation of the lower and upper truths—the intention of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* is as follows:

In the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), the four truths are present before one; in the two higher realms combined, there are likewise four truths to be realized through the Patience of Realization (*abhisamaya-kṣānti*).

This Patience applies both to what is present before one and what is not present before one; the Wisdom of Realization (*abhisamaya-jñāna*) is the same. Patience is the immediate precursor to the Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).

The knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) is the path of liberation through the dharma (*dharmavimuktimārga*). Furthermore, observing the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) of the desire realm is termed the patience for the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*);

observing the truth of suffering of the two higher realms is termed the patience for the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*). Since this is the case for the truth of suffering, it is likewise for the remaining truths.

These sixteen moments of mind all consist of the aspect of the vision of phenomena (*dharmadarśana-bhāga*) taking true suchness (*tathatā*) as their object; therefore, they are called "present realization" (*abhisamaya*) and "patience" (*kṣānti*).

The patience regarding the categories of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the patience regarding the subsequent categories of phenomena (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) belong to the clear realization of wisdom; the category of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the category of subsequent wisdom (*anvayajñāna*). As for "subsequent" (*anvaya*), it refers to the upper realms being the "subsequent" to the lower realms.

[Commentary] Regarding the second stage of clear realization, the meaning is that when the semblance of the knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of subsequent categories arises, this is the subsequently attained wisdom following the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Because this wisdom is subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it is called the second stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*).

That which is termed "the wisdom of patient acceptance and aspiration" refers specifically to the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñānakṣānti*); the same applies to the other truths. The "wisdom of decisive clear realization" refers to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna*);
the other truths are to be understood accordingly. Both of these belong to the subsequently attained wisdom within the path of vision characterized by signs (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga-pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
Because it is wisdom, it is called the "realization of the truths through wisdom at the conclusion of clear observation" (*abhisamaya-anta-jñāna-satya-abhisamaya*).

Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (55), regarding the phrase "the realization of the truths through wisdom at the conclusion of clear observation," the commentary explains: "Clear observation" (*abhisamaya*) refers to true untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*); "conclusion" (*anta*) refers to what follows;

"realization of the truths through wisdom" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*). The intended meaning is that this refers to the subsequently attained [wisdom].

Since "wisdom" (jñāna) refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:
"It should be known that this wisdom arises immediately after the third moment of mind and manifests from the path of seeing;

it takes as its object the previously observed objects of the lower and upper realms, as well as the two types of established truths (*vyavasthāpana-satya*), appearing as the conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that resembles the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)."

This [knowledge] encompasses both the mundane and the supramundane; because it is that which is subsequently attained after supramundane wisdom, two kinds of knowledge arise for each respective truth in their proper order:
first, the knowledge of acceptance and aspiration (*kṣānti-ruci-jñāna*); second, the knowledge of decisive realization (*abhisamaya-niścaya-jñāna*).
Thus, having arisen from the preceding realization, these two pairs of knowledges arise respectively with respect to each of the lower and upper truths. This is the explanation.

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by previous lives," there are briefly two interpretations. The first states that it refers to the conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) within the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Specifically, it refers to the objects of observation—the afflictions of the lower desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the upper form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*), namely the truths of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and origin (*samudaya-satya*)—as well as the two predominant truths of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the path (*mārga-satya*). This is intended to explain the state of the preparatory stage prior [to the path of seeing].
In the middle [stage], one observes the afflictions and so forth of the suffering and origin of the lower desire realm and the suffering and origin of the two upper realms;
furthermore, regarding the establishment of the two superior [truths], these are the untainted truths of cessation and the path.

While conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) does not cling when taking them as its present object, it serves as a superior condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the arising of conventional knowledge that takes the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) as its object. Second, it takes the previously seen reality (*bhūta-darśana*) as its object.

It is also called "having previously observed" because it takes as its object the superior establishment of the Four Truths within the lower and upper stages and within both stages, by means of releasing true vision;
being subsumed under conventional knowledge that resembles dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge, this wisdom is mundane conventional knowledge.
It is called "resembling" because it resembles the other untainted dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge, due to its release.
It is called "resembling" (*sadr̥śa*) because it resembles another; that is to say, it is similar. Furthermore, according to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚聖教論), chapter seventeen, it states:

"From this point of the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) upward, during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), sixteen modes of activity arise as pure mundane and supramundane wisdoms.

That is to say, regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), two kinds of wisdom arise: first, the wisdom of investigative clear observation (*abhisamayavicāra-jñāna*); second, the wisdom of clear observation..."
Regarding the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness, the knowledge of certainty (*niścaya-jñāna*) likewise possesses these two types of knowledge.
Based on this principle, it is said to reside in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The commentary states: The four truths and the two knowledges are likewise fifty-five;

they do not arise from application (*prayoga*), yet there are sixteen distinctions because these distinctions exist according to the specific functions performed in contemplating each truth. Thus, within the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*):
It may also be said that there are sixteen moments of mind.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "this is explained according to the distinctions in practice," the intended meaning is that within this treatise, because the modes of understanding (*ākāra*) and the objects of knowledge differ between the *dharmajñāna* and *anvayajñāna* in relation to the two truths, these constitute exclusively the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

[Commentary]: "The realm present before one" (*pratyakṣa-dhātu*) is discussed in terms of proximity and distance; thus, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is proximate, while the other realms are distant.

Furthermore, it is said that if one enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) while in a body belonging to the desire realm, then the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*) of the desire realm constitute the realm present before one.
[Treatise] If one explains the nine types of mind in the path of seeing according to the principles of the widely disseminated holy teachings (*āgama*), the underlying intention is this:
the Bodhisattva does not actually perform these contemplations; rather, they provisionally establish and designate these nine minds based solely on the terminology of the holy teachings.

This means that there is only verbal expression and no actual meditative practice (*bhāvanā-caryā*). The intention is that although the Bodhisattva does not perform these [contemplations] during the aforementioned path of seeing...
Observing that within the holy teachings there is already the statement establishing nine minds, it follows that Bodhisattvas must also study them;
that is, based upon those two kinds of sixteen minds, the terms "calm abiding" (śamatha) and "insight" (vipaśyanā) are used as provisional designations.
The following passage clarifies the meaning of these provisional designations.
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from the end of fascicle 58 stating "as explained in that manuscript," the meaning is as follows: Previously, there were two sets of sixteen moments of mind;

now, the eight truths are consolidated into four truths. By taking *dharmakṣānti* (dharma-patience) and *anvayakṣānti* (subsequent patience) as one, and *dharmajñāna* (dharma-knowledge) and *anvayajñāna* (subsequent knowledge) as one, there are eight moments of mind beneath the four truths;
that is, each truth possesses two moments of mind. Thus, there are four truths.
Since the eight minds associated with the [four] truths are combined into one as a whole, there are nine minds in total. Question:
Since there are two sets of sixteen types of mind, shouldn't there be sixteen *kṣāntis* (patiences) and sixteen *jñānas* (knowledges) in all?

Why does the commentary state that the eight *kṣāntis* are combined into four and the eight *jñānas* are combined into four, speaking of each patience and knowledge individually? Answer: This is because they are categorized according to the eight truths that are observed.

Question: Since the dharmas and their categories (*jāti*) are identical, the eight truths are combined into four truths; likewise, why are the sixteen moments of mind combined into eight contemplations? Question:
If there are eight contemplations, and since the eight applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) correspond to them, are they not also eight?

Why then do you say they are collectively explained as one moment of mind? Answer: Although there are eight meanings of application corresponding to the contemplations, because the nature of the applications (*śamatha*) is identical, they are combined into one.
Therefore, the Commentary states: "This is based on the distinction of wisdom, while meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is unique, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-ṭīkā*.

[The Treatise] says: "Regarding 'contemplation is superior to cessation' (*śamatha*), 'superior' (*shun*) means excellence; that is, within the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), contemplation is superior and cessation is inferior.
Because it is superior, it is divided into many; because it is inferior, it is unified into one."

[Commentary]: Regarding the meaning of "relying on the truth," the phrase "provisionally designating the Path of Vision (darśanamārga) and so forth as 'uninterrupted' (ānantarya)" means that this text reconciles an apparent contradiction in the treatise’s explanation.
It indicates that while the Path of Vision is said to arise immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma), this is merely a provisional designation;
in reality, it does not have the sense of being a state of "interruption. Therefore, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
Immediately following the first dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), three moments of mind arise which sever the one hundred and twelve types of afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*).

Furthermore, the *Abhidharmapitaka* states: "Immediately following the supreme mundane dharma, sixteen moments of mind arise, beginning with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), which sever the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 55, states: "Immediately following the supreme mundane dharma, three [moments of mind] arise."
Passages such as "the mind severs [afflictions] abandoned through seeing" and so forth all describe the path of seeing based on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by way of its characteristics.

While it is said that [the path of seeing] arises immediately after the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), in reality, it is not the case that there is no interval; nor is it the case that it can truly sever [afflictions].

To speak of "immediacy" and "the ability to sever" is entirely a conventional designation and not a literal fact. This is how this [textual] passage is to be reconciled. If one were to speak according to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then:

Because from the uninterrupted path of the first dharma of the previous life, there arises the true path of seeing; following that, there arise the three moments of the subsequent path of seeing, and subsequently the sixteen moments of the path of seeing.

Therefore, while the Bodhisattva is on the path of seeing, he trains in the matters of abandonment and realization already accomplished by the preceding true path of seeing. Since this is a provisional designation, why must one train? [The answer follows: [Response: Because the true path of seeing has not yet been fully stabilized, and because the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation have not yet been abandoned, one must train in order to bring about their stabilization and to abandon those remaining afflictions. Furthermore, although the true path of seeing has already been realized, it is necessary to train in order to increase its power and to ensure that the fruits of the path are not lost. This is like a king who, though having already conquered his enemies, still maintains his army to prevent future threats.

Thus, even though the true path of seeing has been previously attained, training in its objects is both necessary and appropriate. This is called "training in what has already been realized. It is not as if one were training in something entirely new; rather, it is training for the sake of stabilization and further development. This is why the Bodhisattva must train in the path of seeing. This is the meaning of the teaching.
[This is] because one desires to fully know the two obstacles and the two selves.
[Commentary: The meaning of "there being three reasons" here is to explain the basis for the aforementioned provisional designation;

that is to say, those three minds can only arise after the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and the sixteen moments of mind cannot arise until after the non-conceptual (*avyavasthāpita*) [path]. As the treatise says: "No..."

This is because it is established by way of establishing the subsequent [attainment], and because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) have been truly severed through discernment; therefore, one knows that this is a figurative designation and not a realization of actual severance.
[Commentary]: The reason why the non-established cause does not pervade the three minds is that the three minds of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) are non-established.
Therefore, one cannot use the non-positively established reason (*avyavasthāpita-hetu*) to prove that the three moments of mind are not the true path of seeing;
rather, it can only be used to prove that the sixteen moments of mind are not the true path of seeing.

[Commentary: Why does the root verse speak only of the *tattva-darśana-mārga* (the path of seeing reality) up to this point, whereas here it speaks based on the *darśana-bhāga* (the seeing aspect)? The intention of the question is:

why does the root verse not mention the three minds, the sixteen [moments], and the two types of *lakṣaṇa-darśana-mārga* (the path of seeing characteristics), but speaks only of the *tattva-darśana-mārga*?

The answer is: that which is called the *tattva-darśana-mārga* is for the purpose of realizing the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-svabhāva*). This nature of consciousness is precisely suchness (*tathatā*), which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).

Because it is that which is realized by the *jñāna-darśana-bhāga* (the cognitive-perceptual division), this [text] speaks only in terms of the *darśana-bhāga* and not the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (the self-verifying division).

Furthermore, since the characteristics of the *svasaṃvitti-vijñāna* (self-verifying consciousness) are also one's own mind, it speaks only of the *darśana-bhāga* taking suchness as its object, and does not say that the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* takes suchness as its object.

If one were to say that the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* takes [suchness] as its object, there would be the following problem: it would be taking the *darśana-bhāga* as its object, and the *darśana-bhāga* is comprised within the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
Because it is not said that self-realization takes the seeing-part as its object, but rather that it takes true suchness as its object, true suchness is this Path of Seeing.
If one speaks of the Path of Images, there is this wisdom that takes [the dependent nature] as its object, which is subsumed under the other-dependent nature.
[Treatise] Regarding the question of whether the various subsequently attained wisdoms (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) possess two aspects:

the term "various" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom following the three minds, as well as the subsequently attained wisdom that contemplates the truths of the sixteen moments of mind in their double layers, and furthermore the subsequently attained wisdom that takes phenomena as its object;
for these reasons, it is said to be "various."

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "sounds, forms, and other signs arise upon the consciousness of sentient beings," this means that within the consciousness of sentient beings, sounds, names, phrases, and so forth arise.

Since sound is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), it is said that there is form upon the consciousness of sentient beings. Names, phrases, and so forth are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*);
the same should be understood for the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).

[Treatise] There is an interpretation that this wisdom perceives the existence of the aspect (*nimitta*) and the non-existence of the subject (*darśana*). This second master also agrees with the first master’s explanation, stating:
"The Buddha likewise lacks the fifteen realms; since the Buddha does not preach the Dharma, there is no objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*);

and because the objective aspect is absent, the five sense organs (*indriya*) and the five objects (*viṣaya*) do not exist. Since the sense organs and objects are absent, the five consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), which depend upon them, do not arise."
[Commentary: Regarding the meaning of the two masters in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the intention is as follows:

the first master therein accords with the second master of this treatise, while the latter two masters therein accord with the third master of this treatise. Question: How do the meanings of the latter two masters in that treatise differ? Answer:
The second master therein states generally that untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) possesses both the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) and the aspect of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Whether regarding the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) or the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), according to the third master’s analysis, they are distinguished as two because the fundamental wisdom is held to be without the appearance of objects (*nimitta*), whereas the subsequently attained wisdom is admitted to possess it.

[The Treatise] states: "Because all noble wisdoms (*ārya-jñāna*) are able to directly illuminate their objects. This master’s intention is to say that the subsequently attained wisdom directly apprehends the mind.
Because external essential dharmas do not change and serve as conditions, they lack the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*).

[Commentary: Regarding the detailed explanation according to those four propositions, it is stated in the *Seventy-three* [fascicle] that there is "contemplation of suchness without observing suchness.
This refers to the Bodhisattva in the Path of True Seeing (*tathatā-darśanamārga*) who contemplates suchness by means of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). There is also...

Contemplating suchness and observing suchness refers to the Bodhisattva’s subsequent cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) within the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), wherein there is both contemplation and observation of suchness;
not contemplating and not observing suchness refers to other distracted states of mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).
[Treatise] Furthermore, regarding the statement that this wisdom discriminates all phenomena and so forth, the third master in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says:

Because the mental complex associated with untainted non-conceptual wisdom (*anāsrava-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is non-conceptual, and because the *tathatā* (suchness) which is its object does not exist apart from its own essence, it is like illuminating its own essence without a separate objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
However, the mental complex associated with subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) possesses conceptualization.

Therefore, regarding the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*), because it may be separate from its own substance, just as a contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*) clearly perceives and illuminates an appearance resembling the object, so too an uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) can take an object separate from its substance as its focus even without an appearance resembling that [object].
Otherwise, the *Ālambanaparīkṣā* would not have stated: "Because there is no appearance of atoms upon the five consciousnesses, such an object is not the objective sphere."
Although similar uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds arise from uncontaminated seeds, they possess a semblance of contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena; yet, they are not actually contaminated.
This is because, just as a contaminated mind may manifest a semblance of the uncontaminated but is not thereby uncontaminated, so too is this case.

[Commentary: Regarding "other minds, other bodies, other lands," and so forth, this is a general enumeration of three categories of phenomena: first, other minds, which are the objects perceived by the knowledge of others' minds;

second, the five sense organs (*indriya*) and their auxiliary objects (*bhautika-rūpa*) belonging to other bodies; and third, the four types of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) transformed by other persons.
These phenomena, being distinct from one's own substance, would—lacking the reflection [of consciousness]—not be objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "When one perceives form and so forth, one should perceive sound and so forth, because the cognition perceiving form and so forth does not bear the characteristics of sound and so forth," the formal proof (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
When perceiving form, it should perceive sound and so forth, because it does not bear the characteristics of form and so forth, just like when perceiving sound.

[Treatise] Furthermore, regarding the statement "because there is no causal function for that which takes non-existent dharmas as its object": "non-existent dharmas" refers to the two time periods of the past and future, as well as categories such as sky-flowers.
The term "and so forth" includes those dharmas that are dissociated from mind.

If it were said that subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) does not transform its aspect, then when it takes non-existents and the like as objects, there would be no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because a dharma that lacks substantial reality has no causal function as an object. However...

Since it is accepted that cognition cannot arise with respect to a non-existent object, we know that when subsequently attained cognition (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) takes a non-existent phenomenon as its object, its aspect (*ākāra*) and its vision (*darśana*) are not non-existent.
[Commentary]: However, regarding the threefold distinction between "meaning" (*artha*), "phenomenon" (*vastu*), and "object-condition" (*ālambana*):

"meaning" refers to the meanings such as suffering and impermanence upon the mind of the contemplative subject (*ālambaka*). "Phenomenon" refers to the factors co-arising simultaneously with the contemplative mind, because they share the same functional activity (*kārya*).

The "objects of focus" refer to the Four Truths; "non-establishment" and so forth refers to the meanings of these dharmas as explained extensively in the chapter on the Six Abhisamayas (Sixfold Realization).
Therefore, it says, "as explained in the separate commentary.
[Treatise]: Regarding the "Six Abhisamayas" and so forth, the various treatises explain the distinctions of abhisamaya at length, as narrated in the chapter according to the Abhidharma.

The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* explains ten and eighteen [types of clear realization (*abhisamaya*]); I shall now briefly cite them. Furthermore, the thirteenth chapter of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"The establishment of clear realization is, in brief, of ten kinds. These are: the clear realization of the Dharma, of the meaning, of reality, of subsequent attainment, of the jewels, of non-action, of the ultimate, of the Śrāvaka, of the Pratyekabuddha, and of the Bodhisattva.

Regarding the clear realization of the Dharma: it refers to [the realization] within the teachings of the Sūtras and so forth, which have the Truths as their predominant theme, arising from hearing the voice of another."

By the power of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), one who has attained the superior grade of pure faith and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) subsumed within the final roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya-kuśala-mūla*), and who is designated as "Dharma" by virtue of the Dharma—this is the meaning of the "realization of the Dharma" (*dharma-abhisamaya*).

As for "realization" (*abhisamaya*), it refers to the power of the dominant condition consisting of correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) directed toward the aforementioned Dharma that has the Truths as its object;
having thus [attained] the final [roots of goodness] conducive to liberation regarding the objects such as the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

The true direct realization (*abhisamaya*) consisting of the superior patience in the discernment of phenomena (*dharmavicāra-kṣānti*), which is subsumed under the four roots of goodness of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*),

arises because one has already attained the noble path of sixteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) through the aforementioned predominance of the truths; furthermore, within that path of seeing,
one attains the conventional knowledge of the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) at the conclusion of the direct realization, which is acquired through the increase of supramundane knowledge.
Because it is of this nature, one attains that knowledge and cultivates the stage of the path; it is precisely at this point that the subsequent clear observation (*pṛṣṭhābhisamaya*) is attained.

Regarding "subsequent clear observation," this refers to all paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) following the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); all mundane and supramundane path-knowledges are termed subsequent clear observation.

Regarding "clear observation of the Jewels" (*ratnābhisamaya*), this refers to the fact that the noble disciples of the Buddha have already attained certainty regarding the Three Jewels and have realized purity.
Pure faith consists in knowing that the Blessed One is truly and perfectly enlightened; that the Dharma and Vinaya are truly well-expounded;
and that the community of noble disciples are truly practitioners of the path.

It further consists in knowing that those who have not yet attained realization are practicing the path, while those who have already realized it possess the restraint of the ethical discipline cherished by the noble ones. By attaining this [faith], its opposites—the various states of hell—are abandoned.
Because they have been fully matured and will never again be practiced—being forever exhausted and no longer active—they are called "non-practice" (*apravṛtti*).

Regarding the "ultimate realization" (*niṣṭhā-abhisamaya*), it is as explained in the context of the ultimate path within the Truth of the Path: namely, that all heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) have been stilled and all acquisitions of dissociation (*visamyoga-prāpti*) have been attained.
Such are the realizations of the Śrāvakas. As for the seven types of realization previously mentioned, [they proceed] from...
Because they realize it by hearing the voice [of another], it is called the realization of the śrāvaka (*śrāvakābhisamaya*).

As for the realization of the pratyekabuddha (*pratyekabuddhābhisamaya*), it is so called because they realize the seven kinds of realization previously described without depending on the voice of another; hence, it is called the realization of the pratyekabuddha.

As for the realization of the bodhisattva (*bodhisattvābhisamaya*), it refers to those bodhisattvas who, regarding the seven kinds of realization previously described, feel compassion for sentient beings and—

Because one attains liberation through the lower vehicles, yet enters the bodhisattvas' determination of the correct nature (*samyaktva-niyāma*) within the Bodhisattva Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), this is called the bodhisattva's clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
Furthermore, according to the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (Xianyang shengjiao lun), Chapter 17, there are eighteen types of distinctions in this clear realization, namely:

the wisdom born of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), the wisdom born of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*), and the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), as well as those that are concordant...

The wisdom of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-jñāna*); the wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); the wisdom of the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*);

impure conventional wisdom (*asaṃśuddha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*); pure conventional wisdom (*saṃśuddha-saṃvṛti-jñāna*); ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*); wisdom with conceptualization regarding impure conduct (*asaṃśuddha-caryā-savikalpa-jñāna*); wisdom with conceptualization regarding pure conduct (*saṃśuddha-savikalpa-jñāna*); wisdom without conceptualization regarding pure conduct (*saṃśuddha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*);
wisdom as the preliminary to the fulfillment of what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-pūrvaga-jñāna*); and the fulfillment of what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
The wisdom that accomplishes what is to be done consists of the wisdom of śrāvakas and others, as well as the wisdom of bodhisattvas and others.

However, while the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* briefly indicates their names, it does not explain their characteristics. According to the traditional commentary, the first three types of wisdom correspond to the three kinds of insight (*prajñā*) possessed during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).
The four types that follow should be understood according to their respective names. The eighth is the impure conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) that manifests.

The "observer" refers to the stage of the aids to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); because one has not yet been able to skillfully understand the principle of the Four Noble Truths, it is explained that while one does not understand the principle of the Four Noble Truths, this is termed "unskillful," yet it is not the unskillfulness among the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*).

Ninth, the "wholesome, pure conventional knowledge of clear realization" refers to the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); because one skillfully understands the principle of the Four Noble Truths, it is [termed wholesome].

10. The clear realization of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-abhisamaya*) is the wisdom at the stages of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), and the path of culmination (*niṣṭhā-mārga*).
11. The clear realization of wisdom with conceptual differentiation regarding impure conduct is the wisdom of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
12. The clear realization of wisdom with conceptual differentiation regarding pure conduct is the cultivation of the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu-bhāvanā*).
Thirteenth: the clear realization of non-conceptual wisdom that is perfectly pure conduct through wisdom; Fourteenth:
the clear realization of the wisdom that takes the non-established truths as its object within the path of seeing, the path of meditation, and the path of culmination;

Fifteenth: the clear realization of the wisdom preceding the performance of activities; Sixteenth: the clear realization of the wisdom of performing activities; Seventeenth: the wisdom subsequent to the performance of activities.
Regarding "clear realization" (*abhisamaya*), it is sequentially correlated with the three types of knowledge—preparatory, fundamental, and post-attainment.

The commentary explains that "that which is accomplished" refers to the completion of the task of abandoning [afflictions] and realizing [the truth]; it does not refer to the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (knowledge of accomplishing what is to be done) among the four knowledges.
The seventeenth is the clear realization-knowledge possessed by those śrāvakas; the eighteenth is that possessed by bodhisattvas.
Regarding the wisdom of contemplation, the fourteenth fascicle of that same treatise explains these nine types as follows:
"Among these, impure mundane conventional wisdom refers to the wisdom of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*);

pure mundane conventional wisdom refers to the mundane wisdom attained subsequent to the supramundane [realization]; and ultimate wisdom refers to the wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Furthermore...

The wisdom with conceptual differentiation that has the aspect of thorough purity; the wisdom with conceptual differentiation that has the aspect of thorough purity; the wisdom without conceptual differentiation that has the aspect of thorough purity;

furthermore, the wisdom prior to the wisdom of accomplishing what was to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), the wisdom of accomplishing what was to be done, and the wisdom subsequent to the wisdom of accomplishing what was to be done.
Explanation: This clarifies the distinctions among the nine types of wisdom within the eighteen kinds of clear realization (*abhisamaya*). For now, we shall clarify the former.
This refers to the distinctions among the three types of wisdom, such as the "well-purified" (*suviśuddha*).

Regarding the statement, "arising when afflictions have not been abandoned, it is not an antidote to affliction," the intended meaning is that preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) arises while afflictions have not yet been abandoned;

because this wisdom cannot abandon them, it is not an antidote to affliction. Regarding the statement, "arising when afflictions have already been abandoned, it is not an antidote to affliction": [the same logic applies].
This refers to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which arises after the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).

Regarding the statement that "having already abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*), one gives rise to dharmas that are not antidotes to the afflictions," this is because subsequently attained wisdom cannot abandon the delusions.

To say that "giving rise to [dharmas] after abandoning the afflictions" constitutes an antidote to the afflictions refers precisely to the wisdom of the path of vision. As for the three distinctions within the explanation of the remaining text: it is as follows...
Regarding the distinction between the conventional and ultimate wisdom-natures of these three types based on their being with or without conceptual differentiation (*savikalpa*/*nirvikalpa*):
the explanation states that the term "with conceptual differentiation" includes the first two [types], while the term "without conceptual differentiation" includes only the third;

the term "conventional" also includes the first two, while the term "ultimate" refers only to the third. Thus, the statement regarding the inclusion of the distinctions among the three refers to the distinctions among the latter three.

Regarding the distinction: these three types demonstrate the differences in nature between the prior abandonment (*prahāṇa*), the subsequent knowledge (*jñāna*), and the actual abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa*).
"Prior abandonment" refers to the preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*)—the knowledge prior to the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*). "Actual abandonment" is the fundamental [path] itself (*maula*).

"Subsequent knowledge" is the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*)—the knowledge following true vision (*tattva-darśana*). Thus, there are three distinctions. This is now correlated with the text of the fourteenth chapter of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

Regarding the status as "correct," furthermore, according to the sixth fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is said that there are eleven kinds of distinctions and differences between the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of the Great and Small Vehicles.
Thus, the root treatise states: "The clear realization of a Bodhisattva differs from that of a Śrāvaka; this should be understood through eleven kinds of distinctions.
First, by way of the distinction of the object of focus (*ālambana*), because the Mahāyāna teachings serve as the object of focus. Second, by way of... [text continues]
1. By the distinction of sustenance (*upastambha*), because it takes the two kinds of accumulations—merit and wisdom—as its sustenance; 2.
By the distinction of thorough penetration (*prativedha*), because it is able to thoroughly penetrate the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*);

3. By the distinction of nirvāṇa, because it embraces non-abiding great nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-mahānirvāṇa*); 4. By the distinction of others, because it relies upon the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) for its transcendence.
Therefore, the sixth and seventh [differences] are due to the distinction of purity: because they sever the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions and purify the Buddha-fields.

The commentary explains that while followers of the two vehicles sever the afflictions but cannot purify the lands, Bodhisattvas sever the habitual tendencies of the afflictions and are thus able to purify the lands;
this is the second distinction. The eighth is due to the distinction of attaining a mind of equality toward oneself and others, whereby they bring sentient beings to maturity.
1. By the absence of rest in preparatory application; 2. by the distinction of birth, because of being born into the family of the Tathāgatas; 3.
by the distinction of taking birth, because of being sustained in birth within the great assemblies of all Buddhas; 4.
by the distinction of the fruit, because of the fulfillment of the fruits of immeasurable qualities, such as the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the unique Buddha-dharmas.

[Commentary]: Regarding the question of why *pratisaṃvid* (analytical knowledge), which is characterized by clarity and sharpness, does not correspond with the sensation of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), the answer is as follows:
The "contemplative realization" (*cintā-abhisamaya*) is a wisdom derived from reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Since this wisdom derived from reflection exists only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the sixth consciousness of the desire realm corresponds only to the three sensations of joy (*saumanasya*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); therefore, there is no pleasure within the sixth consciousness.

Regarding feeling: if it is within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) possesses pleasant feeling; furthermore, in the two higher realms, there is no wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Moreover, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when one hears the Dharma and the mental consciousness understands it, it is associated with the feeling of joy (*prīti*); therefore, it is said that joy is capable of clarity and sharpness, as it possesses distinct discernment (*viveka*).

[Treatise] Regarding the statement, "In the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), one observes all phenomena": this text refers to the preceding path of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) as well, because it is also termed the path of application.

Thus, the Treatise states: "It is not that there is no application prior to the path of accumulation. Therefore, this passage does not define the path of application solely by means of the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "reflection (*cintā*) can produce cultivation (*bhāvanā*)," this means that within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*) is able to induce the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "because it comprises the inferior and middling [levels] and does not extensively take objects," the intended meaning is that reflection consists of the inferior and middling grades.

Because it cannot take a broad range of objects but can only spontaneously produce cognition of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is said to concern "specific characteristics"; this is subsumed under the middle and lower grades.
If it can take a broad range of objects such as impermanence and other general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it is then comprised within the superior grade of reflection.
[Commentary]: Although *tathatā* (suchness) is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, prior to its realization, it is regarded as a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
This means that when fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) takes suchness as its object, it directly realizes suchness; therefore, suchness is called a specific characteristic.

However, when the wisdom of application (*prayogamārgajñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdhajñāna*) take suchness as their object, they do not realize it directly; therefore, suchness is merely termed a common characteristic. Thus it is subsumed [under the latter category].
[Commentary]: Although one also contemplates all phenomena as being selfless and so forth, there is a limited scope to this contemplation.

The intention behind this is that although the four roots of goodness—Heat and the others—of this stage of application (prayoga-mārga) contemplate all phenomena as being selfless and so on, they possess limitations;
they either contemplate based on a single phenomenon or take the Four Truths individually as their objects, such as [viewing] suffering as selfless, and are unable to analyze them extensively.
Because they are distinct, they are not established as a single "clear observation" (*abhisamaya*).
[The Treatise] states: "That which takes the Three Jewels as its object is decisive pure faith, whether mundane or supramundane.

This means that mundane faith refers to faith in the causes and effects associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), while supramundane faith refers to that which takes as its object the untainted (*anāsrava*), conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "established as indestructible faith," the intended meaning is that untainted (anāsrava) faith is established as the four indestructible faiths (*akṣaya-śraddhā*).
That is to say, the faith produced toward the Triple Gem and the faith produced toward pure precepts are called the four indestructible faiths.
They are termed "indestructible" because they are not led astray or turned back by their objects of focus (*ālambana*).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "because they are outflows": the four roots of goodness are the outflows of the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), yet they are not identical to that direct realization of the path of vision.

[Treatise] Regarding the phrase "the direct realization of the knowledge of the truths" (*jñāna-satyābhisamaya*): the intent is that "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to the wisdom that is capable of observing, while "truths" (*satya*)...

This is precisely the non-established truth (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*). Because this wisdom takes the non-established truth as its object and realizes it, it is called the "wisdom that realizes the truths" (*abhisamaya-jñāna-satya*).
That which is called "all aspects" (*sarvākāra*) is *tathatā* (suchness); because *tathatā* constitutes the essence of all phenomena, *tathatā* is designated by the name "all aspects."
[Commentary]: This means that at whatever stage one takes as an object only that which is non-established (*apratiṣṭhita*), it is therefore called "all modes" (*sarvākāra*).

This clear realization (*abhisamaya*) consists of both the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Regarding the term "all modes," this refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for fundamental wisdom.
Regarding the term "non-established," this refers to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) consisting of the three minds, which pertains to subsequently attained wisdom.
Since the object is not a subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), both the fundamental (*mūla*) and subsequent attainments are termed non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
What are called the two wisdoms of the paths of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-mārga*) refer to the two wisdoms— fundamental and subsequent— within the paths of seeing and cultivation.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the realization of the truths through the knowledge at the limit of clear observation" (*abhisamayāntika-jñāna-satyābhisamaya*): the "initial realization" refers to the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is the realization of the non-conceptually-constructed truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).
The two characters "realization" (*abhisamaya*) below are the general designation for the six types of realization. "Limit" (*anta*) means the final limit;

this refers to the fact that the conceptually-constructed truths (*pratiṣṭhita-satya*) constitute the final limit of the non-conceptually-constructed truths. That is to say, it is the knowledge of the truths.

Regarding the statement, "The wisdom that subsequently conditions the various established [truths] is mundane and supramundane wisdom," the meaning is as follows: the wisdom of the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) is the true clear realization;

the wisdom that subsequently conditions the various established mundane and supramundane [truths] is the wisdom of the practitioner. This wisdom of the practitioner takes the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*) as its object.
Since this wisdom of the established truths is the subsequent wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) regarding non-established truth (*avyavasthāpita-satya*), it is so designated.
"Cloud" refers to the various mundane and supramundane cognitions that take established truths as their objects, which arise after the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Truths through wisdom.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that this "penetrates both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)," while this fifth realization (*abhisamaya*) is in reality exclusively uncontaminated, the mention of the contaminated is provisional;

for example, it is like the subsequent attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), which is uncontaminated, that follows the wisdom of true vision and takes the ten established truths (*vyavasthāpana-satya*) as its object.

The six minds arise after this, and the contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) is also able to take these sixteen minds as its objects because it establishes them as the truths; therefore, it is said to be "universal" regarding the contaminated.
This occurs within the true path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), where one can fully take the sixteen minds as objects and establish them as the truths.

However, if one were entirely in the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one would not be able to fully know the establishment of the sixteen minds, or would only know them as one mind or two minds.

Because the contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) used for equal contemplation is inferior, and because the initial emergence of the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) upon leaving the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is not yet called the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), being instead subsumed under the path of seeing;
although it is termed "cultivation" when the first moment of contaminated conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) arises, it is not yet called the path of cultivation.
It is only after passing through many moments of wisdom in cultivation that one enters the path of cultivation.

[Commentary]: From "having the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) as its intrinsic nature" up to "having the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) as its intrinsic nature," the ten knowledges refer to:

the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion, and the knowledge of non-arising.
According to the Mahāyāna teachings, it is said that an Arhat does not attain these ten knowledges; however, [the text] merely states...
The state in which the outflows (*āsrava*) of afflictions are exhausted is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*);

furthermore, the arising of knowledge that takes the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its object—the place where afflictions no longer arise—is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Thus, within the Buddha’s body, there are likewise ten knowledges.

Furthermore, among those of the Hīnayāna, Arhats of the non-retrogressive lineage (*aparihāṇadharman*) also possess all ten knowledges, because their afflictions will never arise again. As for those of the retrogressive lineage...
Those of the Arhat lineage possess only nine knowledges and do not possess the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), because they may still regress and give rise to afflictions.

However, while the Hīnayāna asserts that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*), the Mahāyāna asserts that it also extends to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Even if it is uncontaminated, knowledge that takes phenomena as its object is subsumed under conventional knowledge; alternatively, one may take the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) as its basis.
"Dharma is its intrinsic nature.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "as previously explained regarding the grasping...

up to the differences," the intended meaning is that the various treatises explain the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) as being either sixfold, tenfold, or eighteenfold, with varying increases and decreases; these should now be reconciled according to the two previous explanations.

Regarding the fact that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā*, and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* each present different accounts concerning increase and decrease, these do not contradict one another as they are based on distinct interpretations of the meaning.

[Commentary]: The statement "it truly subsumes a small portion of the fourth [knowledge], yet it also extends to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and so forth" means that it subsumes only a small portion of the fundamental knowledge (*mūlajñāna*) of the fourth [level], but does not subsume the subsequently attained knowledge (*prsthalabdhajñāna*);
furthermore, it subsumes only the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and does not subsume the path of cultivation.
"Called 'a small portion'.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "its characteristic is included within the Path of Vision (darśanamārga), from a small portion of the fourth [dhyāna] up to that which also includes cultivation," the intent is as follows:

this Path of Vision subsumes a small portion of the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) of the fourth [dhyāna], but does not subsume the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna); it subsumes only the Path of Vision.
The Path does not include the Path of Cultivation; it includes the entirety of the fifth [type of] subsequently attained wisdom, but does not include the entirety of conventional wisdom.
Furthermore, it includes both the path of vision in its aspects and its seeing, but does not include the path of true vision, the path of cultivation, and so forth.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that the second and third [categories] do not subsume one another because they reach their respective limits:

this explains the underlying principle for why they do not subsume the other four, and since the meaning of this ultimate sense is easy to understand, it is not discussed here. As for the second and third categories, because they define their essential nature (*svabhāva*) by way of simultaneous existence (*sahabhū*), they do not subsume one another;
however, within this context, it is permitted that they may be mutually borrowed and are thus subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The distinctions are as fully detailed in a separate chapter, so they are not described here at length.
[Commentary: "Because it transforms the prior basis and gives rise to another basis" means that "basis" refers to the body.

That is to say, one transforms and discards the body that is the basis for the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), and instead attains the body that is the basis for the nature of a stainless noble one (*ārya*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because this tree of prajñā continues its own succession":

if the four wisdoms of the Buddha’s body are called the flourishing tree of awakening, then the wisdom within the body of a bodhisattva is likewise called a tree. It is termed "succession" because, from the moment it is realized, one attains the stage of non-retrogression.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that the king is the flower and fruit of this continent: if one takes the "fruit" to be the fruit of Buddhahood, it refers to the mental states of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna-citta-varga*) of a Bodhisattva, as well as Great Nirvāṇa, the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), and the fruits of untainted dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-phala*).

All of these are unattainable for a Bodhisattva who has not yet reached completion. As for the "flowers and fruits," these refer to those who have entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and beyond.

Because the power of the untainted (anāsrava) dharma secondarily supports the previous tainted (sāsrava) provisions of the stage prior to the path of equipment, it causes all karma to bring about the ten kings and their respective positions; even the "flower-retribution" of a Bodhisattva is itself the fruit.
Once one reaches the first bhūmi and above, one no longer creates new karma, and thus relies solely upon past karma.
[Treatise] Regarding those who attain the various forms of equality, the *She dacheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha), Chapter Six, states that there are three kinds of attainment of equality:
first, attaining the equality of the mental nature of sentient beings; this is because one universally perceives that all sentient beings are equally devoid of self, as it is said:
"All dharmas are the Tathāgatagarbha. Second, attaining the equality of the mental nature of all Bodhisattvas.
First, because one attains the equality of the bodhisattva’s intention; second, because one attains the equality of the mind of all Buddhas, which is due to attaining the equality of that dharmakāya;
as stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, there are ten kinds of equality, as previously cited.
Furthermore, another interpretation states that "attaining the equality of all sentient beings" means that the bodhisattva contemplates that sentient beings lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Because there is no distinction between kin and stranger, one attains equality with all bodhisattvas;

this is because the bodhisattva views all other bodhisattvas without superiority or inferiority, honoring them with an impartial mind. Because every Buddha is identical, one attains equality with all Tathāgatas.
However, when this treatise states that a bodhisattva on the first stage (bhūmi) attains various forms of equality, it is spoken in reference to three types of equality.
Why is it that this is not yet explained as the ten kinds of equality? This is because these ten equalities are the ten equalities within the seventh consciousness.

Although a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*bhūmi*) attains the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), the afflictive grasping at a self (*kleśa-ātmagrāha*) has not yet been subdued through the path of cultivation;
it is only upon reaching the seventh stage that it is subdued. It is only at the eighth stage that the Bodhisattva fully attains the ten kinds of equality.
"Is it that one is born into the family of the Tathāgata and thoroughly masters the dharma-realm? [The answer is: "Being born into the family of the Tathāgata is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*);

thoroughly mastering the dharma-realm is the function of subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This is because realizing the ultimate while understanding the conventional is the function of subsequently attained wisdom."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that one is constantly born within the Land of Enjoyment for Others (*parasaṃbhogakṣetra*), as explained in the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*:
the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* explains the Bodhisattva precepts for Bodhisattvas of the Second Ground, stating, "I, now as Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal;
upon the thousand petals surrounding it, there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis. This refers to the emanations perceived during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
