or there may be cases where one practices both patience (kṣānti) and wisdom (prajñā)—in all such instances, there are four propositions. Furthermore, regarding those who practice both ethical discipline and meditative concentration as forming four propositions:

there is meditative concentration that is not a perfection, meaning when practicing concentration it is not associated with the seven excellences (saptavidha-prakarsa); and there are perfections that are not concentration.

That is to say, one who maintains the precepts transcends existence (*bhava*) and also attains concentration (*samādhi*); one who possesses concentration is associated with the seven supreme qualities (*saptānuttarya*), yet it should be understood that this is neither transcendence nor concentration.
[Commentary: Within this, there are three sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, regarding merit by way of its categories, there is one set of four propositions as follows:

It has already been stated previously that regarding the two [types of giving], if one does not practice them in sequence according to their categories, the remaining five perfections can each have four permutations as explained before.
Thirdly, regarding those not practiced in sequence, all likewise have four permutations as also explained before;

therefore, it is said here that there are three sets of four permutations. Furthermore, according to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, the four permutations of the fourfold giving are set forth in detail as follows:

This giving is not a perfection (*pāramitā*) refers to the giving of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and bodhisattvas of the first two incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
This giving is a perfection but not giving refers to the other five perfections. It is both a perfection and giving refers to the giving of bodhisattvas of the third incalculable eon.

It is neither a perfection nor giving refers to the five perfections practiced by those of the two vehicles (*yāna*), etc. The remaining perfections may be understood according to these four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the question of what contradiction exists between the Sūtras and the Śāstras: the Sūtras rely on the spontaneous cultivation that progresses without regression and increases in excellence, naming it "pāramitā" (perfection).

The Śāstras, however, establish the name "pāramitā" based on the presence of both general and specific characteristics—whether there is regression or no regression, and whether there is applied effort (*prayoga*) or no applied effort.
Since their intended meanings differ, there is no contradiction.
[Treatise] Regarding the statement "there are only ten here," as explained below, there are eleven obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) and twelve delusions (*moha*).

Why, then, are only ten obstacles mentioned here? Answer: Here, within the context of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), we clarify only ten obstacles in relation to what is counteracted by the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).

[Commentary: "The cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and so forth are all transcended as their respective antidotes" refers to the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) collectively counteracting the cognitive obstructions.

[Commentary: "If one relies on [the perfections] from stinginess (*mātsarya*) up to the obstruction of evil wisdom (*dauṣprajña*)," refers to the individual counteraction of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

There are only six obstructions; what is mentioned below as "obscuration" (*chādana*) refers precisely to these six obstructions that obscure. Herein, it concerns the individual counteraction of the afflictive obstructions.

This is explained solely by way of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and their respective antidotes: for instance, generosity (*dāna*) as the antidote to stinginess (*mātsarya*), up to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as the antidote to distraction (*vikṣepa*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) as the antidote to the obstacle of faulty wisdom (*duṣprajñā*).
If one were to further divide within the category of faulty wisdom to establish five obstacles and apply them to the preceding six to form ten obstacles, that would be incorrect.
Alternatively, if one were to separately extract five obstacles from within faulty wisdom and apply them to the preceding five, such as distraction and so forth, that too would be incorrect.

It is also not the case that the obstructions constitute ten obstructions; for among those specifically remedied by the antidotes to the afflictions (*kleśa*), there are only remedies for six obstructions and none for ten.
However, these present ten obstructions are all considered in relation to the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as ten obstructions, which shall now be explained.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "from the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* up to 'contradictory obstacles' (*viruddhavighna*)," this explains the reason for teaching the six [obstacles]. As the subsequent commentary states:
"Below, according to the text, it refers to stinginess (*mātsarya*) through to corrupt wisdom (*dauṣprajña*); these are the contradictory obstacles."

[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* concerning the causes for not setting out [on the path] and so forth, this explains why there are only six perfections, such as giving (*dāna*) and the rest.
According to the seventh fascicle of the *Saṃgraha*, they are established in order to counteract the obstacles that are their opposites;

specifically, because one wishes to counteract the causes for not setting out, giving and ethical discipline (*śīla*) are established. The causes for not setting out refer to attachment to wealth and status, as well as attachment to the household life.
In order to counteract the causes for retreating even after having set out, patience (*kṣānti*) is established as the cause for not retreating.

This refers to the various sufferings arising from the transgressions of sentient beings within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), as well as the weariness arising from long-term application toward wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa*);
[patience] serves as the cause for not retreating after having set out, thereby preventing the loss and destruction [of the path].
Regarding the causes for the destruction of established concentration and wisdom, these are said to be various forms of distraction and false, evil wisdom;
since these are established as the obstacles to be countered by their respective remedies, only six factors are established.

[Commentary]: Regarding what has been stated above concerning the reason why these ten [perfections] are discussed here in terms of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the three meanings for explaining the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) are as follows.
This particular section of the commentary does not fit within this discussion of the six perfections; rather, it should have been explained earlier when it was said:
"These consist of only ten, neither more nor less. This is what is stated in the commentary text.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the first four causes of non-distraction lead to perfect universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)," this text refers to the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) by means of attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Non-distraction is itself concentration. Greed, stinginess, violation of precepts, anger, and laziness are all capable of obstructing concentration;
for it is due to craving for wealth and status, up to and including laziness, that one is unwilling to cultivate concentration. Thus, stinginess and the other [afflictions] are obstacles.

The obstacle of distraction is so named because the cultivation of the four practices—generosity and the others—as antidotes to the four [faults] such as stinginess, is able to induce meditative concentration;
therefore, the four perfections of generosity and the rest are called the causes of non-distraction, which is to say, the causes of non-diffusion.
Fifth is the actual attainment of concentration, because concentration is perfected. Sixth is the cultivation of wisdom based on concentration, which is able to pervade all objects of focus.
Knowing that by relying on the practice of self-benefit one gradually matures all sentient beings through the cultivation of the six perfections,
this refers to the cultivation of the six perfections for the sake of benefiting others.

[Commentary] "Those already established in concentration are caused to attain liberation" means that from concentration arises wisdom, and wisdom is able to sever delusions and realize *nirvāṇa*, and so forth.
This is called "liberation. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "these latter three causes," the intended meaning is that the six *pāramitās* neither increase nor decrease. These three causes are clarified by means of these three [factors];
as stated in other treatises, they are so designated because they follow the previously mentioned ten [virtues], and thus receive the name "the latter three causes."

[Commentary]: Regarding the "path to higher rebirth" (*abhyudaya-mārga*), the intended meaning is as follows: "higher rebirth" refers to the favorable worldly fruits that are summoned; "path" refers to the cause.
Because fruits such as great wealth arise from causes such as generosity, it is called the "path to higher rebirth.
Furthermore, this retribution is the most excellent within the world: if a bodhisattva practices generosity, they will attain great prosperity and abundant riches.
By upholding the precepts, a Bodhisattva attains a body with upright and handsome features; by practicing patience, they attain a great retinue.

Regarding the phrase "the path of definitive victory" (*niyata-viśeṣa-mārga*): "definitive victory" (*niyata-viśeṣa*) refers to the fruit, specifically the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*) that excels the previous three fruits.

As for the essence of the latter three fruits, it is superior to those [previous fruits] and is thus called the "path of definitive victory," which refers to the cause. [The treatise continues with] diligence and so forth.
Third, being able to subdue afflictions, mature sentient beings, and mature the Buddha-dharma—these are the fruits of diligence and so forth, as explained in detail in the commentary.
These three, in comparison to what preceded them, constitute the supramundane path.
[Commentary]: "To benefit others by gathering material resources for them" means that by giving material wealth to others and thereby gathering them in, one benefits them;
thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says, "Gather the poor through the gift of alms.
Alternatively, it may mean that the Bodhisattva gathers material resources for himself and then uses them to benefit others—that is, to bestow them upon those who come before him.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "encompassing superior rebirth," the intent is as follows: because a Bodhisattva does not abide in *nirvāṇa* but, within the midst of *saṃsāra*, draws forth generosity, ethical discipline, and patience to accomplish worldly wealth, physical form, and retinue, it is said that they "attract superior rebirth.

This is precisely the practice of benefiting others (*parārtha*), and because it consists of the last three of the [six] perfections, it is associated with wisdom, diligence, and meditative concentration. Question: While the sixth perfection may be called wisdom, how can diligence and meditative concentration be considered such?

The wisdom [of the result] is spoken of in conjunction with [the cause] because concentration is essential for wisdom and wisdom is essential for concentration; thus they are designated by their mutual association.
This is also like the three types of *prajñā*, which are established as names through their mutual association. As stated below, the first four are called the "training in morality" (*śīla-śikṣā*);
this should also be understood accordingly. [In this case,] giving is the provision for morality, morality is the essence of morality, patience is the retinue of morality, and diligence is...
The protection of ethical discipline (*śīla*) consists of guarding it through diligent effort; after attaining firmness, the latter two [perfections] each involve individual training.
This explains the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) by way of the three trainings (*triśikṣā*).

[Commentary]: Regarding "the skillful means of the various means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*)," the "various means of integration" refers precisely to the four methods of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*).

The intended meaning is that because the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) assist the three [perfections] beginning with generosity, they cause generosity and the others to become *pāramitās*;
therefore, these means are embraced and established within the category of wholesome qualities. Without skillful means, generosity and the other perfections do not become *pāramitās*.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "it is called 'auxiliary' because it encompasses [the practices] from generosity up to [wisdom] within the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

among the four means of attraction, generosity is precisely the generosity practiced here; because it is characterized by skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), this generosity and the others are able to benefit sentient beings.
Thus, the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of generosity accords with skillful means, and it is through skillful means that—
Because they are able to benefit those [practices] such as giving, it is said that skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) assists them. Question:

Since skillful means is the post-attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) which is untainted (*anāsrava*), how can it assist the preceding scattered practices of giving, ethical discipline, and patience?

Answer: Within the bodhisattva’s untainted post-attainment wisdom, one cultivates the six perfections; since they are supported by untainted skillful means, what fault could there be? It is indeed possible.

In the mind of one with outflows and distractions, following acts such as giving, the subsequent attainment of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and the remote perfuming (*dūravāsana*) of skillful means also increase;
other auxiliary factors should be understood accordingly.
[Commentary: "In the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharme*) refers to practicing in the present. "Weak aspiration" (*hīnāśaya*) refers to that which is inferior.
Regarding "because it is an inferior resolve (*adhimukti*) belonging to the lower realms": "realms" (*dhātu*) refers to natures (*prakṛti*), which are to say seeds (*bīja*).
Thus, within the body of a bodhisattva, there are inferior seeds; therefore, it is said that the internal mind lacks capability.

This is also consistent with what is called the "power of knowledge regarding the higher and lower realms" (*ūrdhvādhodhātu-jñānabala*) among the ten powers. According to such passages, this refers to the power of wisdom, the power of aspiration, the power of effort, and the application of preparatory practice (*prayoga-prayoga*).
A bodhisattva who possesses the accumulations (*sambhāra*) can also perform this within their tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*).
[Commentary: The meaning of the passage in that sutra stating, "If bodhisattvas reach what is called the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*)," is as follows:

among the powers that assist meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), hearing the true Dharma constitutes the power of discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna-bala*), while correct mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) constitutes cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Regarding "one who attains superior resolve (*adhimokṣa*) of the higher realms by means of power": because of this power, one transforms previously inferior seeds and obtains seeds of a superior kind;

this is what is meant by "power. Furthermore, by means of the power of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī* and *cintāmayī prajñā*) within the desire realm, one resolves upon and attains the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of the form realm;

thus, that wisdom of hearing and reflection is called "power," and the absorption of the higher realm is called "meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*). Therefore, it is said that "power assists meditative concentration."

[Commentary]: The meaning of the phrase "if bodhisattvas have already been able to hear and cultivate the object-condition well, thereby reaching the elicitation of supramundane wisdom" is as follows:
it explains the basis by which knowledge assists prajñā. Because one first specifically determines the object-condition, knowledge skillfully elicits meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
subsequently, one is able to elicit dhyāna, and dhyāna can elicit supramundane wisdom. This is based on this successive progression.
Therefore, it is said: "The commentary on the *Prajñāpāramitā* is brief; thus, this [text] is taken as the authority. [Commentary:

Regarding the verse on the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) and the ten obstacles, it further states according to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*: "The obstacles to the fruits of the ten perfections must be understood as in the verse.
The commentary cites the long prose explanation (*vṛtti*), which says: "This explains the obstacles to the fruits obtained through the ten kinds of *pāramitā*."
To clarify the nature of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), it is taught that the ten obstacles to the results are, in fact, the obstacles to the ten perfections themselves.
That is to say, regarding generosity (*dāna*), the obstacle to wealth and status is mentioned;

this refers to the obstacle of stinginess (*mātsarya*) toward generosity, as stinginess constantly obstructs wealth and status through greed for possessions. Thus, these ten obstacles are all established by name according to that which they obstruct.

That is to say, regarding ethical discipline (*śīla*), it is taught that there is an obstacle to the happy realms (*sugati*); because of the violation of ethical discipline, an obstacle arises that prevents birth in the happy realms.

Regarding patience (*kṣānti*), it is taught that there is an obstacle to not abandoning sentient beings; because [patience] increases, one abandons sentient beings, and thus the failure to abandon [sentient beings] acts as an obstacle to patience.

Regarding diligence (*vīrya*), it is taught that there is an obstacle to the reduction of faults and the increase of virtues; this obstacle is precisely laziness (*kausīdya*), for by means of diligence...
Because laziness causes faults to increase and virtues to decrease, while it simultaneously causes virtues to decrease and faults to increase, laziness is an obstacle;

that is to say, regarding meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is an obstacle to the entry of those to be converted into the Dharma. Since it obstructs meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is specifically distraction (*vikṣepa*).

Regarding the wholesome deeds to be performed, one cannot enter into meditative absorption because of this obstacle; that is to say, regarding wisdom (*prajñā*), it is an obstacle to liberation (*vimokṣa*). This obstacle is...
The fruit of liberation through unwholesome wisdom refers to the obstacle to the inexhaustibility of wholesome qualities such as generosity when these are taught as skillful means;
for by dedicating these means toward unsurpassed enlightenment, one causes the wholesome qualities of generosity and so forth to become inexhaustible.

Regarding the vow, it refers to the obstacle to the uninterrupted succession of wholesome qualities throughout all births; for by being sustained by the power of the great vow, one is able to give rise to dharmas that accord with the wholesome.

This refers to what is called the "obstacle to the certainty of accomplishing what is to be done regarding the powers. Because one can subdue those obstacles through the power of discernment (*cintā-bala*) and the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*), rather than being subdued by them;
and because it is called the "obstacle to the accomplishment of the enjoyment of the Dharma for oneself and others regarding wisdom," wherein one does not realize the meaning as it was heard.
These aforementioned and subsequent obstacles are all *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compounds, meaning "the obstacle to wealth and honor" (*aiśvarya-āvaraṇa*).
...up to the obstacles to the accomplishment of the enjoyment of the Dharma for oneself and others.
[Commentary] Regarding the first interpretation: it means that because each preceding stage induces the subsequent one until they become easy to attain, they are not explicitly mentioned.
This clarifies that there are three general interpretations of the sequence of the ten perfections; this is the first, the sequence of induction, which concerns the beginner practitioner.

Furthermore, according to the *Pratipakṣa* (Counteractives), it is said: through the habitual practice of giving, one abandons both internal and external things, disregarding even body and life, and casts away great treasuries;
by upholding the prohibitive precepts (*śīla*), when reviled or insulted by others, one never retaliates, thereby becoming able to endure;
because of this ability to endure sufferings such as cold and heat, one does not cease from application and thus arouses diligent effort (*vīrya*).

Through skillful means, one realizes the ultimate fruit and fulfills meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); having fulfilled meditative concentration, one attains that great intention which is the ultimate emergence of the Buddha into the world.
This explains the sequence by way of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), wherein the latter four perfections are subsumed within the sixth perfection.
[Commentary: Regarding the second explanation, "attaining [the stages] without depending on wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth," this refers to the second sequence of maintaining purity.
This is explained in terms of those who have perfected their cultivation. Furthermore, according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa-śāstra):

"Moreover, because each preceding perfection (*pāramitā*) is sustained by each subsequent one, through possessing ethical discipline (*śīla*), giving (*dāna*) becomes purified; by practicing giving, one benefits sentient beings."
Its nature consists in possessing ethical discipline (*śīla*) so as not to cause harm or injury;
through the power of patience, its precepts become pure, for by being able to endure the non-beneficial actions of others, one never violates the points of training.

Through diligence, patience becomes pure, for by the power of valor, one does not find it difficult to remain long within saṃsāra and is able to endure the opposition and hostility of sentient beings.
Diligence is purified by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because one can diligently practice all wholesome dharmas without rest through the accompaniment of joy and bliss.

Meditative concentration is purified by means of possessing wisdom (*prajñā*), because if one repeatedly examines all phenomena through immeasurable gateways, one can realize internal tranquility and increase the yoga of samādhi.
Thus it is stated at the beginning of the *Samāhitābhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*.
It is not possible to cite too many examples; there is no meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that does not depend upon wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, because one attains the meditative concentrations of the higher realms by means of being led by the non-conceptual wisdom of application (*prayoga-nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it is said that the sixth [perfection], the wisdom of application, can lead to the fifth, the meditative concentration;

this is called "the latter sustaining the former. One might ask: while it is appropriate to say that the six perfections (*pāramitā*) involve the former leading the latter and the latter sustaining the former...

Question: Since the latter four perfections are exclusively subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), why is it said that they "induce the preceding" and "sustain the subsequent," or "the subsequent sustains the preceding"?

Answer: These latter four perfections are subsumed within the sixth perfection (the perfection of wisdom). Therefore, their induction and sustenance are explained in accordance with the sixth perfection.

Alternatively, the essence of these latter four perfections is all wisdom; they are described as four according to their respective functions, and the sequence of their mutual induction and sustenance is likewise established accordingly.
Furthermore, what is the discrepancy? [Commentary]:
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the practice of giving (*dāna*) is the coarsest; because it is the last to be established, it is said that "the practice of giving is the coarsest.

This is because it is a human capacity: one merely takes material wealth and gives it to others, which is called giving. Keeping the precepts (*śīla*) is the subtlest, as it involves guarding the body and speech.

Regarding the three mental karmas, it is easy not to violate the precepts of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) and easy to be patient; however, to be patient with those who are base and lowly is extremely difficult.
Merely practicing patience is easy, but diligence (*vīrya*) is difficult—specifically, to practice with diligent effort for a long duration, day and night without ceasing, is extremely difficult.
Yet, even such diligence can be made easy; whereas meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is extremely difficult, as it is not easy for the mind to remain focused on a single object.
It is difficult because one must focus the mind on a single object; while meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is also easy, wisdom (*prajñā*) is difficult to learn.
A wise person knows nothing that is not known and understands all myriad things—this is truly difficult. For this reason, the sequence of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) is as follows:
alternatively, regarding the latter four perfections, they are described according to their functions, with the preceding being coarse and the succeeding being subtle, following this principle.
[Commentary] Regarding the three interpretations of the forty-nine [factors]: first, by way of antidote (*pratipakṣa*); second, by way of origination (*samutthāna*);

and third, by way of the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*). That which is stated here—"namely, the antidote to hindrances, origination, and thirdly, the ripened fruit"—refers to these. As for "antidote," it refers to:
[the antidote to] stinginess, [the antidote to] malice toward sentient beings, resentment and affliction toward sentient beings, laziness, distraction, dullness, and delusion.
In this way, the six factors such as ignorance can obstruct enlightenment, while the six factors such as generosity serve as their remedies;
accordingly, the six perfections are established. Regarding their origination: origination here refers to the coarse and the subtle, arising first from the coarse and subsequently from the subtle.
Thus, the latter two interpretations are consistent with this treatise, whereas the third [interpretation], regarding the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), is absent.
The sequence is clarified by explaining the resultant maturation (*vipāka*) induced by the six perfections.

Furthermore, it is said that "maturation" refers to the ripening of the six perfections themselves, which is termed maturation; it does not refer to the neutral (*avyākṛta*) nature of karmic maturation.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "factors incompatible with the perfection of non-attachment," what is meant by "non-attachment"?
If one is not attached to wealth or the Dharma while bestowing material gifts upon others, this is called non-attachment. If one is attached to wealth or the Dharma, one is unable to practice giving;
therefore, it acts as a factor incompatible with the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*). The same applies to the [remaining] five perfections. If, regarding these five...
One who is attached to things that are contrary to the perfections cannot practice the five perfections;
such contrary things refer to violations of the precepts, up to and including ignorance and darkness.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "second, being without attachment so that the mind is free from bondage," the meaning is as follows:

A Bodhisattva merely practices giving, yet does not mentally hope for the karmic fruits and rewards produced by the six perfections; furthermore, when practicing giving, they do not expect gratitude or recompense from others.
Because the mind is free from such attachments in these matters, it is called "being without attachment" (*anapekṣa*).
[Commentary]: Regarding "threefold faultlessness" up to "leaving behind non-expedient practices," this refers to the intention of the bodhisattva's practice:
when practicing the six perfections, not allowing the mind to be defiled by afflictions is called "faultlessness.
Furthermore, realizing that both subject and object should be known as they truly are (*yathāvad*), and remaining free from attachment therein, is called "leaving behind non-expedient practices."

[Commentary]: Regarding the four types of non-conceptualization up to the point of "clinging to specific characteristics": the Bodhisattva does not grasp these six perfections as truly existent according to their verbal expressions;
rather, they understand all phenomena to be like illusory things and the like.

[Commentary]: The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that "reaching the other shore" refers to the intention that the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of a bodhisattva, such as giving (*dāna*), are most preeminent because they surpass the giving of worldly beings and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), thereby reaching the other shore.
Those of no-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) do not reach the other shore; thus, this is not the ultimate sense, for the giving of the two vehicles and so forth is not preeminent.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "because it is most supreme," the intended meaning is that it is vast; not only does one not seek worldly pleasures, but it is also the most supreme because it leads to the attainment of the other shore.
Regarding the "four inexhaustibles," this refers to the inexhaustibility of roots of goodness dedicated toward Bodhi.

Regarding the "five uninterrupted [gates]," the meaning is that of being without interval: when a Bodhisattva practices giving, they do not act for their own sake, but extend it universally to all others, causing them to attain it as well.
Because [the perfections of] giving and so forth are swiftly perfected, it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).

[Commentary: Regarding the seven great masteries attained through the realization of the *Gaganagañja* (Space-Treasury) Samādhi, as the sutra says, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* is here termed "Space-Treasury.
Just as space can contain all phenomena, this samādhi is likewise.
This samādhi, which can encompass and store all merits, is attained only by bodhisattvas of great power and by Tathāgatas.
Once a bodhisattva of the first stage attains this, they cause the six perfections, such as generosity, to be swiftly fulfilled.
Thus, the four samādhis explained below are also this very samādhi.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "that which is embraced by the non-conceptual wisdom that embraces," the intended meaning is that this embrace is supreme because it is embraced by signless, non-conceptual wisdom;
thus, it constitutes the most excellent skillful means (*upāya*) of this treatise.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the nine initiations, etc.," the intended meaning is that this most excellent [perfection] is initiated during the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) within the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
[Commentary: This refers to the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment; it is explained as "the perfection of the Tathāgata" because it clarifies the distinction between the Buddha and the Bodhisattva.

Therefore, each is paired with one [of the four categories]. Furthermore, there should be four permutations: there is that which is perfect but not full, referring to the ultimate fruit of the two vehicles;
there is that which is full but not perfect, referring to the giving and so forth of Bodhisattvas in the tenth stage;
there is that which is both perfect and full, referring to the Tathāgata; and there is that which is neither perfect nor full, referring to the giving and so forth practiced by ordinary beings.

[Commentary]: Regarding "that which is reached by the most excellent" and "that which is performed by the most excellent," according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, these refer to all that is done and all that is reached by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;

thus, "that which is done" (*kṛta*) is equivalent to "that which is performed" (*kārya*), and "that which is reached" (*prāpta*) is equivalent to "that which is attained" (*gata*). Another interpretation states:

"that which is performed by the most excellent" refers to what is performed by the Buddha, while "that which is reached by the most excellent" refers to what is reached by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

In detail: it may be that both the Buddha and the Bodhisattva act and arrive together; or, it may be that what the Buddha has arrived at is what the Bodhisattva acts upon—there is no logical fault in this.
[Commentary]: Regarding the meaning of *pāra* as "that which is reached" or "that which is accomplished," and its sense of reaching the capacity to act: *pāra* here is translated as...
"Beyond, beyond" refers both to that which is accomplished and to the place reached.
Regarding the meaning of "Pāramitā" as that which can reach and that which can accomplish, the intent is that *mitā* (the suffix) signifies the capacity to reach and to accomplish.
This section of the commentary is the Master of the Commentary’s own explanation and is not the original treatise.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "reaching the other shore of what is known until abiding in Buddha-nature": this refers to the realization of principle (li), which is termed the "other shore of what is known.
This "principle of the Buddha" is precisely the essence of the other shore; because one is able to abide therein, it is called "reaching.
Furthermore, it is said that "the other shore" (pāra) subsumes the entire Mahāyāna—its supramundane teaching, principle, practice, and fruit.
The four kinds of Buddha-nature are subsumed under the principle (*li*); alternatively, there is no contradiction in extending this to the fruit (*phala*). [Commentary:

Furthermore, regarding the statement that *pāra* means "the other shore of what is known," this explains it in terms of the object (*viṣaya*); that is, knowing all phenomena is called "the other shore.
This passage is the Master of the Commentary’s (*Sū-zhǔ*) explanation of the *Abhidharma* text; it is not the *Abhidharma* itself.

Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that there are three meanings: first, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) constitute this shore, while the six meanings [of the perfections] constitute the other shore;

as that treatise says, "crossing the ocean of afflictions such as stinginess and greed, one reaches the other shore. Second, birth and death (*saṃsāra*) constitute this shore, while nirvāṇa constitutes the other shore;
as that treatise says, "this shore is the world (*loka*), and the other shore is nirvāṇa. Third...
To differentiate between existence and non-existence is called "this shore," while to penetrate the nature of existence and non-existence is called "the other shore. Thus, the Treatise states:
"Objects such as existence and non-existence are called 'this shore,' while the wisdom that knows existence and non-existence is called 'the other shore.'"
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "there should be six explanations," the six characters [of "six"] must be an error; they should be combined into five characters:

1) *yoga* and the five conditions, 2) the twelve supreme factors of the *Abhidharma*, 3) that which is reached by the supreme, etc. The commentary states: "The meaning of 'pāra' is 'that which is reached,' etc.

This is the commentator’s own explanation of the passage concerning "that which is reached" (*prāpta*) found in that treatise; it is not the actual text of the treatise itself. 4) Reaching the destination.
Because they know the "other shore" (*pāra*) and so forth, and because they deliver themselves and others through these five [perfections], there are five interpretations;

alternatively, *pāramitā* may mean "the object of knowledge" (*jñeya*) and so forth, which constitutes one interpretation. Thus, because there are six interpretations in total, the six characters are not erroneous.
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the individual names, up to the point where "the Dharma is named wisdom," according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun), fascicle 7, it says:

"Furthermore, because it can extinguish immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*) and evil destinies (*durgati*), and can acquire good destinies and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called 'precept' (*śīla*).

Alternatively, because it can completely extinguish anger and enmity, and can skillfully abide in the security of oneself and others, it is called 'patience' (*kṣānti*). Furthermore, it can distance [one from]..."
It is called diligence (*vīrya*) because it abandons all laziness and unwholesome states, and gives rise to immeasurable wholesome dharmas so that they may increase;
furthermore, it is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) because it can eliminate all mental distraction and induce the mind to abide in tranquility.
Regarding the two types—wisdom (*prajñā*) and generosity (*dāna*)—they are cited in the commentary as follows: moreover, when a bodhisattva practices generosity...
Furthermore, there are three matters: first, when a bodhisattva practices giving, they are able to destroy stinginess in their present body;
second, practicing giving enables them to eliminate future poverty; third, when practicing giving, they are able to attain vast wealth and status.
When a bodhisattva maintains ethical discipline (*śīla*), there are likewise three matters: first, it can eliminate the fault of violating precepts; second, it can eliminate future [suffering].
Because it can obtain a body in a happy realm in the future and because it can induce meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the bodhisattva’s practice of patience also has three aspects:
first, it can eliminate true anger and the like; second, it eliminates having few attendants in the future;
and third, it induces having a great retinue in the future. The bodhisattva’s practice of diligence also has three aspects.
First, because it can eliminate indolence; second, because it can eliminate future weakness; and third, because it can attain great power.

The bodhisattva’s practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) has three aspects: first, because it can eliminate distraction; second, because it can experience happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*);
and third, because it can attain great merit. Therefore, it is said that meditative concentration is a forest of virtues for the bodhisattva’s practice.
The time of *prajñā* also has three aspects: first, it can eliminate all current evil wisdoms and views;
second, it can eliminate future ignorance; and third, it can attain future true wisdom that is able to know the five fields of knowledge (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

[Commentary]: Regarding "by means of great giving and so forth," according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, "great giving" refers to the relinquishing of all internal and external things and giving for a long duration.
"Free from faults" means being far removed from faults such as seeking in an unequal or improper manner.

"Free from stains" means having permanently severed all stinginess, which is the antithesis [of giving]. The commentary explains that being free from unrighteous greed is what is meant by "free from faults."

The commentary also explains that seeking wealth and possessions is called "unrighteous greed" (*adharma-lobha*); because one is free from this greed at the time of practicing giving, it is termed "free from faults.
Each of the remaining five perfections likewise possesses three meanings, the intent of which is easy to understand.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Treatise on the Abhidharma) further states: "Because they can cause the sense faculties to be eternally tranquil, because they can lead toward pure and auspicious rebirths, and because they can..."

It is called "precept" (*śīla*) because it serves as the basis for purification; because, in its successive order, it guards the doors of the sense faculties, acts as the cause for proceeding to happy realms, and serves as the basis for *nirvāṇa*; and because, by being free from all anger, it is like hot ashes that do not abandon the intent to harm, thereby manifesting constant peace and security for those who cause injury—it is thus called "patience" (*kṣānti*). "Rising with a mind of retribution and not abandoning it" means not discarding this mind; being able to harbor a mind of resentment is called "one who causes harm.
This is stated to manifest fearlessness, for it is called "manifesting one who causes harm" because of constant peace and security.

Because it is associated with the function of increasing harm, it is called "diligence" (*vīrya*). Being associated with the function of harming refers to the first two right abandonments (*samyak-prahāṇa*), as they are capable of...

Regarding the correspondence with the function of growth through the impairment of unwholesome dharmas: this refers to the latter two right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), because they are able to generate all wholesome dharmas.
They are called "meditative concentration" (*dhyāna*) because they can sustain, pacify, still, and discipline [the mind], and furthermore, because they can induce [realization].
"Sustaining" means binding the mind to the object; "pacifying" means calming all distractions; "stilling" means...
"Causing the mind to be tranquil" means it can tame [the mind]; "capable of subduing" means it can suppress the various *paryavasthānas* (obsessions);
"capable of inducing" means it can induce sovereign functioning. Regarding the two passages on giving and wisdom, they have already been cited in the commentary.

In the section on giving, it says "capable of relinquishing giving," etc.; "relinquishing" (*tyāga*) has the meaning of casting off and severing. It is because of giving that one is able to sever [attachment] for the sake of the donor.
Furthermore, the suffering of poverty is removed through giving, which alleviates the heat of affliction caused by the deprivation and oppression experienced in this present life.

Regarding the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the subsequent commentary explains that "wisdom arising from others" refers to the wisdom produced from the vocal sounds of others, as well as the wisdom associated with correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
"Wisdom realized within" refers to the specific seeds of supramundane fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*).

"Wisdom" refers to the wisdom obtained subsequent to supramundane [attainment]. "Wisdom that has attained tranquility" refers to the wisdom within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) that remedies the afflictions;

because it subdues the afflictions so that they do not arise, it is called the excellence of tranquility. "Wisdom of superior capacity" refers to the wisdom capable of inducing superior functional powers.

[Commentary: Regarding "relying on abiding and maintaining" (*niśraya-sthiti-bhāvanā*): "relying" (*niśraya*) has the sense of a staff; that is, one practices the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) by relying on these five kinds of dharmas as a staff.
The term "relying" (*niśraya*) is explained solely in this way. "Sustaining" (*pratiṣṭhā*) has the sense of non-dispersal;

for it is by means of these four [other] kinds that the ten perfections can be maintained so as not to be scattered or lost. Furthermore, these five correct practices have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential substance. Moreover—
It also takes as its essence the mind and mental factors that arise simultaneously with wisdom.
[Commentary] First, regarding "cultivating contemplation based on the cause," this refers exclusively to the seeds;

because one possesses the causal power of the Bodhisattva lineage (*gotra*), one is able to cultivate the correct practice of the *pāramitās*. Since those of the two vehicles lack the Bodhisattva lineage, they are unable to do so.
[He] cultivates the correct practice of the Bodhisattva pāramitās.
[Commentary: Regarding the second, cultivation based on the fruit, this refers to the resultant *vipāka* (ripened fruit) that has been attained.

The meaning is that because the Bodhisattva’s previous body practiced giving, he has now obtained a human body and is likewise able to practice giving; thus it is said that he relies on the power of his own superior physical strength.

Regarding the three bases for the correct practice of the *pāramitās*, first is cultivation based on aspiration: this takes aspiration as the foundation so that the cultivated *pāramitās* may be swiftly fulfilled;
because it is supported by the generation of aspiration, they are quickly brought to fulfillment.

This has as its essence the desire and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that accompany wisdom (*prajñā*). Fourth is cultivation based on discernment (*viveka*): this refers exclusively to taking wisdom as the two supports for action.

When one cultivates these four types of mental attention (*manasikāra*), they are mental attentions that occur simultaneously with wisdom; they are designated by the name "mental attention" as a conventional designation, though in reality they are not devoid of other factors.

[Commentary] First, regarding cultivation based on resolute conviction (*adhimukti*): if a bodhisattva perceives the teachings that express the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), it immediately gives rise to...

The cultivation of the correct practice of the *pāramitās* through the mind of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that accords with realized wisdom has the nature of resolute conviction simultaneous with insight. [Commentary:
Second, cultivation based on relishing refers to giving rise to deep relish for the many perceived qualities of what one has already attained.

The meaning of this is that when a bodhisattva now gives a small amount of wealth and perceives that they will attain the status of one who possesses great wealth, they see it as a great gain for themselves;
thus, they give rise to a profound relish for the correct practice of the *pāramitās*.
While "relish" (*sneha*) in common worldly usage refers merely to affection or attachment, here it refers to a profound mental relish arising from a defiled mind.

The "cultivation through attachment" (*āsvādana-bhāvanā*) refers to the process where, following the current of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one gives small amounts of wealth in a previous life as a bodhisattva and, having attained a position of great wealth and status in this life, develops a deep sense of attachment because one has already obtained many visible merits;
thus, one practices giving and so forth out of such attachment, which is called cultivation through attachment.
[Commentary: Regarding the third point, "cultivation based on sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*)," the *Abhidharma* states:

"It refers to generating deep sympathetic joy toward the acts of giving and so forth performed by all sentient beings in all worlds; this is a feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) conjoined with wisdom (*prajñā*)."

[Commentary]: Regarding the fourth point, "relying on the cultivation of joy and bliss," the Abhidharma states: it refers to generating a profound aspiration and delight toward the superior categories of the *pāramitās* for both oneself and others;
its essence consists of the union of desire, resolute belief (*adhimukti*), and wisdom.
[Commentary] Third, regarding the cultivation based on the aspirational intention (*āśaya*), there are six types; their essence consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) conjoined with desire (*chanda*).

[Commentary] First, the insatiable aspirational intention: according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, it means that all Bodhisattvas, with seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, or even with bodies and lives as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, for a single moment—or for as long as the sands of the Ganges—[offer these to the Buddhas].

When a bodhisattva practices giving to a single sentient being—or even to all beings—so that they may all swiftly accomplish the practice for enlightenment, the bodhisattva’s intention remains unsatiated throughout such differentiated acts of giving; this is called the "intention of non-satiety.
Regarding the two types of "vastness," the Abhidharma states: furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice giving, it proceeds in continuous succession without a single moment's interruption.

That there is regression and abandonment, up to the ultimate sitting upon the seat of enlightenment—this is called the bodhisattva’s third joy regarding the vast mental disposition (*āśaya*) toward the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice generosity, the great joy they produce toward all sentient beings who are included within that generosity is called the mental disposition of joy (*prāmodyāśaya*). (From the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*).

Regarding "gratitude" (*upakāra*): when Bodhisattvas practice generosity, they regard all sentient beings encompassed by that gift as having great kindness toward their own persons, rather than seeing themselves as having any kindness toward those beings;
this is because [those beings] assist them in attaining unsurpassed enlightenment. Furthermore, the solicitor has kindness toward the Bodhisattva; this is what is called a Bodhisattva.
Regarding the five types of untainted resolute intentions toward the grace of the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), the Abhidharma states:

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas practice generosity, although they produce vast merit through great acts of giving toward immeasurable sentient beings, they do not hope for gratitude or for future karmic rewards;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s untainted resolute intention. Sixth is the resolute intention of excellence.

Furthermore, regarding the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, it states that when Bodhisattvas practice generosity, they bestow upon sentient beings the maturation (*vipāka*) obtained from their vast accumulation of giving, rather than for their own sake;
moreover, they dedicate this merit toward enlightenment together with all sentient beings—this is called the Bodhisattva’s excellent intention (*āśaya*).
The other five perfections should be understood accordingly. Regarding this, there is an explanation in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Fearing prolixity, I shall not cite further sources.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the cultivation based on the four reliances up to the three kinds" and so forth, this refers to taking the three wheels as the object of wisdom-observation.
The meaning is that when a Bodhisattva practices giving, it is because it is embraced by non-conceptual wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*).
These three matters are called "purity.
[Commentary: Regarding the fifth, mastery over the support (*āśraya-vaśitā-bhāvanā*), it refers to seeking the support as the object of meditation.

Thus, the practitioner attains mastery over the one body, which consists of the *svābhāvika-kāya* (Essential Body) and the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (Enjoyment Body), because they were cultivated through the practice of the six perfections during the causal stage.
Those who attain the two bodies of the self-nature and enjoyment, or who, having attained these bodies, are also able to practice the six perfections—
the body of sovereign transformation— do so because they cultivated the six perfections in the past and thus all attain the body of others' enjoyment and the body of transformation;

or because, having already attained the body of others' enjoyment and the body of transformation, they are also able to practice the six perfections, and thus [manifest] throughout the lands of the ten directions.

Transformations that accord with the Dharma-practice (*dharmacaryā*) are like those of Śākyamuni Buddha, who was born into a royal palace and transformed immeasurable members of the royal lineage, causing them to attain the fruits of the Path;

or like Maitreya Tathāgata, who was born into a Brahmin family and transformed immeasurable Brahmins and kinsmen, causing them all to attain the fruits of the Path—these are called transformations that accord with the Dharma-practice.
However, because the Bodhisattva seeks these three bodies by means of praising conditions, he relies upon them accordingly.
Because these three bodies practice the six perfections, Wu-xing (Asvabhāva) says: "To practice for their sake is itself called 'practice'.

[Commentary: However, regarding the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* that the five types of cultivation are identical in meaning and intent, if one examines that treatise, it says: "One should know the cultivation..."

Briefly stated, there are five kinds of cultivation: first, the cultivation of manifest application; second, the cultivation of resolute belief; third, the cultivation of mental attention; fourth, the cultivation of skillful means;

and fifth, the cultivation of the accomplishment of tasks. The cultivation of the accomplishment of tasks corresponds to the "cultivation of mastery in reliance" mentioned as the fifth in this treatise.
That treatise states: "That is to say, for all Tathāgatas, the Buddha-activities are spontaneous and without [effort]."

[The text] rests upon the perfection of the *pāramitās* and further cultivates the six *yogas* (six means) to subsume the five [categories] of this treatise; the sequence of these five cultivations corresponds to the five [categories] of that text.
[Commentary]: "That is to say, from the ten *pāramitās* up to their mutual conformity" refers to the eighth section, the gate of mutual inclusion (*saṃgraha*). Within this, there is...
1. Mutual conformity and mutual inclusion of the four [categories] as one; 2. Mutual inclusion through induction; 3. Mutual inclusion through maintaining purity; 4. Fourfold analysis.

Regarding the first, according to what is stated in this treatise, it differs from the *Abhidharma*. The *Abhidharma* states that "one may include all phenomena within True Suchness (*tathatā*)," which is likewise [the case here].
This is the gate of subsuming characteristics into their nature, or the inclusion of the one by means of wisdom as the gate.
"All phenomena" refers to the five kinds of *prajñā*, which encompass all phenomena; this is equivalent to the inclusion of the remaining [factors] through wisdom (*jñāna*).

This is also consistent with the method in the treatises of including the object through consciousness (*vijñāna*), as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other works, such as the inclusion of true thusness (*tathatā*) within wisdom.

[Commentary: However, the intention behind using only the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) here to demonstrate their mutual inclusion is to explain the mutual inclusion of the six perfections as presented in the treatises.

Therefore, when various treatises state that "sometimes the term 'generosity' alone is used to express [all the others]," such that one includes the rest, this refers to the inclusion of the remaining ten perfections under the designation of the ten perfections found within those treatises;
it does not mean that only names, phrases, and so forth constitute the expressive sound (*vyañjana*).
When the expressive words or merely the uttered sounds are mentioned by the speaker, they encompass the conventional designations by subsuming the provisional within the real;
thus, by citing "sound," one includes names, phrases, and so forth. According to various treatises, when the term "generosity" (*dāna*) is cited, it also encompasses the remaining nine perfections;

when the term "ethical discipline" (*śīla*) is cited, it likewise encompasses the remaining nine perfections; and this continues until, when the tenth term, "wisdom" (*jñāna*), is cited, it also encompasses them all.
Regarding the first nine perfections, according to the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, they are also subsumed under the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

This is because they are mutually inclusive within the framework of the six perfections. As Asvabhāva states: "Within the nature of generosity (*dāna*), the six pāramitās are already present," just as it is said that the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) subsumes all six.
Furthermore, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*: "The World-Honored One, regarding all these six..."
Regarding the statement that some *pāramitās* are spoken of by means of the term "giving" (*dāna*) and so forth, the commentary explains:

In certain passages of the sūtras, the single term "giving" subsumes all ten perfections; the same applies to the terms for ethical discipline (*śīla*) and the others. As Asvabhāva’s commentary states:
This means that within each individual application of practice (*prayoga*), there is the assistance of all [the other perfections] one another; that is to say, when practicing giving...
At that time, through restraint, forbearance, endurance, and diligent application of the mind, one is able to skillfully understand the interconnectedness of karma and its results;

thus, within this generosity, there is the inclusion of other [perfections]. When practicing ethical discipline (*śīla*), one remains far removed from stinginess, malice, anger, laziness, distraction, and wrong views;
thus, within this ethical discipline, there is the inclusion of other [perfections]. The same should be said for the cultivation of the remaining [perfections] as well.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the passage from "Moreover, in the Abhidharma... to "...extensively sets forth their characteristics," the intended meaning is that within the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are explained;
moreover, within the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*, they are discussed under three headings: first, the means (*upāya*); second, the distinctions (*prabheda*); and third, the demonstration.

In this treatise, the inclusion of the ten perfections corresponds to what is taught under the heading of "means" in that [text]. As for the "distinctions" heading, that [text] treats them in relation to the six [perfections].
This treatise clarifies that [the perfections] are distinct because there are ten [perfections]. [Commentary:

This relies on the stage of initial practice (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*) regarding the "conformity to the subsequent phrase" (*anuloma-paścāt-pada*) response. For example, if one were asked: "Is that which is the perfection of giving also the perfection of morality?
Or, is that which is the perfection of morality also the perfection of giving? To answer this question, one should employ a response conforming to the subsequent phrase; namely, there is...

The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is necessarily the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*); however, there are cases where it is the perfection of generosity but not the perfection of ethical discipline—namely, generosity that is not subsumed under ethical discipline.
This pattern continues up to the comparison of wisdom (*prajñā*) with generosity, all of which should be answered according to the latter clause.

Now, observing the commentary (*ṭīkā*), there are only the answers and no questions; one should follow this method of composition. Herein, for a person at the stage of a beginner (*ādikarmika*), [the practice proceeds] gradually.

Regarding the subsequent cultivation: if one cultivates, it must depend on each preceding stage and not upon what follows; therefore, all answers follow the "subsequent clause" (paścātpādaka) formula.
If one has already practiced for a long time and suddenly cultivates all six types [of perfections], they are all mutually inclusive, and thus one cannot answer as previously stated;

rather, one should simply say, "both giving and morality. This is because the question asks about the narrow in terms of the broad: giving is broad while morality is narrow. That is to say, within this treatise...
Regarding the statement that the preceding practice induces the subsequent by way of cultivation: the former subsumes the latter because giving subsumes the attainment of ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Thus, giving is broad while ethical discipline is narrow. This is like asking about wisdom (*prajñā*) by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); concentration is broad while wisdom is narrow, because concentration induces wisdom and thus subsumes its attainment, whereas wisdom does not subsume concentration and is therefore narrow.

If one begins to practice for the first time after generating the resolve [for awakening], this is called the stage of the beginner (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*), and all giving performed therein is [of this nature].

Regarding this, the term "ground" (*bhūmi*) is named from the perspective of generating the application of giving within its cause; alternatively, "ground" may refer to a stage (*avasthā*), meaning that within the stages such as the *sambhāra-mārga* (path of equipment), one is called a "beginner" (*ādikarmika*) in reference to the cultivation of the six perfections.

[Commentary] However, regarding the phrase "one should now introduce the *Abhidharma* [treatises], such as the 'conformity to the preceding' (*anuloma-pūrvapada*) and 'conformity to the following' (*anuloma-uttarapada*) phrases," the intended meaning is as follows:
In general, when determining and resolving questions and answers concerning various dharmas, there are differences in their breadth and narrowness.

For this reason, the fifteenth chapter of the *Abhidharma* explains that there are six types of phrases: first, the single-line phrase (*eka-pada*); second, the phrase conforming to what precedes (*pūrvapadaka*); third, the phrase conforming to what follows (*uttarapadaka*).
Regarding the four two-line [verses], five three-line [verses], six four-line [verses], and so forth, they are explained individually as follows. Thus, that treatise states:
"The first type is the method of inquiry (*praśna-vyākaraṇa*), which means that one takes a single dharma and mutually inquires with each of the other dharmas one by one;
having finished inquiring with the first dharma, one then removes it and takes the second dharma to mutually inquire with the others, proceeding in this manner for each one."

Regarding the "single-phrase" formulation concerning all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), it is as if one were to ask: "If one accomplishes the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*), does one also accomplish the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*)?
Or, if one accomplishes the sense-base of form, does one also accomplish the sense-base of the eye? One should answer according to the preceding phrase:

"One who accomplishes the sense-base of the eye necessarily accomplishes the sense-base of form; however, there are those who accomplish the sense-base of form but do not accomplish the sense-base of the eye, such as those who lack the faculty of sight."
There are those who possess both the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), such as a person with eyes;
this corresponds to the first proposition. There are those who possess neither the sense-base of the eye nor the sense-base of visible form, such as the dead, for whom both are useless.
Next, excluding the eye and taking the ear, they inquire of one another in succession, following the same pattern and dividing them into four propositions.
The others should all be explained according to reason in this manner; thus, each subsequent stage should be explained as gradually diminishing according to reason.

With the exception of the first [category], one should pose questions and provide determinations regarding the dharmas by comparing them with the second [category], such as "taking the ear" and so forth. This is a single "formulaic phrase" (*ekapadaka*).

As for the "conformity to the preceding phrase" (*pūrvapādaka*), it refers to taking any two dharmas from among all dharmas and questioning them in relation to one another, based upon the preceding dharma.

To answer such a question as: "If it is wisdom (*jñāna*), is it also an object of knowledge (*jñeya*)? Or if it is an object of knowledge, is it also wisdom?"—one should answer by following the first phrase (*pūrvapādaka*):
"There is that which is both wisdom and an object of knowledge; there is that which is an object of knowledge but not wisdom," namely, other phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth.

There is also [the category of] that which is neither wisdom nor an object of knowledge, and so on; however, this consists of only three phrases. As for the "following the subsequent phrase" (*paścātpādaka*), it refers to the mutual exchange of these two factors.
Regarding the method of answering questions by means of a subsequent term (*uttarapada*), as when one asks: "Is that which is the grasped (*grāhya*) also the grasper (*grāhaka*)?
Or is that which is the grasper also the grasped? This should be answered according to the subsequent term: "All that is the grasper is also the grasped;

however, there is that which is the grasped but not the grasper, namely the five objects such as form (*rūpa*) and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), excluding associated mental factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*)."
There are cases that are neither the grasper (*grāhaka*) nor the grasped (*grāhya*); these also comprise three propositions, the third of which is identical to the first.
Regarding the two propositions, when answering a question, one must respond with exactly two propositions and no more.

For example, regarding the establishment based on the aggregates (*skandha*) and the establishment based on the elements (*dhātu*), if one were to ask: "Is the number of aggregates also the number of elements? [the answer would be restricted to two propositions].

Is the number of *dhātus* also the number of *skandhas*? This should be answered with two propositions: either it is the number of *skandhas* but not the number of *dhātus*. This refers to the *rūpa-skandha* and the *vijñāna-skandha*. Why?
Because there is no single *dhātu* that fully encompasses the characteristics of the *rūpa-skandha*, nor any that fully encompasses the characteristics of the *vijñāna-skandha*.

The commentary explains: because the *dhātus* are narrow while the *skandhas* are broad; thus, a single *rūpa-skandha* encompasses many forms (*rūpas*), and a single *vijñāna-skandha* encompasses many [consciousnesses].
Since the spheres (*dhātu*) of consciousness and so forth are each narrow and limited, the spheres are divided into eighteen.

How could a single sphere of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) or a single sphere of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) fully encompass the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) or the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)? It is for this reason that these are counted as aggregates (*skandha*) but not as spheres;

or rather, there are spheres that are not counted as aggregates, namely the sphere of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*). Although the sphere of phenomena is included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), it cannot encompass everything.

Because they are aggregates (*skandha*), the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) does not include the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) or the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), as stated below. Regarding the enumeration of aggregates rather than the enumeration of bases (*āyatana*):
this is also based on the difference between broad and narrow categories. Because the bases are narrow, they are divided into the twelve internal and external bases;

because the aggregates are broad, "form" encompasses all forms. As for the three propositions regarding attachment: this refers to answering a question with only three propositions. For example, if it is asked: "If [something] is enumerated among the aggregates..."

Are they also included within the bases (*āyatana*)? And if they are included within the bases, are they also included within the aggregates (*skandha*)? This should be answered with three alternatives: 1.

Included within the aggregates but not included within the bases: namely, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). 2. Included within the bases but not included within the aggregates: namely, the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). 3. Included within both the aggregates and the bases:

namely, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) and the mind-base (*manāyatana*). Regarding those that are neither, there are certainly no four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) among the aggregates and bases; that is to say:
Regarding a question, one should provide a fourfold categorical answer (*catuṣkoṭika*). For example, if it is asked: "If one possesses the eye faculty, does one also possess the ear faculty?
Or, if one possesses the ear faculty, does one also possess the eye faculty? One should answer with four alternatives:

(1) there are those who possess the eye faculty but do not possess the ear faculty—namely, the deaf; (2) there are those who possess the ear faculty but do not possess the eye faculty—namely, the blind; and so forth.

One who accomplishes the eye faculty also accomplishes the ear faculty; this refers to those who possess both eyes and ears. There are cases where neither is accomplished, excluding the aforementioned instances.
Regarding the "statement of assent" (*anujñā-vākya*), this refers to answering a question in accordance with it by using such words to express agreement with what was asked.
For example, if one asks: "Are all things that are impermanent conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)? And are all conditioned phenomena [impermanent]? [The answer would be given accordingly.]

Regarding the question "Is it impermanent?", one should answer by affirming the inquiry. As for a "phrase of negation" (*pratiṣedha-pada*), this refers to answering a question with "no," thereby negating the inquiry.
For example, if someone asks, "How many truths (*satya*) do conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) external to the aggregates (*skandha*) subsume?
one should negate the answer by saying, "No; there are no conditioned phenomena external to the aggregates."
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the latter subsumes the former because giving is narrow": since this section concerns the maintenance of purity, the former is subsumed by the latter;
that is, the former is giving and the latter is morality. Because morality can subsume giving, [the sequence continues] until the former is concentration and the latter is wisdom.
Because wisdom can subsume concentration, it is an answer that accords with the preceding statement—that is, it takes up [the previous point] in accordance with it.
The preceding sentence refers to an external question: "Is all giving necessarily precept-keeping? Or is all precept-keeping necessarily giving?

The answer, "All giving is precept-keeping," is an answer that follows the former term (an *anuloma-pada*). This is a case of asking about the narrow [category] of giving in relation to the broad [category] of precepts;
the same applies when asking about meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in relation to wisdom (*prajñā*).

[Treatise]: Regarding the fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*) that should be applied when practicing according to the pure and the mixed, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* (Dafalun shi), in its commentary on this passage, presents two types of fourfold permutations as already cited in the sub-commentary (*śū*). The first set of four permutations concerns the "mixed" (*miśra*);
however, in reality, it consists of only three permutations, lacking the second one, because it does not speak of merit (*puṇya*) in terms of categories, but rather according to what is preeminent.
There are only words of response and no causal inquiry; the second set of four phrases concerns the cultivation of merit by way of its categories (*jāti-puṇya*).

Regarding these four categories of merit: even if one possesses no wealth of one's own, by seeing others practice giving and generating deep sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*), one also attains the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). This is why that treatise states: "Furthermore, all formations..."
Can all acts of giving produce the various types of merit belonging to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*)? This should be analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1.

There is giving that is not the practice of the perfection of giving: this refers to giving that is not dedicated toward enlightenment (*bodhi*). 2. There is the perfection of giving that is not giving:

this refers to such things as exhorting others toward the perfections, praising them, rejoicing in them, and feeling gladness regarding them. 3. There is that which is both giving and [the perfection of giving]. 4. There is that which is neither.
Regarding the phrase "pāramitās," this refers to dedicating all practices toward enlightenment; the fourth line may be understood accordingly. The commentary states:
the first line refers to practicing giving that does not produce the category of pāramitā; the second line refers to merit produced by the category of pāramitā that is not the practice of giving;
the remaining lines may be understood accordingly.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the other five perfections all constitute four propositions because they precede the perfection of morality," this means that prior to morality, the perfection of giving can be established through four propositions.

This does not refer to the four propositions regarding the accumulation of merit through the performance of rituals. It says: there is morality that is not a perfection—namely, upholding the precepts without seeking enlightenment;

there is a perfection that is not morality—namely, the aforementioned third and fourth propositions of the perfection of giving, which are understood as follows. As for those [perfections] that follow:
[This can be] inferred accordingly.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if one practices mixed cultivation" and so forth, the third and fourth phrases are absent in the commentary, which can be understood.
As for the second phrase, its meaning is that mixed cultivation involves mutual intermingling; the second phrase is like saying there is morality that is not [yet] deliverance (*pāramitā*).

If one does not seek awakening, there is a perfection that is not the perfection of morality, but rather the perfection of generosity, and so on, up to the point where there is wisdom that is not a perfection, and perfections that are not wisdom;
all such cases may be understood by analogy.
[Commentary] The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that "up to non-contention, these are outflows. The meaning is that these six perfections are able to encompass the one [perfection of wisdom].

Because it encompasses all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*), it does not merely subsume them through the characteristics of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); rather, it subsumes all meritorious qualities (*guṇa*).

According to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, fascicle seven, Vasubandhu’s commentary on that section regarding mutual subsumption states: "That which is 'because it is their characteristic' refers to the characteristic of the essence of subsumption;

this means that these [perfections], such as giving (*dāna*), and those [perfections], such as giving, mutually subsume one another because they are 'concordant' (*anuloma*). This refers to the concordance of subsumption.

Because wholesome factors such as faith and wholesome mental states such as generosity are cultivated through faith, and because faith follows along within generosity and the other virtues, faith and the rest are themselves the universal wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), such as the foundations of mindfulness; they are their "outflow" (*niṣyanda*).

This refers to the inclusion of the outflows, namely the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), the ten powers (*daśabala*), and so forth, which are the perfections (*pāramitā*) of generosity and the others.
There are many results of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*); therefore, because these are subsumed within the six perfections, they are not merely subsumed by their own specific characteristics.

Even up to the point where wisdom (*prajñā*) subsumes them, this refers to their essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*). Faith is wisdom; that which accords with non-contention (*araṇā*) and so forth is the uniform outflow of wisdom.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "permanently severing [afflictions] through self-governance is disjunction" (visamyoga):
Question—If it is the sixth wisdom (*prajñā*) that can sever afflictions and attain the fruit of disjunction, how can the first five perfections (*pāramitā*) sever afflictions and attain disjunction?
If it is the sixth wisdom that can correctly sever delusions, what is the manner in which the first five perfections assist in the process of severing them? For example:
The preceding giving takes as its nature non-attachment and the three types of karma arising therefrom;

when the sixth fundamental wisdom subsequently arises, it is accompanied by non-attachment and the volition of the three karmas which can assist in severing delusions, while the wisdom itself can directly sever delusions to attain liberation from bondage.
Furthermore, the essence of the precepts also takes the volition of the three karmas as its substance when they arise.

At the time of the sixth fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), there simultaneously exist the path-factors of concentration (*samādhi*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*), which are also capable of assisting in abandonment.

For patience (*kṣānti*) has non-aversion (*adveṣa*) and the three types of action as its essence; diligence (*vīrya*) has the three types of energetic action as its essence; and meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) has meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*) as its essence.
Therefore, when wisdom arises, non-aversion, the three types of action, diligence, and concentration all exist simultaneously and are all capable of abandoning [the afflictions].
Because one attains dissociation from delusion, it is said that the six perfections eternally sever their respective opposites and attain dissociation from their results;
since this treatise states that untainted [attainments] also constitute the four fruits, the same principle applies here as well.
