[Commentary: "From 'embracing oneself and others' up to 'thus possessing the five fruits' clarifies the fruits summoned by the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

Regarding the fact that embracing oneself and others is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*): because the six perfections encompass both self-benefit and the benefit of others, the act of embracing sentient beings so that they attain liberation is called the fruit of human effort.
This is not based on what is realized, but is established solely according to the recipient—the conventional person consisting of the five aggregates."
This is called "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*). Regarding the statement that "the arising of superior excellence in a future life is its outflow" (*niṣyanda*):
this refers to the six perfections inducing one another in succession, which is termed the "fruit of outflow.

Furthermore, it is said that because a bodhisattva is able to practice giving and so forth in the present life, they are able to practice giving and so forth even more extensively in a future life; thus, the subsequent life resembles the present life.
The fact that all [the perfections] can practice giving and so forth is called "equal outflow" (*niṣyanda*). That they draw forth great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) is the "predominant" (*adhipati*);

however, the text here is not exhaustive. Furthermore, regarding the six perfections with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are called "predominant fruits" because they act as remote conditions to draw forth great enlightenment;
in reality, it is the six perfections without outflows (*anāsrava*) that can draw forth great enlightenment, which is termed "attaining the predominant fruit," thereby bringing about great wealth.

Regarding the question: "If these stations are maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*), since they induce great wealth and the external vessel-world (*bhājanaloka*), which are insentient and thus should be categorized as dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*), why are they called maturation fruits?

The answer is: Because the superior maturation fruits to be summoned in the future by the Bodhisattva’s practice of the six perfections—such as generosity—are based upon the ten stages of birth (*daśa-janma-avasthā*) and so forth; in terms of the body and all material requisites, they are entirely [maturation fruits].
It is logically consistent that whatever body one relies upon is termed "conforming to maturation" (*vipākānuparivartin*); this designation should not be subject to error.
[Commentary]: Alternatively, even when uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) factors support contaminated (*sāsrava*) ones, they may still be termed "maturation.

This refers to cases such as when, within the ten stages from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, uncontaminated factors support the contaminated karma of previous lives accumulated during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*) prior to those stages, thereby bringing about its fruition.

The ten royal stations and so forth are called the attainment of the ripened fruit (vipākaphala). Furthermore, because the untainted (anāsrava) sustains the tainted (sāsrava), karma induces the transformational ripened fruit (nairmāṇika-vipākaphala);
or, because the untainted sustains the tainted, it is also the sovereign fruit (adhipatiphala), since the category of the sovereign fruit is broad.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the outflow-free (anāsrava) is also assisted by the outflowing (sāsrava) to attain dissociation from defilements," this is said according to the actual reality.

It means that while it is the outflow-free path that severs delusions and attains dissociation, this is because the outflow-free wisdom—by means of being induced by the outflowing preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) and so forth of the seven stages below—attains the wisdom that severs delusions and thereby achieves dissociation.
Thus, it is said that the outflow-free is assisted by the outflowing to attain dissociation.

Furthermore, within the stage of application (*prayoga*), the contaminated [dharmas] are able to nourish the uncontaminated seeds so as to cause the uncontaminated wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) to arise.
Moreover, the nourishment of the uncontaminated by the contaminated is also a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), because the category of dominant fruits is broad.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that one obtains five fruits because the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) are explained in combination:

if one were to say only that the six perfections obtain five fruits, this would mean that the outflowing and outflow-free are being explained in combination. This is why they are not stated separately—that the four outflowing [perfections] obtain four [fruits] and the outflow-free [perfection] obtains four [fruits].
[Commentary: Regarding the passage from section 78, "nor is it that others are not obtained," according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Section 78), it says:
"O son of good family, you should know that as for the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) of all the pāramitās, there are also briefly six kinds.

As for the meaning of the question, "What is the fruit of maturation?": since there are many types of maturation, one wonders which among them is produced by the cultivation of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*).
Regarding the ripening fruits (*vipākaphala*): first, one attains great wealth; second, one is reborn in a happy realm (*sugati*);
third, one is free from enmity and destruction, possessing much joy and happiness; fourth, one becomes a lord of sentient beings; fifth, one’s body is free from affliction and harm;
sixth, one possesses great branches and leaves from which ripening fruits may mature. These six types clarify that there are no obstructions to obtaining other fruits. Now, this—

The six fruits may be understood as corresponding one-to-one with the six perfections. Because one uses wisdom to discern the meaning of phenomena and bestows them upon others, one will obtain great branches and leaves and vast wealth in the future;
this is called the "ripened fruit" (*vipākaphala*), as has already been explained previously.
As for being a lord of sentient beings, it is through diligence that one gains power over others, thereby becoming a lord of sentient beings in the future without causing affliction or harm.
Because one cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without harming sentient beings, one will obtain freedom from affliction and injury in the future.
"Great branches and leaves" refers to a great retinue; speaking according to the actual reality, it is through patience (*kṣānti*) that one obtains a great retinue.

What is here said regarding obtaining [it] through wisdom (*jñāna*) is because, by teaching the Dharma through wisdom, one extensively benefits sentient beings, and thus they constantly remain close to and attached to one in the future.
[They] become attendants to the Bodhisattvas. [Commentary:
Regarding the statement that this does not contradict the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, if we further consult Vasubandhu’s commentary on the *Saṃgraha*, it says:
"That which is subsumed by wealth and status is the superior benefit obtained through giving; that which is subsumed by noble birth is the superior benefit obtained through ethical discipline."

Regarding "included within the destinies" (*gati-saṃgraha*): it refers to being included within a great birth, a great circle of friends, and a great circle of dependents. "Circle of friends" (*mitra-gaṇa*) refers to the benefits obtained through patience;
"circle of dependents" (*parijana*) refers to slaves and servants. These three are included within the result of maturation (*vipāka-phala*).

Regarding "accomplishment of the application of vast undertakings": this refers to the benefits obtained through diligence. The commentary explains that "vast undertakings" refers to the universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
That which is equivalent to the middle [level of] exertion is called "application" (*prayoga*); because all that is to be done has been accomplished, it is called "attainment" (*siddhi*).
That which is characterized by non-afflictiveness and inclusion within the thinning of the defilements (*rajas*) is the excellence obtained through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*);

because of meditative concentration, one experiences this power and thoroughly knows all things. That which is included within the five fields of knowledge (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*) is the excellence obtained through wisdom (*prajñā*); this follows thereafter.
The three types [of fruits] are subsumed solely within the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*), which does not contradict the previous six types, as those are all maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*).
[Commentary: Regarding the passage in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* that explains [the fruits] up to "all are sovereign fruits," the intended meaning is this:

if one considers the six perfections (*pāramitā*) free from outflows (*anāsrava*) in relation to great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), they should properly be categorized as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), concordant fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*), and so forth; yet, here they are designated as sovereign fruits because the Bodhisattva...
It is said that both the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). The commentary explains:

"The causal condition" refers to the six untainted perfections (*pāramitā*) in relation to Bodhi; "the dominant condition" refers to tainted resources supporting the untainted to bring about the fruit of Bodhi.
Because the dominant fruit is ultimate, they are collectively termed "dominant. Question: According to the treatise, ten fruits of the ten perfections are explained; for what reason [is this said]?

In the commentary (*śāstra*), it is stated that one attains the fruit through the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). As for the four perfections mentioned in the subsequent passage, they are subsumed within the sixth;
the results they induce are identical to those of the sixth, as no distinct results are further specified.

[Commentary]: Regarding the initial statement that the sevenfold precepts of the *saṃgha* constitute the essence, this present exposition of the bodhisattva’s *vinaya-śīla* (precept of discipline) takes the sevenfold precepts as its basis;
however, this is merely a general explanation applicable to all three vehicles. In reality, the bodhisattva also possesses ten branches:
the seven branches of body and speech, plus the three branches of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), which serve to prevent greed, anger, and false views.

[Treatise] Regarding the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint), Asvabhāva’s commentary states: "It refers to the formal undertaking of distancing oneself from all categories of evil and unwholesome dharmas.

Regarding the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of gathering wholesome dharmas), Asvabhāva’s commentary states: "It refers to the correct cultivation of all Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
The commentary explains that "cultivation" here refers to the cultivation of conditioned, untainted (*anāsrava*) wholesome dharmas, and "realization" is their actual attainment.

The ability to realize unconditioned merit (*asaṃskṛta-guṇa*)—according to this treatise and others—is the aspect of all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) in terms of their meaning of abandoning evil;

it is the *śīla* of collecting wholesome dharmas (*saṃgraha-kuśala-dharma-śīla*) in terms of the meaning of progressive cultivation; and it is the *śīla* of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvānugrāhaka-śīla*) in terms of the meaning of benefiting others.

[Treatise] Regarding the statement that this [practice] shares commonalities and differences with the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), according to the seventh fascicle of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are four kinds of excellence that clarify the distinctions between it and the Two Vehicles.
As Vasubandhu’s commentary explains: "First, as for the distinction:

it means that all Bodhisattvas possess the three kinds of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) which universally restrain the three types of action (*trikarma*). This is not shared by the Śrāvakas; the Śrāvaka-yāna and others possess only..."

This single type of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) guards seven branches; therefore, the bodhisattva’s [restraint] is superior to that [of the śrāvaka], and it should be understood that the other three [types of śīla] are likewise superior.
It is also superior when compared to that of the two vehicles (*yāna*).

[Commentary]: This means that regarding all the natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) of Bodhisattvas up to those that are "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*), this present text speaks only as a general overview and does not exhaustively cover the full principle.

For instance, while an ordained Bodhisattva does not commit natural transgressions—thus sharing this with the followers of the Two Vehicles—they still possess what are called "unshared" prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).
Furthermore, if an ordained Bodhisattva were to commit the ten unwholesome actions, these would constitute natural transgressions.

Furthermore, in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-alaṃkāra*, it is asked: "If killing five hundred brāhmaṇas and others constitutes a transgression, why is it that there are cases where a bodhisattva either performs or does not perform such acts?
The answer is: "If one kills with a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*), there is indeed a transgression;
however, if one kills with a virtuous mind (*kuśala-citta*), there is no transgression. Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "That is to say, by means of this..."
Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one may perform the ten paths of unwholesome action, such as taking life, yet remain without fault and generate immeasurable merit, swiftly attaining Bodhi.

[Commentary] Regarding the first point, the various immeasurable precepts (*śikṣāpada*): "Great" refers to the fact that for all Bodhisattvas, there are three thousand modes of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) which serve as prohibitions.
The precepts for guarding the three karmas are vastly different from those of the Two Vehicles, which guard only seven branches and consist of two hundred and fifty rules.

[Commentary: Regarding the fourth point, "profound, supreme, and swift attainment of Bodhi," a sutra states that in the past, during his seventh previous life, a Bodhisattva was a merchant leader who took five hundred merchants into the sea to collect precious jewels and obtained immeasurable wealth.
There was a thief who intended to kill five hundred people in order to seize their treasure. Those five hundred people were fast asleep and did not wake up.
The Bodhisattva became aware of this and reflected: "If I allow these five hundred people to kill the thief, they will all fall into hell.
If I let the thief kill them instead, he will incur two offenses for taking both the lives and the treasure."
Having reflected that there are two offenses—the offense of killing and the offense of stealing—a bodhisattva then says: "I myself possess all merits;
I shall transcend twelve kalpas and attain immeasurable blessings, swiftly realizing Bodhi."
[Commentary]: The meaning of the passage from "Now, by means of the second [category], the common and uncommon... up to "...is precisely that text" is as follows:
Among the four kinds of excellence, the first excellence is this *tri-skandha-viśuddha-śīla* (the threefold pure morality);
the remaining three kinds refer to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Therefore, the treatise states: "The common, the uncommon, and so forth—profound and vast—as explained elsewhere."

[Treatise] Regarding the "Great Vehicle Radiance Samādhi": this samādhi is able to produce the radiance of wisdom that takes as its objects the four spheres, such as the principle within the Great Vehicle.
Regarding the "Samādhi of the King Who Accumulates Merit": this samādhi is able to accumulate merit like the power of a king;
it is named after this metaphor. Regarding the "Samādhi of the Three Sages' Guarding": this samādhi is named after its presiding subject. Question: Regarding these four samādhis...
Regarding which stage among the five stages this belongs to, the ancient masters have provided the following classification: the first four stages are called the "Luminosity of the Mahāyāna";
the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages are called the "Accumulation of Merit King"; the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are called the "Worthy Protector";
and that in which Bodhisattvas such as Vajrapāṇi and all Tathāgatas dwell is called the "Establishment of Practice Samādhi."
[Commentary: However, this [samādhi] exists only in the fourth dhyāna up to the point where it is "inclusive of the outflow-tainted" (*sāsrava*).
Regarding the passage "the Commentary makes this judgment," some have raised an objection, stating: "This judgment made by the Commentary is also not to be relied upon.

Although superior samādhis mostly rely on the fourth dhyāna, there are also those that arise based on other stages as well. Furthermore, one cannot conclude that it is unattainable for those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) to realize it."
The practice undertaken by Bodhisattvas prior to the stage of outflowlessness (*anāsrava-bhūmi*) is likewise not an object of knowledge for the followers of the Two Vehicles.

Furthermore, while the trainings in morality (*śīla*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) may pertain to both the stages prior to and those beyond [the first bhūmi], why is it that the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) is said to apply only to the stages beyond? It is because the training in concentration prior to the stages is taken as superior.
To explain in detail: the Master of the Commentary did not state that the training in concentration refers exclusively to the outflowless [stages]; he merely clarified [this point].

The four concentrations cited in the treatise are not characteristics prior to the stages (*bhūmi*). Furthermore, the two vehicles do not know what is common to both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*);
here, we simply use the fact that they do not know this to prove that the concentration is outflow-free, rather than saying it is outflow-tainted because they would all know it if it were so.

Moreover, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, following the explanation of the distinctions among concentrations, there are four further distinctions: those of counteraction (*pratipakṣa*), capability (*karmanya*), induction (*ākṣepa*), and activity (*kriyā*).

If it were not untainted (*anāsrava*), how could such a capacity exist? Therefore, one knows that the treatise in question relies upon untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*). Since the concentration cited here is identical to that [in the treatise], what contradiction is there?
Furthermore, regarding the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*), since each may be explained according to its own context, why insist on demanding that they all be uniform and equal?
[Commentary: Regarding "that which is obtained by removing hindrances in the third stage": within the third stage, one removes the hindrance to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*).
Once this hindrance to concentration has been removed, concentration is able to bring forth light and so forth.
[Commentary: As for "citing the primary ones": although there are immeasurable gateways of samādhi, these four concentrations are the most preeminent.
Because it is supreme, it is called the "foremost.

[Commentary] Third, regarding the distinction of the remedies: this refers to the cognition that takes characteristics as its object. The intended meaning is that *tathatā* (suchness) is the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena;
thus, the Sūtra says that all phenomena share one common characteristic, namely, "signlessness" (*animitta*). If fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) takes this suchness as its object...
Question: Since it has now been clarified that [this refers to] concentration (*samādhi*), why is wisdom (*prajñā*) cited to explain concentration? Answer:

Although the wisdom that depends upon it is cited, the intention is to manifest the concentration that serves as its basis, because concentration is capable of giving rise to wisdom. Regarding "capability":

when a Bodhisattva wishes to benefit sentient beings according to their needs, they do not regress from meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) in order to take birth; this is not the case for those of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Because there is no such thing within it, it is called "the inducer of unimpeded supernormal powers in all realms," meaning that by means of this meditative concentration,
one can manifest unimpeded supernormal powers for the benefit of sentient beings throughout all worlds.

[Commentary] Regarding "the distinctness of the activities performed" and so forth: the eighteen transformations refer to being able to cause [the earth] to tremble, to blaze, to fill [space], to manifest, to transform, to go and return, to contract and expand, to cause all forms and images to enter one's own body, to travel among similar classes of beings, or to appear and disappear at will;

these are the sovereign powers of subduing the earth and the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), extending even to emitting great radiance and so forth, as well as the ability to induce [other miraculous effects].
Regarding the ten difficult practices (*duṣkaracaryā*), that treatise states: first, the difficult practice of self-vow, because one vows to undertake the aspiration for unsurpassed bodhi;
second, the difficult practice of non-retrogression, because one cannot be turned back by the manifold sufferings of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);

third, the difficult practice of non-abandonment, because one does not forsake any sentient being even if they engage in perverse conduct; fourth, the difficult practice of presence before others, [even] toward sentient beings who are one's enemies...
5. The difficult practice of performing all beneficial activities for sentient beings, because one is not defiled by worldly dharmas while dwelling in the world;
6. The difficult practice of resolute conviction, because one generates profound faith and understanding in the Mahāyāna; 7.

The difficult practice of thorough penetration, because one possesses the capacity to penetrate both the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena; 8. The difficult practice of subsequent realization...
Ninth, the difficult practice of non-separation and non-defilement, because one is able to realize in accordance with the profound and secret words spoken by all Tathāgatas;
tenth, the difficult practice of application, because one can cultivate the liberation in which all Buddhas abide—
free from all obstacles, acting without effort until the end of saṃsāra, and constantly giving rise to a single [mind].

Because it performs all beneficial activities for the sake of all sentient beings, the second of the six types explained above is precisely what is elucidated in this treatise as the essence of the four concentrations (*dhyāna*).
As for the remaining five aspects—such as the objects of focus (*ālambana*) and so forth—the concentration is treated in the same manner as in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Therefore, it is said:
"The objects of focus and other attributes of these four are as explained elsewhere."
[Commentary: Regarding the "esoteric language" (*saṃdhābhāṣya*) of the six perfections and so forth: in Sanskrit, *udāra* means "miserly. This is an esoteric term;
it should be understood as "the great miserliness of a bodhisattva," which refers to not giving away even a small amount of material wealth.

If one understands this esoteric language of the mind, it means that since the beginning of the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the bodhisattva has been able to relinquish kingdoms, cities, wives, and children—let alone small items.
"Named 'Giving Little'—this is a cryptic expression for practicing the six perfections. [The Commentary] explains this extensively, as in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.

[The Sub-commentary] states: Regarding the "ten paths of unwholesome karma," the intended meaning is that if there are sentient beings who first ought to practice unwholesome dharmas, even to the point of giving rise to false views and severing their roots of goodness, and who later wish to resolve upon bodhicitta—at that time, one should first act in accordance with their activities.
Because they subsequently lead others to resolve their minds [on enlightenment], a bodhisattva may remain for immeasurable eons for the sake of even a single sentient being,
employing various diverse means and engaging in their affairs to cause them to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
Since these ten paths of unwholesome action are also explained extensively in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it is said that "it is the same for all."
[Treatise] Question: Regarding "wisdom of non-conceptualization through application," is this wisdom of application itself non-conceptual? Answer:

It is called "wisdom of non-conceptualization through application" because it is free from the conceptualizations of a mind that clings [to objects], a mind that wrongly grasps emptiness (*durgṛhīta-śūnyatā*), and other such inverted states of mind.
If one gives rise to false views, deluded clinging, a wrong grasp of emptiness, or arbitrary speculative constructions, these are termed "conceptual. This refers to the fundamental [wisdom].

Wisdom is defined as non-conceptual. If one were to claim that subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) is called non-conceptual, then there would be no such thing as "wisdom that accords with the object" (yathārtha-jñāna).

This is because all subsequently attained wisdom that adheres to the name "non-conceptual" arises in dependence upon an object; therefore, all three types of wisdom would be termed non-conceptual wisdom.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "The last five are combined into one because they all belong to the sixth," the intent is as follows:

since the last five dharmas are combined to form the sixth, the three types of wisdom—namely, preparatory (*prayoga*) and so forth—are contained within the sixth *pāramitā*. That is to say, among the subsequently attained wisdoms (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), there is the preparatory wisdom;
this "preparatory" refers to that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) when viewed in relation to subsequent superior dharmas, and it is termed "preparatory wisdom. This admits of two interpretations.

[Commentary]: If one explains "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) by means of the other fifteen gates, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She-lun), chapter eight, employs sixteen gates to explain the three types of wisdom (*trividya*).
Regarding the single gate of intrinsic nature, it refers precisely to the three types of wisdom elucidated in this treatise;
the remaining fifteen gates are explained in detail as they appear in the *Saṃgraha*. Now, I shall cite that treatise in its entirety for reference, beginning with the first: intrinsic nature.
Regarding the "gate of nature" (*dharmatā-mukha*), it refers here to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) taking the departure from five characteristics as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

As the root treatise states—and as the commentary (*ṭīkā*) cites—one is the departure from "lack of mental attention" (*amanasikāra*) up to "because it is not that wisdom. Regarding this, Asvabhāva’s commentary explains:
First, if it were merely a lack of mental attention, then deep sleep, intoxication, and the like would also constitute non-conceptual wisdom. Second...
Regarding the phrase "because it is devoid of the stages of vitarka and vicāra up to the non-conceptual," Asvabhāva’s commentary states:

"If [the absence of conceptualization] were merely the transcendence of the stage of vitarka and vicāra, then all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and śrāvakas in the stages from the second dhyāna upward would have to possess non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "because it is devoid of perception and feeling up to the mindless states," Asvabhāva’s commentary states: [As follows:]...

It is said: "If the cessation of perception and feeling were non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), then the essential nature and characteristics of this wisdom would be difficult to establish, because within states such as the absence of perception (*asaṃjñika*), there is no mind apart from the mental factors (*caitta*).

Fourth, regarding the passage "just as the intrinsic nature of form [is not established] up to the great elements," Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "If it were like form, then non-conceptual wisdom would not be attained."
The accomplishment of non-conceptual wisdom is like the derived matter produced from the great elements; because it is of one kind, it is entirely like its own nature.

Regarding the phrase "fifth, because it is free from conceptual construction regarding the distinct aspects of true reality" and "it reaches the state of being non-non-conceptual," Asvabhāva’s commentary states:
"If one were to conceptually construct distinct characteristics within true reality, this would not be non-conceptual wisdom; such wisdom would not be established."
The nature of conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva) involves the mental construction of distinctions based on the cognition of true reality;
because one conceptually determines that "this is true" or "this is false," it is accompanied by conceptualization and therefore does not constitute non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "that which is the basis" up to "it is the mind and so forth," Wu-xing’s commentary states:
This means that the basis of non-conceptual wisdom is neither mind nor volition; yet it is also not a non-mind that serves as its basis, because it belongs to the category of mind.
It takes the mind as its cause, and through the power of repeated cultivation, it attains this state and is thus called "of the category of mind. This clearly demonstrates [the nature of the basis].

"The mind that is the support of wisdom transcends all conceptualization and discrimination. Commentary: The term "mind" (citta) here refers generally to both the thinking mind (*manas*) and the non-thinking [mind].
Furthermore, while the objection specifically challenges the response based on the thinking mind, the answer relies upon both types of mind;

therefore, it is said that the "mind which is the support" refers to the wisdom-supporting mind. Although this mind lacks discrimination, it is of the same category as the immediately preceding mind and thus may be so designated.
The term "mind" (*citta*) is as cited in the *Śū* [Commentary].

Regarding the statement in the *Śū*: "As for 'causal conditions' (*pratyaya*), it means that the hearing-perfuming (*śrutavāsanā*) is the direct causal condition for untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Regarding the statement in the *Śū*:

"As for 'the object-condition' (*ālambana*), it refers to the object of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)," this means that the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is free from conceptualization.
To speak of "thusness" (tathatā) is to say that it is called "ineffable," for it is the object of wisdom (*jñāna*).
Since its nature as thusness consists in the non-existence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is said that the imagined nature is also ineffable.
This very ineffability of the imagined nature reveals the thusness of the two-fold selflessness; this is precisely the threefold non-differentiation.

This is the object of focus for other forms of wisdom. Question: While it may be said that fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) takes true suchness (tathatā) as its object, how do preparatory wisdom (prayoga-jñāna) and subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) take suchness as their object?
Answer: Preparatory wisdom seeks to approach true suchness and induces non-conceptual wisdom; therefore, it is able to take suchness as its object.

As for subsequently attained untainted wisdom, because it universally takes all things as its object, it also takes suchness as its object. There is no error in principle regarding this; the statement that preparatory wisdom [takes suchness as its object] was made with this intention.

Although subsequent attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) does not directly realize suchness as its object, even though correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) realizes suchness, it is still called "taking suchness as its object" because the meaning [of the term] is broad. [Commentary]:
Regarding the statement "the characteristics of speech differ from those of form," the intended meaning is that non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) itself is precisely... [omitted].
The mode of activity (*ākāra*) of conceptualization is also similar to the previously explained mode of activity of the first transformation;

that is, although this cognition possesses both the seeing (*darśana*) and the image (*nimitta*) aspects within its objective referent (*ālambana*), one does not perceive either identity or difference between the subjective and objective aspects.

This is just as when visual consciousness perceives the color blue, it does not differentiate whether the perceiving visual consciousness and the perceived object, the color, are identical or different.
Since this is also the case for [the other] equals, we know that visual consciousness perceives objects without distinguishing between colors such as blue and yellow;

it is only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that these are differentiated into the aspects of blue and so forth. Regarding the six gates above, all are as cited in the commentary (*śāstra*); the remaining eleven gates shall now be cited and explained.
Sixth, "that which is sustained by wisdom" refers to what is attained within the subsequently-attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) induced by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
These various practices of the bodhisattvas all take wisdom as their support; because these practices do not become scattered, they are called "abiding in wisdom.
Regarding the seven non-conceptual wisdoms, what serves as their companions? If there were only one, it would be incapable of anything.

This refers to the first five perfections, which are divided into three paths: the first four constitute the path of accumulation (*sambhāramārga*), and the last one constitutes the path of reliance (*niśrayamārga*).
Because they serve as auxiliary companions, the first five perfections act as companions to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Regarding the question of where this non-conceptual wisdom brings about its maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*), the intent of the question is:
within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), at which stage does the bodhisattva’s non-conceptual wisdom bring about its maturation fruit? The answer is: it is among the Buddhas.

Within the assemblies of the two bodies—the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*)—this is not a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because it serves as an antidote to those [defilements].

Rather, it is a sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*) that is metaphorically designated as "ripening," because it nourishes and perfumes other contaminated (*sāsrava*) karmas so as to cause them to produce ripening results.
The commentary explains: "The Bodhisattva produces ripening within the assemblies of both the transformation body and the other-enjoyment body."

If this is merely a metaphorical designation of the term "ripening" (*vipāka*) within the category of dominant results (*adhipatiphala*), and is not in fact a ripening cause (*vipākahetu*), why is that?
Because it is non-conceptual and capable of counteracting [afflictions], it does not summon a ripened result;

furthermore, because it is not a ripening cause, it does not produce a ripened result. Moreover, due to the powerful function of non-conceptual wisdom, it subsequently supports and nourishes the Bodhisattva's cultivation.

In the past, former karma resulted in the superior and distinct ripened fruits (*vipāka-phala*) of the ten stages and the ten royal positions; because these are directed toward contaminated (*sāsrava*) former karma, they are also termed ripened fruits.
As for the nine types of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), what constitutes their "equal outflow" (*niṣyanda*)?

It refers to the fact that within successive lifetimes, the non-conceptual wisdom of each preceding life induces that of each subsequent life, increasing and becoming more excellent through this continuous succession; this is the equal outflow.
Regarding the result: how is it that the ten non-conceptual wisdoms (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) constitute deliverance?

It means that when one first enters the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) at the stage of the "Extremely Joyful" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one perceives the principle of non-conceptuality across all stages and thus first attains deliverance.

Because this is subsequently fulfilled during the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one perceives the principle of non-conceptuality in its entirety. What is here called "all" refers to a partial totality (*pradeśika-sarva*).

Regarding the question, "Of the eleven types of non-conceptuality (*avikalpa*), which is ultimate? it is said that although the three bodies (*trikāya*) are attained in the first stage (*bhūmi*), they are not yet purified;
it is only upon reaching the tenth stage that they become purified and are then termed "ultimate. The commentary explains:

"Attaining the three bodies in the first stage" means that when a bodhisattva attains the two wisdoms (*jñāna*) in the first stage, they thereby partially attain the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*). This refers to the enjoyment of the body for one's own use.
The four wisdoms constitute its essence; the True Suchness realized therein is the partially realized Dharmakāya, which is the Nirmāṇakāya of the first bhūmi.
Furthermore, it is because one is able to manifest ten billion bodies. Network Sharing:
*Cheng weishi lun shu yi yan*, Fascicle Thirteen, Part One. [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement that "the scope of their essential natures (*tǐxìng*) is neither broader nor narrower and there is no further distinction," the intent is to say that the two obstacles (*èr zhàng*) are the broadest.

This is because the mere mention of the "two obstacles" already encompasses all obstacles—both those arising from discrimination (*fēnbié*) and those arising simultaneously with birth (*jùshēng*). Thus, the two obstacles are broad. If one speaks of the "ten obstacles," then...

The ten obstacles (*daśāvaraṇa*) mentioned in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Cheng weishi lun) are narrow in scope, as they encompass only the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that hinder the entry into the stages (*bhūmi*), but do not include the cognitive obstacles that hinder remaining in the stages or completing the stages.
Furthermore, since the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is also taken to be exclusively a cognitive obstacle, the obstacles in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* are thus restricted.
In contrast, the ten obstacles described in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) encompass only... [the obstacles of the path of cultivation].
The ten innate obstacles (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*) do not include a portion of the distinct nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*) and the two obstacles [of afflictions and the cognizable].

This is because the essence of the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings consists precisely of the two obstacles of afflictions and the cognizable, which are conceptual (*vikalpita*). Since these are not included here, they are said to be "narrow" [in scope].

That is to say, excluding the mind that enters the first stage (*prathamabhūmi-praveśa-citta*), the *Saṃgraha* includes all obstacles within the stages of abiding (*sthiti-bhūmi*) and so forth in the first stage.
This includes the obstacles within the final nine stages and the obstacles residing in the mind of one who has reached fulfillment;

however, since both the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and this treatise do not include the eleventh obstacle—the obstacle of the Buddha-stage—both the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Saṃgraha* are narrow in their scope.

[Commentary]: Although that which is abandoned in the ten stages consists only of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) and does not manifest simultaneously [with afflictions], the intended meaning is that while one correctly abandons the cognitive obstructions during the ten stages, the afflictions that arise together with the cognitive obstructions are likewise suppressed and do not manifest.

Thus, it should be understood that the ten stages also involve the simultaneous abandonment of both obstructions. According to the intent of this passage, one must resolve the following objection: "If..."

Regarding the statement that the "right abandonments" (*samyak-prahāṇa*) do not mention afflictions (*kleśa*), [the objection is] that afflictions should indeed be abandoned. The answer is as stated in the Commentary.
[Commentary]: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (fascicle 58) and other texts state that the worldly path reaches up to the nature of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

The intended meaning of this statement is that the six paths of the worldly, contaminated (*sāsrava*) stage can only suppress the innate (*sahaja*) greed and hatred, as well as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) that subsequently arises in accordance with that greed and hatred.
The neighboring afflictions such as pride and so forth do not subdue the conceptualized afflictions. Why is this?
Because the conceptualized delusions are powerful while the contaminated path is weak; thus, the weak path cannot subdue the powerful delusions, as was already explained in the eighth fascicle.

This is stated in reference to the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) among the two vehicles. Furthermore, it says that when those of the two vehicles wish to attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they also [perform]...
One enters [the path] only after first subduing the afflictions through the contemplation of the six aspects of attraction and aversion.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "If in the stage of the Requisites (*sambhāra-avasthā*), this coarse active manifestation can also be subdued and extinguished, yet up to that point there is no such capacity":

it means that when a Bodhisattva is in the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi—the stages of the Requisites and the Application (*prayoga*)—they are able to correctly know through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) or perform this contemplation of the Truths (*satya*).

One can suppress the active manifestation of conceptual afflictions; alternatively, by practicing the signless contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness), one can suppress the active manifestation of conceptual afflictions.
Furthermore, upon reaching the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), one is able to suddenly suppress and exhaust all conceptual afflictions.

If a follower of the Two Vehicles is able to suppress the coarse conceptual [afflictions] during the stage of accumulation (*sambhāra-avasthā*), they will likewise be able to suppress the conceptual [afflictions] upon reaching the stage of application.
Regarding "subduing individually but not subduing collectively": because one can subdue [defilements] in detail but cannot subdue them all at once, it is said that "one cannot subdue them.
This means that if something is contrary to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it is subdued; if it is not contrary to contemplation, it is not subdued.
This differs from the power of the mundane path of a Bodhisattva, which is not the sixfold path of practice but is merely called a "mundane path" because it is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
[Commentary]: Among those born within the internal Dharma who are negligent, there is none who lacks the "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikāvidyā*).
When a Bodhisattva reaches the seventh mind of the ten stages of faith, it is called the "power of non-retrogression," and only then can they be designated as one born within the internal Dharma.

If such a person born within the internal Dharma is negligent, they indeed possess the unshared ignorance; however, with the remaining three types of ignorance acting as conditions, they initiate [defiled] activity. If internally...
Question: For those who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the Dharma and are not heedless, do they lack the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), or do they possess it?
Is it only the seed-ignorance that serves as the condition for the arising of formations (*saṃskāra*)? Answer:

Regarding the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), although they lack the bodhicitta, according to their own respective stages, once they have fulfilled the stage of the provisions (*sambhāra*) for the two vehicles, they may also be designated as "ordinary beings within the Dharma."
[They are] ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
[Commentary: The fact that only the two stages of conceptualized greed (*vikalpa-rāga*) and so forth do not arise clarifies that the suppression (*vibhava*) extends back to the preceding stage.

Furthermore, another interpretation states that regarding these two stages of conceptualized greed and so forth, they only fail to arise upon reaching the second stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
The preceding section concerned the arising [of afflictions]; as for the subsequent explanation, this subtlety is discussed in terms of conceptualized greed and so forth.

[Commentary]: The "Bodhisattvas of the Three Grades of Worthiness" refers to the thirty minds prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), namely the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*);

these are called the Three Grades of Worthiness. However, since the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*) are subsumed within the initial stage of the Abode of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpādavihāra*), they are included within that Abode of Initial Resolve.
Because it is excluded [from the formal stages], the new sutras and śāstras state that there are thirty minds prior to the bhūmis (*bhūmipūrva*). [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement that "prior to the seventh bhūmi, greed, anger, and so forth still arise," the intended meaning is that when Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh bhūmi give rise to greed or anger for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they do so by the power of intentional effort (*saṃcetanīya-vaśena*);
it does not mean that they act out of ignorance or lack of restraint.
This refers to the arising of [the afflictions].

[Commentary: The question asks: "What is the difference between those who have not yet subdued [the afflictions] prior to the stages (bhūmi) and these [who have subdued them]? The intent of this question is as follows:

while the characteristics of Bodhisattvas prior to the stages—who have not yet subdued the greed for self and the loss of mindfulness—are discernible, they are not discussed here; rather, it refers to what follows below.

Question: Regarding the statement that "a small portion of one's own practice" and so forth refers to the stage prior to the *bhūmis*, how does this differ from the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) subdued on the actual *bhūmis*?
Answer: As the commentary states: "The power of the Path is still slight; therefore, those subdued prior to the *bhūmis* are different from those subdued on the *bhūmis*.
This explains the stage prior to the *bhūmis*, which is for the purpose of restraining the afflictions.

Regarding the phrase "those who practice [only] a small portion": the intention is that because the power of the Path is still weak and they are constrained by craving and so forth, craving and other afflictions manifest to a small degree through their own practice.
Thus it is said that due to craving and so forth, there is the arising of forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), while others do not arise.

This is stated to distinguish them from those on the stages (*bhūmi*) who have already been able to suppress [afflictions] to some extent, yet have not fully suppressed them, as opposed to the afflictions suppressed by those who have entered the stages and beyond.
Regarding the phrase "as for that which is not so," this explains the reason why the afflictions subdued on the stages (*bhūmi*) differ from those [subdued] prior to the stages.

[Commentary]: The meaning of the statement here, from "those abandoned by seeing" up to "both are absent in two ways," is to explain that those abandoned by seeing refer exclusively to the Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment who abandon the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of conceptual construction; whereas those abandoned by cultivation refer to...
Regarding those who progress gradually through the stages of training (*śaikṣa*): among the first three types of trainees, both afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*) obscurations exist;
therefore, within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they are gradually severed and suppressed. Regarding those who progress gradually as non-trainees (*aśaikṣa*):

for those who have already attained the state of a non-trainee in the two vehicles and have not yet turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna], there are no conceptualized afflictions nor innate afflictions; hence it is said that "both are absent."
"Both obstructions are absent.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "for the most part, it is likewise for the category of the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)," this refers to the fact that throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the cognitive obstructions and afflictions (*kleśa*) are either severed or suppressed accordingly;
thus it is said "likewise. It is called "for the most part" because it is taught that they arise from the same substance.

[Commentary]: "Not co-existent with this" means that which arises in a given stage (*bhūmi*) does not arise together with this cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), nor is it suppressed within this [stage].
This implies that in subsequent stages, it may manifest again due to other factors, or it may regress. Alternatively, the interpretation is:
"Not co-existent with this" means it does not arise or become suppressed in this stage, while it is permitted to arise elsewhere in other stages.
[Commentary: By the power of the preceding path, one subdues the manifest cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of the subsequent stages so that they do not function;

this is termed "subduing" (*vibhava*). For instance, when the manifest cognitive obstructions of the latter nine stages enter the untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*) of the first stage, they too can be subdued such that the manifest cognitive obstructions of the latter nine stages do not arise; this is termed "subduing. However, it is merely a subduing...

One cannot suppress the seeds by means of suppressing the manifest activities [of afflictions]. Furthermore, when entering the second bhūmi with an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), one can also suppress the manifest activities [of the cognitive obstructions];
thereafter, throughout the subsequent eight bhūmis, the manifest activities of the cognitive obstructions do not arise, and this remains the case for all that follows.

This is just as in the previous stages of the path of accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*) and the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*): while one was still practicing, upon entering the first bhūmi, one severed the seeds.
"Similar. [Commentary:

This is still not yet fully understood; to what does it refer? The intention of the "Solitary Practitioner" (ekayānika) is that one first provides a general exposition and subsequently analyzes according to the consciousnesses.
Within the general exposition, one first provides a coarse explanation; therefore, it is said, "This is still not yet fully understood," and thus a second [section] is required.
Regarding the analysis according to consciousness:

[The Commentary] states that "the seventh [consciousness], the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*), and its fruit do not contradict one another" because it intends to explain that when one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of persons and its fruit continues from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward,
the cognitive obscuration (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) consisting of the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) within the seventh consciousness still persists.

Because their activities are not mutually contradictory: when the sixth consciousness enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) or when its fruit continues, the seventh [consciousness] does not engage in obstructive grasping;
it would otherwise be able to contradict that state.

[Treatise: Regarding the point that the first five evolving consciousnesses do not manifest as obstructions, this is a further explanation following the difficulty raised, even though the previous [explanation] was general.
Having already explained that for those in the eighth stage and above, the six consciousnesses that accompany [the afflictions] no longer manifest, this still does not fully exhaust the principle.
Why is it that the sixth mental consciousness can give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) without giving rise to grasping, while the obstacles do not function?

Furthermore, since the five sensory consciousnesses are of a different nature and do not contradict the untainted state, how could they obstruct its non-arising? Therefore, we now address these difficulties with a further explanation, stating: "The former..."
"Even if the five evolving consciousnesses have not yet undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), etc.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "there is suppression and there is arising within the ten stages," this refers exclusively to the seventh consciousness among those in the ten stages;

it does not concern the other consciousnesses. The meaning is that although the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the seventh consciousness are severed at the stage of the Diamond-like Mind (*vajropama-citta*), they do not cease immediately upon reaching that point.

Regarding the hindrances within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are both those that are suppressed and those that arise. From the eighth stage onward, one is purely in uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) contemplation;

yet, although the sixth consciousness has predominantly entered the uncontaminated wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), the seventh consciousness still gives rise to the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), which is an obstacle to omniscience (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).

Because this [grasping] is extremely subtle and does not contradict the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of persons, it is not eliminated when the sixth consciousness enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Thus, the obstacle of grasping remains.
The meaning that [the obstacles] are both suppressed and arise prior to the eighth stage can be understood by analogy.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "those associated with the five consciousnesses... are still able to manifest," this refers to the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) associated with the five consciousnesses.
It means that those cognitive obstacles within the five consciousnesses which are capable of obstructing the subsequent stages remain present in the preceding ones.
On the [first] stage, one is able to suppress them. Why? Because the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are coarser than the seeds; therefore, they are said to be "suppressed.

Furthermore, from the eighth stage onward, although the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) are still accompanied by cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because the sixth consciousness constantly enters uncontaminated contemplation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), these obstructions are suppressed and thus prevented from manifesting. As for the five consciousnesses prior to the seventh stage:

Regarding "simultaneously" (*saha*), even when the sixth consciousness’s concomitant cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) arise, if they fluctuate, this is explained according to the treatment of cognitive obstacles within the context of the five sensory consciousnesses. [Commentary:
From "in the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), all evil destinies... up to "...is also included within the Stage of Perfect Fulfillment (*niṣṭhāgata-bhūmi*)," the text is as follows:
This explains the threefold faults of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). The term "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) here refers either to seeds or to the state of unfitness within the afflictions;
it is spoken with this intention. A Bodhisattva, while in the Stage of Supreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), is able to sever all seeds of conceptualized afflictions as well as coarseness.
Furthermore, [they eliminate] the eight difficult conditions, the three evil destinies, and so forth, and they correctly give rise to right view.
When practicing the path, one subdues all afflictions of the path of cultivation—those of superior, middling, and inferior grades—so that they no longer manifest.

Upon reaching the second stage, the signless and effortless dwelling (*animitta-anābhoga-vihāra*), one is able to subdue all afflictions such as craving, pride, ignorance, and the view of a self, preventing them from arising;
furthermore, one is able to sever the "unwieldiness" (*akarmanyatā*) of the superior grade of afflictions—the coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) that acts as an obstacle to the unconditioned.
Because they have produced patience toward sentient beings, they do not sever the seeds of the afflictions;
however, within the third dwelling, the Supreme Fulfillment, they are able to sever the seeds of the afflictions as well as the heavy residues (*dausthulya*).

The intention here is to explain that, having already transcended the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, one has entered the beginning of the second *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* and attained all the portions belonging to the dwelling in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

The two distinct obstacles, the three evil destinies, the eight unfavorable conditions, the five destinies, the body of a *paṇḍaka*, the female body, birth from an egg or moisture, and the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), are all eternally severed; this is called the first dwelling.

While correctly abiding in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), all co-emergent afflictions (*kleśa*) of the upper, middle, and lower grades do not manifest; from this point onward, one gradually transcends through practice.
Having already entered the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa and reached the initial stage of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa—
the dwelling in signlessness and effortlessness— all afflictions within the preceding seven consciousnesses cease to manifest forever,
and the body of segmented existence is also permanently relinquished; this is called the second dwelling, from which one transcends to the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
When the kalpa reaches the stage of the Supreme Fulfillment (parama-paripūrṇa-vihāra), all transformations of the body,
as well as all outflows (sāsrava) and subtle ignorance, along with the seeds of the two obstacles, are forever severed; entering the Tathāgata-vihāra is called the third dwelling.
[Commentary]: The meaning here is that this is also subsumed under the "Supreme Perfected Bodhisattva Abode.

This means that although only the bodhisattvas of the tenth stage constitute the Supreme Perfected Abode, this very Vajra-mind is also termed the "Supreme Perfected Bodhisattva Abode" and is thus included therein.
It is just as the four roots of goodness (catvāri kuśalamūlāni), although they are cultivated at the completion of the first kalpa, are nonetheless still considered part of the first kalpa.
The inclusion of this is likewise so; although it pertains to the final mind of the tenth bhūmi, it is nonetheless subsumed within the tenth bhūmi. [Commentary:
Regarding the statement "the coarse latencies (*dausthulya*) of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are of three kinds... until they are all eternally severed," the intent is as follows:

this clarifies that the coarse latencies of the cognitive obstructions are divided into three types based on the depth of their modes of activity (*ākāra*). Thus, those that are shallow are severed first.
Regarding "deep," later texts remove the term "bone" from the phrase "skin and bone," while other treatises read it as "skin, flesh, and bone. [Commentary:

The meaning here is that it refers to that which has already been severed. Question: If this is based on what has already been severed, then afflictions (*kleśa*) should also be said to be the "abiding in cessation" of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, if it relies on the correct severance of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), it should likewise pertain to the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*). Why is this not the case?
The *Dacheng yizhang tongdalu* (Comprehensive Answers to the Great Treatise) explains that the two obstacles are described according to their shadows and abbreviations:

one resides in the diamond-like mind (*vajropamasamādhi*), and the other resides in the stage of the Tathāgata. This is not contradictory; the intent is that if one refers to the actual severance, it is said to be severed within the diamond-like mind, whereas if one refers to the state where they have already been severed, it is said to be finally eliminated at the stage of the Tathāgata.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because it is the stage where the three *kalpas* are fulfilled, and because one has not yet attained the fulfillment of the signless (*animitta*) within the signful (*sanimitta*)," this section of the commentary contains seven points:
1) concerning the three *kalpas*; 2) concerning the initial arising of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and so forth;

4) concerning the fact that all afflictions (*kleśa*), whether discriminative (*vikalpa*) or innate (*sahaja*), do not function and are ultimately abandoned; 5) concerning the absence... [text truncated]

The first six [stages], beginning with the patience toward sentient beings (*sattvakṣānti*), pertain to the abandonment of the *pudgala* (ordinary being) and the two types of *pariccheda* (segmented and transformational death). The seventh pertains to the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).

Although one may have attained the signless (*animitta*) but not yet the signless-in-itself, or attained the signless-in-itself but not yet its perfection, it is only upon reaching the third stage (*vihāra*) that the signless becomes perfected.

Because the meaning of the three stages is manifested through these seven points, it is specifically stated that there are three types of afflictive latencies (*kleśadausthulya*) abandoned in these three stages.

The *Yijie* (Exegesis on Meaning) states: "Because they constitute the stages of fulfillment within the limits of the three eons (*kalpa*)": this means that having passed the first eon, one attains the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-vihāra*);
having completed the second eon, one attains the second stage, the Stage of Effortlessness (*anābhoga-vihāra*);

and having completed the third eon, one attains the third stage, the Stage of Fulfillment (*pariniṣpanna-vihāra*). Thus, three stages are established based on the completion of the three eons, which transcends the contemplation of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
The initial arising of the mind refers to the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga) of the first bhūmi; "immediately following" refers to the untainted continuity of the eighth bhūmi;
and "perfection" refers to the Buddha-bhūmi. This interpretation explains [the absence of obstacles] in terms of the afflictive hindrance (kleśāvaraṇa).

Regarding the statement that the two hindrances are absent in their manifest form—whether in large measure, small measure, or in their entirety—this interpretation explains it in terms of both hindrances. "In large measure" refers to the beginning.

Abiding therein, one is able to permanently sever all conceptualization such that both the seeds and the manifest forms of the two hindrances are exhausted; this is called "the majority" or "the minor portion.
This means that upon reaching the second stage (*vihāra*), one is only able to suppress the active manifestations of the afflictions so that they do not arise, which is termed the "minor portion.

The "complete portion" refers to being in the third stage, where one is able to exhaustively sever the innate (*sahaja*) aspects of both hindrances; this is termed the "complete portion" of all things.

"Because afflictions (*kleśa*) and conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) are eternally destroyed and do not function due to ultimate detachment" means that all afflictions and conceptual discriminations are eternally destroyed by the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
"Non-functioning of the innate [afflictions]" refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).

"Ultimate detachment" refers to the Buddha-stage (*buddha-bhūmi*). Regarding the distinctions of "slight purity," "much purity," and "extreme purity," these pertain to the Path of Seeing and the innate [afflictions].
The severance of the two obstacles of conceptualization is called "minor purity," wherein innate afflictions do not function from the eighth stage onward as the untainted continuum flows on.

This is called "great purity. At the third dwelling, all tainted states are completely severed and reach ultimate purity; thus one abandons the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), which is the dwelling of supreme joy (*pramuditā*).

Abandoning the death and rebirth of the fragmented body (*paricchinna-śarīra*) is the signless, effortless dwelling (*animitta-anābhoga-vihāra*), and abandoning the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-cyuti*) is [the dwelling of the bodhisattvas].
Regarding the statement that "the Buddha-ground has not yet attained the fulfillment of both the signless and the non-signless within the untainted mind":
if one has reached only up to the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is said that the untainted [mind] has not yet been attained;

if one has reached from the second stage onward, it is said that the signless is fulfilled, because signs are severed at this level; and if one has reached from the third stage onward, it is said that the non-signless is fulfilled.
The full term (*yǎmǎnzì*) encompasses both the aspect (*xiàng*) and the function (*yòng*).
[Commentary: "That which is obstructed differs, and thus that which is severed also varies. Regarding "that which is obstructed differs":

among the six consciousnesses, the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) obstructs the stages of learning (*śaikṣa*) and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the two vehicles; as for the afflictive obstruction within the seventh consciousness, it obstructs...

Regarding the fruit of Buddhahood and the fruit of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), if the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) exclusively obstruct the fruit of Buddhahood and their abandonment also differs,

then for those of the two vehicles, according to what they are obstructed by and what they abandon, the two obstructions within the seventh consciousness must be abandoned all at once upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood and the fruit of No-More-Learning.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the seeds of obstruction within this seventh consciousness lack distinction between coarse and subtle, and thus become perfumers," this first interpretation refers to the fact that within the afflictions of the seventh consciousness, there are nine grades for each stage (*bhūmi*), which results in eighty-one grades.
These eighty-one grades are [identical] to the ninth grade of affliction within the sixth consciousness of the *Bhāvanāmārga* (Stage of Cultivation).
Because they are similar in kind, it is said that there is no distinction between coarse and subtle; however, in reality, there is indeed such a distinction.
This is just as, although wrong views are said to be "one," it is not that the nine grades do not exist. This case should be understood in the same way.

Furthermore, regarding the second interpretation—that since the obstacles are identical, this has already been explained at length—it refers to the nine stages (*bhūmi*) in relation to one another, which collectively constitute the nine [grades].

This chapter, in terms of the three realms (*tridhātu*), comprises nine grades (*navavidha*) in total. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "only taking internal objects as its domain" constitutes the second interpretation;
its text is easy to understand and detailed.

[Commentary] Moreover, although the three minds and nine stages are combined in general to form two distinct grades, they differ from the nine distinct grades of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding the term "sudden" (*tun*) used for abandonment, the commentary explains it as follows: within the three moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one collectively subsumes the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) of the nine stages across the three realms and categorizes them into two grades.
First, the wisdom that internally dispels the conceptualization of sentient beings as real entities is the superior grade of the afflictive obscurations;
second, the wisdom that universally dispels the conceptualization of all sentient beings as real entities is— [the middle grade].

This inferior grade of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*)—the internal cognition that negates the conventional conditions of all phenomena—is itself the superior grade of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The third [grade], the cognition that universally negates the conventional conditions of all phenomena, is the inferior grade of the cognitive hindrance.

For now, we take these two grades—the superior and inferior—of the afflictive hindrance as being "abandoned simultaneously" (*sakṛt-prahīṇa*), which differs from the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are nine grades across the nine stages (*navabhūmi*); within each stage, the nine grades are abandoned one by one. Question:
Since the mind has three types, the afflictions should likewise have three grades. Why, then, is it said that there are only two grades of afflictions? Answer:

At the initial stage, one only abandons the "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) grade; "warmth" is still considered low. When it is now said that this is the "superior" (*adhimātra*) grade, this is based on its mode of activity (*ākāra*).
That which is coarse and shallow is called the "superior grade" and is also able to sever the superior grade [of obstacles]; what is here termed the "inferior grade" refers to this.
Furthermore, that which is subtle in its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is called the "middle grade" and is severed by the second mind;

what is here termed the "superior grade" is spoken of according to the coarseness of its mode of activity, yet according to the principle, it corresponds to the inferior grade of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). This treatise correlates this with the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Because it follows the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), it receives the name "middling. The third category of mental factors to be abandoned should actually be of the "superior" grade;
however, what is here called the "inferior grade" of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is designated as "inferior" based on the subtlety of its mode of activity (*ākāra*).

Thus, although afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obstructions both have superior and inferior grades, those that are abandoned upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) are said to be abandoned "all at once" (*sakṛt*).

[Commentary: Regarding the sincere statement found in the fifty-ninth [section] and elsewhere, the intended meaning is that those three minds of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are also termed "simultaneous abandonment" (*sakṛt-prahāṇa*).
According to that treatise, the afflictions abandoned through seeing are abandoned simultaneously, not gradually. Why is this?

Because by means of the wisdom of clear observation (*abhisamaya-jñāna*), specifically the clear observation of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), one is able to abandon the afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing. However, this clear observation is [identical to] the destruction...

Because the destruction [of afflictions] associated with the mental attention (*manasikāra*) on the truths occurs through the application of the path, the three minds [of the path of seeing] simultaneously sever all views and afflictions to be abandoned through seeing that are deluded regarding the truth of suffering and so forth.
For this reason, this treatise states: "In the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), everything is severed simultaneously.
The commentary on the phrase "there are two types of those to be abandoned by cultivation" means that they are divided into two based on the difference between sharp and dull faculties.
However, regarding this passage in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the first case refers only to those who attain the four fruits through gradual succession;
the second refers to those who, from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), leap over the two intermediate fruits to attain the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*).

To speak according to reality, one should first give rise to the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) to suppress the six grades of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation within the desire realm, and subsequently enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Regarding the case of one who transcends the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) to attain the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*): if they previously used a mundane path (*laukikamārga*) to suppress the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm, then upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they immediately transcend the first two fruits and attain the third fruit (*anāgāmin*).

For now, according to the *Śāstra*, it is not stated that one first gives rise to a mundane path to suppress the afflictions of cultivation and subsequently enters the path of seeing to attain the fruit; as the Commentary (*Vivaraṇa*) states: "Not... [the rest of the citation follows].
This explains the attainment of the second and third fruits by transcendence.

[Commentary: However, this passage does not state that one first suppresses and cultivates the afflictions through the mundane path before entering the path of seeing to leap over the first two fruits.

This is because the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* text does not mention using the mundane path to first suppress and cultivate the afflictions prior to entering the path of seeing and thus transcending the first two fruits.

This treatise clarifies that it is only after one has attained entry into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) that the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārgajñāna*) subsequently arises to abandon the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*).
[Commentary: It does not state that one may leap over to attain the second or third fruits;

indeed, this treatise neither states that one may leap over the first fruit to attain the second fruit, nor does it state that one may leap over the first two fruits to attain the third fruit. This treatise...
The middle section only speaks of transcending the two intermediate fruits to attain the fruit of arhatship (aśaikṣaphala). Therefore, this treatise states:
"The nine stages of the three realms are combined into a single aggregate, which is severed in nine distinct grades.
[Commentary: Regarding the distinction between the two vehicles, as found in that *Chao* (Excerpts), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains only two types of [attainment].
Riding upon the first [vehicle] clarifies those who attain the fruit through gradual stages; the second clarifies those who leap over the middle two fruits.

That treatise does not clarify those who leap over the first two fruits. If other treatises clarify leaping over the first two fruits but do not clarify leaping over the middle two fruits, there is such a distinction as explained in the *Dharmapada-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Thirteenth Fascicle).

[Commentary]: "Must rely on the *anāgamya* stage" means that, according to the intended explanation, those who attain the fruit through the gradual path must rely on the *anāgamya* concentration to give rise to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandons the afflictions and attains the fruit;
this is because their bodies reside in this realm [of desire].

The statement that "the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is likewise" means that for the gradual non-returner, the two types of antidotal paths must arise based on the *anāgamya* stage to abandon the afflictions before the fruit can be attained; thus, they necessarily arise.

Regarding the untainted path of counteraction (*anāsrava-pratipakṣa-mārga*): as clarified above, those who attain the fruits by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) must do so through the untainted path;
this differs from the Sarvāstivāda school, which allows that the two intermediate fruits may be attained through the severance of afflictions via the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*).
[Commentary] Regarding the question, "Is there anyone who enters the dhyānas or the formless attainments and yet [attains] this?"— the intent of this inquiry is as follows: Is it possible that,
by relying on the fundamental dhyānas of the four meditations and the lower three formless attainments to give rise to the path of counteraction and sever the afflictions of the desire realm,
one might first attain the third fruit?

[Commentary]: This is also not the case... up to "it is not sequential. The intent of this response is that it is absolutely impossible to enter the Path of Seeing based on any of the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and thereby abandon the afflictions of the desire realm to attain the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

However, there is indeed the possibility of a "leaping" (*vyutkrāntaka*) Non-returner who has previously used the sixfold worldly path (*laukikamārga*) to suppress the afflictions from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) downward.

Subsequently, relying upon either the fundamental dhyānas of the four meditations or the five stages within the initial threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), one enters the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
