By means of a single uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*), one abandons the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) downward, as well as the afflictions of discrimination within the desire realm, thereby attaining the third fruit; thus, one relies upon the upper four [stages].

Regarding those who enter the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) through either the fundamental dhyāna concentrations or the preparatory stage (anāgamya), they are exclusively those of the "leap-over" (vyutkrāntaka) type and not those of the "gradual" (anupūrvika) type;
only such persons are capable of this.

[Commentary] Second, as for the statement that the nine grades of afflictions across the three realms and nine stages are combined and abandoned until the afflictions are eliminated: this refers to...
The second section clarifies that those of sharp faculties can bypass the two intermediate fruits. The meaning is as follows:

a person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and possesses sharp faculties is able to bypass the two intermediate fruits and directly attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding "deficient in afflictions": this refers to being deficient in the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Specifically, it means one lacks the highest-grade (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) afflictions of the Peak of Existence and the highest-grade afflictions of the eight lower stages.

The reason for establishing the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) by simultaneously and suddenly abandoning the six grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm—

rather than establishing it by abandoning the six grades of the eight higher stages— is the same principle as why one does not establish the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) by abandoning the nine grades of the desire realm.

It is because [the latter] involves the simultaneous abandonment of the nine grades of the desire realm and the nine grades of all eight higher stages, whereby one directly attains the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*).

Since one is not designated as having attained the fruit of a Non-returner [at this stage], we know that only those who have attained the first fruit possess the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) capable of transcending the middle two fruits to attain the fruit of Arhatship.
If one follows this principle, there are only two fruits: namely, the fruit of Stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) and the fruit of Arhatship (*arhat*).

This is also like a person wishing to travel far; although they have not yet stepped out the door, their mind is already directed toward the destination, and they do not remain in any other intermediate dwelling. This refers to the first [fruit].

The fruit is likewise: although one has not yet abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and is thus proceeding toward the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), this person who has attained the first fruit still possesses unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*) because they have not yet abandoned even a single grade of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, and because their number of births is still many.

For these reasons, when a person who has attained the first fruit resolves to leap over the middle two fruits, if they attain the second fruit and so forth, at that time they intend only to proceed toward the third fruit, just as a person [would do].
Upon departing, one looks only toward the proximate dwelling and does not proceed to a distant one;

furthermore, because the person has already abandoned six grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm, and because they have doubly transcended desire and their number of rebirths is few, a person of the second fruit cannot leap over.

Moreover, because a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) has already abandoned the defilements of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation and possesses no unwholesome dharmas, they likewise cannot leap over.

Question: Regarding this person of sharp faculties who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and has already transcended the middle two fruits—if they have already abandoned one or two grades of the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) and then pass away—is this permitted?

Answer: If one distinguishes the intent of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), then such a person would abandon their current body, transcend the middle two fruits, and attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), thereby becoming an Arhat. If one does not distinguish the intent of the Noble Ones, it would be an erroneous abandonment.
If there are those who die while still possessing one or two grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, they cannot be reborn in the higher realms; by the power of their vows,
they return to the desire realm and, within a second lifetime, further sever the remaining afflictions to attain the fruit of a *pratyekabuddha* of the *vargacārin* type,
provided they do not appear in the world during the era of a Buddha.
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, that sūtra uses the tip of a finger to point out the moon; thus it is named the *Aṅguli-sūtra*. "Tip" (*aṅguli*) means "head.

It should properly be called the *Aṅguṣṭha-sūtra* (Finger-head Sūtra). As for the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra*, it is called the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra* because it analyzes various characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth.

[Commentary]: Question: According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, it is accepted that the "leap-over" (*pluta*) non-returner (*anāgāmin*) attains the fruit of non-returning based on five stages (the four fundamental dhyānas and the first *anāgamya* concentration).
Since this [fruit of stream-entry] likewise relies on the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), what fault is there in this? Question:

If it is already accepted that the leap-over non-returner attains the fruit of non-returning based on five stages—the four fundamental dhyānas and the initial *anāgamya*—then since this fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) also transcends the two intermediate fruits, it too should rely on those same four [stages].

If one relies on the fundamental dhyāna concentrations and the lower three formless absorptions—that is, relying on seven locations—one can sever the innate afflictions of the three realms and transcend the middle two fruits to attain the fruit of arhatship; what fault is there in this?

[Commentary]: As for the statement, "However, that the preparatory stage (prayoga) belongs to the form realm (rūpadhātu) while taking the three realms as its general object does not contradict the ultimate principle," the intent of this first interpretation is as follows:

Since it is taught that a "leap-over" non-returner (pluta-anāgāmin) is permitted to enter the path of seeing (darśanamārga) based on any of the five stages of the form realm and thereby sever the afflictions of the desire realm to attain the third fruit, the same applies here—that is, to one who leaps over the two intermediate fruits.

Because they possess sharp faculties, they rely upon the four fundamental dhyānas and the lower three formless attainments; based on these seven stages, they sever the path of preparation for the desire realm.

Since the mind of the form realm can take all three realms as its object in a general manner, once the preparatory mind within the form realm has arisen, the subsequent paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) within the lower three formless stages are able to sever the [afflictions] of the desire realm.

Because one attains the fourth fruit by means of the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) as well as the afflictions of the two upper realms, it is said that within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there exists the path capable of counteracting the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Master Che (Zhe) remarked that this interpretation is incorrect.
[Commentary] Regarding the passage "However, those who have not yet... and so forth, the meaning of the commentary is as follows:

it explains that for those who leap over the two intermediate fruits, they cannot eliminate the afflictions of the second dhyāna and above while relying on the initial *anāgamya* (preparatory stage) within the middle [dhyānas].

Therefore, they must rely on the fundamental stages of the four dhyānas and the three lower formless realms (*ārūpya*) in order to be able to eliminate the afflictions of the higher stages. Thus, this commentary also does not...

To explain this according to principle: if the contaminated (*sāsrava*) meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of a lower stage were unable to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) of a higher stage, then even the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) concentration would likewise be unable to sever the afflictions of a higher stage, because it would lack the power of mastery (*vaśitā*).

However, since the uncontaminated concentration of the initial *anāgamya* (preparatory) stage is able to sever all afflictions of the two upper realms, and even the fundamental uncontaminated concentration of the first *dhyāna* is likewise able to do so.

[The text] states that one abandons all higher afflictions by means of the superior grade; according to this commentary, the statement that "the lower [path] does not abandon the higher" is not yet exhaustive of the principle.

[The commentary] says, "Because of the distinction in the power of the intention (*āśaya*)," which means: although the lower path does not abandon the higher afflictions, according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*,...

Regarding the middle position’s allowance that one may rely on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage or a lower path to abandon higher-level afflictions: this is due to the distinction of intention (*āśaya*) and because of possessing the requisite capacity.
Thus, among the four propositions, the first proposition is not the case; otherwise, the fourfold formulation would not be established.
[Commentary]: One should analyze this by means of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). There are cases where one relies on a lower stage to sever afflictions of a higher stage;

for example, relying on the *anāsrava* (untainted) concentration of the first *dhyāna* or the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage, one can sever the afflictions of the form and formless realms, thereby attaining the fruit of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) or the fourth fruit (*arhat*).
Conversely, there are cases where one relies on a higher stage to sever afflictions of a lower stage; this very passage refers to such a case, relying on the three lower [formless] stages.
The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);

furthermore, there are cases where one relies on a higher stage to sever the delusions of a higher stage, such as when a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) relies on the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) to sever the delusions of the sphere of nothingness. There are also cases where one relies on a lower stage to sever the delusions of a lower stage;
for example, the first two fruits and the third fruit rely on the initial threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) to sever the [delusions] of the desire realm.

Regarding the six grades of afflictions or the nine grades of afflictions and so forth for realizing the second and third fruits, the Venerable Master Guǎnzhé criticized the first interpretation in this commentary, saying:

"If one says that after the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) within the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) has arisen, the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) within the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*) arises;
or if, after the path of preparation in the fourth dhyāna has arisen, it subsequently induces the path of immediate succession in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*)."

It may be that such a principle exists, yet how could one first give rise to the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) within the fourth dhyāna, and subsequently give rise to the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)?
How then can it be said that the preparatory path arises based on the fourth dhyāna and induces the uninterrupted paths of the three lower formless attainments?
Therefore, we know this is incorrect. Furthermore, if one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) has already become detached from the defilements of the form realm, [it would be possible...]

Regarding the three lower formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), since such a person has not yet abandoned the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), how could they attain these three lower formless absorptions?

If it is argued that the person has already abandoned the defilements of the form realm and attained the higher formless absorptions, then since they have severed the defilements of the form realm, they ought to be a non-returner (*anāgāmin*);
how then can this person be said to have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*)? Furthermore, this...
If it is said that one does not give rise to worldly paths (*laukikamārga*) because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower realms have been exhausted,

how can such a person possess the afflictions of the lower realms yet attain the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) of the higher realms? Furthermore, if an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has already given rise to a worldly path and suppressed the defilements of the lower stages can obtain the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) of the form and formless realms,
then a Bodhisattva— who possesses superior capability and does not regress from the dhyānas— should certainly do so as well.

It is certain that one will be reborn in the desire realm; even if one has not yet abandoned the defilements of the lower stages, one may still attain the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the higher stages.
If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a follower of the Two Vehicles possesses the defilements of the lower stages, they cannot attain the meditative absorptions of the higher stages.

Since one who attains the meditative absorptions of the higher stages must necessarily have abandoned the defilements of the lower stages, we know that those who leap over the middle two fruits cannot rely upon the fundamental dhyānas of the four stages or the lower [stages].
Among the three [interpretations] regarding the absence of fixed stages, one attains the fourth fruit; therefore, the second explanation in this commentary is superior. [Commentary]:

It is not so; rather, it is simply that by means of the five stages, one sequentially attains the second and third fruits—this is the second explanation, which represents the intended meaning of the correct doctrine.
As for the statement that if one transcends the middle two fruits and relies on the seven higher stations to attain the fruit of Arhatship (aśaikṣaphala):

That meaning is not so. For one who has already surpassed the first two fruits by means of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*) and suppressed the afflictions (*kleśa*) that have no fixed abode, it is possible to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) based on any of the five stages of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and thereby sever the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to attain the third fruit.

Thus, the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) possess the path that serves as an antidote (*pratipakṣamārga*) to the desire realm; however, this is not the case within the three lower formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Because one does not abandon the afflictions of the desire realm, there is no path that serves as an antidote to the desire realm within the three lower formless attainments.
[Commentary: It is not even admitted that the ninth uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) enters the fundamental dhyāna;

for instance, when a *anupūrvaka-anāgāmin* abandons the nine grades of desire-realm afflictions, all their uninterrupted paths arise based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*). Since the uninterrupted path arises based on the threshold concentration, [the same applies here].
If even the ninth path of liberation of the fruit of non-returning arises based on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration to realize the third fruit,

how much more so for a stream-enterer who attains the four fundamental dhyānas and the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*)— could they not thereby transcend to the two intermediate fruits?
Furthermore, regarding this fruit of stream-entry, within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one has not yet arisen a single grade of the path of antidote that abandons the afflictions.

Because they have severed the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of one grade, it is known that such a person cannot yet give rise to the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) of the four higher dhyānas or the three lower formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) as paths for severing afflictions.
The meaning is as follows: for instance, within the desire realm there are nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

If one relies on the first threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) to give rise to the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) and severs the ninth grade, [the person is considered to have attained the fruit of stream-entry].
Only after having abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm does one obtain the untainted path within the fundamental dhyānas;

if one has not yet abandoned the ninth grade of the afflictions of the desire realm through reflection and cultivation, one will certainly not obtain the untainted path of the fundamental first dhyāna, and this should be understood accordingly for the higher stages as well.
Since a person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) has not yet abandoned the innate afflictions of the desire realm, they have not yet obtained the faculties of the four dhyānas.
How can the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) of the fundamental [dhyānas] give rise to the untainted paths of the lower three formless attainments (*ārūpya*)?

While it may be possible for them to engage in contemplative observation (*paryālocana*), the intention here is to say that although one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) cannot give rise to the untainted paths that abandon afflictions (*kleśa*) through the four dhyānas or the three formless attainments, this person does give rise to the untainted mind of the sevenfold contemplation (*saptasthāna-paryālocana*). This mind, however, is not capable of abandoning afflictions; thus it is so named.

Regarding the practice of *paryāya-darśana* (contemplative observation), someone has raised this objection: "Persons in the first two fruits cannot give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) contemplative observation within the fundamental meditative attainments (*mauladhyāna*).
Only the *kāyasākṣin* (body-witness) and the *anāgāmin* (non-returner) can give rise to the untainted contemplative observation of the eight higher stages. Why is this?

Because they have already suppressed the afflictions from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) downward; thus, they rely upon the untainted contemplative observation as a preliminary application (*prayoga*)."

Since those who have attained the fruit of the third [fruit] and are not yet "bodily witnesses" (kāyasākṣin) are likewise unable to give rise to uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) minds of the higher stages, we know that stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) cannot attain the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*) of the higher stages to practice the observation of the uncontaminated. Question:

Since those in the first and second fruits have already attained the path of counteraction (*pratipakṣamārga*) of the initial "not-yet-arrived" concentration (*anāgamya*), I wonder whether they can also give rise to [the path] within that "not-yet-arrived" state?
Regarding those who possess uncontaminated [paths] (*anāsrava*) but do not attain the arising [of the fruit], such as those who will be reborn seven times at most (*saptakṛtvah-parama*):
it is only during their seventh birth that they are able to give rise to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), and attain the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣaphala*).

If, during the preceding six births, one possesses the uncontaminated path yet does not sever the afflictions—such individuals whose uncontaminated paths do not sever the afflictions are all termed "uncontaminated paths of observation" (*paryāyanirvedhabhāgīya-anāsrava*).
Furthermore, based on this principle, it is called "arising from contemplative observation" (*vīkṣaṇā-vyutthāna*) and is untainted (*anāsrava*).
Now, according to the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, regarding those who attain immediate transcendence (*sakṛd-vyutthāna*): these are persons capable of transcending the two intermediate fruits immediately;

having already entered the clear observation of the truths (*satya-abhisamaya*), they are persons who have transcended the two intermediate fruits and have attained the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). Therefore, such a person...
Relying solely on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration, one can give rise to the supramundane path to sever the afflictions of the three realms and attain the fruit of *aśaikṣa*.
Regarding the establishment of only two fruits: first, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*; subsequently, one attains the untainted fruit, without taking up the two intermediate fruits.
Thus, we know that within this second interpretation, it is stated that a person who transcends the two intermediate fruits relies solely on the initial *anāgamya*.
Within meditative concentration, one can transcend the middle two fruits without relying on the four dhyānas or the lower three formless attainments;
likewise, one does not rely on the four dhyānas or the lower three form realms to attain the second and third fruits in succession.
Therefore, this second interpretation is correct.
[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "taking the previous interpretation up to 'because the intention differs'":

there are those who wish to adopt the first interpretation—that one attains the fourth fruit by leaping over the middle two fruits based on the four dhyānas and three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

However, this would contradict the text of the *Abhidharmakośa*, which states: "In that treatise, it is said that one who leaps over the middle two fruits does not attain the fundamental [dhyānas] of the fourth dhyāna, etc."
Regarding those who attain the fruit of *aśaikṣa*, this is stated based on the majority of cases;

it does not exclude those who do not transcend the middle two fruits, as even a small portion of them are also able to attain the fruit of *aśaikṣa* by relying on the fundamental dhyānas of the four higher stages.

Furthermore, since that treatise does not state that those who transcend the two fruits rely *only* on the *anāgamya* concentration—and there is clearly no word "only" (*mātra*)—it is evident that those who transcend the two fruits may also rely on the higher stages.
If one attains the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*) by means of the fundamental dhyāna of the fourth dhyāna,

yet does not permit those who leap over the intermediate two fruits to rely on the untainted fundamental dhyāna of the fourth dhyāna as support for receiving the body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*), then it must be known that from the point when those in the first fruit turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] onward,
they immediately attain the fundamental dhyāna of the fourth dhyāna and receive the body of transformation; whereas those who leap over the intermediate two fruits [do not].

Furthermore, what contradiction is there in the principle that one may, by relying on the four aforementioned fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), give rise to the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) to abandon the afflictions of the higher realms?
However, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states that the lower paths abandon the afflictions of the higher realms; this is because it refers to a specific power of intention (*āśaya*).

Thus, there should be no contradiction. Some have criticized this, saying: "The first fruit (*srotāpanna*) who turns their mind [toward enlightenment] is immediately called a Bodhisattva; because their power is great, this is possible."
If one attains a transformation body based on the fundamental dhyānas of the four stages, and if this transcends the middle two fruits, it would then be a minor fruit;
how could it possibly be compared to a Bodhisattva? It is like comparing a firefly to the light of the sun; therefore, one knows that such a comparison is impossible.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "because they universally take internal and external objects as their range up to each being universal toward the coarse and the subtle":

if the five internal sense organs are called internal objects and the five external sense-objects are called external objects, then within these internal and external objects, if one takes them in their general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), such as the five organs and so forth, it is called the coarse;
if one takes each individual subtle ultimate atom (paramāṇu) and so forth, it is called the subtle object. According to this commentary, it explains only the [object] that is taken.
Regarding the objection that this is incorrect because it also explains the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), [the author] now provides his own explanation:

the present discussion offers a general explanation for why the afflictive and cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) associated with all six consciousnesses are abandoned gradually, whereas the seventh consciousness is explained as abandoning both hindrances simultaneously.
Thus, one should know that this passage now clarifies the reason for the gradual abandonment of the two hindrances.

If it were not so, how could the afflictions (*kleśa*) not be explained? To explain in detail: first, regarding the seventh consciousness, the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are abandoned simultaneously without distinction;

this clarifies the reason for their simultaneous abandonment. Regarding the six consciousnesses, the two obstacles are explained separately as preceding and following, because within the afflictions there are differences of small and large:

the small are abandoned gradually while the large are abandoned suddenly. Next, it is clarified that the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is exclusively large and exclusively gradual; only after this is that [point] subsequently explained.
Since the textual flow is already interrupted by the phrase "gradually severed," how can it be explained as a gradual process?

Furthermore, since the text itself has already clarified that Bodhisattvas sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) instantaneously, how do the references to internal and external conditions demonstrate this instantaneousness and clarify the gradual process?
For this reason, I shall first distinguish the gradual process regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), merely indicating the general direction.
[Commentary: Regarding the distinction between the three vehicles and the four paths: if the four paths arise separately and individually, their names differ;

if they arise in relation to one another in a temporal sequence, their names are the same—for instance, in relation to what precedes it, it is called "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-gāmin*), while in relation to what follows it, it is called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*) and so forth.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the preparatory application (*prayoga*) and the superior progress (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*) of the two vehicles reach the stage of preparatory application and superior progress," this clarifies that the preparatory application and superior progress must each arise separately.

For instance, once one has given rise to a single grade of preparatory application, one immediately gives rise to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) which abandons a single grade of affliction;

having abandoned the affliction, one immediately gives rise to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), thereby emerging from the meditative observation after a short interval. Furthermore—

Furthermore, having entered [the path], one first gives rise to the preparatory application (*prayoga*), then the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) which eliminates one grade of affliction, then the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and then the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*);

the other grades are to be understood accordingly. Thus, it is clear that for each stage (*bhūmi*), the nine grades of afflictions are abandoned through the arising of nine preparatory paths, nine uninterrupted paths, nine paths of liberation, and nine paths of excellence.

[Commentary]: Alternatively, if one maintains that only a single preparatory application (*prayoga*) is required—lest it contradict the Ninth Chapter of the *Abhidharma*—this refers either to the excellence of the preparatory application or to the process as a whole.
For example, when entering and emerging from meditative absorption to abandon five grades of afflictions (*kleśa*), one first initiates a single path of preparation;

next, one initiates the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) to abandon one grade of affliction; and finally, one initiates the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) to realize cessation (*nirodha*). Furthermore...
Next, one gives rise to a single uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the second grade of afflictions, followed by the arising of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) to realize cessation.

In this manner, up until the fifth grade of afflictions has been abandoned, one subsequently gives rise to only one path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*). That is, for each of the five grades, one gives rise to one uninterrupted path and one path of liberation;

there is one path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and one path of excellence. For the abandonment of the remaining four, three, or other grades, the same principle should be understood accordingly; therefore, they are added here.

The progression of the path of superior advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) is not fixed as being either collective or individual; however, this treatise explains it based on the path of superior advancement that allows for leisure (*sa-vilamba*).

This is because, after abandoning up to five categories [of afflictions], one may subsequently give rise to a single collective path of superior advancement, or at times give rise to five individual paths of superior advancement;
thus, it differs from the *Abhidharma*. The meaning of "allowing for leisure" is that it refers to what is outside the three paths, such as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and so forth.

If one were to separately initiate a distinct path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) that is swift and non-protracted, then the three paths—preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and liberation (*vimukti*)—of the subsequent category would themselves constitute the path of superior progress for the preceding category, leaving no further room for a separate path of superior progress to arise.
Nevertheless, the *Abhidharma-śāstra* speaks of the swift path of superior progress; as that treatise states regarding the abandonment of the nine [levels of affliction]: [it proceeds] as follows.

When abandoning the first category of afflictions (*kleśa*), one first gives rise to one path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), followed by one path of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) which abandons the first category of afflictions;
then, one gives rise to one path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) to realize cessation (*nirodha*).

Without emerging from meditative absorption, one again gives rise to one path of preparation, followed by one path of uninterrupted activity which abandons the second category of afflictions, and then gives rise to one path of liberation to realize cessation. Thus, the second category of afflictions is abandoned.

When the three paths are compared with the first category [of abandonment] mentioned previously, they collectively function as the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) for the abandonment of the second category of afflictions;
this is because these three paths constitute a superior advancement over what preceded them.

Thus, all three paths involved in the abandonment up to the ninth category of affliction collectively function as the path of superior progress for the abandonment of each preceding category of affliction. This is the distinction between the two treatises.
If it were not so, this treatise would contradict the text of the Abhidharma (*Abhidharmapitaka*). Question: What is the meaning of "the path" (*mārga*)? Answer:

According to the ninth chapter of the *Abhidharmapitaka*, it says: "The path of application (*prayoga-mārga*) refers to that path by which one is able to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*). The commentary explains:
"By correctly cultivating such a path, one is able to gradually abandon and distance oneself from the various grades of afflictions, such as the superior (*adhimātra*) grade."

Regarding the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantarya-mārga*) that gradually attains the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) for a portion of the coarse latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the [defilement] category:
this means that by means of this path, one immediately and permanently abandons the afflictions so that none remain.

It is explained that by means of this path, one is able to immediately and permanently eliminate the coarse latencies produced by the category of those afflictions, leaving nothing behind, and furthermore, one attains the transformation of the basis of those coarse latencies.
The path of liberation free from heaviness (*dausthulya*) refers to the liberation said to be attained through this path by means of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is explained that because one realizes the fundamental transformation (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) attained through the permanent abandonment of the afflictions by means of this path, it is so called.

The path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) refers to all preparatory (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), and paths of liberation (*vimukti*) for the purpose of abandoning further categories of afflictions; these are termed the path of superior progress. It is explained as follows.

The preparatory, uninterrupted, and liberative paths directed toward the severance of the remaining afflictions of this category are called the "path of advancement" (*viśeṣa-mārga*) in relation to this category.
Furthermore, what is referred to as the "severance of the heavy impediments" (*dauṣṭhulya*) refers either to the seeds of the afflictions or to the state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*).

What is referred to as "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) refers to the attainment (*prāpti*) of the abandonment of a portion of these heavy impediments from within the eighth consciousness. Or...

The nature of accomplishment (*pariniṣpatti*) also constitutes the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states that the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantarya-mārga*) is so called because, regarding the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa-prāpti*), there is nothing capable of intervening or obstructing it.
The commentary explains: By means of the attainment of the abandonment of afflictions, [the afflictions] are rendered incapable of arising;

because there is no power or capacity to obstruct the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*) such that it cannot realize cessation (*nirodha*), it is named the "uninterrupted path. This is because, by means of the "path of liberation" (*vimukti-mārga*), one has already reached the state of the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), which is certain.
Because the manifest [path] is able to realize cessation.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "both the sequential and the leap-over [attainments] are likewise," this means that when one who practices sequentially abandons the nine grades of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) of each stage (*bhūmi*), they give rise to nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Whether through the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) or the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*), these may occur either collectively or individually.
Regarding those who previously practiced "leaping" (vyutkrāntaka), this refers to the intention of one who has transcended the middle two fruits.

It is explained that since such a person must collectively abandon the afflictions of the nine stages as a whole—comprising nine grades—they must likewise undergo nine paths of uninterrupted activity (ānantarya-mārga) and nine paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga).

Whether the preparatory path (prayoga-mārga) or the path of excellence (viśeṣa-mārga) is practiced collectively or individually, it is as previously stated in the commentary (*śāstra*). This is because there are nine grades [of afflictions]. Up to...
"Arising individually and separately" refers to the distinct arising of practices during the stages of preparation (*prayoga*) and advancement (*viśeṣa*). As the commentary states:

"Entering into contemplation once, up until the final stage of advancement"—this explains the basis for the total arising of the practices of preparation and advancement, whether collectively or individually;
thus it says, "the practices of preparation and advancement, whether collectively or individually. This is the summary.
[Commentary]: The meaning of the statement "when realizing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), there is no room for further abandoning of afflictions" is as follows:

when the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) realizes the principle, there is no further opportunity to abandon remaining afflictions. This makes it clear that the preceding path of liberation cannot serve as the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) for subsequent categories [of afflictions], because its faculties are dull. It is not so for the Bodhisattva.

[Commentary]: Even if one has previously suppressed [the defilements] through the worldly path (*laukikamārga*) such that they do not constitute a separate path, this refers to those of extremely sharp faculties who, having first suppressed the afflictions of the view (*darśana-heya*) and the nine grades of the cultivation path (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) via the worldly path, subsequently enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). At that time, these cultivated [afflictions] are severed simultaneously;
because they do not realize the first fruit but directly attain the third fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), it is said that [this suppression] does not constitute a separate path.
The Path.
[Commentary: Regarding this first stage, the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantarya-mārga*) is intended to mean the "preparatory application" (*prayoga*) in relation to the second moment;

that is, the uninterrupted path of the first stage is intended to be the preparatory application in relation to the second stage. When the commentary says "in relation to the second moment," it intends to express this.
Question: What is the difference between this second moment [of the second category] and the second moment of the preceding [first category]? Answer:
The former refers to the second moment within the first category, whereas this refers to the second moment according to the name of the second category.

Furthermore, it is said that because the second uninterrupted [moment] is viewed in relation to the first category as liberation, it is stated that upon reaching the second moment, one attains liberation. If one follows this explanation, how does it differ from the second moment of the preceding [category]?
There is no difference.

[Commentary: Regarding the second statement, "The second uninterrupted path is merely a path of liberation," the intent is that, in comparison to the first category, the second uninterrupted path is merely a path of liberation and not a path of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
As for the paths of further progress, they all arise subsequent to the path of liberation. In comparison to this...

That which precedes is designated as "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-mārga*). Now, regarding the second uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) in relation to the preceding one, it is merely a path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and is not yet called "superior progress," because it has not yet progressed beyond [the previous state].
For example, when abandoning the fourth grade of afflictions, the fourth uninterrupted path is a "superior progress" path in relation to the preceding second grade;
however, in relation to the third grade, it serves as a path of liberation for that [third grade]. In relation to itself, it is simply an uninterrupted path.
The fourth category constitutes the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) for the subsequent fifth category and the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) up to the abandonment of the fifth category;
viewed in relation to the preceding third category, it is the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*), and viewed in relation to the fourth category, it is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Viewed in relation to its own fifth category, it is the uninterrupted path, and it serves as the preparatory path for the sixth category; the subsequent cases should be understood by analogy.
[Commentary]: This refers to the meaning of "eliminating the dharmas in sequential order" within the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).

It means that although all ten stages possess obstructions, because the Bodhisattva enters the contemplation once and does not emerge until the end, they eliminate them in sequential order; thus, when viewed in relation to the preceding and succeeding moments, it is possible for all four paths (*mārga*) to be present.
Question: For what reason is the first grade of affliction (*kleśa*) not taken [as the object of elimination]?

Question: Are the paths of application (*prayoga-mārga*) within the first stage (*ādikarmika-bhūmi*) classified into four types? Answer: This is based on the Bodhisattva’s entry into meditative observation (*samādhi*). When viewed in relation to what precedes and follows, there can be four paths.
For example, the path of application in the first stage is still contaminated (*sāsrava*); therefore, it is not included [in the category of the path of immediate succession].

Furthermore, it is said that prior to the first stage, one has not yet been able to abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*); thus, the path of application of the first stage, when compared to what precedes it, does not constitute a path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Regarding why this is not accepted, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Moment by moment, as they face one another before and after, all [the paths] may be present;

when each individual category [of affliction] is severed, all four paths are necessarily present. Otherwise, when severing the obstacles to the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*), there would have to be a path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*).

If such a path were admitted, the qualities of the Buddha prior and posterior to it would necessarily possess degrees of superiority and inferiority. Since this is clearly not the case, it is known that [the presence of all four paths] is not an absolute requirement.
"Endowed with the four paths.

[Commentary]: If one were to sever them individually and each arise separately, such that even the four meanings are fully present, this text refers to a bodhisattva within the ten stages who, upon entering meditative observation for a single moment, severs only one grade of hindrance and then immediately arises separately.

The four paths exist because that which can provide verification is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), that which can sever afflictions is the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), and that which follows immediately thereafter with a degree of leisure is the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*);
thus, each stage (*prakāra*) possesses all four paths. Although the knowledge (*jñāna*) is one, it is divided into four paths based on differences in function;
were they not to arise individually, the four paths would be deficient, as for example, the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) is absent in the first stage.
"Finally, there is no further progress, etc.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharmakośa* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa-śāstra), Chapter Nine, "up to each being compared with what precedes it," this reveals that the treatise is based on the explanation of the distinct paths arising in a Bodhisattva;
that is, since each and every chapter contains the four paths, in each chapter, the subsequent...
The three paths are all considered "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-gāmin*) relative to what precedes them; this differs from the present treatise. [Commentary:
Furthermore, it says, "Alternatively, distinguishing the abandonment and severance of afflictions refers to the two vehicles.

This subsequent section corresponds to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, where superior progress is explained based on the two vehicles. According to that treatise: "Furthermore, there is also the distinction of abandoning and severing afflictions..."

The path consisting of preparatory application (*prayoga*), or diligent skillful means in contemplating all phenomena, or diligent application in abiding within all phenomena, or the further cultivation of other *samāpattis*—all such paths are called the "path of superior progress" (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
The commentary states: furthermore, the term "moreover" is used to clarify an additional meaning;

whereas the various paths of application (*prayoga-mārga*) involve the abandonment and severance of afflictions, [this path] involves the correct contemplation of the teachings of the sūtras and so forth.
Alternatively, one may dwell in and observe the dharmas previously contemplated and realized, or enter other superior meditative absorptions (*samādhi*);

such states as these are called the path of superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*). The commentary explains that this clarifies paths of superior progress that do not involve the abandonment of afflictions, thereby distinguishing them from those paths of superior progress that do abandon afflictions;

thus it says "discriminating the abandonment" and so forth, referring to the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for abandoning the afflictions of delusion and the rest. The remainder of the text follows accordingly.
This is easy to understand.

[Commentary]: Alternatively, regarding the general application to the three vehicles (*triyāna*), this is because both sections of the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-lakṣaṇa) text are explained as being applicable to all three vehicles.
Thus, when a Bodhisattva abandons the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), either the latter four paths constitute the "path of excellence" (*viśeṣamārga*) in relation to the preceding four paths.
The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) may also be attained, or alternatively, the path of further progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*) may also be attained.

[Commentary: Since this treatise now discusses the "arrival" (at the stage of *niṣṭhā*), it clarifies that the paths of further progress for the two vehicles mentioned here—where the afflictions are collectively abandoned—are identical to those in the subsequent chapter of the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (the *Prakaraṇapāda*).
Thus, all three paths therein collectively serve as the basis for the four preceding paths.
The application for the stage of superior progress consists in the preparatory effort to abandon the second category of afflictions; this application is exclusively the seeking [of the path].
Since the immediate [attainment] merely abandons the afflictions and the liberation [path] merely realizes cessation, they do not constitute seeking, and therefore are not "application."

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding this present section on the distinct arising of the mode of activity (*ākāra*)—up to the point where the *Cao* (the *Vyākhyā*) provides its explanation—the present treatise here refers to the distinct arising of the superior progress mode (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

Whether taken individually or collectively, as when one abandons the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*), at the very end one may give rise to only a single path of superior progress, or one may give rise to nine distinct paths of superior progress;
therefore, it is said to be "collective or individual" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*). If it concerns a subsequent grade...
Regarding the four paths being "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-mārga*) in relation to preceding categories, this treatise does not mention them.

[Commentary: If it were not so—that is, because they reach superior progress—this further clarifies that the general and specific terminology regarding afflictions (*kleśa*) in this treatise differs from the *Abhidharma* (Dharma-paryāya).

As for the explanation that the *Abhidharma* speaks of the path of superior progress in relation to subsequent categories: for instance, as the *Abhidharma* explains, the path of superior progress is considered in relation to subsequent categories.

Because it is superior to what precedes it, in this treatise, whether the terms are used collectively or individually, they do not anticipate the differences in subsequent chapters as is the case in the Abhidharma.
If that were not so, then all four paths following the first chapter would be superior to this [first chapter], and thus there would be no path—whether individual or collective—that does not arise.
Since the two types of "path of superior progress" (*viśeṣa-mārga*) are not like that, it is clear that they differ from those [in the Abhidharma]. Or...

The general statement indicates that this is indeterminate; the meaning is as explained in the *Śāstra* (Commentary). Since the *Abhidharma* does not speak of either the general or the specific, it is possible that there may be times when the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*) is not produced.

[Commentary]: These four paths, up to the stage of Buddhahood, must possess degrees of superiority and inferiority; this passage refers specifically to the learners (*śaikṣa*) of the three vehicles and the two vehicles.

The four paths—those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*), as well as those of the learner (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*)—are elucidated by means of the "unlearned" (*aśaikṣa*).

These four paths, however, apply universally to the three vehicles and the two vehicles, as well as to those who are learners and non-learners. For those who have attained the first two fruits, there are both the four paths for abandoning afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*) and the four paths for refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

Likewise, for those who have attained the third fruit, there are both the four paths for abandoning afflictions and the four paths for refining the faculties. There are also [the four paths] for the fourth fruit.

There are also four paths for the removal of the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samāpatty-āvaraṇa*), and there are likewise four paths for the cultivation of the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

If one is a *śrāvaka* who has attained the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) through the "group-practitioner" (*gaṇacārin*) method, they possess both the four paths for removing the hindrances to meditative concentration and the four paths for cultivating the supernormal powers; however, because their faculties are dull, they also have the four paths for the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*).

As for the rhinoceros-like solitary realizer (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa pratyekabuddha*), they first exhaust all afflictions (*kleśa*) through the four paths for the abandonment of delusions, and thus do not possess the four paths for the abandonment of further delusions.

Because one has previously attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), there are no four paths for the cultivation of those powers; because the obstructions to meditative concentration (*samādhy-āvaraṇa*) have already been eliminated, there are no four paths [for that purpose];

and because one possesses sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), there are no four paths for the refinement of faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*). There are only the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) and the paths of excellence (*viśeṣamārga*).

All four paths explained above may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); however, only the four paths for the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*) are exclusively uncontaminated, while the others may be either contaminated or uncontaminated.

If one is at the stage prior to the [first] bhūmi, the four paths are exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*); likewise, all four paths involved in the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*), the cultivation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-bhāvanā*), and the removal of hindrances are also contaminated.
From the first bhūmi up to the seventh bhūmi, only the four paths for abandoning afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*) are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);

all other four paths involved in the refinement of faculties and the cultivation of the path for removing the hindrances to meditative concentration (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*) are common to both the contaminated and the uncontaminated.

Regarding those above—namely, the followers of the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage—their paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) and paths of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) comprise both mundane and supramundane wisdoms derived from hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī* and *cintā-mayī prajñā*).

From the eighth stage onward, their four paths for abandoning afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), their four paths for refining the faculties (*indriya-pariśodhana*), and their four paths for removing the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within meditative concentration—all such paths are exclusively supramundane (*anāsrava*). Only a Buddha possesses [all of these].
Regarding the diligence of liberation and progress: compared to the preceding vajra-like mind of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), it is called "progress";

however, from its own perspective, there is no further progress, as there is only the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). If one were to assert that a Buddha possesses a path of progress, it would follow that the Buddha has degrees of superiority and inferiority.
Regarding the four paths of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) in the Hīnayāna, they are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); this applies when a learner (*śaikṣa*) refines their faculties.

That is to say: when one first attains the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and eliminates the afflictions, one gives rise to one uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

If one refines one's faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) while in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one follows the method for eliminating the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and gives rise to nine uninterrupted paths and nine paths of liberation.

Regarding the Mahāyāna explanation of refining the faculties across the three vehicles, this encompasses both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) concentrations as well as the non-concentrated states; thus, there are three categories in total.

1. The determination of the treatise on the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) is as follows: 2. Contemplating all phenomena while in a state of distraction or with outflows (*sāsrava*) is also common to both distraction and the presence of outflows.

3. The meditative observation of the various attainments (*samāpatti*) pertains to both the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) and the outflowing (*sāsrava*). Question: What is meant by "refining the faculties"? Answer:

This refers to a person whose innate faculties are dull who, through repeated cultivation of outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), transforms their dullness into sharpness; this is called "arousing" [the faculties].

Question: How is it that the four paths are all permeated by the contaminated (*sāsrava*)? Answer: If one speaks according to the severing of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), the contaminated path is incapable;

however, if one discusses the suppression of afflictions (*kleśa-vinodana*), the contaminated path is also capable of suppressing them. Therefore, the four paths are all permeated by the contaminated.

As will be explained below, when it is said that "the preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*) is not excluded from being permeated by the contaminated," it does not exclude the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*).

This explains the resolution of an objection. There is an objection that says: "If it is admitted that the four paths can all be contaminated (*sāsrava*), how could a Bodhisattva at the stage of the Diamond-like Mind (*vajropama-citta*) possess contaminated preparatory knowledge (*prayoga-jñāna*)?
Therefore, the explanation states: "It is only the preparatory knowledge of the Bodhisattva at the stage of the Diamond-like Mind that is excluded from being contaminated;
it does not exclude the possibility of the Bodhisattva at the stage of the Diamond-like Mind possessing spontaneous (*anābhoga*) preparatory paths. Thus, the text concludes with "hence" (*iti*).
The Bodhisattva of Firm Mind (*Dṛḍhamati*) also possesses the four paths, yet lacks the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) of seeking.

[Commentary: The four contaminated (*sāsrava*) paths extend through the two upper realms up to the preparatory and superior advancement stages; this explains the reason why these four paths are permeated by the contaminated.
That they exist throughout the ten stages of the two upper realms refers specifically to the intermediate state (*dhyānāntara*) of the desire realm and the four dhyānas.
The "emptiness" refers to the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The meaning is that within these ten stages, there may be four paths; it does not mean that each individual stage possesses all four paths.
However, within the eight *anāgamya* (preliminary) stages, all four contaminated (*sāsrava*) paths are fully present.

This is because within the eight *anāgamya* stages, one can cultivate the contemplations of attraction and aversion, thereby suppressing the defilements of the lower stages. As for other ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they exclude the eight *anāgamya* stages.

Outside of the dhyānas, within the intermediate dhyāna and the four fundamental levels of the four dhyānas, there exist only contaminated paths of preparation (*prayoga*), excellence (*viśeṣa*), and liberation (*vimukti*);
there are no paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), because within the fundamental levels one cannot abandon the defilements of the lower stages.

Furthermore, in this realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), these paths of liberation and excellence consist exclusively of contaminated wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).

If the desire realm itself takes the minds of hearing and reflection wisdom as its paths of preparation (*prayoga*) and superior progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*), then in the desire realm there exists only the mind of aspiration and the subsequent mind of progression, but it lacks both the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Furthermore, it is said that while the desire realm is permitted to have the pursuit [of the object] and the state of leisure (*kramila*), if one suppresses the afflictions or attains realization within the desire realm, then the desire realm itself is non-existent; for the desire realm—[by definition]—is so called because...

Because a distracted mind cannot subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*) nor realize the principle (*tattva*), the desire realm possesses only the paths of application (*prayoga-mārga*) and special progress (*viśeṣa-mārga*).

[Commentary: Regarding the fact that the four untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*) do not exist up to the stage of application and so forth—speaking according to reality—these nine locations, namely the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*), and the first three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), fully possess them.

If the four paths with outflows (*sāsrava*) also rely on the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) cuts off delusions to attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*),

why does the commentary state that the intermediate dhyāna possesses only the three paths— the preparatory (*prayoga*), the path of liberation (*vimukti*), and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa*)— and lacks the four paths?
Regarding the statement that the path of liberation and the path of excellence exist within the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), this refers specifically to the body of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

When one gives rise to the noble path of the lower sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) while at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) in order to sever the afflictions of the level of the Peak of Existence—if one follows what is stated here in this commentary, it says that within the level of the Peak of Existence there is already a "path of liberation" (*vimuktimārga*);

this is called "liberation," but it is not the path of liberation that arises immediately subsequent to the path of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantaryamārga*). This is just as, for example, when a person who has attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) is situated in...

Within the noble path arising from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) directed toward the lower sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) severs the afflictions of the Peak of Existence.
Immediately following that path of uninterrupted transition of Nothingness, one gives rise to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) of Nothingness.
Following the path of liberation of Nothingness, one then gives rise to the untainted path of liberation within the stage of the Peak of Existence.
Because it is not the liberation that follows immediately after [the uninterrupted path], it is called the "liberation-path category" (*vimukti-mārga-jātīya*).
Subsequently, one gives rise to the untainted superior progress path (*viśeṣa-mārga*) within the stage of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

There is an interpretation which states that within the stage of the Peak of Existence there is also a liberation path following the immediate uninterrupted path; this is because a person who has attained the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) has already given rise to it.
The uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) abandons the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).

Immediately thereafter, it is logically consistent that one should give rise to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states: "As for 'arising below,' this is explained according to what is manifest;

it refers specifically to the fact that the uninterrupted path of the sphere of nothingness induces the path of liberation and the path of excellence of the sphere of nothingness. Therefore, it does not mention [the higher stages].
In the Stage of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (asaṃjñisattva-bhūmi), there exists the path of liberation following the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).

[Commentary: Regarding the statement in the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (Dharma-skandha-pāda), chapter fourteen, that [defilements] "no longer manifest," it is as follows: for example, upon attaining the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*), one immediately abandons the stage of being a candidate for the first fruit (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*);

likewise, upon attaining the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), one immediately abandons the previous stage of being a candidate for the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*), and so on, up until the attainment of Arhatship.
The fruit of Arhatship involves the relinquishing of the path leading toward Arhatship as well as the paths of the third fruit and so forth;

thus it is said that at the moment one realizes this fruit and the path included therein is attained, one simultaneously relinquishes the path included in the preceding stage of approach (*pratipannaka*). Because these [lower paths] no longer manifest, they are termed "relinquished";

that is, one attains the superior while relinquishing the inferior. This principle applies even up to the time when the nine grades of afflictions are abandoned, wherein in each case the superior is attained and the inferior is relinquished.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "Although a Bodhisattva does not speak of abandoning the stage of approach (*pratipannaka*) to attain the fruit, they nonetheless attain the superior while abandoning the inferior—just as when one attains the fruit"—the meaning is this:

although a Bodhisattva differs from the Śrāvakas of the Lesser Vehicle in that they do not abandon the stage of approach to attain the fruit, they nevertheless do attain the superior and abandon the inferior.

For example, within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), each stage possesses the mind of entry (*praveśa*), abiding (*sthiti*), and fulfillment (*pūrṇa*); thus, upon attaining the mind of the stage itself, one immediately abandons [the previous level].
Entering the mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*) is like attaining the full mind of that stage, whereby one immediately relinquishes abiding in the mind of the first stage;

likewise, upon attaining the second stage, one relinquishes the first stage, and so forth. This state of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) refers to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) contemplation of the two kinds of emptiness regarding the phenomena of arising.
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement, "Now, based on this text, the meaning of 'equalizing' (zhǐqí) extends to the middle and upper grades," the intent is as follows:
"Equalizing" means that there are three grades—upper, middle, and lower—of untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).

For instance, when one emerges from the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and reaches the dwelling mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*), the untainted seeds of the Path of Seeing become equal in power to the seeds of the untainted mind of the dwelling stage.
Up to and including the mind dwelling in the tenth bhūmi, the untainted seeds (anāsrava-bīja) of the preceding nine bhūmis are equal in power to the untainted seeds of the tenth bhūmi;
likewise, up to and including the fruit of Buddhahood, the untainted seeds within the preceding stages of seeing,
cultivation, and the ten bhūmis are of the same essence as the untainted seeds in the state of the fruit of Buddhahood.

Regarding the equality of power among these, there is an objection which asks: "If the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) of the prior stage are all equal in power to the untainted seeds of the subsequent stage, how is it that at the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) there can exist the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the faculty of 'knowing' (*ājñendriya*)?
The answer is: The faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' and the faculty of 'knowing' from the prior stage persist until the stage of Buddhahood.

Because they are all entirely superior, the various faculties (*indriya*) from the preceding stages up to the stage of Buddhahood are collectively termed the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), and are not termed the faculty of "one who will know what is not yet known" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*). [Commentary]:

Regarding the meaning of transformation and cessation, the intention behind the statement that "a single seed transforms into the middle or superior [levels] until it is called 'abandoning the inferior'" is as follows: [text continues].
If one asks how they are transformed and extinguished: it is that the seeds of a single category are transformed;

specifically, the seeds of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are transformed into the seeds of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and the seeds of the path of cultivation are transformed into the seeds of the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*).

Furthermore, those cultivated in the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) all transform the seeds of the preceding stage into the seeds of the subsequent stage, and so forth. This is explained in detail in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā*. As it says:
When the inferior grade is transformed into the middling grade, and the middling grade is transformed into the superior grade, the preceding inferior and middling grades no longer manifest;
this is termed "cessation," which is why it is called "transformative cessation" (parāvṛtti-nirodha).
[Treatise] Regarding the phrase "the universally pervasive *tathatā* (universal suchness) reaches [all] but does not abide therein": this is a specific explanation of universal suchness.

"Universal" (*sarvatraga*) refers to the fact that *tathatā*, which is revealed by the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), pervades all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) without exception;

therefore, it is called "universally pervasive. In reality, the two types of emptiness extend throughout the other nine stages (*bhūmi*), but here the discussion is based on their initial realization.
Regarding the stage, it is said that the *tathatā* (suchness) of the first ground is called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*). Some say this means the practitioner is present [within it];
that is, because *tathatā* pervades all phenomena, it is named "pervasive suchness" (*sarvatraga-tathatā*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that there are four kinds of "capable realization" (*prativedha*), one asks: how can the ten true suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*) and the ten layers of obstructions (*daśa-āvaraṇa*) be termed "capable of realization"?

Answer: Because it is by means of possessing the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) and the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), severing the ten layers of obstructions, and realizing the ten true suchnesses that one is finally able to realize the *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* of the fruition. Therefore, these four types are all termed "capable of realization."
It is taught that the Buddha-fruit, bodhi, and nirvāṇa are all realized by cultivating these four kinds within the causal stage;
therefore, these four are called "that which realizes.

[Commentary]: Herein, the true suchness (*tathatā*) is distinguished in terms of its essence according to its designation. As for the second point—what dharma it pervades if not explained according to its designation—[it is as follows].
The absence of self is called "realization. Since these two absences of self pervade all phenomena, the principle of the two absences of self likewise pervades all phenomena;
this is an analysis of the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) by way of its designations. Furthermore, it is not that *tathatā* itself can be said to be pervasive.
The meaning is this: if one were not to speak of pervasiveness by way of designations, then since *tathatā* transcends language, it could not even be said to be pervasive.
[Commentary]:

"If one does not rely on the expression to explain what phenomena are pervaded" means that if one does not rely on the expression, True Suchness (tathatā) is beyond words and cannot even be spoken of as being either "excluded" or "not pervasive. When Bodhisattvas of the ten stages realize this True Suchness...
Since the name "True Suchness" (tathatā) is established for all [stages] based on the merit produced therein, the True Suchness of the ten stages all define its essence through its designations;
thus, this "pervasive True Suchness" is a *karmadhāraya* compound (an appositional determinative).
[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "The pervasive suchness" to "there is not a single dharma that is not the two emptinesses," Vasubandhu’s commentary explains:
"This dharma-realm pervades all activities. The sub-commentary states: "Within all worlds and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Since all activities are without self, the true principle of selflessness likewise pervades all dharmas; this explanation focuses specifically on the absence of a person (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
Aseng (Vasubandhu) says that this *tathatā* is the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*);
that is, all phenomena are termed "empty of phenomena," and the principle of the emptiness of phenomena also pervades everything. However, Vasubandhu and Asaṅga each cite one aspect of this meaning.

Yet, their meanings are insufficient because they distinguish between essence (*svabhāva*) and function (*vṛtti*). Regarding "essence": it refers to phenomena; since phenomena themselves are the essence, Asaṅga says this.
The emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is explained in terms of the essence of phenomena by way of their function; that is to say, "self" refers to the functional activity of mastery.
As Vasubandhu stated: "Because there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is not selfless," this is an explanation based on function.
Thus, while essence and function are distinct, both meanings are fully exhausted within this treatise.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "by penetrating this, one realizes the dharma-nature of the equality of self and others," the interpretation states that there are three kinds of equality:

First, the equality of the Buddha. Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), although they practice mindfulness of the Buddha, have not yet attained universal mindfulness;
they take refuge in the West and so forth, yet do not [equally] take the name of Maitreya and others as their object. This is called inequality. If one reaches...
Having realized *tathatā* on the stages (*bhūmi*), because one universally takes refuge in all Buddhas, one makes offerings to ten billion Buddhas and others within a single thought-moment;

this is the second [point], the equality of phenomena (*dharma-samatā*). If a bodhisattva prior to the stages, despite having practices, has not yet been able to cultivate them universally, it is called "inequality";
however, once reaching the stages and having realized the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one gives rise to [realization] regarding all phenomena.

Because the mind practices universally, one practices all modes of conduct within a single mode of conduct, and practices all modes of conduct within every mode of conduct. Regarding these three types of equality:
although Bodhisattvas prior to the Grounds (bhūmi) deliver sentient beings, they do so with only initial conditions and are unable to deliver them universally;
thus, this is called "inequality. Once they reach the First Ground, they realize the Great Compassion of Identical Substance (*sāmbhogika-mahākaruṇā*) and perceive all sentient beings as equal.
Regarding oneself as identical to one's own body, one does not perceive that there are sentient beings existing separately outside the self;
because one vows to deliver all beings in whatever task of delivering beings is undertaken, one is universally equal toward both self and others.

[Commentary] Regarding the question arising from this discussion—namely, "What is the difference between these two practices?"—the intent of the question here is: "In what sense are they called 'two'?"
Furthermore, regarding the two types of emptiness and the two wisdoms of emptiness that correspond to them below, how is there a distinction between the two objects—persons and phenomena?

[Commentary] The answer is: the distinction lies in what is to be remedied; namely, grasping at phenomena as having substantiality versus grasping at phenomena as having functional efficacy. To explain: if one grasps at the substance of phenomena, this is "grasping at phenomena" (*dharmagrāha*);

if one grasps at their function, this is "grasping at usage" (*upayogagrāha*). One employs the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatājñāna*) to eliminate the former, and if one grasps at phenomena as having activity, one employs the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalaśūnyatājñāna*) to eliminate it.
The grasping at function is precisely what is called the clinging to a self (*ātma-grāha*). A bodhisattva cultivates the wisdom of self-emptiness (*ātma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) to sever it.

Although there are also those who cling to functions within phenomena (*dharma*), such as clinging to the function of "discernment" (*vijñapti*) and so forth, here we refer primarily to the clinging that a self possesses function. That which possesses the function of sovereignty is the clinging to a self;
that which possesses the function of sustenance is the clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). These are the two objects to be remedied.
Since their attachments differ, the wisdoms that can remedy them are also distinct.

[Commentary] Now, to set forth the superior cause: "cause" here carries the sense of "reason. The meaning is that because Bodhisattvas in the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*) are able to distance themselves from the defilement of violating precepts, this *tathatā* (suchness) is revealed as possessing boundless virtues.
[Commentary]: The *New Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "By means of penetrating this, one forms this thought:
'Therefore, I shall now universally cultivate and purify all practices that correspond to renunciation. This is what is meant by 'diligently cultivating the correspondence with renunciation.

The commentary explains that the intent of the *Madhyāntavibhāga* is that, having realized the most excellent principle of boundless qualities through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one thereby attains that wisdom.

In this regard, one reflects as follows: "Because I have already realized the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) which encompasses all virtuous qualities, and because I now cultivate all practices within the nature of nirvāṇa that is identical to renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*), it is called 'concordant renunciation. This too is most excellent;

that is, suchness is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound) [meaning] 'the suchness that is itself renunciation. As for 'identical to renunciation,' it refers to the suchness of nirvāṇa, which is the..."
