Because sentient beings share the same point of departure, it is said: "They practice the corresponding conduct regarding the common departure," and so forth. [Treatise] Regarding "the True Suchness of the Superior Flow":
in this third stage (*bhūmi*), one illuminates the Mahāyāna Dharma with the light of the three types of wisdom; therefore, this stage is named "The Radiant" (*Prabhākari*).
This indicates that it is the True Suchness which serves as the basis for the superior flow of the teaching; thus, the superior teaching proceeds from it.
That which flows forth from *tathatā* is *tathatā* itself; it is the teaching that is the "flowing forth," and it is the *tathatā* of the "supreme flowing" (*viśeṣa-niṣyanda*) dharmas.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound).
[The Treatise] says: "The *tathatā* without appropriation. This explains the *tathatā* of the fourth stage, meaning that within this stage, one attains...
Because the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) contemplate detachment from the grasping at "I" and "mine," this suchness has no attachments;
it is not a locus for the grasping at a self, nor is it grasped as a self, and is therefore called "unattached."
[Commentary]: Vasubandhu says: "In this context, there is no admission of 'mine,' no grasping of what belongs to 'me,' and no sense of belonging.
The explanation states: if something were generally subject to me, it would constitute "what belongs to me" (*mama-ka*); therefore, he says there is no reckoning of "mine" and so forth.
This is like the people of Uttarakuru, who have no notions of wife or children and do not reckon them as "my wife" or "my children," thus having no sense of belonging.
[Commentary] Wuxing says: "Reaching that which is not subsumed by self or others" is explained as follows:

the delusion regarding craving for dharmas such as the sūtras and so forth within the third bhūmi is abandoned through the same antidote as the aforementioned grasping at a self; that is, by abandoning craving, one no longer conceives of "mine.
Contemplating this True Suchness (tathatā) of dharmas as being neither subsumed by self nor others, nor grasped as "mine," it is therefore called "unattached" (aniśrita).
[Commentary]: The meaning of the statement, "I merely say that what I have attained does not rely on grasping at suchness," is as follows:

In the case of Vasubandhu, who [asserted] that suchness is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), he merely says that one does not calculate "mine" with respect to this true suchness; thus, his scope is narrow. Why?

Because even [afflictions] such as attachment to phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) are absent, and views of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth do not rely on grasping at suchness. Based on this principle, how could it be that [the absence of grasping] applies only to...?
One does not reckon *tathatā* as "mine," nor do the craving for dharmas, the view of self, pride, and so forth take it as their object;
this is because one does not reckon *tathatā* as "mine" from the very beginning.

[Commentary] This means that although this *tathatā* is called "mine" simply because it serves as an object, this reconciles with the previous [teaching on] the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The passage concerning "what belongs to the self" (*mamakāra*) actually does not speak of views of self, pride, or attachment; rather, it speaks of the absence of "what belongs to the self.
This means that because this *tathatā* (suchness) serves as the object for the self, it is therefore described specifically as "what belongs to the self."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement in other treatises that "even *tathatā* (suchness) is grasped as 'mine'":

this means that within the treatises, *tathatā* is said to be "mine" because it is not separately extracted from the aggregate of the objects of the self; *tathatā* is also included within that aggregate of the objects of the self.
Thus, when the grasping of a self arises, it takes *tathatā* as its object; for this reason, this *tathatā* is called "mine. That is to say—
Other treatises differ from what Vasubandhu has stated.

[Commentary: Regarding the intention behind the statement "one does not give rise to the grasping of 'I' and so forth" toward those [objects], it means that if one were to say "grasping of self" (*ātma-grāha*) instead of merely saying "view of self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and so forth, then the view of "mine" (*mama-kāra-dṛṣṭi*) would not be included; however, by including the term "view," the view of "mine" is indeed subsumed.
Because they are equal, the term "clinging to self" (*ātma-grāha*) is used; thus the treatise says: "It is not the basis for clinging to self and so forth, nor is it that which is grasped;
it is simply *tathatā* (suchness) as the object of its own activity (*karmadhāraya*). This is the explanation.
[Treatise] Regarding the statement, "The five categories have no distinction because True Suchness (tathatā) reaches the point where the categories differ," this is explained as the fifth *tathatā*.

It means that within this stage, one cultivates and attains the path of non-differentiation between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; by means of this, one realizes that the category of True Suchness has no differentiation.
This is unlike the categories of the eye and so forth, which possess distinctions. Thus, this [stage] also has no distinction of category, for it is itself True Suchness.
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound).

[The *Sūtra*] states: "The meaning of 'continuity without differentiation' refers to the fact that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is without differentiation, unlike the continuity of the physical body which possesses distinctions such as self and other.
The *Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "By penetrating this, one attains..."
The equality of the ten intentions: these ten equalities are the ten kinds of pure mind described in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Regarding these ten pure minds, I have carefully consulted the seventh fascicle of the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, which states: first, the profoundly pure mind of equality with the Buddhas of the past;

second, [the same for] the Buddhas of the future; third, the Buddhas of the present; fourth, purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*); fifth, purity of mind (*citta*); sixth, purity through the removal of views, doubt, and regret.

7. Purity of knowledge regarding what is the path and what is not the path; 8. Purity of knowledge regarding the abandonment through practice; 9. Purity of attaining the supreme excellence by contemplating all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
10. Purity of transforming and delivering all sentient beings. The commentary on that treatise explains:

"Attaining purity within equality refers to these qualities of the Buddhas and that which accords with the qualities of the Buddhas—namely, the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Buddhas of the three times."

These are the qualities of the Buddhas; the remaining seven are in accordance with the qualities of the Buddhas. Through these—precept, concentration, and wisdom—the Buddha transforms sentient beings.

Precept corresponds to the fourth [purity]; concentration corresponds to the fifth; and the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth are all subsumed under the purity of knowledge (*jñānaprasāda*). The commentary states:

Regarding the Three Jewels, one is free from doubt and confusion, knowing that what the Buddha has taught is universally capable of leading to liberation. As for "external," it refers to those outside the Buddhist teachings.

If one cannot distinguish between the path and what is not the path, one cannot achieve liberation. Furthermore, it is said that by now severing the middle and lower courses of conduct and initiating the sublime, superior noble practices, these correspond respectively to the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth [stages].
The Master replied: "Even if that were so, what would be lost? Therefore, the treatise restates: "If those characteristics did not exist, how could one designate them as 'conditioned by those'?

This refutes the notion that the cognitions of form and so forth are established through mutual dependence. As for why the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* does not explicitly state that true perception possesses characteristics, it is because it employs skillful brevity.
*Commentary on the Exposition of the Meaning of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirteen, Part One;
*Commentary on the Exposition of the Meaning of the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirteen, Part Two.
[Treatise] From "The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation" up to "all are permitted to manifest," this is the third section, explaining the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Within this, there are two parts: first, the section explaining the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), and second, the section clarifying the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

Within the explanation of the emptiness of persons, there are two further divisions: first, the initial arising, and second, the subsequent arising. Regarding the statement that the contemplation of the emptiness of persons is also "initially arisen" at the stage of the vision of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka-darśana-mārga*):
this clarifies that it is initially attained at the very beginning of the Two Vehicles' stage of vision; thus, the three types of initial arisings are contrasted.

Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattva also attains the realization through the teaching of the meaning," this indicates that it is not only the Bodhisattva who attains the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), but those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) also attain this wisdom.
As for the phrase "subsequently proceeding successively until reaching the higher stages," this clarifies that there are three subsequent stages following the path of seeing:
progressing from after the path of seeing until reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣabhūmi*). This refers to those of the two vehicles with fixed natures (*niyatagotra*).

Regarding the second section, "The Chapter on Arising the Contemplation of the Emptiness of Phenomena": From those who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle from the four fruits [of the śrāvaka] up until the end of the Bodhisattva’s stage of practice (adhimukticaryābhūmi), all are able to give rise to the wisdom of observation;
this is because, during the fulfillment of one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa prior to the [first] bhūmi, they all cause it to arise.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "gradual entry through awakening," up until the end of the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), that which arises here is merely the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) attained at the level of the two vehicles.
This is because [the practitioner] has not yet attained the Bodhisattva path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
From the higher stages of wisdom, beginning from the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) up to the fruit of Buddhahood, this category of wisdom is swiftly produced.
This encompasses both those who turn their minds [from the Lesser Vehicle] and those of sudden enlightenment.
[The Commentary] states: "Sudden enlightenment up to the stage of no-more-learning" means reaching the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a Bodhisattva and so forth;

thus, the "stage of no-more-learning" refers here to the fruit of Buddhahood as no-more-learning, not to the no-more-learning of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Among these three aforementioned stages, only the [stage of] *sopadhiśeṣa* is excluded.

Because Bodhisattvas—whether practicing gradually or suddenly—can all give rise to this wisdom during all other states except for those involving outflows (*āsrava*) and the state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), the Commentary states:

"It is thus for both the gradual and the sudden. Question: For instance, regarding the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-darśana*), it does not arise at three times: namely, during states with outflows, during the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), and during the state of mindlessness of the Bodhisattva.

Does this refer only to the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena among these five stages? Answer: The Tripiṭaka Master [states... *Note: The final answer provided by the Tripiṭaka Master is truncated in the source text.*

The commentary explains: This refers specifically to this passage. According to Dharmapāla’s correct and actual view, when one enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), it must necessarily be accompanied by the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).

However, while there may be the contemplation of the emptiness of persons, it does not necessarily entail the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena. Furthermore, when the grasping at a person arises, it is necessarily accompanied by the grasping at phenomena; yet, at the time of the grasping at phenomena, the grasping at a self is not necessarily present.
For this reason, the meaning and intent of this section on wisdom are also the same.

[Commentary]: Since it does not obstruct the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it clarifies that the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena must necessarily be accompanied by the contemplation of arising.

The meaning of "entering the mind through preparatory practice" (*prayoga*) also contradicts that [previous] statement, because the preceding preparatory mind was intended to perform the subtle contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena;

thus, when entering the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena alone, the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) must serve as the preparatory practice. Furthermore, this contradicts [the claim] that the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena is subtle.
Because the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) does not function within that seventh [consciousness], the seventh consciousness attains the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
[Commentary]: This means that during the aforementioned stages, except for when they are tainted (*sāsrava*) or during states of mindlessness (*acittaka*), it arises in all such instances.
Thus, the intent of the explanation is that within those higher stages, as long as one is not in a state of being tainted or mindless, this wisdom is entirely capable of arising.

[Śāstra]: Regarding the section on the Contemplation of the Emptiness of Dharmas up to the point where it says "all are capable of manifesting," this explains that there are two types of contemplation of the emptiness of dharmas.

First, it clarifies its initial arising; second, it clarifies its subsequent arising. That a Bodhisattva attains its initial arising only at the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) clarifies the initial arising.

According to the correct intention of Dharmapāla, at the time of the first path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), one simultaneously realizes both types of emptiness; they do not arise sequentially. As for the statement that "this subsequently unfolds... [the text continues].

Regarding the statement "it transforms so as to be able to arise in all [states]": this clarifies that, excluding the three states—the state of being with outflows (*sāsrava*), the state of the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), and the state of being without mind (*acittaka*)—this [contemplation] can arise in all other remaining states.

[Commentary: "Only generating the contemplation of [the emptiness of] persons," up to "or contemplating both together"—the meaning of this passage is that from the time one has attained Buddhahood, it is only the sixth consciousness that gives rise to the wondrous wisdom of observation regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
This wisdom may contemplate principle (*li*) rather than phenomena (*shi*), or contemplate phenomena rather than principle, or contemplate both;
in all cases, it attains mastery. Within that sixth consciousness, the wisdom regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) can also arise.

Regarding the wisdom of contemplation—specifically within these two wisdoms, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wisdom of Equality—there exists only the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and never the wisdom of the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
While in the causal stage, if the sixth consciousness gives rise to the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it merely suppresses the ego-clinging within the seventh consciousness;
it cannot, however, induce the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena within the seventh consciousness. As for the sixth consciousness...
Only by giving rise to the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*) can one subsequently give rise to the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) within the seventh consciousness;

therefore, in the state of Buddhahood, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses give rise solely to the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena. Regarding the five consciousnesses in the state of Buddhahood, there are two views:

first, some say they give rise to the subsequently attained wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), because they are induced by the mental consciousness; others say they give rise solely to the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.
The subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arises after the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), subsequent to the sixth wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*).

[Commentary: Although it is said that this can arise even in the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) up until the point where coarse consciousness arises, this explains the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Regarding this, there are two masters' interpretations; this refers to the first master. Although the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that it can arise in the first stage, this is intended to mean that it arises in the mind.

In the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*) of a bodhisattva, [the five consciousnesses] arise; they do not arise within the initial stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The Buddha taught that because these two types of path of seeing occur at that time, there is no room for the five consciousnesses to arise, as coarse external objects would still persist.

Therefore, from the moment of abiding in the mind of the first ground onwards, it is subsumed under the path of cultivation. Question: If the five consciousnesses cannot arise within the path of seeing, how is this so?

This is like the Buddha’s vision during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), where the Bodhisattva suddenly awakens to the "Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas" (*śatadharmaprakāśamukha*) and perceives a hundred Buddha-worlds while exerting his contemplation.

[Treatise] There is an interpretation that one only attains the initial arising [of this state] upon becoming a Buddha; this is the second master, Dharmapāla’s correct position, who states that by means of the ten...
Regarding the phrase "because mental attention arises from the meaning within the stages (*bhūmi*)," the following three reasons establish this statement.
Since, within the ten stages, the support is the *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness) and not the untainted (*anāsrava*), this is the first reason. The explanation is as follows:

from the stage of the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*) upward, that which is reached by maturation—namely, the five sense-faculties such as the eye—is necessarily tainted (*sāsrava*). Consequently, the ten stages do not give rise to the untainted.

Regarding the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, the second reason—that they are not associated with the meaning of being "outflow-tainted" (*sāsrava*) and "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*)—is intended to reinforce the previous reason.

An external objection might state: "Just as the *manas* consciousness, though outflow-tainted, can give rise to the wisdom of sublime observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), so too could tainted sense organs give rise to untainted consciousness.
To address this, it is stated that they are "outflow-tainted" and "unshared."

The *Píngděng jiě* (Equal Explanation) states: "The *manas* is that which does not share the same object as the sense faculties (*indriya*). If the eye and other faculties possess four characteristics:

first, they are *sāsrava* (with outflows), which excludes the fruits of Buddhahood; second, they are 'unshared' (*asādhāraṇa*), which excludes the manifest eighth consciousness, because the manifest eighth consciousness serves as a common support for others;
third, they must be 'simultaneous,' which excludes the immediately preceding ceased faculty; and fourth, they have the 'same object,' which excludes the seventh [consciousness]."

The seventh consciousness and [the five sensory consciousnesses] differ because their objects are not the same; furthermore, it is illogical for the five contaminated sense organs (*āsrava-indriya*) to produce uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousness while possessing the aforementioned four characteristics.
Therefore, it is said that these two differ in terms of clarity and obscurity regarding their objects; this constitutes the third reason. The explanation states:
contaminated sense organs are obscure with respect to their objects, whereas the five uncontaminated consciousnesses are clear regarding their objects. This is established herein.

Regarding the statement that "inference, the elimination of faults, and so forth are all as explained previously in the section on the four conditions, yet [the wisdom] arises through attention that is intermittent," this explains a potential objection.

The objection states: "Since the faculties and objects are ever-present within the state of Buddhahood, the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done) should arise constantly. To resolve this, it is clarified:
"[It does not arise constantly] because it arises through attention that is intermittent. Thus, it is said in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*: "In the stage of the Buddha..."

He also made this statement, questioning the former master: "If you grant that the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) arises from the Vajra-mind (*vajracitta*), then the All-accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) should likewise arise during the Vajra path of immediate succession (*anantaryamārga*), as a wisdom like that of a Buddha at the stage of Buddhahood.

The former master replied: "There are two kinds of Buddhas: first, the Buddha of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbuddha*); second, the Buddha of Wondrous Enlightenment (*pravarasaṃbuddha*). Regarding that...

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* speaks from the perspective of the Buddha of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-buddha*), stating that the fruit of Buddhahood gives rise to the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*);

thus, there is no contradiction. According to the intention of Dharmapāla, however, it is only upon the attainment of the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that the fruit of Buddhahood arises, giving rise to both the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.

[Commentary]: Regarding the seeds that increase prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and the two increases upon entering the stages—although the seeds of the four wisdoms of mental application are all inherently present, they must be awakened by perfuming (*vāsanā*) before they can increase.
Furthermore, because they are perfumed by hearing prior to the stages, the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) increase;
upon entering the stages, untainted manifest activity (*anāsrava-saṃmukhībhāva*) arises. Thus, upon entering the stages, both the seeds and the manifestations are [present].
"Increase. [Commentary:
Before the stages (*bhūmi*), the function increases; upon entering the stages, the essence increases until it reaches the meaning of "protecting the Dharma" alone. The explanation says:

if, prior to the stages, one causes the seeds of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) through the cultivation of much hearing (*bahuśruta*) with outflow (*sāsrava*), the efficacy of these seeds increases; once one has entered the stages, they are outflow-free.
Once the manifest [state] has arisen, it further perfumes and forms untainted seeds; this means that the substance of the untainted seeds increases individually and in multiplicity.

Regarding the phrase "because the manifestations are distinct": once the untainted manifestations have arisen, they further perfume distinct seeds, which differs from the stage prior to the path of seeing where untainted manifestations have not yet arisen.
Now, this commentary first establishes both [the innate and the newly perfumed], because there is indeed new perfuming.
Regarding the statement in the *Dharmapāla-śāstra* that although the substance and function of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) wisdom increase, it is among the four wisdoms the seed of Buddha-wisdom:

the answer is that this refers only to the seeds of the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wonderful observation) and *samatā-jñāna* (equality), and does not speak of the *ādarśa-jñāna* (great perfect mirror) or the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (accomplishment of what is to be done).
According to the correct principle, within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one does not attain the perfect mirror [wisdom].
Because the two wisdoms are cultivated through practice, within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), only the fundamental seeds of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) are perfumed and developed;
therefore, this Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the others are also called "increase of essence" (*svabhāvavṛddhi*) as they exist within the ten stages.

Once these various [wisdoms] have increased, they are also termed "increase of function" (*vṛttivṛddhi*), because they possess the functional capacity to produce their future fruits. Prior to this, when one was unable to perfume the seeds of the two wisdoms, there was no "increase of essence."
Once Buddhahood has been attained, these two seeds of wisdom give rise to the actual manifestation of the two wisdoms; this manifestation is "increase through manifestation" (*samudācāra-vṛddhi*).
Because they do not arise again to perfume new seeds, there is no "increase through essence" (*svabhāva-vṛddhi*).

[Treatise] Regarding the statement "the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom reaches the point of being unknowable," this is the seventh section, the Gate of the Buddha’s Sphere as the Object of Cognition, which explains the four wisdoms.

This is divided into four parts; within the explanation of the objects and wisdoms, two wisdoms are discussed here. This refers to the first master’s view that [Mirror Wisdom] takes only True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object.
It is the non-conceptual Buddha because its mental aspect (*ākāra*) and its cognitive object (*ālambana*) are unknowable.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* that [the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom] is "not deluded with respect to any object," the intended meaning is that the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom takes all objects as its domain and is neither deluded nor confused.
It is called "not deluded" because it lacks false attachment; it is called "not confused" because it is clearly manifest and distinct.
Although the mental aspect (*ākāra*) that arises simultaneously with its preceding objects is likewise unknowable, this does not mean it is not non-deluded.

Therefore, the failure to clearly comprehend the objects of perception is what is termed "delusion. Alternatively, regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), when one speaks merely of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), the consciousnesses are already included within the locations of the faculties;

since both the six faculties and the six consciousnesses are collectively termed "consciousness," it is for this reason that only the twelve bases are mentioned, without further reference to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

[Commentary]: Regarding "aspects" (*ākāra*) and "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*, *so-yuan*), the explanation is as follows: "aspects" refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*), while "objects of cognition" refers to the objective realm.
This is the correct doctrine of Dharmapāla; thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:

"Furthermore, O Subhūti, just as various images appear in dependence upon a round mirror, so too do the images of all sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses appear in dependence upon the mirror of the Tathāgata’s wisdom."
Regarding the fact that the *ādarśa* (polished mirror) alone is used as a metaphor here, one should know that the mirror of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is perfectly equal [to it];
therefore, this mirror of wisdom is called the *ādarśajñāna* (mirror-like wisdom). Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"In this context, the metaphor demonstrates that the Great Mirror-like Wisdom (*mahādarśajñāna*) is the equal and impartial causal condition for the manifestation of the images of all phenomena; that is to say, for all Tathāgatas."
The eighth, the pure consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*), can manifest and give rise to images such as wisdom, just as a great round mirror can manifest all the images of the world.

Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "Just as when a person seeking merit and fortune hangs a great round mirror in a high and excellent place where it is unmoving, immeasurable sentient beings coming and going observe themselves therein and obtain [their own reflections]."

Because one loses [the former] in order to preserve [the latter], and abandons all faults in order to attain [virtue], the Tathāgata thus suspends the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśajñāna) within the pure *dharmadhātu* without interruption;

therefore, it is immovable. This is because he desires to cause immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to contemplate both defilement and purity, so that they may grasp the pure and abandon all defilements.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The 'exalted and superior place' refers to what is high."

"Banner" or "other superior locus" refers to the pure *dharmadhātu*, which is stainless *tathatā*. "Locus" means that it is established there, or [serves as] its support (*āśraya*) or object-condition (*ālambana*), because it is uninterrupted.

"Unwavering" means that because this mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) takes the *dharmadhātu* as its support and object-condition, it constantly follows along with it in a continuous succession without interruption until the end of *saṃsāra*;
therefore, it is unwavering. The intended meaning of this passage is: "The Great Perfect Mirror."
Once the wisdom that is free from all conceptualization and fluctuation has been attained, it continues uninterruptedly until the end of the future;
as for the remaining three types of wisdom, although they lack false conceptualization, they possess the conceptualization of intentional grasping.

After their realization, they may either function or not function. That they are not "non-fluctuating" refers to the fact that, according to the explanation of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), there are times when they do not function.
The fruit of Buddhahood is the constant practice [of wisdom]. Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:

"Just as a perfectly polished and refined round mirror is pure, stainless, and its radiance shines everywhere, so too the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata is utterly refined because it has forever transcended all stains of the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within the Buddha-wisdom;
being sustained by meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it serves as the basis for reliance."

Therefore, it is said that because it is a mirror-like clarity free from defilement, it performs the work of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. The *Fodijing lun* (Treatise on the Buddha-ground) states:
"Mirror-like" means that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is utterly pure; "pure" means being free from adventitious dust;

and "free from defilement" means that, by virtue of being mirror-like and pure, it is free from the two types of obstructions—those of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and those to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Thus, it is called "stainless radiance. As for "radiance":
Because it reflects, it is called "light" (*āloka*); because it is pure, it is called "clarity" (*prabhāsvara*).
Since it is sustained by the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that serves as its support, this supporting concentration is the *vajropama-samādhi*, which is the *śūraṅgama-samādhi*.

Because the power of that concentration is supremely pure and free from conceptual discrimination, when the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) arises, it reflects with purity and stainlessness, illuminating everywhere; though there is no fixed location for this illumination, it is described as "perfect" (*pariṇata*).
Like a mirror that reflects with purity and freedom from defilement, it enables others to perceive the signs of their own gains and losses;
as it performs acts of benefit for others, it is therefore called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom of Pervasive Radiance.

Though its self-nature is pure, clear, and free from defilement such that it cannot be seen, it gives rise to the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), generating all forms of wisdom and accomplishing every kind of benefit for sentient beings.
For this reason, it is called "Universal Illumination. Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:

"Just as various reflected images and appearances arise in dependence upon a round mirror and its objective essence, so too do various cognitive images and appearances arise in the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom in dependence upon all objects and conditions. The intent here is to explain the Great Perfect Mirror [Wisdom].

The pure consciousness associated with mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) has two types of functions: first, the function as a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), which means that within this pure consciousness there exist all the seeds capable of manifesting and generating the bodies, lands, objects, and wisdoms of the pure dharmas;
when it encounters external conditions, it immediately transforms and manifests various images of bodies, lands, and objects.
Second, the function as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), which refers to the excellence of the Buddha’s pure consciousness.

Because it arises through the power of the roots of goodness and vows, when the roots of goodness of sentient beings reach maturity, at that time, the pure consciousness acts as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for manifesting the body and the land.
It is said that "the roots of goodness of sentient beings are fulfilled," and the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, just as a perfect mirror and its various reflected images are neither joined nor separated—because they do not aggregate, it is called 'not joined,' yet it manifests them."

Because they arise through conditions, they are not separate; thus, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) of the Tathāgata and the reflections of the various wisdoms are neither conjoined nor separate.

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Just as a worldly round mirror, though able to act as a cause for the arising of various images, does not become conjoined with those images—because before they have arisen, they lack any substantial entity, so too is the relationship between the round mirror and the images."
It is not that they are separate, because it manifests those objects as its conditions; rather, by being able to act as a condition, it manifests their images.

The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) is likewise: although it can act as the cause for the arising of the images of wisdom and so forth, it is neither conjoined with nor separated from that wisdom.
It is not "conjoined" because, prior to the arising of that [wisdom], it lacks a substantial entity and thus does not aggregate with it. As for saying it is not "separated," it must necessarily...

Because the images produced by the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) arise when [the conditions] exist and do not arise or perish when they do not, this is a brief explanation of the characteristics of the mirror-like wisdom. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "or because it resembles the subsequently attained [wisdom] and arises after reaching true contemplation," this clarifies that there are two interpretations of the subsequently attained wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
Furthermore, the first interpretation states that the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* says: "If the other three wisdoms arise from the fundamental [wisdom], they give rise to the subsequently attained wisdom;

thus, the two wisdoms—fundamental and subsequently attained—are called 'induced. If this accomplishing wisdom (*krtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) previously lacked a fundamental wisdom to induce it, then within this accomplishing wisdom there is subsequently attained wisdom.
Now, the first interpretation further states: "Alternatively, that which resembles the subsequently attained is called 'subsequently attained.'"

Regarding the statement that the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*krtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) at the stage of Buddhahood resembles the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arising after the sublime contemplation of equality during the causal stages of a bodhisattva:
because that subsequently attained wisdom does not realize the ultimate truth, the wisdom of accomplishing activities likewise does not realize the ultimate truth.

Therefore, it is called "subsequently attained" in name; it is called "subsequently attained" because its essence resembles that [subsequently attained wisdom], though its substance is not [identical].

Following this, a second interpretation is presented, which states: "Alternatively, it is as in the case of the subsequently attained [wisdom] (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*). Because within the causal stage, after the true contemplation (*tattva-darśana*) that takes the conventional as its object, the subsequently attained wisdom arises intentionally;

since the subsequently attained wisdom within the causal stage—characterized by the sublime contemplation of equality—takes only the conventional as its object, the subsequently attained wisdom that accomplishes activities (*krtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) at the level of the fruit likewise resembles the subsequently attained wisdom of the causal stage in taking only the conventional as its object. Therefore, the wisdom that accomplishes activities at the level of the fruit is so named."
[This] is obtained subsequently.
[Commentary: Regarding the other cited passages that cross-reference the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, these are texts cited by other wisdoms that cross-reference the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. [Commentary:
There are two types of causes, while the seeds of the fruit always produce only one type; the manifestation of the two functions has not yet been described.

The commentary explains: Because within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), both the fundamental and subsequently attained [wisdoms] each have their own distinct seeds that arise, it is said there are "two types of seeds.

Since the subsequently attained wisdom is perfumed by its own manifest activity, when one reaches the fruit of Buddhahood, there is only one type of seed from which manifest activity arises, yet this activity possesses two functions:

when it takes the ultimate truth as its object, it is called "essentially correct" (*samyag-mūla*); when it takes the conventional truth as its object, it is called "subsequently attained. This is because the subsequently attained wisdom is no longer perfumed [at that stage].
Regarding the seeds: some say that from the first bhūmi through the fifth bhūmi, the two wisdoms—the fundamental and the subsequently attained—arise from their respective distinct seeds;
however, from the fifth bhūmi onwards up to the fruit of Buddhahood, only a single object-condition gives rise to the manifestation of both wisdoms.

This is because within the fifth bhūmi, the practices regarding the ultimate and the conventional are mutually contradictory, yet they are brought into correspondence; thus, there is a combined object-condition of the ultimate and the conventional.

Only the seeds of one [type] arise; furthermore, after the fruit of Buddhahood, the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arises and no longer perfumes various types [of seeds], but possesses only one and not two types.
This meaning is extensively analyzed elsewhere; here, it has not been fully elucidated, but is merely indicated briefly.

It is also like the five feelings (*pañca-vedanā*), each arising from its own distinct seed, which constitute the body. As for the Buddha, he resides within the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Because one knows their names and they further reside on the mental plane—being termed joy (*prīti*), sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and so forth—the five feelings (*vedanā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) each arise from distinct seeds.
If there is joy and equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the first and second preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka-samādhi*), these also each arise from distinct seeds.

If there is joy and bliss (*sukha*) in the third dhyāna, whether in the preparatory stage or the fundamental state, these also each arise from distinct seeds. This is also the case for the fourth dhyāna and above.
The [mental factors] that arise from distinct seeds are identical to those prior to the fifth stage; the two types of wisdom—the fundamental and the subsequent—arise from distinct seeds.
Only in the first two fundamental stages do joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*) arise from the same seed, which is one. Their manifestation in the present consists of two functions:
that which gladdens the mind is called joy, and that which pervades the body is called bliss. Furthermore, because it involves diligent effort (*vīrya*), it is also called "bliss."

This is termed "joy" (*prīti*) because it is tranquil, and it is termed "bliss" (*sukha*) because it is so. The *Śāstra* states that there is a slight distinction in its being even more intensely delightful;
this is identical to the single type of arising and the two types of manifestation from the fifth bhūmi upward, and the same applies to the fruit of Buddhahood.
[Treatise] Regarding the statement in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* that "one reaches the state of equality," this third protection for the Dharma teacher cites two reasons to establish this;
this is the first reason. Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says:
"Furthermore, O Wondrous Birth (*Sujāta*), the wisdom of the knowledge of equality is perfectly accomplished through ten aspects: first, the attainment of supreme delight in all marks."
1. The equality of the perfect accomplishment of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); 2. The equality of dependent origination as the condition for experiencing all things;

3. The equality of distinct characteristics and the absence of characteristics; 4. The equality of great compassion that extensively rescues and aids others; 5. The equality of non-referential great compassion; 6.
The equality of manifesting in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings; 7. The equality with which all sentient beings respectfully receive what is taught. 8. [The equality of]...
1. The world and tranquility are all of one flavor and equal; 2. All phenomena of the nine worlds—suffering and pleasure—are of one flavor and equal;
3. The cultivation and planting of immeasurable merit are ultimately equal. The commentary explains that this passage is interpreted according to the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra*.
Regarding the first point, "attaining the various marks," the treatise states: "The marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*)."
Because they are distinguished by their characteristics, they are all termed "characteristics.

Since these various characteristics are said to be the equality that is free from the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva), a sutra states: "The marks of a Great Being, the Tathāgata explains as being non-marks;
the true characteristic of the imagined is therefore called the mark of a Great Being. Furthermore, "supremacy" refers to wealth and nobility.
Because all such things as mastery and wealth—being free from the nature of imagined construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)—are called "equality," a sutra states:
"O Bhagavān, I now understand that because all things are without self, there is no craving, no wealth, and no fondness.
This means that whatever fondness exists arises toward phenomena conducive to it through the power of imagined construction.
One gives rise to joy regarding that which is contrary to those phenomena, and experiences sorrow and distress regarding them;

yet because all phenomena that are conceptually imputed (*parikalpita*) do not exist, there is likewise no attachment or delight toward any of those conceptually imputed things—this is called "equanimity.

When a Bodhisattva realizes wisdom, they penetrate and understand these aforementioned characteristics as the superior equanimity of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) regarding attachment and delight; therefore, it is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*).
The Wisdom of Equality is first realized by Bodhisattvas at the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*).
Thereafter, through cultivation in the successive grounds, it increases until it reaches full perfection at the Buddha-ground; from this point onward, there is no further increase.

Regarding the second [point], "the equality of all that is grasped as dependent origination," the commentary explains: there are two kinds of dependent origination, namely internal and external. As for internal dependent origination:

This refers to the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*). External dependent origination refers to all external things, such as seeds and sprouts.

Such dependent origination is called "appropriation" (*upādāna*) because its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are what is appropriated; alternatively, it is called "appropriation" because the conventional sentient being is that which appropriates.
All dharmas of dependent origination are what is appropriated, and dependent origination is without volitional action (*anabhisamskāra*).

Because it is empty by virtue of its use, because it is selfless, and because there is no *pudgala*, it is said to be "equality" (*samatā*) as it is far removed from the nature of imaginary construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

When a bodhisattva realizes this wisdom, they penetrate and understand all such explained phenomena—the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the nature of equality—and thus it is called "attainment. Therefore, a sutra states: "O Brahmin, the nature of all phenomena..."
This refers to the realization of the *dharmatā* of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); because of this awakening, it is called *bodhi*. This is explained at length:
not even the slightest phenomenon is seen apart from the nature of dependent origination. Herein, the equal *dharmatā* of dependent origination constitutes the "nature of dependent origination.

Regarding the phrase "threefold separation from distinct characteristics and non-characteristics," the commentary explains: the various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) do not possess characteristics such as transformation and decay [as independent entities].

Because they appear as such, they are called "distinct characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). To be thus distinct from one another is itself the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), namely impermanence and so forth;
or, for example, like blue and so forth. By what characteristic is this common characteristic characterized?

It is characterized by "non-characteristic. As a sūtra says: "The nature of all phenomena has but a single characteristic, which is non-characteristic. This non-characteristic is itself the level (*sama*).

To realize and understand the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as such—that all phenomena, being purely imagined (*parikalpita*), are ultimately and eternally non-existent—is called "attainment," because it is the equality of their nature.

Furthermore, some say that "being free from distinct characteristics" means being free from the characteristic of existence, and "being free from non-characteristics" means being free from the characteristic of non-existence;
thus, being free from both the characteristics of existence and non-existence is the state of equality, which is realized through wisdom.
Regarding this nature—the equality-wisdom (*samatā-jñāna*), the four great vows, the great compassion, and the equality of the dharma-nature—the commentary explains:
The meaning of the Bodhisattva’s equality-wisdom as it truly is (*yathārtha*) is that it takes both the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and sentient beings as its objects;

yet, being free from conceptual discrimination, it realizes the equality of the nature of all conventionally designated sentient beings through its mode of activity of equality, [perceiving] such phenomena as dependent origination.
Because its nature is equal, there is no self; because the *tathatā* (suchness) of its nature is equal, it is called the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).
It is thus named because it equally rescues all sentient beings and [perceives] all sentient beings as equal. These six characters may be explained as follows:
because it transforms into the equality of the *tathatā* of the non-self of all phenomena throughout all sentient beings, it constantly manifests in activity.

Regarding "the equality of the five kinds of non-referential great compassion and the equal nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*), the commentary explains: the compassion of the *śrāvakas* and others is unable to rescue all sentient beings;
it functions only for a brief duration, directed toward a limited range of objects within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

In contrast, the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Tathāgata is universally able to rescue all sentient beings; it functions at all times, directed toward the entire extent of the three realms (*tridhātu*) with a pervasive mode of activity.
Furthermore, it is said that "non-dependent" means being without anything to rely upon; because it constantly rescues and never abandons, it is called non-dependent.

This non-dependence is designated as "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā) because it operates with equality toward all sentient beings, given that the realm of sentient beings is boundless and because there is no temporary cessation when maturing sentient beings.
Great loving-kindness (mahāmaitrī) and great compassion are characterized by non-aversion and non-harming.

Its intrinsic nature is the wholesome root of non-delusion. Its mode of activity consists of bestowing happiness and extracting suffering. Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is non-hatred (*adveṣa*); compassion (*karuṇā*) is non-malevolence (*avihiṃsā*).
Because great compassion functions without dependence and without differentiation, it is called "equanimity.

This is the wisdom of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-jñāna*), or it is called the "wisdom of the nature of equanimity" because it takes the equal nature of phenomena as its object. Furthermore, it accords with the inclinations of all sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "manifesting the equal dharma-nature," the commentary explains: in accordance with the various inclinations of sentient beings to perceive the diverse forms of the Tathāgata’s physical body (*rūpakāya*), the Tathāgata manifests such bodies.

Although the Tathāgata dwells in a state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), by the sovereign power of the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*), the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) manifests subtle and wondrous colors, such as lapis lazuli.

The body causes the roots of virtue of all sentient beings to mature; it is the manifestation of one’s own mind appearing as such bodily forms, meaning that outside of one's own mind, one perceives the body of the Tathāgata.

As stated in the sūtras: "By the power of the roots of virtue of the Tathāgatas’ compassion, they manifest immeasurable transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya) according to the types of beings, causing gods, humans, and others to perceive the body of the Tathāgata within the transformations of their own minds, such as [the body] golden in color."
Manifesting the forms of all Tathāgatas in such a manner is equality; this very equality is the *dharmatā*.
Therefore, it is called the "equality of *dharmatā*. Regarding the phrase "all sentient beings respectfully receive the taught equality of *dharmatā*," the commentary explains:
if there is such a kind of vocal karma (*vākkarman*), it can cause the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of sentient beings to be perfected.
Having heard [the teaching] thoroughly, they give rise to joy and attain pure faith and delight. Then the Tathāgata manifests such verbal activity so that they may hear it.
Although the Tathāgata is free from conceptual proliferation and discrimination, through the power of his compassionate vow he manifests this in such a way.

Due to the power of their own resolute belief (*adhimukti*), the sentient beings to be converted undergo a transformation such that they perceive, as if external to themselves, the sound of the Buddha’s voice coming from the Tathāgata.
Because it issues forth all speech in accordance with the capacities of beings, and because no devas or humans can oppose it, it is called "that which is respectfully received.
Because such speech is manifested identically by all Buddhas, it is called "equality. This equality is itself the *dharmatā*;
therefore, it is termed "the *dharmatā* of equality. This wisdom of equality arises from the prior cultivation of the Buddha...
Because the fruit is perfectly accomplished, the eight worldly dharmas are all of one taste within the equal nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
The commentary explains: the contaminated five aggregates are called "the world" because they are destroyed moment by moment by their respective antidotes;
their cessation is termed "tranquility" (*śānti*). Because one is tranquil through this [cessation], it is precisely the Noble Path and Nirvāṇa.

Because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the world’s quiescence both converge in the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is suchness (*tathatā*), they are called "of one taste" (*ekarasa*).
Furthermore, the "world" refers to that which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*); since its intrinsic nature is non-existent, it is called "quiescent.
Because the suchness revealed by such quiescence is without differentiation, it is called "of one taste. This is precisely what is termed the "equal dharma" (*samatā-dharma*).
Because the nature [of phenomena] is cultivated to perfection as a single flavor through the aforementioned practice, the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is fully accomplished.
Regarding the statement that "the dharmatā of all worldly phenomena is equal in the single flavor of suffering and pleasure," the commentary explains:
there are briefly eight kinds of worldly phenomena: first, gain; second, loss; third, defamation; fourth, praise; fifth, renown; sixth, disparagement; seventh, suffering; and eighth, pleasure.

The attainment of desirable objects is called gain (*lābha*); the loss of desirable objects is called decline (*alābha*). To disparage someone behind their back is called defamation (*nindā*); to fail to praise them behind their back is called disrepute (*praśaṃsā*).
To praise someone in their presence is called fame (*yaśas*); to disparage someone in their presence is called infamy (*ayaśas*).

The affliction of body and mind is called suffering (*duḥkha*); the gratification of body and mind is called pleasure (*sukha*). These eight types are comprised of two categories; the four that are adverse are called the "unfavorable conditions" (*vipakṣa*).

The four types of suffering are designated as "pleasure" because they give rise to joy or sorrow; alternatively, this section provides a brief explanation of the final pair, pleasure and pain, wherein the noble one dwells in a state of constant, uniform flavor:
he is not elated when gaining prosperity, nor dejected when encountering decline.
Thus it continues until there is pleasure without craving and pain without resentment, as the Sūtra says: "The noble one dwells in the world with equanimity and uniformity."

Its flavor is like space; although the foolish in the world conceive of distinctions, because it is free from those, it is of a single flavor in all respects throughout the eight worldly dharmas of the parikalpita nature. This is what is called the "equal dharma-nature.
Because this single flavor is perfected through cultivation as previously described, the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is fully accomplished.
Regarding the phrase "planting ten kinds of seeds of immeasurable merit within the ultimate, equal dharma-nature," the commentary explains:

"Merit" refers to the various meritorious dharmas such as the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). To perfume the seeds, nurture them, and bring them to maturity for liberation is called "cultivating and planting.

Although the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is without conceptual discrimination, through the sovereign power of the wisdom of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
The jewel causes the virtues within other bodies to grow, ripen, and reach liberation; this is called the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

It is termed "ultimate" because it enables the attainment of *parinirvāṇa* through the three vehicles. This wisdom is called the "equality of dharmic nature" (*dharmatāsamatā*) because it is far removed from the nature of imaginary construction (*parikalpitasvabhāva*).
This very state is named the equality of dharmic nature; by virtue of these qualities, one practices as previously described.
Because the cultivation [of this wisdom] is brought to perfection, the Wisdom of Equality is fully accomplished.

As thus described, the Bodhisattvas attain a partial realization of this Wisdom of Equality within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), whereas the Tathāgata attains its full and perfect accomplishment as a Buddha.

[Treatise] Regarding the statement in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* that "one contemplates all sentient beings through the equality of self and other until reaching the image of the Buddha," the explanation is as follows:
"Contemplating all sentient beings" refers to the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) contemplating the Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

"Equality of self and other" means that by means of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), the [Buddha] embraces the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; having heard this, they [the Bodhisattvas] are transformed.
Because there is no sentient being external to one's own body, and no self-body external to sentient beings, they are called "equal.

Regarding "conforming to the superior inclinations of others": this means that according to what the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages desire to hear of the Buddha-dharma or wish to see the Buddha-body, the Tathāgata accordingly preaches the Dharma and manifests his body, displaying infinite images of the Buddha as they have pleased.
This refers to the manifestation of the ten transformations and the *parabhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others) for Bodhisattvas of the ten stages;
according to their respective perceptions and conceptualizations, he manifests a body within each stage.
[Treatise] Because the mental state associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is subsumed under the two wisdoms, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Based on ten kinds of causes, one should understand the tenfold differentiation of the wisdom of sublime observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

The ten causes are: first, the cause of establishment; second, the cause of origination; third, the cause of joy; fourth, the cause of differentiation; fifth, the cause of enjoyment; sixth, the cause of the distinction of destinies; seventh, the cause of the distinction of realms;
eighth, the cause of raining down the great Dharma-rain; ninth, the cause of subduing adversaries; and tenth, the cause of severance.
Regarding the first established cause among all causes for doubt, the commentary explains:

For example, just as the world-system supports the realm of sentient beings, so too does the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom sustain all *dhāraṇī* gates, *samādhi* gates, and unimpeded eloquent expositions of the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas.
Thus, the treatise states: "In this context, the characteristics of the established cause are revealed. This is an analogy.
Just as the world-systems that support the realm of sentient beings— such as the lower wind-circle and other world-system characteristics manifested by the minds of all sentient beings themselves—
support the realms of sentient beings such as the eyes manifested by their own minds; so too,
the Tathāgata’s discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) can support all *dhāraṇī* gates, and so forth, up to the sublime Dharma of all Buddhas.
This wisdom associated with the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is universally associated with all merits and is capable of eliciting all merits;
therefore, it is said to be able to sustain them. This is called the "establishing cause" (*vyavasthāna-hetu*), because it establishes the aforementioned qualities of the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the second, the "generating cause" (*janma-hetu*), the commentary states: The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says, "Furthermore, just as the world..."

In this way, the causes and conditions for sentient beings to suddenly give rise to all manner of infinite consciousnesses of various signs are such that the Tathāgata’s wondrous discerning wisdom can serve as the causes and conditions for suddenly giving rise to all objects of knowledge through unimpeded, wondrous wisdom of various infinite signs.
The treatise states: "This demonstrates the characteristic of the productive cause; it means that the vessel-world (bhājana-loka) is able to [serve as the basis]..."

The causes for the arising of the various perceptions and consciousnesses of sentient beings—whether on the earth, in the immeasurable realms of space, or in such-like forms—are thus simultaneously and instantaneously apprehended by the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom.

Like empty space, it is able to comprehend all objects without obstruction and serves as the cause for the arising of the perceptions and consciousnesses that take as their objective conditions all the various worldly and immeasurable supramundane phenomena; this is what is intended by the teaching.
It is called a "cause" because it arises and can manifest all objective appearances, thereby enabling the consciousness of those appearances to be produced;

that is, it is a causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*) rather than a direct cause (*sākṣāt-hetu*). Thus, the consciousness that grasps these appearances is said to arise from wisdom, and wisdom is designated as the "generative cause" (*janana-hetu*). Third, regarding the characteristics of the cause of joy:
the commentary states that the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says, "Furthermore, it is like the various delightful gardens of the world..."
Just as forests, ponds, and so forth serve as adornments that are exceedingly delightful, so too is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna) exceedingly delightful,

being adorned by the various pāramitās, the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma), the ten powers (bala), the fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), and the unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇikabuddhadharma). In this context,
it is explained that these manifest the characteristics of the causes for joy, just as they do for the receptacle world (bhājanaloka).

Just as various delightful parks, groves, ponds, and other such ornamental features are arranged in succession, radiating intense splendor that causes all sentient beings to feel joy and delight; so too,
the Tathāgata’s wisdom of sublime observation has various delightful perfections (*pāramitā*),
factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and so forth, arranged in succession as its ornaments, radiating intense splendor that causes all bodhisattvas to feel joy and delight.
Because it is blissful, one knows that this is the cause of the Bodhisattva’s joy; thus, the fourth [section] is the "Analysis of the Characteristics of the Cause of Joy.

Regarding the explanation: the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states, "Furthermore, just as in the world there are continents, islands, the sun and moon, the six classes of desire-realm devas, and the Brahma-body devas, all exquisitely arrayed and interspersed, so too is the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna) both worldly and transcendent..."

The *Treatise on the Array of Sublime Observations* (*Miao-shi-jian-lie-lun*), which examines the causes and effects of the world’s decline and prosperity through the complete realization of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas without remainder, states:
"In this context, the characteristics of the causes of conceptualization are revealed, such as the immeasurable continents and the six classes of desire-realm devas, up to the Brahmakāyika devas.
Regarding this, the commentary explains: "That which is free from desire and tranquil is called 'Brahmakāya' (the Brahma-body)."

Regarding the phrase "the multitudes and so forth," this includes all the aforementioned heavens, as well as these islands (*dvīpa*) and the gods dwelling upon them, which are beautifully adorned and arranged without confusion.
These include the four great continents such as Jambudvīpa and the eight smaller sub-continents (*upadvīpa*).

Thus, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is universally able to observe the causes and effects of decline and prosperity within both the mundane and supramundane realms, as well as the perfection of the Three Vehicles.
"Realizing the wondrous adornments arranged without confusion. The commentary explains: the causes and effects of the evil realms are called the decline of the world;

the causes and effects of the good realms are called the prosperity of the world. Furthermore, the causes and effects of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) are called the decline of the supramundane;

the causes and effects of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna) are called the prosperity of the supramundane. "Perfect realization" refers to the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), while "the three vehicles" indicates the stage of cause (*hetu-avasthā*).
Furthermore, regarding "perfect realization," it refers solely to the Buddha-fruit’s wondrous discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).

Because this wisdom observes that the characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) of these various phenomena are distinct, its cognitive aspects (*ākāra*) do not deviate from their objects but manifest clearly and distinctly; for this reason, it is called "wondrously adorned and interspersed.

Because this wisdom discriminates among the various characteristics without confusion, it is named the "discriminating causal characteristic" (*vibhakti-hetu-lakṣaṇa*), the fifth "causal characteristic of enjoyment" (*saṃbhoga-hetu-lakṣaṇa*).

The commentary states: The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says, "Furthermore, just as the world is for the vast enjoyment of all sentient beings, so too does the Tathāgata’s wisdom of sublime observation manifest all the assemblies of Buddhas and rain down the great Dharma rain, in order to cause sentient beings to experience the great joy of the Dharma.
The *Śāstra* states: "This passage reveals the characteristics of the cause of enjoyment, just as the receptacle-world [is the basis for the enjoyment of beings]."

In the interim, by the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, the *ālaya-vijñāna* transforms its seeds of common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-bīja*) to produce various common material requisites,

so that sentient beings may enjoy them extensively. In this way, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) acts as a dominant condition for the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*),
striking and activating the pure consciousness associated with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) to manifest the enjoyment body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).
With various assemblies of bodies, blazing with majestic power, they rain down the great Dharma rain so that the great Bodhisattvas upon the earth may experience the great joy of the Dharma;
furthermore, acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to assist the Tathāgata in accomplishing his *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*,

they strike forth the pure consciousness associated with the *ādarśa-jñāna* (mirror-like wisdom), manifesting transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) with various assemblies blazing with majestic power, raining down the True Dharma.
Regarding the sixth characteristic— the cause for the differentiation of the destinies whereby sentient beings previously transformed by the Buddha enjoy the dharma-pleasure—
the commentary states that the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says: "Just as the five destinies are found within the world— namely, the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals,
the human destiny, and the celestial destiny— so too, upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation, there are five [destinies] of boundless causes and effects."

The *Treatise on the Manifestation of the Distinctions of the Realms of Existence* states: "In this context, the characteristics of the causes for the distinctions among the realms of existence are revealed.

Just as within a world-system, due to the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, the various distinctions of cause and effect of the five realms of existence are perceived as arising from the transformation of the non-common seeds of the ālayavijñāna;
likewise, [the distinctions are produced] by the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom."
Because it takes the causes and effects of the five destinies as its object, it manifests appearing as the two distinct characteristics of those five destinies’ causes and effects;

however, because the various types of *asura* who are not directly born into the five destinies are indeterminate—being sometimes gods, sometimes hungry ghosts, or again, animals—they are not mentioned separately.
Regarding the seventh characteristic, the cause for the differentiation of realms, the commentary states: as the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says: "Just as..."

In the world, the various realms of desire, form, and formlessness can be found; likewise, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation perceives the boundless causes and effects and fully manifests the distinctions of the three realms.
The treatise states: "In this context, the characteristics of the causes for the differentiation of the realms are shown:
just as in the world, by the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, the *ālaya-vijñāna* [arises] together with..."
The seeds of common characteristics transform to produce the various distinctions of cause and effect within the three realms, which can be apprehended herein.
Among these, the "world" encompasses both the sentient and the insentient, namely the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

This is because the receptacle world sustains both the realms of sentient and insentient beings, whereas the world of sentient beings is capable of sustaining only the realm of sentient beings. Thus, the Tathāgata’s wondrous discerning wisdom...

Because the wisdom [of discernment] takes the causes and effects of the three realms as its objective sphere, it manifests appearing as the two distinct aspects of those causes and effects of the three realms;
however, it does not directly produce the causes and effects of the three realms.

The meaning here is that because the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is universally able to observe all objects, it appears everywhere as the aspects of the causes and effects of all realms, destinies, and births, just like a pure mirror.
Question: A circular mirror manifests all various images; all mirror-like appearances manifest within it. What is the difference between this and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*)?

Answer: Because the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is entirely free from delusion, although it can manifest all images and functions spontaneously, it is without conceptual discrimination. This wisdom of observation, however, is able to manifest everything.

The characteristics of objects also possess conceptual differentiation; if there were no such differentiation, one would be unable to contemplate matters such as cause and effect, nor preach the Dharma to assemblies to sever their doubts.

This passage definitively proves that even the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and so forth possess objective aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*), because within the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the infinite causes and effects of the five destinies and the three realms appear in their fullness. [This] is the eighth [chapter], "Raining Down the Great Dharma."
Regarding the "characteristic of the rain," the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* states:

"Just as the great king of mountains, Sumeru, and other such [mountains] are visible and obtainable within the world-system, so too are the vast and profound teachings, drawn forth by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, obtainable upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation.
The treatise further explains: "This passage demonstrates the raining down of the great Dharma-rain."
Regarding the causal characteristic: just as the receptacle world arises through the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings, giving rise to various jewel mountains;

so too does the Tathāgata’s *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (wonderful observing wisdom) arise through the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings who feel for the True Dharma, giving rise to the profound and vast teachings drawn forth by the majestic spiritual power of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. These teachings reveal the mastery of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Majestic power (*prabhāva*) can also induce that majestic power; therefore, it is called "induced by the majestic power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

This explains that the Tathāgata’s discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) can produce the images of the Dharma-teachings within the consciousness associated with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), or can itself manifest the images of the Dharma-teachings.
Taking this as a condition, the roots of virtue of those to be converted reach maturity.
Regarding the ninth sign of the cause for subduing adversaries— the manifestation of the sentient being’s own mind— the commentary states:
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says that just as a vast, profound, and immovable great ocean can be found within the world, so too, upon the Tathāgata’s wisdom of observation,
there exists the profound Dharma which cannot be shaken by any celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, or heterodox arguments.
The *Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra* states: "This passage demonstrates the causal characteristics for subduing adversaries.

Just as the great oceans arise within the receptacle world through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings and remain unshakable, so too does the Tathāgata’s wondrously discerning wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna) arise from the dharmadhātu through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings who perceive the true Dharma."
The teaching that cannot be shaken is the principle of the Dharma-realm as emptiness and signlessness. To speak of the principle of the Dharma-realm is called the "teaching of the Dharma-realm.
All non-Buddhists rely upon various views; the emptiness of the principle of the Dharma-realm serves as the antidote to these views, causing them to leave behind all tendencies toward such views.
Therefore, they cannot fathom this teaching of emptiness, nor can they shake it. The aforementioned teaching of majestic power is sublime in its majesty and power.
Because it is vast, it is likened to a mountain of jewels; because this Dharma-realm teaching is profoundly deep, it is likened to the great ocean.
Since the wisdom of sublime observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) is the cause that illuminates all objects, it is able to give rise to the teachings that expound all dharmas.
To summarize its excellence, a sūtra states: "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is named the Great Wisdom Sun, for he is universally able to illuminate and comprehend all dharmas."
Regarding the tenth [topic], the characteristic of the cause for severing all doubt, the commentary states:

The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says, "Furthermore, just as the world is surrounded by the mountains of the Great and Small Cakravāḍas, so too is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of sublime observation surrounded by all self-characteristics and common characteristics without delusion.
The treatise states that this passage reveals the characteristic of the cause for severing all doubt.
Just as the vessel-world— consisting of one Sumeru, seven great golden mountains, eight great oceans, and the four continents—
is entirely surrounded on its exterior by the Cakravāḍa Mountains, so too, when this count reaches one thousand,
there is another surrounding range of mountains on the outside called the "Small Thousandfold World" (Sāhasracūdika-lokadhatu). This constitutes one such world-system.
Again, when a thousand such units are counted together, they are further encompassed on the outside by a surrounding Cakravāḍa mountain range;

this is called a "Middle Thousandfold World System. When a thousand of these are again counted together, they are encompassed on the outside by a Great Cakravāḍa mountain range, which is supported from below by a great wind-circle;
this is named a "Trichiliocosm" (Great Trichiliocosm). This is what is meant by that term.

Just as Mount Cakravāḍa and Mount Mahācakravāḍa surround [the world], so too does the Tathāgata’s *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (wonderfully discerning wisdom) universally know all specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
It is able to sever all worldly doubts and delusions regarding self and common characteristics;

because it knows self and common characteristics, this delusion does not exist, and thus it is itself free from doubt and can sever the doubts of others. [This is] the *ādarśajñāna* (great perfect mirror wisdom).
